The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and let $d\ge1$ be a finite integer. An
$\mathbb R^d$-valued process $B=(B_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **standard
$d$-dimensional Brownian motion** if:

1. $B_0=0$ almost surely;
2. for every finite list $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_n$, the vector increments
   $$B_{t_j}-B_{t_{j-1}},\qquad 1\le j\le n,$$
   are mutually independent and have laws
   $N_d(0,(t_j-t_{j-1})I_d)$; and
3. there is one measurable event $A$ with $P(A)=1$ such that
   $t\mapsto B_t(\omega)$ is continuous from $[0,\infty)$ to
   $\mathbb R^d$ for every $\omega\in A$.

Equivalently, its $d$ coordinate processes $B^\alpha=(B_t^\alpha)_{t\ge0}$
are independent standard one-dimensional Brownian motions. Here independence
of the processes means the following precise assertion. Put
$I=[0,\infty)$ and equip $\mathbb R^I$ with its cylinder sigma-algebra. The
maps
$$ \Phi_\alpha:\Omega\longrightarrow\mathbb R^I, \qquad \Phi_\alpha(\omega)(t)=B_t^\alpha(\omega), \qquad 1\le\alpha\le d, $$
are independent random elements.

Assume the Axiom of Choice The Axiom of Choice, and fix a probability space
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ with a continuous-time filtration
$(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$
Continuous-time filtrations and all-pairs martingales and a standard
Brownian motion $B$ Brownian motion on it. **Standing hypothesis
(H).** $B$ is adapted to $(\mathcal F_t)$ and for all $0\le s<t$ the increment
$B_t-B_s$ is independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and has law $N(0,t-s)$. The raw
natural filtration and the usual augmented natural filtration
Natural and usual augmented Brownian filtrations both satisfy (H) for a
standard Brownian motion, by
Future-path Markov property; for a general filtration, (H) is
part of the data and is not automatic. Every statement in this development
names (H) when it is used.

Throughout, fix a finite horizon $T>0$. An **elementary predictable Brownian
integrand** on $[0,T]$ is a process of the form
$$H_s(\omega)=\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\xi_k(\omega)\,1_{(t_k,t_{k+1}]}(s),\qquad s\in[0,T],$$
where $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_m=T$ is a finite partition of $[0,T]$, each
$\xi_k$ is a bounded real $\mathcal F_{t_k}$-measurable random variable, and
the values at the partition points are irrelevant because the intervals are
left-open and right-closed. The **mesh** of the representation is
$\max_k(t_{k+1}-t_k)$, and the **supremum norm** of the representation is
$\max_k\|\xi_k\|_\infty$. The integrand itself is the process $H$; a second
list of the same name with different coefficients is the same elementary
integrand only if the two processes coincide in the almost-everywhere sense
made precise below.

The following properties are part of the definition and are used at once.

1. **Predictability.** $H$ is predictable
   Progressively measurable and predictable processes. Indeed, for a
   Borel set $\Gamma\subseteq\mathbb R$,
   $$\{H\in\Gamma\}=Z_\Gamma\cup\bigcup_{k=0}^{m-1}\bigl((t_k,t_{k+1}]\times\{\xi_k\in\Gamma\}\bigr), \qquad Z_\Gamma:=\begin{cases}\{0\}\times\Omega,&0\in\Gamma,\\\varnothing,&0\notin\Gamma,\end{cases}$$
   a finite union of generators of the predictable sigma-algebra because
   $\{\xi_k\in\Gamma\}\in\mathcal F_{t_k}$ and
   $\{0\}\times\Omega$ is a time-zero generator. Consequently $H$ is progressively
   measurable and measurable for the product sigma-algebra
   $\mathcal B([0,T])\otimes\mathcal F$, and $H$ belongs to
   $L^2([0,T]\times\Omega,\mathrm dt\otimes P)$: with
   $c:=\max_k\|\xi_k\|_\infty<\infty$ one has
   $E\int_0^TH_s^2\,ds\le c^2T<\infty$.

2. **Endpoint and null-set conventions.** Replacing the intervals by
   $(t_k,t_{k+1}]$ makes the value at $s=0$ zero for every elementary
   integrand. More generally, if two elementary integrands agree for all
   $s\in[0,T]$ except at finitely many deterministic times, then they agree
   $(\mathrm dt\otimes P)$-almost everywhere, since a finite set of times is
   Lebesgue-null and Tonelli computes
   $\mathrm dt\otimes P(\{u\}\times\Omega)=0$. All integrands and all
   integrals below are therefore elements of the quotient spaces of
   $L^2(\mathrm dt\otimes P)$ and $L^2(P)$; a claim about a process is a claim
   about its almost-everywhere class unless a representative is explicitly
   named, and path statements name the continuous representative.

3. **Deterministic coefficients.** If every $\xi_k$ is a deterministic real
   number, $H$ is a deterministic step function on $[0,T]$, so the elementary
   integrands include all step functions with deterministic coefficients. These
   are the integrands for which the integral is a Gaussian variable below.

The Axiom of Choice is declared because the Brownian construction and the
conditional-expectation interface used in items 6, 7 and 13 assume it; the
definition itself, including the predictability computation of clause 1, uses
no choice. The countable-choice obligations inherited from that interface are declared
as dependencies of this item.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and work under the standing hypothesis (H) of
Elementary predictable Brownian integrands: a filtered probability space
with a standard Brownian motion $B$ adapted to the filtration, with increments
$B_t-B_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ of law $N(0,t-s)$. Fix $T>0$ and an
elementary predictable integrand
$$H_s=\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\xi_k\,1_{(t_k,t_{k+1}]}(s),\qquad 0=t_0<\cdots<t_m=T,$$
with bounded $\mathcal F_{t_k}$-measurable coefficients $\xi_k$. The **Ito
integral of $H$ against $B$** is the process
$$I_t(H):=\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\xi_k\bigl(B_{t\wedge t_{k+1}}-B_{t\wedge t_k}\bigr),\qquad 0\le t\le T,$$
also written $\int_0^tH_s\,dB_s$ or $(H\cdot B)_t$. The sum is finite and is
evaluated with the Brownian path of the given representative; on the event
where $t\mapsto B_t$ is continuous it is continuous in $t$, and $I_0(H)=0$
because $0\wedge t_k=0$ for every $k$.

Three conventions are part of the definition.

1. **Adaptedness and continuity.** For fixed $t$, each summand
   $\xi_k(B_{t\wedge t_{k+1}}-B_{t\wedge t_k})$ is $\mathcal F_t$-measurable:
   if $t<t_k$, the Brownian difference and hence the summand are zero; if
   $t\ge t_k$, then $\mathcal F_{t_k}\subseteq\mathcal F_t$, while
   $B_{t\wedge u}$ is $\mathcal F_t$-measurable for every $u$ because
   $t\wedge u\le t$. Thus
   $I(H)$ is adapted. For each fixed $\omega$ the map
   $t\mapsto B_{t\wedge t_{k+1}}(\omega)-B_{t\wedge t_k}(\omega)$ is continuous
   outside the single exceptional null set of (H) on which the Brownian path is
   discontinuous; the finite sum is therefore continuous on the same event.

2. **Linearity on a common refinement.** If $H$ and $K$ are elementary
   integrands and a partition refines both representations, then the defining
   sums of $H$, $K$, $H+K$ and $aH$ are taken over that common partition, and
   the finite sums give $I_t(H+K)=I_t(H)+I_t(K)$ and $I_t(aH)=aI_t(H)$ for real
   $a$ identically. In particular $I_t(H)-I_t(K)=I_t(H-K)$ for the
   elementary integrand $H-K$ represented on that refinement. This is a
   rearrangement of finitely many terms, not a limiting statement.

3. **Dependence on the representation is temporary.** The definition attaches
   $I_t(H)$ to a *chosen* elementary representation.
   Elementary Ito integrals do not depend on step representation proves that
   two representations that agree $(\mathrm dt\otimes P)$-almost everywhere
   produce the same random variables almost surely at each fixed time, so that
   $I_t(H)$ is a function of the $(\mathrm dt\otimes P)$-class of $H$ alone.
   Until then, every statement about an elementary integrand names the
   representation it uses.

The Axiom of Choice is declared because the standing hypothesis (H) is part of
the Brownian interface of
Elementary predictable Brownian integrands, which assumes it; the
definition of the finite sum uses no choice. The countable-choice obligations
inherited from that interface are declared as dependencies of this item.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
Elementary predictable Brownian integrands. Fix a horizon $T>0$ and let
$\mathcal P_T$ be the predictable sigma-algebra on $[0,T]\times\Omega$
Progressively measurable and predictable processes. Let $H$ be a
predictable process with
$$E\int_0^TH_s^2\,ds=\int_{[0,T]\times\Omega}H^2\,d(\mathrm dt\otimes P)<\infty ,$$
so that $H$ is an element of the quotient space
$L^2(\mathrm dt\otimes P)$ over $\mathcal P_T$; its class is what is integrated.
The **Ito integral** $\int_0^TH_s\,dB_s$, also written $H\cdot B$ or $I_T(H)$,
is defined as follows.

1. **Construction.** By the density theorem
   Density of elementary predictable processes in predictable L2 there
   is a sequence $(H^n)$ of bounded elementary predictable integrands
   Elementary predictable Brownian integrands with
   $\|H^n-H\|_{L^2(\mathrm dt\otimes P)}\to0$. For such a sequence the
   elementary integrals $I_T(H^n)$
   Ito integral of an elementary predictable process form a Cauchy
   sequence in $L^2(P)$: by the elementary isometry
   Ito isometry for elementary integrands and the well-definedness of
   the elementary integral,
   $$E\bigl(I_T(H^n)-I_T(H^m)\bigr)^2=E\int_0^T(H^n-H^m)^2ds=\|H^n-H^m\|^2_{L^2(\mathrm dt\otimes P)} ,$$
   and the right-hand side tends to $0$. Since $L^2(P)$ is complete
   Riesz-Fischer completeness of $L^p$ for $1 \le p \le \infty$, the classes $I_T(H^n)$ converge
   in $L^2(P)$; the limit is a class in $L^2(P)$, and
   $$\int_0^TH_s\,dB_s:=\lim_{n\to\infty}I_T(H^n)\qquad\text{in }L^2(P).$$
   The limit is a random variable only up to almost-sure equality; statements
   about it are statements about that class. The limit does not depend on the
   chosen sequence: if another elementary sequence $K^n\to H$ is used, then
   the elementary isometry and linearity give
   $$\|I_T(H^n)-I_T(K^n)\|_{L^2(P)} =\|H^n-K^n\|_{L^2(\mathrm dt\otimes P)} \le\|H^n-H\|_2+\|K^n-H\|_2\longrightarrow0,$$
   so the two $L^2(P)$ limits agree.

2. **Integrals at a time.** For $t\in[0,T]$ put
   $\int_0^tH_s\,dB_s:=\int_0^TH_s1_{[0,t]}(s)\,dB_s$, the construction of
   clause 1 applied to the truncated process $H1_{[0,t]}$. That process is
   predictable: $H$ is $\mathcal P_T$-measurable and $1_{[0,t]}$ is a
   deterministic predictable indicator, so the product is
   $\mathcal P_T$-measurable; and it is square-integrable because
   $|H1_{[0,t]}|\le|H|$ pointwise. The same construction applied to $H$
   itself gives $t=T$. The family
   $\bigl(\int_0^tH\,dB\bigr)_{t\in[0,T]}$ is a family of $L^2(P)$-classes
   indexed by $t$; its continuous version is supplied by item 13, and no path
   property is asserted by this definition.

3. **Consistency with elementary integrands.** If $H$ is itself elementary,
   then the constant sequence $H^n:=H$ is admissible in clause 1, so
   $\int_0^TH\,dB$ is the limit of the constant sequence of elementary sums,
   namely the elementary sum $I_T(H)$ of
   Ito integral of an elementary predictable process. The same argument
   with $H1_{[0,t]}$ in place of $H$, and the finite telescoping of the
   elementary sum over a refinement containing $t$, gives
   $\int_0^tH\,dB=I_t(H)$ for every $t\in[0,T]$. In particular the general
   definition extends, rather than replaces, the elementary definition.

4. **Linearity in the integrand is not asserted here.** Clause 1 defines each
   integral separately from an arbitrary approximating sequence; the linear and
   isometric properties of the extension are item 12. Until item 12 is proved,
   linearity may be used only for elementary integrands, where it is part of
   Ito integral of an elementary predictable process.

5. **Comparison with deterministic Riemann integration.** The integral is a
   stochastic integral: the integrand is paired with the Brownian path through
   left-endpoint sums and an $L^2(P)$ limit. This definition does not assert
   convergence of arbitrary tagged Riemann--Stieltjes sums for a general
   predictable integrand. Particular integrands can have a pathwise
   interpretation: for $H\equiv1$ every tagged sum telescopes to $B_T-B_0$,
   which is also its Ito integral by clause 3 (the value at time zero is
   irrelevant to its product-measure class). The notation $\int_0^TH\,dB$
   here always refers to the $L^2(P)$-class defined above.

The Axiom of Choice is declared because the construction selects an
approximating sequence and uses the completeness and conditional-expectation
interfaces that assume it; the inherited obligations are declared as
dependencies of this item. An alternative construction that avoids selecting the sequence is
not needed, because clause 1 shows every sequence gives the same class.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
Elementary predictable Brownian integrands. Fix $T>0$. For predictable
$H,K$ with finite energy $E\int_0^TH^2ds,E\int_0^TK^2ds<\infty$ the integrals
$\int_0^TH\,dB$ of
Ito integral for square-integrable predictable processes satisfy
$$\int_0^T(H+K)\,dB=\int_0^TH\,dB+\int_0^TK\,dB,\qquad \int_0^T(aH)\,dB=a\int_0^TH\,dB\quad(a\in\mathbb R),$$
and the identities are equalities of $L^2(P)$-classes (almost sure
equalities). Moreover the map $H\mapsto\int_0^TH\,dB$ is an isometry,
$$E\Bigl(\int_0^TH\,dB\Bigr)^2=E\int_0^TH^2ds=\|H\|^2_{L^2(\mathrm dt\otimes P)},$$
it takes values in the mean-zero subspace of $L^2(P)$, and the bilinear cross
identity
$$E\Bigl[\Bigl(\int_0^TH\,dB\Bigr)\Bigl(\int_0^TK\,dB\Bigr)\Bigr]=E\int_0^TH_sK_s\,ds$$
holds for all such $H,K$. In particular the image of the map is a closed
subspace of $L^2(P)$ isometric to the predictable $L^2$ space of $H$'s, and
$H\mapsto\int_0^TH\,dB$ is injective up to the $(\mathrm dt\otimes P)$-class.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

1. For $1\le p<\infty$, the rule
   $$\|[f]\|_p:=\|f\|_p\qquad([f]\in L^p(\mu))$$
   is well defined on the quotient classes.
2. For $p=\infty$, the rule
   $$\|[f]\|_\infty:=\|f\|_\infty\qquad([f]\in L^\infty(\mu))$$
   is well defined.
3. In either case, with the quotient vector-space operations of
   Coset equality, well-defined quotient operations, and the canonical projection with kernel $W$, the resulting pair
   $(L^p(\mu),\|\cdot\|_p)$ is a normed space in the sense of
   A norm on a real vector space, the induced metric, and the dictionary with the metric axioms.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume AC. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then $$\Phi_X(t):=\mathbb E e^{it\cdot X}=\exp(it\cdot m-t^T\Sigma t/2)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R^d).$$ This transform uniquely determines the law, including singular Sigma.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
Elementary predictable Brownian integrands. Let $H$ be a predictable
process with $E\int_0^TH_s^2ds<\infty$ for every finite $T$. Then there is an
adapted process $M=(M_t)_{t\ge0}$ with continuous paths such that
$M_t=\int_0^tH_s\,dB_s$ almost surely for every $t\ge0$
Ito integral for square-integrable predictable processes, and $M$ is a
square-integrable martingale relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$
Continuous-time adapted processes and martingales: $EM_t^2=E\int_0^tH_s^2ds<\infty$
for every $t$. Any two such continuous versions agree at every time on one
measurable event of probability one; in particular the continuous version is
unique in this common-full-measure-event sense, and it is the only continuous
square-integrable martingale whose value at each deterministic $t$ is the
integral class.

This conclusion is deliberately distinguished from the exact definition of
indistinguishability in
Process law, modification, and indistinguishability. On a
noncomplete probability space the full equality set, although it contains the
measurable probability-one event constructed below, need not itself be
measurable. On a complete probability space the two notions coincide, because
the complement of the equality set is then a measurable subset of a null set.

derivations.claim: Fix $0\le s<t\le T$ and put $H(r)=g(r)1_{(s,t]}(r)$. By [F4], choose elementary predictable approximants $H_n(r,\omega)=\sum_k\xi_{n,k}(\omega)1_{(r_{n,k},r_{n,k+1}]}(r)$ converging to $H$ in $L^2(dr\otimes P)$. On each interval define the deterministic coefficient $\bar\xi_{n,k}=E[\xi_{n,k}]$ and let $\bar H_n=\sum_k\bar\xi_{n,k}1_{(r_{n,k},r_{n,k+1}]}$. Boundedness of the elementary coefficients makes these expectations finite. For every $r$ in the kth interval, nonnegativity of $\operatorname{Var}(\xi_{n,k}-H(r))$ from [F6] gives $|\bar\xi_{n,k}-H(r)|^2\le E|\xi_{n,k}-H(r)|^2$. Integrating and applying [F7], with Tonelli [F8] to exchange the time integral and expectation of this nonnegative integrand, yields $\|\bar H_n-H\|_{L^2([0,T])}^2\le E\int_0^T|H_n-H|^2dr\to0$. Set $H_n^0=\bar H_n1_{(s,t]}$; it remains a deterministic step integrand and its error cannot increase, because $H=0$ outside $(s,t]$.

Write $H_n^0=\sum_j a_{n,j}1_{(u_{n,j},u_{n,j+1}]}$ on a partition of $[s,t]$. By [F3], its vector integral is $Z_n=\sum_j a_{n,j}(W_{u_{n,j+1}}-W_{u_{n,j}})$. For $\theta\in\mathbb R^d$, independence and the Gaussian increment laws in [F1] give $E e^{i\theta\cdot Z_n}=\prod_j\exp(-a_{n,j}^2(u_{n,j+1}-u_{n,j})|\theta|^2/2)=\exp(-|\theta|^2\int_s^t(H_n^0)^2dr/2)$. The same factorization holds with any indicator $1_A$, $A\in\mathcal F_s$, inserted: each increment is independent of the sigma-algebra at its left endpoint, which contains $A$ and all preceding increments, so repeated factorization gives $E[1_Ae^{i\theta\cdot Z_n}]=P(A)E e^{i\theta\cdot Z_n}$.

Let $Z=M_t-M_s$. By [F5] applied to the deterministic step integrands, $E|Z_n-Z|^2=d\int_s^t|H_n^0(r)-g(r)|^2dr\to0$. Since $|e^{i\theta\cdot z}-e^{i\theta\cdot w}|\le|\theta||z-w|$, nonnegativity of the variance of $|Z_n-Z|$ in [F6] gives convergence of both the ordinary and $1_A$-weighted characteristic functions. Also $\int_s^t(H_n^0)^2dr\to\int_s^tg(r)^2dr=v(t)-v(s)$ by the square-integrable norm convergence in step 1.1 and the norm-continuity result [F7]. Passing to the limit in step 1.2 therefore gives $Ee^{i\theta\cdot Z}=\exp(-|\theta|^2(v(t)-v(s))/2)$ and $E[1_Ae^{i\theta\cdot Z}]=P(A)\exp(-|\theta|^2(v(t)-v(s))/2)$ for every $\theta$ and every $A\in\mathcal F_s$.

The multivariate-normal convention [F9] identifies the Gaussian law from its one-dimensional normal projections, and [F10] gives the characteristic function in step 2.1 for those projections. For any $A\in\mathcal F_s$ with $P(A)>0$, the probability measure $B\mapsto P(Z\in B,A)/P(A)$ has the same characteristic function by the second identity, so uniqueness in [F10] identifies it with that same Gaussian law. If $P(A)=0$, the joint probability is zero. Thus $Z$ is independent of $\mathcal F_s$.

By [F11], $M$ has an adapted continuous version. For any finite increasing list $0=t_0<\cdots<t_n$, the increments through time $t_{j-1}$ are $\mathcal F_{t_{j-1}}$-measurable. Step 3.1 makes the next increment independent of that sigma-algebra; induction on $j$ therefore factors the joint probabilities of all increment Borel sets into the product of their marginal probabilities. This proves mutual independence over the list.

finite_smoke.asserts: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix a finite integer $d\ge1$, a horizon $T>0$, and a complete filtered probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{0\le t\le T},P)$. Let $W=(W_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ be a standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion adapted to the filtration, and assume that for every $0\le s<t\le T$ the vector increment $W_t-W_s$ is independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and has law $N_d(0,(t-s)I_d)$. Let $g:[0,T]\to(0,\infty)$ be continuously differentiable with constants $0<g_{\min}\le g(t)\le g_{\max}<\infty$, set $v(t)=\int_0^t g(r)^2\,dr$, and define $M_t=(\int_0^t g(r)\,dW_r^1,\ldots,\int_0^t g(r)\,dW_r^d)$ by coordinatewise scalar Itô integration. For every $0\le s<t\le T$, the increment $M_t-M_s$ is independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and has law $N_d(0,(v(t)-v(s))I_d)$. Consequently, the increments of $M$ over every finite increasing time list are mutually independent.
finite_smoke.claim: The scalar constant-integrand case agrees with the Gaussian variance and independent-increment formulas proved for arbitrary deterministic g.

risk_review.notes: Read all five proof steps and exact statements of all twelve suppliers. Bounded elementary coefficients admit deterministic means; variance nonnegativity and Tonelli contract their L2 approximation error. Truncation to (s,t] preserves predictability. Coordinatewise isometry and norm continuity give Gaussian characteristic-function limits. Weighted characteristic functions for every past event establish filtration independence (including null events); adapted continuous versions then give finite-list independence. Checked d=1, s=0, strictly positive variance and finite T. Full AC is inherited from Ito and Gaussian interfaces. Constant g gives variance g^2(t-s). citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ (Measures on sigma-algebras). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** (Measure spaces); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Assume the Axiom of Choice as required by the stochastic-integral interfaces
below. Fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$ and finite integers $d,m\ge1$. Work on
a complete filtered probability space
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{0\le t\le T},P)$ whose filtration is
right-continuous and contains every $P$-null subset of $\mathcal F$ in
$\mathcal F_0$ (the usual conditions).

Let $W=(W_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ be a standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion
$d$-dimensional Brownian motion adapted to this filtration, with

derivations.claim: For $b(t,x)=0$ and $\sigma(t,x)=g(t)I_d$, the state-Lipschitz constant is zero and $\|\sigma(t,x)\|_F=\sqrt d\,g(t)\le\sqrt d\,g_{\max}$, so the linear-growth bound in [F2] holds with $K=\sqrt d\,g_{\max}$. Since $|X_0|\le R$ almost surely, $E|X_0|^2\le R^2$. The complete usual filtration, Brownian independence, and initial-value hypotheses are exactly those of [F2]; [F3] therefore gives the unique strong solution used in the definition.

Since $g(r)\ge g_{\min}>0$, $v(t)>0$ for $t>0$ and $v(t)-v(s)\ge g_{\min}^2(t-s)>0$ for $s<t$. The one-dimensional density $(2\pi a)^{-1/2}e^{-u^2/(2a)}$ is obtained from the standard normal density in [F8] by the $C^1$ scaling $u\mapsto\sqrt a\,u$ in [F10], so it is positive and has integral one by [F9]. The product formula for $\phi_a$ is therefore positive; Tonelli [F11] gives $\int_{\mathbb R^d}\phi_a(z)\,dz=\prod_{j=1}^d1=1$.

The bound $\phi_{v(t)}(x-z)\le(2\pi v(t))^{-d/2}$ and $\mu(\mathbb R^d)=1$ show $p_t(x)<\infty$. Since $\phi_{v(t)}(x-z)>0$ for every $z$ and $\mu$ has mass one, $p_t(x)>0$. Tonelli and translation change of variables give $\int_{\mathbb R^d}p_t(x)\,dx=\int_{\mathbb R^d}\left(\int_{\mathbb R^d}\phi_{v(t)}(x-z)\,dx\right)\mu(dz)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}1\,\mu(dz)=1.$ The same argument proves that $q(s,x;t,\cdot)$ is positive, finite, and normalized for every $s<t$ and $x$.

Write $Z_t=X_t-X_0=\int_0^t g(r)\,dW_r$. By [F4], $Z_t$ is independent of $X_0$, which is measurable at time zero, and has law $N_d(0,v(t)I_d)$. By [F12] this law is the product of $d$ scalar normal laws of variance $v(t)$; [F8]–[F11] show that this product law has density $\phi_{v(t)}$. The independent-random-elements product law [F6] and the continuous addition map give, for every Borel $A$, $P(X_t\in A)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}\mathbf1_A(z+w)\phi_{v(t)}(w)\,dw\,\mu(dz)=\int_A\left(\int_{\mathbb R^d}\phi_{v(t)}(x-z)\,\mu(dz)\right)dx,$ where Tonelli and translation were used in the last equality. Fix $0\le s<t\le T$. The vector $Z_{s,t}=X_t-X_s$ is independent of $\mathcal F_s$ by [F4], and $X_s$ is $\mathcal F_s$-measurable by the strong-solution conclusion of [F3]. For $0\le s<r<t\le T$, put $a=v(r)-v(s)>0$ and $b=v(t)-v(r)>0$. In one coordinate, completing the square gives $\frac{(z-x)^2}{a}+\frac{(y-z)^2}{b}=\frac{a+b}{ab}\left(z-\frac{bx+ay}{a+b}\right)^2+\frac{(y-x)^2}{a+b}.$ Applying this identity in each of the $d$ coordinates and integrating the centered Gaussian factor using [F9]–[F11] yields $\int\phi_a(z-x)\phi_b(y-z)\,dz=\phi_{a+b}(y-x)$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge1$, $T>0$, and let $\mu$ be a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R^d$ supported in the closed ball $\overline B(0,R)$ for some finite $R\ge0$. Let $g:[0,T]\to(0,\infty)$ be continuously differentiable with $0<g_{\min}\le g(t)\le g_{\max}<\infty$, and set $v(t)=\int_0^t g(r)^2\,dr$. On a complete filtered probability space with the usual conditions, take $X_0$ with law $\mu$, measurable at time zero and independent of the future Brownian increments. Let $W$ be a standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion adapted to the filtration, with $W_t-W_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and distributed as $N_d(0,(t-s)I_d)$ for every $0\le s<t\le T$. Let $X$ be the strong solution of $dX_t=g(t)\,dW_t$ with initial value $X_0$. For $a>0$ define the product Gaussian density $\phi_a(z)=\prod_{j=1}^d(2\pi a)^{-1/2}\exp(-z_j^2/(2a))$. For $t>0$ and $0\le s<t\le T$, define

$$p_t(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}\phi_{v(t)}(x-z)\,\mu(dz),\qquad q(s,x;t,y)=\phi_{v(t)-v(s)}(y-x).$$

Then $p_t$ is a finite, strictly positive, normalized Lebesgue density of the law of $X_t$. For each $x$, $q(s,x;t,\cdot)$ is a finite, strictly positive, normalized Lebesgue density, and for all Borel sets $A,B\subseteq\mathbb R^d$,

$$P(X_s\in A,\ X_t\in B)=\int_A\int_B q(s,x;t,y)\,dy\,\mu_s(dx),\qquad \mu_s:=\operatorname{Law}(X_s).$$

For $0\le s<r<t\le T$, these transition densities satisfy

$$\int_{\mathbb R^d}q(s,x;r,z)q(r,z;t,y)\,dz=q(s,x;t,y)\qquad(x,y\in\mathbb R^d).$$

No Lebesgue density for the initial law $\mu$ is assumed.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

For Borel probability measures $\mu_n,\mu$ on a metric space S, write $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$ if $\int f\,d\mu_n\to\int f\,d\mu$ for every bounded continuous real function f on S. Continuity is Continuity of a map between metric spaces, at a point and globally, in the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ form. Such f is Borel measurable (inverse images of open sets are open) and $\int|f|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\mu(S)<\infty$, so the integrals are finite in Integrable real and complex functions, and their integrals. No completeness or coupling is required.

Assume AC. Two Borel probability laws on $\mathbb R$ with equal characteristic functions are equal. In particular a real random variable has a real-valued characteristic function if and only if its law is symmetric under $x\mapsto-x$.

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$ be a finite integer and $p_\theta(x)=\theta\cdot x$ for $\theta\in\mathbb R^d$. Borel probability laws on $\mathbb R^d$ are determined by all the laws $(p_\theta)_*\mu$. Moreover, if $(p_\theta)_*\mu_n\Rightarrow(p_\theta)_*\mu$ for every $\theta$ and a specified Borel probability law $\mu$, then $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$. If dimension zero is admitted, interpret $\mathbb R^0$ as the singleton empty tuple; both conclusions then hold as well.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element. Its
**law** or **distribution** is the set function
$$\mathbb P_X:\Sigma\to[0,+\infty],\qquad \mathbb P_X(B):=\mathbb P(X^{-1}(B)).$$

Thus the law of $X$ records the probability of each measurable target set by
pulling it back to an event in the original probability space.

Assume AC. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then $$\Phi_X(t):=\mathbb E e^{it\cdot X}=\exp(it\cdot m-t^T\Sigma t/2)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R^d).$$ This transform uniquely determines the law, including singular Sigma.

derivations.claim: For $a>0$, direct differentiation gives $\partial_a\phi_a(z)=\tfrac12\Delta_z\phi_a(z)$. Every finite spatial derivative of $\phi_a(z)$ is a polynomial in $z$ and $a^{-1}$ times $\phi_a(z)$. Fix $\epsilon>0$ and compact sets $K\subset\mathbb R^d$ and $J\subset[\epsilon,T]$. Since $a=v(t)$ is bounded above and away from zero on $J$, and $z$ lies in the compact support of $\mu$, each such derivative is uniformly bounded for $x\in K$, $t\in J$, and $z\in\operatorname{supp}\mu$. Difference quotients are bounded by the same type of constant on a slightly larger compact set, by the one-variable fundamental theorem of calculus. Dominated convergence [F4] therefore permits differentiation under the finite measure $\mu$ to every spatial order and once in time. The chain rule and $v'(t)=g(t)^2$ give $\partial_t p_t(x)=\int \frac{g(t)^2}{2}\Delta_x\phi_{v(t)}(x-z)\,\mu(dz)=\frac{g(t)^2}{2}\Delta_xp_t(x).$ Positivity follows from the positive kernel and the nonzero probability measure.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge1$, $T>0$, and let $\mu$ be a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R^d$ supported in the closed ball $\overline B(0,R)$ for some finite $R\ge0$. Let $g:[0,T]\to(0,\infty)$ be continuously differentiable with $0<g_{\min}\le g(t)\le g_{\max}<\infty$, and set $v(t)=\int_0^t g(r)^2\,dr$. On a complete filtered probability space with the usual conditions, take $X_0$ with law $\mu$, measurable at time zero and independent of the future Brownian increments. Let $W$ be a standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion adapted to the filtration, with $W_t-W_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and distributed as $N_d(0,(t-s)I_d)$ for every $0\le s<t\le T$. Let $X$ be the strong solution of $dX_t=g(t)\,dW_t$ with initial value $X_0$. For $a>0$ define the product Gaussian density $\phi_a(z)=\prod_{j=1}^d(2\pi a)^{-1/2}\exp(-z_j^2/(2a))$. For $t>0$ and $0\le s<t\le T$, define

$$p_t(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}\phi_{v(t)}(x-z)\,\mu(dz),\qquad q(s,x;t,y)=\phi_{v(t)-v(s)}(y-x).$$

Then $p_t$ is a finite, strictly positive, normalized Lebesgue density of the law of $X_t$. For each $x$, $q(s,x;t,\cdot)$ is a finite, strictly positive, normalized Lebesgue density, and for all Borel sets $A,B\subseteq\mathbb R^d$,

$$P(X_s\in A,\ X_t\in B)=\int_A\int_B q(s,x;t,y)\,dy\,\mu_s(dx),\qquad \mu_s:=\operatorname{Law}(X_s).$$

For $0\le s<r<t\le T$, these transition densities satisfy

$$\int_{\mathbb R^d}q(s,x;r,z)q(r,z;t,y)\,dz=q(s,x;t,y)\qquad(x,y\in\mathbb R^d).$$

No Lebesgue density for the initial law $\mu$ is assumed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix $d\ge1$, $T>0$, a finite $R\ge0$, and a Borel probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb R^d$ supported in $\overline B(0,R)$. Let $g:[0,T]\to(0,\infty)$ be continuously differentiable with $0<g_{\min}\le g(t)\le g_{\max}<\infty$, and set $v(t)=\int_0^t g(r)^2\,dr$. On a complete filtered probability space with the usual conditions, let $X_0$ be measurable at time zero with law $\mu$ and independent of future Brownian increments. Let $W$ be a standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion adapted to the filtration, with $W_t-W_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ for every $s<t$, and let $X$ be the unique strong solution of $X_t=X_0+\int_0^t g(r)\,dW_r$. For $a>0$ define $\phi_a(z)=\prod_{j=1}^d(2\pi a)^{-1/2}\exp(-z_j^2/(2a))$. For $t>0$ set

$$p_t(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}\phi_{v(t)}(x-z)\,\mu(dz),$$

and set $\mu_0=\mu$. Let $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$ denote the real infinitely differentiable functions with compact support. For every $t>0$, $p_t$ is positive and infinitely differentiable in $x$. On each interval $[\epsilon,T]$ with $0<\epsilon<T$, it is continuously differentiable in time and satisfies

$$\partial_t p_t(x)=\frac{g(t)^2}{2}\Delta_xp_t(x),\qquad \Delta_x=\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_{x_j}^2.$$

A family $(\nu_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ of Borel probability measures is narrowly continuous when $t\mapsto\int f\,d\nu_t$ is continuous for every bounded continuous real function $f$. It is a weak forward solution with initial law $\mu$ when it is narrowly continuous, $\nu_0=\mu$, and, for every $t\in[0,T]$ and every real-valued function $\psi:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ with continuous first time derivative and continuous spatial derivatives through order two, whose spatial support lies in one compact set for all $s$, it satisfies

$$\int_{\mathbb R^d}\psi(t,x)\,\nu_t(dx)-\int_{\mathbb R^d}\psi(0,x)\,\mu(dx)=\int_0^t\int_{\mathbb R^d}\left(\partial_s\psi(s,x)+\frac{g(s)^2}{2}\Delta_x\psi(s,x)\right)\nu_s(dx)\,ds.$$

Then $(\mu_t)_{0\le t\le T}$, where $\mu_t(dx)=p_t(x)\,dx$ for $t>0$ and $\mu_0=\mu$, is the unique narrowly continuous weak forward solution with initial law $\mu$. No density for $\mu$ at $t=0$ is asserted.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

By [F4], it is supported in $\overline B(0,R)$ and has finite first and second moments. The regularity conclusion [F2] applies on $[\epsilon,T]$. On each compact set of $x$ values, every spatial derivative of $\phi_{v(t)}(x-z)$ is bounded uniformly for $z\in\overline B(0,R)$ because $v(t)>0$ is fixed and the Gaussian derivatives are polynomials times a Gaussian. For each coordinate $i$, differentiation of $p_t$ gives $\partial_i p_t(x)=\int -\frac{x_i-z_i}{v(t)}\phi_{v(t)}(x-z)\,\mu(dz)=-\frac{x_i-m_{t,x,i}}{v(t)}p_t(x).$ Dividing by the positive $p_t(x)$ proves $\nabla\log p_t(x)=-(x-m_{t,x})/v(t)$.

The quotient rule and $\partial_i\phi_{v(t)}(x-z)=-(x_i-z_i)\phi_{v(t)}(x-z)/v(t)$ yield $\partial_i m_{t,x,j}=\frac1{v(t)}\left(\int z_jz_i\,\nu_{t,x}(dz)-m_{t,x,j}m_{t,x,i}\right)=(C_{t,x})_{ji} / v(t).$ All terms are finite by [F4], and the derivative is justified by step 1.1. Differentiating the score identity from step 2.1 therefore gives $D_xs_t=-I_d/v(t)+C_{t,x}/v(t)^2$.

The matrix $C_{t,x}$ is positive semidefinite because for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$, $u^{\mathsf T}C_{t,x}u=\int(u\cdot(z-m_{t,x}))^2\,
u_{t,x}(dz)\ge0$. Also $u^{\mathsf T}C_{t,x}u=\int(u\cdot z)^2\,d
u_{t,x}-\left(\int u\cdot z\,d
u_{t,x}ight)^2\le\int|u|^2|z|^2\,d
u_{t,x}\le R^2|u|^2.$ Thus $\|C_{t,x}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le R^2$. Since $v$ is increasing and $v(t)\ge v(\epsilon)>0$, the Jacobian formula in step 3.1 and the triangle inequality for operator norms give the stated uniform derivative bound. The mean satisfies $|m_{t,x}|\le\int|z|\,d
u_{t,x}\le R$, so the score formula in step 2.1 gives the displayed growth bound.

For any $x,y$, the fundamental theorem of calculus along the segment $y+r(x-y)$ gives $s_t(x)-s_t(y)=\int_0^1D_xs_t(y+r(x-y))(x-y)\,dr$. Taking norms and using step 4.1 proves the global Lipschitz bound uniformly for $t\in[\epsilon,T]$. Since $g\ge g_{\min}>0$, $v(\epsilon)\downarrow0$ as $\epsilon\downarrow0$; the bound therefore supplies no uniform-in-$\epsilon$ constant.

citations.quote: A **supervised prediction problem** consists of nonempty measurable spaces $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$ of instances, $(\mathsf Y,\Sigma_Y)$ of labels, and $(\mathsf A,\Sigma_A)$ of prediction actions; the product measurable space $(\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y,\Sigma_X\otimes\Sigma_Y)$; a probability measure $P$ on that product; a nonempty class $\mathcal F$ of measurable predictors $f:\mathsf X\to\mathsf A$; and a loss $\ell:\mathsf A\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty]$ that is measurable with respect to $\Sigma_A\otimes\Sigma_Y$. The law $P$ need not be supported on a deterministic labeling function, and this definition imposes no assumption that sample observations be independent or share a common law.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
Measurable rectangles in a product of measurable spaces.

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

For a supervised prediction problem with joint law $P$, the **population risk** of any measurable predictor $f:\mathsf X\to\mathsf A$ (in particular, every $f\in\mathcal F$) is the extended nonnegative integral
$$R_P(f):=\int_{\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y}\ell(f(x),y)\,P(d(x,y))\in[0,+\infty].$$
For an ordered sample $S=((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_m,y_m))$ of length $m\ge1$, the **empirical risk** or **training risk** of any such $f$ is
$$\widehat R_S(f):=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\ell(f(x_i),y_i)\in[0,+\infty].$$
Neither definition assumes finite risk. The sum uses extended nonnegative arithmetic; since $m\ge1$, any summand equal to $+\infty$ makes the empirical risk $+\infty$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

1. If $f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ are measurable and $f+g$ is defined
   pointwise, then $f+g$ is measurable.
2. If $c\in\mathbb R$ and $f:X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, then $cf$ is
   measurable.
3. If $f:X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, then $f^+=\max\{f,0\}$,
   $f^-=\max\{-f,0\}$, and $|f|=f^++f^-$ are measurable.
4. If $E\in\mathcal A$ and $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, then
   $f\chi_E$ is measurable, where this function equals $f$ on $E$ and $0$
   off $E$ (in particular, $0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ here).
5. If $(f_n)$ is a sequence of measurable functions $X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$,
   then $\inf_n f_n$ is measurable; if moreover $f_n\uparrow f$ pointwise, then
   $f$ is measurable.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
(Measurable spaces and measurable sets). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space (Measure spaces). Equip
$\overline{\mathbb R}$ (The extended real line $\overline{\mathbb{R}} = \mathbb{R} \cup \{-\infty, +\infty\}$, its order, and the arithmetic that is left undefined) with its order topology and let
$\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$ be the corresponding Borel sigma-algebra
(The Borel sigma-algebra of a topological space).

A function $f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ is **measurable** when
$f^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal A$ for every $B\in\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$.

Equivalently, it is enough to require
$$\{x\in X:f(x)>a\}\in\mathcal A \qquad \text{for every } a\in\mathbb R,$$

For each measurable rectangle $U\times V$ in $\mathsf A\times\mathsf Y$, its preimage is $f^{-1}(U)\times V$, which belongs to $\Sigma_X\otimes\Sigma_Y$ by measurability of $f$. Since the rectangles generate the target product sigma-algebra by [F2], $\Phi_f$ is measurable by [F5]. Therefore $\ell_f:=\ell\circ\Phi_f$ is measurable by successive preimages in [F5] and nonnegative; [F3] defines $R_P(f)=\int\ell_f\,dP$.

For each coordinate $i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$, the sample projection $\pi_i: (\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y)^m\to\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y$ is measurable by the finite product construction in [F2]. Hence $S\mapsto\ell_f(\pi_i(S))$ is measurable by [F5]. The finite sum $s(S):=\sum_{i=1}^m\ell_f(\pi_i(S))$ is a defined nonnegative extended-real function and is measurable by [F4]. Since $m>0$, for every real $a$ we have $\{S:s(S)/m>a\}=\{S:s(S)>ma\}$, including when $s(S)=+\infty$. Thus $s/m$ is measurable by the strict-superlevel criterion [F6], and [F3] gives measurability of $S\mapsto\widehat R_S(f)$.

citations.quote: Given a sample $S$ of length $m\ge1$, an ordered finite nonempty list of measurable predictors $(f_1,\ldots,f_n)$, and a finite tolerance $\eta\ge0$, compute $r_j:=\widehat R_S(f_j)$ for each $j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$. If every $r_j=+\infty$, return index $1$. Otherwise set $r_*:=\min_{1\le j\le n}r_j$ and return the least index $j$ for which $r_j<+\infty$ and $r_j\le r_*+\eta$. The output index denotes the selected predictor from the supplied list. When $\eta=0$, the output is a first exact minimizer, including the all-infinite case. The algorithm evaluates only a finite number of empirical risks and makes no population-risk guarantee.

In a supervised prediction problem, for every measurable predictor $f$, the function $(x,y)\mapsto\ell(f(x),y)$ is measurable, so its population risk is a defined extended nonnegative integral. For every sample size $m\ge1$, the empirical risk $S\mapsto\widehat R_S(f)$ is an extended nonnegative measurable function on the finite product sample space.

Fix a sample $S$ and a nonempty class $\mathcal F$ of predictors. Its **empirical minimum** is $\widehat R_S^*(\mathcal F):=\inf_{f\in\mathcal F}\widehat R_S(f)\in[0,+\infty]$. An **exact empirical risk minimizer** is a predictor $f\in\mathcal F$ with $\widehat R_S(f)=\widehat R_S^*(\mathcal F)$. If the infimum is finite but is not attained, no exact minimizer exists. If the infimum is $+\infty$, nonemptiness implies that every member has infinite empirical risk and is an exact minimizer.

For finite $\eta\ge0$, a predictor $f\in\mathcal F$ is an **$\eta$-approximate empirical risk minimizer** if either the empirical minimum is $+\infty$ and $f$ is an exact minimizer, or the empirical minimum is finite and $f$ has finite empirical risk at most $\widehat R_S^*(\mathcal F)+\eta$. The membership requirement $f\in\mathcal F$ applies in both branches. Thus the definition never forms $+\infty+\eta$. When $\eta=0$ and the finite infimum is not attained, no such predictor exists.

For a fixed sample size $m$, a **measurable prediction rule** with class $\mathcal F$ is a jointly measurable evaluation map from the sample space $((\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y)^m, (\Sigma_X\otimes\Sigma_Y)^{\otimes m})$ and a new instance in $\mathsf X$ to $\mathsf A$, whose slice at each sample belongs to $\mathcal F$. It is an exact or approximate ERM rule when every slice satisfies the corresponding samplewise definition above. This definition asserts no existence of a measurable selector for an arbitrary class.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

1. If $f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ are measurable and $f+g$ is defined
   pointwise, then $f+g$ is measurable.
2. If $c\in\mathbb R$ and $f:X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, then $cf$ is
   measurable.
3. If $f:X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, then $f^+=\max\{f,0\}$,
   $f^-=\max\{-f,0\}$, and $|f|=f^++f^-$ are measurable.
4. If $E\in\mathcal A$ and $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, then
   $f\chi_E$ is measurable, where this function equals $f$ on $E$ and $0$
   off $E$ (in particular, $0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ here).
5. If $(f_n)$ is a sequence of measurable functions $X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$,
   then $\inf_n f_n$ is measurable; if moreover $f_n\uparrow f$ pointwise, then
   $f$ is measurable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
Measurable rectangles in a product of measurable spaces.

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space (Measure spaces). Equip
$\overline{\mathbb R}$ (The extended real line $\overline{\mathbb{R}} = \mathbb{R} \cup \{-\infty, +\infty\}$, its order, and the arithmetic that is left undefined) with its order topology and let
$\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$ be the corresponding Borel sigma-algebra
(The Borel sigma-algebra of a topological space).

A function $f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ is **measurable** when
$f^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal A$ for every $B\in\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$.

Equivalently, it is enough to require
$$\{x\in X:f(x)>a\}\in\mathcal A \qquad \text{for every } a\in\mathbb R,$$
because the rays $(a,+\infty]$ generate $\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
(Measurable spaces and measurable sets). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

derivations.claim: For $j=1,\ldots,n$, put $r_j(S)=\widehat R_S(f_j)$ and $r_*(S)=\min_j r_j(S)$. By [F2] each $r_j$ is measurable. The finite minimum is the infimum of the measurable sequence $r_1,\ldots,r_n,r_n,r_n,\ldots$, so [F4] makes $r_*$ measurable. Thus $E:=\{S:r_*(S)<+\infty\}$ is measurable by [F6].

Define finite nonnegative measurable functions $u_j:=r_j\mathbf1_{\{r_j<+\infty\}}$ and $u_*:=r_*\mathbf1_E$. Their measurability follows from [F4], including the convention $0\cdot(+\infty)=0$. The sets $\{r_j<+\infty\}$ and $E$ are measurable by [F6]. On $E$, $u_*=r_*$ and each finite $r_j$ equals $u_j$, so $C_j:=E\cap\{r_j<+\infty\}\cap\{u_j-u_*\le\eta\}$ is measurable by [F4, F6]. At every $S\in E$ a finite minimizing index lies in some $C_j$.

The algorithm's selected-index events are $\{J=1\}=E^c\cup C_1$ and, for $j>1$, $\{J=j\}=C_j\setminus\bigcup_{k<j}C_k$. They are measurable by step 2.1, so $J$ is measurable into the finite discrete index set by [F7]. For each measurable $B\subseteq\mathsf A$, the evaluation preimage is $\bigcup_{j=1}^n(\{J=j\}\times f_j^{-1}(B))$, a finite union of measurable rectangles by [F5]; hence $(S,x)\mapsto f_{J(S)}(x)$ is jointly measurable by [F7].

On $E^c$ all list risks are $+\infty$, so the returned first predictor is an exact minimizer by [F3]. On $E$, at least one finite minimizer exists in the finite list, belongs to some $C_j$, and the first selected $C_j$ has finite risk at most $r_*+\eta$ by its definition. If $\eta=0$, this inequality forces the selected risk to equal $r_*$. Thus the output has the asserted ERM property in both branches.

citations.quote: A **supervised prediction problem** consists of nonempty measurable spaces $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$ of instances, $(\mathsf Y,\Sigma_Y)$ of labels, and $(\mathsf A,\Sigma_A)$ of prediction actions; the product measurable space $(\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y,\Sigma_X\otimes\Sigma_Y)$; a probability measure $P$ on that product; a nonempty class $\mathcal F$ of measurable predictors $f:\mathsf X\to\mathsf A$; and a loss $\ell:\mathsf A\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty]$ that is measurable with respect to $\Sigma_A\otimes\Sigma_Y$. The law $P$ need not be supported on a deterministic labeling function, and this definition imposes no assumption that sample observations be independent or share a common law.

For a supervised prediction problem with joint law $P$, the **population risk** of any measurable predictor $f:\mathsf X\to\mathsf A$ (in particular, every $f\in\mathcal F$) is the extended nonnegative integral
$$R_P(f):=\int_{\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y}\ell(f(x),y)\,P(d(x,y))\in[0,+\infty].$$
For an ordered sample $S=((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_m,y_m))$ of length $m\ge1$, the **empirical risk** or **training risk** of any such $f$ is
$$\widehat R_S(f):=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\ell(f(x_i),y_i)\in[0,+\infty].$$
Neither definition assumes finite risk. The sum uses extended nonnegative arithmetic; since $m\ge1$, any summand equal to $+\infty$ makes the empirical risk $+\infty$.

A **Dedekind-complete ordered field** is a commutative field $\mathbb R$ with
identity $1>0$, a total order compatible with addition and multiplication, and
the least-upper-bound axiom: every nonempty subset of $\mathbb R$ that is
bounded above has a least upper bound in $\mathbb R$. Throughout this batch,
all real variables, intervals, limits, derivatives and integrals are taken in
such a field. The integers and rationals are interpreted in their usual
embedded copies. For $x\in\mathbb R$, define $|x|=x$ when $x\ge0$ and
$|x|=-x$ when $x<0$.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field (Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property)) and let
$\varepsilon \in F$ with $\varepsilon > 0$. Then there is a natural number
$n \ge 1$ such that

$$\frac{1}{n \cdot 1_F} < \varepsilon ,$$

where $n \cdot 1_F$ is the canonical natural of $F$ (Every complete ordered field is Archimedean) and
$1/(n \cdot 1_F)$ is its multiplicative inverse (Field). As is standard
we abbreviate $n \cdot 1_F$ to $n$ and write the conclusion $1/n < \varepsilon$.

This is the **reciprocal form** of the Archimedean property.
Every complete ordered field is Archimedean on its own delivers only the assertion that the canonical
naturals are cofinal, $x < n \cdot 1_F$; the form actually used in analysis, that
the reciprocals of the naturals get below every positive bound, is the statement
above, and it is recorded separately so that no proof has to reconstruct the
inversion step in passing.

Let $F$ be an ordered field (Ordered field) with positive cone $P$, and
let $a, b \in F$.

1. If $a > 0$ then $a^{-1} > 0$.
2. If $0 < a < b$ then $0 < b^{-1} < a^{-1}$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field, with field structure as in Field, and for
$n \ge 1$ let $n \cdot 1_F$ denote the canonical natural number
$\underbrace{1_F + \cdots + 1_F}_{n}$, defined recursively by $1 \cdot 1_F = 1_F$
and $(n+1) \cdot 1_F = n \cdot 1_F + 1_F$. Then for every $n \ge 1$:

- $n \cdot 1_F > 0$ and $(n+1) \cdot 1_F > n \cdot 1_F$;
- the map $n \mapsto n \cdot 1_F$ is strictly increasing, hence injective, on $\{1, 2, 3, \dots\}$;
- $(m+n) \cdot 1_F = m \cdot 1_F + n \cdot 1_F$ and $(mn) \cdot 1_F = (m \cdot 1_F)(n \cdot 1_F)$ for all $m, n \ge 1$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ be a measurable random element with standard-Borel target, and let $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ be any sub-sigma-algebra. There exists a regular conditional distribution of $X$ given $\mathcal G$. Every section is a probability measure, including at exceptional sample points, and no countable-generation or completeness assumption on $\mathcal G$ is required.

For this necessarily nonempty target, the construction also supplies a bimeasurable bijection $c:E\to B$ onto a Borel set $B\subseteq[0,1]$, and a countable algebra $\mathcal A$ which generates $\mathcal S$, separates points, and determines finite measures.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(T,\Tau)$ be a measurable random element and $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ a sub-sigma-algebra. A **regular conditional distribution of X given $\mathcal G$** is a probability kernel $K:(\Omega,\mathcal G)\to(T,\Tau)$ satisfying
$$\int_H K(\omega,A)\,P(d\omega)=P(H\cap\{X\in A\})\qquad(H\in\mathcal G,\ A\in\Tau).$$

“Probability kernel” has the pointwise meaning of Measure kernel and probability kernel: every $K(\omega,\cdot)$ is a probability measure, and every evaluation is $\mathcal G$-measurable. Its evaluations lie in $[0,1]$ and are integrable. Thus the testing identity says exactly that $K(\cdot,A)$ is a conditional-expectation version of $1_{\{X\in A\}}$ in Conditional expectation given a sigma algebra. Conversely, a probability kernel with these version identities satisfies the displayed definition.

The kernel requirement holds at every sample point. Separate eventwise choices of conditional-expectation versions do not imply it and do not by themselves provide one exceptional set valid for all A. When A is empty the testing identity is zero on both sides, and when A=T it is P(H) on both sides. This defines a property of a supplied kernel and makes no existence or AC assertion.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in Measures on sigma-algebras and A measurable function between measurable spaces; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
Measurable rectangles in a product of measurable spaces.

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
(Measurable spaces and measurable sets). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

Write $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ for the image of $\mathbb{Q}$ in $\mathbb{R}$
under the canonical embedding $q \mapsto \hat q$ (The rationals embed densely in the reals), the
set usually written $\mathbb{Q}$ once the identification is made, and put
$X := \mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ for the irrationals. Then:

1. $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$, that is,
   $\overline{\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}} = \mathbb{R}$ (Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$);
2. $X$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$;
3. every nonempty open subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is uncountable
   (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable).

Claim 2 is not a symmetry of claim 1: the rationals are dense because they are
*constructed* to approximate, whereas the irrationals are dense because there are
too many points in any interval for a countable set to exhaust it, which is why
claim 3 is proved alongside and used for it.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element, let
$\mathbb P_X$ be its law, and let $g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb R$ or
$g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb C$ be measurable.

1. If $g\ge0$, then
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$
2. If $g(X)$ is integrable, then $g$ is integrable with respect to
   $\mathbb P_X$ and the same formula holds:
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

1. If $f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ are measurable and $f+g$ is defined
   pointwise, then $f+g$ is measurable.
2. If $c\in\mathbb R$ and $f:X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, then $cf$ is
   measurable.
3. If $f:X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, then $f^+=\max\{f,0\}$,
   $f^-=\max\{-f,0\}$, and $|f|=f^++f^-$ are measurable.
4. If $E\in\mathcal A$ and $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, then
   $f\chi_E$ is measurable, where this function equals $f$ on $E$ and $0$
   off $E$ (in particular, $0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ here).
5. If $(f_n)$ is a sequence of measurable functions $X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$,
   then $\inf_n f_n$ is measurable; if moreover $f_n\uparrow f$ pointwise, then
   $f$ is measurable.

derivations.claim: Work on $\Omega=\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y$ with sigma-algebra $\mathcal F=\Sigma_X\otimes\Sigma_Y$ and probability $P$. Let $X(x,y)=x$ and $Y(x,y)=y$. These projections are measurable by [F3], and $X$ has law $P_X$. The family $\mathcal G:=\{X^{-1}(C):C\in\Sigma_X\}$ is a sigma-algebra, since inverse images preserve the full set, complements and countable unions; it is contained in $\mathcal F$ and is exactly $\sigma(X)$. Apply [F1] to the label coordinate $Y$ given this exact, uncompleted $\mathcal G$, obtaining a kernel $L$ as in [F2].

Fix one $y_0\in\mathsf Y$ and define $s:\mathsf X\to\Omega$ by $s(x)=(x,y_0)$. As a map into $(\Omega,\mathcal G)$ it is measurable: for every $C\in\Sigma_X$, $s^{-1}(X^{-1}(C))=C$, and step 1.1 describes every set of $\mathcal G$ in this form. Also $X(s(x))=x$ for every $x$.

Every $\mathcal G$-measurable real function $v$ is constant on each $X$-fiber. Indeed, if $X(\omega)=X(\omega')$ but $v(\omega)<v(\omega')$, choose a rational $r$ strictly between these values by [F4]. The measurable set $\{v\le r\}$ equals $X^{-1}(C)$ for some $C\in\Sigma_X$ by step 1.1, and so cannot contain exactly one of $\omega,\omega'$, a contradiction. Reversing the two points rules out the other inequality. Applying this to $v(\omega)=L(\omega,A)\in[0,1]$ separately for each $A\in\Sigma_Y$ gives $L(\omega,A)=L(s(X(\omega)),A)$ for every $\omega$ and every $A$. These are pointwise identities, with no event-dependent null sets.

Define $K(x,A):=L(s(x),A)$. Every $K(x,\cdot)$ is a probability measure by [F2]. For fixed $A$, the evaluation is the composition of the $\mathcal G$-measurable evaluation of $L$ with the measurable map $s$ from step 2.1, so it is $\Sigma_X$-measurable by [F3]. Thus $K$ is an everywhere probability kernel, and step 3.1 gives $K(X(\omega),A)=L(\omega,A)$ for every $\omega,A$.

Fix $C\in\Sigma_X$ and $A\in\Sigma_Y$. The real function $g(x)=\mathbf1_C(x)K(x,A)$ is measurable, nonnegative and bounded by one by [F6] and step 4.1. Apply [F5] and then [F2] to obtain $\int_C K(x,A)P_X(dx)=\int_{X^{-1}(C)}K(X(\omega),A)P(d\omega)=\int_{X^{-1}(C)}L(\omega,A)P(d\omega)=P(X^{-1}(C)\cap Y^{-1}(A))=P(C\times A)$. Since $C,A$ were arbitrary, this proves the Statement on the original arbitrary measurable instance space.

Let $n\ge1$, let $Z_1,\ldots,Z_n$ be IID observations with law $P$, and let $\mathcal F$ be a finite nonempty class of measurable functions $f:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$. For every $\epsilon>0$,

$$P\left(\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}|P_nf-Pf|\ge\epsilon\right)\le2|\mathcal F|e^{-2n\epsilon^2}.$$

Here $P_nf=n^{-1}\sum_i f(Z_i)$ and $Pf=\int f\,dP$. The proof uses only scalar exponential moments and finite independence; it does not assume the Axiom of Choice.

A **supervised prediction problem** consists of nonempty measurable spaces $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$ of instances, $(\mathsf Y,\Sigma_Y)$ of labels, and $(\mathsf A,\Sigma_A)$ of prediction actions; the product measurable space $(\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y,\Sigma_X\otimes\Sigma_Y)$; a probability measure $P$ on that product; a nonempty class $\mathcal F$ of measurable predictors $f:\mathsf X\to\mathsf A$; and a loss $\ell:\mathsf A\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty]$ that is measurable with respect to $\Sigma_A\otimes\Sigma_Y$. The law $P$ need not be supported on a deterministic labeling function, and this definition imposes no assumption that sample observations be independent or share a common law.

For a supervised prediction problem with joint law $P$, the **population risk** of any measurable predictor $f:\mathsf X\to\mathsf A$ (in particular, every $f\in\mathcal F$) is the extended nonnegative integral
$$R_P(f):=\int_{\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y}\ell(f(x),y)\,P(d(x,y))\in[0,+\infty].$$
For an ordered sample $S=((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_m,y_m))$ of length $m\ge1$, the **empirical risk** or **training risk** of any such $f$ is
$$\widehat R_S(f):=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\ell(f(x_i),y_i)\in[0,+\infty].$$
Neither definition assumes finite risk. The sum uses extended nonnegative arithmetic; since $m\ge1$, any summand equal to $+\infty$ makes the empirical risk $+\infty$.

Fix a sample $S$ and a nonempty class $\mathcal F$ of predictors. Its **empirical minimum** is $\widehat R_S^*(\mathcal F):=\inf_{f\in\mathcal F}\widehat R_S(f)\in[0,+\infty]$. An **exact empirical risk minimizer** is a predictor $f\in\mathcal F$ with $\widehat R_S(f)=\widehat R_S^*(\mathcal F)$. If the infimum is finite but is not attained, no exact minimizer exists. If the infimum is $+\infty$, nonemptiness implies that every member has infinite empirical risk and is an exact minimizer.

For finite $\eta\ge0$, a predictor $f\in\mathcal F$ is an **$\eta$-approximate empirical risk minimizer** if either the empirical minimum is $+\infty$ and $f$ is an exact minimizer, or the empirical minimum is finite and $f$ has finite empirical risk at most $\widehat R_S^*(\mathcal F)+\eta$. The membership requirement $f\in\mathcal F$ applies in both branches. Thus the definition never forms $+\infty+\eta$. When $\eta=0$ and the finite infimum is not attained, no such predictor exists.

For a fixed sample size $m$, a **measurable prediction rule** with class $\mathcal F$ is a jointly measurable evaluation map from the sample space $((\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y)^m, (\Sigma_X\otimes\Sigma_Y)^{\otimes m})$ and a new instance in $\mathsf X$ to $\mathsf A$, whose slice at each sample belongs to $\mathcal F$. It is an exact or approximate ERM rule when every slice satisfies the corresponding samplewise definition above. This definition asserts no existence of a measurable selector for an arbitrary class.

Given a sample $S$ of length $m\ge1$, an ordered finite nonempty list of measurable predictors $(f_1,\ldots,f_n)$, and a finite tolerance $\eta\ge0$, compute $r_j:=\widehat R_S(f_j)$ for each $j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$. If every $r_j=+\infty$, return index $1$. Otherwise set $r_*:=\min_{1\le j\le n}r_j$ and return the least index $j$ for which $r_j<+\infty$ and $r_j\le r_*+\eta$. The output index denotes the selected predictor from the supplied list. When $\eta=0$, the output is a first exact minimizer, including the all-infinite case. The algorithm evaluates only a finite number of empirical risks and makes no population-risk guarantee.

For a sample of positive length, a finite ordered nonempty list of measurable predictors, and finite tolerance $\eta\ge0$, let $J(S)$ be the index returned by the finite-list empirical-risk algorithm. Then $J$ is measurable into the finite index set with its discrete sigma-algebra, the evaluation map $(S,x)\mapsto f_{J(S)}(x)$ is jointly measurable, and the returned predictor is an $\eta$-approximate empirical risk minimizer as defined in the algorithm's input conditions. When $\eta=0$, it is an exact minimizer.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in Law or distribution of a random element agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in Independent random elements. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because The exponential is a continuous bijection from $\mathbb{R}$ onto $(0,\infty)$ states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

derivations.claim: For each $h\in\mathcal H$, define $g_h(x,y)=\mathbf1\{h(x)\ne y\}$. Its unit-level set is $(h^{-1}\{0\}\times\{1\})\cup(h^{-1}\{1\}\times\{0\})$, a measurable union of rectangles because $h$ is measurable and $\{0,1\}$ is discrete. Thus $g_h$ is measurable and $[0,1]$-valued; $G:=\{g_h:h\in\mathcal H\}$ is finite and nonempty with $|G|\le|\mathcal H|$. By [F3], $Pg_h=R_P(h)$ and $P_mg_h=\widehat R_S(h)$.

By [F7], the observations meet the IID hypothesis of [F1]. Put $a=a_{m,\mathcal H,\delta}$. Since $|\mathcal H|\ge1$ and $2/\delta>1$, [F8] makes the numerator positive, so $a>0$. Apply [F1] to $G$ at $t=a$. By [F8], $\log|\mathcal H|+\log(2/\delta)=\log(2|\mathcal H|/\delta)$ and $e^{-\log(2|\mathcal H|/\delta)}=\delta/(2|\mathcal H|)$. Hence $2|G|e^{-2ma^2}\le2|\mathcal H|e^{-2ma^2}=\delta$. With probability at least $1-\delta$ every $h\in\mathcal H$ satisfies $|R_P(h)-\widehat R_S(h)|<a$, hence also the asserted non-strict bound.

On that event, [F6] gives $\widehat R_S(\widehat h_\eta)\le\inf_{h\in\mathcal H}\widehat R_S(h)+\eta$. The deviation bound gives $R_P(\widehat h_\eta)\le\widehat R_S(\widehat h_\eta)+a$ and $\widehat R_S(h)\le R_P(h)+a$ for every $h$. Hence $\inf_{g\in\mathcal H}\widehat R_S(g)\le R_P(h)+a$ for every $h\in\mathcal H$, and taking the infimum over $h$ gives $\inf_{g\in\mathcal H}\widehat R_S(g)\le\inf_{h\in\mathcal H}R_P(h)+a$. Combining these inequalities gives $R_P(\widehat h_\eta)-\inf_{h\in\mathcal H}R_P(h)\le2a+\eta$.

The event from step 2.1 has probability at least $1-\delta$, and step 3.1 establishes both stated inequalities on that event. This proves the claim for arbitrary $P$, whether or not the class is realizable.

Let $\mathcal H$ be a finite nonempty class of measurable classifiers $h:\mathcal X\to\{0,1\}$ on a measurable instance space, and let $P$ be a law on $\mathcal X\times\{0,1\}$ for which some $h^*\in\mathcal H$ has zero population zero-one risk. Let $Z_i=(X_i,Y_i)$, $1\le i\le m$, be IID with law $P$, and let $\widehat h_0(S)$ be the measurable exact ERM returned by the finite-list selector on an ordered enumeration of $\mathcal H$. For $0<\epsilon,\delta<1$ and integer $m\ge1$, if

$$m\ge\frac{\log|\mathcal H|+\log(1/\delta)}{\epsilon},$$

then $\mathbb P_S\{R_P(\widehat h_0(S))\le\epsilon\}\ge1-\delta$. This is a realizable guarantee; it makes no claim for distributions without a zero-risk member of $\mathcal H$. The proof is choice-free.

Let $(\mathcal X,\Sigma_X)$ be a measurable space, let $P$ be a probability law on $\mathcal X\times\{0,1\}$, and let $\mathcal H$ be a finite nonempty class of measurable classifiers $h:\mathcal X\to\{0,1\}$. Let $Z_i=(X_i,Y_i)$, $1\le i\le m$, be IID with law $P$, where $m\ge1$, and define $R_P(h)=P\{h(X)\ne Y\}$ and $\widehat R_S(h)=m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m\mathbf 1\{h(X_i)\ne Y_i\}$. With natural logarithms, for $0<\delta<1$ put

$$a_{m,\mathcal H,\delta}:=\sqrt{\frac{\log|\mathcal H|+\log(2/\delta)}{2m}}.$$

Then, with probability at least $1-\delta$, both $|R_P(h)-\widehat R_S(h)|\le a_{m,\mathcal H,\delta}$ for every $h\in\mathcal H$ and

$$R_P(\widehat h_\eta(S))-\inf_{h\in\mathcal H}R_P(h)\le 2a_{m,\mathcal H,\delta}+\eta,$$

for each fixed finite tolerance $\eta\ge0$, where $\widehat h_\eta$ is the measurable finite-list empirical-risk selector applied with tolerance $\eta$ to an ordered list containing every member of $\mathcal H$ exactly once. In particular, exact ERM ($\eta=0$) has excess risk at most $2a_{m,\mathcal H,\delta}$. The conclusion is agnostic: it assumes no zero-risk classifier. No form of the Axiom of Choice is assumed.

Let $(\mathcal X,\Sigma_X)$ be a measurable instance space, let the binary label space $\{0,1\}$ have its discrete sigma-algebra, and let $\mathcal H$ be a finite nonempty class of measurable classifiers $h:\mathcal X\to\{0,1\}$. For a probability law $P$ on $\mathcal X\times\{0,1\}$, write $R_P(h)=P\{(x,y):h(x)\ne y\}$ for the population zero-one risk. A sample of size $m\ge1$ consists of $m$ independent observations with common law $P$; write $\widehat R_S(h)=m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m\mathbf 1\{h(X_i)\ne Y_i\}$ for its empirical zero-one risk. The law $P$ is realizable by $\mathcal H$ if some $h^*\in\mathcal H$ satisfies $R_P(h^*)=0$.

Put $\mathcal Z=\mathcal X\times\{0,1\}$ with its product sigma-algebra. For fixed $m\ge1$, a deterministic learner is a measurable map $A:\mathcal Z^m\to\mathcal H$, where the finite set $\mathcal H$ has its discrete sigma-algebra. For a law $P$ on $\mathcal Z$, let $S=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)$ be an IID sample with common law $P$, and write $\mathbb P_S$ for probability under its joint law. For $0<\epsilon,\delta<1$, the learner is $(\epsilon,\delta)$-PAC realizable if, for every law $P$ realizable by $\mathcal H$, $\mathbb P_S\{R_P(A(S))\le\epsilon\}\ge1-\delta$. It is agnostic $(\epsilon,\delta)$-PAC if, for every law $P$ on $\mathcal Z$, $\mathbb P_S\{R_P(A(S))-\inf_{h\in\mathcal H}R_P(h)\le\epsilon\}\ge1-\delta$.
