Let $(\mathcal X,\Sigma)$ be a nonempty measurable space and let $H$ be a nonempty class of measurable functions $h:\mathcal X\to\{0,1\}$. For an integer $m\ge0$ and an indexed tuple $\mathbf x=(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\in\mathcal X^m$, define its trace by

$$\operatorname{tr}_H(\mathbf x):=\{(h(x_1),\ldots,h(x_m)):h\in H\}\subseteq\{0,1\}^m.$$

The tuple $\mathbf x$ is **shattered by $H$** if $\operatorname{tr}_H(\mathbf x)=\{0,1\}^m$. Its coordinates are indexed: repeated instance points remain distinct coordinates, although their labels must agree for every $h\in H$. For $m=0$, $\mathbf x=()$ and $\{0,1\}^0=\{()\}$, so the empty tuple is shattered. The **VC dimension** of $H$ is

$$\operatorname{VCdim}(H):=\sup\{m\in\mathbb N_0:\text{some }\mathbf x\in\mathcal X^m\text{ is shattered by }H\}\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{+\infty\}.$$

Let $(\mathcal X,\Sigma)$ be a nonempty measurable space and let $H$ be a nonempty class of measurable binary functions on $\mathcal X$. For each integer $m\ge0$, the **growth function** of $H$ is

$$\Pi_H(m):=\sup_{\mathbf x\in\mathcal X^m}|\operatorname{tr}_H(\mathbf x)|.$$

The supremum is a maximum because each trace size is an integer between $1$ and $2^m$ and $\mathcal X^m$ is nonempty. In particular, $\Pi_H(0)=1$. A finite indexed tuple is shattered exactly when its trace has size $2^m$, so $\operatorname{VCdim}(H)=\sup\{m\in\mathbb N_0:\Pi_H(m)=2^m\}$.

Let $(\mathcal X,\Sigma)$ be a nonempty measurable space and let $H$ be a nonempty class of measurable functions $h:\mathcal X\to\{0,1\}$ with finite VC dimension $d$. For every integer $m\ge0$,

$$\Pi_H(m)\le\sum_{j=0}^{d}\binom{m}{j},$$

where $\binom{m}{j}=0$ for $j>m$. Consequently, $\Pi_H(m)=1$ when $d=0$; and when $1\le d\le m$,

$$\Pi_H(m)\le\left(\frac{em}{d}\right)^d,$$

where $e:=\exp(1)$.

For a supervised prediction problem with joint law $P$, the **population risk** of any measurable predictor $f:\mathsf X\to\mathsf A$ (in particular, every $f\in\mathcal F$) is the extended nonnegative integral
$$R_P(f):=\int_{\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y}\ell(f(x),y)\,P(d(x,y))\in[0,+\infty].$$
For an ordered sample $S=((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_m,y_m))$ of length $m\ge1$, the **empirical risk** or **training risk** of any such $f$ is
$$\widehat R_S(f):=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\ell(f(x_i),y_i)\in[0,+\infty].$$
Neither definition assumes finite risk. The sum uses extended nonnegative arithmetic; since $m\ge1$, any summand equal to $+\infty$ makes the empirical risk $+\infty$.

In a supervised prediction problem, for every measurable predictor $f$, the function $(x,y)\mapsto\ell(f(x),y)$ is measurable, so its population risk is a defined extended nonnegative integral. For every sample size $m\ge1$, the empirical risk $S\mapsto\widehat R_S(f)$ is an extended nonnegative measurable function on the finite product sample space.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in Law or distribution of a random element agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in Independent random elements. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   The product measure of two sigma-finite measure spaces is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $n\ge1$, let $Z_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be independent random elements, meaning measurable maps (Random elements and real random variables), with laws $\mu_i$ given by pushforward (Law or distribution of a random element). Put $\mu=\bigotimes_{i=1}^n\mu_i$ on the finite product sigma-algebra (The product sigma-algebra and its finite iterates). Let $f:\prod_{i=1}^nS_i\to\mathbb R$ be product-measurable with $\int|f|\,d\mu<\infty$. Suppose finite deterministic constants $c_i\ge0$ satisfy
$$|f(z_1,\ldots,z_i,\ldots,z_n)-f(z_1,\ldots,z_i',\ldots,z_n)|\le c_i$$
for every fixed setting of the other coordinates and every $z_i,z_i'$. The independent product-law theorem identifies the law of $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)$ as $\mu$. Applying change of variables for expectation first to $|f|$ and then to $f$ makes $f(Z)$ integrable and gives $\mathbb E f(Z)=\int f\,d\mu$. Put $V=\sum_{i=1}^n c_i^2$. For $t>0$, if $V>0$ then
$$\mathbb P\bigl(f(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)-\mathbb E f(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)\ge t\bigr)\le\exp\!\left(-\frac{2t^2}{V}\right),$$
and if $V=0$ this probability is $0$. The same bound holds for the lower tail, so the two-sided probability is at most $2e^{-2t^2/V}$ when $V>0$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $Z_1,\ldots,Z_n$ be IID observations with law $P$, and let $\mathcal F$ be a finite nonempty class of measurable functions $f:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$. For every $\epsilon>0$,

$$P\left(\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}|P_nf-Pf|\ge\epsilon\right)\le2|\mathcal F|e^{-2n\epsilon^2}.$$

Here $P_nf=n^{-1}\sum_i f(Z_i)$ and $Pf=\int f\,dP$. The proof uses only scalar exponential moments and finite independence; it does not assume the Axiom of Choice.

Let $Y$ be a measurable real random variable on a probability space with $0\le Y\le1$ almost surely. Then, for every $\lambda\in\mathbb R$,

$$\mathbb E\exp\{\lambda(Y-\mathbb EY)\}\le \exp(\lambda^2/8).$$

This proof uses only finite product and scalar integral arguments; it does not assume the Axiom of Choice.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because The exponential is a continuous bijection from $\mathbb{R}$ onto $(0,\infty)$ states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

Let $X,Y$ be integrable real or complex random variables on one probability space.
1. For scalars $a,b$, $$\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Y].$$
2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then $$\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y].$$

For all $x,y\in\mathbb R$ and $0\le t\le1$,
$$\exp((1-t)x+ty)\le(1-t)\exp x+t\exp y.$$
If $0<t<1$, equality holds exactly when $x=y$.

derivations.claim: Put $g_h(x,y):=\mathbf1\{h(x)\ne y\}$. Its unit-level set is $(h^{-1}\{0\}\times\{1\})\cup(h^{-1}\{1\}\times\{0\})$, so each $g_h$ is measurable and takes values in $[0,1]$. By [F4]–[F5], $Pg_h=R_P(h)$ and $P_mg_h=\widehat R_S(h)$ are well-defined, measurable risk functions; the assumed supremum measurability applies to their deviations.

For an independent IID copy $S'$ of $S$, every coordinate of $S'$ has law $P$; the product-law and Fubini facts in [F6], together with finite expectation linearity [F11], give $R_P(h)=\mathbb E_{S'}P_m'g_h$ for every $h$. Thus $\Phi(S):=\sup_{h\in H}(R_P(h)-P_mg_h)\le\mathbb E_{S'}\sup_{h\in H}(P_m'g_h-P_mg_h)$. The integrand is bounded and measurable, so product-law invariance and Fubini [F6] allow integration over $S,S'$. For each fixed sign vector $\sigma$, swapping $Z_i$ with $Z_i'$ whenever $\sigma_i=-1$ preserves their joint product law; averaging over the finite sign space therefore leaves this expectation unchanged after inserting $\sigma_i$ into each difference.

Subadditivity of the supremum and expectation linearity [F11] give $\mathbb E\Phi(S)\le2\mathbb E_{S,\sigma}\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(G_H)$, where $\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(G_H)=\mathbb E_\sigma\sup_h m^{-1}\sum_i\sigma_i g_h(Z_i)$. Writing $\widetilde h=2h-1$ and $\widetilde Y_i=2Y_i-1$ gives $g_h(Z_i)=(1-\widetilde h(X_i)\widetilde Y_i)/2$; the sign-only term has mean zero and $-\sigma_i\widetilde Y_i$ are again independent uniform signs, so $\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(G_H)=\tfrac12\mathbb E_\sigma\sup_h m^{-1}\sum_i\sigma_i\widetilde h(X_i)$.

For a fixed sample, the set $V_S=\{(\widetilde h(X_1),\ldots,\widetilde h(X_m)):h\in H\}$ has $|V_S|\le\Pi_H(m)$ and each vector has Euclidean norm $\sqrt m$. For a fixed $v\in\{-1,+1\}^m$, $Y_i=(1+\sigma_i v_i)/2$ is in $[0,1]$ with mean $1/2$; applying [F9] at parameter $2\lambda$ gives $\mathbb E e^{\lambda\sigma_i v_i}\le e^{\lambda^2/2}$. Expanding the finite uniform sign sum factors over coordinates, so $\mathbb E_\sigma e^{\lambda\sum_i\sigma_i v_i}\le e^{m\lambda^2/2}$. For a finite $V$ of size $N$, $e^{\lambda\max_v\sum_i\sigma_iv_i}\le\sum_v e^{\lambda\sum_i\sigma_iv_i}$. On the finite sign space, the two-point convexity inequality [F12] gives $e^{\lambda\mathbb E_\sigma\max_v\sum_i\sigma_iv_i}\le\mathbb E_\sigma e^{\lambda\max_v\sum_i\sigma_iv_i}$; its equal-weight finite form follows by induction over its $q=2^m$ outcomes, applying [F12] to the mean of the first $q-1$ outcomes and the last outcome with weights $(q-1)/q$ and $1/q$. Taking logarithms using [F10] yields $\mathbb E_\sigma\max_{v\in V}m^{-1}\sum_i\sigma_iv_i\le\log N/(m\lambda)+\lambda/2$. Optimizing $\lambda>0$ gives $\sqrt{2\log N/m}$ (and the bound is $0$ if $N=1$). By steps 2.1–3.1, $\mathbb E\Phi(S)\le\sqrt{2\log\Pi_H(m)/m}$.

By [F3], when $1\le d\le m$ the preceding expectation is at most $\sqrt{2d\log(em/d)/m}$. Changing one sample coordinate changes $\Phi(S)$ by at most $1/m$, because every $g_h$ is $[0,1]$-valued. Apply [F7] with $c_i=1/m$ and $t=\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)/(2m)}$; since $\sum_i c_i^2=1/m$, with probability at least $1-\delta$ we have $\Phi(S)\le\mathbb E\Phi(S)+t$, which is the stated VC branch.

If $d=0$, no two distinct functions in $H$ can differ at any point, since that point would be shattered; hence $H$ contains one function. If $H$ is finite, the loss class $\{g_h:h\in H\}$ is finite with size at most $|H|$. Put $t=\sqrt{(\log|H|+\log(2/\delta))/(2m)}$; then $2|H|e^{-2mt^2}=\delta$ by [F10]. Applying [F8] at this $t$ proves the choice-free branch, including the $d=0$ case.

Each coordinate of $S'$ has law $P$, so product-law marginals and Fubini [F4], together with expectation linearity [F8], give $R_P(h)=\mathbb E_{S'}\widehat R_{S'}(h)$ for every $h$. Monotonicity of expectation then gives $\Phi(S)\le\mathbb E_{S'}\sup_h(\widehat R_{S'}(h)-\widehat R_S(h))$. The integrand is bounded and measurable by assumption, hence [F4] allows integration in either sample order. For each fixed sign vector, swapping $Z_i$ with $Z_i'$ at exactly its negative coordinates preserves the joint product law, so the expected supremum is unchanged when each difference is multiplied by $\sigma_i$. Subadditivity of the supremum and expectation linearity [F8] bound it by the sum of the two expected one-sided empirical Rademacher suprema, which are equal because $\sigma$ and $-\sigma$ have the same law. Thus $\mathbb E\Phi(S)\le2\mathbb E_{S,\sigma}\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(G_H)$.

By [F1], $\mathbb E\Phi(S)\le2C_{\rm VC}\sqrt{(d+1)/m}$. Replacing one observation in $S$ changes each $\widehat R_S(h)$ by at most $1/m$, so the supremum $\Phi(S)$ changes by at most $1/m$ as well. Applying [F5] with $c_i=1/m$ and $t=\sqrt{\log(2/\delta)/(2m)}$ gives $\Pr\{\Phi(S)>\mathbb E\Phi(S)+t\}\le\delta/2$.

The complemented class $\bar H=\{1-h:h\in H\}$ has the same trace counts and VC dimension as $H$, and its loss satisfies $g_{1-h}(x,y)=1-g_h(x,y)$. Let $(\mathcal X,\Sigma)$ be a nonempty measurable space, let $H$ be a nonempty class of measurable functions $h:\mathcal X\to\{0,1\}$, put $\mathcal Z=\mathcal X\times\{0,1\}$ with its product sigma-algebra, and let $P$ be a probability law on $\mathcal Z$. For a fixed sample size $m\ge1$, a **risk-measurable learning rule under $P$** is a map $A:\mathcal Z^m\to H$ for which the real-valued maps $S\mapsto R_P(A(S))$ and $S\mapsto\widehat R_S(A(S))$ are measurable; if the class infimum is used, also require $S\mapsto\inf_{h\in H}\widehat R_S(h)$ to be measurable. The **realizable condition** is that some $h^*\in H$ has $R_P(h^*)=0$. The rule is **consistent** on a sample when $\widehat R_S(A(S))=0$, an **exact ERM** when it attains $\inf_{h\in H}\widehat R_S(h)$, and an **$\eta$-approximate ERM** for finite $\eta\ge0$ when $\widehat R_S(A(S))\le\inf_{h\in H}\widehat R_S(h)+\eta$.

In each PAC criterion below, require $A$ to be risk-measurable under every law $P$ quantified over in that criterion. For $0<\epsilon,\delta<1$, $A$ is **realizable $(\epsilon,\delta)$-PAC** on $H$ if for every law $P$ satisfying the realizable condition, $\mathbb P_{S\sim P^m}\{R_P(A(S))\le\epsilon\}\ge1-\delta$. It is **agnostic $(\epsilon,\delta)$-PAC** if for every law $P$ on $\mathcal Z$, $\mathbb P_{S\sim P^m}\{R_P(A(S))-\inf_{h\in H}R_P(h)\le\epsilon\}\ge1-\delta$. These are probability criteria only; no existence, attainment, measurability of a selector beyond the stated risk maps, or computational-efficiency claim is implicit. When $H$ is finite and $A$ is measurable into the discrete space $H$, these probability formulas are the criteria in the finite-class definition.

Let $(\mathcal X,\Sigma)$ be a nonempty measurable space and let $H$ be a nonempty class of measurable functions $h:\mathcal X\to\{0,1\}$. For an integer $m\ge0$ and an indexed tuple $\mathbf x=(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\in\mathcal X^m$, define its trace by

$$\operatorname{tr}_H(\mathbf x):=\{(h(x_1),\ldots,h(x_m)):h\in H\}\subseteq\{0,1\}^m.$$

The tuple $\mathbf x$ is **shattered by $H$** if $\operatorname{tr}_H(\mathbf x)=\{0,1\}^m$. Its coordinates are indexed: repeated instance points remain distinct coordinates, although their labels must agree for every $h\in H$. For $m=0$, $\mathbf x=()$ and $\{0,1\}^0=\{()\}$, so the empty tuple is shattered. The **VC dimension** of $H$ is

$$\operatorname{VCdim}(H):=\sup\{m\in\mathbb N_0:\text{some }\mathbf x\in\mathcal X^m\text{ is shattered by }H\}\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{+\infty\}.$$

Let $(\mathcal X,\Sigma)$ be a nonempty measurable space and let $H$ be a nonempty class of measurable binary functions on $\mathcal X$. For each integer $m\ge0$, the **growth function** of $H$ is

$$\Pi_H(m):=\sup_{\mathbf x\in\mathcal X^m}|\operatorname{tr}_H(\mathbf x)|.$$

The supremum is a maximum because each trace size is an integer between $1$ and $2^m$ and $\mathcal X^m$ is nonempty. In particular, $\Pi_H(0)=1$. A finite indexed tuple is shattered exactly when its trace has size $2^m$, so $\operatorname{VCdim}(H)=\sup\{m\in\mathbb N_0:\Pi_H(m)=2^m\}$.

Let $(\mathcal X,\Sigma)$ be a nonempty measurable space and let $H$ be a nonempty class of measurable functions $h:\mathcal X\to\{0,1\}$ with finite VC dimension $d$. For every integer $m\ge0$,

$$\Pi_H(m)\le\sum_{j=0}^{d}\binom{m}{j},$$

where $\binom{m}{j}=0$ for $j>m$. Consequently, $\Pi_H(m)=1$ when $d=0$; and when $1\le d\le m$,

$$\Pi_H(m)\le\left(\frac{em}{d}\right)^d,$$

where $e:=\exp(1)$.

For a supervised prediction problem with joint law $P$, the **population risk** of any measurable predictor $f:\mathsf X\to\mathsf A$ (in particular, every $f\in\mathcal F$) is the extended nonnegative integral
$$R_P(f):=\int_{\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y}\ell(f(x),y)\,P(d(x,y))\in[0,+\infty].$$
For an ordered sample $S=((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_m,y_m))$ of length $m\ge1$, the **empirical risk** or **training risk** of any such $f$ is
$$\widehat R_S(f):=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\ell(f(x_i),y_i)\in[0,+\infty].$$
Neither definition assumes finite risk. The sum uses extended nonnegative arithmetic; since $m\ge1$, any summand equal to $+\infty$ makes the empirical risk $+\infty$.

In a supervised prediction problem, for every measurable predictor $f$, the function $(x,y)\mapsto\ell(f(x),y)$ is measurable, so its population risk is a defined extended nonnegative integral. For every sample size $m\ge1$, the empirical risk $S\mapsto\widehat R_S(f)$ is an extended nonnegative measurable function on the finite product sample space.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in Law or distribution of a random element agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in Independent random elements. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure

$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,

Let $X,Y$ be integrable real or complex random variables on one probability

2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then

3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$

$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

   If $A_n\downarrow A$, then

derivations.claim: If $d=0$, any two members of $H$ agree at every $x\in\mathcal X$, since otherwise the one-point tuple $(x)$ would be shattered. Thus $H$ has one function. Realizability makes that function have zero risk, and every $H$-valued rule outputs it, proving the $d=0$ clause.

Suppose $d\ge1$ and put $L=\log(64e/\epsilon)>1$ and $D=\log(4/\delta)>0$; the sample-size premise gives $m\epsilon\ge64(dL+D)>8$. Let $E_S:=\{\exists h\in H:R_P(h)>\epsilon,\ \widehat R_S(h)=0\}$ and let $B_{S,S'}$ be the event that some such $h$ also has $\widehat R_{S'}(h)\ge\epsilon/2$, where $S'$ is an independent IID sample. For each fixed $S\in E_S$, fix one witness $h$ for this $S$ only, with no sample-dependent selection function, and let $K_h=\sum_{i=1}^m\mathbf1\{h(X_i')\ne Y_i'\}$. By [F5]–[F8], $K_h$ is a sum of independent Bernoulli indicators with mean $mp$, where $p=R_P(h)>\epsilon$. Factorization [F7] gives $\mathbb E[2^{-K_h}]=(1-p/2)^m\le e^{-mp/2}$ by [F13]. On $K_h<mp/2$, $2^{-K_h}>2^{-mp/2}$, so [F9] gives $\mathbb P(K_h<mp/2)\le\exp[-mp(1-\log2)/2]$. From [F11]–[F12], $1/2\le\log2<4/5$, so this probability is at most $e^{-mp/10}\le e^{-m\epsilon/10}\le e^{-4/5}\le e^{-\log2}=1/2$. Since $mp/2>m\epsilon/2$, this proves $\mathbb P_{S'}(B_{S,S'}\mid S)\ge1/2$ for each $S\in E_S$. Integrating the measurable sections by [F6] yields $\mathbb P(E_S)\le2\mathbb P(B_{S,S'})$.

View $2m$ IID observations as a combined sample $T$. By [F6], permuting its coordinates preserves its product law, so the joint law of the first and second halves equals the average over all uniform choices of an $m$-index training subset $I\subseteq[2m]$ and its complement. For fixed $T$, each $h$ determines an error-index set $J_h=\{i:h(X_i)\ne Y_i\}$, and the number of distinct such sets is at most $\Pi_H(2m)$ because the labels $Y_i$ only flip coordinates of the trace. If $|J_h|=k>m$, no training subset can be disjoint from all errors. If $k\le m$, the fraction of training subsets disjoint from $J_h$ is $\prod_{j=0}^{k-1}(m-j)/(2m-j)\le2^{-k}$: after $j$ specified errors have been assigned to the ghost half, the next specified index lies there with probability $(m-j)/(2m-j)\le1/2$. Therefore only error patterns with $k\ge m\epsilon/2$ can witness $B$, and the finite union bound [F10] gives $\mathbb P(B_{S,S'})\le\Pi_H(2m)2^{-m\epsilon/2}$.

Combining steps 1.2 and 2.1, $\mathbb P(E_S)\le2\Pi_H(2m)2^{-m\epsilon/2}$. The sample-size hypothesis implies $m\ge d$, so [F4] at $n=2m$ gives $\mathbb P(E_S)\le2(2em/d)^d2^{-m\epsilon/2}$. Put $L=\log(64e/\epsilon)$, $D=\log(4/\delta)$, and $M=64(dL+D)/\epsilon$. Then $L>1$, $D>0$, and the hypothesis gives $m\ge M$. For real $t\ge M$, define $q(t)=\log2+d\log(2et/d)-(\log2)\epsilon t/2$. Its derivative is $d/t-(\log2)\epsilon/2\le\epsilon/(64L)-\epsilon/4<0$, using $\log2\ge1/2$ from [F11]–[F12]; hence $q(m)\le q(M)$. The identity $\log(2eM/d)=L+\log2+\log(L+D/d)$, together with $\log(L+D/d)\le\log L+D/(dL)$ (from [F11], [F13]), $\log L\le L$, $\log2\le L$, and $\log2\ge1/2$, gives $q(M)\le L-13dL+D/L-16D$. Consequently $q(M)-\log\delta\le L-13dL+D/L-15D-\log4<0$, because $d\ge1$, $L>1$, and $D>0$. Exponentiating shows $2(2em/d)^d2^{-m\epsilon/2}\le\delta$.

Let $(\mathcal X,\Sigma)$ be a nonempty measurable space, let $H$ be a nonempty class of measurable binary functions with finite VC dimension $d$, put $\mathcal Z=\mathcal X\times\{0,1\}$, and let $P$ be a probability law on $\mathcal Z$. Fix an integer $m\ge1$ and a map $A:\mathcal Z^m\to H$ for which $S\mapsto R_P(A(S))$ and $S\mapsto\widehat R_S(A(S))$ are measurable, where
$$R_P(h):=P\{(x,y):h(x)\ne y\},\qquad \widehat R_S(h):=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\mathbf1\{h(X_i)\ne Y_i\}.$$
Suppose $P$ is realizable by $H$ and $A$ is consistent $P^m$-almost surely. For $0<\epsilon<1$, assume the events
$$E_{m,\epsilon}:=\{S\in\mathcal Z^m:\exists h\in H,\ R_P(h)>\epsilon,\ \widehat R_S(h)=0\}$$
and
$$B_{m,\epsilon}:=\{(S,S')\in\mathcal Z^m\times\mathcal Z^m:\exists h\in H,\ R_P(h)>\epsilon,\ \widehat R_S(h)=0,\ \widehat R_{S'}(h)\ge\epsilon/2\}$$
are measurable in their respective product sigma-algebras; this holds when $H$ is countable. For $0<\epsilon,\delta<1$ and $S\sim P^m$, if $d=0$ then $R_P(A(S))=0$ almost surely for every such rule. If $d\ge1$ and
$$m\ge\frac{64}{\epsilon}\left[d\log\!\left(\frac{64e}{\epsilon}\right)+\log\!\left(\frac4\delta\right)\right],$$
where $\log$ is natural and $e=\exp(1)$, then $\mathbb P\{R_P(A(S))\le\epsilon\}\ge1-\delta$. This is a conditional upper bound for consistent risk-measurable learners; it asserts no existence or computational-efficiency result.

Let $(\mathcal X,\Sigma)$ be a nonempty measurable space, let $H$ be a nonempty class of measurable functions $h:\mathcal X\to\{0,1\}$, put $\mathcal Z=\mathcal X\times\{0,1\}$ with its product sigma-algebra, and let $P$ be a probability law on $\mathcal Z$. For a fixed sample size $m\ge1$, a **risk-measurable learning rule under $P$** is a map $A:\mathcal Z^m\to H$ for which the real-valued maps $S\mapsto R_P(A(S))$ and $S\mapsto\widehat R_S(A(S))$ are measurable; if the class infimum is used, also require $S\mapsto\inf_{h\in H}\widehat R_S(h)$ to be measurable. The **realizable condition** is that some $h^*\in H$ has $R_P(h^*)=0$. The rule is **consistent** on a sample when $\widehat R_S(A(S))=0$, an **exact ERM** when it attains $\inf_{h\in H}\widehat R_S(h)$, and an **$\eta$-approximate ERM** for finite $\eta\ge0$ when $\widehat R_S(A(S))\le\inf_{h\in H}\widehat R_S(h)+\eta$.

In each PAC criterion below, require $A$ to be risk-measurable under every law $P$ quantified over in that criterion. For $0<\epsilon,\delta<1$, $A$ is **realizable $(\epsilon,\delta)$-PAC** on $H$ if for every law $P$ satisfying the realizable condition, $\mathbb P_{S\sim P^m}\{R_P(A(S))\le\epsilon\}\ge1-\delta$. It is **agnostic $(\epsilon,\delta)$-PAC** if for every law $P$ on $\mathcal Z$, $\mathbb P_{S\sim P^m}\{R_P(A(S))-\inf_{h\in H}R_P(h)\le\epsilon\}\ge1-\delta$. These are probability criteria only; no existence, attainment, measurability of a selector beyond the stated risk maps, or computational-efficiency claim is implicit. When $H$ is finite and $A$ is measurable into the discrete space $H$, these probability formulas are the criteria in the finite-class definition.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

For a supervised prediction problem with joint law $P$, the **population risk** of any measurable predictor $f:\mathsf X\to\mathsf A$ (in particular, every $f\in\mathcal F$) is the extended nonnegative integral
$$R_P(f):=\int_{\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y}\ell(f(x),y)\,P(d(x,y))\in[0,+\infty].$$
For an ordered sample $S=((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_m,y_m))$ of length $m\ge1$, the **empirical risk** or **training risk** of any such $f$ is
$$\widehat R_S(f):=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\ell(f(x_i),y_i)\in[0,+\infty].$$
Neither definition assumes finite risk. The sum uses extended nonnegative arithmetic; since $m\ge1$, any summand equal to $+\infty$ makes the empirical risk $+\infty$.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because The exponential is a continuous bijection from $\mathbb{R}$ onto $(0,\infty)$ states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in The exponential series converges absolutely for every real argument. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of The factorial $n!$ and the falling factorial $n^{\underline{k}}$, defined by recursion in $\mathbb{N}$, $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image (The canonical natural $\iota(n) = n \cdot 1_F$ of a field, Canonical naturals are positive and strictly increasing), and powers and series are those of Integer powers $a^m$ and Series, partial sums, convergence and the sum, divergence, and the tail series.

This is a real power series centred at $0$ (A real power series about a centre, its interval of convergence, and its radius in $[0,+\infty]$). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

Suppose $d\ge1$ and write $a_m:=2C_{\rm VC}\sqrt{(d+1)/m}+\sqrt{\log(2/\delta)/(2m)}$. On the event in [F2], [F1] gives $R_P(A(S))\le\widehat R_S(A(S))+a_m\le\inf_{h\in H}\widehat R_S(h)+\eta+a_m$. For every $h\in H$, the same event gives $\widehat R_S(h)\le R_P(h)+a_m$, so $\inf_{h\in H}\widehat R_S(h)\le R_P(h)+a_m$ for every $h$ and therefore $\inf_{h\in H}\widehat R_S(h)\le\inf_{h\in H}R_P(h)+a_m$. Combining proves excess risk at most $2a_m+\eta$.

The event in [F2] has probability at least $1-\delta$, so step 1.2 proves the first inequality. Under the sample-size premise, $2C_{\rm VC}\sqrt{(d+1)/m}\le\epsilon/8$ and $\sqrt{\log(2/\delta)/(2m)}\le\epsilon/8$: the first follows from $m\ge256C_{\rm VC}^2(d+1)/\epsilon^2$, and the second from $m\ge32\log(4/\delta)/\epsilon^2$. Hence $a_m\le\epsilon/4$, and $2a_m+\eta\le\epsilon$ when $\eta\le\epsilon/2$. Under the additional hypotheses for the PAC conclusion, this argument applies to every law $P$ with the same $A,m,\epsilon,\delta$ and $\eta$, so [F1] gives the agnostic PAC criterion.

Let $(\mathcal X,\Sigma)$ be a nonempty measurable space and let $H$ be a nonempty class of measurable functions $h:\mathcal X\to\{0,1\}$. For an integer $m\ge0$ and an indexed tuple $\mathbf x=(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\in\mathcal X^m$, define its trace by

$$\operatorname{tr}_H(\mathbf x):=\{(h(x_1),\ldots,h(x_m)):h\in H\}\subseteq\{0,1\}^m.$$

The tuple $\mathbf x$ is **shattered by $H$** if $\operatorname{tr}_H(\mathbf x)=\{0,1\}^m$. Its coordinates are indexed: repeated instance points remain distinct coordinates, although their labels must agree for every $h\in H$. For $m=0$, $\mathbf x=()$ and $\{0,1\}^0=\{()\}$, so the empty tuple is shattered. The **VC dimension** of $H$ is

$$\operatorname{VCdim}(H):=\sup\{m\in\mathbb N_0:\text{some }\mathbf x\in\mathcal X^m\text{ is shattered by }H\}\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{+\infty\}.$$

Let $(\mathcal X,\Sigma)$ be a nonempty measurable space and let $H$ be a nonempty class of measurable binary functions on $\mathcal X$. For each integer $m\ge0$, the **growth function** of $H$ is

$$\Pi_H(m):=\sup_{\mathbf x\in\mathcal X^m}|\operatorname{tr}_H(\mathbf x)|.$$

The supremum is a maximum because each trace size is an integer between $1$ and $2^m$ and $\mathcal X^m$ is nonempty. In particular, $\Pi_H(0)=1$. A finite indexed tuple is shattered exactly when its trace has size $2^m$, so $\operatorname{VCdim}(H)=\sup\{m\in\mathbb N_0:\Pi_H(m)=2^m\}$.

derivations.claim: If $s<t$, the midpoint $x=(s+t)/2$ satisfies $h_s(x)=0$ and $h_t(x)=1$, so the functions $h_t$ are all distinct as $t$ varies over $\mathbb R$ and the class is infinite. For any single $x$, $t<x$ realizes label $0$ and $t=x$ realizes label $1$, so every one-point tuple is shattered.

For two distinct points $x<y$, the possible trace vectors are only $(0,0)$, $(1,0)$, and $(1,1)$ as the threshold passes from left to right; $(0,1)$ never occurs. If the two indexed points repeat, their labels always agree. Hence no two-point tuple is shattered, and $\operatorname{VCdim}(H_{\rm th})=1$.

For $m$ distinct points ordered $x_1<\cdots<x_m$, a threshold realizes exactly the $m+1$ vectors consisting of $k$ initial ones followed by $m-k$ zeros, for $0\le k\le m$. A tuple with only $r$ distinct points has at most $r+1\le m+1$ traces, while a distinct $m$-tuple attains $m+1$; for $m=0$ the unique empty trace is counted once. Thus $\Pi_{H_{\rm th}}(m)=m+1$.

For any three distinct ordered points, the labeling $(1,0,1)$ is impossible for an interval because containing $x_1$ and $x_3$ forces it to contain every point between them, including $x_2$. On $m$ distinct ordered points, a nonempty interval has as its trace one contiguous block, and every such block is realized by the interval with those two sample endpoints. For a tuple with $r\le m$ distinct points there are at most $1+r(r+1)/2\le1+m(m+1)/2$ traces, while a distinct tuple attains that number. At $m=0$ the formula gives the single empty trace. pointwise operations ([[def-function-space]], [[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). For $i < n$ define the **standard unit vector**
$e_i \in F^{n}$ by

$$e_i(i) = 1_F, \qquad e_i(j) = 0_F \ \text{ for } j < n \text{ with } j \ne i .$$

Then:

1. **Finite sums in a function space are pointwise.** For every set $X$, every
   $p \in \mathbb{N}$, every list $u : p \to F^{X}$ and every $j \in X$,
   $$\Bigl(\sum_{k<p} u_k\Bigr)(j) \;=\; \sum_{k<p} u_k(j),$$

2. $e : n \to F^{n}$ is an ordered basis of $F^{n}$ ([[def-linear-basis]]); in

   basis of $F^{n}$ with $e[n] \approx n$ ([[def-equinumerous]]);

   $\bigl(\sum_{i<n}\lambda_i e_i\bigr)(j) = \lambda_j$; equivalently the
   coordinate list of $x \in F^{n}$ with respect to the ordered basis $e$
   ([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]) is
   $i \mapsto x(i)$;
4. $F^{n}$ is finite-dimensional over $F$ with $\dim_F F^{n} = n$
   ([[def-dimension]]);
5. at $n = 0$ this reads: $F^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
   so $F^{0}$ is the zero space, the empty list is its ordered basis,
   $\varnothing$ is its basis and $\dim_F F^{0} = 0$.

Every index runs from $0$, so the coordinates of an element of $F^{n}$ are
$x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$ and no statement above is restricted to $n \ge 1$.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]) and suppose
$V$ has a spanning subset $S$ ([[def-linear-combination-and-span]]) with
$S \approx n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]). Then:

1. every linearly independent subset $L \subseteq V$
   ([[def-linear-independence]]) is finite ([[def-countable]]), and the unique
   $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $L \approx m$ satisfies $m \le n$;
2. no linearly independent subset of $V$ is equinumerous with $\mathbb{N}$.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]), with finite
sums of vectors as in [[def-linear-combination-and-span]] and linear independence
as in [[def-linear-independence]]. For a function $f$ and a set $A$ we write
$f[A]$ for the image of $A$ ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]).

**Three facts about finite sums.**

1. **Re-indexing along an injection.** Let $n, m \in \mathbb{N}$, let
   $\iota : m \to n$ be injective, and let $u : n \to V$ satisfy $u_j = 0_V$ for
   every $j < n$ with $j \notin \iota[m]$. Then
   $$\sum_{j<n} u_j \;=\; \sum_{i<m} u_{\iota(i)} .$$
2. **Deleting one index.** Let $n' \in \mathbb{N}$ and $k < \sigma(n')$. The map
   $\delta_k : n' \to \sigma(n')$ given by $\delta_k(i) = i$ for $i < k$ and
   $\delta_k(i) = \sigma(i)$ for $k \le i < n'$ is injective with image
   $\sigma(n') \setminus \{k\}$. Consequently, if $u : \sigma(n') \to V$ has
   $u_k = 0_V$, then
   $\sum_{j<\sigma(n')} u_j = \sum_{i<n'} u_{\delta_k(i)}$.
3. **Concatenation.** Let $a, q \in \mathbb{N}$, $y : a \to V$ and
   $z : q \to V$. There is exactly one list $c : a + q \to V$ with $c_i = y_i$ for
   $i < a$ and $c_{a+j} = z_j$ for $j < q$, and it satisfies
   $$\sum_{i<a+q} c_i \;=\; \sum_{i<a} y_i \;+\; \sum_{j<q} z_j .$$
   If moreover $y$ and $z$ are injective with $y[a] \cap z[q] = \varnothing$, then
   $c$ is injective with image $y[a] \cup z[q]$.

**Four facts about independence.**

4. Every linearly independent list $v : n \to V$ is injective, and
   $v_i \ne 0_V$ for every $i < n$.
5. If $v : n \to V$ is linearly independent and $\iota : m \to n$ is injective,
   then the sublist $v \circ \iota : m \to V$ is linearly independent.
6. A list $v : n \to V$ is linearly independent **if and only if** it is
   injective and its image $v[n]$ is a linearly independent subset of $V$; in
   that case $v$ is a bijection $n \to v[n]$, so $v[n] \approx n$
   ([[def-equinumerous]]).
7. Every subset of a linearly independent subset of $V$ is linearly independent.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]). As in
[[def-linear-combination-and-span]], a **finite list** of vectors is a function
$v : n \to V$ on a von Neumann natural $n = \{0, \dots, n-1\}$
([[def-natural-numbers]], [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), written
$v_i := v(i)$, and

$$\sum_{i<n} \lambda_i v_i$$

is the finite sum of [[def-monoid-finite-product]] read additively in the abelian
group $(V,+,0_V)$, applied to the list $i \mapsto \lambda_i v_i$. No second notion
of finite sum is introduced here.

### Independence of a list

A finite list $v : n \to V$ is **linearly independent** when, for every list of
scalars $\lambda : n \to F$,

$$\sum_{i<n} \lambda_i v_i = 0_V \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \lambda_i = 0_F \text{ for every } i < n,$$

and **linearly dependent** otherwise, that is, when some $\lambda : n \to F$ has
$\sum_{i<n}\lambda_i v_i = 0_V$ while $\lambda_j \ne 0_F$ for at least one
$j < n$. Such a $\lambda$ is called a **witness** to the dependence of $v$.

### Independence of a subset

A subset $S \subseteq V$ is **linearly independent** when **every injective**
finite list $v : n \to S$ ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]) is linearly
independent, and **linearly dependent** otherwise, that is, when some injective
finite list into $S$ is linearly dependent.

**The injectivity clause is not decoration.** A linear combination in
[[def-linear-combination-and-span]] is indexed by an arbitrary list $v : n \to S$,
which is **not** required to be injective. If the definition above quantified
over all such lists, then for any $w \in S$ the list $v : 2 \to S$ with
$v_0 = v_1 = w$ and the scalars $\lambda_0 = 1_F$, $\lambda_1 = -1_F$ would give

$$\sum_{i<2}\lambda_i v_i = (0_V + 1_F w) + (-1_F)w = w + (-w) = 0_V$$

with $\lambda_0 = 1_F \ne 0_F$ ([[def-field]],
[[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]), so **every** nonempty subset of
$V$ would be dependent and the notion would be empty. Quantifying over injective
lists is what makes the subset notion the intended one. It costs nothing for
lists: [[lem-independent-list-is-injective]] shows that the vanishing condition
above already forces a list to be injective, so no injectivity hypothesis has to
be carried alongside independence of a list.

### The boundary cases are genuine cases

$\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]), so both of the following are
instances of the definitions and neither is a convention.

- **The empty list is independent.** For $n = 0$ the only list of scalars is the
  empty one, and the condition "$\lambda_i = 0_F$ for every $i < 0$" holds
  vacuously.
- **$\varnothing \subseteq V$ is independent.** The only function $v : n \to
  \varnothing$ is the empty one, with $n = 0$, and it is independent by the
  previous point.
- **$\{0_V\}$ is dependent.** The list $v : 1 \to \{0_V\}$ with $v_0 = 0_V$ is
  injective, and taking $\lambda_0 = 1_F$ gives
  $\sum_{i<1}\lambda_i v_i = 0_V + 1_F 0_V = 0_V$ by the recursion of
  [[def-monoid-finite-product]] and $\lambda 0_V = 0_V$
  ([[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]), while $1_F \ne 0_F$ in a field
  ([[def-field]]). So $\{0_V\}$, and hence every subset of $V$ containing $0_V$,
  is linearly dependent.

Let $(\mathcal X,\Sigma)$ be a nonempty measurable space and let $H$ be a nonempty class of measurable functions $h:\mathcal X\to\{0,1\}$. For an integer $m\ge0$ and an indexed tuple $\mathbf x=(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\in\mathcal X^m$, define its trace by

$$\operatorname{tr}_H(\mathbf x):=\{(h(x_1),\ldots,h(x_m)):h\in H\}\subseteq\{0,1\}^m.$$

The tuple $\mathbf x$ is **shattered by $H$** if $\operatorname{tr}_H(\mathbf x)=\{0,1\}^m$. Its coordinates are indexed: repeated instance points remain distinct coordinates, although their labels must agree for every $h\in H$. For $m=0$, $\mathbf x=()$ and $\{0,1\}^0=\{()\}$, so the empty tuple is shattered. The **VC dimension** of $H$ is

$$\operatorname{VCdim}(H):=\sup\{m\in\mathbb N_0:\text{some }\mathbf x\in\mathcal X^m\text{ is shattered by }H\}\in\mathbb N_0\cup\{+\infty\}.$$

Let $(\mathcal X,\Sigma)$ be a nonempty measurable space and let $H$ be a nonempty class of measurable binary functions on $\mathcal X$. For each integer $m\ge0$, the **growth function** of $H$ is

$$\Pi_H(m):=\sup_{\mathbf x\in\mathcal X^m}|\operatorname{tr}_H(\mathbf x)|.$$

The supremum is a maximum because each trace size is an integer between $1$ and $2^m$ and $\mathcal X^m$ is nonempty. In particular, $\Pi_H(0)=1$. A finite indexed tuple is shattered exactly when its trace has size $2^m$, so $\operatorname{VCdim}(H)=\sup\{m\in\mathbb N_0:\Pi_H(m)=2^m\}$.

For any two distinct points, no member of $H$ labels both points by $1$, so their $(1,1)$ pattern is absent; a repeated two-point tuple also cannot be shattered because both coordinates always agree. Thus no two-point tuple is shattered and $\operatorname{VCdim}(H)=1$.

On $m$ distinct natural numbers, the traces are the empty vector and the $m$ vectors with exactly one positive coordinate, so there are $m+1$. If a tuple repeats values, its trace is determined by its $r\le m$ distinct values and has at most $r+1\le m+1$ patterns. The empty tuple has one trace. Therefore $\Pi_H(m)=m+1$ for every $m\ge0$.

$$\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal F):=\frac1m\,\mathbb E_\sigma\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\sum_{i=1}^m\sigma_i f(z_i).$$

There is no absolute value in this definition and $0$ need not belong to $\mathcal F$. It differs from the absolute-value complexity $m^{-1}\mathbb E_\sigma\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}|\sum_i\sigma_i f(z_i)|$.

Let $m\ge1$, let $z_1,\ldots,z_m$ be fixed, and let $\mathcal F$ be a nonempty finite class of real-valued functions on their domain. For each $i$, let $\Phi_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ satisfy $|\Phi_i(x)-\Phi_i(y)|\le L|x-y|$ for all $x,y\in\mathbb R$, with a common $L\ge0$. Then

$$\frac1m\,\mathbb E_\sigma\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\sum_{i=1}^m\sigma_i\Phi_i(f(z_i))\le L\,\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal F).$$

Here $S=(z_1,\ldots,z_m)$ and $\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal F):=m^{-1}2^{-m}\sum_{\sigma\in\{-1,1\}^m}\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\sum_i\sigma_i f(z_i)$. $$P_mg:=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m g(z_i),\qquad Pg:=\int g\,dP,$$

and define the empirical Rademacher complexity by

$$\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal G):=\mathbb E_\sigma\left[\sup_{g\in\mathcal G}\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\sigma_i g(z_i)\right].$$

Here $\mathbb E_\sigma$ is the uniform average over the $2^m$ sign vectors. If $S=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)$ is an IID sample with common law $P$, and the displayed supremum is measurable as a function of $S$, the expected Rademacher complexity is

$$\mathfrak R_m(\mathcal G):=\mathbb E_{S\sim P^m}\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal G).$$

The class may be finite, countable, or uncountable when the indicated supremum is measurable; a specified countable subclass giving the same supremum for every sign vector for almost every sample suffices. This is the one-sided convention: the definition contains no absolute value, and zero need not belong to $\mathcal G$. Both complexities lie in $[0,1]$: every signed average lies in $[-1,1]$, and for any fixed $g_0\in\mathcal G$ the sign-average supremum is at least the sign-average for $g_0$, which is zero.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(\mathcal Z,\mathcal A,P)$ be a probability space and let $\mathcal G$ be a nonempty class of $\mathcal A$-measurable functions $g:\mathcal Z\to[0,1]$. For a fixed sample $S=(z_1,\ldots,z_m)\in\mathcal Z^m$, where $m\ge1$, let $\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_m$ be independent uniform signs in $\{-1,+1\}$. Define

$$P_mg:=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m g(z_i),\qquad Pg:=\int g\,dP,$$

and define the empirical Rademacher complexity by

$$\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal G):=\mathbb E_\sigma\left[\sup_{g\in\mathcal G}\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\sigma_i g(z_i)\right].$$

Here $\mathbb E_\sigma$ is the uniform average over the $2^m$ sign vectors. If $S=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)$ is an IID sample with common law $P$, and the displayed supremum is measurable as a function of $S$, the expected Rademacher complexity is

$$\mathfrak R_m(\mathcal G):=\mathbb E_{S\sim P^m}\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal G).$$

The class may be finite, countable, or uncountable when the indicated supremum is measurable; a specified countable subclass giving the same supremum for every sign vector for almost every sample suffices. This is the one-sided convention: the definition contains no absolute value, and zero need not belong to $\mathcal G$. Both complexities lie in $[0,1]$: every signed average lies in $[-1,1]$, and for any fixed $g_0\in\mathcal G$ the sign-average supremum is at least the sign-average for $g_0$, which is zero.

Let $(\mathcal Z,\mathcal A,P)$ be a probability space, let $m\ge1$, and let $\mathcal G$ be a nonempty class of measurable functions $g:\mathcal Z\to[0,1]$. Let $S=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)$ be IID with law $P$, let $S'=(Z_1',\ldots,Z_m')$ be an independent IID copy on a finite product probability extension, and let $\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_m$ be independent uniform signs independent of both samples. Write $P_mg=m^{-1}\sum_i g(Z_i)$ and $P_m'g=m^{-1}\sum_i g(Z_i')$. Assume the random suprema $\sup_g(Pg-P_mg)$, $\sup_g(P_m'g-P_mg)$, $\sup_g\sum_i\sigma_i(g(Z_i')-g(Z_i))$, and $\sup_g\sum_i\sigma_i g(Z_i)$ are measurable on their respective product sigma algebras. Then, with $\mathfrak R_m(\mathcal G)$ the expected one-sided Rademacher complexity,

$$\mathbb E_S\sup_{g\in\mathcal G}(Pg-P_mg)\le2\mathfrak R_m(\mathcal G).$$

This is a one-sided expectation inequality; it does not assert a tail bound or an absolute-value deviation bound. No choice axiom is assumed.

Assume AC. Let $n\ge1$, let $Z_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be independent random elements, meaning measurable maps (Random elements and real random variables), with laws $\mu_i$ given by pushforward (Law or distribution of a random element). Put $\mu=\bigotimes_{i=1}^n\mu_i$ on the finite product sigma-algebra (The product sigma-algebra and its finite iterates). Let $f:\prod_{i=1}^nS_i\to\mathbb R$ be product-measurable with $\int|f|\,d\mu<\infty$. Suppose finite deterministic constants $c_i\ge0$ satisfy
$$|f(z_1,\ldots,z_i,\ldots,z_n)-f(z_1,\ldots,z_i',\ldots,z_n)|\le c_i$$
for every fixed setting of the other coordinates and every $z_i,z_i'$. The independent product-law theorem identifies the law of $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)$ as $\mu$. Applying change of variables for expectation first to $|f|$ and then to $f$ makes $f(Z)$ integrable and gives $\mathbb E f(Z)=\int f\,d\mu$. Put $V=\sum_{i=1}^n c_i^2$. For $t>0$, if $V>0$ then
$$\mathbb P\bigl(f(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)-\mathbb E f(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)\ge t\bigr)\le\exp\!\left(-\frac{2t^2}{V}\right),$$
and if $V=0$ this probability is $0$. The same bound holds for the lower tail, so the two-sided probability is at most $2e^{-2t^2/V}$ when $V>0$.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because The exponential is a continuous bijection from $\mathbb{R}$ onto $(0,\infty)$ states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in Law or distribution of a random element agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in Independent random elements. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $A,B\in\mathcal F$,
and let $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be events.

1. $\mathbb P(A^c)=1-\mathbb P(A)$.
2. If $A\subseteq B$, then $\mathbb P(A)\le\mathbb P(B)$.
3. If $A\subseteq B$, then $\mathbb P(B\setminus A)=\mathbb P(B)-\mathbb P(A)$.
4. $\mathbb P(\bigcup_n A_n)\le\sum_{n=0}^\infty \mathbb P(A_n)$, and for every
   natural $m$,
   $$\mathbb P\left(\bigcup_{n<m}A_n\right)\le\sum_{n<m}\mathbb P(A_n).$$
5. $\mathbb P(A\cup B)=\mathbb P(A)+\mathbb P(B)-\mathbb P(A\cap B)$.
6. If $A_n\uparrow A$, then
   $$\mathbb P(A)=\sup_n\mathbb P(A_n).$$
   If $A_n\downarrow A$, then
   $$\mathbb P(A)=\inf_n\mathbb P(A_n).$$

McDiarmid [F3] with $c_i=1/m$ gives $\Psi(S)\le\mathbb E\Psi(S)+t$ with probability at least $1-\delta$, and [F2] bounds its expectation by $2\mathfrak R_m(\mathcal G)$. This proves the first one-sided bound.

For each fixed sample, $\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\overline{\mathcal G})=\mathbb E_\sigma[m^{-1}\sum_i\sigma_i+\sup_{g\in\mathcal G}m^{-1}\sum_i(-\sigma_i)g(Z_i)]$. The first term has mean zero and $-\sigma$ has the same uniform law as $\sigma$, so this equals $\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal G)$; taking expectations gives $\mathfrak R_m(\overline{\mathcal G})=\mathfrak R_m(\mathcal G)$.

For each fixed sign vector, changing one observation changes every $m^{-1}\sum_i\sigma_i g(Z_i)$ by at most $1/m$, since $g$ takes values in $[0,1]$; the same bound holds for the supremum and then for its sign average $\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal G)$. This statistic is bounded and measurable by the Statement. With $t=\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)/(2m)}>0$ as in step 1.1, [F3] applied to its negative gives $\mathfrak R_m(\mathcal G)\le\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal G)+t$ with probability at least $1-\delta$.

For $h=1-g$, $Ph-P_mh=P_mg-Pg$. Apply step 1.1 to $\mathcal G$ and $\overline{\mathcal G}$ with failure probability $\delta/2$ each. By [F7] and step 1.2, both deviations are at most $2\mathfrak R_m(\mathcal G)+\sqrt{\log(2/\delta)/(2m)}$ except on an event of probability at most $\delta$. This proves the first two-sided bound.

Apply step 1.1 with failure probability $\delta/2$ and step 2.1 with failure probability $\delta/2$. By [F7], both events hold with probability at least $1-\delta$. Since $2/\delta>1$, [F5] gives $t:=\sqrt{\log(2/\delta)/(2m)}>0$; combining the two bounds gives $\Psi(S)\le2\mathfrak R_m(\mathcal G)+t\le2\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal G)+3t$. This is the second one-sided guarantee.

Apply step 3.1 to $\mathcal G$ and $\overline{\mathcal G}$ with failure probability $\delta/2$ each. Their complexities agree by step 1.2, and their upper deviations are $\sup_g(Pg-P_mg)$ and $\sup_g(P_mg-Pg)$, respectively. By [F7] the two bounds hold together with probability at least $1-\delta$, giving the last two-sided bound with $\log(4/\delta)$.

A **supervised prediction problem** consists of nonempty measurable spaces $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$ of instances, $(\mathsf Y,\Sigma_Y)$ of labels, and $(\mathsf A,\Sigma_A)$ of prediction actions; the product measurable space $(\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y,\Sigma_X\otimes\Sigma_Y)$; a probability measure $P$ on that product; a nonempty class $\mathcal F$ of measurable predictors $f:\mathsf X\to\mathsf A$; and a loss $\ell:\mathsf A\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty]$ that is measurable with respect to $\Sigma_A\otimes\Sigma_Y$. The law $P$ need not be supported on a deterministic labeling function, and this definition imposes no assumption that sample observations be independent or share a common law.

For a supervised prediction problem with joint law $P$, the **population risk** of any measurable predictor $f:\mathsf X\to\mathsf A$ (in particular, every $f\in\mathcal F$) is the extended nonnegative integral
$$R_P(f):=\int_{\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y}\ell(f(x),y)\,P(d(x,y))\in[0,+\infty].$$
For an ordered sample $S=((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_m,y_m))$ of length $m\ge1$, the **empirical risk** or **training risk** of any such $f$ is
$$\widehat R_S(f):=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\ell(f(x_i),y_i)\in[0,+\infty].$$
Neither definition assumes finite risk. The sum uses extended nonnegative arithmetic; since $m\ge1$, any summand equal to $+\infty$ makes the empirical risk $+\infty$.

Fix a sample $S$ and a nonempty class $\mathcal F$ of predictors. Its **empirical minimum** is $\widehat R_S^*(\mathcal F):=\inf_{f\in\mathcal F}\widehat R_S(f)\in[0,+\infty]$. An **exact empirical risk minimizer** is a predictor $f\in\mathcal F$ with $\widehat R_S(f)=\widehat R_S^*(\mathcal F)$. If the infimum is finite but is not attained, no exact minimizer exists. If the infimum is $+\infty$, nonemptiness implies that every member has infinite empirical risk and is an exact minimizer.

For finite $\eta\ge0$, a predictor $f\in\mathcal F$ is an **$\eta$-approximate empirical risk minimizer** if either the empirical minimum is $+\infty$ and $f$ is an exact minimizer, or the empirical minimum is finite and $f$ has finite empirical risk at most $\widehat R_S^*(\mathcal F)+\eta$. The membership requirement $f\in\mathcal F$ applies in both branches. Thus the definition never forms $+\infty+\eta$. When $\eta=0$ and the finite infimum is not attained, no such predictor exists.

For a fixed sample size $m$, a **measurable prediction rule** with class $\mathcal F$ is a jointly measurable evaluation map from the sample space $((\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y)^m, (\Sigma_X\otimes\Sigma_Y)^{\otimes m})$ and a new instance in $\mathsf X$ to $\mathsf A$, whose slice at each sample belongs to $\mathcal F$. It is an exact or approximate ERM rule when every slice satisfies the corresponding samplewise definition above. This definition asserts no existence of a measurable selector for an arbitrary class.

In a supervised prediction problem, for every measurable predictor $f$, the function $(x,y)\mapsto\ell(f(x),y)$ is measurable, so its population risk is a defined extended nonnegative integral. For every sample size $m\ge1$, the empirical risk $S\mapsto\widehat R_S(f)$ is an extended nonnegative measurable function on the finite product sample space.

Given a nonnegative sequence $(\beta_n)_{n\ge1}$, the rule has uniform deletion stability with coefficients $(\beta_n)$ if, for every $n\ge1$, every $S\in\mathcal Z^n$, every $i\in[n]$, and every $z\in\mathcal Z$,

$$

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

For a supervised prediction problem with joint law $P$, the **population risk** of any measurable predictor $f:\mathsf X\to\mathsf A$ (in particular, every $f\in\mathcal F$) is the extended nonnegative integral
$$R_P(f):=\int_{\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y}\ell(f(x),y)\,P(d(x,y))\in[0,+\infty].$$
For an ordered sample $S=((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_m,y_m))$ of length $m\ge1$, the **empirical risk** or **training risk** of any such $f$ is
$$\widehat R_S(f):=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\ell(f(x_i),y_i)\in[0,+\infty].$$
Neither definition assumes finite risk. The sum uses extended nonnegative arithmetic; since $m\ge1$, any summand equal to $+\infty$ makes the empirical risk $+\infty$.

Let $\mathcal Z$ be an observation set, let $\mathcal H$ be a set of hypotheses, and let $L:\mathcal H\times\mathcal Z\to[0,\infty)$ be a loss. A deterministic size-indexed learning rule consists, for every integer $n\ge1$ and every retained index set $J\subseteq[n]$, of a map $A_{n,J}$ from the indexed observations $(z_j)_{j\in J}$ to $\mathcal H$; the original sample size $n$ remains an input to this rule. For $S=(z_1,\ldots,z_n)$ write $A_S:=A_{n,[n]}(S)$ and $A_{S\setminus i}:=A_{n,[n]\setminus\{i\}}(S|_{[n]\setminus\{i\}})$ for the output after deleting indexed observation $i$. The rule is permutation-invariant if simultaneous reordering of the observations and relabeling of their retained indices leaves each output unchanged. Given a nonnegative sequence $(\beta_n)_{n\ge1}$, the rule has uniform deletion stability with coefficients $(\beta_n)$ if, for every $n\ge1$, every $S\in\mathcal Z^n$, every $i\in[n]$, and every $z\in\mathcal Z$,

$$
|L(A_S,z)-L(A_{S\setminus i},z)|\le\beta_n.
$$

The sequence is nonincreasing when $\beta_{n+1}\le\beta_n$ for every $n\ge1$. This is the deletion convention. If $S'$ differs from $S$ only at coordinate $i$, then $S\setminus i=S'\setminus i$, and the triangle inequality gives $|L(A_S,z)-L(A_{S'},z)|\le2\beta_n$ for every $z$; the resulting replacement bound has coefficient $2\beta_n$.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in Law or distribution of a random element agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in Independent random elements. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$ and $(\mathsf Y,\Sigma_Y)$ be nonempty measurable instance and label spaces, and equip $\mathsf Z=\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y$ with $\Sigma_Z=\Sigma_X\otimes\Sigma_Y$. Let $P$ be a probability measure on $(\mathsf Z,\Sigma_Z)$, let $\mathcal F$ be a nonempty class of measurable functions $f:(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)\to(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$, and let $\ell:\mathbb R\times\mathsf Y\to[0,\infty)$ be measurable with respect to $\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\otimes\Sigma_Y$. For $f\in\mathcal F$ and $z=(x,y)$ write $L_f(z)=\ell(f(x),y)$, $R_P(f)=\int_{\mathsf Z}L_f(z)\,P(dz)$, and $\widehat R_S(f)=m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^mL_f(Z_i)$. Let $S=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)$ have product law $P^m$ on $(\mathsf Z^m,\Sigma_Z^{\otimes m})$, with $m\ge1$, and let $A$ be a deterministic, permutation-invariant size-indexed learning rule that outputs members of $\mathcal F$ and assume the maps $(S,z)\mapsto L_{A_S}(z)$ and $(S,z)\mapsto L_{A_{S\setminus i}}(z)$ for every $i\in[m]$ are jointly measurable with respect to $\Sigma_Z^{\otimes m}\otimes\Sigma_Z$. Assume also that the sample-dependent risk, empirical-risk, and leave-one-out maps in the conclusions are measurable. Assume $0\le L_{A_T}(z)\le M<\infty$ for every full or deleted sample $T$ and every $z\in\mathsf Z$, and assume $A$ has uniform deletion stability with a finite nonincreasing sequence $(\beta_n)_{n\ge1}$. Define $R_{\mathrm{loo}}(A,S)=m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m L_{A_{S\setminus i}}(Z_i)$, using the size-$m$ deletion output. Then

$$\mathbb E_{S\sim P^m}\bigl[R_P(A_S)-\widehat R_S(A_S)\bigr]\le2\beta_m\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathbb E_{S\sim P^m}\bigl[R_P(A_S)-R_{\mathrm{loo}}(A,S)\bigr]\le\beta_m.$$

Moreover, for every sample $S$ and index $i\in[m]$,

$$|R_P(A_S)-R_P(A_{S\setminus i})|\le\beta_m.$$

All three conclusions are choice-free.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because The exponential is a continuous bijection from $\mathbb{R}$ onto $(0,\infty)$ states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

Assume AC. Let $n\ge1$, let $Z_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be independent random elements, meaning measurable maps (Random elements and real random variables), with laws $\mu_i$ given by pushforward (Law or distribution of a random element). Put $\mu=\bigotimes_{i=1}^n\mu_i$ on the finite product sigma-algebra (The product sigma-algebra and its finite iterates). Let $f:\prod_{i=1}^nS_i\to\mathbb R$ be product-measurable with $\int|f|\,d\mu<\infty$. Suppose finite deterministic constants $c_i\ge0$ satisfy
$$|f(z_1,\ldots,z_i,\ldots,z_n)-f(z_1,\ldots,z_i',\ldots,z_n)|\le c_i$$
for every fixed setting of the other coordinates and every $z_i,z_i'$. The independent product-law theorem identifies the law of $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)$ as $\mu$. Applying change of variables for expectation first to $|f|$ and then to $f$ makes $f(Z)$ integrable and gives $\mathbb E f(Z)=\int f\,d\mu$. Put $V=\sum_{i=1}^n c_i^2$. For $t>0$, if $V>0$ then
$$\mathbb P\bigl(f(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)-\mathbb E f(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)\ge t\bigr)\le\exp\!\left(-\frac{2t^2}{V}\right),$$
and if $V=0$ this probability is $0$. The same bound holds for the lower tail, so the two-sided probability is at most $2e^{-2t^2/V}$ when $V>0$.

derivations.claim: Fix an index $k$ and let $S'$ be any sample that differs from $S$ only at coordinate $k$. Their retained samples $S\setminus k$ and $S'\setminus k$ coincide. By [F4], $|R_P(A_S)-R_P(A_{S'})|\le|R_P(A_S)-R_P(A_{S\setminus k})|+|R_P(A_{S'\setminus k})-R_P(A_{S'})|\le2\beta_m$. For every $j\ne k$, the two loss terms at the common test point $Z_j$ differ by at most $2\beta_m$, by [F2] through the same deleted output. The two $k$th loss terms each lie in $[0,M]$, so their difference is at most $M$. Hence $|\widehat R_S(A_S)-\widehat R_{S'}(A_{S'})|\le 2(m-1)\beta_m/m+M/m\le2\beta_m+M/m$. For $\Phi(S)=R_P(A_S)-\widehat R_S(A_S)$ this yields the coordinate oscillation $|\Phi(S)-\Phi(S')|\le4\beta_m+M/m$.

Fix an index $k$ and samples $S,S'$ differing only at coordinate $k$. The risk term in $\Psi(S)=R_P(A_S)-R_{\mathrm{loo}}(A,S)$ changes by at most $2\beta_m$ by [F4]. In the leave-one-out average, the $k$th term uses the same deleted training sample for $S$ and $S'$, and its test losses differ by at most $M$. For $j\ne k$, the two deleted training samples $S\setminus j$ and $S'\setminus j$ have the same $m-2$ common observations and the two alternative $k$th observations. Form a size-$m$ indexed sample $T$ from those $m-2$ common observations and both alternatives. Up to permutation, each of the two deleted training samples is obtained by deleting one of the alternatives from $T$. Permutation invariance and [F2] therefore bound their loss change at the common test point $Z_j$ by $2\beta_m$. When $m=1$ there are no indices $j\ne k$, so only the $k$th term occurs. Thus the leave-one-out average changes by at most $2(m-1)\beta_m/m+M/m\le2\beta_m+M/m$, and $|\Psi(S)-\Psi(S')|\le4\beta_m+M/m$.

Put $c=4\beta_m+M/m$. If $c=0$, then $M=\beta_m=0$ and every loss and both gaps vanish. If $c>0$, then $\Phi$ is bounded, measurable, and integrable by [A2]. Since $0<\delta<1$, [F5]–[F6] give $\log(1/\delta)>0$, so $t=c\sqrt{m\log(1/\delta)/2}>0$. The product law $P^m$ makes the coordinates independent by [F3], and [F7] with all $m$ coordinate bounds equal to $c$ gives $\mathbb P\{\Phi-\mathbb E\Phi\ge t\}\le\exp(-2t^2/(mc^2))=\delta$. By [F4], outside this event $\Phi\le2\beta_m+t=2\beta_m+(4m\beta_m+M)\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)/(2m)}$. Together with the $c=0$ case this proves the first probability bound.

With $c=4\beta_m+M/m$, the case $c=0$ again has zero losses and zero gaps. If $c>0$, [A2] makes $\Psi$ bounded, measurable, and integrable. Since $0<\delta<1$, [F5]–[F6] give $\log(1/\delta)>0$. The product law $P^m$ makes the coordinates independent by [F3], and [F7] with coordinate bounds $c$ gives $\mathbb P\{\Psi-\mathbb E\Psi\ge c\sqrt{m\log(1/\delta)/2}\}\le\delta$. By [F4], $\mathbb E\Psi\le\beta_m$, so outside this event $\Psi\le\beta_m+(4m\beta_m+M)\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)/(2m)}$. This proves the second probability bound, separately from the first.

For a supervised prediction problem with joint law $P$, the **population risk** of any measurable predictor $f:\mathsf X\to\mathsf A$ (in particular, every $f\in\mathcal F$) is the extended nonnegative integral
$$R_P(f):=\int_{\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y}\ell(f(x),y)\,P(d(x,y))\in[0,+\infty].$$
For an ordered sample $S=((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_m,y_m))$ of length $m\ge1$, the **empirical risk** or **training risk** of any such $f$ is
$$\widehat R_S(f):=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\ell(f(x_i),y_i)\in[0,+\infty].$$
Neither definition assumes finite risk. The sum uses extended nonnegative arithmetic; since $m\ge1$, any summand equal to $+\infty$ makes the empirical risk $+\infty$.

Let $\mathcal Z$ be an observation set, let $\mathcal H$ be a set of hypotheses, and let $L:\mathcal H\times\mathcal Z\to[0,\infty)$ be a loss. A deterministic size-indexed learning rule consists, for every integer $n\ge1$ and every retained index set $J\subseteq[n]$, of a map $A_{n,J}$ from the indexed observations $(z_j)_{j\in J}$ to $\mathcal H$; the original sample size $n$ remains an input to this rule. $$
|L(A_S,z)-L(A_{S\setminus i},z)|\le\beta_n.
$$

The sequence is nonincreasing when $\beta_{n+1}\le\beta_n$ for every $n\ge1$. This is the deletion convention. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The law $P$ need not be supported on a deterministic labeling function, and this definition imposes no assumption that sample observations be independent or share a common law.

$$R_P(f):=\int_{\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y}\ell(f(x),y)\,P(d(x,y))\in[0,+\infty].$$

Neither definition assumes finite risk. The sum uses extended nonnegative arithmetic; since $m\ge1$, any summand equal to $+\infty$ makes the empirical risk $+\infty$.

For $S=(z_1,\ldots,z_n)$ write $A_S:=A_{n,[n]}(S)$ and $A_{S\setminus i}:=A_{n,[n]\setminus\{i\}}(S|_{[n]\setminus\{i\}})$ for the output after deleting indexed observation $i$. The rule is permutation-invariant if simultaneous reordering of the observations and relabeling of their retained indices leaves each output unchanged. The sequence is nonincreasing when $\beta_{n+1}\le\beta_n$ for every $n\ge1$. This is the deletion convention. If $S'$ differs from $S$ only at coordinate $i$, then $S\setminus i=S'\setminus i$, and the triangle inequality gives $|L(A_S,z)-L(A_{S'},z)|\le2\beta_n$ for every $z$; the resulting replacement bound has coefficient $2\beta_n$.

Let $(\mathcal Z,\mathcal A,P)$ be a probability space and let $\mathcal G$ be a nonempty class of $\mathcal A$-measurable functions $g:\mathcal Z\to[0,1]$. For a fixed sample $S=(z_1,\ldots,z_m)\in\mathcal Z^m$, where $m\ge1$, let $\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_m$ be independent uniform signs in $\{-1,+1\}$. Define

$$P_mg:=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m g(z_i),\qquad Pg:=\int g\,dP,$$

and define the empirical Rademacher complexity by

$$\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal G):=\mathbb E_\sigma\left[\sup_{g\in\mathcal G}\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\sigma_i g(z_i)\right].$$

Here $\mathbb E_\sigma$ is the uniform average over the $2^m$ sign vectors. If $S=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)$ is an IID sample with common law $P$, and the displayed supremum is measurable as a function of $S$, the expected Rademacher complexity is

$$\mathfrak R_m(\mathcal G):=\mathbb E_{S\sim P^m}\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal G).$$

The class may be finite, countable, or uncountable when the indicated supremum is measurable; a specified countable subclass giving the same supremum for every sign vector for almost every sample suffices. This is the one-sided convention: the definition contains no absolute value, and zero need not belong to $\mathcal G$. Both complexities lie in $[0,1]$: every signed average lies in $[-1,1]$, and for any fixed $g_0\in\mathcal G$ the sign-average supremum is at least the sign-average for $g_0$, which is zero.

Assume the Axiom of Choice (AC). Let $(\mathcal Z,\mathcal A,P)$ be a probability space, let $m\ge1$, and let $\mathcal G$ be a nonempty class of measurable functions $g:\mathcal Z\to[0,1]$. Take $S=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)$ to be the coordinate sample with law $P^m$. Put $P_mg=m^{-1}\sum_i g(Z_i)$ and $\overline{\mathcal G}:=\{1-g:g\in\mathcal G\}$. Assume the sample, independent-copy and sign suprema over $\mathcal G$ and $\overline{\mathcal G}$ used in the displayed claims and the symmetrization argument are measurable. Let $\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_m$ be independent uniform signs, and let

$$\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal G):=\mathbb E_\sigma\sup_{g\in\mathcal G}\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\sigma_i g(Z_i),\qquad \mathfrak R_m(\mathcal G):=\mathbb E_{S\sim P^m}\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal G),$$

where the $\sigma_i$ are independent uniform signs, and let $\delta\in(0,1)$. Each of the following four guarantees holds with probability at least $1-\delta$ over $S$:

$$\forall g\in\mathcal G,\qquad Pg\le P_mg+2\mathfrak R_m(\mathcal G)+\sqrt{\frac{\log(1/\delta)}{2m}},$$

$$\forall g\in\mathcal G,\qquad Pg\le P_mg+2\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal G)+3\sqrt{\frac{\log(2/\delta)}{2m}},$$

$$\sup_{g\in\mathcal G}|Pg-P_mg|\le2\mathfrak R_m(\mathcal G)+\sqrt{\frac{\log(2/\delta)}{2m}},$$

$$\sup_{g\in\mathcal G}|Pg-P_mg|\le2\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal G)+3\sqrt{\frac{\log(4/\delta)}{2m}}.$$

The four guarantees are separate probability statements. The choice axiom is used through the bounded-differences theorem.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in Law or distribution of a random element agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in Independent random elements. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because The exponential is a continuous bijection from $\mathbb{R}$ onto $(0,\infty)$ states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

Under $P$, $h_0\equiv0$ has zero loss at every feature, so its population and empirical risks are both $0$. For $S=((j,0))$, the memorizing learner predicts $0$ at $j$ and $1$ at the other $N-1$ features. Thus its empirical risk is $0$ and its population risk is $(N-1)/N$.

Fix any $z=(j,y)$ and one-point sample $S=(z)$. Since $\mathcal H$ contains every binary labeling, some $h$ has loss $g_h(z)=0$ and some has $g_h(z)=1$. For sign $\sigma=+1$, $\sup_{g\in\mathcal G}\sigma g(z)=1$; for sign $\sigma=-1$, the supremum is $0$. The two equiprobable signs therefore give $\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal G)=1/2$ for every $S$, and averaging over $S\sim P$ gives $\mathfrak R_1(\mathcal G)=1/2$.

The constant learner returns $h_0$ on both $S$ and its deletion, so its size-one stability coefficient is $0$. The empty-sample memorizer predicts $1$ at $j$, whereas the full-sample memorizer predicts $0$ there; at test point $(j,0)$ the loss changes by $1$. Every zero-one loss difference is at most $1$, hence the memorizer's coefficient is exactly $1$.

With $m=1$, [F5] has complexity term $2\mathfrak R_1(\mathcal G)=1$, and [F7]–[F8] make its confidence term positive for every $\delta\in(0,1)$. Every zero-one loss deviation is at most $1$, so this class-wide upper bound is no sharper than the trivial range, while step 1.1 gives the constant learner an exact zero gap and the memorizer zero training risk with a large population risk.

canonical natural of The canonical natural $\iota(n) = n \cdot 1_F$ of a field.
