The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let a supervised prediction problem have a measurable instance space $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$, finite label set $\mathcal Y=\{y_1,\ldots,y_K\}$ with distinct labels, the full power-set sigma-algebra on $\mathcal Y$, and $K\ge2$, and joint probability law $P$ on $\mathsf X\times\mathcal Y$; let $X$ and $Y$ be its coordinate random variables and let $\mathcal G=\{X^{-1}(A):A\in\Sigma_X\}$, the sigma-algebra generated by $X$. There is a measurable function $\eta=(\eta_1,\ldots,\eta_K):\mathsf X\to\Delta_K$, where $\Delta_K=\{p\in[0,1]^K:\sum_jp_j=1\}\subset\mathbb R^K$ has its subspace Borel sigma-algebra, such that for every label index $j$ and $A\in\Sigma_X$,
$$P(X\in A,\ Y=y_j)=\mathbb E[\eta_j(X)\mathbf1_{\{X\in A\}}].$$

Assume AC. Let a supervised prediction problem have a measurable instance space $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$, finite label set $\mathcal Y=\{y_1,\ldots,y_K\}$ with distinct labels, the full power-set sigma-algebra on $\mathcal Y$, and $K\ge2$, and joint probability law $P$ on $\mathsf X\times\mathcal Y$; let $X$ and $Y$ be its coordinate random variables and let $\mathcal G=\{X^{-1}(A):A\in\Sigma_X\}$, the sigma-algebra generated by $X$. There is a measurable function $\eta=(\eta_1,\ldots,\eta_K):\mathsf X\to\Delta_K$, where $\Delta_K=\{p\in[0,1]^K:\sum_jp_j=1\}\subset\mathbb R^K$ has its subspace Borel sigma-algebra, such that for every label index $j$ and $A\in\Sigma_X$,
$$P(X\in A,\ Y=y_j)=\mathbb E[\eta_j(X)\mathbf1_{\{X\in A\}}].$$

Let $Y\in\{-1,+1\}$ be the label in a supervised prediction problem with the full power-set sigma-algebra on this binary label set, and choose the finite-label conditional probability function ordered as $(-1,+1)$; write $\eta(x)=\eta_{+1}(x)$. Let $\Phi:\mathbb R\to[0,\infty)$ be finite, convex and nondecreasing. It is continuous on $\mathbb R$; extend it to $\overline{\mathbb R}=\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty,+\infty\}$ by its one-sided monotone limits, which may equal $+\infty$. The resulting extended function is Borel measurable. For $u\in\overline{\mathbb R}$ define the conditional margin risk
$$L_\Phi(x,u)=\eta(x)\Phi(-u)+(1-\eta(x))\Phi(u),$$
using $0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ at endpoints. A measurable extended-real conditional minimizer is a measurable $h_\Phi^*:\mathsf X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ satisfying $L_\Phi(x,h_\Phi^*(x))\le L_\Phi(x,u)$ for every $x$ and every $u\in\overline{\mathbb R}$. For a measurable real-valued score $h$, its margin loss is $\ell_\Phi(h(x),y)=\Phi(-yh(x))$, its surrogate risk is $L_\Phi(h)=\mathbb E[\Phi(-Yh(X))]$, and its conditional-minimum risk is $L_\Phi^*=\mathbb E[L_\Phi(X,h_\Phi^*(X))]$. Under the zero-score-is-error convention, its classification risk is $R_{01}(h)=P(Yh(X)\le0)$, and the Bayes classification risk is $R_{01}^*=\mathbb E[\min\{\eta(X),1-\eta(X)\}]$. Write $h^*(x)=\eta(x)-\tfrac12$ for the centered conditional class probability.

For a supervised prediction problem with joint law $P$, the **population risk** of any measurable predictor $f:\mathsf X\to\mathsf A$ (in particular, every $f\in\mathcal F$) is the extended nonnegative integral
$$R_P(f):=\int_{\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y}\ell(f(x),y)\,P(d(x,y))\in[0,+\infty].$$
For an ordered sample $S=((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_m,y_m))$ of length $m\ge1$, the **empirical risk** or **training risk** of any such $f$ is
$$\widehat R_S(f):=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\ell(f(x_i),y_i)\in[0,+\infty].$$
Neither definition assumes finite risk. The sum uses extended nonnegative arithmetic; since $m\ge1$, any summand equal to $+\infty$ makes the empirical risk $+\infty$.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then there is an increasing sequence of
nonnegative simple measurable functions $(s_n)$ such that $s_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x\in X$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$
Every convex function $f:U\to\mathbb R$ on an open convex set is continuous on $U$. The assertion is vacuous when $U$ is empty.
For every real $s\ge1$, the function $\varphi_s:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ defined by $\varphi_s(t)=-t^{1/s}$, with $0^{1/s}=0$, is convex.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $X$ be an
integrable real random variable, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval
containing $X(\omega)$ for almost every $\omega$, and let $\varphi:I\to\mathbb R$
be convex.

Assume additionally that $\varphi(X)$ is either integrable or nonnegative, so
its expectation is defined by
[[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. Then
$$\varphi(\mathbb E[X])\le\mathbb E[\varphi(X)].$$
In the nonnegative case the right-hand side may be $+\infty$.

For a binary supervised problem with the full power-set sigma-algebra on $Y\in\{-1,+1\}$, conditional positive-label probability $\eta$, and any measurable real-valued score $h$, use $R_{01}(h)=P(Yh(X)\le0)$ and $R_{01}^*=\mathbb E\min\{\eta(X),1-\eta(X)\}$. Then
$$R_{01}(h)-R_{01}^*=2\mathbb E\!\left[\left|\eta(X)-\tfrac12\right|\mathbf1_{\{h(X)(\eta(X)-\tfrac12)\le0\}}\right]+\mathbb E\!\left[\min\{\eta(X),1-\eta(X)\}\mathbf1_{\{h(X)=0\}}\right].$$

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
(Measurable spaces and measurable sets). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space and let
$f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ be measurable for the Borel sigma-algebra on
the extended real line. Products of functions use
$\odot_X$ from A total pointwise product for extended-real-valued functions, and $cf$
abbreviates $\underline c\odot_X f$ for the constant function $\underline c$.
The magnitude function is $|f|=\max(f,-f)$ as in
The positive and negative parts of a function. Then:

1. $cf$ is measurable for every real scalar $c$;
2. $\max(f,g)$, $\min(f,g)$, $|f|$, $f^+$, and $f^-$ are measurable;
3. if the partial pointwise sum $f+g$ is defined at every point, then it is measurable;
4. the pointwise product $fg:=f\odot_X g$ is measurable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. If $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ are measurable, then
$$\int(f+g)\,d\mu=\int f\,d\mu+\int g\,d\mu.$$

If $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable and $\int f\,d\mu<+\infty$, then
$f(x)<+\infty$ for almost every $x$.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $E$ be measurable with $\mu(E)=0$.
Then
$$\int_E f\,d\mu=0.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

derivations.claim: Under AC [A1], the event identities [F1] imply, first for indicators and finite nonnegative simple functions and then by [F3] for every nonnegative measurable $f:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty]$, that $\mathbb E[\mathbf1_{\{Y=+1\}}f(X)]=\mathbb E[\eta(X)f(X)],\qquad \mathbb E[\mathbf1_{\{Y=-1\}}f(X)]=\mathbb E[(1-\eta(X))f(X)].$ For simple $f$ this follows by finite additivity of the event identities; increasing simple approximation and monotone convergence give the general case.

The function $\Phi$ is continuous by [F4], hence Borel; its endpoint extension by one-sided limits is Borel on the extended real line. Since $h$ is measurable, the measurable-map definition [F7] makes $\Phi\circ h$ and $\Phi\circ(-h)$ measurable and nonnegative. Applying step 1.1 to these functions gives $L_\Phi(h)=\mathbb E[L_\Phi(X,h(X))].$ This identity also verifies measurability of the conditional-risk integrand used below.

Put $m(x)=L_\Phi(x,h_\Phi^*(x))$ and $g(x)=L_\Phi(x,0)-m(x)$. Minimality gives $0\le m(x)\le L_\Phi(x,0)=\Phi(0)$ and $g(x)\ge0$ for every $x$, so $L_\Phi^*=\mathbb E m(X)<\infty$. Here $m$ is measurable: for the endpoint-valued minimizer, each weighted term is the limit of the measurable functions $\eta(x)\min\{\Phi(-h_\Phi^*(x)),n\}$ or $(1-\eta(x))\min\{\Phi(h_\Phi^*(x)),n\}$, respectively; this also implements $0\cdot\infty=0$. For the score $h$, put $R(x)=L_\Phi(x,h(x))$ and $D_0(x)=R(x)-m(x)\ge0$. By step 2.1, $\mathbb E R(X)=L_\Phi(h)$, while $R=D_0+m$ pointwise because $m$ is finite. Additivity [F8] gives $\mathbb E D_0(X)=L_\Phi(h)-L_\Phi^*<\infty$. By [F9], $N=\{D_0=+\infty\}$ is measurable and null. Set $D=D_0$ on $N^c$ and $D=0$ on $N$; [F7] makes this finite representative measurable. Additivity [F8] and [F10] show that it has $\mathbb E D=\mathbb E D_0=L_\Phi(h)-L_\Phi^*$.

Fix $x$, write $a=\eta(x)$, and let $u$ be a real score satisfying $u(a-1/2)\le0$. For all real $u$, convexity gives $\Phi(-u)+\Phi(u)-2\Phi(0)\ge0$. If $a>1/2$ then $u\le0$, so monotonicity gives $\Phi(-u)-\Phi(u)\ge0$; if $a<1/2$ then $u\ge0$, so $\Phi(-u)-\Phi(u)\le0$. The identity $L_\Phi(x,u)-L_\Phi(x,0)=\tfrac12[\Phi(-u)+\Phi(u)-2\Phi(0)]+(a-\tfrac12)[\Phi(-u)-\Phi(u)]$ therefore shows $L_\Phi(x,u)\ge L_\Phi(x,0)$ whenever $a\ne1/2$ and $u(a-1/2)\le0$. When $a=1/2$, the same identity has zero second term and proves $L_\Phi(x,u)\ge L_\Phi(x,0)$ for every $u$, so the conditional minimum is at $0$ and $g(x)=0$. Consequently, on $\{h(x)(a-1/2)\le0\}\setminus N$ one has $D(x)=D_0(x)\ge g(x)\ge0$; the excluded set is null.

Almost surely on the event $h(X)(\eta(X)-1/2)\le0$, we are outside the null set $N$ from step 3.1, so the margin hypothesis and step 4.1 give $|\eta(X)-1/2|^s\le c g(X)\le cD(X)$, hence $|\eta(X)-1/2|\le c^{1/s}D(X)^{1/s}$. For nonnegative measurable integrands, [F8] and [F10] identify each full expectation with its integral on $N^c$; on that set the displayed inequality is pointwise, so monotonicity and positive-scalar homogeneity [F11] pass it to expectations and extract the factor $2c^{1/s}$. Apply the exact excess identity [F6], bound its first integrand in this way, and use $\mathbf1_{\{h=0\}}\le1$ to obtain $R_{01}(h)-R_{01}^*\le2c^{1/s}\mathbb E[D(X)^{1/s}]+\mathbb E[\min\{\eta(X),1-\eta(X)\}\mathbf1_{\{h(X)=0\}}].$

Put $\alpha=1/s\in(0,1]$. For $0\le t\le1$, $t^\alpha\le1$, while for $t\ge1$, $t^\alpha\le t$; hence $D^\alpha\le1+D$. Monotonicity [F11] and additivity [F8] give $\mathbb E[D^\alpha]\le\mathbb E[1+D]=1+\mathbb ED<\infty$ by step 3.1, so $D^\alpha$ is integrable. By [F5], Jensen applied to the integrable convex function $-t^\alpha$ gives $\mathbb E[D^{1/s}]\le(\mathbb ED)^{1/s}=[L_\Phi(h)-L_\Phi^*]^{1/s}$ by step 3.1. Substitution in step 5.1 proves the zero-score-is-error bound.

Under $P(h(X)=0)=0$ the correction has expectation zero. For the label classifier $f_h$, at each $x$ its conditional excess over $\min(\eta(x),1-\eta(x))$ is $2|\eta(x)-1/2|$ on $\{h(x)<0,\eta(x)>1/2\}\cup\{h(x)\ge0,\eta(x)<1/2\}$ and zero elsewhere. This follows by comparing the conditional error $\eta(x)$ for prediction $-1$ and $1-\eta(x)$ for prediction $+1$. This adverse-sign set is contained in the event of step 5.1, so steps 5.1 and 6.1 bound its expectation by $2c^{1/s}[L_\Phi(h)-L_\Phi^*]^{1/s}$ without a tie correction. Finally, replacing $c$ by $a^s$ makes $c^{1/s}=a$ and proves the equivalent source parameterization.

Let $K\ge2$, let $Y$ be a random variable into the finite label set $\{1,\ldots,K\}$ with its full power-set sigma-algebra on a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$, and let $G=(G_1,\ldots,G_K):\Omega\to\Delta_K$ be a measurable forecast, where $\Delta_K=\{p\in[0,1]^K:\sum_jp_j=1\}$. The forecast is **fully reliable** if for every label $j$ and every Borel set $B\subseteq\Delta_K$,
$$\mathbb P(Y=j,\ G\in B)=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_{\{G\in B\}}G_j].$$
It is **classwise calibrated** if for every $j$ and every Borel set $B\subseteq[0,1]$,
$$\mathbb P(Y=j,\ G_j\in B)=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_{\{G_j\in B\}}G_j].$$
For the **top-confidence calibration** condition, define $C=\max_jG_j$ and $\widehat Y=\min\{j:G_j=C\}$, so ties go to the smallest label. The forecast is top-confidence calibrated if for every Borel set $B\subseteq[0,1]$,
$$\mathbb P(Y=\widehat Y,\ C\in B)=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_{\{C\in B\}}C].$$
A measurable function $r:\Delta_K\to\Delta_K$ is a **calibration function** for $G$ if for every $j$ and every Borel set $B\subseteq\Delta_K$,
$$\mathbb P(Y=j,\ G\in B)=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_{\{G\in B\}}r_j(G)].$$
When such a function is supplied and $d:\Delta_K\times\Delta_K\to[0,+\infty)$ is measurable, the **expected calibration error with discrepancy $d$** is $\eta_d=\mathbb E[d(r(G),G)]$.

derivations.claim: Each forecast row and each conditional-label row in Models A, B, and C has nonnegative coordinates summing to one, so all entries define simplex forecasts and conditional label distributions. In each model the three forecast vectors are distinct. Therefore full reliability would require $p_i=g_i$ at every row by [F1], but Model A row 1, Model B row 1, and Model C row 1 each have $p_i\ne g_i$. Full reliability fails in all three models.

In Model A, for each label the groups with forecast coordinate $0.4$ have conditional frequency $0.4$, and the groups with coordinate $0.3$ have average conditional frequency $0.3$: for labels 1, 2, and 3 the latter averages are respectively $(0.2+0.4)/2$, $(0.4+0.2)/2$, and $(0.2+0.4)/2$. Thus Model A is classwise calibrated. Its top confidence is always $0.4$, its predicted labels are $1,2,3$ in the three rows, and each corresponding conditional correctness probability is $0.4$, so it is top-confidence calibrated.

In Model B the top confidence is always $0.5$, the predicted labels are $1,2,3$, and the average conditional correctness is $(0.7+0.5+0.3)/3=0.5$, so top-confidence calibration holds. Classwise calibration fails because forecast coordinate $G_1=0.5$ occurs only in row 1, where $P(Y=1\mid X=1)=0.7\ne0.5$.

In Model C, for each label the forecast coordinate $0.5$ group has average conditional frequency $0.5$, and the coordinate $0$ group has frequency $0$: the three nonzero-group averages are $(0.8+0.2)/2$, $(0.2+0.8)/2$, and $(0.8+0.2)/2$. Thus classwise calibration holds. All top confidences equal $0.5$; the tie-broken predicted labels are $1,1,2$, with conditional correctness probabilities $0.8,0.2,0.8$. Their average is $0.6\ne0.5$, so top-confidence calibration fails. Steps 1.1, 1.2, and 1.3 establish the other model claims; the Model C calculation completes the pairwise distinctions.

Let $K\ge2$, let $Y$ be a random variable into the finite label set $\{1,\ldots,K\}$ with its full power-set sigma-algebra on a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$, and let $G=(G_1,\ldots,G_K):\Omega\to\Delta_K$ be a measurable forecast, where $\Delta_K=\{p\in[0,1]^K:\sum_jp_j=1\}$. The forecast is **fully reliable** if for every label $j$ and every Borel set $B\subseteq\Delta_K$,
$$\mathbb P(Y=j,\ G\in B)=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_{\{G\in B\}}G_j].$$
It is **classwise calibrated** if for every $j$ and every Borel set $B\subseteq[0,1]$,
$$\mathbb P(Y=j,\ G_j\in B)=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_{\{G_j\in B\}}G_j].$$
For the **top-confidence calibration** condition, define $C=\max_jG_j$ and $\widehat Y=\min\{j:G_j=C\}$, so ties go to the smallest label. The forecast is top-confidence calibrated if for every Borel set $B\subseteq[0,1]$,
$$\mathbb P(Y=\widehat Y,\ C\in B)=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_{\{C\in B\}}C].$$
A measurable function $r:\Delta_K\to\Delta_K$ is a **calibration function** for $G$ if for every $j$ and every Borel set $B\subseteq\Delta_K$,
$$\mathbb P(Y=j,\ G\in B)=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_{\{G\in B\}}r_j(G)].$$
When such a function is supplied and $d:\Delta_K\times\Delta_K\to[0,+\infty)$ is measurable, the **expected calibration error with discrepancy $d$** is $\eta_d=\mathbb E[d(r(G),G)]$.

Let $Y$ be a random variable into $\{1,\ldots,K\}$ with its full power-set sigma-algebra, $K\ge2$, and let $G\in\Delta_K$ be a random forecast with measurable calibration function $r:\Delta_K\to\Delta_K$. Let $d:\Delta_K\times\Delta_K\to[0,\infty)$ be continuous and satisfy $d(p,p)=0$. For a finite data-independent Borel partition $\mathcal P$ of $\Delta_K$, draw an iid sequence $(G_i,Y_i)$ from the joint law of $(G,Y)$, let $V_i=e_{Y_i}$ be the corresponding standard basis vector, and form the empirical estimator
$$\widehat E_{n,\mathcal P}=\sum_{B\in\mathcal P}\frac{N_B}{n}\,d(\bar V_B,\bar G_B),$$
where $N_B=\#\{i\le n:G_i\in B\}$ and, when $N_B>0$, $\bar V_B$ and $\bar G_B$ are the sample averages in bin $B$; when $N_B=0$, set both to any fixed $q_0\in\Delta_K$. Define
$$E_{\mathcal P}=\sum_{B\in\mathcal P:P(G\in B)>0}P(G\in B)\,d\!\left(\mathbb E[r(G)\mid G\in B],\mathbb E[G\mid G\in B]\right).$$
For each fixed $\mathcal P$, $\widehat E_{n,\mathcal P}\to E_{\mathcal P}$ almost surely. If $d$ is additionally jointly convex, then $E_{\mathcal P}\le\mathbb E[d(r(G),G)]$. Without requiring convexity, if $\mathcal P_m$ is a sequence of finite data-independent Borel partitions whose mesh $\max_{B\in\mathcal P_m}\operatorname{diam}_2(B)$ tends to zero, where $\operatorname{diam}_2(B)=\sup_{u,v\in B}\|u-v\|_2$, and $r$ is Lipschitz with respect to the Euclidean metric on $\Delta_K$, then $E_{\mathcal P_m}\to\mathbb E[d(r(G),G)]$. Thus the iterated limit $\lim_{m\to\infty}\lim_{n\to\infty}\widehat E_{n,\mathcal P_m}$ equals the expected calibration error almost surely; no diagonal rate is asserted.
For IID real $(X_n)_{n\ge1}$ with $\mathbb E|X_1|<\infty$, $S_n/n\to\mu=\mathbb EX_1$ almost surely.

derivations.claim: For any randomized test, its average error is at least $\bigl(1-\operatorname{TV}(P_-^k,P_+^k)\bigr)/2$: writing the two error expectations over the common finite sample space gives $e_k(\psi)=\frac12\left(1-\sum_\omega\psi(\omega)(P_+^k(\omega)-P_-^k(\omega))\right)$. Each $\psi(\omega)\in[0,1]$ makes the signed sum at most the sum of the positive differences; these differences sum to $\frac12\sum_\omega|P_+^k(\omega)-P_-^k(\omega)|$ because their total signed sum is zero. This is $\operatorname{TV}(P_-^k,P_+^k)$ by the definition in the statement.

For any finite laws $Q,R$, write $|Q(\omega)-R(\omega)|=|\sqrt Q-\sqrt R|(\sqrt Q+\sqrt R)$. The finite Cauchy–Schwarz inequality follows by expanding $\sum_i(a_i-\lambda b_i)^2\ge0$ with $\lambda=(\sum_i a_i b_i)/(\sum_i b_i^2)$ when the denominator is positive, and is immediate when it is zero. Apply it to $a_\omega=|\sqrt{Q(\omega)}-\sqrt{R(\omega)}|$ and $b_\omega=\sqrt{Q(\omega)}+\sqrt{R(\omega)}$ to obtain $\operatorname{TV}(Q,R)^2\le\frac14\left(\sum_\omega(\sqrt Q-\sqrt R)^2\right)\left(\sum_\omega(\sqrt Q+\sqrt R)^2\right)=1-\operatorname{aff}(Q,R)^2$. Thus $e_k(\psi)\ge\frac12(1-\sqrt{1-\operatorname{aff}(P_-^k,P_+^k)^2})$.

The single-observation affinity is $2\sqrt{(1-u^2)/4}=\sqrt{1-u^2}$. Finite product distributivity makes the $k$-observation affinity its $k$th power, $(1-u^2)^{k/2}$; substituting gives the first displayed lower bound.

For $0\le x<1$, $g(x)=\log(1-x)+x/(1-x)$ satisfies $g(0)=0$ and $g'(x)=x/(1-x)^2\ge0$, so $(1-u^2)^k\ge\exp(-ku^2/(1-u^2))$. Since $2\lceil k/2\rceil\ge k$, the exponential with exponent $-ku^2/(1-u^2)$ is at least the one with exponent $-2\lceil k/2\rceil u^2/(1-u^2)$. The map $s\mapsto1-\sqrt{1-s}$ is increasing on $[0,1]$, so the first lower bound is at least $2\Phi(2\lceil k/2\rceil,u)$.
With no observations the test's decision distribution is the same under both signs, so its equal-prior error is $\frac12(q+(1-q))=\frac12$ for its probability $q$ of deciding $+$.

derivations.claim: Splitting the expectation on $\{Z\le t\}$ and $\{Z>t\}$ and using $Z\le t$ on the first event and $Z\le1$ on the second gives $\mathbb E Z\le t\Pr\{Z\le t\}+\Pr\{Z>t\}=t+(1-t)\Pr\{Z>t\}$.

Let $(\mathcal X,\Sigma)$ be a measurable instance space and let $\mathcal H$ be a nonempty class of measurable functions $h:\mathcal X\to\{0,1\}$. Give $\{0,1\}$ its full power-set sigma-algebra; all joint and sample spaces below carry the corresponding product sigma-algebras. For a finite set of distinct points $T=\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}$, its indexed trace family is
$$\mathcal F_{\mathcal H,T}:=\left\{\{j\in[n]:h(x_j)=1\}:h\in\mathcal H\right\}\subseteq\mathcal P([n]).$$
The set $T$ is shattered by $\mathcal H$ when $\mathcal F_{\mathcal H,T}=\mathcal P([n])$, and $\operatorname{VCdim}(\mathcal H)$ is the supremum of the integers $n\ge0$ for which some $n$ distinct points are shattered; the value is $+\infty$ if these integers are unbounded. This definition is independent of the chosen ordering of $T$, since a reordering bijects the index sets and all their subsets.

For a probability law $D$ on $\mathcal X\times\{0,1\}$, the zero-one risk of a measurable binary predictor $g$ is $R_D(g):=D\{(x,y):g(x)\ne y\}\in[0,1]$, and the class benchmark is $R_D^*(\mathcal H):=\inf_{h\in\mathcal H}R_D(h)\in[0,1]$. The class excess risk of $g\in\mathcal H$ is $\Delta_D(g):=R_D(g)-R_D^*(\mathcal H)\in[0,1]$; no attainment of the infimum is asserted. A law $D$ is realizable by $\mathcal H$ when there is an $f\in\mathcal H$ with $D\{(x,y):y=f(x)\}=1$. For such a pair $(D,f)$, define its target risk by $R_D(g,f):=D_X\{x:g(x)\ne f(x)\}$, where $D_X:=D\circ\pi_X^{-1}$ is the instance marginal under the projection $\pi_X(x,y)=x$. On the probability-one event $Y=f(X)$, the indicators of $g(X)\ne Y$ and $g(X)\ne f(X)$ agree; hence $R_D(g)=R_D(g,f)$ for every measurable binary $g$, and $R_D^*(\mathcal H)=0$.

Let $\mathcal D$ be the class of all probability laws on $\mathcal X\times\{0,1\}$, and let $\mathcal D_{\rm real}(\mathcal H):=\{D\in\mathcal D:\text{there is }f\in\mathcal H\text{ with }D\{(x,y):y=f(x)\}=1\}$. For integer $m\ge1$, an admissible possibly randomized learner $A$ is a rule that depends on $\mathcal H$ and $m$, not on $D$. Its seed space and law are fixed as part of $A$, independently of $D$: a probability space $(\Omega_A,\mathscr F_A,\nu_A)$ and a seed $U\sim\nu_A$ independent of the sample. Given an ordered sample $S\in(\mathcal X\times\{0,1\})^m$, $A(S,U)$ outputs a measurable member of $\mathcal H$. For every fixed $x\in\mathcal X$, the evaluation $(S,U)\mapsto A(S,U)(x)$ must be measurable on $\big((\mathcal X\times\{0,1\})^m\times\Omega_A,(\Sigma\otimes2^{\{0,1\}})^{\otimes m}\otimes\mathscr F_A\big)$, and for every $D\in\mathcal D$ the risk $R_D(A(S,U))$ must be measurable as a function of the sample and seed. The sample law $D^m$ is the $m$-fold product law, so its coordinates are independent and each has law $D$. Probabilities and expectations involving $A$ use the product law $D^m\otimes\nu_A$. Let $\mathcal A_m(\mathcal H)$ denote this class of learners, and write $A(S)$ for $A(S,U)$ when the random seed is suppressed. These measurability conditions make each displayed expectation and probability well defined. Define the expected minimax excess risks by
$$\mathfrak M_{\rm real}(m,\mathcal H):=\inf_{A\in\mathcal A_m(\mathcal H)}\sup_{D\in\mathcal D_{\rm real}(\mathcal H)}\mathbb E_{S\sim D^m,A}R_D(A(S)),$$
$$\mathfrak M_{\rm agn}(m,\mathcal H):=\inf_{A\in\mathcal A_m(\mathcal H)}\sup_{D\in\mathcal D}\mathbb E_{S\sim D^m,A}\left[R_D(A(S))-R_D^*(\mathcal H)\right].$$
For a tolerance $\eta\ge0$, their high-probability tail versions are
$$\mathfrak T_{\rm real}(m,\mathcal H,\eta):=\inf_{A\in\mathcal A_m(\mathcal H)}\sup_{D\in\mathcal D_{\rm real}(\mathcal H)}\Pr_{S\sim D^m,A}\{R_D(A(S))>\eta\},$$
$$\mathfrak T_{\rm agn}(m,\mathcal H,\eta):=\inf_{A\in\mathcal A_m(\mathcal H)}\sup_{D\in\mathcal D}\Pr_{S\sim D^m,A}\{R_D(A(S))-R_D^*(\mathcal H)>\eta\}.$$
The lower bounds below are high-probability statements; their expectation consequences follow by integrating the nonnegative excess risk.

Let $\mathcal{F}\subseteq\mathcal{P}([n])$ and let $T\subseteq[n]$.

The **trace** of $\mathcal{F}$ on $T$ is

$$\mathcal{F}\vert_T:=\{\,F\cap T:F\in\mathcal{F}\,\}.$$

The family $\mathcal{F}$ **shatters** $T$ when

$$\mathcal{F}\vert_T=\mathcal{P}(T).$$

The **VC dimension** of $\mathcal{F}$ is the greatest integer $d\ge0$ such that
some subset $T\subseteq[n]$ with $\lvert T\rvert=d$ is shattered. For the empty
family we set $\operatorname{VC}(\varnothing):=0$ by convention.

This maximum is well defined: every shattered set is a subset of the finite set
$[n]$, so its size lies in $\{0,\dots,n\}$, and for any nonempty family the empty
set is shattered because every trace on $\varnothing$ is $\varnothing$.

On any probability space, if a random variable $Z$ satisfies $0\le Z\le1$ almost surely and $0\le t<1$, then
$$\Pr\{Z>t\}\ge\frac{\mathbb E Z-t}{1-t}.$$

derivations.claim: Since $d$ is the finite VC dimension, choose distinct $x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_{d-1}$ shattered by $\mathcal H$. For each of the finitely many label vectors $\theta\in\{0,1\}^d$, shattering supplies a target $f_\theta\in\mathcal H$ with those labels on these points; finite choice suffices for this finite family. Put $\epsilon=(d-1)/(32m)$ and define the finite mixture $\mu=(1-8\epsilon)\delta_{x_0}+\sum_{i=1}^{d-1}\frac{8\epsilon}{d-1}\delta_{x_i}$. The range on $m$ gives $8\epsilon=(d-1)/(4m)\le1$, so all mixture weights are nonnegative and sum to one. For each $\theta$, let $D_\theta$ be the law of $(X,f_\theta(X))$ for $X\sim\mu$.

Let $M$ count sample positions drawn from the rare atoms $x_1,\ldots,x_{d-1}$. Then $M\sim\operatorname{Bin}(m,8\epsilon)$ and $\mu_0:=\mathbb EM=(d-1)/4\ge1/4$. Since $e^p=\sum_{j=0}^\infty p^j/j!\ge1+p$ for $p\ge0$, $\mathbb E2^M=(1+8\epsilon)^m\le e^{\mu_0}$. For any nonnegative random variable $X$ and $b>0$, $\mathbb EX\ge b\Pr\{X\ge b\}$ because $X\ge b\mathbf1_{\{X\ge b\}}$; apply this to $X=2^M$ and $b=2^{2\mu_0}$. On $\{M\ge2\mu_0\}$, $2^M\ge2^{2\mu_0}$, hence $\Pr\{M\ge2\mu_0\}\le e^{\mu_0-2\mu_0\log2}\le e^{-\mu_0/3}$, where $\log2\ge2/3$ because $g(x)=\log x-2(x-1)/(x+1)$ has $g(1)=0$ and $g'(x)=(x-1)^2/(x(x+1)^2)\ge0$ for $x\ge1$. Since $2\mu_0=(d-1)/2$, $\Pr\{M\le(d-1)/2\}\ge1-e^{-\mu_0/3}\ge1-e^{-1/12}\ge1/13$; the last inequality follows from $e^{1/12}\ge1+1/12=13/12$.

Fix any vector of sample atom indices and observed labels for which $M\le(d-1)/2$. At least $(d-1)/2$ rare atoms were not observed. Under the uniform prior on $\theta$, each unseen label $\theta_i$ is still an independent fair bit, independent of the learner's output at $x_i$, because the learner depends only on the observed sample and independent internal randomness. Therefore, if $W$ is the learner's risk contribution from $x_1,\ldots,x_{d-1}$, then $\mathbb E_{\theta,A}[W\mid\text{observed data}]\ge\frac12\frac{d-1}{2}\frac{8\epsilon}{d-1}=2\epsilon$, while $0\le W\le8\epsilon$. Applying [F2] to $W/(8\epsilon)$ at $t=1/8$ yields $\Pr_{\theta,A}\{W>\epsilon\mid\text{observed data}\}\ge1/7$.

Each $D_\theta$ is realizable by $f_\theta$, so [F4] gives $R_{D_\theta}^*(\mathcal H)=0$. By [F3] and the event $Y=f_\theta(X)$ of probability one, the zero-one risk and target risk of the learner's output agree. The full target risk is at least $W$. Averaging step 1.3 over sample locations and labels, then using step 1.2, gives $\Pr_{\theta,S\sim D_\theta^m,A}\{R_{D_\theta}(A(S),f_\theta)>\epsilon\}\ge\frac1{7}\cdot\frac1{13}=\frac1{91}>\frac1{100}$. This is an average over the finite set $\{0,1\}^d$, so at least one $\theta$ has conditional failure probability at least $1/91$. Its $D_\theta$ and $f_\theta$ satisfy the statement.

Let $\mathcal{F}\subseteq\mathcal{P}([n])$ and let $T\subseteq[n]$.

The **trace** of $\mathcal{F}$ on $T$ is

$$\mathcal{F}\vert_T:=\{\,F\cap T:F\in\mathcal{F}\,\}.$$

The family $\mathcal{F}$ **shatters** $T$ when

$$\mathcal{F}\vert_T=\mathcal{P}(T).$$

The **VC dimension** of $\mathcal{F}$ is the greatest integer $d\ge0$ such that
some subset $T\subseteq[n]$ with $\lvert T\rvert=d$ is shattered. For the empty
family we set $\operatorname{VC}(\varnothing):=0$ by convention.

On any probability space, if a random variable $Z$ satisfies $0\le Z\le1$ almost surely and $0\le t<1$, then

Let $(\mathcal X,\Sigma)$ be a measurable instance space and let $\mathcal H$ be a nonempty class of measurable functions $h:\mathcal X\to\{0,1\}$. $$\mathcal F_{\mathcal H,T}:=\left\{\{j\in[n]:h(x_j)=1\}:h\in\mathcal H\right\}\subseteq\mathcal P([n]).$$
The set $T$ is shattered by $\mathcal H$ when $\mathcal F_{\mathcal H,T}=\mathcal P([n])$, and $\operatorname{VCdim}(\mathcal H)$ is the supremum of the integers $n\ge0$ for which some $n$ distinct points are shattered; the value is $+\infty$ if these integers are unbounded. This definition is independent of the chosen ordering of $T$, since a reordering bijects the index sets and all their subsets.

On the probability-one event $Y=f(X)$, the indicators of $g(X)\ne Y$ and $g(X)\ne f(X)$ agree; hence $R_D(g)=R_D(g,f)$ for every measurable binary $g$, and $R_D^*(\mathcal H)=0$.

$$\mathfrak M_{\rm real}(m,\mathcal H):=\inf_{A\in\mathcal A_m(\mathcal H)}\sup_{D\in\mathcal D_{\rm real}(\mathcal H)}\mathbb E_{S\sim D^m,A}R_D(A(S)),$$
$$\mathfrak M_{\rm agn}(m,\mathcal H):=\inf_{A\in\mathcal A_m(\mathcal H)}\sup_{D\in\mathcal D}\mathbb E_{S\sim D^m,A}\left[R_D(A(S))-R_D^*(\mathcal H)\right].$$

derivations.claim: For a nonnegative random variable $X$ and $t\ge0$, $X\ge t\mathbf1_{\{X>t\}}$ pointwise, so $\mathbb EX\ge t\Pr\{X>t\}$. For each learner, [F1] supplies a realizable law with target risk exceeding $(d-1)/(32m)$ with probability at least $1/100$; since the supremum over realizable laws is at least this expectation, [F3] gives $\mathfrak M_{\rm real}\ge\frac1{100}\frac{d-1}{32m}=\frac{d-1}{3200m}\ge\frac{d}{6400m}$ because $d-1\ge d/2$. Likewise [F2], nonnegativity in [F5], and the supremum over all laws in [F4] give $\mathfrak M_{\rm agn}\ge\frac1{64}\sqrt{d/(320m)}$.

If $m<(d-1)/(32\eta)$ then $(d-1)/(32m)>\eta$, so the event in [F1] is contained in the event of error exceeding $\eta$. Its probability is at least $1/100>\delta$. If $m<d/(320\eta^2)$ then $\sqrt{d/(320m)}>\eta$, so [F2] similarly gives failure probability at least $1/64>\delta$. For $0<u<1$, let $P_-$ and $P_+$ be the Bernoulli laws on $\{0,1\}$ with success probabilities $(1-u)/2$ and $(1+u)/2$. For an integer $k\ge1$, a randomized test is a function $\psi:\{0,1\}^k\to[0,1]$, interpreted as the probability of deciding $+$. Its equal-prior average error is
$$e_k(\psi):=\frac12\left(E_{P_-^k}\psi+E_{P_+^k}(1-\psi)\right).$$
For finite probability laws $Q,R$ on a common finite set, define $\operatorname{aff}(Q,R):=\sum_\omega\sqrt{Q(\omega)R(\omega)}$ and $\operatorname{TV}(Q,R):=\frac12\sum_\omega|Q(\omega)-R(\omega)|$. Set
$$\Phi(t,u):=\frac14\left(1-\sqrt{1-\exp\left(-\frac{tu^2}{1-u^2}\right)}\right)\qquad(t\ge0).$$
Then every such test satisfies
$$e_k(\psi)\ge\frac12\left(1-\sqrt{1-(1-u^2)^k}\right)\ge2\Phi(2\lceil k/2\rceil,u).$$
With no observations ($k=0$), every equal-prior test has average error exactly $1/2$.

Let $(\mathcal X,\Sigma)$ be a measurable instance space and let $\mathcal H$ be a nonempty class of measurable functions $h:\mathcal X\to\{0,1\}$. Give $\{0,1\}$ its full power-set sigma-algebra; all joint and sample spaces below carry the corresponding product sigma-algebras. For a finite set of distinct points $T=\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}$, its indexed trace family is
$$\mathcal F_{\mathcal H,T}:=\left\{\{j\in[n]:h(x_j)=1\}:h\in\mathcal H\right\}\subseteq\mathcal P([n]).$$
The set $T$ is shattered by $\mathcal H$ when $\mathcal F_{\mathcal H,T}=\mathcal P([n])$, and $\operatorname{VCdim}(\mathcal H)$ is the supremum of the integers $n\ge0$ for which some $n$ distinct points are shattered; the value is $+\infty$ if these integers are unbounded. This definition is independent of the chosen ordering of $T$, since a reordering bijects the index sets and all their subsets.

For a probability law $D$ on $\mathcal X\times\{0,1\}$, the zero-one risk of a measurable binary predictor $g$ is $R_D(g):=D\{(x,y):g(x)\ne y\}\in[0,1]$, and the class benchmark is $R_D^*(\mathcal H):=\inf_{h\in\mathcal H}R_D(h)\in[0,1]$. The class excess risk of $g\in\mathcal H$ is $\Delta_D(g):=R_D(g)-R_D^*(\mathcal H)\in[0,1]$; no attainment of the infimum is asserted. A law $D$ is realizable by $\mathcal H$ when there is an $f\in\mathcal H$ with $D\{(x,y):y=f(x)\}=1$. For such a pair $(D,f)$, define its target risk by $R_D(g,f):=D_X\{x:g(x)\ne f(x)\}$, where $D_X:=D\circ\pi_X^{-1}$ is the instance marginal under the projection $\pi_X(x,y)=x$. On the probability-one event $Y=f(X)$, the indicators of $g(X)\ne Y$ and $g(X)\ne f(X)$ agree; hence $R_D(g)=R_D(g,f)$ for every measurable binary $g$, and $R_D^*(\mathcal H)=0$.

Let $\mathcal D$ be the class of all probability laws on $\mathcal X\times\{0,1\}$, and let $\mathcal D_{\rm real}(\mathcal H):=\{D\in\mathcal D:\text{there is }f\in\mathcal H\text{ with }D\{(x,y):y=f(x)\}=1\}$. For integer $m\ge1$, an admissible possibly randomized learner $A$ is a rule that depends on $\mathcal H$ and $m$, not on $D$. Its seed space and law are fixed as part of $A$, independently of $D$: a probability space $(\Omega_A,\mathscr F_A,\nu_A)$ and a seed $U\sim\nu_A$ independent of the sample. Given an ordered sample $S\in(\mathcal X\times\{0,1\})^m$, $A(S,U)$ outputs a measurable member of $\mathcal H$. For every fixed $x\in\mathcal X$, the evaluation $(S,U)\mapsto A(S,U)(x)$ must be measurable on $\big((\mathcal X\times\{0,1\})^m\times\Omega_A,(\Sigma\otimes2^{\{0,1\}})^{\otimes m}\otimes\mathscr F_A\big)$, and for every $D\in\mathcal D$ the risk $R_D(A(S,U))$ must be measurable as a function of the sample and seed. The sample law $D^m$ is the $m$-fold product law, so its coordinates are independent and each has law $D$. Probabilities and expectations involving $A$ use the product law $D^m\otimes\nu_A$. Let $\mathcal A_m(\mathcal H)$ denote this class of learners, and write $A(S)$ for $A(S,U)$ when the random seed is suppressed. These measurability conditions make each displayed expectation and probability well defined. Define the expected minimax excess risks by
$$\mathfrak M_{\rm real}(m,\mathcal H):=\inf_{A\in\mathcal A_m(\mathcal H)}\sup_{D\in\mathcal D_{\rm real}(\mathcal H)}\mathbb E_{S\sim D^m,A}R_D(A(S)),$$
$$\mathfrak M_{\rm agn}(m,\mathcal H):=\inf_{A\in\mathcal A_m(\mathcal H)}\sup_{D\in\mathcal D}\mathbb E_{S\sim D^m,A}\left[R_D(A(S))-R_D^*(\mathcal H)\right].$$
For a tolerance $\eta\ge0$, their high-probability tail versions are
$$\mathfrak T_{\rm real}(m,\mathcal H,\eta):=\inf_{A\in\mathcal A_m(\mathcal H)}\sup_{D\in\mathcal D_{\rm real}(\mathcal H)}\Pr_{S\sim D^m,A}\{R_D(A(S))>\eta\},$$
$$\mathfrak T_{\rm agn}(m,\mathcal H,\eta):=\inf_{A\in\mathcal A_m(\mathcal H)}\sup_{D\in\mathcal D}\Pr_{S\sim D^m,A}\{R_D(A(S))-R_D^*(\mathcal H)>\eta\}.$$
The lower bounds below are high-probability statements; their expectation consequences follow by integrating the nonnegative excess risk.

The family $\mathcal{F}$ **shatters** $T$ when

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$, $(\mathsf Y,\Sigma_Y)$, and $(\mathsf A,\Sigma_A)$ be nonempty measurable spaces. A **source/target pair of joint laws** consists of probability measures $P_S$ and $P_T$ on $(\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y,\Sigma_X\otimes\Sigma_Y)$. For $D\in\{S,T\}$, its input marginal is the probability measure $\mu_D$ on $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$ defined by $\mu_D(A)=P_D(A\times\mathsf Y)$. If $h:\mathsf X\to\mathsf A$ is measurable and $\ell:\mathsf A\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty]$ is product-measurable, then $(x,y)\mapsto(h(x),y)$ is measurable: the preimage of a measurable rectangle $U\times V$ is $h^{-1}(U)\times V$, and such rectangles generate the product sigma-algebra. Taking preimages once more shows that $(x,y)\mapsto\ell(h(x),y)$ is measurable. The domain risk is the extended nonnegative integral
$$R_D(h):=\int_{\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y}\ell(h(x),y)\,P_D(d(x,y)).$$

A **conditional label kernel** for $P_D$ is a specified probability kernel $K_D$ from $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$ to $(\mathsf Y,\Sigma_Y)$ such that, for every nonnegative product-measurable $g:\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty]$,
$$\int g(x,y)\,P_D(d(x,y))=\int_{\mathsf X}\left(\int_{\mathsf Y}g(x,y)\,K_D(x,dy)\right)\mu_D(dx).$$
The pair is under **covariate shift** when conditional label kernels $K_S,K_T$ are supplied, there is a measurable set $N$ with $\mu_T(N)=0$ such that $K_S(x,\cdot)=K_T(x,\cdot)$ as probability measures for every $x\notin N$, and $\mu_T\ll\mu_S$. No existence of conditional kernels is asserted by this definition.

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be dominated by the fixed sigma-finite positive measure $\mu$. For each
$\theta$, the Radon–Nikodym theorem gives the almost-everywhere class
$dP_\theta/d\mu$; a sigma-finite exhaustion for $\mu$ is also finite for the
probability measure $P_\theta$. Under AC, select simultaneously a
finite-valued measurable nonnegative representative $p_\theta$ from each
class. The nonnegative version exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].

For fixed observed $x\in\mathcal X$, the function
$$L_x:\Theta\to[0,+\infty),\qquad L_x(\theta):=p_\theta(x),$$
is the **likelihood at $x$**. This is a function on the parameter labels, not
a probability distribution on $\Theta$. No sigma-algebra on $\Theta$ or
measurability of $L_x$ is implied. Each density is determined only
$\mu$-almost everywhere; there is no canonical pointwise version and, for
arbitrary uncountable $\Theta$, no common exceptional null set is asserted.

Let $P_0$ and $P_1$ be probability measures on the same measurable space.
Assume AC. Their Lebesgue decomposition relative to $P_0$ is the unique
decomposition
$P_1=P_{1,\mathrm{ac}}+P_{1,\mathrm{s}}$ with
$P_{1,\mathrm{ac}}\ll P_0$ and $P_{1,\mathrm{s}}\perp P_0$
([[thm-lebesgue-decomposition-exists-for-sigma-finite-signed-measures]],
[[thm-lebesgue-decomposition-is-unique-for-sigma-finite-signed-measures]]).
Both components are positive by
[[lem-positive-lebesgue-components-of-a-positive-measure]], and
$P_{1,\mathrm{ac}}$ is finite because their sum has mass one. Define the
**likelihood-ratio density** of $P_1$ against $P_0$ to be the
$P_0$-almost-everywhere class
$$
\frac{dP_{1,\mathrm{ac}}}{dP_0}
$$
of [[def-radon-nikodym-derivative]]. Under AC this class has a nonnegative
measurable representative by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].

This is a full density of $P_1$ with respect to $P_0$ only in the
absolutely continuous case $P_1\ll P_0$. If that condition fails, the
singular component remains separate. A displayed representative is not a
canonical pointwise function: its values are determined only
$P_0$-almost everywhere.

Assume AC and let $P_0,P_1$ be probability measures on one measurable space.
Let $r$ be a nonnegative measurable representative of the likelihood-ratio
class for $P_1$ versus $P_0$. If $P_1\ll P_0$, then
$$
E_{P_0}[g r]=E_{P_1}[g]
$$
for every nonnegative measurable $g$, and also for every real-valued
$P_1$-integrable measurable $g$. Here $E_{P_i}[h]$ means
$\int h\,dP_i$. Without $P_1\ll P_0$, this identity need not hold because the
singular component may be nonzero.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. The **measure with density $f$ relative
to $\mu$** is the measure
$$f\,d\mu:\mathcal A\to[0,+\infty],\qquad (f\,d\mu)(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu,$$
whose measure property is supplied by
The indefinite integral of a nonnegative measurable function is a measure.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
(Measurable spaces and measurable sets). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

1. If $f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ are measurable and $f+g$ is defined
   pointwise, then $f+g$ is measurable.
2. If $c\in\mathbb R$ and $f:X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, then $cf$ is
   measurable.
3. If $f:X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, then $f^+=\max\{f,0\}$,
   $f^-=\max\{-f,0\}$, and $|f|=f^++f^-$ are measurable.
4. If $E\in\mathcal A$ and $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, then
   $f\chi_E$ is measurable, where this function equals $f$ on $E$ and $0$
   off $E$ (in particular, $0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ here).
5. If $(f_n)$ is a sequence of measurable functions $X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$,
   then $\inf_n f_n$ is measurable; if moreover $f_n\uparrow f$ pointwise, then
   $f$ is measurable.

Let $X$ be a set. A **pi-system on $X$** is a nonempty family
$\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal P(X)$ closed under binary intersections: if
$A,B\in\mathcal P$, then $A\cap B\in\mathcal P$.

The nonempty-family requirement is the convention used here. It does not require
$X\in\mathcal P$ and it does not add an empty-intersection axiom.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
Measurable rectangles in a product of measurable spaces.

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$ and let $\mathcal A=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. If finite measures $\mu$ and $
u$ on $(X,\mathcal A)$ agree on $\mathcal P$ and satisfy $\mu(X)=
u(X)$, then $\mu=
u$ on $\mathcal A$.

The total-mass equality is separate because this library's pi-system convention does not require $X\in\mathcal P$.

Let $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$, $(\mathsf Y,\Sigma_Y)$, and $(\mathsf A,\Sigma_A)$ be nonempty measurable spaces. A **source/target pair of joint laws** consists of probability measures $P_S$ and $P_T$ on $(\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y,\Sigma_X\otimes\Sigma_Y)$. For $D\in\{S,T\}$, its input marginal is the probability measure $\mu_D$ on $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$ defined by $\mu_D(A)=P_D(A\times\mathsf Y)$. Taking preimages once more shows that $(x,y)\mapsto\ell(h(x),y)$ is measurable. The domain risk is the extended nonnegative integral

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in Measures on sigma-algebras and A measurable function between measurable spaces; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in Measures on sigma-algebras and A measurable function between measurable spaces; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $E$ be measurable with $\mu(E)=0$.
Then
$$\int_E f\,d\mu=0.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

u_0:=(w_0\circ\pi_X)\,dP_S$; [F4] makes $
u_0$ a measure. Since $K_S(x,\mathsf Y)=1$ by [F11], [F1] and [F13] give $
u_0(\mathsf X	imes\mathsf Y)=\int w_0\,d\mu_S$. Applying [F3] to $q=1$ yields $\int w_0\,d\mu_S=\int 1\,d\mu_T=1$. Thus $
u_0$ and $P_T$ are finite measures of equal total mass.

For $A\in\Sigma_X$ and $B\in\Sigma_Y$, the function $g(x,y)=\mathbf1_{A\times B}(x,y)w_0(x)$ is nonnegative and product-measurable by [F5]–[F7]. By [F10], $x\mapsto K_S(x,B)$ is measurable, and by [F6] the function $q(x)=\mathbf1_A(x)K_S(x,B)$ is measurable. Since $w_0(x)$ is finite, [F13] pulls this scalar through the section integral in [F1]. Applying [F3] to $q$ gives
$$\nu_0(A\times B)=\int_A w_0(x)K_S(x,B)\,\mu_S(dx)=\int_A K_S(x,B)\,\mu_T(dx)=\int_A K_T(x,B)\,\mu_T(dx)=P_T(A\times B).$$
The middle equality uses the $\mu_T$-almost-everywhere equality of the specified kernels, and the last equality uses their target disintegration [F1].

The measurable rectangles form the generating $\pi$-system in [F7], so [F8] and steps 1.1–1.2 give $\nu_0=P_T$ on the entire product sigma-algebra. Since [F2] identifies $w_0$ as a representative of $d\mu_T/d\mu_S$, the setwise equality makes $w_0\circ\pi_X$ a Radon–Nikodym representative of $P_T$ with respect to $P_S$.

Let $w$ be the arbitrary representative in the Statement. The same preimage argument as in step 1.1, using [F5] and [F7], shows $w\circ\pi_X$ is measurable. By [F2], there is a measurable $N\in\Sigma_X$ with $\mu_S(N)=0$ outside of which $w=w_0$. By [F14], $P_S(N\times\mathsf Y)=0$. For each $D\in\{S,T\}$, the given measurable spaces, joint law $P_D$, measurable predictor $h$, and product-measurable loss $\ell$ form a supervised prediction problem with predictor class $\{h\}$. For $D\in\{S,T\}$, its input marginal is the probability measure $\mu_D$ on $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$ defined by $\mu_D(A)=P_D(A\times\mathsf Y)$. If $h:\mathsf X\to\mathsf A$ is measurable and $\ell:\mathsf A\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty]$ is product-measurable, then $(x,y)\mapsto(h(x),y)$ is measurable: the preimage of a measurable rectangle $U\times V$ is $h^{-1}(U)\times V$, and such rectangles generate the product sigma-algebra. $$\int g(x,y)\,P_D(d(x,y))=\int_{\mathsf X}\left(\int_{\mathsf Y}g(x,y)\,K_D(x,dy)\right)\mu_D(dx).$$

$$A_{h,h'}:=\bigl(h^{-1}(\{0\})\cap h'^{-1}(\{1\})\bigr)\cup\bigl(h^{-1}(\{1\})\cap h'^{-1}(\{0\})\bigr).$$
The **$\mathcal H\Delta\mathcal H$ divergence** of the two input laws is
$$d_{\mathcal H\Delta\mathcal H}(\mu_S,\mu_T):=2\sup_{h,h'\in\mathcal H}\left|\mu_S(A_{h,h'})-\mu_T(A_{h,h'})\right|\in[0,2].$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $d,n\ge1$ be integers, let $\sigma>0$, let $\theta\in\mathbb R^d$ satisfy $\|\theta\|_2=\sqrt d$, and draw independent observations $(X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^n$ from the two-class spherical Gaussian model with parameters $\theta,\sigma$. Put $W=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nY_iX_i$, and define $\widehat W=W/\|W\|_2$ when $W\ne0$ and $\widehat W=e_1$ when $W=0$. Then
$$\mathbb P\!\left(\langle\widehat W,\theta\rangle\le\frac{2\sqrt n-1}{2\sqrt n+4\sigma}\sqrt d\right)\le2\exp\!\left(-\frac{d}{8(\sigma^2+1)}\right).$$

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume AC. If $X$ has law $N(m,\sigma^2)$ with $\sigma\ge0$, then $\varphi_X(t)=\exp(imt-\sigma^2t^2/2)$ for every real $t$. Moreover $\mathbb EX=m$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\sigma^2$, including $\sigma=0$.

For real $a,b,t$, $\varphi_{aX+b}(t)=e^{itb}\varphi_X(at)$. For a finite mutually independent family $(X_j)_{j=1}^n$ of real random variables, $\varphi_{\sum_jX_j}(t)=\prod_j\varphi_{X_j}(t)$. The empty sum has characteristic function one.

Assume AC. Two Borel probability laws on $\mathbb R$ with equal characteristic functions are equal. In particular a real random variable has a real-valued characteristic function if and only if its law is symmetric under $x\mapsto-x$.

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$ be an integer, $\sigma>0$, and $G\sim N_d(0,\sigma^2I_d)$. For every $t\ge0$ and $s\ge0$,
$$\mathbb P(\|G\|_2\ge \sigma\sqrt d+t)\le \exp\!\left(-\frac{t^2}{2\sigma^2}\right),\qquad \mathbb P(\|G\|_\infty>s)\le 2d\exp\!\left(-\frac{s^2}{2\sigma^2}\right).$$
For every unit vector $u\in\mathbb R^d$ and $s\ge0$, each one-sided projection tail satisfies
$$\mathbb P(\langle u,G\rangle\ge s)\le \exp\!\left(-\frac{s^2}{2\sigma^2}\right),\qquad \mathbb P(\langle u,G\rangle\le-s)\le \exp\!\left(-\frac{s^2}{2\sigma^2}\right).$$
Consequently, for $d\ge2$,
$$\mathbb P\!\left(\|G\|_\infty\le 2\sigma\sqrt{2\log d}\right)\ge1-\frac1d.$$

Assume AC. If $X$ has law $N(m,\sigma^2)$ with $\sigma\ge0$, then $\varphi_X(t)=\exp(imt-\sigma^2t^2/2)$ for every real $t$. Moreover $\mathbb EX=m$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\sigma^2$, including $\sigma=0$.

Assume AC. Two Borel probability laws on $\mathbb R$ with equal characteristic functions are equal. In particular a real random variable has a real-valued characteristic function if and only if its law is symmetric under $x\mapsto-x$.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because The exponential is a continuous bijection from $\mathbb{R}$ onto $(0,\infty)$ states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in The Euclidean inner product $\langle x,y\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k y_k$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Then:

   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   (A norm on a real vector space, the induced metric, and the dictionary with the metric axioms), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

Let $(\mathcal X,\Sigma_X)$ and $(\mathcal Y,\Sigma_Y)$ be measurable spaces, let $\mathcal A$ be a measurable action space, and let $P$ be a probability measure on $(\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y,\Sigma_X\otimes\Sigma_Y)$. A threat correspondence is a map $\Delta:\mathcal X\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X)$ with $\Delta(x)\ne\varnothing$ for every $x$. It is measurable when its graph $\{(x,x')\in\mathcal X^2:x'\in\Delta(x)\}$ belongs to $\Sigma_X\otimes\Sigma_X$. For a measurable predictor $f:\mathcal X\to\mathcal A$ and a nonnegative measurable loss $\ell:\mathcal A\times\mathcal Y\to[0,+\infty]$, the pointwise robust loss is
$$L_{\Delta,f}(x,y)=\sup_{x'\in\Delta(x)}\ell(f(x'),y).$$
Its robust risk is the outer expectation
$$R^{\mathrm{rob}}_{P,\Delta}(f)=\mathbb E_P^*[L_{\Delta,f}(X,Y)] :=\inf\{\mathbb E_P[g(X,Y)]:g\ge L_{\Delta,f}\text{ and }g\text{ is nonnegative measurable}\}.$$
If $L_{\Delta,f}$ is measurable, this is its ordinary expectation. The supremum need not be attained. For a metric $\rho$ on $\mathcal X$ and a radius $\epsilon\ge0$, the closed-ball threat is $\Delta_\epsilon(x)=\{x'\in\mathcal X:\rho(x,x')\le\epsilon\}$. On $\mathbb R^d$, $\|u\|_\infty:=\max_{1\le j\le d}|u_j|$ and the $\ell_\infty$ threat is $\Delta_\epsilon(x)=\{x+\delta:\|\delta\|_\infty\le\epsilon\}$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$, $m\in\mathbb R^d$, and let $\Sigma$ be a real symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then its law has Lebesgue density
$$f_{m,\Sigma}(x)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\det(\Sigma)^{-1/2} \exp\!\left(-\tfrac12(x-m)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x-m)\right), \qquad x\in\mathbb R^d.$$

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
Independent sigma-algebras and independent events.

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from The sigma-algebra generated by a function.

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$, $m\in\mathbb R^d$, and let $\Sigma$ be a real symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then its law has Lebesgue density
$$f_{m,\Sigma}(x)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\det(\Sigma)^{-1/2} \exp\!\left(-\tfrac12(x-m)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x-m)\right), \qquad x\in\mathbb R^d.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Indeed, the prior density and each conditional Gaussian density are given by [F2], and their product is the joint density by conditional independence and [F1]. The independent labels contribute a constant factor $2^{-n}$, so conditioning on their observed values does not change the $\theta$-dependent factor.

Write $\bar z=n^{-1}\sum_i z_i$. Expanding squares gives $\sum_i\|z_i-\theta\|_2^2=\sum_i\|z_i-\bar z\|_2^2+n\|\theta-\bar z\|_2^2$. Completing the remaining square in $\theta$ yields $\|\theta\|_2^2+\frac n{\sigma^2}\|\theta-\bar z\|_2^2 =\frac{\sigma^2+n}{\sigma^2}\left\|\theta-\frac n{\sigma^2+n}\bar z\right\|_2^2 +\frac n{\sigma^2+n}\|\bar z\|_2^2$. The final term is independent of $\theta$. The normalized conditional density is therefore the Gaussian density in the Statement, with positive covariance $\frac{\sigma^2}{\sigma^2+n}I_d$.

The density ratio in step 2.1 defines a measurable probability kernel in the observed vectors because its mean is linear in $\bar z$ and its covariance is fixed; [F2] gives unit mass. Applying [F3] to the nonnegative joint density verifies the conditional-law identity on every pair of Borel sets. Since the labels are independent of $(\Theta,Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)$, the same kernel is the conditional law after adjoining the labels.

This law is independent of $y$; scalar uniqueness [F1] identifies each projection, and Cramer–Wold [F1] gives $Y_iX_i\sim N_d(\theta,\sigma^2I_d)$ independent of $Y_i$. Independence of the training pairs and measurable coordinate transformations preserve independence across $i$, so the class-weighted observations have the independent Gaussian likelihood and labels required by [F2].

The map $S\mapsto m(S)$ is Borel because it is a finite sum of coordinate products and division by the positive constant $\sigma^2+n$.

This indicator is measurable in the test pair, so every measurable majorant in [F3] has expectation at least its probability; therefore the fixed-parameter robust risk is at least that probability.

The classifier family and $m$ are Borel, so the shifted error indicator is product-measurable in $(S,\theta,Y,G)$; [F5] makes $H$ measurable. Step 1.3 gives $H(S,\theta)\le R^{\mathrm{rob}}_{P_{\theta,\sigma},\Delta_\epsilon}(f_S)$ pointwise. By [F4], taking the outer expectation over $(\Theta,S)$ yields a lower bound by $\mathbb E[H(\Theta,S)]$.

For either sign $y$, $yR+G$ has law $N_d(0,(v+\sigma^2)I_d)$: each projection has the product characteristic function of independent centered scalar normals, and [F1] identifies the vector law. This conditional law is the same for both labels, so $U:=YR+G$ is independent of the uniform label. By [F6], $\mathbb P(F(S,U)\ne Y\mid S)=1/2$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $d,n\ge1$ be integers, let $\theta\in\mathbb R^d$ satisfy $\|\theta\|_2=\sqrt d$, let $\sigma>0$, and draw independent training pairs $(X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^n$ from the two-class spherical Gaussian model with parameters $\theta,\sigma$. Set $W=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nY_iX_i$ and let $f_W(x)=+1$ when $\langle W,x\rangle\ge0$ and $f_W(x)=-1$ otherwise. For $0<\beta<1$, if
$$0\le\epsilon\le\frac{2\sqrt n-1}{2\sqrt n+4\sigma}-\frac{\sigma\sqrt{2\log(1/\beta)}}{\sqrt d},$$
then with probability at least $1-2\exp(-d/(8(\sigma^2+1)))$ over the training sample, the $\ell_\infty$ robust risk of $f_W$ under $P_{\theta,\sigma}$ at radius $\epsilon$ is at most $\beta$.

In particular, if $\sigma\le d^{1/4}/32$, then each of the following two conditions is sufficient for $\ell_\infty$ robust risk at most $1/100$ with the same training-sample probability:

- $0\le\epsilon\le(1/4)d^{-1/4}$ and $n\ge1$;
- $(1/4)d^{-1/4}\le\epsilon\le1/4$ and $n\ge64\epsilon^2\sqrt d$.

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$ be an integer, let $n\ge0$ be an integer, let $\sigma>0$ and $\epsilon\ge0$, draw $\Theta\sim N_d(0,I_d)$, and, conditional on $\Theta$, draw $n$ independent training pairs $S=((X_i,Y_i))_{i=1}^n$ from the two-class spherical Gaussian model with parameters $\Theta,\sigma$. Let $\mathcal S_n=(\mathbb R^d\times\{-1,+1\})^n$, and let $F:\mathcal S_n\times\mathbb R^d\to\{-1,+1\}$ be a Borel learning rule; write $f_S(x)=F(S,x)$. Define $m(S)=(\sigma^2+n)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nY_iX_i$, with the empty sum equal to zero. Define the expected robust risk as the outer expectation over $(\Theta,S)$ of $R^{\mathrm{rob}}_{P_{\Theta,\sigma},\Delta_\epsilon}(f_S)$, using the same measurable-majorant convention as robust risk; when this random robust risk is measurable, this is its ordinary expectation. Then
$$\mathbb E^*_{\Theta,S}\!\left[R^{\mathrm{rob}}_{P_{\Theta,\sigma},\Delta_\epsilon}(f_S)\right]\ge\frac12\,\mathbb P_{V\sim N_d(0,I_d)}\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{n}{\sigma^2+n}}\,\|V\|_\infty\le\epsilon\right).$$Consequently, if $d\ge2$ and $n\le\epsilon^2\sigma^2/(8\log d)$, then$$\mathbb E^*_{\Theta,S}\!\left[R^{\mathrm{rob}}_{P_{\Theta,\sigma},\Delta_\epsilon}(f_S)\right]\ge\frac12\left(1-\frac1d\right).$$

Let $d\ge1$ be an integer, let $\theta\in\{-1,+1\}^d$, and let $0<\tau\le1/2$. The $(\theta,\tau)$ binary-feature Bernoulli model is the probability law $P_{\theta,\tau}$ on $\{-1,+1\}^d\times\{-1,+1\}$ defined by
$$P_{\theta,\tau}(\{(x,y)\})=\frac12\prod_{j=1}^d\left[\left(\frac12+\tau\right)\mathbf1_{\{x_j=y\theta_j\}}+\left(\frac12-\tau\right)\mathbf1_{\{x_j=-y\theta_j\}}\right].$$
Thus $Y$ is uniform on $\{-1,+1\}$ and, conditional on $Y=y$, the feature coordinates are independent, with $X_j=y\theta_j$ with probability $1/2+\tau$ and $X_j=-y\theta_j$ with probability $1/2-\tau$. The displayed masses sum to one because each coordinate factor sums to one over its two possible signs and the label weights sum to one. The uniform-prior experiment used below draws $\Theta$ uniformly from $\{-1,+1\}^d$ and then draws observations conditionally independently from $P_{\Theta,\tau}$.

Input: an integer $d\ge1$ and a vector $x\in\mathbb R^d$. Output $T(x)\in\{-1,+1\}^d$ with
$$T(x)_i= \begin{cases} +1,&x_i\ge0,\\ -1,&x_i<0 \end{cases} \qquad (1\le i\le d).$$

Let $(\mathcal X,\Sigma_X)$ and $(\mathcal Y,\Sigma_Y)$ be measurable spaces, let $\mathcal A$ be a measurable action space, and let $P$ be a probability measure on $(\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y,\Sigma_X\otimes\Sigma_Y)$. A threat correspondence is a map $\Delta:\mathcal X\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X)$ with $\Delta(x)\ne\varnothing$ for every $x$. It is measurable when its graph $\{(x,x')\in\mathcal X^2:x'\in\Delta(x)\}$ belongs to $\Sigma_X\otimes\Sigma_X$. For a measurable predictor $f:\mathcal X\to\mathcal A$ and a nonnegative measurable loss $\ell:\mathcal A\times\mathcal Y\to[0,+\infty]$, the pointwise robust loss is
$$L_{\Delta,f}(x,y)=\sup_{x'\in\Delta(x)}\ell(f(x'),y).$$
Its robust risk is the outer expectation
$$R^{\mathrm{rob}}_{P,\Delta}(f)=\mathbb E_P^*[L_{\Delta,f}(X,Y)] :=\inf\{\mathbb E_P[g(X,Y)]:g\ge L_{\Delta,f}\text{ and }g\text{ is nonnegative measurable}\}.$$
If $L_{\Delta,f}$ is measurable, this is its ordinary expectation. The supremum need not be attained. For a metric $\rho$ on $\mathcal X$ and a radius $\epsilon\ge0$, the closed-ball threat is $\Delta_\epsilon(x)=\{x'\in\mathcal X:\rho(x,x')\le\epsilon\}$. On $\mathbb R^d$, $\|u\|_\infty:=\max_{1\le j\le d}|u_j|$ and the $\ell_\infty$ threat is $\Delta_\epsilon(x)=\{x+\delta:\|\delta\|_\infty\le\epsilon\}$. When $\mathcal A=\mathcal Y=\{-1,+1\}$ with their discrete sigma-algebras and $\ell(a,y)=\mathbf1_{\{a\ne y\}}$, the robust zero-one loss of a measurable classifier $f:\mathcal X\to\{-1,+1\}$ is $\mathbf1\{\exists x'\in\Delta_\epsilon(x):f(x')\ne y\}$.

For $w\in\mathbb R^d$, let $f_w(x)=+1$ when $\langle w,x\rangle\ge0$ and $f_w(x)=-1$ otherwise. In the following lower-bound branch, let $d\ge1$, $0<\tau\le1/4$, $0<\gamma<1/2$, and $0\le\epsilon<3\tau$. Draw $\Theta$ uniformly from $\{-1,+1\}^d$ and, conditional on $\Theta$, draw $n\ge0$ independent training observations $S$ from the binary-feature Bernoulli model with parameters $\Theta,\tau$. Let $g_n$ be any function from the finite sample space to $\mathbb R^d$, set $w=g_n(S)$, and use $f_w$. If
$$n\le\frac{\epsilon^2\gamma^2}{5000\tau^4\log(4d/\gamma)},$$
then the expected robust risk for the closed threat $\Delta_\epsilon(x)=\{x+\delta:\|\delta\|_\infty\le\epsilon\}$ of $f_w$, averaged over $\Theta,S$, and a fresh test pair from $P_{\Theta,\tau}$, is at least $1/2-\gamma$.

In the separate thresholded upper-bound branch, let $d\ge1$, $0<\tau\le1/2$, $0<\beta<1$, and let $\theta\in\{-1,+1\}^d$ satisfy $\tau\ge(\log(1/\beta)/(2d))^{1/4}$. Draw one training pair $(X_0,Y_0)$ from $P_{\theta,\tau}$, set $W=Y_0X_0$, and define $T:\mathbb R^d\to\{-1,+1\}^d$ by $T(x)_j=+1$ when $x_j\ge0$ and $T(x)_j=-1$ otherwise. Then for every $0\le\epsilon<1$, with training-sample probability at least $1-e^{-\tau^2d/2}$, the robust risk for the closed threat $\Delta_\epsilon(x)=\{x+\delta:\|\delta\|_\infty\le\epsilon\}$ of $f_W\circ T$ under $P_{\theta,\tau}$ is at most $\beta$.

derivations.claim: Fix $x\in\{-1,+1\}^d$ and any $\delta$ with $\|\delta\|_\infty\le\epsilon<1$. If $x_j=+1$, then $x_j+\delta_j\ge1-\epsilon>0$, so [F2] gives $T(x+\delta)_j=+1=x_j$. If $x_j=-1$, then $x_j+\delta_j\le-1+\epsilon<0$, so $T(x+\delta)_j=-1=x_j$. Hence $T(x+\delta)=x$ for every admissible perturbation.

For each support point $(x,y)$, every allowed perturbation therefore makes $g(T(x+\delta))=g(x)$. The robust zero-one loss of $g\circ T$ equals $\mathbf1\{g(x)\ne y\}$ pointwise. Taking expectation under $P_{\theta,\tau}$ proves the displayed equality.

Under the final $\tau,\beta$ condition, [F4] gives the one-sample risk bound for $f_{Y_0X_0}\circ T$ with the stated probability. The pointwise identity in step 2.1 explains why every radius $\epsilon<1$ has the same risk.

Let $\Sigma$ and $\mathcal B$ be nonempty finite sets of feature types and score bins. For each group $t\in\{1,2\}$, let $N_t>0$ be its total mass and let $a_{t\sigma}\ge0$ satisfy $\sum_{\sigma\in\Sigma}a_{t\sigma}=1$. Let $p_\sigma\in[0,1]$ be the probability of the positive binary outcome $Y=1$ for feature type $\sigma$, with the same $p_\sigma$ in both groups. A randomized risk assignment consists of scores $v_b\in[0,1]$ for $b\in\mathcal B$ and a single matrix $X_{\sigma b}\ge0$ with $\sum_{b\in\mathcal B}X_{\sigma b}=1$ for each $\sigma$; conditional on feature type $\sigma$, the assignment chooses bin $b$ with probability $X_{\sigma b}$, independently of group and outcome. Thus, for a group-$t$ individual chosen according to its feature distribution, $\Pr_t(\Sigma=\sigma,Y=1,B=b)=a_{t\sigma}p_\sigma X_{\sigma b}$ and $\Pr_t(\Sigma=\sigma,Y=0,B=b)=a_{t\sigma}(1-p_\sigma)X_{\sigma b}$, and the assigned score is $S=v_B$. The expected positive mass is $\mu_t=N_t\sum_\sigma a_{t\sigma}p_\sigma$, and the group base rate is $\rho_t=\mu_t/N_t$.

The assignment is **calibrated within group $t$** if for every $b\in\mathcal B$,
$$
\sum_{\sigma\in\Sigma}a_{t\sigma}p_\sigma X_{\sigma b}=v_b\sum_{\sigma\in\Sigma}a_{t\sigma}X_{\sigma b}.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By The standard normal density has total mass one and The indefinite integral of a nonnegative measurable function is a measure, gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Take independent standard normals $Z_j$, independent also of all active variables, and define the inactive coordinates by $$T_j=c(U_j-V_j)+\sqrt r Z_j,\qquad r=1-(1-\epsilon)^2(1-\delta/2).$$ Take independent observations and independent standard-normal noise $w_i$; set $\beta_i^*=n$ on $S$ and zero off $S$. These finite Gaussian constructions define the model in the Statement, with $\sigma^2=1$ and no intercept.

The eigenvalues of $B$ are $\delta$ and $2-\delta$, and each row of $B^{-1}$ has absolute sum $1/\delta$. Thus $C_{\min}=\delta$ and $D_{\max}=1/\delta$ work. Each inactive coordinate regresses on its pair with coefficients $(c,-c)$, so $\|\Sigma_{S^cS}\Sigma_{SS}^{-1}\|_\infty=2c=1-\epsilon$. Its variance is one by the definition of $r$, and $0<r<2\epsilon+\delta/2<3\cdot10^{-6}$. The full covariance, after reordering, is a direct sum of positive-definite three-dimensional covariance blocks and singleton identity blocks: each triple is an invertible linear image of $(U_j,V_j,Z_j)$ because $r>0$. Every triple has trace three, so every eigenvalue is at most three. Consequently $C_{\max}=3$ bounds the maximum eigenvalue of the full covariance, and all its diagonal entries are one.

For these constants, $$\sqrt3-\sqrt{8/3}=\frac{1/3}{\sqrt3+\sqrt{8/3}}>\frac1{12},\qquad 3(2-\epsilon)^2<12,$$ so the precise claimed constant satisfies $\theta_\ell>1/1728$ and $2(\theta_\ell-\nu)>2(1/1728-1/100000)>a$. Since $\lceil a s\log N\rceil\le a s\log N+1$, the claimed failure inequality $n<2(\theta_\ell-\nu)s\log N+s+1$ holds. Also $s,n-s,N\to\infty$ and $s/n\to0$. The constant penalty is positive and non-increasing. The lower claim puts no restriction on $\rho_n=n$.

Write $X_S=Z\Sigma_{SS}^{1/2}$, with $Z$ an $n\times s$ iid standard-Gaussian matrix, and put $G=X_S^{\mathsf T}X_S$ and $A=G/n$. By [F1] and $s/n\to0$, with probability tending to one the minimum eigenvalue of $A$ is at least $\delta/2$ and $\|A^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le2/\delta$. On this event define $$\widehat\beta_S=n\mathbf1+\eta-A^{-1}\mathbf1,\qquad \eta=A^{-1}X_S^{\mathsf T}w/n,\qquad \widehat\beta_{S^c}=0.$$ The shrinkage term satisfies $\|A^{-1}\mathbf1\|_\infty\le2\sqrt{s}/\delta=o(n)$. Conditional on $X_S$, $\eta$ is centered Gaussian with covariance $A^{-1}/n$, so [F5] and a finite union bound give $$\mathbb P(\|\eta\|_\infty\ge1\mid X_S)\le2s e^{-n\delta/4}\longrightarrow0$$ uniformly on the spectral event. Put $b=\mathbf1_s$ and $T=b^{\mathsf T}\Sigma_{SS}^{-1}b=s-2N+2N/\delta$, so $T/s\to1$. For each fixed full-rank $H$, the projector $I-P_H$ has rank $n-s+1$, so orthogonal invariance gives the conditional law $D\sim\chi^2_{n-s+1}$. This conditional law is the same for every such $H$; the projector is a measurable function of $H$, and no random basis is selected. Expanding the squared norm and using $X^{\mathsf T}X=I_p$ gives $\frac{1}{2n}\|y-X\beta\|_2^2+\lambda\|\beta\|_1=\frac{\|y\|_2^2-\|z\|_2^2}{2n}+\sum_{j=1}^p\left(\frac{(\beta_j-z_j)^2}{2n}+\lambda|\beta_j|\right)$. For a scalar $z$, the derivative of $(t-z)^2/(2n)+\lambda|t|$ on $t>0$ is $(t-z)/n+\lambda$, and on $t<0$ it is $(t-z)/n-\lambda$. The positive stationary point is $t=z-n\lambda$ exactly when $z>n\lambda$; the negative stationary point is $t=z+n\lambda$ exactly when $z<-n\lambda$. When $|z|\le n\lambda$, the one-sided derivatives at zero satisfy $(-z/n-\lambda)\le0\le(-z/n+\lambda)$, so zero minimizes.
