If an optimizer $\widehat\beta$ of $\|y-X\beta\|_2^2/(2n)+\lambda\|\beta\|_1$ has support exactly $S$ and sign vector $b=\operatorname{sgn}(\widehat\beta_S)\in\{-1,1\}^{|S|}$, then
$$\widehat\beta_S=(X_S^{\mathsf T}X_S/n)^{-1}(X_S^{\mathsf T}y/n-\lambda b).$$
This is a necessary active-coordinate condition only; it does not assert that the candidate satisfies any inactive-coordinate condition.

Assume AC. Let $d_k,n_k\ge1$ be integer sequences with $d_k/n_k\to0$. For each $k$, let $G_k\in\mathbb R^{n_k\times d_k}$ have mutually independent $N(0,1)$ entries. Then

$$\left\|\frac{G_k^{\mathsf T}G_k}{n_k}-I_{d_k}\right\|_{\mathrm{op}}\xrightarrow[k\to\infty]{\mathbb P}0.$$

Assume AC. Let $r_k,n_k$ be positive integers with $n_k\to\infty$ and $r_k/n_k\to1$. For each $k$, let $Z_{k,1},\ldots,Z_{k,r_k}$ be independent $N(0,1)$ random variables and set $D_k=\sum_{j=1}^{r_k}Z_{k,j}^2$. Then $D_k/n_k\to1$ in probability.

Assume AC. Let $m\ge2$, and let $X,Y\in\mathbb R^m$ be independent, centered Gaussian vectors with finite covariance matrices. If

$$\mathbb E[(X_i-X_j)^2]\ge\mathbb E[(Y_i-Y_j)^2]\qquad(i,j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}),$$

then $\mathbb E[\max_iX_i]\ge\mathbb E[\max_iY_i]$.

Assume AC. There is an integer $m_0$ such that for every $m\ge m_0$ and independent standard-normal random variables $G_1,\ldots,G_m$,
$$\mathbb E\max_{1\le i\le m}G_i\ge\frac14\sqrt{\log m}.$$

Assume AC, DC, and countable choice. Let $Z\sim\gamma_d$ be standard Gaussian
on $\mathbb R^d$ and let
$f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be $L$-Lipschitz. If $L>0$, then for every $r>0$,
$$P\{f(Z)\ge E f(Z)+r\}\le e^{-r^2/(2L^2)}.$$
If $L=0$, the probability on the left is zero.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$, $m\in\mathbb R^d$, and let $\Sigma$ be a real symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then its law has Lebesgue density
$$f_{m,\Sigma}(x)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\det(\Sigma)^{-1/2} \exp\!\left(-\tfrac12(x-m)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x-m)\right), \qquad x\in\mathbb R^d.$$

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By The standard normal density has total mass one and The indefinite integral of a nonnegative measurable function is a measure, gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. The law of a random element is a probability measure makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in The Dirac set function at a point.

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   The product measure of two sigma-finite measure spaces is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: For integers $n\le\lceil e^e\rceil$, set $\lambda_n=1$, and for $n>\lceil e^e\rceil$ set $\lambda_n=(\log\log n)^{-1/2}$. Since $\log\log n>1$ in the latter range and is increasing, this defines a positive non-increasing sequence. For $k\ge2$, set $N_k=\lceil e^k\rceil$, $s_k=\lceil e^{k^2}\rceil$, $n_k=\lceil5s_kk\rceil$, and $p_k=s_k+N_k$. Use the model subsequence at sample sizes $n_k$, with $\Sigma_k=I_{p_k}$, $\beta_k^*=(\mathbf1_{s_k},0_{N_k})$, $\sigma^2=1$, and $\lambda_k=\lambda_{n_k}$. Then $C_{\min}=C_{\max}=D_{\max}=\epsilon=1$, $\rho_{n_k}=1$, and $\theta_u=1$, while $\log N_k\sim k$, $\log s_k\sim k^2$, $n_k/s_k\sim5k$, and $\log\log n_k\sim2\log k$. For $\nu=1/2$, $n_k>3s_k\log N_k+s_k$ eventually; also $\lambda_k\to0$, $n_k\lambda_k^2/\log N_k\to\infty$, and $\lambda_k+\sqrt{\log s_k/n_k}\to0$, so the claimed upper hypotheses hold.

Let $X_S$ be the active design, $A=X_S^{\mathsf T}X_S/n_k$, and $v=X_S^{\mathsf T}w/n_k$. Choose an orthogonal $R$ with first column $q=\mathbf1_{s_k}/\sqrt{s_k}$ and write $X_SR=[h,H]$. Each row keeps its $N(0,I_{s_k})$ projection laws under $R$; [F7]–[F10] give its factorized standard-normal density and [F9] gives independent rows, so entries of $h,H$ are mutually independent standard normals. Set $B=H^{\mathsf T}H$, $P_H=HB^{-1}H^{\mathsf T}$ when $B$ is invertible, and $d=h^{\mathsf T}(I-P_H)h$. Conditional on $H$, $d$ is chi-square with $n_k-s_k+1$ degrees of freedom.

Since $s_k/n_k\to0$ and $(n_k-s_k+1)/n_k\to1$, [F2] applied to $X_S$ and $H$ and [F3] applied conditionally to $d$ show that $E_{A,k}=\{\|A-I\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le1/2\}$, $E_{B,k}=\{\|B/n_k-I\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le1/2\}$, and $E_{d,k}=\{n_k/2\le d\le2n_k\}$ each have probability tending to one. Their intersection $E_k=E_{A,k}\cap E_{B,k}\cap E_{d,k}$ therefore has probability tending to one.

On $E_{A,k}$, $\|A^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le2$. Given $X_S$, $A^{-1}v$ is centered Gaussian with covariance $A^{-1}/n_k$, so each coordinate variance is at most $2/n_k$. Completing the square in [F10] gives moment-generating function $e^{\tau_i^2t^2/2}$; [F11] at $t=n_k/2$ yields $\mathbb P(|(A^{-1}v)_i|\ge1\mid X_S)\le2e^{-n_k/4}$. A union bound gives $\mathbb P(\|A^{-1}v\|_\infty\ge1\mid X_S)\le2s_ke^{-n_k/4}$ on $E_{A,k}$, hence $\mathbb P(E_{A,k}\cap\{\|A^{-1}v\|_\infty\ge1\})\le2s_ke^{-n_k/4}\to0$.

For fixed full-rank $H$, the Gaussian coordinates of $h$ along $\operatorname{im}H$ and its orthogonal complement are independent by the factorized density [F8]–[F10]; hence $H^{\mathsf T}h\sim N(0,B)$ is independent of $d$, and $B^{-1}H^{\mathsf T}h$ has covariance $B^{-1}$. This conditional law is measurable because $B^{-1}$ and $P_H$ are Borel on $\det B>0$. Direct multiplication gives $\begin{pmatrix}h^{\mathsf T}h&h^{\mathsf T}H\\H^{\mathsf T}h&B\end{pmatrix}\binom{1}{-B^{-1}H^{\mathsf T}h}=\binom d0$; since $R^{\mathsf T}\mathbf1=\sqrt{s_k}e_1$, it follows that $A^{-1}\mathbf1=(n_k/d)\mathbf1+Z$, where $Z=-(n_k\sqrt{s_k}/d)R\binom0{B^{-1}H^{\mathsf T}h}$ is conditionally centered Gaussian with covariance $\Gamma=(n_k^2s_k/d^2)R\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&B^{-1}\end{pmatrix}R^{\mathsf T}$. On $E_{B,k}\cap E_{d,k}$, $\|\Gamma\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le8s_k/n_k$ and, for $i\ne j$, $\mathbb E[(Z_i-Z_j)^2\mid H,d]\ge(n_k^2s_k/d^2)(1/(2n_k))\|e_i-e_j\|_2^2\ge s_k/(4n_k)$.

Conditional on $H,d$ when $E_{B,k}\cap E_{d,k}$ holds, use [F12] to put the law of $Z$ and an independent standard Gaussian vector $G$ on a product space, and set $Y_i=\sqrt{s_k/(8n_k)}G_i$. By [F4], their increment variances, and [F5], $\mathbb E[\max_iZ_i\mid H,d]\ge\mathbb E\max_iY_i\ge(4\sqrt8)^{-1}\sqrt{s_k\log s_k/n_k}$.

The map $z\mapsto-\max_i z_i$ is 1-Lipschitz. By [F7], represent $Z=\Gamma^{1/2}G$ conditionally and apply [F6] with Lipschitz constant $\sqrt{\|\Gamma\|_{\mathrm{op}}}$ and deviation half the mean bound in step 5.1; uniformly when $E_{B,k}\cap E_{d,k}$ holds, $\mathbb P(\max_iZ_i<\tfrac12\mathbb E[\max_iZ_i\mid H,d]\mid H,d)\le e^{-c\log s_k}\to0$ for some fixed $c>0$. Hence $\max_iZ_i\ge(8\sqrt8)^{-1}\sqrt{s_k\log s_k/n_k}$ with probability tending to one.

On $E_{d,k}$, $n_k/d\ge1/2$. Step 6.1 gives $\max_iZ_i\ge(8\sqrt8)^{-1}\sqrt{s_k\log s_k/n_k}$ with probability tending to one, and $\mathbb P(E_{B,k}\cap E_{d,k})\to1$. Since $A^{-1}\mathbf1=(n_k/d)\mathbf1+Z$ on this event, and step 1.1 gives $\log s_k\sim k^2$, $n_k/s_k\sim5k$, and $\lambda_k\sim(2\log k)^{-1/2}$, it follows that $\lambda_k\max_i(A^{-1}\mathbf1)_i\ge\lambda_k(1/2+(8\sqrt8)^{-1}\sqrt{s_k\log s_k/n_k})\to\infty$ in probability; the diverging term has order $\sqrt{k/\log k}$.

By steps 3.1, 4.1, and 7.1 and a union bound, with probability tending to one $E_{A,k}$ holds, $\|A^{-1}v\|_\infty<1$, and $\lambda_k\max_i(A^{-1}\mathbf1)_i>2$. If an optimizer had the correct signed support, [F1] would force $\widehat\beta_S=A^{-1}(X_S^{\mathsf T}y/n_k-\lambda_k\mathbf1)=\mathbf1+A^{-1}v-\lambda_kA^{-1}\mathbf1$. At an index attaining the maximum, these events imply $\widehat\beta_i<0$, contradicting the required positive sign. Thus exact signed-support success probability tends to zero, refuting the upper implication and the combined threshold statement.

risk_review.notes: Independently checked all nine refutation steps and every cited supplier interface. Identity covariance gives exact constants; log N~k, log s~k^2 and n/s~5k satisfy every upper hypothesis, with a globally non-increasing lambda sequence. Fixed rotation and Schur elimination yield A^-1 1=(n/d)1+Z. Conditional on H,d, the Gaussian Z covariance has norm <=8s/n and pairwise increment variance >=s/(4n), since e_i-e_j is perpendicular to 1. Sudakov-Fernique and the directly proved Gaussian-max lower bound give mean >=sqrt(s log s/n)/(4sqrt8). Applying the stated upper-tail concentration to minus the maximum gives the required lower tail uniformly on E_B intersect E_d, without conditioning on E_A. The separate active-noise union bound is on E_A; their final intersection needs no independence. Lambda times the maximum diverges like sqrt(k/log k); active stationarity therefore forces a negative coefficient for every putative correct-sign optimizer. AC, DC and countable choice are explicitly carried. The refutation disproves the upper branch and hence conjunction, without claiming the separate lower branch here. Reader/refuter have no findings.

citations.quote:
Let $n,p\ge1$, $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$, and $y\in\mathbb R^n$. The ordinary least-squares minimizers of $\|y-X\beta\|_2^2$ are exactly the solutions of $X^{\mathsf T}X\beta=X^{\mathsf T}y$; if $\beta_0$ is one such solution, the full minimizer set is $\beta_0+\ker X$. It is a singleton if and only if the columns of $X$ are linearly independent. For every $\lambda>0$, the ridge objective $\|y-X\beta\|_2^2+\lambda\|\beta\|_2^2$ has the unique minimizer
$$\widehat\beta_{\mathrm{ridge}}=(X^{\mathsf T}X+\lambda I_p)^{-1}X^{\mathsf T}y.$$

Let $n,p\ge1$, let $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$ be a fixed design matrix, let $y\in\mathbb R^n$, and let $\beta\in\mathbb R^p$. The empirical squared loss is

$$\ell_n(\beta)=\frac{1}{2n}\|y-X\beta\|_2^2.$$

Ordinary least squares minimizes $\ell_n(\beta)$ over $\mathbb R^p$. For $\lambda>0$, the ridge (Tikhonov) objective is

$$J^{\mathrm{ridge}}_\lambda(\beta)=\|y-X\beta\|_2^2+\lambda\|\beta\|_2^2.$$

For $\lambda>0$, the lasso objective in the empirical-loss convention is

$$J^{\mathrm{lasso}}_\lambda(\beta)=\ell_n(\beta)+\lambda\|\beta\|_1,\qquad \|\beta\|_1=\sum_{j=1}^p|\beta_j|.$$

This lasso has the same minimizers as $n^{-1}\|y-X\beta\|_2^2+2\lambda\|\beta\|_1$, the fixed-design convention with penalty parameter $\tau=\lambda$.

For a partition $G_1,\ldots,G_m$ of $\{1,\ldots,p\}$, fixed weights $w_g>0$, and $\lambda\ge0$, the group-lasso objective is

$$J^{\mathrm{group}}_{\lambda}(\beta)=\ell_n(\beta)+\lambda\sum_{g=1}^m w_g\|\beta_{G_g}\|_2.$$

For a fixed matrix $D\in\mathbb R^{q\times p}$ and $\lambda_1,\lambda_2\ge0$, a fused-lasso objective is

$$J^{\mathrm{fused}}_{\lambda_1,\lambda_2}(\beta)=\ell_n(\beta)+\lambda_1\|\beta\|_1+\lambda_2\|D\beta\|_1.$$

These group and fused formulas define objectives only; no existence, uniqueness, or algorithm guarantee is asserted for them here. The formulas use the displayed feature scales, so rescaling a column changes the penalty unless its coefficient and penalty weight are adjusted. If a separate intercept is included, write $X=[\mathbf 1\;X_0]$ and $\beta=(\beta_0,\gamma)$, and define the loss by $\|y-\beta_0\mathbf1-X_0\gamma\|_2^2/(2n)$. In this convention replace the ridge penalty by $\lambda\|\gamma\|_2^2$, the lasso penalty by $\lambda\|\gamma\|_1$, the group penalty by $\lambda\sum_g w_g\|\gamma_{G_g}\|_2$ with the groups partitioning only the coordinates of $\gamma$, and the fused penalty by $\lambda_1\|\gamma\|_1+\lambda_2\|D_0\gamma\|_1$ with $D=[0\;D_0]$. The ridge loss remains unaveraged. Each penalty then acts only on $\gamma$ and the intercept coordinate $\beta_0$ is unpenalized.

derivations.claim: Here $X^{\mathsf T}X=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $X^{\mathsf T}y=(1,1)^{\mathsf T}$. The OLS normal equations reduce to $\beta_1+\beta_2=1$, giving the stated full line.
For ridge parameter $1$, $X^{\mathsf T}X+I_2=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$, whose inverse sends $(1,1)^{\mathsf T}$ to $(1/3,1/3)^{\mathsf T}$.

Write $t=\beta_1+\beta_2$. Since $|\beta_1|+|\beta_2|\ge|t|$, the Lasso objective is at least $\tfrac12(1-t)^2+\tfrac14|t|$, with equality exactly when the coordinates have the same weak sign. The scalar function decreases up to $t=3/4$ and increases after it: on $t>0$ its derivative is $t-3/4$, and on $t<0$ its derivative is $t-5/4<0$. Thus its unique minimizing sum is $t=3/4>0$, where equality in the triangle inequality requires both coordinates nonnegative. This gives exactly the stated segment of minimizers.

Let $n,p\ge1$, $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$ satisfy $X^{\mathsf T}X=I_p$, and let $y\in\mathbb R^n$ and $\lambda>0$. The objective
$$\frac{1}{2n}\|y-X\beta\|_2^2+\lambda\|\beta\|_1$$
has the unique minimizer $\widehat\beta_j=S_{n\lambda}((X^{\mathsf T}y)_j)$, where $S_a(t)=\operatorname{sgn}(t)(|t|-a)_+$, $(u)_+=\max\{u,0\}$, and $\operatorname{sgn}(0)=0$. Thus the threshold is $n\lambda$ under this loss normalization.

Let $n,p\ge1$, $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$, and $y\in\mathbb R^n$. The ordinary least-squares minimizers of $\|y-X\beta\|_2^2$ are exactly the solutions of $X^{\mathsf T}X\beta=X^{\mathsf T}y$; if $\beta_0$ is one such solution, the full minimizer set is $\beta_0+\ker X$. It is a singleton if and only if the columns of $X$ are linearly independent. For every $\lambda>0$, the ridge objective $\|y-X\beta\|_2^2+\lambda\|\beta\|_2^2$ has the unique minimizer
$$\widehat\beta_{\mathrm{ridge}}=(X^{\mathsf T}X+\lambda I_p)^{-1}X^{\mathsf T}y.$$

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional inner product spaces and let $b\in W$. A vector $x\in V$ minimises $\lVert Tx-b\rVert$ if and only if

$$T^*(Tx-b)=0,$$

equivalently $T^*Tx=T^*b$. Minimisers exist, and if $x_0$ is one minimiser, then the full set of minimisers is $x_0+\ker T$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

such that

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The LDA subfamily imposes one common covariance matrix, $\Sigma_k=\Sigma$ for every $k$; the QDA subfamily permits the covariance matrices to differ by class.

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$, $m\in\mathbb R^d$, and let $\Sigma$ be a real symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then its law has Lebesgue density
$$f_{m,\Sigma}(x)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\det(\Sigma)^{-1/2} \exp\!\left(-\tfrac12(x-m)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x-m)\right), \qquad x\in\mathbb R^d.$$

Let $d\ge1$ and $K\ge2$ be finite integers, with ordered labels $1<2<\cdots<K$. A finite linear-score classifier on $\mathbb R^d$ is specified by vectors $a_k\in\mathbb R^d$ and constants $b_k\in\mathbb R$, one pair for each label, and assigns score $s_k(x)=a_k^Tx+b_k$ to $x\in\mathbb R^d$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

A **real kernel** on a set $X$ is a function $k:X\times X\to\mathbb R$. It is **positive semidefinite** if it is symmetric and, for every integer $n\ge1$, every $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in X$, and every $c_1,\ldots,c_n\in\mathbb R$,

$$\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n c_i c_j k(x_i,x_j)\ge0.$$

A **real reproducing kernel Hilbert space with kernel $k$** is a real Hilbert space $\mathcal H$ of functions $X\to\mathbb R$ such that, for each $x\in X$, the section $k_x:=k(\cdot,x)$ lies in $\mathcal H$ and $\langle f,k_x\rangle_{\mathcal H}=f(x)$ for every $f\in\mathcal H$. Consequently $\langle k_z,k_x\rangle_{\mathcal H}=k(z,x)=k(x,z)$.

For the canonical construction, let $E_0$ be the real vector space of finitely supported functions $a:X\to\mathbb R$, write $\delta_x$ for the function supported at $x$ with value $1$, and put

$$B(a,b):=\sum_{x\in\operatorname{supp}(a)}\sum_{z\in\operatorname{supp}(b)}a(x)b(z)k(x,z).$$

Let $N:=\{a\in E_0:B(a,a)=0\}$. Under the Axiom of Countable Choice, the canonical space is formed by giving $E_0/N$ its induced inner product and taking a norm completion; the image of $\delta_x$ is denoted $k_x$. For an element $h$ of that completion, its associated function is $x\mapsto\langle h,k_x\rangle$. The quotient, completed inner product, and function identification are justified by the local construction theorem.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]). A **completion** of $(X,d)$
is a pair $\big((\widehat{X}, \widehat{d}),\, \iota\big)$ in which

- $(\widehat{X}, \widehat{d})$ is a **complete** metric space
  ([[def-complete-metric-space]]);
- $\iota : X \to \widehat{X}$ is an **isometric embedding**, that is
  $\widehat{d}(\iota(x), \iota(y)) = d(x,y)$ for all $x,y \in X$
  ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]);
- $\iota[X]$ is **dense** in $\widehat{X}$, that is
  $\overline{\iota[X]} = \widehat{X}$
  ([[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]]).

**The embedding is part of the data, not an afterthought.** A completion is a
pair, and two completions of the same space are compared through their embeddings
([[thm-metric-completion-unique]]); the underlying complete space alone carries
no information about where $X$ sits inside it. This is the same discipline as for
the metric itself: a metric space is a pair, not a set.

**$\iota$ identifies $X$ with a subspace of $\widehat{X}$, metric and topology
included.** An isometric embedding is injective, is an isometry onto its image,
and carries the metric topology of $X$ onto the subspace topology of $\iota[X]$
([[lem-isometry-is-an-embedding]]). So "$X$ is a dense subspace of a complete
space" is an accurate reading of the definition, and the pedantic version with
$\iota$ written out is used only where two completions have to be compared.

**Existence and uniqueness are theorems, not part of the definition.** Under
Countable Choice, every metric space has a completion
([[thm-metric-completion-exists]]) and any two are isometric by a unique
isometry commuting with the embeddings
[[thm-metric-completion-unique]]. Until the first of those is proved, the phrase
*the* completion is not licensed, and it is not used here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice for assertion 5 and the consequent
existence claim ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space
([[def-metric-space]]) and let $\mathcal{C}$ be the set of all Cauchy sequences
in $X$ ([[def-cauchy-in-metric]]). Then:

1. For all $x = (x_n)$ and $y = (y_n)$ in $\mathcal{C}$ the real sequence
   $\big(d(x_n,y_n)\big)_n$ converges, so
   $$\rho(x,y) \;:=\; \lim_{n} d(x_n,y_n)$$
   is a single well-determined real ([[thm-cauchy-criterion-via-lub]],
   [[lem-limit-unique]]).
2. The relation $x \sim y :\Longleftrightarrow \rho(x,y) = 0$ is an equivalence
   relation on $\mathcal{C}$. Write $\widehat{X} := \mathcal{C}/\!\sim$ for the
   set of its classes and $[x]$ for the class of $x$.
3. $\widehat{d}\big([x],[y]\big) := \rho(x,y)$ does not depend on the chosen
   representatives, and $\widehat{d}$ is a metric on $\widehat{X}$.
4. The map $\iota : X \to \widehat{X}$ sending $p$ to the class of the constant
   sequence at $p$ is an isometric embedding with dense image
   ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]],
   [[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]]).
5. $(\widehat{X}, \widehat{d})$ is complete.

Consequently $\big((\widehat{X},\widehat{d}), \iota\big)$ is a completion of
$(X,d)$ ([[def-metric-completion]]), and **every metric space has a
completion**.

**The notation is kept honest.** A Cauchy sequence in $X$ need not converge in
$X$, so no symbol $\lim_n x_n$ appears anywhere below; the only limits taken are
limits of *real* sequences, and each is written only after its existence has been
proved. The equivalence relation is defined and verified here rather than cited, as was
done for [[def-integers]], so that the construction is self-contained and its
transitivity argument is visible at the point of use.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $X$ be a
normed space. The published metric completion of the norm metric on $X$ admits
a unique vector-space structure and norm whose induced metric is the
published completion metric and such that the constant sequence embedding
$i:X\to \widehat X$ is a dense linear isometry. With this structure,
$\widehat X$ is a Banach space.

Let $X$ be a normed space. A **completion of $X$** is a pair
$\bigl(\widehat X,\iota\bigr)$ such that

- $\widehat X$ is a Banach space ([[def-banach-space]]);
- $\iota:X\to \widehat X$ is a linear isometry
  ([[def-linear-isometry-and-isometric-isomorphism]]);
- $\iota[X]$ is dense in $\widehat X$
  ([[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]]).

Equivalently, a completion of a normed space is a completion of its norm metric
([[def-metric-completion]]) together with compatible linear structure on the
complete space.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $X$ be a real or complex inner-product space and let $(\widehat X,\kappa)$ be its norm completion ([[def-completion-of-a-normed-space]]). Then $\widehat X$ carries a unique inner product that extends the given one along $\kappa$ and whose induced length is the completion norm; with it $\widehat X$ is a Hilbert space, and the extension is unique among inner products that extend the given pairing and induce the completion norm.

For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.

derivations.claim: Let $E_0$ be the finitely supported functions on $X$ and define $B(a,b)=\sum_{x,z}a(x)b(z)k(x,z)$, where each sum is over the finite supports. Symmetry and bilinearity follow from symmetry of $k$ and finite-sum algebra. For any $a$, listing its finite support gives $B(a,a)\ge0$ by [F1].

For $a,b\in E_0$ and $t\in\mathbb R$, $0\le B(a+tb,a+tb)=B(a,a)+2tB(a,b)+t^2B(b,b)$. If $B(b,b)>0$, nonnegativity of this quadratic for all $t$ gives $B(a,b)^2\le B(a,a)B(b,b)$; if $B(b,b)=0$, its linear coefficient must vanish, so $B(a,b)=0$.

It follows that every $a\in N:=\{a:B(a,a)=0\}$ satisfies $B(a,b)=0$ for every $b\in E_0$. Hence $N$ is a subspace and the form descends to a well-defined positive definite inner product on $Q:=E_0/N$: changing a representative by an element of $N$ does not change any pairing, and a quotient class has zero squared norm exactly when it is the zero class.

The induced inner product makes $Q$ a real inner-product space. By [F2] and [A1], its norm metric has a metric completion with compatible Banach structure, hence a norm completion; the inner product extends uniquely and makes the completion $\widehat Q$ a real Hilbert space.

For each $x\in X$, the image $k_x$ of $[\delta_x]\in Q$ satisfies $\|k_x\|^2=B(\delta_x,\delta_x)=k(x,x)\ge0$. Thus the finite kernel sections are elements of $\widehat Q$, and their span is dense because the image of $Q$ is dense in its completion.

For $a\in E_0$, the quotient pairing gives $\langle[a],k_x\rangle=\sum_{z\in\operatorname{supp}(a)}a(z)k(z,x)$, independently of the representative by [step 3.1]. Given $h\in\widehat Q$, density in [step 4.1] provides an approximating sequence $[a_m]\to h$. By [F3], the real sequence $\langle[a_m],k_x\rangle$ is Cauchy, and if $[b_m]\to h$ is another such sequence then $|\langle[a_m-b_m],k_x\rangle|\le\|[a_m-b_m]\|\|k_x\|\to0$, so its limit is independent of the approximants. The extended inner product also satisfies [F3], hence this limit equals $\langle h,k_x\rangle$.

Define the associated function of $h\in\widehat Q$ by $h(x):=\langle h,k_x\rangle$. Applying the extended pairing to $k_z$ gives $k_z(x)=\langle k_z,k_x\rangle=B(\delta_z,\delta_x)=k(z,x)=k(x,z)$, so $k_x$ is exactly the section $k(\cdot,x)$ and $\langle h,k_x\rangle=h(x)$ for every $h$.

If $h(x)=0$ for every $x\in X$, then $h$ is orthogonal to every section $k_x$ and therefore to their dense span from [step 5.1]. Continuity of the inner product gives $\langle h,h\rangle=0$, so positive definiteness gives $h=0$. Thus the associated-function map is injective and identifies $\widehat Q$ with a Hilbert space of functions having reproducing kernel $k$.

derivations.claim: Regard $K$ as an endomorphism of $\mathbb R^n$ with its usual dot product. By [A1], $K$ is symmetric, hence self-adjoint. By [F1], there are an orthonormal eigenbasis $q_1,\ldots,q_n$ and real eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n$ with $Kq_\ell=\lambda_\ell q_\ell$.
Since $\|q_\ell\|_2=1$, [A1] gives $\lambda_\ell=q_\ell^TKq_\ell\ge0$ for each $\ell$. Thus each $\sqrt{\lambda_\ell}$ is a real number, including when $\lambda_\ell=0$.

For $1\le i\le n$, define $z_i=(\sqrt{\lambda_1}(q_1)_i,\ldots,\sqrt{\lambda_n}(q_n)_i)\in\mathbb R^n$. The spectral decomposition $K=\sum_{\ell=1}^n\lambda_\ell q_\ell q_\ell^T$ then gives $z_i^Tz_j=\sum_{\ell=1}^n\lambda_\ell(q_\ell)_i(q_\ell)_j=K_{ij}=k(x_i,x_j)$ for all $i,j$.

derivations.claim: Let $M:=\operatorname{span}\{k_{x_i}:1\le i\le n\}$. It is finite-dimensional. Apply [F2] to $f$ and $M$, and write $f=p+h$ with $p\in M$ and $h\perp M$.
For every $i$, [F1] gives $h(x_i)=\langle h,k_{x_i}\rangle=0$, so $p(x_i)=f(x_i)$. Hence the loss terms in $J(p)$ and $J(f)$ agree.
The norm-contraction clause of [F2] gives $\|p\|_{\mathcal H}\le\|f\|_{\mathcal H}$. Monotonicity of $\Omega$ therefore gives $J(p)\le J(f)$.
Since $f$ is a minimizer, $J(f)\le J(p)$. Thus $J(p)=J(f)$ and $p$ is also a minimizer; by its definition $p$ is a finite linear combination of the sample kernel sections.

Let $X$ be a set, let $\mathcal H$ be a real Hilbert space, and let $\phi:X\to\mathcal H$ be a feature map. Define its kernel by $k(x,z):=\langle\phi(x),\phi(z)\rangle_{\mathcal H}$. For a finite labeled sample $(x_i,y_i)_{i=1}^n$ with $n\ge1$, $x_i\in X$, and $y_i\in\{-1,+1\}$, the **soft-margin support-vector machine** with cost $C>0$ is

$$\min_{w\in\mathcal H,\ b\in\mathbb R,\ \xi\in\mathbb R^n}\ \frac12\|w\|_{\mathcal H}^2+C\sum_{i=1}^n\xi_i$$

subject to

$$y_i\bigl(\langle w,\phi(x_i)\rangle_{\mathcal H}+b\bigr)\ge1-\xi_i,\qquad \xi_i\ge0\quad(1\le i\le n).$$

The bias $b$ is unpenalized. The associated real score is $s_{w,b}(x):=\langle w,\phi(x)\rangle_{\mathcal H}+b$. If a binary label is required, use the deterministic rule $+1$ when $s_{w,b}(x)\ge0$ and $-1$ otherwise. The score is not defined as a probability, and this optimization includes no probability-calibration map.

The **hard-margin** problem removes the slack variables and minimizes $\frac12\|w\|_{\mathcal H}^2$ subject to $y_i(\langle w,\phi(x_i)\rangle_{\mathcal H}+b)\ge1$ for every $i$. In this library, “margin-separable sample” means exactly that this hard-margin feasible set is nonempty; no hard-margin conclusion is asserted for a sample that fails this condition.

This vector is the unique nearest point in $M$ to $f$, and it satisfies $\|p\|\le\|f\|$. The conclusion does not require $E$ to be complete.

For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.
Every finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space has an orthonormal basis. In dimension zero, this is the empty basis.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty. The following are equivalent.

1. $A$ is compact.
2. $A$ is closed and bounded.
3. $A$ is pseudocompact.
4. Every continuous $f:A\to\mathbb{R}$ attains a maximum and a minimum on $A$.

This theorem is a ZF statement. The nonemptiness hypothesis is necessary for condition 4, because the empty image has neither a maximum nor a minimum.

derivations.claim: The tuple $w=0$, $b=0$, and $\xi_i=1$ is feasible and has objective $Cn$. Every feasible objective is nonnegative, so the primal infimum lies in $[0,Cn]$.

Let $M=\operatorname{span}\{\phi(x_i):1\le i\le n\}$. For any feasible tuple, project $w$ onto $M$ using [F1]. The residual is orthogonal to every $\phi(x_i)$, so all sample scores and constraints are unchanged, while the norm does not increase. Thus minimizing over $M\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ has the same infimum as minimizing over the full feature space.

If all labels are $+1$, then $w=0$, $b=1$, and $\xi=0$ is feasible with objective $0$, which is globally minimal by step 1.1. If all labels are $-1$, then $w=0$, $b=-1$, and $\xi=0$ gives the same conclusion.

Suppose both labels occur. Set $R=\max_i\|\phi(x_i)\|$ and let $S$ be the subset of $M\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ consisting of feasible tuples with objective at most $Cn$. By step 1.1, $S$ is nonempty. It is closed because the constraints are continuous affine inequalities and the objective is continuous; continuity of each score follows from [F2]. Every tuple in $S$ satisfies $\|w\|\le\sqrt{2Cn}$ and $0\le\xi_i\le n$. Choose indices $i_+$ and $i_-$ with labels $+1$ and $-1$. Their constraints and [F2] give $b\ge1-n-\sqrt{2Cn}R$ and $b\le n-1+\sqrt{2Cn}R$, so $b$ is bounded. Equip the product space with the inner product $\langle(w,b,\xi),(w',b',\xi')\rangle=\langle w,w'\rangle+bb'+\xi^T\xi'$. It has finite dimension $d=\dim M+1+n\ge1$, so [F3] gives an orthonormal basis identifying it with $\mathbb R^d$. Hence $S$ is a nonempty closed bounded subset of that Euclidean space. By [F4], the continuous objective attains a minimum on $S$. Any feasible tuple outside $S$ has objective greater than $Cn$, whereas $S$ contains a feasible tuple of objective $Cn$; therefore this minimum is also the global primal minimum. By step 1.2 it is a full-space minimizer with $w\in M$.

citations.quote: Let $n\ge1$, let $C>0$, and let $(x_i,y_i)_{i=1}^n$ be a finite labeled sample with $y_i\in\{-1,+1\}$ in a real Hilbert feature space $\mathcal H$, with feature map $\phi$. The soft-margin SVM primal has a finite attained minimum. At least one minimizing tuple has its weight vector in $M:=\operatorname{span}\{\phi(x_i):1\le i\le n\}$. This conclusion includes samples with only one label and does not assert uniqueness of the bias or slack variables.

Let $E$ be a real inner-product space, let $M\subseteq E$ be a finite-dimensional subspace, and let $f\in E$. There is a unique $p\in M$ such that $f-p$ is orthogonal to every vector of $M$. This vector is the unique nearest point in $M$ to $f$, and it satisfies $\|p\|\le\|f\|$. The conclusion does not require $E$ to be complete.

Let $k$ be a real positive semidefinite kernel on a set $X$, let $n\ge1$, and let $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in X$. There are vectors $z_1,\ldots,z_n\in\mathbb R^n$ such that $k(x_i,x_j)=z_i^Tz_j$ for every $1\le i,j\le n$. The vectors may be zero and need not be linearly independent.

A subset is convex when it contains the segment joining each pair of its
points ([[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]]). A function
$F:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ is proper if it never equals
$-\infty$ and is finite at at least one point. Its domain is
$\operatorname{dom}F=\{x:F(x)<+\infty\}$. Its epigraph is
$\operatorname{epi}F=\{(x,t):F(x)\le t\}$. It is closed convex when its
epigraph is a closed convex set. For a nonempty convex set $S$,
$\operatorname{aff}S$ is its smallest containing affine subspace and
$\operatorname{ri}S$ is its interior relative to $\operatorname{aff}S$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $m,p\in\mathbb N$ with zero allowed, let
$f_0,g_1,\ldots,g_m$ be proper closed convex functions on $\mathbb R^n$,
let $A\in\mathbb R^{p\times n}$ have full row rank, and let
$b\in\mathbb R^p$. Full row rank means that the rows are linearly
independent, vacuously when $p=0$. The common domain is
$D=\operatorname{dom}f_0\cap\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{dom}g_i$. The primal
problem is to minimize $f_0(x)$ over $x\in D$ satisfying $Ax=b$ and
$g_i(x)\le0$. An inequality is removable if, with
$D_{-i}=\operatorname{dom}f_0\cap\bigcap_{j\ne i}\operatorname{dom}g_j$,
$D_{-i}\subseteq\operatorname{dom}g_i$ and $g_i(x)\le0$ for every $x\in D_{-i}$.
Then $D=D_{-i}$, so removing that function and its inequality leaves the
feasible set unchanged. While a removable inequality exists, delete the one
with smallest original index, recomputing $D_{-i}$ using the currently retained
family after each deletion. Stop when none is removable, then relabel the
remaining inequalities consecutively in their original order and let $m$
denote their number. An inequality that is nonpositive only on $D$
but whose function domain restricts $D$ is not removable. Unless stated
otherwise, the inequalities below are the remaining ones after only these
domain-preserving deletions. The primal value is
$$
p^*=\inf\{f_0(x):x\in D,\ Ax=b,\ g_i(x)\le0\text{ for all }i\}.
$$

For $\lambda\in\mathbb R^m_+$ and $\nu\in\mathbb R^p$, the extended
Lagrangian is
$$
L(x,\lambda,\nu)=\begin{cases}f_0(x)+\lambda^Tg(x)+\nu^T(Ax-b),&x\in D,\\+\infty,&x\notin D.\end{cases}
$$
The dual function and dual value are
$$
q(\lambda,\nu)=\inf_{x\in\mathbb R^n}L(x,\lambda,\nu),\qquad d^*=\sup_{\lambda\ge0,\ \nu\in\mathbb R^p}q(\lambda,\nu).
$$
The dual supremum is attained when some admissible $(\lambda,\nu)$ has
$q(\lambda,\nu)=d^*$; the optimal duality gap is $p^*-d^*$ when both values
are finite.

Slater's condition means that there is
$x_s\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f_0)\cap
\bigcap_i\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}g_i)$ with $Ax_s=b$ and
$g_i(x_s)<0$ for every remaining inequality. Relative interior is used in
the affine hull of each domain, so the domain need not have ambient interior.

Consider the finite-dimensional convex program of
[[def-convex-program-duality-and-slater-condition]]. Assume its equality
matrix has independent rows, Slater's condition holds, and the finite primal
value $p^*\in\mathbb R$ is attained at $x_*$. Then there are
$\lambda_*\ge0$ and $\nu_*$ such that
$$q(\lambda_*,\nu_*)=d^*=p^*.$$
Moreover, every inequality multiplier satisfies
$\lambda_{*,i}g_i(x_*)=0$. The Slater and attainment hypotheses do not assert
that a primal minimizer is unique.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$
be $C^2$. Let $p,m\in\mathbb N$ with zero allowed; when the target
dimension is positive, let $h:U\to\mathbb R^p$ and
$g=(g_1,\ldots,g_m):U\to\mathbb R^m$ be componentwise $C^2$, and when it
is zero use the unique empty map. The $C^2$ convention for positive
dimensions is [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]].
The $C^2$ inequality program is to minimize $f(x)$ subject to
$h(x)=0$ and $g_i(x)\le0$ for every $i$. Its feasible set is
$C=\{x\in U:h(x)=0,\ g_i(x)\le0\ (1\le i\le m)\}$. A feasible point $x_*$ is
a local minimizer if some open neighborhood $V$ of $x_*$ satisfies
$f(x_*)\le f(y)$ for every $y\in C\cap V$.

At a feasible $x$, the active set is
$I(x)=\{i:g_i(x)=0\}$. The Bouligand tangent cone and linearized cone are,
respectively,
$$
T_C(x)=\{d:\exists\,t_k>0,\ t_k\downarrow0,\ d_k\to d,\ x+t_kd_k\in C\},
$$
and
$$
\mathcal L_C(x)=\{d:Dh(x)d=0,\ Dg_i(x)d\le0\text{ for every }i\in I(x)\}.
$$
Gradients are column vectors and $Dg_i(x)d=\nabla g_i(x)^Td$.

The linear independence constraint qualification (LICQ) holds at $x$ when the rows of $Dh(x)$ together with
$\{\nabla g_i(x)^T:i\in I(x)\}$ are linearly independent. MFCQ holds at $x$
when $Dh(x)$ has full row rank (its rows are linearly independent) and there is $w\in\ker Dh(x)$ with
$Dg_i(x)w<0$ for every active $i$; the latter condition is vacuous if
$I(x)=\varnothing$. Here full row rank for a matrix with zero rows is
understood vacuously.

The Mangasarian–Fromovitz constraint qualification (MFCQ) is the condition
just stated. The Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) system is the stationarity,
feasibility, dual-feasibility, and complementarity system below.

For $\nu\in\mathbb R^p$ and $\lambda\in\mathbb R^m$, the Lagrangian and KKT
system are
$$
L(x,\nu,\lambda)=f(x)+\nu^Th(x)+\lambda^Tg(x),
$$
$$
h(x)=0,\quad g(x)\le0,\quad \lambda\ge0,\quad \lambda_i g_i(x)=0\ (1\le i\le m),\quad \nabla_xL(x,\nu,\lambda)=0.
$$
The critical cone for a KKT tuple is
$\mathcal K(x,\nu,\lambda)=\mathcal L_C(x)\cap
\{d:\nabla f(x)^Td=0\}$. These definitions use the differentiability and
gradient conventions of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]],
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]].

Let $m\ge0$ be an integer. Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and convex,
and suppose the objective $f:U\to\mathbb R$ and inequalities
$g_i:U\to\mathbb R$ $(1\le i\le m)$ are differentiable and convex.
Let the equalities be $Ax=b$ and define the feasible set
$C=\{x\in U:Ax=b,\ g_i(x)\le0\ (1\le i\le m)\}$. If a feasible tuple
$(x_*,\nu,\lambda)$ satisfies the KKT conditions with $\lambda\ge0$, then
$x_*$ is a global minimizer over the feasible set $C$. Moreover,
$-\nabla f(x_*)\in N_C(x_*)$, where the normal cone has the convention of
[[def-kkt-residual-and-normal-cone]].

derivations.claim: Let $(w_*,b_*,\xi_*)$ be any primal minimizer, which exists by [F1], and let $M=\operatorname{span}\{\phi(x_i):1\le i\le n\}$. Project $w_*$ onto $M$ using [F2]; its residual is orthogonal to every $\phi(x_i)$, so the projection preserves all margins and slacks. If the residual were nonzero, [F3] would give a strictly smaller squared norm and hence a strictly smaller objective, contradicting minimality because the regularization coefficient is $1/2>0$. Thus every primal minimizer has $w_*\in M$.

Identify $M$ with a Euclidean space using an orthonormal basis. In the finite-dimensional variable space $M\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$, the objective is a proper continuous convex function and the $2n$ inequality constraints are continuous affine functions with the sign convention [F7]. No inequality is removed by the domain-preserving convention in [F5]: all functions have full domain, and sending the corresponding $\xi_i\to-\infty$ makes either constraint function positive. There are no primal equality rows, so the full-row-rank condition in [F5] holds vacuously.

The point $w=0$, $b=0$, $\xi_i=2$ has strict slack in every constraint: $1-\xi_i-y_i(\langle w,\phi(x_i)\rangle+b)=-1<0$ and $-\xi_i=-2<0$. The objective and all constraint domains are the whole finite-dimensional variable space, so this point lies in their relative interiors. Together with the finite attained primal value from [F1], this verifies every hypothesis of [F6].

Write the margin constraints as $g_i^{(m)}:=1-\xi_i-y_i(\langle w,\phi(x_i)\rangle+b)\le0$ and the nonnegative-slack constraints as $g_i^{(s)}:=-\xi_i\le0$. Give them multipliers $\alpha_i\ge0$ and $\mu_i\ge0$, respectively. The Lagrangian is $L=\frac12\|w\|^2+C\sum_i\xi_i+\sum_i\alpha_i g_i^{(m)}+\sum_i\mu_i g_i^{(s)}$.

Put $v:=\sum_i\alpha_i y_i\phi(x_i)$. The terms of $L$ depending on $w$ are $\frac12\|w\|^2-\langle w,v\rangle=\frac12\|w-v\|^2-\frac12\|v\|^2$, so their infimum is $-\frac12\|v\|^2$. The infimum over the unrestricted bias $b$ is finite exactly when $\sum_i\alpha_i y_i=0$, and the infimum over each unrestricted $\xi_i$ is finite exactly when $C-\alpha_i-\mu_i=0$. Thus the dual-feasible conditions are $\sum_i\alpha_i y_i=0$ and $0\le\alpha_i\le C$.

Apply [F6] using the verified hypotheses in [step 3.1]. It gives an attained dual optimum $(\alpha,\mu)$ with the same value as the primal optimum and complementarity for both families $g_i^{(m)}$ and $g_i^{(s)}$. At any fixed primal minimizer, these equal values and complementarity make $L$ attain its unconstrained infimum; its derivatives in $w$, $b$, and each $\xi_i$ therefore vanish.

For any finite list $u_1,\ldots,u_m\in X$ and $c_1,\ldots,c_m\in\mathbb R$, symmetry and bilinearity of the real inner product give $\sum_{r,s}c_rc_sk(u_r,u_s)=\langle\sum_r c_r\phi(u_r),\sum_s c_s\phi(u_s)\rangle=\|\sum_r c_r\phi(u_r)\|^2\ge0$. Thus the feature-induced kernel $k$ is real positive semidefinite, so its sample Gram matrix satisfies the hypothesis of [F4]. Since $k(x_i,x_j)=\langle\phi(x_i),\phi(x_j)\rangle$, $\|v\|^2=\sum_{i,j}\alpha_i\alpha_jy_iy_jk(x_i,x_j)$. By [F4], the matrix $(y_iy_jk(x_i,x_j))_{i,j}$ is the Gram matrix of $y_i z_i$, so its quadratic form is nonnegative. Hence the displayed dual objective is concave. Its equality row has coefficient vector $y\ne0$, because $n\ge1$ and each $y_i\in\{-1,+1\}$, so that row is independent.

Differentiating the Lagrangian of [step 3.2] gives $w=\sum_i\alpha_i y_i\phi(x_i)$, $\sum_i\alpha_i y_i=0$, and $C-\alpha_i-\mu_i=0$. The last equation and $\mu_i\ge0$ give $\alpha_i\le C$; together with $\alpha_i\ge0$ these are the dual box constraints. The complementarity equations supplied by [F6] are $\alpha_i g_i^{(m)}=0$ and $\mu_i g_i^{(s)}=0$, which are exactly the two equations in the Statement.

The finite-dimensional primal has differentiable convex objective and affine convex constraints on the open convex variable space identified in [step 2.1]. Thus [F8] certifies that any feasible tuple satisfying the stationarity and complementarity equations is a global primal minimizer. If $0<\alpha_i<C$, then $\mu_i=C-\alpha_i>0$, so $\mu_i\xi_i=0$ forces $\xi_i=0$; then $\alpha_i g_i^{(m)}=0$ forces the signed margin to equal $1$. Finally, for any input $x$, stationarity gives the score $s(x)=\sum_i\alpha_i y_i k(x_i,x)+b$.

A **real kernel** on a set $X$ is a function $k:X\times X\to\mathbb R$. It is **positive semidefinite** if it is symmetric and, for every integer $n\ge1$, every $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in X$, and every $c_1,\ldots,c_n\in\mathbb R$,

$$\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n c_i c_j k(x_i,x_j)\ge0.$$

A **real reproducing kernel Hilbert space with kernel $k$** is a real Hilbert space $\mathcal H$ of functions $X\to\mathbb R$ such that, for each $x\in X$, the section $k_x:=k(\cdot,x)$ lies in $\mathcal H$ and $\langle f,k_x\rangle_{\mathcal H}=f(x)$ for every $f\in\mathcal H$. Consequently $\langle k_z,k_x\rangle_{\mathcal H}=k(z,x)=k(x,z)$.

For the canonical construction, let $E_0$ be the real vector space of finitely supported functions $a:X\to\mathbb R$, write $\delta_x$ for the function supported at $x$ with value $1$, and put

$$B(a,b):=\sum_{x\in\operatorname{supp}(a)}\sum_{z\in\operatorname{supp}(b)}a(x)b(z)k(x,z).$$

Let $N:=\{a\in E_0:B(a,a)=0\}$. Under the Axiom of Countable Choice, the canonical space is formed by giving $E_0/N$ its induced inner product and taking a norm completion; the image of $\delta_x$ is denoted $k_x$. For an element $h$ of that completion, its associated function is $x\mapsto\langle h,k_x\rangle$. The quotient, completed inner product, and function identification are justified by the local construction theorem.

derivations.claim: For any finite sample $x_1,\ldots,x_m\in\mathbb R^p$ and coefficients $c_1,\ldots,c_m\in\mathbb R$, the linear Gram quadratic form is $\sum_{i,j}c_ic_jx_i^Tx_j=\|\sum_i c_ix_i\|_2^2\ge0$. Thus $k_{\rm lin}$ satisfies the nonnegative-form condition in [F1], and it is symmetric because $x^Tz=z^Tx$.

For $\alpha=(\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_p)\in\mathbb N_0^{p+1}$ with $|\alpha|=d$, define $\psi_\alpha(x)=\sqrt{d!/\alpha_0!\cdots\alpha_p!}\prod_{r=1}^p x_r^{\alpha_r}$. The multinomial theorem gives $(1+x^Tz)^d=\sum_{|\alpha|=d}\psi_\alpha(x)\psi_\alpha(z)$.

Therefore, for every finite sample and coefficients, $\sum_{i,j}c_ic_jk_d(x_i,x_j)=\sum_{|\alpha|=d}(\sum_i c_i\psi_\alpha(x_i))^2\ge0$. The polynomial kernel is symmetric and positive semidefinite by [F1].
When $p=2$ and $d=2$, the six multi-indices in [step 1.2] give $h(x)=(1,\sqrt2x_1,\sqrt2x_2,x_1^2,x_2^2,\sqrt2x_1x_2)$, so the stated feature identity holds.

derivations.claim: For each sample point put $a_i=c_i\exp(-\|x_i\|_2^2/(2\sigma^2))$. The identity $\|x_i-x_j\|_2^2=\|x_i\|_2^2+\|x_j\|_2^2-2x_i^Tx_j$ gives $\sum_{i,j}c_ic_jk_\sigma(x_i,x_j)=\sum_{i,j}a_i a_j\exp(x_i^Tx_j/\sigma^2)$.

For each fixed pair $i,j$, the exponential series has the absolutely convergent multi-index expansion $\exp(x_i^Tx_j/\sigma^2)=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^p}(x_i^\alpha x_j^\alpha)/(\sigma^{2|\alpha|}\alpha!)$, since the corresponding series of absolute values is $\prod_{r=1}^p\exp(|x_{ir}x_{jr}|/\sigma^2)<\infty$. The sample sums are finite, so they can be interchanged with this absolutely convergent series.

Substitution into [step 1.1] yields $\sum_{i,j}c_ic_jk_\sigma(x_i,x_j)=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^p}\frac{1}{\sigma^{2|\alpha|}\alpha!}(\sum_i a_ix_i^\alpha)^2\ge0$. Symmetry of $k_\sigma$ is immediate from $\|x-z\|_2=\|z-x\|_2$, so [F1] proves positive semidefiniteness; zero eigenvalues or repeated points do not affect the sum-of-squares argument.

Let $X$ be a set, let $\mathcal H$ be a real Hilbert space, and let $\phi:X\to\mathcal H$ be a feature map. Define its kernel by $k(x,z):=\langle\phi(x),\phi(z)\rangle_{\mathcal H}$. For a finite labeled sample $(x_i,y_i)_{i=1}^n$ with $n\ge1$, $x_i\in X$, and $y_i\in\{-1,+1\}$, the **soft-margin support-vector machine** with cost $C>0$ is

$$\min_{w\in\mathcal H,\ b\in\mathbb R,\ \xi\in\mathbb R^n}\ \frac12\|w\|_{\mathcal H}^2+C\sum_{i=1}^n\xi_i$$

subject to

$$y_i\bigl(\langle w,\phi(x_i)\rangle_{\mathcal H}+b\bigr)\ge1-\xi_i,\qquad \xi_i\ge0\quad(1\le i\le n).$$

The bias $b$ is unpenalized. The associated real score is $s_{w,b}(x):=\langle w,\phi(x)\rangle_{\mathcal H}+b$. If a binary label is required, use the deterministic rule $+1$ when $s_{w,b}(x)\ge0$ and $-1$ otherwise. The score is not defined as a probability, and this optimization includes no probability-calibration map.

The **hard-margin** problem removes the slack variables and minimizes $\frac12\|w\|_{\mathcal H}^2$ subject to $y_i(\langle w,\phi(x_i)\rangle_{\mathcal H}+b)\ge1$ for every $i$. In this library, “margin-separable sample” means exactly that this hard-margin feasible set is nonempty; no hard-margin conclusion is asserted for a sample that fails this condition.

For $x,z\in\mathbb R^p$ with $p\ge1$, the linear kernel $k_{\rm lin}(x,z)=x^Tz$ and, for each integer $d\ge0$, the inhomogeneous polynomial kernel $k_d(x,z)=(1+x^Tz)^d$ are positive semidefinite. When $p=2$ and $d=2$, the polynomial kernel has the explicit feature map $h(x)=(1,\sqrt2x_1,\sqrt2x_2,x_1^2,x_2^2,\sqrt2x_1x_2)$ with $k_2(x,z)=h(x)^Th(z)$.

derivations.claim: The feature map realizes the stated kernel directly: $\langle\phi(x),\phi(z)\rangle=xz=k(x,z)$; [F2] also verifies that this kernel is positive semidefinite. With $w,b\in\mathbb R$, the two hard-margin constraints are $w-b\ge1$ and $w+b\ge1$. Adding them gives $w\ge1$.
Hence every feasible objective satisfies $\frac12w^2\ge\frac12$. The candidate $w=1,b=0$ satisfies both constraints with equality and has objective $1/2$, so it attains the minimum.
For this minimizer, $s(x)=wx+b=x$. Thus the signed margins at $(-1,-1)$ and $(1,+1)$ are both $1$, as stated.

Let $n\ge1$, $C>0$, let $\mathcal H$ be a real Hilbert space, and let $\phi:X\to\mathcal H$ be a feature map with kernel $k(x,z)=\langle\phi(x),\phi(z)\rangle_{\mathcal H}$. For any finite sample $(x_i,y_i)_{i=1}^n$ with $y_i\in\{-1,+1\}$, the soft-margin SVM primal attains its minimum. Its Lagrangian dual is

$$\max_{\alpha\in\mathbb R^n}\ \sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i-\frac12\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n\alpha_i\alpha_jy_iy_jk(x_i,x_j)$$

subject to $0\le\alpha_i\le C$ for every $i$ and $\sum_i\alpha_i y_i=0$. The dual maximum is attained and equals the primal minimum. For every primal minimizer there are dual multipliers $\alpha_i$ and $\mu_i$ such that

$$w=\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i y_i\phi(x_i),\qquad \sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i y_i=0,\qquad C-\alpha_i-\mu_i=0,$$

$$\alpha_i\bigl(1-\xi_i-y_i(\langle w,\phi(x_i)\rangle+b)\bigr)=0,\qquad \mu_i\xi_i=0,$$

with $\alpha_i\ge0$ and $\mu_i\ge0$. Conversely, any primal-feasible tuple and nonnegative multipliers satisfying these stationarity and complementarity equations are globally optimal. An index with $\alpha_i>0$ is a support vector; if $0<\alpha_i<C$, then $\xi_i=0$ and its signed margin equals $1$. The single dual equality row is independent because $(y_1,\ldots,y_n)\ne0$.

For $x,z\in\mathbb R^p$ with $p\ge1$, the linear kernel $k_{\rm lin}(x,z)=x^Tz$ and, for each integer $d\ge0$, the inhomogeneous polynomial kernel $k_d(x,z)=(1+x^Tz)^d$ are positive semidefinite. derivations.claim: The feature map in [F3] realizes the stated linear kernel. At $w=0$, $b=-1$, the scores at all three observations equal $-1$. Their signed margins are respectively $1,-1,1$, so $\xi=(0,2,0)$ satisfies every soft-margin constraint, with objective $2C$.

For any feasible tuple, let $t=w+b$, the score at $x=1$. The two observations at $x=1$ require $\xi_2\ge\max(0,1-t)$ and $\xi_3\ge\max(0,1+t)$. If $-1\le t\le1$ these lower bounds sum to $2$; if $t>1$, the second is $1+t>2$; and if $t<-1$, the first is $1-t>2$. Thus $\xi_2+\xi_3\ge2$ for every feasible tuple, and its objective is at least $C(\xi_2+\xi_3)\ge2C$.

The candidate in [step 1.1] is therefore globally optimal. For $\alpha=(0,C,C)$ and $\mu=(C,0,0)$, $\sum_i\alpha_i y_i\phi(x_i)=C-C=0=w$, $\sum_i\alpha_i y_i=C-C=0$, and $C-\alpha_i-\mu_i=0$ for all three indices. Each margin constraint is active, so $\alpha_i g_i^{(m)}=0$; also $\mu_i\xi_i=0$ for each $i$. These are the KKT conditions in [F2].

The dual objective is $\sum_i\alpha_i-\frac12\|\sum_i\alpha_i y_i\phi(x_i)\|^2=2C$, equal to the primal value. The score at $x=1$ is $-1$, while the empirical positive-label frequency among the two observations at $x=1$ is $1/2$. The logistic transform of the score is $(1+e)^{-1}\ne1/2$; the SVM optimization does not assert that this transformed value is a probability.

citations.quote: Every finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space has an orthonormal basis. In dimension zero, this is the empty basis.

derivations.claim: Choose an orthonormal basis $e_1,\ldots,e_r$ of $V$ by [F1], allowing $r=0$, and set $p=\sum_{j=1}^r\langle f,e_j\rangle e_j$. For each $\ell$, orthonormality gives $\langle f-p,e_\ell\rangle=\langle f,e_\ell\rangle-\sum_{j=1}^r\langle f,e_j\rangle\langle e_j,e_\ell\rangle=0$; since the basis spans $V$, $f-p$ is orthogonal to $V$.

For any $v\in V$, $p-v\in V$ and $f-p$ is orthogonal to $V$. Expanding the squared norm of $f-v=(f-p)+(p-v)$ therefore gives $\|f-v\|^2=\|f-p\|^2+\|p-v\|^2$. If $q\in V$ also has $f-q$ orthogonal to $V$, then $p-q=(f-q)-(f-p)$ lies in $V^\perp$ and in $V$, hence $\|p-q\|^2=0$ and $p=q$. Taking $v=0$ gives the stated norm identity.

By [F2], choose an orthonormal eigenbasis $e_1,\ldots,e_n$ of $A$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_j\ge0$. In this basis, $A$ is invertible exactly when no $\lambda_j$ is zero, while $z^TAz=\sum_j\lambda_j c_j^2$ for $z=\sum_j c_je_j$ is positive for every nonzero $z$ exactly when all $\lambda_j>0$. In the same basis, $A^*A=A^2$ has eigenvalues $\lambda_j^2$. By [F4], its unique nonnegative square root has eigenvalues $\lambda_j$, so [F3] says the singular values of $A$ are precisely these $\lambda_j$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a set, let $m:T\to\mathbb R$, and let
$k:T\times T\to\mathbb R$ be symmetric and positive semidefinite, meaning that
for every finite list $t_1,\ldots,t_n\in T$ and every $a\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$\sum_{i,j=1}^n a_i a_j k(t_i,t_j)\ge0.$$
There is a unique probability measure $\mu$ on the cylinder sigma-algebra
$\mathcal C_T$ of $\mathbb R^T$ whose marginal on each finite-coordinate space
$\mathbb R^F$, for $F\subseteq T$ finite, is the Gaussian law with mean
$(m(t))_{t\in F}$ and covariance matrix $(k(s,t))_{s,t\in F}$. The coordinate
process $X_t(x)=x(t)$ is Gaussian, has mean function $m$, and has covariance
kernel $k$. This construction gives only the cylinder-space process; it
asserts no sample-path continuity, joint measurability in $(t,x)$, or tight
Banach-valued law.

$X=(X_t)_{t\in I}$ Stochastic processes and their finite-dimensional distributions
is a **Gaussian process** if, for every integer $n\ge 1$, every time list
$t_1,\ldots,t_n\in I$, and every $a_1,\ldots,a_n\in\mathbb R$, the random

symmetric positive semidefinite, and set $Y=f_X+\epsilon$. Assume the
observed covariance $C=K_{XX}+R$ is positive definite. Then a version of the
conditional law of $f_{X_*}$ given $Y=y$ is, for every $y\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$N_p\!\left(m_*+K_{*X}C^{-1}(y-m_X),\;K_{**}-K_{*X}C^{-1}K_{X*}\right).$$
The displayed conditional covariance is positive semidefinite and may be
singular; $K_{XX}$ and $K_{**}$ may also be singular. If a prediction-noise
vector $\eta_*\sim N_p(0,R_*)$ jointly independent of the process and
$\epsilon$ is added to $f_{X_*}$, with $R_*$ symmetric positive semidefinite,
the conditional mean is unchanged and
$R_*$ is added to the conditional covariance. The displayed kernel is a
version defined at every $y$; conditional-law versions are determined only
$P_Y$-almost surely.

For computation, the occurrences of $C^{-1}v$ mean solving $Cu=v$. Since
$C$ is positive definite, its Cholesky factorization and forward/back
substitution evaluate these solves without forming $C^{-1}$.

In the finite observation model, let $K=K_{XX}$ and let $R$ be symmetric and
positive semidefinite. Then $A=K+R$ is symmetric and positive semidefinite.
Its ordinary inverse exists if and only if $A$ is positive definite,
equivalently if and only if all singular values of $A$ are positive. Thus the
standard inverse formulas are defined exactly under $A\succ0$; no ordinary
inverse formula applies when $A$ is singular.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $\mathcal X$ be a set, let $m:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R$, and let
$k:\mathcal X\times\mathcal X\to\mathbb R$ be symmetric and positive
semidefinite, meaning that for every finite ordered list $t_1,\ldots,t_r$
in $\mathcal X$ and every $a\in\mathbb R^r$,
$$\sum_{i,j=1}^r a_i a_j k(t_i,t_j)\ge0.$$
For finite ordered lists $A=(a_i)_{i=1}^r$ and $B=(b_j)_{j=1}^s$ in
$\mathcal X$, define
$$K_{AB}=(k(a_i,b_j))_{i,j};$$
repeated indices are allowed.

Given a real Gaussian process $f=(f_t)_{t\in\mathcal X}$ with mean
$m(t)=\mathbb E[f_t]$ and covariance
$k(s,t)=\mathbb E[(f_s-m(s))(f_t-m(t))]$, and a nonempty finite training list
$X=(x_i)_{i=1}^n$ in $\mathcal X$, define $f_X=(f_{x_i})_{i=1}^n$ and
$m_X=(m(x_i))_{i=1}^n$. For a centered Gaussian noise vector
$\varepsilon\sim N_n(0,R)$ with symmetric positive-semidefinite covariance
$R$ that is independent of $f$, define the observation vector
$Y=f_X+\varepsilon$ and the matrix
$A_X=K_{XX}+R$.

For a nonempty finite test list $X_*=(x_j^*)_{j=1}^p$ in $\mathcal X$,
define the latent test
vector $f_*=f_{X_*}$. If a centered Gaussian vector
$\eta_*\sim N_p(0,R_*)$ with symmetric positive-semidefinite covariance
$R_*$ is independent of the pair $(f,\varepsilon)$, define the noisy test
vector $Y_*=f_*+\eta_*$.

Let $H$ be a real inner-product space and $V\subseteq H$ a finite-dimensional
subspace. For each $f\in H$ there is a unique $p\in V$ such that $f-p$ is
orthogonal to $V$, meaning $\langle f-p,v\rangle=0$ for every $v\in V$.
For every $v\in V$,
$$\|f-v\|^2=\|f-p\|^2+\|p-v\|^2.$$
In particular, $\|f\|^2=\|p\|^2+\|f-p\|^2$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be non-negative. Then there exists a unique non-negative operator
$R:V\to V$ such that

$$R^2=T.$$

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional inner product spaces and let $b\in W$. A vector $x\in V$ minimises $\lVert Tx-b\rVert$ if and only if

$$T^*(Tx-b)=0,$$

equivalently $T^*Tx=T^*b$. Minimisers exist, and if $x_0$ is one minimiser, then the full set of minimisers is $x_0+\ker T$.

Assume AC. Let $\mathcal X$ be a set, $m:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R$, and
$k:\mathcal X\times\mathcal X\to\mathbb R$ a symmetric kernel whose every
finite Gram quadratic form on points of $\mathcal X$ is nonnegative. Let
$f=(f_t)_{t\in\mathcal X}$ be the canonical Gaussian process with
$m(t)=\mathbb E[f_t]$ and
$k(s,t)=\mathbb E[(f_s-m(s))(f_t-m(t))]$. For finite ordered lists
$A=(a_i)_{i=1}^r$ and $B=(b_j)_{j=1}^s$ in $\mathcal X$, set
$K_{AB}=(k(a_i,b_j))$; repetitions are allowed. Take
$X=(x_i)_{i=1}^n\in\mathcal X^n$ and
$X_*=(x_j^*)_{j=1}^p\in\mathcal X^p$ with $n,p\ge1$, and write
$m_X=(m(x_i))$, $m_*=(m(x_j^*))$, $f_X=(f_{x_i})$, and
$f_*=(f_{x_j^*})$. Let $\varepsilon\sim N_n(0,R)$ be independent of $f$,
where $R$ is symmetric positive semidefinite, and set $Y=f_X+\varepsilon$ and
$A_X=K_{XX}+R$. Suppose $A_X$ is positive definite. Then for every
$y\in\mathbb R^n$ the conditional law of $f_*$ given $Y=y$ has mean
$$m_*+K_{*X}A_X^{-1}(y-m_X)$$
and covariance
$$K_{**}-K_{*X}A_X^{-1}K_{X*}.$$
This covariance is positive semidefinite and may be singular. If
$\eta_*\sim N_p(0,R_*)$ is independent of the pair $(f,\varepsilon)$, where
$R_*$ is symmetric positive semidefinite, then the conditional law of
$f_*+\eta_*$ has the same mean and covariance with $R_*$ added. The displayed
kernel is defined for every $y$, although regular conditional versions are
determined only $P_Y$-almost surely.

In the finite observation model, let $K=K_{XX}$ and let $R$ be symmetric and
positive semidefinite. Then $A=K+R$ is symmetric and positive semidefinite.
Its ordinary inverse exists if and only if $A$ is positive definite,
equivalently if and only if all singular values of $A$ are positive. Thus the
standard inverse formulas are defined exactly under $A\succ0$; no ordinary
inverse formula applies when $A$ is singular.

derivations.claim: Define the linear evaluation map $S:H\to\mathbb R^n$ by $(Sh)_i=h(x_i)$. It is bounded because $\lVert Sh\rVert_2^2=\sum_i|\langle h,k_{x_i}\rangle_H|^2\le\lVert h\rVert_H^2\sum_i\lVert k_{x_i}\rVert_H^2$. The reproducing identities then give its adjoint $S^*\beta=\sum_i\beta_i k_{x_i}$, since $\langle Sh,\beta\rangle=\sum_i\beta_i\langle h,k_{x_i}\rangle_H=\langle h,S^*\beta\rangle_H$. Consequently $SS^*=K$ and $V=\operatorname{ran}(S^*)=\operatorname{span}\{k_{x_i}:1\le i\le n\}$.

For every $c\in\mathbb R^n$, $c^T(K+\sigma^2I_n)c=c^TKc+\sigma^2\lVert c\rVert^2\ge\sigma^2\lVert c\rVert^2$, because $K$ is a Gram matrix of the positive-semidefinite kernel. Hence $A=K+\sigma^2I_n$ is positive definite and, by [F6], its ordinary inverse exists. Put $r=y-m_X$, $\alpha=A^{-1}r$, and $h_0=S^*\alpha$.

Write $g=m+h$, so $J(m+h)=\lVert r-Sh\rVert^2+\sigma^2\lVert h\rVert_H^2$. By [F2], each $h$ decomposes uniquely as $p+q$ with $p\in V$ and $q\perp V$. Then $Sq=0$ by the reproducing identities, and $\lVert p+q\rVert_H^2=\lVert p\rVert_H^2+\lVert q\rVert_H^2$. Thus $J(m+p+q)=J(m+p)+\sigma^2\lVert q\rVert_H^2$, so minimization reduces to $V$.

Let $B=K^{1/2}$ be supplied by [F3], and define $C:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\oplus\mathbb R^n$ by $C\beta=(K\beta,\sigma B\beta)$. For $h=S^*\beta$, its objective is $\lVert C\beta-(r,0)\rVert^2$, because $Sh=K\beta$ and $\lVert S^*\beta\rVert_H^2=\beta^TK\beta=\lVert B\beta\rVert^2$. The normal equation is $C^*C\beta=C^*(r,0)$, that is $(K^2+\sigma^2K)\beta=Kr$. Our $\alpha$ satisfies it because $(K^2+\sigma^2K)\alpha=K(K+\sigma^2I_n)\alpha=Kr$. Therefore [F4] makes $h_0$ a minimizer on $V$.

For any $d\in H$, $Sh_0-r=K\alpha-r=-\sigma^2\alpha$ and $S^*(Sh_0-r)=-\sigma^2h_0$. Expanding both squared norms and using the adjoint identity gives $J(m+h_0+d)-J(m+h_0)=\lVert Sd\rVert^2+\sigma^2\lVert d\rVert_H^2$. This is nonnegative and is zero only for $d=0$, so the minimizer is unique on all of $H$, not just on $V$.

The minimizing function is $g_*=m+h_0=m+\sum_i\alpha_i k_{x_i}$, and $S h_0=K\alpha$, giving the displayed evaluation vector. For Gaussian observations with $R=\sigma^2I_n$, [F5] at test list $X_*=X$ gives the same conditional-mean vector; $A=K+R\succ0$ by step 1.2, so its inverse hypothesis holds.

boundaries.evidence: Step 2.1 handles V={0}; the finite-span projection lemma gives p=0 and the objective still has a minimizer.
When y=m_X, step 1.2 gives r=0 and α=0, so the minimizer is g=m.
The positive shift in step 1.2 proves invertibility also when n=1.
Step 1.2 makes A positive definite even when K is singular, and step 2.3 proves uniqueness.

boundaries.evidence: Steps 1.1–2.3 are finite and choice-free; AC is needed only for the GP comparison in step 3.1.

risk_review.notes: Read all six proof steps and eight direct suppliers. Reproducing identities bound S and explicitly construct its adjoint; SS*=K. For sigma>0, K+sigma^2 I is positive definite even with repeated points or K=0. Finite-span projection handles V=0 and needs no infinite-dimensional projection theorem. B=K^(1/2) and the finite C normal equation prove existence without cancelling a possibly singular K; coefficient representations need not be unique. At X*=X the posterior supplier matches exactly, including AC and independent noise. There is a unique probability measure $\mu$ on the cylinder sigma-algebra

$(m(t))_{t\in F}$ and covariance matrix $(k(s,t))_{s,t\in F}$. The coordinate
process $X_t(x)=x(t)$ is Gaussian, has mean function $m$, and has covariance
kernel $k$. This construction gives only the cylinder-space process; it
asserts no sample-path continuity, joint measurability in $(t,x)$, or tight

derivations.claim: Cholesky factorization costs $n^3/3+O(n^2)$ by [F5]. For one test point, the posterior variance formula requires solving $A_Xu=k_{X*}$ and forming $k_{**}-k_{*X}u$. Factoring $A_X=L L^T$ reduces this to two triangular solves, each with $O(n^2)$ cost by [F5], followed by an $O(n)$ inner product. Therefore the variance calculation after factorization is $O(n^2)$.

The spectral norm of $A_\epsilon=\operatorname{diag}(1,\epsilon)$ is $1$, its smallest singular value is $\epsilon$, and therefore its spectral condition number is $1/\epsilon$. The perturbation $E=\operatorname{diag}(0,-\epsilon)$ has norm $\epsilon$, so $\lVert E\rVert_2/\lVert A_\epsilon\rVert_2=\epsilon$, while $A_\epsilon+E=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$ is singular. Thus operation counts alone do not control sensitivity to finite-precision perturbations near singularity.

The scalar kernel $k_\theta(t,t)=\theta$ is positive semidefinite for $\theta\ge0$, and the observed covariance is $A_\theta=1+\theta>0$. Apply [F1] with $m=0$ and $y=0$ to get $L(\theta)=\tfrac12\log(1+\theta)+\tfrac12\log(2\pi)$. Differentiating twice gives $L''(\theta)=-1/(2(1+\theta)^2)<0$ for every $\theta>0$, so this negative log marginal likelihood is not convex on its parameter domain.

Write $\sigma(z)=(1+e^{-z})^{-1}$; then $0<\sigma(z)<1$ for all $z$, so $\int_{\mathbb R}\phi(z)\sigma(z)\,dz$ is finite and positive. The logistic posterior is therefore a positive density whose log, up to an additive constant, is $q(z)=-z^2/2-\log(1+e^{-z})$. Differentiation gives $q'''(z)=-\sigma(z)(1-\sigma(z))(1-2\sigma(z))$. At $z=\log 3$ this equals $3/32\ne0$. A positive density on all of $\mathbb R$ cannot be a degenerate Gaussian; every nondegenerate univariate Gaussian log density is quadratic and has third derivative zero, so this posterior is not Gaussian.

Since $0<\Phi(z)<1$ for all $z$, the probit posterior normalizer $\int_{\mathbb R}\phi(z)\Phi(z)\,dz$ is finite and positive. Its positive log density, up to an additive constant, is $q(z)=-z^2/2+\log\Phi(z)$. Put $h=\phi/\Phi$ and $c=h(0)=\sqrt{2/\pi}$. Since $(\log\Phi)'=h$ and $h'=-zh-h^2$, differentiation yields $(\log\Phi)'''(0)=h''(0)=-c+2c^3=c(4/\pi-1)\ne0$; the last inequality uses $\pi<4$. A positive density on all of $\mathbb R$ cannot be a degenerate Gaussian; every nondegenerate univariate Gaussian log density is quadratic and has third derivative zero, so this posterior is not Gaussian.

Let $D=\{t_i:1\le i\le r\}$ for any finite list $t_1,\ldots,t_r\in[0,1]$. The equality kernel has Gram form $\sum_{t\in D}(\sum_{i:t_i=t}a_i)^2\ge0$. Therefore it is positive semidefinite, and by [A1, F2] it defines a cylinder-space Gaussian process with standard normal coordinates and covariance $1_{s=t}$.

For any finite list of distinct inputs in $[0,1]$, [F3] gives a centered Gaussian vector with covariance identity. By [F4] its characteristic function is $\exp(-\tfrac12\sum_i u_i^2)$, which factors into the univariate standard-normal characteristic functions; uniqueness therefore gives independent standard-normal coordinates.

Let $q_j=1/(j+2)$. If a continuous modification $G$ existed, the equalities $G_{q_j}=f_{q_j}$ for all $j$ and $G_0=f_0$ would hold simultaneously almost surely, since there are countably many coordinates. Let $E_0=\{|f_0|<1\}$, which has positive probability, and $E_j=\{|f_{q_j}|>2\}$, each of probability $p>0$ by [F2]. The finite-coordinate independence from step 2.1 gives $\Pr(E_0\cap\bigcap_{j=N}^M E_j^c)=\Pr(E_0)(1-p)^{M-N+1}$. By [F7], letting $M\to\infty$ gives $\Pr(E_0\cap\bigcap_{j=N}^\infty E_j^c)=0$ for each $N$; the countable union over $N$ then shows $E_0$ and infinitely many $E_j$ occur together with probability $\Pr(E_0)>0$. On that event $|G_0|<1$ while $|G_{q_j}|>2$ infinitely often, contradicting continuity at $0$. No continuous modification exists.

The scope distinction in [F6] concerns a Gaussian observation likelihood; the explicit logistic and probit posterior calculations in steps 1.4 and 1.5 have nonzero third derivatives and are not Gaussian. Thus the exact finite Gaussian regression formula does not give an exact Gaussian posterior for those classification models.
