Every scalar projection of a finite affine image of $W=(W_1,\ldots,W_m)$ is such a sum, so [F3] proves that every such image is multivariate normal, including when a projection has variance zero.

The chain model's density is $\phi(x)\phi(y-x)\phi(z-y)$, where $\phi$ is the standard-normal density. Its factors are exactly the parent probability kernels $K_X(dx)=N(0,1)(dx)$, $K_Y(x,dy)=N(x,1)(dy)$, and $K_Z(y,dz)=N(y,1)(dz)$, so the full-joint law factorizes in the topological order $X,Y,Z$. All three vertices are observed and [F8] gives the Markovian SCM condition. Its moments are $\operatorname{Var}(X)=1$, $\operatorname{Var}(Y)=2$, $\operatorname{Var}(Z)=3$, and distinct covariances $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=1$, $\operatorname{Cov}(Y,Z)=2$, $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Z)=1$. The vector is multivariate normal by step 1.1, and its covariance matrix is positive definite because $(X,Y,Z)$ is an invertible triangular linear transform of $(U_X,U_Y,U_Z)$. The conditional covariance formula gives $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Z\mid Y)=1-\frac{1\cdot2}{2}=0,\quad \operatorname{Cov}(X,Y\mid Z)=1-\frac{1\cdot2}{3}=\frac13,\quad \operatorname{Cov}(Y,Z\mid X)=2-\frac{1\cdot1}{1}=1.$ Together with the nonzero marginal covariances, [F4] shows that the only conditional independence between distinct variables is $X\perp Z\mid Y$. By [F10], the only d-separated vertex pair is also $X,Z$ given $Y$: the adjacent pairs have an active one-edge path, and the $X$–$Z$ path is blocked only by conditioning on $Y$. Any conditional independence between vertex sets would imply the corresponding coordinate independences, so the set-level independence and d-separation models also agree. This verifies faithfulness in [F7].

The collider model's density is $\phi(x)\phi(z)\phi(y-x-z)$. Its factors are exactly the parent probability kernels $K_X(dx)=N(0,1)(dx)$, $K_Z(dz)=N(0,1)(dz)$, and $K_Y(x,z,dy)=N(x+z,1)(dy)$, so the full-joint law factorizes in the topological order $X,Z,Y$. Its variances are $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\operatorname{Var}(Z)=1$, $\operatorname{Var}(Y)=3$, its covariances are $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\operatorname{Cov}(Z,Y)=1$, and $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Z)=0$. The vector is multivariate normal by step 1.1, and this covariance matrix is positive definite by the invertible triangular map from the exogenous variables. Fix a finite DAG $G=(V,E)$ and a specified topological ordering
$v_1,\ldots,v_n$ (every arrow points from an earlier to a later vertex).
Partition $V=O\sqcup H$ into **observed** vertices $O$ and **latent** vertices
$H$. For each $v\in V$, specify a measurable state space $(S_v,\mathcal
S_v)$, a measurable exogenous space $(E_v,\mathcal E_v)$, a jointly
measurable structural function
$$f_v:\prod_{u\in\operatorname{pa}(v)}S_u\times E_v\to S_v,$$
and an exogenous random element $U_v$ with values in $E_v$. Here
$\operatorname{pa}(v)=\{u:(u,v)\in E\}$; the empty product is a singleton.
The model is **Markovian** when the finite family $(U_v)_{v\in V}$ is mutually
independent. No parametric form or distributional truth is asserted. Correlated
disturbances may be represented by adding their common causes as latent
vertices, after which the exogenous family in the expanded model is required
to be mutually independent.

Recursion in the topological order defines the endogenous random elements
uniquely by $X_v=f_v(X_{\operatorname{pa}(v)},U_v)$. The full-joint law is the
law of $(X_v)_{v\in V}$; the observed law is its marginal law on $O$. An
observed-only DAG factorization is asserted only when $H=\varnothing$ or when
an additional stated latent-variable condition proves it.

For $I\subseteq V$ and a value $a=(a_v)_{v\in I}\in\prod_{v\in I}S_v$,
**$do(X_I=a)$** means replace only the equations indexed by $I$ by the
constants $X_v=a_v$, leaving every other structural function and every
exogenous law unchanged. Recursion then defines counterfactual values
$X_w^a$ for every vertex $w$; the interventional law is their joint law. The
response map $(a,\omega)\mapsto X_w^a(\omega)$ is jointly measurable, by
induction through the finite topological order and joint measurability of each
$f_v$. This permits evaluation at a random treatment value, such as
$X_w^{M^a}$. When $I=\{A\}$, write $X_w^a$ for the response under
$do(A=a)$. If the factual treatment is $A$, then on $\{A=a\}$ recursion
gives $X_w=X_w^a$ for every vertex $w$.

Let $V$ be a finite set of observed vertices, let $G$ be a directed acyclic graph
on $V$, and let $(X_v)_{v\in V}$ be the endogenous variables of a finite
recursive structural causal model whose observed set is all of $V$ and whose
latent set is empty. The model is Markovian: its exogenous random elements are
mutually independent. Require that the full-joint law $P$ of $(X_v)_{v\in V}$
has a topological probability-kernel factorization: for a topological order
$v_1,\ldots,v_p$, its joint law is formed by composing probability kernels
$K_{v_r}(x_{\operatorname{pa}(v_r)},dx_{v_r})$ that depend only on the parents
of $v_r$. Also require that $P$ is faithful to $G$, meaning its conditional
independences among vertex subvectors are exactly the d-separations in $G$.
Assume AC for these probability interfaces.

A **perfect conditional-independence oracle** for this regime accepts any
pairwise disjoint $A,B,S\subseteq V$ and returns “independent” exactly when
$\sigma(X_A)$ and $\sigma(X_B)$ are conditionally independent given
$\sigma(X_S)$. The **causally sufficient perfect-oracle regime** consists of
the finite observed DAG, its Markovian recursive model and full-joint law, the
faithfulness condition, and this exact oracle. No latent vertex is omitted
from the graph supplied to the oracle.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
Independent sigma-algebras and independent events.

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from The sigma-algebra generated by a function.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By The standard normal density has total mass one and The indefinite integral of a nonnegative measurable function is a measure, gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. The law of a random element is a probability measure makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in The Dirac set function at a point.

For real $a,b,t$, $\varphi_{aX+b}(t)=e^{itb}\varphi_X(at)$. For a finite mutually independent family $(X_j)_{j=1}^n$ of real random variables, $\varphi_{\sum_jX_j}(t)=\prod_j\varphi_{X_j}(t)$. The empty sum has characteristic function one.

Assume AC. If $X$ has law $N(m,\sigma^2)$ with $\sigma\ge0$, then $\varphi_X(t)=\exp(imt-\sigma^2t^2/2)$ for every real $t$. Moreover $\mathbb EX=m$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\sigma^2$, including $\sigma=0$.

Assume AC. Two Borel probability laws on $\mathbb R$ with equal characteristic functions are equal. In particular a real random variable has a real-valued characteristic function if and only if its law is symmetric under $x\mapsto-x$.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume AC. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then $$\Phi_X(t):=\mathbb E e^{it\cdot X}=\exp(it\cdot m-t^T\Sigma t/2)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R^d).$$ This transform uniquely determines the law, including singular Sigma.

Two finite DAGs on the same vertex set are Markov equivalent, meaning that they
induce the same d-separation relations, if and only if they have the same
skeleton and the same unshielded colliders.

Fix a finite vertex set $V$. For a DAG $G$ on $V$, its **skeleton** is the
undirected graph with edge $\{i,j\}$ exactly when $G$ contains $i\to j$ or
$j\to i$. An **unshielded triple** is a triple of distinct vertices $i,k,j$
with edges $i-k$ and $k-j$ in the skeleton and no edge between $i$ and $j$.
It is an **unshielded collider** (also called a v-structure) when its arrows are
$i\to k\leftarrow j$. Two DAGs on $V$ are **Markov equivalent** when they
induce the same d-separation relations: for every pairwise disjoint
$A,B,S\subseteq V$, $A$ and $B$ are d-separated by $S$ in one DAG exactly
when they are d-separated by $S$ in the other. The equivalence class of $G$ is
denoted $[G]$.

A **partially directed acyclic graph** (PDAG) on $V$ is a simple mixed graph
whose directed edges contain no directed cycle. A **consistent DAG extension**
of a PDAG preserves every directed edge, orients every undirected edge, is
acyclic, and creates no unshielded collider absent from the PDAG. For an
equivalence class with a common skeleton, its **completed pattern** directs an
edge exactly when that orientation occurs in every DAG of the class and leaves
the edge undirected when both orientations occur. A **completed partially
directed acyclic graph** (CPDAG) for $[G]$ is this unique completed pattern
when its consistent DAG extensions are exactly $[G]$. Thus its directed edges
are compelled, while each undirected edge occurs in both directions among its
consistent extensions.

**Input:** A finite vertex set $V$, a perfect conditional-independence oracle
for a law in the causally sufficient discovery regime, and a fixed total order
of $V$. For every adjacent pair and conditioning set $S$ tested below, the
oracle returns whether $X_i$ and $X_j$ are conditionally independent given
$X_S$.

**Output:** An undirected skeleton $C$, a separator record $\operatorname{Sep}(i,j)$
for each deleted edge, and a partially directed graph $P$.

1. Initialize $C$ to the complete undirected graph on $V$ and set the level
$\ell=0$.

2. In the fixed lexicographic order of unordered vertex pairs, process each
pair $i-j$ that is still an edge of $C$. First test every $\ell$-element
subset of $\operatorname{Adj}_C(i)\setminus\{j\}$ in lexicographic order;
then test every $\ell$-element subset of
$\operatorname{Adj}_C(j)\setminus\{i\}$ in lexicographic order. On the first
oracle result of conditional independence given a tested set $S$, delete
$i-j$, record $\operatorname{Sep}(i,j)=\operatorname{Sep}(j,i)=S$, and do
not test that pair again. If no set separates the pair, leave it adjacent.
Adjacency sets are read from the current graph, including deletions already
made at level $\ell$.

3. If at least one remaining edge has an endpoint with at least $\ell+1$
neighbors other than the other endpoint, increment $\ell$ and repeat step 2.
Otherwise stop the skeleton search.

4. Copy the completed skeleton $C$ to a separate graph $P$. For each
unshielded triple $i-k-j$ in $C$, orient its incident edges in $P$ as
$i\to k\leftarrow j$ exactly when $k\notin\operatorname{Sep}(i,j)$,
retaining any orientations already made. Keep $C$ unchanged.

5. Repeatedly orient edges of $P$ to closure under the following background-free rules,
using fixed lexicographic order on rule instances:

   - **R1:** If $i\to j-k$ and $i,k$ are nonadjacent, orient $j-k$ as $j\to k$.
   - **R2:** If $i-j$ is undirected and $i\to k\to j$, orient $i-j$ as $i\to j$.
   - **R3:** If $i-j$, $i-k$, and $i-\ell$ are undirected, $k\to j$,
     $\ell\to j$, and $k,\ell$ are nonadjacent, orient $i-j$ as $i\to j$.

Do not apply a background-knowledge rule. Return $C$, the separator record,
and $P$.

Every scalar projection of a finite affine image of $W=(W_1,\ldots,W_m)$ is such a sum, so [F4] proves that every such image is multivariate normal, including when a projection has variance zero.

In the latent model, $\mathbb E(X,Y)=(0,0)$, $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\operatorname{Var}(Y)=2$, and $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=1$, by independence of $L,U_X,U_Y$. In the direct-edge model, $\mathbb E(X,Y)=(0,0)$, $\operatorname{Var}(X)=2$, $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\tfrac12\operatorname{Var}(X)=1$, and $\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\tfrac14(2)+\tfrac32=2$. Both vectors are Gaussian by step 1.1 and have the same positive-definite covariance matrix $\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$, whose leading principal minors are $2$ and $3$. By [F5], both vector characteristic functions equal $\exp(-t^T\Sigma t/2)$ for every $t\in\mathbb R^2$; the uniqueness clause of [F5] gives equality of the full observed laws.

The latent model is a finite recursive Markovian SCM with observed set $\{X,Y\}$ and omitted latent vertex $L$, so it does not satisfy [F2]. The direct-edge model has observed set $\{X,Y\}$ and independent exogenous variables; its full-joint law factors as $N(0,2)(dx)N(x/2,3/2)(dy)$, the root probability kernel for $X$ followed by the probability kernel for $Y$ given its parent $X$. In its two-vertex graph $X\to Y$, the only pair of nonempty disjoint endpoint sets is $\{X\},\{Y\}$, which is not d-separated because of the direct path; step 2.1 gives $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=1$, so they are not independent. Thus this law is faithful to the direct-edge DAG, and the direct-edge model satisfies the observed-only Markovian factorization and faithfulness conditions in the discovery regime. Since the observed laws agree by step 2.1, no procedure using only that law can distinguish the two causal explanations.

The common observed law has $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=1\ne0$, so $X,Y$ are dependent and the perfect oracle does not delete their only edge. With only two vertices there is no unshielded triple and none of R1–R3 applies; by [F9] the regime-compliant run terminates, and its computed output is $X-Y$. Reversing the single edge in the direct-edge DAG keeps the same skeleton and no unshielded collider, so [F6] proves the reverse DAG is equivalent; [F7] therefore gives the same undirected CPDAG. The PC output reports adjacency but cannot recover the latent-versus-direct causal distinction.

citations.quote:
A **finite directed acyclic graph** (DAG) is a finite vertex set $V$ with an
arrow set $E\subseteq V\times V$ and no directed cycle. A **path** from $u$ to
$v$ is a finite sequence of distinct vertices beginning at $u$ and ending at
$v$ in which each consecutive pair is joined by an arrow in either direction;
the arrows are not required to point along the sequence. An internal vertex of
a path is a **collider on that path** when the two arrows on the path both point
into it, and is a **noncollider** otherwise. A vertex $w$ is a **descendant** of
$v$ if there is a directed path from $v$ to $w$; for this definition
$\operatorname{De}^+(v)$ includes $v$ itself as well as its descendants.

For pairwise disjoint vertex sets $X,Y,C\subseteq V$, a path joining $X$ to
$Y$ is **active given $C$** when every internal noncollider is outside $C$ and
every internal collider has at least one member of $\operatorname{De}^+(v)$ in
$C$. The set $C$ **d-separates** $X$ and $Y$ in $G$ when no path joining $X$ to
$Y$ is active given $C$; write $X\perp_d Y\mid C$ in $G$. The empty set of
vertices is allowed for any of $X,Y,C$; in particular d-separation is vacuous
if either endpoint set is empty.

For $T\subseteq V$, $G_{\underline T}$ is obtained by deleting every arrow
whose tail lies in $T$, and $G_{\overline T}$ by deleting every arrow whose
head lies in $T$. These are graph operations only; they do not by themselves
specify a probability law under intervention.

Two finite DAGs on the same vertex set are Markov equivalent, meaning that they
induce the same d-separation relations, if and only if they have the same
skeleton and the same unshielded colliders.

Fix a finite vertex set $V$. For a DAG $G$ on $V$, its **skeleton** is the
undirected graph with edge $\{i,j\}$ exactly when $G$ contains $i\to j$ or
$j\to i$. An **unshielded triple** is a triple of distinct vertices $i,k,j$
with edges $i-k$ and $k-j$ in the skeleton and no edge between $i$ and $j$.
It is an **unshielded collider** (also called a v-structure) when its arrows are
$i\to k\leftarrow j$. Two DAGs on $V$ are **Markov equivalent** when they
induce the same d-separation relations: for every pairwise disjoint
$A,B,S\subseteq V$, $A$ and $B$ are d-separated by $S$ in one DAG exactly
when they are d-separated by $S$ in the other. The equivalence class of $G$ is
denoted $[G]$.

A **partially directed acyclic graph** (PDAG) on $V$ is a simple mixed graph
whose directed edges contain no directed cycle. A **consistent DAG extension**
of a PDAG preserves every directed edge, orients every undirected edge, is
acyclic, and creates no unshielded collider absent from the PDAG. For an
equivalence class with a common skeleton, its **completed pattern** directs an
edge exactly when that orientation occurs in every DAG of the class and leaves
the edge undirected when both orientations occur. A **completed partially
directed acyclic graph** (CPDAG) for $[G]$ is this unique completed pattern
when its consistent DAG extensions are exactly $[G]$. Thus its directed edges
are compelled, while each undirected edge occurs in both directions among its
consistent extensions.

**Input:** A finite vertex set $V$, a perfect conditional-independence oracle
for a law in the causally sufficient discovery regime, and a fixed total order
of $V$. For every adjacent pair and conditioning set $S$ tested below, the
oracle returns whether $X_i$ and $X_j$ are conditionally independent given
$X_S$.

**Output:** An undirected skeleton $C$, a separator record $\operatorname{Sep}(i,j)$
for each deleted edge, and a partially directed graph $P$.

1. Initialize $C$ to the complete undirected graph on $V$ and set the level
$\ell=0$.

2. In the fixed lexicographic order of unordered vertex pairs, process each
pair $i-j$ that is still an edge of $C$. First test every $\ell$-element
subset of $\operatorname{Adj}_C(i)\setminus\{j\}$ in lexicographic order;
then test every $\ell$-element subset of
$\operatorname{Adj}_C(j)\setminus\{i\}$ in lexicographic order. On the first
oracle result of conditional independence given a tested set $S$, delete
$i-j$, record $\operatorname{Sep}(i,j)=\operatorname{Sep}(j,i)=S$, and do
not test that pair again. If no set separates the pair, leave it adjacent.
Adjacency sets are read from the current graph, including deletions already
made at level $\ell$.

3. If at least one remaining edge has an endpoint with at least $\ell+1$
neighbors other than the other endpoint, increment $\ell$ and repeat step 2.
Otherwise stop the skeleton search.

4. Copy the completed skeleton $C$ to a separate graph $P$. For each
unshielded triple $i-k-j$ in $C$, orient its incident edges in $P$ as
$i\to k\leftarrow j$ exactly when $k\notin\operatorname{Sep}(i,j)$,
retaining any orientations already made. Keep $C$ unchanged.

5. Repeatedly orient edges of $P$ to closure under the following background-free rules,
using fixed lexicographic order on rule instances:

   - **R1:** If $i\to j-k$ and $i,k$ are nonadjacent, orient $j-k$ as $j\to k$.
   - **R2:** If $i-j$ is undirected and $i\to k\to j$, orient $i-j$ as $i\to j$.
   - **R3:** If $i-j$, $i-k$, and $i-\ell$ are undirected, $k\to j$,
     $\ell\to j$, and $k,\ell$ are nonadjacent, orient $i-j$ as $i\to j$.

Do not apply a background-knowledge rule. Return $C$, the separator record,
and $P$.

Let $G$ be a finite DAG. Start with its skeleton, orient exactly the edges in
its unshielded colliders, and leave all other edges undirected. Repeatedly apply
the background-free rules R1–R3 from the PC algorithm until no rule applies.
The resulting partially directed graph is the CPDAG for the Markov-equivalence
class of $G$.

Let $V$ be a finite set of observed vertices, let $G$ be a directed acyclic graph
on $V$, and let $(X_v)_{v\in V}$ be the endogenous variables of a finite
recursive structural causal model whose observed set is all of $V$ and whose
latent set is empty. The model is Markovian: its exogenous random elements are
mutually independent. Require that the full-joint law $P$ of $(X_v)_{v\in V}$
has a topological probability-kernel factorization: for a topological order
$v_1,\ldots,v_p$, its joint law is formed by composing probability kernels
$K_{v_r}(x_{\operatorname{pa}(v_r)},dx_{v_r})$ that depend only on the parents
of $v_r$. Also require that $P$ is faithful to $G$, meaning its conditional
independences among vertex subvectors are exactly the d-separations in $G$.
Assume AC for these probability interfaces.

A **perfect conditional-independence oracle** for this regime accepts any
pairwise disjoint $A,B,S\subseteq V$ and returns “independent” exactly when
$\sigma(X_A)$ and $\sigma(X_B)$ are conditionally independent given
$\sigma(X_S)$. The **causally sufficient perfect-oracle regime** consists of
the finite observed DAG, its Markovian recursive model and full-joint law, the
faithfulness condition, and this exact oracle. No latent vertex is omitted
from the graph supplied to the oracle.

citations.quote: A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ (Measures on sigma-algebras). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** (Measure spaces); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $n\ge 1$, let $E\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, and let $a\in\mathbb R^n$ (The Euclidean inner product $\langle x,y\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k y_k$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$). The **translate** of $E$ by $a$ is

$$E+a:=\{x+a:x\in E\}.$$

Translation by $a$ is the bijection $\tau_a(x)=x+a$, whose inverse is $\tau_{-a}$. In particular, $\varnothing+a=\varnothing$.

A **Dedekind-complete ordered field** is a commutative field $\mathbb R$ with
identity $1>0$, a total order compatible with addition and multiplication, and
the least-upper-bound axiom: every nonempty subset of $\mathbb R$ that is
bounded above has a least upper bound in $\mathbb R$. Throughout this batch,
all real variables, intervals, limits, derivatives and integrals are taken in
such a field. The integers and rationals are interpreted in their usual
embedded copies. For $x\in\mathbb R$, define $|x|=x$ when $x\ge0$ and
$|x|=-x$ when $x<0$.

Every complete ordered field $F$ (Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property)) is Archimedean:
for every $x \in F$ there is a natural number $n \ge 1$ with $x < n \cdot 1_F$,
where $n \cdot 1_F$ is the canonical natural of the ordered field $F$
(Ordered field). Equivalently, the canonical naturals are cofinal in $F$.

If $c>0$, choose a natural $n>1/c$ by [F3]. The first $n$ intervals are disjoint, so finite additivity gives $1\ge\mu(\bigcup_{k=0}^{n-1}I_k)=nc>1$, a contradiction. Hence $c=0$.
Countable additivity over the partition $(I_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z}$ now gives $1=\mu(\mathbb R)=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\mu(I_k)=0$, again a contradiction. Therefore $a=0$.

Let $n \ge 1$, let $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and let $E + h$ be the translate of
$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ (Translation of a subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$). Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(E+h) = \lambda_n^*(E)$ for **every** subset $E$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $E+h$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(E+h) = \lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

**No choice principle is used.** Lebesgue outer measure is defined as an infimum
and the Carathéodory condition is a family of equations between its values, so
all three clauses are statements about objects that exist in ZF; countable
choice is needed to know that $\lambda_n$ is a measure, not to know that it is
translation invariant.

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim: The coordinate change $(y,c)\mapsto(r,c)=(y-m(c),c)$ is a translation in each fixed $c$-section. By [F1] and iterated integration [F3], the law of $(R,C)$ has density $h(r,c)=p(r+m(c),c)$. Since $p$ and $m$ are $C^3$ and $p>0$, $h$ is a strictly positive $C^3$ function.

Independence and [F2] make the law with density $h(r,c)$ from step 1.1 the product of the marginal laws of $R$ and $C$. Tonelli [F3] gives marginal density versions, and therefore $h(r,c)=q_R(r)p_C(c)$ almost everywhere. Choose $c_0$ for which $0<p_C(c_0)<\infty$ and this equality holds for almost every $r$. Then $q_R(r)=h(r,c_0)/p_C(c_0)$ almost everywhere, so this formula supplies a strictly positive $C^3$ version of $q_R$.

By Fubini choose $r_0$ with $q_R(r_0)>0$ such that $h(r_0,c)=q_R(r_0)p_C(c)$ for almost every $c$. Set $p_C^*(c)=h(r_0,c)/q_R(r_0)$. This is a strictly positive $C^3$ function and equals $p_C$ almost everywhere. Thus $h(r,c)=q_R(r)p_C^*(c)$ almost everywhere; both sides are continuous, so the equality holds everywhere.
Substituting $r=y-m(c)$ into step 3.1 yields $p(y,c)=q_R(y-m(c))p_C^*(c)$ for every $(y,c)$. Renaming $p_C^*$ as $p_C$ proves the Statement.

Fix a nonempty finite directed acyclic graph $G=(V,E)$ with a specified
topological order $v_1,\ldots,v_p$; every arrow points from an earlier to a
later vertex. For $j\in V$, let
$\operatorname{pa}(j)=\{i\in V:(i,j)\in E\}$ be its parent set, and let
$\operatorname{nd}(j)$ be the vertices other than $j$ that are not descendants
of $j$. A **continuous additive-noise model** on $G$ consists of real random
variables $X_j,N_j$ on a common probability space and continuous Borel
functions $f_j:\mathbb R^{\operatorname{pa}(j)}\to\mathbb R$ such that
$$X_j=f_j(X_{\operatorname{pa}(j)})+N_j$$
recursively in the topological order. The finite family of noises is mutually
independent, and each $N_j$ has a strictly positive Lebesgue density $q_j$.
All vertices of $G$ are observed; no latent vertices are omitted from the
model. The **observational law** is the law of the vector
$X=(X_j)_{j\in V}$.

The model is **causally minimal** when every parent input is essential: for
each edge $i\to j$, there are values of the other parent coordinates and two
distinct real values of the $i$-coordinate at which $f_j$ takes different
values. A root has no parent-coordinate minimality condition.

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. The **measure with density $f$ relative
to $\mu$** is the measure
$$f\,d\mu:\mathcal A\to[0,+\infty],\qquad (f\,d\mu)(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu,$$
whose measure property is supplied by
The indefinite integral of a nonnegative measurable function is a measure.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   The product measure of two sigma-finite measure spaces is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $n \ge 1$, let $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and let $E + h$ be the translate of
$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ (Translation of a subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$). Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(E+h) = \lambda_n^*(E)$ for **every** subset $E$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $E+h$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(E+h) = \lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

**No choice principle is used.** Lebesgue outer measure is defined as an infimum
and the Carathéodory condition is a family of equations between its values, so
all three clauses are statements about objects that exist in ZF; countable
choice is needed to know that $\lambda_n$ is a measure, not to know that it is
translation invariant.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space and let
$f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ be measurable for the Borel sigma-algebra on
the extended real line. Products of functions use
$\odot_X$ from A total pointwise product for extended-real-valued functions, and $cf$
abbreviates $\underline c\odot_X f$ for the constant function $\underline c$.
The magnitude function is $|f|=\max(f,-f)$ as in
The positive and negative parts of a function. Then:

1. $cf$ is measurable for every real scalar $c$;
2. $\max(f,g)$, $\min(f,g)$, $|f|$, $f^+$, and $f^-$ are measurable;
3. if the partial pointwise sum $f+g$ is defined at every point, then it is measurable;
4. the pointwise product $fg:=f\odot_X g$ is measurable.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$, $(Y,\mathcal{B})$, and $(Z,\mathcal{C})$ be measurable
spaces. If $f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Y,\mathcal{B})$ is measurable and
$g : (Y,\mathcal{B}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable, then
$g \circ f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable.

In particular, if $f$ is measurable and $g$ is a Borel measurable function on
its codomain, then $g \circ f$ is measurable.

Let $m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
one has
$$\mathcal B(\mathbb R^m)\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n) = \mathcal B(\mathbb R^{m+n}).$$

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Write $\beta_n$ for the restriction of $\lambda_n$ to
the Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n)$
([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). Then $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is exactly the
completion domain of $(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n), \beta_n)$
([[def-completion-of-a-measure-space]]), and $\lambda_n$ is the completed measure
there. Explicitly,

$$E \in \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n) \iff E = A\cup N \text{ for some } A, Z \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n) \text{ with } N \subseteq Z \text{ and } \beta_n(Z) = 0,$$

and then $\lambda_n(E) = \beta_n(A)$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $(X,\mathcal{A}_0,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$(X,\overline{\mathcal{A}_0},\overline{\mu})$ be its completion. If
$f : X \to \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ is measurable with respect to
$\overline{\mathcal{A}_0}$, then there is an $\mathcal{A}_0$-measurable function
$g : X \to \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ such that $f=g$ almost everywhere.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, and let $(X,\overline{\mathcal A},\overline\mu)$ be its completion construction. Then $\overline\mu$ is a complete measure on $\overline{\mathcal A}$ extending $\mu$. It is the unique complete measure on $\overline{\mathcal A}$ that extends $\mu$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: First suppose every $q_j$ is Borel measurable. For each $j$, let $Q_j=q_j\,d\lambda$ on Borel sets; [F1, F3] makes $Q_j$ a probability measure. The function $g(n)=\prod_{r=1}^p q_{v_r}(n_{v_r})$ is Borel, hence product-measurable, by [F7, F8]. Repeated Tonelli gives $\int g\,d\rho=1$ and, on every Borel rectangle, $\int_{\prod B_j}g\,d\rho=\prod_j Q_j(B_j)$. Uniqueness of product measures identifies this Borel density measure with the joint law of the independent noises.

Recursion in topological order defines a Borel map $T:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R^p$ from the noise vector to $X$. Its inverse has coordinates $n_j=x_j-f_j(x_{\operatorname{pa}(j)})$, so the observational law is the Borel pushforward under $T$.

Start from step 1.1 and change one coordinate at a time in topological order. With earlier endogenous coordinates fixed, $x_{v_r}=n_{v_r}+f_{v_r}(x_{\operatorname{pa}(v_r)})$ is a fixed translation. Translation invariance changes its density factor to $q_{v_r}(x_{v_r}-f_{v_r}(x_{\operatorname{pa}(v_r)}))$. Every intermediate integrand for a nonnegative Borel test function is product-measurable by [F7, F8], so Tonelli justifies the successive one-dimensional substitutions. The resulting identity $\mathbb E[h(X)]=\int h(x)p_X(x)\,d\rho(x)$ for every nonnegative Borel $h$ proves the density assertion on Borel sets. The product is Borel and strictly positive. No choice principle was used in this case.

Now assume Countable Choice and allow arbitrary Lebesgue-measurable $q_j$. By [F9] choose Borel representatives, replace their values outside $(0,\infty)$ by $1$, and call the resulting functions $\bar q_j$. Since each original density is positive and finite almost everywhere, this changes it only on a null set and preserves its integral and noise law. Choose a Borel null hull $Z_j$ of $\{q_j\ne\bar q_j\}$. These are only finitely many applications of [F9]. Step 2.1 applied to $\bar q_j$ gives the positive Borel density $\bar p_X$ relative to $\rho$.

For each $j$, let $E_j=\{x:x_j-f_j(x_{\operatorname{pa}(j)})\in Z_j\}$. It is Borel by [F8]. With all coordinates except $x_j$ fixed, its $x_j$-section is a translate of $Z_j$ and has measure zero by [F6]; for $p>1$, Tonelli gives $\rho(E_j)=0$, and for $p=1$ this follows directly from translation invariance. Off the finite union $E=\bigcup_jE_j$, the products $p_X$ and $\bar p_X$ agree. Completeness [F10] therefore makes $p_X$ measurable for $\bar\rho$, with the same integral on every completed measurable set as $\bar p_X$. Every original factor is positive, proving strict positivity as well.

In the Countable Choice case, the density measures in steps 2.1 and 4.1 extend the Borel observational law. To see uniqueness among absolutely continuous extensions, first note that every product-measurable set differs from a Borel set by a subset of a Borel $\rho$-null set: the sets with this property form a sigma-algebra under Countable Choice and contain every Lebesgue rectangle by [F9]; Borel null coordinate slabs have product measure zero by Tonelli. A product-null set has a Borel null hull by the same representation, so every $\bar\rho$-measurable set has such a representation too. Any absolutely continuous extension assigns zero to the exceptional set and is determined by the Borel core. Thus the stated extensions and both density conclusions hold.

derivations.claim: For each $k\in S$, define $A_k$ to be $k$ together with all vertices having a directed path to $k$, and put $A=\bigcup_{k\in S}A_k$. Let a finite additive-noise model have topological order $v_1,\ldots,v_p$,
equations $X_j=f_j(X_{\operatorname{pa}(j)})+N_j$, and strictly positive
Lebesgue densities $q_j$ for its mutually independent noises. Write
$\rho=\lambda^{\otimes p}$ for the finite product of one-dimensional Lebesgue
measure. If all $q_j$ are Borel measurable, the observational law has the
strictly positive Borel density
$$p_X(x)=\prod_{r=1}^p q_{v_r}\!\left(x_{v_r}-f_{v_r}(x_{\operatorname{pa}(v_r)})\right)$$
with respect to $\rho$ on Borel sets.

For arbitrary Lebesgue-measurable $q_j$, assume Countable Choice. There are
strictly positive finite Borel density versions $\bar q_j=q_j$ almost
everywhere. Their product
$$\bar p_X(x)=\prod_{r=1}^p \bar q_{v_r}\!\left(x_{v_r}-f_{v_r}(x_{\operatorname{pa}(v_r)})\right)$$
is a strictly positive Borel density with respect to $\rho$. The original
product $p_X$ is measurable for the completion $\bar\rho$ of $\rho$, agrees
with $\bar p_X$ $\bar\rho$-almost everywhere, and is a strictly positive
density with respect to $\bar\rho$. In this Countable Choice case, on non-Borel sets these density measures
refer to the unique absolutely continuous extensions of the Borel
observational law to the indicated sigma-algebras.

Fix a nonempty finite directed acyclic graph $G=(V,E)$ with a specified
topological order $v_1,\ldots,v_p$; every arrow points from an earlier to a
later vertex. For $j\in V$, let
$\operatorname{pa}(j)=\{i\in V:(i,j)\in E\}$ be its parent set, and let
$\operatorname{nd}(j)$ be the vertices other than $j$ that are not descendants
of $j$. A **continuous additive-noise model** on $G$ consists of real random
variables $X_j,N_j$ on a common probability space and continuous Borel
functions $f_j:\mathbb R^{\operatorname{pa}(j)}\to\mathbb R$ such that
$$X_j=f_j(X_{\operatorname{pa}(j)})+N_j$$
recursively in the topological order. The finite family of noises is mutually
independent, and each $N_j$ has a strictly positive Lebesgue density $q_j$.
All vertices of $G$ are observed; no latent vertices are omitted from the
model. The **observational law** is the law of the vector
$X=(X_j)_{j\in V}$.

The model is **causally minimal** when every parent input is essential: for
each edge $i\to j$, there are values of the other parent coordinates and two
distinct real values of the $i$-coordinate at which $f_j$ takes different
values. A root has no parent-coordinate minimality condition.

Let $n \ge 1$, let $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and let $E + h$ be the translate of
$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ (Translation of a subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$). Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(E+h) = \lambda_n^*(E)$ for **every** subset $E$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $E+h$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(E+h) = \lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

**No choice principle is used.** Lebesgue outer measure is defined as an infimum
and the Carathéodory condition is a family of equations between its values, so
all three clauses are statements about objects that exist in ZF; countable
choice is needed to know that $\lambda_n$ is a measure, not to know that it is
translation invariant.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

For disjoint $X,Y,C\subseteq V$, $C$ d-separates $X$ and $Y$ in $G$ if and
only if deleting $C$ from $\operatorname{mor}_G(X\cup Y\cup C)$ leaves no
undirected path from $X$ to $Y$.

For $S\subseteq V$, its **ancestral set** is
$$\operatorname{An}_G(S):=\{v\in V:\text{there is a directed path from }v\text{ to some }s\in S\},$$
where paths of length zero are allowed, so $S\subseteq\operatorname{An}_G(S)$.
The induced directed subgraph on this set keeps exactly the arrows of $G$
whose two endpoints lie in $\operatorname{An}_G(S)$. Its **moral graph** is
the undirected simple graph obtained by replacing every arrow by an
undirected edge and joining every distinct pair of parents of a common child
by an undirected edge; loops and duplicate edges are discarded. This
undirected graph is the **ancestral moral graph** on $S$ and is denoted
$\operatorname{mor}_G(S)$.

derivations.claim: For Borel noise densities use the displayed product. Otherwise [F1] supplies positive finite Borel versions under the assumed Countable Choice; use their Borel product throughout the integrations below. It has the same observational law, and its marginal densities agree almost everywhere with the stipulated marginal versions, so the final almost-everywhere identity transfers to those versions. Put $H=\operatorname{An}_G(A\cup B\cup C)$. No vertex outside $H$ is a parent of a vertex in $H$, since that would make it an ancestor of $A\cup B\cup C$. Integrate the product density [F1] over $V\setminus H$ in reverse topological order. At each elimination, all child factors have already been integrated and no child lies in $H$, so the only remaining factor involving the current coordinate $x_v$ is $q_v(x_v-f_v(x_{\operatorname{pa}(v)}))$. Its section integral is one by [F2]. Tonelli [F3] justifies each section integral; consequently the marginal density on $H$ is $\prod_{v\in H}q_v(x_v-f_v(x_{\operatorname{pa}(v)}))$.

By [F4], deleting $C$ from the moral graph on $H$ leaves no path from $A$ to $B$. Partition its connected components into $L$, the union of components meeting $A$, and $R$, the union of the remaining components. Then $A\subseteq L$, $B\subseteq R$, and there is no moral edge between $L$ and $R$. For each $v\in H$, the factor indexed by $v$ in step 1.1 depends only on $\{v\}\cup\operatorname{pa}(v)\subseteq H$; this set is a clique in that moral graph by [F5]. Hence no such factor involves both an $L$-coordinate and an $R$-coordinate. Assign factors involving an $L$-coordinate to $U$, and assign all other factors to $W$. Their finite products give a factorization of the density on $H$ as $U(x_L,x_C)W(x_R,x_C)$.

Integrate the factorization in step 2.1 over the hidden coordinates $L\setminus A$ and $R\setminus B$. Since the factors separate and are nonnegative, Tonelli [F3] yields measurable functions $u(x_A,x_C)$ and $w(x_B,x_C)$ such that $p_{A\cup B\cup C}(x_A,x_B,x_C)=u(x_A,x_C)w(x_B,x_C)$ almost everywhere. Each function is strictly positive because it integrates a strictly positive factor over its hidden coordinates; if that coordinate set is empty, it is the original strictly positive factor.

Define $\alpha(x_C)=\int u(x_A,x_C)\,dx_A$ and $\beta(x_C)=\int w(x_B,x_C)\,dx_B$. Tonelli makes these measurable and gives $p_{A\cup C}=u\beta$ and $p_{B\cup C}=w\alpha$ almost everywhere. Also $p_C(x_C)=\int u(x_A,x_C)w(x_B,x_C)\,dx_A dx_B$ for almost every $x_C$. The marginal $p_C$ is positive, since it integrates the everywhere-positive density over any unit box in the remaining coordinates, and it is finite almost everywhere since $\int p_C=1$. For almost every such $x_C$, strict positivity of $u,w$ gives $\alpha,\beta>0$. If, for example, $\alpha=\infty$, then $\beta>0$ supplies a set of $b$-values of positive measure where $w(b,x_C)>1/n$ for some $n$, so Tonelli makes $\int u(a,x_C)w(b,x_C)\,da\,db=\infty$; the same argument applies if $\beta=\infty$. Hence both integrals are finite almost everywhere, Tonelli factors the last integral as $p_C=\alpha\beta$, and multiplying the finite marginal identities gives the claimed conditional-density factorization.

derivations.claim: Use the supplied Borel noise densities, or their positive finite Borel versions from [F2] under Countable Choice. Work with their Borel shifted-noise product and its integrated marginals; changing density versions does not change an almost-everywhere conditional-independence factorization. Every variable in $\{i\}\cup P\cup Q$ is a nondescendant of $j$. By [F3], $N_j$ is independent of the vector $(X_i,X_P,X_Q)$. Conditional on $(X_i=x,X_P=p,X_Q=q)$, the structural equation therefore gives the density $p_{X_j\mid X_i,X_P,X_Q}(y\mid x,p,q)=q_j(y-f_j(p,x))$ for almost every $(x,p,q,y)$. This density does not depend on $q$, so the joint conditional density of $(X_j,X_Q)$ given $(X_i,X_P)$ factors; hence $X_j\perp_d X_Q\mid(X_i,X_P)$.

Suppose, for contradiction, that $X_j\perp_d X_i\mid X_P$. Since $N_j$ is independent of the parent vector $(X_i,X_P)$, its conditional density is $q_j(y-f_j(p,x))$. The assumed factorization says this density is independent of $x$ for almost every $p$ and almost every $x$. The conditional density of $X_i$ given $X_P=p$ is positive for almost every $x$ at almost every $p$ with $0<p_P(p)<\infty$, because the full joint density is strictly positive. Therefore, for almost every such $p$, for almost every pair $x,x'$, the two translates $q_j(y-f_j(p,x))$ and $q_j(y-f_j(p,x'))$ agree for almost every $y$.

A positive integrable density cannot have a nonzero period: if $q_j(y-a)=q_j(y-b)$ almost everywhere with $a\ne b$, then $q_j$ repeats on every translate of an interval of length $|a-b|$; that interval has positive integral, so the integral over the disjoint translates is infinite, contradicting $\int q_j=1$. Thus step 1.2 forces $f_j(p,x)=f_j(p,x')$ for almost every pair $x,x'$ and almost every $p$. Continuity of $f_j$ extends this constancy to every setting of the other parent coordinates: any two unequal values would persist on open neighborhoods of positive Lebesgue measure. This contradicts [F1], so $X_j\not\perp_d X_i\mid X_P$.

If $Q$ is empty, $S=P$ and step 2.1 is the required conclusion. Otherwise, suppose $X_j\perp_d X_i\mid X_{P,Q}$. By the conditional-density equality in step 1.1 and this supposition, for almost every $(p,y)$ one has $p_{X_j\mid X_i=x,X_P=p}(y)=p_{X_j\mid X_P=p,X_Q=q}(y)$ for almost every pair $(x,q)$. The left side depends only on $x$ and the right side only on $q$; by Fubini, each is therefore almost everywhere constant in its varying coordinate. Hence $X_j\perp_d X_i\mid X_P$, contradicting step 2.1. Thus the factorization given $X_S$ fails.

Hence each density factor in [F2] for a vertex outside $D$ depends only on $(y,s,z)$, while each factor for a vertex in $D$ depends only on $(d,s,z)$. citations.quote:
Fix a nonempty finite directed acyclic graph $G=(V,E)$ with a specified
topological order $v_1,\ldots,v_p$; every arrow points from an earlier to a
later vertex. For $j\in V$, let
$\operatorname{pa}(j)=\{i\in V:(i,j)\in E\}$ be its parent set, and let
$\operatorname{nd}(j)$ be the vertices other than $j$ that are not descendants
of $j$. A **continuous additive-noise model** on $G$ consists of real random
variables $X_j,N_j$ on a common probability space and continuous Borel
functions $f_j:\mathbb R^{\operatorname{pa}(j)}\to\mathbb R$ such that
$$X_j=f_j(X_{\operatorname{pa}(j)})+N_j$$
recursively in the topological order. The finite family of noises is mutually
independent, and each $N_j$ has a strictly positive Lebesgue density $q_j$.
All vertices of $G$ are observed; no latent vertices are omitted from the
model. The **observational law** is the law of the vector
$X=(X_j)_{j\in V}$.

The model is **causally minimal** when every parent input is essential: for
each edge $i\to j$, there are values of the other parent coordinates and two
distinct real values of the $i$-coordinate at which $f_j$ takes different
values. A root has no parent-coordinate minimality condition.

Let a finite additive-noise model have topological order $v_1,\ldots,v_p$,
equations $X_j=f_j(X_{\operatorname{pa}(j)})+N_j$, and strictly positive
Lebesgue densities $q_j$ for its mutually independent noises. Write
$\rho=\lambda^{\otimes p}$ for the finite product of one-dimensional Lebesgue
measure. If all $q_j$ are Borel measurable, the observational law has the
strictly positive Borel density
$$p_X(x)=\prod_{r=1}^p q_{v_r}\!\left(x_{v_r}-f_{v_r}(x_{\operatorname{pa}(v_r)})\right)$$
with respect to $\rho$ on Borel sets.

For arbitrary Lebesgue-measurable $q_j$, assume Countable Choice. There are
strictly positive finite Borel density versions $\bar q_j=q_j$ almost
everywhere. Their product
$$\bar p_X(x)=\prod_{r=1}^p \bar q_{v_r}\!\left(x_{v_r}-f_{v_r}(x_{\operatorname{pa}(v_r)})\right)$$
is a strictly positive Borel density with respect to $\rho$. The original
product $p_X$ is measurable for the completion $\bar\rho$ of $\rho$, agrees
with $\bar p_X$ $\bar\rho$-almost everywhere, and is a strictly positive
density with respect to $\bar\rho$. In this Countable Choice case, on non-Borel sets these density measures
refer to the unique absolutely continuous extensions of the Borel
observational law to the indicated sigma-algebras.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

In a finite additive-noise model on a DAG $G$, for every vertex $j$ and every
set $S\subseteq\operatorname{nd}(j)$ of nondescendants, the noise $N_j$ is
independent of the random vector $X_S=(X_k)_{k\in S}$.

Let $X$ follow a finite additive-noise model with a strictly positive joint
density and continuous structural functions that are causally minimal in each
parent coordinate. For positive joint densities, write
$Y\perp_d A\mid Z$ when the conditional-density factorization
$$p_{Y,A,Z}(y,a,z)p_Z(z)=p_{Y,Z}(y,z)p_{A,Z}(a,z)$$
holds almost everywhere. For every edge $i\to j$ and every set $S$ such that
$$\operatorname{pa}(j)\setminus\{i\}\subseteq S\subseteq\operatorname{nd}(j)\setminus\{i\},$$
the density conditional-independence factorization
$X_j\perp_d X_i\mid X_S$ fails.

A **finite directed acyclic graph** (DAG) is a finite vertex set $V$ with an
arrow set $E\subseteq V\times V$ and no directed cycle. A **path** from $u$ to
$v$ is a finite sequence of distinct vertices beginning at $u$ and ending at
$v$ in which each consecutive pair is joined by an arrow in either direction;
the arrows are not required to point along the sequence. An internal vertex of
a path is a **collider on that path** when the two arrows on the path both point
into it, and is a **noncollider** otherwise. A vertex $w$ is a **descendant** of
$v$ if there is a directed path from $v$ to $w$; for this definition
$\operatorname{De}^+(v)$ includes $v$ itself as well as its descendants.

For pairwise disjoint vertex sets $X,Y,C\subseteq V$, a path joining $X$ to
$Y$ is **active given $C$** when every internal noncollider is outside $C$ and
every internal collider has at least one member of $\operatorname{De}^+(v)$ in
$C$. The set $C$ **d-separates** $X$ and $Y$ in $G$ when no path joining $X$ to
$Y$ is active given $C$; write $X\perp_d Y\mid C$ in $G$. The empty set of
vertices is allowed for any of $X,Y,C$; in particular d-separation is vacuous
if either endpoint set is empty.

For $T\subseteq V$, $G_{\underline T}$ is obtained by deleting every arrow
whose tail lies in $T$, and $G_{\overline T}$ by deleting every arrow whose
head lies in $T$. These are graph operations only; they do not by themselves
specify a probability law under intervention.

In a finite DAG, a **route** is a finite sequence of vertices with consecutive vertices adjacent by an arrow in either direction; repeated vertices are allowed. Collider and noncollider status is assigned to each internal occurrence using its two incident route arrows. A route is **active given $C$** if each noncollider occurrence is outside $C$ and each collider occurrence is an ancestor of $C$, including membership in $C$. If an active route joins vertices $x,y\notin C$ with $x\ne y$, then an active distinct-vertex path joins $x$ and $y$ given $C$.

Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite DAG, and let $X$ follow a recursive additive-noise
model on $G$ in a fixed topological order, with continuous Borel structural
functions $f_v:\mathbb R^{\operatorname{pa}(v)}\to\mathbb R$ and equations
$$X_v=f_v(X_{\operatorname{pa}(v)})+N_v,$$
mutually independent noises with strictly positive Lebesgue densities $q_v$,
and joint density
$$p_X(x)=\prod_{v\in V}q_v\!\left(x_v-f_v(x_{\operatorname{pa}(v)})\right).$$
For $T\subseteq V$, let
$$p_T(x_T)=\int_{\mathbb R^{V\setminus T}}p_X(x)\,dx_{V\setminus T}$$
be the marginal density relative to finite product Lebesgue measure. Let
$A,B,C\subseteq V$ be pairwise disjoint with $A$ and $B$ nonempty. If $C$
d-separates $A$ and $B$ (every path from $A$ to $B$ has an internal
noncollider in $C$ or an internal collider with no descendant in $C$), then
$$p_{A\cup B\cup C}(x_A,x_B,x_C)p_C(x_C)=p_{A\cup C}(x_A,x_C)p_{B\cup C}(x_B,x_C)$$
for Lebesgue-almost every $(x_A,x_B,x_C)$. This identity is the
conditional-density factorization expressing conditional independence.

Let $n \ge 1$, let $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and let $E + h$ be the translate of
$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ (Translation of a subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$). Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(E+h) = \lambda_n^*(E)$ for **every** subset $E$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $E+h$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(E+h) = \lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

**No choice principle is used.** Lebesgue outer measure is defined as an infimum
and the Carathéodory condition is a family of equations between its values, so
all three clauses are statements about objects that exist in ZF; countable
choice is needed to know that $\lambda_n$ is a measure, not to know that it is
translation invariant.

derivations.claim: Use the Borel noise densities supplied in the hypotheses, or choose their positive finite Borel versions under Countable Choice by [F1]. Repeatedly delete a vertex that is a sink in both graphs and has the same parent set in both. At each deletion, its equation contributes a single shifted noise-density factor, which integrates to one by [F7]; no remaining equation uses the deleted vertex, so the remaining law still has the positive ANM product density and all remaining edges remain causally minimal. The process cannot delete every vertex, since then the graphs would be equal. It stops only when no common sink with equal parent sets remains; therefore choose a remaining sink $l$ of $G$, which either has a different parent set in $G'$ or has a child in $G'$.

Partition the incident vertices by $Z=\operatorname{pa}_G(l)\cap\operatorname{pa}_{G'}(l)$, $Y=\operatorname{pa}_G(l)\cap\operatorname{ch}_{G'}(l)$, $W=\operatorname{pa}_G(l)\setminus(Z\cup Y)$, $D=\operatorname{pa}_{G'}(l)\setminus\operatorname{pa}_G(l)$, and $E=\operatorname{ch}_{G'}(l)\setminus\operatorname{pa}_G(l)$. These sets are pairwise disjoint, $\operatorname{pa}_G(l)=Z\cup Y\cup W$, $\operatorname{pa}_{G'}(l)=Z\cup D$, and $\operatorname{ch}_{G'}(l)=Y\cup E$. Put $T=Y\cup W$.

Suppose $T=\varnothing$ and $D\ne\varnothing$, and choose $d\in D$. Since $l$ is a sink in $G$, all vertices in $D\cup Z$ are nondescendants of $l$. By [F2], $N_l$ is independent of $(X_D,X_Z)$; the equation $X_l=f_l(X_Z)+N_l$ therefore makes the conditional density of $X_l$ given $(X_D,X_Z)$ independent of $X_D$. Its density factorization gives $X_l\perp_d X_D\mid X_Z$. Weak union follows directly by writing this factorization for the split $D=\{d\}\cup(D\setminus\{d\})$ and dividing by the positive marginal density: $X_l\perp_d X_d\mid X_{Z\cup(D\setminus\{d\})}$. This conditioning set contains all other parents of $l$ in $G'$ and contains no descendant of $l$ there, contradicting [F3] for $d\to l$ in $G'$.

Suppose $T=D=\varnothing$ and $E\ne\varnothing$. Choose $e\in E$ and put $R=\operatorname{pa}_{G'}(e)\setminus\{l\}$. Since $l$ is a sink in $G$, every vertex of $\{e\}\cup Z\cup R$ is a nondescendant of $l$. By [F2], $N_l$ is independent of $(X_e,X_R,X_Z)$; hence the conditional density of $X_l$ given these variables depends only on $X_Z$. Splitting off $X_e$ and dividing by the positive marginal density gives $X_l\perp_d X_e\mid X_{Z\cup R}$. In $G'$, $l\to e$, the set $Z\cup R$ contains all other parents of $e$, and each $z\in Z$ is an ancestor of $e$ along $z\to l\to e$, so this set contains no descendant of $e$. This contradicts [F3] for $l\to e$. If also $E=\varnothing$, then $l$ is a common sink with the same parent set and would have been deleted in step 1.1.

It remains that $T\ne\varnothing$. Choose $t\in T$ with no directed path in $G'$ from $t$ to any other member of $T$; such a vertex exists by taking a maximal element of the directed-reachability partial order on the finite nonempty set $T$. We show that $t\notin W$. For contradiction suppose $t=w\in W$, and form $\widetilde G'$ by adding arrows $y'\to w$ for all $y'\in Y$ and $w'\to w$ for all $w'\in W\setminus\{w\}$. The graph is still acyclic: a new arrow could create a cycle only if $w$ already reached its tail, contrary to the choice of $w$. Also $l$ and $w$ are nonadjacent in $\widetilde G'$.

In $\widetilde G'$, choose a d-separating set $S_0$ for the nonadjacent vertices $l,w$ as follows. For any vertex $v$ and nondescendant nonparent $u$, its parent set d-separates $v$ from $u$: a path starting $v\leftarrow a$ is blocked by the conditioned noncollider $a$; a path starting with an arrow out of $v$ must have a first edge traversed backward, since $u$ is not a descendant. At that first turn there is a collider reached by a directed path from $v$. Neither this collider nor any of its descendants can be a parent of $v$, since that would give a directed cycle; thus it is blocked given the parents of $v$. If $l$ is an ancestor of $w$, then $l$ is a nondescendant nonparent of $w$; apply this argument from $w$ and take $S_0=\operatorname{pa}_{\widetilde G'}(w)$. It covers paths through a child of $w$ as well as paths through a parent. Otherwise $w$ is a nondescendant nonparent of $l$; take $S_0=\operatorname{pa}_{\widetilde G'}(l)$.

Put $W_0=W\setminus\{w\}$ and $S=S_0\cup Y\cup Z\cup W_0$. Each $y'\in Y$ belongs to $S_0$, since $l\to y'\to w$ is a path with noncollider $y'$. Suppose a path $\pi$ from $l$ to $w$ is active given $S$. Its noncolliders lie outside $S_0$, and every collider with a descendant in $S_0$ is active given $S_0$. Since $S_0$ d-separates the endpoints, at least one collider on $\pi$ is not an ancestor of $S_0$; its descendant in $S$ must lie in $Z$ or $W_0$. Label every such collider by one such type, $Z$ or $W_0$. A labeled $Z$-collider $v$ has a directed path to some $z\in Z$, followed by $z\to l$; traversing this chain backward connects $l$ to $v$. The chain avoids $S_0$, since otherwise $v$ would be an ancestor of $S_0$. A labeled $W_0$-collider $u$ has a directed path to some $w'\in W_0$, followed by the added arrow $w'\to w$; this chain also avoids $S_0$. If only $Z$ labels occur, use the one nearest $w$, replace the prefix of $\pi$ by its backward chain from $l$, and retain the suffix. If only $W_0$ labels occur, use the one nearest $l$, retain the prefix, and replace the suffix by its forward chain to $w$. If both labels occur, take consecutive labeled colliders of different types; connect $l$ to the $Z$-collider by its backward chain, retain the segment between the two colliders in either direction, and connect the $W_0$-collider to $w$ by its forward chain. The resulting finite route has no conditioned noncollider: original noncolliders avoid $S_0$, connector interiors avoid $S_0$, and each selected collider becomes a noncollider at its junction. Every remaining collider has a descendant in $S_0$, because there is no differently labeled collider between the selected ones, and in the one-label cases the retained side contains no other newly opened collider. This is an active route given $S_0$, so [F5] gives an active path, contradicting the choice of $S_0$. Thus $S$ d-separates $l,w$ in $\widetilde G'$, and also in its subgraph $G'$.

By [F6], $X_l\perp_d X_w\mid X_S$ in $G'$. In $G$, $w\to l$, and $S$ contains all other parents of $l$ and only nondescendants of the sink $l$. This contradicts [F3]. Therefore the selected maximal member $t$ cannot lie in $W$; it lies in $Y$.

Let the selected $y=t\in Y$, and set $Q=\operatorname{pa}_G(l)\setminus\{y\}$, $R=\operatorname{pa}_{G'}(y)\setminus\{l\}$, and $S=Q\cup R$. In $G$, $l$ is a sink, so every member of $S$ is a nondescendant of $l$, and $Q\subseteq S$. In $G'$, every member of $R$ is a parent of $y$. A vertex $z\in Z$ cannot be a descendant of $y$, since $z\to l\to y$ and a path $y\to\cdots\to z$ would create a directed cycle. Every vertex of $Y\setminus\{y\}\cup W$ is another member of $T$, so none is a descendant of $y$ by the choice of $t$. Hence $S$ is contained in the nondescendants of $y$ in $G'$ and contains all parents of $y$ other than $l$. A vertex deleted in step 1.1 cannot be an ancestor of a surviving vertex in either original graph: when it was deleted it had no outgoing edge to any then-remaining vertex. Consequently all original parents of surviving vertices survive, and every original directed path between surviving vertices stays in the reduced graph. The parent sets and nondescendant inclusions just proved therefore hold in the original graphs too. The edges are $y\to l$ in $G$ and $l\to y$ in $G'$, so the vertices and $S$ satisfy the Statement.

citations.quote:
Fix a nonempty finite directed acyclic graph $G=(V,E)$ with a specified
topological order $v_1,\ldots,v_p$; every arrow points from an earlier to a
later vertex. For $j\in V$, let
$\operatorname{pa}(j)=\{i\in V:(i,j)\in E\}$ be its parent set, and let
$\operatorname{nd}(j)$ be the vertices other than $j$ that are not descendants
of $j$. A **continuous additive-noise model** on $G$ consists of real random
variables $X_j,N_j$ on a common probability space and continuous Borel
functions $f_j:\mathbb R^{\operatorname{pa}(j)}\to\mathbb R$ such that
$$X_j=f_j(X_{\operatorname{pa}(j)})+N_j$$
recursively in the topological order. The finite family of noises is mutually
independent, and each $N_j$ has a strictly positive Lebesgue density $q_j$.
All vertices of $G$ are observed; no latent vertices are omitted from the
model. The **observational law** is the law of the vector
$X=(X_j)_{j\in V}$.

The model is **causally minimal** when every parent input is essential: for
each edge $i\to j$, there are values of the other parent coordinates and two
distinct real values of the $i$-coordinate at which $f_j$ takes different
values. A root has no parent-coordinate minimality condition.

Let a finite additive-noise model have topological order $v_1,\ldots,v_p$,
equations $X_j=f_j(X_{\operatorname{pa}(j)})+N_j$, and strictly positive
Lebesgue densities $q_j$ for its mutually independent noises. Write
$\rho=\lambda^{\otimes p}$ for the finite product of one-dimensional Lebesgue
measure. If all $q_j$ are Borel measurable, the observational law has the
strictly positive Borel density
$$p_X(x)=\prod_{r=1}^p q_{v_r}\!\left(x_{v_r}-f_{v_r}(x_{\operatorname{pa}(v_r)})\right)$$
with respect to $\rho$ on Borel sets.

For arbitrary Lebesgue-measurable $q_j$, assume Countable Choice. There are
strictly positive finite Borel density versions $\bar q_j=q_j$ almost
everywhere. Their product
$$\bar p_X(x)=\prod_{r=1}^p \bar q_{v_r}\!\left(x_{v_r}-f_{v_r}(x_{\operatorname{pa}(v_r)})\right)$$
is a strictly positive Borel density with respect to $\rho$. The original
product $p_X$ is measurable for the completion $\bar\rho$ of $\rho$, agrees
with $\bar p_X$ $\bar\rho$-almost everywhere, and is a strictly positive
density with respect to $\bar\rho$. In this Countable Choice case, on non-Borel sets these density measures
refer to the unique absolutely continuous extensions of the Borel
observational law to the indicated sigma-algebras.

For a smooth bivariate additive-noise model $Y=f(X)+N$, let $f$ be three
times continuously differentiable, and let $X$ and $N$ have strictly positive
three-times continuously differentiable densities $p_X$ and $p_N$. Put
$\xi(x)=\log p_X(x)$ and $\nu(z)=\log p_N(z)$. The triple $(f,p_X,p_N)$
satisfies **Condition 19** when there are $x,y\in\mathbb R$ with
$\nu''(y-f(x))f'(x)\ne0$ at which
$$\xi'''(x)\ne \xi''(x)\left(-\frac{\nu'''(y-f(x))f'(x)}{\nu''(y-f(x))}+\frac{f''(x)}{f'(x)}\right) -2\nu''(y-f(x))f''(x)f'(x) +\nu'(y-f(x))f'''(x) +\frac{\nu'(y-f(x))\nu'''(y-f(x))f''(x)f'(x)}{\nu''(y-f(x))} -\frac{\nu'(y-f(x))(f''(x))^2}{f'(x)}.$$
Here every derivative of $\nu$ is evaluated at $y-f(x)$ and every derivative
of $f$ at $x$. The nonzero-domain condition makes both denominators in this
formula well defined.

A finite additive-noise model is a **restricted additive-noise model** when
every structural function $f_j$ is $C^3$ and every noise has a strictly
positive $C^3$ Lebesgue density, and when for every vertex $j$, every parent
$i\in\operatorname{pa}(j)$, and every set
$S$ satisfying
$$\operatorname{pa}(j)\setminus\{i\}\subseteq S\subseteq\operatorname{nd}(j)\setminus\{i\},$$
there is a value $s$ with $0<p_S(s)<\infty$ such that the
conditional law of $X_i$ given $X_S=s$, together with the structural slice
$u\mapsto f_j(s_{\operatorname{pa}(j)\setminus\{i\}},u)$ and the noise $N_j$,
is a smooth bivariate additive-noise model satisfying Condition 19. The
conditional density is the ratio
$p_{X_i,X_S}(u,s)/p_S(s)$ for the finite positive-density version supplied
by the joint-density formula. The structural slice and conditional input
density have the smoothness and strict positivity required in the preceding
Condition 19 definition. If the model has no edges, the restricted condition
is vacuous.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $n \ge 1$, let $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and let $E + h$ be the translate of
$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ (Translation of a subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$). Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(E+h) = \lambda_n^*(E)$ for **every** subset $E$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $E+h$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(E+h) = \lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

**No choice principle is used.** Lebesgue outer measure is defined as an infimum
and the Carathéodory condition is a family of equations between its values, so
all three clauses are statements about objects that exist in ZF; countable
choice is needed to know that $\lambda_n$ is a measure, not to know that it is
translation invariant.

Let $\mu$ be a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R$. If a real number
$a$ satisfies $\mu(A+a)=\mu(A)$ for every Borel set $A\subseteq\mathbb R$,
then $a=0$.

Put $\xi=\log p_X$, $
u=\log p_N$, and $\pi(x,y)=\log p(x,y)$. By [F2], $\pi(x,y)=\xi(x)+
u(y-f(x))$ is a $C^3$ function. The chain rule gives $\pi_{xy}=-
u''(y-f(x))f'(x),\qquad \pi_{xx}=
u''(y-f(x))(f'(x))^2-
u'(y-f(x))f''(x)+\xi''(x).$ Thus both derivatives are defined, and $\pi_{xy}
e0$ exactly on the Condition 19 domain.

Suppose a reverse representation as in the Statement exists. By [F4] and [F2], $p_Y(y)=\int_{\mathbb R}p(x,y)\,dx$ is positive and finite for almost every $y$. The sectionwise translation $m=x-g(y)$ gives the joint density $p_{M,Y}(m,y)=p(m+g(y),y)$ by [F5]; independence makes it equal to $p_M(m)p_Y(y)$ almost everywhere. Choose $y_0$ for which $0<p_Y(y_0)<\infty$ and this factorization holds for almost every $m$. Then $p_M(m)= rac{p(m+g(y_0),y_0)}{p_Y(y_0)}\quad	ext{for almost every }m.$ The right side is a strictly positive $C^3$ function of $m$, so choose it as the density version of $M$ and put $\widetilde
u=\log p_M$. Consequently the forward and reverse density formulas agree almost everywhere: $p(x,y)=p_Y(y)p_M(x-g(y)).$ For almost every $y$ with $0<p_Y(y)<\infty$, the two sides as functions of $x$ are continuous and agree almost everywhere, hence agree for every $x$. Taking logarithmic $x$-derivatives gives $\pi_x(x,y)=\widetilde
u'(x-g(y))$ for almost every $(x,y)$. Both sides are continuous on $\mathbb R^2$, so this identity holds everywhere. Differentiating in $x$ and $y$ gives $\pi_{xx}=\widetilde
u''(x-g(y))$ and $\pi_{xy}=-\widetilde
u''(x-g(y))g'(y)$. Wherever $\pi_{xy}
e0$, it follows that $ rac{\pi_{xx}}{\pi_{xy}}=- rac1{g'(y)},$ which is independent of $x$; hence $\partial_x(\pi_{xx}/\pi_{xy})=0$.
Step 3.1 forces Condition 19's differential equation at every point where $\nu''(y-f(x))f'(x)\ne0$, contrary to [F3]. Therefore no reverse representation in the stated class exists.

The law cannot be independent: if $X$ and $Y$ were independent, positivity of $p_X$ and the forward density formula [F2] would make $p_N(y-f(x))$ equal $p_Y(y)$ for almost every $(x,y)$. By Fubini, for almost every pair $x,x'$, the translates $p_N(y-f(x))$ and $p_N(y-f(x'))$ agree for almost every $y$. Their probability laws are translates of the law of $N$; [F6] forces $f(x)=f(x')$ for almost every pair. Continuity of $f$ makes it constant everywhere, contradicting the hypothesis. Thus the empty graph is excluded as well, and the only smooth bivariate ANM direction in the class is $X\to Y$.
