with the same vertex set have the same observational law, a strictly positive
joint density, and causal minimality in each model. If their DAGs are $G$ and $G'$, then there
are vertices $y,l$ and a set $S$ such that $y\to l$ in $G$, $l\to y$ in $G'$, and
$$\operatorname{pa}_G(l)\setminus\{y\}\subseteq S\subseteq \operatorname{nd}_G(l)\setminus\{y\},\qquad \operatorname{pa}_{G'}(y)\setminus\{l\}\subseteq S\subseteq \operatorname{nd}_{G'}(y)\setminus\{l\}.$$

In a finite additive-noise model on a DAG $G$, for every vertex $j$ and every
set $S\subseteq\operatorname{nd}(j)$ of nondescendants, the noise $N_j$ is
independent of the random vector $X_S=(X_k)_{k\in S}$.

For a smooth bivariate additive-noise model $Y=f(X)+N$, let $f$ be three
times continuously differentiable, and let $X$ and $N$ have strictly positive
three-times continuously differentiable densities $p_X$ and $p_N$. Put
$\xi(x)=\log p_X(x)$ and $\nu(z)=\log p_N(z)$. The triple $(f,p_X,p_N)$
satisfies **Condition 19** when there are $x,y\in\mathbb R$ with
$\nu''(y-f(x))f'(x)\ne0$ at which
$$\xi'''(x)\ne \xi''(x)\left(-\frac{\nu'''(y-f(x))f'(x)}{\nu''(y-f(x))}+\frac{f''(x)}{f'(x)}\right) -2\nu''(y-f(x))f''(x)f'(x) +\nu'(y-f(x))f'''(x) +\frac{\nu'(y-f(x))\nu'''(y-f(x))f''(x)f'(x)}{\nu''(y-f(x))} -\frac{\nu'(y-f(x))(f''(x))^2}{f'(x)}.$$
Here every derivative of $\nu$ is evaluated at $y-f(x)$ and every derivative
of $f$ at $x$. The nonzero-domain condition makes both denominators in this
formula well defined.

A finite additive-noise model is a **restricted additive-noise model** when
every structural function $f_j$ is $C^3$ and every noise has a strictly
positive $C^3$ Lebesgue density, and when for every vertex $j$, every parent
$i\in\operatorname{pa}(j)$, and every set
$S$ satisfying
$$\operatorname{pa}(j)\setminus\{i\}\subseteq S\subseteq\operatorname{nd}(j)\setminus\{i\},$$
there is a value $s$ with $0<p_S(s)<\infty$ such that the
conditional law of $X_i$ given $X_S=s$, together with the structural slice
$u\mapsto f_j(s_{\operatorname{pa}(j)\setminus\{i\}},u)$ and the noise $N_j$,
is a smooth bivariate additive-noise model satisfying Condition 19. The
conditional density is the ratio
$p_{X_i,X_S}(u,s)/p_S(s)$ for the finite positive-density version supplied
by the joint-density formula. The structural slice and conditional input
density have the smoothness and strict positivity required in the preceding
Condition 19 definition. If the model has no edges, the restricted condition
is vacuous.

Let a finite additive-noise model have topological order $v_1,\ldots,v_p$,
equations $X_j=f_j(X_{\operatorname{pa}(j)})+N_j$, and strictly positive
Lebesgue densities $q_j$ for its mutually independent noises. Write
$\rho=\lambda^{\otimes p}$ for the finite product of one-dimensional Lebesgue
measure. If all $q_j$ are Borel measurable, the observational law has the
strictly positive Borel density
$$p_X(x)=\prod_{r=1}^p q_{v_r}\!\left(x_{v_r}-f_{v_r}(x_{\operatorname{pa}(v_r)})\right)$$
with respect to $\rho$ on Borel sets.

For arbitrary Lebesgue-measurable $q_j$, assume Countable Choice. There are
strictly positive finite Borel density versions $\bar q_j=q_j$ almost
everywhere. Their product
$$\bar p_X(x)=\prod_{r=1}^p \bar q_{v_r}\!\left(x_{v_r}-f_{v_r}(x_{\operatorname{pa}(v_r)})\right)$$
is a strictly positive Borel density with respect to $\rho$. The original
product $p_X$ is measurable for the completion $\bar\rho$ of $\rho$, agrees
with $\bar p_X$ $\bar\rho$-almost everywhere, and is a strictly positive
density with respect to $\bar\rho$. In this Countable Choice case, on non-Borel sets these density measures
refer to the unique absolutely continuous extensions of the Borel
observational law to the indicated sigma-algebras.

Assume Countable Choice, or suppose the specified noise densities are Borel measurable.
Let a finite causally sufficient additive-noise model have graph $G$, and let
$y\to z$ be an edge such that there is no directed path from $z$ to any other
child of $y$. Write $D=\operatorname{de}_G(z)$ for the strict descendants of
$z$ and $S=V\setminus(D\cup\{y,z\})$. Use the supplied Borel noise densities, or fix positive finite Borel versions under Countable Choice, and let $p$ be their shifted-noise product density. Then
there are positive measurable functions $A(y,s,z)$ and $B(d,s,z)$ such that
$p(d,y,s,z)=A(y,s,z)B(d,s,z)$, where $A$ does not depend on $d$ and $B$ does
not depend on $y$. Use marginal density versions obtained by iterated
integration. Then
$$p_{X_D,X_y,X_S,X_z}(d,y,s,z)\,p_{X_S,X_z}(s,z)=p_{X_D,X_S,X_z}(d,s,z)\,p_{X_y,X_S,X_z}(y,s,z)$$
for almost every $(d,y,s,z)$. This is the density conditional-independence
factorization of $X_D$ and $X_y$ given $(X_S,X_z)$. Moreover, for every $s$
with $0<p_{X_S}(s)<\infty$, the conditional law of $(X_D,X_y)$ given
$X_S=s$ satisfies the density conditional-independence factorization given
$X_z$.

Let $C$ be a finite-dimensional real random vector, let $(Y,C)$ have a
strictly positive $C^3$ joint density $p(y,c)$, and let
$m:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be $C^3$. If $R=Y-m(C)$ is independent of $C$, then there are
strictly positive $C^3$ Lebesgue density versions $q_R$ and $p_C$ such that
$$p(y,c)=q_R(y-m(c))p_C(c)$$
for every $(y,c)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$.

Let $\mu$ be a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R$. If a real number
$a$ satisfies $\mu(A+a)=\mu(A)$ for every Borel set $A\subseteq\mathbb R$,
then $a=0$.

Let $X,N$ be independent real random variables, let $Y=f(X)+N$, and suppose
$f\in C^3(\mathbb R)$ is nonconstant while $X$ and $N$ have strictly positive
$C^3$ Lebesgue densities. If the triple of $f$ and these two densities
satisfies Condition 19, then there is no reverse additive-noise representation
$X=g(Y)+M$ with $M$ independent of $Y$ and $g\in C^3(\mathbb R)$. No density
regularity for $M$ is assumed; the proof derives a strictly positive $C^3$
density version from the forward joint density and reverse independence. Hence
the direction $X\to Y$ is identified from the observational law among these
smooth bivariate additive-noise models.

Let $X$ follow a finite additive-noise model with a strictly positive joint
density and continuous structural functions that are causally minimal in each
parent coordinate. For positive joint densities, write
$Y\perp_d A\mid Z$ when the conditional-density factorization
$$p_{Y,A,Z}(y,a,z)p_Z(z)=p_{Y,Z}(y,z)p_{A,Z}(a,z)$$
holds almost everywhere. For every edge $i\to j$ and every set $S$ such that
$$\operatorname{pa}(j)\setminus\{i\}\subseteq S\subseteq\operatorname{nd}(j)\setminus\{i\},$$
the density conditional-independence factorization
$X_j\perp_d X_i\mid X_S$ fails.

Fix a finite nonempty ordered vertex set $V$ and a population law of a real
vector $X=(X_j)_{j\in V}$ generated by an additive-noise model. A **population
regression rule** $\mathcal R$ assigns to each target $j\in V$ and predictor
set $C\subseteq V\setminus\{j\}$ a Borel function
$m_{j,C}:\mathbb R^C\to\mathbb R$. A **perfect independence oracle** returns
“independent” exactly when the tested random variable and random vector are
independent under this population law. For a given ANM, $\mathcal R$ is
**population-consistent on that model** if for every $j$ and every
$C$ with $\operatorname{pa}(j)\subseteq C\subseteq\operatorname{nd}(j)$,
there is a constant $c_{j,C}\in\mathbb R$ such that
$$m_{j,C}(X_C)=f_j(X_{\operatorname{pa}(j)})+c_{j,C}\quad\text{almost surely}.$$
This consistency condition concerns only the population regression target and
does not assert a finite-sample guarantee. The procedure itself is defined for
any supplied regression rule and oracle.

RESIT takes $X$, $\mathcal R$, and the perfect independence oracle and
performs the following steps, using a fixed total order on $V$ for every tie
and loop order.

1. Set the remaining set $S:=V$ and an empty sink list. While $S\ne\varnothing$,
   for each $j\in S$ form
   $$R_j:=X_j-m_{j,S\setminus\{j\}}(X_{S\setminus\{j\}}).$$
   Retain the vertices for which the oracle declares
   $R_j$ independent of $X_{S\setminus\{j\}}$. If there is no such vertex,
   return `failure`. Otherwise choose the least retained vertex $k$, record
   the provisional parent set $\widehat{\operatorname{pa}}(k):=S\setminus\{k\}$,
   append $k$ to the sink list, and remove $k$ from $S$.
2. Reverse the sink list to obtain an order $\pi$. In that order, for each
   vertex $j$ and each candidate $\ell$ in its provisional parent set, in the
   fixed order, let
   $C:=\widehat{\operatorname{pa}}(j)\setminus\{\ell\}$ and form
   $$R_{j,\ell}:=X_j-m_{j,C}(X_C).$$
   If the oracle declares $R_{j,\ell}$ independent of the vector of all
   vertices preceding $j$ in $\pi$, delete $\ell$ from
   $\widehat{\operatorname{pa}}(j)$; otherwise retain it.
3. Return the DAG with arrow $i\to j$ exactly when
   $i\in\widehat{\operatorname{pa}}(j)$ after pruning.

derivations.claim: Suppose another causally minimal restricted ANM on the same vertices gives the same observational law but has a different DAG $G'$. By [F1], there are vertices $y,l$ and a set $S$ such that $y\to l$ in $G$, $l\to y$ in $G'$, and $S$ contains the other parents of $l$ in $G$ and is contained in its nondescendants; also $S$ contains the other parents of $y$ in $G'$ and is contained in its nondescendants.

Consider Phase 1 on a current vertex set $J$ obtained by deleting true sinks. A deleted sink cannot be a parent of a remaining vertex, so $J$ is parent-closed and its marginal law is the ANM product over $J$ by [F4]; consequently every original directed path between vertices still in $J$ stays in $J$. A finite DAG on nonempty $J$ has a sink $j$. Every other current vertex is a nondescendant of $j$ in the original graph: if one were a descendant, its path from $j$ would remain in the parent-closed current graph, contradicting that $j$ is a sink there. Thus for $C=J\setminus\{j\}$, $\operatorname{pa}(j)\subseteq C\subseteq\operatorname{nd}(j)$.

Both models in step 1.1 are restricted ANMs. By [F3] their structural functions and noise densities are $C^3$, so the product density versions supplied by [F4] are $C^3$. Since the models have the same observational law, these continuous densities agree almost everywhere and hence everywhere; denote their common pointwise version by $p$. Define the marginal versions needed below by iterated integration of this same $p$, and define conditional-density versions at each finite positive value of $p_{X_S}$ by the corresponding ratios. Apply the restricted-model definition in $G$ to the edge $y\to l$ and this exact set $S$. It supplies $s$ with $0<p_{X_S}(s)<\infty$ such that the pair $Y^*=X_y\mid X_S=s$, $L^*=X_l\mid X_S=s$, using these common density versions, is a smooth bivariate ANM satisfying Condition 19. In particular, the definition gives the forward equation $L^*=f_l(s_{\operatorname{pa}(l)\setminus\{y\}},Y^*)+N_l$ with $N_l$ independent of $Y^*$.

Population consistency gives $m_{j,C}(X_C)=f_j(X_{\operatorname{pa}(j)})+c_{j,C}$ almost surely, so the tested residual is $N_j-c_{j,C}$. By [F2] it is independent of $X_C$, and the perfect oracle accepts $j$. Hence every iteration has at least one accepted candidate and cannot return failure.

In $G'$, the reverse edge is $l\to y$ and $S$ contains all other parents of $y$. Since $S\cup\{l\}\subseteq\operatorname{nd}_{G'}(y)$, [F2] gives $N'_y$ independent of $(X_l,X_S)$. Let $q_{N'_y}$ be its density and choose the product density version $$p_{N'_y,X_l,X_S}(n,l,s):=q_{N'_y}(n)p_{X_l,X_S}(l,s),$$ using the common marginal version fixed in step 2.1. Because $0<p_{X_S}(s)<\infty$, dividing this version by $p_{X_S}(s)$ shows that, conditional on $X_S=s$, $N'_y$ and $X_l$ are independent. The reverse structural equation at that section is $$Y^*=g_y(s_{\operatorname{pa}_{G'}(y)\setminus\{l\}},L^*)+N'_y,$$ and its structural slice is $C^3$ by [F3]. In the $G'$ product-density formula, the factor for $X_y$ depends only on $y,l,s$, because all other parents of $y$ lie in $S$; integrating the remaining coordinates by the same iterated-integral convention in step 2.1 gives the common section density $$p_{X_y,X_l,X_S}(y,l,s)=q_{N'_y}\!\left(y-g_y(s_{\operatorname{pa}_{G'}(y)\setminus\{l\}},l)\right)p_{X_l,X_S}(l,s).$$ Thus the reverse conditional pair at this exact $s$ is formed from the same density $p_{X_y,X_l,X_S}(\cdot,\cdot,s)/p_{X_S}(s)$ as the forward pair in step 2.1. They have the same law, and this is a reverse representation forbidden by [F8], proving population graph identifiability.

Now suppose a candidate $y\in J$ is not a sink. By the current-set invariant in step 1.2, choose a child $z$ of $y$ in $G[J]$ with no directed path to any other child of $y$ in $G[J]$; finiteness and acyclicity give such a child. Every parent of $z$ other than $y$ lies in $T$, and $T\subseteq\operatorname{nd}(z)\setminus\{y,z\}$ in the original graph as well as in $G[J]$. The predictor set tested for $y$ is $C=J\setminus\{y\}=T\cup\{z\}\cup D$. Suppose the oracle accepts it, and set $R_y=X_y-m_{y,C}(X_C)$. Then $R_y$ is independent of $X_C$. The current joint density is positive $C^3$ by [F3]–[F4], and $m_{y,C}$ is $C^3$ by hypothesis, so [F6] gives a pointwise density version $p_{X_y,X_C}(u,c)=q_{R_y}(u-m_{y,C}(c))p_{X_C}(c).$ By [F5], at the exact witness $t$, for almost every $(z,d)$ the conditional density of $Y^*$ given $(Z^*=z,X_D=d,X_T=t)$ does not depend on $d$. Combining this with the pointwise factorization above shows that the probability laws of $R_y+m_{y,C}(t,z,d)$ and $R_y+m_{y,C}(t,z,d')$ are equal for almost every $z,d,d'$.

If $D\ne\varnothing$, [F7] forces $m_{y,C}(t,z,d)=m_{y,C}(t,z,d')$ for almost every $(z,d,d')$. Fubini supplies a fixed $d_0$ for which $m_{y,C}(t,z,d)=m_{y,C}(t,z,d_0)$ for almost every $(z,d)$. Define $g_t(z)=m_{y,C}(t,z,d_0)$; this is $C^3$ by the Phase 1 smoothness hypothesis. If $D=\varnothing$, define $g_t(z)=m_{y,C}(t,z)$, which is also $C^3$. In either case the accepted residual equation yields $Y^*=g_t(Z^*)+R_y$ almost surely. The pointwise factorization [F6], restricted to $X_T=t$ and integrated over $X_D$, shows that $R_y$ is independent of $Z^*$ in this conditional law. This is a reverse representation of the Condition 19 pair from step 3.2, contradicting [F8]. Therefore no nonsink candidate is accepted.

Phase 1 therefore removes only true sinks. Reversing their removal order gives a topological order: for every edge $i\to j$, $j$ must be removed before $i$ while both remain, so $i$ precedes $j$ in the reversed list. The provisional parent set of each vertex is exactly the set of vertices preceding it in that order.

Fix a vertex $j$ and consider its candidate parents in the fixed loop order. We prove by induction through that list that no true parent is deleted. At a true-parent candidate $\ell$, all other true parents are still present: they were either untested or retained by the induction hypothesis. The current set $C$ contains them and is contained in the preceding vertices, hence in $\operatorname{nd}(j)\setminus\{\ell\}$. If the oracle accepted deletion, the residual $U=X_j-m_{j,C}(X_C)$ would be independent of the full preceding vector, in particular of $(X_\ell,X_C)$. Since $X_j=m_{j,C}(X_C)+U$, its conditional law given $(X_\ell,X_C)$ would not depend on $X_\ell$, yielding $X_j\perp_d X_\ell\mid X_C$. This contradicts [F9]. Thus every true parent is retained.

If the tested candidate $\ell$ is not a true parent, step 7.1 ensures that every true parent remains in the predictor set $C$ after deleting $\ell$. This set is contained in $\operatorname{nd}(j)$, so [F10] makes the residual $N_j$ minus a constant; [F2] makes it independent of all vertices preceding $j$. The oracle accepts and the algorithm deletes this superfluous edge.
Steps 7.1 and 8.1 show that pruning removes exactly the superfluous preceding vertices and retains every parent. Each returned parent set is therefore the true parent set, so RESIT returns $G$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Fix a finite DAG $G=(V,E)$ and a specified topological ordering
$v_1,\ldots,v_n$ (every arrow points from an earlier to a later vertex).
Partition $V=O\sqcup H$ into **observed** vertices $O$ and **latent** vertices
$H$. For each $v\in V$, specify a measurable state space $(S_v,\mathcal
S_v)$, a measurable exogenous space $(E_v,\mathcal E_v)$, a jointly
measurable structural function
$$f_v:\prod_{u\in\operatorname{pa}(v)}S_u\times E_v\to S_v,$$
and an exogenous random element $U_v$ with values in $E_v$. Here
$\operatorname{pa}(v)=\{u:(u,v)\in E\}$; the empty product is a singleton.
The model is **Markovian** when the finite family $(U_v)_{v\in V}$ is mutually
independent. No parametric form or distributional truth is asserted. Correlated
disturbances may be represented by adding their common causes as latent
vertices, after which the exogenous family in the expanded model is required
to be mutually independent.

Recursion in the topological order defines the endogenous random elements
uniquely by $X_v=f_v(X_{\operatorname{pa}(v)},U_v)$. The full-joint law is the
law of $(X_v)_{v\in V}$; the observed law is its marginal law on $O$. An
observed-only DAG factorization is asserted only when $H=\varnothing$ or when
an additional stated latent-variable condition proves it.

For $I\subseteq V$ and a value $a=(a_v)_{v\in I}\in\prod_{v\in I}S_v$,
**$do(X_I=a)$** means replace only the equations indexed by $I$ by the
constants $X_v=a_v$, leaving every other structural function and every
exogenous law unchanged. Recursion then defines counterfactual values
$X_w^a$ for every vertex $w$; the interventional law is their joint law. The
response map $(a,\omega)\mapsto X_w^a(\omega)$ is jointly measurable, by
induction through the finite topological order and joint measurability of each
$f_v$. This permits evaluation at a random treatment value, such as
$X_w^{M^a}$. When $I=\{A\}$, write $X_w^a$ for the response under
$do(A=a)$. If the factual treatment is $A$, then on $\{A=a\}$ recursion
gives $X_w=X_w^a$ for every vertex $w$.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By The standard normal density has total mass one and The indefinite integral of a nonnegative measurable function is a measure, gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. The law of a random element is a probability measure makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in The Dirac set function at a point.
Assume AC. The function $\phi(x)=e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}$ is positive and Borel measurable on $\mathbb R$, with Lebesgue integral one.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
(The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)) and let $T : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be linear
with matrix $A$ (Linear map between vector spaces over the same field,
Every Euclidean linear map has a unique matrix and satisfies $\|Lh\|_2\le K\|h\|_2$ for some $K\ge0$).

1. **Invertible case.** If $\det A \ne 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable for
   every Lebesgue measurable $E$ and
   $$\lambda_n\big(T[E]\big) \;=\; |\det A|\;\lambda_n(E),$$
   both sides possibly $+\infty$; the product is defined in
   $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ because $|\det A| > 0$.
2. **Singular case.** If $\det A = 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ for **every** $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$.

**The singular clause is stated as nullity and not as a product.** When
$\det A = 0$ and $\lambda_n(E) = +\infty$ the expression
$|\det A|\,\lambda_n(E)$ is $0\cdot(+\infty)$, which The extended real line $\overline{\mathbb{R}} = \mathbb{R} \cup \{-\infty, +\infty\}$, its order, and the arithmetic that is left undefined
leaves undefined; writing the conclusion as $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ says the same
thing wherever the product is defined and remains a statement where it is not.
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-x^2}\,dx=\sqrt\pi.$$

Fix a nonempty finite directed acyclic graph $G=(V,E)$ with a specified
topological order $v_1,\ldots,v_p$; every arrow points from an earlier to a
later vertex. For $j\in V$, let
$\operatorname{pa}(j)=\{i\in V:(i,j)\in E\}$ be its parent set, and let
$\operatorname{nd}(j)$ be the vertices other than $j$ that are not descendants
of $j$. A **continuous additive-noise model** on $G$ consists of real random
variables $X_j,N_j$ on a common probability space and continuous Borel
functions $f_j:\mathbb R^{\operatorname{pa}(j)}\to\mathbb R$ such that
$$X_j=f_j(X_{\operatorname{pa}(j)})+N_j$$
recursively in the topological order. The finite family of noises is mutually
independent, and each $N_j$ has a strictly positive Lebesgue density $q_j$.
All vertices of $G$ are observed; no latent vertices are omitted from the
model. The **observational law** is the law of the vector
$X=(X_j)_{j\in V}$.

The model is **causally minimal** when every parent input is essential: for
each edge $i\to j$, there are values of the other parent coordinates and two
distinct real values of the $i$-coordinate at which $f_j$ takes different
values. A root has no parent-coordinate minimality condition.

Let a finite additive-noise model have topological order $v_1,\ldots,v_p$,
equations $X_j=f_j(X_{\operatorname{pa}(j)})+N_j$, and strictly positive
Lebesgue densities $q_j$ for its mutually independent noises. Write
$\rho=\lambda^{\otimes p}$ for the finite product of one-dimensional Lebesgue
measure. If all $q_j$ are Borel measurable, the observational law has the
strictly positive Borel density
$$p_X(x)=\prod_{r=1}^p q_{v_r}\!\left(x_{v_r}-f_{v_r}(x_{\operatorname{pa}(v_r)})\right)$$
with respect to $\rho$ on Borel sets.

For arbitrary Lebesgue-measurable $q_j$, assume Countable Choice. There are
strictly positive finite Borel density versions $\bar q_j=q_j$ almost
everywhere. Their product
$$\bar p_X(x)=\prod_{r=1}^p \bar q_{v_r}\!\left(x_{v_r}-f_{v_r}(x_{\operatorname{pa}(v_r)})\right)$$
is a strictly positive Borel density with respect to $\rho$. The original
product $p_X$ is measurable for the completion $\bar\rho$ of $\rho$, agrees
with $\bar p_X$ $\bar\rho$-almost everywhere, and is a strictly positive
density with respect to $\bar\rho$. In this Countable Choice case, on non-Borel sets these density measures
refer to the unique absolutely continuous extensions of the Borel
observational law to the indicated sigma-algebras.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim: Under AC [A1], treat the full Model A vector $(U,X,Y)$ as an ANM with noises $(N_U,\epsilon_X,\epsilon_Y)$. By [F4]–[F5], its density is $\phi(u)\phi(x-u)\phi(y-u)$; marginalizing the latent $U$ gives $p_A(x,y)=\int_{\mathbb R}\phi(u)\phi(x-u)\phi(y-u)\,du.$ Completing the square, $u^2+(x-u)^2+(y-u)^2=3\left(u-\frac{x+y}{3}\right)^2+\frac23(x^2-xy+y^2).$ Thus [F3] and the substitution $t=\sqrt{3/2}\,(u-(x+y)/3)$ give $p_A(x,y)=\frac1{2\pi\sqrt3}\exp\!\left(-\frac{x^2-xy+y^2}{3}\right).$

The scaled standard normal variables in Model B have densities $q_2(x)=\frac1{2\sqrt\pi}e^{-x^2/4}$ and $q_{3/2}(e)=\frac1{\sqrt{3\pi}}e^{-e^2/3}$ by [F2]. The Model B equation is an ANM, so [F4] gives $p_B(x,y)=q_2(x)q_{3/2}(y-x/2)=\frac1{2\pi\sqrt3}\exp\!\left(-\frac{x^2-xy+y^2}{3}\right),$ where the last equality follows by expanding $x^2/4+(y-x/2)^2/3=(x^2-xy+y^2)/3$. Hence $p_A=p_B$ pointwise.

Under $do(X=1)$ in Model A, [F1] replaces only the equation for $X$; the unchanged $Y$ equation remains $Y=U+\epsilon_Y$. Its density is the convolution $\int\phi(u)\phi(y-u)\,du=\frac1{2\sqrt\pi}e^{-y^2/4}$, by completing the square and [F3]. In Model B the intervention gives $Y=1/2+E$, whose density is $\frac1{\sqrt{3\pi}}e^{-(y-1/2)^2/3}$ by [F2]. At $y=1/2$ the second density is larger than the first by the factor $\frac2{\sqrt3}e^{1/16}>1$, so the intervention laws differ although the observational densities agree.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $U,\epsilon_X,\epsilon_Y$ be mutually
independent standard normal random variables. In Model A, set
$U=N_U$, $X=U+\epsilon_X$, and $Y=U+\epsilon_Y$, with $U$ latent and $X,Y$
observed. In Model B, let $Z_1,Z_2$ be independent standard normal variables,
set $X=\sqrt2 Z_1$, $E=\sqrt{3/2}Z_2$, and $Y=X/2+E$, with both vertices
observed. In each model the observed vector $(X,Y)$ has density
$$p(x,y)=\frac1{2\pi\sqrt3}\exp\!\left(-\frac{x^2-xy+y^2}{3}\right).$$
Under $do(X=1)$, Model A gives $Y=U+\epsilon_Y$ with density
$\frac1{2\sqrt\pi}e^{-y^2/4}$, while Model B gives $Y=1/2+E$ with density
$\frac1{\sqrt{3\pi}}e^{-(y-1/2)^2/3}$. The two intervention densities
differ at $y=1/2$, so the same observational law is compatible with different
causal effects when a latent common cause is allowed.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. The law of a random element is a probability measure makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in The Dirac set function at a point.

Fix a nonempty finite directed acyclic graph $G=(V,E)$ with a specified
topological order $v_1,\ldots,v_p$; every arrow points from an earlier to a
later vertex. For $j\in V$, let
$\operatorname{pa}(j)=\{i\in V:(i,j)\in E\}$ be its parent set, and let
$\operatorname{nd}(j)$ be the vertices other than $j$ that are not descendants
of $j$. A **continuous additive-noise model** on $G$ consists of real random
variables $X_j,N_j$ on a common probability space and continuous Borel
functions $f_j:\mathbb R^{\operatorname{pa}(j)}\to\mathbb R$ such that
$$X_j=f_j(X_{\operatorname{pa}(j)})+N_j$$
recursively in the topological order. The finite family of noises is mutually
independent, and each $N_j$ has a strictly positive Lebesgue density $q_j$.
All vertices of $G$ are observed; no latent vertices are omitted from the
model. The **observational law** is the law of the vector
$X=(X_j)_{j\in V}$.

The model is **causally minimal** when every parent input is essential: for
each edge $i\to j$, there are values of the other parent coordinates and two
distinct real values of the $i$-coordinate at which $f_j$ takes different
values. A root has no parent-coordinate minimality condition.

For a smooth bivariate additive-noise model $Y=f(X)+N$, let $f$ be three
times continuously differentiable, and let $X$ and $N$ have strictly positive
three-times continuously differentiable densities $p_X$ and $p_N$. Put
$\xi(x)=\log p_X(x)$ and $\nu(z)=\log p_N(z)$. The triple $(f,p_X,p_N)$
satisfies **Condition 19** when there are $x,y\in\mathbb R$ with
$\nu''(y-f(x))f'(x)\ne0$ at which
$$\xi'''(x)\ne \xi''(x)\left(-\frac{\nu'''(y-f(x))f'(x)}{\nu''(y-f(x))}+\frac{f''(x)}{f'(x)}\right) -2\nu''(y-f(x))f''(x)f'(x) +\nu'(y-f(x))f'''(x) +\frac{\nu'(y-f(x))\nu'''(y-f(x))f''(x)f'(x)}{\nu''(y-f(x))} -\frac{\nu'(y-f(x))(f''(x))^2}{f'(x)}.$$
Here every derivative of $\nu$ is evaluated at $y-f(x)$ and every derivative
of $f$ at $x$. The nonzero-domain condition makes both denominators in this
formula well defined.

A finite additive-noise model is a **restricted additive-noise model** when
every structural function $f_j$ is $C^3$ and every noise has a strictly
positive $C^3$ Lebesgue density, and when for every vertex $j$, every parent
$i\in\operatorname{pa}(j)$, and every set
$S$ satisfying
$$\operatorname{pa}(j)\setminus\{i\}\subseteq S\subseteq\operatorname{nd}(j)\setminus\{i\},$$
there is a value $s$ with $0<p_S(s)<\infty$ such that the
conditional law of $X_i$ given $X_S=s$, together with the structural slice
$u\mapsto f_j(s_{\operatorname{pa}(j)\setminus\{i\}},u)$ and the noise $N_j$,
is a smooth bivariate additive-noise model satisfying Condition 19. The
conditional density is the ratio
$p_{X_i,X_S}(u,s)/p_S(s)$ for the finite positive-density version supplied
by the joint-density formula. The structural slice and conditional input
density have the smoothness and strict positivity required in the preceding
Condition 19 definition. If the model has no edges, the restricted condition
is vacuous.

Assume AC. Let $X,N$ be independent standard normal random variables and set
$Y=X+N$. The forward model $Y=X+N$ is an additive-noise model, and the same
joint law also has the reverse representation
$$X=\frac12Y+M,\qquad M:=\frac{X-N}{2},$$
where $M$ is independent of $Y$. Indeed, the joint density of $(Y,M)$ is
$$p_{Y,M}(y,m)=\frac1{2\pi}\exp\!\left(-\frac{y^2}{4}-m^2\right)=\left(\frac1{2\sqrt\pi}e^{-y^2/4}\right)\left(\frac1{\sqrt\pi}e^{-m^2}\right).$$
The forward structural function $f(x)=x$ and the two Gaussian log densities
satisfy the differential equation in Condition 19 at every point of its
nonzero domain, so Condition 19 fails. Thus this reversible case lies outside
the bivariate identifiability theorem's hypothesis.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. For $b>0$, let $\mu_b$ be the probability measure on $\mathbb R$ concentrated on $(0,+\infty)$ with Lebesgue density $x\mapsto b^{-1}e^{-x/b}$ there and zero elsewhere. For every Borel set $A\subseteq\mathbb R$, define

$$
\operatorname{Lap}(b)(A)=\frac12\mu_b(A\cap(0,+\infty))+\frac12\mu_b(\{x>0:-x\in A\}).
$$

Thus $\operatorname{Lap}(b)$ is the equal mixture of the positive exponential law and its reflection in the origin. Define $\operatorname{Lap}(0)$ to be the point mass at $0$.

Assume Countable Choice. For $\lambda>0$, the density
$$f_\lambda(t)=\begin{cases}\lambda e^{-\lambda t},&t>0,\\0,&t\le0\end{cases}$$
defines a probability law on $\mathbb R$ with survival
$S(t)=e^{-\lambda t}$ for $t\ge0$. For $k,\eta>0$, the density
$$f_{k,\eta}(t)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{k}{\eta}(t/\eta)^{k-1}e^{-(t/\eta)^k},&t>0,\\0,&t\le0\end{cases}$$
defines a probability law with survival $S(t)=e^{-(t/\eta)^k}$ for $t\ge0$.
Each law is unique among probability laws on $[0,\infty)$ with that survival.
The density hazards are respectively $\lambda$ and
$\dfrac{k}{\eta}(t/\eta)^{k-1}$ for $t>0$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice (The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
(The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

(Axis-parallel rectangles in $\mathbb{R}^m$ and their volume). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of Half-open boxes in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and their volume, and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ (Assuming countable choice, $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra containing every elementary set and $\lambda_n$ is a complete measure extending elementary volume).

derivations.claim: Put $A_+=A\cap(0,+\infty)$ and $A_-=A\cap(-\infty,0)$. By [F1] and [F2], the positive mixture half contributes $\frac12\int_{A_+}b^{-1}e^{-x/b}\,d\lambda(x)$. Applying [F3] to reflection $T(x)=-x$ and $y\mapsto\mathbf1_{A_-}(y)b^{-1}e^{y/b}$ shows that the reflected half contributes $\frac12\int_{A_-}b^{-1}e^{y/b}\,d\lambda(y)$. On $A_+$, $e^{-x/b}=e^{-|x|/b}$; on $A_-$, $e^{y/b}=e^{-|y|/b}$. The singleton at zero has Lebesgue measure zero by [F4]. Hence $\operatorname{Lap}(b)(A)=\int_A(2b)^{-1}e^{-|z|/b}\,d\lambda(z)$.

The identity in step 1.1 holds for every Borel set $A$. Its integrand is nonnegative and measurable; thus every Lebesgue-null Borel set has zero $\operatorname{Lap}(b)$ measure, and the displayed function is the claimed Radon–Nikodym density.

> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

For every $b>0$, the probability measure $\operatorname{Lap}(b)$ is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R$ and has density

$$
z\longmapsto \frac{1}{2b}e^{-|z|/b}.
$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
Measurable rectangles in a product of measurable spaces.

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   The product measure of two sigma-finite measure spaces is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and define

Then $\nu_f$ is a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$.

derivations.claim: Define $f(z)=\prod_{i=1}^d f_b(z_i)=(2b)^{-d}\exp(-\|z\|_1/b)$; the equality factoring the exponential of a finite sum uses [F8]. Repeated application of [F4] gives $\int_{\mathbb R^d} f(z)\,d\lambda^d(z)=\prod_{i=1}^d\int_{\mathbb R}f_b(x)\,d\lambda(x)=1$, using [F1] for each one-dimensional integral. By [F5], $\nu(A)=\int_A f\,d\lambda^d$ is therefore a probability measure.

For a measurable rectangle $A=\prod_{i=1}^d A_i$, repeated Tonelli integration [F4] gives $\nu(A)=\prod_{i=1}^d\int_{A_i}f_b\,d\lambda=\prod_{i=1}^d\operatorname{Lap}(b)(A_i)$. The finite product law has this same rectangle value by [F3]. Rectangles form a generating pi-system by [F2], and the constant sequence of whole-space rectangles is an increasing exhaustion with mass one for both measures, so [F6] identifies $\nu$ with $\operatorname{Lap}(b)^{\otimes d}$ on the entire product sigma-algebra. Taking unrestricted factors equal to $\mathbb R$ gives the stated coordinate marginals and factorization for every finite subfamily of coordinate events. These are exactly the events in the generated coordinate sigma-algebras, so the projections are independent by [F7].

Let $U$ be a nonempty set of possible records and let $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$. A database is a function $D:U\to\mathbb N_0$ with finite support $\operatorname{supp}(D)=\{u\in U:D(u)\ne0\}$; $D(u)$ is the number of occurrences of record $u$. Let $\mathcal D$ be the set of databases and equip it with the power-set sigma-algebra. For $u\in U$, let $\mathbf 1_{\{u\}}$ be the function that is one at $u$ and zero elsewhere. Two databases $D,D'\in\mathcal D$ are neighbors, written $D\sim D'$, when $D'=D+\mathbf 1_{\{u\}}$ or $D=D'+\mathbf 1_{\{u\}}$ for some $u\in U$.

A randomized mechanism with output measurable space $(Y,\mathcal B)$ is a probability kernel $K$ from $\mathcal D$ to $Y$: for each $D\in\mathcal D$, $A\mapsto K(D,A)$ is a probability measure on $(Y,\mathcal B)$, and for each $A\in\mathcal B$, $D\mapsto K(D,A)$ is measurable. Given $\varepsilon\ge0$ and $0\le\delta\le1$, the mechanism is $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-differentially private if, for every ordered neighboring pair $D\sim D'$ and every output event $A\in\mathcal B$,

$$
K(D,A)\le e^{\varepsilon}K(D',A)+\delta.
$$

The mechanism is $\varepsilon$-differentially private, or pure $\varepsilon$-differentially private, when $\delta=0$. The ordered-pair quantifier includes both directions because $\sim$ is symmetric.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

Let $d\ge1$ and let $f:\mathcal D\to\mathbb R^d$ be a query on databases with the add/remove adjacency relation. Write $\|x\|_1=\sum_{j=1}^d|x_j|$. When the set of adjacent-pair differences has an attained finite maximum, the global $L^1$ sensitivity of $f$ is

$$
\Delta_1 f=\max_{D\sim D'}\|f(D)-f(D')\|_1.
$$

The sensitivity is finite when this maximum is finite.

Assume Countable Choice. For $b>0$, let $\mu_b$ be the probability measure on $\mathbb R$ concentrated on $(0,+\infty)$ with Lebesgue density $x\mapsto b^{-1}e^{-x/b}$ there and zero elsewhere. For every Borel set $A\subseteq\mathbb R$, define

$$
\operatorname{Lap}(b)(A)=\frac12\mu_b(A\cap(0,+\infty))+\frac12\mu_b(\{x>0:-x\in A\}).
$$

Thus $\operatorname{Lap}(b)$ is the equal mixture of the positive exponential law and its reflection in the origin. Define $\operatorname{Lap}(0)$ to be the point mass at $0$.

Let $(S,\Sigma)$ and $(T_i,\Tau_i)$ for $i<n$ be measurable spaces, with
$n<\infty$, and let $K_i:S\to T_i$ be probability kernels with the same
source. There is a unique probability kernel
$$K:S\to\prod_{i<n}T_i$$
whose evaluation on every measurable rectangle is
$$K(s,\prod_{i<n}B_i)=\prod_{i<n}K_i(s,B_i).$$
For $n=0$, the target is the empty-product singleton and $K$ is its point
mass. For $n>0$, the product sigma-algebra is the recursive finite product
sigma-algebra.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space (Topology on a set, open and closed sets, clopen sets, the closed-set axiomatisation, and the coarser/finer comparison). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by Nonempty intersections of sigma-algebras are sigma-algebras, so the generated sigma-algebra exists and is minimal.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $n,m\ge1$. Every continuous map
$f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is Borel measurable in
the sense of Borel measurable and Lebesgue measurable functions on $\mathbb{R}^n$.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in Measures on sigma-algebras and A measurable function between measurable spaces; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let $\mathcal D$ be the finite-support count functions on a nonempty record universe, with add/remove-one-occurrence adjacency. Let $R$ be a nonempty finite set independent of the database, and let $u:\mathcal D\times R\to\mathbb R$ be a real-valued utility. When the set of adjacent-pair utility differences has an attained finite maximum, the global utility sensitivity of $u$ is
$$
\Delta_u=\max_{D\sim D',\,r\in R}|u(D,r)-u(D',r)|.
$$
The sensitivity is positive when $\Delta_u>0$; the exponential mechanism on this page uses that positive-sensitivity case.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in The exponential series converges absolutely for every real argument. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of The factorial $n!$ and the falling factorial $n^{\underline{k}}$, defined by recursion in $\mathbb{N}$, $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image (The canonical natural $\iota(n) = n \cdot 1_F$ of a field, Canonical naturals are positive and strictly increasing), and powers and series are those of Integer powers $a^m$ and Series, partial sums, convergence and the sum, divergence, and the tail series.

This is a real power series centred at $0$ (A real power series about a centre, its interval of convergence, and its radius in $[0,+\infty]$). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ (Measures on sigma-algebras). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** (Measure spaces); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $U$ be a nonempty set of possible records and let $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$. A database is a function $D:U\to\mathbb N_0$ with finite support $\operatorname{supp}(D)=\{u\in U:D(u)\ne0\}$; $D(u)$ is the number of occurrences of record $u$. Let $\mathcal D$ be the set of databases and equip it with the power-set sigma-algebra. For $u\in U$, let $\mathbf 1_{\{u\}}$ be the function that is one at $u$ and zero elsewhere. Two databases $D,D'\in\mathcal D$ are neighbors, written $D\sim D'$, when $D'=D+\mathbf 1_{\{u\}}$ or $D=D'+\mathbf 1_{\{u\}}$ for some $u\in U$.

A randomized mechanism with output measurable space $(Y,\mathcal B)$ is a probability kernel $K$ from $\mathcal D$ to $Y$: for each $D\in\mathcal D$, $A\mapsto K(D,A)$ is a probability measure on $(Y,\mathcal B)$, and for each $A\in\mathcal B$, $D\mapsto K(D,A)$ is measurable. Given $\varepsilon\ge0$ and $0\le\delta\le1$, the mechanism is $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-differentially private if, for every ordered neighboring pair $D\sim D'$ and every output event $A\in\mathcal B$,

$$
K(D,A)\le e^{\varepsilon}K(D',A)+\delta.
$$

The mechanism is $\varepsilon$-differentially private, or pure $\varepsilon$-differentially private, when $\delta=0$. The ordered-pair quantifier includes both directions because $\sim$ is symmetric.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in Measures on sigma-algebras and A measurable function between measurable spaces; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

derivations.claim: Since $\Delta_u>0$ and each score $u(D,r)$ is real, [F2] makes every weight $w_D(r)$ finite and positive. The nonempty finite sum $Z_D$ is therefore finite and strictly positive. For $A\subseteq R$, define $K(D,A)=\sum_{r\in A}w_D(r)/Z_D$. This is nonnegative, equals one on $R$, and is countably additive because a disjoint family of subsets of finite $R$ has only finitely many nonempty members. For every $A\subseteq R$, $D\mapsto K(D,A)$ is measurable because every subset of the database domain is measurable by [F4]. Hence the assignment satisfies both conditions in [F5] and is a probability kernel.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because The exponential is a continuous bijection from $\mathbb{R}$ onto $(0,\infty)$ states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

derivations.claim: For every $r\in R$, [F2] and monotonicity and addition for $\exp$ from [F6] give $w_D(r)\le e^{\varepsilon/2}w_{D'}(r)$; summing gives $Z_D\le e^{\varepsilon/2}Z_{D'}$. Applying the same argument with $D,D'$ interchanged gives $Z_{D'}\le e^{\varepsilon/2}Z_D$. Since the weights and normalizers are positive, [F6] then yields $(w_D(r)/Z_D)/(w_{D'}(r)/Z_{D'})\le e^\varepsilon$. Interchanging $D,D'$ gives the reverse point-mass bound. Summing over any event $A\subseteq R$ gives both $(\varepsilon,0)$ event inequalities, so [F4] proves privacy.

By [F3], the maximizing set is nonempty and its elements each have weight $e^{\varepsilon\operatorname{OPT}_u(D)/(2\Delta_u)}$. Let $B$ be the event in the Statement. For each $r\in B$, its defining score inequality, monotonicity and addition for $\exp$ from [F6], and [F5] imply $w_D(r)\le e^{\varepsilon\operatorname{OPT}_u(D)/(2\Delta_u)}(|R_{\operatorname{OPT}}|/|R|)e^{-t}$. There are at most $|R|$ such elements, while the normalizer is at least the sum of the maximizing weights, namely $|R_{\operatorname{OPT}}|e^{\varepsilon\operatorname{OPT}_u(D)/(2\Delta_u)}$. Therefore the probability of $B$ is at most $e^{-t}$. If $B$ is empty its probability is zero and the same bound holds.

finite_smoke.asserts:
Let $\mathcal D$ be the set of finite-support record-count databases, with neighbors defined by adding or removing one record occurrence. Let $R$ be a nonempty finite set independent of the database, and let $u:\mathcal D\times R\to\mathbb R$ be a real-valued utility with finite positive attained global utility sensitivity $\Delta_u$. For $\varepsilon>0$, use weights $w_D(r)=\exp(\varepsilon u(D,r)/(2\Delta_u))$ and normalize them over $R$ as in the exponential mechanism. Its output law is $(\varepsilon,0)$-differentially private. For a fixed database $D$, let
$$ \operatorname{OPT}_u(D)=\max_{r\in R}u(D,r),\qquad R_{\operatorname{OPT}}=\{r\in R:u(D,r)=\operatorname{OPT}_u(D)\}. $$
For every $t>0$, if $M(D)$ denotes the random output, then
$$
\Pr\!\left[u(D,M(D))\le\operatorname{OPT}_u(D)-\frac{2\Delta_u}{\varepsilon}\left(\ln\frac{|R|}{|R_{\operatorname{OPT}}|}+t\right)\right]\le e^{-t}.
$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of Integrable real and complex functions, and their integrals, its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

Let $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\chi_{E_j}$ be a simple representation of a
nonnegative simple measurable function
(Nonnegative simple measurable functions) on a measure space
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$, so the $E_j\in\mathcal A$ are pairwise disjoint and
$c_j\ge0$. Its
**simple integral** is
$$\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mu(E_j),$$
where $\mu$ is the given measure (Measures on sigma-algebras) and the convention
$0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ is fixed once and for all.

The next lemma proves that this value is independent of the chosen simple
representation.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: For each integer $m\ge0$, put $n=2^m$ and define $g_m=\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n\mathbf1_{\{g\ge j/n\}}$. Each $g_m$ is a measurable simple function and $0\le g_m\le g$. Every level $j/n$ counted at stage $m$ contributes the two levels $(2j-1)/(2n)$ and $2j/(2n)$ at stage $m+1$, so $g_{m+1}\ge g_m$. The largest dyadic level not exceeding any fixed $g(x)$ differs from $g(x)$ by less than $2^{-m}$, so $g_m(x)\uparrow g(x)$.

Apply the given event inequality to the $n$ level sets in step 1.1 and use [F3] on disjoint simple representations. Partition the range into $B_k=\{k/n\le g<(k+1)/n\}$ for $0\le k<n$ and $B_n=\{g=1\}$. Then $g_m=\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}(k/n)\mathbf1_{B_k}+\mathbf1_{B_n}$, while each level set $\{g\ge j/n\}$ is the disjoint union of $B_j,\ldots,B_n$. Rearranging these finite sums gives $\int g_m\,dP=\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^nP(g\ge j/n)\le\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n(e^\varepsilon Q(g\ge j/n)+\delta)=e^\varepsilon\int g_m\,dQ+\delta$. This holds for every $m$.
Let $m\to\infty$ in step 2.1. By [F4] and step 1.1, both nonnegative integrals converge to the corresponding integrals of $g$, so $\int g\,dP\le e^\varepsilon\int g\,dQ+\delta$.

Let $U$ be a nonempty set of possible records and let $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$. A database is a function $D:U\to\mathbb N_0$ with finite support $\operatorname{supp}(D)=\{u\in U:D(u)\ne0\}$; $D(u)$ is the number of occurrences of record $u$. Let $\mathcal D$ be the set of databases and equip it with the power-set sigma-algebra. For $u\in U$, let $\mathbf 1_{\{u\}}$ be the function that is one at $u$ and zero elsewhere. Two databases $D,D'\in\mathcal D$ are neighbors, written $D\sim D'$, when $D'=D+\mathbf 1_{\{u\}}$ or $D=D'+\mathbf 1_{\{u\}}$ for some $u\in U$.

A randomized mechanism with output measurable space $(Y,\mathcal B)$ is a probability kernel $K$ from $\mathcal D$ to $Y$: for each $D\in\mathcal D$, $A\mapsto K(D,A)$ is a probability measure on $(Y,\mathcal B)$, and for each $A\in\mathcal B$, $D\mapsto K(D,A)$ is measurable. Given $\varepsilon\ge0$ and $0\le\delta\le1$, the mechanism is $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-differentially private if, for every ordered neighboring pair $D\sim D'$ and every output event $A\in\mathcal B$,

$$
K(D,A)\le e^{\varepsilon}K(D',A)+\delta.
$$

The mechanism is $\varepsilon$-differentially private, or pure $\varepsilon$-differentially private, when $\delta=0$. The ordered-pair quantifier includes both directions because $\sim$ is symmetric.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in Measures on sigma-algebras and A measurable function between measurable spaces; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let $P$ and $Q$ be probability measures on a measurable space. Suppose $\varepsilon\ge0$, $0\le\delta\le1$, and $P(A)\le e^\varepsilon Q(A)+\delta$ for every measurable set $A$. Then every measurable function $g$ with $0\le g\le1$ satisfies

$$
\int g\,dP\le e^\varepsilon\int g\,dQ+\delta.
$$

For probability kernels $K:(S,\Sigma)\to(T,\Tau)$ and $L:(T,\Tau)\to(U,\Upsilon)$, their **composition**, in the order K then L, is
$$(KL)(s,A)=\int_T L(t,A)\,K(s,dt),\qquad s\in S,\quad A\in\Upsilon.$$

The kernel convention is Measure kernel and probability kernel. The integrand is measurable in t and lies in $[0,1]$, so the displayed number exists in $[0,1]$. As a function of s it is measurable by Measurability of integration against a kernel, applied to the product-measurable function $(s,t)\mapsto L(t,A)$: its threshold preimages are rectangles $S\times\{t:L(t,A)>a\}$. The probability-kernel assertion and associativity are justified by Kernel composition is well defined and associative.

Composition refers to specified pointwise kernels. Almost-everywhere classes alone do not define this formula until representatives and the relevant measures are specified. For an empty source the candidate is the empty map. No choice of versions or assumption of AC enters this definition.

The composition KL of probability kernels $K:S\to T$ and $L:T\to U$ is a probability kernel $S\to U$. If $M:U\to V$ is another probability kernel, then $(KL)M=K(LM)$ at every source point and every measurable subset of V. Equality concerns the specified kernels, not unspecified almost-everywhere classes.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

A measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$ is **standard Borel** if there are a Polish space $P$ and a bijection $h:E\to P$ such that $A\in\mathcal E$ exactly when $h[A]$ is Borel in $P$. Thus the measurable structure is part of the datum; no particular compatible Polish topology on $E$ is selected.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mu$ be a positive measure and let $
u$ be a signed measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. Assume there is an increasing measurable exhaustion $(X_n)$ with $ igcup_nX_n=X$, $\mu(X_n)<+\infty$, and $|
u|(X_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$. If $
u\ll\mu$, then there exists a measurable real-valued function $f$, unique up to $\mu$-almost-everywhere equality, such that
$$
u(E)=\int_Ef\,d\mu\qquad(E\in\mathcal A).$$
If in addition $|
u|(X)<+\infty$, then $f\in L^1(\mu)$.

Let $\mu$ be a sigma-finite positive measure and let $\nu$ be a signed measure or a finite complex measure with $\nu\ll\mu$. If $h$ is a representative of $d\nu/d\mu$, then
$$\nu(E)=\int_E h\,d\mu\qquad(E\in\mathcal A).$$
More generally, if
$$g=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mathbf 1_{E_j}$$
is the canonical disjoint representation of a simple measurable function and $|\nu|(E_j)<+\infty$ for every $j$, then
$$\int g\,d\nu=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\int_{E_j} h\,d\mu.$$
In particular, whenever the Lebesgue integral of $gh$ is defined, one has
$$\int g\,d\nu=\int gh\,d\mu.$$

The definition is independent of the representative: two representatives

The function $\psi$ is continuous at zero: for $s\ge1$,

Thus $t\log t\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$; here $L=\log$ by

This convention is directional: the first argument must be absolutely
continuous with respect to the second for the integral formula to apply.

Kullback–Leibler divergence. For probability measures $P,Q$ on one
measurable space, $D(P\|Q)\ge0$, and $D(P\|Q)=0$ if and only if $P=Q$.

There is also the following normalized-density identity. Let
$(\mathsf X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a sigma-finite measure space: it is a set
with a sigma-algebra and measure (Measure spaces), and there is a
countable measurable cover by sets of finite $\mu$-measure
(Finite, sigma-finite, and semifinite measures). Let
$\gamma:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ be a finite-valued measurable function with
$Z:=\int\gamma\,d\mu\in(0,\infty)$, and put $\pi=\gamma/Z$. Let
$q:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ be a finite-valued measurable probability density,
so $\int q\,d\mu=1$, and suppose $q=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on
$\{\gamma=0\}$. Assume
$$\int q\bigl(|\log\gamma|+|\log q|\bigr)\,d\mu<\infty,$$
where each term with $q=0$ is defined to be zero. Then
$$\log Z =\int q(\log\gamma-\log q)\,d\mu +D(q\,\mu\|\pi\,\mu).$$
In particular, the first integral is at most $\log Z$. This identity concerns
normalized densities only; it does not assert posterior existence for an
unspecified statistical model.
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$, $(Y,\mathcal{B})$, and $(Z,\mathcal{C})$ be measurable
spaces. If $f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Y,\mathcal{B})$ is measurable and
$g : (Y,\mathcal{B}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable, then
$g \circ f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable.

In particular, if $f$ is measurable and $g$ is a Borel measurable function on
its codomain, then $g \circ f$ is measurable.

derivations.claim: The standard-Borel hypotheses are explicit as required by [F1]. Since $P(A)\le aQ(A)$ for every measurable $A$, $P\ll Q$. Choose a Radon–Nikodym density $r=dP/dQ$ using [A1] and [F2].

By [F6], $a=e^\varepsilon\ge1$ and $a^{-1}>0$. The inequality $P(A)\le aQ(A)$ forces $r\le a$ $Q$-almost everywhere: otherwise some set $E_n=\{r\ge a+1/n\}$ has positive $Q$-measure and violates the inequality after integration. Similarly $Q(A)\le aP(A)=a\int_A r\,dQ$ forces $r\ge a^{-1}$ $Q$-almost everywhere, since any positive-measure set where $r\le a^{-1}-1/n$ violates that inequality. Thus $a^{-1}\le r\le a$ almost everywhere.

Let $E=\{r\ge1\}$, $p=P(E)$, $q=Q(E)$, and $t=p-q$. Since $P(A)-Q(A)=\int_A(r-1)\,dQ$, the set $E$ maximizes this difference and $E^c$ gives its negative. Hence $t=\sup_A|P(A)-Q(A)|=\frac12\int|r-1|\,dQ$. The event inequalities on $E$ and $E^c$ give $t\le(a-1)q$ and $at\le(a-1)(1-q)$, respectively. Adding yields $(a+1)t\le a-1$, so $t\le(a-1)/(a+1)$.

The lower bound in step 2.1 makes $P$ and $Q$ equivalent. Define $s=1/r$ on $\{r>0\}$ and $s=0$ on its null complement; [F7] makes it measurable. By [F3], $\int_A s\,dP=\int_A sr\,dQ=Q(A)$ for every measurable $A$, so $s=dQ/dP$. The logarithm reciprocal identity in [F6] gives $\log s=-\log r$ almost everywhere, and both log densities are bounded in absolute value by $\varepsilon$; [F4] therefore gives finite divergences and $D(P\|Q)+D(Q\|P)=\int(r-1)\log r\,dQ\le\varepsilon\int|r-1|\,dQ=2\varepsilon t$. By [F5], $D(Q\|P)\ge0$, and step 3.1 gives $2\varepsilon t\le2\varepsilon(a-1)/(a+1)\le\varepsilon(a-1)$. Therefore $D(P\|Q)\le\varepsilon(a-1)=\varepsilon(e^\varepsilon-1)$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

A measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$ is **standard Borel** if there are a Polish space $P$ and a bijection $h:E\to P$ such that $A\in\mathcal E$ exactly when $h[A]$ is Borel in $P$. Thus the measurable structure is part of the datum; no particular compatible Polish topology on $E$ is selected.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in Measures on sigma-algebras and A measurable function between measurable spaces; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Assume AC. Let $(E,\mathcal E)$ and $(F,\mathcal F)$ be standard Borel spaces, let $\lambda$ be a probability measure on $E$, and let $M$ and $R$ be probability kernels from $E$ to $F$. Suppose $M(x,\cdot)\ll R(x,\cdot)$ for $\lambda$-almost every $x$. Then there is an $(\mathcal E\otimes\mathcal F)$-measurable function $r:E\times F\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for $\lambda$-almost every $x$ and every $B\in\mathcal F$,
$$M(x,B)=\int_B r(x,y)\,R(x,dy).$$
The exceptional set in $x$ is a single null set, independent of $B$.

Assume AC. Every standard-Borel space $(E,\mathcal S)$ has a countable algebra $\mathcal A$ which generates $\mathcal S$, separates points, and determines finite measures: if finite measures $\mu,\nu$ agree on $\mathcal A$, then $\mu=\nu$. In particular it determines probability measures.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and define
$$\nu_f(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu \qquad (A\in\mathcal A).$$
Then $\nu_f$ is a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces, and let
$$f : X \times Y \to \overline{\mathbb R}$$
be $(\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B,\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R}))$-measurable.
Then $f_x : Y \to \overline{\mathbb R}$ is $\mathcal B$-measurable for every
$x \in X$, and $f^y : X \to \overline{\mathbb R}$ is $\mathcal A$-measurable
for every $y \in Y$.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$, $(Y,\mathcal{B})$, and $(Z,\mathcal{C})$ be measurable
spaces. If $f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Y,\mathcal{B})$ is measurable and
$g : (Y,\mathcal{B}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable, then
$g \circ f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable.

In particular, if $f$ is measurable and $g$ is a Borel measurable function on
its codomain, then $g \circ f$ is measurable.

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

derivations.claim: Let $M(h,A)=(K(h,A)+L(h,A))/2$, which is a probability kernel by [F2]. For every $h$, $M(h,A)=0$ implies $K(h,A)=L(h,A)=0$, so both sections are absolutely continuous with respect to $M(h,\cdot)$. Apply [F3] twice to obtain jointly measurable densities. Replace any value $+\infty$ by $0$ in each density; this Borel operation preserves measurability by [F8] and changes no section measure on the common conull representation set, since each density has integral one. Call the resulting finite-valued functions $p(h,y)$ and $q(h,y)$. Let $\mathcal C$ be the countable generating algebra in [F4], containing $Y$. Define $G$ to be the set of $h$ for which, for every $C\in\mathcal C$, both $K(h,C)=\int_Cp(h,y)M(h,dy)$ and $L(h,C)=\int_Cq(h,y)M(h,dy)$ hold, and both DP inequalities hold for $C$. By [F2], [F5], and countability of $\mathcal C$, $G$ is measurable. It has full $\lambda$-measure by the joint representation property and the hypothesis. For $h\in G$, [F6] and [F7] make the density integrals finite measures; they agree with $K(h,\cdot)$ and $L(h,\cdot)$ on $\mathcal C$, so [F4] gives the density representations on every measurable event.

For fixed $h\in G$, put $\rho=K(h,\cdot)+L(h,\cdot)$, a finite measure. Let $\mathcal E_\rho$ be the measurable sets approximable in $\rho$-measure by members of $\mathcal C$. Complements preserve symmetric-difference measure, and $(A\cup B)\mathbin\triangle(C\cup D)\subseteq(A\mathbin\triangle C)\cup(B\mathbin\triangle D)$ proves closure under finite unions. If $A_n\in\mathcal E_\rho$ and $A=\bigcup_nA_n$, put $U_N=\bigcup_{n\le N}A_n$ and $D_1=U_1$, $D_N=U_N\setminus U_{N-1}$ for $N>1$. The $D_N$ are disjoint and $A=\bigcup_ND_N$, so countable additivity and finiteness of $\rho(A)$ give $\rho(A\setminus U_N)=\sum_{j>N}\rho(D_j)\to0$. Approximate each of the first $N$ sets closely enough that their finite union has arbitrarily small symmetric-difference measure from $U_N$. Thus $\mathcal E_\rho$ is a sigma-algebra containing $\mathcal C$, so it is the full target sigma-algebra. For any measurable $B$, choose $C_n\in\mathcal C$ with $\rho(B\mathbin\triangle C_n)\to0$. Then both $K(h,C_n)\to K(h,B)$ and $L(h,C_n)\to L(h,B)$, so the two inequalities on $\mathcal C$ pass to every measurable $B$.

Write $a=\exp(\varepsilon)\ge1$ and $c=\exp(-\varepsilon)=1/a>0$ by [F9]. On $G$, set $p_0=\min\{\max\{p,cq\},aq\}$, $\alpha=\int(p-aq)_+\,dM$, and $\beta=\int(cq-p)_+\,dM$. These quantities are finite and measurable in $h$ by [F5] and [F8]. The sets $A_h=\{y:p(h,y)>aq(h,y)\}$ and $B_h=\{y:p(h,y)<cq(h,y)\}$ are measurable by [F7]. Step 2.1 and the density identities give $\alpha=K(h,A_h)-aL(h,A_h)\le\delta$ and $a\beta=L(h,B_h)-aK(h,B_h)\le\delta$. Also $p_0=p-(p-aq)_++(cq-p)_+$, so $m:=\int p_0\,dM=1-\alpha+\beta$. Hence $\max\{\alpha,\beta\}\le\delta$.

Define a corrected density on $G$ as follows. If $m<1$, let $t_+=(1-m)/(a-m)$ and $r=p_0+t_+(aq-p_0)$. Its denominator is positive and $0\le t_+\le1$ because $a\ge1$, so $p_0\le r\le aq$ and $\int r\,dM=m+t_+(a-m)=1$. If $m>1$, let $t_-=(m-1)/(m-c)$ and $r=p_0-t_-(p_0-cq)$. Here $m-c>0$ and $0\le t_-\le1$ because $c\le1$, so $cq\le r\le p_0$ and $\int r\,dM=m-t_-(m-c)=1$. If $m=1$, set $r=p_0$. These formulas are product-measurable by [F8], and in every case $cq\le r\le aq$ and $\int r\,dM=1$. Set $r=0$ off $G$ and define $K^*(h,A)=\int_A r(h,y)M(h,dy)+\mathbf1_{G^c}(h)L(h,A)$. By [F5], this is measurable in $h$ for each $A$; for each $h\in G$ it is a probability measure by [F6] and the normalization, and for $h\notin G$ it equals the probability measure $L(h,\cdot)$. Thus $K^*$ is a probability kernel. For $h\in G$, integrate $cq\le r\le aq$ and use the density representation of L to obtain the claimed two-sided pure-DP inequalities.

For $h\in G$, clipping changes $p$ by total integral $\int|p-p_0|\,dM=\alpha+\beta$, while correction moves $p_0$ in one direction and changes its integral by $|m-1|=|\alpha-\beta|$. Thus $\int|p-r|\,dM\le\alpha+\beta+|\alpha-\beta|=2\max\{\alpha,\beta\}\le2\delta$. For probability densities with equal integral, $\sup_A|\int_A(p-r)\,dM|=\tfrac12\int|p-r|\,dM$: every event integral is bounded by the positive-part integral and $\{p\ge r\}$ attains it. Hence $\operatorname{TV}(K(h,\cdot),K^*(h,\cdot))\le\delta$ on $G$. This TV function is measurable: applying the approximation argument of step 2.1 to $K+K^*$ shows its supremum may be taken over $\mathcal C$, whose kernel evaluations are measurable. Since $G$ is conull, integration proves the asserted bound.

Assume AC. Let $H$ and $Y$ be measurable spaces measurably isomorphic to Polish spaces, let $\lambda$ be a probability measure on $H$, and let $K,L$ be probability kernels from $H$ to $Y$. Let $\varepsilon\ge0$ and $0\le\delta\le1$. Suppose that for $\lambda$-almost every $h$, both inequalities
$$
K(h,A)\le e^\varepsilon L(h,A)+\delta,\qquad L(h,A)\le e^\varepsilon K(h,A)+\delta
$$
hold for every measurable $A\subseteq Y$. Then there is a probability kernel $K^*$ from $H$ to $Y$ such that for $\lambda$-almost every $h$ and every measurable $A\subseteq Y$,
$$
e^{-\varepsilon}L(h,A)\le K^*(h,A)\le e^\varepsilon L(h,A),
$$
and
$$
\int_H \operatorname{TV}(K(h,\cdot),K^*(h,\cdot))\,\lambda(dh)\le\delta,
$$
where $\operatorname{TV}(P,Q)=\sup_A|P(A)-Q(A)|$ over measurable events.

Let $U$ be a nonempty set of possible records and let $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$. A database is a function $D:U\to\mathbb N_0$ with finite support $\operatorname{supp}(D)=\{u\in U:D(u)\ne0\}$; $D(u)$ is the number of occurrences of record $u$. Let $\mathcal D$ be the set of databases and equip it with the power-set sigma-algebra. For $u\in U$, let $\mathbf 1_{\{u\}}$ be the function that is one at $u$ and zero elsewhere. Two databases $D,D'\in\mathcal D$ are neighbors, written $D\sim D'$, when $D'=D+\mathbf 1_{\{u\}}$ or $D=D'+\mathbf 1_{\{u\}}$ for some $u\in U$.

A randomized mechanism with output measurable space $(Y,\mathcal B)$ is a probability kernel $K$ from $\mathcal D$ to $Y$: for each $D\in\mathcal D$, $A\mapsto K(D,A)$ is a probability measure on $(Y,\mathcal B)$, and for each $A\in\mathcal B$, $D\mapsto K(D,A)$ is measurable. Given $\varepsilon\ge0$ and $0\le\delta\le1$, the mechanism is $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-differentially private if, for every ordered neighboring pair $D\sim D'$ and every output event $A\in\mathcal B$,

$$
K(D,A)\le e^{\varepsilon}K(D',A)+\delta.
$$

The mechanism is $\varepsilon$-differentially private, or pure $\varepsilon$-differentially private, when $\delta=0$. The ordered-pair quantifier includes both directions because $\sim$ is symmetric.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
Measurable rectangles in a product of measurable spaces.

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

be $(\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B,\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R}))$-measurable.
Then $f_x : Y \to \overline{\mathbb R}$ is $\mathcal B$-measurable for every
