$f_i:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be differentiable client objectives and
$f=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^Nf_i$. Run SCAFFOLD for $R$ rounds with local step count
$K$, client sample size $S$, server iterates $x_0,\ldots,x_R$, and client
controls $c_i^r$ after round $r$. In each round, extend the local trajectory
$y_{i,0}^r=x_{r-1},y_{i,1}^r,\ldots,y_{i,K}^r$ to every client using the
same local update rule, including hypothetical paths for clients not selected
in that round. Generate these counterfactual paths using fresh local oracle randomness independently of the fresh client sample, so a selected path agrees with its actual local execution. Local paths use only the round-start model and controls and their own successive oracle draws. Oracle moment conditions in the results below are conditional on the full prequery history, including any earlier revealed draws in the current round. All expectations below are over client samples and local
stochastic-gradient draws.

The **round-$r$ client drift at gradient-query points** is
$$ E_r=\frac1{KN}\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{k=1}^K \mathbb E\|y_{i,k-1}^r-x_{r-1}\|_2^2. $$
For every client and local-step index, initialize a stored anchor
$\alpha_{i,k}^0=x_0$ and stored gradient $\gamma_{i,k}^0=\nabla f_i(x_0)$.

$\alpha_{i,k}^r=y_{i,k-1}^r$ and let $\gamma_{i,k}^r$ be the actual
stochastic gradient draw used at that local query. If client $i$ was not
selected, retain both previous stored values. Thus the anchors and stored
gradients record the most recent query and its realized oracle output for
each local-step index.

When $f$ is convex with minimizer $x^\star$, the **round-$r$ convex control
lag** is the average second moment of the mean full-gradient error at the
stored anchors:
$$ C_r=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\mathbb E\left\| \frac1K\sum_{k=1}^K\nabla f_i(\alpha_{i,k}^r) -\nabla f_i(x^\star)\right\|_2^2. $$
For the nonconvex analysis, the **round-$r$ control-tracking error** is
$$ \Xi_r=\frac1{KN}\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{k=1}^K \mathbb E\|\alpha_{i,k}^r-x_r\|_2^2. $$
Thus $\Xi_0=0$ and each stored anchor records the point at which that client's
corresponding control-gradient sample was evaluated.

The query-point indexing in $E_r$ is deliberate: the gradient-difference

$y_{i,k}^r$.

$$ v_i=c-c_i+\nabla f_i(x) =\nabla f(x)+\bar a-a_i+\bar e-e_i. $$
For each realization,
$N^{-1}\sum_i\|\bar a-a_i\|_2^2\le N^{-1}\sum_i\|a_i\|_2^2$;
the same holds for $e_i$. Lipschitzness and Jensen give
$N^{-1}\sum_i\mathbb E\|a_i\|_2^2\le\beta^2\Xi_{r-1}$, and [F3] gives

$$ \frac1N\sum_i\mathbb E\|v_i\|_2^2 \le3\left(\mathbb E\|\nabla f(x)\|_2^2 +\beta^2\Xi_{r-1}+\frac{\sigma^2}{K}\right). $$

Put $d_{i,k}=y_{i,k}^r-x$. Define [given]
$T_i(y)=y-\eta_l(\nabla f_i(y)-\nabla f_i(x))$ and
$\xi_{i,k}=g_i(y_{i,k-1}^r)-\nabla f_i(y_{i,k-1}^r)$. The update is

Conditional centering of $\xi_{i,k}$ removes its cross term with the
pre-draw vector. Use [F4] with $a=1/(K-1)$ to get
$$ \mathbb E\|d_{i,k}\|_2^2 \le q\,\mathbb E\|d_{i,k-1}\|_2^2 +K\eta_l^2\mathbb E\|v_i\|_2^2+\eta_l^2\sigma^2, \qquad q=\left(1+\frac1{K-1}\right)(1+\eta_l\beta)^2. $$
The step bound implies $\eta_l\beta\le1/(24K)$. For $K\ge2$,
$1+1/(K-1)\le1+2/K$ and
$(1+1/(24K))^2\le1+1/(10K)$, hence $q\le1+3/K$. Therefore

$$ E_r\le24K^2\eta_l^2\frac1N\sum_i\mathbb E\|v_i\|_2^2 +24K\eta_l^2\sigma^2. $$

Substitute the control-vector bound from step 1.1 into step 1.2. [given]

$$ E_r\le72K^2\eta_l^2\left( \mathbb E\|\nabla f(x_{r-1})\|_2^2+\beta^2\Xi_{r-1}\right) +96K\eta_l^2\sigma^2, $$
which is the Statement.

The inputs are positive integers $N,d,R,K,S$ with $1\le S\le N$, objective
functions $f_i:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$, an initial
server model $x_0\in\mathbb R^d$, client controls $c_i^0\in\mathbb R^d$,
positive step sizes $\eta_l,\eta_g$, a local stochastic-gradient oracle
$g_i$, and a control-update option from $\{\mathrm I,\mathrm{II}\}$. Set
$c^0=N^{-1}\sum_i c_i^0$. The random client sample in each round is
independent of that round's fresh local-oracle randomness; no independence
among distinct clients' oracle draws is required here.

For each round $r=1,\ldots,R$, independently sample a uniform fixed-size
subset $\mathcal S_r$ of $S$ clients. At the start of this round, write
$x=x_{r-1}$, $c=c^{r-1}$, and $c_i=c_i^{r-1}$. For every selected client
$i$, initialize $y_{i,0}=x$ and, for $k=1,\ldots,K$, call $g_i$ at
$y_{i,k-1}$ and update
$$ y_{i,k}=y_{i,k-1}-\eta_l\bigl(g_i(y_{i,k-1})-c_i+c\bigr). $$
After its $K$ local steps, a selected client updates its control using either

- **Option I:** call $g_i$ at the round-start model $x_{r-1}$ and set
  $c_i^+=g_i(x)$; or
- **Option II:** set
  $c_i^+=c_i-c+(K\eta_l)^{-1}(x-y_{i,K})$.

The client sends $\Delta x_i=y_{i,K}-x$ and
$\Delta c_i=c_i^+-c_i$. Unselected clients retain their controls. The server
forms
$$ \Delta x=\frac1S\sum_{i\in\mathcal S_r}\Delta x_i,\qquad \Delta c=\frac1S\sum_{i\in\mathcal S_r}\Delta c_i $$
and updates
$$x_r=x+\eta_g\Delta x,\qquad c^r=c^{r-1}+\frac SN\Delta c.$$
The selected clients set $c_i^r=c_i^+$ and unselected clients set
$c_i^r=c_i^{r-1}$. Thus $c^r=N^{-1}\sum_i c_i^r$ whenever
$c^{r-1}=N^{-1}\sum_i c_i^{r-1}$ held before the round. The general
procedure permits zero initial controls; the convergence rates stated below
use the explicitly stated gradient-consistent initialization
$c_i^0=\nabla f_i(x_0)$. Repeat through round $R$ and return the model and
control trajectories $((x_r,c^r,(c_i^r)_{i=1}^N))_{r=0}^R$.

The following schematic records only the communication flow. Its vertices are
the server and the selected clients; the arrow labels are exactly the
quantities sent in each direction. The local updates and server equations above,
not the schematic, define the procedure.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=stealth]
\node[draw,rounded corners] (server) at (0,0) {Server: $(x,c)$};
\node[draw,rounded corners] (clients) at (5,0) {Selected clients $i\in\mathcal S$};
\draw[->] (server) to[bend left=18] node[above] {$(x,c)$} (clients);
\draw[->] (clients) to[bend left=18] node[below] {$(\Delta x_i,\Delta c_i)$} (server);
\end{tikzpicture}
```

Let $N,d,K,R\ge1$ be positive integers and let $1\le S\le N$. Let
$f_i:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be differentiable client objectives and
$f=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^Nf_i$. Run SCAFFOLD for $R$ rounds with local step count
$K$, client sample size $S$, server iterates $x_0,\ldots,x_R$, and client
controls $c_i^r$ after round $r$. In each round, extend the local trajectory
$y_{i,0}^r=x_{r-1},y_{i,1}^r,\ldots,y_{i,K}^r$ to every client using the
same local update rule, including hypothetical paths for clients not selected
in that round. Generate these counterfactual paths using fresh local oracle randomness independently of the fresh client sample, so a selected path agrees with its actual local execution. Local paths use only the round-start model and controls and their own successive oracle draws. Oracle moment conditions in the results below are conditional on the full prequery history, including any earlier revealed draws in the current round. All expectations below are over client samples and local
stochastic-gradient draws.

The **round-$r$ client drift at gradient-query points** is
$$ E_r=\frac1{KN}\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{k=1}^K \mathbb E\|y_{i,k-1}^r-x_{r-1}\|_2^2. $$
For every client and local-step index, initialize a stored anchor
$\alpha_{i,k}^0=x_0$ and stored gradient $\gamma_{i,k}^0=\nabla f_i(x_0)$.
After round $r$, if client $i$ was selected, set
$\alpha_{i,k}^r=y_{i,k-1}^r$ and let $\gamma_{i,k}^r$ be the actual
stochastic gradient draw used at that local query. If client $i$ was not
selected, retain both previous stored values. Thus the anchors and stored
gradients record the most recent query and its realized oracle output for
each local-step index.

When $f$ is convex with minimizer $x^\star$, the **round-$r$ convex control
lag** is the average second moment of the mean full-gradient error at the
stored anchors:
$$ C_r=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\mathbb E\left\| \frac1K\sum_{k=1}^K\nabla f_i(\alpha_{i,k}^r) -\nabla f_i(x^\star)\right\|_2^2. $$
For the nonconvex analysis, the **round-$r$ control-tracking error** is
$$ \Xi_r=\frac1{KN}\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{k=1}^K \mathbb E\|\alpha_{i,k}^r-x_r\|_2^2. $$
Thus $\Xi_0=0$ and each stored anchor records the point at which that client's
corresponding control-gradient sample was evaluated.

The query-point indexing in $E_r$ is deliberate: the gradient-difference
terms in the variance and drift recurrences are evaluated at $y_{i,k-1}^r$.
It is not interchangeable with an average over the post-update endpoints
$y_{i,k}^r$.

Let $f_i:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be differentiable with $\beta$-Lipschitz
gradients and let $f=N^{-1}\sum_i f_i$. Run Option II SCAFFOLD with
$1\le S\le N$ uniformly sampled clients, $K\ge1$ local steps, and
conditionally unbiased local stochastic gradients of variance at most
$\sigma^2$. Initialize $c_i^0=\nabla f_i(x_0)$ and
$c^0=N^{-1}\sum_i c_i^0$, and set $\widetilde\eta=K\eta_l\eta_g$. Let
$E_r$ and $\Xi_{r-1}$ be the drift and tracking errors in the SCAFFOLD
analysis-trajectory definition, and let $\mathcal F_{r-1}$ be the history
before the fresh round-$r$ client sample. All outer expectations below include
that history and the current round. Then
$$ \mathbb E\left\|\mathbb E[x_r\mid\mathcal F_{r-1}]-x_{r-1}\right\|_2^2 \le2\widetilde\eta^2\beta^2E_r +2\widetilde\eta^2\mathbb E\|\nabla f(x_{r-1})\|_2^2, $$
and
$$ \mathbb E\|x_r-x_{r-1}\|_2^2 \le6\widetilde\eta^2\beta^2E_r +12\widetilde\eta^2\beta^2\Xi_{r-1} +3\widetilde\eta^2\mathbb E\|\nabla f(x_{r-1})\|_2^2 +\frac{18\widetilde\eta^2\sigma^2}{KS}. $$

Let $v_1,\ldots,v_N\in\mathbb R^d$, let $1\le S\le N$, and choose
$\mathcal S$ uniformly from the $S$-element subsets of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$. Put
$\bar v=N^{-1}\sum_i v_i$ and
$\bar v_{\mathcal S}=S^{-1}\sum_{i\in\mathcal S}v_i$. If $N>1$, then
$$ \mathbb E[\bar v_{\mathcal S}]=\bar v,\qquad \mathbb E\|\bar v_{\mathcal S}-\bar v\|_2^2 =\left(1-\frac SN\right)\frac{1}{S(N-1)} \sum_{i=1}^N\|v_i-\bar v\|_2^2. $$
In particular,
$$ \mathbb E\|\bar v_{\mathcal S}-\bar v\|_2^2 \le2\left(1-\frac SN\right)\frac1S \frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\|v_i\|_2^2. $$
If $N=1$, necessarily $S=1$ and $\bar v_{\mathcal S}=\bar v$.

For vectors $u,v\in\mathbb R^d$ and $a>0$,
$$ \|u+v\|_2^2\le(1+a)\|u\|_2^2+(1+a^{-1})\|v\|_2^2, \qquad 2|\langle u,v\rangle|\le a\|u\|_2^2+a^{-1}\|v\|_2^2. $$
For $m\ge1$ vectors $u_1,\ldots,u_m\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$ \left\|\sum_{j=1}^m u_j\right\|_2^2\le m\sum_{j=1}^m\|u_j\|_2^2. $$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ (The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann),
On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of The vector space $F^{X}$ of all functions $X \to F$ with pointwise operations, and $F^{n}$ as the case $X = n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
(Vector space over a field). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of Finite sums and finite products, by recursion applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 4 and
Squares of nonzero elements are positive, the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
Integer powers $a^m$) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root (Square roots exist: a unique $\sqrt{a} \ge 0$ with $(\sqrt{a})^2 = a$; the positives are $\{x^2 : x \neq 0\}$).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space (The standard list $e : n \to F^{n}$ with $e_i(i) = 1_F$ and $e_i(j) = 0_F$ for $j \ne i$ is an ordered basis of $F^{n}$; hence $\dim_F F^{n} = n$, and $F^{0}$ is the zero space with basis $\varnothing$ and dimension $0$ clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
$\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and Conventions of this page, the standing $n \ge 1$ hypothesis, and what is taken up elsewhere in the reading order lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ (Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   (Squares of nonzero elements are positive), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of A norm on a real vector space, the induced metric, and the dictionary with the metric axioms
is proved in Cauchy-Schwarz $\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \le \lVert x\rVert_2\lVert y\rVert_2$ with its equality case, the triangle inequality for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$, the parallelogram law and polarisation, where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

A **discrete filtered probability space** is $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_n)_{n\in\mathbb N_0},P)$, where $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ is a probability space Probability measures and probability spaces, each $\mathcal F_n$ is a sigma-algebra on $\Omega$ Sigma-algebras, and $\mathcal F_n\subseteq\mathcal F_{n+1}\subseteq\mathcal F$. The sequence $(\mathcal F_n)$ is a **filtration**. Time starts at zero. Neither completeness nor triviality of $\mathcal F_0$ is required.

Restriction of $P$ to $\mathcal F_n$ has total mass one and is countably additive: a disjoint sequence in $\mathcal F_n$ is also such a sequence in $\mathcal F$, with the same union and the same values of $P$. Thus each restriction is a probability measure. This specifies a structure and uses no choice principle. Real-valued processes will be the default.

Assume AC for the supplied existence theorem. Write $E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ for the unique class in $L^1(\Omega,\mathcal G,P|_{\mathcal G})$ consisting of conditional-expectation versions of $X$. A chosen real $\mathcal G$-measurable representative is a **version**. Equalities and inequalities involving these classes mean almost-sure equalities and inequalities.

Existence is Conditional expectation exists by radon nikodym and uniqueness is Conditional expectation is unique almost surely, applied to Conditional expectation given a sigma algebra. The quotient is The space $L^p(\mu)$ as the quotient by null functions. If $X=X^{\ast}$ almost surely, Two integrable functions are equal almost everywhere exactly when all of their indefinite integrals agree gives identical event integrals, so the output class is independent of the input representative. The The Axiom of Choice assumption is inherited from RN existence.

Assume AC for existence. For real $X,Y\in L^1(P)$ and $a,b\in\mathbb R$, $E[aX+bY\mid\mathcal G]=aE[X\mid\mathcal G]+bE[Y\mid\mathcal G]$. Conditional expectation is positive, preserves order and constants, satisfies $E(E[X\mid\mathcal G])=EX$, and $|E[X\mid\mathcal G]|\le E[|X|\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. Also $X<Y$ almost surely implies $E[X\mid\mathcal G]<E[Y\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely.

Assume AC for existence. If $X\in L^1(P)$ and $Z$ is bounded real $\mathcal G$-measurable, then $E[ZX\mid\mathcal G]=ZE[X\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. The identity also holds for finite real $\mathcal G$-measurable $Z$ whenever $ZX$ and $ZE[X\mid\mathcal G]$ are integrable. In fact $X,ZX\in L^1$ imply the latter integrability.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of Integrable real and complex functions, and their integrals, its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

Let $X,Y$ be integrable real or complex random variables on one probability
space.

1. For scalars $a,b$,
   $$\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Y].$$
2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y].$$
3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$

derivations.claim: Put $x=x_{r-1}$, $\Delta=x_r-x$, $I_i=\mathbf1_{\{i\in\mathcal S_r\}}$, $z_{i,k}=\alpha_{i,k}^{r-1}-x$, and $w_{i,k}=y_{i,k-1}^r-x$. Let $Z=(KN)^{-1}\sum_{i,k}z_{i,k}$, $U=(KN)^{-1}\sum_{i,k}I_iw_{i,k}$, and $V=(KN)^{-1}\sum_{i,k}I_iz_{i,k}$. The actual anchor update is $\alpha_{i,k}^r-x=z_{i,k}+I_i(w_{i,k}-z_{i,k})$. The inputs are positive integers $N,d,R,K,S$ with $1\le S\le N$, objective
functions $f_i:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$, an initial
server model $x_0\in\mathbb R^d$, client controls $c_i^0\in\mathbb R^d$,
positive step sizes $\eta_l,\eta_g$, a local stochastic-gradient oracle
$g_i$, and a control-update option from $\{\mathrm I,\mathrm{II}\}$. Set
$c^0=N^{-1}\sum_i c_i^0$. The random client sample in each round is
independent of that round's fresh local-oracle randomness; no independence
among distinct clients' oracle draws is required here.

For each round $r=1,\ldots,R$, independently sample a uniform fixed-size
subset $\mathcal S_r$ of $S$ clients. At the start of this round, write
$x=x_{r-1}$, $c=c^{r-1}$, and $c_i=c_i^{r-1}$. For every selected client
$i$, initialize $y_{i,0}=x$ and, for $k=1,\ldots,K$, call $g_i$ at
$y_{i,k-1}$ and update
$$ y_{i,k}=y_{i,k-1}-\eta_l\bigl(g_i(y_{i,k-1})-c_i+c\bigr). $$
After its $K$ local steps, a selected client updates its control using either

- **Option I:** call $g_i$ at the round-start model $x_{r-1}$ and set
  $c_i^+=g_i(x)$; or
- **Option II:** set
  $c_i^+=c_i-c+(K\eta_l)^{-1}(x-y_{i,K})$.

The client sends $\Delta x_i=y_{i,K}-x$ and
$\Delta c_i=c_i^+-c_i$. Unselected clients retain their controls. The server
forms
$$ \Delta x=\frac1S\sum_{i\in\mathcal S_r}\Delta x_i,\qquad \Delta c=\frac1S\sum_{i\in\mathcal S_r}\Delta c_i $$
and updates
$$x_r=x+\eta_g\Delta x,\qquad c^r=c^{r-1}+\frac SN\Delta c.$$
The selected clients set $c_i^r=c_i^+$ and unselected clients set
$c_i^r=c_i^{r-1}$. Thus $c^r=N^{-1}\sum_i c_i^r$ whenever
$c^{r-1}=N^{-1}\sum_i c_i^{r-1}$ held before the round. The general
procedure permits zero initial controls; the convergence rates stated below
use the explicitly stated gradient-consistent initialization
$c_i^0=\nabla f_i(x_0)$. Repeat through round $R$ and return the model and
control trajectories $((x_r,c^r,(c_i^r)_{i=1}^N))_{r=0}^R$.

The following schematic records only the communication flow. Its vertices are
the server and the selected clients; the arrow labels are exactly the
quantities sent in each direction. The local updates and server equations above,
not the schematic, define the procedure.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=stealth]
\node[draw,rounded corners] (server) at (0,0) {Server: $(x,c)$};
\node[draw,rounded corners] (clients) at (5,0) {Selected clients $i\in\mathcal S$};
\draw[->] (server) to[bend left=18] node[above] {$(x,c)$} (clients);
\draw[->] (clients) to[bend left=18] node[below] {$(\Delta x_i,\Delta c_i)$} (server);
\end{tikzpicture}
```

Let $N,d,K,R\ge1$ be positive integers and let $1\le S\le N$. Let
$f_i:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be differentiable client objectives and
$f=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^Nf_i$. Run SCAFFOLD for $R$ rounds with local step count
$K$, client sample size $S$, server iterates $x_0,\ldots,x_R$, and client
controls $c_i^r$ after round $r$. In each round, extend the local trajectory
$y_{i,0}^r=x_{r-1},y_{i,1}^r,\ldots,y_{i,K}^r$ to every client using the
same local update rule, including hypothetical paths for clients not selected
in that round. Generate these counterfactual paths using fresh local oracle randomness independently of the fresh client sample, so a selected path agrees with its actual local execution. Local paths use only the round-start model and controls and their own successive oracle draws. Oracle moment conditions in the results below are conditional on the full prequery history, including any earlier revealed draws in the current round. All expectations below are over client samples and local
stochastic-gradient draws.

The **round-$r$ client drift at gradient-query points** is
$$ E_r=\frac1{KN}\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{k=1}^K \mathbb E\|y_{i,k-1}^r-x_{r-1}\|_2^2. $$
For every client and local-step index, initialize a stored anchor
$\alpha_{i,k}^0=x_0$ and stored gradient $\gamma_{i,k}^0=\nabla f_i(x_0)$.
After round $r$, if client $i$ was selected, set
$\alpha_{i,k}^r=y_{i,k-1}^r$ and let $\gamma_{i,k}^r$ be the actual
stochastic gradient draw used at that local query. If client $i$ was not
selected, retain both previous stored values. Thus the anchors and stored
gradients record the most recent query and its realized oracle output for
each local-step index.

When $f$ is convex with minimizer $x^\star$, the **round-$r$ convex control
lag** is the average second moment of the mean full-gradient error at the
stored anchors:
$$ C_r=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\mathbb E\left\| \frac1K\sum_{k=1}^K\nabla f_i(\alpha_{i,k}^r) -\nabla f_i(x^\star)\right\|_2^2. $$
For the nonconvex analysis, the **round-$r$ control-tracking error** is
$$ \Xi_r=\frac1{KN}\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{k=1}^K \mathbb E\|\alpha_{i,k}^r-x_r\|_2^2. $$
Thus $\Xi_0=0$ and each stored anchor records the point at which that client's
corresponding control-gradient sample was evaluated.

The query-point indexing in $E_r$ is deliberate: the gradient-difference
terms in the variance and drift recurrences are evaluated at $y_{i,k-1}^r$.
It is not interchangeable with an average over the post-update endpoints
$y_{i,k}^r$.

Let $f_i:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be differentiable with $\beta$-Lipschitz
gradients and let $f=N^{-1}\sum_i f_i$. Run Option II SCAFFOLD with
$1\le S\le N$ uniformly sampled clients, $K\ge1$ local steps, and
conditionally unbiased local stochastic gradients of variance at most
$\sigma^2$. Initialize $c_i^0=\nabla f_i(x_0)$ and
$c^0=N^{-1}\sum_i c_i^0$, and set $\widetilde\eta=K\eta_l\eta_g$. Let
$E_r$ and $\Xi_{r-1}$ be the drift and tracking errors in the SCAFFOLD
analysis-trajectory definition, and let $\mathcal F_{r-1}$ be the history
before the fresh round-$r$ client sample. All outer expectations below include
that history and the current round. Then
$$ \mathbb E\left\|\mathbb E[x_r\mid\mathcal F_{r-1}]-x_{r-1}\right\|_2^2 \le2\widetilde\eta^2\beta^2E_r +2\widetilde\eta^2\mathbb E\|\nabla f(x_{r-1})\|_2^2, $$
and
$$ \mathbb E\|x_r-x_{r-1}\|_2^2 \le6\widetilde\eta^2\beta^2E_r +12\widetilde\eta^2\beta^2\Xi_{r-1} +3\widetilde\eta^2\mathbb E\|\nabla f(x_{r-1})\|_2^2 +\frac{18\widetilde\eta^2\sigma^2}{KS}. $$

Let U be open in R^d, let x in U, let n>=1, and let f_1,...,f_n:U->R be totally differentiable at x. Put F=n^{-1}sum_{i=1}^n f_i. Then F is totally differentiable at x and

$$
\nabla F(x)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\nabla f_i(x).
$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $f_i:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ have $\beta$-Lipschitz gradients with $\beta>0$ and let $f=N^{-1}\sum_i f_i$. Run Option II SCAFFOLD with $1\le S\le N$ uniformly sampled clients, $K\ge1$ local steps, server scale $\eta_g\ge1$, and fresh conditionally unbiased local stochastic gradients with within-client variance at most $\sigma^2$. Initialize $c_i^0=\nabla f_i(x_0)$ and $c^0=N^{-1}\sum_i c_i^0$. Current client samples are independent of the past and of the counterfactual local oracle draws. Write $p=S/N$, $t=\widetilde\eta=K\eta_l\eta_g$, and let $E_r,\Xi_r$ be the query-point drift and anchor-tracking errors. Then
$$ \Xi_r\le\left(1-\frac p2+72\beta^2t^2\right)\Xi_{r-1}+\left(2p+\left(36+\frac8p\right)\beta^2t^2\right)E_r+\left(18+\frac8p\right)t^2\mathbb E\|\nabla f(x_{r-1})\|_2^2+\frac{108t^2\sigma^2}{KS}. $$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $f_i:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ have $\beta$-Lipschitz gradients with $\beta>0$ and
let $f=N^{-1}\sum_i f_i$ be bounded below. Run Option II SCAFFOLD with
$1\le S\le N$ uniformly sampled clients, $K\ge1$ local steps, server scale
$\eta_g\ge1$, and fresh conditionally unbiased local stochastic gradients
with within-client variance at most $\sigma^2$. Initialize
$c_i^0=\nabla f_i(x_0)$ and $c^0=N^{-1}\sum_i c_i^0$. Let
$\widetilde\eta=K\eta_l\eta_g$ and let $E_r,\Xi_{r-1}$ be the query-point
drift and anchor-tracking errors in the SCAFFOLD analysis-trajectory
definition. If
$$ 0<\widetilde\eta\le\frac{(S/N)^{2/3}}{24\beta}, $$
then
$$ E_r\le72K^2\eta_l^2\left( \mathbb E\|\nabla f(x_{r-1})\|_2^2 +\beta^2\Xi_{r-1}\right)+96K\eta_l^2\sigma^2. $$

Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be continuously differentiable and suppose $\nabla f$ is Lipschitz with constant $L\ge0$ in the Euclidean norm. Then
$$f(y)\le f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle+\frac{L}{2}\|y-x\|_2^2\qquad(x,y\in\mathbb R^n).$$

For vectors $u,v\in\mathbb R^d$ and $a>0$,
$$ \|u+v\|_2^2\le(1+a)\|u\|_2^2+(1+a^{-1})\|v\|_2^2, \qquad 2|\langle u,v\rangle|\le a\|u\|_2^2+a^{-1}\|v\|_2^2. $$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $f_i:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be differentiable, $\mu$-strongly
convex and $\beta$-smooth, with $0\le\mu\le\beta$, and let
$f=N^{-1}\sum_i f_i$ attain $f^\star=f(x^\star)$. Run Option II SCAFFOLD
with $1\le S\le N$ clients sampled uniformly without replacement, $K\ge1$
local steps, local step $\eta_l$, server scale $\eta_g\ge1$, and fresh
conditionally unbiased local stochastic gradients with variance at most
$\sigma^2$. Assume $c=N^{-1}\sum_i c_i$, initialize
$c_i^0=\nabla f_i(x_0)$ and $c^0=N^{-1}\sum_i c_i^0$, and define
$\widetilde\eta=K\eta_l\eta_g$. If
$$ \widetilde\eta\le\frac1{81\beta}, \qquad \text{and, when }\mu>0,\quad \widetilde\eta\le\frac{S}{15\mu N}, $$
then, with $E_r,C_r$ as in the SCAFFOLD analysis-trajectory definition and
$\rho=(2+34\beta\widetilde\eta)/3$,
$$ \begin{aligned} \mathbb E\|x_r-x^\star\|_2^2 +\frac{14N\widetilde\eta^2}{S}C_r &\le\left(1-\frac{\mu\widetilde\eta}{2}\right) \left(\mathbb E\|x_{r-1}-x^\star\|_2^2 +\frac{14N\widetilde\eta^2}{S}C_{r-1}\right)\\ &\quad-\widetilde\eta\mathbb E[f(x_{r-1})-f^\star] +\left(\frac{18}{KS}+\frac{\rho}{K\eta_g^2}\right) \widetilde\eta^2\sigma^2. \end{aligned} $$
For $\mu=0$ this is a general-convex descent inequality; for $\mu>0$ it
also contracts the distance-and-control potential.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $f_i:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ have $\beta$-Lipschitz gradients with $\beta>0$, and let $f=N^{-1}\sum_i f_i$ be bounded below by $f^\star$. Run Option II SCAFFOLD with $1\le S\le N$ uniformly sampled clients, $K\ge1$ local steps, server scale $\eta_g\ge1$, and fresh conditionally unbiased local stochastic gradients of within-client variance at most $\sigma^2$. Initialize $c_i^0=\nabla f_i(x_0)$ and $c^0=N^{-1}\sum_i c_i^0$. Client samples are fresh and independent of prior history and counterfactual oracle draws. Let $p=S/N$, $t=\widetilde\eta=K\eta_l\eta_g$, and let $\Xi_r$ be the control-anchor tracking error. If
$$ 0<t\le\frac{p^{2/3}}{100\beta}, $$
then the potential
$$ P_r=\mathbb E[f(x_r)-f^\star]+\frac{24\beta^3t^2}{p}\Xi_r $$
satisfies
$$ P_r\le P_{r-1}-\frac t3\mathbb E\|\nabla f(x_{r-1})\|_2^2+\frac{10\beta t^2\sigma^2}{KS}\left(1+\frac S{\eta_g^2}\right). $$

Let $R\ge1$ and let $d_0,\ldots,d_R\ge0$, $q_0,\ldots,q_{R-1}\ge0$.

1. If $a,\eta>0$, $b,c\ge0$, and
$$ d_r+a\eta q_{r-1}\le d_{r-1}+b\eta^2+c\eta^3 \quad(1\le r\le R), $$
then
$$ \frac1R\sum_{r=1}^R q_{r-1} \le\frac{d_0}{a\eta R}+\frac{b\eta+c\eta^2}{a}. $$

2. If $0<\rho\eta<1$, $a>0$, $b,c\ge0$, and
$$ d_r\le(1-\rho\eta)d_{r-1}-a\eta q_{r-1} +b\eta^2+c\eta^3, $$
then for $w_r=(1-\rho\eta)^{-r}$ and $W_R=\sum_{r=1}^Rw_r$,
$$ \frac1{W_R}\sum_{r=1}^Rw_rq_{r-1} \le\frac{d_0}{a\eta W_R}+\frac{b\eta+c\eta^2}{a}. $$
The left side in part 2 is the expectation of $q_{r-1}$ when an index
$r\in\{1,\ldots,R\}$ is selected with probability $w_r/W_R$.

Let $h_1,\ldots,h_N:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be convex and continuously
differentiable, with $\beta$-Lipschitz gradients for $\beta>0$. Put
$f=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^Nh_i$, and let $x^\star$ minimize $f$. Then
$$ \frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N \|\nabla h_i(x)-\nabla h_i(x^\star)\|_2^2 \le2\beta\bigl(f(x)-f(x^\star)\bigr) \qquad(x\in\mathbb R^d). $$

Let U be open in R^d, let x in U, let n>=1, and let f_1,...,f_n:U->R be totally differentiable at x. Put F=n^{-1}sum_{i=1}^n f_i. Then F is totally differentiable at x and

$$
\nabla F(x)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\nabla f_i(x).
$$

Let $N,d\ge1$, let each client $i\in\{1,\ldots,N\}$ have a positive integer
sample count $n_i$, and put $n=\sum_{i=1}^N n_i$. For differentiable client
objectives $F_i:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$, the sample-count-weighted deployment
objective is
$$ f_{\rm wt}(w)=\sum_{i=1}^N\frac{n_i}{n}F_i(w). $$
For differentiable client objectives $f_i:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$, the
equal-client objective is
$$ f(w)=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N f_i(w). $$
The symbols $F_i$ and $f_i$ denote separate families; they are not identified
unless an application states $F_i=f_i$. In general, $f_{\rm wt}$ and $f$ are
different objectives.

For integers $1\le S\le N$, a uniform fixed-size client sample is a random
subset $\mathcal S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}$ of cardinality $S$ for which every
$S$-element subset has probability $\binom NS^{-1}$. This is sampling without
replacement. When several communication rounds are used, the sampled subsets
are independent across rounds unless a theorem states a different sampling
law.

The inputs are positive integers $N,d,R,K,S$ with $1\le S\le N$, objective
functions $f_i:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$, an initial
server model $x_0\in\mathbb R^d$, client controls $c_i^0\in\mathbb R^d$,
positive step sizes $\eta_l,\eta_g$, a local stochastic-gradient oracle
$g_i$, and a control-update option from $\{\mathrm I,\mathrm{II}\}$. Set
$c^0=N^{-1}\sum_i c_i^0$. The random client sample in each round is
independent of that round's fresh local-oracle randomness; no independence
among distinct clients' oracle draws is required here.

For each round $r=1,\ldots,R$, independently sample a uniform fixed-size
subset $\mathcal S_r$ of $S$ clients. At the start of this round, write
$x=x_{r-1}$, $c=c^{r-1}$, and $c_i=c_i^{r-1}$. For every selected client
$i$, initialize $y_{i,0}=x$ and, for $k=1,\ldots,K$, call $g_i$ at
$y_{i,k-1}$ and update
$$ y_{i,k}=y_{i,k-1}-\eta_l\bigl(g_i(y_{i,k-1})-c_i+c\bigr). $$
After its $K$ local steps, a selected client updates its control using either

- **Option I:** call $g_i$ at the round-start model $x_{r-1}$ and set
  $c_i^+=g_i(x)$; or
- **Option II:** set
  $c_i^+=c_i-c+(K\eta_l)^{-1}(x-y_{i,K})$.

The client sends $\Delta x_i=y_{i,K}-x$ and
$\Delta c_i=c_i^+-c_i$. Unselected clients retain their controls. The server
forms
$$ \Delta x=\frac1S\sum_{i\in\mathcal S_r}\Delta x_i,\qquad \Delta c=\frac1S\sum_{i\in\mathcal S_r}\Delta c_i $$
and updates
$$x_r=x+\eta_g\Delta x,\qquad c^r=c^{r-1}+\frac SN\Delta c.$$
The selected clients set $c_i^r=c_i^+$ and unselected clients set
$c_i^r=c_i^{r-1}$. Thus $c^r=N^{-1}\sum_i c_i^r$ whenever
$c^{r-1}=N^{-1}\sum_i c_i^{r-1}$ held before the round. The general
procedure permits zero initial controls; the convergence rates stated below
use the explicitly stated gradient-consistent initialization
$c_i^0=\nabla f_i(x_0)$. Repeat through round $R$ and return the model and
control trajectories $((x_r,c^r,(c_i^r)_{i=1}^N))_{r=0}^R$.

The following schematic records only the communication flow. Its vertices are
the server and the selected clients; the arrow labels are exactly the
quantities sent in each direction. The local updates and server equations above,
not the schematic, define the procedure.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=stealth]
\node[draw,rounded corners] (server) at (0,0) {Server: $(x,c)$};
\node[draw,rounded corners] (clients) at (5,0) {Selected clients $i\in\mathcal S$};
\draw[->] (server) to[bend left=18] node[above] {$(x,c)$} (clients);
\draw[->] (clients) to[bend left=18] node[below] {$(\Delta x_i,\Delta c_i)$} (server);
\end{tikzpicture}
```

Let $N,d,K,R\ge1$ be positive integers and let $1\le S\le N$. Let
$f_i:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be differentiable client objectives and
$f=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^Nf_i$. Run SCAFFOLD for $R$ rounds with local step count
$K$, client sample size $S$, server iterates $x_0,\ldots,x_R$, and client
controls $c_i^r$ after round $r$. In each round, extend the local trajectory
$y_{i,0}^r=x_{r-1},y_{i,1}^r,\ldots,y_{i,K}^r$ to every client using the
same local update rule, including hypothetical paths for clients not selected
in that round. Generate these counterfactual paths using fresh local oracle randomness independently of the fresh client sample, so a selected path agrees with its actual local execution. Local paths use only the round-start model and controls and their own successive oracle draws. Oracle moment conditions in the results below are conditional on the full prequery history, including any earlier revealed draws in the current round. All expectations below are over client samples and local
stochastic-gradient draws.

The **round-$r$ client drift at gradient-query points** is
$$ E_r=\frac1{KN}\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{k=1}^K \mathbb E\|y_{i,k-1}^r-x_{r-1}\|_2^2. $$
For every client and local-step index, initialize a stored anchor
$\alpha_{i,k}^0=x_0$ and stored gradient $\gamma_{i,k}^0=\nabla f_i(x_0)$.
After round $r$, if client $i$ was selected, set
$\alpha_{i,k}^r=y_{i,k-1}^r$ and let $\gamma_{i,k}^r$ be the actual
stochastic gradient draw used at that local query. If client $i$ was not
selected, retain both previous stored values. Thus the anchors and stored
gradients record the most recent query and its realized oracle output for
each local-step index.

When $f$ is convex with minimizer $x^\star$, the **round-$r$ convex control
lag** is the average second moment of the mean full-gradient error at the
stored anchors:
$$ C_r=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\mathbb E\left\| \frac1K\sum_{k=1}^K\nabla f_i(\alpha_{i,k}^r) -\nabla f_i(x^\star)\right\|_2^2. $$
For the nonconvex analysis, the **round-$r$ control-tracking error** is
$$ \Xi_r=\frac1{KN}\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{k=1}^K \mathbb E\|\alpha_{i,k}^r-x_r\|_2^2. $$
Thus $\Xi_0=0$ and each stored anchor records the point at which that client's
corresponding control-gradient sample was evaluated.

The query-point indexing in $E_r$ is deliberate: the gradient-difference
terms in the variance and drift recurrences are evaluated at $y_{i,k-1}^r$.
It is not interchangeable with an average over the post-update endpoints
$y_{i,k}^r$.

A **discrete filtered probability space** is $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_n)_{n\in\mathbb N_0},P)$, where $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ is a probability space Probability measures and probability spaces, each $\mathcal F_n$ is a sigma-algebra on $\Omega$ Sigma-algebras, and $\mathcal F_n\subseteq\mathcal F_{n+1}\subseteq\mathcal F$. The sequence $(\mathcal F_n)$ is a **filtration**. Time starts at zero. Neither completeness nor triviality of $\mathcal F_0$ is required.

Restriction of $P$ to $\mathcal F_n$ has total mass one and is countably additive: a disjoint sequence in $\mathcal F_n$ is also such a sequence in $\mathcal F$, with the same union and the same values of $P$. Thus each restriction is a probability measure. This specifies a structure and uses no choice principle. Real-valued processes will be the default.

Assume AC for the supplied existence theorem. Write $E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ for the unique class in $L^1(\Omega,\mathcal G,P|_{\mathcal G})$ consisting of conditional-expectation versions of $X$. A chosen real $\mathcal G$-measurable representative is a **version**. Equalities and inequalities involving these classes mean almost-sure equalities and inequalities.

Existence is Conditional expectation exists by radon nikodym and uniqueness is Conditional expectation is unique almost surely, applied to Conditional expectation given a sigma algebra. The quotient is The space $L^p(\mu)$ as the quotient by null functions. If $X=X^{\ast}$ almost surely, Two integrable functions are equal almost everywhere exactly when all of their indefinite integrals agree gives identical event integrals, so the output class is independent of the input representative. The The Axiom of Choice assumption is inherited from RN existence.

Assume AC for existence. For real $X,Y\in L^1(P)$ and $a,b\in\mathbb R$, $E[aX+bY\mid\mathcal G]=aE[X\mid\mathcal G]+bE[Y\mid\mathcal G]$. Conditional expectation is positive, preserves order and constants, satisfies $E(E[X\mid\mathcal G])=EX$, and $|E[X\mid\mathcal G]|\le E[|X|\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. Also $X<Y$ almost surely implies $E[X\mid\mathcal G]<E[Y\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely.

Assume AC for existence. If $X\in L^1(P)$ and $Z$ is bounded real $\mathcal G$-measurable, then $E[ZX\mid\mathcal G]=ZE[X\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. The identity also holds for finite real $\mathcal G$-measurable $Z$ whenever $ZX$ and $ZE[X\mid\mathcal G]$ are integrable. In fact $X,ZX\in L^1$ imply the latter integrability.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of Integrable real and complex functions, and their integrals, its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

Let $X,Y$ be integrable real or complex random variables on one probability
space.

1. For scalars $a,b$,
   $$\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Y].$$
2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y].$$
3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$

derivations.claim: In the strongly convex case, put $\widetilde\eta=K\eta_l\sqrt S$ and [given] apply [F1]. Since $\eta_g^2=S$, the variance term in [F1] is at most $19\widetilde\eta^2\sigma^2/(KS)$. The geometric recurrence lemma [F3] with gap coefficient one and weights $w_r=(1-\mu\widetilde\eta/2)^{-r}$ gives $$ \mathbb E[f(\bar x_R)-f^\star] \le\frac{V_0}{\widetilde\eta W_R} +\frac{19\widetilde\eta\sigma^2}{KS}, \qquad V_0=\mathbb E\|x_0-x^\star\|_2^2 +\frac{14N\widetilde\eta^2}{S}C_0. $$ This is the strongly convex bound in the Statement.

In the general convex case, apply [F1] with $\mu=0$ and [given] $\eta_g=\sqrt S$. It gives $V_r\le V_{r-1}-\widetilde\eta\mathbb E[f(x_{r-1})-f^\star] +19\widetilde\eta^2\sigma^2/(KS)$. Sum over $r=1,\ldots,R$ and drop the nonnegative terminal potential. For independent uniform $J$ this yields $$ \frac1R\sum_{r=0}^{R-1}\mathbb E[f(x_r)-f^\star] \le\frac{V_0}{\widetilde\eta R} +\frac{19\widetilde\eta\sigma^2}{KS}, \qquad V_0=D^2+\frac{14N\widetilde\eta^2}{S}C_0. $$ Substitution of $C_0\le2\beta F$ proves the exact bound in the Statement.

In the nonconvex case use [F2] with $\eta_g^2=S$. The initialization in [F6] gives $\Xi_0=0$, so $P_0=F$. Its variance term is at most $20\beta\widetilde\eta^2\sigma^2/(KS)$. Sum over rounds and drop $P_R\ge0$ to obtain $$ \frac{\widetilde\eta}{3}\sum_{r=1}^R\mathbb E\|\nabla f(x_{r-1})\|_2^2\le F+\frac{20R\beta\widetilde\eta^2\sigma^2}{KS}. $$ Dividing by $R\widetilde\eta/3$ and choosing the uniform independent output index gives precisely the nonconvex finite-round bound.

In the strongly convex case, by convex smoothness, [F4] gives $C_0\le2\beta F$, hence [given] $V_0\le D^2+28\beta N\widetilde\eta^2F/S$. citations.quote:
The inputs are positive integers $N,d,R,K,S$ with $1\le S\le N$, objective
functions $f_i:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$, an initial
server model $x_0\in\mathbb R^d$, client controls $c_i^0\in\mathbb R^d$,
positive step sizes $\eta_l,\eta_g$, a local stochastic-gradient oracle
$g_i$, and a control-update option from $\{\mathrm I,\mathrm{II}\}$. Set
$c^0=N^{-1}\sum_i c_i^0$. The random client sample in each round is
independent of that round's fresh local-oracle randomness; no independence
among distinct clients' oracle draws is required here.

For each round $r=1,\ldots,R$, independently sample a uniform fixed-size
subset $\mathcal S_r$ of $S$ clients. At the start of this round, write
$x=x_{r-1}$, $c=c^{r-1}$, and $c_i=c_i^{r-1}$. For every selected client
$i$, initialize $y_{i,0}=x$ and, for $k=1,\ldots,K$, call $g_i$ at
$y_{i,k-1}$ and update
$$ y_{i,k}=y_{i,k-1}-\eta_l\bigl(g_i(y_{i,k-1})-c_i+c\bigr). $$
After its $K$ local steps, a selected client updates its control using either

- **Option I:** call $g_i$ at the round-start model $x_{r-1}$ and set
  $c_i^+=g_i(x)$; or
- **Option II:** set
  $c_i^+=c_i-c+(K\eta_l)^{-1}(x-y_{i,K})$.

The client sends $\Delta x_i=y_{i,K}-x$ and
$\Delta c_i=c_i^+-c_i$. Unselected clients retain their controls. The server
forms
$$ \Delta x=\frac1S\sum_{i\in\mathcal S_r}\Delta x_i,\qquad \Delta c=\frac1S\sum_{i\in\mathcal S_r}\Delta c_i $$
and updates
$$x_r=x+\eta_g\Delta x,\qquad c^r=c^{r-1}+\frac SN\Delta c.$$
The selected clients set $c_i^r=c_i^+$ and unselected clients set
$c_i^r=c_i^{r-1}$. Thus $c^r=N^{-1}\sum_i c_i^r$ whenever
$c^{r-1}=N^{-1}\sum_i c_i^{r-1}$ held before the round. The general
procedure permits zero initial controls; the convergence rates stated below
use the explicitly stated gradient-consistent initialization
$c_i^0=\nabla f_i(x_0)$. Repeat through round $R$ and return the model and
control trajectories $((x_r,c^r,(c_i^r)_{i=1}^N))_{r=0}^R$.

The following schematic records only the communication flow. Its vertices are
the server and the selected clients; the arrow labels are exactly the
quantities sent in each direction. The local updates and server equations above,
not the schematic, define the procedure.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=stealth]
\node[draw,rounded corners] (server) at (0,0) {Server: $(x,c)$};
\node[draw,rounded corners] (clients) at (5,0) {Selected clients $i\in\mathcal S$};
\draw[->] (server) to[bend left=18] node[above] {$(x,c)$} (clients);
\draw[->] (clients) to[bend left=18] node[below] {$(\Delta x_i,\Delta c_i)$} (server);
\end{tikzpicture}
```

derivations.claim: Fix $N\ge2$ and $\beta>0$. Take $d=K=S=1$, $\eta_g=1$, $x_0=1$, $f_i(x)=\beta x^2/2$ for every client, and the exact oracle $g_i(x)=\beta x$. Every client is convex and $\beta$-smooth, the equal-client objective has minimizer $x^\star=0$ and minimum zero, and $D=1$, $F=\beta/2$, $\sigma=0$. Initialize $c_i^0=\beta$ and $c^0=\beta$, as required. Sample one independent uniform client in every round. These deterministic exact oracles satisfy every conditional unbiasedness and variance hypothesis; all moments at a finite time are finite because there are finitely many sample histories.

Let $t=\beta\eta_l\in(0,1/81]$, put $a_i^r=c_i^r/\beta$ and $m_r=N^{-1}\sum_i a_i^r$, and let $I_r$ be the client sampled to pass from time $r$ to time $r+1$. The updates [F1] become $$ x_{r+1}=(1-t)x_r+t(a_{I_r}^r-m_r),\qquad a_{I_r}^{r+1}=x_r,\qquad a_j^{r+1}=a_j^r\quad(j\ne I_r),\qquad a_i^0=1. $$ Conditioning on the history through time $r$, the sampled difference has mean zero. Therefore, for $z_r=\mathbb E x_r^2$ and $V_r=\mathbb E[N^{-1}\sum_i(a_i^r-m_r)^2]$, $$ \mathbb E x_r=(1-t)^r,\qquad z_{r+1}=(1-t)^2z_r+t^2V_r,\qquad z_r\ge(1-t)^{2r}. $$ The claimed uniform output has expected objective gap $F R^{-1}\sum_{r=0}^{R-1}z_r$.

Put $L=\lfloor1/(4t)\rfloor$. Since $t\le1/81$, we have $L\ge1/(8t)$. For every integer $0\le r<L$, Bernoulli's inequality gives $(1-t)^{2r}\ge1-2rt\ge1/2$. The bias lower bound in step 2.1 thus implies, for every $R\ge1$, $$ \frac1R\sum_{r=0}^{R-1}z_r\ge\frac{\min\{R,L\}}{2R}\ge\min\left\{\frac12,\frac1{16tR}\right\}. $$ This argument uses only the scalar inequality $(1-t)^n\ge1-nt$ for integers $n\ge0$, which follows by induction.

After $r$ updates, at least $N-r$ table entries are still equal to their initial value 1. If $U$ is their set, the pairwise variance identity gives $$ \frac1N\sum_i(a_i^r-m_r)^2=\frac1{2N^2}\sum_{i,j}(a_i^r-a_j^r)^2\ge\frac{|U|}{N^2}\sum_i(a_i^r-1)^2\ge\left(1-\frac rN\right)\frac1N\sum_i(a_i^r-1)^2 $$ whenever $r\le N$. Indeed, retain in the double sum the pairs with exactly one index in $U$; pairs with both indices in $U$ contribute zero, and the two orientations cancel the factor 2.

For a fixed client $i$ and $0\le s<r$, the event that its last update before time $r$ occurs at time $s$ has probability $N^{-1}(1-1/N)^{r-1-s}$. On this event $a_i^r=x_s$. The event involves only $I_s,\ldots,I_{r-1}$, which are independent of $x_s$; hence its conditional law of $x_s$ is the unconditional law. If the client was never updated, $a_i^r=1$. Consequently, taking expectations in step 3.2 and using $\mathbb E(x_s-1)^2\ge(\mathbb E x_s-1)^2$, we obtain $$ V_r\ge\left(1-\frac rN\right)\frac1N\sum_{s=0}^{r-1}\left(1-\frac1N\right)^{r-1-s}\left(1-(1-t)^s\right)^2. $$ The expectation inequality follows by expanding the nonnegative variance $\mathbb E(x_s-\mathbb E x_s)^2$.

Suppose $2\lceil1/t\rceil\le r\le N/2$. In step 4.1 restrict to $s\ge\lceil1/t\rceil$, leaving at least $r/2$ indices. Since $(1-t)^s\le e^{-ts}\le e^{-1}<1/2$, each squared factor is at least $1/4$. Bernoulli's inequality gives $(1-1/N)^{r-1-s}\ge1-r/N\ge1/2$; the prefactor $1-r/N$ is also at least $1/2$. Thus $$ V_r\ge\frac r{32N}. $$ Here $1-t\le e^{-t}$ follows, for example, because the derivative of $e^{-t}-(1-t)$ is $1-e^{-t}\ge0$ for $t\ge0$, and its value at zero is zero.

Assume $R\le N/2$ and set $q=tR$. If $q<16$, step 3.1 gives $R^{-1}\sum_{r<R}z_r\ge1/256$. If $q\ge16$, then $R\ge16/t\ge1296$. Consider all integers $r\in[\lceil R/2\rceil,\lfloor3R/4\rfloor]$. There are at least $R/8$ such integers; each satisfies $2\lceil1/t\rceil\le r\le N/2$, so step 5.1 gives $V_r\ge R/(96N)$. Also $r+L\le3R/4+1/(4t)\le R-1$: the final inequality follows from $R/4-1/(4t)\ge15/(4t)>1$.

Iterating the exact nonnegative recurrence in step 2.1, each $t^2V_r$ from step 6.1 contributes $t^2V_r(1-t)^{2j}$ to $z_{r+1+j}$ for $0\le j<L$. These indices all lie below $R$ by step 6.1. Their weights sum to at least $L/2\ge1/(16t)$, by the Bernoulli estimate in step 3.1. All contributions are nonnegative, so they can be summed, including when their target indices overlap. It follows that $$ \frac1R\sum_{r<R}z_r\ge\frac1R\,t^2\frac R8\frac R{96N}\frac1{16t}=\frac{q}{12288N}\qquad(q\ge16). $$ Combining this with step 3.1 and using $\max\{u,v\}\ge\sqrt{uv}$ gives $R^{-1}\sum_{r<R}z_r\ge1/\sqrt{196608N}>1/(1024\sqrt N)$. The $q<16$ bound in step 6.1 gives the same conclusion. Thus, for every admissible constant stepsize and every $1\le R\le N/2$, $$ \mathbb E[f(x_J)-f^\star]\ge\frac F{1024\sqrt N}. $$

Now take $\beta=N^{-2}$ and $\epsilon=FN^{-3/4}=\tfrac12N^{-11/4}$. On this family the claimed round expression is exactly $$ 1+\frac{\sigma^2D^2}{KS\epsilon^2}+\frac{\beta D^2}{\epsilon}+\frac{NF}{S}=1+2N^{3/4}+\frac1{2N}. $$ For any proposed universal constant $C>0$, choose an integer $N$ large enough that $C(1+2N^{3/4}+1/(2N))\le N/2$ and $N^{1/4}>1024$. Such integers exist because the displayed expression divided by $N$ tends to zero. Every round count allowed by the claim then satisfies $R\le N/2$, but step 7.1 gives $\mathbb E[f(x_J)-f^\star]\ge F/(1024\sqrt N)>FN^{-3/4}=\epsilon$, for every admissible constant step. This contradicts the asserted accuracy and refutes the Statement.

Let $n,d,K,T,b,m$ be positive integers, let $f_j:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be
differentiable for $1\le j\le n$, and define
$f(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^n f_j(x)$. The inputs are a starting point
$x_0\in\mathbb R^d$, positive step sizes $\eta_0,\ldots,\eta_{T-1}$, and
integer synchronization times
$$ 0<t_1<\cdots<t_m=T,\qquad \mathcal I_T=\{t_1,\ldots,t_m\}. $$
Set $t_0=0$ and
$$ H=\max_{1\le j\le m}(t_j-t_{j-1}). $$
Initialize $x_0^k=x_0$ for each worker $k\in\{1,\ldots,K\}$. For each
$t=0,\ldots,T-1$, each worker $k$ and each within-step draw
$q=1,\ldots,b$, draw $i_{t,q}^k$ uniformly from $\{1,\ldots,n\}$, with all
draws mutually independent, and form
$$g_t^k(x)=\frac1b\sum_{q=1}^b\nabla f_{i_{t,q}^k}(x),\qquad z_{t+1}^k=x_t^k-\eta_t g_t^k(x_t^k).$$
For $b=1$ this is a single stochastic gradient. If
$t+1\notin\mathcal I_T$, set $x_{t+1}^k=z_{t+1}^k$ for every worker. If
$t+1\in\mathcal I_T$, set
$$x_{t+1}^k=\frac1K\sum_{\ell=1}^Kz_{t+1}^{\ell} \quad\text{for every }k.$$
The procedure returns the worker trajectories
$(x_t^k)_{0\le t\le T,\,1\le k\le K}$. The common initialization at time
$0$ is included when measuring the largest synchronization gap, and a
convergence statement must specify any particular average or iterate it
analyzes.

derivations.claim: The gradients are $\nabla f_1(x)=x$ and $\nabla f_2(x)=2x$. Without an intermediate synchronization, worker 1 follows $1\mapsto1/2\mapsto1/4$ and worker 2 follows $1\mapsto0\mapsto0$. Their arithmetic mean is $(1/4+0)/2=1/8$.

With synchronization after the first step, the worker states are first $1/2$ and $0$, so their common synchronized value is $1/4$. On the second step, the same coupled draws give worker states $1/4-(1/2)(1/4)=1/8$ and $1/4-(1/2)(2)(1/4)=0$. Their mean is $(1/8+0)/2=1/16$.
Since $1/8\ne1/16$ and the draw sequence in [A1] has positive probability under the algorithm, the two schedules can produce different final worker means.

intermediate synchronization their mean is $1/8$. If they instead synchronize

Let $U$ be a nonempty set of possible records and let $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$. A database is a function $D:U\to\mathbb N_0$ with finite support $\operatorname{supp}(D)=\{u\in U:D(u)\ne0\}$; $D(u)$ is the number of occurrences of record $u$. Let $\mathcal D$ be the set of databases and equip it with the power-set sigma-algebra. For $u\in U$, let $\mathbf 1_{\{u\}}$ be the function that is one at $u$ and zero elsewhere. Two databases $D,D'\in\mathcal D$ are neighbors, written $D\sim D'$, when $D'=D+\mathbf 1_{\{u\}}$ or $D=D'+\mathbf 1_{\{u\}}$ for some $u\in U$.

A randomized mechanism with output measurable space $(Y,\mathcal B)$ is a probability kernel $K$ from $\mathcal D$ to $Y$: for each $D\in\mathcal D$, $A\mapsto K(D,A)$ is a probability measure on $(Y,\mathcal B)$, and for each $A\in\mathcal B$, $D\mapsto K(D,A)$ is measurable. Given $\varepsilon\ge0$ and $0\le\delta\le1$, the mechanism is $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-differentially private if, for every ordered neighboring pair $D\sim D'$ and every output event $A\in\mathcal B$,

$$
K(D,A)\le e^{\varepsilon}K(D',A)+\delta.
$$

The mechanism is $\varepsilon$-differentially private, or pure $\varepsilon$-differentially private, when $\delta=0$. The ordered-pair quantifier includes both directions because $\sim$ is symmetric.

A **measurable space** is a pair $(X,\mathcal A)$ consisting of a set $X$ and a
sigma-algebra $\mathcal A$ on $X$ (Sigma-algebras). The members of
$\mathcal A$ are the **measurable subsets** of $X$.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ (Measures on sigma-algebras). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** (Measure spaces); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in Measures on sigma-algebras and A measurable function between measurable spaces; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

derivations.claim: Let $D=\varnothing$, $D'=\{r\}$, and let $M(E)=|E|$. These databases are add/remove neighbors. For the measurable event $A=\{1\}$, $\Pr[M(D)\in A]=0$ and $\Pr[M(D')\in A]=1$.

The required privacy inequality in the order $(D',D)$ would read $1\le e^\varepsilon\cdot0+\delta=\delta$, which is false whenever $\delta<1$. Therefore the exact count mechanism is not $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-differentially private for the stated parameters.

Let $n,p\ge1$, let $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$ be a fixed design matrix, let $y\in\mathbb R^n$, and let $\beta\in\mathbb R^p$. The empirical squared loss is

$$\ell_n(\beta)=\frac{1}{2n}\|y-X\beta\|_2^2.$$

Ordinary least squares minimizes $\ell_n(\beta)$ over $\mathbb R^p$. For $\lambda>0$, the ridge (Tikhonov) objective is

$$J^{\mathrm{ridge}}_\lambda(\beta)=\|y-X\beta\|_2^2+\lambda\|\beta\|_2^2.$$

For $\lambda>0$, the lasso objective in the empirical-loss convention is

$$J^{\mathrm{lasso}}_\lambda(\beta)=\ell_n(\beta)+\lambda\|\beta\|_1,\qquad \|\beta\|_1=\sum_{j=1}^p|\beta_j|.$$

This lasso has the same minimizers as $n^{-1}\|y-X\beta\|_2^2+2\lambda\|\beta\|_1$, the fixed-design convention with penalty parameter $\tau=\lambda$.

For a partition $G_1,\ldots,G_m$ of $\{1,\ldots,p\}$, fixed weights $w_g>0$, and $\lambda\ge0$, the group-lasso objective is

$$J^{\mathrm{group}}_{\lambda}(\beta)=\ell_n(\beta)+\lambda\sum_{g=1}^m w_g\|\beta_{G_g}\|_2.$$

For a fixed matrix $D\in\mathbb R^{q\times p}$ and $\lambda_1,\lambda_2\ge0$, a fused-lasso objective is

$$J^{\mathrm{fused}}_{\lambda_1,\lambda_2}(\beta)=\ell_n(\beta)+\lambda_1\|\beta\|_1+\lambda_2\|D\beta\|_1.$$

These group and fused formulas define objectives only; no existence, uniqueness, or algorithm guarantee is asserted for them here. The formulas use the displayed feature scales, so rescaling a column changes the penalty unless its coefficient and penalty weight are adjusted. If a separate intercept is included, write $X=[\mathbf 1\;X_0]$ and $\beta=(\beta_0,\gamma)$, and define the loss by $\|y-\beta_0\mathbf1-X_0\gamma\|_2^2/(2n)$. In this convention replace the ridge penalty by $\lambda\|\gamma\|_2^2$, the lasso penalty by $\lambda\|\gamma\|_1$, the group penalty by $\lambda\sum_g w_g\|\gamma_{G_g}\|_2$ with the groups partitioning only the coordinates of $\gamma$, and the fused penalty by $\lambda_1\|\gamma\|_1+\lambda_2\|D_0\gamma\|_1$ with $D=[0\;D_0]$. The ridge loss remains unaveraged. Each penalty then acts only on $\gamma$ and the intercept coordinate $\beta_0$ is unpenalized.

Let $N,d\ge1$, let each client $i\in\{1,\ldots,N\}$ have a positive integer
sample count $n_i$, and put $n=\sum_{i=1}^N n_i$. For differentiable client
objectives $F_i:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$, the sample-count-weighted deployment
objective is
$$ f_{\rm wt}(w)=\sum_{i=1}^N\frac{n_i}{n}F_i(w). $$
For differentiable client objectives $f_i:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$, the
equal-client objective is
$$ f(w)=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N f_i(w). $$
The symbols $F_i$ and $f_i$ denote separate families; they are not identified
unless an application states $F_i=f_i$. In general, $f_{\rm wt}$ and $f$ are
different objectives.

For integers $1\le S\le N$, a uniform fixed-size client sample is a random
subset $\mathcal S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,N\}$ of cardinality $S$ for which every
$S$-element subset has probability $\binom NS^{-1}$. This is sampling without
replacement. When several communication rounds are used, the sampled subsets
are independent across rounds unless a theorem states a different sampling
law.

The inputs are positive integers $N,d,R,K,S$ with $1\le S\le N$, an initial
server model $x_0\in\mathbb R^d$, client objectives for the chosen mode and
their local oracle procedures $g_i$, positive step sizes $\eta_l,\eta_g$,
and one aggregation mode from the two modes below. In count-weighted
deployment mode the objectives are $F_i$ and the inputs also include positive
integer record counts $n_1,\ldots,n_N$, with
$n=\sum_i n_i$. A call to $g_i$ returns a gradient vector according to its
supplied deterministic or stochastic local-oracle rule; the client-sample
randomness in a round is independent of that round's fresh oracle randomness.
In uniform-client analysis mode the objectives are $f_i$.

For each round $r=1,\ldots,R$, independently draw a uniform fixed-size subset
$\mathcal S_r$ of $S$ clients from $\{1,\ldots,N\}$. For every selected client $i$, initialize
$y_{i,0}=x_{r-1}$ and for $k=1,\ldots,K$ call $g_i$ at $y_{i,k-1}$ and update
$$ y_{i,k}=y_{i,k-1}-\eta_l g_i(y_{i,k-1}),\qquad 1\le k\le K, $$
The client sends its model difference $y_{i,K}-x_{r-1}$ to the server. Use one
of the following aggregation branches in every round:

1. **Count-weighted deployment mode.** With positive client record counts
   $n_i$ and $n=\sum_i n_i$, set
$$ x_r=x_{r-1}+\eta_g\sum_{i\in\mathcal S_r}\frac{n_i}{n} (y_{i,K}-x_{r-1}). $$
   Equivalently, each unselected client contributes its unchanged model
   $x_{r-1}$ to the full count-weighted average.

2. **Uniform-client analysis mode.** Set
$$ x_r=x_{r-1}+\frac{\eta_g}{S} \sum_{i\in\mathcal S_r}(y_{i,K}-x_{r-1}). $$
   The equal-client convergence result on this page uses this mode and the
   objective $f=N^{-1}\sum_i f_i$.

After the selected clients finish the round, apply the chosen branch to obtain
$x_r$. Repeat through round $R$. Return the finite server trajectory
$x_0,\ldots,x_R$.

derivations.claim: By [F1], client 1 has derivative $w-1$ and minimizer $1$; client 2 has derivative $4(w+1)$ and minimizer $-1$. The equal-client derivative is $(w-1+4(w+1))/2=(5w+3)/2$, so its unique zero and minimizer is $-3/5$.
From $w_0=0$, the two local trajectories are $0\mapsto1/4\mapsto7/16$ and $0\mapsto-1\mapsto-1$. Averaging the two final local models gives $(7/16-1)/2=-9/32$.
Since $-9/32\ne-3/5$, this one-round FedAvg output is not the minimizer of the equal-client objective, although the clients' optima are shifted in opposite directions.

The inputs are positive integers $N,d,R,K,S$ with $1\le S\le N$, objective
functions $f_i:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$, an initial
server model $x_0\in\mathbb R^d$, client controls $c_i^0\in\mathbb R^d$,
positive step sizes $\eta_l,\eta_g$, a local stochastic-gradient oracle
$g_i$, and a control-update option from $\{\mathrm I,\mathrm{II}\}$. Set
$c^0=N^{-1}\sum_i c_i^0$. The random client sample in each round is
independent of that round's fresh local-oracle randomness; no independence
among distinct clients' oracle draws is required here.

For each round $r=1,\ldots,R$, independently sample a uniform fixed-size
subset $\mathcal S_r$ of $S$ clients. At the start of this round, write
$x=x_{r-1}$, $c=c^{r-1}$, and $c_i=c_i^{r-1}$. For every selected client
$i$, initialize $y_{i,0}=x$ and, for $k=1,\ldots,K$, call $g_i$ at
$y_{i,k-1}$ and update
$$ y_{i,k}=y_{i,k-1}-\eta_l\bigl(g_i(y_{i,k-1})-c_i+c\bigr). $$
After its $K$ local steps, a selected client updates its control using either

- **Option I:** call $g_i$ at the round-start model $x_{r-1}$ and set
  $c_i^+=g_i(x)$; or
- **Option II:** set
  $c_i^+=c_i-c+(K\eta_l)^{-1}(x-y_{i,K})$.

The client sends $\Delta x_i=y_{i,K}-x$ and
$\Delta c_i=c_i^+-c_i$. Unselected clients retain their controls. The server
forms
$$ \Delta x=\frac1S\sum_{i\in\mathcal S_r}\Delta x_i,\qquad \Delta c=\frac1S\sum_{i\in\mathcal S_r}\Delta c_i $$
and updates
$$x_r=x+\eta_g\Delta x,\qquad c^r=c^{r-1}+\frac SN\Delta c.$$
The selected clients set $c_i^r=c_i^+$ and unselected clients set
$c_i^r=c_i^{r-1}$. Thus $c^r=N^{-1}\sum_i c_i^r$ whenever
$c^{r-1}=N^{-1}\sum_i c_i^{r-1}$ held before the round. The general
procedure permits zero initial controls; the convergence rates stated below
use the explicitly stated gradient-consistent initialization
$c_i^0=\nabla f_i(x_0)$. Repeat through round $R$ and return the model and
control trajectories $((x_r,c^r,(c_i^r)_{i=1}^N))_{r=0}^R$.

The inputs are positive integers $N,d,R,K,S$ with $1\le S\le N$, objective
functions $f_i:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$, an initial
server model $x_0\in\mathbb R^d$, client controls $c_i^0\in\mathbb R^d$,
positive step sizes $\eta_l,\eta_g$, a local stochastic-gradient oracle
$g_i$, and a control-update option from $\{\mathrm I,\mathrm{II}\}$. Set
$c^0=N^{-1}\sum_i c_i^0$. The random client sample in each round is
independent of that round's fresh local-oracle randomness; no independence
among distinct clients' oracle draws is required here.

For each round $r=1,\ldots,R$, independently sample a uniform fixed-size
subset $\mathcal S_r$ of $S$ clients. At the start of this round, write
$x=x_{r-1}$, $c=c^{r-1}$, and $c_i=c_i^{r-1}$. For every selected client
$i$, initialize $y_{i,0}=x$ and, for $k=1,\ldots,K$, call $g_i$ at
$y_{i,k-1}$ and update
$$ y_{i,k}=y_{i,k-1}-\eta_l\bigl(g_i(y_{i,k-1})-c_i+c\bigr). $$
After its $K$ local steps, a selected client updates its control using either

- **Option I:** call $g_i$ at the round-start model $x_{r-1}$ and set
  $c_i^+=g_i(x)$; or
- **Option II:** set
  $c_i^+=c_i-c+(K\eta_l)^{-1}(x-y_{i,K})$.

The client sends $\Delta x_i=y_{i,K}-x$ and
$\Delta c_i=c_i^+-c_i$. Unselected clients retain their controls. The server
forms
$$ \Delta x=\frac1S\sum_{i\in\mathcal S_r}\Delta x_i,\qquad \Delta c=\frac1S\sum_{i\in\mathcal S_r}\Delta c_i $$
and updates
$$x_r=x+\eta_g\Delta x,\qquad c^r=c^{r-1}+\frac SN\Delta c.$$

$c_i^r=c_i^{r-1}$. Thus $c^r=N^{-1}\sum_i c_i^r$ whenever
$c^{r-1}=N^{-1}\sum_i c_i^{r-1}$ held before the round. The general

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**

3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$

Let $N,d\ge1$ be positive integers, let $f_i:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$

dissimilarity if
$$ \frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\|\nabla f_i(x)\|_2^2\le G^2+B^2\|\nabla f(x)\|_2^2 \qquad(x\in\mathbb R^d). $$

$$ \frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\|\nabla f_i(x)\|_2^2\le G^2+2\beta B^2(f(x)-f^\star) \qquad(x\in\mathbb R^d). $$
In the convex-client FedAvg results, $\beta$ is a common gradient Lipschitz
constant and $f^\star$ is the attained minimum of $f$; this is the relaxed
convex form of the source's assumption. These conditions bound the population
second moment of deterministic client gradients. They are separate from the
within-client stochastic-gradient noise bound
$\mathbb E\|g_i(x)-\nabla f_i(x)\|_2^2\le\sigma^2$.

2. the measure space $(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n), \lambda_n)$ is
   complete (Complete measure spaces), and every $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   with $\lambda_n^*(S) = 0$ is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(S) = 0$;
3. every elementary set is Lebesgue measurable and

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice (The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)). Let

(The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)) and let $T : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be linear
with matrix $A$ (Linear map between vector spaces over the same field,
Every Euclidean linear map has a unique matrix and satisfies $\|Lh\|_2\le K\|h\|_2$ for some $K\ge0$).

1. **Invertible case.** If $\det A \ne 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable for

$\det A = 0$ and $\lambda_n(E) = +\infty$ the expression

Let $n \ge 1$, let $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and let $E + h$ be the translate of

1. $\lambda_n^*(E+h) = \lambda_n^*(E)$ for **every** subset $E$;

and the Carathéodory condition is a family of equations between its values, so

derivations.claim: Put $u=w/\lVert w\rVert_2$. For $d\ge2$, start with $u$ and inspect the standard basis vectors in their finite order; for each $e_i$, subtract its orthogonal projection onto the span of the vectors already retained, and append and normalize the residual exactly when it is nonzero. Since the standard basis spans $\mathbb R^d$, this finite Gram–Schmidt procedure produces an orthonormal basis whose first vector is $u$. Let $Q$ be the associated orthogonal coordinate map. If $d=1$, take $Qx=ux$. In either case the first coordinate of $Qx$ is $u\cdot x$, and [F4] says $Q$ preserves Lebesgue measure.

Fix an integer $R\ge1$. Since $Q$ is a finite matrix, choose $C_R<\infty$ greater than $R$ times the largest sum of absolute entries in any row; then $Q([-R,R]^d)\subseteq[-C_R,C_R]^d$. Since $E$ has outer measure zero, [F1] makes it Lebesgue measurable and null. Thus $E_R=((E-b)/\lVert w\rVert_2)\cap[-C_R,C_R]$ is a one-dimensional measurable null set by [F5]. By [F1], choose a Borel null set $B_R\supseteq E_R$. If $d=1$, the image under $Q$ of the set in the Statement intersected with $[-R,R]$ is contained in $B_R$. If $d\ge2$, that image is contained in $B_R\times[-C_R,C_R]^{d-1}$.

If $d=1$, the bounded pullback image is contained in the Borel null set $B_R$, and the inverse orthogonal map preserves nullity by [F4]. If $d\ge2$, the Borel set $B_R\times[-C_R,C_R]^{d-1}$ is Lebesgue measurable by [F7]; both Lebesgue factors are $\sigma$-finite by [F8], so Tonelli [F2] gives it product measure zero because its one-dimensional section factor $B_R$ has measure zero, and [F3] identifies that product measure with $\lambda_d$. Applying the inverse orthogonal map preserves nullity by [F4]. In either case the ridge pullback inside $[-R,R]^d$ is contained in a Borel null set.

The full pullback is the countable union of its intersections with $[-R,R]^d$, $R\ge1$. Each intersection is a subset of the Borel null set from step 3.1, hence is measurable and null by [F6]. The full pullback is measurable by [F6] and null by countable subadditivity [F9]. If two functions differ only on $E$, their compositions differ only on this pullback, proving the consequence.

citations.quote:
For an integer $n\ge1$, a compact $K\subseteq\Omega$, and an open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, put $\mathcal D_K=\{\varphi\in\mathcal D(\Omega):\operatorname{supp}\varphi\subseteq K\}$, using [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]. For integers $m\ge0$ set

$$p_m(\varphi)=\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_{x\in K}|\partial^\alpha\varphi(x)|,\qquad d(\varphi,\psi)=\sum_{m=0}^\infty2^{-m-1}\min(1,p_m(\varphi-\psi)).$$

The topology is generated by the seminorms $p_m$: neighborhoods at zero contain finite intersections of $p_m<\varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon>0$. Derivatives are continuous on $K$, so these suprema are finite; for $K=\varnothing$ all suprema are defined as zero and $\mathcal D_K=\{0\}$. For nonempty $K$, $p_0$ separates functions because all functions vanish off $K$. These are increasing seminorms and the displayed series converges since its terms are at most $2^{-m-1}$.

The term **fixed-support Fréchet space** refers to this topology and metric. Their agreement and completeness are established by the registered justifier [[lem-fixed-support-test-function-spaces-are-complete]], rather than included as unproved consequences of the name. If $K$ has empty interior, every test supported in $K$ is zero: a nonzero continuous value would have a neighborhood of nonzero values inside $K$.

For $n\ge1$, there exists $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$, $\chi=1$ on $|x|\le1$, and $\chi=0$ on $|x|\ge2$. For $R>0$, $\chi_R(x)=\chi(x/R)$ satisfies $\partial^\beta\chi_R(x)=R^{-|\beta|}(\partial^\beta\chi)(x/R)$. The construction requires no choice.
For $a\le b$, every continuous real function on $[a,b]$ is a uniform limit of polynomials.

Let $n\ge0$, let $f$ have continuous derivatives through order $n+1$ on an
open interval containing the closed interval between $c$ and $x$, and define
$P_n(t)=\sum_{j=0}^n f^{(j)}(c)(t-c)^j/j!$. If $x\ne c$, there is a point
$\xi$ strictly between $c$ and $x$ such that
$$
f(x)-P_n(x)=\frac{f^{(n+1)}(\xi)}{(n+1)!}(x-c)^{n+1}.
$$
For $x=c$, the remainder is zero.

Let $a,b$ lie in an open interval $J$, and let $f$ be continuously
differentiable on $J$. Then
$$
\int_a^b f'(t)\,dt=f(b)-f(a).
$$
If $f,g$ are continuously differentiable on $J$, then
$$\int_a^b f(t)g'(t)\,dt =f(b)g(b)-f(a)g(a)-\int_a^b f'(t)g(t)\,dt.$$
Both identities hold for oriented endpoints.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field (Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property)) and let
$\varepsilon \in F$ with $\varepsilon > 0$. Then there is a natural number
$n \ge 1$ such that

$$\frac{1}{n \cdot 1_F} < \varepsilon ,$$

where $n \cdot 1_F$ is the canonical natural of $F$ (Every complete ordered field is Archimedean) and
$1/(n \cdot 1_F)$ is its multiplicative inverse (Field). As is standard
we abbreviate $n \cdot 1_F$ to $n$ and write the conclusion $1/n < \varepsilon$.

This is the **reciprocal form** of the Archimedean property.
Every complete ordered field is Archimedean on its own delivers only the assertion that the canonical
naturals are cofinal, $x < n \cdot 1_F$; the form actually used in analysis, that
the reciprocals of the naturals get below every positive bound, is the statement
above, and it is recorded separately so that no proof has to reconstruct the
inversion step in passing.

If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and $a\le b$, then $f$ is bounded and
attains both a maximum and a minimum on $[a,b]$.

Every function differentiable at $c$ is continuous at $c$.
If $f,g$ are real functions differentiable at $c$, then $f+g$ and $fg$ are
differentiable there and
$$
(f+g)'(c)=f'(c)+g'(c),\qquad (fg)'(c)=f'(c)g(c)+f(c)g'(c).
$$
If $g(c)\ne0$, then $f/g$ is differentiable at $c$ and
$$
(f/g)'(c)=\frac{f'(c)g(c)-f(c)g'(c)}{g(c)^2}.
$$
If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, $g$ is differentiable at $f(c)$, and the
composition is defined near $c$, then $g\circ f$ is differentiable at $c$ and
$(g\circ f)'(c)=g'(f(c))f'(c)$. For every integer $m\ge1$,
$(x^m)'=mx^{m-1}$.

Every complete ordered field $F$ (Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property)) is Archimedean:
for every $x \in F$ there is a natural number $n \ge 1$ with $x < n \cdot 1_F$,
where $n \cdot 1_F$ is the canonical natural of the ordered field $F$
(Ordered field). Equivalently, the canonical naturals are cofinal in $F$.

derivations.claim: For each integer $n>2/(b-a)$ define $\chi_n(x)=\theta(n(x-a))\theta(n(b-x))$; such integers exist by [F6], and can tend to infinity by [F8]. By [F2], $\chi_n$ is smooth, vanishes off $I$, and equals one on $[a+1/n,b-1/n]$. Every derivative of $\theta$ is continuous and vanishes outside $[0,1]$ in positive order, so [F7] bounds it on $[0,1]$; repeated chain and product rules [F7] bound $\chi_n^{(j)}$ by a constant times $n^j$. For every $\varphi\in D_I$, all derivatives of its zero extension vanish at $a$ and $b$. Fix $M$. Taylor's formula [F4] gives, for every $N\ge1$ and each $0\le r\le M$, bounds $|\varphi^{(r)}(x)|\le C_{r,N}|x-a|^N$ near $a$ and $|\varphi^{(r)}(x)|\le C'_{r,N}|b-x|^N$ near $b$. Applying the product rule on the two boundary strips, and taking $N>M$, shows $p_M(\varphi-\chi_n\varphi)\to0$.

Fix $n$ and $M$. By [F3], choose a real polynomial $p$ uniformly approximating $\varphi^{(M)}$ on $I$, and integrate it $M$ times while matching the values $\varphi^{(j)}(a)$ for $0\le j<M$ to obtain a polynomial $q_0$. Put $e=\varphi-q_0$. Then $e^{(M)}=\varphi^{(M)}-p$ and $e^{(j)}(a)=0$ for $j<M$. Repeated application of [F5], inducting downward from $j=M-1$, gives $$\sup_I|e^{(j)}|\le (b-a)^{M-j}\sup_I|e^{(M)}|\qquad(0\le j<M);$$ for $j=M$ the error is just $\sup_I|e^{(M)}|$. Thus sufficiently accurate approximation at order $M$ makes every derivative through order $M$ uniformly close. Approximating the finitely many coefficients of $q_0$ by rational numbers gives $q\in\mathbb Q[x]$ with the same approximation to any prescribed tolerance. Since the finitely many derivatives of $\chi_n$ are bounded on $I$, the product rule makes $p_M(\chi_n(q-\varphi))$ arbitrarily small. Thus $\chi_nq\in D_I$ approximates $\chi_n\varphi$ in $p_M$.

The set $\{\chi_nq:n\in\mathbb N,\ n>2/(b-a),\ q\in\mathbb Q[x]\}$ is countable. Given a metric neighborhood of $\varphi\in D_I$, the summable metric weights reduce it to finitely many seminorms, bounded by $p_M$ for the largest index. Choose $n$ in step 1.1 so that $p_M(\varphi-\chi_n\varphi)$ is less than half the target tolerance, then choose $q$ in step 1.2 so that $p_M(\chi_n\varphi-\chi_nq)$ is less than the other half. The triangle inequality places $\chi_nq$ in the neighborhood. Hence this countable set is dense.
