citations.quote: Assume Countable Choice for the Lebesgue regular-distribution convention. If $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ is nonempty, open and connected and $\partial_j u=0$ for every $1\le j\le n$, then there is a unique $c\in\mathbb C$ such that $u(\psi)=c\int\psi$ for every test. Conversely every constant regular distribution has zero first derivatives. On a disconnected open set constants may differ on different connected components.

For a distribution $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ in the convention of [[def-distribution]] and a multi-index $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, its **distributional derivative** is
$$\langle\partial^\alpha u,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\langle u,\partial^\alpha\varphi\rangle\qquad(\varphi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)).$$
The test derivative is a continuous linear endomorphism by [[thm-test-function-operations-are-continuous]]. Its composition with $u$, multiplied by the indicated sign, is therefore a continuous complex-linear functional, so this definition produces a distribution. The pairing is bilinear, with no complex conjugation. For $\alpha=0$ the operation is the identity; for one coordinate derivative its sign is minus. Every derivative of the zero distribution is zero, including on the empty domain. No choice axiom enters this construction. Compatibility with classical derivatives requires an integration-by-parts argument where it is used; it is not part of the definition.

Distributional derivatives satisfy $\partial^\alpha\partial^\beta u=\partial^{\alpha+\beta}u$ and are continuous linear maps on $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ for both the weak and strong distribution topologies. These claims hold in ZF. Assuming Countable Choice for the cited Riemann-to-Lebesgue comparison, if $f\in C^k(\Omega;\mathbb C)$ and $|\alpha|\le k$, then $\partial^\alpha u_f=u_{\partial^\alpha f}$. In particular distributional differentiation extends classical smooth differentiation.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $f=\sum_{i\ge0}a_i x^i\in R[x]$. Its **formal derivative** is

$$ f':=\sum_{i\ge1} i a_i x^{i-1}. $$

Here $i a_i$ means the sum of $i$ copies of $a_i$ in the additive group of $R$. Equivalently, the coefficient of $x^n$ in $f'$ is $(n+1)a_{n+1}$. The sequence defining $f'$ has finite support because the coefficient sequence of $f$ does ([[def-polynomial-ring-over-a-commutative-ring]]). This is an algebraic operation and does not use a limit.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

In ZF, for compact $K\subseteq\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\Omega$ open, there is $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$ and $\chi=1$ on a neighborhood of $K$. Every open cover of $\Omega$ admits an at most countable locally finite smooth partition of unity with compact supports, each support contained in some cover member. Subordination here asserts existence of such a member for each support; it does not select cover labels.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
(The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

(Axis-parallel rectangles in $\mathbb{R}^m$ and their volume). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of Half-open boxes in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and their volume, and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ (Assuming countable choice, $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra containing every elementary set and $\lambda_n$ is a complete measure extending elementary volume).

derivations.claim: Base case $n=0$: the hypothesis is $DT=0$, so [F1] gives a constant regular distribution with some value $c\in\mathbb C$. Choose a real test function $\eta$ with integral one by [F5]. Since $c=\langle T,\eta\rangle$ and $T$ is real, $c\in\mathbb R$. Thus $T$ is represented by a real polynomial of degree at most zero.

Inductive step: let $n\ge1$ and assume the result for $n-1$. The distribution $S=D^nT$ satisfies $DS=D^{n+1}T=0$ and is real by [F2]. By [F1], $S$ is the constant distribution with some value $c\in\mathbb C$. Choose a real test function $\eta$ with integral one by [F5]. Since $c=\langle S,\eta\rangle$ and $S$ is real, $c\in\mathbb R$.

The smooth polynomial $q(x)=c x^n/n!$ has $D^nq=c$ as a regular distribution by [F3] and [F4]. Thus $U=T-q$ satisfies $D^nU=0$. The induction hypothesis applied with index $n-1$ gives a polynomial $r$ of degree at most $n-1$ whose regular distribution is $U$.
The polynomial $p=q+r$ has degree at most $n$ and its regular distribution is $T$, since regular distributions and distributional derivatives are linear. This completes the induction.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $p$ be a real number with
$0<p<\infty$. Write $\mathcal M(X,\mu)$ for the measurable functions
$f:X\to\mathbb R$. For $f\in\mathcal M(X,\mu)$ define the extended-valued
$p$-functional

$$\|f\|_p:=\begin{cases}\left(\int |f|^p\,d\mu\right)^{1/p},&\displaystyle\int |f|^p\,d\mu<\infty,\\+\infty,&\displaystyle\int |f|^p\,d\mu=+\infty.\end{cases}$$

The finite power uses [[def-real-power]], while the second clause avoids
applying real powers to the extended value $+\infty$. The integral is the
nonnegative Lebesgue integral of [[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]].

The class

$$\mathcal L^p(\mu):=\{f\in\mathcal M(X,\mu): \|f\|_p<\infty\}$$

is the measurable-function space used on this page before passing to
almost-everywhere equivalence classes.

For $1\le p<\infty$, the pointwise operations make $\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ a real
vector space by
[[thm-calligraphic-l-p-and-l-infinity-are-vector-spaces-for-p-at-least-one]].

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

- For $0<p<\infty$, define an equivalence relation on $\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ by
  $$f\sim g\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f-g\in\mathcal N(\mu),$$
  and write $L^p(\mu)$ for the set of classes $[f]$.
- For $p=\infty$, define the same relation on $L^\infty(\mu)$ and again write
  $L^\infty(\mu)$ for the set of classes.

Thus an element of $L^p(\mu)$ is an almost-everywhere equivalence class of
measurable representatives.

When $1\le p\le\infty$, the displayed set quotient agrees with the usual
quotient-vector-space construction of
The quotient vector space $V/W$ and its canonical projection.

For $0<p<1$, the same class notation is used; under its stated choice hypothesis, the later item
The $L^p$ distance for $0 < p < 1$ is a complete translation-invariant metric
supplies the metric structure rather than a normed-space structure.

Let $X$ be a set and let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on $X$ (Sigma-algebras). A **measure** on $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a function

$$\mu:\mathcal A\longrightarrow[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$$

such that:

1. $\mu(\varnothing)=0$;
2. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$,
   $$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k),$$
   where the right side is the nonnegative extended sum of Series in the nonnegative extended real line.

The second condition is **countable additivity**. It begins at index $0$ and includes the case in which some term or the total sum is $+\infty$.

In ZF, for compact $K\subseteq\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\Omega$ open, there is $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$ and $\chi=1$ on a neighborhood of $K$. Every open cover of $\Omega$ admits an at most countable locally finite smooth partition of unity with compact supports, each support contained in some cover member. Subordination here asserts existence of such a member for each support; it does not select cover labels.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

1. For $1\le p<\infty$, the rule
   $$\|[f]\|_p:=\|f\|_p\qquad([f]\in L^p(\mu))$$
   is well defined on the quotient classes.
2. For $p=\infty$, the rule
   $$\|[f]\|_\infty:=\|f\|_\infty\qquad([f]\in L^\infty(\mu))$$
   is well defined.
3. In either case, with the quotient vector-space operations of
   Coset equality, well-defined quotient operations, and the canonical projection with kernel $W$, the resulting pair
   $(L^p(\mu),\|\cdot\|_p)$ is a normed space in the sense of
   A norm on a real vector space, the induced metric, and the dictionary with the metric axioms.

derivations.claim: Choose a measurable representative $f$ of $[f]$. Truncate it to $f_M=\max(-M,\min(f,M))$. Since $|f-f_M|^p\le |f|^p$ and $f_M\to f$ pointwise wherever $f$ is finite, [F4] makes $\|f-f_M\|_{L^p(\mu)}<\varepsilon/2$ for some large $M$. Partition $[-M,M]$ into finitely many intervals of length at most $\delta$ and replace each value of $f_M$ by a fixed endpoint of its interval. If $\mu(K)>0$, choose $\delta$ with $\delta\mu(K)^{1/p}<\varepsilon/2$; if $\mu(K)=0$, any $\delta>0$ suffices. The resulting finite-valued Borel simple function $s$ satisfies $|s-f_M|\le\delta$ pointwise, so $\|s-f_M\|_{L^p(\mu)}\le\delta\,\mu(K)^{1/p}$. By [F5] and the triangle inequality, $\|s-f\|_{L^p(\mu)}<\varepsilon$. Since $\mu$ is concentrated on $K$, replace $s$ by $\mathbf1_Ks$: this finite Borel simple function represents the same class and admits a representation with every set $E_j\subseteq K$. Thus such supported simple functions are dense in $L^p(\mu)$.

Write such a simple function as $s=\sum_{j=1}^N c_j\mathbf 1_{E_j}$ with Borel $E_j\subseteq K$. For any $\eta>0$, regularity [F2] gives compact $F_j\subseteq E_j$ and open $O_j\supseteq E_j$ with $\mu(O_j\setminus F_j)<\eta$. By [F3] choose $\psi_j\in C_c^\infty(O_j)$ with $0\le\psi_j\le1$ and $\psi_j=1$ on $F_j$. Outside $O_j\setminus F_j$ the functions $\psi_j$ and $\mathbf1_{E_j}$ agree; everywhere their difference has magnitude at most one. Therefore $\|\psi_j-\mathbf1_{E_j}\|_{L^p(\mu)}^p\le\mu(O_j\setminus F_j)<\eta$.

The triangle inequality [F5] gives $\left\|\sum_{j=1}^N c_j\psi_j-s\right\|_{L^p(\mu)}\le\sum_{j=1}^N|c_j|\eta^{1/p}$. Choose $\eta$ small enough that this is below $\varepsilon/2$, and choose $s$ from step 1.1 within $\varepsilon/2$ of $f$. Then the compactly supported continuous function $\sum_jc_j\psi_j$ is within $\varepsilon$ of $f$ in $L^p(\mu)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice (The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)). Let
$m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
the product measure $\lambda_m \times \lambda_n$ and the Euclidean Lebesgue
measure $\lambda_{m+n}$ agree on every Borel subset of $\mathbb R^{m+n}$.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Every at most countable subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
([[def-countable]]) is Lebesgue measurable with

$$\lambda_n(E) \;=\; 0,$$

so $E$ is a $\lambda_n$-null set ([[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]]).
In particular every singleton is null, and on the real line the set
$\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ of rational reals ([[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]) satisfies
$\lambda_1(\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}) = 0$.

Let $\mu$ be a measure and let $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be measurable. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k).$$

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ one also has

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k<m}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k<m}\mu(E_k),$$

including $m=0$, where both sides are $0$.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
(The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)). Then

$$\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n) \;\subseteq\; \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n) :$$

every Borel subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ (The Borel sigma-algebra of a topological space) is Lebesgue
measurable (Lebesgue measurable sets, the family $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$, and the restricted set function $\lambda_n$). In
particular every open set, every closed set and every countable intersection of
open sets is Lebesgue measurable.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

derivations.claim: Base case $d=1$: [F1] makes the zero set finite, hence countable and null by [F4].

Inductive step: let $d\ge2$ and assume the claim in dimension $d-1$. Write $P(x',t)=\sum_{j=0}^m Q_j(x')t^j$, where $x'\in\mathbb R^{d-1}$ and the highest coefficient $Q_m$ is a nonzero polynomial. By the induction hypothesis, $Z=\{x':Q_m(x')=0\}$ is null. For every $x'\notin Z$, the section $t\mapsto P(x',t)$ is a nonzero univariate polynomial, so its zero set is finite by [F1] and null by [F4].

Fix $R\ge1$. The set $\{(x',t)\in[-R,R]^d:P(x',t)=0\}$ is Borel because $P$ is continuous. Its section has measure at most $2R$ when $x'\in Z$ and measure zero otherwise. Both Lebesgue factors are $\sigma$-finite by [F6], so Tonelli [F2] shows that its product measure is zero, since $Z$ is null; [F3] identifies this with its Euclidean Lebesgue measure.

The full zero set is the countable union of these Borel null intersections over integers $R\ge1$. Countable subadditivity [F4] makes it measurable and null. The base case and induction step prove the assertion for every $d\ge1$.

Assume Countable Choice for the Lebesgue-measure convention. A real-valued function $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ belongs to the activation class $\mathcal M$ when it is Lebesgue measurable, is locally essentially bounded, and the closure of its discontinuity set has one-dimensional Lebesgue measure zero. Here locally essentially bounded means that for every compact interval $J\subset\mathbb R$ there is a finite $M_J$ such that $|\sigma(t)|\le M_J$ for Lebesgue-almost every $t\in J$. The discontinuity set is $\{t:\sigma\text{ is not continuous at }t\}$. The function is a polynomial almost everywhere when there is a real algebraic polynomial $p$ such that $\sigma=p$ outside a Lebesgue-null set.

The subclass $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{pt}}$ consists of those $\sigma\in\mathcal M$ that are also pointwise locally bounded: $\sup_{t\in J}|\sigma(t)|<\infty$ for every compact interval $J$. This extra condition distinguishes pointwise uniform approximation from approximation in the essential-supremum norm.

For open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, write $f\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ when $f:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is Lebesgue measurable and $\int_K|f|<\infty$ for every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$. This extends [[def-locally-integrable-function-on-r-n]]: equivalently, require integrability on every ball whose closure is a compact subset of $\Omega$. Such balls finitely cover each compact $K$, and conversely their closures are compact; on all of $\mathbb R^n$, any ball lies in a larger compact closed ball.

For a test $\varphi$ as in [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]], define the **regular functional**

$$\langle u_f,\varphi\rangle=\int_\Omega f(x)\varphi(x)\,dx.$$

This is well-defined since $|\int f\varphi|\le\sup_K|\varphi|\int_K|f|$ for $K=\operatorname{supp}\varphi$. It is complex-linear in $f$ and in $\varphi$ and depends only on the almost-everywhere class of $f$. For an empty support the integral is zero. The subsequent embedding theorem establishes continuity, so that this is a distribution, and injectivity modulo almost-everywhere equality. That theorem states the Countable Choice cost of its injectivity proof; no choice is needed to define the displayed pairing.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. The map $f\mapsto u_f$, $u_f(\varphi)=\int_\Omega f\varphi$, is a complex-linear injection from $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ modulo almost-everywhere equality into $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$. It is continuous from the local $L^1$ topology, generated by $f\mapsto\int_K|f|$ for compact $K\subseteq\Omega$, to the strong distribution topology. In particular local $L^1$ convergence implies strong distribution convergence. The continuity estimate itself is choice-free; Countable Choice is used in the cited $L^1$ approximate-identity theorem proving injectivity.

For an integer $n\ge1$, a compact $K\subseteq\Omega$, and an open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, put $\mathcal D_K=\{\varphi\in\mathcal D(\Omega):\operatorname{supp}\varphi\subseteq K\}$, using [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]. For integers $m\ge0$ set

$$p_m(\varphi)=\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_{x\in K}|\partial^\alpha\varphi(x)|,\qquad d(\varphi,\psi)=\sum_{m=0}^\infty2^{-m-1}\min(1,p_m(\varphi-\psi)).$$

The topology is generated by the seminorms $p_m$: neighborhoods at zero contain finite intersections of $p_m<\varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon>0$. Derivatives are continuous on $K$, so these suprema are finite; for $K=\varnothing$ all suprema are defined as zero and $\mathcal D_K=\{0\}$. For nonempty $K$, $p_0$ separates functions because all functions vanish off $K$. These are increasing seminorms and the displayed series converges since its terms are at most $2^{-m-1}$.

The term **fixed-support Fréchet space** refers to this topology and metric. Their agreement and completeness are established by the registered justifier [[lem-fixed-support-test-function-spaces-are-complete]], rather than included as unproved consequences of the name. If $K$ has empty interior, every test supported in $K$ is zero: a nonzero continuous value would have a neighborhood of nonzero values inside $K$.

For every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$ with $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ open, the space $\mathcal D_K$ is Hausdorff, locally convex and complete for
$$d(f,g)=\sum_{m=0}^\infty2^{-m-1}\min(1,p_m(f-g)).$$
This metric induces exactly its derivative-seminorm topology. Multiplying the metric by two gives the equivalent convention with weights $2^{-m}$. These assertions require no choice axiom.

Let $I=[a,b]$ with $a<b$. Let $D_I$ be the real-valued smooth functions $\varphi:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ that vanish outside $I$, with seminorms

$$p_M(\varphi)=\max_{0\le j\le M}\sup_{x\in I}|\varphi^{(j)}(x)|,\qquad M\in\mathbb N_0,$$

and metric

$$d(\varphi,\psi)=\sum_{M=0}^{\infty}2^{-M-1}\min(1,p_M(\varphi-\psi)).$$

Then $D_I$ is separable in this metric.

In $\mathrm{ZF}$, every separable ([[def-separable-space]]) complete
([[def-complete-metric-space]]) metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) is a Baire
space ([[def-baire-space]]).

**The form of the conclusion used below.** A space $X$ is Baire exactly when
$W \cap \bigcap_{n} U_n \ne \varnothing$ for every sequence $(U_n)$ of dense open
subsets and every nonempty open $W \subseteq X$. No choice principle is spent:
separability supplies a single at most countable dense set, the padding lemma
turns it into a fixed sequence, and the recursion below selects a least
index-radius pair at each stage, a definable operation.

Let $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ and $\varphi\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^n)$. On the open safe domain $V=\{x:x-\operatorname{supp}\varphi\subseteq\Omega\}$, the convolution $u*\varphi$ is smooth and
$$\partial^\alpha(u*\varphi)=(\partial^\alpha u)*\varphi=u*(\partial^\alpha\varphi).$$
The last expression is restricted to $V$ if its own safe domain is larger. For $\Omega=\mathbb R^n$ the domain is all of $\mathbb R^n$. This holds in ZF.

For an integer $n\ge1$, $u\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n)$ as in [[def-distribution]], and $\varphi\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^n)$, define

$$(u*\varphi)(x)=\langle u(y),\varphi(x-y)\rangle.$$

The variable $y$ is the distribution variable: for fixed $x$, the smooth test $y\mapsto\varphi(x-y)$ has compact support $x-\operatorname{supp}\varphi$. The pairing is complex bilinear, with no conjugation; the displayed test, not the pairing convention itself, includes reflection of $\varphi$.

More generally, if $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$, the same formula is defined on the open set $\{x:x-\operatorname{supp}\varphi\subseteq\Omega\}$. Openness follows by covering the compact set $x-\operatorname{supp}\varphi$ by finitely many balls whose closures lie in $\Omega$, giving a positive translation margin. If $\varphi=0$, its support is empty and the formula defines zero everywhere. The subsequent smoothness theorem proves differentiability and its signs; the definition only pairs legitimate compactly supported tests.

For open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, write $f\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ when $f:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is Lebesgue measurable and $\int_K|f|<\infty$ for every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$. This extends [[def-locally-integrable-function-on-r-n]]: equivalently, require integrability on every ball whose closure is a compact subset of $\Omega$. Such balls finitely cover each compact $K$, and conversely their closures are compact; on all of $\mathbb R^n$, any ball lies in a larger compact closed ball.

For a test $\varphi$ as in [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]], define the **regular functional**

$$\langle u_f,\varphi\rangle=\int_\Omega f(x)\varphi(x)\,dx.$$

This is well-defined since $|\int f\varphi|\le\sup_K|\varphi|\int_K|f|$ for $K=\operatorname{supp}\varphi$. It is complex-linear in $f$ and in $\varphi$ and depends only on the almost-everywhere class of $f$. For an empty support the integral is zero. The subsequent embedding theorem establishes continuity, so that this is a distribution, and injectivity modulo almost-everywhere equality. That theorem states the Countable Choice cost of its injectivity proof; no choice is needed to define the displayed pairing.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ (Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point, Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Let $X=D_{[-1,1]}$ with its fixed-support Fréchet topology. For each $n\in\mathbb N_0$, set $E_n=\{\varphi\in X:g_\varphi^{(n+1)}(x)=0\text{ for every }x\in\mathbb R\}$. Linearity of convolution makes $E_n$ a linear subspace. For fixed $x$, its defining functional is continuous: on the compact interval $x-[-1,1]$, local essential boundedness of $\sigma$ gives a finite bound $M_x$, and $|g_{\varphi}^{(n+1)}(x)-g_{\psi}^{(n+1)}(x)|\le 2M_xp_{n+1}(\varphi-\psi)$. Thus $E_n$, an intersection of kernels of continuous functionals, is closed.

If a smooth function $g$ has $(n+1)$st derivative zero, [F6] first makes $g^{(n)}$ constant; subtracting its corresponding multiple of $x^n/n!$ leaves an $n$th derivative equal to zero. Repeating this argument down to order zero shows $g$ is a polynomial of degree at most $n$. Conversely every such polynomial has $(n+1)$st derivative zero. Thus the hypothesis gives $X=\bigcup_{n=0}^\infty E_n$.

By [F2]–[F4], the Baire theorem applies to $X$. Let $d\ge1$ and let $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be an activation function. For a finite width $m\in\mathbb N_0$, output weights $a_1,\ldots,a_m\in\mathbb R$, input weights $w_1,\ldots,w_m\in\mathbb R^d$, hidden biases $b_1,\ldots,b_m\in\mathbb R$, and output bias $c\in\mathbb R$, the scalar single-hidden-layer realization is

$$N(x)=c+\sum_{j=1}^{m}a_j\sigma(w_j\cdot x+b_j),\qquad x\in\mathbb R^d.$$

The family $\mathcal N_\sigma^{(d)}$ consists of all such functions as $m$ and the real parameters vary; $m=0$ is allowed and gives constant functions. This is the scalar-output, one-hidden-layer specialization of a layered multilayer perceptron with linear output.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\ge1$, $w\in\mathbb R^d\setminus\{0\}$, $b\in\mathbb R$, and let $E\subseteq\mathbb R$ have Lebesgue outer measure zero. Then

$$\{x\in\mathbb R^d:w\cdot x+b\in E\}$$

is Lebesgue measurable and has $d$-dimensional Lebesgue measure zero. Consequently, if two Lebesgue measurable real functions on $\mathbb R$ agree outside a null set, their compositions with the same nonconstant affine form $x\mapsto w\cdot x+b$ agree almost everywhere on $\mathbb R^d$.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
(The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

(Axis-parallel rectangles in $\mathbb{R}^m$ and their volume). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of Half-open boxes in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and their volume, and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ (Assuming countable choice, $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra containing every elementary set and $\lambda_n$ is a complete measure extending elementary volume).

Let $\mu$ be a measure and let $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be measurable. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k).$$

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ one also has

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k<m}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k<m}\mu(E_k),$$

including $m=0$, where both sides are $0$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Restrict each unit of $N$ to $te_1$. If its first weight coordinate is zero, that unit is constant in $t$. If that coordinate is nonzero, [F2] says the set of $t$ for which its preactivation lies in $E$ is null. There are finitely many units, so their union is null by [F4] and cannot contain a nondegenerate interval by [F3]. Every nonempty relatively open subset of $[0,1]$ contains a nondegenerate interval, so the complement is dense in $[0,1]$. On this dense complement every nonconstant unit equals $p(w_{j1}t+b_j)$. Thus $N(te_1)$ agrees there with a polynomial $P_N(t)$ of degree at most $q$; the constant units are absorbed into its constant term.

Suppose $\sup_{0\le t\le1}|N(te_1)-t^{q+1}|<\varepsilon_q$. On the dense subset from step 1.1, $|P_N(t)-t^{q+1}|<\varepsilon_q$; continuity of both polynomials extends the weak bound $\le\varepsilon_q$ to all of $[0,1]$.

Put $h=1/(q+1)$ and evaluate the $(q+1)$st forward difference at $t=0$. Its nodes are $jh$ for $0\le j\le q+1$, all in $[0,1]$. The forward-difference operation $Q(t)\mapsto Q(t+h)-Q(t)$ lowers the degree of every nonconstant polynomial by one and multiplies its leading coefficient by its degree times $h$. Iterating it $q+1$ times therefore annihilates $P_N$ and gives $(q+1)!h^{q+1}$ on $t^{q+1}$. The approximation bound [step 2.1] makes the absolute value of the resulting error sum at most $2^{q+1}\varepsilon_q$, since the binomial coefficients sum to $2^{q+1}$. But this is half of $(q+1)!h^{q+1}$ by the definition of $\varepsilon_q$, a contradiction.

Hence no network attains the stated error on this target, so the family is not uniformly dense on $K$. The argument includes $q=0$, where it says constants cannot approximate $t$ to arbitrary accuracy.

$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ (Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point, Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which

differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and

derivations.claim: Fix $k\ge1$ and $w\in\mathbb R^d$. If a smooth function has $g^{(k)}\equiv0$, induction on $k$ shows it is a polynomial of degree at most $k-1$: for $k=1$, [F4] makes it constant; for $k\ge2$, [F4] makes $g^{(k-1)}$ constant $c$, and subtracting $cx^{k-1}/(k-1)!$ reduces to the induction hypothesis. Since $g$ is not a polynomial, choose $b_k$ with $g^{(k)}(b_k)\ne0$. For $\delta\ne0$, repeated application of [F4] gives the finite-difference identity $$\Delta_\delta^k g(y)=\delta^k g^{(k)}(\xi)$$ for some $\xi$ between $y$ and $y+k\delta$, where $\Delta_\delta g(y)=g(y+\delta)-g(y)$. Indeed, the case $k=1$ is [F4]; for the induction step apply [F4] to $x\mapsto\Delta_\delta^{k-1}g(x)$ between $y$ and $y+\delta$, then apply the induction hypothesis to $g'$ at the resulting point. The binomial expansion of $\Delta_\delta^kg(y)$ is $\sum_{j=0}^{k}(-1)^{k-j}\binom{k}{j}g(y+j\delta)$. For $h>0$, define $$R_{k,h}(x)=\frac{1}{g^{(k)}(b_k)h^k}\sum_{j=0}^{k}(-1)^{k-j}\binom{k}{j}g(b_k+jh\,w\cdot x),$$ a finite linear combination of units from [F1]. If $w\cdot x=0$ then $R_{k,h}(x)=0=(w\cdot x)^k$. Otherwise the identity with $\delta=h(w\cdot x)$ gives $$R_{k,h}(x)=\frac{(w\cdot x)^k}{g^{(k)}(b_k)}g^{(k)}(\xi_{x,h}),\qquad |\xi_{x,h}-b_k|\le kh|w\cdot x|.$$ By [F3], choose $M<\infty$ with $|w\cdot x|\le M$ on $K$. Continuity of $g^{(k)}$ at $b_k$ makes $g^{(k)}(\xi_{x,h})\to g^{(k)}(b_k)$ uniformly over $x\in K$ as $h\downarrow0$, since $|\xi_{x,h}-b_k|\le khM$. Therefore $R_{k,h}\to(w\cdot x)^k$ uniformly on $K$.

A real-valued function $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ belongs to the activation class $\mathcal M$ when it is Lebesgue measurable, is locally essentially bounded, and the closure of its discontinuity set has one-dimensional Lebesgue measure zero. Here locally essentially bounded means that for every compact interval $J\subset\mathbb R$ there is a finite $M_J$ such that $|\sigma(t)|\le M_J$ for Lebesgue-almost every $t\in J$. The discontinuity set is $\{t:\sigma\text{ is not continuous at }t\}$. The function is a polynomial almost everywhere when there is a real algebraic polynomial $p$ such that $\sigma=p$ outside a Lebesgue-null set.

The subclass $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{pt}}$ consists of those $\sigma\in\mathcal M$ that are also pointwise locally bounded: $\sup_{t\in J}|\sigma(t)|<\infty$ for every compact interval $J$. This extra condition distinguishes pointwise uniform approximation from approximation in the essential-supremum norm.

**Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice** ([[def-countable-choice]]).

1. Let $a<b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be bounded, with
   discontinuity set $D$. Then $f$ is Riemann integrable on $[a,b]$ if and only
   if $D$ is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_1(D) = 0$.
2. Let $m \ge 1$ and let $f$ be a bounded real function on a closed
   nondegenerate rectangle in $\mathbb{R}^m$, with discontinuity set $D$. Then
   $f$ is Riemann integrable if and only if $D$ is Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_m(D) = 0$.

of [[thm-lebesgue-criterion]] are now proved in ZF. The translation between
elementary interval-cover nullity and Lebesgue-measure nullity used here rests
on the construction of $\lambda$ and requires countable choice in the cited
suppliers, so the statement above retains that hypothesis throughout.

bounded and Riemann integrable. Then $f$ is Lebesgue measurable on $[a,b]$ and
is integrable there, and its Lebesgue integral equals its Riemann integral:
$$\int_{[a,b]} f\,d\lambda_1=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx.$$

This is the point at which the completeness of Lebesgue measure is used
essentially: the proof obtains a Borel function equal to $f$ almost everywhere,
and measurability of $f$ itself is then a completeness statement.

([[def-countable-choice]]). For **every** subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$,
measurable or not,

$$\lambda_n^*(E) \;=\; \inf\,\{\, \lambda_n(U) \;:\; U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n \text{ open and } E \subseteq U \,\},$$

$\mathbb{R}^n$ is open.

1. $\lambda_n^*(E+h) = \lambda_n^*(E)$ for **every** subset $E$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $E+h$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(E+h) = \lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

and the Carathéodory condition is a family of equations between its values, so

translation invariant.

On the compact set $J\setminus U$, $\sigma$ is continuous and therefore uniformly continuous by [F5]; it is also bounded on $J$ by [F1]. Both $\varphi_R$ and $\varphi_I$ are uniformly continuous by [F5]. Hence the two products $\sigma(x-t)\varphi_\alpha(t)$, $\alpha\in\{R,I\}$, have a common modulus of continuity on every grid cell for which $x-t\notin U$, uniformly over $x\in K$.

Their total integral and sum error is at most twice this length times $\sup_J|\sigma|\max_{\alpha}\sup|\varphi_\alpha|$. On all other cells the common modulus from step 2.1 bounds the total error by $2R$ times that modulus at $h_n$. derivations.claim: Let $T_\sigma$ be the regular distribution induced by $\sigma$. It is real by [F9]. The hypothesis of the Statement includes all real-valued test functions. Applying [F2] to that subclass gives $N\in\mathbb N_0$ such that every real-test convolution supported in $[-1,1]$ is a polynomial of degree at most $N$. By [F7], choose a nonnegative smooth bump supported in $(-1,1)$ and divide by its positive finite integral to obtain the real unit-mass test $\rho$. Its rescalings $\rho_\varepsilon$ for $0<\varepsilon\le1$ remain supported in $[-1,1]$, so $g_\varepsilon=\sigma*\rho_\varepsilon$ is a polynomial of degree at most $N$.

By [F3], the regular distributions induced by $g_\varepsilon$ converge to $T_\sigma$ on every test function. For every $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$, the definition [F8] and this convergence give $\langle D^{N+1}T_\sigma,\psi\rangle=(-1)^{N+1}\langle T_\sigma,\psi^{(N+1)}\rangle=\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}(-1)^{N+1}\int g_\varepsilon(x)\psi^{(N+1)}(x)\,dx=0$, because [F6] makes each integral zero for the polynomial $g_\varepsilon$ of degree at most $N$. Thus $D^{N+1}T_\sigma=0$.

By [F4], $T_\sigma$ is the regular distribution of a polynomial $p$. Since both $\sigma$ and $p$ are locally integrable, injectivity [F5] implies $\sigma=p$ almost everywhere. This proves the forward implication; its contrapositive is the equivalent existence assertion.

The last expression is restricted to $V$ if its own safe domain is larger. For $\Omega=\mathbb R^n$ the domain is all of $\mathbb R^n$. This holds in ZF.

derivations.claim: By [F2] and the hypothesis on $\sigma$, some real test function $\varphi_*$ supported in $[-1,1]$ has a nonpolynomial convolution $g_*=\sigma*\varphi_*$. Indeed, if every real test had polynomial convolution, then for every complex test $\varphi=\varphi_R+i\varphi_I$ both real convolutions would be polynomials, making every complex convolution polynomial; [F2] would then imply that $\sigma$ is polynomial almost everywhere. Summing the finitely many approximants yields a $\sigma$-network $N$ with $\sup_K|N-G|<\varepsilon/2$.

The family $\mathcal N_\sigma^{(d)}$ consists of all such functions as $m$ and the real parameters vary; $m=0$ is allowed and gives constant functions. This is the scalar-output, one-hidden-layer specialization of a layered multilayer perceptron with linear output.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\ge1$, let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be compact, and let $\sigma\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{pt}}$ not agree almost everywhere with any polynomial. Then the finite scalar single-hidden-layer networks with activation $\sigma$ are uniformly dense in $C(K,\mathbb R)$.

Let $\mu$ be a finite regular Borel measure on $\mathbb R^d$ concentrated on a compact set $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, and let $1\le p<\infty$. Form the real $L^p(\mu)$ space using the Borel $\sigma$-algebra. Then restrictions to $K$ of real-valued compactly supported continuous functions on $\mathbb R^d$ are dense in $L^p(\mu;\mathbb R)$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\ge1$, $w\in\mathbb R^d\setminus\{0\}$, $b\in\mathbb R$, and let $E\subseteq\mathbb R$ have Lebesgue outer measure zero. Then

$$\{x\in\mathbb R^d:w\cdot x+b\in E\}$$

is Lebesgue measurable and has $d$-dimensional Lebesgue measure zero. Consequently, if two Lebesgue measurable real functions on $\mathbb R$ agree outside a null set, their compositions with the same nonconstant affine form $x\mapsto w\cdot x+b$ agree almost everywhere on $\mathbb R^d$.

Assume Countable Choice. For every integer $d\ge1$, if

$$P(x_1,\ldots,x_d)=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^d}c_\alpha x_1^{\alpha_1}\cdots x_d^{\alpha_d},$$

is a nonzero real polynomial with finitely many nonzero coefficients, then its zero set $\{x\in\mathbb R^d:P(x)=0\}$ is Lebesgue measurable and has $d$-dimensional Lebesgue measure zero.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\ge1$, $q\in\mathbb N_0$, and let $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be measurable and equal almost everywhere to a polynomial of degree at most $q$ (including the zero polynomial). For every finite single-hidden-layer network with activation $\sigma$, its restriction to the segment $K=\{te_1:0\le t\le1\}\subset\mathbb R^d$ cannot approximate the target $f(te_1)=t^{q+1}$ uniformly with error less than

$$\varepsilon_q=\frac{(q+1)!}{2^{q+2}(q+1)^{q+1}}>0.$$

Consequently these networks are not uniformly dense in $C(K,\mathbb R)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $p$ be a real number with
$0<p<\infty$. Write $\mathcal M(X,\mu)$ for the measurable functions
$f:X\to\mathbb R$. For $f\in\mathcal M(X,\mu)$ define the extended-valued
$p$-functional

$$\|f\|_p:=\begin{cases}\left(\int |f|^p\,d\mu\right)^{1/p},&\displaystyle\int |f|^p\,d\mu<\infty,\\+\infty,&\displaystyle\int |f|^p\,d\mu=+\infty.\end{cases}$$

The finite power uses [[def-real-power]], while the second clause avoids
applying real powers to the extended value $+\infty$. The integral is the
nonnegative Lebesgue integral of [[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]].

The class

$$\mathcal L^p(\mu):=\{f\in\mathcal M(X,\mu): \|f\|_p<\infty\}$$

is the measurable-function space used on this page before passing to
almost-everywhere equivalence classes.

For $1\le p<\infty$, the pointwise operations make $\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ a real
vector space by
[[thm-calligraphic-l-p-and-l-infinity-are-vector-spaces-for-p-at-least-one]].

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

- For $0<p<\infty$, define an equivalence relation on $\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ by
  $$f\sim g\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f-g\in\mathcal N(\mu),$$
  and write $L^p(\mu)$ for the set of classes $[f]$.
- For $p=\infty$, define the same relation on $L^\infty(\mu)$ and again write
  $L^\infty(\mu)$ for the set of classes.

Thus an element of $L^p(\mu)$ is an almost-everywhere equivalence class of
measurable representatives.

When $1\le p\le\infty$, the displayed set quotient agrees with the usual
quotient-vector-space construction of
The quotient vector space $V/W$ and its canonical projection.

For $0<p<1$, the same class notation is used; under its stated choice hypothesis, the later item
The $L^p$ distance for $0 < p < 1$ is a complete translation-invariant metric
supplies the metric structure rather than a normed-space structure.

Let $\mu$ be a positive measure and let $
u$ be a signed measure or a complex measure on the same measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$. We say that $
u$ is **absolutely continuous with respect to $\mu$**, and write
$$
u\ll\mu,$$
if every measurable $\mu$-null set is also $
u$-null:
$$\mu(E)=0\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 
u(E)=0\qquad(E\in\mathcal A).$$
Because every measurable subset of a $\mu$-null set is again $\mu$-null, this is equivalent to requiring $
u(F)=0$ for every measurable $F\subseteq E$ whenever $\mu(E)=0$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $X$ be a set and let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on $X$ (Sigma-algebras). A **measure** on $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a function

$$\mu:\mathcal A\longrightarrow[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$$

such that:

1. $\mu(\varnothing)=0$;
2. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$,
   $$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k),$$
   where the right side is the nonnegative extended sum of Series in the nonnegative extended real line.

The second condition is **countable additivity**. It begins at index $0$ and includes the case in which some term or the total sum is $+\infty$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

1. For $1\le p<\infty$, the rule
   $$\|[f]\|_p:=\|f\|_p\qquad([f]\in L^p(\mu))$$
   is well defined on the quotient classes.
2. For $p=\infty$, the rule
   $$\|[f]\|_\infty:=\|f\|_\infty\qquad([f]\in L^\infty(\mu))$$
   is well defined.
3. In either case, with the quotient vector-space operations of
   Coset equality, well-defined quotient operations, and the canonical projection with kernel $W$, the resulting pair
   $(L^p(\mu),\|\cdot\|_p)$ is a normed space in the sense of
   A norm on a real vector space, the induced metric, and the dictionary with the metric axioms.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space with $\mu(X)<\infty$.

1. If $1\le p<r<\infty$ and $f\in\mathcal L^r(\mu)$, then
   $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $$\|f\|_p\le\mu(X)^{1/p-1/r}\|f\|_r.$$
2. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $$\|f\|_p\le\mu(X)^{1/p}\|f\|_\infty.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, and let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be
measurable. The **essential supremum of $|f|$ with respect to $\mu$** is

$$\|f\|_{\infty,\mu}:=\inf\{M\in[0,\infty] : |f|\le M \text{ }\mu\text{-almost everywhere}\}.$$

When the measure is fixed from context, this is written $\|f\|_\infty$. The
phrase **essentially bounded** means $\|f\|_\infty<\infty$.

The later proposition
[[prop-essential-supremum-is-attained-as-the-least-essential-bound]] proves
that when $\|f\|_\infty<\infty$, the inequality $|f|\le\|f\|_\infty$ itself
holds almost everywhere and that this bound is the least essential bound.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space,
Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
(Continuity of a map between metric spaces, at a point and globally, in the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ form), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below (Lower bound, bounded below, bounded set), and it has a
maximum and a minimum (Maximum and minimum of a set): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
(Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property), Greatest lower bound (infimum)).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

Every Cauchy sequence of real numbers (Limits and Cauchy sequences of reals) converges to a real
number. Together with The reals form a totally ordered field, this completes the
construction: $\mathbb{R}$ is a complete totally ordered field.
The proof uses no form of the axiom of choice.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
(The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

(Axis-parallel rectangles in $\mathbb{R}^m$ and their volume). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of Half-open boxes in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and their volume, and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ (Assuming countable choice, $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra containing every elementary set and $\lambda_n$ is a complete measure extending elementary volume).

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$. Then $E$ is
Lebesgue measurable ([[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]) if
and only if each of the following four conditions holds, and the four are
equivalent to one another.

1. **Open excess.** For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is an open
   $U \supseteq E$ with $\lambda_n^*(U\setminus E) < \varepsilon$.
2. **$G_\delta$ minus null.** There are a $G_\delta$ set $G$ and a set $Z$ with
   $\lambda_n^*(Z) = 0$ and $E = G\setminus Z$
   ([[def-g-delta-and-f-sigma-in-a-topological-space]]).
3. **Closed deficit.** For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a closed
   $F \subseteq E$ with $\lambda_n^*(E\setminus F) < \varepsilon$.
4. **$F_\sigma$ plus null.** There are an $F_\sigma$ set $H$ and a set $W$ with
   $\lambda_n^*(W) = 0$ and $E = H\cup W$.

Each condition is stated for sets of infinite measure as well as finite ones,
which is why the excess and the deficit are measured by the outer measure of a
difference rather than by a difference of measures.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
(The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)). Then

$$\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n) \;\subseteq\; \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n) :$$

every Borel subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ (The Borel sigma-algebra of a topological space) is Lebesgue
measurable (Lebesgue measurable sets, the family $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$, and the restricted set function $\lambda_n$). In
particular every open set, every closed set and every countable intersection of
open sets is Lebesgue measurable.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). For every Lebesgue measurable
$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$,

$$\lambda_n(E) \;=\; \sup\,\{\, \lambda_n(K) \;:\; K \subseteq E \text{ and } K \text{ is a compact subset of } \mathbb{R}^n \,\}$$

([[def-metric-compactness]]), the supremum being over a nonempty family since
$\varnothing$ is compact.

**The choice hypothesis is inherited, not decorative.** The proof runs through
[[thm-littlewood-characterisations-of-lebesgue-measurability]], which is itself
stated under countable choice, so the conclusion carries the same hypothesis and
says so.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: If $\sigma\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{pt}}$ is nonpolynomial almost everywhere, [F3] proves pointwise uniform density on every compact $K$. If $\sigma$ is polynomial almost everywhere, [F7] gives a specific compact segment on which density fails.

Now let $\sigma\in\mathcal M$ and put $C=\overline{D_\sigma}$, its closed null discontinuity set. Definition [F1] supplies the local essential bound and null-closure hypotheses. Define $\widetilde\sigma=\sigma$ off $C$ and $\widetilde\sigma=0$ on $C$. This is measurable and equals $\sigma$ almost everywhere. For a compact interval $J$, choose a larger compact interval $J'$ containing $J$ in its interior and an essential bound $M_{J'}$ for $\sigma$ there. At any $t\in J\setminus C$, continuity of $\sigma$ implies $|\sigma(t)|\le M_{J'}$: a strict violation would, by continuity, give an interval of positive measure inside $J'$ on which $|\sigma|>M_{J'}$. Thus $\widetilde\sigma$ is pointwise locally bounded; outside $C$ it is continuous, so the closure of its discontinuities is contained in $C$. It belongs to $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{pt}}$; if $\sigma$ is nonpolynomial almost everywhere, so is $\widetilde\sigma$. For any nonconstant affine form $T(x)=w\cdot x+b$ and any Lebesgue measurable $A\subseteq\mathbb R$, [F16] writes $A=H\cup W$ with $H$ an $F_\sigma$ set and $W$ outer null. Then $T^{-1}(H)$ is Borel, hence Lebesgue measurable by [F17], and $T^{-1}(W)$ is measurable and null by [F5]. Thus $\sigma\circ T$ is Lebesgue measurable, as is every finite network; constant affine forms give constant measurable units. This makes the essential-supremum seminorm in the Statement well-defined for raw networks.

For the converse, suppose $\sigma=p_0$ almost everywhere for a polynomial $p_0$ of degree $q$. By [F5] and [F8], every nonconstant unit equals $p_0(w_j\cdot x+b_j)$ for $\mu$-almost every $x$; constant-input units can be absorbed into the output bias. Hence every network represents, in $L^p(\mu)$, a polynomial of total degree at most $q$.

For any finite $\widetilde\sigma$-network, a unit with $w_j\ne0$ differs from the corresponding $\sigma$-unit only on the null pullback $\{x:w_j\cdot x+b_j\in C\}$, null by [F5]. Replace the output bias by $c+\sum_{w_j=0}a_j(\widetilde\sigma(b_j)-\sigma(b_j))$ to absorb the constant-input units. The resulting $\sigma$-network equals the $\widetilde\sigma$-network almost everywhere in $\mathbb R^d$, and hence defines the same Borel $L^p(\mu)$ class under the representative convention when $\mu\ll\lambda_d$. For nonpolynomial-almost-everywhere $\sigma$, applying [F3] to $\widetilde\sigma$ and transferring these approximants proves essential-supremum density for $\mathcal M$ on every compact $K$.

Assume $\mu(K)>0$ and let $P_q$ be the vector space of real polynomials in $d$ variables of total degree at most $q$. In a monomial basis its coefficient space is $\mathbb R^s$ for some finite $s\ge1$, with its Euclidean norm. Every monomial is bounded on compact $K$, so for coefficient vectors $a,b$ one has $\sup_K|P_a-P_b|\le\sum_{|\alpha|\le q}|a_\alpha-b_\alpha|\sup_K|x^\alpha|$, which tends to zero as $a-b\to0$. By [F12], $\|P_a-P_b\|_{L^p(\mu)}\le\mu(K)^{1/p}\sup_K|P_a-P_b|$; the reverse triangle inequality from [F11] therefore makes $P\mapsto\|P\|_{L^p(\mu)}$ continuous in the coefficients. For a nonzero coefficient vector, $P$ is a nonzero polynomial; by [F6] its zero set is Lebesgue null, hence $\mu$-null by [F8]. If its $L^p$ norm were zero, [F11] would make its class zero, so $P=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere. This would give $\mu(K\setminus\{P=0\})=0$, whereas [F8] and [F10] give $\mu(K\setminus\{P=0\})=\mu(K)>0$, a contradiction. Thus the norm is positive on the coefficient unit sphere. That sphere is nonempty and compact by [F9], and [F13] gives a minimum $a>0$; homogeneity yields $\|P\|_{L^p(\mu)}\ge a|\operatorname{coeff}(P)|$. Any $L^p$-Cauchy sequence in $P_q$ therefore has Cauchy coefficient vectors. By [F14], their finitely many coordinates converge to those of a polynomial $P\in P_q$; the coefficient estimate above and [F12] imply convergence to $P$ in $L^p$. If a class lies in the closure of $P_q$, Countable Choice [A1] supplies a sequence from $P_q$ converging to it; the preceding argument and uniqueness of norm limits [F11] put that class in $P_q$. Hence $P_q$ is closed in $L^p(\mu)$.

To justify the Borel convention, $C$ is closed, $\widetilde\sigma=0$ on $C$, and $\widetilde\sigma$ is continuous on the open complement of $C$, so $\widetilde\sigma$ is Borel measurable. For any raw $\sigma$-network $N$, replace only its nonconstant units by $\widetilde\sigma$-units and keep each constant-input value $a_j\sigma(b_j)$ in the output bias. The resulting Borel function $N^*$ is bounded on $K$ by pointwise local boundedness of $\widetilde\sigma$ and compactness of each affine image. It equals $N$ outside the finite union of the closed Lebesgue-null sets $\{x:w_j\cdot x+b_j\in C\}$ with $w_j\ne0$, by [F5]. Hence $N^*$ lies in $L^p(\mu)$. Any two Borel representatives of $N$ agreeing with it Lebesgue-almost everywhere differ on a Borel Lebesgue-null set, which is $\mu$-null by [F8], so they define the same class. This also justifies the polynomial representatives in step 1.3 and the transfers in step 2.1 without assuming raw networks are Borel measurable.

The polynomial $r(x)=x_1^{q+1}$ is not in $P_q$ modulo $\mu$-almost-everywhere equality: for every $P\in P_q$, $r-P$ is a nonzero polynomial, so [F6]–[F8] imply $\mu(\{x\in K:r(x)=P(x)\})=0<\mu(K)$. Thus the closed subspace $P_q$ is proper and cannot be dense. Step 1.3 places the whole network family inside it, proving failure of $L^p$ density for polynomial-almost-everywhere activations.

Suppose $\mu(K)>0$. By [F10], $\mu$ is a measure, and the real Borel $L^p$ convention is fixed in the Statement. To prove the positive $L^p$ sufficiency, choose any real class $[f]\in L^p(\mu;\mathbb R)$ and $\varepsilon>0$. By [F4], choose $u\in C_c(\mathbb R^d,\mathbb R)$ with $\|f-u\|_{L^p(\mu)}<\varepsilon/2$. Apply [F3] to $\widetilde\sigma$ on $K$ to choose a network $N_{\widetilde\sigma}$ with $\sup_{x\in K}|N_{\widetilde\sigma}(x)-u(x)|<\varepsilon/(2\mu(K)^{1/p})$. By step 2.1 replace it by a $\sigma$-network equal $\mu$-almost everywhere. Using the Borel representative supplied by steps 2.1 and 3.1, equality of classes and [F12] give $\|N-u\|_{L^p(\mu)}=\|N_{\widetilde\sigma}-u\|_{L^p(\mu)}\le\mu(K)^{1/p}\sup_K|N_{\widetilde\sigma}-u|$. The triangle inequality [F11] yields $\|N-f\|_{L^p(\mu)}<\varepsilon$.

If $\mu=0$, every measurable real function represents the zero class in $L^p(\mu;\mathbb R)$, and the network family contains zero by width zero and output bias zero. Thus it is dense regardless of $\sigma$. Together with steps 4.1 and 3.2, this proves the stated $L^p$ equivalence and its zero-measure boundary.

Let $K=[0,1]^d$, which is compact by [F9], and define $\mu(A)=\lambda_d(A\cap K)$ for Borel $A$. By [F15], $\mu(K)=1$. This is a finite Borel measure concentrated on $K$ and absolutely continuous with respect to $\lambda_d$. It is regular: inner regularity follows by applying [F18] to $A\cap K$; for outer regularity, apply [F18] to $K\setminus A$ to choose a compact $F\subseteq K\setminus A$ with $\lambda_d((K\setminus A)\setminus F)<\varepsilon$, and use the open set $\mathbb R^d\setminus F\supseteq A$, for which $\mu((\mathbb R^d\setminus F)\setminus A)<\varepsilon$. Thus this $\mu$ satisfies the theorem's measure hypotheses. If a polynomial-almost-everywhere activation gave essential-supremum approximation to every continuous target there, [F12] and $\mu(K)=1$ would turn those approximations into $L^p(\mu)$ approximations, contradicting step 3.2 for $f(x)=x_1^{q+1}$. This proves the essential-supremum obstruction on the cube and completes both compact-set equivalences.

Step 5.1 proves Lp(0)={0}; step 1.1 and its polynomial supplier include q=0. Constant-input units are preserved in steps 2.1 and 3.1.

risk_review.notes: Independently checked all ten Proof steps and the 23 direct supplier Statements/Definitions. F1-F18/A1 are sufficient: zeroing sigma on its closed null discontinuity closure yields a Borel pointwise locally bounded representative, since continuity rules out an essential-bound violation off that set. Littlewood decomposes measurable sets into F_sigma plus outer-null sets; affine pullbacks are Borel plus null, establishing raw-network measurability. Replacing nonconstant units transfers a.e. approximants, and the explicit output-bias correction exactly preserves constant units. Borel representatives agree modulo a Borel Lebesgue-null set, hence modulo mu, without assuming mu is complete. Positive finite absolutely continuous mu makes every nonzero polynomial have positive Lp norm; the compact coefficient sphere therefore gives a positive norm lower bound. Coefficient completeness and Countable Choice for a closure sequence prove P_q closed; x_1^(q+1) is outside it. Zero polynomial uses degree bound q=0 (the same P_q argument). Continuous density plus the finite-mass sup-to-Lp inequality proves sufficiency. Zero measure, empty/null K, constants, finite widths and both directions of both compact-set equivalences are covered. The restricted cube measure is regular by compact inner approximants to A intersect K and K minus A; this yields the essential-supremum obstruction. p is kept in (1,infinity); no endpoint beyond the stated range is claimed. The delta_0 remark correctly explains absolute continuity. Leshno Definitions 3-5/Theorem 1 and proof Steps 1-7 were consulted with the essential-norm and zero-mass qualifications kept explicit. Statement links occur only after the complete section. No diagram or routed finding.

Let $d\ge1$ and let $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be an activation function. derivations.claim: Since sine is odd, $S(0)=c$ and $\bigl(S(1)+S(-1)\bigr)/2=c$.

Let $d\ge1$ and let $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be an activation function. For a finite width $m\in\mathbb N_0$, output weights $a_1,\ldots,a_m\in\mathbb R$, input weights $w_1,\ldots,w_m\in\mathbb R^d$, hidden biases $b_1,\ldots,b_m\in\mathbb R$, and output bias $c\in\mathbb R$, the scalar single-hidden-layer realization is

$$N(x)=c+\sum_{j=1}^{m}a_j\sigma(w_j\cdot x+b_j),\qquad x\in\mathbb R^d.$$

The family $\mathcal N_\sigma^{(d)}$ consists of all such functions as $m$ and the real parameters vary; $m=0$ is allowed and gives constant functions. This is the scalar-output, one-hidden-layer specialization of a layered multilayer perceptron with linear output.

A nonzero real polynomial of degree $n$ has at most $n$ distinct real roots. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-real-polynomial-degree-leading-coefficient-and-monic]], [[lem-real-polynomial-factor-at-a-root]], [[thm-induction-principle]].

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Every at most countable subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
([[def-countable]]) is Lebesgue measurable with

$$\lambda_n(E) \;=\; 0,$$

so $E$ is a $\lambda_n$-null set ([[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]]).
In particular every singleton is null, and on the real line the set
$\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ of rational reals ([[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]) satisfies
$\lambda_1(\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}) = 0$.

Assume Countable Choice for the Lebesgue-measure convention. A real-valued function $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ belongs to the activation class $\mathcal M$ when it is Lebesgue measurable, is locally essentially bounded, and the closure of its discontinuity set has one-dimensional Lebesgue measure zero. Here locally essentially bounded means that for every compact interval $J\subset\mathbb R$ there is a finite $M_J$ such that $|\sigma(t)|\le M_J$ for Lebesgue-almost every $t\in J$. The discontinuity set is $\{t:\sigma\text{ is not continuous at }t\}$. The function is a polynomial almost everywhere when there is a real algebraic polynomial $p$ such that $\sigma=p$ outside a Lebesgue-null set.

The subclass $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{pt}}$ consists of those $\sigma\in\mathcal M$ that are also pointwise locally bounded: $\sup_{t\in J}|\sigma(t)|<\infty$ for every compact interval $J$. This extra condition distinguishes pointwise uniform approximation from approximation in the essential-supremum norm.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: The spike set $\{1/n:n\in\mathbb N,\ n\ge1\}$ is countable and null by [F3]. Thus $\sigma=H$ almost everywhere and $\sigma$ is locally essentially bounded. Its discontinuities are exactly $\{0\}\cup\{1/n:n\in\mathbb N,\ n\ge1\}$, a closed null set: away from this set the step part is locally constant and there are no spikes nearby. Hence the activation satisfies [F4].

Consider a finite network $N(x)=c+\sum_j a_j\sigma(w_jx+b_j)$ on $[-1,1]$. Absorb constant affine units into $c$, combine terms with identical affine maps and discard groups with zero combined coefficient. Call a nonconstant affine map active when its zero lies in $[-1,1]$ and it takes positive values arbitrarily close to that zero at points of $[-1,1]$. If an active group remains, fix its zero $x_0$ and choose, among active groups at $x_0$ with nonzero coefficient, one with minimal $|w_0|$; write its combined coefficient as $A_0\ne0$.

The function $\sigma$ is not polynomial almost everywhere. If a polynomial agreed with it almost everywhere, it would vanish almost everywhere on $(-\infty,0)$, so [F2] would force it to be the zero polynomial; this contradicts $\sigma=1$ almost everywhere on $(0,1)$.

Set $x_n=x_0+1/(nw_0)$, choosing $n$ sufficiently large that $x_n\in[-1,1]$. The chosen unit has preactivation $1/n$ and contributes $A_0(n^2+1)$. For a unit with a different zero, its preactivation tends to a nonzero value; if the limit is negative the unit is eventually negative, and if positive it lies near only finitely many reciprocals, each attained at most once by the nonconstant affine sequence. Thus it spikes at only finitely many $x_n$. At the same zero, an active group with opposite sign has negative preactivation on this sequence; one with the same sign and a distinct affine map has slope ratio $r=|w|/|w_0|>1$. If $r$ is irrational the equation $r/n=1/m$ is impossible; if $r=p/q>1$ in lowest terms it requires $p\mid n$. Choose the infinite sequence $n=1+kP$, where $P$ is the product of the finitely many such numerators $p$ (take $P=1$ if there are none); then none of those other groups spikes. Along a tail of this sequence all other spike terms vanish and all Heaviside contributions remain bounded, so $|N(x_n)|\to\infty$. Thus a bounded network can have no active group with nonzero coefficient.

For a bounded network, every nonconstant group that remains has no positive threshold crossing in $[-1,1]$. Its Heaviside part is constant on $(-1,1)$, and its spike set in $[-1,1]$ is finite because its positive preactivation values stay bounded away from zero. Constant units are constant as well. Hence $N$ is constant outside a finite subset of $[-1,1]$.

If $N$ is unbounded, it cannot approximate the bounded target $f(x)=x$ uniformly. If it is bounded, choose $x_-,x_+$ outside the finite exceptional set with $x_+-x_->1$; then $N(x_-)=N(x_+)$, so at least one of $|N(x_-)-x_-|$ and $|N(x_+)-x_+|$ exceeds $1/2$. Thus no network approximates $x$ on $[-1,1]$ with error below $1/2$, refuting the pointwise-uniform claim.

Let $X$ be a set and let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on $X$ (Sigma-algebras). A **measure** on $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a function

$$\mu:\mathcal A\longrightarrow[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$$

such that:

1. $\mu(\varnothing)=0$;
2. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$,
   $$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k),$$

The second condition is **countable additivity**. It begins at index $0$ and includes the case in which some term or the total sum is $+\infty$.

Assume Countable Choice for the Lebesgue-measure convention. A real-valued function $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ belongs to the activation class $\mathcal M$ when it is Lebesgue measurable, is locally essentially bounded, and the closure of its discontinuity set has one-dimensional Lebesgue measure zero. Here locally essentially bounded means that for every compact interval $J\subset\mathbb R$ there is a finite $M_J$ such that $|\sigma(t)|\le M_J$ for Lebesgue-almost every $t\in J$. The discontinuity set is $\{t:\sigma\text{ is not continuous at }t\}$. The function is a polynomial almost everywhere when there is a real algebraic polynomial $p$ such that $\sigma=p$ outside a Lebesgue-null set.

The subclass $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{pt}}$ consists of those $\sigma\in\mathcal M$ that are also pointwise locally bounded: $\sup_{t\in J}|\sigma(t)|<\infty$ for every compact interval $J$. This extra condition distinguishes pointwise uniform approximation from approximation in the essential-supremum norm.

Assume Countable Choice. Fix $d\ge1$ and use the finite scalar single-hidden-layer family

$$\mathcal N_\sigma^{(d)}=\left\{x\mapsto c+\sum_{j=1}^m a_j\sigma(w_j\cdot x+b_j):m\in\mathbb N_0,\ c,a_j,b_j\in\mathbb R,\ w_j\in\mathbb R^d\right\}.$$

For every compact $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, if $\sigma\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{pt}}$ is not equal almost everywhere to a polynomial, then $\mathcal N_\sigma^{(d)}$ is uniformly dense in $C(K,\mathbb R)$. More generally, if $\sigma\in\mathcal M$ is not polynomial almost everywhere, this family is dense for the essential-supremum seminorm on each such $K$ with respect to $d$-dimensional Lebesgue measure. If instead $\sigma$ agrees almost everywhere with a polynomial of degree at most $q$ for some $q\in\mathbb N_0$ (including the zero polynomial), the family is not uniformly dense on the segment $\{te_1:0\le t\le1\}$, and is not dense in the Lebesgue essential-supremum seminorm on $[0,1]^d$. Thus pointwise compact-uniform density for $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{pt}}$, and essential-supremum density for $\mathcal M$, each hold on every compact set if and only if $\sigma$ is not polynomial almost everywhere.

Let $1<p<\infty$, and let $\mu$ be a finite regular Borel measure concentrated on a compact $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ and absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure. Form the real $L^p(\mu)$ space using the Borel $\sigma$-algebra. For $\sigma\in\mathcal M$, a network is interpreted in this space through any Borel representative agreeing with it outside a Lebesgue-null set; these representatives exist, are integrable on $K$, and give a unique $L^p(\mu)$ class. This convention does not alter the actual pointwise network used in the uniform clause. For $\sigma\in\mathcal M$ and $\mu(\mathbb R^d)>0$, $\mathcal N_\sigma^{(d)}$ is dense in $L^p(\mu;\mathbb R)$ if and only if $\sigma$ is not polynomial almost everywhere. If $\mu=0$, then $L^p(\mu;\mathbb R)=\{0\}$ and the network family is dense for every $\sigma\in\mathcal M$, including polynomial activations.

These are existence statements without a quantitative width bound. They imply neither trainability nor statistical generalization, and compact-uniform approximation does not mean uniform approximation on all of $\mathbb R^d$.

derivations.claim: ReLU and logistic sigmoid are continuous, hence their discontinuity sets are empty; ReLU is bounded on each compact interval and sigmoid is globally bounded between zero and one. Thus both lie in the pointwise locally bounded activation class.

Neither is a polynomial almost everywhere. If a continuous function equals a polynomial almost everywhere on $\mathbb R$, their difference is continuous and must vanish everywhere, since any nonzero value would persist on an open interval of positive measure. ReLU vanishes on $(-\infty,0)$ but is positive on $(0,\infty)$; the sigmoid is bounded and nonconstant. These properties exclude a polynomial identity for each.

Applying the pointwise $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{pt}}$ branch of [F2] separately to each activation proves the stated compact-uniform approximation property. Both activations and their networks are continuous, so they are already Borel representatives when the theorem's $L^p$ clause is used. The theorem is an existence statement only and supplies no uniform width bound.

Fix integers $d,r\ge1$. A ReLU feedforward network with $d$ input coordinates and $r$ affine output units is a finite acyclic computation graph whose hidden units apply $\rho(z)=\max\{0,z\}$ to real affine combinations of input coordinates and earlier hidden-unit values, and whose output units apply real affine combinations of input coordinates and hidden-unit values. There are no edges into input vertices or out of output vertices. For each hidden unit $v$, define its canonical level by
$$\ell(v)=1+\max\bigl(\{\ell(u):u\text{ is a hidden unit with an edge }u\to v\}\cup\{0\}\bigr).$$
Thus units with no hidden-unit predecessor have level $1$, and edges between hidden units may skip levels. Let $H$ be the largest hidden-unit level, with $H=0$ when there are no hidden units. The network depth is $H+2$, counting an input layer and a final affine output layer; equivalently, it is two plus the maximum number of hidden units on a directed path in the hidden-unit graph. A network on $[0,1]^d$ means the restriction to that domain of the graph's globally defined formula on $\mathbb R^d$; an approximation domain restricts evaluation, not the formula. Its computation units are its hidden and output vertices; its connections are its directed weighted edges; its weights are all connection coefficients and unit biases. Units and connections are counted as vertices and edges, while weights are counted as scalar entries, with zero-valued entries counted only when the architecture explicitly includes them. $$\ell(v)=1+\max\bigl(\{\ell(u):u\text{ is a hidden unit with an edge }u\to v\}\cup\{0\}\bigr).$$
Thus units with no hidden-unit predecessor have level $1$, and edges between hidden units may skip levels. Let $H$ be the largest hidden-unit level, with $H=0$ when there are no hidden units. Its computation units are its hidden and output vertices; its connections are its directed weighted edges; its weights are all connection coefficients and unit biases.
