$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
The space $L^p(\mu)$ as the quotient by null functions and
Complex Lp classes and Euclidean test-function conventions. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
The $L^p$ norm descends to the quotient and makes $L^p$ a normed space for $1 \le p \le \infty$
for real scalars and
Complex Holder, Minkowski, and the quotient norm for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
Weak derivative of a locally integrable function. Under
The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
Weak differentiation ignores null-set changes, while
Uniqueness of a weak derivative as an almost-everywhere class gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Assume the Axiom of Choice (The Axiom of Choice). Let $n\ge1$ and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, bounded and convex. If $u\in W^{1,\infty}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, then $u$ has a representative $u^{*}$ with
$$|u^{*}(x)-u^{*}(y)|\le\|Du\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}\,|x-y|\qquad(x,y\in\Omega),$$
and $u^{*}=u$ almost everywhere on $\Omega$. Conversely, every Lipschitz function $f:\Omega\to\mathbb K$ with constant $L$ lies in $W^{1,\infty}(\Omega)$ and $\|Df\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}\le L$ for real scalars, while $\|Df\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}\le\sqrt2 L$ for complex scalars. In both cases the real-linear derivative has operator norm at most $L$ almost everywhere.

**Gradient convention.** For a weak gradient $Dv=(D_1v,\ldots,D_nv)$ we write $|Dv|=(\sum_{i=1}^n|D_iv|^2)^{1/2}$ for its Euclidean norm and $\|Dv\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}:=\||Dv|\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}$ for the essential supremum of that norm, as in Pointwise potential bound for compactly supported smooth functions. For real scalars this norm equals the derivative operator norm. For complex scalars it is the Frobenius norm of the real-linear map $\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^2$ and can exceed its operator norm: $f(x)=x_1+ix_2$ is $1$-Lipschitz but $|Df|=\sqrt2$. If $\Omega=\varnothing$ both assertions hold vacuously.

In ZF, assume the Axiom of Choice. Then the Axiom of Countable Choice holds.
Moreover, if $R\subseteq X\times X$ is a serial relation on a nonempty set
$X$ and $a\in X$, there is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ such that
$x_0=a$ and $x_nRx_{n+1}$ for every $n$. Thus AC supplies the
prescribed-initial-point form of Dependent Choice.

$\rho\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ of unit mass with
$\operatorname{supp}\rho\subseteq\overline B_1(0)$, put
$\rho_\varepsilon(x)=\varepsilon^{-n}\rho(x/\varepsilon)$, and define the
interior mollification
$$u_\varepsilon(x)=(\rho_\varepsilon*\widetilde u)(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\widetilde u(y)\,\rho_\varepsilon(x-y)\,dy,$$
where $\widetilde u$ is a representative of $u$ extended by zero to
$\mathbb R^n$. Then $u_\varepsilon\to u$ in $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every
open $U\subset\subset\Omega$; equivalently $u_\varepsilon\to u$ in
$W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. The exponent $p=1$ is included, and

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
The space $L^p(\mu)$ as the quotient by null functions and
Complex Lp classes and Euclidean test-function conventions. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
The $L^p$ norm descends to the quotient and makes $L^p$ a normed space for $1 \le p \le \infty$
for real scalars and
Complex Holder, Minkowski, and the quotient norm for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
Weak derivative of a locally integrable function. Under
The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
Weak differentiation ignores null-set changes, while
Uniqueness of a weak derivative as an almost-everywhere class gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Assume the Axiom of Choice (The Axiom of Choice). Let $n\ge1$ and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, bounded and convex. If $u\in W^{1,\infty}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, then $u$ has a representative $u^{*}$ with
$$|u^{*}(x)-u^{*}(y)|\le\|Du\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}\,|x-y|\qquad(x,y\in\Omega),$$
and $u^{*}=u$ almost everywhere on $\Omega$. Conversely, every Lipschitz function $f:\Omega\to\mathbb K$ with constant $L$ lies in $W^{1,\infty}(\Omega)$ and $\|Df\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}\le L$ for real scalars, while $\|Df\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}\le\sqrt2 L$ for complex scalars. In both cases the real-linear derivative has operator norm at most $L$ almost everywhere.

**Gradient convention.** For a weak gradient $Dv=(D_1v,\ldots,D_nv)$ we write $|Dv|=(\sum_{i=1}^n|D_iv|^2)^{1/2}$ for its Euclidean norm and $\|Dv\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}:=\||Dv|\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}$ for the essential supremum of that norm, as in Pointwise potential bound for compactly supported smooth functions. For real scalars this norm equals the derivative operator norm. For complex scalars it is the Frobenius norm of the real-linear map $\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^2$ and can exceed its operator norm: $f(x)=x_1+ix_2$ is $1$-Lipschitz but $|Df|=\sqrt2$. If $\Omega=\varnothing$ both assertions hold vacuously.

In ZF, assume the Axiom of Choice. Then the Axiom of Countable Choice holds.
Moreover, if $R\subseteq X\times X$ is a serial relation on a nonempty set
$X$ and $a\in X$, there is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ such that
$x_0=a$ and $x_nRx_{n+1}$ for every $n$. Thus AC supplies the
prescribed-initial-point form of Dependent Choice.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Fix integers $d,r\ge1$. A ReLU feedforward network with $d$ input coordinates and $r$ affine output units is a finite acyclic computation graph whose hidden units apply $\rho(z)=\max\{0,z\}$ to real affine combinations of input coordinates and earlier hidden-unit values, and whose output units apply real affine combinations of input coordinates and hidden-unit values. There are no edges into input vertices or out of output vertices. For each hidden unit $v$, define its canonical level by
$$\ell(v)=1+\max\bigl(\{\ell(u):u\text{ is a hidden unit with an edge }u\to v\}\cup\{0\}\bigr).$$
Thus units with no hidden-unit predecessor have level $1$, and edges between hidden units may skip levels. Let $H$ be the largest hidden-unit level, with $H=0$ when there are no hidden units. The network depth is $H+2$, counting an input layer and a final affine output layer; equivalently, it is two plus the maximum number of hidden units on a directed path in the hidden-unit graph. A network on $[0,1]^d$ means the restriction to that domain of the graph's globally defined formula on $\mathbb R^d$; an approximation domain restricts evaluation, not the formula. Its computation units are its hidden and output vertices; its connections are its directed weighted edges; its weights are all connection coefficients and unit biases. Units and connections are counted as vertices and edges, while weights are counted as scalar entries, with zero-valued entries counted only when the architecture explicitly includes them. A layered fully connected ReLU network with $L$ hidden layers is the specialization in which every edge joins consecutive layers and every such edge is present; its depth is $L+2$.

derivations.claim: By [A1] and [F2], the Countable Choice convention in [F1] holds. Choose the Lipschitz representative on $(0,1)$ and extend it uniquely to $[0,1]$: values along any sequence approaching an endpoint are Cauchy and any two such limits agree by the Lipschitz bound. The continuous representative satisfies $|f|\le1$ everywhere, since any interior value with modulus greater than $1$ would by continuity violate the almost-everywhere bound on an interval of positive measure. Let $T\ge1$ be an integer and let $f_1$ linearly interpolate $f$ at $t/T$, $0\le t\le T$. Then $f_1$ is $1$-Lipschitz, and $f_2=f-f_1$ vanishes at every grid endpoint and is $2$-Lipschitz. Indeed, both summands are $1$-Lipschitz.

Let $m\ge1$ and let $\Gamma$ be the set of piecewise-linear functions on the grid $r/m$, $0\le r\le m$, with endpoint values zero and successive increments in $\{-2/m,0,2/m\}$. Thus $|\Gamma|\le3^m$. For each coarse interval $I_t=[t/T,(t+1)/T)$, rescale $g_t(y)=Tf_2((t+y)/T)$. This function is $2$-Lipschitz and vanishes at both endpoints. Quantize each node value down to the nearest multiple of $2/m$; adjacent quantized values differ by one of the three allowed increments. At a fraction $\theta$ of a grid subinterval, a $2$-Lipschitz function differs from its endpoint chord by at most $4\theta(1-\theta)/m\le1/m$; quantizing both endpoint values changes that chord by at most $2/m$. Hence some $\gamma_t\in\Gamma$ satisfies $\sup_{x\in I_t}|f_2(x)-T^{-1}\gamma_t(Tx-t)|\le3/(Tm)$.

Define the discontinuous selector $\chi(z)=z$ for $0\le z<1$ and $0$ otherwise. For $x\in[0,1)$, exactly the index $t$ with $x\in I_t$ has $\chi(Tx-t)=Tx-t$; all other terms vanish. Therefore $$\widetilde f_2(x)=\frac1T\sum_{\gamma\in\Gamma}\gamma\!\left(\sum_{t:\gamma_t=\gamma}\chi(Tx-t)\right)$$ equals the local interpolant $T^{-1}\gamma_t(Tx-t)$ and has error at most $3/(Tm)$. If $s_{\gamma,r}$ is the slope of $\gamma$ on $[r/m,(r+1)/m]$, then its zero value at $0$ gives $$\gamma(z)=s_{\gamma,0}\rho(z)+\sum_{r=1}^{m-1}(s_{\gamma,r}-s_{\gamma,r-1})\rho(z-r/m),\qquad 0\le z\le1,$$ by matching the initial slope and each slope jump. This uses $m$ ReLU hinges. The cache is a depth-five mixed-gate network with $O(T+m3^m)$ units and weights: $T$ selector units, at most $3^m$ grouped sums, $m3^m$ ReLU hinge units, and an affine output. For the coarse interpolant, set $s_t=T(f((t+1)/T)-f(t/T))$ for $0\le t<T$; then $$f_1(x)=f(0)+s_0\rho(x)+\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}(s_t-s_{t-1})\rho(x-t/T)$$ on $[0,1]$. This slope-jump identity has $T$ ReLU units and one affine output, so $f_1$ is a depth-three ReLU network of size $O(T)$.

Replace each discontinuous selector by $$\chi_\delta(z)=\rho(z)-\delta^{-1}\rho(z-(1-\delta))+(\delta^{-1}-1)\rho(z-1).$$ This continuous piecewise-linear function agrees with $\chi$ on $[0,1-\delta]$, decreases linearly to zero on $[1-\delta,1]$, and is zero outside $[0,1]$. Let $\varphi_\delta$ be the piecewise-linear tent that is zero outside $[0,1-\delta]$, rises from $0$ to $1$ on $[0,\delta]$, equals $1$ on $[\delta,1-2\delta]$, and falls to $0$ on $[1-2\delta,1-\delta]$. Its four slope jumps give a representation by at most four ReLU hinges as in step 3.1. Put $\Phi_\delta(x)=\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\varphi_\delta(Tx-t)$; this comb is a ReLU spline with $O(T)$ units and weights. Replacing the $T$ selectors by three ReLU units each and adding the comb keeps the cache size $O(T+m3^m)$ independently of $\delta$.

Let $\widetilde f_{2,\delta}$ be the cache network using $\chi_\delta$, and set $$f_{2,\delta}(x)=\rho(\widetilde f_{2,\delta}(x)+2\Phi_\delta(x)-1)-\rho(2\Phi_\delta(x)-1).$$ At most one selector is nonzero at any $x$, its value lies in $[0,1]$, and each rescaled $\gamma_t$ vanishes at both endpoints and is $2$-Lipschitz; hence $|\widetilde f_{2,\delta}(x)|\le1$. On each plateau where $\Phi_\delta=1$, the selector is unchanged and the gate outputs the cache. Where $\Phi_\delta=0$, the two ReLU terms cancel. On the transition strips $y\in[0,\delta]$ or $y\in[1-2\delta,1-\delta]$ in a coarse coordinate $y=Tx-t$, $\chi_\delta(y)=\chi(y)$, so the cache equals the continuous piecewise-linear spline $\widetilde f_2$ from step 3.1. For $0\le p\le1$, the map $a\mapsto\rho(a+2p-1)-\rho(2p-1)$ is $1$-Lipschitz and vanishes at $a=0$, hence its output has modulus at most $|a|$. Every point where $0<\Phi_\delta<1$ is within $2\delta/T$ of a coarse endpoint; both $f_2$ and $\widetilde f_2$ vanish there and are $2$-Lipschitz, so on those strips $|f_2-f_{2,\delta}|\le8\delta/T$. Where $\Phi_\delta=0$, $f_{2,\delta}=0$ and $|f_2|\le4\delta/T$, which is also within this bound. On plateaus the quantization error is at most $3/(Tm)$ by step 2.1. Thus $$\|f_2-f_{2,\delta}\|_\infty\le 8\delta/T+3/(Tm).$$ The two final ReLU preactivations absorb the former affine cache output, followed by a shared affine output, so depth increases from five to six; complexity remains $O(T+m3^m)$.

Choose $m=\lceil\tfrac12\log_3(1/\varepsilon)\rceil$, $T=\lceil6/(m\varepsilon)\rceil$, and $0<\delta\le\min\{1/4,\varepsilon T/16\}$. Then both error terms in step 5.1 are at most $\varepsilon/2$, while $T+m3^m\le C/[\varepsilon\log(1/\varepsilon)]$: here $T=O(1/(\varepsilon m))$, $3^m=O(\varepsilon^{-1/2})$, and $m\varepsilon^{-1/2}=O(1/(\varepsilon m))$ because $\varepsilon^{1/2}(\log(1/\varepsilon))^2$ is bounded on $(0,1/2)$. The sum $f_1+f_{2,\delta}$ is the required ReLU approximation.

citations.quote: Let a scalar-input ReLU network have $H\ge0$ hidden layers of widths $n_1,\ldots,n_H$ and an affine output. On any interval, its output is affine on at most $\prod_{\ell=1}^H(n_\ell+1)$ subintervals. In particular, if it has $U=\sum_\ell n_\ell$ hidden units, the number of affine intervals is at most $(1+U/H)^H$ for $H\ge1$, and is $1$ when $H=0$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d,n\ge1$ be integers, $Q=[0,1]^d$, and let $F_{d,n}\subset C(Q;\mathbb R)$ consist of the continuous functions whose restrictions represent members of $W^{n,\infty}((0,1)^d)$ satisfying
$$\max_{|\alpha|\le n}\|D^\alpha f\|_{L^\infty((0,1)^d)}\le1.$$
There exists $c_{d,n}>0$ such that, for every integer $W\ge1$, every map $\eta:\mathbb R^W\to C(Q;\mathbb R)$, and every map $M:F_{d,n}\to\mathbb R^W$ continuous for the uniform norm on $F_{d,n}$,
$$\sup_{f\in F_{d,n}}\|f-\eta(M(f))\|_\infty\ge c_{d,n}(W+1)^{-n/d}.$$
No continuity or measurability assumption is imposed on $\eta$. In particular, if this supremum is at most $\varepsilon>0$, then $W\ge C_{d,n}\varepsilon^{-d/n}$ for some $C_{d,n}>0$ depending only on $d,n$.

Fix a scalar-output ReLU feedforward architecture on $[0,1]^d$, permitting skip edges, with $W\ge1$ scalar connection coefficients and unit biases, and depth at most $L$. Fix a real threshold $a$. For its realizations $f_\theta$, let $\mathcal H_a=\{\{x:f_\theta(x)>a\}:\theta\in\mathbb R^W\}$. There is an absolute constant $C$ such that $\operatorname{VC}(\mathcal H_a)\le CW^2$ and $\operatorname{VC}(\mathcal H_a)\le CW L\log(2W)$. In particular, for $W\ge2$ the bound $\operatorname{VC}(\mathcal H_a)\le C L^2W\log W$ holds. The same assertions hold for $f_\theta(x)\ge a$. The parameter count includes every hidden and output bias, even when its chosen value is zero.

derivations.claim: By [F2], the hypotheses of clause (i) imply $\varepsilon\ge c_{d,n}(W+1)^{-n/d}$. Since $W\ge1$, we have $W+1\le2W$, hence $W\ge\tfrac12 c_{d,n}^{d/n}\varepsilon^{-d/n}$. The decoder needs no continuity; exactly the selector topology in the statement is used.

For clause (ii), write $p(t)=(4t(1-t))^{n+1}$ on $[0,1]$, extended by zero, and $\psi(x)=\prod_{r=1}^d p(x_r)$. The polynomial has endpoint zeros of order $n+1$, so its zero extension is $C^n$. Put $B=\max_{|\alpha|\le n}\|D^\alpha\psi\|_\infty\ge1$. Partition the cube into $K^d$ cubes of side $1/K$, with lower vertices $v_j$, and define $\phi_j(x)=B^{-1}K^{-n}\psi(K(x-v_j))$. All derivatives through order $n$ vanish at support boundaries, so the weak derivatives of these finite sums are their classical derivatives, as follows by integration by parts with zero boundary terms. Disjoint support interiors imply that every $f_\sigma=\sum_{j=1}^{K^d}\sigma_j\phi_j$, $\sigma_j\in\{-1,1\}$, belongs to $F_{d,n}$, since $\|D^\alpha f_\sigma\|_\infty\le K^{|\alpha|-n}\le1$ for $|\alpha|\le n$. At the center $x_j$ of cube $j$, $f_\sigma(x_j)=\sigma_jB^{-1}K^{-n}$.

For clause (iii), nonlinearity of $f$ implies that its Hessian is nonzero at an interior point; otherwise all first derivatives are constant on the connected cube and $f$ is affine. A symmetric nonzero Hessian has a direction with nonzero second directional derivative. By continuity choose a short interior segment and parameterize it by $t\in[0,1]$, so $g(t)=f(a+tv)$ has either $g''\ge c_0>0$ throughout or $g''\le-c_0<0$ throughout. The approximating network restricts to a scalar-input network of at most the same depth and unit count.

For sufficiently small $\varepsilon>0$, choose $K=\lfloor(1/(4B\varepsilon))^{1/n}\rfloor\ge\tfrac12(1/(4B\varepsilon))^{1/n}$. Then the center amplitude $B^{-1}K^{-n}$ is at least $4\varepsilon$. Every approximant to $f_\sigma$ within $\varepsilon$ has positive output at centers with $\sigma_j=1$ and negative output at centers with $\sigma_j=-1$. Thus the threshold classifiers from the one fixed architecture shatter these $K^d\ge c_{d,n}\varepsilon^{-d/n}$ centers.

Combining step 2.1 with the first bound in [F3] gives $c_{d,n}\varepsilon^{-d/n}\le CW^2$, hence $W\ge c\varepsilon^{-d/(2n)}$. Shrinking the constant covers the remaining non-small accuracies, because any scalar-output architecture has $W\ge1$.

If $L\le c_1(\log(1/\varepsilon))^p$, the second bound in [F3] gives $c_{d,n}\varepsilon^{-d/n}\le Cc_1^2W(\log(1/\varepsilon))^{2p}\log(2W)$. For sufficiently small $\varepsilon$, if $W\ge\varepsilon^{-d/n}$ the desired conclusion follows directly since $\log(1/\varepsilon)\ge1$. Otherwise $\log(2W)\le\log2+(d/n)\log(1/\varepsilon)\le C_{d,n}\log(1/\varepsilon)$, and rearrangement gives $W\ge c_2\varepsilon^{-d/n}(\log(1/\varepsilon))^{-2p-1}$. No assumption on continuity of the targetwise weight choices was made in either shattering argument.

Write $H=L-2$ and let $U$ be its hidden unit count. Discard units with no path to the output and absorb input-independent units into their downstream biases; this preserves the restricted function and does not increase the remaining hidden unit count. Partition the remaining hidden units by topological rank, where rank is the greatest number of hidden units on an input-to-that-unit path. Every rank is at most $H$, and every predecessor hidden unit has smaller rank. Let $n_\ell$ count rank $\ell$, setting $n_\ell=0$ for unused ranks; these are counts in a partition, not inserted computation layers. Maintain a common affine partition for the input and all earlier unit outputs, retaining those outputs when the next rank is processed. Every preactivation at that rank is affine on each existing interval, including all skip-edge terms, so its at most $n_\ell$ zeros split that interval into at most $n_\ell+1$ pieces. Thus the interval count in [F1] applies to this rank partition, and $\sum_\ell n_\ell\le U$. By AM–GM, the restricted network has at most $M\le\prod_{\ell=1}^{H}(n_\ell+1)\le(1+U/H)^H$ affine intervals. One has length $h\ge1/M$. On this interval the network output $r$ is affine. Fix integers $d,r\ge1$. A ReLU feedforward network with $d$ input coordinates and $r$ affine output units is a finite acyclic computation graph whose hidden units apply $\rho(z)=\max\{0,z\}$ to real affine combinations of input coordinates and earlier hidden-unit values, and whose output units apply real affine combinations of input coordinates and hidden-unit values. There are no edges into input vertices or out of output vertices. For each hidden unit $v$, define its canonical level by
$$\ell(v)=1+\max\bigl(\{\ell(u):u\text{ is a hidden unit with an edge }u\to v\}\cup\{0\}\bigr).$$

Its computation units are its hidden and output vertices; its connections are its directed weighted edges; its weights are all connection coefficients and unit biases. Units and connections are counted as vertices and edges, while weights are counted as scalar entries, with zero-valued entries counted only when the architecture explicitly includes them. Put $y_i=0$ for even $i$ and $y_i=1$ for odd $i$, and define $s_i=(y_{i+1}-y_i)/(t_{i+1}-t_i)$ for $0\le i\le n$. It follows that the threshold classifier $1[g(z)\ge1/2]$ is constant on at most $C=(1+\beta^\ell)\prod_{i=1}^{\ell}(1+tm_i\alpha\beta^{i-1})$ open intervals. Identically zero threshold polynomials contribute no roots. Since every factor's nonconstant term is at least one, $C\le2(2t\alpha)^\ell\beta^{\ell(\ell+1)/2}\prod_i m_i\le2(2t\alpha m/\ell)^\ell\beta^{\ell(\ell+1)/2}\le B$, where the penultimate inequality is AM–GM. The same partition argument applies for every fixed offset of the remaining coordinates.

Put $T=2^q$. By [F1], the target threshold classifier alternates on $N=T+1$ intervals in $[0,1]$. Its two end intervals have length $1/(2T)$ and each of the others length $1/T$. The integral of $|f-1/2|$ is $1/(8T)$ on each end interval and $1/(4T)$ on each other interval. A comparator classifier with at most $C$ intervals has at most $C-1$ internal boundaries. Discard target intervals containing such a boundary. At most $C-1$ intervals are discarded; in each of the at most $C$ remaining runs the alternating target labels disagree with the constant comparator on at least half the run length minus $1/2$. Hence at least $(N-2C)/2$ target intervals disagree throughout, whenever this quantity is positive. Their contribution gives $\int_0^1|f-g|\,dz\ge\max\{0,(N-2C)/(16T)\}$. Endpoint equalities have no effect on the integral. Integrating in the other coordinates gives the displayed bound and its $B\le T/4$ consequence.

Write $s=t\alpha\beta$. For $\ell=1$, the bound in step 2.1 is $4sm$. For $\ell\ge2$, use $(2/\ell)^\ell\le1$, $\ell(\ell+1)/2\le\ell^2$, and $\ell\le\ell^2$ to bound it by $2(sm)^{\ell^2}$. Therefore $B\le4(sm)^{k^2}$. If $m\le2^{k/s}$ and $s2^{k/s}\le2^k$, then $B\le2^{k^3+2}=T/4$. For $s=1$ the condition is equality; for fixed $s>1$ it is equivalent to $k\ge s\log_2(s)/(s-1)$, so it eventually holds. This proves the exponential-budget assertion with all its indicated parameter cases.

Remove any unary branches and branches whose two outcomes compute the same subtree function, replacing them by their sole or common continuation; these reductions preserve the represented function and never increase the node count. A decision tree is then full binary: every internal branch has exactly two children. If it has $I$ internal nodes and $J$ leaves, its edge count is both $2I$ and $I+J-1$, so $J=I+1$ and $r=2I+1$. Consequently a full binary decision tree with at most $r$ total nodes has at most $(r-1)/2$ internal branch nodes. On a fixed line each nonconstant affine test has at most one zero. A sum of at most $t$ such trees, with $r\le2^{A/t}$ and $A=k^3$, is constant away from at most $t(2^{A/t}-1)/2$ thresholds. Convexity of $u\mapsto2^u$ yields $t(2^{A/t}-1)\le2^A-1$ for $t\ge1$. Thus its threshold classifier has at most $(2^A+1)/2\le2^{A+2}=T/4$ intervals. Step 3.1 proves the tree assertion. Finally at $k=d=t=\alpha=1$, the target $h^5$ is $32$-Lipschitz; its degree-$2^{22}$ Bernstein polynomial has uniform error at most $32/(2\sqrt{2^{22}})=1/128$ by [F2]. This polynomial is one $(1,1,2^{22})$ gate, allowed by the node budget $2^{1/2^{22}}>1$, so the parameter restriction cannot be omitted.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
The space $L^p(\mu)$ as the quotient by null functions and
Complex Lp classes and Euclidean test-function conventions. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
The $L^p$ norm descends to the quotient and makes $L^p$ a normed space for $1 \le p \le \infty$
for real scalars and
Complex Holder, Minkowski, and the quotient norm for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
Weak derivative of a locally integrable function. Under
The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
Weak differentiation ignores null-set changes, while
Uniqueness of a weak derivative as an almost-everywhere class gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d,n\ge1$, let $Q=(0,1)^d$, and let $F_{d,n}$ be the unit ball of $W^{n,\infty}(Q;\mathbb R)$ for the norm given by the maximum of the essential suprema of all weak derivatives of order at most $n$. There is a constant $C=C(d,n)$ such that for every $0<\varepsilon<1/2$ one can choose a ReLU network architecture, independent of $f\in F_{d,n}$, for which every $f\in F_{d,n}$ has weights producing a representative $\Phi_f$ with $$\|f-\Phi_f\|_{L^\infty(Q)}\le\varepsilon,$$ depth at most $C(1+\log(1/\varepsilon))$, and at most $C\varepsilon^{-d/n}(1+\log(1/\varepsilon))$ weights and computation units.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $F_{1,1}$ be the unit ball of $W^{1,\infty}((0,1);\mathbb R)$ under the maximum norm of the function and its weak derivative, using the Lipschitz representative on $[0,1]$. There is an absolute constant $C$ such that for every $f\in F_{1,1}$ and $0<\varepsilon<1/2$, an architecture depending on $f$ computes a ReLU approximation with uniform error at most $\varepsilon$, depth $6$ counting input and output layers, and at most $C/[\varepsilon\log(1/\varepsilon)]$ weights, connections, and computation units.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

citations.quote: For integers $m\ge0$ and $d\ge1$, the complement of any $m$ affine hyperplanes in $\mathbb R^d$ has at most $\sum_{j=0}^{d}\binom mj$ connected components, with $\binom mj=0$ for $j>m$. If the hyperplanes are in general position, meaning every $q\le d$ of them meet in codimension $q$ and no $d+1$ have a common point, the number of components is exactly this sum; such arrangements exist for every $m,d$. On a zero-dimensional affine image there is at most one full-dimensional activation cell.

Fix integers $d,r\ge1$. A ReLU feedforward network with $d$ input coordinates and $r$ affine output units is a finite acyclic computation graph whose hidden units apply $\rho(z)=\max\{0,z\}$ to real affine combinations of input coordinates and earlier hidden-unit values, and whose output units apply real affine combinations of input coordinates and hidden-unit values. There are no edges into input vertices or out of output vertices. For each hidden unit $v$, define its canonical level by
$$\ell(v)=1+\max\bigl(\{\ell(u):u\text{ is a hidden unit with an edge }u\to v\}\cup\{0\}\bigr).$$
Thus units with no hidden-unit predecessor have level $1$, and edges between hidden units may skip levels. Let $H$ be the largest hidden-unit level, with $H=0$ when there are no hidden units. The network depth is $H+2$, counting an input layer and a final affine output layer; equivalently, it is two plus the maximum number of hidden units on a directed path in the hidden-unit graph. A network on $[0,1]^d$ means the restriction to that domain of the graph's globally defined formula on $\mathbb R^d$; an approximation domain restricts evaluation, not the formula. Its computation units are its hidden and output vertices; its connections are its directed weighted edges; its weights are all connection coefficients and unit biases. Units and connections are counted as vertices and edges, while weights are counted as scalar entries, with zero-valued entries counted only when the architecture explicitly includes them. A layered fully connected ReLU network with $L$ hidden layers is the specialization in which every edge joins consecutive layers and every such edge is present; its depth is $L+2$.

Assume AC. Infinite real projective space has
$$H^*(\mathbb {RP}^{\infty};\mathbb F_2)\cong\mathbb F_2[a],\qquad |a|=1.$$

For every integer $n\geq0$, restriction along the standard skeletal inclusion
$i_n:\mathbb {RP}^n\hookrightarrow\mathbb {RP}^{\infty}$ is an isomorphism in
degrees at most $n$. For $n\geq1$ it sends $a$ to the unique nonzero
degree-one class on $\mathbb {RP}^n$; for $n=0$ it sends $a$ to zero.

For each integer $m\ge0$, $\mathbb{RP}^m=S^m/(x\sim-x)$ has a CW structure with one cell in each dimension $0,\ldots,m$. Orientations can be chosen so its integral cellular complex has $C_j=\mathbb Z$ in these degrees, $d_j=2$ for positive even $j$, and $d_j=0$ for odd $j$. Consequently its integral homology is $\mathbb Z$ in degree zero, $\mathbb Z/2$ in odd degrees $0<j<m$, $\mathbb Z$ in degree $j=m$ when $m$ is odd, and zero otherwise. For $m=0$ only the degree-zero copy occurs.

The quotient $q:\mathbb{RP}^2\to\mathbb{RP}^2/\mathbb{RP}^1\cong S^2$ induces an isomorphism $H_2(\mathbb{RP}^2;\mathbb F_2)\to H_2(S^2;\mathbb F_2)$. Assuming AC, it therefore induces an isomorphism $q^*:H^2(S^2;\mathbb F_2)\to H^2(\mathbb{RP}^2;\mathbb F_2)$, both groups being $\mathbb F_2$.

Assume AC. Let $X$ be a nonempty finite CW complex of dimension $d$, and let
$R$ be a commutative ring. For every $n>d$ the singular cohomology vanishes:
$$H^n(X;R)=0.$$
More generally, for a CW pair $(X,A)$ with $X$ finite of dimension $d$ one has
$H^n(X,A;R)=0$ for every $n>d$.
If $f,g:X\to Y$ are homotopic continuous maps, then $f^*=g^*:H^n(Y;G)\to H^n(X;G)$ for every integer $n$ and every abelian coefficient group $G$.

For continuous $f:X\to Y$ and a commutative unital ring $R$, pullback on singular cohomology satisfies
$$f^*(a\smile b)=f^*a\smile f^*b,\qquad f^*(1)=1.$$
Cup product is associative already on cochains. Consequently $f^*:H^*(Y;R)\to H^*(X;R)$ is a unital graded-ring homomorphism. Homotopic maps give the same homomorphism.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function

there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that

derivations.claim: We first rule out a continuous odd map $g:S^m\to S^{m-1}$ for $m\ge1$. Such a map descends to $b:\mathbb{RP}^m\to\mathbb{RP}^{m-1}$, $b([x])=[g(x)]$. This is continuous by the quotient topology, since the composite with the sphere quotient is continuous and $g(-x)=-g(x)$.

In the coordinate subspace $\mathbb R^{m+1}\oplus\mathbb R^m\subset\mathbb R^{\infty}$, define $$H([x],t)=[\cos(\pi t/2)x,\ \sin(\pi t/2)g(x)],\qquad 0\le t\le1.$$ Its representing vector has norm one. Replacing $x$ by $-x$ negates the whole vector, so the projective point is independent of representative. Continuity can be checked on each chart where a chosen coordinate of $x$ is nonzero: choose the unit representative with that coordinate positive, which varies continuously in the ratios of the remaining coordinates, and use the displayed formula. These charts cover projective space, proving joint continuity in $([x],t)$. Thus $H$ is a homotopy from $i_m$ to $j\circ b$, where $j([y])=[0,y]$ is the inclusion in the second block. The same formula with $y$ in the first $m$ coordinates and $y$ in the second block, namely $[\cos(\pi t/2)y,0,\sin(\pi t/2)y]$, is a homotopy from $i_{m-1}$ to $j$. Both homotopies lie in the finite projective subspace $\mathbb{RP}^{2m}$ of the infinite space and therefore are continuous there as well.

Put $a_k=i_k^*a$. By [F3] and step 2.1, $a_m=b^*a_{m-1}$, including $m=1$ when $a_0=0$. Consequently $$a_m^m=b^*(a_{m-1}^m)=0,$$ since $H^m(\mathbb{RP}^{m-1};\mathbb F_2)=0$ by [F2]. On the other hand, [F1] says $a^m\ne0$ and that $i_m^*$ is an isomorphism in degree $m$, so $a_m^m=i_m^*(a^m)\ne0$. These incompatible conclusions rule out every such odd map.

For $m\ge1$, if $h(x)-h(-x)$ never vanished, then $$g(x)=\frac{h(x)-h(-x)}{\|h(x)-h(-x)\|_2}$$ would be continuous, take values in $S^{m-1}$ and satisfy $g(-x)=-g(x)$. Let $F$ be a field. Every polynomial in the iterated ring
$F[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ has a unique finite expansion

$$f=\sum_{\mathbf{t}}c_{\mathbf{t}}x^{\mathbf{t}},\qquad x^{\mathbf{t}}:=x_1^{t_1}\cdots x_n^{t_n},$$

over finitely many multi-indices $\mathbf{t}=(t_1,\dots,t_n)\in\mathbb{N}^n$.

For such an index, the scalar $c_{\mathbf{t}}$ is the **coefficient**
$[x^{\mathbf{t}}]f$ of the monomial $x^{\mathbf{t}}$.

The **degree in $x_i$** is the largest $t_i$ with $c_{\mathbf{t}}\ne0$, and the
**total degree** is the largest value of $t_1+\cdots+t_n$ with
$c_{\mathbf{t}}\ne0$. For the zero polynomial, every degree is left undefined.

Evaluation at a point $(a_1,\dots,a_n)\in F^n$ is the iterated substitution
supplied by the universal property of the polynomial ring.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty. The following are equivalent.

1. $A$ is compact.
2. $A$ is closed and bounded.
3. $A$ is pseudocompact.
4. Every continuous $f:A\to\mathbb{R}$ attains a maximum and a minimum on $A$.

This theorem is a ZF statement. The nonemptiness hypothesis is necessary for condition 4, because the empty image has neither a maximum nor a minimum.
If $f:U\subseteq\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R$ is differentiable at an interior local maximum or minimum $a$, then $\nabla f(a)=0$.

derivations.claim: First establish an elementary zero-counting fact. If $D\ge1$ and $r_i(x)=x_i^D+s_i(x)$ with $\deg s_i<D$ for $1\le i\le k$, then these $k$ polynomials have at most $D^k$ distinct common real zeros. In the quotient vector space $V=\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_k]/(r_1,\ldots,r_k)$, every monomial is a linear combination of the $D^k$ monomials $x_1^{a_1}\cdots x_k^{a_k}$ with $0\le a_i<D$. Indeed, if some exponent is at least $D$, replace its factor $x_i^D$ by $-s_i$ modulo the ideal. Every resulting monomial has strictly smaller total degree, so induction on total degree terminates and proves the spanning assertion. Thus $\dim V\le D^k$.

If no strict sign vector occurs, its bound is immediate. Otherwise choose one representative $a_\sigma$ for each attained strict vector $\sigma$. Only finitely many choices are involved, since there are at most $2^m$ vectors. Set $P=\prod_{i=1}^m p_i$ and $D=2md+1$. Then $P(a_\sigma)\ne0$. Choose a single $\delta>0$ so small that $H(a_\sigma)>0$ for every representative, where $H(x)=P(x)^2-\delta\sum_{i=1}^k x_i^{D+1}$. Such a choice exists: there are finitely many positive numbers $P(a_\sigma)^2$, and the other term has a fixed finite value at each representative. Since $D+1$ is even and greater than $2\deg P$, $H(x)\to-\infty$ as $\|x\|\to\infty$. Explicitly, $|P(x)|^2\le C(1+\|x\|^{2md})$ and $\sum_i x_i^{D+1}\ge k^{-(D+1)/2}\|x\|^{D+1}$.

For any finite list of distinct common zeros $z_1,\ldots,z_t$, evaluation defines a surjective linear map $V\to\mathbb R^t$. To see surjectivity, for every ordered pair $j\ne h$ choose a coordinate $i(j,h)$ in which $z_j$ and $z_h$ differ, and set $h_j(x)=\prod_{h\ne j}(x_{i(j,h)}-(z_h)_{i(j,h)})/((z_j)_{i(j,h)}-(z_h)_{i(j,h)})$. Then $h_j(z_h)$ is $1$ for $h=j$ and $0$ otherwise. Evaluation vanishes on the ideal because all its generators vanish at these zeros, so it is well defined on $V$ and the classes of $h_j$ map onto the standard coordinate vectors. The classes of $h_1,\ldots,h_t$ are linearly independent: applying evaluation to any relation gives the same relation among the standard coordinate vectors, so every coefficient is zero. A vector space spanned by $D^k$ vectors contains at most $D^k$ independent vectors. Explicitly, insert the independent vectors successively into the given spanning list: express the next one in the current spanning list, replace a listed vector with a nonzero coefficient outside the previously inserted independent vectors, and solve that expression for the replaced vector. The list still spans and has the same length. If there were no such outside coefficient, the new vector would lie in the span of the previously inserted ones, contradicting independence. Thus at most $D^k$ independent vectors can be inserted. This proves $t\le\dim V\le D^k$ using only finite linear algebra. If there were more than $D^k$ zeros, choosing a finite list of $D^k+1$ of them would contradict this inequality. This proves the zero-counting fact without a genericity or multiplicity assumption.

For an attained strict vector $\sigma$, put $S_\sigma=\{x:\operatorname{sgn}p_i(x)=\sigma_i\text{ for all }i\}$. This is open. Its closure has a maximum of $H$: choose a closed ball containing $a_\sigma$ outside which $H<0$, and apply [F2] to its nonempty closed bounded intersection with $\overline{S_\sigma}$. The resulting maximum is positive, because $H(a_\sigma)>0$, and it is also the maximum over the full closure. Any point in $\overline{S_\sigma}\setminus S_\sigma$ has $p_i=0$ for some $i$ by continuity, so there $H=-\delta\sum_i x_i^{D+1}\le0$. Therefore the positive maximum is attained at a point $b_\sigma\in S_\sigma$, which is an interior local maximum of $H$. Distinct strict vectors give distinct such points.

By [F3] every $b_\sigma$ is a common zero of the $k$ polynomials $\partial_i H=2P\partial_iP-\delta(D+1)x_i^D$. After division by the nonzero coefficient $-\delta(D+1)$, each has the form $x_i^D+s_i(x)$ with $\deg s_i\le2md-1<D$. The zero-counting fact therefore bounds their distinct common zeros, and hence the number of strict sign vectors, by $D^k=(2md+1)^k$.

For binary vectors with $>0$, choose one representative per attained vector. Choose $\varepsilon>0$ smaller than every nonzero $|p_i|$ occurring at these finitely many representatives; if there are no such values, choose any positive $\varepsilon$. The strict signs of $p_i-\varepsilon$ at the representatives now encode their original binary vectors: positive values remain positive, and nonpositive values become negative. Applying the strict bound to the $m$ shifted polynomials gives the binary bound. For $\ge0$, use $p_i+\varepsilon$: nonnegative values become positive, and negative values remain negative. For ternary vectors choose representatives and $\varepsilon$ in the same way, and use the $2m$ polynomials $p_i-\varepsilon,p_i+\varepsilon$. Their strict sign pairs are $(-,-)$, $(-,+)$, and $(+,+)$ for the original negative, zero, and positive values, respectively, so distinct ternary vectors give distinct strict vectors. The strict bound with $2m$ polynomials gives $(4md+1)^k$. Restriction of the domain only removes vectors.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
The space $L^p(\mu)$ as the quotient by null functions and
Complex Lp classes and Euclidean test-function conventions. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
The $L^p$ norm descends to the quotient and makes $L^p$ a normed space for $1 \le p \le \infty$
for real scalars and
Complex Holder, Minkowski, and the quotient norm for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
Weak derivative of a locally integrable function. Under
The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
Weak differentiation ignores null-set changes, while
Uniqueness of a weak derivative as an almost-everywhere class gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For every integer $m\ge0$ and every continuous map $h:S^m\to\mathbb R^m$, there exists $x\in S^m$ with $h(x)=h(-x)$. Here $S^m$ is the Euclidean unit sphere in $\mathbb R^{m+1}$.

derivations.claim: Define $p(t)=(4t(1-t))^{n+1}$ for $0\le t\le1$ and $p(t)=0$ otherwise, and put $\psi(x)=\prod_{r=1}^d p(x_r)$. The one-sided derivatives of $p$ of orders $0,\ldots,n$ vanish at each endpoint because the polynomial has a zero of multiplicity $n+1$ there. Hence the zero extension is $C^n(\mathbb R)$, and $\psi\in C^n(\mathbb R^d)$ is supported in $[0,1]^d$, is one at its center, and lies between zero and one. Set $$B=\max_{|\alpha|\le n}\|D^\alpha\psi\|_\infty\ge1.$$ This is finite since the derivatives are continuous polynomials on the compact cube and zero outside it. Their classical derivatives are weak derivatives: integrate by parts successively in each coordinate against a compactly supported smooth test function; endpoint terms vanish because the derivatives below order $n$ match their zero extensions. This also verifies the weak derivative identity after every scaling and finite sum used below.

Set $N=W+1$ and $k=\lceil N^{1/d}\rceil$. Partition $Q$ into $k^d$ closed coordinate cubes of side $1/k$, and take the first $N$ in lexicographic order. Write $v_j$ for their lower vertices and put $$\phi_j(x)=B^{-1}k^{-n}\psi(k(x-v_j)),\qquad j=1,\ldots,N.$$ Distinct supports have disjoint interiors; all derivatives of orders at most $n$ vanish on their boundaries. Thus, for $u=(u_1,\ldots,u_N)\in[-1,1]^N$, the sum $T(u)=\sum_j u_j\phi_j$ satisfies $\|D^\alpha T(u)\|_\infty\le B^{-1}k^{|\alpha|-n}\|D^\alpha\psi\|_\infty\le1$. The weak derivative verification in step 1.1 proves $T(u)\in F_{d,n}$. Disjoint interiors, and evaluation at the centers, give the exact identity $$\|T(u)\|_\infty=B^{-1}k^{-n}\max_j|u_j|.$$ In particular $T$ is linear, odd and continuous into $C(Q)$ with its uniform norm.

For $z\in S^{N-1}=S^W$, put $R(z)=z/\|z\|_\infty$. Its denominator is nonzero, and $R$ is continuous and odd with $\|R(z)\|_\infty=1$. Therefore $z\mapsto M(T(R(z)))$ is continuous into $\mathbb R^W$. By [F2], some antipodal pair has equal images. Setting $f=T(R(z))$, we obtain $M(f)=M(-f)$ and $\|f\|_\infty=B^{-1}k^{-n}$.

Let $q=\eta(M(f))=\eta(M(-f))$. The triangle inequality yields $$2B^{-1}k^{-n}=\|f-(-f)\|_\infty\le\|f-q\|_\infty+\|-f-q\|_\infty.$$ At least one of the two errors is at least $B^{-1}k^{-n}$. Because $k\le2N^{1/d}$, this is at least $c_{d,n}N^{-n/d}$ with $c_{d,n}=2^{-n}B^{-1}>0$. This proves the asserted supremum bound without any regularity of $\eta$.

If every error is at most $\varepsilon$, step 4.1 gives $W+1\ge(c_{d,n}/\varepsilon)^{d/n}$. Since $W\ge1$ implies $W+1\le2W$, we obtain $W\ge\tfrac12 c_{d,n}^{d/n}\varepsilon^{-d/n}$. The construction works at $W=1$, $d=1$, $n=1$, on cubes touching the boundary and when $N=k^d$, with exactly the same vanishing-derivative argument. AC is inherited from [F2] and subsumes the countable choice in [F1]; choosing finitely many indexed cubes or derivatives introduces no new choice principle.

citations.quote:
Fix integers $d,r\ge1$. A ReLU feedforward network with $d$ input coordinates and $r$ affine output units is a finite acyclic computation graph whose hidden units apply $\rho(z)=\max\{0,z\}$ to real affine combinations of input coordinates and earlier hidden-unit values, and whose output units apply real affine combinations of input coordinates and hidden-unit values. There are no edges into input vertices or out of output vertices. For each hidden unit $v$, define its canonical level by
$$\ell(v)=1+\max\bigl(\{\ell(u):u\text{ is a hidden unit with an edge }u\to v\}\cup\{0\}\bigr).$$
Thus units with no hidden-unit predecessor have level $1$, and edges between hidden units may skip levels. Let $H$ be the largest hidden-unit level, with $H=0$ when there are no hidden units. The network depth is $H+2$, counting an input layer and a final affine output layer; equivalently, it is two plus the maximum number of hidden units on a directed path in the hidden-unit graph. A network on $[0,1]^d$ means the restriction to that domain of the graph's globally defined formula on $\mathbb R^d$; an approximation domain restricts evaluation, not the formula. Its computation units are its hidden and output vertices; its connections are its directed weighted edges; its weights are all connection coefficients and unit biases. Units and connections are counted as vertices and edges, while weights are counted as scalar entries, with zero-valued entries counted only when the architecture explicitly includes them. A layered fully connected ReLU network with $L$ hidden layers is the specialization in which every edge joins consecutive layers and every such edge is present; its depth is $L+2$.

Let $k,m,d\ge1$ be integers and let $p_1,\ldots,p_m$ be real polynomials in $k$ variables, each of total degree at most $d$ (including the zero polynomial). The number of strict sign vectors $(\operatorname{sgn}p_1(x),\ldots,\operatorname{sgn}p_m(x))\in\{-1,1\}^m$ attained at points where all polynomials are nonzero is at most $(2md+1)^k$. The number of binary vectors $(\mathbf1_{p_i(x)>0})_{i=1}^m$ is also at most $(2md+1)^k$, and the same bound holds with $\ge0$ in place of $>0$. The number of ternary sign vectors in $\{-1,0,1\}^m$ is at most $(4md+1)^k$. Each assertion remains valid when $x$ is restricted to any subset of $\mathbb R^k$.

Let $\mathcal C\subseteq\mathcal P(X)$ be a family of subsets of an arbitrary set $X$. For a finite $T\subseteq X$, its trace is

$$\mathcal C|_T:=\{C\cap T:C\in\mathcal C\}.$$

The family $\mathcal C$ **shatters** $T$ when $\mathcal C|_T=\mathcal P(T)$. This extends the finite-ground-set trace convention of Shattering and the Vapnik–Chervonenkis dimension of a set family: any finite $T$ can be relabeled by $[|T|]$, and relabeling preserves all traces and their cardinalities.

For a nonempty class, its **VC dimension** $d(\mathcal C)$ is the greatest size of a finite shattered set if those sizes are bounded, is $0$ if no singleton is shattered, and is $+\infty$ if finite shattered sets have unbounded size. When the dimension is finite, its **VC index** is

$$V(\mathcal C):=d(\mathcal C)+1,$$

equivalently the least positive integer $V$ such that no $V$-point subset is shattered. The empty class is assigned $V=0$ by convention and is treated separately in the entropy theorem.

derivations.claim: Remove all hidden units that have no path to the output. Also remove all hidden units having no input ancestor: for each fixed parameter assignment their values are constants in $x$, and their contributions to a remaining unit or the output can be added to its existing bias. Allowing these new biases to vary independently produces a fixed reduced architecture whose realization class contains the original class. No new coefficient slots are needed, because every surviving computation unit already has a bias; edges and removed units only disappear. If the output has no input ancestor, the original class consists of constant functions and has VC dimension at most $1$, which satisfies the conclusions. Otherwise the reduced graph has $w\le W$ counted slots, $U$ hidden units, and $U+1\le w$ because the output and every hidden unit have counted biases. Every remaining unit lies on an input-to-output path. Rank each hidden unit by the maximum number of computation units on an input-to-that-unit path, and give the output its analogous rank $K$. Then each edge increases rank, and $K\le L-1$ and $K\le U+1\le w$. Empty ranks can be omitted. It suffices to bound the reduced class.

Fix arbitrary sample points $x_1,\ldots,x_m$. For any prescribed binary mask $b\in\{0,1\}^U$, replace the ReLU at hidden unit $v$ by multiplication of its preactivation by $b_v$. Its preactivation and the final output are now polynomials in the $w$ parameters. By induction along the graph, a unit of rank $j$ has polynomial degree at most $j$: input values have degree zero, multiplication by an edge coefficient raises degree by one, addition of a bias has degree one, and multiplication by a fixed mask entry changes no degree. Thus every such polynomial has degree at most $K\le w$. On any actual parameter vector the convention $b_v=\mathbf1_{z_v>0}$ gives a unique mask, even when a preactivation is zero, and the masked polynomials then reproduce every actual unit value.

For each sample point and each of the $2^U$ masks, form the $U$ preactivation polynomials and the output polynomial minus $a$. There are $M=m(U+1)2^U$ polynomials, all of degree at most $w$. Their strict-positivity vector determines the actual output classification at every sample point: evaluate units in topological order, determining their actual mask by the relevant preactivation entry, then read the output entry for that mask. Hence the number of label vectors is at most $(2Mw+1)^w\le(3mw^2 2^w)^w$ by [F2]. If the classifier uses $\ge a$, take the hidden-unit mask $\mathbf1_{z_v\ge0}$ and use nonnegativity vectors throughout; at zero, multiplying by either mask value still gives the ReLU value, so the same count holds.

For a second count, start with the single parameter-space cell $\mathbb R^w$. At stage $j$, refine every existing cell by the activation bits of all units of rank $j$ at all $m$ sample points; at the final stage refine by the output threshold bits. Within a cell, all earlier mask bits are fixed, so the relevant $mN_j$ preactivation polynomials, or output-minus-threshold polynomials, have degree at most $j\le K$ by step 2.1, where $N_j$ is the number of units at that rank, with $N_K=1$ for the output. By [F2] there are at most $(2mN_jK+1)^w\le(3mwK)^w$ refinements of each cell. This estimate holds on an arbitrary cell; no connectedness or openness is needed. After $K$ stages, the number of cells, hence the number of output label vectors, is at most $(3mwK)^{wK}$. The construction using $\ge0$ activation bits and nonnegativity output bits proves the identical bound for the other threshold convention.

Put $m_0=64w^2$. At this sample size the base-two logarithm of the last bound is $w(\log_2 3+\log_2m_0+2\log_2w+w)=w(w+\log_2 3+6+4\log_2w)\le13w^2<m_0$, using $\log_2w\le w$ for integers $w\ge1$. Thus no $m_0$-point set can be shattered, and [F3] rules out all larger shattered sets. Consequently $\operatorname{VC}(\mathcal H_a)<64w^2\le64W^2$.

Write $A=wK$ and $B=\log_2(2w)\ge1$, and take the integer $m_1=\lceil64AB\rceil\le65AB$. Since $K\le w$, one has $\log_2 A\le2\log_2w$ and $\log_2B\le B$. The base-two logarithm of the label-count bound at $m=m_1$ is at most $A\log_2(195A^2B)\le A(8+4\log_2w+\log_2B)\le A(4+5B)\le9AB< m_1$. No set of $m_1$ points is shattered. Therefore $\operatorname{VC}(\mathcal H_a)<m_1\le65wK\log_2(2w)\le65WL\log_2(2W)$. Conversion between logarithm bases changes only an absolute constant. For $W\ge2$, $\log(2W)\le2\log W$ and $L\ge1$, so this implies the requested $CL^2W\log W$ estimate. Together with step 4.1 and the constant-output case, this proves every assertion.

citations.quote: Let $\rho(z)=\max\{0,z\}$ and define $\tau(x)=2\rho(x)-4\rho(x-1/2)$ for $x\in[0,1]$. Let $G$ be a group with identity $e$ and let $X$ be a set. A **left action** of
$G$ on $X$ is a function $G\times X\to X$, written $(g,x)\mapsto g\cdot x$,
such that

$$e\cdot x=x,\qquad (gh)\cdot x=g\cdot(h\cdot x)$$

for all $g,h\in G$ and $x\in X$. Then $X$ is a **$G$-set**. The action is
**transitive** when every $x,y\in X$ satisfy $g\cdot x=y$ for some $g\in G$.
It is **faithful** when $g\cdot x=x$ for every $x\in X$ implies $g=e$.

A **group** is a monoid $(G,*,e)$ (Semigroup and monoid) in which every
element is invertible (Left inverse, right inverse, and invertible element of a monoid). Written out, a group is a set
$G$ with a binary operation $*$ (Binary operation on a set; associativity, commutativity, and a subset closed under the operation) and an element
$e \in G$ such that

- **(G1)** $(x * y) * z = x * (y * z)$ for all $x, y, z \in G$;
- **(G2)** $e * x = x = x * e$ for every $x \in G$;
- **(G3)** for every $x \in G$ there is $y \in G$ with $y * x = e = x * y$.

By A left identity and a right identity for the same binary operation are equal; hence there is at most one two-sided identity the element $e$ of (G2) is unique, and by
In a monoid, a left inverse and a right inverse of the same element are equal; hence an invertible element has exactly one inverse, and it is two-sided the element $y$ of (G3) is unique for each $x$ and is
determined by either one of the two equations alone. So the notations $e$ for the
identity and $x^{-1}$ for the inverse of $x$ are legitimate, and asserting
$y * x = e$ alone already says $y = x^{-1}$.

A group is **abelian**, or **commutative**, when its operation is commutative:
$x * y = y * x$ for all $x, y \in G$.

**Notation.** The operation is usually written multiplicatively, $xy$ for
$x * y$, with identity $e$ (or $1$) and inverse $x^{-1}$. For an abelian group it
is often written additively, $x + y$, with identity $0$ and inverse $-x$; the two
notations describe the same notion and nothing below depends on the choice. We
write $G$ for the group when the operation is understood.

The rotation matrices are $I,\rho,-I,-\rho$, hence distinct; their products add exponents modulo $4$, and $(\rho^j)^{-1}=\rho^{-j}$. The four matrices $\sigma,\rho\sigma,-\sigma,-\rho\sigma$ are distinct, have determinant $-1$, and differ from the rotations, which have determinant $1$. Writing elements of $D_4$ as $\rho^j\sigma^\epsilon$ with $\epsilon\in\{0,1\}$, the relation $\sigma\rho^j=\rho^{-j}\sigma$ shows products stay in $D_4$, and $(\rho^j\sigma^\epsilon)^{-1}=\rho^{-(-1)^\epsilon j}\sigma^\epsilon$ also lies in $D_4$. For either matrix group $A$, the pair multiplication is closed on $\mathbb Z^2\times A$. It is associative because both parenthesizations of three factors $(t,M),(s,N),(r,Q)$ equal $(t+Ms+MN r,MNQ)$. Its identity is $(0,I)$. For every pair $(t,M)$, the pair $(-M^{-1}t,M^{-1})$ belongs to the same set by 1.1, and $(t,M)(-M^{-1}t,M^{-1})=(0,I)=(-M^{-1}t,M^{-1})(t,M)$. Let $G$ be a group (Group and abelian group) with identity $e$. A subset $H \subseteq G$ is
a **subgroup** of $G$, written $H \le G$, when

- **(S1)** $e \in H$;
- **(S2)** $H$ is closed under the operation: $x, y \in H$ implies $xy \in H$
  (Binary operation on a set; associativity, commutativity, and a subset closed under the operation);
- **(S3)** $H$ is closed under inverses: $x \in H$ implies $x^{-1} \in H$.

By (S2) the operation of $G$ restricts to a binary operation on $H$; it is
associative there because it is associative on $G$, the element $e$ of (S1) is a
two-sided identity for it (Left identity, right identity, and two-sided identity for a binary operation), and (S3) supplies for each
$x \in H$ a two-sided inverse lying in $H$ (Left inverse, right inverse, and invertible element of a monoid). So a
subgroup, with the restricted operation, is itself a group, and its identity and
its inverses are those of $G$.

Every group $G$ has the two **trivial subgroups** $\{e\}$ and $G$ itself; a
subgroup $H$ with $H \ne G$ is called **proper**.

Let $G$ be a group and let $H\le G$ be a subgroup (Group and abelian group,
Subgroup). For $g\in G$, the **left coset** and **right coset** of $H$
represented by $g$ are

$$gH:=\{gh:h\in H\},\qquad Hg:=\{hg:h\in H\}.$$

The element $g$ is a **representative** of these cosets. The notation denotes
subsets of $G$; it does not assert that either subset is a subgroup.

Let $G$ be a group with identity $e$ and let $X$ be a set. A **left action** of
$G$ on $X$ is a function $G\times X\to X$, written $(g,x)\mapsto g\cdot x$,
such that

$$e\cdot x=x,\qquad (gh)\cdot x=g\cdot(h\cdot x)$$

for all $g,h\in G$ and $x\in X$. Then $X$ is a **$G$-set**. The action is
**transitive** when every $x,y\in X$ satisfy $g\cdot x=y$ for some $g\in G$.
It is **faithful** when $g\cdot x=x$ for every $x\in X$ implies $g=e$.

Let $G$ be a group with identity $e$ and let $X$ be a set. A **left action** of
$G$ on $X$ is a function $G\times X\to X$, written $(g,x)\mapsto g\cdot x$,
such that

$$e\cdot x=x,\qquad (gh)\cdot x=g\cdot(h\cdot x)$$

for all $g,h\in G$ and $x\in X$. Then $X$ is a **$G$-set**. The action is
**transitive** when every $x,y\in X$ satisfy $g\cdot x=y$ for some $g\in G$.
It is **faithful** when $g\cdot x=x$ for every $x\in X$ implies $g=e$.

A **group** is a monoid $(G,*,e)$ (Semigroup and monoid) in which every
element is invertible (Left inverse, right inverse, and invertible element of a monoid). Written out, a group is a set
$G$ with a binary operation $*$ (Binary operation on a set; associativity, commutativity, and a subset closed under the operation) and an element
$e \in G$ such that

- **(G1)** $(x * y) * z = x * (y * z)$ for all $x, y, z \in G$;
- **(G2)** $e * x = x = x * e$ for every $x \in G$;
- **(G3)** for every $x \in G$ there is $y \in G$ with $y * x = e = x * y$.

By A left identity and a right identity for the same binary operation are equal; hence there is at most one two-sided identity the element $e$ of (G2) is unique, and by
In a monoid, a left inverse and a right inverse of the same element are equal; hence an invertible element has exactly one inverse, and it is two-sided the element $y$ of (G3) is unique for each $x$ and is
determined by either one of the two equations alone. So the notations $e$ for the
identity and $x^{-1}$ for the inverse of $x$ are legitimate, and asserting
$y * x = e$ alone already says $y = x^{-1}$.

A group is **abelian**, or **commutative**, when its operation is commutative:
$x * y = y * x$ for all $x, y \in G$.

**Notation.** The operation is usually written multiplicatively, $xy$ for
$x * y$, with identity $e$ (or $1$) and inverse $x^{-1}$. For an abelian group it
is often written additively, $x + y$, with identity $0$ and inverse $-x$; the two
notations describe the same notion and nothing below depends on the choice. We
write $G$ for the group when the operation is understood.

Let $G$ be a group acting on the left on a set $S$, and let $V$ be a set of feature values. A feature map is a function $f:S\to V$. For $u\in G$, the induced transformation of feature maps is

$$
(L_u f)(x)=f(u^{-1}\cdot x)\qquad(x\in S).
$$

It is a left action on the set of feature maps: the group acts by reindexing sites and leaves the feature values unchanged. In particular, for maps $F:G\to V$ on the group itself with its left multiplication action, $(L_uF)(g)=F(u^{-1}g)$.

Let $G$ be a discrete group acting on the lattice $\mathbb Z^2$ on the left. Let $C_{\rm in},C_{\rm out}$ be positive integers, and regard channel vectors as row vectors. For a feature map $f:G\to\mathbb R^{C_{\rm in}}$ and a filter $\Psi:G\to\mathbb R^{C_{\rm in}\times C_{\rm out}}$, the group-to-group cross-correlation is the map $C_\Psi f:G\to\mathbb R^{C_{\rm out}}$ defined by

$$
(C_\Psi f)(g)=\sum_{h\in G} f(h)\Psi(g^{-1}h).
$$

For an image feature map $f:\mathbb Z^2\to\mathbb R^{C_{\rm in}}$ and a lattice filter $\Psi:\mathbb Z^2\to\mathbb R^{C_{\rm in}\times C_{\rm out}}$, the first-layer image-to-group cross-correlation is the map $E_\Psi f:G\to\mathbb R^{C_{\rm out}}$ defined by

$$
(E_\Psi f)(g)=\sum_{x\in\mathbb Z^2} f(x)\Psi(g^{-1}\cdot x).
$$

Each displayed sum is required to have finite support or to converge absolutely in every output coordinate. The first operation takes group-indexed features and filters; the second takes lattice-indexed image features and filters and returns group-indexed features. These are cross-correlations, with the filter argument displayed as written; they need not be commutative, and no finiteness of $G$ is assumed.

u:\mathbb R	o\mathbb R$ is $N_

The left-coset set is $G/H=\{gH:g\in G\}$, where $gH=\{gh:h\in H\}$. Its left $G$-action is $a\cdot(gH)=(ag)H$. Let a group $G$ act on sets $X$ and $Y$ by left actions $T$ and $T'$, respectively. A layer is a function $\Phi:X\to Y$. It is $G$-equivariant when

$$
\Phi(T_gx)=T'_g\Phi(x)\qquad(g\in G,\ x\in X).
$$

The input and output actions need not be the same. The layer is $G$-invariant when $\Phi(T_gx)=\Phi(x)$ for every $g\in G$ and $x\in X$; equivalently, it is equivariant into $Y$ equipped with the trivial action.

Let $D,O\subseteq\mathbb Z^2$ be input and output index sets, let $C_{\rm in},C_{\rm out}$ be positive integers, and let $x:D\to\mathbb R^{C_{\rm in}}$ assign a row vector of input channels to each input site. A boundary extension is a function $\widetilde x:\mathbb Z^2\to\mathbb R^{C_{\rm in}}$ whose restriction to $D$ is $x$; zero padding is the extension that is zero off $D$. Choose a finite receptive-field offset set $K\subseteq\mathbb Z^2$, a positive integer stride vector $s\in\mathbb Z_{>0}^2$, an origin $a\in\mathbb Z^2$, one matrix $W_\delta\in\mathbb R^{C_{\rm in}\times C_{\rm out}}$ for each $\delta\in K$, and an output bias row vector $b\in\mathbb R^{C_{\rm out}}$. The discrete convolutional layer is the map $y:O\to\mathbb R^{C_{\rm out}}$ given by

$$
y(p)=b+\sum_{\delta\in K}\widetilde x(a+s\odot p+\delta)W_\delta\qquad(p\in O),
$$

where $s\odot p$ is coordinatewise multiplication. Thus each output uses only the input sites in its receptive field, mixes input channels by matrix multiplication, and uses the same weights and bias at every output site. With unit stride on the full lattice and no boundary truncation, this formula is a discrete cross-correlation; many machine-learning software packages call it convolution. Mathematical convolution instead reverses the kernel offsets. The choices of $O$, the extension $\widetilde x$, and the stride specify cropping, padding, and subsampling, and need not preserve a symmetry of the full lattice.

Let $\rho=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ be the quarter-turn matrix and $\sigma=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$ a reflection matrix. Let $C_4=\{\rho^j:j=0,1,2,3\}$ and $D_4=\{\rho^j,\rho^j\sigma:j=0,1,2,3\}$, with matrix multiplication. For $A=C_4$ or $D_4$, define $P_A=\mathbb Z^2\times A$ with multiplication

$$
(t,M)(s,N)=(t+Ms,MN).
$$

Each pair $(t,M)$ acts on lattice sites by $x\mapsto Mx+t$. The p4 lattice-symmetry group is $P_{C_4}$, generated by integer translations and quarter-turns. The p4m lattice-symmetry group is $P_{D_4}$, generated by integer translations, quarter-turns, and reflections. The point groups $C_4$ and $D_4$ have four and eight elements, respectively, but both full groups are infinite because they contain every integer translation.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be $G$-sets (Left group actions, transitive actions, and faithful actions). A function
$f:X\to Y$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain) is **$G$-equivariant** when

$$f(g\cdot x)=g\cdot f(x)$$

for every $g\in G$ and $x\in X$. An **isomorphism of $G$-sets** is an
equivariant bijection (Injection, surjection, bijection). Two actions are
**equivariantly isomorphic** when such a bijection exists between their
$G$-sets.

Let $G$ be a group (Group and abelian group) with identity $e$. A subset $H \subseteq G$ is
a **subgroup** of $G$, written $H \le G$, when

- **(S1)** $e \in H$;
- **(S2)** $H$ is closed under the operation: $x, y \in H$ implies $xy \in H$
  (Binary operation on a set; associativity, commutativity, and a subset closed under the operation);
- **(S3)** $H$ is closed under inverses: $x \in H$ implies $x^{-1} \in H$.

By (S2) the operation of $G$ restricts to a binary operation on $H$; it is
associative there because it is associative on $G$, the element $e$ of (S1) is a
two-sided identity for it (Left identity, right identity, and two-sided identity for a binary operation), and (S3) supplies for each
$x \in H$ a two-sided inverse lying in $H$ (Left inverse, right inverse, and invertible element of a monoid). So a
subgroup, with the restricted operation, is itself a group, and its identity and
its inverses are those of $G$.

Every group $G$ has the two **trivial subgroups** $\{e\}$ and $G$ itself; a
subgroup $H$ with $H \ne G$ is called **proper**.

Let $G$ be a group and let $H\le G$ be a subgroup (Group and abelian group,
Subgroup). For $g\in G$, the **left coset** and **right coset** of $H$
represented by $g$ are

$$gH:=\{gh:h\in H\},\qquad Hg:=\{hg:h\in H\}.$$

The element $g$ is a **representative** of these cosets. The notation denotes
subsets of $G$; it does not assert that either subset is a subgroup.

Choose a finite receptive-field offset set $K\subseteq\mathbb Z^2$, a positive integer stride vector $s\in\mathbb Z_{>0}^2$, an origin $a\in\mathbb Z^2$, one matrix $W_\delta\in\mathbb R^{C_{\rm in}\times C_{\rm out}}$ for each $\delta\in K$, and an output bias row vector $b\in\mathbb R^{C_{\rm out}}$. The discrete convolutional layer is the map $y:O\to\mathbb R^{C_{\rm out}}$ given by

$$
y(p)=b+\sum_{\delta\in K}\widetilde x(a+s\odot p+\delta)W_\delta\qquad(p\in O),
$$

where $s\odot p$ is coordinatewise multiplication. Thus each output uses only the input sites in its receptive field, mixes input channels by matrix multiplication, and uses the same weights and bias at every output site. With unit stride on the full lattice and no boundary truncation, this formula is a discrete cross-correlation; many machine-learning software packages call it convolution. Mathematical convolution instead reverses the kernel offsets. The choices of $O$, the extension $\widetilde x$, and the stride specify cropping, padding, and subsampling, and need not preserve a symmetry of the full lattice.

Let $G$ be a discrete group acting on the lattice $\mathbb Z^2$ on the left. Let $C_{\rm in},C_{\rm out}$ be positive integers, and regard channel vectors as row vectors. For a feature map $f:G\to\mathbb R^{C_{\rm in}}$ and a filter $\Psi:G\to\mathbb R^{C_{\rm in}\times C_{\rm out}}$, the group-to-group cross-correlation is the map $C_\Psi f:G\to\mathbb R^{C_{\rm out}}$ defined by

$$
(C_\Psi f)(g)=\sum_{h\in G} f(h)\Psi(g^{-1}h).
$$

For an image feature map $f:\mathbb Z^2\to\mathbb R^{C_{\rm in}}$ and a lattice filter $\Psi:\mathbb Z^2\to\mathbb R^{C_{\rm in}\times C_{\rm out}}$, the first-layer image-to-group cross-correlation is the map $E_\Psi f:G\to\mathbb R^{C_{\rm out}}$ defined by

$$
(E_\Psi f)(g)=\sum_{x\in\mathbb Z^2} f(x)\Psi(g^{-1}\cdot x).
$$

Each displayed sum is required to have finite support or to converge absolutely in every output coordinate. The first operation takes group-indexed features and filters; the second takes lattice-indexed image features and filters and returns group-indexed features. Let $G$ be a discrete group acting on the left on the square lattice $\mathbb Z^2$, and let feature maps take values in finite-dimensional row-vector channel spaces. Let $G$ be a group (Group and abelian group) with identity $e$. A subset $H \subseteq G$ is
a **subgroup** of $G$, written $H \le G$, when

- **(S1)** $e \in H$;
- **(S2)** $H$ is closed under the operation: $x, y \in H$ implies $xy \in H$
  (Binary operation on a set; associativity, commutativity, and a subset closed under the operation);
- **(S3)** $H$ is closed under inverses: $x \in H$ implies $x^{-1} \in H$.

By (S2) the operation of $G$ restricts to a binary operation on $H$; it is
associative there because it is associative on $G$, the element $e$ of (S1) is a
two-sided identity for it (Left identity, right identity, and two-sided identity for a binary operation), and (S3) supplies for each
$x \in H$ a two-sided inverse lying in $H$ (Left inverse, right inverse, and invertible element of a monoid). So a
subgroup, with the restricted operation, is itself a group, and its identity and
its inverses are those of $G$.

Every group $G$ has the two **trivial subgroups** $\{e\}$ and $G$ itself; a
subgroup $H$ with $H \ne G$ is called **proper**.

citations.quote: Let $G=(V,E,\ell)$ and $H=(W,F,m)$ be finite vertex-labeled simple undirected graphs with labels in the same set $\Sigma$. A label-preserving graph isomorphism from $G$ to $H$ is a bijection $\varphi:V\to W$ such that $\ell(v)=m(\varphi(v))$ for every $v\in V$, and for all distinct $u,v\in V$, $\{u,v\}\in E$ if and only if $\{\varphi(u),\varphi(v)\}\in F$. The graphs are isomorphic when such a bijection exists, and nonisomorphic otherwise.

Let $G=(V,E,\ell)$ and $H=(W,F,m)$ be finite vertex-labeled simple undirected graphs with labels in a common set $\Sigma$. Define color sets recursively by $C_0=\Sigma$ and $C_{t+1}=C_t\times\mathsf M_{\mathrm{fin}}(C_t)$ for each integer $t\ge0$. Set $c_0^G(v)=\ell(v)$ and $c_0^H(w)=m(w)$; for $t\ge0$, update

$$ c_{t+1}^G(v)=\left(c_t^G(v),\{\!\{c_t^G(u):u\in N_G(v)\}\!\}\right),\qquad c_{t+1}^H(w)=\left(c_t^H(w),\{\!\{c_t^H(z):z\in N_H(w)\}\!\}\right). $$

The graph color multiset at round $t$ is $C_t(G)=\{\!\{c_t^G(v):v\in V\}\!\}$, and likewise for $H$. One-dimensional Weisfeiler–Leman color refinement distinguishes $G$ and $H$ at round $t$ when $C_t(G)\ne C_t(H)$; it distinguishes the pair when this holds for some finite $t$. If no finite round distinguishes them, they are one-WL-indistinguishable. In the unlabeled case, take $\Sigma$ to be a singleton. The tuple update is the canonical collision-free color encoding.

Let $X$ be a set. A finite multiset on $X$ is a function $m:X\to\mathbb N_0$ with finite support $\operatorname{supp}(m)=\{x\in X:m(x)>0\}$. The multiplicity $m(x)$ is the number of occurrences of $x$, and the size is $|m|=\sum_{x\in\operatorname{supp}(m)}m(x)$. Two finite multisets are equal exactly when their multiplicity functions agree at every element of $X$. We write $\{\!\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}\!\}$ for the multiset whose multiplicity at $x$ is the number of indices $i$ with $x_i=x$; $n=0$ denotes the empty multiset.

derivations.claim: By induction on $t$, $c_t^G(v)=c_t^H(\varphi(v))$ for every $v\in V(G)$. At $t=0$ this is label preservation from [F1]. If it holds at $t$, bijectivity and adjacency preservation in [F1] give a bijection $N_G(v)\to N_H(\varphi(v))$, and corresponding neighbors have equal round-$t$ colors by the induction hypothesis. Thus the neighbor-color multisets agree; the center colors agree as well, so the ordered-pair update [F2] gives equality at round $t+1$.

The same vertex bijection therefore sends every occurrence of each round-$t$ color in $G$ to an occurrence of that color in $H$, and its inverse gives the reverse correspondence. Hence the two graph color multisets have equal multiplicities for each color by [F3]. Their round-$t$ histograms agree for every finite $t$, so no round distinguishes them.
