Fix a finite vertex-labeled simple undirected graph $G=(V,E,\ell)$, a finite nonnegative depth $K$, feature sets $H_0,\ldots,H_K$, and an initial map $\eta:\Sigma\to H_0$. For each $k=1,\ldots,K$, choose a set $Z_k$, an aggregation function $A_k:\mathsf M_{\mathrm{fin}}(H_{k-1})\to Z_k$ on finite multisets, and an update function $U_k:H_{k-1}\times Z_k\to H_k$. Initialize $h_v^0=\eta(\ell(v))$ and recursively set

$$
a_v^k=A_k\!\left(\{\!\{h_u^{k-1}:u\in N_G(v)\}\!\}\right),\qquad h_v^k=U_k(h_v^{k-1},a_v^k).
$$

For a chosen output set $Y$, a graph readout is a function $R:\mathsf M_{\mathrm{fin}}(H_K)\to Y$; the graph output is $z_G=R(\{\!\{h_v^K:v\in V\}\!\})$. The same maps are used on every graph being compared. The model has no vertex-identity input and uses no graph-wide information before the readout. It distinguishes two graphs when their outputs differ.

derivations.claim: By induction on $t=0,\ldots,K$, equal round-$t$ WL colors of vertices from either graph imply equal GNN states after $t$ layers. At $t=0$, the shared initial embedding gives this implication. If it holds at $t$ and two vertices have equal round-$(t+1)$ colors, [F2] says their center colors and neighbor-color multisets agree. By the induction hypothesis, equal neighbor colors have equal GNN states; applying this correspondence occurrence by occurrence gives equal neighbor-state multisets. The shared aggregation and update functions in [F1] therefore give equal next-layer states. Thus a well-defined map from each round-$t$ color occurring in either graph to its common GNN state exists.

At round $K$, the assumed equal WL color multisets become equal multisets of GNN states when each color is sent to its common state from step 1.1; multiplicities are preserved by [F3]. The shared graph readout in [F4] receives equal multisets, so the two graph outputs are equal. The contrapositive gives the stated distinguishing implication.

Let $\mathcal X$ be a countable set and let $M\in\mathbb N_0$. There is a map $\phi:\mathcal X\to\mathbb N_{>0}\subset\mathbb Q$ such that the sum $S\mapsto\sum_{x\in S}\phi(x)$ is injective on finite multisets $S$ of total multiplicity at most $M$. For every irrational $\varepsilon\in\mathbb R\setminus\mathbb Q$, the map

$$
(c,S)\longmapsto(1+\varepsilon)\phi(c)+\sum_{x\in S}\phi(x)
$$

is injective on pairs with $c\in\mathcal X$ and $S$ a finite multiset of total multiplicity at most $M$. For $M=0$, the only allowed neighbor multiset is empty.

Fix a finite depth $K\in\mathbb N_0$, positive integer dimensions $d_0,\ldots,d_K$, an initial embedding $\eta:\Sigma\to\mathbb R^{d_0}$, scalars $\varepsilon_1,\ldots,\varepsilon_K\in\mathbb R$, and maps $M_k:\mathbb R^{d_{k-1}}\to\mathbb R^{d_k}$ for $1\le k\le K$. Each $M_k$ is a multilayer perceptron, meaning a finite composition of affine maps between finite-dimensional real vector spaces and coordinatewise applications of a fixed scalar activation. On a finite vertex-labeled simple undirected graph $G$, initialize $h_v^0=\eta(\ell(v))$ and update

$$
h_v^k=M_k\!\left((1+\varepsilon_k)h_v^{k-1}+\sum_{u\in N_G(v)}h_u^{k-1}\right)\qquad(1\le k\le K).
$$

For a chosen output set $Y$, the graph readout is a map $R:\mathsf M_{\mathrm{fin}}(\mathbb R^{d_K})\to Y$ on the multiset of final vertex features. The neighbor sum counts each neighbor vertex once, so equal feature vectors at different neighbors contribute with their multiplicity. This definition imposes no injectivity condition on the perceptrons or the readout and makes no claim that a fixed finite architecture realizes an arbitrary injection.

derivations.claim: For each $k\le K$, we prove that there is an injective map $\psi_k$ from the WL colors occurring at round $k$ in either graph to their GNN states. For $k=0$, use the initial embedding and [A1]. If this holds at $k-1$, a round-$k$ WL color has the form $(c,S)$ by [F1]. The injective map $\psi_{k-1}$ sends different center colors to different center states and, occurrence by occurrence, different neighbor-color multisets to different neighbor-state multisets. By [A2], their aggregates and then their updated states remain different whenever $(c,S)$ differs. Equal WL colors give equal states because the layer maps are shared functions. Thus the resulting round-$k$ state map $\psi_k$ is well-defined and injective.

The WL histograms at round $K$ differ by hypothesis. Applying the injective map $\psi_K$ to each color occurrence preserves multiplicities and keeps these two multisets different. The final node-state multisets therefore differ, and [A3] makes their graph readouts different by [F5].

If the active feature set is countable and neighbor multisets have size at most $\Delta$, apply [F3] with $M=\Delta$ to obtain the stated center/multiset preactivation code for any irrational $\varepsilon$. If each graph has at most $N$ vertices, apply the multiset part of [F3] with $M=N$ to obtain an injective sum code for final node-state multisets. Formula [F4] identifies the first code with the GIN preactivation when the current features use $\phi$; the injectivity of any post-MLP or readout realizing the full theorem remains the separate hypothesis [A2]–[A3].

The radix-two procedure returns this vector by the following exact recursion. If $M=1$, return $(a_0)$. derivations.claim: Put $w_n=\sqrt{2n+1}$ and define the real skew-symmetric matrix $S$ by $S_{nk}=-w_nw_k/2$ for $n>k$, $S_{nk}=w_nw_k/2$ for $n<k$, and $S_{nn}=0$. The transpose is $-S$, so over $\mathbb C$ its conjugate transpose is also $-S$; hence $S$ is normal. With $v=w/\sqrt2$, entrywise comparison gives $G^S=(S-\tfrac12I)-vv^*$: below the diagonal the entries are $-w_nw_k$, above they cancel to zero, and on the diagonal they are $-\tfrac12-(2n+1)/2=-(n+1)$. Since a scalar shift of a normal matrix is normal and $vv^*$ has rank at most one, this is the required LegS decomposition. This assertion concerns the finite coefficient matrix only; the factor $1/t$ in the LegS ODE remains time-dependent.

Define $S$ with entries $-1/2$ below the diagonal, $+1/2$ above it, and zero on the diagonal. It is real skew-symmetric and therefore normal. For $e=(1,\ldots,1)^T$, entrywise comparison gives $G^L=(S-\tfrac12I)-\tfrac12ee^*$: below the diagonal the two terms sum to $-1$, above they sum to zero, and on the diagonal they sum to $-1$. Thus the original LagT generator is a normal matrix minus a rank-at-most-one matrix.

For LegT let $D=\operatorname{diag}(2n+1)_{n=0}^{N-1}$ and $E=\operatorname{diag}((-1)^n)_{n=0}^{N-1}$. Define $T_{nk}=1$ for $n\ge k$, and $T_{nk}=(-1)^{k-n}$ for $n<k$. Then direct entry evaluation gives $G^T=-DETE/\theta$: for $n\ge k$, $(-1)^n(-1)^k=(-1)^{n-k}$, while for $n<k$, $(-1)^n(-1)^{k-n}(-1)^k=1$. Write $T=S+R$, where $R_{nk}=1$ when $n$ and $k$ have the same parity and is zero otherwise. The matrix $R$ is the sum of the outer products of the even-index and odd-index indicator vectors, so its rank is at most two. For opposite parities, $S_{nk}=1$ below the diagonal and $S_{nk}=-1$ above it; for equal parities and on the diagonal, $S_{nk}=0$. Thus $S^T=-S$. The invertible diagonal matrix $S_0=D^{1/2}E$ gives $S_0^{-1}G^TS_0=-\theta^{-1}D^{1/2}SD^{1/2}-\theta^{-1}D^{1/2}RD^{1/2}$. The first term is real skew-symmetric and hence normal; the second has rank at most two. The diagonal similarity is essential: this proves the claim for an equivalent state-space matrix, not unitary similarity of the raw LegT matrix.

In each case write the resulting generator as $H-UV^*$ with $H$ normal: for LegS and LagT the factors are the displayed real vectors divided by $\sqrt2$, and for LegT use the even and odd indicator columns multiplied by $D^{1/2}/\sqrt\theta$ as both factors. By [F2], choose a unitary matrix $V_0$ with $V_0^*HV_0=\Lambda$ diagonal. Then $V_0^*(H-UV^*)V_0=\Lambda-(V_0^*U)(V_0^*V)^*$, preserving the low-rank bound. If the original coordinates were changed by $S_0$, the total state change is $x=S_0V_0z$; substitution into $x'=Gx+Bu$, $y=C^*x$ gives $z'=(V_0^*S_0^{-1}GS_0V_0)z+V_0^*S_0^{-1}Bu$ and output vector $V_0^*S_0^*C$. These are exactly the state-coordinate transformations required for an equivalent DPLR model.

Input an integer $M=2^q$ with $q\ge0$, a primitive $M$th root of unity $\omega$, a finite list of poles $\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_n\in\mathbb C$, and weights $a_1,\ldots,a_n\in\mathbb C$. The required output is $y_k=\sum_{j=1}^n a_j/(\omega^k-\mu_j)$ for $0\le k<M$, provided no denominator is zero. If $n=0$, return the zero vector.

Here a primitive $M$th root means $\omega^M=1$ and $\omega^k\ne1$ for $1\le k<M$. For $n\ge1$, form a balanced binary tree on the pole indices, splitting each consecutive index interval into two intervals whose sizes differ by at most one. At a leaf containing index $j$, store polynomials $D_j(z)=z-\mu_j$ and $P_j(z)=a_j$. At an internal node with disjoint child index sets $I_1,I_2$, store
$$ D_I(z)=D_{I_1}(z)D_{I_2}(z),\qquad P_I(z)=P_{I_1}(z)D_{I_2}(z)+D_{I_1}(z)P_{I_2}(z). $$
At the root, fold the coefficients of each polynomial modulo $z^M-1$: the coefficient at degree $r$ is replaced by the sum of coefficients at degrees congruent to $r$ modulo $M$. Let $\omega_0=e^{-2\pi i/M}$, which equals $1$ when $M=1$. Apply the radix-two DFT procedure to each folded coefficient vector to evaluate $P_I$ and $D_I$ at $\omega_0^j$, $0\le j<M$. If $M>1$, find the unique odd integer $s\in\{1,3,\ldots,M-1\}$ with $\omega=\omega_0^s$ by generating and comparing the $M$ powers of $\omega_0$, then place the value at index $sk\bmod M$ at output index $k$; this is the supplied root order because $\omega^k=\omega_0^{sk}$. For $M=1$, the only root is $1$ and no reindexing is needed. This root search and reindexing use $O(M)$ operations. If some reindexed $D_I(\omega^k)=0$, return status `collision`; otherwise return $y_k=P_I(\omega^k)/D_I(\omega^k)$.

Let $M=2^q$ for an integer $q\ge0$, and let $\omega=e^{-2\pi i/M}$ (with $\omega=1$ when $M=1$). Define the forward DFT matrix $F\in\mathbb C^{M\times M}$ by $F_{kj}=\omega^{jk}$, where $^*$ denotes conjugate transpose. Then $F^*F=MI$, so the inverse DFT is $M^{-1}F^*$. The radix-two procedure defined on this page computes either transform exactly in $O(M\log(2+M))$ complex arithmetic operations and $O(M)$ space. Consequently, for every integer $n\ge1$, two polynomials of degree less than $n$ can be multiplied exactly in $O(n\log(2+n))$ complex arithmetic operations and $O(n)$ space by zero-padding to a radix-two transform length at least $2n-1$.

derivations.claim: For a leaf containing index $j$, $P_j(z)/D_j(z)=a_j/(z-\mu_j)$ whenever $z\ne\mu_j$. If the identity $P_I/D_I=\sum_{j\in I}a_j/(z-\mu_j)$ holds for the two child sets, then the internal-node formulas in [F1] give $P_I/D_I=P_{I_1}/D_{I_1}+P_{I_2}/D_{I_2}$. Induction up the finite tree therefore gives $P_I(z)/D_I(z)=\sum_{j=1}^{n}a_j/(z-\mu_j)$ at the root wherever its denominator is nonzero.

The balanced tree has height at most $\lceil\log_2 n\rceil$. At a node whose index set has size $s$, its three polynomial products have operand degrees at most $s$; by [F2] they cost $O(s\log(2+s))$ operations. At a fixed height, the node index sets are disjoint and their sizes sum to at most $n$, so that height costs at most $O(n\log(2+n))$. Summing over the height gives $O(n\log^2(2+n))$ operations, including the coefficient additions. A depth-first evaluation stores at most one completed sibling subtree per level; their coefficient-array sizes form a geometric sum bounded by $O(n)$, so the product-tree workspace is $O(n)$.

Write the root coefficients as $P_I(z)=\sum_j p_jz^j$ and $D_I(z)=\sum_j d_jz^j$. For each $0\le r<M$, fold them to $p'_r=\sum_{j\equiv r\pmod M}p_j$ and $d'_r=\sum_{j\equiv r\pmod M}d_j$. Since $\omega^{kM}=1$, evaluating the folded polynomials at $\omega^k$ gives exactly $P_I(\omega^k)$ and $D_I(\omega^k)$. The algorithm evaluates both folded arrays with two radix-two DFTs on the standard grid $\omega_0^j=e^{-2\pi i j/M}$; if $M>1$, the supplied primitive root is $\omega=\omega_0^s$ for a unique odd $s$, so reindexing the standard outputs at $sk\bmod M$ gives their values at $\omega^k$. For $M=1$ the grids coincide. By [F2] the two transforms cost $O(M\log(2+M))$ operations and $O(M)$ additional space; finding $s$ and reindexing cost $O(M)$ operations and space, within the same bounds. Folding costs $O(n)$ operations and $O(n+M)$ space.

The noncollision hypothesis makes $D_I(\omega^k)=\prod_j(\omega^k-\mu_j)\ne0$ for every $k$. Thus the divisions in [F1] are defined, and step 1.1 identifies each quotient with the required Cauchy sum. Adding the product-tree, folding, transform, and division costs gives $O((n+M)\log^2(2+n+M))$ operations and $O(n+M)$ space.

$$ H(z)=\frac{2}{1+z}\left(\widetilde C^*R(z)B-\widetilde C^*R(z)P\,W(z)^{-1}Q^*R(z)B\right). $$

Suppose $s\le r$ and consider a homogeneous solution $(z,x_Z)$ of the bordered system in [F3]. Set $x_J=-\alpha D_J^{-1}P_Jz$. The first bordered row gives $z=Q_J^*x_J+Q_Z^*x_Z=Q^*x$, while its lower row gives $\alpha P_Zz=0$. Therefore the $J$ rows of $Gx$ equal $D_Jx_J+\alpha P_JQ^*x=0$, and the $Z$ rows equal $\alpha P_ZQ^*x=\alpha P_Zz=0$. Invertibility of $G$ implies $x=0$, hence $z=Q^*x=0$ and $x_Z=0$. The square bordered matrix has trivial kernel and is therefore invertible.

For any right-hand side, solve the bordered system, define $x_J=D_J^{-1}(b_J-\alpha P_Jz)$, and keep the solved $x_Z$. Its first row states $z=Q^*x$; the upper coordinate equations then give $(Gx)_J=b_J$, and the lower row gives $(Gx)_Z=\alpha P_Zz=b_Z$. Thus $x=x'$ is the unique solution to $Gx'=b$. The bordered dimension is $r+s\le2r$; forming it and its right-hand side costs $O(Nr^2)$ operations and $O(Nr+r^2)$ space, and factoring/solving it costs $O(r^3)$. Computing $C^*x'$ adds $O(N)$. Both branches satisfy the claimed fixed-rank linear bounds.

An $N$-state single-input, single-output complex linear state-space model has $B,C\in\mathbb C^N$, state equation $x'(t)=Ax(t)+Bu(t)$, and output $y(t)=C^*x(t)$; its direct term is set to zero in the S4 convolution convention. Here $X^*$ denotes conjugate transpose; a square complex matrix $H$ is normal when $H^*H=HH^*$; and a square matrix $V$ is unitary when $V^*V=VV^*=I$. A matrix is in diagonal-plus-low-rank (DPLR) form of rank $r$ if
$$
A=\Lambda-PQ^*,
$$
where $\Lambda\in\mathbb C^{N\times N}$ is diagonal and $P,Q\in\mathbb C^{N\times r}$. It is in normal-plus-low-rank (NPLR) form of rank $r$ if
$$
A=V\Lambda V^*-PQ^*,
$$
where $V\in\mathbb C^{N\times N}$ is unitary, $\Lambda$ is diagonal, and $P,Q\in\mathbb C^{N\times r}$. The unitary state change $\widetilde x=V^*x$ converts this NPLR representation to DPLR form and changes $B,C$ to $V^*B,V^*C$, respectively.

For a step size $\Delta>0$ such that $I-\Delta A/2$ is invertible, the bilinear recurrent matrices are
$$ \overline A=(I-\Delta A/2)^{-1}(I+\Delta A/2),\qquad \overline B=(I-\Delta A/2)^{-1}\Delta B,\qquad \overline C=C. $$
With initial state $x_{-1}=0$, the discrete recurrence is $x_t=\overline A x_{t-1}+\overline B u_t$, $y_t=\overline C^*x_t$. Its length-$L$ impulse kernel is the vector $K_L=(\overline C^*\overline A^j\overline B)_{j=0}^{L-1}$. For a nonzero direct term $D$, the output has the additional separate skip term $Du_t$.

For a filter evaluation of transform length $M\ge L$, the output vector for the length-$M$ truncated generating function is $\widetilde C_M=(I-\overline A^M)^*C$. A filter procedure may receive $\widetilde C_M$ as given data; an operation count for evaluating the filter from this transformed vector does not include the separate work of forming it from $C$.

Let $D\in\mathbb C^{N\times N}$ be invertible, let $U,V\in\mathbb C^{N\times r}$, and set $W=I_r+V^*D^{-1}U$, where $^*$ denotes conjugate transpose. Then $D+UV^*$ is invertible if and only if $W$ is invertible. When these matrices are invertible,
$$
(D+UV^*)^{-1}=D^{-1}-D^{-1}U W^{-1}V^*D^{-1}.
$$

Input an integer $M=2^q$ with $q\ge0$, a primitive $M$th root of unity $\omega$, a finite list of poles $\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_n\in\mathbb C$, and weights $a_1,\ldots,a_n\in\mathbb C$. The required output is $y_k=\sum_{j=1}^n a_j/(\omega^k-\mu_j)$ for $0\le k<M$, provided no denominator is zero. If $n=0$, return the zero vector.

Here a primitive $M$th root means $\omega^M=1$ and $\omega^k\ne1$ for $1\le k<M$. For $n\ge1$, form a balanced binary tree on the pole indices, splitting each consecutive index interval into two intervals whose sizes differ by at most one. At a leaf containing index $j$, store polynomials $D_j(z)=z-\mu_j$ and $P_j(z)=a_j$. At an internal node with disjoint child index sets $I_1,I_2$, store
$$ D_I(z)=D_{I_1}(z)D_{I_2}(z),\qquad P_I(z)=P_{I_1}(z)D_{I_2}(z)+D_{I_1}(z)P_{I_2}(z). $$
At the root, fold the coefficients of each polynomial modulo $z^M-1$: the coefficient at degree $r$ is replaced by the sum of coefficients at degrees congruent to $r$ modulo $M$. Let $\omega_0=e^{-2\pi i/M}$, which equals $1$ when $M=1$. Apply the radix-two DFT procedure to each folded coefficient vector to evaluate $P_I$ and $D_I$ at $\omega_0^j$, $0\le j<M$. If $M>1$, find the unique odd integer $s\in\{1,3,\ldots,M-1\}$ with $\omega=\omega_0^s$ by generating and comparing the $M$ powers of $\omega_0$, then place the value at index $sk\bmod M$ at output index $k$; this is the supplied root order because $\omega^k=\omega_0^{sk}$. For $M=1$, the only root is $1$ and no reindexing is needed. This root search and reindexing use $O(M)$ operations. If some reindexed $D_I(\omega^k)=0$, return status `collision`; otherwise return $y_k=P_I(\omega^k)/D_I(\omega^k)$.

derivations.claim: Put $\alpha=\Delta/2$. For every root $z\ne-1$, substitution of $\bar A=G^{-1}(I+\alpha A)$ gives $I-z\bar A=G^{-1}((1-z)I-\alpha(1+z)A)=G^{-1}\alpha(1+z)(s(z)I-A)$. By [A1] and [F2], $s(z)I-A=(s(z)I-\Lambda)+PQ^*$ is invertible; inversion and multiplication by $\bar B=G^{-1}\Delta B$ give $(I-z\bar A)^{-1}\bar B=\frac{2}{1+z}(s(z)I-A)^{-1}B$. At $z=-1$, $I+\bar A=G^{-1}(G+I+\alpha A)=2G^{-1}$ is invertible.

For any root $z\ne-1$, put $a=1/\alpha=2/\Delta$. For $\lambda_j\ne-a$, direct algebra gives $s(z)-\lambda_j=\frac{(a-\lambda_j)-(a+\lambda_j)z}{1+z}=\frac{(a+\lambda_j)(\mu_j-z)}{1+z}$, hence $\frac{2}{1+z}(s(z)-\lambda_j)^{-1}=-\frac{2}{a+\lambda_j}(z-\mu_j)^{-1}$. For $\lambda_j=-a$, $s(z)-\lambda_j=2a/(1+z)$ and the scaled reciprocal is $1/a=\Delta/2$. No nonexceptional pole equals $-1$, since $\mu_j=-1$ would imply $2a=0$ although $a>0$.

At each root, $z^M=1$ and step 1.1 makes $I-z\bar A$ invertible. The finite geometric identity gives $(I-\bar A^M)(I-z\bar A)^{-1}=\sum_{j=0}^{M-1}z^j\bar A^j$. If $M$ is even, $-1$ is a root. Step 1.1 gives $(I+\bar A)^{-1}\bar B=(1/2)G(G^{-1}\Delta B)=(\Delta/2)B$; applying the finite geometric identity from step 2.1 yields $H_M(-1)=\widetilde C_M^*(I+\bar A)^{-1}\bar B=(\Delta/2)\widetilde C_M^*B$.

By step 1.2, each scaled diagonal-resolvent entry in step 3.1 is one scalar roots-of-unity Cauchy sum, with the $\lambda_j=-a$ entries supplied by their explicit constants. Let $N,r\ge1$ and $A=\Lambda-PQ^*$ with $\Lambda\in\mathbb C^{N\times N}$ diagonal and $P,Q\in\mathbb C^{N\times r}$, where $^*$ denotes conjugate transpose; let $B,C\in\mathbb C^N$, let $\Delta>0$, and put $\alpha=\Delta/2$. The bilinear step is defined only when $G=I-\alpha A$ is invertible. Given an input sequence $(u_t)$ and state $x_{-1}$, its recurrent mode computes
$$ b_t=(I+\alpha A)x_{t-1}+\Delta Bu_t,\qquad Gx_t=b_t,\qquad y_t=C^*x_t. $$
For a zero initial state, the equivalent matrices and length-$L$ kernel are $\bar A=G^{-1}(I+\alpha A)$, $\bar B=G^{-1}\Delta B$, and $K_j=C^*\bar A^j\bar B$ for $0\le j<L$; a direct term $Du_t$, if present, is added separately.

For the filter mode, fix an integer $L\ge1$, let $M$ be the least power of two with $M\ge L$, let $\omega=e^{-2\pi i/M}$, and let $\widetilde C\in\mathbb C^N$ be supplied as the length-$M$ truncated-output parameter. When a conventional output vector $C$ is used, this parameter is $\widetilde C=(I-\bar A^M)^*C$. Define the $M$ root values $z_k=\omega^k$. The algorithm returns the first $L$ coefficients of the inverse radix-two transform of the values $H(z_k)$ below.

For $z_k=-1$, set $H(z_k)=(\Delta/2)\widetilde C^*B$. For each $z=z_k\ne-1$, put $s(z)=(2/\Delta)(1-z)/(1+z)$. If $s(z)-\lambda_j=0$ for some diagonal entry $\lambda_j$ of $\Lambda$, return status `resonant-diagonal`. If no diagonal resonance is present, write $R(z)=\operatorname{diag}((s(z)-\lambda_j)^{-1})$ and $W(z)=I_r+Q^*R(z)P$. If $W(z)$ is singular, return status `resonant-correction`. When this correction is invertible, the target root value is
$$ H(z)=\frac{2}{1+z}\left(\widetilde C^*R(z)B-\widetilde C^*R(z)P\,W(z)^{-1}Q^*R(z)B\right). $$
The preceding resolvent expression specifies the target root values. The filter evaluation computes them using $1+2r+r^2=(r+1)^2$ scalar Cauchy products as follows. Put $a=2/\Delta$, and for each $j$ with $\lambda_j\ne-a$ define $\mu_j=(a-\lambda_j)/(a+\lambda_j)$. For any pair of vectors $u,v\in\mathbb C^N$, compute on the root grid
$$ S_{uv}(z)=\frac{2}{1+z}u^*R(z)v =\frac{\Delta}{2}\sum_{j:\lambda_j=-a}\overline{u_j}v_j-2\sum_{j:\lambda_j\ne-a}\frac{\overline{u_j}v_j}{a+\lambda_j}\frac{1}{z-\mu_j} $$
by calling the roots-of-unity Cauchy procedure with poles $\mu_j$ and weights $-2\overline{u_j}v_j/(a+\lambda_j)$, then adding the displayed constant. A collision $\mu_j=z_k$ returns status `resonant-diagonal`. For $z=z_k\ne-1$, set
$$ W(z)=I_r+\frac{1+z}{2}S_{Q,P}(z),\qquad H(z)=S_{\widetilde C,B}(z)-\frac{1+z}{2}S_{\widetilde C,P}(z)W(z)^{-1}S_{Q,B}(z). $$
If $W(z)$ is singular, return status `resonant-correction`. The four families $S_{\widetilde C,B}$, $S_{\widetilde C,P}$, $S_{Q,B}$, and $S_{Q,P}$ contain $1$, $r$, $r$, and $r^2$ scalar products, respectively. The root $-1$ is handled directly and is never included in this Cauchy evaluation. Matrix products and inversions of the $r\times r$ corrections are performed separately at each root.

The recurrent solver may exploit the diagonal-plus-low-rank structure as follows. Write $d_j=1-\alpha\lambda_j$, let $J=\{j:d_j\ne0\}$ and $Z=\{j:d_j=0\}$. If $Z$ is empty, use the Woodbury inverse with $D=\operatorname{diag}(d_j)$ and correction $I_r+\alpha Q^*D^{-1}P$; if this correction is singular, return status `singular-bilinear-matrix`. If $s=|Z|>0$, then when $s\le r$ solve the bordered system
$$ \begin{bmatrix} I_r+\alpha Q_J^*D_J^{-1}P_J&-Q_Z^*\\ \alpha P_Z&0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}z\\x_Z\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}Q_J^*D_J^{-1}b_J\\b_Z\end{bmatrix}, \qquad x_J=D_J^{-1}(b_J-\alpha P_Jz), $$
where $D_J=\operatorname{diag}(d_j)_{j\in J}$; if $s>r$ or the bordered system is singular, return status `singular-bilinear-matrix`. Here $z=Q^*x$. This branch solves $Gx=b$ without assuming the diagonal base is invertible.

Let $N,r\ge1$, $M=2^q\ge1$, $1\le L\le M$, $A=\Lambda-PQ^*$ with diagonal $\Lambda\in\mathbb C^{N\times N}$ and $P,Q\in\mathbb C^{N\times r}$, where $^*$ denotes conjugate transpose, $B,C\in\mathbb C^N$, and $\Delta>0$. Assume $G=I-\Delta A/2$ is invertible, define $\bar A=G^{-1}(I+\Delta A/2)$, $\bar B=G^{-1}\Delta B$, and put $\widetilde C_M=(I-\bar A^M)^*C$. For each $M$th root of unity $z\ne-1$, let $s(z)=(2/\Delta)(1-z)/(1+z)$, $R(z)=(s(z)I-\Lambda)^{-1}$, and $W(z)=I_r+Q^*R(z)P$. Assume all these $R(z)$ and $W(z)$ are invertible. The length-$M$ truncated generating value $H_M(z)=\sum_{j=0}^{M-1}C^*\bar A^j\bar B z^j$ then satisfies
$$
H_M(z)=\frac{2}{1+z}\left(\widetilde C_M^*R(z)B-\widetilde C_M^*R(z)P\,W(z)^{-1}Q^*R(z)B\right)\quad(z\ne-1).
$$
If $M$ is even, the root $z=-1$ has the finite value $H_M(-1)=(\Delta/2)\widetilde C_M^*B$. For $a=2/\Delta$ and each diagonal entry $\lambda_j\ne-a$, put $\mu_j=(a-\lambda_j)/(a+\lambda_j)$. For any $u,v\in\mathbb C^N$ and root $z\ne-1$,
$$
\frac{2}{1+z}u^*R(z)v=\frac{\Delta}{2}\sum_{\lambda_j=-a}\overline{u_j}v_j-2\sum_{\lambda_j\ne-a}\frac{\overline{u_j}v_j}{a+\lambda_j}\frac{1}{z-\mu_j}.
$$
Thus the four families of scalar products $\widetilde C_M^*RB$, $\widetilde C_M^*RP$, $Q^*RB$, and $Q^*RP$ reduce to $1+2r+r^2=(r+1)^2$ roots-of-unity Cauchy products; when $r=1$ there are four.

Let $n\ge1$, $M=2^q\ge1$, $\omega$ be a primitive $M$th root of unity, and let $\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_n\in\mathbb C$ and $a_1,\ldots,a_n\in\mathbb C$ satisfy $\mu_j\ne\omega^k$ for every $j$ and $0\le k<M$. Then the Cauchy matrix-vector product $y_k=\sum_{j=1}^{n}a_j/(\omega^k-\mu_j)$, $0\le k<M$, is computed exactly by the balanced product-tree procedure using $O((n+M)\log^2(2+n+M))$ complex arithmetic operations and $O(n+M)$ space. Repeated poles are allowed.

Let $M=2^q$ for an integer $q\ge0$, and let $\omega=e^{-2\pi i/M}$ (with $\omega=1$ when $M=1$). Define the forward DFT matrix $F\in\mathbb C^{M\times M}$ by $F_{kj}=\omega^{jk}$, where $^*$ denotes conjugate transpose. Then $F^*F=MI$, so the inverse DFT is $M^{-1}F^*$. The radix-two procedure defined on this page computes either transform exactly in $O(M\log(2+M))$ complex arithmetic operations and $O(M)$ space. Consequently, for every integer $n\ge1$, two polynomials of degree less than $n$ can be multiplied exactly in $O(n\log(2+n))$ complex arithmetic operations and $O(n)$ space by zero-padding to a radix-two transform length at least $2n-1$.

Index rows and columns by $0,\ldots,N-1$. Define the real LegS coefficient matrix $G^S$ by $G^S_{nk}=-\sqrt{(2n+1)(2k+1)}$ when $n>k$, $G^S_{nn}=-(n+1)$, and $G^S_{nk}=0$ when $n<k$. In the LegS coefficient ODE for $t>0$ this matrix is multiplied by the time-dependent scalar $1/t$; the matrix assertion below does not make that ODE time-invariant. For $\theta>0$, define the LegT state generator by $G^T_{nk}=-(2n+1)(-1)^{n-k}/\theta$ when $n\ge k$ and $G^T_{nk}=-(2n+1)/\theta$ when $n<k$. Define the original HiPPO LagT state generator by $G^L_{nk}=-1$ when $n\ge k$ and $G^L_{nk}=0$ when $n<k$. Here $X^*$ is conjugate transpose, a complex matrix $H$ is normal when $H^*H=HH^*$, and a square matrix $V$ is unitary when $V^*V=VV^*=I$. For LegS and LagT use the identity similarity; for LegT use the invertible diagonal similarity $S_0=\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt{2n+1})_{n=0}^{N-1}\operatorname{diag}((-1)^n)_{n=0}^{N-1}$. Each transformed matrix is a difference $H-UV^*$ with $H$ normal and $\operatorname{rank}(UV^*)\le1$ for LegS and LagT and $\operatorname{rank}(UV^*)\le2$ for LegT. Consequently the equivalent finite-dimensional complex state-space matrix has a normal-plus-low-rank representation, and a unitary change of state coordinates gives diagonal-plus-low-rank form. Under any state change $x=S\widetilde x$, the input and output vectors change to $S^{-1}B$ and $S^*C$, respectively.

Let $n\ge0$, $M=2^q\ge1$, $z_k=\exp(2\pi i k/M)$, and let $a_j,\mu_j\in\mathbb C$ satisfy $|z_k-\mu_j|\ge d>0$ for every $j,k$. Repeated poles are allowed. Let $A\ge\sum_j|a_j|$ and $s=\max(1,A/d)$. For $0<\eta\le1/2$, the products $y_k=\sum_j a_j/(z_k-\mu_j)$ have numerical approximations satisfying
$$ \max_k|\widehat y_k-y_k|\le\eta s $$
using $O((n+M)\log(2+M)\log(1/\eta))$ scalar operations and $O(n+M)$ scalar words. Consequently absolute error $\delta$, for $0<\delta\le1/2$, costs $O((n+M)\log(2+M)\log(s/\delta))$ operations with the same word space.

The model is variable-precision arithmetic with unrestricted exponent range, supplied certified approximations to the inputs, roots and arc-center constants, and certified bounds for the finite computation specified in the proof. Each real comparison, word access and scalar arithmetic operation has unit cost; the latter has absolute rounding error at most $u$. A word stores one scalar at the selected precision. Input approximation, working precision and word lengths may depend on $n,M,d,A,\eta$ and intermediate magnitudes. This is neither a bit-complexity bound nor a bound at fixed word length. All preprocessing, geometric routing and numerical summation operations are included; computing the supplied constants or certificates from other representations is excluded.

Here is a sufficient explicit precision certificate. For the selected finite rational summation circuit, include its input constants among its exact intermediates, let $T$ bound its arithmetic gates, let $V\ge1$ bound their moduli, and let $0<D\le1$ bound below the modulus of every divisor. Set $K=64(V+1)^2/D^2$. With $\tau=\eta s/2$, it suffices to take
$$ u\le\frac{\min(1,D/2,\tau)}{2K^{T+1}}. $$
The geometric decisions additionally use certified interval enclosures narrow enough to choose between the overlapping near and far tests described below. Such enclosures require only finite precision, including at threshold equalities. These certificate assumptions hold for each particular noncollision input, but have no uniform bound as pole/root separation tends to zero.

derivations.claim: By [F5], each fixed matrix $G^S,G^T,G^L$ admits equivalent DPLR coordinates of bounded rank. When such a matrix is used as a constant state matrix and satisfies the stated invertibility hypotheses, it is an admissible input here. This does not identify the original time-dependent LegS ODE with a constant-matrix model. The operation argument applies to any supplied DPLR matrices of the same dimensions. By [F2], each required root value has the stated Cauchy-product expression, including the direct value at $-1$. Under the noncollision and correction-invertibility assumptions, the filter procedure in [F1] therefore computes all $M$ generating values exactly.

For $z\ne-1$, $R=\beta D$. Substitution in [F2] gives $H_M(z)=x-\beta u(I_r+\beta T)^{-1}v$ and $W=I_r+\beta T$. Also $|\beta|\le1$. The pole mapping in [F2] expresses each entry of $D$ as $-2/(a+\lambda_j)(z-\mu_j)^{-1}$ for $\lambda_j\ne-a$, and as the constant $\Delta/2$ otherwise. Thus the weights in [F6] are exactly $-2\overline{f_j}g_j/(a+\lambda_j)$ for the applicable vector pair $f,g$. Their preparation and the exceptional constant sums cost $O(N)$ for fixed $r$. At $-1$, retain the direct value $(\Delta/2)\widetilde C_M^*B$ from [F2], without a resolvent division.

Each scalar product has at most $N$ poles and is evaluated on $M$ roots. If it has at least one pole, [F3] bounds its cost by $O((N+M)\log^2(2+N+M))$ operations and $O(N+M)$ space; if it has no poles, its constant value is formed by a single finite sum in $O(N+M)$ operations and space. There are at most $(r+1)^2$ such products by [F2], a constant number because $r$ is fixed. The per-root correction matrix products and inversions cost $O(M(r+1)^3)$ operations by finite-dimensional elimination, which is $O(M)$ for fixed $r$.

The generating values are the DFT of the $M$ coefficients $C^*\bar A^j\bar B$ for $0\le j<M$. By [F4], the inverse radix-two transform recovers these coefficients exactly; [F1] then returns their first $L$ entries, which are precisely the length-$L$ filter.

Let $\delta=\varepsilon/[32r w^2(b+1)^2]$ and first consider exact arithmetic on truncated Cauchy sums having scalar entry errors at most $\delta$, with finite constant sums exact. Denote the resulting blocks by $\widehat x,\widehat u,\widehat v,\widehat T$. Each of their infinity-norm errors is at most $e=r\delta$, since each row has at most $r$ entries and $r\ge1$. Hence $\|\widehat W-W\|_\infty\le e$, $we<1/2$ and $e\le1$. Writing $E=W^{-1}(\widehat W-W)$, the geometric series $\sum_{j\ge0}(-E)^j$ converges in infinity norm because $\|E\|_\infty\le we<1/2$, is the inverse of $I+E$ by finite geometric identities and passage to the norm limit, and has norm at most $2$. Therefore $\|\widehat W^{-1}\|_\infty\le2w$. The identity $\widehat W^{-1}-W^{-1}=-W^{-1}(\widehat W-W)\widehat W^{-1}$ gives $\|\widehat W^{-1}-W^{-1}\|_\infty\le2w^2e$.

Since $M$ is the least power of two at least $L$, $M<2L$ for every integer $L\ge1$. Combining the Cauchy products, per-root corrections, and inverse transform gives $O((N+L)\log^2(2+N+L))$ exact complex arithmetic operations. Fix positive finite dimensions $d_x,d_h$, inputs $x_t\in\mathbb R^{d_x}$, hidden states $h_t\in\mathbb R^{d_h}$, cell states $c_t\in\mathbb R^{d_h}$, and initial values $h_0,c_0$. A standard long short-term memory (LSTM) cell without peephole connections or projection has shared matrices $W_i,W_f,W_o,W_c\in\mathbb R^{d_h\times d_x}$, $U_i,U_f,U_o,U_c\in\mathbb R^{d_h\times d_h}$, and biases $b_i,b_f,b_o,b_c\in\mathbb R^{d_h}$. Apply $\sigma(s)=(1+e^{-s})^{-1}$ and $\tanh(s)=(e^s-e^{-s})/(e^s+e^{-s})$ coordinatewise. At each time $t\ge1$, set

$$ i_t=\sigma(W_i x_t+U_i h_{t-1}+b_i),\qquad f_t=\sigma(W_f x_t+U_f h_{t-1}+b_f),\qquad o_t=\sigma(W_o x_t+U_o h_{t-1}+b_o), $$

$$ g_t=\tanh(W_c x_t+U_c h_{t-1}+b_c),\qquad c_t=f_t\odot c_{t-1}+i_t\odot g_t,\qquad h_t=o_t\odot\tanh(c_t), $$

where $\odot$ is coordinatewise multiplication. The same matrices and biases are reused at every time step. The vectors $i_t,f_t,o_t$ are the input, forget, and output gates, and $g_t$ is the candidate state update.

derivations.claim: Every gate's affine argument is zero because all weights and biases vanish. By [F1], $\sigma(0)=1/(1+1)=1/2$ and $\tanh(0)=0$, so $i_t=f_t=o_t=1/2$ and $g_t=0$. Substitution into the cell recurrence gives $c_t=c_{t-1}/2$ and $h_t=\tfrac12\tanh(c_t)$.

The recurrence in step 1.1 gives $c_1=2^{-1}c_0$. If $c_{t-1}=2^{-(t-1)}c_0$, then $c_t=c_{t-1}/2=2^{-t}c_0$; induction proves this for every $t\ge1$. Substituting this expression into the hidden-state identity in step 1.1 gives $h_t=\tfrac12\tanh(2^{-t}c_0)$.

An $N$-state single-input, single-output complex linear state-space model has $B,C\in\mathbb C^N$, state equation $x'(t)=Ax(t)+Bu(t)$, and output $y(t)=C^*x(t)$; its direct term is set to zero in the S4 convolution convention. Here $X^*$ denotes conjugate transpose; a square complex matrix $H$ is normal when $H^*H=HH^*$; and a square matrix $V$ is unitary when $V^*V=VV^*=I$. A matrix is in diagonal-plus-low-rank (DPLR) form of rank $r$ if
$$
A=\Lambda-PQ^*,
$$
where $\Lambda\in\mathbb C^{N\times N}$ is diagonal and $P,Q\in\mathbb C^{N\times r}$. It is in normal-plus-low-rank (NPLR) form of rank $r$ if
$$
A=V\Lambda V^*-PQ^*,
$$
where $V\in\mathbb C^{N\times N}$ is unitary, $\Lambda$ is diagonal, and $P,Q\in\mathbb C^{N\times r}$. The unitary state change $\widetilde x=V^*x$ converts this NPLR representation to DPLR form and changes $B,C$ to $V^*B,V^*C$, respectively.

For a step size $\Delta>0$ such that $I-\Delta A/2$ is invertible, the bilinear recurrent matrices are
$$ \overline A=(I-\Delta A/2)^{-1}(I+\Delta A/2),\qquad \overline B=(I-\Delta A/2)^{-1}\Delta B,\qquad \overline C=C. $$
With initial state $x_{-1}=0$, the discrete recurrence is $x_t=\overline A x_{t-1}+\overline B u_t$, $y_t=\overline C^*x_t$. Its length-$L$ impulse kernel is the vector $K_L=(\overline C^*\overline A^j\overline B)_{j=0}^{L-1}$. For a nonzero direct term $D$, the output has the additional separate skip term $Du_t$.

For a filter evaluation of transform length $M\ge L$, the output vector for the length-$M$ truncated generating function is $\widetilde C_M=(I-\overline A^M)^*C$. A filter procedure may receive $\widetilde C_M$ as given data; an operation count for evaluating the filter from this transformed vector does not include the separate work of forming it from $C$.

Let $N,r\ge1$ and $A=\Lambda-PQ^*$ with $\Lambda\in\mathbb C^{N\times N}$ diagonal and $P,Q\in\mathbb C^{N\times r}$, where $^*$ denotes conjugate transpose; let $B,C\in\mathbb C^N$, let $\Delta>0$, and put $\alpha=\Delta/2$. The bilinear step is defined only when $G=I-\alpha A$ is invertible. Given an input sequence $(u_t)$ and state $x_{-1}$, its recurrent mode computes
$$ b_t=(I+\alpha A)x_{t-1}+\Delta Bu_t,\qquad Gx_t=b_t,\qquad y_t=C^*x_t. $$
For a zero initial state, the equivalent matrices and length-$L$ kernel are $\bar A=G^{-1}(I+\alpha A)$, $\bar B=G^{-1}\Delta B$, and $K_j=C^*\bar A^j\bar B$ for $0\le j<L$; a direct term $Du_t$, if present, is added separately.

For the filter mode, fix an integer $L\ge1$, let $M$ be the least power of two with $M\ge L$, let $\omega=e^{-2\pi i/M}$, and let $\widetilde C\in\mathbb C^N$ be supplied as the length-$M$ truncated-output parameter. When a conventional output vector $C$ is used, this parameter is $\widetilde C=(I-\bar A^M)^*C$. Define the $M$ root values $z_k=\omega^k$. The algorithm returns the first $L$ coefficients of the inverse radix-two transform of the values $H(z_k)$ below.

For $z_k=-1$, set $H(z_k)=(\Delta/2)\widetilde C^*B$. For each $z=z_k\ne-1$, put $s(z)=(2/\Delta)(1-z)/(1+z)$. If $s(z)-\lambda_j=0$ for some diagonal entry $\lambda_j$ of $\Lambda$, return status `resonant-diagonal`. If no diagonal resonance is present, write $R(z)=\operatorname{diag}((s(z)-\lambda_j)^{-1})$ and $W(z)=I_r+Q^*R(z)P$. If $W(z)$ is singular, return status `resonant-correction`. When this correction is invertible, the target root value is
$$ H(z)=\frac{2}{1+z}\left(\widetilde C^*R(z)B-\widetilde C^*R(z)P\,W(z)^{-1}Q^*R(z)B\right). $$
The preceding resolvent expression specifies the target root values. The filter evaluation computes them using $1+2r+r^2=(r+1)^2$ scalar Cauchy products as follows. Put $a=2/\Delta$, and for each $j$ with $\lambda_j\ne-a$ define $\mu_j=(a-\lambda_j)/(a+\lambda_j)$. For any pair of vectors $u,v\in\mathbb C^N$, compute on the root grid
$$ S_{uv}(z)=\frac{2}{1+z}u^*R(z)v =\frac{\Delta}{2}\sum_{j:\lambda_j=-a}\overline{u_j}v_j-2\sum_{j:\lambda_j\ne-a}\frac{\overline{u_j}v_j}{a+\lambda_j}\frac{1}{z-\mu_j} $$
by calling the roots-of-unity Cauchy procedure with poles $\mu_j$ and weights $-2\overline{u_j}v_j/(a+\lambda_j)$, then adding the displayed constant. A collision $\mu_j=z_k$ returns status `resonant-diagonal`. For $z=z_k\ne-1$, set
$$ W(z)=I_r+\frac{1+z}{2}S_{Q,P}(z),\qquad H(z)=S_{\widetilde C,B}(z)-\frac{1+z}{2}S_{\widetilde C,P}(z)W(z)^{-1}S_{Q,B}(z). $$
If $W(z)$ is singular, return status `resonant-correction`. The four families $S_{\widetilde C,B}$, $S_{\widetilde C,P}$, $S_{Q,B}$, and $S_{Q,P}$ contain $1$, $r$, $r$, and $r^2$ scalar products, respectively. The root $-1$ is handled directly and is never included in this Cauchy evaluation. Matrix products and inversions of the $r\times r$ corrections are performed separately at each root.

The recurrent solver may exploit the diagonal-plus-low-rank structure as follows. Write $d_j=1-\alpha\lambda_j$, let $J=\{j:d_j\ne0\}$ and $Z=\{j:d_j=0\}$. If $Z$ is empty, use the Woodbury inverse with $D=\operatorname{diag}(d_j)$ and correction $I_r+\alpha Q^*D^{-1}P$; if this correction is singular, return status `singular-bilinear-matrix`. If $s=|Z|>0$, then when $s\le r$ solve the bordered system
$$ \begin{bmatrix} I_r+\alpha Q_J^*D_J^{-1}P_J&-Q_Z^*\\ \alpha P_Z&0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}z\\x_Z\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}Q_J^*D_J^{-1}b_J\\b_Z\end{bmatrix}, \qquad x_J=D_J^{-1}(b_J-\alpha P_Jz), $$
where $D_J=\operatorname{diag}(d_j)_{j\in J}$; if $s>r$ or the bordered system is singular, return status `singular-bilinear-matrix`. Here $z=Q^*x$. This branch solves $Gx=b$ without assuming the diagonal base is invertible.

derivations.claim: If $n=0$, return zero; if $M=1$, sum the $n$ nonzero-denominator fractions directly, using $O(n+1)$ operations and space, and use the rounding argument below. Otherwise construct a binary tree on consecutive root indices. Its root covers all roots, with center $0$ and radius $1$. At depth $\ell\ge1$, a node contains $m=M/2^\ell$ consecutive roots starting at index $b$; its center is $c=\exp(2\pi i(b+(m-1)/2)/M)$ and its covering radius is $R=2\sin(\pi(m-1)/(2M))\le\pi 2^{-\ell}$. These disks contain their roots because the largest angular distance from the arc midpoint is $\pi(m-1)/M$. Singleton leaves have radius zero. For each pole start at the root: at a nonleaf stop at a far node if $|c-\mu_j|\ge3R/2$, or descend into both children if $|c-\mu_j|\le2R$. In the overlap either choice is valid. A singleton is evaluated directly if reached. Certified interval tests terminate: for $R>0$, the two thresholds have a positive gap $R/2$, so enclosures of width less than $R/4$ distinguish at least one admissible choice, even when one threshold is an equality. Squared-distance comparisons implement the same test with a positive gap and finitely accurate supplied coordinates.

At a fixed depth put $J=2^\ell$. The $J$ arc centers are equally spaced on the unit circle and have mutual distance at least $2\sin(\pi/J)\ge4/J$ for $J\ge2$, by concavity of sine on $[0,\pi/2]$. Every near center lies within $2\pi/J$ of its pole. Disks of radius $2/J$ about these centers have disjoint interiors and lie in the disk of radius $(2\pi+2)/J$ about that pole. Comparing their areas bounds the number of near centers by $(\pi+1)^2<18$. Thus there are fewer than $36$ candidate children per pole at the next depth, including all far stops. The root contributes one candidate. The $q+1$ depths therefore contain $O(n\log(2+M))$ pole/node pairs. Each root follows exactly one stopped or singleton node for each pole, so these pairs partition all pole/root interactions without duplication. Repeated poles obey the same argument separately.

For a stopped pair put $t=-(z-c)/(c-\mu_j)$. Its targets satisfy $|t|\le2/3$. The finite geometric identity gives $1/(z-\mu_j)=\sum_{h=0}^{p-1}(-(z-c))^h/(c-\mu_j)^{h+1}+t^p/(z-\mu_j)$. Therefore the error in this pair is at most $(2/3)^p|a_j|/|z-\mu_j|$. Summing the partition from step 2.1 gives error at each root at most $(2/3)^p\sum_j|a_j|/|z-\mu_j|\le(2/3)^p A/d$. Choose $p\ge1$ with $(2/3)^p\le\eta/2$; then $p=O(\log(1/\eta))$ and the truncation error is at most $\eta s/2$. Direct singleton interactions have zero truncation error.

Process depths successively, keeping the bounded near list per pole for the next depth and the bounded far list for the current depth. At a fixed depth, store $v_{j,I}=1/(c_I-\mu_j)$ and initially $w_{j,I}=a_jv_{j,I}$ for each far pair. Initialize one target power $t_k=1$ per root. For degrees $h=0,\ldots,p-1$, clear one coefficient $g_I$ per current-depth node, add every current $w_{j,I}$ to its node's $g_I$, and add $g_{I(k)}t_k$ to each target accumulator, where $I(k)$ is its unique ancestor at this depth. Update $w_{j,I}\leftarrow w_{j,I}v_{j,I}$ and $t_k\leftarrow-(z_k-c_{I(k)})t_k$. A node without stopped pairs has coefficient zero. Discard the depth's arrays before advancing; at leaves add all direct pairs. The sums are exactly the polynomials in step 3.1. Each depth/degree uses $O(n+M)$ operations and words by step 2.1; the near/far lists, current coefficients, powers and output arrays occupy $O(n+M)$ words. No array of $p$ moments and no list across all depths is stored. The binary root tree has fewer than $2M$ nodes, so its supplied constants and routing data also occupy $O(M)$ words. Routing costs $O(n\log(2+M)+M)$ operations; fixed-width certified interval arithmetic for each overlapping test has constant scalar cost at its supplied sufficient precision. Total cost is $O((n+M)\log(2+M)p)$, with $O(n+M)$ words independently of $p$.

Fix the certified routing and the exact truncated rational circuit just constructed. Nonleaf far denominators are nonzero by their distance test; leaf denominators are nonzero by [A1]. Its finite exact intermediates and denominators admit the stated $V,D$. Suppose all already formed operands have error at most $e\le\min(1,D/2)$. Addition or subtraction increases error by at most $2e+u$. Multiplication increases it by at most $(2V+1)e+u$. For division, writing exact operands as $x,y$, approximate operands as $x',y'$, and $|y|\ge D$, gives $|y'|\ge D/2$ and $|x'/y'-x/y|\le2e/D+2Ve/D^2$; the final rounding adds $u$. Induction over the $T$ gates bounds every operand error by $2uK^{T+1}$: more precisely after $t$ gates the maximum error is at most $u(1+K+\cdots+K^t)\le2uK^t$. The stated choice of $u$ keeps this within $\min(1,D/2,\tau)$, so every division remains defined and the output rounding error is at most $\tau$. Root and pole approximation errors are included as input errors in this recurrence. The certified routing uses exact admissible inequalities, so rounding cannot route a pair outside its valid geometric estimate; the positive overlapping gap in step 1.1 permits finite enclosures, whose sufficient precision can be selected together with this $u$.

Combine the truncation and rounding errors to obtain $\max_k|\widehat y_k-y_k|\le\eta s$. derivations.claim: In a left-to-right grammar expansion, expanding the current $S$ nontrivially emits its opening bracket and leaves an inner $S$, its matching closing bracket, and a following $S$. Choosing $\epsilon$ finishes the current $S$ and either emits the pending matching close or, when no close is pending, ends the word. Thus each token is generated by precisely the stack transition stated above. The remaining choices after any finite emitted prefix are fresh independent choices. This constructs the stream law directly, including on nonterminating samples. Each valid prefix uniquely specifies the transition choices so far: every opening requires its type choice and every closing requires an epsilon choice. Their product is $w_p(x)$. In particular $s_{p,k}$ is the probability of reaching $k$ bracket tokens, is positive (all-open prefixes have positive probability), and is nonincreasing in $k$. Conditioning on reaching $k$ does not constrain the fresh choice after the prefix.

The grammar is unambiguous: a nonempty Dyck word has a unique first opening, its matching closing, and the resulting inside and following Dyck words, which recursively determine the derivation. A word with $m$ bracket pairs has $m$ nonempty choices and $m+1$ epsilon leaves, proving its stated finite-word mass. To calculate total termination mass, the probabilities of trees having height below successive finite bounds start at $q_0=0$ and satisfy $q_{j+1}=1-p+pq_j^2$. Their increasing limit is the probability of a finite tree: every finite binary tree has finite height, and an infinite finitely branching tree cannot have bounded height. The limit is the least fixed point in $[0,1]$, since iteration from zero stays below any nonnegative fixed point. The roots are $1$ and $(1-p)/p$, giving the stated $q_p$. The stream is finite exactly when the derivation is finite: every nonempty expansion emits an opening and any derivation with only finitely many nonempty expansions has only finitely many nodes.

Each prefix in $E_k$ is uniquely $u\,a\,b\,\overline b$, where $u$ is a valid prefix of length $k-3$. Such an extension is always valid, has height $h(u)+1$, and has the $a$-opening as its top unmatched opening. Its cylinder weight is $w_p(u)(p/2)^2(1-p)$. Summing the four choices of $a,b$ and then all $u$ gives $p^2(1-p)s_{p,k-3}$. Divide by $s_{p,k}$ and use monotonicity from step 1.1 to obtain the bound. Flipping $a$ changes no count, leaves the suffix pattern valid, and changes only position $k-2$; applying the flip twice restores the prefix. There are no fixed points, so its orbits are disjoint equal-mass pairs with swapped closing targets.

After a valid prefix of height $h$, the left-to-right residual derivation contains exactly $h+1$ still independent $S$ subtrees (and $h$ pending closing brackets). Its probability of eventual termination is therefore $q_p^{h+1}$. Consequently the termination-conditioned prefix cylinder is $w_p(x)q_p^{h(x)+1}/q_p=(pq_p/2)^{o(x)}((1-p)/q_p)^{c(x)}$. The fixed-point equation gives $(1-p)/q_p=1-pq_p$. This is exactly $w_a(x)$ with $a=pq_p$. The finite-word laws likewise agree, either by the same calculation including the final epsilon or directly from step 1.2. Applying step 2.1 with $a$ gives its pairing bound. Finally all typed Dyck words of a fixed length have the same mass by step 1.2 and there are finitely many of them, proving the uniform exact-length law and the asserted distinction of conditioning.

Let $\Sigma$ be a finite token alphabet, let $\mathtt{eos}\notin\Sigma$ be an end-of-sequence symbol, and let $d,L,H\ge1$ be fixed integers. For each length $n\ge1$, an input is $(x_1,\ldots,x_{n-1},\mathtt{eos})$. A symbol embedding assigns a vector $v_a\in\mathbb R^d$ to each $a\in\Sigma\cup\{\mathtt{eos}\}$; a positional embedding sequence assigns $p_i\in\mathbb R^d$ independent of the input symbols. A fixed shared input map gives $y_i^{(0)}=f_{\rm in}(v_{x_i},p_i)$. For each layer $k=1,\ldots,L$ and head $h=1,\ldots,H$, a fixed score map $s_{k,h}:\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ gives scores $a_{i,j}^{(k,h)}=s_{k,h}(y_i^{(k-1)},y_j^{(k-1)})$ for every query position $i$ and key position $j$. In the soft model, $\widehat a_{i,\cdot}^{(k,h)}=\operatorname{softmax}(a_{i,\cdot}^{(k,h)})$. In the hard model, $\widehat a_{i,j}^{(k,h)}=1$ at the smallest index $j$ attaining $\max_{r\le n}a_{i,r}^{(k,h)}$ and is $0$ at other indices. With fixed value maps $V_{k,h}:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ and fixed positionwise maps $F_k:(\mathbb R^d)^{H+1}\to\mathbb R^d$, the update is

$$
b_{i,k,h}=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\widehat a_{i,j}^{(k,h)}V_{k,h}(y_j^{(k-1)}),\qquad y_i^{(k)}=F_k(y_i^{(k-1)},b_{i,k,1},\ldots,b_{i,k,H}).
$$

Each score, value, and positionwise map is shared across positions and is fixed independently of $n$. In the hard-attention limit theorem, the score, value, and positionwise maps may be arbitrary fixed maps; no activation-function or parameter-norm bound is imposed. For the soft-influence theorem below, each score is a scaled dot product of fixed linear query and key projections, each value map is a fixed linear map, the token and positional embeddings are uniformly bounded over all positions and lengths, the combined initial states satisfy $\sup_{i\ge1,\ a\in\Sigma\cup\{\mathtt{eos}\}}\|f_{\rm in}(v_a,p_i)\|_2<\infty$, and every positionwise map is globally Lipschitz. The initial-state bound holds for addition or concatenation of bounded embeddings, but must be imposed separately for an arbitrary input map. A hard-attention recognizer classifies the input from $y_n^{(L)}$ after reading $\mathtt{eos}$. A soft next-token predictor applies a fixed linear logit map and softmax to $y_n^{(L)}$ to obtain a probability vector on a fixed finite alphabet.

Let $D$ be a dependency digraph for finite events $(A_i)_{i\in I}$. If there are reals $0\le x_i<1$ such that
$$\mathbb P(A_i)\le x_i\prod_{j\in N_D^+(i)}(1-x_j)$$
for every $i$, then
$$\mathbb P\!\left(\bigcap_{i\in I}A_i^c\right)\ge\prod_{i\in I}(1-x_i)>0.$$

derivations.claim: Choose $0<\eta<1/4$ so that $(1-2\eta)C>C'$, then choose $0<\delta<1$ and $0<q<1/(1+\delta)$ so that $(1-(1+\delta)q)(1-2\eta)C>C'$. Put $D=\lceil c/(\eta C)\rceil$ and regard $k\ge1$ as an integer parameter whose finitely many lower bounds will be fixed after the local-lemma estimates. For each position $j$, choose a support $S_j$ of at most $c$ currently free input positions determining its layer-zero activation. There are at most $cn$ incidences between supports and positions. Fix every free input position occurring in more than $D$ supports, using any fixed symbol. At most $cn/D\le\eta Cn$ positions are fixed; afterwards every free input position belongs to at most $D$ supports.

For a current restriction and query triple $(i,h,z)$, where $h$ is a head at position $i$ and $z$ is a possible layer-zero activation at $i$, at most $cD$ key positions have supports intersecting $S_i$; call these exceptional. For every other key position $j$, its support is disjoint from $S_i$, so the maximum score $m_j$ for query value $z$ is attainable by assigning its free support. Order these eligible positions by decreasing $m_j$, breaking ties by position, and put $R=\lceil cD(k+1)\rceil$. For all sufficiently large $n$, at least $R$ eligible positions exist. Greedily select $k$ among the first $R$ with pairwise disjoint supports: each choice removes at most $cD$ candidates because its support has at most $c$ symbols and each symbol occurs in at most $D$ supports. Record for each selected position a support assignment attaining its maximum.

If a selected support is fixed to its recorded maximum-attaining assignment, that key's score is at least $m_R$. Every eligible position after the first $R$ has maximum score at most $m_R$; equality is resolved in favor of a position among the first $R$ by the chosen tie order. Hence a head's winner lies among the exceptional positions or the first $R$ eligible positions. The first-layer output at position $i$ is therefore determined by $S_i$ and the supports of at most $Hs^c(cD+R)$ candidate key positions, one set for each possible query activation, head, and key. It depends on at most $c'=c+Hs^c c(cD+R)$ original input positions.

Starting from the restriction in step 1.1, repeatedly recompute the candidate sets in step 2.1 for every still-uncaptured triple. When a triple is captured, retain its current exceptional set and first-$R$ eligible positions as its candidate set. Its assigned cutoff key remains at least as highly scored as every later position in the old eligible ordering, since refinements leave its score fixed and can only decrease other attainable maxima; any position that later leaves the eligible set was already in the retained exceptional set. If some key activation is selected in more than $s^c kH$ uncaptured triples, one of its at most $s^c$ possible values is a recorded maximum for more than $kH$ of them. Fix its at most $c$ free input symbols to a support assignment producing that value. The query values of those triples remain unchanged, so all become captured. There are at most $s^cHn$ triples, so this process has at most $s^c n/k$ refinements and fixes at most $s^c c n/k$ additional symbols. Require $k$ large enough that $s^c c/k\le\eta C$. At termination at least $(1-2\eta)Cn$ inputs remain free, and each key activation is selected in at most $T=s^c kH$ uncaptured triples.

For each uncaptured triple $t=(i,h,z)$, let $X_t$ be the event that none of its $k$ selected supports is fixed to its recorded maximum-attaining assignment by the random restriction [A1]. An assignment on $r\le c$ free symbols has probability $(q/s)^r\ge(q/s)^c$. The selected supports are pairwise disjoint, so these assignment events are independent and $\mathbb P(X_t)\le a^k$, where $a=1-(q/s)^c<1$.

Let $m$ be the number of free inputs after step 3.2 and let $X_0$ be the event that more than $(1+\delta)qm$ of them are fixed by [A1]. For $Z\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(m,q)$ and $\mu=mq$, exponential Markov at $t=\log(1+\delta)$ gives $\mathbb P(Z\ge(1+\delta)\mu)\le e^{-t(1+\delta)\mu}(1-q+qe^t)^m\le e^{-\mu((1+\delta)\log(1+\delta)-\delta)}\le e^{-\delta^2\mu/3}$. The middle inequality uses $1+u\le e^u$. For the last, $g(\delta)=(1+\delta)\log(1+\delta)-\delta-\delta^2/3$ has $g(0)=0$ and $g'(\delta)=\log(1+\delta)-2\delta/3\ge0$ on $[0,1]$, since $\log(1+\delta)\ge2\delta/(2+\delta)\ge2\delta/3$. Consequently $\mathbb P(X_0)\le e^{-\alpha n}$, where $\alpha=\delta^2q(1-2\eta)C/3>0$.

For each event $X_t$, take its defining-coordinate set to be the union of its query support and its $k$ selected key supports. Join two $X_t$ events when these sets overlap, and join $X_0$ to every $X_t$. Each coordinate occurs in at most $DHs^c$ query supports: at most $D$ position supports contain it, and each such position has at most $Hs^c$ head-and-query-value triples. It occurs in at most $Ds^cT$ selected key supports: each of at most $D$ position supports has at most $s^c$ possible key activations, and each activation is selected in at most $T$ triples by step 3.2. Each event uses at most $c(k+1)$ coordinates, so its degree is at most $f=1+c(k+1)D(Hs^c+s^cT)=O(k^2)$. Non-neighbours' defining-coordinate sets are disjoint from the event's set; product independence therefore gives independence from every conjunction of their complements, as required by [F2]. Set $x_{X_0}=1/2$ and $x_{X_t}=1/k^2$. Since $a=1-(q/s)^c<1$ and $f=O(k^2)$, the quantity $k^{-2}(1/2)(1-k^{-2})^f$ is bounded below by a positive constant times $k^{-2}$ for large $k$, whereas $a^k$ decays exponentially. Thus the local-lemma condition holds for every $X_t$ once $k$ is sufficiently large.

There are at most $s^cHn$ events other than $X_0$. Its local-lemma condition follows if $e^{-\alpha n}\le\tfrac12(1-k^{-2})^{s^cHn}$. Choose $k$ large enough that $s^cH[-\log(1-k^{-2})]<\alpha$; the inequality then holds for all sufficiently large $n$. The stage-two, local-event, and $X_0$ requirements are finitely many eventual lower bounds on $k$, so they hold simultaneously for sufficiently large $k$. By [F2], a refinement avoiding $X_0$ and every $X_t$ exists.

Avoiding $X_0$ leaves at least $(1-(1+\delta)q)m\ge(1-(1+\delta)q)(1-2\eta)Cn>C'n$ free inputs by the choices in step 1.1. Avoiding every $X_t$ captures each remaining triple. For a captured triple, its retained cutoff key and candidate set from step 3.2 continue to block every later eligible position; for an uncaptured triple, step 6.1 fixes a cutoff key from its final candidate set. Step 3.1 therefore confines each head's winner to at most $cD+R$ candidate positions for each query value. Taking the union over at most $s^c$ query values and $H$ heads, together with the query support, gives the dependence bound $c'=c+Hs^c c(cD+R)$. Replacing each layer-zero activation by its first-layer output absorbs one layer while preserving the model's restricted computation.

Apply the one-layer reduction successively to the fixed $L$ layers, choosing intermediate fractions $C=C_0>C_1>\cdots>C_L=C'$. Each stage has a finite dependence bound and a finite length threshold. Since $L$ is finite, their maximum threshold is finite; beyond it, the final restriction leaves at least $C'n$ inputs free and the final output depends on a bounded number of original inputs. This proves the Statement.

citations.quote: Fix a finite content alphabet $\Sigma$ with $s=|\Sigma|\ge2$, a hard-attention model with fixed $H\ge1$ heads per position and $L\ge1$ layers, and an integer $c\ge1$. At length $n$, the model input is $(x_1,\ldots,x_{n-1},\mathtt{eos})$, with the end marker fixed at position $n$. An input restriction assigns each content position $i<n$ either $*$ (free) or a fixed symbol of $\Sigma$; its free positions are precisely the content positions marked $*$. Say that a layer-zero activation, including the activation at the end-marker position, depends on at most $c$ free positions if, with the restriction fixed, its value is determined by at most $c$ of the remaining free input symbols. Suppose the current restriction leaves at least $Cn$ content positions free for every sufficiently large $n$, where $0<C\le1$, and every layer-zero activation depends on at most $c$ free positions. For every $0<C'<C$, there are an integer $c'\ge1$ and a refinement, for every sufficiently large $n$, that leaves at least $C'n$ content positions free and preserves the model's output on every completion, while absorbing the first remaining attention layer into new layer-zero activations that each depend on at most $c'$ original content positions. Repeating this conclusion through the fixed $L$ layers gives a restriction with at least $C'n$ free content positions on which the output depends on at most a constant number of original content positions. The constants and the length threshold may depend on the fixed model, $c,C,C'$, but not on $n$.

Let $\Sigma$ be a finite token alphabet, let $\mathtt{eos}\notin\Sigma$ be an end-of-sequence symbol, and let $d,L,H\ge1$ be fixed integers. For each length $n\ge1$, an input is $(x_1,\ldots,x_{n-1},\mathtt{eos})$. A symbol embedding assigns a vector $v_a\in\mathbb R^d$ to each $a\in\Sigma\cup\{\mathtt{eos}\}$; a positional embedding sequence assigns $p_i\in\mathbb R^d$ independent of the input symbols. A fixed shared input map gives $y_i^{(0)}=f_{\rm in}(v_{x_i},p_i)$. For each layer $k=1,\ldots,L$ and head $h=1,\ldots,H$, a fixed score map $s_{k,h}:\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ gives scores $a_{i,j}^{(k,h)}=s_{k,h}(y_i^{(k-1)},y_j^{(k-1)})$ for every query position $i$ and key position $j$. In the soft model, $\widehat a_{i,\cdot}^{(k,h)}=\operatorname{softmax}(a_{i,\cdot}^{(k,h)})$. In the hard model, $\widehat a_{i,j}^{(k,h)}=1$ at the smallest index $j$ attaining $\max_{r\le n}a_{i,r}^{(k,h)}$ and is $0$ at other indices. With fixed value maps $V_{k,h}:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ and fixed positionwise maps $F_k:(\mathbb R^d)^{H+1}\to\mathbb R^d$, the update is

$$
b_{i,k,h}=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\widehat a_{i,j}^{(k,h)}V_{k,h}(y_j^{(k-1)}),\qquad y_i^{(k)}=F_k(y_i^{(k-1)},b_{i,k,1},\ldots,b_{i,k,H}).
$$

Each score, value, and positionwise map is shared across positions and is fixed independently of $n$. In the hard-attention limit theorem, the score, value, and positionwise maps may be arbitrary fixed maps; no activation-function or parameter-norm bound is imposed. For the soft-influence theorem below, each score is a scaled dot product of fixed linear query and key projections, each value map is a fixed linear map, the token and positional embeddings are uniformly bounded over all positions and lengths, the combined initial states satisfy $\sup_{i\ge1,\ a\in\Sigma\cup\{\mathtt{eos}\}}\|f_{\rm in}(v_a,p_i)\|_2<\infty$, and every positionwise map is globally Lipschitz. The initial-state bound holds for addition or concatenation of bounded embeddings, but must be imposed separately for an arbitrary input map. A hard-attention recognizer classifies the input from $y_n^{(L)}$ after reading $\mathtt{eos}$. A soft next-token predictor applies a fixed linear logit map and softmax to $y_n^{(L)}$ to obtain a probability vector on a fixed finite alphabet.

derivations.claim: Let the model have $L$ layers and let $N=n+1$ be the number of input positions for a word of length $n$, including its fixed end marker. Initially each free layer-zero state depends on its own input symbol. For all sufficiently large $n$, at least $0.99N$ positions are free, since only the end-marker position is fixed. Apply [F1] successively through the $L$ layers, using free fractions $0.99=C_0>C_1>\cdots>C_L=0.9$. For every sufficiently large $n$, this gives a restriction leaving at least $0.9N$ free word positions and a constant $c_L$ such that the classification output depends on at most $c_L$ input positions.

Now suppose the model recognizes $\mathrm{2DYCK}$. Its restriction to the two-symbol subalphabet consisting of one opening bracket and its matching closing bracket would recognize the one-type Dyck language, whose words have equal numbers of opening and closing brackets and nonnegative opening-minus-closing count at every prefix. Fix an even word length $n$, put $N=n+1$, and let $m=\lfloor n/5\rfloor$. Initially fix the first $m$ word symbols to the opening bracket and the last $m$ word symbols to the closing bracket; leave the middle symbols free and keep the end marker fixed. For all sufficiently large even $n$, at least $0.59N$ positions are free. By [F1], with final free fraction $0.55$, refine this restriction so the model output depends on at most $c_L$ input positions and at least $0.55N$ word positions remain free. If $t$ middle positions were additionally fixed, then $$ t\le n-2m-0.55N\le0.06N $$ for all sufficiently large $N$. Also $m\ge N/5-6/5$, so $m>t$.

Choose $n$ large enough that $0.9N>c_L$. Some free bit position $i$ is not among the at most $c_L$ positions determining the output. Complete the restriction arbitrarily to a word $w$, and let $w'$ be obtained by flipping bit $i$. Their model outputs agree because all input positions on which the output depends agree, but exactly one of $w,w'$ has an even number of ones. Thus no such model classifies all length-$n$ words exactly as $\mathrm{PARITY}$.

Let $f_o$ be the number of additionally fixed middle symbols that are opening brackets, and let $M=n-2m-t$ be the number of still-free middle positions. Assign an opening bracket to the first $r=n/2-m-f_o$ still-free positions in their order, and assign a closing bracket to the rest. Since $m+t<n/2$, we have $r\ge0$ and $$ M-r=n/2-m-t+f_o>0. $$ The completed word has exactly $n/2$ opening brackets, hence total balance zero. A prefix before the last of the assigned free opening brackets has height at least $m-t>0$, because at most $t$ fixed middle symbols are closings. After that last free opening, every still-free middle symbol is a closing. For any later prefix ending in the middle segment, its remaining suffix contains the final $m$ fixed closings and at most $t$ fixed openings, so its net opening-minus-closing count is at most $t-m<0$. Since the whole word has total balance zero, every such middle prefix has positive height. The final $m$ closing brackets decrease the height from $m$ to zero. Thus this completion is a valid one-type Dyck word.

At least $0.55N$ positions remain free, so for sufficiently large $n$ there is a free word position $i$ outside the at most $c_L$ positions determining the model output. Flip its bracket in the valid completion from step 2.2. The new word is unbalanced, while the model output is unchanged because position $i$ does not affect that output. This contradicts recognition of the one-type Dyck language. Any exact recognizer for $\mathrm{2DYCK}$ would restrict to an exact recognizer for this one-type sublanguage, so no such hard-attention model recognizes $\mathrm{2DYCK}$.

derivations.claim: There are constants $B_k<\infty$ such that $\|y_j^{(k)}\|_2\le B_k$ for every position $j$, input length $n$, and input pair. At layer zero this follows from $y_j^{(0)}=v_{x_j}+p_j$ and the bounded token and positional embeddings. If it holds at layer $k-1$, each value vector has norm at most $\|V_{k,h}\|B_{k-1}$ and each attention output is a convex combination of those values by [F1]; the fixed globally Lipschitz positionwise map is bounded on this resulting bounded set. Induction gives all $B_k$.

Consequently every dot-product score at every layer has absolute value at most some $A_k<\infty$. For any row with $n$ keys, its softmax weight $a_j$ is at most $e^{2A_k}/n$, since its numerator is at most $e^{A_k}$ and its denominator is at least $n e^{-A_k}$.

We prove by induction on $k$ that for constants $D_k,E_k$ independent of $n$, the changed position satisfies $\|y_i^{(k)}-y_i'^{(k)}\|_2\le D_k$, while every $j
e i$ satisfies $\|y_j^{(k)}-y_j'^{(k)}\|_2\le E_k/n$. This holds at $k=0$ because only the bounded token embedding at $i$ changes. Assume it holds at $k-1$ and fix a query position $j
e i$ and one head. Its query changes by $O(1/n)$. Its key at position $i$ can change by $O(1)$, while all other keys change by $O(1/n)$, using the fixed linear matrices and the induction hypothesis. Hence its score-difference vector $\Delta$ has $|\Delta_i|\le K$ and $|\Delta_r|\le K/n$ for $r
e i$, for a constant $K$ independent of $n$.

Interpolate the two score vectors linearly. All interpolated scores remain in $[-A_k,A_k]$, so the distinguished key has softmax weight at most $e^{2A_k}/n$ throughout by step 2.1. For softmax probabilities $a_r(t)$, differentiation gives $a_r'(t)=a_r(t)(\Delta_r-\sum_s a_s(t)\Delta_s)$; therefore $\sum_r|a_r'(t)|\le2\sum_r a_r(t)|\Delta_r|=O(1/n)$, and integration yields $\|a-a'\|_1=O(1/n)$.

The head values are uniformly bounded by step 1.1. Splitting the difference of the two weighted sums into (i) the change of values under the first attention row and (ii) the change of attention weights applied to the second value list gives $\|b_{j,k,h}-b'_{j,k,h}\|_2=O(1/n)$: the changed value at $i$ has weight $O(1/n)$, all other value changes are $O(1/n)$, and the total weight change is $O(1/n)$ by step 4.1. Let $h,d_q,d_k,d_v,d_h,d_{vh},d_o,n_q,n_k$ be positive integers. For query, key, and value matrices $Q\in\mathbb R^{n_q\times d_q}$, $K\in\mathbb R^{n_k\times d_k}$, and $V\in\mathbb R^{n_k\times d_v}$, choose matrices $W_i^Q\in\mathbb R^{d_q\times d_h}$, $W_i^K\in\mathbb R^{d_k\times d_h}$, and $W_i^V\in\mathbb R^{d_v\times d_{vh}}$ for each head $i=1,\ldots,h$, and choose $W^O\in\mathbb R^{h d_{vh}\times d_o}$. The $i$-th head is

$$
H_i=\operatorname{Attn}(QW_i^Q,KW_i^K,VW_i^V)\in\mathbb R^{n_q\times d_{vh}},
$$

where $\operatorname{Attn}$ is scaled dot-product attention, with any chosen mask applied to its score matrix. Multi-head attention is

$$
\operatorname{MHA}(Q,K,V)=\operatorname{Concat}_{\rm feature}(H_1,\ldots,H_h)W^O\in\mathbb R^{n_q\times d_o}.
$$

Self-attention is the specialization $Q=K=V=X$ for a single token matrix $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$; each row is one token representation. Unmasked self-attention permits every query row to use every key row. Masked self-attention applies one specified mask to every head.

derivations.claim: For one head, write $Q=XW^Q$, $K=XW^K$, and $V=XW^V$. On input $PX$, the projections are $PQ$, $PK$, and $PV$. The unmasked score matrix therefore becomes $(PQ)(PK)^{\mathsf T}=P(QK^{\mathsf T})P^{\mathsf T}$.

Row softmax commutes with simultaneous row and column permutation: every row's logits are merely reordered, so its normalized entries are reordered by the same permutation. Thus $\operatorname{softmax}_{\rm row}(PSP^{\mathsf T})=P\operatorname{softmax}_{\rm row}(S)P^{\mathsf T}$; multiplying by $PV$ gives $P\operatorname{softmax}_{\rm row}(S)V$. Concatenation and the shared output projection preserve this identity, and so does the residual addition.

A shared positionwise map applies the same function to each row, hence maps $PX$ to the permutation of its outputs. Rowwise layer normalization has the same property because each row's mean and variance are unchanged by reordering rows. Combining these identities with the attention and residual identity in step 2.1 shows that one encoder layer is equivariant; induction over the finite stack gives $T(PX)=PT(X)$.

For a masked head, transforming the mask to $PMP^{\mathsf T}$ gives the same score-and-weight calculation as steps 1.1–2.1, proving the stated mask identity. A permutation preserving the causal mask must preserve the relation $j\le i$ on the finite chain $1<\cdots<n$; its unique least element must map to itself, and then induction on the remaining ordered positions makes every position fixed. Therefore only the identity preserves the standard causal mask.

citations.quote: Let $\mathrm{PARITY}=\{w\in\{0,1\}^*: w\text{ contains an even number of }1\text{s}\}$. Let $\mathrm{2DYCK}$ be the language over $\{(,),[,]\}$ of words whose brackets are correctly balanced and properly nested by type. No fixed finite-depth hard-attention sequence model with a fixed finite number of heads, fixed maps independent of input length, and a fixed classification readout from its end-marker state classifies every sufficiently long input exactly as a member or nonmember of $\mathrm{PARITY}$; no such model recognizes $\mathrm{2DYCK}$ either. Exact recognition means that the model's binary output equals the language membership indicator for every input word, with the end marker appended before the model is evaluated.

Fix $p\in(0,1)$. Generate a bit string by a two-state process whose state is the parity of the number of emitted $1$s: in the even state it terminates with probability $p$, and otherwise emits $0$ or $1$ with probability $(1-p)/2$ each; in the odd state it emits $0$ or $1$ with probability $1/2$ each and cannot terminate. For each $n\ge2$, let $D_n$ be the law of length-$(n-1)$ prefixes conditional on the process emitting at least $n-1$ bits, and ask a fixed soft-attention model to predict the next symbol in $\{\mathtt{eos},0,1\}$ from that prefix followed by the end marker. Let $r_x$ be the true next-symbol distribution and let $q_n(x)$ be the model's predicted distribution. Define cross-entropy by $\operatorname{CE}(r,q)=-\sum_a r(a)\log q(a)$, with value $+\infty$ if $r(a)>0=q(a)$, and entropy by $H(r)=-\sum_{a:r(a)>0}r(a)\log r(a)$. Then every fixed soft-attention model satisfying the one-symbol influence hypotheses has

$$\liminf_{n\to\infty}\mathbb E_{x\sim D_n}\operatorname{CE}(r_x,q_n(x))\ge H(u),\qquad u(\mathtt{eos})=p/2,\quad u(0)=u(1)=(2-p)/4.$$
A constant predictor $q_n(x)=u$ attains $H(u)$ for every $n$, so $H(u)$ is the sharp unigram chance level. An arbitrary fixed predictor may have greater cross-entropy; this result gives no soft-attention exact-classification impossibility theorem.

Fix $p\in(0,1)$ and let $D_n$ be a probability law on valid length-$(n-1)$ prefixes over $\{(,),[, ]\}$. Let $E_n$ be a union of disjoint equal-mass pairs $\{x,x'\}$ in the support of $D_n$ such that each prefix in a pair ends in a closing bracket and has positive stack height after that bracket; $x'$ is obtained by changing the type of the top unmatched opening bracket in $x$, at a position before the final prefix symbol. Assume that, conditional on $x$, the next-symbol law assigns probability $p/2$ to each opening bracket and probability $1-p$ to the closing bracket matching its top unmatched opening, and that the law conditional on $x'$ swaps the two possible closing-bracket types while leaving the opening probabilities unchanged. If $D_n(E_n)\ge P_0>0$ for all sufficiently large $n$, then every fixed soft-attention predictor satisfying the one-symbol influence hypotheses has

$$
\liminf_{n\to\infty}\bigl(\mathcal L_n-\mathcal L_n^*\bigr)\ge P_0(1-p)\log 2,
$$

where $\mathcal L_n$ is expected next-symbol cross-entropy and $\mathcal L_n^*=\mathbb E_{x\sim D_n}H(r_x)$ is the optimal conditional cross-entropy. This lemma requires the positive-mass paired-prefix hypothesis; it does not assert that a particular PCFG supplies that hypothesis.

Fix $p\in(0,1)$. Independently expand each nonterminal of the grammar $S\to(S)S$, $S\to[S]S$, $S\to\epsilon$ with respective probabilities $p/2,p/2,1-p$, and read the yield from left to right. Equivalently, start with an empty bracket stack and repeatedly choose an opening bracket of either type with probability $p/2$ each, pushing its type; with probability $1-p$, close the top bracket when the stack is nonempty, or emit $\mathtt{eos}$ and stop when it is empty. This defines a probability law on finite words followed by $\mathtt{eos}$ and on infinite bracket streams. For a valid bracket prefix $x$, let $o(x),c(x)$ and $h(x)=o(x)-c(x)$ denote its opening count, closing count and final stack height. Its cylinder probability is
$$
w_p(x)=(p/2)^{o(x)}(1-p)^{c(x)}.
$$
For every $k\ge0$, let $s_{p,k}=\sum_{|x|=k}w_p(x)$, summing over valid prefixes, and define $D_{p,k}(x)=w_p(x)/s_{p,k}$. Thus $D_{p,k}$ conditions only on having emitted at least $k$ bracket tokens, without conditioning on eventual termination or exact total length. The target after a sampled prefix is its ordinary next token in the same process. At positive height its law assigns $p/2$ to each opening type and $1-p$ to the matching closing type.

For $k\ge3$, let $E_k$ consist of prefixes whose last three symbols are an opening of type $a$, an opening of type $b$, and the closing of type $b$, with $a,b$ independently ranging over the two types. These prefixes have positive final height and end in a closing bracket. Flipping the opening type $a$ at position $k-2$ is a fixed-point-free involution of $E_k$ into equal-mass pairs; paired prefixes differ only at this nonfinal position and their top unmatched opening types are opposite. Moreover,
$$
D_{p,k}(E_k)=p^2(1-p)\frac{s_{p,k-3}}{s_{p,k}}\ge p^2(1-p)>0.
$$

The finite-word mass of a typed Dyck word of length $2m$ is $(p/2)^m(1-p)^{m+1}$. The total finite-word mass is $q_p=1$ for $p\le1/2$ and $q_p=(1-p)/p$ for $p>1/2$. After conditioning on eventual termination, the finite-word probability law and all its prefix laws are exactly those of the preceding process with parameter $a=pq_p=\min(p,1-p)$; consequently its survival-conditioned prefixes have the same pairing bound $a^2(1-a)$. Conditioning instead on exact word length $2m$ yields the uniform law on typed Dyck words of that length, independently of $p$; that conditioning is different and does not retain the displayed next-token probabilities.

Put $n=k+1$ and append the fixed readout end marker to each sampled length-$k$ prefix. By [F4], every prefix in the paired event ends with a closing bracket and has positive stack height; the flipped opening at position $k-2$ is nonfinal. The pair members have equal probability and ordinary next-token laws assigning $p/2$ to each opening and $1-p$ to opposite matching closing types. Hence all hypotheses of [F3] hold with $P_0=p^2(1-p)$. It gives excess cross-entropy at least $p^2(1-p)^2\log2$ in the lower limit. Under conditioning on eventual termination, [F4] identifies the entire prefix and target process with parameter $a=\min(p,1-p)$. Repeat step 1.3 with $a$ to prove the finite-word bound. The finite-word mass and extinction calculation in [F4] give the stated distinction between the two laws. At $p=1/2$, let $G_j$ be the nodes in generation $j$ of the derivation tree. A finite-generation induction gives $\mathbb E|G_j|=(2p)^j=1$ for every $j$. Hence the number $Z_N=\sum_{j=0}^{N}|G_j|$ of nodes through generation $N$ has expectation $N+1$. The total node count $Z$ is at least $Z_N$, so monotonicity of expectation gives $\mathbb E Z\ge N+1$ for every $N$ and therefore $\mathbb E Z=\infty$, without interchanging an expectation with an infinite sum. Finite derivations are full binary trees, and their word length is their node count minus one; thus the finite-word law has infinite expected length. Neither pairing proof uses finite expected length.
