Let $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$ be a sequence matrix whose rows are token representations, and let $P$ be any $n\times n$ permutation matrix. Every finite composition $T$ of position-shared encoder layers built from unmasked multi-head self-attention, residual additions, rowwise layer normalization, and a shared positionwise feedforward map, with no positional encoding, satisfies

$$
T(PX)=P\,T(X).
$$

For a fixed attention mask $M$, the corresponding layer satisfies $\operatorname{Layer}_{PMP^{\mathsf T}}(PX)=P\operatorname{Layer}_{M}(X)$. Hence every permutation that leaves a fixed mask $M$ unchanged is an equivariance of the corresponding layer. The standard causal mask $M_{ij}=0$ for $j\le i$ and $M_{ij}=-\infty$ for $j>i$ is preserved only by the identity permutation.

For a sequence of length $n$ with $d$-dimensional token representations, a positional encoding is a fixed or trainable matrix $P\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$ added rowwise to the token matrix $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$, giving $X+P$. One fixed choice, with positions $s\in\mathbb N_0$ and coordinates indexed from $0$, is $P_{s,2r}=\sin(s/10000^{2r/d})$ and $P_{s,2r+1}=\cos(s/10000^{2r/d})$ whenever the indicated coordinate is less than $d$.

For decoder self-attention on $n$ positions indexed by $0,\ldots,n-1$, the causal mask is $M\in(\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty\})^{n\times n}$ with $M_{ij}=0$ when $j\le i$ and $M_{ij}=-\infty$ when $j>i$. Thus query position $i$ can use keys at positions $0,\ldots,i$ and cannot use a future position; every row has an allowed key because $M_{ii}=0$.

derivations.claim: Put $u=(1,\delta^{-1},\ldots,\delta^{-d+1})$. For a grid column $x=(a_1\delta,\ldots,a_d\delta)$, where $a_i\in\{0,\ldots,m-1\}$, its scalar code is $$\ell(x)=u^{\mathsf T}x,\qquad \ell(x)/\delta=a_1+a_2m+\cdots+a_dm^{d-1}.$$ Thus the valid column codes are distinct multiples of $\delta$ in $[0,B]$, where $B=\delta(q-1)$. If a column has a sentinel coordinate $-\delta^{-nd}$, the sum of all its other coordinate contributions is at most $\delta^{-d+1}-1$, so its code is at most $-\delta^{-nd}+\delta^{-d+1}-1<0$.

For a scalar threshold $b$, the single-head update $$ \psi(Z;b)=e_1(u^{\mathsf T}Z)\operatorname{hmax}\!\left((u^{\mathsf T}Z)^{\mathsf T}(u^{\mathsf T}Z-b\mathbf1_n^{\mathsf T})\right) $$ is an allowed attention update contribution: its key and value projections are $u$, its query projection is $u$ with bias $-b$, and its output vector is $e_1$. In query column $j$, if $\ell_j>b$ it returns the largest current scalar code, and if $\ell_j<b$ it returns the smallest. If $\ell_j=b$, all query scores are zero and equal-weight hardmax returns the mean $\bar\ell=n^{-1}\sum_k\ell_k$. Thus, writing $\ell_{\max}=\max_k\ell_k$ and $\ell_{\min}=\min_k\ell_k$, the contribution $\psi(Z;b)-\psi(Z;b')$ for $b<b'$ is $\ell_{\max}-\ell_{\min}$ in the first coordinate when $b<\ell_j<b'$, $\bar\ell-\ell_{\min}$ when $\ell_j=b$, $\ell_{\max}-\bar\ell$ when $\ell_j=b'$, and zero when $\ell_j<b$ or $\ell_j>b'$. In particular, if no current code equals either threshold, it shifts exactly the columns strictly between them by $\ell_{\max}-\ell_{\min}$.

Sweep the valid scalar codes $0,\delta,\ldots,B$ in increasing order, using the two-head update $\;Z\mapsto Z+q(\psi(Z;\ell-\delta/2)-\psi(Z;\ell+\delta/2))\;$ at code $\ell$. All initial codes, including sentinel codes, are multiples of $\delta$: every grid coordinate lies in $\delta\mathbb Z$ and every entry of $u$ is an integer. Since $q=m^d$ is an integer, each strict selective shift preserves this lattice; inductively no current code can equal any half-grid threshold $\ell\pm\delta/2$. This also applies to duplicate-column inputs and to the position-tagged lattice. For $L\in\widehat G_\delta$, order its distinct column codes as $\ell_1<\cdots<\ell_n$. The first sweep shifts only $\ell_1$ to $\widetilde\ell_1=\ell_1+q(\ell_n-\ell_1)>B$, since $\ell_n-\ell_1\ge\delta$ and $q\delta=B+\delta$. Each later sweep shifts the next unmodified code and gives $$ \widetilde\ell_j=\ell_j+q(\widetilde\ell_{j-1}-\ell_j)>\widetilde\ell_{j-1}\qquad(2\le j\le n). $$ Thus shifted columns leave all later threshold intervals, and the final scalar codes satisfy $0<\widetilde\ell_1<\cdots<\widetilde\ell_n$.

Write $g_j=\ell_{j+1}-\ell_j\ge\delta$. Unrolling the recurrence in step 2.1 gives $$ t:=\widetilde\ell_n=\ell_n+\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}(q^n-q^{n-j})g_j. $$ Consequently $$\delta q^{n-1}(q-1)\le t\le \delta q^n(q-1)-\delta(q-1)^2.$$ The lower bound follows from the $j=1$ term; the upper bound follows from $\ell_n\le B$ and $\sum_jg_j\le B$. The map $(\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_n)\mapsto t$ is injective: if two ordered tuples give the same $t$, put $a_j=(\ell_j-\ell'_j)/\delta\in\mathbb Z$, so $|a_j|\le q-1$. The difference equation is $$ a_n+q(a_{n-1}-a_n)+\cdots+q^{n-1}(a_1-a_2)+q^n(a_n-a_1)=0. $$ Reduction modulo $q$ first gives $a_n=0$; division by $q$ and repeated reduction modulo $q$ then gives $a_{n-1}=0,\ldots,a_1=0$. Hence distinct unordered column multisets have distinct $t$ values, separated by at least $\delta$.

Apply one final single-head update $Z\mapsto Z+K\psi(Z;0)$, with a positive integer $K$. For valid $L$, all $\widetilde\ell_j>0$, so it adds $Kt$ to every first coordinate and changes the scalar codes to $$ c_{L,j}=Kt+\widetilde\ell_j. $$ For different column multisets, their $t$ values differ by at least $\delta$, while $0<\widetilde\ell_j\le t$. Choose $K$ so that $K\delta>\max t$ over the finite valid grid. The intervals $[Kt,Kt+t]$ for different multisets are disjoint, and codes within one multiset are distinct by step 2.1. All resulting codes are multiples of $\delta$, hence distinct codes are at least $\delta$ apart.

If $L$ has duplicate columns but no sentinel, its scalar codes have only $r<n$ distinct levels. The same sweep shifts these $r$ levels, and its largest value is at most $\delta q^r(q-1)-\delta(q-1)^2\le\delta q^{n-1}(q-1)-\delta(q-1)^2$, strictly below the lower bound for valid $t$ in step 3.1. A sentinel column has a negative code by step 1.1 and remains the minimum throughout the sweep. If all codes are negative, the final update in step 4.1 shifts every code further negative. If some codes are nonnegative, the first nonnegative code is shifted by at least $q(q^n-B)>\delta q^{n+1}$; the later positive codes are shifted by still larger amounts. This exceeds every valid $t$ in step 3.1. Thus, after the final update, each invalid scalar code has one of three forms: below every valid code, above every valid code, or negative. Since there are finitely many grid inputs and all codes are multiples of $\delta$, choose $K$ large enough that every invalid code lies at least $\delta$ outside the interval from the least to the greatest valid code.

The preceding construction gives a finite scalar code for each token of each valid context; these codes are all distinct, and column permutations carry each code and its token to the corresponding permuted token by [F2]. Let $\lambda_-$ and $\lambda_+$ be the least and greatest valid codes. Because the table $A$ and grid are finite, enlarge $K$ so that $|u^{\mathsf T}A(L)_{:,j}|<\lambda_- -\delta/3$ for every valid $L,j$. A three-piece constant activation that is zero on $[\lambda_- -\delta/3,\lambda_+ +\delta/3]$ and one outside this interval detects exactly the invalid codes. Subtracting a constant larger than the maximum absolute coordinate of every encoded grid state makes every invalid state strictly negative; for each coordinate $r$, the allowed residual update $Z\mapsto Z+e_r\operatorname{ReLU}(-e_r^{\mathsf T}Z)$ replaces that coordinate by $z_r+\max(0,-z_r)=\max(0,z_r)$. These $d$ updates send every invalid state to zero and leave every valid, coordinatewise nonnegative state unchanged. For each valid code $c_{L,j}$, a three-piece pulse equal to one on $[-\delta/3,\delta/3]$ and zero outside, applied to $u^{\mathsf T}Z-c_{L,j}$, selects exactly its token. Add the vector $A(L)_{:,j}-Z_{:,j}$ at that token. The updated token has scalar value $u^{\mathsf T}A(L)_{:,j}$ below every code, so later pulses cannot select it; the remaining tokens retain their codes until selected. Equivariance of $A$ makes each update correct for every permutation of $L$. This yields $A(L)$ on $\widehat G_\delta$ and zero on every other point of $G_\delta^+$.

For the position-tagged grid, the scalar code of column $j$ has the form $$ \ell_j=(j-1)S+r_j,\qquad S=\sum_{k=0}^{d-1}\delta^{-k},\quad 0\le r_j\le B,\quad r_j\in\delta\mathbb Z. $$ Since $S-B\ge\delta$, codes in a matrix satisfy $\ell_1<\cdots<\ell_n$ and each individual code identifies its column vector. Choose an integer $Q\ge q$ with $Q\delta>(n-1)S+B$. Sweep all possible position-tagged scalar codes in increasing order, replacing the shift multiplier $q$ in step 2.1 by $Q$. All codes remain in $\delta\mathbb Z$, so none equals a half-grid threshold. Since distinct initial codes differ by at least $\delta$, the first shifted code exceeds the largest possible initial code, and each subsequent shifted code exceeds its predecessor. Thus the recurrence of step 2.1 holds with $Q$ in place of $q$, and different matrices give different ordered tuples $(\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_n)$. The divisibility argument in step 3.1 applies modulo $Q$: for each fixed position, the offsets $(j-1)S$ cancel and the difference of two $r_j$ values divided by $\delta$ has magnitude at most $q-1<Q$. Thus the final maxima $t$ distinguish all position-tagged matrices, and the codes $Kt+\widetilde\ell_j$ distinguish every token in every matrix when $K\delta>\max t$. Choose $K$ still larger so these positive codes exceed all finitely many target values $|u^{\mathsf T}A(L)_{:,j}|+\delta/3$. The pulse layers of step 6.1 then implement the arbitrary table $A$; no permutation condition is needed because the position offsets distinguish columns.

Each update used above is either a two-head attention update, a single-head attention update with the second head set to zero, or a tokenwise scalar piecewise-affine update; an unused attention or feedforward sublayer is made the identity by setting its output weights to zero. Therefore the finite constructions are compositions of the modified Yun blocks specified in the Statement, proving both lookup assertions.

citations.quote:
**Inputs:** A nonempty source token sequence $(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$, a target prefix $(y_0,\ldots,y_{m-1})$ with $m\ge1$ and a start token $y_0$, source and target embedding maps into $\mathbb R^d$, positional encoding matrices of compatible shapes, a finite encoder stack, a finite decoder stack, and a linear output map to a finite vocabulary of logits. Each layer has the parameters and conventions in the transformer encoder/decoder definition. All self-attention and cross-attention masks must leave at least one allowed key in every query row.

**Procedure:**

1. Embed each source token and add its positional vector to form $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$.
2. Apply the encoder layers in order to $X$ and call the final matrix $E\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$.
3. Embed each target-prefix token and add its positional vector to form $U\in\mathbb R^{m\times d}$.
4. Apply each decoder layer in order. In every decoder layer, use the causal mask on decoder self-attention, use the current decoder rows as queries and $E$ as keys and values for cross-attention, and then apply the positionwise feedforward sublayer.
5. Apply the output linear map to each final decoder row and apply softmax over vocabulary coordinates. Return the encoder matrix $E$, the final decoder hidden matrix, and the rowwise next-token probability matrix.

**Outputs:** The source representations, decoder representations, and one probability vector for each target-prefix position. At position $i$, the decoder self-attention calculation uses only target-prefix positions $j\le i$; the encoder cross-attention may use every source position.

derivations.claim: For one head of width $d_h$, the score product has dimensions $(n\times d_h)(d_h\times n)$ and therefore uses $O(n^2d_h)$ scalar multiply-adds. The value product has dimensions $(n\times n)(n\times d_h)$ and also uses $O(n^2d_h)$ operations.

For finite real scores, every softmax weight is strictly positive, so each output row uses the value row of every input position. This is one direct attention edge; composing $L$ layers yields at most one such edge per layer, hence at most $L$ attention edges independent of $n$.
Summing over $h$ heads with total width $\sum_{a=1}^h d_h^{(a)}=d$ gives $O(n^2d)$ score and value work. Normalizing $n$ rows of $n$ scores costs $O(n^2)$, which is at most $O(n^2d)$ because $d\ge1$.

A dense projection of an $n\times d$ matrix by a $d\times d$ matrix costs $O(nd^2)$, and a two-map positionwise feedforward network of hidden width $d_{\rm ff}$ costs $O(ndd_{\rm ff})$. Adding these separate terms gives the full-layer operation count stated in the Statement.

citations.quote:
Let $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$ be a sequence matrix whose rows are token representations, and let $P$ be any $n\times n$ permutation matrix. Every finite composition $T$ of position-shared encoder layers built from unmasked multi-head self-attention, residual additions, rowwise layer normalization, and a shared positionwise feedforward map, with no positional encoding, satisfies

$$
T(PX)=P\,T(X).
$$

For a fixed attention mask $M$, the corresponding layer satisfies $\operatorname{Layer}_{PMP^{\mathsf T}}(PX)=P\operatorname{Layer}_{M}(X)$. Hence every permutation that leaves a fixed mask $M$ unchanged is an equivariance of the corresponding layer. The standard causal mask $M_{ij}=0$ for $j\le i$ and $M_{ij}=-\infty$ for $j>i$ is preserved only by the identity permutation.

Let $d\ge1$, $n\ge2$, $m\ge2$ be integers, set $\delta=1/m$ and $q=\delta^{-d}$, and assume $n\le q$. Define
$$G_\delta=\{0,\delta,\ldots,1-\delta\}^{d\times n},\qquad G_\delta^+=\{-\delta^{-nd},0,\delta,\ldots,1-\delta\}^{d\times n}.$$
Let $\widehat G_\delta$ consist of those $L\in G_\delta$ whose columns are pairwise distinct. For column-token matrices $Z\in\mathbb R^{d\times n}$, consider finite compositions of residual attention updates
$$Z\longmapsto Z+\sum_{h=1}^{2}o_h(v_h^{\mathsf T}Z)\, \operatorname{hmax}\!\left((k_h^{\mathsf T}Z)^{\mathsf T}(r_h^{\mathsf T}Z+b_h\mathbf1_n^{\mathsf T})\right)$$
and residual tokenwise updates
$$
Z\longmapsto Z+w\,\phi(v^{\mathsf T}Z+b\mathbf1_n^{\mathsf T}),
$$
where all displayed vectors and scalars are fixed across columns, $\operatorname{hmax}$ assigns equal weights to all maximizing entries in each column, and each scalar $\phi$ is piecewise affine on at most three intervals with at least one constant piece. If $A:\widehat G_\delta\to\mathbb R^{d\times n}$ satisfies $A(LP)=A(L)P$ for every column-permutation matrix $P$, then such a composition maps each $L\in\widehat G_\delta$ to $A(L)$ and each $L\in G_\delta^+\setminus\widehat G_\delta$ to $0$.

There is also a position-tagged version. For each $j=1,\ldots,n$, let
$$J_j=\{j-1,j-1+\delta,\ldots,j-\delta\}^d,\qquad G_{\delta,\mathrm{pos}}=J_1\times\cdots\times J_n,$$
where the $j$th factor specifies column $j$. For every function $A:G_{\delta,\mathrm{pos}}\to\mathbb R^{d\times n}$, with no permutation condition, a finite composition of the same updates maps each $L\in G_{\delta,\mathrm{pos}}$ to $A(L)$.

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space), let
$(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space (Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric) and let $f : X \to Y$ be
continuous (Continuity of a map between metric spaces, at a point and globally, in the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ form). Then $f$ is uniformly continuous
(Uniform continuity of a map of metric spaces: one $\delta$ serving every point).

No choice principle is used: the cover built below is cut out by a property, and
the Lebesgue number lemma it is fed to is itself choice free
(Every open cover of a compact metric space has a Lebesgue number: a $\delta > 0$ such that every nonempty subset of diameter less than $\delta$ lies inside a single member of the cover).

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
(The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)). Then:

1. $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and
   $\lambda_n$ is a measure on it (Measures on sigma-algebras);
2. the measure space $(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n), \lambda_n)$ is
   complete (Complete measure spaces), and every $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   with $\lambda_n^*(S) = 0$ is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(S) = 0$;
3. every elementary set is Lebesgue measurable and
   $\lambda_n(A) = \mu_0(A)$ for every $A \in \mathcal{E}_n$; in particular
   $\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ for every half-open box $B$,
   $\lambda_n(\varnothing) = 0$ and $\lambda_n(\mathbb{R}^n) = +\infty$.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
(The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

(Axis-parallel rectangles in $\mathbb{R}^m$ and their volume). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of Half-open boxes in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and their volume, and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ (Assuming countable choice, $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra containing every elementary set and $\lambda_n$ is a complete measure extending elementary volume).

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
(The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)). Then

$$\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n) \;\subseteq\; \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n) :$$

every Borel subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ (The Borel sigma-algebra of a topological space) is Lebesgue
measurable (Lebesgue measurable sets, the family $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$, and the restricted set function $\lambda_n$). In
particular every open set, every closed set and every countable intersection of
open sets is Lebesgue measurable.

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a decreasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$. If $\mu(E_{n_0})<+\infty$ for some $n_0$, then

$$\mu\left(\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\inf_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

derivations.claim: First consider the compactly supported equivariant map. If $f=0$, the zero Transformer suffices. Otherwise its support $K$ is a nonempty compact permutation-invariant set. Compactness bounds all scalar entries of matrices in $K$; choose real $a<b$ with every entry in $[a,b]$. Since a nonzero continuous function is nonzero on an open set, $K$ has positive measure and the bounds can be chosen with $a<b$. The common affine map $T(X)=(X-a\mathbf1)/(b-a)$ sends $K$ into $[0,1]^{d\times n}$ and commutes with column permutations. A residual width-four ReLU sublayer implements $z\mapsto\alpha z+\beta$ on every feature by $$ z+(\alpha-1)\bigl(\operatorname{ReLU}(z)-\operatorname{ReLU}(-z)\bigr)+\beta=\alpha z+\beta; $$ two hidden units handle one feature and finitely many layers handle all $d$ features. Thus $T$ can be inserted in the Yun architecture.

Now consider continuous $f$ on compact $K$ without symmetry. If $K$ has zero Lebesgue measure, the integral is zero for any network. Otherwise let $a,b$ be the minimum and maximum of its scalar entries; again $a<b$. Put $\alpha=(b-a)^{-1}$ and choose $$ E_{rj}=(b-a)(j-1)-a\qquad(1\le r\le d,\ 1\le j\le n). $$ The first residual width-four sublayers scale $X+E$ by $\alpha$, producing entries $(X_{rj}-a)/(b-a)+(j-1)$. For any mesh $\delta=1/m$ used below, put $\eta_\delta(t)=-t$ for $0\le t<\delta$ and $\eta_\delta(t)=0$ otherwise. For each feature row, apply the residual updates $t\mapsto t+\eta_\delta(t-k)$ in increasing order for $k=0,\delta,\ldots,n-\delta$. The $k$th update sends exactly $[k,k+\delta)$ to $k$ and leaves values outside that interval unchanged; hence every column-$j$ value in $[j-1,j)$ is mapped to one of $j-1,j-1+\delta,\ldots,j-\delta$. Entries exactly at an upper endpoint lie on finitely many coordinate hyperplanes of measure zero and do not affect the integral. Thus the quantized matrices lie in $G_{\delta,\mathrm{pos}}$ from [F3], where position offsets make every column distinct. For each grid cell meeting $K$, choose a representative $X_L\in K$ and set $A(L)=f(X_L)$; set arbitrary values, for example zero, on cells disjoint from $K$. The position-tagged assertion of [F3] realizes this finite table exactly.

It remains to replace the modified gates and uniform hardmax in [F3] by the standard ReLU and softmax of $\mathcal T^{2,1,4}$. Consider any scalar gate $\phi$ that is affine on the three intervals cut by $c_1<c_2$, with formulas $a_1t+b_1$, $a_2t+b_2$, and $a_3t+b_3$, and with at least one $a_i=0$. Fix $0<\rho<(c_2-c_1)/2$. Replace the parts on $[c_1-\rho,c_1]$ and $[c_2-\rho,c_2]$ by linear ramps joining the left, middle, and right affine pieces, and leave $\phi$ unchanged elsewhere. The resulting continuous piecewise-affine map has knots $r_1=c_1-\rho$, $r_2=c_1$, $r_3=c_2-\rho$, $r_4=c_2$ and successive slopes $s_0=a_1$, $s_1$, $s_2=a_2$, $s_3$, $s_4=a_3$. Put $\Delta_i=s_i-s_{i-1}$. It is a constant plus four ReLUs: use $\Delta_i\operatorname{ReLU}(t-r_i)$ at knots not in $S$ and $\Delta_i\operatorname{ReLU}(r_i-t)$ at knots in $S$, choosing any applicable case $S=\varnothing$ if $a_1=0$, $S=\{1,2\}$ if $a_2=0$, or $S=\{1,2,3,4\}$ if $a_3=0$; add the constant that matches the left affine piece. In each case the left-tail slope is $-\sum_{i\in S}\Delta_i=a_1$ and the right-tail slope is $\sum_{i\notin S}\Delta_i=a_3$, while the slope jump at each knot is $\Delta_i$, so this formula is exact outside the two ramp intervals. It covers the middle-constant sentinel gate as well as the constant-ended pulse and clamp gates used below. The two-piece clipping gate $\phi(t)=-t$ for $t<0$ and $0$ for $t\ge0$ is exactly $\operatorname{ReLU}(-t)$. A width-four ReLU sublayer realizes each ramped scalar gate, including its constant bias, in the modified residual update. On bounded input regions the ramp error is confined to strips whose widths tend to zero with $\rho$. For any finite score vector $s$, softmax of $\lambda s$ converges as $\lambda\to\infty$ to equal weights on its maximizing coordinates and zero elsewhere; hence it converges to the uniform hardmax used in [F3].

Choose $\delta=1/m$ with integer $m$ large enough that $n\le\delta^{-d}$, the duplicate-cell bound below is small, and $M=\delta^{-nd}>d+1+\log(n)/\lambda$ for a fixed $\lambda>0$. Let $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$ be a sequence matrix whose rows are token representations, and let $P$ be any $n\times n$ permutation matrix. Every finite composition $T$ of position-shared encoder layers built from unmasked multi-head self-attention, residual additions, rowwise layer normalization, and a shared positionwise feedforward map, with no positional encoding, satisfies

$$
T(PX)=P\,T(X).
$$

For a fixed attention mask $M$, the corresponding layer satisfies $\operatorname{Layer}_{PMP^{\mathsf T}}(PX)=P\operatorname{Layer}_{M}(X)$. Hence every permutation that leaves a fixed mask $M$ unchanged is an equivariance of the corresponding layer. The standard causal mask $M_{ij}=0$ for $j\le i$ and $M_{ij}=-\infty$ for $j>i$ is preserved only by the identity permutation.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice, fix integers $d\ge1$ and $n\ge2$, and fix $1\le p<\infty$. For a matrix $Y\in\mathbb R^{d\times n}$, let $\|Y\|_p=(\sum_{r=1}^d\sum_{j=1}^n|Y_{rj}|^p)^{1/p}$, and for measurable maps on $\mathbb R^{d\times n}$ define
$$
d_p(f,g)=\left(\int_{\mathbb R^{dn}}\|f(X)-g(X)\|_p^p\,dX\right)^{1/p},
$$
using $dn$-dimensional Lebesgue measure. Let $\mathcal T^{2,1,4}$ be the finite compositions of the two-head, head-size-one Yun blocks with tokenwise ReLU feedforward width four and no layer normalization. If $f:\mathbb R^{d\times n}\to\mathbb R^{d\times n}$ is continuous, has compact support, and satisfies $f(XP)=f(X)P$ for every $n\times n$ permutation matrix $P$, then for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $g\in\mathcal T^{2,1,4}$ with $d_p(f,g)<\varepsilon$.

For every compact $K\subseteq\mathbb R^{d\times n}$ and every continuous $f:K\to\mathbb R^{d\times n}$, with no permutation condition, there are a trainable positional matrix $E\in\mathbb R^{d\times n}$ and $g\in\mathcal T^{2,1,4}$ such that
$$
\left(\int_K\|f(X)-g(X+E)\|_p^p\,dX\right)^{1/p}<\varepsilon.
$$

The map $f$ is continuous on $K=[0,1]^{1\times2}$, which is compact, and $n=2,d=1$ meet the size hypotheses. Under the assumed Countable Choice, the position-encoded compact-domain branch of [F2] with any prescribed $\varepsilon>0$ gives a position-encoded stack whose integrated $L_p$ error from $f$ is less than $\varepsilon$. Thus positional tags remove the equivariance restriction for this fixed-length approximation problem.

Let $n_q,n_k,d_k,d_v$ be positive integers, let $Q\in\mathbb R^{n_q\times d_k}$ and $K\in\mathbb R^{n_k\times d_k}$ be query and key matrices, and let $V\in\mathbb R^{n_k\times d_v}$ be a value matrix. For a real matrix $S$ with $n_q$ rows and $n_k$ columns, define its row softmax by $\operatorname{softmax}_{\rm row}(S)_{ij}=\exp(S_{ij})/\sum_{\ell=1}^{n_k}\exp(S_{i\ell})$. The scaled dot-product attention output is

$$
\operatorname{Attn}(Q,K,V)=\operatorname{softmax}_{\rm row}\!\left(\frac{QK^{\mathsf T}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V\in\mathbb R^{n_q\times d_v}.
$$

Each output row is the weighted average of the value rows, with weights given by the softmax of that query's scaled dot products with all keys. A mask is an array $M\in(\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty\})^{n_q\times n_k}$ whose entries are $0$ for allowed query-key pairs and $-\infty$ for disallowed pairs; masked attention replaces the score matrix by $QK^{\mathsf T}/\sqrt{d_k}+M$ before row softmax and is defined only when every row has at least one allowed key. Here $\exp(-\infty)=0$.

For a sequence of length $n$ with $d$-dimensional token representations, a positional encoding is a fixed or trainable matrix $P\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$ added rowwise to the token matrix $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$, giving $X+P$. One fixed choice, with positions $s\in\mathbb N_0$ and coordinates indexed from $0$, is $P_{s,2r}=\sin(s/10000^{2r/d})$ and $P_{s,2r+1}=\cos(s/10000^{2r/d})$ whenever the indicated coordinate is less than $d$.

For decoder self-attention on $n$ positions indexed by $0,\ldots,n-1$, the causal mask is $M\in(\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty\})^{n\times n}$ with $M_{ij}=0$ when $j\le i$ and $M_{ij}=-\infty$ when $j>i$. Thus query position $i$ can use keys at positions $0,\ldots,i$ and cannot use a future position; every row has an allowed key because $M_{ii}=0$.

In the second row the mask leaves logits $(0,0)$, whose row-softmax is $(1/2,1/2)$; multiplying by $(1,3)^{\mathsf T}$ gives output $2$. Both rows have at least one allowed key, so the masked attention is defined.

Let $\mathrm{PARITY}=\{w\in\{0,1\}^*: w\text{ contains an even number of }1\text{s}\}$. Let $\mathrm{2DYCK}$ be the language over $\{(,),[,]\}$ of words whose brackets are correctly balanced and properly nested by type. No fixed finite-depth hard-attention sequence model with a fixed finite number of heads, fixed maps independent of input length, and a fixed classification readout from its end-marker state classifies every sufficiently long input exactly as a member or nonmember of $\mathrm{PARITY}$; no such model recognizes $\mathrm{2DYCK}$ either. Exact recognition means that the model's binary output equals the language membership indicator for every input word, with the end marker appended before the model is evaluated.

Fix $p\in(0,1)$. Generate a bit string by a two-state process whose state is the parity of the number of emitted $1$s: in the even state it terminates with probability $p$, and otherwise emits $0$ or $1$ with probability $(1-p)/2$ each; in the odd state it emits $0$ or $1$ with probability $1/2$ each and cannot terminate. For each $n\ge2$, let $D_n$ be the law of length-$(n-1)$ prefixes conditional on the process emitting at least $n-1$ bits, and ask a fixed soft-attention model to predict the next symbol in $\{\mathtt{eos},0,1\}$ from that prefix followed by the end marker. Let $r_x$ be the true next-symbol distribution and let $q_n(x)$ be the model's predicted distribution. Define cross-entropy by $\operatorname{CE}(r,q)=-\sum_a r(a)\log q(a)$, with value $+\infty$ if $r(a)>0=q(a)$, and entropy by $H(r)=-\sum_{a:r(a)>0}r(a)\log r(a)$. Then every fixed soft-attention model satisfying the one-symbol influence hypotheses has

$$\liminf_{n\to\infty}\mathbb E_{x\sim D_n}\operatorname{CE}(r_x,q_n(x))\ge H(u),\qquad u(\mathtt{eos})=p/2,\quad u(0)=u(1)=(2-p)/4.$$
A constant predictor $q_n(x)=u$ attains $H(u)$ for every $n$, so $H(u)$ is the sharp unigram chance level. An arbitrary fixed predictor may have greater cross-entropy; this result gives no soft-attention exact-classification impossibility theorem.

The collection

$$\mathcal{T}_d := \{\, U \subseteq X : U \text{ is open in } (X,d) \,\}$$

of all open subsets is the **metric topology** of $d$ on $X$. A subset of $X$
that is both open and closed is called **clopen**.

**Two sets are open for trivial reasons.** $\emptyset$ is open, because the
defining condition quantifies over no points; and $X$ is open, because
$B(x,r) \subseteq X$ for every $x$ and every $r > 0$. Consequently $X$ and
$\emptyset$ are also closed, and both are clopen.

**A neighbourhood of a point $x$** is any set containing an open set that
contains $x$; an **open neighbourhood** is an open set containing $x$. In a
metric space, a set is a neighbourhood of $x$ exactly when it contains some
ball $B(x,r)$ with $r>0$. Thus $U$ is open exactly when it is a neighbourhood of
each of its points, and metric balls suffice to test this condition.

**The metric, not the set, determines $\mathcal{T}_d$.** Two metrics on the same
set may have different metric topologies, and two different metrics may have the
same one; the systematic comparison is Topologically, uniformly and Lipschitz equivalent metrics on a set.

This family covers $f[K]$ by openness and [F3], so [F1] gives a finite subcover with centers $y_1,\ldots,y_s$ and radii $r_1,\ldots,r_s$. Since $f[K]\ne\emptyset$, $s\ge1$; let $\delta=\min_i r_i>0$. Assume Countable Choice. Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded Lipschitz open set, with $d\ge1$, and let $m\in\mathbb N_0$. Let $X$ be either $W^{m,p}(D;\mathbb R)$ for $1\le p<\infty$, including $W^{0,p}(D)=L^p(D)$, or $C^m(\bar D;\mathbb R)$. In the latter space derivatives in $D$ extend continuously to $\bar D$, and the norm is $\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_{\bar D}|D^\alpha u|$. For every norm-compact $K\subseteq X$ and every $\varepsilon>0$, there is a bounded finite-rank linear map $F:X\to X$ such that $\sup_{u\in K}\|Fu-u\|_X<\varepsilon$ and whose range is contained in the restrictions to $D$ of functions in $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$, with their continuous boundary values in the $C^m$ case. In particular, such smooth restrictions are norm-dense in $X$.

Moreover, there are finitely many ambient smooth cutoffs $\psi_j$, vectors $v_j$, a unit-mass $\rho\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$, and $t_0>0$ such that for $0<t<t_0$ the kernel $k_t(x,y)=\sum_j\psi_j(x)\rho_t(x+tv_j-y)$, with $\rho_t(z)=t^{-d}\rho(z/t)$, defines bounded linear smoothing maps $S_tu(x)=\int_Dk_t(x,y)u(y)\,dy$. They satisfy $\sup_{0<t<t_0}\|S_t\|_{X\to X}<\infty$ and $\sup_{u\in K}\|S_tu-u\|_X\to0$ for every norm-compact $K\subset X$. Each kernel is ambient smooth with fixed compact support in its first variable.

Let $X$ be a Banach space. It has the **approximation property** (AP) if for
every norm-compact set $C\subseteq X$ and every $\varepsilon>0$ there is a
bounded finite-rank operator $T:X\to X$ such that

$$\sup_{x\in C}\|Tx-x\|<\varepsilon.$$

Here finite rank means that $T(X)$ is finite-dimensional.

For $\lambda\ge0$, $X$ has the **$\lambda$-bounded approximation property**
($\lambda$-BAP) if the same assertion holds with the additional operator-norm
bound $\|T\|\le\lambda$, where the norm is that of [[def-operator-norm]]. It
has the **bounded approximation property** (BAP) if it has $\lambda$-BAP for
some finite $\lambda$.

No sequence of approximating operators is required; this matters in
nonseparable spaces. Plainly $\lambda$-BAP implies AP.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
The space $L^p(\mu)$ as the quotient by null functions and
Complex Lp classes and Euclidean test-function conventions. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
The $L^p$ norm descends to the quotient and makes $L^p$ a normed space for $1 \le p \le \infty$
for real scalars and
Complex Holder, Minkowski, and the quotient norm for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
Weak derivative of a locally integrable function. Under
The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
Weak differentiation ignores null-set changes, while
Uniqueness of a weak derivative as an almost-everywhere class gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Assume Countable Choice for the weak-derivative uniqueness interface. Let
$\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, and
$1\le p\le\infty$. For either real or complex scalars, the displayed
$W^{k,p}(\Omega)$ formula from
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]] is independent of the representatives
of its Sobolev and derivative classes and defines a norm: it is finite,
absolutely homogeneous, subadditive, and zero exactly on the zero $L^p$ class.
This holds at $p=1$ and $p=\infty$, and when $k=0$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the only class is zero and the formula is zero.

Assume countable choice (in particular, the Axiom of Choice suffices). Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $1\le p\le\infty$. Then
$L^p(\mu)$, with the norm of
The $L^p$ norm descends to the quotient and makes $L^p$ a normed space for $1 \le p \le \infty$, is
complete. Equivalently, the metric induced by that norm is a complete metric in
the sense of Complete metric space: every Cauchy sequence converges in the space.

Moreover, if a sequence in $L^p(\mu)$ converges in norm, then some subsequence
admits measurable representatives converging almost everywhere in the sense of
Convergence almost everywhere relative to a measure.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the Lebesgue-measure interfaces. Let $X$ be a real or complex Banach space, let $a<b$, and let $f:[a,b]\to X$ be continuous. Differentiation uses the underlying real structure. Then $G(t):=\int_a^t f(s)\,ds$ is differentiable on $(a,b)$ and has the corresponding one-sided derivatives at $a,b$, with $G'(t)=f(t)$, and this derivative extends continuously to $[a,b]$. Consequently, if $\varphi:[a,b]\to X$ is continuous, differentiable on $(a,b)$ with $\varphi'$ continuous on $(a,b)$ and extendable to a continuous $X$-valued function on $[a,b]$, then $\int_a^b\varphi'(s)\,ds=\varphi(b)-\varphi(a)$. The Bochner integral here is the one of [[def-bochner-integrable-function]]; the identities also hold for continuous curves on $[0,\infty)$ restricted to compact subintervals.

derivations.claim: The listed Sobolev spaces are Banach under the stated Countable Choice hypothesis. Indeed, let $(u_n)$ be Cauchy in $W^{m,p}(D)$. By [F3], for each of the finitely many $|\alpha|\le m$, $D^\alpha u_n$ converges in $L^p$ to a class $v_\alpha$; put $u=v_0$. For any $\phi\in C_c^\infty(D)$, its derivatives are bounded with compact support, hence belong to the conjugate $L^{p'}$ space, including $p'=\infty$ when $p=1$. By [F4], both integrals in $\int_Du_nD^\alpha\phi=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_DD^\alpha u_n\phi$ converge to the corresponding integrals of $u$ and $v_\alpha$. Thus $v_\alpha$ is the weak derivative $D^\alpha u$ by [F3], so $u\in W^{m,p}(D)$, and the finite norm sum gives $u_n\to u$ in that norm. This includes $m=0$, which gives $L^p(D)$.

The listed $C^m(\bar D)$ spaces are Banach as well. If $(u_n)$ is Cauchy in their norm, every derivative sequence has a uniform limit $g_\alpha$ on $\bar D$: pointwise real completeness gives the limit, and the uniform Cauchy estimate gives uniform convergence. Each $g_\alpha$ is continuous, since for a positive error one first approximates it uniformly by a fixed continuous $D^\alpha u_n$ and then applies continuity of that fixed function. Put $u=g_0$. For $|\alpha|<m$, an interior point $x$, and a coordinate direction $e_i$, take $h$ small enough that the segment $x+[0,h]e_i$ lies in $D$. By [F5], $D^\alpha u_n(x+he_i)-D^\alpha u_n(x)=\int_0^hD^{\alpha+e_i}u_n(x+se_i)\,ds$. Uniform convergence passes this identity to $g_\alpha(x+he_i)-g_\alpha(x)=\int_0^h g_{\alpha+e_i}(x+se_i)\,ds$, since the integral error is bounded by $|h|$ times the uniform error. By [F5], $\partial_i g_\alpha=g_{\alpha+e_i}$. Induction in $|\alpha|$ yields $D^\alpha u=g_\alpha$ in $D$ through order $m$, with the continuous extensions already supplied on $\bar D$. Thus $u\in C^m(\bar D)$ and $u_n\to u$ in norm. For $m=0$ only the uniform-limit continuity argument is needed. The displayed maximum is a norm because its order-zero term detects zero functions and the remaining norm axioms hold termwise.

Fix one listed space $X$, a norm-compact $K\subseteq X$, and $\varepsilon>0$. Its Banach-space status was established in the two preceding steps. Apply [F1], using $W^{0,p}=L^p$ in the Lebesgue case, to obtain a bounded finite-rank $F:X\to X$ with $\sup_{u\in K}\|Fu-u\|_X<\varepsilon$. These are exactly the quantified requirements of [F2], so every listed space has AP, including every $p=1$ case.

The argument in step 2.1 holds for every Euclidean dimension, every nonnegative integer regularity and every finite exponent in the stated ranges. Applying it with the output dimension and output regularity parameters proves the output-space clause. The proof establishes AP for $C^m(\bar D)$ without any basis assertion.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of

Choose $\kappa>0$ large enough that $\kappa^2\lambda_0-\kappa B-C_0\ge1$. For $\psi(x)=e^{\kappa x_1}$, [F1] gives $$L[\psi](x)=e^{\kappa x_1}\bigl(\kappa^2a_{11}(x)+\kappa\widetilde b_1(x)+\widetilde c(x)\bigr)\ge e^{\kappa a_1}>0.$$ Choose $M>e^{\kappa b_1}$ and set $\Phi=M-\psi$. Then $\Phi>0$ on $\bar U$ and $L[\Phi]=M\widetilde c-L[\psi]\le-e^{\kappa a_1}$.

Put $R=\|L[w]\|_{C^0(U)}$, $Q=\|w\|_{C^0(\partial U)}$, and $\eta=e^{\kappa a_1}$. For $z=w-Q-(R/\eta)\Phi$, the boundary values satisfy $z\le0$. In $U$, $$L[z]=L[w]-Q\widetilde c-(R/\eta)L[\Phi]\ge -R+R=0,$$ because $-Q\widetilde c\ge0$.

Suppose $z(x_0)>0$ at some $x_0\in U$. Since $z\le0$ on $\partial U$ and $z$ is continuous on $\bar U$, its positive maximum is attained at an interior point. statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(V,H,V^*)$ be the real evolution triple of
[[def-parabolic-evolution-triple-and-energy-space]], and let
$u,v\in W(0,T;V)$. Each has a unique representative in $C([0,T];H)$, and
for all $0\le s\le t\le T$,
$$\|u(t)\|_H^2-\|u(s)\|_H^2 =2\int_s^t\langle u'(r),u(r)\rangle_{V^*,V}\,dr,$$
$$(u(t),v(t))_H-(u(s),v(s))_H =\int_s^t\bigl(\langle u'(r),v(r)\rangle_{V^*,V} +\langle v'(r),u(r)\rangle_{V^*,V}\bigr)\,dr.$$
Writing $c_i=\|i:V\to H\|$, the trace obeys
$$\sup_{0\le t\le T}\|u(t)\|_H^2 \le \frac{c_i^2}{T}\|u\|_{L^2(0,T;V)}^2 +2\|u'\|_{L^2(0,T;V^*)}\|u\|_{L^2(0,T;V)}.$$

Let $V$ and $H$ be real Hilbert spaces and let $i:V\to H$ be an injective,
continuous linear map with dense range. Let $V^*$ be the continuous real linear
dual of $V$. Identify $H$ with its Hilbert dual by its inner product and embed
$H$ into $V^*$ by
$$h\longmapsto\bigl(v\longmapsto (h,i v)_H\bigr).$$
The resulting dense continuous embeddings are written
$$V\hookrightarrow H\cong H^*\hookrightarrow V^*$$
and $(V,H,V^*)$ is called an **evolution triple**. The pairing between $V^*$
and $V$ is denoted $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{V^*,V}$.

For a Hilbert space $X$, $L^2(0,T;X)$ is the space of equivalence classes of
strongly measurable $X$-valued functions $w$ with
$$\int_0^T\|w(t)\|_X^2\,dt<\infty.$$
Strong measurability means being an almost-everywhere pointwise limit of
measurable simple functions. For $u\in L^2(0,T;V)$ and $g\in L^2(0,T;V^*)$,
say that $g$ is the **weak time derivative** of $u$ when
$$\int_0^T (i u(t),i v)_H\,\phi'(t)\,dt =-\int_0^T\langle g(t),v\rangle_{V^*,V}\,\phi(t)\,dt$$
for every $v\in V$ and every $\phi\in C_c^\infty(0,T)$. The derivative is
unique up to equality almost everywhere. The **parabolic energy space** is
$$W(0,T;V):=\{u\in L^2(0,T;V):u'\in L^2(0,T;V^*)\},$$
with norm
$$\|u\|_{W(0,T;V)}:=\bigl(\|u\|_{L^2(0,T;V)}^2+ \|u'\|_{L^2(0,T;V^*)}^2\bigr)^{1/2}.$$
No endpoint values are part of this definition; they are assigned only after
a continuous $H$ trace representative has been proved. Separability is an
additional hypothesis when it is needed by a later result.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ be bounded and open, $d\ge1$, and put $H=L^2(U;\mathbb R)$ and $V=H^1_0(U;\mathbb R)$, where the latter is the $H^1$-closure of $C_c^\infty(U)$. Then $V$ is a separable real Hilbert space, its inclusion into $H$ is continuous, injective and dense, and $(V,H,V^*)$ is a real evolution triple. The gradient norm and the full $H^1$ norm are equivalent on $V$. No regularity of $\partial U$ is required.

Let $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty, bounded, and open, let $T>0$, and set $Q=U\times(0,T)$ and
$$\Gamma_T=(\bar U\times\{0\})\cup(\partial U\times[0,T]).$$
The final-time face $U\times\{T\}$ is excluded from $\Gamma_T$. For time-dependent coefficients define
$$L_t[u]=\sum_{i,j=1}^dD_i(a_{ij}(x,t)D_j u)+\sum_{i=1}^dD_i(b_i(x,t)u)+\sum_{i=1}^d c_i(x,t)D_i u+d(x,t)u.$$
Where the coefficient derivatives exist, write its nondivergence expansion as
$$L_t[u]=\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}D_iD_j u+\sum_i\widetilde b_iD_i u+\widetilde c\,u,$$
where $\widetilde b_i=\sum_jD_j a_{ji}+b_i+c_i$ and $\widetilde c=\sum_iD_i b_i+d$. For symmetric $a$, the drift also equals $\sum_jD_j a_{ij}+b_i+c_i$, the form used by the symmetric source consumers. The initial-boundary value problem uses the sign convention
$$-u_t+L_t[u]=f\quad\hbox{in }Q,\qquad u=\varphi\quad\hbox{on }\partial U\times[0,T],\qquad u=g\quad\hbox{on }\bar U\times\{0\},$$
with compatibility $g(x)=\varphi(x,0)$ on $\partial U$. Its residual for a trial function $h$ is $f+h_t-L_t[h]$, and its prescribed-data error is measured on $\Gamma_T$.

For the source notation $C_{2+\alpha}(Q)$, use the parabolic distance
$$d_p((x,t),(y,s))=(|x-y|^2+|t-s|)^{1/2}.$$
Let $B=U\times\{0\}$ and $S_\tau=\partial U\times[0,\tau]$. For $P=(x,\tau)\in Q$, set $\delta(P)=\inf_{R\in B\cup S_\tau}d_p(P,R)$ and $\delta_{P,Q}=\min\{\delta(P),\delta(Q)\}$. For an integer $m\ge0$, define
$$|v|_{m,\alpha}=\sup_{P\in Q}\delta(P)^m|v(P)|+\sup_{P\ne Q\in Q}\delta_{P,Q}^{m+\alpha}\frac{|v(P)-v(Q)|}{d_p(P,Q)^\alpha}.$$
The class $C_{2+\alpha}(Q)$ consists of functions for which
$$|u|_{0,\alpha}+\sum_i|D_i u|_{1,\alpha}+\sum_{i,j}|D_{ij}u|_{1,\alpha}+|u_t|_{2,\alpha}<\infty,$$
with the indicated derivatives continuous in $Q$. This fixes the source's weighted parabolic Hölder convention.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

derivations.claim: For almost every $t$, by [F4], approximate $e(\cdot,t)$ in $H^1(U)$ by compactly supported smooth functions. For each approximant the distributional definition of the divergence terms gives the spatial integration-by-parts identity; the coefficient bounds make every pairing continuous in $H^1$, so passing to the limit produces no boundary term because $e(\cdot,t)\in H^1_0(U)$. Pair the weak equation $-e_t+L_t[e]=r$ against $e$ in $V^*,V$ and use [F1] and [F2]. Moving the time derivative to the left gives $$\tfrac12 E'(t)+\lambda_0\|\nabla e(t)\|_2^2\le (\|b\|_\infty+\|c\|_\infty)\|e(t)\|_2\|\nabla e(t)\|_2+\|d\|_\infty E(t)+\|r(t)\|_2\|e(t)\|_2,$$ where $E(t)=\|e(t)\|_2^2$.

By Young's inequality, the first product on the right is at most $\frac{\lambda_0}{4}\|\nabla e\|_2^2+C_1E(t)$ and the last product is at most $\frac12\|r(t)\|_2^2+\frac12E(t)$, for a finite $C_1$ depending only on the coefficient bounds and $\lambda_0$. Hence for $C_2=C_1+\|d\|_\infty+\frac12$, $$E'(t)+\lambda_0\|\nabla e(t)\|_2^2\le 2C_2E(t)+\|r(t)\|_2^2.$$

Dropping the nonnegative gradient term in step 2.1 and multiplying by $e^{-2C_2t}$ gives $\frac{d}{dt}(e^{-2C_2t}E(t))\le e^{-2C_2t}\|r(t)\|_2^2$. Integrating from $0$ to any $s\le T$ yields $$\sup_{0\le s\le T}E(s)\le e^{2C_2T}\left(E(0)+\|r\|_{L^2(Q)}^2\right).$$

Integrating step 2.1 from $0$ to $T$ and using step 3.1 gives $$\lambda_0\int_0^T\|\nabla e(t)\|_2^2dt\le E(0)+2C_2T\sup_{0\le t\le T}E(t)+\|r\|_{L^2(Q)}^2.$$ Combining this with step 3.1 and dividing by $\lambda_0>0$ proves the stated estimate after increasing the constant.

Let $n\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be a nonempty bounded open set with
closure $\overline\Omega$ and boundary $\partial\Omega$ in the sense of
[[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]], and let $T>0$. Write
$Q:=\Omega\times(0,T]$ for the **space-time cylinder** and
$$\overline Q:=\overline\Omega\times[0,T]\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}$$
for its closure in the space-time variable; the **final-time face** is
$\Omega\times\{T\}$, while the **parabolic boundary** of $Q$ is
$$\partial_pQ:=(\overline\Omega\times\{0\})\cup(\partial\Omega\times[0,T]).$$
No point of the final-time face belongs to $\partial_pQ$: the intersections
$\bigl(\Omega\times\{T\}\bigr)\cap\bigl(\overline\Omega\times\{0\}\bigr)$ and
$\bigl(\Omega\times\{T\}\bigr)\cap\bigl(\partial\Omega\times[0,T]\bigr)$ are
empty because $T>0$ and $\Omega\cap\partial\Omega=\varnothing$.

A function $u$ on $\overline Q$ is of class $C^{2,1}(\overline Q)$ if it is
continuous there, is $C^2$ in $x$ and $C^1$ in $t$ on $Q$, and the functions
$u_t$ and $D_x^\alpha u$ for $|\alpha|\le2$ extend continuously to
$\overline Q$; the multi-index notation and the classes $C^k$ are those of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], and at $t=T$ the time
derivative means the left one-sided limit. The relevant operator is
$\partial_t-\Delta_x$, the heat operator of
[[def-heat-equation-heat-operator-and-cauchy-problem]], and the phrase
"$u_t-\Delta u\le0$ in $Q$" always refers to that cylinder, with the one-sided
interpretation of $u_t$ on the final-time face.

On this page a **classical heat solution** means a function with the stated $C^{2,1}$ regularity satisfying the equation pointwise; no second time derivative is required. Formulas that put time first use the canonical coordinate permutation $(x,t)\leftrightarrow(t,x)$; regularity and derivatives always refer to the named spatial and time variables. The analogous interior class has the same continuous derivatives without an up-to-boundary requirement.

Two elementary topological facts are part of the vocabulary. First,
$\overline Q$ is compact: $\Omega$ is bounded, so $\overline\Omega$ is closed and
bounded in $\mathbb R^n$, hence compact ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]); then
$\overline Q=\overline\Omega\times[0,T]$ is closed and bounded in
$\mathbb R^{n+1}$, hence compact by the same theorem
([[def-metric-compactness]]). Second, $\partial_pQ$ is closed in
$\mathbb R^{n+1}$, being the union of the two closed sets
$\overline\Omega\times\{0\}$ and $\partial\Omega\times[0,T]$; in particular it
is a closed subset of $\overline Q$
([[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]]).

derivations.claim: Choose $a_1<b_1$ with $a_1\le x_1\le b_1$ on $\bar U$. Let $B=\|\widetilde b_1\|_\infty$, $C_0=\|\widetilde c\|_\infty$, and choose $\kappa>0$ so that $\kappa^2\lambda_0-\kappa B-C_0\ge1$. For $\psi(x,t)=e^{\kappa x_1}$, [F1] gives $P[\psi]=e^{\kappa x_1}(\kappa^2a_{11}+\kappa\widetilde b_1+\widetilde c)\ge\eta:=e^{\kappa a_1}>0$. Choose $M>e^{\kappa b_1}$ and put $\Phi=M-\psi$. Then $\Phi>0$ and $P[\Phi]=M\widetilde c-P[\psi]\le-\eta$.
Let $R=\|P[w]\|_\infty$, $Q_0=\|w\|_{C^0(\Gamma_T)}$, and $z=w-Q_0-(R/\eta)\Phi$. On $\Gamma_T$, $z\le0$, and in $Q$, $$P[z]=P[w]-Q_0\widetilde c-(R/\eta)P[\Phi]\ge-R+R=0.$$

Fix any $0<\tau<T$ and work on $\bar U\times[0,\tau]$, where the time derivatives at spatial interior points at $t=\tau$ exist because $\tau<T$. Suppose $z>0$ somewhere on this stopped cylinder. Since $z\le0$ on $\Gamma_T$, a positive maximum occurs at a spatial interior point and at a time in $(0,\tau]$. For sufficiently small $\delta>0$, $z+\delta\psi$ still has a positive maximum away from $\Gamma_T$. At this maximum, the spatial gradient is zero and the spatial Hessian is negative semidefinite; the time derivative is zero for $t<\tau$ and nonnegative from the left if $t=\tau$. Thus [F2] and $\widetilde c\le0$ imply $P[z+\delta\psi]\le0$, while step 2.1 and step 1.1 give $P[z+\delta\psi]>0$. This contradiction shows $z\le0$ on every stopped cylinder; let $\tau\uparrow T$ and use continuity at the final face. Hence $w\le Q_0+(R/\eta)\|\Phi\|_\infty$.

Apply the same argument to $-w$, for which $P[-w]=-P[w]$ and the boundary norm is still $Q_0$. Combining the upper and lower bounds gives the asserted estimate with $C_P=\max\{1,\|\Phi\|_\infty/\eta\}$.

Inputs are a dimension $d\ge1$, the data and operators specified in the physics-informed residual loss definition, $0<\alpha\le1$, positive weights $\lambda_r,\lambda_b$, and an admissible trial function $h$. The procedure returns the scalar empirical objective value $J_m(h)$. It uses the realized sample points and target values as inputs; it does not generate random samples.

For $d\ge2$, also supply positive integer counts $m_r,m_b$, residual samples $x_r^1,\ldots,x_r^{m_r}\in U$ with their observed values $f(x_r^i)$, boundary samples $x_b^1,\ldots,x_b^{m_b}\in\Gamma$ with their observed values $g(x_b^j)$, constants $c_r,c_b,C_r,C_b>0$, and small-scale cutoffs $\ell_{0,i},\rho_{0,i}>0$. At the selected partition scales $0<\ell_i\le\ell_{0,i}$, require cells $U_j^{\ell_r}$ and $\Gamma_j^{\ell_b}$ with masses at least $c_r\ell_r^d$ and $c_b\ell_b^{d-1}$, each contained in a cube of side $\ell_i$. Require upper ball-mass bounds $\mu_r(\overline B_\rho(x)\cap U)\le C_r\rho^d$ and $\mu_b(\overline B_\rho(y)\cap\Gamma)\le C_b\rho^{d-1}$ for every center and for all $0<\rho\le\rho_{0,i}$. The admissible counts satisfy, for $i\in\{r,b\}$,
$$m_i\ge\max\{1,c_i^{-2}\ell_{0,i}^{-2s_i},c_i^{-2}d^{s_i}\rho_{0,i}^{-2s_i}\},$$
so the computed partition scales and fill radii lie in the specified ranges.

For $d=1$, supply a positive integer $m_r$, residual samples $x_r^1,\ldots,x_r^{m_r}\in U$ with observed values $f(x_r^i)$, constants $c_r,C_r>0$, and cutoffs $\ell_{0,r},\rho_{0,r}>0$. At the residual scale $\ell_r$ below, require a finite measurable partition with each cell contained in an interval of length $\ell_r$ and mass at least $c_r\ell_r$, and require upper ball-mass bounds $\mu_r(\overline B_\rho(x)\cap U)\le C_r\rho$ for every center $x\in U$ and all $0<\rho\le\rho_{0,r}$. The admissible count satisfies
$$m_r\ge\max\{1,c_r^{-2}\ell_{0,r}^{-2},c_r^{-2}\rho_{0,r}^{-2}\},$$
so $\ell_r=\delta_r$ is in the specified ranges. Supply the observed boundary values at every point of the finite set $\Gamma$ with their masses $\mu_b(\{y\})$. No random boundary sample or boundary sample count is used.

For $d\ge2$, set $s_r=d$, $s_b=d-1$, and, for $i\in\{r,b\}$, compute
$$\ell_i=(c_i\sqrt{m_i})^{-1/s_i},\qquad \delta_i=\sqrt d\,\ell_i,\qquad \kappa_i=C_i/c_i,$$
$$C_m=3\max_{i\in\{r,b\}}\{\kappa_i d^{s_i/2}m_i^{1/2}\},\qquad \widehat\lambda^R_{i,m}=\frac{3\lambda_i\delta_i^{2\alpha}}{C_m}.$$
For $d=1$, compute
$$\ell_r=\delta_r=(c_r\sqrt{m_r})^{-1},\qquad \kappa_r=C_r/c_r,\qquad C_m=3\kappa_r m_r^{1/2},$$
$$\widehat\lambda^R_{r,m}=\frac{3\lambda_r\delta_r^{2\alpha}}{C_m} =\frac{\lambda_r c_r^{-2\alpha}}{\kappa_r}m_r^{-\alpha-1/2},\qquad \widehat\lambda^R_{b,m}=0.$$
For $d\ge2$, use supplied regularization weights $\lambda^R_{i,m}$ satisfying $\lambda^R_{i,m}\ge\widehat\lambda^R_{i,m}$ componentwise; for a sequence of sample counts also require $\|\lambda_m^R\|_\infty=O(\|\widehat\lambda_m^R\|_\infty)$. For $d=1$, set $\lambda^R_{b,m}=0$ and choose $\lambda^R_{r,m}\ge\widehat\lambda^R_{r,m}$, with the corresponding one-coordinate max-norm order condition across a sequence of counts. If no residual weights are supplied, set them equal to their thresholds.

Finally evaluate and return $J_m(h)=\operatorname{Loss}_m(h;\lambda,\lambda_m^R)$ using the realized residual values, the realized boundary values when $d\ge2$, the exact weighted full-boundary contribution when $d=1$, and the residual seminorm penalty when $d=1$ or both seminorm penalties when $d\ge2$. The regularization thresholds are the source's exact thresholds and cannot be replaced by a generic positive penalty.

Cancelling the common factor $C_m$ in [F1] gives $$\frac{\lambda^R_{r,m}}{\lambda^R_{b,m}}=\frac{\widehat\lambda^R_{r,m}}{\widehat\lambda^R_{b,m}}=\frac{\lambda_r c_r^{-2\alpha/d}}{\lambda_b c_b^{-2\alpha/(d-1)}}\,n^{\alpha/(d-1)-\alpha/d}=C\,n^{\alpha/(d(d-1))},$$ where $C>0$ is independent of $n$. Let $n\ge1$ be an integer, let $k\ge0$ be an integer, let $0<\alpha<1$ and let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Fix an open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and a function $u\in C^k(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, where $C^k$ and the canonical-order derivatives $D^\beta u$ are those of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. Put
$$[u]_{k,\alpha;\Omega}:=\sum_{|\beta|=k}\ \sup_{\substack{x,y\in\Omega\\ x\ne y}}\frac{|D^\beta u(x)-D^\beta u(y)|}{|x-y|^{\alpha}},\qquad \|u\|_{C^{k,\alpha}(\Omega)}:=\sum_{j=0}^{k}\ \sup_{x\in\Omega}\ \max_{|\beta|=j}|D^\beta u(x)|+[u]_{k,\alpha;\Omega},$$
where the sums and maxima run over the finitely many multi-indices of the stated order. The quantity $[u]_{k,\alpha;\Omega}$ is the **$k$-th order $\alpha$-Hölder seminorm** of $u$ and the quantity $\|u\|_{C^{k,\alpha}(\Omega)}$ the **$C^{k,\alpha}$ norm** of $u$; both are taken in $[0,+\infty]$, so the "norm" may be $+\infty$ and only the class below carries a genuine normed-space structure.

The **local Hölder class** $C^{k,\alpha}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ consists of the $u\in C^k(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $[u]_{k,\alpha;\Omega'}<+\infty$ for every $\Omega'\Subset\Omega$. The **bounded class** $C^{k,\alpha}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=C^{k,\alpha}_b(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ consists of the $u\in C^k(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $\|u\|_{C^{k,\alpha}(\Omega)}<+\infty$. Thus $C^{k,\alpha}(\Omega;\mathbb K)\subseteq C^{k,\alpha}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, and the inclusion may be strict: on $\Omega=\mathbb R^n$ the function $u(x)=\sin(|x|^2)$ lies in the local class (it is $C^1$, hence locally $\alpha$-Hölder on every compact set), while $[u]_{0,\alpha;\mathbb R^n}=+\infty$, because at the points $x_j=\sqrt{2\pi j}\,e_1$ and $y_j=x_j+(2\sqrt{2\pi j})^{-1}e_1$ the difference quotients are $\asymp(2\sqrt{2\pi j})^{\alpha}\to\infty$. On the bounded class the displayed formula is a norm, and the assignment $u\mapsto\|u\|_{C^{k,\alpha}(\Omega)}$ is that norm.

**Scaled interior norm.** For a ball $B_R(x_0)\subseteq\Omega$ of radius $R>0$ and centre $x_0$, write $[v]_{0,\alpha;B}:=\sup\{|v(x)-v(y)|/|x-y|^{\alpha}:x,y\in B,\ x\ne y\}$ for the plain Hölder seminorm on a set $B$, and put
$$\|u\|^{*}_{k,\alpha;B_R(x_0)}:=\sum_{j=0}^{k}R^{j}\max_{|\beta|=j}\ \sup_{B_R(x_0)}|D^\beta u|+R^{k+\alpha}\max_{|\beta|=k}[D^\beta u]_{0,\alpha;B_R(x_0)}.$$
On every ball, $C^{2,\alpha}(B_R(x_0))$ therefore agrees with the finite-scaled-norm class of that dependency. This is the **scaled interior norm** of $u$ on the ball; for $k=2$ it is exactly the scaled quantity of [[def-local-holder-and-c-two-alpha-norms-on-euclidean-balls]], and it takes values in $[0,+\infty]$ as well. It is read off the open ball alone.

**Bounded $C^{k,\alpha}$ domains.** A **bounded $C^{k,\alpha}$ domain** in $\mathbb R^n$ is a bounded nonempty open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with the following local graph property: for every $x\in\partial\Omega$ there are an open neighbourhood $W$ of $x$, a rigid motion $R(p)=Qp+b$ with orthogonal $Q$ and $b\in\mathbb R^n$, an open ball $B\subseteq\mathbb R^{n-1}$ and a function $\varphi\in C^{k,\alpha}(B;\mathbb R)$ such that, after shrinking $W$ so that $R(W)\subseteq B\times\mathbb R$,
$$R(\Omega\cap W)=R(W)\cap\{y=(y',y_n)\in B\times\mathbb R:\ y_n<\varphi(y')\}.$$
This generalises the integer-order notion of [[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]] to the Hölder scale, with the same one-sided graph convention; the regularity $\varphi\in C^{k,\alpha}(B)$ is the only strengthening, connectedness is not required, and no boundary seminorm is attached to the interior norms above. In dimension $n=1$ the corresponding sets are finite disjoint unions of bounded open intervals.

**The boundary-extension class.** Let $\Omega$ be bounded and let $u\in C^{k,\alpha}_b(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Say that $u$ lies in $C^{k,\alpha}(\overline\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when each derivative field $D^\beta u$ with $|\beta|\le k$ extends continuously to $\overline\Omega$. The extension of each field is then unique, since $\Omega$ is dense in $\overline\Omega$, and the sup and Hölder quantities formed with the extended fields and suprema over $\overline\Omega$ agree with those displayed above, formed over $\Omega$: a supremum over the dense subset $\Omega$ already computes the supremum of the extension, and for the seminorm the inequality $[\tilde v]_{0,\alpha;\overline\Omega}\le[v]_{0,\alpha;\Omega}$ follows by approximating a pair in $\overline\Omega$ by pairs in $\Omega$, so the two seminorms are equal. We equip $C^{k,\alpha}(\overline\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with this common norm. This is the Hölder-scale analogue of the interior-up-to-boundary convention for integer order $C^m(\overline\Omega)$ fixed in [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]].

Let $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ be bounded and open, and let
$$L[u]=\sum_{i,j=1}^d a_{ij}D_iD_j u+\sum_{j=1}^d\widetilde b_jD_j u+\widetilde c\,u$$
on $U$, where $a(x)$ is symmetric, $\xi^Ta(x)\xi\ge\lambda_0|\xi|^2$ for all $x\in U$ and $\xi\in\mathbb R^d$ with $\lambda_0>0$, the coefficients are continuous and bounded, and $\widetilde c\le0$. There is a constant $C_L<\infty$, depending only on $U$, $\lambda_0$, and the coefficient bounds, such that every $w\in C^2(U)\cap C^0(\bar U)$ with $L[w]\in C^0(U)$ satisfies
$$\|w\|_{C^0(U)}\le C_L\left(\|L[w]\|_{C^0(U)}+\|w\|_{C^0(\partial U)}\right).$$
In particular, for any two functions $u^*,h\in C^2(U)\cap C^0(\bar U)$,
$$\|u^*-h\|_{C^0(U)}\le C_L\left(\|L[u^*]-L[h]\|_{C^0(U)}+\|u^*-h\|_{C^0(\partial U)}\right).$$

There exists $b\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$ with $0\le b\le1$, $b(x)=1$ for $|x|\le1$, and $b(x)=0$ for $|x|\ge2$, such that the profile $\chi:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ defined by $\chi(r)=b(4r)$ is the restriction of a smooth function on $\mathbb R$, equals $1$ for $0\le r\le1/4$, and equals $0$ for $r\ge1/2$.

Here $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$ denotes the infinitely differentiable, compactly supported real-valued functions.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$ in the sense of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. Then $\nabla f$ is a $C^1$ field on $U$ by [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], since each of its components $\partial_if$ has continuous first partial derivatives, so its divergence is defined; the **Laplacian** of $f$ is

$$\Delta f:=\operatorname{div}\nabla f=\sum_{i<n}\partial_i\partial_if,$$

with the gradient of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]] and the divergence of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]. A $C^2$ function with $\Delta f=0$ on $U$ is called **harmonic** on $U$.

For a $C^2$ map $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{q-1}):U\to\mathbb R^q$, whose components are $C^2$ by [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], $\Delta F$ is the field whose $i$th coordinate is $\Delta F_i$. In the three-coordinate naming of this page, $\Delta f=\partial_x\partial_xf+\partial_y\partial_yf+\partial_z\partial_zf$ and $\Delta F=(\Delta F_x,\Delta F_y,\Delta F_z)$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

derivations.claim: Let $U=\{(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta):0<r<1,\ 0<\theta<2\pi/3\}$. It is bounded and Lipschitz: its boundary consists of two line segments and a circular arc, meeting at finitely many corners of angles $2\pi/3$ and $\pi/2$. At a smooth boundary point, a sufficiently small ball tangent on the exterior side is disjoint from $U$; on the circular arc one can use a ball outside the unit disk. At a corner of interior angle $\beta<\pi$, choose a ball tangent at the corner with its center on the exterior angle bisector. Directions from the vertex to points in this ball lie within angle $\pi/2$ of the center direction, while the sector directions are at angular distance at least $\pi-\beta/2>\pi/2$; hence the ball is exterior. Therefore $U$ satisfies the exterior sphere condition everywhere.

Let $\chi$ be the profile supplied by [F3]. Set $$u(r,\theta)=\chi(r)r^{3/2}\sin(3\theta/2),\qquad L=\Delta,\qquad f=\Delta u,\qquad g=0.$$ Since $r>0$ on $U$, $u\in C^\infty(U)$. It extends continuously by zero at the vertex, vanishes on both straight sides because the sine factor vanishes, and vanishes on the circular arc because $\chi(1)=0$. To compute $\Delta w$ for any $C^2$ function in local polar coordinates, write $c=\cos\theta$ and $s=\sin\theta$. The chain rule [F5] gives $$w_{xx}=c^2w_{rr}+\frac{s^2}{r}w_r+\frac{s^2}{r^2}w_{\theta\theta}-\frac{2sc}{r}w_{r\theta}+\frac{2sc}{r^2}w_\theta,\quad w_{yy}=s^2w_{rr}+\frac{c^2}{r}w_r+\frac{c^2}{r^2}w_{\theta\theta}+\frac{2sc}{r}w_{r\theta}-\frac{2sc}{r^2}w_\theta.$$ By [F4], adding yields $\Delta w=w_{rr}+r^{-1}w_r+r^{-2}w_{\theta\theta}$. For $w=r^{3/2}\sin(3\theta/2)$, these derivatives are $w_r=\frac32r^{1/2}\sin(3\theta/2)$, $w_{rr}=\frac34r^{-1/2}\sin(3\theta/2)$, and $w_{\theta\theta}=-\frac94r^{3/2}\sin(3\theta/2)$, so the polar Laplacian is zero on $r<1/4$. On the annulus where $\chi$ varies, $r$ is bounded away from zero and all factors are smooth; outside $r<1/2$, $u=0$. Thus $f$ is smooth and supported in $1/4\le r\le1/2$. The domain $U$ is convex, so boundedness of $\nabla f$ gives a Lipschitz bound on $f$ along each segment in $U$; since $U$ is bounded and $0<\alpha<1$, this implies $f\in C^{0,\alpha}(U)$.

Along the ray $\theta=\pi/3$ and for $0<r<1/4$, $\partial_{rr}u=(3/4)r^{-1/2}$, which is unbounded as $r\downarrow0$. A bounded global $C^{2,\alpha}$ norm bounds every Cartesian second derivative and hence every unit-direction second derivative, so [F1] implies $u\notin C^{2,\alpha}(U)$. The coefficients of $L=\Delta$ are smooth, the ellipticity constant is $1$, and the expanded zero-order coefficient is $0\le0$.

The displayed $u$ is a classical solution in $C^2(U)\cap C^0(\bar U)$ of $\Delta u=f$ with zero Dirichlet data. Any other solution in that class differs from $u$ by a zero-boundary harmonic function, which vanishes by [F2]. Hence it is the unique classical solution, and no solution in the asserted global $C^{2,\alpha}(U)\cap C^0(\bar U)$ class exists. This refutes the assertion.

Fix an input dimension $q\ge1$ and an integer $m\ge0$. Let $\mathcal A_m^{(q)}$ be the class of continuous scalar activations $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ for which there is one depth $n\in\mathbb N$ such that, for every compact $K\subset\mathbb R^q$, the scalar-output depth-$n$ multilayer perceptrons with activation $\sigma$ are dense in $C^m(K)$ in the $C^m$ norm. For $m=0$, $C^0(K)$ has the supremum norm. For $m>0$, $C^m(K)$ means jets of functions defined and $C^m$ on an open neighborhood of $K$: identify two functions when all their derivatives of orders at most $m$ agree on $K$, and use the norm $\max_{|\beta|\le m}\sup_{x\in K}|D^\beta f(x)|$. Only networks that are $C^m$ near $K$ enter this density assertion. For vector outputs, stack scalar-output networks of that same depth. The source notation $\mathcal A_m$ suppresses the input dimension fixed by the finite-dimensional network under consideration. Let $\mathcal A_m^{L,(q)}$ be the subclass whose members are Borel measurable and have at most linear growth, meaning
$$\sup_{s\in\mathbb R}\frac{|\sigma(s)|}{1+|s|}<\infty.$$
For an integer $q\ge1$, define $\mathrm{BA}_q$ to consist of those $\sigma\in\mathcal A_0^{(q)}$ for which, for every compact $K\subset\mathbb R^q$, every $\varepsilon>0$, and every $C\ge\operatorname{diam}_2(K)$, there is a finite multilayer perceptron $f:\mathbb R^q\to\mathbb R^q$ with
$$|f(x)-x|_2\le\varepsilon\quad(x\in K),\qquad |f(x)|_2\le C\quad(x\in\mathbb R^q).$$
Here $\operatorname{diam}_2(K)=\sup_{x,y\in K}|x-y|_2$, with diameter and all displayed approximation seminorms equal to zero on the empty set. The diameter-based global bound is part of this definition and is retained verbatim; whether it has any members is checked separately.

derivations.claim: Suppose $\sigma\in\mathrm{BA}_q$. Choose $x_0\in\mathbb R^q$ with $x_0\ne0$, set $K=\{x_0\}$, choose $C=0$, and choose $0<\varepsilon<|x_0|_2$. Since a singleton has diameter zero, these choices satisfy the quantifiers in [F1].

The required network would satisfy $|f(x)|_2\le0$ for every $x\in\mathbb R^q$, hence $f(x_0)=0$. It would also satisfy $|f(x_0)-x_0|_2\le\varepsilon$, which becomes $|x_0|_2\le\varepsilon$, contrary to the choice of $\varepsilon$. Therefore no $\sigma$ belongs to $\mathrm{BA}_q$.
