citations.quote:
Let $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$ be metric spaces, let $K\subseteq X$ be compact, and let $f,f_n:X\to Y$ be continuous for every integer $n\ge1$. Suppose that for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $N\ge1$ such that $d_Y(f_n(x),f(x))<\varepsilon$ for all $n\ge N$ and all $x\in K$.
Then
$$W=f[K]\cup\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}f_n[K]$$
is compact in $Y$. The empty-set case is included, and the proof uses no choice principle.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space), let
$(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space (Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric) and let $f : X \to Y$ be
continuous (Continuity of a map between metric spaces, at a point and globally, in the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ form). Then $f$ is uniformly continuous
(Uniform continuity of a map of metric spaces: one $\delta$ serving every point).

No choice principle is used: the cover built below is cut out by a property, and
the Lebesgue number lemma it is fed to is itself choice free
(Every open cover of a compact metric space has a Lebesgue number: a $\delta > 0$ such that every nonempty subset of diameter less than $\delta$ lies inside a single member of the cover).

Let $(X,d)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]). Then $(X,d)$ is totally bounded
([[def-totally-bounded]]) and complete ([[def-complete-metric-space]]).

**Both implications are theorems of ZF.** Completeness is obtained here from the
finite intersection characterisation ([[thm-compact-iff-finite-intersection-property]])
applied to the closures of the tails of a Cauchy sequence, and not from the
extraction of a convergent subsequence, which would route the argument through
sequential compactness. What matters for the ledger is that the route taken below
selects nothing at all; the first remark below says why the other route was not
taken.

Let $A$ and $U$ be real Banach spaces of functions on bounded domains $D$ and $D'$, with the input point evaluations used below defined. For every $n\ge1$, choose finite-dimensional normed spaces $E_n,F_n$, an exactly defined sampling map $S_n:A\to E_n$ (for example, $S_n(a)=(a(\xi_{n,1}),\ldots,a(\xi_{n,N_n}))$ at specified input points), a finite-dimensional map $\widetilde G_n:E_n\to F_n$, and an output reconstruction map $R_n:F_n\to U$. The reconstruction supplies a function with a defined value at every point of $D'$. The corresponding continuum-valued discrete map is
$$G_n(a):=R_n\bigl(\widetilde G_n(S_n(a))\bigr)\in U.$$
A family $(G_n)_{n\ge1}$ is a **discretization-invariant approximation** of an operator $G:A\to U$ if its sampling maps and output reconstructions are part of the family and it approximates this single continuum operator as the input discretization is refined. In the compact-uniform version, for every compact $K\subset A$,
$$\sup_{a\in K}\|G_n(a)-G(a)\|_U\longrightarrow0.$$
For $K=\emptyset$, the supremum of this nonnegative error is defined to be $0$. When $A$ consists of almost-everywhere equivalence classes, the sampling map must be explicitly defined on those classes or use a specified representative convention; point evaluation is not inferred from the equivalence class alone. This definition does not identify unrelated grid-specific maps as one operator family.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), let $A \subseteq X$ and let
$(A,d_A)$ be the metric subspace ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]). Then:

1. **Relative openness is a trace.** A set $V \subseteq A$ is open in $(A,d_A)$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) if and only if $V = U \cap A$ for some $U$ open in
   $(X,d)$.
2. **Compactness read in the ambient space.** $A$ is a compact subset of $X$
   ([[def-metric-compactness]]), that is $(A,d_A)$ is a compact metric space, if
   and only if for every family $\mathcal{U}$ of open subsets of $X$ with
   $A \subseteq \bigcup \mathcal{U}$ there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and
   $U_0, \dots, U_n \in \mathcal{U}$ with $A \subseteq U_0 \cup \dots \cup U_n$,
   or else $A = \emptyset$.
3. **The same in indexed form.** $A$ is a compact subset of $X$ if and only if
   for every set $I$ and every family $(U_i)_{i \in I}$ of open subsets of $X$
   with $A \subseteq \bigcup_{i \in I} U_i$ there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and
   indices $i_0, \dots, i_n \in I$ with
   $A \subseteq U_{i_0} \cup \dots \cup U_{i_n}$, or else $A = \emptyset$.

Claim 3 is the form used by almost every later proof on this page, because a
cover is usually produced by a rule that attaches an open set to each point or to
each index, and a set of open sets forgets that rule. No choice principle is used
anywhere below; the one place a selection is made is over a finite index set, and
[[lem-finite-choice]] is a theorem of ZF.

derivations.claim: Fix compact $K\subset X$. If $K$ is empty the conclusion is vacuous. Otherwise put $A_n=J_nS_n$ and $L=K\cup\bigcup_{n\ge1}A_n(K)$. The maps $A_n$ are continuous and converge uniformly on $K$ to the identity. Thus [F1] makes $L$ compact in the actual $X$ norm. By hypothesis $\sup_{b\in L}\|H_n(b)-H(b)\|_U\to0$.

In the concrete branch $0\le h_n<\infty$. If $h_n=0$, every cell is its singleton tag, so their finite union $D$ is finite. A nonempty open subset of $\mathbb R^d$ with $d\ge1$ contains a ball and hence infinitely many points; therefore this case forces $d=0$ and $D=\bar D$ is the singleton of $\mathbb R^0$. All tags are that point, and $J_n(z)(x)=z_1$ is a bounded linear reconstruction of norm at most one, with $J_nS_n(a)=a$ and reconstruction error $0=\omega_a(0)$. Now suppose $h_n>0$. Every point of $D$ is within $h_n$ of some tag in its cell. The distance to the finite tag set is continuous, so the same inequality holds on $\bar D$. Consequently $\sum_jw_{n,j}(x)>0$ there. The normalized weights are continuous, nonnegative and sum to one. Thus $J_n$ is a bounded linear map from the finite sample space with its maximum norm into $C(\bar D;\mathbb R^q)$, of norm at most one. The sampling map is bounded with norm at most one. A positive weight implies $|x-\xi_{n,j}|<2h_n$, so $\|J_nS_n(a)-a\|_\infty\le\omega_a(2h_n)$, where $\omega_a(r)=\sup_{|x-y|\le r}|a(x)-a(y)|$.

Continuity of $H$ controls uniform perturbations of the compact set $K$. Explicitly, for $\varepsilon>0$ collect every ball $B(x,r)$ with $x\in K$ and $r>0$ such that $\|H(z)-H(x)\|_U<\varepsilon/2$ for $\|z-x\|_X<3r$. These balls cover $K$; choose a finite subcover and take $\delta$ to be its smallest radius. If $a\in K$ and $\|b-a\|_X<\delta$, both points lie within $3r$ of one selected center, so $\|H(b)-H(a)\|_U<\varepsilon$. Hence $\sup_K\|H(A_n(a))-H(a)\|_U\to0$. Combining this with step 1.1 gives $\sup_K\|G_n-H\|_U\to0$. The maps $S_n$, identity on $E_n$, and $R_n=H_nJ_n$ provide the asserted finite-dimensional factorization, and [F4] applies when its function-space conventions hold; no access to the original input is used by $R_n$.

For a compact $K\subset C(\bar D;\mathbb R^q)$ and $\eta>0$, [F3] gives a finite $\eta$-net $a_1,\ldots,a_s$. By [F2] their moduli tend to zero. For $a\in K$ within $\eta$ of $a_i$, $\omega_a(r)\le2\eta+\omega_{a_i}(r)$. Therefore $\sup_{a\in K}\omega_a(r)\to0$. Step 1.2 supplies the reconstruction hypotheses of steps 1.1–2.1 and proves the whole concrete branch. The general argument measured every reconstruction error in $X$ and every output error in $U$, so it also proves the first clause without any unproved norm upgrade.

For the last assertion set $E_n=F_n=(\mathbb R^{q_0})^{N_n}$ and let $S_n(a)$ be its prescribed sample vector. For $z\in E_n$, construct $v_{1,n}(z)(x)=\sum_j\omega_{n,j}\kappa_n(x,\xi_{n,j})P(z_j)+b_n(x)$ and apply the subsequent raw stages to this field; call the resulting output $R_n(z)$. The first field belongs to its designated auxiliary space because it is a finite sum of its kernel sections and bias with finite scalar/vector coefficients. Every subsequent field belongs to its designated space by the stated compatibility assumptions. The finite sum and continuity of the lift make the first field continuous in $z$, and continuity of the subsequent maps makes $R_n:E_n\to U$ continuous. Induction through those stages proves $H_n(a)=R_n(S_n(a))$ exactly. The identity finite map between $E_n$ and $F_n$ gives [F4], and the assumed compact-uniform raw limit proves its convergence in the actual $U$ norm. No off-grid original input is requested at any stage of this construction.

derivations.claim: For the specified layer, the continuum operator and every raw quadrature map are $H(a)=H_n(a)=a$: the integral term is zero, so replacing it by any tagged sum changes nothing. In particular, an arbitrary output query still asks for $a(x)$ in the local term.

The zero function and the polynomial $a(x)=\prod_{j=1}^N(x-\xi_j)^2$ have the same zero sample vector. The polynomial is not identically zero: any point of the interval outside the finite sampling set has strictly positive value. For $N=0$ use the empty product $a=1$. Let $U \subseteq X$ be open in a real Banach space $X$, and let $Y$, $Z$, $W$ be

2. **Bounded-bilinear product rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ and $g : U \to Z$ are

Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
(Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Given $d\ge1$, a continuously differentiable objective $f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$, a discrete filtered probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0},P)$, an initial iterate $x_1$ measurable with respect to $\mathcal F_1$, an integer horizon $N\ge1$, deterministic finite stepsizes $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_N>0$, and a stochastic-gradient oracle whose output at $x_t$ is a random vector $G_t:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$ measurable with respect to $\mathcal F_{t+1}$, the procedure returns the trajectory $(x_t)_{t=1}^{N+1}$. For each iteration $t=1,\ldots,N$, query the oracle at $x_t$ and set
$$x_{t+1}=x_t-\alpha_tG_t.$$
No conditional mean, variance, or independence-across-iterations property is part of this procedure's definition.

Fix a finite dimension $d\ge1$ and a discrete filtered probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_k)_{k\ge0},P)$ as in Filtration and filtered probability space. A sequence $x_k:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$ is an iterate process when each coordinate is $\mathcal F_k$-measurable; a sequence $G_k:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$ is an oracle process when each coordinate is $\mathcal F_{k+1}$-measurable. These are coordinatewise instances of Random elements and real random variables and Adapted and integrable stochastic process. Assume the coordinates used in a conditional moment are square-integrable.

For deterministic stepsizes $\alpha_k>0$, the unconstrained Robbins–Monro/SGD update is
$$x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_kG_k.$$
For a differentiable objective $f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$, the oracle is conditionally unbiased when $\mathbb E[G_k\mid\mathcal F_k]=\nabla f(x_k)$ coordinatewise almost surely; it has conditional bias $b_k$ when $\mathbb E[G_k\mid\mathcal F_k]=\nabla f(x_k)+b_k$. The conditional variance of a vector is the sum of the scalar conditional variances of its coordinates, using Conditional variance. By Conditional variance is well-defined and has the second-moment formula, it satisfies
$$\mathbb E[\|G_k\|_2^2\mid\mathcal F_k]=\|\mathbb E[G_k\mid\mathcal F_k]\|_2^2+\operatorname{Var}(G_k\mid\mathcal F_k)$$
almost surely. All conditional expectations are coordinatewise instances of Conditional expectation as an ae class, whose existence assumes the The Axiom of Choice. No independence across iterations is part of this definition.

The conditional second-moment bound $\mathbb E[\|G_k\|_2^2\mid\mathcal F_k]\le M_k^2$ and the conditional variance bound $\operatorname{Var}(G_k\mid\mathcal F_k)\le\sigma_k^2$ are distinct hypotheses; the latter combines with conditional unbiasedness through the displayed identity.

A **discrete filtered probability space** is $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_n)_{n\in\mathbb N_0},P)$, where $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ is a probability space Probability measures and probability spaces, each $\mathcal F_n$ is a sigma-algebra on $\Omega$ Sigma-algebras, and $\mathcal F_n\subseteq\mathcal F_{n+1}\subseteq\mathcal F$. The sequence $(\mathcal F_n)$ is a **filtration**. Time starts at zero. Neither completeness nor triviality of $\mathcal F_0$ is required.

Restriction of $P$ to $\mathcal F_n$ has total mass one and is countably additive: a disjoint sequence in $\mathcal F_n$ is also such a sequence in $\mathcal F$, with the same union and the same values of $P$. Thus each restriction is a probability measure. This specifies a structure and uses no choice principle. Real-valued processes will be the default.

On a filtered probability space Filtration and filtered probability space, a **real stochastic process** is a sequence $(X_n)_{n\in\mathbb N_0}$ of real random variables Random elements and real random variables on the same space. It is **adapted** when $X_n^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal F_n$ for every $n$ and every real Borel set $B$. It is **integrable** when $E|X_n|<\infty$ for every $n$, using Expectation of a nonnegative or integrable random variable.

An integrable adapted process satisfies both conditions at each fixed time. Integrability here does not mean $\sup_nE|X_n|<\infty$: the deterministic process $X_n=n$ has $E|X_n|=n<\infty$ at every time but unbounded supremum. Measurability and finiteness of each integral are separate requirements. No versions, limits or choices are selected.

Assume AC for existence. If $X\in L^1(P)$ and $Z$ is bounded real $\mathcal G$-measurable, then $E[ZX\mid\mathcal G]=ZE[X\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. The identity also holds for finite real $\mathcal G$-measurable $Z$ whenever $ZX$ and $ZE[X\mid\mathcal G]$ are integrable. In fact $X,ZX\in L^1$ imply the latter integrability.

Assume AC for existence. For real $X,Y\in L^1(P)$ and $a,b\in\mathbb R$, $E[aX+bY\mid\mathcal G]=aE[X\mid\mathcal G]+bE[Y\mid\mathcal G]$. The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

Integer powers $a^m$) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space (The standard list $e : n \to F^{n}$ with $e_i(i) = 1_F$ and $e_i(j) = 0_F$ for $j \ne i$ is an ordered basis of $F^{n}$; hence $\dim_F F^{n} = n$, and $F^{0}$ is the zero space with basis $\varnothing$ and dimension $0$ clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
$\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and Conventions of this page, the standing $n \ge 1$ hypothesis, and what is taken up elsewhere in the reading order lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ (Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   (Squares of nonzero elements are positive), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of A norm on a real vector space, the induced metric, and the dictionary with the metric axioms
is proved in Cauchy-Schwarz $\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \le \lVert x\rVert_2\lVert y\rVert_2$ with its equality case, the triangle inequality for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$, the parallelogram law and polarisation, where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in The Euclidean inner product $\langle x,y\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k y_k$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   (A norm on a real vector space, the induced metric, and the dictionary with the metric axioms), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for finite sums, stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
The Euclidean inner product $\langle x,y\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k y_k$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of Integrable real and complex functions, and their integrals, its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

Let $d\ge1$, let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space, and let $f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be continuously differentiable with an $L$-Lipschitz gradient for some finite $L\ge0$. Fix an integer $N\ge1$, measurable maps $x_0,G_0,\ldots,G_{N-1}:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$, and finite real stepsizes $\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{N-1}$. Suppose $\mathbb E\|x_0\|_2^2<\infty$ and $\mathbb E\|G_k\|_2^2<\infty$ for every $k<N$, and define $x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_kG_k$. Then every $x_k$ and $\nabla f(x_k)$ for $0\le k\le N$ has finite second moment, and every $f(x_k)$ has finite absolute expectation.

derivations.claim: Fix $t\ge1$ and write $g_t=\nabla f(x_t)$, $m_t=\mathbb E[G_t\mid\mathcal F_t]$, and $\varepsilon_t=G_t-m_t$. The filtration and adapted-process conventions [F3, F4], together with the random-element convention [F5], make the time-indexed measurability explicit. By [F16], the objective values, gradients, and oracle vectors used below are integrable. The vector $\varepsilon_t$ is $\mathcal F_{t+1}$-measurable and has conditional mean zero given $\mathcal F_t$, so each coordinate, after shifting the filtration to $\mathcal H_n=\mathcal F_{n+1}$, is a martingale difference by [F8]. The conditional variance identity [F2, F7] and [A3]–[A4] give $\mathbb E[\|G_t\|_2^2\mid\mathcal F_t]=\|m_t\|_2^2+\operatorname{Var}(G_t\mid\mathcal F_t)\le M+(M_V+\mu_G^2)\|g_t\|_2^2=M+M_G\|g_t\|_2^2$.

Apply [F9] with $x=x_t$ and $y=x_{t+1}=x_t-\alpha_tG_t$, condition on $\mathcal F_t$, and use [F10] to take the $\mathcal F_t$-measurable gradient factor outside. Each coordinate product is integrable because $2|g_{t,j}G_{t,j}|\le g_{t,j}^2+G_{t,j}^2$, with finite expectations by [F16] and the stated oracle moments. Conditional linearity and order [F11] give $\mathbb E[f(x_{t+1})\mid\mathcal F_t]\le f(x_t)-\alpha_t\langle g_t,m_t\rangle+\frac{L\alpha_t^2}{2}\mathbb E[\|G_t\|_2^2\mid\mathcal F_t]\le f(x_t)-\left(\mu\alpha_t-\frac{LM_G\alpha_t^2}{2}\right)\|g_t\|_2^2+\frac{LM\alpha_t^2}{2}$. All remaining terms are integrable by [F15]–[F16] and the second-moment bound in step 1.1.

For constant $\alpha\le\mu/(LM_G)$, $\mu\alpha-LM_G\alpha^2/2\ge\mu\alpha/2$. Take ordinary expectations in step 2.1, using [F11]–[F12], and sum from $t=1$ to $T$. The objective terms telescope and [A5] gives $\frac{\mu\alpha}{2}\sum_{t=1}^T\mathbb E\|g_t\|_2^2\le f(x_1)-F_{\inf}+\frac{L\alpha^2MT}{2}$. Divide by $T\mu\alpha/2$ to obtain the stated constant-step average bound.

In the diminishing-step regime, $\sum_t\alpha_t^2<\infty$ implies $\alpha_t\to0$: otherwise some $\epsilon>0$ would satisfy $\alpha_t\ge\epsilon$ at infinitely many indices, forcing the square sum to diverge. Since $\mu/(LM_G)>0$, choose $K$ so that $\alpha_t\le\mu/(LM_G)$ for every $t\ge K$. Apply step 2.1 on this tail, take expectations, and telescope through $T\ge K$; then $\frac\mu2\sum_{t=K}^T\alpha_t\mathbb E\|g_t\|_2^2\le\mathbb E f(x_K)-F_{\inf}+\frac{LM}{2}\sum_{t=K}^T\alpha_t^2$. The right side is bounded independently of $T$ by [F15], [F16], and square summability. The omitted finite prefix has finite weighted sum by [F16]. Thus $\sum_{t=1}^T\alpha_t\mathbb E\|g_t\|_2^2$ stays bounded while $A_T=\sum_{t=1}^T\alpha_t\to\infty$. Their ratio tends to zero, which is the claimed expectation of the weighted average because each $\alpha_t$ is deterministic.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Given $d\ge1$, a continuously differentiable objective $f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$, a discrete filtered probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0},P)$, an initial iterate $x_1$ measurable with respect to $\mathcal F_1$, an integer horizon $N\ge1$, deterministic finite stepsizes $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_N>0$, and a stochastic-gradient oracle whose output at $x_t$ is a random vector $G_t:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$ measurable with respect to $\mathcal F_{t+1}$, the procedure returns the trajectory $(x_t)_{t=1}^{N+1}$. For each iteration $t=1,\ldots,N$, query the oracle at $x_t$ and set
$$x_{t+1}=x_t-\alpha_tG_t.$$
No conditional mean, variance, or independence-across-iterations property is part of this procedure's definition.

Fix a finite dimension $d\ge1$ and a discrete filtered probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_k)_{k\ge0},P)$ as in Filtration and filtered probability space. A sequence $x_k:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$ is an iterate process when each coordinate is $\mathcal F_k$-measurable; a sequence $G_k:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$ is an oracle process when each coordinate is $\mathcal F_{k+1}$-measurable. These are coordinatewise instances of Random elements and real random variables and Adapted and integrable stochastic process. Assume the coordinates used in a conditional moment are square-integrable.

For deterministic stepsizes $\alpha_k>0$, the unconstrained Robbins–Monro/SGD update is
$$x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_kG_k.$$
For a differentiable objective $f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$, the oracle is conditionally unbiased when $\mathbb E[G_k\mid\mathcal F_k]=\nabla f(x_k)$ coordinatewise almost surely; it has conditional bias $b_k$ when $\mathbb E[G_k\mid\mathcal F_k]=\nabla f(x_k)+b_k$. The conditional variance of a vector is the sum of the scalar conditional variances of its coordinates, using Conditional variance. By Conditional variance is well-defined and has the second-moment formula, it satisfies
$$\mathbb E[\|G_k\|_2^2\mid\mathcal F_k]=\|\mathbb E[G_k\mid\mathcal F_k]\|_2^2+\operatorname{Var}(G_k\mid\mathcal F_k)$$
almost surely. All conditional expectations are coordinatewise instances of Conditional expectation as an ae class, whose existence assumes the The Axiom of Choice. No independence across iterations is part of this definition.

The conditional second-moment bound $\mathbb E[\|G_k\|_2^2\mid\mathcal F_k]\le M_k^2$ and the conditional variance bound $\operatorname{Var}(G_k\mid\mathcal F_k)\le\sigma_k^2$ are distinct hypotheses; the latter combines with conditional unbiasedness through the displayed identity.

A **discrete filtered probability space** is $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_n)_{n\in\mathbb N_0},P)$, where $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ is a probability space Probability measures and probability spaces, each $\mathcal F_n$ is a sigma-algebra on $\Omega$ Sigma-algebras, and $\mathcal F_n\subseteq\mathcal F_{n+1}\subseteq\mathcal F$. The sequence $(\mathcal F_n)$ is a **filtration**. Time starts at zero. Neither completeness nor triviality of $\mathcal F_0$ is required.

Restriction of $P$ to $\mathcal F_n$ has total mass one and is countably additive: a disjoint sequence in $\mathcal F_n$ is also such a sequence in $\mathcal F$, with the same union and the same values of $P$. Thus each restriction is a probability measure. This specifies a structure and uses no choice principle. Real-valued processes will be the default.

On a filtered probability space Filtration and filtered probability space, a **real stochastic process** is a sequence $(X_n)_{n\in\mathbb N_0}$ of real random variables Random elements and real random variables on the same space. It is **adapted** when $X_n^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal F_n$ for every $n$ and every real Borel set $B$. It is **integrable** when $E|X_n|<\infty$ for every $n$, using Expectation of a nonnegative or integrable random variable.

An integrable adapted process satisfies both conditions at each fixed time. Integrability here does not mean $\sup_nE|X_n|<\infty$: the deterministic process $X_n=n$ has $E|X_n|=n<\infty$ at every time but unbounded supremum. Measurability and finiteness of each integral are separate requirements. No versions, limits or choices are selected.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and let
$(S,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space. A **random element** of $S$ is a measurable
map
$$X:(\Omega,\mathcal F)\to(S,\Sigma)$$
in the sense of A measurable function between measurable spaces.

When $S=\mathbb R$ and $\Sigma=\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$ from
The Borel sigma-algebra of a topological space, the map $X$ is a **real random variable**.

Assume AC for the supplied existence theorem. Write $E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ for the unique class in $L^1(\Omega,\mathcal G,P|_{\mathcal G})$ consisting of conditional-expectation versions of $X$. A chosen real $\mathcal G$-measurable representative is a **version**. Equalities and inequalities involving these classes mean almost-sure equalities and inequalities.

Existence is Conditional expectation exists by radon nikodym and uniqueness is Conditional expectation is unique almost surely, applied to Conditional expectation given a sigma algebra. The quotient is The space $L^p(\mu)$ as the quotient by null functions. If $X=X^{\ast}$ almost surely, Two integrable functions are equal almost everywhere exactly when all of their indefinite integrals agree gives identical event integrals, so the output class is independent of the input representative. The The Axiom of Choice assumption is inherited from RN existence.

Assume AC. For real $X\in L^2(P)$ define $\operatorname{Var}(X\mid\mathcal G)=E[(X-E[X\mid\mathcal G])^2\mid\mathcal G]$ as an almost-sure class. Its integrability, nonnegativity, representative independence and second-moment formula are justified by the following lemma.

The conditional class is Conditional expectation as an ae class, with The Axiom of Choice inherited from existence. By Conditional lp contraction, a version of the conditional mean is square integrable. The unbounded-factor rule Taking out what is known will apply to products whose integrability is verified in the well-definedness lemma, recorded under `justified_by`.

Assume AC. For real $X\in L^2(P)$, conditional variance is an integrable nonnegative class independent of representatives and satisfies $\operatorname{Var}(X\mid\mathcal G)=E[X^2\mid\mathcal G]-(E[X\mid\mathcal G])^2$ almost surely.

Assume AC The Axiom of Choice for conditional-expectation existence. A **martingale difference sequence** relative to $(\mathcal F_n)_{n\ge0}$ is a sequence $(D_n)_{n\ge1}$ of real integrable variables such that $D_n$ is $\mathcal F_n$-measurable and
$$E[D_n\mid\mathcal F_{n-1}]=0\quad\text{a.s. for every }n\ge1.$$
Integrability and adaptedness have the timewise meanings of Adapted and integrable stochastic process. Conditional expectations have the class convention of Conditional expectation as an ae class, which is the exact inherited use of AC here. No representative is selected by this definition. There is no $D_0$, and $\mathcal F_0$ need not be trivial or generated by the differences.

Let $d\ge1$, let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space, and let $f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be continuously differentiable with an $L$-Lipschitz gradient for some finite $L\ge0$. Fix an integer $N\ge1$, measurable maps $x_0,G_0,\ldots,G_{N-1}:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$, and finite real stepsizes $\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{N-1}$. Suppose $\mathbb E\|x_0\|_2^2<\infty$ and $\mathbb E\|G_k\|_2^2<\infty$ for every $k<N$, and define $x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_kG_k$. Then every $x_k$ and $\nabla f(x_k)$ for $0\le k\le N$ has finite second moment, and every $f(x_k)$ has finite absolute expectation.

Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be continuously differentiable and suppose $\nabla f$ is Lipschitz with constant $L\ge0$ in the Euclidean norm. Then
$$f(y)\le f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle+\frac{L}{2}\|y-x\|_2^2\qquad(x,y\in\mathbb R^n).$$

Assume AC for existence. If $X\in L^1(P)$ and $Z$ is bounded real $\mathcal G$-measurable, then $E[ZX\mid\mathcal G]=ZE[X\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. The identity also holds for finite real $\mathcal G$-measurable $Z$ whenever $ZX$ and $ZE[X\mid\mathcal G]$ are integrable. In fact $X,ZX\in L^1$ imply the latter integrability.

Assume AC for existence. For real $X,Y\in L^1(P)$ and $a,b\in\mathbb R$, $E[aX+bY\mid\mathcal G]=aE[X\mid\mathcal G]+bE[Y\mid\mathcal G]$. Conditional expectation is positive, preserves order and constants, satisfies $E(E[X\mid\mathcal G])=EX$, and $|E[X\mid\mathcal G]|\le E[|X|\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. Also $X<Y$ almost surely implies $E[X\mid\mathcal G]<E[Y\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely.

Assume AC for existence. If $\mathcal H\subseteq\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ and $X\in L^1(P)$, then $E[E[X\mid\mathcal G]\mid\mathcal H]=E[X\mid\mathcal H]$ and $E[E[X\mid\mathcal H]\mid\mathcal G]=E[X\mid\mathcal H]$ almost surely. Also, if a version of $E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ is $\mathcal H$-measurable, it is a version of $E[X\mid\mathcal H]$.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space, let $N\ge1$, and let $p_1,\ldots,p_N\ge0$ satisfy $\sum_{k=1}^N p_k=1$. There is a probability-space extension carrying an independent random index $R\in\{1,\ldots,N\}$ with $P(R=k)=p_k$. For any integrable real random variables $H_1,\ldots,H_N$ on the original space, the lifted random variable $H_R(\omega,k)=H_k(\omega)$ is integrable on the extension and satisfies $\mathbb E[H_R]=\sum_{k=1}^N p_k\mathbb E[H_k]$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ (The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann),
On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of The vector space $F^{X}$ of all functions $X \to F$ with pointwise operations, and $F^{n}$ as the case $X = n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
(Vector space over a field). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of Finite sums and finite products, by recursion applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 4 and
Squares of nonzero elements are positive, the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
Integer powers $a^m$) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root (Square roots exist: a unique $\sqrt{a} \ge 0$ with $(\sqrt{a})^2 = a$; the positives are $\{x^2 : x \neq 0\}$).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space (The standard list $e : n \to F^{n}$ with $e_i(i) = 1_F$ and $e_i(j) = 0_F$ for $j \ne i$ is an ordered basis of $F^{n}$; hence $\dim_F F^{n} = n$, and $F^{0}$ is the zero space with basis $\varnothing$ and dimension $0$ clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
$\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and Conventions of this page, the standing $n \ge 1$ hypothesis, and what is taken up elsewhere in the reading order lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ (Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   (Squares of nonzero elements are positive), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of A norm on a real vector space, the induced metric, and the dictionary with the metric axioms
is proved in Cauchy-Schwarz $\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \le \lVert x\rVert_2\lVert y\rVert_2$ with its equality case, the triangle inequality for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$, the parallelogram law and polarisation, where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in The Euclidean inner product $\langle x,y\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k y_k$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   (A norm on a real vector space, the induced metric, and the dictionary with the metric axioms), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for finite sums, stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
The Euclidean inner product $\langle x,y\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k y_k$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of Integrable real and complex functions, and their integrals, its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

derivations.claim: Fix $k$ and put $g_k=\nabla f(x_k)$ and $\varepsilon_k=G_k-g_k$. The filtration and adapted-process convention [F3] puts $x_k$ and $G_k$ at their stated time indices, and [F4] records their random-element measurability. Under AC [A1], the conditional-expectation classes used here are the almost-sure classes in [F5]. By [F8], the objective values, gradients, and directions used in the descent calculation are integrable. The residual $\varepsilon_k$ has conditional mean zero given $\mathcal F_k$; after shifting the filtration by one index, its coordinates form martingale differences by [F3, F7]. The conditional variance identity [F2, F6] and [A3] yield $\mathbb E[\|G_k\|_2^2\mid\mathcal F_k]=\|g_k\|_2^2+\operatorname{Var}(G_k\mid\mathcal F_k)\le\|g_k\|_2^2+\sigma^2$.

Apply the smoothness inequality [F9] to $x_{k+1}=x_k-\gamma_kG_k$ and condition on $\mathcal F_k$. The products are integrable because $2|g_{k,j}G_{k,j}|\le g_{k,j}^2+G_{k,j}^2$ coordinatewise, with finite expectations by [F8]. Take the $\mathcal F_k$-measurable gradient factor outside conditional expectation by [F10], then use [A2], [F11], and step 1.1 to obtain $\mathbb E[f(x_{k+1})\mid\mathcal F_k]\le f(x_k)-\left(\gamma_k-\frac{L}{2}\gamma_k^2\right)\|g_k\|_2^2+\frac{L\gamma_k^2\sigma^2}{2}$.

Take ordinary expectations in step 2.1 using the tower property [F11, F12], and sum from $k=1$ to $N$. The objective terms telescope; by [A4], $\mathbb E f(x_{N+1})\ge f^*$. Therefore $\sum_{k=1}^N\left(\gamma_k-\frac{L}{2}\gamma_k^2\right)\mathbb E\|g_k\|_2^2\le f(x_1)-f^*+\frac{L\sigma^2}{2}\sum_{k=1}^N\gamma_k^2$. Multiplying by $2$ gives $\sum_{k=1}^Na_k\mathbb E\|g_k\|_2^2\le2(f(x_1)-f^*)+L\sigma^2\sum_{k=1}^N\gamma_k^2$.

Since $a_k=\gamma_k(2-L\gamma_k)>0$, $S_N>0$ and $(a_k/S_N)_{k=1}^N$ is a probability vector. Apply [F13] to the integrable random variables $H_k=\|g_k\|_2^2$; it gives $\mathbb E\|\nabla f(x_R)\|_2^2=S_N^{-1}\sum_ka_k\mathbb E\|g_k\|_2^2$. Dividing step 3.1's bound by $LS_N$ yields the claimed weighted estimate.

Suppose $D_f,\sigma>0$ and set $\gamma=\min\{1/L,D_f/(\sigma\sqrt N)\}$. If $\gamma=D_f/(\sigma\sqrt N)\le1/L$, then $2\gamma-L\gamma^2\ge\gamma$ and $D_f^2+N\sigma^2\gamma^2=2D_f^2$, so the weighted bound is at most $2D_f\sigma/\sqrt N$. If $\gamma=1/L$, the bound equals $LD_f^2/N+\sigma^2/L$, and the clipping condition implies $\sigma^2/L\le LD_f^2/N$, giving at most $2LD_f^2/N$. Thus it is bounded by the stated sum of the two terms. If $\sigma=0$, use $\gamma=1/L$ in the formula to obtain $LD_f^2/N$. If $D_f=0<\sigma$, use $\gamma=1/(L\sqrt N)$; then $S_N=(2\sqrt N-1)/L$ and the right side is $\sigma^2/[L(2\sqrt N-1)]$. These cases prove the asserted constant-step rate and handle the zero boundaries.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

A **supervised prediction problem** consists of nonempty measurable spaces $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$ of instances, $(\mathsf Y,\Sigma_Y)$ of labels, and $(\mathsf A,\Sigma_A)$ of prediction actions; the product measurable space $(\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y,\Sigma_X\otimes\Sigma_Y)$; a probability measure $P$ on that product; a nonempty class $\mathcal F$ of measurable predictors $f:\mathsf X\to\mathsf A$; and a loss $\ell:\mathsf A\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty]$ that is measurable with respect to $\Sigma_A\otimes\Sigma_Y$. The law $P$ need not be supported on a deterministic labeling function, and this definition imposes no assumption that sample observations be independent or share a common law.

For a supervised prediction problem with joint law $P$, the **population risk** of any measurable predictor $f:\mathsf X\to\mathsf A$ (in particular, every $f\in\mathcal F$) is the extended nonnegative integral
$$R_P(f):=\int_{\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y}\ell(f(x),y)\,P(d(x,y))\in[0,+\infty].$$
For an ordered sample $S=((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_m,y_m))$ of length $m\ge1$, the **empirical risk** or **training risk** of any such $f$ is
$$\widehat R_S(f):=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\ell(f(x_i),y_i)\in[0,+\infty].$$
Neither definition assumes finite risk. The sum uses extended nonnegative arithmetic; since $m\ge1$, any summand equal to $+\infty$ makes the empirical risk $+\infty$.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
(Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property)), neighbourhoods are those of
The $\varepsilon$-neighbourhood and the punctured $\varepsilon$-neighbourhood of a point of $\mathbb{R}$ and limit points those of Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that The $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ limit $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a limit point $c$ of $A$ defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by At a limit point of the domain a function has at most one limit applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why The $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ limit $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a limit point $c$ of $A$ leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
(The $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ limit $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a limit point $c$ of $A$). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of The limit at $c$ depends only on the restriction of $f$ to a punctured neighbourhood of $c$, and passes to any subset of the domain having $c$ as a limit point carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex (Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
(Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$).

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Given $d\ge1$, a continuously differentiable objective $f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$, a discrete filtered probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0},P)$, an initial iterate $x_1$ measurable with respect to $\mathcal F_1$, an integer horizon $N\ge1$, deterministic finite stepsizes $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_N>0$, and a stochastic-gradient oracle whose output at $x_t$ is a random vector $G_t:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$ measurable with respect to $\mathcal F_{t+1}$, the procedure returns the trajectory $(x_t)_{t=1}^{N+1}$. For each iteration $t=1,\ldots,N$, query the oracle at $x_t$ and set
$$x_{t+1}=x_t-\alpha_tG_t.$$
No conditional mean, variance, or independence-across-iterations property is part of this procedure's definition.

For each $t\ge1$, put $g_t=\nabla f(x_t)$ and $m_t=\mathbb E[G_t\mid\mathcal F_t]$, with conditional expectations interpreted coordinatewise almost surely. Let the conditional variance of a vector be the sum of its coordinate conditional variances. Suppose there are constants $\mu_G\ge\mu>0$, $M\ge0$, $M_V\ge0$, and $F_{\inf}\in\mathbb R$ such that, almost surely for every $t$,
$$\langle g_t,m_t\rangle\ge\mu\|g_t\|_2^2,\qquad \|m_t\|_2\le\mu_G\|g_t\|_2,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(G_t\mid\mathcal F_t)\le M+M_V\|g_t\|_2^2,\qquad f(x_t)\ge F_{\inf}.$$
Set $M_G=M_V+\mu_G^2>0$.

If the stepsize is constant, $\alpha_t=\alpha$ with $0<\alpha\le\mu/(LM_G)$, then for every integer $T\ge1$,
$$\mathbb E\left[\frac1T\sum_{t=1}^T\|\nabla f(x_t)\|_2^2\right]\le\frac{\alpha LM}{\mu}+\frac{2(f(x_1)-F_{\inf})}{T\mu\alpha}.$$

If instead the deterministic stepsizes satisfy $\alpha_t>0$, $\sum_{t=1}^{\infty}\alpha_t=\infty$, and $\sum_{t=1}^{\infty}\alpha_t^2<\infty$, then, with $A_T=\sum_{t=1}^T\alpha_t$,
$$\mathbb E\left[\frac1{A_T}\sum_{t=1}^T\alpha_t\|\nabla f(x_t)\|_2^2\right]\longrightarrow0\qquad(T\to\infty).$$
Conditional unbiasedness is the special case $\mu=\mu_G=1$; a uniform conditional-variance bound $\sigma^2$ then gives $M=\sigma^2$ and $M_V=0$. No convexity or minimizer attainment is assumed.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
(Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property)), neighbourhoods are those of
The $\varepsilon$-neighbourhood and the punctured $\varepsilon$-neighbourhood of a point of $\mathbb{R}$ and limit points those of Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that The $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ limit $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a limit point $c$ of $A$ defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by At a limit point of the domain a function has at most one limit applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why The $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ limit $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a limit point $c$ of $A$ leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
(The $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ limit $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a limit point $c$ of $A$). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of The limit at $c$ depends only on the restriction of $f$ to a punctured neighbourhood of $c$, and passes to any subset of the domain having $c$ as a limit point carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex (Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real

Consequently, for $f$ defined on a nondegenerate interval $I$, the symbol

$$p_\lambda(r;\alpha,\beta):=r^2-(1+\beta-\alpha\lambda)r+\beta,\qquad \rho_\lambda(\alpha,\beta):=\max\{|r|:p_\lambda(r;\alpha,\beta)=0\}.$$

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ and $m \in \mathbb{R}$.

- $m$ is a **maximum** (or *greatest element*) of $S$ if $m \in S$ and $s \le m$
  for every $s \in S$.
- $m$ is a **minimum** (or *least element*) of $S$ if $m \in S$ and $m \le s$
  for every $s \in S$.

A set has at most one maximum: if $m_1$ and $m_2$ are both maxima then
$m_1 \in S$ gives $m_1 \le m_2$ and $m_2 \in S$ gives $m_2 \le m_1$, so
$m_1 = m_2$ by antisymmetry of the order, which is immediate from the trichotomy
axiom of an ordered field (Ordered field, Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property)).
The same argument applies to minima, so we may write $\max S$ and $\min S$.

An **ordered field** is a field $F$ (Field) together with a subset
$P \subseteq F$, the set of **positive** elements (the *positive cone*),
satisfying:

- **(O1) Trichotomy.** For each $x \in F$, exactly one of the following holds:
  $x \in P$, or $x = 0$, or $-x \in P$.
- **(O2) Closure.** If $x, y \in P$ then $x + y \in P$ and $x \cdot y \in P$.

We write $x > 0$ for $x \in P$ (read "$x$ is positive"), and define the order by

$$a < b \;:\Longleftrightarrow\; b - a \in P, \qquad a \le b \;:\Longleftrightarrow\; a < b \text{ or } a = b.$$

Thus $a > b$ means $b < a$, and $a \ge b$ means $b \le a$. An element $x$ with
$-x \in P$ (equivalently $x < 0$) is called **negative**.

Let $F$ be an ordered field (Ordered field) with positive cone $P$, and
let $a, b, c \in F$.

1. If $a > 0$ and $b > 0$ then $ab > 0$.
2. If $a > 0$ and $b < 0$ then $ab < 0$.
3. If $a < 0$ and $b < 0$ then $ab > 0$.
4. If $c > 0$ then $a < b \iff ac < bc$.
5. If $c < 0$ then $a < b \iff bc < ac$ (multiplication by a negative reverses order).

The set of **natural numbers** is the **smallest inductive set**
(Inductive set),

$$\mathbb{N} = \omega := \bigcap\,\{\, I : I \text{ is inductive} \,\},$$

which exists and is itself inductive by The natural numbers exist: a smallest inductive set (the
Axiom of Infinity, The Axiom of Infinity: there is a set containing a set with no elements and closed under $y \mapsto y \cup \{y\}$, supplies one inductive set to
intersect within, and Separation, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$, makes the
intersection a set). On $\mathbb{N}$ we take

$$0 := \varnothing, \qquad \sigma(n) := n \cup \{n\},$$

the distinguished element and the successor function. Thus
$0 = \varnothing$, $1 = \{0\}$, $2 = \{0, 1\}$, $3 = \{0, 1, 2\}$, and in general
$n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ is the set of its predecessors.

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. If $0 \in S$ and $\sigma(n) \in S$ whenever $n \in S$, then $S = \mathbb{N}$. Equivalently (property form): if a property $P$ satisfies $P(0)$ and ($P(n) \Rightarrow P(\sigma(n))$) for all $n$, then $P(n)$ holds for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. This is the induction principle, the basis of proof by induction.

Throughout this page $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
(Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property)), in particular an ordered field
(Ordered field) and a field (Field), and $\mathbb{N}$ is the set
of natural numbers (The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with successor $\sigma(n) = n + 1$
(Addition of natural numbers).

Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a sequence of reals, written $a_k$ for
$a(k)$. **Finite sums and finite products of $a$ are defined by recursion on the
upper index**, which is legitimate because of the recursion theorem
(The recursion theorem). That theorem produces a function of one variable, so the
running index has to be carried along inside the value: applying it to the set
$A = \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$, the starting element $(0, 0)$ and the function
$f(n, s) = (\sigma(n),\, s + a_n)$ gives a unique
$g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{R}$ with

$$g(0) = (0, 0), \qquad g(\sigma(n)) = f(g(n)) \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

Write $g(n) = \big(\pi_1(g(n)),\, \Sigma_n\big)$ for its two coordinates.

**The first coordinate is the index itself, and that is a small induction, not an
observation** (The principle of mathematical induction). Indeed $\pi_1(g(0)) = 0$; and if
$\pi_1(g(n)) = n$, then
$g(\sigma(n)) = f\big(\pi_1(g(n)), \Sigma_n\big) = \big(\sigma(\pi_1(g(n))),\, \Sigma_n + a_{\pi_1(g(n))}\big) = \big(\sigma(n),\, \Sigma_n + a_n\big)$,
so $\pi_1(g(\sigma(n))) = \sigma(n)$. By induction $\pi_1(g(n)) = n$ for every
$n \in \mathbb{N}$. Only now may the second coordinate of the two displayed
clauses be read off, and doing so gives

$$\Sigma_0 = 0, \qquad \Sigma_{\sigma(n)} = \Sigma_n + a_n .$$

$\Sigma$ is moreover the **unique** function $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with those
two properties: if $\Sigma'$ also has them then $n \mapsto (n, \Sigma'_n)$ satisfies
the two clauses defining $g$, hence equals $g$ by the uniqueness clause of
The recursion theorem, so $\Sigma' = \Sigma$.

We write $\sum_{k < n} a_k := \Sigma_n$. The same construction with starting
element $(0, 1)$ and $f(n, p) = (\sigma(n),\, p \cdot a_n)$, with the same
induction on the first coordinate and the same uniqueness argument, gives the
unique $\Pi : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with

$$\Pi_0 = 1, \qquad \Pi_{\sigma(n)} = \Pi_n \cdot a_n ,$$

and we write $\prod_{k < n} a_k := \Pi_n$.

**Notation.** For $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ we abbreviate

$$\sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \sum_{k < n+1} a_k, \qquad \prod_{k=0}^{n} a_k := \prod_{k < n+1} a_k,$$

and, for a general lower index $m$ with $m \le n + 1$, let $d$ be the
unique natural number satisfying $m+d=n+1$. Existence is the definition of
natural order (Order on the natural numbers); if $m+d=m+e$, commutativity
(Addition is commutative) gives $d+m=e+m$, so cancellation
(Addition is cancellative) gives $d=e$. On these admissible bounds only,
we may write this unique additive gap as $d=n+1-m$; no total natural subtraction
operation is presupposed. With $d$ thus fixed, define

$$\sum_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \sum_{j < d} a_{m+j}, \qquad \prod_{k=m}^{n} a_k := \prod_{j < d} a_{m+j} .$$

When $m = n + 1$ we have $d = 0$ and the sum is **empty**, with value $0$, while
the empty product has value $1$. In the same spirit $\sum_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ is
notation for the empty sum $\Sigma_0 = 0$ and $\prod_{k=0}^{-1} a_k$ for the
empty product $\Pi_0 = 1$; the index $-1$ never occurs as an element of
$\mathbb{N}$ and is only a way of writing "no terms".

Equivalently, for naturals $m \le r$, the half-open endpoint notation
$\sum_{k=m}^{r-1}a_k$ and $\prod_{k=m}^{r-1}a_k$ means
$\sum_{j<d}a_{m+j}$ and $\prod_{j<d}a_{m+j}$, respectively, where $d$ is the
unique natural with $m+d=r$. Here $r-1$ is an endpoint label for the terms
before $r$, so this notation needs no total subtraction operation. For $m=r$,
the unique gap is $0$ because $m+0=m$, giving the empty sum and product; the
case $m=r=0$ is the $-1$ endpoint convention just stipulated.

Only finitely many values of $a$ enter $\sum_{k<n} a_k$, so the notation
$\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ is also used for a list
$a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ of reals given without reference to any extension of the
list to all of $\mathbb{N}$: extend the list by $a_k = 0$ (respectively
$a_k = 1$) for $k \ge n$ and apply the definition above.

Let $a, b, c : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be sequences of reals, let
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, and let $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, with finite sums and
finite products as in Finite sums and finite products, by recursion. Then:

1. **Additivity.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}(a_k + b_k) = \sum_{k<n} a_k + \sum_{k<n} b_k$.
2. **Scaling.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda a_k = \lambda \sum_{k<n} a_k$; in particular $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda = n\lambda$, where $n$ denotes the canonical field image $n\cdot1_{\mathbb{R}}$ of the natural n (The unique embedding of ℚ into an ordered field, Canonical naturals are positive and strictly increasing).
3. **Splitting.** If $m \le n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k = \sum_{k<m} a_k + \sum_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k$, and $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n} a_k = \Big(\prod_{k<m} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k\Big)$.
4. **Monotonicity.** If $a_k \le b_k$ for all $k < n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k \le \sum_{k<n} b_k$. In particular, if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\sum_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, every single term satisfies $a_j \le \sum_{k<n} a_k$ for $j < n$, and $\sum_{k<n} a_k = 0$ forces $a_k = 0$ for every $k < n$.
5. **Telescoping.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}\big(c_{k+1} - c_k\big) = c_n - c_0$.
6. **Products.** $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n}(a_k b_k) = \Big(\prod_{k<n} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k<n} b_k\Big)$; if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, and if $a_k > 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k > 0$.

derivations.claim: Put $s_j=x_0+\sum_{i=1}^j\delta_i$ and $s_0=x_0$. For $0\le j\le k$, induction gives $x_j\ge s_j$ and $x_j\le1$: the base is $x_0=s_0\in[-1,1]$; at a next nonpositive increment, $x_{j-1}+\delta_j\le1$, so clipping replaces it only by its maximum with $-1$, which is no smaller than $x_{j-1}+\delta_j\ge s_j$.

For $k\le j\le n$, induction gives $x_j\ge\min\{1,s_j\}$. The base follows from step 1.1 and $x_k\le1$. If $s_{j-1}\le1$, then $x_{j-1}\ge s_{j-1}$ and $\delta_j\ge0$, so $y:=x_{j-1}+\delta_j\ge s_j$. If $s_j<-1$, then $c(y)\ge-1>s_j$. If $-1\le s_j\le1$, both $1$ and $y$ are at least $s_j$, so $\min\{1,y\}\ge s_j$ and then $c(y)=\max\{-1,\min\{1,y\}\}\ge s_j$. If $s_j>1$, then $y>1$ and $c(y)=1$. In all cases $c(y)\ge\min\{1,s_j\}$. If instead $s_{j-1}>1$, the induction bound and $x_{j-1}\le1$ imply $x_{j-1}=1$; a nonnegative increment keeps the clipped value at $1$. Taking $j=n$ proves the Statement.

Fix a dimension $d\ge1$, an initial vector $x_1\in\mathbb R^d$, a finite or infinite sequence of finite gradient vectors $g_t\in\mathbb R^d$, positive step sizes $\eta_t>0$, a decay parameter $\rho\in[0,1)$, and a denominator constant $\epsilon>0$. Use one-based coordinate notation $z_i:=z(i-1)$ for every vector $z\in\mathbb R^d$ and $1\le i\le d$. Set $r_0=0$. At each integer round $t\ge1$, update the second-moment estimate coordinatewise by

$$r_{t,i}=\rho r_{t-1,i}+(1-\rho)g_{t,i}^2\qquad(1\le i\le d),$$

and then set

$$x_{t+1,i}=x_{t,i}-\eta_t\frac{g_{t,i}}{\sqrt{r_{t,i}}+\epsilon}\qquad(1\le i\le d).$$

For a finite gradient sequence of length $T\ge0$, perform rounds $1\le t\le T$ and return the trajectory $(x_1,\ldots,x_{T+1})$; when $T=0$, return $(x_1)$. For an infinite gradient sequence, perform every round $t\ge1$, thereby defining and returning the iterate sequence $(x_t)_{t\ge1}$. The root, addition, and division in the update are coordinatewise. The procedure makes no convergence or regret claim.

Fix a finite horizon $T\ge1$, an initial scalar $x_1\in[-1,1]$, a step parameter $\alpha>0$, moment parameters $\beta_1\in[0,1)$ and $\beta_2\in(0,1)$, a denominator parameter $\epsilon\ge0$, and a sequence of scalar gradients $g_1,\ldots,g_T$. Set $m_0=v_0=0$. At round $t$, update

$$m_t=\beta_1m_{t-1}+(1-\beta_1)g_t,\qquad v_t=\beta_2v_{t-1}+(1-\beta_2)g_t^2.$$

The input is admissible only when $v_t+\epsilon>0$ at every update. Set $\alpha_t=\alpha/\sqrt t$, compute $y_{t+1}=x_t-\alpha_t m_t/\sqrt{v_t+\epsilon}$, and set $x_{t+1}=\max(-1,\min(1,y_{t+1}))$. Thus the iterate is projected onto $[-1,1]$ after the update. Return the trajectory $(x_1,\ldots,x_{T+1})$, whose final iterate is $x_{T+1}$. derivations.claim: For each procedure, induction over its finite horizon shows that every moment is a finite real and each second moment is nonnegative. The initial moments are zero. At a successor round, each recurrence is a finite sum of products of finite reals by [F1]–[F3] and [F9]; the coefficients $\rho,1-\rho,\beta_2,1-\beta_2$ are nonnegative, and each squared gradient is nonnegative by [F5], so the next second moment remains nonnegative.

For RMSProp, [F6] supplies $\sqrt{r_{t,i}}\ge0$, so $\sqrt{r_{t,i}}+\epsilon>0$ by [F1]. For Adam, [F6] supplies $\sqrt{v_t+\epsilon}$ because $v_t\ge0$ and $\epsilon\ge0$; its positivity is the explicit admissibility condition in [F2]. Thus each stated quotient has a positive denominator.

In AMSGrad, both entries in each maximum are finite and nonnegative by [F3], [F5], and step 1.1. The maximum exists by [F7] and is nonnegative. If $\widehat v_{t,i}=0$, then $\widehat v_{t-1,i}=v_{t,i}=0$. Since $\beta_2>0$, $1-\beta_2>0$, and both summands defining $v_{t,i}$ are nonnegative, $v_{t-1,i}=0$ and $g_{t,i}=0$. Repeating this argument back to time zero gives every earlier $g_{s,i}=0$; the first-moment recurrence then gives $m_{t,i}=m_{t-1,i}=0$. Conversely, if $\widehat v_{t,i}>0$, some $v_{s,i}>0$ for $s\le t$, and then $v_{u+1,i}\ge\beta_2v_{u,i}>0$ for each $u\ge s$, so $v_{t,i}>0$. The zero-ratio convention in [F3] is therefore consistent with the recurrence.

Fix a round and its finite vector $y$ and nonnegative weights $q_i=\sqrt{\widehat v_{t,i}}$. Since $F$ is compact, [F8] bounds $\|x\|_2$ by some $B$ for $x\in F$. For $x,z\in F$, coordinatewise expansion and [F9] give $$\left|\sum_i q_i(x_i-y_i)^2-\sum_i q_i(z_i-y_i)^2\right|\le\|x-z\|_2\sum_i q_i(2B+2\|y\|_2).$$ Thus the objective is continuous on $F$. Since $F$ is nonempty and compact, [F8] gives a minimizer. The objective can be constant along zero-weight coordinates, so allowing any minimizer is necessary and sufficient. This proves the remaining well-definedness claim.

Fix a dimension $d\ge1$, a finite horizon $T\ge1$, a nonempty compact convex set $F\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, an initial point $x_1\in F$, positive step sizes $\alpha_t>0$, a fixed parameter $\beta_2\in(0,1)$, and parameters $\beta_{1,t}\in[0,1)$ for $1\le t\le T$. Use one-based coordinate notation $z_i:=z(i-1)$ for every vector $z\in\mathbb R^d$ and $1\le i\le d$. At round $t$, receive a finite subgradient vector $g_t\in\mathbb R^d$. Set $m_0=v_0=\widehat v_0=0$ and update coordinatewise by

$$m_{t,i}=\beta_{1,t}m_{t-1,i}+(1-\beta_{1,t})g_{t,i},\qquad v_{t,i}=\beta_2v_{t-1,i}+(1-\beta_2)g_{t,i}^2,$$

$$\widehat v_{t,i}=\max\{\widehat v_{t-1,i},v_{t,i}\}.$$

If $\widehat v_{t,i}>0$, set $y_{t+1,i}=x_{t,i}-\alpha_t m_{t,i}/\sqrt{\widehat v_{t,i}}$; if $\widehat v_{t,i}=0$, set $y_{t+1,i}=x_{t,i}$. Choose any minimizer

$$x_{t+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in F}\sum_{i=1}^d\sqrt{\widehat v_{t,i}}(x_i-y_{t+1,i})^2.$$

Return the trajectory through $x_{T+1}$. The procedure uses the uncorrected first and second moments and the coordinatewise running maximum of the raw second moment. It contains no denominator stabilizer.

For every finite admissible run of the RMSProp, uncorrected Adam, or uncorrected AMSGrad procedures defined on this page, all moment coordinates are finite and all second-moment coordinates are nonnegative. Every denominator specified by the procedure is positive. For AMSGrad, a zero historical-maximum coordinate has zero current and previous first moments, and the raw second moment is positive whenever its historical maximum is positive; the zero-ratio convention is therefore consistent. Each weighted minimization over the compact feasible set attains a minimum.
