Assume AC, DC and countable choice for the Gaussian probability-law constructions below. The displayed finite real network recurrences and empirical loss are deterministic definitions for fixed parameters. Fix positive integers $d,n,H,m$, training inputs $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R^d$ with $\|x_i\|_2=1$, labels $y_1,\ldots,y_n\in\mathbb R$, an analytic nonpolynomial activation $\sigma$ satisfying $|\sigma(0)|<\infty$ and finite Lipschitz constants for $\sigma$ and $\sigma'$, and the positive finite normalization $c_\sigma=(\mathbb E_{Z\sim N(0,1)}[\sigma(Z)^2])^{-1}$. A fully connected network of width $m$ and depth $H$ is the finite feedforward recurrence

$$x^{(0)}=x,\qquad x^{(h)}=\sqrt{c_\sigma/m}\,\sigma(W^{(h)}x^{(h-1)})\quad(1\le h\le H),\qquad f_{\rm fc}(x,\theta)=a^Tx^{(H)},$$

where $W^{(1)}\in\mathbb R^{m\times d}$, $W^{(h)}\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ for $h\ge2$, $a\in\mathbb R^m$, and $\sigma$ acts coordinatewise. The residual network uses the same first layer and then

$$x^{(1)}=\sqrt{c_\sigma/m}\,\sigma(W^{(1)}x),\qquad x^{(h)}=x^{(h-1)}+\frac{c_{\rm res}}{H\sqrt m}\,\sigma(W^{(h)}x^{(h-1)})\quad(2\le h\le H),\qquad f_{\rm res}(x,\theta)=a^Tx^{(H)},$$

with $0<c_{\rm res}<1$. In either architecture, random initialization means all entries of all matrices $W^{(h)}$ and of $a$ are independent $N(0,1)$ random variables; all these entries are trained by full-batch gradient descent. The empirical quadratic loss is $L(\theta)=\frac12\sum_{i=1}^n(f(x_i,\theta)-y_i)^2$.

For the fully connected architecture and the same fixed data, define the population matrices by

$$K_{ij}^{(0)}=\langle x_i,x_j\rangle.$$

For $1\le h<H$, let $(U_{ij}^{(h)},V_{ij}^{(h)})$ be a centered bivariate normal vector with covariance

$$A_{ij}^{(h)}=\begin{pmatrix}K_{ii}^{(h-1)}&K_{ij}^{(h-1)}\\K_{ji}^{(h-1)}&K_{jj}^{(h-1)}\end{pmatrix},$$

and put $K_{ij}^{(h)}=c_\sigma\mathbb E[\sigma(U_{ij}^{(h)})\sigma(V_{ij}^{(h)})]$. For $h=H$, use the same bivariate-normal definition with $A_{ij}^{(H)}$ formed from $K^{(H-1)}$, and set

$$K_{ij}^{(H)}=c_\sigma K_{ij}^{(H-1)}\mathbb E[\sigma'(U_{ij}^{(H)})\sigma'(V_{ij}^{(H)})].$$

When $H=1$, this last formula uses $K^{(0)}$ directly and there are no intermediate activation-covariance matrices. For the fully connected theorem, this terminal matrix is denoted $K_{\rm fc}^{(H)}$.

For the residual architecture with $H\ge2$, use a separate sequence $S^{(h)}$ and mean vector $b^{(h)}$. Set $S^{(0)}=K^{(0)}$. For $G^{(0)}\sim N_n(0,S^{(0)})$, put

$$S_{ij}^{(1)}=c_\sigma\mathbb E[\sigma(G_i^{(0)})\sigma(G_j^{(0)})],\qquad b_i^{(1)}=\sqrt{c_\sigma}\mathbb E[\sigma(G_i^{(0)})].$$

Write $\alpha=c_{\rm res}/H$. For $2\le h<H$, take a fresh centered Gaussian vector $G^{(h-1)}$ with covariance $S^{(h-1)}$, put $\mu_i^{(h-1)}=\mathbb E[\sigma(G_i^{(h-1)})]$, and define

$$S_{ij}^{(h)}=S_{ij}^{(h-1)}+\alpha\bigl(b_i^{(h-1)}\mu_j^{(h-1)}+b_j^{(h-1)}\mu_i^{(h-1)}\bigr)+\alpha^2\mathbb E[\sigma(G_i^{(h-1)})\sigma(G_j^{(h-1)})],\qquad b_i^{(h)}=b_i^{(h-1)}+\alpha\mu_i^{(h-1)}.$$

For $G\sim N_n(0,S^{(H-1)})$, define the residual terminal matrix by

$$K_{{\rm res},ij}^{(H)}=\frac{c_{\rm res}^2}{H^2}S_{ij}^{(H-1)}\mathbb E[\sigma'(G_i)\sigma'(G_j)].$$

The fully connected and residual convergence statements use $K_{\rm fc}^{(H)}$ and $K_{\rm res}^{(H)}$, respectively. At $H=1$, the two architectures coincide; define $K_{\rm res}^{(1)}=K_{\rm fc}^{(1)}$. The residual recursion above is the scalar specialization of the source's general mean/second-moment recursion, equation (16); in particular it includes the mean cross terms. Its terminal Gaussian covariance is $S^{(H-1)}$, as determined by the finite-width last-layer Gram formula (14).

The residual recurrence has one identity contribution from $x^{(h-1)}$ and one nonlinear contribution at every layer $2\le h\le H$; the arrows below depict that convention for one generic layer and do not enter any proof.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=stealth,node distance=1.3cm]
  \node (in) {$x^{(h-1)}$};
  \node[draw,rectangle,right=1.7cm of in] (act) {$\frac{c_{\rm res}}{H\sqrt m}\sigma(W^{(h)}x^{(h-1)})$};
  \node[draw,circle,right=2.0cm of act] (sum) {$+$};
  \node[right=1.2cm of sum] (out) {$x^{(h)}$};
  \draw[->] (in) -- (act);
  \draw[->] (act) -- (sum);
  \draw[->] (in) to[bend right=28] (sum);
  \draw[->] (sum) -- (out);
\end{tikzpicture}
```

Assume AC. Let $Z$ have the standard normal law on $\mathbb R$. Suppose $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is analytic, nonpolynomial, satisfies $|\sigma(0)|\le B$ for some finite $B$, and is $L$-Lipschitz for a finite $L$. Then $0<\mathbb E[\sigma(Z)^2]<\infty$. Consequently the normalization constant

$$c_\sigma:=\bigl(\mathbb E[\sigma(Z)^2]\bigr)^{-1}$$

is a well-defined positive finite real number.

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. If $0 \in S$ and $\sigma(n) \in S$ whenever $n \in S$, then $S = \mathbb{N}$. Equivalently (property form): if a property $P$ satisfies $P(0)$ and ($P(n) \Rightarrow P(\sigma(n))$) for all $n$, then $P(n)$ holds for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. This is the induction principle, the basis of proof by induction.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

Assume countable choice and dependent choice. Every probability measure $\nu$
on $(S,\Sigma)$ is the common law of a countable independent family of
$S$-valued random elements.

Let $n\ge1$, let $X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}$ be independent real random variables on a
common probability space, and let $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Borel
measurable for each $i<n$.

1. If every $g_i$ is nonnegative, then
   $$\mathbb E\left[\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)\right]=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$$
   in $[0,+\infty]$. In this finite product of expectations, a zero factor
   makes the product zero even when another factor is $+\infty$; otherwise
   multiplication has its usual extended nonnegative meaning.
2. If every $g_i(X_i)$ is integrable, then $\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)$ is integrable
   and the same factorization holds in $\mathbb R$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   The product measure of two sigma-finite measure spaces is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

derivations.claim: The input matrix $K^{(0)}$ is symmetric, and for $v\in\mathbb R^n$, $v^TK^{(0)}v=\|\sum_i v_ix_i\|_2^2\ge0$. Its diagonal entries are $\|x_i\|_2^2=1$, giving the base case.

Assume the induction hypothesis that $K^{(h-1)}$ is finite, symmetric positive semidefinite, and has diagonal $1$, for some $1\le h<H$. By [F2]–[F3], take $G\sim N_n(0,K^{(h-1)})$; each pair $(G_i,G_j)$ has covariance $A_{ij}^{(h)}$. The growth bound $|\sigma(z)|\le|\sigma(0)|+L|z|$ and finite Gaussian second moments put each $\sigma(G_i)$ in $L^2$; [F8] then makes every product $\sigma(G_i)\sigma(G_j)$ integrable. Thus $K^{(h)}$ is finite and symmetric, and for every $v$, $v^TK^{(h)}v=c_\sigma\mathbb E[(\sum_i v_i\sigma(G_i))^2]\ge0$. Because $G_i\sim N(0,1)$, its diagonal is $c_\sigma\mathbb E[\sigma(Z)^2]=1$ by [F5]. This establishes the induction step.

For the fixed $H$, let $P(h)$ mean that $K^{(h)}$ is finite, symmetric positive semidefinite, and has diagonal $1$, for $0\le h<H$. Define $Q(k)$ to mean $P(j)$ for every $j\le\min(k,H-1)$. Step 1.1 gives $Q(0)$. If $Q(k)$ and $k+1<H$, step 2.1 applied with $h=k+1$ gives $P(k+1)$ and hence $Q(k+1)$; if $k+1\ge H$, $Q(k+1)$ adds no new index. By [F6], $Q(H-1)$ holds, so $K^{(H-1)}$ is finite, symmetric positive semidefinite, and has diagonal $1$; when $H=1$, this is exactly the base matrix $K^{(0)}$. By [F4], take independent $G,G'$ both distributed as $N_n(0,K^{(H-1)})$. The vector with coordinates $Y_i=\sqrt{c_\sigma}\,G'_i\sigma'(G_i)$ has finite second moments; $\sigma'$ is bounded because it is the derivative of a Lipschitz differentiable function. Factoring expectations of independent variables gives $\mathbb E[Y_iY_j]=c_\sigma K_{ij}^{(H-1)}\mathbb E[\sigma'(G_i)\sigma'(G_j)]=K_{ij}^{(H)}$. Therefore $K^{(H)}$ is finite and symmetric, and $v^TK^{(H)}v=\mathbb E[(\sum_i v_iY_i)^2]\ge0$ for every $v$. This proves the fully connected terminal claim and discharges that induction.

For the residual base layer let $G_0\sim N_n(0,S^{(0)})$ and $V^{(1)}=\sqrt{c_\sigma}\,\sigma(G_0)$, with activation applied coordinatewise. Then $EV^{(1)}=b^{(1)}$ and $E[V^{(1)}(V^{(1)})^T]=S^{(1)}$ by [F1]. The growth bound used in step 2.1 proves finite second moments. For every $v$, $v^TS^{(1)}v=E[(v^TV^{(1)})^2]\ge0$, while $S^{(1)}-b^{(1)}(b^{(1)})^T$ is its covariance and has quadratic form $E[(v^T(V^{(1)}-EV^{(1)}))^2]\ge0$. Thus both matrices are symmetric positive semidefinite.

Suppose a finite-second-moment vector $V^{(h-1)}$ has mean $b^{(h-1)}$ and second-moment matrix $S^{(h-1)}$. Let $\mu$ be the Borel law of this generally non-Gaussian vector and let $
u=N_n(0,S^{(h-1)})$, which exists by [F2]. Both are probability measures and hence sigma-finite. By [F7], on $(\mathbb R^n	imes\mathbb R^n,\mu	imes
u)$ the coordinate projections $V$ and $G$ have laws $\mu$ and $
u$ and are independent: for Borel sets $A,B$, the probability of $\{V\in A,G\in B\}$ is $\mu(A)
u(B)$. Put $V^{(h)}=V+\alpha\sigma(G)$. Finite second moments follow from the growth bound and $(u+v)^2\le2u^2+2v^2$. Independence gives $EV^{(h)}=b^{(h-1)}+\alpha\mu^{(h-1)}$ and $E[V_i^{(h)}V_j^{(h)}]=S_{ij}^{(h-1)}+\alpha(b_i^{(h-1)}\mu_j^{(h-1)}+b_j^{(h-1)}\mu_i^{(h-1)})+\alpha^2E[\sigma(G_i)\sigma(G_j)]=S_{ij}^{(h)}$. For every $v$, $v^TS^{(h)}v=E[(v^TV^{(h)})^2]\ge0$, and $S^{(h)}-b^{(h)}(b^{(h)})^T$ is the covariance of $V^{(h)}$, so its quadratic form is also an expectation of a square. Thus both matrices are finite, symmetric positive semidefinite at this stage, which supplies the covariance hypothesis for the next stage. Iterating through the finitely many layers is justified by [F6].

For $H\ge2$, take independent $G,G'\sim N_n(0,S^{(H-1)})$ and set $Y_i=(c_{\rm res}/H)G'_i\sigma'(G_i)$. The boundedness $|\sigma'|\le L$ gives finite second moments, and independence gives $E[Y_iY_j]=K_{{\rm res},ij}^{(H)}$. Consequently this terminal matrix is symmetric positive semidefinite. At $H=1$ it equals the already proved fully connected matrix by definition. This proves all residual assertions.

Assume AC, DC and countable choice for the Gaussian probability-law constructions below. The displayed finite real network recurrences and empirical loss are deterministic definitions for fixed parameters. Fix positive integers $d,n,H,m$, training inputs $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R^d$ with $\|x_i\|_2=1$, labels $y_1,\ldots,y_n\in\mathbb R$, an analytic nonpolynomial activation $\sigma$ satisfying $|\sigma(0)|<\infty$ and finite Lipschitz constants for $\sigma$ and $\sigma'$, and the positive finite normalization $c_\sigma=(\mathbb E_{Z\sim N(0,1)}[\sigma(Z)^2])^{-1}$. A fully connected network of width $m$ and depth $H$ is the finite feedforward recurrence

$$x^{(0)}=x,\qquad x^{(h)}=\sqrt{c_\sigma/m}\,\sigma(W^{(h)}x^{(h-1)})\quad(1\le h\le H),\qquad f_{\rm fc}(x,\theta)=a^Tx^{(H)},$$

where $W^{(1)}\in\mathbb R^{m\times d}$, $W^{(h)}\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ for $h\ge2$, $a\in\mathbb R^m$, and $\sigma$ acts coordinatewise. The residual network uses the same first layer and then

$$x^{(1)}=\sqrt{c_\sigma/m}\,\sigma(W^{(1)}x),\qquad x^{(h)}=x^{(h-1)}+\frac{c_{\rm res}}{H\sqrt m}\,\sigma(W^{(h)}x^{(h-1)})\quad(2\le h\le H),\qquad f_{\rm res}(x,\theta)=a^Tx^{(H)},$$

with $0<c_{\rm res}<1$. In either architecture, random initialization means all entries of all matrices $W^{(h)}$ and of $a$ are independent $N(0,1)$ random variables; all these entries are trained by full-batch gradient descent. The empirical quadratic loss is $L(\theta)=\frac12\sum_{i=1}^n(f(x_i,\theta)-y_i)^2$.

For the fully connected architecture and the same fixed data, define the population matrices by

$$K_{ij}^{(0)}=\langle x_i,x_j\rangle.$$

For $1\le h<H$, let $(U_{ij}^{(h)},V_{ij}^{(h)})$ be a centered bivariate normal vector with covariance

$$A_{ij}^{(h)}=\begin{pmatrix}K_{ii}^{(h-1)}&K_{ij}^{(h-1)}\\K_{ji}^{(h-1)}&K_{jj}^{(h-1)}\end{pmatrix},$$

and put $K_{ij}^{(h)}=c_\sigma\mathbb E[\sigma(U_{ij}^{(h)})\sigma(V_{ij}^{(h)})]$. For $h=H$, use the same bivariate-normal definition with $A_{ij}^{(H)}$ formed from $K^{(H-1)}$, and set

$$K_{ij}^{(H)}=c_\sigma K_{ij}^{(H-1)}\mathbb E[\sigma'(U_{ij}^{(H)})\sigma'(V_{ij}^{(H)})].$$

When $H=1$, this last formula uses $K^{(0)}$ directly and there are no intermediate activation-covariance matrices. For the fully connected theorem, this terminal matrix is denoted $K_{\rm fc}^{(H)}$.

For the residual architecture with $H\ge2$, use a separate sequence $S^{(h)}$ and mean vector $b^{(h)}$. Set $S^{(0)}=K^{(0)}$. For $G^{(0)}\sim N_n(0,S^{(0)})$, put

$$S_{ij}^{(1)}=c_\sigma\mathbb E[\sigma(G_i^{(0)})\sigma(G_j^{(0)})],\qquad b_i^{(1)}=\sqrt{c_\sigma}\mathbb E[\sigma(G_i^{(0)})].$$

Write $\alpha=c_{\rm res}/H$. For $2\le h<H$, take a fresh centered Gaussian vector $G^{(h-1)}$ with covariance $S^{(h-1)}$, put $\mu_i^{(h-1)}=\mathbb E[\sigma(G_i^{(h-1)})]$, and define

$$S_{ij}^{(h)}=S_{ij}^{(h-1)}+\alpha\bigl(b_i^{(h-1)}\mu_j^{(h-1)}+b_j^{(h-1)}\mu_i^{(h-1)}\bigr)+\alpha^2\mathbb E[\sigma(G_i^{(h-1)})\sigma(G_j^{(h-1)})],\qquad b_i^{(h)}=b_i^{(h-1)}+\alpha\mu_i^{(h-1)}.$$

For $G\sim N_n(0,S^{(H-1)})$, define the residual terminal matrix by

$$K_{{\rm res},ij}^{(H)}=\frac{c_{\rm res}^2}{H^2}S_{ij}^{(H-1)}\mathbb E[\sigma'(G_i)\sigma'(G_j)].$$

The fully connected and residual convergence statements use $K_{\rm fc}^{(H)}$ and $K_{\rm res}^{(H)}$, respectively. At $H=1$, the two architectures coincide; define $K_{\rm res}^{(1)}=K_{\rm fc}^{(1)}$. The residual recursion above is the scalar specialization of the source's general mean/second-moment recursion, equation (16); in particular it includes the mean cross terms. Its terminal Gaussian covariance is $S^{(H-1)}$, as determined by the finite-width last-layer Gram formula (14).

The residual recurrence has one identity contribution from $x^{(h-1)}$ and one nonlinear contribution at every layer $2\le h\le H$; the arrows below depict that convention for one generic layer and do not enter any proof.

Let $p,q\ge1$, let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $H\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be open, and let $T$ be a nonnegative integer. Suppose $h_0:\Theta\to H$, $\Phi_t:\Theta\times H\to H$ for $1\le t\le T$, and $\ell:\Theta\times H\to\mathbb R$ are continuously differentiable on open domains containing the trajectory at $\theta\in\Theta$. A continuously differentiable map is totally differentiable at each point and has a derivative matrix continuous on its domain. Define $h_0=h_0(\theta)$, $h_t=\Phi_t(\theta,h_{t-1})$, and $J(\theta)=\ell(\theta,h_T)$. Write $A_t=D_\theta\Phi_t(\theta,h_{t-1})$ and $B_t=D_h\Phi_t(\theta,h_{t-1})$, with each partial derivative holding the other argument fixed. Set $\lambda_T=(D_h\ell(\theta,h_T))^T$ and, in descending order, $\lambda_{t-1}=B_t^T\lambda_t$. Then the backpropagation algorithm returns $J(\theta)$ and

$$\nabla_\theta J(\theta)=(D_\theta\ell(\theta,h_T))^T+\sum_{t=1}^{T}A_t^T\lambda_t+(Dh_0(\theta))^T\lambda_0,$$

where the sum is empty when $T=0$. The statement also applies when every primitive is evaluated on one fixed strict $C^1$ branch; it makes no assertion at a branch boundary.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be continuously
Fréchet differentiable. The gradient $\nabla f(x)$ is the vector of partial
derivatives in the Euclidean coordinates, with the convention of
The Jacobian matrix of partial derivatives and the gradient in the scalar-valued case; differentiability is the Fréchet
condition of The real Frechet derivative on real and complex matrix spaces with the Frobenius norm.

**Inputs:** an initial point $x_0\in U$; either a positive fixed-step
sequence $(t_k)_{k\ge0}$ or backtracking parameters $\alpha\in(0,1)$ and
$\beta\in(0,1)$; and an optional caller stopping predicate
$S(k,x,g)\in\{\mathrm{false},\mathrm{true}\}$, with
$S:\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\times U\times\mathbb R^d\to\{\mathrm{false},\mathrm{true}\}$.
If no predicate is supplied, use $S\equiv\mathrm{false}$. **Output:** when the
procedure stops, return the last valid iterate $x_k$ and the status
`stationary`, `caller-stop`, or `domain-failure`.
If no stopping status occurs, the sequence continues and there is no finite
return.
For example, an outer procedure's at-most-$M$-updates limit, for finite real
$M\ge0$, is implemented by $S(k,x,g):=(k+1>M)$.

At iteration $k$, where $k$ is the number of accepted updates so far and the
current iterate is $x_k$:

1. Compute $g_k:=\nabla f(x_k)$ and set $p_k:=-g_k$. If $g_k=0$, return
   $(x_k,\texttt{stationary})$.
2. If $S(k,x_k,g_k)$ is true, return $(x_k,\texttt{caller-stop})$. Check this
   predicate at the current iterate after its gradient is computed and before
   any step is selected.
3. In fixed-step mode, set $t=t_k$. If $x_k+tp_k\notin U$, return
   $(x_k,\texttt{domain-failure})$ without accepting that candidate.
4. In backtracking mode, start with $t=1$ and repeatedly replace $t$ by
   $\beta t$ until $x_k+tp_k\in U$ and
   $f(x_k+tp_k)\le f(x_k)+\alpha t\,\langle g_k,p_k\rangle$.
5. Set $x_{k+1}:=x_k+t p_k$ and continue at iteration $k+1$.

The fixed-step update map is $x\mapsto x-t_k\nabla f(x)$; at a stationary
point its value is $x$, which is the returned iterate. A backtracking search
that is reached at a nonstationary iterate is well-defined by
Armijo backtracking terminates for strict descent directions. The
procedure asserts no convergence or global-minimization property for an
arbitrary objective.

Let $U$ be an open subset of a real matrix space $\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ or of
a complex matrix space $\mathbb C^{m\times n}$ viewed as a real vector space,
and let $F:U\to W$ take values in a finite-dimensional real normed vector
space $(W,\|\,\cdot\,\|_W)$.
We say that $F$ is **real Fr\'echet differentiable** at $A\in U$ if there is a real-linear map $L$ such that for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ for which

$$\|F(A+H)-F(A)-L[H]\|_W\le\varepsilon\|H\|_F\qquad\text{whenever }A+H\in U\text{ and }\|H\|_F<\delta.$$

That map $L$ is the **real Fr\'echet derivative** of $F$ at $A$ and is denoted $DF(A)$. At $H=0$ the remainder is zero because $L[0]=0$. When the source matrix space has at least one entry, this is equivalently

$$\frac{\|F(A+H)-F(A)-L[H]\|_W}{\|H\|_F}\longrightarrow0\qquad(H\to0,\ H\ne0),$$

since a nonempty open neighborhood supplies nonzero increments arbitrarily close to zero. Thus the original positive-dimensional notion is unchanged. A source with zero entries is the zero vector space with its zero Frobenius norm ([[def-frobenius-matrix-norm]]). Its only increment is $H=0$, and the unique real-linear map from it to $W$ is zero; the displayed normwise estimate holds identically. No punctured quotient limit at an isolated point is asserted.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

Assume AC, DC, and countable choice. Let $Z\sim\gamma_d$ be standard Gaussian
on $\mathbb R^d$ and let
$f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be $L$-Lipschitz. If $L>0$, then for every $r>0$,
$$P\{f(Z)\ge E f(Z)+r\}\le e^{-r^2/(2L^2)}.$$
If $L=0$, the probability on the left is zero.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in The Euclidean inner product $\langle x,y\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k y_k$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   (A norm on a real vector space, the induced metric, and the dictionary with the metric axioms), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for finite sums, stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
The Euclidean inner product $\langle x,y\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k y_k$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. If $0 \in S$ and $\sigma(n) \in S$ whenever $n \in S$, then $S = \mathbb{N}$. Equivalently (property form): if a property $P$ satisfies $P(0)$ and ($P(n) \Rightarrow P(\sigma(n))$) for all $n$, then $P(n)$ holds for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. This is the induction principle, the basis of proof by induction.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: The rows $i,j$ of $K^{(0)}$ coincide because $K_{i\ell}^{(0)}=\langle x_i,x_\ell\rangle=\langle x_j,x_\ell\rangle=K_{j\ell}^{(0)}$ for every $\ell$. This is the base case.

Assume rows $i,j$ of $K^{(h-1)}$ coincide. By [F2], the matrix is symmetric, so the corresponding columns coincide as well. For each $\ell$, the covariance matrices $A_{i\ell}^{(h)}$ and $A_{j\ell}^{(h)}$ are equal. Thus the Gaussian activation expectations agree for $h<H$, and for $h=H$ both the derivative expectations and prefactors $K_{i\ell}^{(H-1)}$, $K_{j\ell}^{(H-1)}$ agree. Hence rows $i,j$ of the fully connected $K^{(h)}$ coincide.

For the fixed $H$, let $P(h)$ assert that rows $i,j$ of $K^{(h)}$ coincide for $0\le h\le H$. Step 1.1 gives the base, and step 1.2 proves $P(h)$ from $P(h-1)$ for every $1\le h\le H$. By [F4], the fully connected terminal rows coincide. For $H=1$, the residual terminal matrix equals this fully connected terminal matrix by definition, so its rows also coincide.

Now assume $H\ge2$. For $1\le h<H$, let $Q(h)$ assert both that rows $i,j$ of $S^{(h)}$ coincide and that $b_i^{(h)}=b_j^{(h)}$. The base $S^{(0)}=K^{(0)}$ has equal rows by step 1.1. At layer $1$, this equality and symmetry from [F2] make the pair covariance matrices for indices $(i,\ell)$ and $(j,\ell)$ identical for every $\ell$, and give $S_{ii}^{(0)}=S_{jj}^{(0)}$. Hence the Gaussian marginal means agree, so the defining formulas give $S_{i\ell}^{(1)}=S_{j\ell}^{(1)}$ for every $\ell$ and $b_i^{(1)}=b_j^{(1)}$; this proves $Q(1)$. For $2\le h<H$, assume $Q(h-1)$. Symmetry from [F2] and equal rows of $S^{(h-1)}$ give equal columns, so the covariance matrices for $(i,\ell)$ and $(j,\ell)$ coincide and $\mu_i^{(h-1)}=\mu_j^{(h-1)}$. In the mean recursion this gives $b_i^{(h)}=b_j^{(h)}$. In the second-moment recursion, the old-row terms agree, the terms $b_i^{(h-1)}\mu_\ell^{(h-1)}+b_\ell^{(h-1)}\mu_i^{(h-1)}$ agree with their $j$-row counterparts, and the Gaussian activation expectations agree; thus $S_{i\ell}^{(h)}=S_{j\ell}^{(h)}$ for every $\ell$. This proves $Q(h)$. Finite induction gives $Q(H-1)$. The terminal residual formula then has equal prefactors $S_{i\ell}^{(H-1)}=S_{j\ell}^{(H-1)}$ and equal derivative expectations because the corresponding pair covariance matrices coincide. Therefore the terminal residual rows coincide.

For either terminal matrix, let $v=e_i-e_j\ne0$. Symmetry and equal rows imply $K^{(H)}v=0$. By [F2]–[F3], this matrix is positive semidefinite and has a nonzero null vector, so zero is an eigenvalue and the smallest eigenvalue is zero. This proves the residual branch and completes the example.

Assume AC, DC and countable choice for the Gaussian probability-law constructions below. The displayed finite real network recurrences and empirical loss are deterministic definitions for fixed parameters. Fix positive integers $d,n,H,m$, training inputs $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R^d$ with $\|x_i\|_2=1$, labels $y_1,\ldots,y_n\in\mathbb R$, an analytic nonpolynomial activation $\sigma$ satisfying $|\sigma(0)|<\infty$ and finite Lipschitz constants for $\sigma$ and $\sigma'$, and the positive finite normalization $c_\sigma=(\mathbb E_{Z\sim N(0,1)}[\sigma(Z)^2])^{-1}$. A fully connected network of width $m$ and depth $H$ is the finite feedforward recurrence

$$x^{(0)}=x,\qquad x^{(h)}=\sqrt{c_\sigma/m}\,\sigma(W^{(h)}x^{(h-1)})\quad(1\le h\le H),\qquad f_{\rm fc}(x,\theta)=a^Tx^{(H)},$$

where $W^{(1)}\in\mathbb R^{m\times d}$, $W^{(h)}\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ for $h\ge2$, $a\in\mathbb R^m$, and $\sigma$ acts coordinatewise. The residual network uses the same first layer and then

$$x^{(1)}=\sqrt{c_\sigma/m}\,\sigma(W^{(1)}x),\qquad x^{(h)}=x^{(h-1)}+\frac{c_{\rm res}}{H\sqrt m}\,\sigma(W^{(h)}x^{(h-1)})\quad(2\le h\le H),\qquad f_{\rm res}(x,\theta)=a^Tx^{(H)},$$

with $0<c_{\rm res}<1$. In either architecture, random initialization means all entries of all matrices $W^{(h)}$ and of $a$ are independent $N(0,1)$ random variables; all these entries are trained by full-batch gradient descent. The empirical quadratic loss is $L(\theta)=\frac12\sum_{i=1}^n(f(x_i,\theta)-y_i)^2$.

For the fully connected architecture and the same fixed data, define the population matrices by

$$K_{ij}^{(0)}=\langle x_i,x_j\rangle.$$

For $1\le h<H$, let $(U_{ij}^{(h)},V_{ij}^{(h)})$ be a centered bivariate normal vector with covariance

$$A_{ij}^{(h)}=\begin{pmatrix}K_{ii}^{(h-1)}&K_{ij}^{(h-1)}\\K_{ji}^{(h-1)}&K_{jj}^{(h-1)}\end{pmatrix},$$

and put $K_{ij}^{(h)}=c_\sigma\mathbb E[\sigma(U_{ij}^{(h)})\sigma(V_{ij}^{(h)})]$. For $h=H$, use the same bivariate-normal definition with $A_{ij}^{(H)}$ formed from $K^{(H-1)}$, and set

$$K_{ij}^{(H)}=c_\sigma K_{ij}^{(H-1)}\mathbb E[\sigma'(U_{ij}^{(H)})\sigma'(V_{ij}^{(H)})].$$

When $H=1$, this last formula uses $K^{(0)}$ directly and there are no intermediate activation-covariance matrices. For the fully connected theorem, this terminal matrix is denoted $K_{\rm fc}^{(H)}$.

For the residual architecture with $H\ge2$, use a separate sequence $S^{(h)}$ and mean vector $b^{(h)}$. Set $S^{(0)}=K^{(0)}$. For $G^{(0)}\sim N_n(0,S^{(0)})$, put

$$S_{ij}^{(1)}=c_\sigma\mathbb E[\sigma(G_i^{(0)})\sigma(G_j^{(0)})],\qquad b_i^{(1)}=\sqrt{c_\sigma}\mathbb E[\sigma(G_i^{(0)})].$$

Write $\alpha=c_{\rm res}/H$. For $2\le h<H$, take a fresh centered Gaussian vector $G^{(h-1)}$ with covariance $S^{(h-1)}$, put $\mu_i^{(h-1)}=\mathbb E[\sigma(G_i^{(h-1)})]$, and define

$$S_{ij}^{(h)}=S_{ij}^{(h-1)}+\alpha\bigl(b_i^{(h-1)}\mu_j^{(h-1)}+b_j^{(h-1)}\mu_i^{(h-1)}\bigr)+\alpha^2\mathbb E[\sigma(G_i^{(h-1)})\sigma(G_j^{(h-1)})],\qquad b_i^{(h)}=b_i^{(h-1)}+\alpha\mu_i^{(h-1)}.$$

For $G\sim N_n(0,S^{(H-1)})$, define the residual terminal matrix by

$$K_{{\rm res},ij}^{(H)}=\frac{c_{\rm res}^2}{H^2}S_{ij}^{(H-1)}\mathbb E[\sigma'(G_i)\sigma'(G_j)].$$

The fully connected and residual convergence statements use $K_{\rm fc}^{(H)}$ and $K_{\rm res}^{(H)}$, respectively. At $H=1$, the two architectures coincide; define $K_{\rm res}^{(1)}=K_{\rm fc}^{(1)}$. The residual recursion above is the scalar specialization of the source's general mean/second-moment recursion, equation (16); in particular it includes the mean cross terms. Its terminal Gaussian covariance is $S^{(H-1)}$, as determined by the finite-width last-layer Gram formula (14).

The residual recurrence has one identity contribution from $x^{(h-1)}$ and one nonlinear contribution at every layer $2\le h\le H$; the arrows below depict that convention for one generic layer and do not enter any proof.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=stealth,node distance=1.3cm]
  \node (in) {$x^{(h-1)}$};
  \node[draw,rectangle,right=1.7cm of in] (act) {$\frac{c_{\rm res}}{H\sqrt m}\sigma(W^{(h)}x^{(h-1)})$};
  \node[draw,circle,right=2.0cm of act] (sum) {$+$};
  \node[right=1.2cm of sum] (out) {$x^{(h)}$};
  \draw[->] (in) -- (act);
  \draw[->] (act) -- (sum);
  \draw[->] (in) to[bend right=28] (sum);
  \draw[->] (sum) -- (out);
\end{tikzpicture}
```

Assume AC. Let $Z$ have the standard normal law on $\mathbb R$. Suppose $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is analytic, nonpolynomial, satisfies $|\sigma(0)|\le B$ for some finite $B$, and is $L$-Lipschitz for a finite $L$. Then $0<\mathbb E[\sigma(Z)^2]<\infty$. Consequently the normalization constant

$$c_\sigma:=\bigl(\mathbb E[\sigma(Z)^2]\bigr)^{-1}$$

is a well-defined positive finite real number.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By The standard normal density has total mass one and The indefinite integral of a nonnegative measurable function is a measure, gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. The law of a random element is a probability measure makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in The Dirac set function at a point.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. If $0\le s,t$ and a real random variable
$X_t-X_s$ has law $N(0,|t-s|)$, then, for every integer $m\ge1$,
$$E|X_t-X_s|^{2m}=c_m|t-s|^m,$$
where
$$c_m=E|Z|^{2m}=(2m-1)!!=1\cdot3\cdots(2m-1)<\infty$$
for $Z\sim N(0,1)$. In particular, when $m\ge2$, this is the moment hypothesis
of the one-parameter Kolmogorov criterion with
$\alpha=2m$, $\beta=m-1$, and $C_T=c_m$.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

If $W$ is a subspace of a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space $V$, then

$$V=W\oplus W^\perp.$$

Thus every $v\in V$ has unique vectors $w\in W$ and $z\in W^\perp$ with $v=w+z$.
Every finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space has an orthonormal basis. In dimension zero, this is the empty basis.

Assume Countable Choice for the finite-dimensional Gaussian probability law.
Let $G\in F^{a\times b}$ have the iid Gaussian law of
[[def-standard-real-and-normalized-complex-gaussian-matrix-law]]. If $U,V$
are compatible orthogonal matrices for $F=\mathbb R$ or unitary matrices for
$F=\mathbb C$, then $U^*GV$ has the same iid law as $G$. In particular, if
$W\in F^{n\times n}$ is orthogonal/unitary and $\Omega\in F^{n\times\ell}$
is iid Gaussian, then any two disjoint row blocks of $W^*\Omega$ are
independent standard Gaussian matrices.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Softplus is positive and nonconstant. It is analytic, has derivative in $(0,1)$, and its second derivative is at most $1/4$, so it satisfies the activation regularity assumptions. By [F2] and [F4], $\mu$ is finite; because $\sigma(Z)\ge\log 2$ when $Z\ge0$ and the standard normal density is positive on $(0,1)$, $\mu>0$. Since softplus is nonconstant, choose $z_0$ with $\sigma(z_0)\ne\mu$; continuity and the positive Gaussian density give $\mathbb E[(s-\mu)^2]>0$. Expanding this finite square and using $\mathbb E s=\mu$ yields $\mathbb E[s^2]>\mu^2$. Therefore $0<\rho<1$.

Let $U=\operatorname{span}\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}$. By [F5], $\mathbb R^d=U\oplus U^\perp$, and [F6] supplies an orthonormal basis of $U^\perp$. Joining it to $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ gives the columns of an orthogonal matrix $Q$. By [F7], $W^{(1)}Q$ has the same iid Gaussian law as $W^{(1)}$, so all coordinates $W^{(1)}_{r\cdot}x_i$ are independent standard normals. Thus $\mathbb E[(\Phi\Phi^T)_{ii}]=c_\sigma\mathbb E[s^2]=1$, while for $i\ne j$, $\mathbb E[(\Phi\Phi^T)_{ij}]=c_\sigma\mu^2=\rho$. Therefore $\mathbb E[\Phi\Phi^T]=(1-\rho)I_n+\rho\mathbf1\mathbf1^T$, and its quadratic form in the unit vector $e$ is $1+(n-1)\rho$.

Conditional on the hidden weights, $e^Tu=e^T\Phi a$ is a centered normal random variable with variance $S=e^T\Phi\Phi^Te\ge0$, by [F1] and [F3]. The nonnegative random variable $S$ has expectation $1+(n-1)\rho>\rho n/2$, so the event $S>\rho n/2$ has positive probability; otherwise its expectation would be at most $\rho n/2$. On this event, for any fixed $C>0$, the conditional probability of $|e^Tu|>C\sqrt n$ is at least $P\{|Z|>C\sqrt{2/\rho}\}>0$. Averaging over the hidden weights proves positive unconditional probability. Since $e$ is a unit vector, write $u=(e^Tu)e+(u-(e^Tu)e)$; the summands are orthogonal, so $\|u\|_2^2=|e^Tu|^2+\|u-(e^Tu)e\|_2^2\ge|e^Tu|^2$. This proves the asserted absence of one confidence-uniform constant by a local projection calculation.

Assume AC, DC and countable choice for the Gaussian probability-law constructions below. The displayed finite real network recurrences and empirical loss are deterministic definitions for fixed parameters. Fix positive integers $d,n,H,m$, training inputs $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathbb R^d$ with $\|x_i\|_2=1$, labels $y_1,\ldots,y_n\in\mathbb R$, an analytic nonpolynomial activation $\sigma$ satisfying $|\sigma(0)|<\infty$ and finite Lipschitz constants for $\sigma$ and $\sigma'$, and the positive finite normalization $c_\sigma=(\mathbb E_{Z\sim N(0,1)}[\sigma(Z)^2])^{-1}$. A fully connected network of width $m$ and depth $H$ is the finite feedforward recurrence

$$x^{(0)}=x,\qquad x^{(h)}=\sqrt{c_\sigma/m}\,\sigma(W^{(h)}x^{(h-1)})\quad(1\le h\le H),\qquad f_{\rm fc}(x,\theta)=a^Tx^{(H)},$$

where $W^{(1)}\in\mathbb R^{m\times d}$, $W^{(h)}\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ for $h\ge2$, $a\in\mathbb R^m$, and $\sigma$ acts coordinatewise. The residual network uses the same first layer and then

$$x^{(1)}=\sqrt{c_\sigma/m}\,\sigma(W^{(1)}x),\qquad x^{(h)}=x^{(h-1)}+\frac{c_{\rm res}}{H\sqrt m}\,\sigma(W^{(h)}x^{(h-1)})\quad(2\le h\le H),\qquad f_{\rm res}(x,\theta)=a^Tx^{(H)},$$

with $0<c_{\rm res}<1$. In either architecture, random initialization means all entries of all matrices $W^{(h)}$ and of $a$ are independent $N(0,1)$ random variables; all these entries are trained by full-batch gradient descent. The empirical quadratic loss is $L(\theta)=\frac12\sum_{i=1}^n(f(x_i,\theta)-y_i)^2$.

For the fully connected architecture and the same fixed data, define the population matrices by

$$K_{ij}^{(0)}=\langle x_i,x_j\rangle.$$

For $1\le h<H$, let $(U_{ij}^{(h)},V_{ij}^{(h)})$ be a centered bivariate normal vector with covariance

$$A_{ij}^{(h)}=\begin{pmatrix}K_{ii}^{(h-1)}&K_{ij}^{(h-1)}\\K_{ji}^{(h-1)}&K_{jj}^{(h-1)}\end{pmatrix},$$

and put $K_{ij}^{(h)}=c_\sigma\mathbb E[\sigma(U_{ij}^{(h)})\sigma(V_{ij}^{(h)})]$. For $h=H$, use the same bivariate-normal definition with $A_{ij}^{(H)}$ formed from $K^{(H-1)}$, and set

$$K_{ij}^{(H)}=c_\sigma K_{ij}^{(H-1)}\mathbb E[\sigma'(U_{ij}^{(H)})\sigma'(V_{ij}^{(H)})].$$

When $H=1$, this last formula uses $K^{(0)}$ directly and there are no intermediate activation-covariance matrices. For the fully connected theorem, this terminal matrix is denoted $K_{\rm fc}^{(H)}$.

For the residual architecture with $H\ge2$, use a separate sequence $S^{(h)}$ and mean vector $b^{(h)}$. Set $S^{(0)}=K^{(0)}$. For $G^{(0)}\sim N_n(0,S^{(0)})$, put

$$S_{ij}^{(1)}=c_\sigma\mathbb E[\sigma(G_i^{(0)})\sigma(G_j^{(0)})],\qquad b_i^{(1)}=\sqrt{c_\sigma}\mathbb E[\sigma(G_i^{(0)})].$$

Write $\alpha=c_{\rm res}/H$. For $2\le h<H$, take a fresh centered Gaussian vector $G^{(h-1)}$ with covariance $S^{(h-1)}$, put $\mu_i^{(h-1)}=\mathbb E[\sigma(G_i^{(h-1)})]$, and define

$$S_{ij}^{(h)}=S_{ij}^{(h-1)}+\alpha\bigl(b_i^{(h-1)}\mu_j^{(h-1)}+b_j^{(h-1)}\mu_i^{(h-1)}\bigr)+\alpha^2\mathbb E[\sigma(G_i^{(h-1)})\sigma(G_j^{(h-1)})],\qquad b_i^{(h)}=b_i^{(h-1)}+\alpha\mu_i^{(h-1)}.$$

For $G\sim N_n(0,S^{(H-1)})$, define the residual terminal matrix by

$$K_{{\rm res},ij}^{(H)}=\frac{c_{\rm res}^2}{H^2}S_{ij}^{(H-1)}\mathbb E[\sigma'(G_i)\sigma'(G_j)].$$

The fully connected and residual convergence statements use $K_{\rm fc}^{(H)}$ and $K_{\rm res}^{(H)}$, respectively. At $H=1$, the two architectures coincide; define $K_{\rm res}^{(1)}=K_{\rm fc}^{(1)}$. The residual recursion above is the scalar specialization of the source's general mean/second-moment recursion, equation (16); in particular it includes the mean cross terms. Its terminal Gaussian covariance is $S^{(H-1)}$, as determined by the finite-width last-layer Gram formula (14).

The residual recurrence has one identity contribution from $x^{(h-1)}$ and one nonlinear contribution at every layer $2\le h\le H$; the arrows below depict that convention for one generic layer and do not enter any proof.

  \node (in) {$x^{(h-1)}$};
  \node[draw,rectangle,right=1.7cm of in] (act) {$\frac{c_{\rm res}}{H\sqrt m}\sigma(W^{(h)}x^{(h-1)})$};

Let $p,q\ge1$, let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $H\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be open, and let $T$ be a nonnegative integer. Suppose $h_0:\Theta\to H$, $\Phi_t:\Theta\times H\to H$ for $1\le t\le T$, and $\ell:\Theta\times H\to\mathbb R$ are continuously differentiable on open domains containing the trajectory at $\theta\in\Theta$. A continuously differentiable map is totally differentiable at each point and has a derivative matrix continuous on its domain. Define $h_0=h_0(\theta)$, $h_t=\Phi_t(\theta,h_{t-1})$, and $J(\theta)=\ell(\theta,h_T)$. Write $A_t=D_\theta\Phi_t(\theta,h_{t-1})$ and $B_t=D_h\Phi_t(\theta,h_{t-1})$, with each partial derivative holding the other argument fixed. Set $\lambda_T=(D_h\ell(\theta,h_T))^T$ and, in descending order, $\lambda_{t-1}=B_t^T\lambda_t$. Then the backpropagation algorithm returns $J(\theta)$ and

$$\nabla_\theta J(\theta)=(D_\theta\ell(\theta,h_T))^T+\sum_{t=1}^{T}A_t^T\lambda_t+(Dh_0(\theta))^T\lambda_0,$$

where the sum is empty when $T=0$. The statement also applies when every primitive is evaluated on one fixed strict $C^1$ branch; it makes no assertion at a branch boundary.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in The Euclidean inner product $\langle x,y\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k y_k$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   (A norm on a real vector space, the induced metric, and the dictionary with the metric axioms), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for finite sums, stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
The Euclidean inner product $\langle x,y\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k y_k$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Let $n\ge0$, let $f$ have continuous derivatives through order $n+1$ on an
open interval containing the segment between $c$ and $x$, and put
$$
P_n(x)=\sum_{j=0}^n\frac{f^{(j)}(c)}{j!}(x-c)^j.
$$
Then
$$
f(x)-P_n(x)=\frac1{n!}\int_c^x f^{(n+1)}(t)(x-t)^n\,dt.
$$
If $M\ge0$ and $|f^{(n+1)}(t)|\le M$ between $c$ and $x$, then
$$
|f(x)-P_n(x)|\le\frac{M|x-c|^{n+1}}{(n+1)!}.
$$
The formula and bound include $x=c$ and oriented endpoints.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$ and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$.

1. **Fundamental theorem, second part, in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as
   a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and
   suppose $f' : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is integrable. Then
   $$\int_a^b f' \;=\; f(b) - f(a).$$
2. **A bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz function.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at
   every point of $(a,b)$, and let $M \ge 0$ satisfy
   $\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \le M$ for every $t \in (a,b)$. Then
   $$\lVert f(t) - f(s)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,|t-s| \qquad \text{for all } s,t \in [a,b],$$
   that is, $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $M$ as a map
   $([a,b], d_{\mathbb{R}}) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]],
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

$$\lVert A\rVert_F\;:=\;\Bigl(\,\sum_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|^{2}\Bigr)^{1/2},$$

where $|\cdot|$ is the absolute value on $\mathbb R$
(Absolute value in an ordered field) for $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ and the modulus on $\mathbb C$
(Real and imaginary parts, complex conjugation, and modulus) for
$\mathbb F=\mathbb C$, and the outer power is the nonnegative real square root.

**The displayed quantity is a norm.** Regard $A$ as the element of the
coordinate space $\mathbb F^{mn}$ whose $j+in$-th entry is $a_{ij}$. The
standard coordinate inner product of The standard formulas $\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_{k<n}x_k y_k$ on $\mathbb R^n$ and $\sum_{k<n}x_k\overline{y_k}$ on $\mathbb C^n$ are inner products
satisfies $\langle A,A\rangle=\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}\overline{a_{ij}}$, which equals
$\sum_{i,j}|a_{ij}|^{2}$ because $z\overline z=|z|^{2}$
(Conjugation is an involutive real-field automorphism, $z\overline z=|z|^2$, and modulus is definite, multiplicative, and subadditive). Thus $\lVert A\rVert_F$ is
exactly the inner-product norm of The norm $\lVert v\rVert=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ induced by a real or complex inner product evaluated at $A$,
and the three norm axioms hold for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_F$ because they hold for
every inner-product norm. For real matrices the same sum is
$\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}^{2}$, since $|x|^{2}=x^{2}$ for real $x$ by the two cases of
Absolute value in an ordered field.

The Frobenius norm is the Euclidean norm of the full entry list, not the
largest factor by which the matrix stretches a single vector. It can coincide
with an induced $2$-norm in one-row or one-column cases, but in general it is a
different matrix norm from the induced operator norms used on this page. Its
relation to the spectral norm, its unitary invariance and its singular-value
formula are
Spectral and Frobenius norms are unitarily invariant, are given by singular values, and satisfy the sharp rank comparison.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ be the function space of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]], with $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$.

### The $p$-norm, for a rational exponent $p \ge 1$

Let $p \in \mathbb{Q}$ with $p \ge 1$. For $x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ put

$$\lVert x\rVert_p \;:=\; \Bigl(\sum_{k<n} |x_k|^{p}\Bigr)^{1/p},$$

where $|\cdot|$ is the absolute value ([[def-abs-value]]), the sum is the finite
sum of [[def-finite-sum]], and both powers are the **rational** powers of
[[def-rational-power]].

**Every power written here is defined.** Each base $|x_k|$ is a nonnegative real
and $p > 0$, so $|x_k|^{p}$ is given by [[def-rational-power]] for $|x_k| > 0$
and by its supplementary clause $0^{p} = 0$ for $|x_k| = 0$; the sum of these
nonnegative terms is nonnegative ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), and
$1/p$ is a positive rational, so the outer power is defined for the same two
reasons. The value does not depend on which representative of $p$ or of $1/p$ is
used ([[lem-rational-power-well-defined]]).

**The exponent is rational in this definition.**
[[def-rational-power]] supplies the nonnegative-base powers used here, and
[[thm-minkowski-finite]] supplies the corresponding triangle inequality for
rational $p \ge 1$. This item makes no claim with $p$ ranging over a real
interval; its rational domain is unchanged.

### The maximum norm

For $n \ge 1$ and $x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ put

$$\lVert x\rVert_\infty \;:=\; \max\{\, |x_k| \;:\; k < n \,\},$$

the maximum of a nonempty finite set of reals, which exists and is one of its
elements ([[lem-finite-set-has-max]], [[def-max-min]]).

**The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is required and propagates.** At $n = 0$ the set
$\{|x_k| : k<n\}$ is empty and has no maximum ([[def-max-min]]). This is the same
restriction the published [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] carries, for the same reason, and
**every statement on this page that mentions $\lVert\cdot\rVert_\infty$ inherits
it**. The $p$-norms for rational $p \ge 1$ carry no such restriction: at $n = 0$
each is the empty sum raised to a positive rational power, hence $0$.

### The three cases the rest of the page uses

- $\lVert x\rVert_1 = \sum_{k<n}|x_k|$, since $t^{1} = t$ for $t \ge 0$
  ([[lem-rational-power-laws]], and $0^{1} = 0$ by the supplementary clause).
- $\lVert x\rVert_2 = \bigl(\sum_{k<n}|x_k|^{2}\bigr)^{1/2} = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}x_k^{2}}$,
  which is exactly the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]: the
  exponent $2$ agrees with the integer power, so $|x_k|^{2} = x_k^{2}$
  ([[lem-of-abs-value]]), and $t^{1/2}$ is the unique nonnegative square root of
  $t$, which is $\sqrt{t}$ ([[def-rational-power]], [[thm-of-square-roots]]).
  **The two notations denote the same function and no second Euclidean norm is
  introduced.**
- $\lVert x\rVert_\infty$ as above, for $n \ge 1$.

That each of these is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]], and
that the metrics they induce are exactly the published $d_1$, $d_2$ and
$d_\infty$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], is
[[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]; it is proved there
and is not assumed here.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be continuously
Fréchet differentiable. The gradient $\nabla f(x)$ is the vector of partial
derivatives in the Euclidean coordinates, with the convention of
The Jacobian matrix of partial derivatives and the gradient in the scalar-valued case; differentiability is the Fréchet
condition of The real Frechet derivative on real and complex matrix spaces with the Frobenius norm.

**Inputs:** an initial point $x_0\in U$; either a positive fixed-step
sequence $(t_k)_{k\ge0}$ or backtracking parameters $\alpha\in(0,1)$ and
$\beta\in(0,1)$; and an optional caller stopping predicate
$S(k,x,g)\in\{\mathrm{false},\mathrm{true}\}$, with
$S:\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\times U\times\mathbb R^d\to\{\mathrm{false},\mathrm{true}\}$.
If no predicate is supplied, use $S\equiv\mathrm{false}$. **Output:** when the
procedure stops, return the last valid iterate $x_k$ and the status
`stationary`, `caller-stop`, or `domain-failure`.
If no stopping status occurs, the sequence continues and there is no finite
return.
For example, an outer procedure's at-most-$M$-updates limit, for finite real
$M\ge0$, is implemented by $S(k,x,g):=(k+1>M)$.

At iteration $k$, where $k$ is the number of accepted updates so far and the
current iterate is $x_k$:

1. Compute $g_k:=\nabla f(x_k)$ and set $p_k:=-g_k$. If $g_k=0$, return
   $(x_k,\texttt{stationary})$.
2. If $S(k,x_k,g_k)$ is true, return $(x_k,\texttt{caller-stop})$. Check this
   predicate at the current iterate after its gradient is computed and before
   any step is selected.
3. In fixed-step mode, set $t=t_k$. If $x_k+tp_k\notin U$, return
   $(x_k,\texttt{domain-failure})$ without accepting that candidate.
4. In backtracking mode, start with $t=1$ and repeatedly replace $t$ by
   $\beta t$ until $x_k+tp_k\in U$ and
   $f(x_k+tp_k)\le f(x_k)+\alpha t\,\langle g_k,p_k\rangle$.
5. Set $x_{k+1}:=x_k+t p_k$ and continue at iteration $k+1$.

The fixed-step update map is $x\mapsto x-t_k\nabla f(x)$; at a stationary
point its value is $x$, which is the returned iterate. A backtracking search
that is reached at a nonstationary iterate is well-defined by
Armijo backtracking terminates for strict descent directions. The
procedure asserts no convergence or global-minimization property for an
arbitrary objective.

Let $n\ge0$, let $f$ have continuous derivatives through order $n+1$ on an
open interval containing the segment between $c$ and $x$, and put
$$
P_n(x)=\sum_{j=0}^n\frac{f^{(j)}(c)}{j!}(x-c)^j.
$$
Then
$$
f(x)-P_n(x)=\frac1{n!}\int_c^x f^{(n+1)}(t)(x-t)^n\,dt.
$$
If $M\ge0$ and $|f^{(n+1)}(t)|\le M$ between $c$ and $x$, then
$$
|f(x)-P_n(x)|\le\frac{M|x-c|^{n+1}}{(n+1)!}.
$$

product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in The Euclidean inner product $\langle x,y\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k y_k$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   (A norm on a real vector space, the induced metric, and the dictionary with the metric axioms), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for finite sums, stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
The Euclidean inner product $\langle x,y\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k y_k$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

$$x^{(0)}=x,\qquad x^{(h)}=\sqrt{c_\sigma/m}\,\sigma(W^{(h)}x^{(h-1)})\quad(1\le h\le H),\qquad f_{\rm fc}(x,\theta)=a^Tx^{(H)},$$

where $W^{(1)}\in\mathbb R^{m\times d}$, $W^{(h)}\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ for $h\ge2$, $a\in\mathbb R^m$, and $\sigma$ acts coordinatewise. The residual network uses the same first layer and then

$$x^{(1)}=\sqrt{c_\sigma/m}\,\sigma(W^{(1)}x),\qquad x^{(h)}=x^{(h-1)}+\frac{c_{\rm res}}{H\sqrt m}\,\sigma(W^{(h)}x^{(h-1)})\quad(2\le h\le H),\qquad f_{\rm res}(x,\theta)=a^Tx^{(H)},$$

with $0<c_{\rm res}<1$. In either architecture, random initialization means all entries of all matrices $W^{(h)}$ and of $a$ are independent $N(0,1)$ random variables; all these entries are trained by full-batch gradient descent. The empirical quadratic loss is $L(\theta)=\frac12\sum_{i=1}^n(f(x_i,\theta)-y_i)^2$.

For the fully connected architecture and the same fixed data, define the population matrices by

$$K_{ij}^{(0)}=\langle x_i,x_j\rangle.$$

For $1\le h<H$, let $(U_{ij}^{(h)},V_{ij}^{(h)})$ be a centered bivariate normal vector with covariance

$$A_{ij}^{(h)}=\begin{pmatrix}K_{ii}^{(h-1)}&K_{ij}^{(h-1)}\\K_{ji}^{(h-1)}&K_{jj}^{(h-1)}\end{pmatrix},$$

and put $K_{ij}^{(h)}=c_\sigma\mathbb E[\sigma(U_{ij}^{(h)})\sigma(V_{ij}^{(h)})]$. For $h=H$, use the same bivariate-normal definition with $A_{ij}^{(H)}$ formed from $K^{(H-1)}$, and set

$$K_{ij}^{(H)}=c_\sigma K_{ij}^{(H-1)}\mathbb E[\sigma'(U_{ij}^{(H)})\sigma'(V_{ij}^{(H)})].$$

When $H=1$, this last formula uses $K^{(0)}$ directly and there are no intermediate activation-covariance matrices. For the fully connected theorem, this terminal matrix is denoted $K_{\rm fc}^{(H)}$.

For the residual architecture with $H\ge2$, use a separate sequence $S^{(h)}$ and mean vector $b^{(h)}$. Set $S^{(0)}=K^{(0)}$. For $G^{(0)}\sim N_n(0,S^{(0)})$, put

$$S_{ij}^{(1)}=c_\sigma\mathbb E[\sigma(G_i^{(0)})\sigma(G_j^{(0)})],\qquad b_i^{(1)}=\sqrt{c_\sigma}\mathbb E[\sigma(G_i^{(0)})].$$

Write $\alpha=c_{\rm res}/H$. For $2\le h<H$, take a fresh centered Gaussian vector $G^{(h-1)}$ with covariance $S^{(h-1)}$, put $\mu_i^{(h-1)}=\mathbb E[\sigma(G_i^{(h-1)})]$, and define

$$S_{ij}^{(h)}=S_{ij}^{(h-1)}+\alpha\bigl(b_i^{(h-1)}\mu_j^{(h-1)}+b_j^{(h-1)}\mu_i^{(h-1)}\bigr)+\alpha^2\mathbb E[\sigma(G_i^{(h-1)})\sigma(G_j^{(h-1)})],\qquad b_i^{(h)}=b_i^{(h-1)}+\alpha\mu_i^{(h-1)}.$$

For $G\sim N_n(0,S^{(H-1)})$, define the residual terminal matrix by

$$K_{{\rm res},ij}^{(H)}=\frac{c_{\rm res}^2}{H^2}S_{ij}^{(H-1)}\mathbb E[\sigma'(G_i)\sigma'(G_j)].$$

The fully connected and residual convergence statements use $K_{\rm fc}^{(H)}$ and $K_{\rm res}^{(H)}$, respectively. At $H=1$, the two architectures coincide; define $K_{\rm res}^{(1)}=K_{\rm fc}^{(1)}$. The residual recursion above is the scalar specialization of the source's general mean/second-moment recursion, equation (16); in particular it includes the mean cross terms. Its terminal Gaussian covariance is $S^{(H-1)}$, as determined by the finite-width last-layer Gram formula (14).

The residual recurrence has one identity contribution from $x^{(h-1)}$ and one nonlinear contribution at every layer $2\le h\le H$; the arrows below depict that convention for one generic layer and do not enter any proof.
