derivations.claim: By [A1], [F1], and [F2], the Gaussian kernel has the real RKHS used in the Statement, with evaluation property [F3]. Let $X_n=\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}$ and $V_n=\operatorname{span}\{k_\sigma(\cdot,x_i):1\le i\le n\}$. For any interpolant $h$, put $g=h-h^*$. Then $g(x_i)=0$, so [F3] gives $\langle g,k_\sigma(\cdot,x_i)\rangle=0$ for each $i$ and hence $g\perp V_n$. By [F6] the projection $\Pi_{V_n}$ exists; therefore $$g(x)=\langle g,k_\sigma(\cdot,x)\rangle =\langle g,k_\sigma(\cdot,x)-\Pi_{V_n}k_\sigma(\cdot,x)\rangle.$$ The inner-product Cauchy--Schwarz inequality follows by expanding $\|u-tv\|^2\ge0$ and minimizing over real $t$ (with the zero-vector case immediate). The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Then countable choice holds. Moreover, if $R\subseteq X\times X$ is serial on a nonempty set X and $a\in X$, there is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\ge0}$ with $x_0=a$ and $x_n R x_{n+1}$ for every n. Thus the countable and dependent choices required by the probability-product suppliers are available under AC.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By The standard normal density has total mass one and The indefinite integral of a nonnegative measurable function is a measure, gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. The law of a random element is a probability measure makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in The Dirac set function at a point.

The **monic probabilists' Hermite polynomials** are the polynomials $H_m\in\mathbb R[x]$ defined by
$$H_0=1,\qquad H_1(x)=x,\qquad xH_m(x)=H_{m+1}(x)+m\,H_{m-1}(x)\quad(m\ge1).$$
The recurrence is solved for the higher polynomial, $H_{m+1}(x)=xH_m(x)-mH_{m-1}(x)$, so it determines $H_m$ uniquely by induction on $m$. Each $H_m$ is monic of degree $m$: $H_2=x^2-1$, $H_3=x^3-3x$ and $H_4=x^4-6x^2+3$; in general $H_m(x)=m!\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor m/2\rfloor}\frac{(-1/2)^j x^{m-2j}}{j!\,(m-2j)!}$.

Under the AC assumption of the Gaussian-law supplier, these are the monic orthogonal polynomials for the standard normal law of [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]]: they form an orthogonal system for the measure $(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}dx$; orthogonality and the expansion of monomials in this system are proved separately on this page. The moments of that law are those of [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]], and the polynomial calculus used below is that of [[def-derivative]]. The defining property used in this batch is the recurrence; no choice principle is used.

Assume countable choice. On every measure space, complex $L^p$ is complete for $1\le p\le\infty$, and every norm-convergent sequence has a subsequence of measurable representatives converging a.e. to its limit. For finite $p$, finite simple functions with finite-measure support are dense, and on $\mathbb R^n$ with Lebesgue measure, $n\ge1$, complex $C_c^\infty$ is dense. Complex $L^2$ has the first-variable-linear inner product $\int f\overline g$, its norm is $\|\cdot\|_2$, and Cauchy–Schwarz has the following equality criterion: if $g\ne0$, equality iff $f=cg$ a.e.; if $g=0$, equality for all $f$. The finite-tuple version uses a common scalar across components.

Let $n\ge1$ and $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, with the componentwise integral and quotient conventions of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]. Define
$$\widehat f(\xi)=\mathcal Ff(\xi):=\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(x)\exp(-2\pi i x\cdot\xi)\,dx,\qquad \xi\in\mathbb R^n.$$
Here $x\cdot\xi=\sum_{j=1}^n x_j\xi_j$, Lebesgue measure is used, and the exponential is [[def-complex-exponential]]. Its unit modulus follows from [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]. The integral is evaluated using any measurable representative. Absolute convergence and representative independence are the obligations discharged by [[lem-l-one-fourier-transform-is-well-defined]]. The output is a function defined at every frequency, not merely an almost-everywhere class. At frequency zero the formula reads $\widehat f(0)=\int f$. No choice selection of representatives for a family of classes is part of this definition.

For every $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$, $n\ge1$, the integral defining $\widehat f(\xi)$ is absolutely convergent for every $\xi$ and unchanged by null-set modifications. Moreover $|\widehat f(\xi)|\le\|f\|_1$.
Assume countable choice. If $f,g\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$ and $\widehat f=\widehat g$, then $f=g$ almost everywhere. Equality of the transforms almost everywhere already suffices.

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].
For every $z\in\mathbb C$, the series $\sum z^n/n!$ converges absolutely.

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Assume AC and let $G\sim N(0,\sigma^2)$ for $\sigma\ge0$. Then $\mathbb E[G^2]=\sigma^2$ and $\mathbb E[G^4]=3\sigma^4$; in particular the fourth moment is finite. For independent centered normal coordinates $G_j\sim N(0,\sigma_j^2)$, every finite linear combination of the variables $G_j^2$ has finite second moment.

derivations.claim: Let $r\in L^2(\gamma)$ be orthogonal to every $h_m$. Each monomial $x^j$ is a finite linear combination of $H_0,\ldots,H_j$ by [F2], and each fixed polynomial is square-integrable under $\gamma$ because a polynomial times $e^{-x^2/2}$ has an integrable tail. Therefore $\int r(x)x^j\,d\gamma(x)=0$ for every $j\ge0$.

Put $v(x)=r(x)\phi(x)$, so $v\in L^1(\mathbb R)$ by [F1] and [F6]. For every $a\ge0$, Cauchy–Schwarz and completion of the square give $\int |r(x)|e^{a|x|}\,d\gamma(x)\le\|r\|_2(\int e^{2a|x|}\,d\gamma)^{1/2}<\infty$, since each half-line integral is at most $e^{2a^2}$.

Fix $\xi\in\mathbb R$. The partial sums $S_M(x)=\sum_{j=0}^M(-2\pi i\xi x)^j/j!$ converge pointwise to $e^{-2\pi i\xi x}$ and satisfy $|S_M(x)|\le e^{2\pi|\xi||x|}$ by [F5]. Applying [F7] with the integrable majorant from step 1.2 gives $\widehat v(\xi)=\lim_{M\to\infty}\int r(x)S_M(x)\,d\gamma(x)=0$, because every term is a scalar multiple of a zero moment from step 1.1.

By [F4], $\widehat v=0$ implies $v=0$ Lebesgue-almost everywhere. Since $\phi(x)>0$ for all $x$, $r=0$ $\gamma$-almost everywhere. Thus the only $L^2(\gamma)$ function orthogonal to all the $h_m$ is zero.

For arbitrary real $f\in L^2(\gamma)$, set $a_m=\int f h_m\,d\gamma$ and $S_M=\sum_{m=0}^M a_mh_m$. Orthogonality in [F2] gives $\|f-S_M\|_2^2=\|f\|_2^2-\sum_{m=0}^M a_m^2\ge0$ and, for $M>K$, $\|S_M-S_K\|_2^2=\sum_{K<m\le M}a_m^2$; hence the partial sums are Cauchy. View them in complex $L^2(\gamma)$; by [F3] and [A1] they converge there, and their limit is real because every $S_M$ is real. The residual $f-S$ is orthogonal to each $h_m$, hence zero by step 3.1. Therefore $f=S$ in $L^2(\gamma)$ and taking norms yields Parseval’s identity.

If only finitely many $a_m$ are nonzero, step 4.1 makes $f$ equal almost everywhere to a polynomial $p$. If $f$ is continuous and differs from $p$ at some point, it differs on a nonempty open interval, which has positive $\gamma$ measure by [F1]; hence $f=p$ everywhere, contrary to nonpolynomiality. Thus a continuous nonpolynomial $f$ has unbounded coefficient support. A globally Lipschitz $f$ obeys $|f(x)|\le |f(0)|+L|x|$; [F8] gives $\int |x|^2\,d\gamma<\infty$, so this growth bound implies $f\in L^2(\gamma)$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

A **real kernel** on a set $X$ is a function $k:X\times X\to\mathbb R$. It is **positive semidefinite** if it is symmetric and, for every integer $n\ge1$, every $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in X$, and every $c_1,\ldots,c_n\in\mathbb R$,

$$\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n c_i c_j k(x_i,x_j)\ge0.$$

A **real reproducing kernel Hilbert space with kernel $k$** is a real Hilbert space $\mathcal H$ of functions $X\to\mathbb R$ such that, for each $x\in X$, the section $k_x:=k(\cdot,x)$ lies in $\mathcal H$ and $\langle f,k_x\rangle_{\mathcal H}=f(x)$ for every $f\in\mathcal H$. Consequently $\langle k_z,k_x\rangle_{\mathcal H}=k(z,x)=k(x,z)$.

For the canonical construction, let $E_0$ be the real vector space of finitely supported functions $a:X\to\mathbb R$, write $\delta_x$ for the function supported at $x$ with value $1$, and put

$$B(a,b):=\sum_{x\in\operatorname{supp}(a)}\sum_{z\in\operatorname{supp}(b)}a(x)b(z)k(x,z).$$

Let $N:=\{a\in E_0:B(a,a)=0\}$. Under the Axiom of Countable Choice, the canonical space is formed by giving $E_0/N$ its induced inner product and taking a norm completion; the image of $\delta_x$ is denoted $k_x$. For an element $h$ of that completion, its associated function is $x\mapsto\langle h,k_x\rangle$. The quotient, completed inner product, and function identification are justified by the local construction theorem.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$. Then a unique local solution of the IVP exists on some interval around the initial time. More quantitatively, if $h,r>0$ make

$$[t_0-h,t_0+h]\times\overline B(x_0,r)\subseteq D,$$

if $\|F\|_2\le M$ and $F$ has state-Lipschitz constant $L$ on this cylinder, and if $hM\le r$ and $Lh<1$, then there is exactly one solution on $[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ through $(t_0,x_0)$ whose graph lies in the cylinder. Any two solutions through the same initial data agree on every common subinterval containing $t_0$.

In particular, a unique local solution exists on an interval around the initial time.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Then countable choice holds. Moreover, if $R\subseteq X\times X$ is serial on a nonempty set X and $a\in X$, there is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\ge0}$ with $x_0=a$ and $x_n R x_{n+1}$ for every n. Thus the countable and dependent choices required by the probability-product suppliers are available under AC.

Assume AC. Let $\gamma$ be the standard Gaussian probability measure on $\mathbb R$ with density $\phi(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}$, let $H_m$ be the monic probabilists’ Hermite polynomial defined by $H_0=1$, $H_1(x)=x$, and $H_{m+1}(x)=xH_m(x)-mH_{m-1}(x)$, and put $h_m=H_m/\sqrt{m!}$. Then $(h_m)_{m\ge0}$ is a complete orthonormal basis of real $L^2(\gamma)$. Every $f\in L^2(\gamma)$ has the norm-convergent expansion $f=\sum_{m\ge0}a_mh_m$, where $a_m=\int f h_m\,d\gamma$, and $\sum_{m\ge0}a_m^2=\|f\|_{L^2(\gamma)}^2$. If $f$ is continuous and nonpolynomial, then $a_m\ne0$ for an unbounded set of indices $m$. Every globally Lipschitz real function belongs to $L^2(\gamma)$, so this conclusion applies to every globally Lipschitz nonpolynomial activation.

Assume AC. Let $\gamma$ be standard Gaussian measure, let $h_m=H_m/\sqrt{m!}$ be the normalized probabilists’ Hermite basis, and let $f,g\in L^2(\gamma)$ have coefficients $a_m=\int f h_m\,d\gamma$ and $b_m=\int g h_m\,d\gamma$. For $\rho\in[-1,1]$, let $(X,Y)$ have the centered bivariate normal law with unit variances and correlation $\rho$. Then
$$\mathbb E[f(X)g(Y)]=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}a_mb_m\rho^m.$$
The series is absolutely convergent, including at $\rho=\pm1$. In particular, the Gaussian dual kernel of $f$ is $\sum_{m\ge0}a_m^2\rho^m$, and $\sum_{m\ge0}a_m^2=\|f\|_{L^2(\gamma)}^2$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Applying [F2] to $\mu$ gives $k(x,y)=\beta^2+\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}a_r^2(\alpha x\cdot y+\delta)^r.$ The series is absolutely convergent since $|r(x,y)|\le1$ and $\sum_r a_r^2<\infty$.

Expanding by the binomial theorem, for each $x,y$ on the sphere the absolute double series is $\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}a_r^2\sum_{m=0}^r\binom rm\alpha^m\delta^{r-m}|x\cdot y|^m=\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}a_r^2(\alpha|x\cdot y|+\delta)^r\le\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}a_r^2<\infty$, since $|x\cdot y|\le1$ and $\alpha+\delta=1$. Tonelli applied to this nonnegative absolute series justifies reordering the sign-changing binomial terms. Define $d_m=\mathbf1_{\{m=0\}}\beta^2+\alpha^m\sum_{r=m}^{\infty}a_r^2\binom rm\delta^{r-m}\quad(m\ge0)$; then $k(x,y)=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}d_m(x\cdot y)^m$. The rescaled function $\mu(z)=\sigma(\sqrt q z)$ is continuous and nonpolynomial: if it were a polynomial, then $\sigma(u)=\mu(u/\sqrt q)$ would be a polynomial because $q>0$. It is globally Lipschitz, so [F1] supplies its $L^2(\gamma)$ membership and Parseval. The function $\mu$ has infinitely many nonzero Hermite coefficients: otherwise [F1] would make it equal almost everywhere to a polynomial, and continuity would make that equality hold everywhere, contradicting nonpolynomiality. Thus for each $m$ there is an $r\ge m$ with $a_r\ne0$, and the corresponding term in [F3]’s sum is strictly positive because $\alpha,\delta>0$. Hence $d_m>0$ for every $m$, including $m=0$ because $\beta>0$.

For any $c\in\mathbb R^N$, the quadratic form is $\sum_{i,j}c_ic_jk(x_i,x_j)=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}d_m\left\|\sum_{i=1}^N c_i x_i^{\otimes m}\right\|_2^2\ge0.$ Indeed, $\langle x_i^{\otimes m},x_j^{\otimes m}\rangle=(x_i\cdot x_j)^m$ by the induced tensor inner product, and the convergent series may be evaluated termwise because $|x_i\cdot x_j|\le1$ and $\sum_m d_m<\infty$.

If this quadratic form were zero, positivity of every $d_m$ would force $\sum_i c_i x_i^{\otimes m}=0$ for every $m\ge0$. Consequently $\sum_i c_i p(x_i)=0$ for every polynomial $p$ on $\mathbb R^{n_0}$: each monomial of degree $m$ is a coordinate linear functional on $x^{\otimes m}$, and constants correspond to $m=0$. For each index $j$, take $p_j(x)=\prod_{i
e j}\|x-x_i\|_2^2$, with the empty product equal to $1$. Then $p_j(x_i)=0$ for $i
e j$ and $p_j(x_j)>0$, so $c_j=0$. This holds for every $j$, contradicting $c
e0$. Thus the quadratic form in step 3.2 is strictly positive.

Let $p,q\ge1$, let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $H\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be open, and let $T$ be a nonnegative integer. Suppose $h_0:\Theta\to H$, $\Phi_t:\Theta\times H\to H$ for $1\le t\le T$, and $\ell:\Theta\times H\to\mathbb R$ are continuously differentiable on open domains containing the trajectory at $\theta\in\Theta$. A continuously differentiable map is totally differentiable at each point and has a derivative matrix continuous on its domain. Define $h_0=h_0(\theta)$, $h_t=\Phi_t(\theta,h_{t-1})$, and $J(\theta)=\ell(\theta,h_T)$. Write $A_t=D_\theta\Phi_t(\theta,h_{t-1})$ and $B_t=D_h\Phi_t(\theta,h_{t-1})$, with each partial derivative holding the other argument fixed. Set $\lambda_T=(D_h\ell(\theta,h_T))^T$ and, in descending order, $\lambda_{t-1}=B_t^T\lambda_t$. Then the backpropagation algorithm returns $J(\theta)$ and

$$\nabla_\theta J(\theta)=(D_\theta\ell(\theta,h_T))^T+\sum_{t=1}^{T}A_t^T\lambda_t+(Dh_0(\theta))^T\lambda_0,$$

where the sum is empty when $T=0$. The statement also applies when every primitive is evaluated on one fixed strict $C^1$ branch; it makes no assertion at a branch boundary.

Let $P,q\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^P$ be open, let $X$ be a set, and let $f:\Omega\times X\to\mathbb R^q$. Fix $\theta\in\Omega$ and suppose that for each $x\in X$ the map $\vartheta\mapsto f(\vartheta,x)$ is totally differentiable at $\theta$, meaning it has a linear first-order approximation with remainder $o(\|\vartheta-\theta\|_2)$. Write $D_\theta f(\theta,x)\in\mathbb R^{q\times P}$ for its derivative matrix in the standard Euclidean coordinates. The matrix-valued neural tangent kernel at $\theta$ is

$$K_\theta(x,x'):=D_\theta f(\theta,x)\,D_\theta f(\theta,x')^{T}\in\mathbb R^{q\times q}.$$

Equivalently, for $1\le a,b\le q$,
$$\bigl(K_\theta(x,x')\bigr)_{ab}=\sum_{p=1}^{P}\partial_{\theta_p}f_a(\theta,x)\,\partial_{\theta_p}f_b(\theta,x').$$
For a scalar-output model this is the scalar kernel $\sum_{p=1}^{P}\partial_{\theta_p}f(\theta,x)\partial_{\theta_p}f(\theta,x')$.

Assume AC. Fix integers $L,n_0,\ldots,n_L\ge1$, a bias scale $\beta>0$, and an activation $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$. For each layer $\ell=0,\ldots,L-1$, let $W^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb R^{n_{\ell+1}\times n_\ell}$ and $b^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb R^{n_{\ell+1}}$. At initialization all entries of all matrices and bias vectors are mutually independent and each has the standard normal law $N(0,1)$. These finite collections of entries have the corresponding finite-dimensional multivariate normal product law.

For an input $x\in\mathbb R^{n_0}$, put $z^{(0)}(x)=x$ and, for $\ell=0,\ldots,L-1$, define the preactivation
$$u^{(\ell+1)}(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n_\ell}}W^{(\ell)}z^{(\ell)}(x)+\beta b^{(\ell)}.$$
For $\ell+1<L$, set $z^{(\ell+1)}(x)=\sigma(u^{(\ell+1)}(x))$ coordinatewise; the output layer is linear and $f_\theta(x):=u^{(L)}(x)\in\mathbb R^{n_L}$. The parameter vector $\theta$ consists of every entry of the matrices and biases. The width $n_L$ is the fixed output dimension; the hidden widths are $n_1,\ldots,n_{L-1}$. A sequential hidden-width limit takes $n_1\to\infty$ first, then $n_2\to\infty$, and so on through $n_{L-1}\to\infty$.

Let $(X_k)_{k\ge1}$ be IID square-integrable real random variables, with $\mu=\mathbb EX_1$ and $\sigma^2=\operatorname{Var}(X_1)$. For $S_n=\sum_{k=1}^nX_k$,
$$\mathbb E|S_n/n-\mu|^2=\sigma^2/n,$$
and $S_n/n\to\mu$ in $L^2$ and in probability. Also $\mathbb P(|S_n/n-\mu|\ge\varepsilon)\le\sigma^2/(n\varepsilon^2)$ for $\varepsilon>0$.

Assume AC and let $G\sim N(0,\sigma^2)$ for $\sigma\ge0$. Then $\mathbb E[G^2]=\sigma^2$ and $\mathbb E[G^4]=3\sigma^4$; in particular the fourth moment is finite. For independent centered normal coordinates $G_j\sim N(0,\sigma_j^2)$, every finite linear combination of the variables $G_j^2$ has finite second moment.

For real random variables $(X_n)$ and $X$ on one probability space, write
$X_n\to X$ **in probability** when, for every $\varepsilon>0$,
$$\mathbb P(|X_n-X|>\varepsilon)\longrightarrow0.$$
This is precisely [[def-convergence-in-measure]] for the probability measure.

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

Let $X,Y$ be integrable real or complex random variables on one probability
space.

1. For scalars $a,b$,
   $$\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Y].$$
2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y].$$
3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ (Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point, Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. If $F:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous, differentiable except at countably
many points, and $F'\in L^1[a,b]$, then $F$ is absolutely continuous and
$$F(x)-F(a)=\int_a^xF'(t)\,dt$$
for every $x\in[a,b]$.

derivations.claim: Regard the network as a finite composition of $C^1$ maps on its Euclidean parameter space; [F1] gives the shared-parameter gradients. Let $J_f(\theta(t))$ be the Jacobian of $(f_\theta(x_i))_{i=1}^N$. It is continuous in $\theta$ because $\sigma$ is $C^2$, and it is bounded on the compact image of the continuous path $\theta([0,T])$. The flow equation and $d\in L^1([0,T];\mathbb R^N)$ therefore imply $\dot\theta\in L^1([0,T])$. By [F8], applied to each of the finitely many parameter coordinates, $\theta$ is absolutely continuous and its increments equal the integrals of its derivative. Define the terminal array by $D^L_{1i}(t)=d_i(t)$, and obtain each hidden backpropagated array $D^{\ell+1}(t)\in\mathbb R^{n_{\ell+1}\times N}$ by weighting the derivative of each data-point output with $d_i(t)$. If $Z^\ell(t)\in\mathbb R^{n_\ell\times N}$ is the activation array, the weight and bias equations are $\dot W^{(\ell)}=-D^{\ell+1}(Z^\ell)^T/(N\sqrt{n_\ell})$ and $\dot b^{(\ell)}=-\beta D^{\ell+1}\mathbf1/N$, while hidden backpropagation is $D^\ell=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma\prime(U^\ell))(W^{(\ell)})^TD^{\ell+1}/\sqrt{n_\ell}$. Here division by $N$ acts on the data sum.

For an array $R\in\mathbb R^{m\times N}$ write $\|R\|_{F,N}=\|R\|_F/\sqrt N$. Let $c=\sup|\sigma'|$ and $M_2=\sup|\sigma''|$, both finite by the hypotheses (taking a difference-quotient limit in the global Lipschitz inequality gives $c\le\operatorname{Lip}(\sigma)$), and set $w_\ell(t)=\|W^{(\ell)}(t)\|_{op}/\sqrt{n_\ell}$ and $a_\ell(t)=\|Z^\ell(t)\|_{F,N}/\sqrt{n_\ell}$ for $1\le\ell<L$. Let $K^\ell$ be the tangent-kernel block for the preactivation array $U^\ell$, acting on direction arrays by $(\mathcal K^\ell D)_{ai}=N^{-1}\sum_{b,j}K^\ell_{(i,a),(j,b)}D_{bj}$, and put $B_\ell=\|\mathcal K^\ell\|_{op}$ using $\|\cdot\|_{F,N}$. The initial block and layerwise chain rule give $B_1\le\|X\|_F^2/(n_0N)+\beta^2$ and $B_{\ell+1}\le c^2w_\ell^2B_\ell+a_\ell^2+\beta^2$ for $1\le\ell<L$: the current-layer weight-and-bias Gram has operator norm at most $a_\ell^2+\beta^2$, while the preceding Jacobian is composed with $W^{(\ell)}/\sqrt{n_\ell}$ and diagonal activation derivatives of norm at most $c$. The backpropagation identity in step 1.1 also gives $\|D^\ell(t)\|_{F,N}\le c^{L-\ell}(\prod_{k=\ell}^{L-1}w_k(t))\|d(t)\|_N$. Recursively, each $B_\ell$ is bounded by a polynomial in the finitely many $a_k,w_k,c,\beta$, and each backpropagation norm is bounded by such a polynomial times $\|d(t)\|_N$.

Cauchy–Schwarz in the data index and step 1.1 give, for $1\le\ell<L$, $\|\dot W^{(\ell)}\|_{op}/\sqrt{n_\ell}\le a_\ell\|D^{\ell+1}\|_{F,N}/\sqrt{n_\ell}$. For hidden layers the chain rule gives $\dot U^\ell=-\mathcal K^\ell D^\ell$, so $\|\dot U^\ell\|_{F,N}/\sqrt{n_\ell}\le B_\ell\|D^\ell\|_{F,N}/\sqrt{n_\ell}$; for $\ell=1$ this is the first-layer parameter Gram. The hidden-bias equation gives $\beta\|\dot b^{(\ell-1)}\|_2/\sqrt{n_\ell}\le\beta^2\|D^\ell\|_{F,N}/\sqrt{n_\ell}$, and the first-layer matrix gives $\|\dot W^{(0)}\|_F/\sqrt{n_1}\le C\|D^1\|_{F,N}/\sqrt{n_1}$ with $C=\|X\|_F/\sqrt{n_0N}$. The output bias is excluded because its derivative contributes only the constant feature $\beta$ and changes no later feature or parameter derivative. By [F7], $|\sigma'(u)-\sigma\prime(v)|\le M_2|u-v|$; global Lipschitz continuity gives $\|\dot Z^\ell\|_{F,N}\le c\|\dot U^\ell\|_{F,N}$. Whenever $a_\ell(t),w_\ell(t)\le R$ for every hidden layer, the recurrence in step 2.1 gives $B_\ell\le P_\ell(R)$, where $P_1(R)=\|X\|_F^2/(n_0N)+\beta^2$ and $P_{\ell+1}(R)=c^2R^2P_\ell(R)+R^2+\beta^2$; backpropagation gives $\|D^\ell\|_{F,N}\le(cR)^{L-\ell}\|d\|_N$. Substituting these bounds in the displayed rates shows that each normalized activation, preactivation, hidden-bias, and weight change rate is at most a polynomial in $R$ times $\|d(t)\|_N/\sqrt{n_{\min}}$, with $n_{\min}=\min_{1\le k<L}n_k$.

For $1\le\ell<L$ define $\widetilde a_\ell=\|Z^\ell(t)-Z^\ell(0)\|_{F,N}/\sqrt{n_\ell}$, $\widetilde u_\ell=\|U^\ell(t)-U^\ell(0)\|_{F,N}/\sqrt{n_\ell}$, and $\widetilde w_\ell=\|W^{(\ell)}(t)-W^{(\ell)}(0)\|_{op}/\sqrt{n_\ell}$; for $0\le\ell<L-1$ put $\widetilde b_\ell=\beta\|b^{(\ell)}(t)-b^{(\ell)}(0)\|_2/\sqrt{n_{\ell+1}}$, and put $\widetilde w_0=\|W^{(0)}(t)-W^{(0)}(0)\|_F/\sqrt{n_1}$. Define $A(t)=\sum_{\ell=1}^{L-1}(a_\ell(0)+w_\ell(0)+\widetilde a_\ell+\widetilde u_\ell+\widetilde w_\ell+\widetilde b_{\ell-1})+\widetilde w_0$. Since $a_\ell(t)\le a_\ell(0)+\widetilde a_\ell(t)$ and $w_\ell(t)\le w_\ell(0)+\widetilde w_\ell(t)$, all $a_\ell,w_\ell$ are bounded by $A(t)$. Each term of $A$ is absolutely continuous by [F8] and the norm/Lipschitz inequalities; the preceding estimates and the polynomial bounds in step 3.1 give, with $n_{\min}=\min_{1\le\ell<L}n_\ell$, $|\dot A(t)|\le Q(A(t))\|d(t)\|_N/\sqrt{n_{\min}}$ for a polynomial $Q$ with nonnegative coefficients depending only on $L,N,c,M_2,\beta$ and the fixed inputs. Initially $A(0)$ is stochastically bounded in the sequential limit: each $a_\ell(0)^2$ is an empirical second moment of a Lipschitz function of a finite Gaussian vector, and at each width limit [F4] applies after conditioning on earlier layers; for each fixed next-layer width, $W^{(\ell)}W^{(\ell)T}/n_\ell\to I$ entrywise by [F4], so $w_\ell(0)$ is bounded in that iterated limit.

Fix probability tolerance $\varepsilon>0$. Stochastic boundedness of $A(0)$ and of $\int_0^T\|d(t)\|_Ndt$ lets us restrict, except on a set of probability at most $2\varepsilon$, to $A(0)\le R$ and this integral at most $M$ for finite $R,M$. On this event, the differential inequality in step 4.1 implies $A(t)\le R+1$ for all $t\le T$ once $n_{\min}$ is large: on $[0,R+1]$, $Q$ is bounded by some $Q_*$, so $|A(t)-A(0)|\le Q_*M/\sqrt{n_{\min}}<1$; a first-exit argument justifies the bound on the whole interval. Since the normalized changes are nonnegative summands of $A(t)-A(0)$, each tends uniformly to zero.

For each layer, the exact tangent-kernel block recursion is $K^{\ell+1}_{(i,c),(j,d)}=\delta_{cd}(n_\ell^{-1}\sum_a Z^\ell_{ai}Z^\ell_{aj}+\beta^2)+n_\ell^{-1}\sum_{a,b}W^{(\ell)}_{ca}W^{(\ell)}_{db}\sigma'(U^\ell_{ai})\sigma'(U^\ell_{bj})K^\ell_{(i,a),(j,b)}$. It follows by applying the chain rule to each coordinate and splitting parameter derivatives into the current layer and earlier shared parameters, as in [F1]. The first term varies uniformly by the activation and hidden-bias estimates in step 5.1. For the second term, for each output index $c$ and data index $i$ use the vector $v_{c,i}(t)\in\mathbb R^{n_\ell}$ with entries $W^{(\ell)}_{ca}(t)\sigma'(U^\ell_{ai}(t))$. Their normalized Euclidean norms stay bounded. Their changes tend to zero in normalized Euclidean norm: the weight-change part is bounded by $c\|\Delta W_c\|_2/\sqrt{n_\ell}$, while Cauchy–Schwarz for the initial-weight part gives $n_\ell^{-1}\sum_a|W^{(\ell)}_{ca}(0)|^2|\Delta\sigma'_{ai}|^2\le(n_\ell^{-1}\sum_a|W^{(\ell)}_{ca}(0)|^4)^{1/2}(n_\ell^{-1}\sum_a|\Delta\sigma'_{ai}|^4)^{1/2}$. The first factor is stochastically bounded by [F3]–[F4]; the second tends uniformly to zero because [F7] gives $|\Delta\sigma'|\le M_2|\Delta U|$ and $|\Delta\sigma'|\le2c$, hence $|\Delta\sigma'|^4\le(2c)^2M_2^2|\Delta U|^2$; normalized preactivation changes tend to zero by step 5.1. For each fixed next-layer width, the finitely many output-index blocks have uniformly bounded subnetwork Gram operators by step 2.1, and induction from the constant first-layer Gram makes their changes tend uniformly to zero; applying $|\langle v,Kv'\rangle-\langle w,K_0w'\rangle|\le\|v-w\|\|K\|\|v'\|+\|w\|\|K-K_0\|\|v'\|+\|w\|\|K_0\|\|v'-w'\|$ at each of the finitely many layers proves uniform convergence of the finite-data kernel blocks. The output layer has fixed scalar dimension, so this is exactly $\sup_{t\le T}\|K_t-K_0\|_{op}\to0$ in probability.

A zero training horizon is allowed: there is no time increment to integrate, the kernel equals its initialization at the only time, and the displayed supremum of their difference is zero. Statement: The estimates hold for N=1; the empirical norm then is absolute value and all finite-data matrix bounds remain valid.
Statement: The inputs may repeat or have singular covariance; the finite-data Jacobian Gram and drift estimates do not require distinct data.

Statement: The supremum includes both t=0 and t=T; at T=0 the conclusion is the identity K0=K0. Joint measurability is also assumed, and continuity of the kernel paths makes the supremum event measurable. risk_review.notes: Checked 1.1–6.1 with network/backpropagation interfaces and Jacot Appendix A.2–A.3. Differentiable paths and integrable directions give integrable parameter derivatives on their compact images, hence absolute continuity. Array norm bounds give a polynomial first-exit estimate with factor 1/sqrt(n_min); Gaussian empirical moments and fixed-next-width weight Gram bounds give sequential tightness. In 6.1 the depth induction is in fixed next-layer output dimensions, not a simultaneous-width assertion: bounded backpropagated directions permit the smaller-network induction; the fourth-moment estimate controls weighted derivative changes in the final contraction. Probability truncation uses A(0)<=R and integrated direction<=M before taking sequential limits. Continuous kernel paths make supremum events measurable. T=0 and constant activation cause no division by a zero derivative bound. Accepted law/measurability clarification with confidence 1.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Then countable choice holds. Moreover, if $R\subseteq X\times X$ is serial on a nonempty set X and $a\in X$, there is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\ge0}$ with $x_0=a$ and $x_n R x_{n+1}$ for every n. Thus the countable and dependent choices required by the probability-product suppliers are available under AC.

Assume AC. Fix integers $L,n_0,\ldots,n_L\ge1$, a bias scale $\beta>0$, and an activation $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$. For each layer $\ell=0,\ldots,L-1$, let $W^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb R^{n_{\ell+1}\times n_\ell}$ and $b^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb R^{n_{\ell+1}}$. At initialization all entries of all matrices and bias vectors are mutually independent and each has the standard normal law $N(0,1)$. These finite collections of entries have the corresponding finite-dimensional multivariate normal product law.

For an input $x\in\mathbb R^{n_0}$, put $z^{(0)}(x)=x$ and, for $\ell=0,\ldots,L-1$, define the preactivation
$$u^{(\ell+1)}(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n_\ell}}W^{(\ell)}z^{(\ell)}(x)+\beta b^{(\ell)}.$$
For $\ell+1<L$, set $z^{(\ell+1)}(x)=\sigma(u^{(\ell+1)}(x))$ coordinatewise; the output layer is linear and $f_\theta(x):=u^{(L)}(x)\in\mathbb R^{n_L}$. The parameter vector $\theta$ consists of every entry of the matrices and biases. The width $n_L$ is the fixed output dimension; the hidden widths are $n_1,\ldots,n_{L-1}$. A sequential hidden-width limit takes $n_1\to\infty$ first, then $n_2\to\infty$, and so on through $n_{L-1}\to\infty$.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume AC. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then $$\Phi_X(t):=\mathbb E e^{it\cdot X}=\exp(it\cdot m-t^T\Sigma t/2)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R^d).$$ This transform uniquely determines the law, including singular Sigma.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By The standard normal density has total mass one and The indefinite integral of a nonnegative measurable function is a measure, gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. The law of a random element is a probability measure makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in The Dirac set function at a point.

Let $n\ge1$, let $X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}$ be independent real random variables on a
common probability space, and let $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Borel
measurable for each $i<n$.

1. If every $g_i$ is nonnegative, then
   $$\mathbb E\left[\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)\right]=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$$
   in $[0,+\infty]$. In this finite product of expectations, a zero factor
   makes the product zero even when another factor is $+\infty$; otherwise
   multiplication has its usual extended nonnegative meaning.
2. If every $g_i(X_i)$ is integrable, then $\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)$ is integrable
   and the same factorization holds in $\mathbb R$.

Let $(X_k)_{k\ge1}$ be IID square-integrable real random variables, with $\mu=\mathbb EX_1$ and $\sigma^2=\operatorname{Var}(X_1)$. For $S_n=\sum_{k=1}^nX_k$,
$$\mathbb E|S_n/n-\mu|^2=\sigma^2/n,$$
and $S_n/n\to\mu$ in $L^2$ and in probability. Also $\mathbb P(|S_n/n-\mu|\ge\varepsilon)\le\sigma^2/(n\varepsilon^2)$ for $\varepsilon>0$.

Assume AC and let $G\sim N(0,\sigma^2)$ for $\sigma\ge0$. Then $\mathbb E[G^2]=\sigma^2$ and $\mathbb E[G^4]=3\sigma^4$; in particular the fourth moment is finite. For independent centered normal coordinates $G_j\sim N(0,\sigma_j^2)$, every finite linear combination of the variables $G_j^2$ has finite second moment.

Assume AC. Let $C_n$ be real symmetric positive-semidefinite $2\times2$ matrices converging entrywise to $C$, and suppose both diagonal entries of $C_n$ and of $C$ are positive. Let $(U_n,V_n)$ and $(U,V)$ have centered bivariate normal laws with covariance matrices $C_n$ and $C$, respectively; singular covariance matrices are allowed. For every globally Lipschitz $\tau:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$,
$$\mathbb E[\tau(U_n)\tau(V_n)]\longrightarrow\mathbb E[\tau(U)\tau(V)].$$
For every bounded Borel function $g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$,
$$\mathbb E[g(U_n)g(V_n)]\longrightarrow\mathbb E[g(U)g(V)].$$
The second conclusion applies to any bounded measurable representative of an almost-everywhere derivative, including when the limiting pair is supported on a line.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Assume AC. Fix a finite data set $x_1,\ldots,x_N\in\mathbb R^{n_0}$ with $N,n_0\ge1$, a depth $L\ge2$, a bias scale $\beta>0$, and a horizon $T\ge0$. Let $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be globally Lipschitz, twice continuously differentiable, and have bounded second derivative. Use the network parameterization and independent standard-normal initialization in the width-normalized network definition, with scalar output $n_L=1$. For each hidden-width tuple $\mathbf n=(n_1,\ldots,n_{L-1})$, let $\mathbb P_{\mathbf n}$ be a probability law carrying this product standard-normal initialization marginal and any auxiliary randomness used by training. For each $\mathbf n$, take the training direction $d_{\mathbf n}$ and parameter path $\theta_{\mathbf n}$ to be jointly measurable in the probability outcome and time; for $\mathbb P_{\mathbf n}$-almost every outcome, assume $d_{\mathbf n}$ is integrable on $[0,T]$ and $\theta_{\mathbf n}$ is differentiable there and satisfies

$$\dot\theta_p(t)=-\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\partial_{\theta_p}f_{\theta(t)}(x_i)\,d_i(t),$$

where, for each fixed tuple, the width and probability-outcome subscripts are suppressed and the displayed path equation holds almost surely. Write $K_t=(K_{\theta(t)}(x_i,x_j))_{i,j=1}^N$ for the finite-data scalar neural tangent kernel. Suppose $\int_0^T\|d_{\mathbf n}(t)\|_N\,dt$ is stochastically bounded in the prescribed sequential hidden-width limit, where $\|v\|_N=(N^{-1}\sum_i|v_i|^2)^{1/2}$ and stochastic boundedness means that for every $\varepsilon>0$ some $M<\infty$ satisfies $\limsup_{n_{L-1}\to\infty}\cdots\limsup_{n_1\to\infty}\mathbb P_{\mathbf n}(\int_0^T\|d_{\mathbf n}(t)\|_Ndt>M)<\varepsilon$. The sample paths of $K_t$ are continuous, so joint measurability makes the supremum events below measurable. Then, as $n_1\to\infty$ first and then $n_2,\ldots,n_{L-1}\to\infty$, for every $\varepsilon>0$,

$$\mathbb P_{\mathbf n}\left(\sup_{0\le t\le T}\|K_t-K_0\|_{\mathrm{op}}>\varepsilon\right)\longrightarrow0.$$

For real random variables $(X_n)$ and $X$ on one probability space, write
$X_n\to X$ **in probability** when, for every $\varepsilon>0$,
$$\mathbb P(|X_n-X|>\varepsilon)\longrightarrow0.$$
This is precisely [[def-convergence-in-measure]] for the probability measure.

Let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$.

1. If $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, differentiable on $(a,b)$, and $f'$ extends
   continuously to $[a,b]$, then $f$ is Lipschitz.
2. Every Lipschitz $f$ is absolutely continuous.
3. Every absolutely continuous $f$ is continuous and has bounded variation.

Thus, with $C^1$ understood in the endpoint-extension sense of claim 1,
$C^1\subseteq\mathrm{Lipschitz}\subseteq AC\subseteq C\cap BV$ on a compact
interval.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. If $F\in AC[a,b]$, then $F'$ exists almost everywhere on $(a,b)$ and belongs to
$L^1[a,b]$.

derivations.claim: By [F8], $\sigma$ is absolutely continuous on every compact interval; applying [F9] on $[-m,m]$ for each positive integer $m$ shows that it is differentiable outside a Lebesgue-null set. The forward difference quotients $s_0(x)=\limsup_{k\to\infty}k(\sigma(x+1/k)-\sigma(x))$ define a bounded Borel function and equal $\sigma\prime(x)$ wherever the derivative exists. Since the given representative $s$ also equals $\sigma\prime$ almost everywhere, there is a Lebesgue-null set $E$ outside which $\sigma$ is differentiable and $s=s_0=\sigma\prime$. For any fixed finite width tuple, condition on the preceding layers: every coordinate of every data-point preactivation is normal with variance $\|z^\ell(x_i)\|_2^2/n_\ell+\beta^2\ge\beta^2$. Thus each avoids $E$ almost surely, and a finite union shows all preactivations at initialization avoid $E$ almost surely. The finite network is therefore parameter-differentiable at initialization for every data point, and [F5] applies with derivative values $s(U)$. The first-layer covariance is $\Sigma^1$; its diagonal is positive, and its Jacobian Gram block is exactly $K^1_{(i,a),(j,b)}=\delta_{ab}\Sigma^1_{ij}$ because different neurons use disjoint parameters.

Let $C_n$ be the conditional empirical covariance of the layer-$(r-1)$ preactivation vectors across the $n_{r-1}$ neurons. By induction $C_n\to\Sigma^{r-1}$ in probability; conditional on the preceding layer, these vectors are iid centered Gaussian with covariance $C_n$ and diagonal entries at least $\beta^2$. Choose $R>1+\max_i\Sigma^{r-1}_{ii}$, so $\mathbb P(\max_i(C_n)_{ii}>R)\to0$. Write $L_\sigma$ for a global Lipschitz constant. If $Y_a=\sigma(U^{r-1}_a(x_i))\sigma(U^{r-1}_a(x_j))$, the Lipschitz bound $|\sigma(u)|\le|\sigma(0)|+L_\sigma|u|$, Gaussian fourth moments, and Cauchy--Schwarz give $\mathbb E[Y_a^2\mid C_n]\le M_R$ whenever all diagonal entries of $C_n$ are at most $R$, for a finite constant $M_R$. The conditional variance bound in [F3] therefore gives $\mathbb P(|n_{r-1}^{-1}\sum_aY_a-\mathbb E[Y_a\mid C_n]|>\eta)\le\mathbb P(\max_i(C_n)_{ii}>R)+M_R/(n_{r-1}\eta^2)\to0$. The conditional mean is a bivariate Gaussian feature expectation and converges by [F4] to $\mathbb E[\sigma(U_i)\sigma(U_j)]$. For $V_a=s(U^{r-1}_a(x_i))s(U^{r-1}_a(x_j))$, the same conditional variance estimate holds with $M_R=\|s\|_\infty^4$, and [F4] makes its conditional mean converge to $\dot\Sigma^r_{ij}$. Adding the bias Gram gives $\Sigma^r$. Each empirical feature Gram plus that bias Gram is positive semidefinite with diagonal at least $\beta^2$; the cone of positive-semidefinite matrices is closed, so its deterministic limit $\Sigma^r$ is positive semidefinite and defines the next Gaussian pairs. This proves the covariance and derivative recursions at every layer.

For a finite network, [F5] gives the exact tangent-kernel block recursion $K^{r}_{(i,c),(j,d)}=\delta_{cd}(n_{r-1}^{-1}\sum_a Z^{r-1}_{ai}Z^{r-1}_{aj}+\beta^2)+n_{r-1}^{-1}\sum_{a,b}W^{(r-1)}_{ca}W^{(r-1)}_{db}s(U^{r-1}_{ai})s(U^{r-1}_{bj})K^{r-1}_{(i,a),(j,b)}$. The first term is the current-layer weight-and-bias Gram, and the second is the contribution of all earlier shared parameters. At the first layer this block is the one in step 1.1.

At this sequential stage the previous widths have already been taken to their limits while $n_{r-1}$ and $n_r$ are fixed, so the inductive block has limit $K^{r-1}_{(i,a),(j,b)}=\delta_{ab}\Theta^{r-1}_{ij}$ for the finitely many $a,b$. Substituting this block in the Jacobian term of step 2.2 leaves $\Theta^{r-1}_{ij}n_{r-1}^{-1}\sum_a W^{(r-1)}_{ca}W^{(r-1)}_{da}q_a$, where $q_a=s(U^{r-1}_a(x_i))s(U^{r-1}_a(x_j))$ and $|q_a|\le\|s\|_\infty^2$. The current weights are independent standard normals, independent of the preceding $U$ values. Conditional on those values, for $c=d$ the mean is $\Theta^{r-1}_{ij}n_{r-1}^{-1}\sum_aq_a$ and the variance is at most $2(\Theta^{r-1}_{ij})^2\|s\|_\infty^4/n_{r-1}$, using $\operatorname{Var}(W^2)=2$; for $c\ne d$ the mean is zero and the variance is at most $(\Theta^{r-1}_{ij})^2\|s\|_\infty^4/n_{r-1}$, using independence of the two rows. The empirical average of $q_a$ converges to $\dot\Sigma^r_{ij}$ by step 2.1, so the Jacobian term converges to $\delta_{cd}\Theta^{r-1}_{ij}\dot\Sigma^r_{ij}$. The covariance term converges to $\delta_{cd}\Sigma^r_{ij}$ by steps 2.1–2.2. Hence the limiting block is $\delta_{cd}(\Sigma^r_{ij}+\Theta^{r-1}_{ij}\dot\Sigma^r_{ij})=\delta_{cd}\Theta^r_{ij}$. Since the final layer has one output, its scalar block is $K_\infty$.

Under the additional $C^2$ training hypotheses, [F6] and the initialization convergence from step 3.1 give $\sup_{t\le T}\|K_t-K_\infty\|_{op}\le\sup_{t\le T}\|K_t-K_0\|_{op}+\|K_0-K_\infty\|_{op}\to0$ in probability. The parameter-flow equation and [F5] give $\dot f_t(x_i)=-N^{-1}\sum_jK_t(i,j)d_j(t)$. Integrating and subtracting the equation with $K_\infty$ yields $\sup_{t\le T}\|f_t-f_0+N^{-1}\int_0^tK_\infty d(s)\,ds\|_N\le N^{-1}\sup_{t\le T}\|K_t-K_\infty\|_{op}\int_0^T\|d(s)\|_Nds$. For any $M>0$ and $\delta>0$, the product exceeds $\delta$ only if $\int_0^T\|d(s)\|_Nds>M$ or $\sup_{t\le T}\|K_t-K_\infty\|_{op}>\delta N/M$; first use stochastic boundedness to choose $M$, then use kernel convergence. Thus the right side tends to zero in probability.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Then countable choice holds. Moreover, if $R\subseteq X\times X$ is serial on a nonempty set X and $a\in X$, there is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\ge0}$ with $x_0=a$ and $x_n R x_{n+1}$ for every n. Thus the countable and dependent choices required by the probability-product suppliers are available under AC.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume AC. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then $$\Phi_X(t):=\mathbb E e^{it\cdot X}=\exp(it\cdot m-t^T\Sigma t/2)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R^d).$$ This transform uniquely determines the law, including singular Sigma.

Let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$.

1. If $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, differentiable on $(a,b)$, and $f'$ extends
   continuously to $[a,b]$, then $f$ is Lipschitz.
2. Every Lipschitz $f$ is absolutely continuous.
3. Every absolutely continuous $f$ is continuous and has bounded variation.

Thus, with $C^1$ understood in the endpoint-extension sense of claim 1,
$C^1\subseteq\mathrm{Lipschitz}\subseteq AC\subseteq C\cap BV$ on a compact
interval.

Assume AC. Let $\gamma$ be the standard Gaussian probability measure on $\mathbb R$ with density $\phi(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}$, let $H_m$ be the monic probabilists’ Hermite polynomial defined by $H_0=1$, $H_1(x)=x$, and $H_{m+1}(x)=xH_m(x)-mH_{m-1}(x)$, and put $h_m=H_m/\sqrt{m!}$. Then $(h_m)_{m\ge0}$ is a complete orthonormal basis of real $L^2(\gamma)$. Every $f\in L^2(\gamma)$ has the norm-convergent expansion $f=\sum_{m\ge0}a_mh_m$, where $a_m=\int f h_m\,d\gamma$, and $\sum_{m\ge0}a_m^2=\|f\|_{L^2(\gamma)}^2$. If $f$ is continuous and nonpolynomial, then $a_m\ne0$ for an unbounded set of indices $m$. Every globally Lipschitz real function belongs to $L^2(\gamma)$, so this conclusion applies to every globally Lipschitz nonpolynomial activation.

Assume AC. Let $\gamma$ be standard Gaussian measure, let $h_m=H_m/\sqrt{m!}$ be the normalized probabilists’ Hermite basis, and let $f,g\in L^2(\gamma)$ have coefficients $a_m=\int f h_m\,d\gamma$ and $b_m=\int g h_m\,d\gamma$. For $\rho\in[-1,1]$, let $(X,Y)$ have the centered bivariate normal law with unit variances and correlation $\rho$. Then
$$\mathbb E[f(X)g(Y)]=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}a_mb_m\rho^m.$$
The series is absolutely convergent, including at $\rho=\pm1$. In particular, the Gaussian dual kernel of $f$ is $\sum_{m\ge0}a_m^2\rho^m$, and $\sum_{m\ge0}a_m^2=\|f\|_{L^2(\gamma)}^2$.

Assume AC. Fix an integer $n_0\ge1$, a number $\beta>0$, and a globally Lipschitz function $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ that is not a polynomial. Let $S^{n_0-1}=\{x\in\mathbb R^{n_0}:\|x\|_2=1\}$, put $q=n_0^{-1}+\beta^2$, and define $\mu(z)=\sigma(\sqrt q\,z)$. Let $a_m=\int \mu(z)h_m(z)\,d\gamma(z)$ be its coefficients in the normalized probabilists’ Hermite basis $h_m=H_m/\sqrt{m!}$ of standard Gaussian measure $\gamma$. For $x,y\in S^{n_0-1}$, let $(U_{x,y},V_{x,y})$ be a centered Gaussian pair with variances $q$ and covariance $\beta^2+x\cdot y/n_0$, and set $k(x,y)=\mathbb E[\sigma(U_{x,y})\sigma(V_{x,y})]+\beta^2$. Then $k$ is strictly positive definite on $S^{n_0-1}$: for every finite list of pairwise distinct points $x_1,\ldots,x_N$ and every nonzero $c\in\mathbb R^N$, $\sum_{i,j=1}^N c_i c_j k(x_i,x_j)>0$. The conclusion includes $n_0=1$, for which the sphere consists of the two points $-1$ and $1$.

Assume AC. Let $m\ge1$, let $C\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ be symmetric positive definite, let $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)$ have the centered multivariate normal law with covariance $C$, let $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be globally Lipschitz and nonconstant, and let $\beta>0$. Let $s$ be a bounded Borel representative of the almost-everywhere derivative of $\sigma$: it agrees with the ordinary derivative wherever that derivative exists, and its values on the remaining Lebesgue-null set are arbitrary. Define
$$S_{ij}:=\mathbb E[\sigma(Z_i)\sigma(Z_j)]+\beta^2,\qquad D_{ij}:=\mathbb E[s(Z_i)s(Z_j)]\quad(1\le i,j\le m).$$
Then $S$ is strictly positive definite and $D$ is positive semidefinite. Consequently, for every positive-semidefinite matrix $T\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$, the matrix $T\circ D+S$ is strictly positive definite, where $\circ$ denotes entrywise multiplication.

Let $P,q\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^P$ be open, let $X$ be a set, and let $f:\Omega\times X\to\mathbb R^q$. Fix $\theta\in\Omega$ and suppose that for each $x\in X$ the map $\vartheta\mapsto f(\vartheta,x)$ is totally differentiable at $\theta$, meaning it has a linear first-order approximation with remainder $o(\|\vartheta-\theta\|_2)$. Write $D_\theta f(\theta,x)\in\mathbb R^{q\times P}$ for its derivative matrix in the standard Euclidean coordinates. The matrix-valued neural tangent kernel at $\theta$ is

$$K_\theta(x,x'):=D_\theta f(\theta,x)\,D_\theta f(\theta,x')^{T}\in\mathbb R^{q\times q}.$$

Equivalently, for $1\le a,b\le q$,
$$\bigl(K_\theta(x,x')\bigr)_{ab}=\sum_{p=1}^{P}\partial_{\theta_p}f_a(\theta,x)\,\partial_{\theta_p}f_b(\theta,x').$$
For a scalar-output model this is the scalar kernel $\sum_{p=1}^{P}\partial_{\theta_p}f(\theta,x)\partial_{\theta_p}f(\theta,x')$.

Assume AC. Fix integers $L,n_0,\ldots,n_L\ge1$, a bias scale $\beta>0$, and an activation $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$. For each layer $\ell=0,\ldots,L-1$, let $W^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb R^{n_{\ell+1}\times n_\ell}$ and $b^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb R^{n_{\ell+1}}$. At initialization all entries of all matrices and bias vectors are mutually independent and each has the standard normal law $N(0,1)$. These finite collections of entries have the corresponding finite-dimensional multivariate normal product law.

For an input $x\in\mathbb R^{n_0}$, put $z^{(0)}(x)=x$ and, for $\ell=0,\ldots,L-1$, define the preactivation
$$u^{(\ell+1)}(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n_\ell}}W^{(\ell)}z^{(\ell)}(x)+\beta b^{(\ell)}.$$
For $\ell+1<L$, set $z^{(\ell+1)}(x)=\sigma(u^{(\ell+1)}(x))$ coordinatewise; the output layer is linear and $f_\theta(x):=u^{(L)}(x)\in\mathbb R^{n_L}$. The parameter vector $\theta$ consists of every entry of the matrices and biases. The width $n_L$ is the fixed output dimension; the hidden widths are $n_1,\ldots,n_{L-1}$. A sequential hidden-width limit takes $n_1\to\infty$ first, then $n_2\to\infty$, and so on through $n_{L-1}\to\infty$.

Assume AC. Fix a finite list $x_1,\ldots,x_N\in\mathbb R^{n_0}$ with $N,n_0\ge1$, a depth $L\ge2$, a bias scale $\beta>0$, and a globally Lipschitz activation $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$. Let $s$ be any bounded Borel representative of the almost-everywhere derivative of $\sigma$, meaning that it agrees with the ordinary derivative outside a Lebesgue-null set; such a representative exists and is bounded by the Lipschitz constant. For each tuple of positive integer hidden widths $\mathbf n=(n_1,\ldots,n_{L-1})$, let $\mathbb P_{\mathbf n}$ be a probability law carrying the product standard-normal initialization marginal and any auxiliary randomness used by training; take all probabilities in the width limit under these laws. Use the width-normalized network with scalar linear output.

Put

$$\Sigma^1_{ij}=\frac{x_i\cdot x_j}{n_0}+\beta^2.$$

For $r=2,\ldots,L$, let $(U_i,U_j)$ have the centered Gaussian law with variances $\Sigma^{r-1}_{ii},\Sigma^{r-1}_{jj}$ and covariance $\Sigma^{r-1}_{ij}$, and define

$$\Sigma^r_{ij}=\mathbb E[\sigma(U_i)\sigma(U_j)]+\beta^2,\qquad \dot\Sigma^r_{ij}=\mathbb E[s(U_i)s(U_j)].$$

These Gaussian laws may be singular; their marginal variances are at least $\beta^2$, and their laws and expectations depend only on the displayed covariance. Define $\Theta^1_{ij}=\Sigma^1_{ij}$ and, for $r=2,\ldots,L$,

$$\Theta^r_{ij}=\Theta^{r-1}_{ij}\dot\Sigma^r_{ij}+\Sigma^r_{ij},\qquad K_\infty=(\Theta^L_{ij})_{i,j=1}^N.$$

At initialization, the finite-data neural tangent Gram matrix $K_0$ converges in probability to $K_\infty$ under the sequential hidden-width limit $n_1\to\infty$ first, then $n_2\to\infty$, and so on through $n_{L-1}$.

For the training conclusion, fix a horizon $T\ge0$. In addition, assume that $\sigma$ is twice continuously differentiable with bounded second derivative. For each width tuple, let $d_{\mathbf n}$ and $\theta_{\mathbf n}$ be jointly measurable in the probability outcome and time; for $\mathbb P_{\mathbf n}$-almost every outcome, assume $d_{\mathbf n}$ is integrable on $[0,T]$ and $\theta_{\mathbf n}$ is differentiable there and satisfies, with width and probability-outcome subscripts suppressed in the equation,

$$\dot\theta_p(t)=-\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\partial_{\theta_p}f_{\theta(t)}(x_i)d_i(t).$$

Write $f_t(x)=f_{\theta(t)}(x)$ and $K_t(i,j)=K_{\theta(t)}(x_i,x_j)$, where $K_\theta$ is the finite-network neural tangent kernel; width and probability-outcome subscripts are suppressed. The sample paths of $K_t$ are continuous, so joint measurability makes the supremum events below measurable. Define $\|v\|_N=(N^{-1}\sum_i|v_i|^2)^{1/2}$. Suppose $\int_0^T\|d_{\mathbf n}(t)\|_Ndt$ is stochastically bounded in the prescribed sequential limit, meaning that for every $\varepsilon>0$ some $M<\infty$ satisfies $\limsup_{n_{L-1}\to\infty}\cdots\limsup_{n_1\to\infty}\mathbb P_{\mathbf n}(\int_0^T\|d_{\mathbf n}(t)\|_Ndt>M)<\varepsilon$. Then

$$\sup_{0\le t\le T}\|K_t-K_\infty\|_{op}\longrightarrow0\quad\text{in probability},$$

where $\|\cdot\|_{op}$ is the Euclidean operator norm. Along the path,

$$\dot f_t(x_i)=-\frac1N\sum_{j=1}^N K_t(i,j)d_j(t),$$

and

$$\sup_{0\le t\le T}\left\|f_t-f_0+\frac1N\int_0^tK_\infty d(s)\,ds\right\|_N\longrightarrow0\quad\text{in probability}.$$

Thus the finite-time output equation has the deterministic limiting kernel as its generator in the precise integrated-error sense displayed above.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. If $F\in AC[a,b]$, then $F'$ exists almost everywhere on $(a,b)$ and belongs to
$L^1[a,b]$.

derivations.claim: Fix pairwise distinct $x_1,\ldots,x_N$ on the sphere. The matrix $\Sigma^1$ is a Gram matrix because $\Sigma^1_{ij}=\langle(x_i/\sqrt{n_0},\beta),(x_j/\sqrt{n_0},\beta)\rangle$; it may be singular. Its diagonal is $q=n_0^{-1}+\beta^2>0$. By [F2] and [F6], on each compact interval $\sigma$ is absolutely continuous and differentiable almost everywhere; a countable union gives a null exceptional set, and the pointwise upper limit of bounded continuous difference quotients defines a bounded Borel representative $s_0$ equal to $\sigma\prime$ wherever it exists. The given representative $s$ agrees with $s_0$ outside a null set; include this set and the nondifferentiability set in one null set $E$. The multivariate Gaussian with covariance $\Sigma^1$ exists by [F1], and every coordinate has a positive-variance normal density and hence avoids $E$ almost surely, so the choice of representative does not change any expectation.

The covariance $\Sigma^2$ is strictly positive definite by [F3], applied to this finite set, with the same $n_0,\beta,\sigma$. The derivative matrix $D^2$ is positive semidefinite directly: for every $c\in\mathbb R^N$, $c^TD^2c=\mathbb E[(\sum_i c_i s(U_i))^2]\ge0$ for a common Gaussian vector $U$ of covariance $\Sigma^1$. Also, writing $u_i=(x_i/\sqrt{n_0},\beta)$, finite expansion gives $c^T(\Sigma^1\circ D^2)c=\mathbb E\left\|\sum_i c_i s(U_i)u_i\right\|_2^2\ge0,$ so $\Sigma^1\circ D^2$ is positive semidefinite. Hence $\Theta^2=\Sigma^2+\Sigma^1\circ D^2$ is strictly positive definite.

Let $r\ge3$ and suppose $\Sigma^{r-1}$ is strictly positive definite. Its Gaussian vector therefore satisfies the nondegenerate-covariance hypothesis of [F4]; the activation is nonconstant because a nonpolynomial function cannot be constant. Thus $\Sigma^r$ is strictly positive definite and $D^r$ is positive semidefinite. If $\Theta^{r-1}$ is positive semidefinite, [F4] makes $\Theta^{r-1}\circ D^r$ positive semidefinite; adding $\Sigma^r$ makes $\Theta^r$ strictly positive definite.

Step 2.1 initializes the induction with both $\Sigma^2$ and $\Theta^2$ strictly positive definite. Repeated step 3.1 proves $\Theta^L$ strictly positive definite for each $L\ge2$. By [F5], this recursively defined kernel is the limiting NTK of the stated network on the chosen finite data set. Since the list was arbitrary, the claimed strict positive definiteness holds for every finite set of distinct sphere points, including the two points of $S^0$.

The recursion never divides by the list length.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Assume AC. Fix $n_0\ge1$, $L\ge2$, $\beta>0$, and a globally Lipschitz activation $\sigma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ that is not a polynomial. For $x,y$ on the unit sphere $S^{n_0-1}=\{x\in\mathbb R^{n_0}:\|x\|_2=1\}$, define $\Sigma^1(x,y)=x\cdot y/n_0+\beta^2$. Recursively, for $r=2,\ldots,L$, let $(U,V)$ be a centered Gaussian pair whose covariance entries are $\Sigma^{r-1}(x,x),\Sigma^{r-1}(y,y),\Sigma^{r-1}(x,y)$, and set

$$\Sigma^r(x,y)=\mathbb E[\sigma(U)\sigma(V)]+\beta^2,\qquad D^r(x,y)=\mathbb E[s(U)s(V)],$$

where $s$ is any bounded Borel representative of the almost-everywhere derivative of $\sigma$. Set $\Theta^1=\Sigma^1$ and $\Theta^r(x,y)=\Theta^{r-1}(x,y)D^r(x,y)+\Sigma^r(x,y)$. Then for every finite list of pairwise distinct points $x_1,\ldots,x_N\in S^{n_0-1}$ and every nonzero $c\in\mathbb R^N$,

$$\sum_{i,j=1}^N c_ic_j\Theta^L(x_i,x_j)>0.$$

Thus the scalar limiting neural tangent kernel is strictly positive definite on every finite set of distinct sphere points, for every $n_0\ge1$ and $L\ge2$. In dimension $n_0=1$ this includes both antipodal points of $S^0=\{-1,1\}$.

derivations.claim: For any finite-width parameters $\theta$ and coefficients $c_i$, [F1] gives $c^TK_\theta c=\left\|\sum_{i=1}^Nc_i\nabla_\theta f_\theta(x_i)\right\|_2^2\ge0.$ Thus every $K_\theta$ is symmetric positive semidefinite. Taking the finite-dimensional probability limit in [F2] preserves symmetry and each quadratic inequality, so $K_\infty$ is symmetric positive semidefinite.

Apply [F3] to $K_\infty$. In the orthogonal coordinates $r(t)=Q^T(f(t)-y)$, the flow equation becomes $\dot r_i(t)=-(\lambda_i/N)r_i(t)$. vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$

derivations.claim: Put $a=e^{2u}>0$. Then $|a-1|<a+1$, so $|\sigma(u)|<1$. The derivative rules in [F1] give $\sigma'(u)=4e^{2u}/(e^{2u}+1)^2=1-\sigma(u)^2$ and $\sigma''(u)=-2\sigma(u)\sigma'(u)$. Thus $|\sigma'|\le1$ and $|\sigma''|\le2$. By [F2], $|\sigma(u)-\sigma(v)|\le|u-v|$, so $\sigma$ is globally Lipschitz. Since $\sigma'(u)>0$, it is nonconstant; a polynomial of degree $m\ge1$ with leading coefficient $a_m\ne0$ satisfies $p(u)/u^m\to a_m$ as $u\to+\infty$, so its absolute value is unbounded. The bounded nonconstant $\sigma$ is therefore nonpolynomial.

For each finite network, the parameter vector field for the constant direction is smooth and locally Lipschitz, so a local solution exists by [F3]. The output-layer weights and bias have bounded speed because all hidden activations are bounded by $1$, so they remain bounded on every compact time interval. Suppose the parameters in layers $k+1,\ldots,L-1$ are bounded on such an interval. Backpropagating through those layers multiplies the direction by their finite weight matrices and factors $\sigma'$ of modulus at most $1$, so each coordinate of the backpropagated direction at layer $k+1$ is bounded. The gradient formulas in [F4], together with $|\sigma|\le1$, then bound every derivative in layer $k$; integration bounds its weights and biases. Descending induction bounds all parameters on every compact interval. If the maximal local solution had a finite endpoint, the smooth vector field would be bounded on a compact ball containing the trajectory, so the trajectory would be Lipschitz in time and have a limit as the endpoint is approached. Applying [F3] at that limit extends the solution, a contradiction. Hence the path exists on $[0,1]$. On any compact tube around a finite solution segment the vector field is Lipschitz; subtracting the integral equations for two solutions gives $u(t)\le u(0)+M\int_0^tu(s)\,ds$ on the tube for a Lipschitz constant $M$; iterating this inequality gives $u(t)\le e^{Mt}u(0)$, proving local continuous dependence on the initial parameters. A finite cover of $[0,1]$ patches these local flow maps. Thus the global path is measurable as a function of initialization and time. For this direction, $\|d(t)\|_N=1$ at every time, so its integral is $1$.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

derivations.claim: For each integer $k\ge1$, the Cauchy property gives a threshold N_k such that $W_2(\mu_n,\mu_m)<2^{-k}$ whenever $n,m\ge N_k$. Set $n_1=N_1$ and recursively $n_{k+1}=\max\{N_{k+1},n_k+1\}$. Then $n_k<n_{k+1}$ and $W_2(\mu_{n_k},\mu_{n_{k+1}})\le2^{-k}$. By AC choose an optimal coupling $\pi_k$ of these consecutive laws for each k using [F1].

Put $S=(\mathbb R^d)^{\{1,2,\ldots\}}$, the set of sequences of Euclidean vectors indexed by positive integers, and equip $S$ with $D(x,y)=\sum_{j\ge1}2^{-j}\min(1,|x_j-y_j|)$. This metric induces the product topology: each coordinate projection is continuous from the bound on its summand, and a product neighborhood restricting finitely many coordinates contains a sufficiently small D-ball. Conversely, given a D-ball radius, make the geometric tail less than half that radius and restrict the finitely many remaining coordinates so their summands total less than the other half; this gives a product neighborhood inside the D-ball. A D-Cauchy sequence is Cauchy in each coordinate, so coordinate completeness gives a limit in S; bounding the first finitely many coordinate terms and then the geometric tail proves convergence in D. Sequences of rational vectors which are zero after finitely many coordinates form a countable dense subset, since the tail is arbitrarily small and each of finitely many coordinates can be approximated by rationals. Thus S is complete and separable, hence Polish by definition.

Set $Q_1=\pi_1$, the probability on the first two coordinates. For $N\ge2$, assume $Q_{N-1}$ is a probability on coordinates $1,\ldots,N$ with adjacent pair marginals $\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_{N-1}$ and last marginal $\mu_{n_N}$. Regard it as a law on $\mathbb R^{d(N-1)}\times\mathbb R^d$, and regard $\pi_N$ as a law on $\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^d$; they have the common second/first marginal $\mu_{n_N}$. The gluing statement [F1] gives $Q_N$ on coordinates $1,\ldots,N+1$ preserving all earlier adjacent marginals and adding $\pi_N$. Let $I_N:(\mathbb R^d)^{N+1}\to S$ send $(x_1,\ldots,x_{N+1})$ to $(x_1,\ldots,x_{N+1},0,0,\ldots)$; this map is continuous for the product topology. Define $\eta_N=(I_N)_\#Q_N$, that is, $\eta_N(B)=Q_N(I_N^{-1}(B))$ for Borel $B\subset S$. By [F7] it is a Borel probability, and its first $N+1$ coordinates have law $Q_N$ while every later coordinate equals zero.

The $j$th marginal of any $\eta_N$ is either $\mu_{n_j}$ (when $N+1\ge j$) or $\delta_0$. Each fixed probability $\mu_{n_j}$ is tight by [F2]; AC chooses a compact $K_j\subset\mathbb R^d$ containing zero with $\mu_{n_j}(K_j^c)<\varepsilon2^{-j-1}$. Countable subadditivity gives $\eta_N((\prod_jK_j)^c)\le\sum_{j\ge1}\varepsilon2^{-j-1}<\varepsilon$ for every $N$. The product $K=\prod_jK_j$ is compact in $S$: it is closed and complete, and it is totally bounded because for any radius one first makes the metric tail small and then takes finite nets in the finitely many compact coordinates; [F5] applies. Hence $(\eta_N)$ is tight. By [F2] and Prokhorov, a subsequence converges weakly to a probability $\eta$ on $S$.

For fixed $k$, all sufficiently late $\eta_N$ have their $(k,k+1)$ coordinate marginal equal to $\pi_k$. The coordinate projection $S\to\mathbb R^{2d}$ is continuous, so the projected laws of $\eta_N$ converge weakly to the corresponding marginal of $\eta$; because they are eventually exactly $\pi_k$, uniqueness of weak limits [F6] shows that this marginal is $\pi_k$. > Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
