derivations.claim: Suppose $W_2(\mu_n,\mu)\to0$. For each $n$ choose an optimal coupling $\pi_n$ and regard its coordinates as $X_n,Y$ with laws $\mu_n,\mu$. The cost gives $\int|X_n-Y|^2d\pi_n\to0$. For bounded continuous $\varphi$, choose a ball $B(0,K)$ with $\mu(B(0,K)^c)$ small. On the event $|Y|\le K$ and $|X_n-Y|\le\delta<1$, both points lie in the compact ball $\overline B(0,K+1)$, where $\varphi$ is uniformly continuous. The complement has probability at most $\mu(B(0,K)^c)+\delta^{-2}\int|X_n-Y|^2d\pi_n$. First choose $K$, then $δ$, and then $n$; the boundedness of $\varphi$ shows $\int\varphi d\mu_n-\int\varphi d\mu\to0$. Thus $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$.

Conversely suppose narrow convergence and the stated uniform tail condition. Fix $\varepsilon>0$. Choose $R$ so that the second-moment tails outside $Q=[-R,R]^d$ of all $\mu_n$ and of $\mu$ are less than $\varepsilon$; the tail of $\mu$ vanishes because $\mu\in\mathcal P_2$. Enlarge R slightly if necessary so its coordinate faces have zero $\mu$-mass. Partition each coordinate interval $[-R,R]$ by finitely many levels that are not atoms of the corresponding one-dimensional marginal of $\mu$, with mesh small enough that each resulting rectangular cell has diameter at most $\varepsilon$. Such levels exist because each probability has at most countably many atoms. Together with $Q^c$, these cells form a finite Borel partition $(C_i)_{i=0}^N$ whose boundaries have $\mu$-measure zero. By [F2], $a_{n,i}:=\mu_n(C_i)\to a_i:=\mu(C_i)$ for each $i$.

Write $Z_n=X_n-Y$ and $a_n=\int|Z_n|^2d\pi_n\to0$. For $R>K$, on $\{|X_n|>R\}$ either $|Y|>K$ or $|Z_n|>R-K$. Since $|X_n|^2\le2|Y|^2+2|Z_n|^2$, for every $n$, $\int_{|X_n|>R}|X_n|^2d\pi_n\le 2\int_{|Y|>K}|Y|^2d\pi_n+2K^2\frac{a_n}{(R-K)^2}+2a_n.$ Given a target $\eta>0$, first choose K so the first term is below $\eta/4$; then choose N so $a_n<\eta/8$ for $n\ge N$; then choose R>K so the middle term is below $\eta/8$ for all $n\ge N$. The last term is below $\eta/4$. Finally enlarge R so the finitely many tails for $n<N$ are below $\eta$. This proves the required uniform tail limit.

For each bounded cell $C_i\subset Q$, match mass $r_{n,i}=\min(a_{n,i},a_i)$. If $r_{n,i}>0$, take $r_{n,i}$ times the product of the probability measures $\mu_n|_{C_i}/a_{n,i}$ and $\mu|_{C_i}/a_i$; if $r_{n,i}=0$, use the zero measure. This gives a coupling piece supported on $C_i\times C_i$ with cost at most $\varepsilon^2r_{n,i}$. Subtract its two marginals from $\mu_n$ and $\mu$. The residual measures have equal mass. If that mass is positive, their normalized product, multiplied by that mass, couples them; if it is zero there is no residual piece. The sum is a coupling $\pi_n$ of $\mu_n,\mu$. Its matched cost is at most $\varepsilon^2$. For the residual coupling, $|x-y|^2\le2|x|^2+2|y|^2$. Its residual second moments are bounded by the two tails outside $Q$ plus $dR^2\sum_{i=1}^N|a_{n,i}-a_i|$ on each side: inside a bounded cell, unmatched mass is exactly the positive part of the difference of its two cell masses. Therefore $W_2(\mu_n,\mu)^2\le\int|x-y|^2d\pi_n\le\varepsilon^2+4\varepsilon+4dR^2\sum_{i=1}^N|a_{n,i}-a_i|.$ For this fixed finite partition the sum tends to zero, so $\limsup_nW_2(\mu_n,\mu)^2\le\varepsilon^2+4\varepsilon$. Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ proves $W_2(\mu_n,\mu)\to0$.

For the witness, the mass outside a ball of radius $R$ is at most $n^{-2}$ for indices $n>R$ and is zero for indices $n\le R$; hence the family is tight. For bounded continuous $\varphi$, $\int\varphi d\mu_n=(1-n^{-2})\varphi(0)+n^{-2}\varphi(ne_1)\to\varphi(0)$, proving narrow convergence. Every coupling with second marginal $\delta_0$ is concentrated on $\mathbb R^d\times\{0\}$, so its cost is forced to be $\int|x|^2d\mu_n=1$. The asserted failure of W2 convergence follows.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> (Choice function).

Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

citations.quote: Let $T>0$ and let $t\mapsto\mu_t$ be a narrowly continuous curve of Borel probability measures on $\mathbb R^d$, where narrow continuity means convergence against every bounded continuous real test function. For a product-Borel set $E\subseteq[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d$, write $E_t=\{x:(t,x)\in E\}$ and define $M(E)=\int_0^T\mu_t(E_t)dt$. Then $t\mapsto\mu_t$ is a probability kernel, $M$ is a finite Borel measure of total mass $T$, and for every nonnegative product-Borel $f$, $\int f\,dM=\int_0^T\int f(t,x)d\mu_t(x)dt$.

Fix $T>0$ and an integer $d\ge1$. Let $t\mapsto\mu_t$ be a narrowly continuous curve in $\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)$ (so $t\mapsto\int f\,d\mu_t$ is continuous for every bounded continuous $f$), let $M$ be its space-time measure $M(dt,dx)=dt\,\mu_t(dx)$, and let $v:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ be Borel. Its squared action is $A(\mu,v)=\int|v(t,x)|^2dM(t,x)$. If $A(\mu,v)<\infty$, say that $v$ solves the continuity equation for $\mu$ when
$$\int_0^T\!\int_{\mathbb R^d}(\partial_t\varphi(t,x)+\nabla_x\varphi(t,x)\cdot v(t,x))\,d\mu_t(x)\,dt=0$$
for every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty((0,T)\times\mathbb R^d)$. This is the distributional meaning of $\partial_t\mu_t+\nabla\cdot(v_t\mu_t)=0$; the continuous representative fixes the endpoint laws.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure

$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

For this page, a Borel measure $\mu$ on a locally compact Hausdorff space is
**Radon** when $\mu(K)<\infty$ for every compact $K$, and, for every Borel
$E$ and every open $U$,
$$\mu(E)=\inf_{E\subseteq V\text{ open}}\mu(V),\qquad \mu(U)=\sup_{K\subseteq U\text{ compact}}\mu(K).$$
Cohn calls this convention regular. It does not assert compact inner
approximation for arbitrary Borel $E$.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

The $L^p$ norm descends to the quotient and makes $L^p$ a normed space for $1 \le p \le \infty$, is
complete. Equivalently, the metric induced by that norm is a complete metric in
the sense of Complete metric space: every Cauchy sequence converges in the space.

Moreover, if a sequence in $L^p(\mu)$ converges in norm, then some subsequence
admits measurable representatives converging almost everywhere in the sense of
Convergence almost everywhere relative to a measure.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and let $f$ be a bounded linear functional on $H$ (The dual space X^* of a normed space and its dual norm). Then there is a unique $y\in H$ with

$$f(x)=\langle x,y\rangle\qquad\text{for every }x\in H,$$

and $\|f\|=\|y\|$, where $\|f\|$ is the dual norm (The operator norm as the least bound and as the unit-sphere or unit-ball supremum). Under the first-variable-linear convention the representing vector depends conjugate-linearly and isometrically on $f$: if $f_i$ is represented by $y_i$ and $a,b$ are scalars, then $af_1+bf_2$ is represented by $\overline a\,y_1+\overline b\,y_2$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice (The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)).

Let $a<b$ and let $f\in L^1([a,b])$. Define
$$F(x):=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt\qquad(a\le x\le b).$$
Then $F$ is differentiable for almost every $x\in(a,b)$ and
$$F'(x)=f(x)$$
at every such point.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

derivations.claim: For a partition $P=(t_i)_{i=0}^N$, write $Q_P(\gamma)=\sum_i|\gamma(t_{i+1})-\gamma(t_i)|^2/(t_{i+1}-t_i)$ and set $C=\sup_PQ_P(\gamma)$. If $\gamma$ is absolutely continuous with square-integrable derivative, Cauchy--Schwarz [F4] on each interval gives $Q_P(\gamma)\le\int_0^T|\dot\gamma|^2dt$.

Suppose $C<\infty$. On interval-step functions $f(t)=c_i$ for $t_i<t<t_{i+1}$ define $\Lambda(f)=\sum_i c_i\cdot(\gamma(t_{i+1})-\gamma(t_i))$. Refinement leaves this value unchanged, so the functional is well-defined. Cauchy--Schwarz for the finite sums gives $|\Lambda(f)|\le\left(\sum_i|c_i|^2\Delta t_i\right)^{1/2}Q_P(\gamma)^{1/2}\le\sqrt C\|f\|_{L^2}.$ By [F1], interval-step functions are dense in $L^2$, so $\Lambda$ extends uniquely to a bounded linear functional on the real Hilbert space $L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^d)$.

By [F2]–[F3], Riesz represents $\Lambda$ by some $u\in L^2(0,T;\mathbb R^d)$. Taking the step function equal to a fixed vector c on $(s,t)$ and zero elsewhere gives $c\cdot(\gamma(t)-\gamma(s))=\int_s^t c\cdot u(r)dr$ for every $c$ and every interval. Hence $\gamma(t)-\gamma(s)=\int_s^t u(r)dr$. The scalar FTC [F3] coordinatewise shows that $\gamma$ is absolutely continuous and $\dot\gamma=u$ almost everywhere. Thus $\mathcal E(\gamma)<\infty$.

For this absolutely continuous path, the functional $\Lambda$ is integration against $\dot\gamma$ on interval-step functions. Since those functions are dense, its norm is $\|\dot\gamma\|_{L^2}$; for each fixed partition the squared norm of the restriction of $\Lambda$ to step functions constant on its intervals is exactly $Q_P(\gamma)$. Taking the supremum over partitions therefore gives $C=\|\dot\gamma\|_{L^2}^2=\mathcal E(\gamma)$. Conversely, steps 2.1–3.1 prove that finite C forces finite energy, so if $\mathcal E(\gamma)=+\infty$ then C is also infinite. Each $Q_P$ is continuous in the uniform topology because it uses finitely many point evaluations; their supremum is lower semicontinuous.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ and every real $a>0$,
$$\frac{x^m}{\exp(ax)}\longrightarrow0\qquad(x\to+\infty).$$

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ (Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$) at which $g$ is differentiable
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
(Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of If $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L \ne 0$ then $|f| > |L|/2$ on a punctured neighbourhood of $c$; in particular if $L > 0$ then $f > L/2 > 0$ there applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
Carathéodory's characterisation: $f$ is differentiable at $c$ if and only if there is $\varphi : A \to \mathbb{R}$, continuous at $c$, with $f(x) - f(c) = \varphi(x)(x - c)$ for every $x \in A$, and then $\varphi$ is unique and $\varphi(c) = f'(c)$.** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of Sums, scalar multiples, products, absolute values, maxima, minima and quotients with nonvanishing denominator of continuous functions are continuous, as are constants, the identity and every polynomial function.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
(The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

(Axis-parallel rectangles in $\mathbb{R}^m$ and their volume). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of Half-open boxes in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and their volume, and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ (Assuming countable choice, $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra containing every elementary set and $\lambda_n$ is a complete measure extending elementary volume).

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $A$
([[def-continuity-real]]) and let $K \subseteq A$ be **nonempty** and compact
([[def-open-cover-r]]). Then $\sup f[K]$ and $\inf f[K]$ exist and are
**attained**: there are $p, q \in K$ with

$$f(q) \;=\; \inf f[K] \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; \sup f[K] \;=\; f(p) \qquad \text{for every } x \in K .$$

Equivalently, the set $f[K]$ has a maximum and a minimum
([[def-max-min]]), namely $\max f[K] = f(p)$ and $\min f[K] = f(q)$.

**Nonemptiness of $K$ is a hypothesis, not an oversight.** For $K = \varnothing$
the set $f[K]$ is empty, and neither a supremum nor a maximum of the empty set
exists in this library ([[def-complete-ordered-field]] supplies suprema of
nonempty sets bounded above only).

**This theorem is stated twice in this library, on purpose.** Its metric-space
twin is [[thm-extreme-value-metric]], proved from the cover machinery of metric
spaces; the proof below is $\mathbb{R}$-native, running through Heine-Borel for
$\mathbb{R}$ and the order-completeness of $\mathbb{R}$, and it uses no cover
argument beyond the one already spent in
[[thm-continuous-image-of-a-compact-set-r]]. That the two statements are the
same statement in two vocabularies is proved in
[[lem-real-and-metric-notions-agree]], later on this page.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that

countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice (The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)). Let
$m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
the product measure $\lambda_m \times \lambda_n$ and the Euclidean Lebesgue
measure $\lambda_{m+n}$ agree on every Borel subset of $\mathbb R^{m+n}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Define $\phi(t)=e^{-1/t}$ for $t>0$ and $\phi(t)=0$ for $t\le0$. For each $k\ge0$, repeated chain and product rules give $\phi^{(k)}(t)=P_k(1/t)e^{-1/t}$ on $t>0$ for a polynomial $P_k$: it holds with $P_0=1$, and if $u=1/t$ then differentiation replaces $P_k(u)$ by the polynomial $u^2(P_k(u)-P_k'(u))$. By [F1], this derivative tends to $0$ as $t\downarrow0$. Its difference quotient at $0$ is $uP_k(u)e^{-u}$ with $u=1/t$, which also tends to $0$ by [F1]; from the left it is zero. Induction therefore gives every derivative at $0$ equal to $0$ and continuous there, so $\phi$ is smooth on $\mathbb R$.

Set $\Phi(t)=\phi(t+1)\phi(1-t)$. By [F2], $\Phi$ is smooth. It vanishes for $t\notin[-1,1]$ and is positive for $-1<t<1$, so its support is $[-1,1]$. Let $I=\int_{\mathbb R}\Phi(t)\,dt$. The extreme-value bound [F3] makes $\Phi$ bounded on $[-1,1]$, so $I<\infty$. Since $\Phi(0)=e^{-2}>0$, continuity gives $\delta\in(0,1)$ with $\Phi(t)\ge e^{-2}/2$ on $[-\delta,\delta]$; [F3] gives $I\ge\delta e^{-2}>0$. Hence $\psi=\Phi/I$ is smooth, supported on $[-1,1]$, positive on $(-1,1)$, and has integral one.

Define $\rho_d(x_1,\ldots,x_d)=\prod_{j=1}^d\psi(x_j)$. Repeated coordinatewise chain and product rules give every partial derivative as $\prod_{j=1}^d\psi^{(\alpha_j)}(x_j)$ for its multi-index $\alpha$, so all partial derivatives are continuous. The function is nonnegative, vanishes outside $[-1,1]^d$, and is positive at every point of $(-1,1)^d$; therefore its support is exactly that closed cube.

For $d=1$, $\int\rho_1=1$ by step 2.1. By step 3.1, $\rho_d$ is a nonnegative Borel function supported in the compact cube. For $d\ge2$, split $\mathbb R^d=\mathbb R^{d-1}\times\mathbb R$. By [F4] and Tonelli, $\int\rho_d\,dx=(\int\rho_{d-1}\,dx)(\int\psi\,dt)$; the second factor is $1$ by step 2.1. Induction on $d$ proves $\int_{\mathbb R^d}\rho_d\,dx=1$.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

For this page, a Borel measure $\mu$ on a locally compact Hausdorff space is
**Radon** when $\mu(K)<\infty$ for every compact $K$, and, for every Borel
$E$ and every open $U$,
$$\mu(E)=\inf_{E\subseteq V\text{ open}}\mu(V),\qquad \mu(U)=\sup_{K\subseteq U\text{ compact}}\mu(K).$$
Cohn calls this convention regular. It does not assert compact inner
approximation for arbitrary Borel $E$.
Assume Dependent Choice ([[def-dependent-choice]]). If $\mu$ is a Radon measure on an LCH space $X$ and $1\le p<\infty$, then $C_c(X)$ is dense in $L^p(\mu)$.

In ZF, the Axiom of Dependent Choice implies the Axiom of Countable Choice:
every at most countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-choice-function]],
[[def-dependent-choice]]).

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. For every integer $d\ge1$ there is a nonnegative function $\rho_d:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ with continuous partial derivatives of every order, support exactly $[-1,1]^d$, strictly positive on $(-1,1)^d$, and Lebesgue integral $\int_{\mathbb R^d}\rho_d(x)\,dx=1$. Here the support is the closure of the set where the function is nonzero.

Let $\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ satisfy

$$ \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \varphi(x)\,dx = 1. $$

For $\varepsilon > 0$, define

$$ \varphi_\varepsilon(x) := \varepsilon^{-n}\varphi(x/\varepsilon) \qquad(x \in \mathbb{R}^n). $$

The family $(\varphi_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ is the **mollifier family
generated by $\varphi$**.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{C}$ be locally integrable, let
$\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ have mass $1$, and let
$\varphi_\varepsilon$ be the associated mollifier. Then for every
$\varepsilon > 0$, the convolution

$$ (f*\varphi_\varepsilon)(x) := \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(y)\varphi_\varepsilon(x-y)\,dy $$

is smooth, and for every multi-index $\alpha$,

$$ \partial^\alpha(f*\varphi_\varepsilon) = f*(\partial^\alpha \varphi_\varepsilon). $$

derivations.claim: By [F1], given $\epsilon>0$ choose $g\in C_c(\mathbb R^n)$ with $\|f-g\|_{L^2(M)}<\epsilon/2$. Extend g by zero on $\mathbb R^n$; it is bounded and uniformly continuous. Let $\rho_\delta$ be the mollifier generated by [F3]. Since $\rho$ has compact support, for some $R<\infty$ its support is contained in $B_R(0)$, and $\sup_x|(g*\rho_\delta)(x)-g(x)|\le\sup_{|z|\le R\delta,x}|g(x-z)-g(x)|\longrightarrow0$ by uniform continuity.

The function $g*\rho_\delta$ is smooth by [F2], and its support lies in the sum of the compact supports of g and $\rho_\delta$, hence is compact. Since M is finite, $\|g*\rho_\delta-g\|_{L^2(M)}\le M(\mathbb R^n)^{1/2}\|g*\rho_\delta-g\|_\infty.$ Choose $\delta$ small enough that this is below $\epsilon/2$ (if $M$ is zero, every $L^2(M)$ class is zero and the conclusion is immediate). The triangle inequality gives $\|f-g*\rho_\delta\|_{L^2(M)}<\epsilon$, proving density.

Let $J$ be a nonempty compact interval and $n\ge1$. Continuous $\mathbb R^n$-valued curves on $J$ are complete in the supremum metric

$$d_\infty(x,y):=\sup_{t\in J}\|x(t)-y(t)\|_2.$$

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty complete metric space ([[def-complete-metric-space]])
and let $f : X \to X$ be a contraction with constant $q$, so
$d(f(u),f(v)) \le q\,d(u,v)$ for all $u,v \in X$ and $0 \le q < 1$
([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]]). Then:

1. There is exactly one $x^{*} \in X$ with $f(x^{*}) = x^{*}$.
2. For every $x_0 \in X$ the sequence of **iterates**, defined by recursion
   ([[thm-recursion]]) by $x_{n+1} := f(x_n)$, converges to $x^{*}$ in $(X,d)$
   ([[def-metric-convergence]]). In particular the limit does not depend on
   $x_0$.
3. For all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge n$,
   $$d(x_m, x_n) \;\le\; \frac{q^{\,n}\, d(x_1,x_0)}{1-q},$$
   with the integer power of [[def-integer-power]].

Claim 3 is the quantitative form of the argument that proves claims 1 and 2, and
it is recorded in the statement because the error estimates
([[cor-banach-error-estimates]]) are read off from it.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice (The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)).

Let $a<b$ and let $f\in L^1([a,b])$. Define
$$F(x):=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt\qquad(a\le x\le b).$$
Then $F$ is differentiable for almost every $x\in(a,b)$ and
$$F'(x)=f(x)$$
at every such point.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ (The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ (The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice (The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)).

Let $f\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^n)$. Then
$$\lim_{r\to0^+}A_rf(x)=f(x)$$
for Lebesgue-almost every $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.
For $f\in L^1[a,b]$, the function $I_f(x)=\int_a^x f$ is absolutely continuous.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Every absolutely continuous
$F:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ has property $(N)$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $A$
([[def-continuity-real]]) and let $K \subseteq A$ be compact in the sense of
[[def-open-cover-r]], that is, every family of open subsets of $\mathbb{R}$
whose union contains $K$ has a finite subfamily whose union contains $K$. Then
the image

$$f[K] \;:=\; \{\, f(x) : x \in K \,\}$$

is a compact subset of $\mathbb{R}$.

**This theorem is stated twice in this library, on purpose.** Its metric-space
twin is [[thm-continuous-image-of-a-compact-space-is-compact]], proved from the
cover machinery of metric spaces; the proof below is $\mathbb{R}$-native and
uses only open subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ and the definition of continuity of this
page. The duplication is deliberate and is acknowledged in exactly one place,
[[lem-real-and-metric-notions-agree]] later on this page, which proves that the
two notions of "compact subset of $\mathbb{R}$" and the two notions of
"continuous" coincide, so that the two theorems really are the same statement in
two vocabularies.

**No choice principle is used.** The covering family built below is cut out by a
property rather than selected point by point, and the only selection made is
from a *finite* list, which needs no axiom.

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be an increasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$, so $E_n\subseteq E_{n+1}$. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\sup_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

No finiteness hypothesis is required.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on the closed bounded interval $[a,b]$ (Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length,
Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point), and let $y \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy

$$f(a) \le y \le f(b) \qquad \text{or} \qquad f(b) \le y \le f(a) .$$

Then there is $c \in [a,b]$ with $f(c) = y$.

**The construction is canonical, so no choice principle is used.** The bisection
below tests the left half first and takes the right half only when the left one
has been ruled out, so the passage from one interval to the next is a *function*
of that interval, and The recursion theorem applies with nothing selected. This is
the same discipline the library uses wherever a sequence is built one term at a
time.

derivations.claim: Fix an initial pair $(s,x_0)$ and a closed ball $K=\overline B(x_0,r)$. On a sufficiently short one-sided interval $J$ adjoining $s$, absolute continuity of the integrals of $m_K,L_K$ gives $\int_Jm_K\le r$ and $\int_JL_K<1$. On continuous curves taking values in $K$, define $\Phi(X)(t)=x_0+\int_s^t b(q,X(q))dq,$ with the oriented integral when J lies to the left of s. The integrand is measurable because $q\mapsto(q,X(q))$ is continuous and b is Borel; it is integrable because $|b(q,X(q))|\le m_K(q)$ almost everywhere. The map preserves the closed sup-norm ball of radius r about the constant curve $x_0$, and $\|\Phi(X)-\Phi(Y)\|_\infty\le(\int_JL_K)\|X-Y\|_\infty$. By [F1] it has a unique fixed point. The integral FTC [F2] makes this curve absolutely continuous and a solution almost everywhere.

We first prove the scalar zero-derivative implication needed for uniqueness. Let $H:[a,c]\to\mathbb R$ be absolutely continuous with $H'=0$ outside a null set $N$ containing the endpoints. For $\varepsilon>0$ and $n\ge1$, let $E_n$ consist of all $x\in[a,c]$ such that $|H(y)-H(x)|\le\varepsilon|y-x|$ whenever $y\in[a,c]$ and $|y-x|<1/n$. Continuity of $H$ makes $E_n$ closed: pass to the limit in this inequality for each fixed y with $|y-x|<1/n$. These compact sets increase with n and cover $[a,c]\setminus N$. Partition $[a,c]$ into finitely many closed intervals of length less than $1/n$. On each interval I, the compact image $H(E_n\cap I)$ has diameter at most $\varepsilon|I|$, so covering it by its smallest containing interval gives $\lambda(H(E_n))\le\varepsilon(c-a)$. By [F8], the increasing union of the compact images has measure at most $\varepsilon(c-a)$, hence $\lambda^*(H([a,c]\setminus N))\le\varepsilon(c-a)$. Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ makes this image null; [F7] makes $H(N)$ null as well. Thus the whole range of H is null, and the intermediate value theorem [F8] makes H constant. The singleton interval is immediate.

Any absolutely continuous solution Y on a compact interval with image in K satisfies its integral equation. Indeed, $f(q)=b(q,Y(q))$ is measurable and bounded almost everywhere by $m_K$, hence integrable. By [F2], $I(t)=\int_a^t f(q)dq$ is absolutely continuous and $I'=f$ almost everywhere. Each component of $Y-I$ is absolutely continuous by the finite-family definition (split a given tolerance between the two summands), and has derivative zero almost everywhere. Step 1.2 makes it constant. Therefore $Y(t)-Y(a)=\int_a^t b(q,Y(q))dq$ for every t, and subtraction gives the oriented version with any base time.

If two solutions have the same value at one time and remain in a compact K on a common compact interval, partition that interval into finitely many subintervals on which $\int L_K<1$. By step 2.1 both satisfy their integral equations. On each subinterval beginning at a time where the solutions agree, these equations bound their sup-norm difference by $(\int L_K)$ times itself, so the difference is zero. Induction over the partition proves uniqueness throughout the common interval. Their compatible union therefore defines a unique maximal locally absolutely continuous solution: every compact subinterval of its domain is covered by finitely many local solution intervals, on which the integral equation holds. Suppose a maximal endpoint $\tau$ lies in $(0,T)$ and there are times $t_n\uparrow\tau$ with $X(t_n)$ in a compact set K. Choose R with K contained in the ball $B_R(0)$, put $K_1=\overline B_{R+1}(0)$, and take n large enough that $\int_{t_n}^{\tau}m_{K_1}<1$. If the path first reaches the boundary of $K_1$ at some $r\in(t_n,\tau)$, it stays in $K_1$ on $[t_n,r]$, so $|X(r)-X(t_n)|\le\int_{t_n}^r m_{K_1}<1$, while $|X(r)-X(t_n)|\ge |X(r)|-|X(t_n)|\ge1$, a contradiction. Thus it stays in $K_1$ up to $\tau$; the same integrable bound makes it Cauchy there, and its finite limit lets step 1.1 extend it past $\tau$, again a contradiction. Hence the path eventually leaves every compact set at an interior right maximal endpoint. Time reversal gives the same conclusion at an interior left maximal endpoint.

Assume the spatial derivative hypothesis. On a short interval and compact ball as in step 1.1, solutions from nearby initial points remain in a common compact ball. The contraction estimate gives $\|X(\cdot;s,x_0+h)-X(\cdot;s,x_0)\|_\infty\le C|h|$. Write $\Delta_h(t)=X(t;s,x_0+h)-X(t;s,x_0)$. The state-variable fundamental theorem of calculus [F3] gives $\Delta_h(t)=h+\int_s^t A_h(q)\Delta_h(q)dq,\quad A_h(q)=\int_0^1D_xb(q,X(q;s,x_0)+\theta\Delta_h(q))d\theta.$ Put $A(q)=D_xb(q,X(q;s,x_0))$ at the almost-everywhere times where the spatial differential exists, with value zero on its exceptional time set. The matrix equation $V(t)=I_d+\int_s^tA(q)V(q)dq$ has a unique continuous solution by the contraction argument of step 1.1, since $\int_JL_K<1$. Subtracting its product with h from the equation for $\Delta_h$ gives $\Delta_h(t)-V(t)h=\int_s^t A_h(q)(\Delta_h(q)-V(q)h)dq+\int_s^t(A_h(q)-A(q))V(q)h\,dq.$ Taking sup norms and absorbing the first term bounds the left side by $C|h|\int_J\|A_h-A\|dq=o(|h|)$. Thus $D_{x_0}X=V$; dominated convergence in the same integral equation proves continuity of V in $x_0$. The integral FTC [F2] yields $\dot V=A(t)V$ almost everywhere. Repeating on a finite cover by overlapping short intervals gives $C^1$ dependence throughout each common flow domain and continuous dependence in the uniform path norm on trajectories existing through the full interval.

Uniqueness makes the time map from s to t injective. Continuous dependence makes its domain open; solving backward from time t shows its image is open and its inverse is the backward flow, which is $C^1$ by step 3.1. The chain rule [F5] says the derivative of the inverse times V is the identity. Thus the time map is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism between its open domain and image.

Fix a compact flow tube and a compact set K of states it visits. For a fixed target time t, choose a compact time interval J containing t and the varying start times, with all trajectories in the flow identity remaining in K. For trajectories with the same starting time, the integral equation gives $|X(r;s,y)-X(r;s,z)|\le|y-z|+\int_{\min\{s,r\}}^{\max\{s,r\}}L_K(q)|X(q;s,y)-X(q;s,z)|dq$; iterating this inequality yields the spatial Lipschitz bound $|X(t;s,y)-X(t;s,z)|\le e^{\int_JL_K}|y-z|$. For $s,s+h\in J$, the flow identity and the integral equation along the short backward segment give $X(t;s+h,x)=X(t;s,X(s;s+h,x))$ and $|X(s;s+h,x)-x|\le\int_{[s,s+h]}m_K(q)dq$, where the integral is over the unoriented interval. Hence $|X(t;s+h,x)-X(t;s,x)|\le e^{\int_JL_K}\int_{[s,s+h]}m_K(q)dq$. Summing over any disjoint adjacent intervals shows that $s\mapsto X(t;s,x)$ is locally absolutely continuous, uniformly for x in the tube. To identify its derivative, choose a countable dense subset Q of K. Apply [F2] to the indefinite integrals of $m_K,L_K$ and each component of $s\mapsto b(s,q)$ for $q\in Q$; their differentiability gives the corresponding one-sided interval averages at almost every s. By Countable Choice select exceptional null sets for this countable family, and take their union with the exceptional set for the spatial Lipschitz bound. Outside this union all these averages converge to the values at s; [F6] also gives the centered-average conclusion there after enlarging the null set. Approximation by q and the common Lipschitz bound show that the averages of $b(r,x)$ over intervals shrinking to s converge to $b(s,x)$ uniformly for $x\in K$. For the solution started at x at time $s+h$, the magnitude bound gives $|X(r;s+h,x)-x|\le\int_{[s,s+h]}m_K=O(|h|)$ uniformly between s and s+h at these Lebesgue points. Replacing $b(r,x)$ by $b(r,X(r;s+h,x))$ in the average contributes at most $|h|^{-1}O(|h|)\int_{[s,s+h]}L_K(r)dr=O(|h|)$. The integral equation therefore gives $[X(s;s+h,x)-x]/h\to-b(s,x)$ uniformly on K. The flow identity $X(t;s+h,x)=X(t;s,X(s;s+h,x))$ and the spatial derivative from step 4.1 yield $\partial_sX(t;s,x)=-D_xX(t;s,x)b(s,x)$ almost everywhere on the tube. The right side has the integrable local bound $e^{\int_JL_K}m_K(s)$, consistent with and also giving the local absolute continuity.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T>0$, $d\ge1$, and let $(\mu_t,v_t)$ be a narrowly continuous finite-action solution of the continuity equation on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d$, with space-time law $M(dt,dx)=dt\,\mu_t(dx)$. Put $a(t)=\int|v_t(y)|^2d\mu_t(y)$ and $N=\{t:a(t)=+\infty\}$. Then $a$ is measurable, $N$ is Borel and Lebesgue-null, and the Borel representative $\bar v(t,x)=0$ for $t\in N$ and $\bar v(t,x)=v(t,x)$ for $t\notin N$ agrees with $v$ $M$-almost everywhere. For $\varepsilon>0$, let $\rho_\varepsilon$ be the strictly positive centered Gaussian probability density with covariance $\varepsilon I_d$, and define
$$p_t^\varepsilon(x)=\int\rho_\varepsilon(x-y)d\mu_t(y),\quad j_t^\varepsilon(x)=\int\rho_\varepsilon(x-y)\bar v_t(y)d\mu_t(y),\quad v_t^\varepsilon(x)=j_t^\varepsilon(x)/p_t^\varepsilon(x).$$
Then $p_t^\varepsilon$ is a strictly positive smooth probability density for each $t$, $t\mapsto\mu_t^\varepsilon$ is narrowly continuous, $v_t^\varepsilon$ is Borel and locally Lipschitz in $x$ with local magnitude and Lipschitz bounds integrable in time, and $(\mu_t*\rho_\varepsilon,v_t^\varepsilon)$ solves the continuity equation. For almost every $t$,
$$\int|v_t^\varepsilon(x)|^2p_t^\varepsilon(x)dx\le\int|v_t(y)|^2d\mu_t(y).$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $T>0$, let $d\ge1$, and let $b:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ be Borel. Suppose that for every compact $K\subset\mathbb R^d$ there are nonnegative $m_K,L_K\in L^1(0,T)$ such that for almost every $t$, $|b(t,x)|\le m_K(t)$ and $|b(t,x)-b(t,y)|\le L_K(t)|x-y|$ for all $x,y\in K$. For each $(s,x_0)$ there is a unique maximal locally absolutely continuous solution $X(\cdot;s,x_0)$ of $\dot X=b(t,X)$ with $X(s)=x_0$, defined on an interval $I\subseteq[0,T]$ containing $s$. Here locally absolutely continuous means absolutely continuous on every compact subinterval of $I$, and maximal means that it has no locally absolutely continuous solution extension to a strictly larger interval in $[0,T]$; any maximal endpoint lying in $(0,T)$ can occur only if the trajectory leaves every compact subset of $\mathbb R^d$. If, in addition, $b(t,\cdot)$ is continuously differentiable for almost every $t$ and $D_xb$ has integrable local bounds, then the set of initial points whose trajectories exist between any fixed pair of times is open, its time map is one-to-one onto an open image with both map and inverse continuously differentiable, and the path map into the uniform path space is continuous on the set of trajectories existing through the full interval. On compact flow tubes the dependence on the starting time is locally absolutely continuous and satisfies $\partial_sX(t;s,x)=-D_xX(t;s,x)b(s,x)$ for almost every s, simultaneously for x in the tube. The spatial derivative $V_t=D_{x_0}X(t;s,x_0)$ satisfies $\dot V_t=D_xb(t,X_t)V_t$, $V_s=I_d$, almost everywhere.

Assume countable choice. If $P$ is Polish and $\mu$ is a Borel probability measure on $P$, then for every Borel $A\subseteq P$ and $\varepsilon>0$ there is a compact $K\subseteq A$ with $\mu(A\setminus K)<\varepsilon$.

Assume Countable Choice. For every integer $d\ge1$ there is a nonnegative function $\rho_d:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ with continuous partial derivatives of every order, support exactly $[-1,1]^d$, strictly positive on $(-1,1)^d$, and Lebesgue integral $\int_{\mathbb R^d}\rho_d(x)\,dx=1$. Here the support is the closure of the set where the function is nonzero.

Let $\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ satisfy

$$ \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \varphi(x)\,dx = 1. $$

For $\varepsilon > 0$, define

$$ \varphi_\varepsilon(x) := \varepsilon^{-n}\varphi(x/\varepsilon) \qquad(x \in \mathbb{R}^n). $$

The family $(\varphi_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ is the **mollifier family
generated by $\varphi$**.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{C}$ be locally integrable, let
$\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ have mass $1$, and let
$\varphi_\varepsilon$ be the associated mollifier. Then for every
$\varepsilon > 0$, the convolution

$$ (f*\varphi_\varepsilon)(x) := \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(y)\varphi_\varepsilon(x-y)\,dy $$

is smooth, and for every multi-index $\alpha$,

$$ \partial^\alpha(f*\varphi_\varepsilon) = f*(\partial^\alpha \varphi_\varepsilon). $$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

Assume countable choice. If $P$ is Polish and $\mu$ is a Borel probability measure on $P$, then for every Borel $A\subseteq P$ and $\varepsilon>0$ there is a compact $K\subseteq A$ with $\mu(A\setminus K)<\varepsilon$.

A topological space is **Polish** when it is separable ([[def-separable-space]]) and completely metrizable: its topology is induced by some complete metric ([[lem-complete-remetrisation]]). No particular compatible complete metric or countable dense subset is part of the structure.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: Apply [F2] to $v^\varepsilon$ and denote by $D_t$ the open set of initial points whose trajectories exist from time 0 through t, and by $E_t=X_t^\varepsilon(D_t)$ its open image. Fix $t\in(0,T]$ and $f\in C_c^\infty(E_t)$. For $0\le r\le t$ and $x\in D_{r,t}$, the set of states whose trajectories exist from r to t, define $\psi(r,x)=f(X^\varepsilon(t;r,x))$; extend it by zero outside $D_{r,t}$. Since $\operatorname{supp}f$ is compactly contained in $E_t$, its backward images form a compact subset of the flow domain. Thus $\psi$ has compact spatial support uniformly in r, is continuously differentiable in x, and is absolutely continuous in r locally. The start-time derivative from [F2] and the flow identity give $\partial_r\psi=\nabla f(X(t;r,x))\cdot[-D_xX(t;r,x)v_r^\varepsilon(x)]=-v_r^\varepsilon(x)\cdot\nabla_x\psi$ almost everywhere.

For this fixed t define the restricted finite pushforward $
u_t$ on $E_t$ by $
u_t(B)=\mu_0^\varepsilon(\{x\in D_t:X_t^\varepsilon(x)\in B\})$ for Borel $B\subseteq E_t$. The set is Borel because $X_t^\varepsilon$ is continuous on the open domain $D_t$; preimages preserve disjoint unions, so $
u_t$ is a finite Borel measure of mass $\mu_0^\varepsilon(D_t)$. The weak continuity-equation identity extends from smooth compact tests to compactly supported tests that are $C^1$ in x and absolutely continuous in r with locally integrable time derivative: multiply by a time cutoff, convolve in time and space on a fixed compact neighborhood, and pass to the limit. The terms converge because $p^\varepsilon$ is locally bounded, $p^\varepsilon v^\varepsilon$ is locally integrable in time and space by finite action, and the test and its spatial gradient converge uniformly while its time derivative converges in $L^1$. Apply this extension to $\eta(r)\psi(r,x)$ from step 1.1 for every smooth compactly supported time cutoff $\eta$. The transport equation leaves $\int\eta'(r)F(r)dr=0$, so $F(r)=\int\psi(r,x)d\mu_r^\varepsilon(x)$ is constant on $(0,t)$. Continuity of the flow and of $\mu_r^\varepsilon$ extends the identity to r=0,t, giving $\int f(y)d\mu_t^\varepsilon(y)=\int f(X_t^\varepsilon(x))d\mu_0^\varepsilon(x)$ for every $f\in C_c^\infty(E_t)$. Uniform mollification extends equality to every $f\in C_c(E_t)$; both measures are finite, so uniform limits pass through their integrals. For a compact $K\subset E_t$, choose n sufficiently large that the closed $1/n$-neighborhood of K is compactly contained in $E_t$ and set $f_n(x)=\max\{0,1-n\operatorname{dist}(x,K)\}$. Then $f_n\in C_c(E_t)$ and $f_n\downarrow\mathbf1_K$, so [F6] gives $
u_t(K)=\mu_t^\varepsilon(K)$. By [F5], both finite Borel measures on the Polish space $E_t$ are inner regular; their agreement on compact sets therefore proves $
u_t=\mu_t^\varepsilon|_{E_t}$.

For every $r\in(0,T]$, step 2.1 gives equality of the restricted finite measures on $E_r$. Applying it to $y\mapsto\min\{N,|v_r^\varepsilon(y)|^2\}$ and letting $N\uparrow\infty$ by [F7] yields $\int_{D_r}|v_r^\varepsilon(X_r^\varepsilon(x))|^2d\mu_0^\varepsilon(x)=\int_{E_r}|v_r^\varepsilon(y)|^2d\mu_r^\varepsilon(y)\le\int|v_r^\varepsilon(y)|^2d\mu_r^\varepsilon(y)$. Let $\mathscr D=\{(r,x):x\in D_r\}$. This domain is relatively open in $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d$ and $(r,x)\mapsto X_r^\varepsilon(x)$ is continuous on it: cover any compact trajectory segment through $(r,x)$ by finitely many local flow neighborhoods from [F2] and patch their continuous dependence on the initial point; time continuity follows from the integral equation. Thus the integrand is Borel; extend it by zero off $\mathscr D$. Tonelli [F4] then gives $\int\!\int_0^{\min\{T,\tau(x)\}}|v_r^\varepsilon(X_r^\varepsilon(x))|^2dr\,d\mu_0^\varepsilon(x)\le\int_0^T\!\int|v_r^\varepsilon(y)|^2d\mu_r^\varepsilon(y)dr<\infty.$ Thus for $\mu_0^\varepsilon$-almost every x the path has finite squared speed integral up to its maximal endpoint. Holder then makes its total path length finite. Such a path is Cauchy at any finite endpoint; it cannot escape every compact set, contradicting [F2] if an endpoint lies in $(0,T)$. At T it has a finite limit and extends continuously to T. Thus $\mu_0^\varepsilon(D_T)=1$.

Let $T>0$, $d\ge1$, and let $(\mu_t,v_t)$ be a narrowly continuous finite-action solution of the continuity equation on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d$, with space-time law $M(dt,dx)=dt\,\mu_t(dx)$. Put $a(t)=\int|v_t(y)|^2d\mu_t(y)$ and $N=\{t:a(t)=+\infty\}$. Then $a$ is measurable, $N$ is Borel and Lebesgue-null, and the Borel representative $\bar v(t,x)=0$ for $t\in N$ and $\bar v(t,x)=v(t,x)$ for $t\notin N$ agrees with $v$ $M$-almost everywhere. For $\varepsilon>0$, let $\rho_\varepsilon$ be the strictly positive centered Gaussian probability density with covariance $\varepsilon I_d$, and define
$$p_t^\varepsilon(x)=\int\rho_\varepsilon(x-y)d\mu_t(y),\quad j_t^\varepsilon(x)=\int\rho_\varepsilon(x-y)\bar v_t(y)d\mu_t(y),\quad v_t^\varepsilon(x)=j_t^\varepsilon(x)/p_t^\varepsilon(x).$$
Then $p_t^\varepsilon$ is a strictly positive smooth probability density for each $t$, $t\mapsto\mu_t^\varepsilon$ is narrowly continuous, $v_t^\varepsilon$ is Borel and locally Lipschitz in $x$ with local magnitude and Lipschitz bounds integrable in time, and $(\mu_t*\rho_\varepsilon,v_t^\varepsilon)$ solves the continuity equation. $$\int|v_t^\varepsilon(x)|^2p_t^\varepsilon(x)dx\le\int|v_t(y)|^2d\mu_t(y).$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

It is unique as a kernel outside a single measurable $\beta$-null set. For every nonnegative product-measurable $f:E\times T\to[0,\infty]$,

$$\int f(x,y)\,\lambda(d(x,y))=\int_T\left(\int_E f(x,y)K(y,dx)\right)\beta(dy).$$

For this page, a Borel measure $\mu$ on a locally compact Hausdorff space is
