In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

derivations.claim: Set $\varepsilon_n=1/n$. For each n, let $D_n$ be the Borel full-$\mu_0^{\varepsilon_n}$-measure set of initial points whose regularized flow paths exist on all of $[0,T]$. The map $F_n:D_n\to C([0,T];\mathbb R^d)$, $F_n(x)(t)=X_t^{\varepsilon_n}(x)$, is Borel by [F1]. Extend it by the zero path off $D_n$ and define $\eta_n=(F_n)_\#\mu_0^{\varepsilon_n}$; this is the law of a Borel random element and is a Borel probability. For every t, composition with evaluation gives $(e_t)_\#\eta_n=(X_t^{\varepsilon_n})_\#\mu_0^{\varepsilon_n}=\mu_t^{\varepsilon_n}$ by [F1]. The flow equation, the same marginal identity, and Tonelli give $\int\mathcal E(\gamma)d\eta_n(\gamma)=\int_0^T\!\int|v_t^{\varepsilon_n}(x)|^2d\mu_t^{\varepsilon_n}(x)dt\le A,$ where $A=\int_0^T\!\int|v_t(x)|^2d\mu_t(x)dt<\infty$. For every fixed t, $\mu_t^{\varepsilon_n}\Rightarrow\mu_t$: for bounded continuous f, first restrict y to a compact set carrying all but arbitrarily small $\mu_t$-mass using [F8], then use uniform continuity of f on a one-neighborhood of that compact and concentration of the Gaussian kernels at zero.

The path space C with the uniform metric is Polish: it is complete by the continuous-curve completeness fact, and rational polygonal paths are countable and dense. By [F2], the sequence of initial laws is tight. Given $\delta>0$, choose compact K with $\mu_0^{\varepsilon_n}(K^c)<\delta/2$ for all n, and choose R so $A/R<\delta/2$. The set $K_R=\{\gamma:\gamma(0)\in K,\ \mathcal E(\gamma)\le R\}$ is closed by [F3] and compact by Arzela–Ascoli: its paths obey $|\gamma(t)-\gamma(s)|\le\sqrt{R|t-s|}$ and $\sup_t|\gamma(t)|\le\sup_{x\in K}|x|+\sqrt{RT}$. Markov's inequality, which follows from $\mathbf1_{\{\mathcal E>R\}}\le\mathcal E/R$, gives $\eta_n(K_R)\ge1-\delta$. Thus $(\eta_n)$ is tight; [F2] gives a weakly convergent subsequence, still denoted $\eta_n$, with Borel probability limit $\eta$.

For each t, evaluation $e_t:C\to\mathbb R^d$ is continuous, so weak convergence and the marginal convergence $\mu_t^{\varepsilon_n}\Rightarrow\mu_t$ imply $(e_t)_\#\eta=\mu_t$. By [F3], $\mathcal E$ is nonnegative and lower semicontinuous. For each integer k define $g_k(\gamma)=\min\{k,\inf_{\zeta\in C}[\mathcal E(\zeta)+k\|\gamma-\zeta\|_\infty]\}$. The triangle inequality makes $g_k$ k-Lipschitz, $0\le g_k\le\mathcal E$, and $g_k$ increases with k. If $a<\mathcal E(\gamma)$, lower semicontinuity gives a neighborhood of $\gamma$ where $\mathcal E>a$; outside that neighborhood the term $k\|\gamma-\zeta\|_\infty$ exceeds a for all sufficiently large k. Thus $g_k(\gamma)\uparrow\mathcal E(\gamma)$. By [F9], weak convergence gives $\int g_kd\eta=\lim_n\int g_kd\eta_n\le\liminf_n\int\mathcal E d\eta_n$ for every k. Monotone convergence [F9] yields $\int\mathcal E d\eta\le\liminf_n\int\mathcal E d\eta_n\le A$. In particular $\eta$-almost every path is absolutely continuous with square-integrable derivative.

Give $[0,T]\times C$ the probability measure $\lambda=(dt/T)\otimes\eta$ and define the Borel random element $Z(t,\gamma)=(t,\gamma(t),\dot\gamma(t))$, setting the last coordinate to zero wherever the derivative limit is undefined. Measurability follows by expressing the derivative as the limit of measurable difference quotients; it agrees with the path derivative for $\lambda$-almost every pair. The law $\Pi$ of Z has $(t,x)$ marginal $M/T$ by the time-marginal identity in step 2.1. Disintegrate with the velocity as the conditioned coordinate, and put $b(t,x)=\int u\,K_{t,x}(du)$ where defined, zero otherwise. It is Borel by [F4]. Conditional Jensen and step 2.1 give $\int|b|^2dM\le T\int|u|^2d\Pi=\int\!\int_0^T|\dot\gamma(t)|^2dt\,d\eta(\gamma)\le A.$ The factor T cancels because $\Pi$ uses normalized time.

Fix a smooth compactly supported vector field $\xi(t,x)$. For a finite partition $P=(t_i)$ of mesh h, set $S_P(\gamma)=\sum_i\xi(t_i,\gamma(t_i))\cdot(\gamma(t_{i+1})-\gamma(t_i)).$ For every $AC^2$ path, bounded derivatives of $\xi$ imply $\left|\int_0^T\xi(t,\gamma(t))\cdot\dot\gamma(t)dt-S_P(\gamma)\right|\le C_\xi\left(h\sqrt T\,\mathcal E(\gamma)^{1/2}+h\mathcal E(\gamma)\right).$ Indeed on each interval $|\xi(t,\gamma_t)-\xi(t_i,\gamma_{t_i})|\le C_\xi(h+|\gamma_t-\gamma_{t_i}|)$, while Cauchy--Schwarz gives $\int_{t_i}^{t_{i+1}}|\dot\gamma|\le\sqrt{hE_i}$ and $|\gamma_t-\gamma_{t_i}|\le\sqrt{hE_i}$; summing yields the bound. Its expectation is uniform over $\eta_n$ and $\eta$ by the action bound. For fixed P with N intervals, $S_P$ is continuous and $|S_P|^2\le N\|\xi\|_\infty^2\sum_i|\gamma(t_{i+1})-\gamma(t_i)|^2$. Pathwise Cauchy--Schwarz gives $\int|\gamma(t_{i+1})-\gamma(t_i)|^2d\eta_n\le(t_{i+1}-t_i)A$, so these sums have uniformly bounded second moments under $\eta_n$ and $\eta$. Thus $S_P$ is uniformly integrable, and weak convergence plus bounded truncations gives $\int S_Pd\eta_n\to\int S_Pd\eta$. Letting h tend to zero proves convergence of the expected path integrals.

Under $\eta_n$, the path derivative is $v_t^{\varepsilon_n}(\gamma(t))$; hence its expected $\xi$-pairing is $\int\xi(t,x)\cdot v_t^{\varepsilon_n}(x)d\mu_t^{\varepsilon_n}(x)dt$. By the convolution definitions, $\int\xi\cdot v^{\varepsilon_n}dM^{\varepsilon_n}=\int_0^T\!\int v_t(y)\cdot(\xi_t*\rho_{\varepsilon_n})(y)d\mu_t(y)dt\longrightarrow\int\xi\cdot v\,dM,$ since $\xi_t*\rho_{\varepsilon_n}\to\xi_t$ uniformly and $v\in L^1(M)$ by finite action and Holder. Combining with step 3.2 and the conditional-mean definition of b gives $\int\xi\cdot b\,dM=\int\xi\cdot v\,dM$. Smooth-test density [F5] implies $b=v$ M-almost everywhere.

The time marginals of $\eta$ are $\mu_t$, so $\int|v(t,\gamma(t))|^2dt\,d\eta=A$. By step 3.1 the conditional mean of $\dot\gamma$ given $(t,\gamma(t))$ is b, which equals v by step 4.1. Therefore $\int\!\int_0^T|\dot\gamma(t)-v_t(\gamma(t))|^2dt\,d\eta=\int\mathcal E\,d\eta+A-2\int v\cdot b\,dM=\int\mathcal E\,d\eta-A\le0.$ The left side is nonnegative, so it is zero. Thus $\dot\gamma=v_t(\gamma(t))$ for $dt\,d\eta$-almost every pair, and the expected path action equals A. Together with the time marginals this is the claimed superposition law.

$$|\dot\mu_t|=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{W_2(\mu_{t+h},\mu_t)}{|h|}$$
exists for almost every $t\in(0,T)$, is measurable and belongs to $L^2(0,T)$. For all $0\le s\le t\le T$,
$$W_2(\mu_s,\mu_t)\le\int_s^t|\dot\mu_r|dr.$$
It is the least nonnegative square-integrable upper control: if $g\in L^2(0,T)$ and $W_2(\mu_s,\mu_t)\le\int_s^t g(r)dr$ for all $s\le t$, then $|\dot\mu_t|\le g(t)$ almost everywhere.

$$\mu:\mathcal A\longrightarrow[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$$

such that:

1. $\mu(\varnothing)=0$;
2. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$,
   $$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k),$$
   where the right side is the nonnegative extended sum of Series in the nonnegative extended real line.

The second condition is **countable additivity**. It begins at index $0$ and includes the case in which some term or the total sum is $+\infty$.

1. If $g\ge0$, then

Define $\pi_{s,t}(B)=\eta(E_{s,t}^{-1}(B))$ for Borel $B\subseteq\mathbb R^{2d}$; by [F4] this is a Borel probability. Its coordinate marginals are $(e_s)_\#\eta=\mu_s$ and $(e_t)_\#\eta=\mu_t$, so $\pi_{s,t}$ is a coupling. Its quadratic cost satisfies $\int|x-y|^2d\pi_{s,t}(x,y)=\int|\gamma(t)-\gamma(s)|^2d\eta(\gamma)$ by [F4]. For $\eta$-almost every path, absolute continuity gives $|\gamma(t)-\gamma(s)|\le\int_s^t|\dot\gamma(r)|dr$. Minkowski [F2], applied with the path probability space and Lebesgue measure on $[s,t]$, yields $W_2(\mu_s,\mu_t)\le\left(\int\left(\int_s^t|\dot\gamma(r)|dr\right)^2d\eta\right)^{1/2}\le\int_s^t\left(\int|\dot\gamma(r)|^2d\eta\right)^{1/2}dr.$ The marginal identity and the pathwise velocity identity in [F1] identify the inner integral for almost every r as $\int|v_r(x)|^2d\mu_r(x)$. Put $g(r)=(\int|v_r|^2d\mu_r)^{1/2}$. Finite action gives $g\in L^2(0,T)$, and the displayed bound for every interval implies W2-continuity and the defining $AC^2$ upper-control inequality.

By [F3], the metric derivative exists almost everywhere and is no larger than any nonnegative $L^2$ upper control. Applying it to $g$ from step 1.1 gives $|\dot\mu_t|\le g(t)$ almost everywhere, as claimed.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
(Real and imaginary parts, complex conjugation, and modulus). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of Real and complex inner product spaces, with the inner product linear in the first argument: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published The norm $\lVert v\rVert=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ induced by a real or complex inner product: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ (Real and complex inner-product spaces and their induced length) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of Complete metric space: every Cauchy sequence converges in the space: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ (The induced length is a norm) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm (Banach space).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
Banach space defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and let $f$ be a bounded linear functional on $H$ (The dual space X^* of a normed space and its dual norm). Then there is a unique $y\in H$ with

$$f(x)=\langle x,y\rangle\qquad\text{for every }x\in H,$$

and $\|f\|=\|y\|$, where $\|f\|$ is the dual norm (The operator norm as the least bound and as the unit-sphere or unit-ball supremum). Under the first-variable-linear convention the representing vector depends conjugate-linearly and isometrically on $f$: if $f_i$ is represented by $y_i$ and $a,b$ are scalars, then $af_1+bf_2$ is represented by $\overline a\,y_1+\overline b\,y_2$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

Finite sigma-algebras are countably generated as well. These observations do not identify the label dimension $k$ with the output dimension $d$.

The functions $\sum_{j=1}^m q_j\mathbf1_{A_j}$, with $q_j\in\mathbb Q$ and $A_j\in\mathcal A_0$, form a countable subset of scalar $L^2(\sigma)$. It is dense: by [F2], approximate any $f$ by a finite-measure simple function $\sum_j c_j\mathbf1_{E_j}$; approximate each $E_j$ in measure using [F4], then approximate each coefficient by a rational. The error satisfies $\|c\mathbf1_E-q\mathbf1_A\|_2\le |c-q|\sqrt{\sigma(E)}+|q|\sqrt{\sigma(E\triangle A)}$, so the finitely many choices make the total error arbitrarily small.

The vector space $K$ is the finite product of $d$ copies of scalar $L^2(\sigma)$. By pointwise [F5], $2|X\cdot Y|\le |X|^2+|Y|^2$, so its displayed pairing is integrable and independent of representatives. Linearity of the integral and the Euclidean dot product give bilinearity and symmetry. Its value on $(X,X)$ is $\int|X|^2\ge0$, and equality forces $|X|=0$ almost everywhere, precisely the zero class. Thus it is an inner product, with the stated norm. A Cauchy sequence for that norm is Cauchy in each of the finitely many scalar coordinates; [F1] gives coordinate limits, and the sum of their squared errors tends to zero. This proves completeness for every probability space, without a countable-generation hypothesis. derivations.claim: Pointwise Cauchy–Schwarz and scalar Cauchy–Schwarz show that the displayed pairing is integrable and bounded by $\|u\|_Z\|v\|_Z$. It is bilinear and symmetric; if $\int\|u\|_H^2=0$, then $\|u(t)\|_H=0$ almost everywhere, so the equivalence class is zero. Thus it is a real inner product.

Let $(u_n)$ be Cauchy in $Z$. By [F4], choose a subsequence $(u_{n_k})$ with $\|u_{n_{k+1}}-u_{n_k}\|_Z\le2^{-k}$. Use [F4] to choose strongly measurable representatives and modify them to zero on their exceptional null sets. Put $g_m(t)=\sum_{k=1}^m\|u_{n_{k+1}}(t)-u_{n_k}(t)\|_H$. Minkowski gives $\|g_m\|_2\le\sum_{k\ge1}2^{-k}=1$; monotone convergence then gives $g=\sum_k\|u_{n_{k+1}}-u_{n_k}\|_H\in L^2$. Hence $g<\infty$ almost everywhere, and completeness of $H$ gives a pointwise limit $u(t)$ there; put $u=0$ on the null set.

The limit $u$ is strongly measurable: the chosen representatives are strongly measurable and converge pointwise off a measurable null set, so their simple approximations give a strongly measurable limit. The tail estimate $\|u-u_{n_m}\|_H\le\sum_{k\ge m}\|u_{n_{k+1}}-u_{n_k}\|_H$ and [F2] show $\|u-u_{n_m}\|_Z\le\sum_{k\ge m}2^{-k}\to0$. Thus $u\in Z$ and the subsequence converges in norm. Since the original sequence is Cauchy, the full sequence converges to the same class; $Z$ is complete.

Fix the given countable dense set $D\subset H$. From strong measurability choose finite-valued simple functions $s_n$ converging pointwise almost everywhere to a representative $u$. Replace $s_n$ by $t_n=s_n\mathbf1_{\{\|s_n\|_H\le2\|u\|_H\}}$; then $t_n\to u$ pointwise and $\|u-t_n\|_H^2\le9\|u\|_H^2$, so dominated convergence makes finite-valued simple functions dense in $Z$. Let $\mathcal A$ be the algebra generated by rational intervals restricted to $(0,T)$. It is countable and generates the Borel sigma-algebra. To verify approximation by this particular algebra, let $\mathcal M$ consist of Borel sets approximable in symmetric-difference measure by members of $\mathcal A$. It contains $\mathcal A$, is closed under complements because symmetric differences are preserved by complements, and is closed under finite unions by subadditivity. For a countable union, first approximate it by a finite subunion: the measure of the omitted part tends to zero since $(0,T)$ has finite measure. Then approximate that finite union by $\mathcal A$. Thus $\mathcal M$ is a sigma-algebra and contains all Borel sets. For a simple function on a finite measurable partition, approximate its cells by $\mathcal A$, disjointify the approximating cells, and assign the complement to the last cell. The new and old partitions disagree only inside the union of the cellwise symmetric differences. Replace each value by a nearby element of $D$. The integral squared error is bounded by a constant times the measure of that disagreement plus $T$ times the maximal squared value error. It tends to zero. The resulting functions take values in $D$ and have finitely many rational breakpoints within $(0,T)$; there are only countably many of them. They are dense, proving separability.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a separable real Hilbert space and $T>0$, and equip $(0,T)$ with its Borel sigma-algebra and Lebesgue measure. Let $Z=L^2((0,T);H)$ consist of strongly measurable $H$-valued functions modulo equality almost everywhere with $\int_0^T\|u(t)\|_H^2\,dt<\infty$. Then
$$\langle u,v\rangle_Z=\int_0^T\langle u(t),v(t)\rangle_H\,dt$$
is a well-defined real inner product and its induced norm is complete. If $D\subset H$ is any countable dense set, the finite-valued step functions with values in $D$ and finitely many rational interval endpoints are dense in $Z$; in particular $Z$ is separable.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and let $f$ be a bounded linear functional on $H$ (The dual space X^* of a normed space and its dual norm). Then there is a unique $y\in H$ with

$$f(x)=\langle x,y\rangle\qquad\text{for every }x\in H,$$

and $\|f\|=\|y\|$, where $\|f\|$ is the dual norm (The operator norm as the least bound and as the unit-sphere or unit-ball supremum). Under the first-variable-linear convention the representing vector depends conjugate-linearly and isometrically on $f$: if $f_i$ is represented by $y_i$ and $a,b$ are scalars, then $af_1+bf_2$ is represented by $\overline a\,y_1+\overline b\,y_2$.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and $X$ a real or complex
Banach space. A strongly measurable function $f:\Omega\to X$ is
**Bochner integrable** if there is a sequence of integrable $X$-valued simple
functions $(s_n)$ such that

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_\Omega\|f-s_n\|\,d\mu=0.$$

For such a sequence define

$$\int_\Omega f\,d\mu:=\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_\Omega s_n\,d\mu.$$

The displayed norm limit exists: the simple integral inequality gives

$$\left\|\int s_n-\int s_m\right\|\leq\int\|s_n-s_m\|\leq\int\|s_n-f\|+\int\|f-s_m\|,$$

so the simple integrals form a Cauchy sequence, and $X$ is complete. The next
theorem proves that the value is independent of the approximating sequence and
characterizes existence by integrability of $\|f\|$.

For $E\in\mathcal A$, write
$\int_Ef\,d\mu:=\int_\Omega\mathbf1_Ef\,d\mu$ whenever this function is
Bochner integrable.

Let $f:\Omega\to X$ be strongly measurable. Then $f$ is Bochner integrable if
and only if

$$\int_\Omega\|f\|\,d\mu<\infty.$$

Here an a.e.-defined scalar function is integrated through any measurable
representative supplied by the strong simple approximation. Moreover the
Bochner integral is independent of the approximating sequence in its
definition.

Let $X,Y$ be Banach spaces, let $T:X\to Y$ be bounded and linear, and let $f$
be Bochner integrable. Then $T\circ f$ is Bochner integrable and, for every
measurable $E$,

$$T\left(\int_Ef\,d\mu\right)=\int_E Tf\,d\mu.$$

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice (The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)).

Let $f\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^n)$. Then
$$\lim_{r\to0^+}A_rf(x)=f(x)$$
for Lebesgue-almost every $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $t>0$. Then
$$\mu(\{f\ge t\})\le\frac1t\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $\mu$ be a measure and let $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be measurable. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k).$$

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ one also has

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k<m}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k<m}\mu(E_k),$$

including $m=0$, where both sides are $0$.

derivations.claim: Let $S$ be the vector space of all finite $H$-valued interval step functions. It contains the dense family in [F1], hence is dense in $Z$. If $f(t)=\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}c_i\mathbf1_{(t_i,t_{i+1})}(t)$ on a partition $P$, define $\Lambda(f)=\sum_i\langle c_i,x(t_{i+1})-x(t_i)\rangle_H$. Refining $P$ leaves this sum unchanged, so $\Lambda$ is well-defined and linear on $S$. Finite-sum Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|\Lambda(f)|\le\|f\|_Z Q_P(x)^{1/2}\le\sqrt C\,\|f\|_Z$. By [F1], $\Lambda$ extends uniquely to a bounded linear functional on $Z$, and [F2] represents it by $u\in Z$.

Fix $0\le s<t\le T$ and $c\in H$. The function $c\mathbf1_{(s,t)}$ belongs to $S$, so its defining value is $\Lambda(c\mathbf1_{(s,t)})=\langle c,x(t)-x(s)\rangle_H$. By the Riesz representation in step 1.1 and commutation of bounded linear functionals with Bochner integrals, this equals $\int_s^t\langle c,u(r)\rangle_Hdr$. The identity holds for every $c\in H$; take $c$ equal to the difference of $x(t)-x(s)$ and $\int_s^tu(r)dr$ to see that its squared norm is zero. Thus $x(t)-x(s)=\int_s^t u(r)dr$ in $H$.

By [F3], choose simple $H$-valued functions $s_n$ with $\int_0^T\|u-s_n\|_Hdt<2^{-3n}$ and put $g_n(t)=\|u(t)-s_n(t)\|_H$. Markov's inequality gives $\operatorname{Leb}\{g_n>2^{-n}\}\le2^{-2n}$; [F7] shows that outside a null set $g_n(t)\le2^{-n}$ eventually. Remove also the countable union of differentiation exceptional sets for all scalar functions $g_n$ and the finitely many indicators defining each $s_n$, using [F5] and [F6]. At each remaining interior $t$, the average of $g_n$ over either one-sided interval with endpoint $t$ has limsup at most $2g_n(t)$, since that interval lies in the centered interval of twice its length. The average of $\|s_n(q)-s_n(t)\|_H$ tends to zero: $s_n$ has finitely many values and each level-set indicator has density $1$ or $0$ at $t$. Therefore $\displaystyle \limsup_{h\to0}\left\|\frac1h\int_t^{t+h}u(q)dq-u(t)\right\|_H\le3g_n(t)$ for every $n$, and letting $n\to\infty$ proves the limit is zero. Step 2.1 identifies this average with $(x(t+h)-x(t))/h$, proving norm differentiability of $x$ with derivative $u$ almost everywhere.

The norm of $\Lambda$ is exactly $\sqrt C$. The upper bound is step 1.1. For any partition $P$ with $Q_P(x)>0$, take the step function $f$ with $c_i=(x(t_{i+1})-x(t_i))/(t_{i+1}-t_i)$ on each interval. It belongs to $S$ and satisfies $\Lambda(f)=\|f\|_Z^2=Q_P(x)$, so $\|\Lambda\|_Z\ge|\Lambda(f)|/\|f\|_Z=\sqrt{Q_P(x)}$. If $Q_P(x)=0$, this lower bound is automatic. Taking the supremum over partitions gives $\|\Lambda\|_Z^2=C$. By [F2], $\|u\|_Z=\|\Lambda\|_Z$, proving the displayed energy identity.

order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Let $(f_n)$ be nonnegative measurable functions. Then
$$\int \liminf_{n\to\infty}f_n\,d\mu\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}\int f_n\,d\mu.$$

For each $k \in \mathbb{N}$ let $I_k = [a_k, b_k]$ be a closed bounded interval
with $a_k \le b_k$ (Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length), and suppose the family is **nested**:

$$I_{k+1} \subseteq I_k \qquad (k \in \mathbb{N}).$$

Write $\ell_k = b_k - a_k \ge 0$ for the length of $I_k$. Then:

1. $\displaystyle\bigcap_{k \in \mathbb{N}} I_k$ is **nonempty**. More precisely,
   with $a = \sup\{a_k : k \in \mathbb{N}\}$ and
   $b = \inf\{b_k : k \in \mathbb{N}\}$, both of which exist, one has $a \le b$
   and $$\bigcap_{k \in \mathbb{N}} I_k = [a, b].$$
2. $\displaystyle\bigcap_{k \in \mathbb{N}} I_k$ is a **single point** if and only
   if $\ell_k \to 0$ (Limits and Cauchy sequences of reals).

Every hypothesis is load bearing. Dropping closedness makes the intersection
empty; dropping boundedness does the same; and dropping nonemptiness of the
individual intervals is vacuously fatal.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice (The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)).

Let $f\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^n)$. Then
$$\lim_{r\to0^+}A_rf(x)=f(x)$$
for Lebesgue-almost every $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$.
For $f\in L^1[a,b]$, the function $I_f(x)=\int_a^x f$ is absolutely continuous.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice (The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)).

Let $a<b$ and let $f\in L^1([a,b])$. Define
$$F(x):=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt\qquad(a\le x\le b).$$
Then $F$ is differentiable for almost every $x\in(a,b)$ and
$$F'(x)=f(x)$$
at every such point.

derivations.claim: For $0<\tau$ with $1+\lambda\tau>0$ and $z\in H$, set $\Psi_{\tau,z}(y)=E(y)+\|y-z\|_H^2/(2\tau)$. It is lower semicontinuous and $(\lambda+1/\tau)$-strongly convex, with positive strong-convexity coefficient. It is bounded below and coercive because $E$ is bounded below. Choose a minimizing sequence $(y_n)$ using [F4]. The midpoint inequality $\displaystyle \Psi_{\tau,z}\!\left(\frac{y_n+y_m}{2}\right)\le\frac{\Psi_{\tau,z}(y_n)+\Psi_{\tau,z}(y_m)}{2}-\frac{1+\lambda\tau}{8\tau}\|y_n-y_m\|_H^2$ and the lower bound by the infimum show that $(y_n)$ is Cauchy. Completeness of $H$ and lower semicontinuity give a minimizer, and strong convexity makes it unique. Call it $J_\tau z$. For $0<h<1$, set $y_h=(1-h)J_\tau z+hy$. Minimality at $y_h$, the $\lambda$-convex inequality, and expansion of the quadratic term give $\displaystyle 0\le h(E(y)-E(J_\tau z))-\frac{\lambda}{2}h(1-h)\|y-J_\tau z\|_H^2-\frac h\tau\langle z-J_\tau z,y-J_\tau z\rangle_H+\frac{h^2}{2\tau}\|y-J_\tau z\|_H^2.$ Divide by $h$ and let $h\downarrow0$ to obtain $\displaystyle E(y)\ge E(J_\tau z)+\left\langle\frac{z-J_\tau z}{\tau},y-J_\tau z\right\rangle_H+\frac{\lambda}{2}\|y-J_\tau z\|_H^2,$ so $(z-J_\tau z)/\tau\in\partial_\lambda E(J_\tau z)$.

Starting at $x_0$, iterate $x_n=J_\tau x_{n-1}$. Comparison with the admissible point $x_{n-1}$ gives $\displaystyle E(x_n)+\frac{\|x_n-x_{n-1}\|_H^2}{2\tau}\le E(x_{n-1}).$ Thus $E(x_n)$ decreases and, for $m=\inf_HE$, $\sum_n\tau\|(x_{n-1}-x_n)/\tau\|_H^2\le2(E(x_0)-m)$.

Let $x_\tau$ be the linear interpolation between the iterates and $\bar x_\tau(t)=x_n$ on $(t_{n-1},t_n]$; then $\dot x_\tau=-\xi_\tau$ and $\xi_\tau(t)\in\partial_\lambda E(\bar x_\tau(t))$. The action bound in step 2.1 gives $\|\xi_\tau\|_{L^2(0,T;H)}^2\le2(E(x_0)-m)$ and $\|x_\tau-\bar x_\tau\|_{L^\infty(0,T;H)}\le\sqrt{\tau}\|\xi_\tau\|_{L^2(0,T;H)}$. For two uniform meshes $\tau,\sigma$, put $\delta_\tau=x_\tau-\bar x_\tau$ and $q(t)=\|x_\tau(t)-x_\sigma(t)\|_H^2$. The subgradient monotonicity obtained by adding the defining inequalities for $\partial_\lambda E$ gives $\displaystyle \frac12q'(t)\le-\lambda\|\bar x_\tau(t)-\bar x_\sigma(t)\|_H^2+(\|\xi_\tau(t)\|_H+\|\xi_\sigma(t)\|_H)(\|\delta_\tau(t)\|_H+\|\delta_\sigma(t)\|_H).$ Using $\|\delta_\tau(t)\|_H\le\tau\|\xi_\tau(t)\|_H$ on each step and Cauchy–Schwarz in time, the interpolation-error terms obey $\displaystyle \int_0^T(\|\xi_\tau\|+\|\xi_\sigma\|)(\|\delta_\tau\|+\|\delta_\sigma\|)dt\le 2(\tau+\sigma)(\|\xi_\tau\|_{L^2}^2+\|\xi_\sigma\|_{L^2}^2),\quad\int_0^T\|\delta_\tau-\delta_\sigma\|^2dt\le2\tau^2\|\xi_\tau\|_{L^2}^2+2\sigma^2\|\xi_\sigma\|_{L^2}^2.$ When $\lambda\ge0$ its term in the differential inequality is nonpositive; when $\lambda<0$, $\|\bar x_\tau-\bar x_\sigma\|^2\le2q+2\|\delta_\tau-\delta_\sigma\|^2$ bounds it by $2|\lambda|q+2|\lambda|\|\delta_\tau-\delta_\sigma\|^2$. Since the action norms are uniformly bounded by step 2.1, for $0<\tau,\sigma\le1$ the differential inequality has the form $q'(t)\le4|\lambda|q(t)+r(t)$, $q(0)=0$, with $\int_0^T r(t)dt\le C(\tau+\sigma)$ and $C$ depending only on $T,\lambda,E(x_0)-m$. Multiplying by $e^{-4|\lambda|t}$ and integrating yields $\sup_{t\le T}q(t)\le C_T(\tau+\sigma)$, so the interpolants converge uniformly on every bounded time interval.

Let $x$ be the uniform limit. Every finite partition $P$ satisfies $\sum_{[a,b]\in P}\|x(b)-x(a)\|_H^2/(b-a)\le\liminf_{\tau\downarrow0}\int_0^T\|\dot x_\tau\|_H^2\le2(E(x_0)-m)$, by Cauchy–Schwarz on each mesh interval and uniform convergence. [F2] gives $x\in AC^2$ and a derivative. The step functions $\xi_\tau$ are bounded in the separable Hilbert space [F1]; apply [F7] successively to their inner products with a countable dense family and take a diagonal subsequence. The limits define a bounded linear functional on the dense span, hence on the whole space, and [F3] represents its extension by $\xi\in L^2(0,T;H)$. Thus $\xi_\tau\rightharpoonup\xi$. Since $x_\tau(t)-x_0=-\int_0^t\xi_\tau(r)dr$ and the Bochner integral on $(0,t)$ is a bounded linear map, weak convergence and uniform convergence imply $\dot x=-\xi$. Also $\bar x_\tau\to x$ uniformly.

For each fixed $y$ with $E(y)<\infty$, integrate the discrete inequality from step 1.1 over any measurable $A\subset(0,T)$. Weak convergence of $\xi_\tau$ and uniform convergence of $\bar x_\tau$ pass the linear term to its limit; lower semicontinuity of $E$ and Fatou's lemma [F6], applied to $E(\bar x_\tau)-m\ge0$, pass the energy term. Thus the subgradient inequality holds for almost every $t$, first for a countable dense subset of the graph (choose one graph point from each nonempty member of a countable base of $H\times\mathbb R$, using [F4]) $\{(y,E(y)):E(y)<\infty\}$ and then for every such $y$ by continuity in the graph variables. Hence $\xi(t)\in\partial_\lambda E(x(t))$ almost everywhere.

Work on $[0,T]$, choosing the construction on $[0,T+1]$ to allow small time translations. Put $u=\dot x=-\xi$ and $e(t)=E(x(t))$. The discrete bound $E(\bar x_\tau(t))\le E(x_0)$, uniform convergence and lower semicontinuity give $m\le e(t)\le E(x_0)$ for every $t$, where $m=\inf_HE$. As a lower-semicontinuous function of time, $e$ is measurable and bounded. Extend $u$ and $\xi$ by zero outside $(0,T+1)$. Time translations are continuous in $L^2(\mathbb R;H)$: this is immediate for interval step functions because the measure of the symmetric difference of an interval with its translate tends to zero, and holds for every $L^2$ function by the density in [F1] and the isometry of translations. For $0<a<b<T$ and sufficiently small $h>0$, put $q_h(r)=(x(r+h)-x(r-h))/(2h)=(2h)^{-1}\int_{-h}^h u(r+s)ds$ for $a<r<b$. Cauchy–Schwarz in the averaging variable and translation continuity give $q_h\to u$ in $L^2(a,b;H)$ and $\sup_h\|q_h\|_{L^2(a,b;H)}<\infty$. Indeed, $\int_a^b\|q_h-u\|_H^2dr\le(2h)^{-1}\int_{-h}^h\int_a^b\|u(r+s)-u(r)\|_H^2drds\to0$.

For each sufficiently small fixed $h$, the subgradient inequalities at $x(r-h)$ and $x(r+h)$ hold for almost every $r\in(a,b)$ and imply $\langle\xi(r-h),q_h(r)\rangle_H+\lambda h\|q_h(r)\|_H^2\le(e(r+h)-e(r-h))/(2h)\le\langle\xi(r+h),q_h(r)\rangle_H-\lambda h\|q_h(r)\|_H^2$. Both pairings converge in $L^1(a,b)$ to $g(r)=\langle\xi(r),u(r)\rangle_H$, since translations of $\xi$ and $q_h$ converge in $L^2$ and Cauchy–Schwarz bounds their products. The quadratic remainder has $L^1$ norm at most $|\lambda|h\|q_h\|_{L^2(a,b;H)}^2\to0$. The sandwich therefore implies convergence of the entire centered energy quotient to $g$ in $L^1(a,b)$: if $L_h\le d_h\le U_h$, then $|d_h-g|\le|L_h-g|+|U_h-g|$ almost everywhere.

For every $0<a<b<T$ the exact integral identity is $\int_a^b(e(r+h)-e(r-h))/(2h)dr=(2h)^{-1}(\int_{b-h}^{b+h}e(r)dr-\int_{a-h}^{a+h}e(r)dr)$. By [F8] there is a full-measure set $B\subset(0,T)$ on which centered averages recover $e$. For any $a,b\in B$ with $a<b$, Step 6.1 and this exact identity give $e(b)-e(a)=\int_a^b g(r)dr$. Fix $a_*\in B$ and define $\widetilde e(t)=e(a_*)+\int_{a_*}^t g(r)dr$ on $[0,T]$. Here $g\in L^1(0,T)$ by Cauchy–Schwarz. Thus [F9] makes $\widetilde e$ absolutely continuous and [F10] gives $\widetilde e'=g$ almost everywhere, while the preceding equality implies $e=\widetilde e$ on $B$. This proves an absolutely continuous representative by an integral identity, without inferring it from an almost-everywhere derivative.

Lower semicontinuity of $e$ and continuity of $\widetilde e$ give $e(t)\le\widetilde e(t)$ for every $t\in[0,T]$ by approaching $t$ through $B$. Fix $t\in(0,T]$. For sufficiently large $n$, put $I_n=(t-2^{-n},t-2^{-n-1})\subset(0,T)$ and choose $s_n\in I_n\cap B$ where the subgradient inclusion holds and $\|\xi(s_n)\|_H^2\le2|I_n|^{-1}\int_{I_n}\|\xi(r)\|_H^2dr$. Such points exist since the excluded set is null and the upper threshold exceeds the mean, with the zero-integral case treated by choosing a point where $\xi=0$. Since $(t-s_n)/|I_n|\le2$, one has $(t-s_n)\|\xi(s_n)\|_H^2\le4\int_{I_n}\|\xi\|_H^2\to0$. Consequently $|\langle\xi(s_n),x(t)-x(s_n)\rangle_H|\le((t-s_n)\|\xi(s_n)\|_H^2)^{1/2}(\int_{s_n}^t\|u\|_H^2)^{1/2}\to0$. The subgradient inequality at $s_n$ gives $e(t)\ge e(s_n)+\langle\xi(s_n),x(t)-x(s_n)\rangle_H+(\lambda/2)\|x(t)-x(s_n)\|_H^2$; using $e(s_n)=\widetilde e(s_n)$ and continuity of $x,\widetilde e$ yields $e(t)\ge\widetilde e(t)$. At $t=0$, the bound $e(r)\le E(x_0)$ for all $r$ and equality on $B$ give $\widetilde e(0)\le E(x_0)=e(0)$, proving equality there too. Thus $e=\widetilde e$ on $[0,T]$ and, for every $0\le s\le t\le T$, $E(x(t))-E(x(s))=\int_s^t\langle\xi(r),u(r)\rangle_Hdr=-\int_s^t\|\dot x(r)\|_H^2dr$. Since $T$ is arbitrary this holds for all finite endpoints.

At almost every $t$, let $\zeta\in\partial_\lambda E(x(t))$. Applying its defining inequality to $x(t+h)$ for positive and negative $h$, then using differentiability of $x$ and $e$, gives $\langle\zeta,\dot x(t)\rangle_H=-\|\dot x(t)\|_H^2$. Since $\xi=-\dot x\in\partial_\lambda E(x(t))$, this says $\langle\zeta-\xi,\xi\rangle_H=0$ and hence $\|\zeta\|_H^2=\|\xi\|_H^2+\|\zeta-\xi\|_H^2$. Thus $\xi$ is the unique minimum-norm subgradient almost everywhere.

For two solutions, $\lambda$-semiconvexity implies $\langle\xi-\tilde\xi,x-\tilde x\rangle_H\ge\lambda\|x-\tilde x\|_H^2$. Therefore $\frac12\frac d{dt}\|x-\tilde x\|_H^2=-\langle\xi-\tilde\xi,x-\tilde x\rangle_H\le-\lambda\|x-\tilde x\|_H^2$ almost everywhere. Grönwall proves the stated estimate and uniqueness.

Let $X,Y$ be Banach spaces, let $T:X\to Y$ be bounded and linear, and let $f$
be Bochner integrable. Then $T\circ f$ is Bochner integrable and, for every
measurable $E$,

$$T\left(\int_Ef\,d\mu\right)=\int_E Tf\,d\mu.$$

Let $f:\Omega\to X$ be strongly measurable. Then $f$ is Bochner integrable if
and only if

$$\int_\Omega\|f\|\,d\mu<\infty.$$

Here an a.e.-defined scalar function is integrated through any measurable
representative supplied by the strong simple approximation. Moreover the
Bochner integral is independent of the approximating sequence in its
definition.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and $X$ a real or complex
Banach space. A strongly measurable function $f:\Omega\to X$ is
**Bochner integrable** if there is a sequence of integrable $X$-valued simple
functions $(s_n)$ such that

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_\Omega\|f-s_n\|\,d\mu=0.$$

For such a sequence define

$$\int_\Omega f\,d\mu:=\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_\Omega s_n\,d\mu.$$

The displayed norm limit exists: the simple integral inequality gives

$$\left\|\int s_n-\int s_m\right\|\leq\int\|s_n-s_m\|\leq\int\|s_n-f\|+\int\|f-s_m\|,$$

so the simple integrals form a Cauchy sequence, and $X$ is complete. The next
theorem proves that the value is independent of the approximating sequence and
characterizes existence by integrability of $\|f\|$.

For $E\in\mathcal A$, write
$\int_Ef\,d\mu:=\int_\Omega\mathbf1_Ef\,d\mu$ whenever this function is
Bochner integrable.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and let $f$ be a bounded linear functional on $H$ (The dual space X^* of a normed space and its dual norm). Then there is a unique $y\in H$ with

$$f(x)=\langle x,y\rangle\qquad\text{for every }x\in H,$$

and $\|f\|=\|y\|$, where $\|f\|$ is the dual norm (The operator norm as the least bound and as the unit-sphere or unit-ball supremum). Under the first-variable-linear convention the representing vector depends conjugate-linearly and isometrically on $f$: if $f_i$ is represented by $y_i$ and $a,b$ are scalars, then $af_1+bf_2$ is represented by $\overline a\,y_1+\overline b\,y_2$.

Let $d\ge1$, let $\mathcal H$ be a separable real Hilbert space, and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be the closure of a nonempty convex open set. Let $R:\mathcal H\to[0,\infty)$ be differentiable, with differential Lipschitz on bounded sets in the uniform sense that for every bounded $B\subseteq\mathcal H$ there is a finite $L_B$ such that
$$\|dR_z-dR_{z'}\|_{\mathcal H^*}\le L_B\|z-z'\|_{\mathcal H}\qquad(z,z'\in B),$$
and with differential bounded on every sublevel set of $R$: for each $c\ge0$,
$$\sup\{\|dR_z\|_{\mathcal H^*}:z\in\mathcal H,\ R(z)\le c\}<\infty.$$ In particular, on each closed convex hull of a bounded feature image $\Phi(Q_r)$, both a finite Lipschitz constant $L_r$ and a finite norm bound $N_r$ for $dR$ are available. Let $\Phi:\Omega\to\mathcal H$ be Fréchet differentiable and let $V:\Omega\to[0,\infty)$ be $\lambda_V$-semiconvex, with the convention that $V(u)-\frac{\lambda_V}{2}|u|^2$ is convex on $\Omega$. For a semiconvex function $f$ on a convex domain $D$ with coefficient $\lambda$, define
$$\partial_\lambda f(u)=\{\xi\in\mathbb R^d:f(v)\ge f(u)+\xi\cdot(v-u)+\tfrac{\lambda}{2}|v-u|^2\text{ for every }v\in D\}.$$
For a locally semiconvex function $g$ on $D$, define its local Fréchet subdifferential by
$$\partial g(u)=\left\{\xi\in\mathbb R^d:\liminf_{\substack{v\to u,\ v\in D\\v\ne u}}\frac{g(v)-g(u)-\xi\cdot(v-u)}{|v-u|}\ge0\right\}.$$
When $g$ is globally $\lambda$-semiconvex, this local subdifferential agrees with the convexified supporting set $\partial_\lambda g(u)$.
For every $r>0$, require a nonempty closed convex set $Q_r\subseteq\Omega$, nested increasingly in $r$, such that
$$\{u\in\Omega:\operatorname{dist}(u,Q_r)\le r'\}\subseteq Q_{r+r'}\qquad(r,r'>0),$$
such that $\Phi$ and $V$ are bounded on $Q_r$, $d\Phi$ is Lipschitz on $Q_r$, and there are fixed constants $C_1,C_2>0$ with
$$\sup_{u\in Q_r}\bigl(\|d\Phi_u\|+\|\partial V(u)\|\bigr)\le C_1+C_2r.$$
Here $\partial V(u)=\partial_{\lambda_V}V(u)$ is the supporting set on $\Omega$, and in the growth bound $\|\partial V(u)\|$ means its minimum element norm, equivalently the bound requires a supporting vector of norm at most $C_1+C_2r$ at every $u\in Q_r$. No bound is imposed on the domain normal cone. This is a bounded-selection variant of the source assumptions: Assumption 2.1(iii)(c) in Chizat and Bach explicitly uses the maximal element norm, which implies the minimum-norm bound wherever the supporting set is nonempty. The source does not specify that its maximal bound excludes domain normals. The bounded-selection convention here allows relative-domain supporting sets with unbounded normal vectors; results using this variant require their own proofs. For a Borel set $A\subseteq\Omega$, write $\mathcal P_2(A)$ for the Borel probability measures on $\mathbb R^d$ concentrated on $A$ and having finite second moment.
For a finite nonnegative Borel measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb R^d$, set
$$F(\mu)=R\!\left(\int_\Omega\Phi(u)\,d\mu(u)\right)+\int_\Omega V(u)\,d\mu(u)$$
when $\mu$ is concentrated on $\Omega$, the Bochner integral exists, and the scalar integral is finite; set $F(\mu)=+\infty$ otherwise. For $\mu\in\mathcal P_2(\Omega)$ with finite $F(\mu)$, write $m_\mu=\int_\Omega\Phi\,d\mu$ and define its first-variation potential on $\Omega$ by
$$F'(\mu)(u)=dR_{m_\mu}[\Phi(u)]+V(u).$$
No convexity of $R$ is required by this definition.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

citations.quote: Assume AC and the hypotheses of the feature-measure energy definition. Fix an arbitrary probability label space $(S,\Sigma,\sigma)$, let $K=L^2(\sigma;\mathbb R^d)$, and let $C_r=\{X:X(s)\in Q_r\text{ for }\sigma\text{-almost every }s\}$. Write $A_r=\sup_{Q_r}\|d\Phi\|$, $B_r=\operatorname{Lip}_{Q_r}(d\Phi)$, $M_r=\sup_{Q_r}\|\partial V\|$, and let $L_r$ and $N_r$ be, respectively, a Lipschitz constant and a norm bound for $dR$ on the closed convex hull of $\Phi(Q_r)$. For all $X,Y\in C_r$, the smooth part $G_r(X)=R(\int\Phi(X)d\sigma)$ has the first-order expansion on $C_r$ with gradient $\nabla G_r(X)(s)=d\Phi_{X(s)}^*\nabla R(\int\Phi(X)d\sigma)$, and this gradient is Lipschitz with constant $L_rA_r^2+N_rB_r$. No separability of the label space is required for these estimates. Consequently $E_r(X)=G_r(X)+\int V(X)d\sigma+\iota_{C_r}(X)$ is $(\lambda_V-L_rA_r^2-N_rB_r)$-semiconvex on $K$.

Let $d\ge1$, let $\mathcal H$ be a separable real Hilbert space, and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be the closure of a nonempty convex open set. Let $R:\mathcal H\to[0,\infty)$ be differentiable, with differential Lipschitz on bounded sets in the uniform sense that for every bounded $B\subseteq\mathcal H$ there is a finite $L_B$ such that
$$\|dR_z-dR_{z'}\|_{\mathcal H^*}\le L_B\|z-z'\|_{\mathcal H}\qquad(z,z'\in B),$$
and with differential bounded on every sublevel set of $R$: for each $c\ge0$,
$$\sup\{\|dR_z\|_{\mathcal H^*}:z\in\mathcal H,\ R(z)\le c\}<\infty.$$ In particular, on each closed convex hull of a bounded feature image $\Phi(Q_r)$, both a finite Lipschitz constant $L_r$ and a finite norm bound $N_r$ for $dR$ are available. Let $\Phi:\Omega\to\mathcal H$ be Fréchet differentiable and let $V:\Omega\to[0,\infty)$ be $\lambda_V$-semiconvex, with the convention that $V(u)-\frac{\lambda_V}{2}|u|^2$ is convex on $\Omega$. For a semiconvex function $f$ on a convex domain $D$ with coefficient $\lambda$, define
$$\partial_\lambda f(u)=\{\xi\in\mathbb R^d:f(v)\ge f(u)+\xi\cdot(v-u)+\tfrac{\lambda}{2}|v-u|^2\text{ for every }v\in D\}.$$
For a locally semiconvex function $g$ on $D$, define its local Fréchet subdifferential by
$$\partial g(u)=\left\{\xi\in\mathbb R^d:\liminf_{\substack{v\to u,\ v\in D\\v\ne u}}\frac{g(v)-g(u)-\xi\cdot(v-u)}{|v-u|}\ge0\right\}.$$
When $g$ is globally $\lambda$-semiconvex, this local subdifferential agrees with the convexified supporting set $\partial_\lambda g(u)$.
For every $r>0$, require a nonempty closed convex set $Q_r\subseteq\Omega$, nested increasingly in $r$, such that
$$\{u\in\Omega:\operatorname{dist}(u,Q_r)\le r'\}\subseteq Q_{r+r'}\qquad(r,r'>0),$$
such that $\Phi$ and $V$ are bounded on $Q_r$, $d\Phi$ is Lipschitz on $Q_r$, and there are fixed constants $C_1,C_2>0$ with
$$\sup_{u\in Q_r}\bigl(\|d\Phi_u\|+\|\partial V(u)\|\bigr)\le C_1+C_2r.$$
Here $\partial V(u)=\partial_{\lambda_V}V(u)$ is the supporting set on $\Omega$, and in the growth bound $\|\partial V(u)\|$ means its minimum element norm, equivalently the bound requires a supporting vector of norm at most $C_1+C_2r$ at every $u\in Q_r$. No bound is imposed on the domain normal cone. This is a bounded-selection variant of the source assumptions: Assumption 2.1(iii)(c) in Chizat and Bach explicitly uses the maximal element norm, which implies the minimum-norm bound wherever the supporting set is nonempty. The source does not specify that its maximal bound excludes domain normals. The bounded-selection convention here allows relative-domain supporting sets with unbounded normal vectors; results using this variant require their own proofs. For a Borel set $A\subseteq\Omega$, write $\mathcal P_2(A)$ for the Borel probability measures on $\mathbb R^d$ concentrated on $A$ and having finite second moment.
For a finite nonnegative Borel measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb R^d$, set
$$F(\mu)=R\!\left(\int_\Omega\Phi(u)\,d\mu(u)\right)+\int_\Omega V(u)\,d\mu(u)$$
when $\mu$ is concentrated on $\Omega$, the Bochner integral exists, and the scalar integral is finite; set $F(\mu)=+\infty$ otherwise. For $\mu\in\mathcal P_2(\Omega)$ with finite $F(\mu)$, write $m_\mu=\int_\Omega\Phi\,d\mu$ and define its first-variation potential on $\Omega$ by
$$F'(\mu)(u)=dR_{m_\mu}[\Phi(u)]+V(u).$$
No convexity of $R$ is required by this definition.

Let $(f_n)$ be nonnegative measurable functions. Then
$$\int \liminf_{n\to\infty}f_n\,d\mu\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}\int f_n\,d\mu.$$
Every convex function $f:U\to\mathbb R$ on an open convex set is continuous on $U$. The assertion is vacuous when $U$ is empty.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim: The set $C_r$ is convex because $Q_r$ is convex. To show it is closed, take $X_n\in C_r$ with $X_n\to X$ in $K$. Countable Choice [F3] gives a subsequence with $\|X_{n_k}-X\|_K^2\le2^{-k}$ and strongly measurable representatives; discard their countably many exceptional null sets. Tonelli [F6] implies $\sum_k|X_{n_k}(s)-X(s)|^2<\infty$ for almost every $s$, so $X_{n_k}(s)\to X(s)$ there; closedness of $Q_r$ gives $X\in C_r$. For lower semicontinuity of $E_r$, consider a sequence with finite energy liminf and pass to a subsequence of finite energies, so every term lies in $C_r$ and its limit lies there by the closure just proved. For any $u\in Q_r$, a vector $\zeta\in\partial_{\lambda_V}V(u)$ supplied by [F2] gives $V(y)\ge V(u)+\zeta\cdot(y-u)+\frac{\lambda_V}{2}|y-u|^2$ for $y\in\Omega$, proving lower semicontinuity of $V$ at $u$. Fatou [F4] makes the potential integral lower semicontinuous along this sequence, and the smooth term is continuous by [F1]. A constant $Q_r$-valued function has finite energy because $Q_r$ is nonempty and $\Phi,V$ are bounded on it, while $R,V\ge0$ make $E_r$ bounded below. Thus $E_r$ is proper, lower semicontinuous, and lower bounded.

Let $f=V+\iota_{Q_r}$. Since every point of $Q_r$ has a subgradient by [F2], the supporting inequality implies that $f$ is lower semicontinuous at every point of $Q_r$. The function $g(u)=f(u)-\frac{\lambda_V}{2}|u|^2$ is proper, lower semicontinuous and convex, with $\partial g(u)=\partial_{\lambda_V}f(u)-\lambda_Vu$. For $\varepsilon>0$ small enough that $1+\varepsilon\lambda_V>0$, minimize $f(y)+|x-y|^2/(2\varepsilon)$. This is strongly convex and coercive, so it has a unique minimizer $J_\varepsilon x$. Its optimality inequality says $z_\varepsilon(x)=(x-J_\varepsilon x)/\varepsilon\in\partial_{\lambda_V}f(J_\varepsilon x)$; this follows by testing minimality at $(1-h)J_\varepsilon x+hy$, using semiconvexity of $f$, dividing by $h$, and letting $h\downarrow0$. Comparing the two optimality inequalities at $x$ and $x'$ and adding gives $\|J_\varepsilon x-J_\varepsilon x'\|\le(1+\varepsilon\lambda_V)^{-1}\|x-x'\|$, so $z_\varepsilon$ is continuous. For fixed $x\in Q_r$, comparison with $y=x$ shows $J_\varepsilon x\to x$. Monotonicity of $\partial g$ between $z_\varepsilon(x)-\lambda_VJ_\varepsilon x\in\partial g(J_\varepsilon x)$ and any $z-\lambda_Vx\in\partial g(x)$ gives $(1+\varepsilon\lambda_V)\|z_\varepsilon(x)\|^2\le\langle z,z_\varepsilon(x)\rangle$. Thus $z_\varepsilon(x)$ is bounded by every candidate norm in the limit. Passing to a limit in the defining subgradient inequalities shows the graph of $\partial g$ is closed; every convergent subsequence therefore limits to an element of $\partial_{\lambda_V}f(x)$. The norm inequality makes that limit the unique minimum-norm element. Finite-dimensional compactness gives convergence of the full sequence $\varepsilon_n\downarrow0$, so the minimum section is a pointwise limit of continuous maps and hence Borel.

The selected section has norm at most $M_r$ by [F2], so composition with a strongly measurable $X$ is measurable and square integrable; call it $\zeta_X\in K$. For any $Y\in C_r$, its pointwise supporting inequality integrates to $\displaystyle \int f(Y)d\sigma\ge\int f(X)d\sigma+\langle\zeta_X,Y-X\rangle_K+\frac{\lambda_V}{2}\|Y-X\|_K^2.$ Together with [F1], this proves that $\nabla G_r(X)+\zeta_X\in\partial_{\lambda_E}E_r(X)$ and establishes nonemptiness.

Conversely, let $\eta\in\partial_{\lambda_E}E_r(X)$. Put $C=L_rA_r^2+N_rB_r$ and $\lambda_E=\lambda_V-C$. Then $E_r- rac{\lambda_E}{2}\|\cdot\|_K^2$ is the sum of the convex integral $X\mapsto\int g(X)d\sigma$ and the differentiable convex function $G_r(X)+ rac C2\|X\|_K^2$. The latter has gradient $
abla G_r(X)+CX$. The convex sum rule here follows directly from one-sided directional derivatives: if $q$ is convex and $h$ is differentiable convex, a supporting vector $w$ of $q+h$ satisfies $q'(X;H)\ge\langle w-
abla h(X),Hangle$ for every feasible direction $H$; convex secant slopes dominate $q'(X;H)$, so $w-
abla h(X)$ supports $q$. Apply this with $w=\eta-\lambda_EX$ to conclude that $\eta-
abla G_r(X)-\lambda_VX$ supports the convex integral. Testing with $Y=X$ off a measurable set $A$ and $Y=y$ on $A$ gives a pointwise supporting inequality for every $y$ in a countable dense subset of $Q_r$, outside a common null set by [F3]. The relative interior is nonempty by [F5]; on it, continuity [F5] extends the inequality from the dense subset. For a boundary point $y$, choose $y_0$ in the relative interior and let $B(y_0,ho)$ be a relative ball contained in $Q_r$. For $y_n=(1-1/n)y+(1/n)y_0$, convexity gives a relative ball of radius $ho/n$ around $y_n$ contained in $Q_r$, so $y_n$ is in the relative interior. Convexity gives $g(y_n)\le(1-1/n)g(y)+(1/n)g(y_0)$, and lower semicontinuity gives $g(y)\le\liminf_n g(y_n)$; hence $g(y_n)	o g(y)$ and the supporting inequality passes to $y$. Undoing the quadratic shift proves $\eta-
abla G_r(X)$ is a $K$-section of $\partial_{\lambda_V}f(X(s))$, proving the reverse inclusion.

For the shifted selection, apply step 1.2 to $f_a(u)=\langle a,\Phi(u)\rangle+V(u)+\iota_{Q_r}(u)$, whose semiconvexity coefficient is $\alpha_a=\lambda_V-B_r\|a\|$. Its resolvent $J_\varepsilon^a x$ is jointly continuous in $(a,x)$ where $1+\varepsilon\alpha_a>0$: comparison of the two optimality inequalities gives $(1+\varepsilon\alpha_a)|J_\varepsilon^a x-J_\varepsilon^{a\prime}x\prime|\le |x-x\prime|+\varepsilon A_r\|a-a\prime\|$ when the coefficient is taken as a common lower bound for the two parameters. Hence $(x-J_\varepsilon^a x)/\varepsilon$ is jointly continuous there. On each bounded parameter ball, step 1.2 proves its pointwise limit at $u\in Q_r$ is the minimum of $\partial f_a(u)=b_a(u)+\partial_{\lambda_V}f(u)$; the sum formula follows by subtracting the smooth Taylor remainder in the local supporting inequality. The parameter balls exhaust $\mathcal H$, so the limit is jointly Borel. A bounded potential subgradient gives an admissible shifted vector of norm $A_r\|a\|+M_r$, proving the bound. The pointwise projection inequality $|S(a,u)|\le|z|$ for every $z$ in the shifted set integrates over labels. The exact subdifferential formula from step 3.1 therefore proves that this measurable section is the unique minimum-norm Hilbert subgradient.

Assume AC. Let $T>0$ and let $(\mu_t,v_t)$ be a narrowly continuous finite-action solution of the continuity equation on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d$. There is a Borel probability law $\eta$ on $C([0,T];\mathbb R^d)$ such that $(e_t)_\#\eta=\mu_t$ for every $t$, and for $\eta$-almost every path $\gamma$, $\gamma$ is absolutely continuous and $\dot\gamma(t)=v_t(\gamma(t))$ for almost every $t$. Its expected path action equals the Eulerian action:
$$\int\!\int_0^T|\dot\gamma(t)|^2dt\,d\eta(\gamma)=\int_0^T\!\int|v_t(x)|^2d\mu_t(x)dt.$$

Assume AC. Let $\lambda$ be a probability on $(E\times T,\mathcal S\otimes\mathcal T)$, where E and T are standard-Borel spaces, and let $\beta(B)=\lambda(E\times B)$ be its second marginal. There is a probability kernel $K:(T,\mathcal T)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ such that

$$\lambda(A\times B)=\int_B K(y,A)\,\beta(dy)\quad(A\in\mathcal S,\ B\in\mathcal T).$$

It is unique as a kernel outside a single measurable $\beta$-null set. For every nonnegative product-measurable $f:E\times T\to[0,\infty]$,

$$\int f(x,y)\,\lambda(d(x,y))=\int_T\left(\int_E f(x,y)K(y,dx)\right)\beta(dy).$$

In particular this applies to the joint law of random elements $(X,Y)$, with $\beta=P_Y$; the direction is the law of X given Y.

A measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$ is **standard Borel** if there are a Polish space $P$ and a bijection $h:E\to P$ such that $A\in\mathcal E$ exactly when $h[A]$ is Borel in $P$. Thus the measurable structure is part of the datum; no particular compatible Polish topology on $E$ is selected.
Every finite product of standard Borel spaces, with its finite product sigma-algebra, is standard Borel.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in Measures on sigma-algebras and A measurable function between measurable spaces; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

**Assume the Axiom of Choice.** Let $X$ be a nonempty compact metric space, let $Y$ be a proper metric space, and let $(f_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be an equicontinuous sequence in $C(X,Y)$. If $\{f_k(x):k\in\mathbb N\}$ is bounded for every $x\in X$, then some subsequence converges uniformly to a member of $C(X,Y)$.

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. For $F\in AC[a,b]$ and $L\ge0$, $F$ is $L$-Lipschitz if and only if
$|F'|\le L$ almost everywhere.

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. For $F:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$, the following are equivalent:

1. $F$ is absolutely continuous.
2. $F'$ exists almost everywhere, $F'\in L^1[a,b]$, and
$$F(x)-F(a)=\int_a^xF'(t)\,dt\quad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$
