All other terms converge uniformly by step 2.2, yielding $(|X(c)-z|^2-|X(b)-z|^2)/2+\int_b^c[V(X)+\langle g(t,X),X-z\rangle+(\lambda/2)|X-z|^2]dt\le(c-b)V(z)$. Choose countably many dense $z\in D$ and differentiate this interval inequality where the scalar absolutely continuous functions and coordinates of $X$ are differentiable. Outside their common null set the inequality says $-X'-g(t,X)\in\partial_\lambda f(X)$, first for these tests and then for every $z\in D$ by continuity of $V$ on bounded sets. This proves the inclusion without any continuity or convergence assertion for the nonsmooth minimum field.

Two solutions $X,Y$ to the same forcing have bounded images in a common $Q_s$. Monotonicity gives $(|X-Y|^2/2)'\le(MB_s-\lambda)|X-Y|^2$, so multiplication by the scalar integrating factor proves uniqueness. Therefore all converging Euler subsequences have the same limit and compactness gives uniform convergence of the entire family. For all starts in $D\cap Q_r$, step 2.2 gives the same radius $R$ and time-Lipschitz constant $K$; the same distance estimate gives $|X(t,u)-X(t,w)|\le e^{(MB_R-\lambda)t}|u-w|$. Together these prove joint continuity in $(t,u)$ and uniform Lipschitz dependence on the initial point. Nearby starts lie in a common $Q_s$ by the neighborhood property. For different forcings $a,b$ and paths in $Q_s$, monotonicity gives $(|X-Y|^2/2)'\le c|X-Y|^2+A_s\|a-b\||X-Y|$, $c=(\max\|a\|)B_s-\lambda$. Apply this to $\sqrt{|X-Y|^2+\varepsilon^2}$ and let $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ to obtain $|X(t)-Y(t)|\le e^{ct}|X(0)-Y(0)|+A_s\int_0^t e^{c(t-q)}\|a(q)-b(q)\|dq$. This is forcing stability. All finite horizons patch uniquely.

Since $V\circ X$ is Lipschitz, at a time where it and $X$ are differentiable and the inclusion holds, test any $\eta\in\partial_\lambda f(X(t))$ against $X(t+h)$ for both signs of $h$. Division by $h$ and passage to zero give $(V\circ X)'=\langle\eta,X'\rangle$ for every such $\eta$ simultaneously. For $\xi=-X'-g(t,X)$ this gives $\langle\eta-\xi,X'\rangle=0$, so $|g+\eta|^2=|-X'|^2+|\eta-\xi|^2$. Thus $-X'$ is the full shifted minimum. Its Borel measurability for fixed forcing follows directly from $q_\varepsilon(t,x)=(x-J_\varepsilon(x-\varepsilon g(t,x)))/\varepsilon$: these are continuous, and monotonicity gives $(1+\varepsilon\lambda)|q_\varepsilon|^2\le\langle g(t,x)+\eta,q_\varepsilon\rangle$ for every $\eta\in\partial_\lambda f(x)$. Therefore $q_\varepsilon$ is bounded and its prox point tends to $x$. Continuity of $V$ passes the supporting inequalities to every cluster point $q$, placing it in the shifted subdifferential; the displayed inequality becomes its minimum-norm projection inequality. All cluster points equal the unique minimum, so the entire sequence converges. The pointwise limit of the continuous $q_\varepsilon$ is Borel.

For any finite-action PDE solution with this velocity and fixed continuous forcing, [F1] represents it by absolutely continuous paths. Their positions lie in closed $D$ at every rational time and hence every time. Each path solves the inclusion, so uniqueness from step 4.1 identifies it with $X(\cdot,u)$, where $u$ is its initial point. Thus $\mu_t=X(t,\cdot)_\#\mu_0$, with the same radius bound from step 2.2 whenever $\mu_0$ is concentrated on $Q_r$. This argument uses neither a backward inverse nor continuity of the minimum field. With $a(t)=\nabla R(m(t))$ it proves the characteristic assertion in the Statement; steps 1.1–2.1 prove the self-consistent law stability assertion.

Assume AC. Let $\lambda$ be a probability on $(E\times T,\mathcal S\otimes\mathcal T)$, where E and T are standard-Borel spaces, and let $\beta(B)=\lambda(E\times B)$ be its second marginal. There is a probability kernel $K:(T,\mathcal T)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ such that

$$\lambda(A\times B)=\int_B K(y,A)\,\beta(dy)\quad(A\in\mathcal S,\ B\in\mathcal T).$$

It is unique as a kernel outside a single measurable $\beta$-null set. For every nonnegative product-measurable $f:E\times T\to[0,\infty]$,

$$\int f(x,y)\,\lambda(d(x,y))=\int_T\left(\int_E f(x,y)K(y,dx)\right)\beta(dy).$$

In particular this applies to the joint law of random elements $(X,Y)$, with $\beta=P_Y$; the direction is the law of X given Y.

A measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$ is **standard Borel** if there are a Polish space $P$ and a bijection $h:E\to P$ such that $A\in\mathcal E$ exactly when $h[A]$ is Borel in $P$. Thus the measurable structure is part of the datum; no particular compatible Polish topology on $E$ is selected.
Every finite product of standard Borel spaces, with its finite product sigma-algebra, is standard Borel.

Assume AC. Let $H$ be a separable real Hilbert space, $T>0$, and $x:[0,T]\to H$ be continuous. For a finite partition $P=(t_i)_{i=0}^N$ with $0=t_0<\cdots<t_N=T$, set
$$Q_P(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}\frac{\|x(t_{i+1})-x(t_i)\|_H^2}{t_{i+1}-t_i},\qquad C(x)=\sup_P Q_P(x).$$
If $C(x)<\infty$, then there is a strongly measurable $u\in L^2((0,T);H)$ such that $x(t)=x(0)+\int_0^t u(s)\,ds$ for every $t$, $x$ is norm-differentiable almost everywhere with derivative $u$, and
$$\int_0^T\|u(t)\|_H^2\,dt=C(x).$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

citations.quote: Assume AC and the hypotheses of the feature-measure energy definition. Fix an arbitrary probability label space $(S,\Sigma,\sigma)$, let $K=L^2(\sigma;\mathbb R^d)$, and let $C_r=\{X:X(s)\in Q_r\text{ for }\sigma\text{-almost every }s\}$. Write $A_r=\sup_{Q_r}\|d\Phi\|$, $B_r=\operatorname{Lip}_{Q_r}(d\Phi)$, $M_r=\sup_{Q_r}\|\partial V\|$, and let $L_r$ and $N_r$ be, respectively, a Lipschitz constant and a norm bound for $dR$ on the closed convex hull of $\Phi(Q_r)$. For all $X,Y\in C_r$, the smooth part $G_r(X)=R(\int\Phi(X)d\sigma)$ has the first-order expansion on $C_r$ with gradient $\nabla G_r(X)(s)=d\Phi_{X(s)}^*\nabla R(\int\Phi(X)d\sigma)$, and this gradient is Lipschitz with constant $L_rA_r^2+N_rB_r$. No separability of the label space is required for these estimates. Consequently $E_r(X)=G_r(X)+\int V(X)d\sigma+\iota_{C_r}(X)$ is $(\lambda_V-L_rA_r^2-N_rB_r)$-semiconvex on $K$.

Assume AC and the hypotheses of the feature-measure energy definition. Fix any probability label space $(S,\Sigma,\sigma)$ and use the localized lift $E_r$ on $K=L^2(\sigma;\mathbb R^d)$. Separability of $K$ is not assumed or needed for the subdifferential formula and minimum-section conclusion. For a semiconvex functional $J:K\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ with coefficient $\alpha$, define
$$\partial_\alpha J(X)=\{\eta\in K:J(Y)\ge J(X)+\langle\eta,Y-X\rangle_K+\tfrac{\alpha}{2}\|Y-X\|_K^2\text{ for all }Y\in K\}.$$
The set $C_r$ is closed and convex, and $E_r$ is proper, lower semicontinuous, and lower bounded. Write $A_r=\sup_{Q_r}\|d\Phi\|$, $B_r=\operatorname{Lip}_{Q_r}(d\Phi)$, $M_r=\sup_{Q_r}\|\partial V\|$ in the bounded-selection convention, and let $L_r,N_r$ bound the Lipschitz constant and norm of $dR$ on the closed convex hull of $\Phi(Q_r)$. Let $C_r^{\rm sm}=L_rA_r^2+N_rB_r$ and $\lambda_E=\lambda_V-C_r^{\rm sm}$. For $X\in C_r$, its Hilbert subdifferential with coefficient $\lambda_E$ is exactly
$$\partial_{\lambda_E} E_r(X)=\left\{s\mapsto d\Phi_{X(s)}^*\nabla R\!\left(\int\Phi(X)d\sigma\right)+\zeta(s):\ \zeta\in K,\ \zeta(s)\in\partial_{\lambda_V}(V+\iota_{Q_r})(X(s))\text{ for }\sigma\text{-almost every }s\right\}.$$
The pointwise minimum-norm selection $u\mapsto\operatorname{argmin}\{|z|:z\in\partial_{\lambda_V}(V+\iota_{Q_r})(u)\}$ is Borel on $Q_r$ and has norm at most $M_r$; hence its composition with any $X\in C_r$ is a measurable member of $K$. More generally, for $a\in\mathcal H$ put $b_a(u)=d\Phi_u^*a$ and $S(a,u)=\operatorname{argmin}\{|z|:z\in b_a(u)+\partial_{\lambda_V}(V+\iota_{Q_r})(u)\}$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $f_n:\Omega\to X$ be strongly measurable,
suppose $f_n(\omega)\to f(\omega)$ in norm for almost every $\omega$, and let
$g$ be a nonnegative integrable scalar function with
$\|f_n(\omega)\|\leq g(\omega)$ almost everywhere for every $n$. Then $f$ and
all $f_n$ are Bochner integrable,

$$\int\|f_n-f\|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$

and $\int f_n\,d\mu\to\int f\,d\mu$ in norm.

derivations.claim: On $(\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^d,\gamma)$, set $X(x,y)=x$ and $Y(x,y)=y$. This is a Euclidean Borel probability label space of dimension $2d$, with output dimension $d$; the arbitrary-label lift and subdifferential formula therefore apply. These are admissible lifts because both marginals are concentrated on $Q_r$. Their laws are $\mu$ and $\eta$ by [F3], so their lifted energies are $F(\mu)$ and $F(\eta)$. The pointwise minimum section and smooth gradient in [F2] give the lifted subgradient $s(x,y)=g_\mu(x)\in L^2(\gamma;\mathbb R^d)$.

Apply the semiconvex subgradient inequality [F1] to the two lifts. The Hilbert inner product is $\int g_\mu(x)\cdot(y-x)d\gamma$ and the squared displacement norm is $\int|y-x|^2d\gamma$. Substitution gives exactly the asserted inequality for this coupling. Since $\gamma$ was arbitrary, it holds for every coupling and proves the strong-subgradient claim.

Conversely let $h\in L^2(\mu)$ satisfy the all-coupling strong-subgradient inequality. Lift on $(\mathbb R^d,\mu)$ with $X(x)=x$, and take the coupling $(X,(1-t)X+tY)_\#\mu$ for any admissible $Y$. Its displacement norm is $t\|Y-X\|_2$. Dividing the strong inequality by $t$ gives the lower bound $\langle h,Y-X\rangle$ for the directional derivative of $E_r$ at $X$ in direction $Y-X$. Semiconvexity of $E_r$ implies its secant slope is at least that directional derivative plus $\lambda_r\|Y-X\|_2^2/2$; consequently $h\in\partial_{\lambda_r}E_r(X)$. The pointwise formula [F2] gives $h(x)\in d\Phi_x^*\nabla R(m_\mu)+\partial_{\lambda_V}(V+\iota_{Q_r})(x)$ almost everywhere. The full shifted minimum has norm no larger pointwise, so $\|g_\mu\|_2\le\|h\|_2$. Equality forces equality pointwise by strict convexity and the projection inequality. This proves the claimed minimality and uniqueness.

Assume AC. Let $H$ be a separable real Hilbert space and let $E:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper, lower semicontinuous, bounded below, and $\lambda$-convex, meaning
$$E((1-t)x+ty)\le(1-t)E(x)+tE(y)-\frac{\lambda}{2}t(1-t)\|x-y\|_H^2\quad(0\le t\le1).$$
For $x\in\operatorname{dom}E$, define
$$\partial_\lambda E(x)=\{\xi\in H:E(y)\ge E(x)+\langle\xi,y-x\rangle_H+\tfrac{\lambda}{2}\|y-x\|_H^2\text{ for every }y\in H\}.$$
For every $x_0\in\operatorname{dom}E$, there is a unique curve $x:[0,\infty)\to H$ which is absolutely continuous with square-integrable derivative on every bounded interval, satisfies $x(0)=x_0$ and $-\dot x(t)\in\partial_\lambda E(x(t))$ for almost every $t$, and obeys
$$E(x(t))-E(x(s))=-\int_s^t\|\dot x(r)\|_H^2\,dr\quad(0\le s\le t<\infty).$$
For almost every $t$, $-\dot x(t)$ is the unique minimum-norm element of $\partial_\lambda E(x(t))$. For two such curves $x,\widetilde x$ with initial values $x_0,\widetilde x_0$,
$$\|x(t)-\widetilde x(t)\|_H\le e^{-\lambda t}\|x_0-\widetilde x_0\|_H.$$

Assume AC and the hypotheses of the feature-measure energy definition. Fix any probability label space $(S,\Sigma,\sigma)$ and use the localized lift $E_r$ on $K=L^2(\sigma;\mathbb R^d)$. Separability of $K$ is not assumed or needed for the subdifferential formula and minimum-section conclusion. For a semiconvex functional $J:K\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ with coefficient $\alpha$, define
$$\partial_\alpha J(X)=\{\eta\in K:J(Y)\ge J(X)+\langle\eta,Y-X\rangle_K+\tfrac{\alpha}{2}\|Y-X\|_K^2\text{ for all }Y\in K\}.$$
The set $C_r$ is closed and convex, and $E_r$ is proper, lower semicontinuous, and lower bounded. Write $A_r=\sup_{Q_r}\|d\Phi\|$, $B_r=\operatorname{Lip}_{Q_r}(d\Phi)$, $M_r=\sup_{Q_r}\|\partial V\|$ in the bounded-selection convention, and let $L_r,N_r$ bound the Lipschitz constant and norm of $dR$ on the closed convex hull of $\Phi(Q_r)$. Let $C_r^{\rm sm}=L_rA_r^2+N_rB_r$ and $\lambda_E=\lambda_V-C_r^{\rm sm}$. For $X\in C_r$, its Hilbert subdifferential with coefficient $\lambda_E$ is exactly
$$\partial_{\lambda_E} E_r(X)=\left\{s\mapsto d\Phi_{X(s)}^*\nabla R\!\left(\int\Phi(X)d\sigma\right)+\zeta(s):\ \zeta\in K,\ \zeta(s)\in\partial_{\lambda_V}(V+\iota_{Q_r})(X(s))\text{ for }\sigma\text{-almost every }s\right\}.$$
The pointwise minimum-norm selection $u\mapsto\operatorname{argmin}\{|z|:z\in\partial_{\lambda_V}(V+\iota_{Q_r})(u)\}$ is Borel on $Q_r$ and has norm at most $M_r$; hence its composition with any $X\in C_r$ is a measurable member of $K$. More generally, for $a\in\mathcal H$ put $b_a(u)=d\Phi_u^*a$ and $S(a,u)=\operatorname{argmin}\{|z|:z\in b_a(u)+\partial_{\lambda_V}(V+\iota_{Q_r})(u)\}$. This full shifted minimum is jointly Borel in $(a,u)$, has $|S(a,u)|\le A_r\|a\|+M_r$, and the minimum-norm element of $\partial_{\lambda_E}E_r(X)$ is exactly $s\mapsto S(\nabla R(\int\Phi(X)d\sigma),X(s))$. It is generally different from the smooth gradient plus the minimum of the potential subdifferential alone.

Assume AC. Let $H$ be a separable real Hilbert space, $T>0$, and $x:[0,T]\to H$ be continuous. For a finite partition $P=(t_i)_{i=0}^N$ with $0=t_0<\cdots<t_N=T$, set
$$Q_P(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}\frac{\|x(t_{i+1})-x(t_i)\|_H^2}{t_{i+1}-t_i},\qquad C(x)=\sup_P Q_P(x).$$
If $C(x)<\infty$, then there is a strongly measurable $u\in L^2((0,T);H)$ such that $x(t)=x(0)+\int_0^t u(s)\,ds$ for every $t$, $x$ is norm-differentiable almost everywhere with derivative $u$, and
$$\int_0^T\|u(t)\|_H^2\,dt=C(x).$$

Let $X,Y$ be Banach spaces, let $T:X\to Y$ be bounded and linear, and let $f$
be Bochner integrable. Then $T\circ f$ is Bochner integrable and, for every
measurable $E$,

$$T\left(\int_Ef\,d\mu\right)=\int_E Tf\,d\mu.$$

Assume AC. Let $T>0$ and let $(\mu_t,v_t)$ be a narrowly continuous finite-action solution of the continuity equation on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d$. Then $t\mapsto\mu_t$ belongs to $AC^2([0,T];\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d))$ and, for almost every $t$,
$$|\dot\mu_t|\le\left(\int|v_t(x)|^2d\mu_t(x)\right)^{1/2}.$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $T>0$ and $\mu\in AC^2([0,T];\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d))$. There is a Borel vector field $v$ of finite action that solves the continuity equation and satisfies
$$\int|v_t(x)|^2d\mu_t(x)=|\dot\mu_t|^2$$
for almost every $t$. Every other Borel finite-action solution $w$ of the same continuity equation obeys the pointwise Pythagorean identity
$$\int|w_t(x)|^2d\mu_t(x)=|\dot\mu_t|^2+\int|w_t(x)-v_t(x)|^2d\mu_t(x)$$
for almost every $t$. Consequently $v$ is the unique minimum-action velocity up to $dt\,\mu_t(dx)$-null sets and
$$\int_0^T|\dot\mu_t|^2dt=\min_w\int_0^T\!\int|w_t(x)|^2d\mu_t(x)dt,$$
where the minimum ranges over Borel finite-action fields solving the same continuity equation.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: Since $m_t$ is the image of $X_t$ under Bochner integration, [F3] and the Lipschitz bound on $\Phi$ show $t\mapsto m_t$ is continuous. The full shifted selection $S(a,u)$ is jointly Borel on $\mathcal H\times Q_r$ by [F2]; extending $v_t=-S(a(t),u)$ by zero outside the closed set $Q_r$ gives a Borel field on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d$. Here $a(t)=\nabla R(m_t)$ is continuous. By [F1] and [F2], a representative of the Hilbert derivative satisfies $\dot X(t,s)=v_t(X(t,s))$ for almost every $(t,s)$. Its squared integral is $\int_0^T\int|v_t(u)|^2d\mu_t(u)dt=\int_0^T\|\dot X(t)\|_K^2dt<\infty$.

For $\varphi\in C_c^\infty((0,T)\times\mathbb R^d)$, the scalar chain rule along the almost-everywhere absolutely continuous label paths gives $\displaystyle \frac d{dt}\varphi(t,X(t,s))=\partial_t\varphi(t,X(t,s))+\nabla_x\varphi(t,X(t,s))\cdot v_t(X(t,s))$ for almost every $(t,s)$. The right side is integrable: the test derivatives are bounded, $\mu_t$ is a probability, and [F1] gives finite $L^1$ velocity action on $[0,T]$. Integrating in $s$ and $t$, Fubini and the vanishing of $\varphi$ near $t=0,T$ give the weak continuity-equation identity for $\mu_t$.

The coupling $(X(s),X(t))_\#\mu_0$ gives $W_2(\mu_s,\mu_t)^2\le\|X(s)-X(t)\|_K^2$. Cauchy–Schwarz in time and [F1] imply $W_2(\mu_s,\mu_t)\le\int_s^t\|\dot X(q)\|_K\,dq$ for $s<t$. Thus $\mu\in AC^2$ on $[0,T]$. Alternatively [F4] applies to the continuity equation and the action bound from step 1.1.

Fix a time $t$ and put $f_t(u)=\langle\nabla R(m_t),\Phi(u)\rangle+V(u)+\iota_{Q_r}(u)$. On $Q_r$ this function is bounded, lower semicontinuous and semiconvex, with a nonempty subdifferential and minimum section $g_t=-v_t$ bounded uniformly on compact time intervals by [F2]. For small $\varepsilon>0$ let $J_\varepsilon x$ minimize $f_t(y)+|x-y|^2/(2\varepsilon)$ and let $f_{t,\varepsilon}$ be the minimum value. The resolvent proof in [F2] gives $J_\varepsilon$ Lipschitz. Comparing the envelope at $x+h$ using $J_\varepsilon x$, and at $x$ using $J_\varepsilon(x+h)$, bounds the difference from $\langle(x-J_\varepsilon x)/\varepsilon,h\rangle$ by $O(|h|^2)$ locally. Thus $f_{t,\varepsilon}$ is $C^1$ and its gradient is $(x-J_\varepsilon x)/\varepsilon$. The monotonicity estimate from [F2] gives $|\nabla f_{t,\varepsilon}(x)|\le |g_t(x)|/(1+\varepsilon\alpha_t)$ on $Q_r$, with $\alpha_t$ a semiconvexity coefficient; the same proof gives pointwise convergence to $g_t(x)$. Dominated convergence yields convergence in $L^2(\mu_t)$. Each gradient belongs to the closure of gradients of compactly supported smooth functions: multiply the $C^1$ envelope by smooth cutoffs equal to one on $B_N$, with derivative $O(1/N)$, and then mollify. On $Q_r$ the envelope stays between the fixed lower bound and upper bound of $f_t$, so the cutoff derivative term tends to zero in $L^2(\mu_t)$; the other tail tends to zero by the bound just proved. Mollification converges uniformly in $C^1$ on each compact set. Therefore $g_t$ belongs to the spatial gradient closure in $L^2(\mu_t)$.

Let $w$ be a minimum-action field for $\mu$ as in the AC² minimal-velocity theorem. Subtracting its continuity equation from that of $v$ and using time tensor tests shows $\int(v_t-w_t)\cdot\nabla\psi\,d\mu_t=0$ for almost every $t$, simultaneously for a countable set of compactly supported smooth $\psi$ dense in $C^1$ on each compact ball. Such a set is obtained by rational polynomial approximations and fixed smooth cutoffs; extend the equality to every compactly supported smooth test by uniform gradient approximation. By step 2.3, $v_t$ belongs to the $L^2(\mu_t)$ closure of these gradients. Hence $\langle v_t-w_t,v_t\rangle_{L^2(\mu_t)}=0$, and therefore $\|w_t\|_{L^2(\mu_t)}^2=\|v_t\|_{L^2(\mu_t)}^2+\|w_t-v_t\|_{L^2(\mu_t)}^2$ almost everywhere. Thus $v$ is a minimum-action field; [F6] identifies its action with $\int_0^T|\dot\mu_t|_{W_2}^2dt$. The constraint is included: for any absolutely continuous label path in $Q_r$, at a two-sided differentiability time and every $n\in N_{Q_r}(X_t)$, the inequalities $n\cdot(X_{t+h}-X_t)\le0$ for both signs of $h$ give $n\cdot\dot X_t=0$. Thus normal-cone terms contribute no velocity pairing, and the constrained minimum cannot be replaced by an unconstrained selection.

derivations.claim: Form the label Hilbert space $K=L^2(\mu_0;\mathbb R^d)$ and the initial vector $X_0(s)=s$. This Euclidean Borel label space is countably generated, so its $d$-vector $L^2$ space is separable under the generalized label-space interface. It has finite $E_r$ because $F(\mu_0)<\infty$. [F1] yields the unique Hilbert gradient flow $X_t$ for all $t\ge0$. Define $\mu_t=(X_t)_\#\mu_0$. By [F2] this curve solves the localized continuity equation with the prescribed minimum-norm velocity and is in $AC^2_{\mathrm{loc}}$.

The Hilbert energy identity in [F1] is $E_r(X_t)-E_r(X_s)=-\int_s^t\|\dot X_q\|_K^2dq$. By [F2], $\dot X_q(s)=v_q(X_q(s))$ almost everywhere and $E_r(X_q)=F(\mu_q)$. The change-of-variables identity for the pushforward therefore gives the displayed Wasserstein energy identity.

Fix $\eta\in\mathcal P_2(Q_r)$ and a time where [F4] applies. Choose an optimal coupling $\gamma_t$ of $\mu_t,\eta$. The derivative estimate [F4] gives $\displaystyle \frac12\frac d{dt}W_2^2(\mu_t,\eta)\le\int(x-y)\cdot v_t(x)d\gamma_t=-\int g_{\mu_t}(x)\cdot(x-y)d\gamma_t.$ By [F3], $F(\eta)\ge F(\mu_t)+\int g_{\mu_t}(x)\cdot(y-x)d\gamma_t+\frac{\lambda_r}{2}W_2^2(\mu_t,\eta)$. Combining the inequalities proves the EVI.

If $\mu$ and $\nu$ are two such solutions, [F5] gives their stability estimate; equal initial data imply $W_2(\mu_t,\nu_t)=0$ for every $t$, hence equality of the measures and uniqueness. The construction in step 1.1 proves existence.

Assume AC and the feature-measure energy hypotheses. Let $r>0$ and let $\mu_0\in\mathcal P_2(\Omega)$ have finite energy and be concentrated on $Q_r$. There is a unique curve $\mu:[0,\infty)\to\mathcal P_2(Q_r)$ in $AC^2_{\mathrm{loc}}$ that starts at $\mu_0$, solves the continuity equation with velocity equal almost everywhere to the negative minimum-norm element of $\partial(F'(\mu_t)+\iota_{Q_r})$, and satisfies
$$F(\mu_t)-F(\mu_s)=-\int_s^t\int|v_q(u)|^2d\mu_q(u)dq\qquad(0\le s\le t<\infty).$$
Writing $\lambda_r=\lambda_V-L_rA_r^2-N_rB_r$, it also satisfies the evolution variational inequality
$$\frac12\frac d{dt}W_2^2(\mu_t,\eta)+\frac{\lambda_r}{2}W_2^2(\mu_t,\eta)\le F(\eta)-F(\mu_t)$$
for each fixed $\eta\in\mathcal P_2(Q_r)$ and almost every $t>0$ (with the exceptional null set allowed to depend on $\eta$). Any two such localized flows obey $W_2(\mu_t,\nu_t)\le e^{-\lambda_r t}W_2(\mu_0,\nu_0)$.

Let $d\ge1$, let $\mathcal H$ be a separable real Hilbert space, and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be the closure of a nonempty convex open set. Let $R:\mathcal H\to[0,\infty)$ be differentiable, with differential Lipschitz on bounded sets in the uniform sense that for every bounded $B\subseteq\mathcal H$ there is a finite $L_B$ such that
$$\|dR_z-dR_{z'}\|_{\mathcal H^*}\le L_B\|z-z'\|_{\mathcal H}\qquad(z,z'\in B),$$
and with differential bounded on every sublevel set of $R$: for each $c\ge0$,
$$\sup\{\|dR_z\|_{\mathcal H^*}:z\in\mathcal H,\ R(z)\le c\}<\infty.$$ In particular, on each closed convex hull of a bounded feature image $\Phi(Q_r)$, both a finite Lipschitz constant $L_r$ and a finite norm bound $N_r$ for $dR$ are available. Let $\Phi:\Omega\to\mathcal H$ be Fréchet differentiable and let $V:\Omega\to[0,\infty)$ be $\lambda_V$-semiconvex, with the convention that $V(u)-\frac{\lambda_V}{2}|u|^2$ is convex on $\Omega$. For a semiconvex function $f$ on a convex domain $D$ with coefficient $\lambda$, define
$$\partial_\lambda f(u)=\{\xi\in\mathbb R^d:f(v)\ge f(u)+\xi\cdot(v-u)+\tfrac{\lambda}{2}|v-u|^2\text{ for every }v\in D\}.$$
For a locally semiconvex function $g$ on $D$, define its local Fréchet subdifferential by
$$\partial g(u)=\left\{\xi\in\mathbb R^d:\liminf_{\substack{v\to u,\ v\in D\\v\ne u}}\frac{g(v)-g(u)-\xi\cdot(v-u)}{|v-u|}\ge0\right\}.$$
When $g$ is globally $\lambda$-semiconvex, this local subdifferential agrees with the convexified supporting set $\partial_\lambda g(u)$.
For every $r>0$, require a nonempty closed convex set $Q_r\subseteq\Omega$, nested increasingly in $r$, such that
$$\{u\in\Omega:\operatorname{dist}(u,Q_r)\le r'\}\subseteq Q_{r+r'}\qquad(r,r'>0),$$
such that $\Phi$ and $V$ are bounded on $Q_r$, $d\Phi$ is Lipschitz on $Q_r$, and there are fixed constants $C_1,C_2>0$ with
$$\sup_{u\in Q_r}\bigl(\|d\Phi_u\|+\|\partial V(u)\|\bigr)\le C_1+C_2r.$$
Here $\partial V(u)=\partial_{\lambda_V}V(u)$ is the supporting set on $\Omega$, and in the growth bound $\|\partial V(u)\|$ means its minimum element norm, equivalently the bound requires a supporting vector of norm at most $C_1+C_2r$ at every $u\in Q_r$. No bound is imposed on the domain normal cone. This is a bounded-selection variant of the source assumptions: Assumption 2.1(iii)(c) in Chizat and Bach explicitly uses the maximal element norm, which implies the minimum-norm bound wherever the supporting set is nonempty. The source does not specify that its maximal bound excludes domain normals. The bounded-selection convention here allows relative-domain supporting sets with unbounded normal vectors; results using this variant require their own proofs. For a Borel set $A\subseteq\Omega$, write $\mathcal P_2(A)$ for the Borel probability measures on $\mathbb R^d$ concentrated on $A$ and having finite second moment.
For a finite nonnegative Borel measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb R^d$, set
$$F(\mu)=R\!\left(\int_\Omega\Phi(u)\,d\mu(u)\right)+\int_\Omega V(u)\,d\mu(u)$$
when $\mu$ is concentrated on $\Omega$, the Bochner integral exists, and the scalar integral is finite; set $F(\mu)=+\infty$ otherwise. For $\mu\in\mathcal P_2(\Omega)$ with finite $F(\mu)$, write $m_\mu=\int_\Omega\Phi\,d\mu$ and define its first-variation potential on $\Omega$ by
$$F'(\mu)(u)=dR_{m_\mu}[\Phi(u)]+V(u).$$
No convexity of $R$ is required by this definition.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: By [F1], $m_{\mu_t}$ stays in the $R$-sublevel set used to define $M_0$. The unconstrained part of the negative velocity has norm at most $M_0(C_1+C_2R)+(C_1+C_2R)=(a+bR)$. Since $0$ belongs to the normal cone of $Q_R$ at each point of $Q_R$, adding the cutoff constraint and taking the minimum norm cannot increase this bound by [F2]. Thus every localized label path has speed at most $a+bR$ before leaving $Q_R$.

Fix $R>r(T)$ and a label path starting at $u_0\in Q_{r_0}$. Let $s_R(t)=\int_0^t|\dot X_q|dq$. By [F3], its displacement from $u_0$ gives $\operatorname{dist}(X_t,Q_{r_0})\le s_R(t)$ and hence $X_t\in Q_{r_0+s_R(t)}$. At almost every time apply [F2] at its current radius (the bounded potential supporting vector at the current point remains admissible after restriction to $Q_R$), obtaining $s_R'(t)\le a+b(r_0+s_R(t))$ almost everywhere. If $b>0$, multiply by $e^{-bt}$ and integrate to get $r_0+s_R(t)\le(r_0+a/b)e^{bt}-a/b$; if $b=0$, integration gives $r_0+s_R(t)\le r_0+at$. Thus $r_0+s_R(t)\le r(t)$. This estimate holds for the entire localized path; in particular $r(T)<R$ places it in the relative $\Omega$-interior of $Q_R$ on this interval. The bound holds for almost every label, so the measure flow stays in $Q_{r(T)}$.

For $x\in Q_{r(T)}$, the relative-neighborhood condition places an $\Omega$-neighborhood of $x$ inside $Q_R$ because $R>r(T)$. Thus the cutoff and $\Omega$ constraints have the same local normal cone along these paths, so each localized flow solves the equation with the common $\Omega$-constrained field. If two cutoffs exceed $r(T)$, [F5] gives equality for the common initial law. Taking $T$ arbitrary and increasing the cutoff constructs a compatible global flow, so finite-time escape from all cutoffs is impossible.

Assume AC. Fix an arbitrary probability label space $(S,\Sigma,\sigma)$ and $r>0$. Let $K=L^2(\sigma;\mathbb R^d)$ with its usual real Hilbert inner product, and let
$$C_r=\{X\in K:X(s)\in Q_r\text{ for }\sigma\text{-almost every }s\}.$$
Define the indicator $\iota_{C_r}$ to be $0$ on $C_r$ and $+\infty$ outside it. For $X\in C_r$, the compositions $\Phi\circ X$ and $V\circ X$ are measurable and bounded, and $\Phi\circ X$ is strongly measurable; hence the scalar integral is finite and the Bochner integral exists. Define
$$E_r(X)=\begin{cases} R\!\left(\int_S\Phi(X(s))\,d\sigma(s)\right)+\int_SV(X(s))\,d\sigma(s),&X\in C_r,\\ +\infty,&X\notin C_r. \end{cases}$$
The formula evaluates neither integral when $X\notin C_r$. The space $K$ is Hilbert for every probability label space and is separable when $\Sigma$ is countably generated. The latter condition holds for finite labels and for Euclidean Borel labels of any dimension, including joint and triple transport-plan labels. For the flow from a law $\mu_0\in\mathcal P_2(\Omega)$ concentrated on $Q_r$, the particular choice is $(S,\Sigma,\sigma)=(\Omega,\mathcal B(\Omega),\mu_0)$ and $X_0(s)=s\in C_r\subseteq K$. Values of representatives on $\sigma$-null sets do not affect $C_r$ or $E_r$.

$$\|dR_z-dR_{z'}\|_{\mathcal H^*}\le L_B\|z-z'\|_{\mathcal H}\qquad(z,z'\in B),$$
and with differential bounded on every sublevel set of $R$: for each $c\ge0$,
$$\sup\{\|dR_z\|_{\mathcal H^*}:z\in\mathcal H,\ R(z)\le c\}<\infty.$$ In particular, on each closed convex hull of a bounded feature image $\Phi(Q_r)$, both a finite Lipschitz constant $L_r$ and a finite norm bound $N_r$ for $dR$ are available. Let $\Phi:\Omega\to\mathcal H$ be Fréchet differentiable and let $V:\Omega\to[0,\infty)$ be $\lambda_V$-semiconvex, with the convention that $V(u)-\frac{\lambda_V}{2}|u|^2$ is convex on $\Omega$. For a semiconvex function $f$ on a convex domain $D$ with coefficient $\lambda$, define
$$\partial_\lambda f(u)=\{\xi\in\mathbb R^d:f(v)\ge f(u)+\xi\cdot(v-u)+\tfrac{\lambda}{2}|v-u|^2\text{ for every }v\in D\}.$$
For a locally semiconvex function $g$ on $D$, define its local Fréchet subdifferential by
$$\partial g(u)=\left\{\xi\in\mathbb R^d:\liminf_{\substack{v\to u,\ v\in D\\v\ne u}}\frac{g(v)-g(u)-\xi\cdot(v-u)}{|v-u|}\ge0\right\}.$$
When $g$ is globally $\lambda$-semiconvex, this local subdifferential agrees with the convexified supporting set $\partial_\lambda g(u)$.
For every $r>0$, require a nonempty closed convex set $Q_r\subseteq\Omega$, nested increasingly in $r$, such that
$$\{u\in\Omega:\operatorname{dist}(u,Q_r)\le r'\}\subseteq Q_{r+r'}\qquad(r,r'>0),$$
such that $\Phi$ and $V$ are bounded on $Q_r$, $d\Phi$ is Lipschitz on $Q_r$, and there are fixed constants $C_1,C_2>0$ with
$$\sup_{u\in Q_r}\bigl(\|d\Phi_u\|+\|\partial V(u)\|\bigr)\le C_1+C_2r.$$
Here $\partial V(u)=\partial_{\lambda_V}V(u)$ is the supporting set on $\Omega$, and in the growth bound $\|\partial V(u)\|$ means its minimum element norm, equivalently the bound requires a supporting vector of norm at most $C_1+C_2r$ at every $u\in Q_r$. No bound is imposed on the domain normal cone. This is a bounded-selection variant of the source assumptions: Assumption 2.1(iii)(c) in Chizat and Bach explicitly uses the maximal element norm, which implies the minimum-norm bound wherever the supporting set is nonempty. The source does not specify that its maximal bound excludes domain normals. The bounded-selection convention here allows relative-domain supporting sets with unbounded normal vectors; results using this variant require their own proofs. For a Borel set $A\subseteq\Omega$, write $\mathcal P_2(A)$ for the Borel probability measures on $\mathbb R^d$ concentrated on $A$ and having finite second moment.
For a finite nonnegative Borel measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb R^d$, set
$$F(\mu)=R\!\left(\int_\Omega\Phi(u)\,d\mu(u)\right)+\int_\Omega V(u)\,d\mu(u)$$

$$F'(\mu)(u)=dR_{m_\mu}[\Phi(u)]+V(u).$$
No convexity of $R$ is required by this definition.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

u\in\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)$, the infimum of $\int|x-y|^2d\pi(x,y)$ over couplings $\pi$ of $\mu$ and $
u$ is finite and is attained. If $\mu_n,
u_n,\mu,
u\in\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)$, $\mu_n$ converges narrowly to $\mu$, and $
u_n$ converges narrowly to $
u$, then
$$W_2(\mu,
u)^2\le\liminf_{n	o\infty}W_2(\mu_n,
u_n)^2.$$

derivations.claim: Put the finite labels on the probability space $\{1,\ldots,m\}$ with mass $1/m$. The finite label sigma-algebra is countably generated, so the generalized label lemma gives a separable Hilbert space. Then $K=L^2(\{1,\ldots,m\};\mathbb R^d)$ has inner product $m^{-1}\sum_i x_i\cdot y_i$. For each cutoff $r$, its localized energy $E_r$ equals $F(m^{-1}\sum_i\delta_{x_i})=F_m$ on $Q_r^m$ and is $+\infty$ outside that set by [F1]. A Euclidean subgradient $p$ represents the functional derivative in the weighted metric by $mp$, since $m^{-1}\sum_i(mp_i)\cdot h_i=\sum_i p_i\cdot h_i$. This gives the normalization of the two inclusions; the local supporting-set argument below proves their local subdifferential identification and the converse for every particle path.

Fix $m$, a finite interval $[0,T]$, and any classical particle path from the Statement. Its coordinate image is compact. Fix $q\in Q_1$ and first choose $r>1+\max_{i,t}|x_i^{(m)}(t)-q|$. The cutoff enlargement condition then puts the image in $Q_r^m$. Choose $R>r$; the same condition gives a relative $\Omega^m$-neighborhood of the image inside $Q_R^m$. Set $A_R=\sup_{Q_R}\|d\Phi\|$, $B_R=\operatorname{Lip}_{Q_R}(d\Phi)$, and choose the finite Lipschitz and norm bounds $L_R,N_R$ for $dR$ on the closed convex hull of $\Phi(Q_R)$. On the atomic label space write $G_R(X)=R(\int\Phi(X)d\sigma)$. Its gradient in the weighted Hilbert metric is $s\mapsto d\Phi_{X(s)}^*
abla R(\int\Phi(X)d\sigma)$. Also $\|\int\Phi(X)d\sigma-\int\Phi(Y)d\sigma\|\le A_R\|X-Y\|_K$. Adding and subtracting $d\Phi_{X(s)}^*
abla R(\int\Phi(Y)d\sigma)$ therefore gives the Lipschitz bound $$\|
abla G_R(X)-
abla G_R(Y)\|_K\le (L_RA_R^2+N_RB_R)\|X-Y\|_K.$$ Writing $C_R=L_RA_R^2+N_RB_R$, the smooth term is therefore $(-C_R)$-semiconvex in the weighted Hilbert metric, while the averaged potential is $\lambda_V$-semiconvex there. Since $\|X-Y\|_K^2=m^{-1}\sum_i|x_i-y_i|^2$, the corresponding Euclidean product coefficient for $F_m$ is $(\lambda_V-C_R)/m$. Because $Q_R^m$ and $\Omega^m$ agree locally along the path, the local Fréchet subdifferential in the Statement is the supporting subdifferential on $Q_R^m$ with this coefficient. Under the weighted Hilbert norm, $p\in\partial F_m(x)$ corresponds exactly to $mp\in\partial_{\lambda_V-C_R}E_R(x)$.

On a bounded neighborhood of the compact path image, the smooth feature gradient is bounded, and the two supporting inequalities for $V$ together with its bounded supporting selections give a local Lipschitz bound for the potential. Hence $F_m$ is locally Lipschitz there, so $e(t)=F_m(x^{(m)}(t))$ is absolutely continuous. At almost every time when $e$ and $x^{(m)}$ are differentiable and the inclusion holds, apply the semiconvex supporting inequality at $x^{(m)}(t)$ to $x^{(m)}(t+h)$ for positive and negative $h$. Dividing by $h$ and letting $h\to0$ gives $$e'(t)=\sum_i p_i(t)\cdot\dot x_i^{(m)}(t)=-m\sum_i|p_i(t)|^2=-\|\dot x^{(m)}(t)\|_K^2.$$ Since $F_m\ge0$, integration shows that the path has square-integrable derivative on $[0,T]$. Step 2.1 therefore identifies it as a solution of the localized Hilbert gradient-flow inclusion, and uniqueness of that flow identifies it with the atomic localized flow. The escape estimate [F3] consequently applies to every particle path in the Statement.

By [F3], for each fixed $T$ the particle flows, now identified with localized flows, and the measure flow remain inside a common larger cutoff $Q_R$ and solve the same localized equation. Apply [F4] on that cutoff to get $W_2(\mu_{m,t},\mu_t)\le e^{K_Tt}W_2(\mu_{m,0},\mu_0)$ for $0\le t\le T$. Since $e^{K_Tt}\le e^{K_TT}$ when $K_T\ge0$ (replace it by $\max(K_T,0)$ otherwise), taking the supremum and using the assumed initial convergence proves the result.

Assume AC. Let $\mu_0,\mu_1\in\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)$. A generalized $W_2$ geodesic from $\mu_0$ to $\mu_1$ with base $
u\in\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)$ is a probability measure $\pi$ on triples $(z,x,y)$ whose $(z,x)$ marginal is an optimal coupling of $
u$ and $\mu_0$ and whose $(z,y)$ marginal is an optimal coupling of $
u$ and $\mu_1$; its interpolating curve is $\mu_t=((1-t)x+ty)_\#\pi$. A functional $F$ is $\lambda$-convex along generalized geodesics if for every such $\pi$ its values satisfy $F(\mu_t)\le(1-t)F(\mu_0)+tF(\mu_1)- rac{\lambda}{2}t(1-t)\int|x-y|^2d\pi$. A vector field $g_\mu\in L^2(\mu;\mathbb R^d)$ is a strong Wasserstein subgradient of $F$ at $\mu$ if for every $\eta\in\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d)$ and every coupling $\gamma$ of $\mu$ and $\eta$, $F(\eta)\ge F(\mu)+\int g_\mu(x)\cdot(y-x)d\gamma+o\!\left((\int|y-x|^2d\gamma)^{1/2}ight)$ as the coupling action tends to zero, with a remainder uniform over all such couplings. The definition imposes no global displacement-convexity claim.

For finite nonnegative measures $\mu_0,\mu_1$, write $a=\int\sin x\,d\mu_0$ and $b=\int\sin x\,d\mu_1$. Linearity of integration gives $F((1-t)\mu_0+t\mu_1)=((1-t)a+tb)^2\le(1-t)a^2+tb^2=(1-t)F(\mu_0)+tF(\mu_1)$ by step 1.1. Thus $F$ is mixture-convex.

For $\mu_0=\delta_0$ and $\mu_1=\delta_\pi$, [F2] gives the geodesic $\mu_t=\delta_{\pi t}$. Then $F(\mu_0)=F(\mu_1)=0$, whereas $F(\mu_{1/2})=\sin^2(\pi/2)=1$. The convexity inequality at $t=1/2$ would require $1\le0$, which is false. Hence mixture convexity does not imply displacement convexity.

Let $d\ge1$, let $\mathcal H$ be a separable real Hilbert space, and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be the closure of a nonempty convex open set. Let $R:\mathcal H\to[0,\infty)$ be differentiable, with differential Lipschitz on bounded sets in the uniform sense that for every bounded $B\subseteq\mathcal H$ there is a finite $L_B$ such that
$$\|dR_z-dR_{z'}\|_{\mathcal H^*}\le L_B\|z-z'\|_{\mathcal H}\qquad(z,z'\in B),$$
and with differential bounded on every sublevel set of $R$: for each $c\ge0$,
$$\sup\{\|dR_z\|_{\mathcal H^*}:z\in\mathcal H,\ R(z)\le c\}<\infty.$$ In particular, on each closed convex hull of a bounded feature image $\Phi(Q_r)$, both a finite Lipschitz constant $L_r$ and a finite norm bound $N_r$ for $dR$ are available. Let $\Phi:\Omega\to\mathcal H$ be Fréchet differentiable and let $V:\Omega\to[0,\infty)$ be $\lambda_V$-semiconvex, with the convention that $V(u)-\frac{\lambda_V}{2}|u|^2$ is convex on $\Omega$. For a semiconvex function $f$ on a convex domain $D$ with coefficient $\lambda$, define
$$\partial_\lambda f(u)=\{\xi\in\mathbb R^d:f(v)\ge f(u)+\xi\cdot(v-u)+\tfrac{\lambda}{2}|v-u|^2\text{ for every }v\in D\}.$$
For a locally semiconvex function $g$ on $D$, define its local Fréchet subdifferential by
$$\partial g(u)=\left\{\xi\in\mathbb R^d:\liminf_{\substack{v\to u,\ v\in D\\v\ne u}}\frac{g(v)-g(u)-\xi\cdot(v-u)}{|v-u|}\ge0\right\}.$$
When $g$ is globally $\lambda$-semiconvex, this local subdifferential agrees with the convexified supporting set $\partial_\lambda g(u)$.
For every $r>0$, require a nonempty closed convex set $Q_r\subseteq\Omega$, nested increasingly in $r$, such that
$$\{u\in\Omega:\operatorname{dist}(u,Q_r)\le r'\}\subseteq Q_{r+r'}\qquad(r,r'>0),$$
such that $\Phi$ and $V$ are bounded on $Q_r$, $d\Phi$ is Lipschitz on $Q_r$, and there are fixed constants $C_1,C_2>0$ with
$$\sup_{u\in Q_r}\bigl(\|d\Phi_u\|+\|\partial V(u)\|\bigr)\le C_1+C_2r.$$
Here $\partial V(u)=\partial_{\lambda_V}V(u)$ is the supporting set on $\Omega$, and in the growth bound $\|\partial V(u)\|$ means its minimum element norm, equivalently the bound requires a supporting vector of norm at most $C_1+C_2r$ at every $u\in Q_r$. No bound is imposed on the domain normal cone. This is a bounded-selection variant of the source assumptions: Assumption 2.1(iii)(c) in Chizat and Bach explicitly uses the maximal element norm, which implies the minimum-norm bound wherever the supporting set is nonempty. The source does not specify that its maximal bound excludes domain normals. The bounded-selection convention here allows relative-domain supporting sets with unbounded normal vectors; results using this variant require their own proofs. For a Borel set $A\subseteq\Omega$, write $\mathcal P_2(A)$ for the Borel probability measures on $\mathbb R^d$ concentrated on $A$ and having finite second moment.
For a finite nonnegative Borel measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb R^d$, set
$$F(\mu)=R\!\left(\int_\Omega\Phi(u)\,d\mu(u)\right)+\int_\Omega V(u)\,d\mu(u)$$
when $\mu$ is concentrated on $\Omega$, the Bochner integral exists, and the scalar integral is finite; set $F(\mu)=+\infty$ otherwise. For $\mu\in\mathcal P_2(\Omega)$ with finite $F(\mu)$, write $m_\mu=\int_\Omega\Phi\,d\mu$ and define its first-variation potential on $\Omega$ by
$$F'(\mu)(u)=dR_{m_\mu}[\Phi(u)]+V(u).$$
No convexity of $R$ is required by this definition.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $T>0$ and let $(\mu_t,v_t)$ be a narrowly continuous finite-action solution of the continuity equation on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d$. There is a Borel probability law $\eta$ on $C([0,T];\mathbb R^d)$ such that $(e_t)_\#\eta=\mu_t$ for every $t$, and for $\eta$-almost every path $\gamma$, $\gamma$ is absolutely continuous and $\dot\gamma(t)=v_t(\gamma(t))$ for almost every $t$. Its expected path action equals the Eulerian action:
$$\int\!\int_0^T|\dot\gamma(t)|^2dt\,d\eta(\gamma)=\int_0^T\!\int|v_t(x)|^2d\mu_t(x)dt.$$

derivations.claim: The characteristic equation $\dot x=-x$ with $x(0)=x_0$ has the solution $x(t)=e^{-t}x_0$, as direct differentiation verifies. Pushing $\mu_0$ forward by this map gives a continuity-equation solution with velocity $v_t(x)=-x$. Its action on $[0,T]$ is finite because $\int|x|^2d\mu_t=e^{-2t}\int|x|^2d\mu_0$. For compactly supported initial laws it is the flow identified by the global uniqueness theorem. For arbitrary $\mu_0\in\mathcal P_2$, the same conclusion follows directly: every finite-action PDE solution with the prescribed smooth velocity $-x$ is represented by its unique characteristics via superposition, so it equals this pushforward, even when $\mu_0$ lies in no finite cutoff.

The metric $m^{-1}\sum_i x_i\cdot y_i$ gives the particle gradient of $m^{-1}\sum_i|x_i|^2/2$ equal to $(x_1,\dots,x_m)$, so the same scalar ODE gives $x_i(t)=e^{-t}x_i(0)$. Consequently $\mu_{m,t}=(e^{-t}\operatorname{id})_\#\mu_{m,0}$.

For $a>0$, pushing both marginals of any coupling forward by $x\mapsto ax$ multiplies its quadratic cost by $a^2$; applying the inverse scaling gives the reverse inequality for the infimum. Thus $W_2(a_\#\alpha,a_\#\beta)=aW_2(\alpha,\beta)$. Apply this with $a=e^{-t}$, $\alpha=\mu_{m,0}$, and $\beta=\mu_0$ to obtain the displayed identity. Since $e^{-t}\le1$, its supremum for $0\le t\le T$ is at most the initial W2 error, proving compact-time uniform convergence.

Let $M$ be a boundaryless $n$-manifold, $R$ a commutative unital ring, and $K\subseteq M$ compact. Then $H_i(M,M\setminus K;R)=0$ for $i>n$, and restriction from $H_n(M,M\setminus K;R)$ to all local stalks at points of $K$ is injective. Every continuous section $s$ of the local $R$-homology system on $M$ is realized by a unique class $s_K$ in this relative group.

In particular an $R$-orientation determines a unique $[M]_K$ restricting to its generator at each point of $K$. These classes commute with restriction for compact-set inclusions and split over the finitely many components meeting $K$. No AC is needed.

A continuous map of pairs $f:(X,A)\to(Y,B)$, meaning $f(A)\subseteq B$,
induces $f_*:H_n(X,A;G)\to H_n(Y,B;G)$ for every $n$. Identity maps and
composites induce identity maps and composites.

The **relative singular homology group** of $(X,A)$ in degree $n$ is
$$H_n(X,A;G):=H_n(C_\bullet(X,A;G))=\ker\bar\partial_n/\operatorname{im}\bar\partial_{n+1}.$$
Equivalently, a relative cycle is an ordinary finite chain $c$ with
$\partial c\in C_{n-1}(A;G)$, modulo adding a chain in $A$ and an ordinary
boundary.

If $Z\subseteq X$ and $\overline Z\subseteq\operatorname{int}_X(A)$, then
inclusion $(X-Z,A-Z)\to(X,A)$ induces isomorphisms
$H_n(X-Z,A-Z;G)\cong H_n(X,A;G)$ for every $n$.

Let $M$ be an $n$-manifold with boundary and $x\in M$. For any commutative unital coefficient ring $R$,
$$H_k(M,M\setminus\{x\};R)\cong\begin{cases}R,&x\in\operatorname{int}M\text{ and }k=n,\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}$$
The boundary subset is independent of charts, and a nonempty manifold's dimension is intrinsic. Homeomorphisms preserve boundary and, for nonempty manifolds, dimension. A manifold is boundaryless exactly when it is locally Euclidean of its specified dimension. Dimension is not intrinsic for the empty space, and the zero coefficient ring cannot detect boundary or dimension; use integral coefficients for these conclusions. No AC is assumed.

derivations.claim: If $f^{-1}(y)\cap U=\varnothing$, then $K=\varnothing$ and $H_d(U,U\setminus K)=H_d(U,U)=0$, so $D(f,U,y)=0$. For the identity and $y\in U$, $K=\{y\}$ and the induced map sends the chosen local orientation generator to itself, so $D(\operatorname{id},U,y)=1$.

Under the additivity hypotheses, $K$ is the disjoint union of $K_i=K\cap U_i$. The closed set $Z=U\setminus(U_1\cup U_2)$ has closure in $U$ disjoint from $K$: the compact set $K$ lies in the open set $U_1\cup U_2$. Excision [F3] identifies $H_d(U,U\setminus K)$ with $H_d(U_1\cup U_2,(U_1\cup U_2)\setminus K)$. Since $U_1,U_2$ are disjoint open sets, every singular simplex in their union lies in exactly one of them, so this relative group and its chains split as the direct sum of the two relative groups. The unique orientation class [F1] therefore corresponds to $[U_1]_{K_1}+[U_2]_{K_2}$. The restrictions of $f$ commute with the inclusions of these pairs, so functoriality [F2] maps this sum to the sum of the two target classes. Their integer coefficients consequently satisfy $D(f,U,y)=D(f,U_1,y)+D(f,U_2,y)$.

For moving-target invariance set $g_t(x)=H_t(x)-y(t)$; translation identifies the target generator with the standard generator at $0$. The zero set $S=\{(t,x):g_t(x)=0\}$ is a closed subset of compact $[0,1]\times\overline U$ and is disjoint from $[0,1]\times\partial U$. Thus its projection $K_*\subset U$ is compact. Every $g_t$ defines a map of the fixed pair $(U,U\setminus K_*)$ into $(\mathbb R^d,\mathbb R^d\setminus\{0\})$. The singular prism operator for the homotopy satisfies $\partial P+P\partial=(g_1)_\#-(g_0)_\#$; each prism over a simplex in $U\setminus K_*$ avoids $0$, so the chain homotopy descends to relative chains. Hence $(g_0)_*=(g_1)_*$ on $H_d(U,U\setminus K_*)$. Restriction compatibility in [F1] sends $[U]_{K_*}$ to $[U]_{K_t}$ for the actual time-$t$ zero set, so these two induced integers are exactly $D(H_0,U,y(0))$ and $D(H_1,U,y(1))$. They are equal, proving moving-target invariance.

The target group is $\mathbb Z$ by [F4]; the source class is unique by [F1]; and the induced map exists by [F2]. Thus the integer in the Statement is well-defined. Steps 1.1–3.1 establish all asserted properties.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and define
$$\nu_f(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu \qquad (A\in\mathcal A).$$
Then $\nu_f$ is a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space. A **signed measure** on
$(X,\mathcal A)$ is a function
$$\nu:\mathcal A\longrightarrow \overline{\mathbb R}$$
such that:

1. $\nu(\varnothing)=0$;
2. $\nu$ takes at most one infinite sign: either $\nu(E)\neq-\infty$ for every
   $E\in\mathcal A$, or $\nu(E)\neq+\infty$ for every $E\in\mathcal A$;
3. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in
   $\mathcal A$,
   the series on the right is defined in the extended reals and
   $$\nu\left(\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty \nu(E_n)$$
   ([[def-extended-reals]]).

The second and third clauses are load-bearing, not stylistic: together they
rule out the undefined form $(+\infty)+(-\infty)$ and require the disjoint
series to exist before countable additivity is asserted.

The next proposition proves the extra fact that if
$\nu(\bigcup_n E_n)$ is finite, then the real series $\sum_n \nu(E_n)$
converges absolutely in the sense of
[[def-absolute-and-conditional-convergence]].

Let $\nu$ be a signed measure or a complex measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. For
$E\in\mathcal A$, define its **total variation on $E$** by
$$|\nu|(E):=\sup\left\{\sum_{n=0}^\infty |\nu(E_n)|:\ (E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\text{ is a countable measurable partition of }E\right\},$$
where, for a signed measure, the term $|\nu(E_n)|$ means the ordinary absolute
value when $\nu(E_n)\in\mathbb R$ and means $+\infty$ when
$\nu(E_n)\in\{+\infty,-\infty\}$; for a complex measure it is the usual complex
modulus. A countable measurable partition of $E$ means:

1. each $E_n$ lies in $\mathcal A$;
2. the sets $E_n$ are pairwise disjoint;
3. $E=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n$.

The sum on the right is a nonnegative extended series, so it is always defined
in $[0,+\infty] \subseteq \overline{\mathbb R}$.

For signed measures, a later proposition shows that finite partitions already
suffice. For complex measures, that finite-partition shortcut is not built into
the definition here.

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

Let $f:\Omega\to X$ be strongly measurable. Then $f$ is Bochner integrable if
and only if

$$\int_\Omega\|f\|\,d\mu<\infty.$$

Here an a.e.-defined scalar function is integrated through any measurable
representative supplied by the strong simple approximation. Moreover the
Bochner integral is independent of the approximating sequence in its
definition.

Let $X,Y$ be Banach spaces, let $T:X\to Y$ be bounded and linear, and let $f$
be Bochner integrable. Then $T\circ f$ is Bochner integrable and, for every
measurable $E$,

$$T\left(\int_Ef\,d\mu\right)=\int_E Tf\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: The coordinate $w$ is measurable, so $w_+$ and $w_-$ are nonnegative measurable functions. By [F1], $\alpha_\mu$ and $\beta_\mu$ are measures, and [F2] gives $\alpha_\mu(\Theta),\beta_\mu(\Theta)\le\int|w|d\mu<\infty$.

For each measurable $B$, $w=w_+-w_-$ and both integrals are finite, so $\int_{\mathbb R\times B}w d\mu=\alpha_\mu(B)-\beta_\mu(B)$. Countable additivity of both finite measures makes their difference countably additive with finite real values, hence a finite signed measure by [F3]. For every $B\in\mathcal T$ and every countable measurable partition $(B_j)$ of $B$, $\sum_j|h^1(\mu)(B_j)|\le\sum_j(\alpha_\mu(B_j)+\beta_\mu(B_j))=\alpha_\mu(B)+\beta_\mu(B)$; taking the supremum in [F4] proves the stated pointwise total-variation bound. The weighted penalty inequality follows by monotonicity of the nonnegative integral, first for simple nonnegative weights and then by increasing simple approximation. For a finite-valued simple $\varphi$, linearity [F5] and the definitions of $\alpha_\mu,\beta_\mu$ give $\int\varphi d\alpha_\mu-\int\varphi d\beta_\mu=\int w\varphi d\mu$. For general bounded measurable $\varphi$, choose $M$ with $|\varphi|\le M$ and partition $[-M,M]$ into finitely many intervals of length at most $1/n$; assigning one endpoint on each measurable inverse image gives a finite-valued simple $\varphi_n$ with $\|\varphi_n-\varphi\|_\infty\le1/n$. The errors in the two $\alpha_\mu,\beta_\mu$ integrals are at most $(\alpha_\mu(\Theta)+\beta_\mu(\Theta))/n$, and the error in the $w\varphi$ integral is at most $\int|w|d\mu/n$. Letting $n\to\infty$ proves the identity.

Let $\varphi:\Theta\to\mathcal H$ have the bounded everywhere simple approximation specified in the Definition. Its approximants pulled back to the product, multiplied by scalar simple functions converging everywhere to $w$, show that $w\varphi(\theta)$ is strongly measurable; moreover $\|w\varphi(\theta)\|\le|w|\|\varphi\|_\infty$, so [F6] makes it Bochner integrable. For each $z\in\mathcal H$, [F7] moves the bounded functional $x\mapsto\langle z,x\rangle$ inside that Bochner integral, and step 2.1 identifies the resulting scalar integral with the pairing in the Definition. Equality of all inner products proves the displayed feature-moment factorization.

Let $d\ge1$, let $\mathcal H$ be a separable real Hilbert space, and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be the closure of a nonempty convex open set. Let $R:\mathcal H\to[0,\infty)$ be differentiable, with differential Lipschitz on bounded sets in the uniform sense that for every bounded $B\subseteq\mathcal H$ there is a finite $L_B$ such that
$$\|dR_z-dR_{z'}\|_{\mathcal H^*}\le L_B\|z-z'\|_{\mathcal H}\qquad(z,z'\in B),$$
and with differential bounded on every sublevel set of $R$: for each $c\ge0$,
$$\sup\{\|dR_z\|_{\mathcal H^*}:z\in\mathcal H,\ R(z)\le c\}<\infty.$$ In particular, on each closed convex hull of a bounded feature image $\Phi(Q_r)$, both a finite Lipschitz constant $L_r$ and a finite norm bound $N_r$ for $dR$ are available. Let $\Phi:\Omega\to\mathcal H$ be Fréchet differentiable and let $V:\Omega\to[0,\infty)$ be $\lambda_V$-semiconvex, with the convention that $V(u)-\frac{\lambda_V}{2}|u|^2$ is convex on $\Omega$. For a semiconvex function $f$ on a convex domain $D$ with coefficient $\lambda$, define
$$\partial_\lambda f(u)=\{\xi\in\mathbb R^d:f(v)\ge f(u)+\xi\cdot(v-u)+\tfrac{\lambda}{2}|v-u|^2\text{ for every }v\in D\}.$$
For a locally semiconvex function $g$ on $D$, define its local Fréchet subdifferential by
$$\partial g(u)=\left\{\xi\in\mathbb R^d:\liminf_{\substack{v\to u,\ v\in D\\v\ne u}}\frac{g(v)-g(u)-\xi\cdot(v-u)}{|v-u|}\ge0\right\}.$$
When $g$ is globally $\lambda$-semiconvex, this local subdifferential agrees with the convexified supporting set $\partial_\lambda g(u)$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: First, $\Phi$ is Borel measurable with values in the separable space $\mathcal H$. Fix a countable dense sequence $(h_j)$ in $\mathcal H$; the map assigning to $\Phi(u)$ a nearest point among $h_1,\ldots,h_k$, breaking ties by least index, is finite-valued and measurable, and its error tends to zero as $k\to\infty$. Thus $\Phi$ is strongly measurable. Moreover, $\|\Phi(w,\theta)\|\le\|\varphi\|_\infty|w|$. A probability law with finite second moment has $\int|w|d\mu\le(\int|w|^2d\mu)^{1/2}<\infty$ by Cauchy–Schwarz. Thus [F3] gives existence of its feature moment, while $0\le V\le\|\widetilde V\|_\infty|w|$ gives a finite penalty; $R$ is finite-valued. This proves the asserted well-definedness for every law in the Statement. By [A1] and [F1] choose couplings $\pi_n$ of $\mu_n$ and $\mu$ with $\delta_n^2=\int(|w-w'|^2+|\theta-\theta'|^2)d\pi_n\to0$. By [F2], the coupling marginal identities hold also for these Bochner feature integrals: apply a bounded linear functional, use the scalar marginal identity, and identify the vectors by all such evaluations. Consequently [F4] and the pointwise bound $$\|w\varphi(\theta)-w'\varphi(\theta')\|\le\|\varphi\|_\infty|w-w'|+\operatorname{Lip}(\varphi)|w'|\,|\theta-\theta'|$$ give $$\|m_{\mu_n}-m_\mu\|\le\left(\|\varphi\|_\infty+\operatorname{Lip}(\varphi)\Bigl(\int|w'|^2d\mu(w',\theta')\Bigr)^{1/2}\right)\delta_n\longrightarrow0.$$ The second-moment factor belongs to the fixed limit marginal and is finite, with no bound on the diameter or interior of $\Theta$ required.

Since $\bigl||w|-|w'|\bigr|\le|w-w'|$, the same estimate with scalar $\widetilde V$ in place of $\varphi$ gives $\int Vd\mu_n\to\int Vd\mu$. Step 1.1 gives convergence of feature moments in $\mathcal H$; continuity of $R$ therefore gives convergence of the risk terms. Adding the two limits proves $F(\mu_n)\to F(\mu)$. Under the full feature-energy hypotheses, the identical feature and penalty integrals are finite by step 1.1, so the finite branch in that definition gives exactly this $F$. If $\Theta=\varnothing$, no law in the Statement exists and the assertion is vacuous; zero maps, zero weights and singleton or lower-dimensional $\Theta$ are included in the estimates.

derivations.claim: On $\mathbb R^d\setminus\{0\}$, write $u=|u|\rho(u)$. Positive two-homogeneity gives $\Phi(u)=|u|^2\Phi(\rho(u))$ and $V(u)=|u|^2V(\rho(u))$; at $u=0$ both vanish. Integrating these identities and applying the definition of $h^2$ proves both displayed projection identities.

For weak convergence on the compact sphere, the masses $h^2(\mu_n)(\mathbb S^{d-1})$ are bounded. The continuous map $\Phi|_{\mathbb S^{d-1}}$ has compact image in $\mathcal H$. Given $\epsilon>0$, choose finitely many vectors $g_j=\Phi(\theta_j)$ whose open $\epsilon$-balls cover that image and put $U_j=\{\theta:\|\Phi(\theta)-g_j\|<\epsilon\}$. Define $r_j(\theta)=\operatorname{dist}(\theta,\mathbb S^{d-1}\setminus U_j)$ when the complement is nonempty, and $r_j\equiv1$ when $U_j=\mathbb S^{d-1}$. The continuous functions $\psi_j=r_j/(\sum_i r_i)$ are well-defined because the finite open sets cover the sphere, and $\psi_j(\theta)>0$ only when $\theta\in U_j$. Therefore $\|\Phi(\theta)-\sum_j\psi_j(\theta)g_j\|<\epsilon$ uniformly. Weak convergence gives convergence of each scalar coefficient $\int\psi_jdh^2(\mu_n)$, hence strong convergence of the approximating vector integrals. The uniform approximation error is at most $\epsilon$ times the uniformly bounded masses, so $\int\Phi dh^2(\mu_n)\to\int\Phi d\nu$ in norm. Since $V|_{\mathbb S^{d-1}}$ is continuous, weak convergence also gives $\int Vdh^2(\mu_n)\to\int Vd\nu$. Continuity of $R$ proves the energy limit.

If $\Theta=\varnothing$, the only finite measures on $\Theta$ and $\mathbb R\times\Theta$ are zero, so all partial feature moments and penalties vanish and all asserted convergence conclusions hold directly. Otherwise $\Theta$ is nonempty. In this case, fix $z\in\mathcal H$ and apply [F2] to the bounded scalar function $\psi(\theta)=\langle z,\varphi(\theta)\rangle$. This gives the displayed feature identity for every $z$, hence equality of the Hilbert-valued feature moments because inner products determine vectors. For the penalty, $|w|-w=2w_-\ge0$, and [F2] applied to $\widetilde V$ gives $\int |w|\widetilde V(\theta)d\mu-\int\widetilde Vdh^1(\mu)=2\int w_-\widetilde V(\theta)d\mu\ge0.$ If $h^1(\mu_n)$ converges against bounded continuous scalar tests, testing against $\langle z,\varphi(\cdot)\rangle$ for each $z\in\mathcal H$ proves weak convergence of the feature moments. Under the additional AC, closed-Euclidean, separable-Hilbert assumptions in the Statement, [F4] improves this to norm convergence. For the claimed failure of penalty determination, take any nonempty $\Theta$ and fix $\theta\in\Theta$. Let $\mu_1$ assign mass one to $(1,\theta)$ and let $\mu_2$ assign mass two to $(1,\theta)$ and mass one to $(-1,\theta)$. and with differential bounded on every sublevel set of $R$: for each $c\ge0$,
$$\sup\{\|dR_z\|_{\mathcal H^*}:z\in\mathcal H,\ R(z)\le c\}<\infty.$$ In particular, on each closed convex hull of a bounded feature image $\Phi(Q_r)$, both a finite Lipschitz constant $L_r$ and a finite norm bound $N_r$ for $dR$ are available. Let $\Phi:\Omega\to\mathcal H$ be Fréchet differentiable and let $V:\Omega\to[0,\infty)$ be $\lambda_V$-semiconvex, with the convention that $V(u)-\frac{\lambda_V}{2}|u|^2$ is convex on $\Omega$. For a semiconvex function $f$ on a convex domain $D$ with coefficient $\lambda$, define
$$\partial_\lambda f(u)=\{\xi\in\mathbb R^d:f(v)\ge f(u)+\xi\cdot(v-u)+\tfrac{\lambda}{2}|v-u|^2\text{ for every }v\in D\}.$$
For a locally semiconvex function $g$ on $D$, define its local Fréchet subdifferential by
$$\partial g(u)=\left\{\xi\in\mathbb R^d:\liminf_{\substack{v\to u,\ v\in D\\v\ne u}}\frac{g(v)-g(u)-\xi\cdot(v-u)}{|v-u|}\ge0\right\}.$$
When $g$ is globally $\lambda$-semiconvex, this local subdifferential agrees with the convexified supporting set $\partial_\lambda g(u)$.
For every $r>0$, require a nonempty closed convex set $Q_r\subseteq\Omega$, nested increasingly in $r$, such that
$$\{u\in\Omega:\operatorname{dist}(u,Q_r)\le r'\}\subseteq Q_{r+r'}\qquad(r,r'>0),$$
such that $\Phi$ and $V$ are bounded on $Q_r$, $d\Phi$ is Lipschitz on $Q_r$, and there are fixed constants $C_1,C_2>0$ with
$$\sup_{u\in Q_r}\bigl(\|d\Phi_u\|+\|\partial V(u)\|\bigr)\le C_1+C_2r.$$
Here $\partial V(u)=\partial_{\lambda_V}V(u)$ is the supporting set on $\Omega$, and in the growth bound $\|\partial V(u)\|$ means its minimum element norm, equivalently the bound requires a supporting vector of norm at most $C_1+C_2r$ at every $u\in Q_r$. No bound is imposed on the domain normal cone. This is a bounded-selection variant of the source assumptions: Assumption 2.1(iii)(c) in Chizat and Bach explicitly uses the maximal element norm, which implies the minimum-norm bound wherever the supporting set is nonempty. The source does not specify that its maximal bound excludes domain normals. The bounded-selection convention here allows relative-domain supporting sets with unbounded normal vectors; results using this variant require their own proofs. For a Borel set $A\subseteq\Omega$, write $\mathcal P_2(A)$ for the Borel probability measures on $\mathbb R^d$ concentrated on $A$ and having finite second moment.
For a finite nonnegative Borel measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb R^d$, set
$$F(\mu)=R\!\left(\int_\Omega\Phi(u)\,d\mu(u)\right)+\int_\Omega V(u)\,d\mu(u)$$
when $\mu$ is concentrated on $\Omega$, the Bochner integral exists, and the scalar integral is finite; set $F(\mu)=+\infty$ otherwise. For $\mu\in\mathcal P_2(\Omega)$ with finite $F(\mu)$, write $m_\mu=\int_\Omega\Phi\,d\mu$ and define its first-variation potential on $\Omega$ by
$$F'(\mu)(u)=dR_{m_\mu}[\Phi(u)]+V(u).$$
No convexity of $R$ is required by this definition.

Assume AC and the feature-measure energy hypotheses. Write $AC^2_{\mathrm{loc}}([0,\infty);\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d))$ for curves whose restriction to every finite interval $[0,T]$ belongs to $AC^2([0,T];\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d))$ in the $W_2$ metric. For $\mu\in\mathcal P_2(\Omega)$ with finite energy, define $F'(\mu)(u)=dR_{m_\mu}[\Phi(u)]+V(u)$ on $\Omega$, and extend this potential by $+\infty$ off $\Omega$. Its constrained subdifferential at $u$ is the local Fréchet subdifferential of $F'(\mu)+\iota_\Omega$ defined in the feature-measure-energy convention. A Wasserstein gradient flow from $\mu_0\in\mathcal P_2(\Omega)$ is a curve $t\mapsto\mu_t$ in $AC^2_{\mathrm{loc}}([0,\infty);(\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d),W_2))$, with $\mu_{t=0}=\mu_0$, for which there is a Borel velocity $v_t(u)$ satisfying the finite-action continuity equation and $v_t(u)$ equals the negative minimum-norm element of $\partial(F'(\mu_t)+\iota_\Omega)(u)$ for $dt\,d\mu_t(u)$-almost every $(t,u)$. This definition does not assert that the energy is displacement convex.

Assume DC. Let $X$ be a Banach space, $Y$ a normed space, and let $\mathcal F$ be a family of bounded linear operators $X\to Y$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). If $\sup_{T\in\mathcal F}\|Tx\|<\infty$ for every $x\in X$, then $\sup_{T\in\mathcal F}\|T\|<\infty$, where the norm is [[def-operator-norm]].

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

derivations.claim: The natural partial-model cutoffs $Q_r=[-r,r]\times\Theta$ satisfy the feature-energy conditions: their distance enlargement is $Q_{r+r'}$, boundedness of $\varphi,\widetilde V$ bounds $\Phi,V$ there, and the bounded Lipschitz first derivatives give Lipschitz $d\Phi$ on each slab. The ambient potential has a local supporting vector $(\operatorname{sign}(w)\widetilde V,|w|\nabla\widetilde V)$ off $w=0$, and $(0,0)$ at $w=0$; its norm is bounded by $C(1+r)$. These vectors belong to the relative supporting set by global semiconvexity, so no bound on normal vectors is needed. Thus bounded initial weights supply the common-cutoff hypothesis of [F1]. The path $t\mapsto m_{\mu_t}$ is continuous on $[0,T]$, so its differential image $\{dR_{m_{\mu_t}}:0\le t\le T\}$ is compact and bounded. Boundedness of $\varphi,\widetilde V$ and [F4] give a finite $B_T$ with $|\dot w|\le B_T$ for every characteristic. Choose $\alpha>r_0+B_TT$. Characteristics from $K_0$ have $|w_t|<\alpha$ for $0\le t\le T$, while characteristics starting on either plane $w=\pm\beta$ remain outside the slab $|w|\le\alpha$ for every $\beta>\alpha+B_TT$.

In the bounded branch, $K_0$ is compact because it is closed and contained in the compact set $[-r_0,r_0]\times\Theta$. Thus $X_t(K_0)$ is compact and closed, so [F1]–[F2] give $\operatorname{spt}\mu_t=X_t(K_0)$. The Neumann premise makes the angular characteristic tangent to $\partial\Theta$. In local boundary charts the characteristic equation restricted to $\mathbb R\times\partial\Theta$ therefore has a solution starting at every boundary point; ambient uniqueness identifies it with the characteristic from that point. This proves the forward invariance of the boundary used below.

In the unbounded branch use $\psi(	heta)=	anh|	heta|\,	heta/|	heta|$ for $	heta
e0$ and $\psi(0)=0$. This maps $\mathbb R^{d-1}$ diffeomorphically onto the open unit ball. Its radial and tangential differential eigenvalues are $\operatorname{sech}^2|	heta|$ and $	anh|	heta|/|	heta|$, both tending to zero at infinity. A bounded $C^1$ function with Lipschitz derivative has bounded derivative: Taylor's inequality in the unit direction of its derivative would otherwise force its bounded range to grow without bound. Apply this to scalar evaluations of $\varphi$ and to $\widetilde V$; hence the angular gradients $
abla G_f$ are bounded on bounded sets of $f$. For each $f$, the assumed $C^1$ limit of $G_f(r\cdot)$ gives pointwise convergence of bounded linear operators $f\mapsto\langle f,\varphi(r\cdot)angle$ into $C^1(\mathbb S^{d-2})$. On bounded radial intervals their operator norms are bounded by local $C^1$ regularity; convergence at infinity makes the family pointwise bounded. By [F5] the operator norms are uniformly bounded, and the convergence is uniform on the compact set $\{dR_{m_{\mu_t}}:0\le t\le T\}$ by finite-net approximation. The partial characteristic equations for $w>0$ and $w<0$ are $\dot w=-G_{a_t,+}(	heta)$, $\dot	heta=-w
abla G_{a_t,+}(	heta)$ and $\dot w=G_{a_t,-}(	heta)$, $\dot	heta=-|w|
abla G_{a_t,-}(	heta)$, respectively, where $G_{a_t,+}=a_t[\varphi]+\widetilde V$ and $G_{a_t,-}=-a_t[\varphi]+\widetilde V$. At $w=0$, the scalar inclusion is $\dot w\in-\partial_w(a_t[\varphi(	heta)]w+\widetilde V(	heta)|w|)$ and $\dot	heta=0$; the pointwise minimum-norm choice is used by the flow definition, but the vector-field selection can jump across $w=0$. The compactified angular speed is $D\psi(	heta)\dot	heta$, which tends uniformly to zero as $|	heta|	o\infty$ for bounded $w$. The coefficients of the limiting scalar inclusion converge uniformly on the compact set of risk gradients. Monotonicity of the subdifferential of the convex function $w\mapsto aw+V|w|$ gives $|w_1(t)-w_2(t)|\le |w_1(0)-w_2(0)|+\int_0^t(|a_1-a_2|+|V_1-V_2|)ds$ for two solutions, so the scalar characteristics converge continuously to their unique boundary limit. Write $Y_t$ for the characteristic flow in $(w,\psi(	heta))$ coordinates; it extends continuously to the closed unit ball, with lateral angular coordinate fixed at the boundary.

In the unbounded branch the original map $X_t$ is closed on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{d-1}$. If $X_t(w_n,\theta_n)$ converges to a finite point, [F4] bounds $w_n$; compactness of the closed unit ball gives a convergent subsequence of $\psi(\theta_n)$. Its limit cannot lie on the boundary because $Y_t$ preserves that boundary, while the image limit is finite. Hence a subsequence of $(w_n,\theta_n)$ converges in the original domain; closedness follows. Now [F1]–[F2] give $\operatorname{spt}\mu_t=X_t(K_0)$ in this branch as well.

Fix any $\beta>\alpha+B_TT$. In either branch, use $Y_s=X_s$ in the bounded case and the compactified characteristic $Y_s$ from step 3.1 in the unbounded case. Put $\widehat K_0^{\beta}=K_0$ in the bounded case and let $\widehat K_0^{\beta}$ be the closure of $(\mathrm{id}\times\psi)(K_0)$ in $[-\beta,\beta]\times\overline D$ in the unbounded case. This is closed; any added limit points lie on the lateral boundary because $K_0$ is closed in the original domain. Work in $U_\beta=(-\beta,\beta)\times D$, where $D=\operatorname{int}\Theta$ in the bounded case and $D$ is the open unit ball in the compactified case. Let $A_\beta$ be the component of $U_\beta\setminus\widehat K_0^{\beta}$ containing the connected positive face $\{\alpha\}\times D$. The positive face lies in $A_\beta$ because it misses $\widehat K_0^{\beta}$. No point of the negative face lies in $A_\beta$: a path in $A_\beta$ from $-\alpha$ to $+\alpha$ would have a subpath between its last crossing of $w=-r_0$ and its first later crossing of $w=r_0$, wholly inside the original box and disjoint from $K_0$, contrary to the assumed separation. Here components of an open subset of Euclidean space are path connected, since each path component is open and its complement is a union of open path components. The boundary satisfies $\partial A_\beta\subseteq\widehat K_0^{\beta}\cup\partial U_\beta$. At time $s\in[0,T]$, the image of the original part of $\widehat K_0^{\beta}$ lies in $|w|<\alpha$, the horizontal boundary planes $w=\pm\beta$ map outside $|w|\le\alpha$, and the lateral boundary maps into itself by steps 2.1–3.1. The added compactification points are on that lateral boundary. Therefore every target on either $\alpha$ face avoids $Y_s(\partial A_\beta)$. The definition and properties of $D$ in [F3] give $D(Y_t,A_\beta,y)=1$ on the positive face and $D(Y_t,A_\beta,y)=0$ on the negative face.

Suppose a path in $\mathbb R\times\Theta$ joins the negative to the positive $\alpha$ face without meeting $X_t(K_0)$. In the bounded branch, compactness and positive distance from the closed support let us perturb the path by an arbitrarily small convex interpolation toward a fixed interior point of $\Theta$; the perturbed path stays disjoint from the support and has endpoints in $D$. In the unbounded branch its compact image already lies in the open ball after applying $\psi$. Stop the path at its first visit to the positive face, and let $m$ be its minimum $w$-coordinate. Choose $\beta>\max\{\alpha,-m\}+B_TT$ and use the construction of step 5.1 with this $\beta$. The target path is contained in $U_\beta$ and avoids the images of the horizontal boundary planes. In the unbounded case it lies in the open ball, so it also avoids the added lateral limit points of $Y_t(\widehat K_0^{\beta})$; its remaining points avoid that image by the assumption that the original path misses $X_t(K_0)$. Degree invariance along this target path would make its endpoint values of $D(Y_t,A_\beta,\cdot)$ equal, contradicting the values $0$ and $1$ from step 5.1. Thus every such path intersects $X_t(K_0)=\operatorname{spt}\mu_t$.
