Assume AC and the full feature-measure energy hypotheses. Let $\mu_0\in\mathcal P_2(\Omega)$ have finite energy and be concentrated on $Q_{r_0}$. There is a unique global curve $\mu:[0,\infty)	o\mathcal P_2(\Omega)$ in $AC^2_{\mathrm{loc}}$ with $\mu_{t=0}=\mu_0$ that solves the continuity equation with the negative minimum-norm subgradient velocity of the extended potential $F'(\mu_t)+\iota_\Omega$. For every finite $T$, the curve is concentrated on some $Q_{r(T)}$ and satisfies
$$F(\mu_t)-F(\mu_s)=-\int_s^t\int|v_q(u)|^2d\mu_q(u)dq\qquad(0\le s\le t\le T).$$
For any $\mu_0,
u_0\in\mathcal P_2(\Omega)$ concentrated on the same $Q_{r_0}$, their flows obey $\sup_{0\le t\le T}W_2(\mu_t,
u_t)\le e^{K_TT}W_2(\mu_0,
u_0)$ for a finite constant $K_T$ depending only on $T$, $r_0$, and a common upper bound for the initial energies. Consequently, W2-convergent initial laws in a common $Q_{r_0}$ have flows converging uniformly in W2 on every compact time interval.

Assume AC and the feature-measure energy hypotheses. Fix $r>0$ and a nonempty closed convex constraint $D\subseteq\Omega$. For every continuous moment path $m:[0,T]	o\mathcal H$, the nonautonomous inclusion
$$\dot X(t)\in-\partial_{\lambda_V}(V+\iota_D)(X(t))-d\Phi_{X(t)}^*
abla R(m(t))$$
has a unique forward solution from each $X(0)\in D\cap Q_r$; its characteristic map is jointly continuous in $(t,X(0))$ and locally Lipschitz in the initial point on each $Q_r$. Let $\mu_t$ and $
u_t$ be two finite-action solutions on $[0,T]$ of the continuity equation with laws concentrated on $D\cap Q_r$ and velocities
$$v_t^\alpha(x)=-\operatorname{argmin}\{|q|:q\in d\Phi_x^*
abla R(m_{\alpha_t})+\partial_{\lambda_V}(V+\iota_D)(x)\},\qquad\alpha\in\{\mu,
u\},$$
where $m_\alpha=\int\Phi\,d\alpha$. The full shifted minimum selection is Borel; it need not be continuous in position. Each finite-action PDE solution with a continuous prescribed feature moment is the pushforward by its unique characteristic map. For starts in $D\cap Q_r$, these characteristics remain in a larger $Q_R$ uniformly on compact time intervals, and their velocity is the negative full shifted minimum almost everywhere. The same construction applies directly to any continuous forcing $a(t)\in\mathcal H$ in place of $
abla R(m(t))$. Then for all $t\in[0,T]$,
$$W_2(\mu_t,
u_t)\le e^{(C_r-\lambda_V)t}W_2(\mu_0,
u_0),\qquad C_r=L_rA_r^2+N_rB_r.$$
Here $A_r=\sup_{Q_r}\|d\Phi\|$, $B_r=\operatorname{Lip}_{Q_r}(d\Phi)$, $M_r=\sup_{Q_r}\|\partial V\|$ in the bounded-selection convention, and $L_r,N_r$ are respectively a Lipschitz constant and a norm bound for $dR$ on the closed convex hull of $\Phi(Q_r)$. In particular, the localized measure-valued flow is unique for each initial law. The estimate does not assume that $v_t$ is continuous in position.

Assume AC. Let $T>0$ and let $(\mu_t,v_t)$ be a narrowly continuous finite-action solution of the continuity equation on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d$. There is a Borel probability law $\eta$ on $C([0,T];\mathbb R^d)$ such that $(e_t)_\#\eta=\mu_t$ for every $t$, and for $\eta$-almost every path $\gamma$, $\gamma$ is absolutely continuous and $\dot\gamma(t)=v_t(\gamma(t))$ for almost every $t$. Its expected path action equals the Eulerian action:
$$\int\!\int_0^T|\dot\gamma(t)|^2dt\,d\eta(\gamma)=\int_0^T\!\int|v_t(x)|^2d\mu_t(x)dt.$$

Let $X\subseteq\mathbb R^k$ and $Y\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be closed Euclidean subspaces. Let $\mu$ be a finite nonnegative Borel measure on $X$, define $\operatorname{spt}\mu=\{x:\mu(U)>0\text{ for every relatively open neighborhood }U\text{ of }x\}$, and let $f:X\to Y$ be continuous. Define the pushforward by $f_\#\mu(A)=\mu(f^{-1}(A))$ for Borel $A$. Then

$$\operatorname{spt}(f_\#\mu)=\overline{f(\operatorname{spt}\mu)}.$$

Let $d\ge1$, let $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ be bounded and open, and let $f:\overline U\to\mathbb R^d$ be continuous. For $y\notin f(\partial U)$, put $K=f^{-1}(\{y\})\cap U$ and define $D(f,U,y)$ by

$$f_*[U]_K=D(f,U,y)[\mathbb R^d]_{\{y\}}\quad\text{in }H_d(\mathbb R^d,\mathbb R^d\setminus\{y\};\mathbb Z),$$

where $[U]_K$ is the unique relative orientation class restricting to the standard local generator on $K$, and $[\mathbb R^d]_{\{y\}}$ is the positive local generator. This integer is well-defined. It is nonzero only if $f^{-1}(y)\cap U\ne\varnothing$, and $D(\operatorname{id},U,y)=1$ whenever $y\in U$. If $U_1,U_2\subset U$ are disjoint bounded open sets, $y\notin f(\partial U_i)$ for $i=1,2$, and every point of $f^{-1}(y)\cap U$ lies in $U_1\cup U_2$, then

$$D(f,U,y)=D(f,U_1,y)+D(f,U_2,y).$$

If $H:[0,1]\times\overline U\to\mathbb R^d$ and $y:[0,1]\to\mathbb R^d$ are continuous and $y(t)\notin H_t(\partial U)$ for every $t$, then $D(H_0,U,y(0))=D(H_1,U,y(1))$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Since $R(m_{\mu_t})\le F(\mu_0)$, $\|dR_{m_{\mu_t}}\|$ is bounded on $[0,T]$ by [F1]. Differentiating $\Phi(ru)=r^2\Phi(u)$ gives $d\Phi_{ru}=r\,d\Phi_u$. If $\zeta\in\partial_{\lambda_V}V(u)$, substitute $y=rz$ into its defining inequality and use $V(rz)=r^2V(z)$; division by $r^2$ shows $r\zeta\in\partial_{\lambda_V}V(ru)$, and applying the same argument with $1/r$ proves equality of the scaled subdifferentials. The feature-energy bounds on the unit sphere therefore imply $|v_t(u)|\le C|u|$ uniformly on $[0,T]$. Along a characteristic, $r(t)=|X_t(u_0)|$ obeys $|r'(t)|\le Cr(t)$ whenever $r(t)>0$. Grönwall gives $e^{-Ct}|u_0|\le|X_t(u_0)|\le e^{Ct}|u_0|$; the lower bound prevents a nonzero trajectory from reaching zero, while two-homogeneity fixes the zero trajectory.

By [F3], the flow law has a path-space representation concentrated on AC trajectories solving its velocity equation, with initial law $\mu_0$. Each such path solves the nonautonomous characteristic inclusion for the moment path $m_{\mu_t}$; uniqueness in [F2] makes it $t\mapsto X_t(x)$ from its initial point $x$. Therefore $\mu_t=(X_t)_\#\mu_0$. The compact set $K$ has compact image $X_t(K)$; [F4] gives $\operatorname{spt}\mu_t=\overline{X_t(K)}=X_t(K)$. Continuity on $[0,T]\times K$ makes $M_K=\sup_{s\le T,u\in K}|X_s(u)|$ finite.

Let $C_\infty$ be the unbounded component of $\mathbb R^d\setminus K$. It is unique because the complement of a sufficiently large ball is connected. It is an open connected subset of Euclidean space, hence path connected: small open balls show that each path component is open, and its complement, being a union of the other path components, is open as well. No point of $C_\infty$ lies in $B(0,r_a)$: a path in $C_\infty$ from such a point to a point outside $B(0,r_b)$ would contain a subpath from $r_a\mathbb S^{d-1}$ to $r_b\mathbb S^{d-1}$ lying in $C_\infty$ and avoiding $K$, contrary to the initial separation. Choose $\alpha>\max(r_b,M_K)$ and then $\beta>e^{CT}\alpha$. Set $A=B(0,\beta)\cap C_\infty$. Its boundary lies in $K\cup\beta\mathbb S^{d-1}$, and $A\cap B(0,r_a)=\partial A\cap B(0,r_a)=\varnothing$.

For $y\in\alpha\mathbb S^{d-1}$, $y\in A$ and $X_s(\partial A)$ avoids $y$ for all $s\le T$: $X_s(K)\subset B(0,M_K)\subset B(0,\alpha)$, while the radial lower bound sends $\beta\mathbb S^{d-1}$ outside $B(0,\alpha)$. Homotopy invariance [F5] gives $D(X_t,A,y)=D(\operatorname{id},A,y)=1$. Choose $0<\eta<e^{-CT}r_a$. For every $y\in B(0,\eta)$ and $x\in\partial A$, $|X_s(x)|\ge e^{-Cs}|x|\ge e^{-CT}r_a>\eta$, so the target avoids $X_s(\partial A)$. Since $B(0,r_a)\cap A=\varnothing$, the identity degree there is zero; hence $D(X_t,A,y)=0$.

Consider any path from $\eta\mathbb S^{d-1}$ to $\alpha\mathbb S^{d-1}$ and stop it the first time it reaches $\alpha\mathbb S^{d-1}$. Before that time it stays in $\overline{B(0,\alpha)}$, which is disjoint from $X_t(\beta\mathbb S^{d-1})$. If the stopped path avoided $X_t(K)$, then $\partial A\subset K\cup\beta\mathbb S^{d-1}$ would imply that it avoided $X_t(\partial A)$. The degree along that moving target path would be constant by [F5], contradicting its endpoint values $0$ and $1$ from step 4.1. Thus every such path meets $X_t(K)=\operatorname{spt}\mu_t$, proving separation.

For d>=2 the exterior component is unique; initial separation excludes the inner ball. Choose beta>exp(CT)alpha and eta<exp(-CT)ra to avoid boundary images uniformly. Homotopy degree is 1 on the outer target and 0 on the inner one, forcing every joining path to hit support. No backward inverse is used.

citations.quote: Let $W:\Theta\to[0,\infty)$ be bounded and $C^1$, and suppose $V(w,\theta)=|w|W(\theta)$ is globally $\lambda$-semiconvex on $\mathbb R\times\Theta$ for one finite coefficient $\lambda$. Suppose either $\Theta=\mathbb R^q$, or $\Theta$ is the closure of a nonempty bounded connected open convex set with $C^1$ boundary and $dW(n)=0$ on that boundary. Then $W\equiv c$ for some $c\ge0$. In the full partial-model hypotheses, the Neumann assumption for $G_f=\langle f,\varphi\rangle+W$ at $f=0$ supplies the latter condition. Consequently, writing $H_+=\langle f,\varphi\rangle+c$ and $H_-=-\langle f,\varphi\rangle+c$, one has $H_-=2c-H_+$ and $\nabla H_-=-\nabla H_+$.

Assume AC. Let $\mathcal H$ be a real Hilbert space, let $q\ge1$, let $c\ge0$, and let $\varphi:\Theta\to\mathcal H$ be bounded and continuously differentiable with bounded Lipschitz differential. For $s\in\{-1,1\}$ and $f\in\mathcal H$ put
$$H_{s,f}(\theta)=s\langle f,\varphi(\theta)\rangle+c.$$
Assume one of the following alternatives. In the bounded alternative, $\Theta$ is the closure of a bounded nonempty open convex subset of $\mathbb R^q$ with $C^1$ boundary, and $\partial_nH_{s,f}=0$ on its boundary for every $f$. In the unbounded alternative, $\Theta=\mathbb R^q$ and, for every $f$, $H_{s,f}(r\cdot)$ has a limit $H_{s,f}^\infty$ uniformly in $C^1(\mathbb S^{q-1})$ as $r\to\infty$.

Fix $s,f_0$ and $a_0<0$. Suppose $H:=H_{s,f_0}$ has dense regular values in its range and, in the unbounded alternative, the same holds for $H^\infty:=H_{s,f_0}^\infty$. Values whose level sets are empty count as regular. There exist numbers $a,b$ and $\epsilon>0$ with
$$a_0<a<b<0$$
such that the following two assertions hold on every finite interval $[t_0,t_1]$. Let $f:[t_0,t_1]\to\mathcal H$ be Borel with $\|f(t)-f_0\|\le\epsilon$ for every $t$, and let $\rho:[t_0,t_1]\to(0,\infty)$ be continuous. Every absolutely continuous path $\theta:[t_0,t_1]\to\Theta$ satisfying
$$\dot\theta(t)=-\rho(t)\nabla H_{s,f(t)}(\theta(t))\quad\text{for almost every }t$$
and $H(\theta(t_0))\le a$ satisfies $H(\theta(t))<b$ for all $t$. Every absolutely continuous path satisfying the equation with the opposite sign and $H(\theta(t_1))\le a$ satisfies $H(\theta(t))<b$ throughout the same interval. The constants do not depend on the interval, on $\rho$, or on the order in which the forcing values occur. In particular they apply after reversing time and reversing the forcing path. By decreasing $\epsilon$ if necessary, one also has $H_{s,f(t)}(\theta)\le b/2<0$ whenever $H(\theta)<b$.

$$F(\mu_t)-F(\mu_s)=-\int_s^t A(q)dq,\qquad S(t)-S(s)=-2\int_s^t(\langle f_q,m_q\rangle+P_q)dq.$$

Assume AC. Let $T>0$ and let $(\mu_t,v_t)$ be a narrowly continuous finite-action solution of the continuity equation on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d$. There is a Borel probability law $\eta$ on $C([0,T];\mathbb R^d)$ such that $(e_t)_\#\eta=\mu_t$ for every $t$, and for $\eta$-almost every path $\gamma$, $\gamma$ is absolutely continuous and $\dot\gamma(t)=v_t(\gamma(t))$ for almost every $t$. Its expected path action equals the Eulerian action:
$$\int\!\int_0^T|\dot\gamma(t)|^2dt\,d\eta(\gamma)=\int_0^T\!\int|v_t(x)|^2d\mu_t(x)dt.$$

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ be a measurable space and let $\mu$ be a finite nonnegative measure on $(\mathbb R\times\Theta,\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\otimes\mathcal T)$ such that $\int|w|d\mu(w,\theta)<\infty$. Set $w_+=\max(w,0)$ and $w_-=\max(-w,0)$, and define finite nonnegative measures on $\Theta$ by

$$\alpha_\mu(B)=\int_{\mathbb R\times B}w_+d\mu,\qquad\beta_\mu(B)=\int_{\mathbb R\times B}w_-d\mu\quad(B\in\mathcal T).$$

The partially one-homogeneous signed projection is

$$h^1(\mu)=\alpha_\mu-\beta_\mu,\qquad h^1(\mu)(B)=\int_{\mathbb R\times B}w\,d\mu(w,\theta).$$

It is a finite signed measure. For every bounded measurable $\varphi:\Theta\to\mathbb R$, define its integral against this signed projection by

$\int_\Theta\varphi\,dh^1(\mu):=\int_\Theta\varphi d\alpha_\mu-\int_\Theta\varphi d\beta_\mu=\int_{\mathbb R\times\Theta}w\varphi(\theta)d\mu(w,\theta).$

Put $\lambda_\mu=\alpha_\mu+\beta_\mu$, so $\lambda_\mu(B)=\int_{\mathbb R\times B}|w|d\mu$. Its total variation satisfies $|h^1(\mu)|(B)\le\lambda_\mu(B)$ for every $B\in\mathcal T$. Therefore $\int\widetilde Vd|h^1(\mu)|\le\int |w|\widetilde V(\theta)d\mu$ for every bounded nonnegative measurable $\widetilde V$.

If $\mathcal H$ is a separable real Hilbert space and $\varphi:\Theta\to\mathcal H$ is bounded and is the pointwise norm limit on all of $\Theta$ of a sequence of $\mathcal T$-measurable finite-valued simple functions, then for every $z\in\mathcal H$ the feature moment satisfies $\langle z,\int w\varphi(\theta)d\mu\rangle=\int\langle z,\varphi(\theta)\rangle dh^1(\mu)$, with the scalar integral defined above. The raw measures $\alpha_\mu$ and $\beta_\mu$ record positive and negative parameter weights before cancellation and need not be mutually singular; for example, if $\mu$ assigns mass one to each of $(1,\theta_0)$ and $(-1,\theta_0)$ and zero elsewhere, then $\alpha_\mu=\beta_\mu$ both assign mass one to $\theta_0$ while $h^1(\mu)=0$. Thus the signed projection does not by itself determine a penalty of the form $\int|w|\widetilde V(\theta)d\mu$.

By [F1] write $\widetilde V=c$. Apply [F2] to each nonempty $K_s$ using its level $-\eta_s$ as the inner threshold; if necessary choose a regular outer level strictly between that threshold and zero, also regular for the sphere limit in the unbounded case. Choose $\epsilon>0$ so that step 1.1 sends BL distance less than $\epsilon$ into the forcing ball in step 2.1. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC and the feature-measure energy hypotheses. Write $AC^2_{\mathrm{loc}}([0,\infty);\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d))$ for curves whose restriction to every finite interval $[0,T]$ belongs to $AC^2([0,T];\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d))$ in the $W_2$ metric. For $\mu\in\mathcal P_2(\Omega)$ with finite energy, define $F'(\mu)(u)=dR_{m_\mu}[\Phi(u)]+V(u)$ on $\Omega$, and extend this potential by $+\infty$ off $\Omega$. Its constrained subdifferential at $u$ is the local Fréchet subdifferential of $F'(\mu)+\iota_\Omega$ defined in the feature-measure-energy convention. A Wasserstein gradient flow from $\mu_0\in\mathcal P_2(\Omega)$ is a curve $t\mapsto\mu_t$ in $AC^2_{\mathrm{loc}}([0,\infty);(\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d),W_2))$, with $\mu_{t=0}=\mu_0$, for which there is a Borel velocity $v_t(u)$ satisfying the finite-action continuity equation and $v_t(u)$ equals the negative minimum-norm element of $\partial(F'(\mu_t)+\iota_\Omega)(u)$ for $dt\,d\mu_t(u)$-almost every $(t,u)$. This definition does not assert that the energy is displacement convex.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

$$F(\lambda):=R\!\left(\int_{\mathbb R^d}\Phi(u)d\lambda(u)\right)+\int_{\mathbb R^d}V(u)d\lambda(u).$$

$$\int_{\mathbb R^d}\Phi(u)d\mu(u)=\int_{\mathbb S^{d-1}}\Phi(\theta)dh^2(\mu)(\theta),\qquad\int_{\mathbb R^d}V(u)d\mu(u)=\int_{\mathbb S^{d-1}}V(\theta)dh^2(\mu)(\theta).$$

Let $d\ge1$, let $\mathcal H$ be a separable real Hilbert space, and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be the closure of a nonempty convex open set. Let $R:\mathcal H\to[0,\infty)$ be differentiable, with differential Lipschitz on bounded sets in the uniform sense that for every bounded $B\subseteq\mathcal H$ there is a finite $L_B$ such that
$$\|dR_z-dR_{z'}\|_{\mathcal H^*}\le L_B\|z-z'\|_{\mathcal H}\qquad(z,z'\in B),$$
and with differential bounded on every sublevel set of $R$: for each $c\ge0$,
$$\sup\{\|dR_z\|_{\mathcal H^*}:z\in\mathcal H,\ R(z)\le c\}<\infty.$$ In particular, on each closed convex hull of a bounded feature image $\Phi(Q_r)$, both a finite Lipschitz constant $L_r$ and a finite norm bound $N_r$ for $dR$ are available. Let $\Phi:\Omega\to\mathcal H$ be Fréchet differentiable and let $V:\Omega\to[0,\infty)$ be $\lambda_V$-semiconvex, with the convention that $V(u)-\frac{\lambda_V}{2}|u|^2$ is convex on $\Omega$. For a semiconvex function $f$ on a convex domain $D$ with coefficient $\lambda$, define
$$\partial_\lambda f(u)=\{\xi\in\mathbb R^d:f(v)\ge f(u)+\xi\cdot(v-u)+\tfrac{\lambda}{2}|v-u|^2\text{ for every }v\in D\}.$$
For a locally semiconvex function $g$ on $D$, define its local Fréchet subdifferential by
$$\partial g(u)=\left\{\xi\in\mathbb R^d:\liminf_{\substack{v\to u,\ v\in D\\v\ne u}}\frac{g(v)-g(u)-\xi\cdot(v-u)}{|v-u|}\ge0\right\}.$$
When $g$ is globally $\lambda$-semiconvex, this local subdifferential agrees with the convexified supporting set $\partial_\lambda g(u)$.
For every $r>0$, require a nonempty closed convex set $Q_r\subseteq\Omega$, nested increasingly in $r$, such that
$$\{u\in\Omega:\operatorname{dist}(u,Q_r)\le r'\}\subseteq Q_{r+r'}\qquad(r,r'>0),$$
such that $\Phi$ and $V$ are bounded on $Q_r$, $d\Phi$ is Lipschitz on $Q_r$, and there are fixed constants $C_1,C_2>0$ with
$$\sup_{u\in Q_r}\bigl(\|d\Phi_u\|+\|\partial V(u)\|\bigr)\le C_1+C_2r.$$
Here $\partial V(u)=\partial_{\lambda_V}V(u)$ is the supporting set on $\Omega$, and in the growth bound $\|\partial V(u)\|$ means its minimum element norm, equivalently the bound requires a supporting vector of norm at most $C_1+C_2r$ at every $u\in Q_r$. No bound is imposed on the domain normal cone. This is a bounded-selection variant of the source assumptions: Assumption 2.1(iii)(c) in Chizat and Bach explicitly uses the maximal element norm, which implies the minimum-norm bound wherever the supporting set is nonempty. The source does not specify that its maximal bound excludes domain normals. The bounded-selection convention here allows relative-domain supporting sets with unbounded normal vectors; results using this variant require their own proofs. For a Borel set $A\subseteq\Omega$, write $\mathcal P_2(A)$ for the Borel probability measures on $\mathbb R^d$ concentrated on $A$ and having finite second moment.
For a finite nonnegative Borel measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb R^d$, set
$$F(\mu)=R\!\left(\int_\Omega\Phi(u)\,d\mu(u)\right)+\int_\Omega V(u)\,d\mu(u)$$
when $\mu$ is concentrated on $\Omega$, the Bochner integral exists, and the scalar integral is finite; set $F(\mu)=+\infty$ otherwise. For $\mu\in\mathcal P_2(\Omega)$ with finite $F(\mu)$, write $m_\mu=\int_\Omega\Phi\,d\mu$ and define its first-variation potential on $\Omega$ by
$$F'(\mu)(u)=dR_{m_\mu}[\Phi(u)]+V(u).$$
No convexity of $R$ is required by this definition.

Let $d\ge2$, let $\rho_X$ be a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R^{d-1}$ with finite second moment, and define $s(t)=t|t|$ and $\sigma(t)=\max(t,0)$. For $\theta=(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_d)\in\mathbb R^d$, define the signed-square ReLU feature in $L^2(\rho_X)$ by

$$\Phi(\theta)(x)=\sigma\!\left(\sum_{j=1}^{d-1}s(\theta_j)x_j+s(\theta_d)\right).$$

The two-copy parameterization uses this feature on one copy of $\mathbb R^d$ and its negative on the other copy; nonnegative measures on the disjoint union represent signed linear combinations of these features. The scalar signed-square map is continuously differentiable with derivative $s'(t)=2|t|$. This definition asserts differentiability of the resulting $L^2$ feature map only when its data law has the additional regularity needed for that conclusion; it does not assert that its differential is locally Lipschitz.

derivations.claim: On a small neighborhood of $(1,1)$ with $w,b>0$, the root $c(w,b)$ is a smooth function of parameters. For an increment $h=(h_1,h_2)$, $$r_{(w,b)+h}(x)-r_{w,b}(x)=2wh_1x+2bh_2+h_1^2x+h_2^2.$$ The candidate differential is $D\Phi_{(w,b)}h=\mathbf1_{x>c(w,b)}(2wh_1x+2bh_2)$. Outside the interval between $c(w,b)$ and $c((w,b)+h)$, the two preactivations have the same sign; there the ReLU remainder is either zero or $h_1^2x+h_2^2$, whose $L^2(pdx)$ norm is $O(|h|^2)$ by the finite second moment in [F1]. The interval between the two roots has length $O(|h|)$ and lies in a fixed bounded neighborhood of $-1$; on it the pointwise remainder is $O(|h|)$, so its $L^2(pdx)$ norm is $O(|h|^{3/2})$. Thus the full remainder is $o(|h|)$, proving Fréchet differentiability and the displayed differential.

At $(1,1)$ the derivative in direction $e_w=(1,0)$ is $2x\mathbf1_{x>-1}$. At $(1,1+\delta)$ it is $2x\mathbf1_{x>-(1+\delta)^2}$. For $0<\delta\le1/4$, their squared $L^2$ distance is $$4\int_{-(1+\delta)^2}^{-1}x^2p(x)\,dx\ge8p(2)\delta,$$ because the interval lies in $[-2,-1]$, where $x^2\ge1$ and $p(x)\ge p(2)$, and has length $2\delta+\delta^2\ge2\delta$. The operator norm difference of the two differentials is at least their difference on the unit vector $e_w$. Dividing by the parameter distance $\delta$ gives a quotient at least $\sqrt{8p(2)}/\sqrt\delta$, which diverges as $\delta\downarrow0$. Therefore the differential is not locally Lipschitz at $(1,1)$.

There is a Borel probability law $\eta$ on $C([0,T];\mathbb R^d)$ such that $(e_t)_\#\eta=\mu_t$ for every $t$, and for $\eta$-almost every path $\gamma$, $\gamma$ is absolutely continuous and $\dot\gamma(t)=v_t(\gamma(t))$ for almost every $t$. Assume AC. Let $H$ be a separable real Hilbert space, $T>0$, and $x:[0,T]\to H$ be continuous. For a finite partition $P=(t_i)_{i=0}^N$ with $0=t_0<\cdots<t_N=T$, set
$$Q_P(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}\frac{\|x(t_{i+1})-x(t_i)\|_H^2}{t_{i+1}-t_i},\qquad C(x)=\sup_P Q_P(x).$$
If $C(x)<\infty$, then there is a strongly measurable $u\in L^2((0,T);H)$ such that $x(t)=x(0)+\int_0^t u(s)\,ds$ for every $t$, $x$ is norm-differentiable almost everywhere with derivative $u$, and
$$\int_0^T\|u(t)\|_H^2\,dt=C(x).$$

Let $X,Y$ be Banach spaces, let $T:X\to Y$ be bounded and linear, and let $f$
be Bochner integrable. Then $T\circ f$ is Bochner integrable and, for every
measurable $E$,

$$T\left(\int_Ef\,d\mu\right)=\int_E Tf\,d\mu.$$

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. For $F:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$, the following are equivalent:

1. $F$ is absolutely continuous.
2. $F'$ exists almost everywhere, $F'\in L^1[a,b]$, and
$$F(x)-F(a)=\int_a^xF'(t)\,dt\quad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

**Assume the Axiom of Choice.** Let $X$ be a nonempty compact metric space, let $Y$ be a proper metric space, and let $(f_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be an equicontinuous sequence in $C(X,Y)$. If $\{f_k(x):k\in\mathbb N\}$ is bounded for every $x\in X$, then some subsequence converges uniformly to a member of $C(X,Y)$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. For $F:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$, the following are equivalent:

1. $F$ is absolutely continuous.
2. $F'$ exists almost everywhere, $F'\in L^1[a,b]$, and
$$F(x)-F(a)=\int_a^xF'(t)\,dt\quad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

derivations.claim: We first prove a scalar gluing fact, without inferring absolute continuity of a composition with a merely continuous function. Let $I=[u,v]$, let $C\subseteq I$ be closed, let $h:I\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, and let $Q:I\to\mathbb R$ be absolutely continuous with $h=Q$ on $C$. Suppose that $Q'\le-\kappa$ a.e. on $C$, for some $\kappa>0$, and that $h(t)+\kappa t$ is nonincreasing on every component interval of $I\setminus C$, including its endpoints by continuity. Put $U=h+\kappa t$ and $Z=Q+\kappa t$. If $x<y$ both belong to $C$, the complementary open intervals $(\alpha_j,\beta_j)$ of $C$ inside $(x,y)$ have endpoints in $C$. Absolute continuity of $Z$ and countable additivity of its integrable derivative give $Z(y)-Z(x)=\int_{C\cap[x,y]}Z'(t)\,dt+\sum_j\int_{\alpha_j}^{\beta_j}Z'(t)\,dt$. The series is absolutely convergent because the intervals are disjoint and $Z'\in L^1$. Each gap integral equals $Z(\beta_j)-Z(\alpha_j)=U(\beta_j)-U(\alpha_j)\le0$, and the integral over $C$ is nonpositive. Thus $U(y)\le U(x)$. For arbitrary $x<y$, if $[x,y]$ misses $C$ they lie in one gap. Otherwise let $x_*=\min(C\cap[x,y])$ and $y_*=\max(C\cap[x,y])$; monotonicity on the two possible end gaps and the preceding inequality yield $U(y)\le U(y_*)\le U(x_*)\le U(x)$. Hence $h(y)-h(x)\le-\kappa(y-x)$ on all of $I$. This explicitly excludes positive singular variation on the closed contact set; no absolute continuity of $h$ has been assumed or concluded.

Let $d\ge1$, let $\mathcal H$ be a separable real Hilbert space, and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be the closure of a nonempty convex open set. Let $R:\mathcal H\to[0,\infty)$ be differentiable, with differential Lipschitz on bounded sets in the uniform sense that for every bounded $B\subseteq\mathcal H$ there is a finite $L_B$ such that
$$\|dR_z-dR_{z'}\|_{\mathcal H^*}\le L_B\|z-z'\|_{\mathcal H}\qquad(z,z'\in B),$$
and with differential bounded on every sublevel set of $R$: for each $c\ge0$,
$$\sup\{\|dR_z\|_{\mathcal H^*}:z\in\mathcal H,\ R(z)\le c\}<\infty.$$ In particular, on each closed convex hull of a bounded feature image $\Phi(Q_r)$, both a finite Lipschitz constant $L_r$ and a finite norm bound $N_r$ for $dR$ are available. Let $\Phi:\Omega\to\mathcal H$ be Fréchet differentiable and let $V:\Omega\to[0,\infty)$ be $\lambda_V$-semiconvex, with the convention that $V(u)-\frac{\lambda_V}{2}|u|^2$ is convex on $\Omega$. For a semiconvex function $f$ on a convex domain $D$ with coefficient $\lambda$, define
$$\partial_\lambda f(u)=\{\xi\in\mathbb R^d:f(v)\ge f(u)+\xi\cdot(v-u)+\tfrac{\lambda}{2}|v-u|^2\text{ for every }v\in D\}.$$
For a locally semiconvex function $g$ on $D$, define its local Fréchet subdifferential by
$$\partial g(u)=\left\{\xi\in\mathbb R^d:\liminf_{\substack{v\to u,\ v\in D\\v\ne u}}\frac{g(v)-g(u)-\xi\cdot(v-u)}{|v-u|}\ge0\right\}.$$
When $g$ is globally $\lambda$-semiconvex, this local subdifferential agrees with the convexified supporting set $\partial_\lambda g(u)$.
For every $r>0$, require a nonempty closed convex set $Q_r\subseteq\Omega$, nested increasingly in $r$, such that
$$\{u\in\Omega:\operatorname{dist}(u,Q_r)\le r'\}\subseteq Q_{r+r'}\qquad(r,r'>0),$$
such that $\Phi$ and $V$ are bounded on $Q_r$, $d\Phi$ is Lipschitz on $Q_r$, and there are fixed constants $C_1,C_2>0$ with
$$\sup_{u\in Q_r}\bigl(\|d\Phi_u\|+\|\partial V(u)\|\bigr)\le C_1+C_2r.$$
Here $\partial V(u)=\partial_{\lambda_V}V(u)$ is the supporting set on $\Omega$, and in the growth bound $\|\partial V(u)\|$ means its minimum element norm, equivalently the bound requires a supporting vector of norm at most $C_1+C_2r$ at every $u\in Q_r$. No bound is imposed on the domain normal cone. This is a bounded-selection variant of the source assumptions: Assumption 2.1(iii)(c) in Chizat and Bach explicitly uses the maximal element norm, which implies the minimum-norm bound wherever the supporting set is nonempty. The source does not specify that its maximal bound excludes domain normals. The bounded-selection convention here allows relative-domain supporting sets with unbounded normal vectors; results using this variant require their own proofs. For a Borel set $A\subseteq\Omega$, write $\mathcal P_2(A)$ for the Borel probability measures on $\mathbb R^d$ concentrated on $A$ and having finite second moment.
For a finite nonnegative Borel measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb R^d$, set
$$F(\mu)=R\!\left(\int_\Omega\Phi(u)\,d\mu(u)\right)+\int_\Omega V(u)\,d\mu(u)$$
when $\mu$ is concentrated on $\Omega$, the Bochner integral exists, and the scalar integral is finite; set $F(\mu)=+\infty$ otherwise. For $\mu\in\mathcal P_2(\Omega)$ with finite $F(\mu)$, write $m_\mu=\int_\Omega\Phi\,d\mu$ and define its first-variation potential on $\Omega$ by
$$F'(\mu)(u)=dR_{m_\mu}[\Phi(u)]+V(u).$$
No convexity of $R$ is required by this definition.

derivations.claim: Fix $s>0$ and two points $\theta_0,\theta_1\in\Theta$. Restrict the semiconvex inequality [F1] to the slice $w=s$ and divide it by $s$. Its quadratic error is bounded by $|\lambda|t(1-t)|\theta_1-\theta_0|^2/(2s)$. Letting $s\to\infty$ gives the convexity inequality for $W$, for every $0\le t\le1$.

If $\Theta=\mathbb R^q$, restrict $W$ to any line. A nonzero secant slope of a convex function forces its values to grow without bound in one of the two directions: for $a<b<c$, convexity makes the secant slope on $[b,c]$ at least that on $[a,b]$, and the reversed assertion treats a negative slope. Boundedness therefore makes every secant slope zero. Any two points lie on a line, so $W$ is constant.

In the bounded case $W$ attains its maximum at a point $x$ of the compact closure. At an interior maximum $dW_x=0$. At a boundary maximum its tangential differential is zero, because local $C^1$ boundary charts give two-sided differentiable curves in every tangent direction, while the Neumann hypothesis gives zero normal differential. These tangent and normal directions span the ambient space, so again $dW_x=0$. For any $y\in\Theta$, the one-variable convex function $t\mapsto W(x+t(y-x))$ has right derivative $dW_x(y-x)=0$; its secant slope is at least this derivative. Hence $W(y)\ge W(x)$, and maximality gives equality. The final reflected formulas follow by direct differentiation.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,

> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $(\mathcal Z,\mathcal A,P)$ be a probability space and let $\mathcal G$ be a nonempty class of $\mathcal A$-measurable functions $g:\mathcal Z\to[0,1]$. For a fixed sample $S=(z_1,\ldots,z_m)\in\mathcal Z^m$, where $m\ge1$, let $\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_m$ be independent uniform signs in $\{-1,+1\}$. Define

$$P_mg:=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m g(z_i),\qquad Pg:=\int g\,dP,$$

and define the empirical Rademacher complexity by

$$\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal G):=\mathbb E_\sigma\left[\sup_{g\in\mathcal G}\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\sigma_i g(z_i)\right].$$

Here $\mathbb E_\sigma$ is the uniform average over the $2^m$ sign vectors. If $S=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)$ is an IID sample with common law $P$, and the displayed supremum is measurable as a function of $S$, the expected Rademacher complexity is

$$\mathfrak R_m(\mathcal G):=\mathbb E_{S\sim P^m}\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal G).$$

The class may be finite, countable, or uncountable when the indicated supremum is measurable; a specified countable subclass giving the same supremum for every sign vector for almost every sample suffices. This is the one-sided convention: the definition contains no absolute value, and zero need not belong to $\mathcal G$. Both complexities lie in $[0,1]$: every signed average lies in $[-1,1]$, and for any fixed $g_0\in\mathcal G$ the sign-average supremum is at least the sign-average for $g_0$, which is zero.

Let $n,m\ge1$, let $U$ be a nonempty subset of the real matrix space $\mathbb R^{n\times m}$, and let $\epsilon>0$. A **proper $\epsilon$-cover** of $U$ in Frobenius norm is a finite subset $V\subseteq U$ such that every $X\in U$ has some $Y\in V$ with $\lVert X-Y\rVert_F\le\epsilon$. The **proper Frobenius covering number** $N_F(U,\epsilon)$ is the least cardinality of such a cover when one exists, and is $+\infty$ otherwise. The cover is proper because its centers belong to $U$.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\sinh x:=\frac{\exp x-\exp(-x)}2,\qquad\cosh x:=\frac{\exp x+\exp(-x)}2,$$
$$\tanh x:=\frac{\sinh x}{\cosh x},\qquad\operatorname{sech}x:=\frac1{\cosh x}.$$
For $x\ne0$, define
$$\coth x:=\frac{\cosh x}{\sinh x},\qquad\operatorname{csch}x:=\frac1{\sinh x}.$$

The positivity of $\exp$ makes $\cosh x>0$ for every $x$. If $x\ne0$, then
$x\ne-x$, so strict increase of $\exp$ makes $\exp x\ne\exp(-x)$; hence
$\sinh x\ne0$. Thus all four quotients above are defined on exactly their
stated domains ([[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]],
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]]).

For all real $x,y$,
$$\sinh(x+y)=\sinh x\cosh y+\cosh x\sinh y,\qquad\cosh(x+y)=\cosh x\cosh y+\sinh x\sinh y,$$
$$\cosh^2x-\sinh^2x=1,\qquad(\sinh x)'=\cosh x,\qquad(\cosh x)'=\sinh x.$$
Moreover $\sinh:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is odd, strictly increasing, and onto;
$\cosh:\mathbb R\to[1,\infty)$ is even and positive, and its restriction
to $[0,\infty)$ is strictly increasing and onto $[1,\infty)$; and
$\tanh:\mathbb R\to(-1,1)$ is strictly increasing and onto. On their declared domains,
$$(\tanh x)'=\operatorname{sech}^2x,\quad(\coth x)'=-\operatorname{csch}^2x,\quad(\operatorname{sech}x)'=-\operatorname{sech}x\tanh x,\quad(\operatorname{csch}x)'=-\operatorname{csch}x\coth x.$$

Assume additionally that $\varphi(X)$ is either integrable or nonnegative, so

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because The exponential is a continuous bijection from $\mathbb{R}$ onto $(0,\infty)$ states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ (Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point, Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ (Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$) at which $g$ is differentiable
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
(Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of If $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L \ne 0$ then $|f| > |L|/2$ on a punctured neighbourhood of $c$; in particular if $L > 0$ then $f > L/2 > 0$ there applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
Carathéodory's characterisation: $f$ is differentiable at $c$ if and only if there is $\varphi : A \to \mathbb{R}$, continuous at $c$, with $f(x) - f(c) = \varphi(x)(x - c)$ for every $x \in A$, and then $\varphi$ is unique and $\varphi(c) = f'(c)$.** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.

Write $U:=(\mathcal G|S)-v_0$; it contains $0$, and each vector has norm at most $\sqrt n$. For any $\epsilon>0$, partition $[-1,1]^n$ into finitely many boxes of side at most $\epsilon/\sqrt n$; from each box meeting $U$ take one member of that intersection. The resulting finite set is a proper $\epsilon$-cover, since two points in one box differ in Euclidean norm by at most $\epsilon$. Set $\epsilon_j=\sqrt n\,2^{-(j-1)}$. The singleton $V_1=\{0\}$ is a proper $\epsilon_1$-cover of $U$, so $|V_1|=N_F(U,\epsilon_1)=1$. For each finite truncation $N\ge2$ and each $2\le j\le N$, choose a proper $\epsilon_j$-cover $V_j$ of $U$ with the least possible cardinality, so $|V_j|=N_F(U,\epsilon_j)$; such a least cardinality exists because a finite cover exists and cover cardinalities are positive integers. Enumerate each finite cover and map every sample vector to the first center within $\epsilon_j$.

For $T_v=\sum_i\varepsilon_i v_i$, independence of the signs and step 1.1 give $\mathbb E e^{\lambda T_v}=\prod_i\cosh(\lambda v_i)\le e^{\lambda^2R^2/2}$. If $R=0$ or $|V|=1$, $\mathbb E\max_{v\in V}T_v=0$. Otherwise, for $\lambda>0$, [F4] and $e^{\lambda\max_v T_v}\le\sum_{v\in V}e^{\lambda T_v}$ imply $\mathbb E\max_vT_v\le\log|V|/\lambda+\lambda R^2/2$. Choosing $\lambda=\sqrt{2\log|V|}/R$ gives $\mathbb E\max_vT_v\le R\sqrt{2\log|V|}$.

Therefore step 3.1 gives $\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal G)\le\epsilon_N/\sqrt n+(12/n)\int_{\epsilon_{N+1}}^{\sqrt n}f(\epsilon)\,d\epsilon$.

$$\lVert A\rVert_F\;:=\;\Bigl(\,\sum_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|^{2}\Bigr)^{1/2},$$

where $|\cdot|$ is the absolute value on $\mathbb R$
(Absolute value in an ordered field) for $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ and the modulus on $\mathbb C$
(Real and imaginary parts, complex conjugation, and modulus) for
$\mathbb F=\mathbb C$, and the outer power is the nonnegative real square root.

coordinate space $\mathbb F^{mn}$ whose $j+in$-th entry is $a_{ij}$. The
standard coordinate inner product of The standard formulas $\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_{k<n}x_k y_k$ on $\mathbb R^n$ and $\sum_{k<n}x_k\overline{y_k}$ on $\mathbb C^n$ are inner products

(Conjugation is an involutive real-field automorphism, $z\overline z=|z|^2$, and modulus is definite, multiplicative, and subadditive). Thus $\lVert A\rVert_F$ is
exactly the inner-product norm of The norm $\lVert v\rVert=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ induced by a real or complex inner product evaluated at $A$,
and the three norm axioms hold for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_F$ because they hold for
every inner-product norm. For real matrices the same sum is

Absolute value in an ordered field.

The Frobenius norm is the Euclidean norm of the full entry list, not the
largest factor by which the matrix stretches a single vector. It can coincide
with an induced $2$-norm in one-row or one-column cases, but in general it is a
different matrix norm from the induced operator norms used on this page. Its

formula are
Spectral and Frobenius norms are unitarily invariant, are given by singular values, and satisfy the sharp rank comparison.

For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.

The function induced by an inner product satisfies, for all vectors $u,v$ and scalars $\lambda$,

$$\lVert v\rVert\ge0,\qquad \lVert v\rVert=0\Longleftrightarrow v=0,$$

$$\lVert\lambda v\rVert=|\lambda|\lVert v\rVert,\qquad \lVert u+v\rVert\le\lVert u\rVert+\lVert v\rVert.$$

Let $n,m\ge1$, let $U$ be a nonempty subset of the real matrix space $\mathbb R^{n\times m}$, and let $\epsilon>0$. A **proper $\epsilon$-cover** of $U$ in Frobenius norm is a finite subset $V\subseteq U$ such that every $X\in U$ has some $Y\in V$ with $\lVert X-Y\rVert_F\le\epsilon$. The **proper Frobenius covering number** $N_F(U,\epsilon)$ is the least cardinality of such a cover when one exists, and is $+\infty$ otherwise. The cover is proper because its centers belong to $U$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because The exponential is a continuous bijection from $\mathbb{R}$ onto $(0,\infty)$ states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

Let $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$ be metric spaces ([[def-metric-space]]) and let
$f : X \to Y$ be continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then:

1. If $(X,d_X)$ is compact ([[def-metric-compactness]]), the image
   $f[X] \subseteq Y$ is a compact subset of $Y$.
2. More generally, if $K \subseteq X$ is a compact subset of $X$, then $f[K]$ is
   a compact subset of $Y$.

No choice principle is used.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space,
Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
(Continuity of a map between metric spaces, at a point and globally, in the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ form), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below (Lower bound, bounded below, bounded set), and it has a
maximum and a minimum (Maximum and minimum of a set): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
(Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property), Greatest lower bound (infimum)).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

derivations.claim: For any $B\in\mathbb R^{d\times m}$, write its columns as $b_j$ and the columns of $X$ as $x_r$. By [F2], $\lVert Xb_j\rVert_2^2=\sum_i|\sum_rX_{ir}(b_j)_r|^2\le\lVert X\rVert_F^2\lVert b_j\rVert_2^2$. Summing over $j$ gives $\lVert XB\rVert_F\le\lVert X\rVert_F(\sum_j\lVert b_j\rVert_2^2)^{1/2}\le\lVert X\rVert_F\sum_j\lVert b_j\rVert_2=\lVert X\rVert_F\lVert B\rVert_{2,1}$; the middle inequality follows by squaring, since all column norms are nonnegative. Thus $\lVert A-A'\rVert_{2,1}\le2a$ for $A,A'\in C$, and the diameter of $U$ is at most $2a\lVert X\rVert_F$. If $a\lVert X\rVert_F=0$, $U$ is a singleton; if $\epsilon\ge2a\lVert X\rVert_F$, any one point of nonempty $U$ covers it.

Assume $a\lVert X\rVert_F>0$ and $0<\epsilon<2a\lVert X\rVert_F$. For each nonzero column $x_r$, each output coordinate $j$, and each sign $\eta\in\{-1,+1\}$, form the rank-one atom $V_{rj\eta}=\eta(x_r/\lVert x_r\rVert_2)e_j^\top$, where $e_j$ is the $j$th standard basis vector in $\mathbb R^m$. There are at most $2dm$ atoms and each has Frobenius norm $1$. For $B=A-M$, the expansion $XB=\sum_{r,j}(B)_{rj}x_re_j^\top$ has coefficient mass $\beta:=\sum_{r,j}|B_{rj}|\lVert x_r\rVert_2\le\lVert B\rVert_{2,1}\lVert X\rVert_F\le a\lVert X\rVert_F=:c$, by [F2] column by column. Hence $XB/c$ lies in the convex hull of these signed atoms: if $\beta<c$, fill the remaining weight with $0$, which is the midpoint of an atom and its negative. If $\beta=0$, the product is $0$.

For an integer $k\ge1$, sample $k$ atoms independently from the finite convex representation of $XB/c$ constructed in step 1.2. If $V_1,\ldots,V_k$ are these atoms and $\mathbb E V_1=XB/c$, expansion of the squared Frobenius norm and independence give $\mathbb E\lVert c k^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^kV_t-XB\rVert_F^2=(c^2/k)(\mathbb E\lVert V_1\rVert_F^2-\lVert\mathbb EV_1\rVert_F^2)\le c^2/k$. Therefore some ordered $k$-tuple gives a center within $c/\sqrt k$, and all such centers number at most $(2dm)^k$. Taking $k=\lceil c^2/\epsilon^2\rceil$ yields an external $\epsilon$-cover of the translated relaxed product set $XM+\{XB:\lVert B\rVert_{2,1}\le a\}$.

The mixed-norm constraint set is convex: for $A,A'\in C$ and $0\le t\le1$, the column triangle inequality [F3] gives $\lVert t(A-M)+(1-t)(A'-M)\rVert_{2,1}\le ta+(1-t)a=a$. The operator-norm constraint is convex because for each unit vector $v$, $\lVert(tA+(1-t)A')v\rVert_2\le t\lVert Av\rVert_2+(1-t)\lVert A'v\rVert_2\le s$, and taking the supremum over $v$ preserves the bound. The mixed norm is continuous as a finite sum of continuous column norms. From [F7] and the Euclidean triangle inequality, $|\lVert A\rVert_\sigma-\lVert A'\rVert_\sigma|\le\lVert A-A'\rVert_\sigma\le\lVert A-A'\rVert_F$, where the last inequality follows from the rowwise Cauchy estimate in step 1.1; hence the operator norm is continuous and $C$ is closed. Also $\lVert A-M\rVert_F\le\lVert A-M\rVert_{2,1}\le a$, so $C$ is bounded. Identify the real matrix space with $\mathbb R^{dm}$ by its entries; its Euclidean norm is the Frobenius norm, so [F5] makes $C$ compact. The map $T(A)=XA$ is continuous because step 1.1 and [F2] give $\lVert T(A)-T(A')\rVert_F\le\lVert X\rVert_F\lVert A-A'\rVert_{2,1}\le\sqrt m\lVert X\rVert_F\lVert A-A'\rVert_F$. Hence [F8] makes $U=T(C)$ compact; it is convex because $C$ is convex and $T$ is linear. For each of the finitely many external centers $z$ from step 2.1, the function $u\mapsto\lVert z-u\rVert_F$ is continuous on the nonempty compact metric space $U$, since the reverse triangle inequality bounds its change by $\lVert u-u'\rVert_F$. Thus [F9] gives a nearest point $p\in U$ for each center; enumerate the finite center set and choose these minimizers successively. For any $u\in U$, convexity gives $p+t(u-p)\in U$ for $0\le t\le1$. Put $\langle P,Q\rangle_F:=\sum_{i,j}P_{ij}Q_{ij}$. Minimality implies $0\le\lVert z-p-t(u-p)\rVert_F^2-\lVert z-p\rVert_F^2=-2t\langle z-p,u-p\rangle_F+t^2\lVert u-p\rVert_F^2$ for $0<t\le1$; division by $t$ and passage to $t\downarrow0$ give $\langle z-p,u-p\rangle_F\le0$. Expanding $\lVert z-u\rVert_F^2$ then gives $\lVert p-u\rVert_F^2\le\lVert z-u\rVert_F^2$. Thus projection does not increase distance to any point of $U$, and the cover becomes proper without increasing its size.

Put $q=a^2\lVert X\rVert_F^2/\epsilon^2>1/4$. Then $k=\lceil q\rceil\le q+1\le5q$, so step 2.1 and [F6] imply $\log N_F(U,\epsilon)\le k\log(2dm)\le5q\log(2dm)$. Together with step 1.1 this proves both cases of the Statement.

Let $K\ge2$, let $D$ be a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R^d\times\{1,\ldots,K\}$, and let $F:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^K$ be a continuous score map. At $(x,y)$ its **multiclass margin** is
$$m_F(x,y):=F(x)_y-\max_{j\ne y}F(x)_j.$$
The predicted label is
$$\widehat y_F(x):=\min\{j\in\{1,\ldots,K\}:F(x)_j=\max_{1\le l\le K}F(x)_l\}.$$
Its population zero-one error is
$$L_0(F):=D\bigl(\{(x,y):\widehat y_F(x)\ne y\}\bigr).$$
For $\gamma>0$, the **ramp loss** is
$$\ell_\gamma(r):=\begin{cases}0,&r< -\gamma,\\1+r/\gamma,&-\gamma\le r\le0,\\1,&r>0.\end{cases}$$
The population ramp risk is $R_\gamma(F):=\int\ell_\gamma(-m_F(x,y))\,D(d(x,y))$. For a sample $S=((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_n,y_n))$ of length $n\ge1$, the empirical ramp risk and empirical margin loss are
$$\widehat R_{\gamma,S}(F):=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\ell_\gamma(-m_F(x_i,y_i)),\qquad\widehat L_{\gamma,S}(F):=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf1\{m_F(x_i,y_i)\le\gamma\}.$$
The score coordinates are continuous, and finite maxima, comparisons, and the piecewise-linear ramp preserve Borel measurability. Thus the classification event and ramp loss in the displayed integrals are Borel sets or functions, so the risks are well-defined for $D$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it

2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of

   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in Law or distribution of a random element agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in Independent random elements. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
Measurable rectangles in a product of measurable spaces.

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element, let
$\mathbb P_X$ be its law, and let $g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb R$ or
$g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb C$ be measurable.

1. If $g\ge0$, then
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$
2. If $g(X)$ is integrable, then $g$ is integrable with respect to
   $\mathbb P_X$ and the same formula holds:
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $n\ge1$, let $Z_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be independent random elements, meaning measurable maps (Random elements and real random variables), with laws $\mu_i$ given by pushforward (Law or distribution of a random element). Put $\mu=\bigotimes_{i=1}^n\mu_i$ on the finite product sigma-algebra (The product sigma-algebra and its finite iterates). Let $f:\prod_{i=1}^nS_i\to\mathbb R$ be product-measurable with $\int|f|\,d\mu<\infty$. Suppose finite deterministic constants $c_i\ge0$ satisfy
$$|f(z_1,\ldots,z_i,\ldots,z_n)-f(z_1,\ldots,z_i',\ldots,z_n)|\le c_i$$
for every fixed setting of the other coordinates and every $z_i,z_i'$. The independent product-law theorem identifies the law of $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)$ as $\mu$. Applying change of variables for expectation first to $|f|$ and then to $f$ makes $f(Z)$ integrable and gives $\mathbb E f(Z)=\int f\,d\mu$. Put $V=\sum_{i=1}^n c_i^2$. For $t>0$, if $V>0$ then
$$\mathbb P\bigl(f(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)-\mathbb E f(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)\ge t\bigr)\le\exp\!\left(-\frac{2t^2}{V}\right),$$
and if $V=0$ this probability is $0$. The same bound holds for the lower tail, so the two-sided probability is at most $2e^{-2t^2/V}$ when $V>0$.

Let $(\mathcal Z,\mathcal A,P)$ be a probability space and let $\mathcal G$ be a nonempty class of $\mathcal A$-measurable functions $g:\mathcal Z\to[0,1]$. For a fixed sample $S=(z_1,\ldots,z_m)\in\mathcal Z^m$, where $m\ge1$, let $\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_m$ be independent uniform signs in $\{-1,+1\}$. Define

$$P_mg:=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m g(z_i),\qquad Pg:=\int g\,dP,$$

and define the empirical Rademacher complexity by

$$\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal G):=\mathbb E_\sigma\left[\sup_{g\in\mathcal G}\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\sigma_i g(z_i)\right].$$

Here $\mathbb E_\sigma$ is the uniform average over the $2^m$ sign vectors. If $S=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)$ is an IID sample with common law $P$, and the displayed supremum is measurable as a function of $S$, the expected Rademacher complexity is

$$\mathfrak R_m(\mathcal G):=\mathbb E_{S\sim P^m}\widehat{\mathfrak R}_S(\mathcal G).$$

The class may be finite, countable, or uncountable when the indicated supremum is measurable; a specified countable subclass giving the same supremum for every sign vector for almost every sample suffices. This is the one-sided convention: the definition contains no absolute value, and zero need not belong to $\mathcal G$. Both complexities lie in $[0,1]$: every signed average lies in $[-1,1]$, and for any fixed $g_0\in\mathcal G$ the sign-average supremum is at least the sign-average for $g_0$, which is zero.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because The exponential is a continuous bijection from $\mathbb{R}$ onto $(0,\infty)$ states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

Write $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ for the image of $\mathbb{Q}$ in $\mathbb{R}$
under the canonical embedding $q \mapsto \hat q$ (The rationals embed densely in the reals), the
set usually written $\mathbb{Q}$ once the identification is made, and put
$X := \mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ for the irrationals. Then:

1. $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$, that is,
   $\overline{\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}} = \mathbb{R}$ (Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$);
2. $X$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$;
3. every nonempty open subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is uncountable
   (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable).

Claim 2 is not a symmetry of claim 1: the rationals are dense because they are
*constructed* to approximate, whereas the irrationals are dense because there are
too many points in any interval for a countable set to exhaust it, which is why
claim 3 is proved alongside and used for it.

derivations.claim: Let $\Theta$ be the set of all feasible tuples $(A_1,\ldots,A_L)$. The mixed-norm constraints are closed because each is a finite sum of continuous Euclidean column norms. For each layer, $\lVert A_i\rVert_\sigma\le s_i$ is the intersection, over all unit vectors $v$, of the closed conditions $\lVert A_iv\rVert_2\le s_i$, by the induced-operator-norm definition. Each column $A_ie_j$ then has norm at most $s_i$, so all matrix entries are bounded. Hence $\Theta$ is closed and bounded in finite-dimensional Euclidean space and is compact by [F2].

For fixed $x$, induction over the layers shows that the score vector depends continuously on the matrix tuple: matrix multiplication is jointly continuous and each Lipschitz activation is continuous. Finite maxima, coordinate differences, and the ramp preserve continuity, so for fixed $(x,y)$ the loss $A\mapsto\ell_\gamma(-m_{F_A}(x,y))$ is continuous. If $A^{(r)}\to A$, these losses converge pointwise in $(x,y)$ and are bounded by one, so [F3] shows that $A\mapsto R_\gamma(F_A)$ is continuous. Each empirical loss and each finite signed sum of losses is also continuous in $A$.

Identify the parameter tuples with $\mathbb R^p$, where $p:=\sum_{i=1}^L d_i d_{i-1}$. The balls $B(q,r)$ with $q\in\mathbb Q^p$ and $r\in\mathbb Q_{>0}$ form a countable family: each rational is a quotient of an integer by a positive integer, the integers have the enumeration $0,1,-1,2,-2,\ldots$, and finite tuples of natural numbers are enumerated by iterating the diagonal pairing $\pi(a,b):=(a+b)(a+b+1)/2+b$.
