Assume the axiom of choice.

Fix a finite network architecture with $L\ge1$, widths $d_0,\ldots,d_L\ge1$, output size $K=d_L\ge2$, activations, and reference matrices as in the spectral-network-complexity definition. Let $s_i>0$, $b_i\ge0$, and let $\mathcal F$ be the nonempty class with layer constraints $\lVert A_i\rVert_\sigma\le s_i$ and $\lVert A_i^\top-M_i^\top\rVert_{2,1}\le b_i$. Let $S=((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_n,y_n))$ be an iid sample from any Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R^{d_0}\times\{1,\ldots,K\}$, let $X$ be its input matrix with rows $x_i^\top$, and fix $n\ge1$, $\gamma>0$, and $0<\delta<1$. Set $W:=\max_{0\le i\le L}d_i$. With probability at least $1-\delta$, every $F_A\in\mathcal F$ satisfies
$$L_0(F_A)\le\widehat L_{\gamma,S}(F_A)+\frac8n+\frac{36\sqrt{20}\,\lVert X\rVert_F\sqrt{\log(2W^2)}\log n}{\gamma n}\left(\prod_{i=1}^L\rho_i s_i\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^L(b_i/s_i)^{2/3}\right)^{3/2}+3\sqrt{\frac{\log(2/\delta)}{2n}}.$$
All logarithms are natural. The matrix norm on $X$ is the Frobenius norm, and the empirical margin loss uses the threshold convention $m_{F_A}(x_i,y_i)\le\gamma$.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$ and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$. The **Frobenius norm** of $A$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_F\;:=\;\Bigl(\,\sum_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|^{2}\Bigr)^{1/2},$$

where $|\cdot|$ is the absolute value on $\mathbb R$
(Absolute value in an ordered field) for $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ and the modulus on $\mathbb C$
(Real and imaginary parts, complex conjugation, and modulus) for
$\mathbb F=\mathbb C$, and the outer power is the nonnegative real square root.

**The displayed quantity is a norm.** Regard $A$ as the element of the
coordinate space $\mathbb F^{mn}$ whose $j+in$-th entry is $a_{ij}$. The
standard coordinate inner product of The standard formulas $\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_{k<n}x_k y_k$ on $\mathbb R^n$ and $\sum_{k<n}x_k\overline{y_k}$ on $\mathbb C^n$ are inner products
satisfies $\langle A,A\rangle=\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}\overline{a_{ij}}$, which equals
$\sum_{i,j}|a_{ij}|^{2}$ because $z\overline z=|z|^{2}$
(Conjugation is an involutive real-field automorphism, $z\overline z=|z|^2$, and modulus is definite, multiplicative, and subadditive). Thus $\lVert A\rVert_F$ is
exactly the inner-product norm of The norm $\lVert v\rVert=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ induced by a real or complex inner product evaluated at $A$,
and the three norm axioms hold for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_F$ because they hold for
every inner-product norm. For real matrices the same sum is
$\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}^{2}$, since $|x|^{2}=x^{2}$ for real $x$ by the two cases of
Absolute value in an ordered field.

The Frobenius norm is the Euclidean norm of the full entry list, not the
largest factor by which the matrix stretches a single vector. It can coincide
with an induced $2$-norm in one-row or one-column cases, but in general it is a
different matrix norm from the induced operator norms used on this page. Its
relation to the spectral norm, its unitary invariance and its singular-value
formula are
Spectral and Frobenius norms are unitarily invariant, are given by singular values, and satisfy the sharp rank comparison.

Let $K\ge2$, let $D$ be a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R^d\times\{1,\ldots,K\}$, and let $F:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^K$ be a continuous score map. At $(x,y)$ its **multiclass margin** is
$$m_F(x,y):=F(x)_y-\max_{j\ne y}F(x)_j.$$
The predicted label is
$$\widehat y_F(x):=\min\{j\in\{1,\ldots,K\}:F(x)_j=\max_{1\le l\le K}F(x)_l\}.$$
Its population zero-one error is
$$L_0(F):=D\bigl(\{(x,y):\widehat y_F(x)\ne y\}\bigr).$$
For $\gamma>0$, the **ramp loss** is
$$\ell_\gamma(r):=\begin{cases}0,&r< -\gamma,\\1+r/\gamma,&-\gamma\le r\le0,\\1,&r>0.\end{cases}$$
The population ramp risk is $R_\gamma(F):=\int\ell_\gamma(-m_F(x,y))\,D(d(x,y))$. For a sample $S=((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_n,y_n))$ of length $n\ge1$, the empirical ramp risk and empirical margin loss are
$$\widehat R_{\gamma,S}(F):=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\ell_\gamma(-m_F(x_i,y_i)),\qquad\widehat L_{\gamma,S}(F):=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf1\{m_F(x_i,y_i)\le\gamma\}.$$
The score coordinates are continuous, and finite maxima, comparisons, and the piecewise-linear ramp preserve Borel measurability. Thus the classification event and ramp loss in the displayed integrals are Borel sets or functions, so the risks are well-defined for $D$.

If $A$ and $B$ are at most countable (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) then so is
$A \times B$.

**No choice principle is used**: the two enumerations are given, and the
enumeration of the product is written down from them.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $A,B\in\mathcal F$,
and let $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be events.

1. $\mathbb P(A^c)=1-\mathbb P(A)$.
2. If $A\subseteq B$, then $\mathbb P(A)\le\mathbb P(B)$.
3. If $A\subseteq B$, then $\mathbb P(B\setminus A)=\mathbb P(B)-\mathbb P(A)$.
4. $\mathbb P(\bigcup_n A_n)\le\sum_{n=0}^\infty \mathbb P(A_n)$, and for every
   natural $m$,
   $$\mathbb P\left(\bigcup_{n<m}A_n\right)\le\sum_{n<m}\mathbb P(A_n).$$
5. $\mathbb P(A\cup B)=\mathbb P(A)+\mathbb P(B)-\mathbb P(A\cap B)$.
6. If $A_n\uparrow A$, then
   $$\mathbb P(A)=\sup_n\mathbb P(A_n).$$
   If $A_n\downarrow A$, then
   $$\mathbb P(A)=\inf_n\mathbb P(A_n).$$

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because The exponential is a continuous bijection from $\mathbb{R}$ onto $(0,\infty)$ states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in Law or distribution of a random element agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in Independent random elements. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: For each integer $j\in\mathbb Z$, put $\gamma_j:=2^j/n$ and $v_j:=2^{-|j|}/3$. Then $\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}v_j=(1+2\sum_{m\ge1}2^{-m})/3=1$, since $\sum_{m=1}^N2^{-m}=1-2^{-N}\to1$. Every $\gamma>0$ belongs to exactly one interval $[\gamma_j,2\gamma_j)$. For each positive integer $m$, put $w_m:=1/(m(m+1))=1/m-1/(m+1)$; the finite partial sum is $\sum_{m=1}^Nw_m=1-1/(N+1)$, so $\sum_{m\ge1}w_m=1$.

The integers are countable by the enumeration $0,1,-1,2,-2,\ldots$; the other factors are positive integers, so repeated use of [F4] shows that the tuples indexed by $j\in\mathbb Z$, a positive integer $q$, and positive integers $k_i,l_i$ for $1\le i\le L$ form a countable set. For such a tuple set $\eta_{j,q,k,l}:=\delta v_j w_q\prod_iw_{k_i}w_{l_i}$. Let $J_N=\{-N,\ldots,N\}$ and $M_N=\{1,\ldots,N\}$. Finite distributivity gives the sum over $J_N\times M_N^{1+2L}$ as $\delta(\sum_{j\in J_N}v_j)(\sum_{q\in M_N}w_q)\prod_i(\sum_{k_i\in M_N}w_{k_i})(\sum_{l_i\in M_N}w_{l_i})$, which tends to $\delta$ by step 1.1. These finite boxes increase to the countable index set and contain every finite subset for large enough $N$; since all terms are nonnegative, their partial sums establish $\sum_{j,q,k,l}\eta_{j,q,k,l}=\delta$. For each tuple consider the layer class with caps $s_i=l_i/L$ and $b_i=k_i/L$; if it is empty its event is vacuous. Otherwise [F1] gives a fixed-margin result at $\gamma_j$ and confidence $\eta_{j,q,k,l}$, with its displayed sample-norm term evaluated at the realized $X$.

Apply countable subadditivity [F4] to the failure events from step 2.1. Their union has probability at most $\sum_{j,q,k,l}\eta_{j,q,k,l}=\delta$. Thus outside that union, all fixed-margin inequalities for every tuple hold simultaneously.

Fix any realized sample, any network with nonzero layer matrices, and any $\gamma>0$. Choose its unique $j$ from step 1.1 with $\gamma_j\le\gamma<2\gamma_j$, and set $q=\lfloor\lVert X\rVert_F\rfloor+1,\qquad k_i=\lfloor L\lVert A_i^\top-M_i^\top\rVert_{2,1}\rfloor+1,\qquad l_i=\lfloor L\lVert A_i\rVert_\sigma\rfloor+1.$ These positive integers satisfy $\lVert X\rVert_F<q$, $\lVert A_i^\top-M_i^\top\rVert_{2,1}<k_i/L$, and $0<\lVert A_i\rVert_\sigma<l_i/L$. The network belongs to the corresponding constrained class. Also $\widehat L_{\gamma_j,S}(F_A)\le\widehat L_{\gamma,S}(F_A)$ by [F3], and $1/(\gamma_j n)<2/(\gamma n)$.

In the leading term of [F1], the cap expression satisfies $\left(\prod_i s_i\right)\left(\sum_i(b_i/s_i)^{2/3}\right)^{3/2}=\left(\sum_i\left(b_i\prod_{r\ne i}s_r\right)^{2/3}\right)^{3/2}.$ For the tuple selected in step 4.1, $q\le1+\lVert X\rVert_F$, $k_i/L\le\lVert A_i^\top-M_i^\top\rVert_{2,1}+1/L$, and $l_i/L\le\lVert A_i\rVert_\sigma+1/L$. Monotonicity of the sums and products therefore bounds [F1]'s leading term by the leading term in the Statement, using $1/(\gamma_jn)<2/(\gamma n)$.

The confidence logarithm for this tuple equals $\log(2/\eta_{j,q,k,l})=\log(6/\delta)+|j|\log2+\log(q(q+1))+\sum_i\bigl(\log(k_i(k_i+1))+\log(l_i(l_i+1))\bigr).$ Put $t=n\gamma$. If $j\ge0$, then $2^j\le t$ and $|j|\log2\le\log(2+t)$. If $j<0$, then $t<2^{j+1}\le1$, so $\log(2+t)\ge\log2$ and $\log(2+1/t)\ge\log(1/t)$; their sum is at least $\log(2/t)>|j|\log2$. For each positive integer bin chosen as $m=\lfloor u\rfloor+1$, one has $m\le u+1$ and $m+1\le u+2$, hence $\log(m(m+1))\le2\log(u+2)$. Apply this with $u=\lVert X\rVert_F$ and $u=L\lVert A_i^\top-M_i^\top\rVert_{2,1}$ or $L\lVert A_i\rVert_\sigma$. By [F5], the result is $\log(2/\eta_{j,q,k,l})\le Q(A,X,\gamma,n,\delta)$.

On the probability-$1-\delta$ event from step 3.1, apply the selected fixed-margin inequality. Steps 4.1–5.2 replace its empirical margin loss, leading term, and confidence term by the respective terms displayed in the Statement. The choices in step 4.1 were arbitrary, so this holds simultaneously for every network with nonzero layer matrices and every $\gamma>0$.

$$m_F(x,y):=F(x)_y-\max_{j\ne y}F(x)_j.$$
The predicted label is
$$\widehat y_F(x):=\min\{j\in\{1,\ldots,K\}:F(x)_j=\max_{1\le l\le K}F(x)_l\}.$$
Its population zero-one error is
$$L_0(F):=D\bigl(\{(x,y):\widehat y_F(x)\ne y\}\bigr).$$
For $\gamma>0$, the **ramp loss** is
$$\ell_\gamma(r):=\begin{cases}0,&r< -\gamma,\\1+r/\gamma,&-\gamma\le r\le0,\\1,&r>0.\end{cases}$$
The population ramp risk is $R_\gamma(F):=\int\ell_\gamma(-m_F(x,y))\,D(d(x,y))$. For a sample $S=((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_n,y_n))$ of length $n\ge1$, the empirical ramp risk and empirical margin loss are
$$\widehat R_{\gamma,S}(F):=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\ell_\gamma(-m_F(x_i,y_i)),\qquad\widehat L_{\gamma,S}(F):=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf1\{m_F(x_i,y_i)\le\gamma\}.$$

$$h_u(x):=\min\{k\in\mathcal Y:u_k(x)=\max_{j\in\mathcal Y}u_j(x)\}$$

Let $(\mathcal X,\Sigma_X)$ be a nonempty measurable instance space, let $\mathcal Y=\{1,\ldots,K\}$ have its discrete sigma-algebra with $K\ge2$, and equip $\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y$ and its finite powers with their product sigma-algebras. Let $P$ be a probability law on $\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y$. For an integer $m\ge1$, write a sample as $S=((X_1,Y_1),\ldots,(X_m,Y_m))$. A score map $u=(u_1,\ldots,u_K):\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^K$ is **coordinatewise measurable** when each $u_k:(\mathcal X,\Sigma_X)\to(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$ is measurable. Define its classifier by the least-index tie rule

$$h_u(x):=\min\{k\in\mathcal Y:u_k(x)=\max_{j\in\mathcal Y}u_j(x)\}$$

and its margin on label $y$ by

$$M_u(x,y):=u_y(x)-\max_{j\in\mathcal Y,\ j\ne y}u_j(x).$$

For each $k\in\mathcal Y$,
$$\{x:h_u(x)=k\}=\bigcap_{j<k}\{x:u_k(x)>u_j(x)\}\cap\bigcap_{j>k}\{x:u_k(x)\ge u_j(x)\},$$
and each comparison set is measurable; an intersection over no indices means $\mathcal X$. Since $\mathcal Y$ is finite, $M_u$ is measurable on $\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y$ as well. The population zero-one risk is
$$R_P(h_u):=P\{(x,y):h_u(x)\ne y\}.$$
For a sample $S$ of length $m$ and $\gamma\ge0$, the empirical margin loss is
$$\widehat L_\gamma(u;S):=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\mathbf1\{M_u(X_i,Y_i)\le\gamma\}.$$
The event defining $R_P(h_u)$ is measurable by measurability of $h_u$.

Fix integers $q\ge0$ and $r\ge1$. A fixed-helper finite parameter codebook consists of a helper string $s$ fixed independently of the sample, finite nonempty sets $D_1,\ldots,D_q$ with $|D_j|\le r$, a nonempty code set $\mathcal A\subseteq\prod_{j=1}^qD_j$, and one coordinatewise measurable decoder score map $g_{s,a}:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^K$ for each $a\in\mathcal A$. For $q=0$, the empty product is the singleton containing the empty tuple. The codebook and all its decoders are fixed independently of the sample, so $|\mathcal A|\le r^q$.

Let $F:(\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y)^m\times\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^K$ be measurable for the product sigma-algebra on its domain and the Borel sigma-algebra on $\mathbb R^K$. Let $\alpha:(\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y)^m\to\mathcal A$ be measurable, where $\mathcal A$ has its discrete sigma-algebra, and write $f_S(x):=F(S,x)$. For $\epsilon>0$, the sample-dependent trained score map $f_S$ is $\epsilon$-compressible by this codebook on a sample $S$ if
$$\max_{k\in\mathcal Y}|f_S(X_i)_k-g_{s,\alpha(S)}(X_i)_k|\le\epsilon\qquad(1\le i\le m).$$
The code $\alpha(S)$ may depend on $S$; the helper string, codebook, and decoders remain fixed independently of the sample.

The following corrected finite-description form of Arora, Ge, Neyshabur, and Zhang's compression bound applies to a measurable sample-dependent score classifier. Let $(\mathcal X,\Sigma_X)$ be a nonempty measurable space, let $\mathcal Y=\{1,\ldots,K\}$ have the discrete sigma-algebra with $K\ge2$, put $\Sigma_Z=\Sigma_X\otimes2^{\mathcal Y}$ on $Z=\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y$, and let $P$ be a probability law on $(Z,\Sigma_Z)$. Let $m\ge1$ and draw $S=((X_1,Y_1),\ldots,(X_m,Y_m))$ independently and identically distributed (IID) with law $P$, with sample space $Z^m$ carrying $\Sigma_Z^{\otimes m}$. Fix integers $q\ge0$, $r\ge1$, a helper string $s$ independent of $S$, finite nonempty parameter sets $D_1,\ldots,D_q$ with $|D_j|\le r$, a nonempty code set $\mathcal A\subseteq\prod_{j=1}^qD_j$ (with the empty product a singleton when $q=0$), a distortion tolerance $\epsilon>0$, and a confidence level $0<\delta<1$. For any score map $u$ with measurable coordinates, write $h_u(x)$ for the classifier that chooses the least index attaining the largest coordinate of $u(x)$. For each $a\in\mathcal A$, let $g_{s,a}:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^K$ have measurable coordinates and put $h_{s,a}:=h_{g_{s,a}}$. Equip $\mathbb R^K$ with its Borel sigma-algebra. Let $F:Z^m\times\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^K$ be measurable for $\Sigma_Z^{\otimes m}\otimes\Sigma_X$, write $f_S(x)=F(S,x)$, and let $\alpha:Z^m\to\mathcal A$ be measurable for the discrete sigma-algebra on $\mathcal A$. Suppose that, for $P^m$-almost every $S$,
$$\max_{k\in\mathcal Y}|f_S(X_i)_k-g_{s,\alpha(S)}(X_i)_k|\le\epsilon\qquad(1\le i\le m)$$
With natural logarithms, define
$$R_P(h):=P\{(x,y):h(x)\ne y\},\qquad \widehat R_S(h):=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\mathbf1\{h(X_i)\ne Y_i\},$$
$$M_{f_S}(x,y):=f_S(x)_y-\max_{j\ne y}f_S(x)_j,\qquad \widehat L_\gamma(f_S;S):=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\mathbf1\{M_{f_S}(X_i,Y_i)\le\gamma\},\qquad \gamma\ge0.$$
Then, with probability at least $1-\delta$ over $S$,
$$R_P\bigl(h_{s,\alpha(S)}\bigr)\le\widehat L_{2\epsilon}(f_S;S)+\sqrt{\frac{q\log r+\log(1/\delta)}{2m}}.$$
In particular, the coordinatewise distortion $\epsilon$ only guarantees preservation of an observed label when its original score margin is strictly greater than $2\epsilon$. The conclusion bounds the selected compressed classifier $h_{s,\alpha(S)}$; it does not bound the original classifier $h_{f_S}$ unless a separate all-domain loss-preservation argument is supplied. The theorem assumes a suitable fixed-helper compressor and makes no claim that a network compression construction exists or that layer-stability or cushion hypotheses hold.

derivations.claim: Let the two hidden ReLU units for $f$ be $u_1(x)=\rho(x)$ and $u_2(x)=\rho(1-x)$, with output coordinates $(10u_2,u_1)$. Let $g$ use one hidden unit $u_1(x)=\rho(x)$, output weights zero, and output biases $(10,0)$. These are finite one-hidden-layer graphs with hidden activation $\rho$ and identity output activation, as in [F1]. Direct evaluation gives $f(0)=g(0)=(10,0)$ and $f(1)=(0,1)$, $g(1)=(10,0)$.

The least-index argmax rule predicts class $1$ for both maps at $x=0$; at $x=1$, $f$ predicts class $2$ and $g$ predicts class $1$. Under $P$, $f$ is correct on both support points, while $g$ errs exactly at $(1,2)$, so $R_P(h_f)=0$ and $R_P(h_g)=1/2$. Also $P^1\{S=((0,1))\}=1/2$.

Let $\mathcal A=\{a_0\}$ with one parameter slot whose only possible value is $a_0$, fix the helper string, decode $a_0$ to $g$, and let the compressor choose $a_0$ on every sample. On $S=((0,1))$, the maximum coordinate error is $0\le1/10$, so this sample is compressed and the predictions agree on the observed point. On $S'=((1,2))$, the maximum coordinate error is $10>1/10$, so this fixed compressor fails the almost-sure premise of the theorem under $P$. Therefore this example establishes only that single-sample agreement can coexist with different off-sample predictions and population risks; it does not contradict or invoke the theorem's high-probability conclusion.

citations.quote: A **supervised prediction problem** consists of nonempty measurable spaces $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$ of instances, $(\mathsf Y,\Sigma_Y)$ of labels, and $(\mathsf A,\Sigma_A)$ of prediction actions; the product measurable space $(\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y,\Sigma_X\otimes\Sigma_Y)$; a probability measure $P$ on that product; a nonempty class $\mathcal F$ of measurable predictors $f:\mathsf X\to\mathsf A$; and a loss $\ell:\mathsf A\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty]$ that is measurable with respect to $\Sigma_A\otimes\Sigma_Y$. The law $P$ need not be supported on a deterministic labeling function, and this definition imposes no assumption that sample observations be independent or share a common law.

For a supervised prediction problem with joint law $P$, the **population risk** of any measurable predictor $f:\mathsf X\to\mathsf A$ (in particular, every $f\in\mathcal F$) is the extended nonnegative integral
$$R_P(f):=\int_{\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y}\ell(f(x),y)\,P(d(x,y))\in[0,+\infty].$$
For an ordered sample $S=((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_m,y_m))$ of length $m\ge1$, the **empirical risk** or **training risk** of any such $f$ is
$$\widehat R_S(f):=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\ell(f(x_i),y_i)\in[0,+\infty].$$
Neither definition assumes finite risk. The sum uses extended nonnegative arithmetic; since $m\ge1$, any summand equal to $+\infty$ makes the empirical risk $+\infty$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of Finite sums and finite products, by recursion applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum

Squares of nonzero elements are positive, the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
Integer powers $a^m$) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space (The standard list $e : n \to F^{n}$ with $e_i(i) = 1_F$ and $e_i(j) = 0_F$ for $j \ne i$ is an ordered basis of $F^{n}$; hence $\dim_F F^{n} = n$, and $F^{0}$ is the zero space with basis $\varnothing$ and dimension $0$ clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
$\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such

exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ (Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   (Squares of nonzero elements are positive), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of A norm on a real vector space, the induced metric, and the dictionary with the metric axioms
is proved in Cauchy-Schwarz $\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \le \lVert x\rVert_2\lVert y\rVert_2$ with its equality case, the triangle inequality for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$, the parallelogram law and polarisation, where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in The Euclidean inner product $\langle x,y\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k y_k$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   (A norm on a real vector space, the induced metric, and the dictionary with the metric axioms), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for finite sums, stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
The Euclidean inner product $\langle x,y\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k y_k$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Fix a supervised prediction problem with observation space $\mathsf Z=\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y$, measurable predictor class $\mathcal F$, and nonnegative measurable loss $\ell$. Write $L_f(x,y)=\ell(f(x),y)$ for $f\in\mathcal F$. Fix a sample size $n\ge1$. A randomized learning rule at this sample size consists of internal randomness $U_n$ with law $Q_n$, independent of the sample, and an output $A_n(S,U_n)\in\mathcal F$ for every ordered sample $S\in\mathsf Z^n$. Assume the expected test losses below are finite. For $\varepsilon\ge0$, the rule has **uniform replacement stability at level $\varepsilon$** if, for every pair $S,S'\in\mathsf Z^n$ differing in at most one coordinate, and every test observation $z\in\mathsf Z$,

$$\left|\mathbb E_{U_n}L_{A_n(S,U_n)}(z)-\mathbb E_{U_n}L_{A_n(S',U_n)}(z)\right|\le\varepsilon.$$

The absolute value is outside expectation over the internal randomness. No permutation-invariance condition is imposed on the learning rule.

Let $n\ge1$ and consider a supervised prediction problem with measurable observation space $\mathsf Z=\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y$, probability law $P$, measurable predictor class $\mathcal F$, and nonnegative measurable loss $\ell$. For $f\in\mathcal F$ and $z=(x,y)$, write $L_f(z)=\ell(f(x),y)$, $R_P(f)=\int L_f(z)\,P(dz)$, and, for $S=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)$, $\widehat R_S(f)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nL_f(Z_i)$. Let $Z_1,\ldots,Z_n$ be IID with law $P$, and let $U_n$ be internal randomness independent of the sample. Suppose the randomized learning rule $A_n(S,U_n)$ takes values in $\mathcal F$, the joint loss map $(S,U_n,z)\mapsto L_{A_n(S,U_n)}(z)$ is measurable, and all displayed risks are integrable. If $A_n$ has uniform replacement stability at level $\varepsilon$, then

$$\left|\mathbb E_{S,U_n}\left[R_P(A_n(S,U_n))-\widehat R_S(A_n(S,U_n))\right]\right|\le\varepsilon.$$

The expectation is over both the IID sample and the algorithm's internal randomness. No permutation-invariance assumption on $A_n$ is required.

For every real $x$,
$$1+x\le\exp(x).$$
Consequently, if $0\le p\le1$ and $m\in\mathbb N$, then
$$ (1-p)^m\le\exp(-mp). $$
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

For all real $x,y$,
$$\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y).$$

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

For $a>0$ and $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$a^x:=\exp(x\log a).$$
For the supplementary zero-base convention, define $0^x:=0$ when $x>0$.

The expressions $0^0$ and $0^x$ for $x<0$ are left undefined. Negative bases are not assigned arbitrary real powers.

For $a>0$, the function $x\mapsto a^x$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and
$$(a^x)'=a^x\log a.$$
For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with
$$(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}.$$

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ (The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ (The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ (Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point). Then $f$ is bounded (Lower bound, bounded below, bounded set) and Riemann integrable on $[a,b]$ (The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$).

Let $a < c < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be bounded
(Lower bound, bounded below, bounded set). Then:

1. $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ (The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$) **if and only if** its
   restrictions to $[a,c]$ and to $[c,b]$ are integrable;
2. and in that case
   $$\int_a^b f \;=\; \int_a^c f \;+\; \int_c^b f .$$
3. **Oriented form.** Let $\alpha < \beta$ be reals, let $f : [\alpha,\beta] \to
   \mathbb{R}$ be integrable, and let $u, v, w \in [\alpha,\beta]$ be arbitrary.
   Then, with the convention of The integral with oriented limits: $\int_a^a f := 0$ and $\int_b^a f := -\int_a^b f$,
   $$\int_u^v f \;+\; \int_v^w f \;=\; \int_u^w f .$$

Claim 3 is where The integral with oriented limits: $\int_a^a f := 0$ and $\int_b^a f := -\int_a^b f$ earns its place: it holds for every
arrangement of the three points, including the degenerate ones, and it is the
form used everywhere below.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
(The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$). Then:

1. **Nonnegativity.** If $f(x) \ge 0$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $\int_a^b f \ge 0$.
2. **Monotonicity.** If $f(x) \le g(x)$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $$\int_a^b f \;\le\; \int_a^b g .$$
3. **Two-sided bound.** If $m \le f(x) \le M$ for every $x \in [a,b]$, with
   $m, M$ real, then
   $$m\,(b-a) \;\le\; \int_a^b f \;\le\; M\,(b-a) .$$

**Equality in claim 1 does not force $f$ to vanish.** A nonnegative integrable
function with integral $0$ may be positive at infinitely many points; that is
FALSE: a nonnegative Riemann integrable function on $[a,b]$ with $\int_a^b f = 0$ is identically zero on the previous page's
companion. Under the additional hypothesis of continuity the conclusion does
hold, and that is A continuous $f \ge 0$ on $[a,b]$ with $\int_a^b f = 0$ is identically $0$
below.

**Claim 2 is stated for $a < b$ and is not orientation-invariant.** With the
convention of The integral with oriented limits: $\int_a^a f := 0$ and $\int_b^a f := -\int_a^b f$, $f \le g$ gives
$\int_u^v f \le \int_u^v g$ when $u \le v$ and the reverse inequality when
$u \ge v$, since both sides change sign together.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in Law or distribution of a random element agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in Independent random elements. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

A **supervised prediction problem** consists of nonempty measurable spaces $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$ of instances, $(\mathsf Y,\Sigma_Y)$ of labels, and $(\mathsf A,\Sigma_A)$ of prediction actions; the product measurable space $(\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y,\Sigma_X\otimes\Sigma_Y)$; a probability measure $P$ on that product; a nonempty class $\mathcal F$ of measurable predictors $f:\mathsf X\to\mathsf A$; and a loss $\ell:\mathsf A\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty]$ that is measurable with respect to $\Sigma_A\otimes\Sigma_Y$. The law $P$ need not be supported on a deterministic labeling function, and this definition imposes no assumption that sample observations be independent or share a common law.

For a supervised prediction problem with joint law $P$, the **population risk** of any measurable predictor $f:\mathsf X\to\mathsf A$ (in particular, every $f\in\mathcal F$) is the extended nonnegative integral
$$R_P(f):=\int_{\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y}\ell(f(x),y)\,P(d(x,y))\in[0,+\infty].$$
For an ordered sample $S=((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_m,y_m))$ of length $m\ge1$, the **empirical risk** or **training risk** of any such $f$ is
$$\widehat R_S(f):=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\ell(f(x_i),y_i)\in[0,+\infty].$$
Neither definition assumes finite risk. The sum uses extended nonnegative arithmetic; since $m\ge1$, any summand equal to $+\infty$ makes the empirical risk $+\infty$.

Let $n,T,d\ge1$, let $\beta>0$ and $L\ge0$, and let $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$, $(\mathsf Y,\Sigma_Y)$, and $(\mathsf A,\Sigma_A)$ be measurable spaces. Let $P$ be a probability measure on $\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y$, let $\ell:\mathsf A\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty)$ be a measurable loss, and let $f_w:\mathsf X\to\mathsf A$ be a measurable predictor for every $w\in\mathbb R^d$. For $z=(x,y)$ set $g(w,z)=\ell(f_w(x),y)$ and assume this map and $(w,z)\mapsto\nabla_wg(w,z)$ are jointly measurable. For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because The exponential is a continuous bijection from $\mathbb{R}$ onto $(0,\infty)$ states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in The exponential series converges absolutely for every real argument. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of The factorial $n!$ and the falling factorial $n^{\underline{k}}$, defined by recursion in $\mathbb{N}$, $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image (The canonical natural $\iota(n) = n \cdot 1_F$ of a field, Canonical naturals are positive and strictly increasing), and powers and series are those of Integer powers $a^m$ and Series, partial sums, convergence and the sum, divergence, and the tail series.

This is a real power series centred at $0$ (A real power series about a centre, its interval of convergence, and its radius in $[0,+\infty]$). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and

derivations.claim: The positive-part function is nondecreasing and $1$-Lipschitz: if two inputs have the same sign, the positive-part difference is either their difference or zero; if they have opposite signs, the positive part of the nonnegative input is at most the distance between them. It is convex as the maximum of the affine functions $0$ and $1+t$. Therefore $\ell_{\rm h}$ is nondecreasing, convex, and $1$-Lipschitz, and $\ell_{\rm h}(0)=1$.
By [F2]–[F3] and the chain rule, $$\ell_{\rm log}'(t)=\frac{e^t}{(1+e^t)\ln2},\qquad \ell_{\rm log}''(t)=\frac{e^t}{(1+e^t)^2\ln2}.$$

By [F1], $\ln2>0$, and [F2] gives $e^t>0$. Step 1.2 therefore shows that $0<\ell_{\rm log}'(t)\le1/\ln2$ for every real $t$. The derivative is positive, so the logistic loss is strictly increasing; applying [F5] on each closed interval gives the global $1/\ln2$ Lipschitz bound.

The second derivative in step 1.2 is nonnegative because its numerator and denominator are positive. The convexity criterion [F4] gives convexity of $\ell_{\rm log}$. Also $\ell_{\rm log}(0)=\log_2(2)=1$ from the definition of $\log_2$.

Since $L_0$ exceeds both Lipschitz constants, steps 1.1 and 2.1 give the common $L_0$-Lipschitz bound. For the hinge loss, if $0<R<1/\sqrt2$, then $B_{\ell_{\rm h},R}=(1+2R^2)-(1-2R^2)=4R^2>0$; if $R\ge1/\sqrt2$, then $B_{\ell_{\rm h},R}=1+2R^2>0$. The logistic loss is strictly increasing by step 2.1, so $B_{\ell_{\rm log},R}>0$ as well. In either case, the interval has length $4R^2$, so the Lipschitz bound gives $B_{\ell,R}\le4L_0R^2$.

Let $(\mathcal C,\mathcal C_0,\rho)$ be a measurable probability space and $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ a measurable space. For each class $c\in\mathcal C$, let $D_c$ be a probability measure on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ and assume $c\mapsto D_c(A)$ is measurable for every $A\in\mathcal A$. Assume the displayed mixtures define probability measures. The positive-pair law $D_{\rm sim}$ and negative marginal $D_{\rm neg}$ are specified by

$$D_{\rm sim}(A\times B):=\int_{\mathcal C}D_c(A)D_c(B)\,\rho(dc),\qquad D_{\rm neg}(A):=\int_{\mathcal C}D_c(A)\,\rho(dc)$$

for measurable $A,B\in\mathcal A$. Equivalently, draw $C\sim\rho$ and then draw $X,X^+$ independently with law $D_C$ for a positive pair; draw a fresh independent class $C'\sim\rho$ and $X^-\sim D_{C'}$ for one negative. The class labels are latent: the learner observes the pair and negative data, not their classes.

Let $d\ge1$, $R>0$, and let $\mathcal F$ be a nonempty class of measurable maps $f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^d$ satisfying $\sup_{x\in\mathcal X}\lVert f(x)\rVert_2\le R$. Use either one-negative loss $\ell_{\rm h}(t)=(1+t)_+$ or $\ell_{\rm log}(t)=\log_2(1+e^t)$ from the immediately preceding loss-properties lemma. The contrastive score and population loss are

$$q_f(x,x^+,x^-):=f(x)^\top\bigl(f(x^-)-f(x^+)\bigr),\qquad L_{\rm un}(f):=\mathbb E_{(X,X^+)\sim D_{\rm sim},\,X^-\sim D_{\rm neg}}\bigl[\ell(q_f(X,X^+,X^-))\bigr].$$

For $M\ge1$, an observed sample is $S=((x_j,x_j^+,x_j^-))_{j=1}^M$ of $M$ independent triplets with common law $D_{\rm sim}\otimes D_{\rm neg}$, and its empirical loss is $\widehat L_{\rm un}(f):=M^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^M\ell(q_f(x_j,x_j^+,x_j^-))$. For this sample define the unnormalized vector Rademacher complexity

$$\mathcal R_S(\mathcal F):=\mathbb E_\varepsilon\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\sum_{j=1}^M\sum_{t=1}^d\bigl(\varepsilon_{jt0}f_t(x_j)+\varepsilon_{jt+}f_t(x_j^+)+\varepsilon_{jt-}f_t(x_j^-)\bigr),$$

where every $\varepsilon_{jt0},\varepsilon_{jt+},\varepsilon_{jt-}$ is an independent uniform sign. This is the one-sided convention with no absolute value and no $1/M$ factor.

All vector and matrix expectations in this definition are taken entrywise in finite dimensions. The bound on $f$ makes each coordinate of $f(X)$ and every product defining a covariance entry integrable.

Let $C_+,C_-\sim\rho$ be independent class draws and set $\tau:=\Pr(C_+=C_-)<1$. Assume the diagonal $\Delta:=\{(c,c):c\in\mathcal C\}$ and each $\Delta_A:=\{(c,c):c\in A\}$, $A\in\mathcal C_0$, are measurable. The average binary task draws $(C_+,C_-)$ conditional on $C_+\ne C_-$, then samples a label $Y$ uniformly from $\{+1,-1\}$ and an input $X$ from $D_{C_+}$ if $Y=+1$ or $D_{C_-}$ if $Y=-1$. For a vector representation $f$, a binary linear classifier uses a weight vector $w\in\mathbb R^d$ and loss $\ell(-Yw^\top f(X))$. Define $L_{\rm sup}(f)$ as the average over tasks of the infimum of this risk over $w\in\mathbb R^d$. Write $\mu_c:=\mathbb E_{X\sim D_c}f(X)$ and define the class-mean classifier by $w_\mu=\mu_{C_+}-\mu_{C_-}$; its average risk is $L^\mu_{\rm sup}(f)$. For $\gamma>0$, write $L^\mu_{\gamma,\rm sup}(f)$ for the same mean-classifier risk with margin loss $\ell_\gamma(t):=(1+t/\gamma)_+$ in place of $\ell$.

For $\tau>0$, let $L^=_{\rm un}(f)$ and $L^\ne_{\rm un}(f)$ be the conditional contrastive risks given $C_+=C_-$ and $C_+\ne C_-$, respectively. Let $\nu$ be the class law conditioned on the collision event, namely $\nu(A):=(\rho\otimes\rho)(\Delta_A)/\tau$ for $A\in\mathcal C_0$; for an atomic class law this gives $\nu(\{c\})=\rho(\{c\})^2/\tau$. Define $\Sigma_f(c):=\mathbb E_{X\sim D_c}[(f(X)-\mu_c)(f(X)-\mu_c)^\top]$ and

$$s(f):=\mathbb E_{C\sim\nu}\left[\sqrt{\lVert\Sigma_f(C)\rVert_{\rm op}}\,\mathbb E_{X\sim D_C}\lVert f(X)\rVert_2\right],\qquad \lVert\Sigma\rVert_{\rm op}:=\max_{\lVert u\rVert_2=1}\lVert\Sigma u\rVert_2.$$

The assumed measurability of $\Delta$ and every $\Delta_A$ makes the displayed collision event and conditional class law well-defined; disjoint class sets give disjoint $\Delta_A$, so the formula for $\nu$ is countably additive and has total mass one. Assume also that $c\mapsto\mu_c$ and $c\mapsto\Sigma_f(c)$ are measurable for each $f$, and that the displayed class-conditional risks and random suprema used below are measurable.

If $\tau=0$, there is no collision term; set $s(f):=0$ and use $L_{\rm un}(f)=L^\ne_{\rm un}(f)$. Any empirical minimizer or approximate minimizer used below is separately assumed to be a measurable selector; no selector-existence claim is part of this definition.

Write $\ln$ for the natural logarithm and $\log_2 u:=\ln(u)/\ln(2)$ for $u>0$. Define the one-negative hinge and logistic losses by $\ell_{\rm h}(t):=(1+t)_+$ and $\ell_{\rm log}(t):=\log_2(1+e^t)$ for $t\in\mathbb R$, where $r_+:=\max\{r,0\}$. Put $L_0:=1+1/\ln(2)$. Each loss is convex, nondecreasing, $L_0$-Lipschitz, and has value $1$ at $0$. For $R>0$ and either loss $\ell$, define $B_{\ell,R}:=\ell(2R^2)-\ell(-2R^2)$. Then $0<B_{\ell,R}\le4L_0R^2$.

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

derivations.claim: Fix distinct classes $c_+,c_-$ and an anchor $x\in\mathcal X$. Conditional on these classes and $x$, the random score $Z=f(x)^\top(f(X^-)-f(X^+))$ is integrable and has mean $\mathbb E[Z]=f(x)^\top(\mu_{c_-}-\mu_{c_+})$ by independence and [F5] applied to the bounded coordinates. Jensen's inequality [F2] gives $\mathbb E[\ell(Z)]\ge\ell(f(x)^\top(\mu_{c_-}-\mu_{c_+}))$. Integrating over $x\sim D_{c_+}$ and then over distinct ordered class pairs shows that $L^\ne_{\rm un}(f)$ is at least the average mean-classifier loss on the positive label.

By [F4], swapping $(c_+,c_-)$ preserves the conditional ordered-pair law. Therefore the average mean-classifier loss on the negative label equals its average on the positive label: swapping the classes turns its margin $f(x)^\top(\mu_{c_+}-\mu_{c_-})$ into the positive-label margin from step 1.1. Since the task label is uniform, the average of the two label risks is exactly the positive-label average. Thus $L^\mu_{\rm sup}(f)\le L^\ne_{\rm un}(f)$.

derivations.claim: Partition the independent class-pair law into the collision event, of probability $\tau$, and its complement, of probability $1-\tau$. The conditional loss on these two events is respectively $L^=_{\rm un}(f)$ and $L^\ne_{\rm un}(f)$, giving the displayed decomposition when $\tau>0$. If $\tau=0$, the collision event is null and $L_{\rm un}(f)=L^\ne_{\rm un}(f)$.

Suppose $\tau>0$. Fix a collision class $c$ and anchor $x$. Conditional on $x,c$, let $Y_+=f(X^+)$ and $Y_-=f(X^-)$ be independent copies with mean $\mu_c$. Then $\mathbb E[f(x)^\top(Y_--Y_+)]=0$ by [F4] and [F6]. Jensen's inequality [F9], using convexity [F2], gives $\mathbb E[\ell(f(x)^\top(Y_--Y_+))]\ge\ell(0)=1$. Averaging over $x\sim D_c$ and $c\sim\nu$ proves $L^=_{\rm un}(f)\ge1$.

With $Z_+:=f(X^+) -\mu_c$ and $Z_-:=f(X^-) -\mu_c$, the conditional vectors are independent, centered, and have covariance $\Sigma_f(c)$. For each matrix entry, Fubini and product-law independence factor the cross expectation as $\mathbb E[(Z_-)_{r}(Z_+)_{s}]=\mathbb E[(Z_-)_{r}]\mathbb E[(Z_+)_{s}]=0$, and likewise with $+$ and $-$ exchanged. Linearity therefore gives $\mathbb E[(Z_--Z_+)(Z_--Z_+)^\top]=2\Sigma_f(c)$. By [F3], $\Sigma_f(c)$ is positive semidefinite; by [F7] and the operator-norm definition, $f(x)^\top\Sigma_f(c)f(x)\le\lVert f(x)\rVert_2\lVert\Sigma_f(c)f(x)\rVert_2\le\lVert\Sigma_f(c)\rVert_{\rm op}\lVert f(x)\rVert_2^2$. Thus $$\mathbb E\bigl[(f(x)^\top(Y_--Y_+))^2\bigr]=2f(x)^\top\Sigma_f(c)f(x)\le2\lVert\Sigma_f(c)\rVert_{\rm op}\lVert f(x)\rVert_2^2.$$

Apply [F8] to the bounded score in step 1.3 to get $\mathbb E|f(x)^\top(Y_--Y_+)|\le\sqrt2\sqrt{\lVert\Sigma_f(c)\rVert_{\rm op}}\lVert f(x)\rVert_2$. By [F2], $\mathbb E[\ell(f(x)^\top(Y_--Y_+))]-1\le L_0\mathbb E|f(x)^\top(Y_--Y_+)|$. Average over $x\sim D_c$ and $c\sim\nu$ to obtain $L^=_{\rm un}(f)-1\le\sqrt2L_0s(f)$.
Steps 1.2 and 2.1 establish both bounds on $L^=_{\rm un}(f)$, while step 1.1 gives the unconditional decomposition and the zero-collision case.

$$q_f(x,x^+,x^-):=f(x)^\top\bigl(f(x^-)-f(x^+)\bigr),\qquad L_{\rm un}(f):=\mathbb E_{(X,X^+)\sim D_{\rm sim},\,X^-\sim D_{\rm neg}}\bigl[\ell(q_f(X,X^+,X^-))\bigr].$$

$$\mathcal R_S(\mathcal F):=\mathbb E_\varepsilon\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\sum_{j=1}^M\sum_{t=1}^d\bigl(\varepsilon_{jt0}f_t(x_j)+\varepsilon_{jt+}f_t(x_j^+)+\varepsilon_{jt-}f_t(x_j^-)\bigr),$$

where every $\varepsilon_{jt0},\varepsilon_{jt+},\varepsilon_{jt-}$ is an independent uniform sign. This is the one-sided convention with no absolute value and no $1/M$ factor.

All vector and matrix expectations in this definition are taken entrywise in finite dimensions. The bound on $f$ makes each coordinate of $f(X)$ and every product defining a covariance entry integrable.

Applying [F4] to $e^{\lambda Z}$ with $\lambda=t/v>0$ and using step 1.1 gives $p:=\Pr(Z\ge t)\le e^{-t^2/(2v)}=e^{-t^2/(4R^2\sigma^2)}\le\epsilon/(3R^2)$ for $R\ge1$, and $p\le\epsilon/3$ for $0<R<1$. On $\{Z\ge t\}$, the score bound in step 1.1 gives $(1+m+Z)_+=(1+q)_+\le1+2R^2$. Therefore $\mathbb E_Z(1+m+Z)_+\le(\gamma+m)_++p(1+2R^2)\le(\gamma+m)_++\epsilon$, because $1+2R^2\le3R^2$ for $R\ge1$ and $1+2R^2\le3$ for $R<1$. When $\sigma=0$, step 2.1 gives $Z\le0=t$ almost surely, so $(1+m+Z)_+\le(1+m)_+=(\gamma+m)_+$ and the same inequality follows. Since $\gamma\ge1$, $(\gamma+m)_+=\gamma(1+m/\gamma)_+$.

Integrate the conditional inequality in step 3.1 over $x\sim D_{c_+}$ and the ordered class-pair law conditioned on inequality. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. In the one-negative latent-class model, fix $R>0$, a source loss $\ell\in\{\ell_{\rm h},\ell_{\rm log}\}$, a sample size $M\ge1$, and a sample $S$ of $M$ IID triplets. Assume the loss risks and all sample, independent-copy, and sign suprema below are measurable. Let $B_{\ell,R}=\ell(2R^2)-\ell(-2R^2)$ and define

$$\Gamma_M(S,\delta):=\frac{2\sqrt{18}L_0R\,\mathcal R_S(\mathcal F)}{M}+3B_{\ell,R}\sqrt{\frac{\ln(4/\delta)}{2M}},\qquad 0<\delta<1.$$

With probability at least $1-\delta$ over $S$,

$$\forall f\in\mathcal F,\qquad |L_{\rm un}(f)-\widehat L_{\rm un}(f)|\le\Gamma_M(S,\delta).$$

Here $\mathcal R_S(\mathcal F)$ is the unnormalized vector Rademacher complexity of the three embeddings in each triplet.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. In the one-negative latent-class model, fix $R>0$, a source loss $\ell\in\{\ell_{\rm h},\ell_{\rm log}\}$, a sample size $M\ge1$, and a sample $S$ of $M$ IID triplets. Assume the loss risks and all sample, independent-copy, and sign suprema below are measurable. Let $B_{\ell,R}=\ell(2R^2)-\ell(-2R^2)$ and define

$$\Gamma_M(S,\delta):=\frac{2\sqrt{18}L_0R\,\mathcal R_S(\mathcal F)}{M}+3B_{\ell,R}\sqrt{\frac{\ln(4/\delta)}{2M}},\qquad 0<\delta<1.$$

With probability at least $1-\delta$ over $S$,

$$\forall f\in\mathcal F,\qquad |L_{\rm un}(f)-\widehat L_{\rm un}(f)|\le\Gamma_M(S,\delta).$$

Here $\mathcal R_S(\mathcal F)$ is the unnormalized vector Rademacher complexity of the three embeddings in each triplet.

Let $(\mathcal C,\mathcal C_0,\rho)$ be a measurable probability space and $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ a measurable space. For each class $c\in\mathcal C$, let $D_c$ be a probability measure on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ and assume $c\mapsto D_c(A)$ is measurable for every $A\in\mathcal A$. Assume the displayed mixtures define probability measures. The positive-pair law $D_{\rm sim}$ and negative marginal $D_{\rm neg}$ are specified by

$$D_{\rm sim}(A\times B):=\int_{\mathcal C}D_c(A)D_c(B)\,\rho(dc),\qquad D_{\rm neg}(A):=\int_{\mathcal C}D_c(A)\,\rho(dc)$$

for measurable $A,B\in\mathcal A$. Equivalently, draw $C\sim\rho$ and then draw $X,X^+$ independently with law $D_C$ for a positive pair; draw a fresh independent class $C'\sim\rho$ and $X^-\sim D_{C'}$ for one negative. The class labels are latent: the learner observes the pair and negative data, not their classes.

Let $d\ge1$, $R>0$, and let $\mathcal F$ be a nonempty class of measurable maps $f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^d$ satisfying $\sup_{x\in\mathcal X}\lVert f(x)\rVert_2\le R$. Use either one-negative loss $\ell_{\rm h}(t)=(1+t)_+$ or $\ell_{\rm log}(t)=\log_2(1+e^t)$ from the immediately preceding loss-properties lemma. The contrastive score and population loss are

$$q_f(x,x^+,x^-):=f(x)^\top\bigl(f(x^-)-f(x^+)\bigr),\qquad L_{\rm un}(f):=\mathbb E_{(X,X^+)\sim D_{\rm sim},\,X^-\sim D_{\rm neg}}\bigl[\ell(q_f(X,X^+,X^-))\bigr].$$

For $M\ge1$, an observed sample is $S=((x_j,x_j^+,x_j^-))_{j=1}^M$ of $M$ independent triplets with common law $D_{\rm sim}\otimes D_{\rm neg}$, and its empirical loss is $\widehat L_{\rm un}(f):=M^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^M\ell(q_f(x_j,x_j^+,x_j^-))$. For this sample define the unnormalized vector Rademacher complexity

$$\mathcal R_S(\mathcal F):=\mathbb E_\varepsilon\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\sum_{j=1}^M\sum_{t=1}^d\bigl(\varepsilon_{jt0}f_t(x_j)+\varepsilon_{jt+}f_t(x_j^+)+\varepsilon_{jt-}f_t(x_j^-)\bigr),$$

where every $\varepsilon_{jt0},\varepsilon_{jt+},\varepsilon_{jt-}$ is an independent uniform sign. This is the one-sided convention with no absolute value and no $1/M$ factor.

All vector and matrix expectations in this definition are taken entrywise in finite dimensions. The bound on $f$ makes each coordinate of $f(X)$ and every product defining a covariance entry integrable.

Let $C_+,C_-\sim\rho$ be independent class draws and set $\tau:=\Pr(C_+=C_-)<1$. Assume the diagonal $\Delta:=\{(c,c):c\in\mathcal C\}$ and each $\Delta_A:=\{(c,c):c\in A\}$, $A\in\mathcal C_0$, are measurable. The average binary task draws $(C_+,C_-)$ conditional on $C_+\ne C_-$, then samples a label $Y$ uniformly from $\{+1,-1\}$ and an input $X$ from $D_{C_+}$ if $Y=+1$ or $D_{C_-}$ if $Y=-1$. For a vector representation $f$, a binary linear classifier uses a weight vector $w\in\mathbb R^d$ and loss $\ell(-Yw^\top f(X))$. Define $L_{\rm sup}(f)$ as the average over tasks of the infimum of this risk over $w\in\mathbb R^d$. Write $\mu_c:=\mathbb E_{X\sim D_c}f(X)$ and define the class-mean classifier by $w_\mu=\mu_{C_+}-\mu_{C_-}$; its average risk is $L^\mu_{\rm sup}(f)$. For $\gamma>0$, write $L^\mu_{\gamma,\rm sup}(f)$ for the same mean-classifier risk with margin loss $\ell_\gamma(t):=(1+t/\gamma)_+$ in place of $\ell$.

For $\tau>0$, let $L^=_{\rm un}(f)$ and $L^\ne_{\rm un}(f)$ be the conditional contrastive risks given $C_+=C_-$ and $C_+\ne C_-$, respectively. Let $\nu$ be the class law conditioned on the collision event, namely $\nu(A):=(\rho\otimes\rho)(\Delta_A)/\tau$ for $A\in\mathcal C_0$; for an atomic class law this gives $\nu(\{c\})=\rho(\{c\})^2/\tau$. Define $\Sigma_f(c):=\mathbb E_{X\sim D_c}[(f(X)-\mu_c)(f(X)-\mu_c)^\top]$ and

$$s(f):=\mathbb E_{C\sim\nu}\left[\sqrt{\lVert\Sigma_f(C)\rVert_{\rm op}}\,\mathbb E_{X\sim D_C}\lVert f(X)\rVert_2\right],\qquad \lVert\Sigma\rVert_{\rm op}:=\max_{\lVert u\rVert_2=1}\lVert\Sigma u\rVert_2.$$

The assumed measurability of $\Delta$ and every $\Delta_A$ makes the displayed collision event and conditional class law well-defined; disjoint class sets give disjoint $\Delta_A$, so the formula for $\nu$ is countably additive and has total mass one. Assume also that $c\mapsto\mu_c$ and $c\mapsto\Sigma_f(c)$ are measurable for each $f$, and that the displayed class-conditional risks and random suprema used below are measurable.

If $\tau=0$, there is no collision term; set $s(f):=0$ and use $L_{\rm un}(f)=L^\ne_{\rm un}(f)$. Any empirical minimizer or approximate minimizer used below is separately assumed to be a measurable selector; no selector-existence claim is part of this definition.

derivations.claim: On the event in [F1], apply its uniform bound to the random selector $\widehat f$ (which belongs to $\mathcal F$ almost surely) to obtain $L_{\rm un}(\widehat f)\le\widehat L_{\rm un}(\widehat f)+\Gamma_M(S,\delta)$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the hypotheses of the one-negative uniform-generalization lemma for a sample $S$ of size $M$. Let $\widehat f$ be a measurable selector taking values in $\mathcal F$ almost surely and satisfying, almost surely, $\widehat L_{\rm un}(\widehat f)\le\widehat L_{\rm un}(f)+\eta$ for every $f\in\mathcal F$, where $\eta\ge0$. For every $0<\delta<1$, with probability at least $1-\delta$,

$$\forall f\in\mathcal F,\qquad L_{\rm un}(\widehat f)\le L_{\rm un}(f)+2\Gamma_M(S,\delta)+\eta,$$

where

$$\Gamma_M(S,\delta):=\frac{2\sqrt{18}L_0R\,\mathcal R_S(\mathcal F)}{M}+3B_{\ell,R}\sqrt{\frac{\ln(4/\delta)}{2M}}$$

is the uniform-deviation quantity for the same sample and loss. The case $\eta=0$ includes any attained measurable empirical minimizer; the statement does not assert that such a selector exists.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the hypotheses of the one-negative uniform-generalization lemma for a sample $S$ of size $M$. Let $\widehat f$ be a measurable selector taking values in $\mathcal F$ almost surely and satisfying, almost surely, $\widehat L_{\rm un}(\widehat f)\le\widehat L_{\rm un}(f)+\eta$ for every $f\in\mathcal F$, where $\eta\ge0$. For every $0<\delta<1$, with probability at least $1-\delta$,

$$\forall f\in\mathcal F,\qquad L_{\rm un}(\widehat f)\le L_{\rm un}(f)+2\Gamma_M(S,\delta)+\eta,$$

where

$$\Gamma_M(S,\delta):=\frac{2\sqrt{18}L_0R\,\mathcal R_S(\mathcal F)}{M}+3B_{\ell,R}\sqrt{\frac{\ln(4/\delta)}{2M}}$$

is the uniform-deviation quantity for the same sample and loss. The case $\eta=0$ includes any attained measurable empirical minimizer; the statement does not assert that such a selector exists.

Assume the one-negative latent-class model has $\tau<1$. Let $C_+,C_-$ be independent with law $\rho$, conditioned on $C_+\ne C_-$, let $X,X^+$ be independent with law $D_{C_+}$, and let $X^-$ be independent with law $D_{C_-}$. For every measurable bounded representation $f$ and either source hinge or logistic loss, the average binary-task mean-classifier risk satisfies

$$L^\mu_{\rm sup}(f)\le L^\ne_{\rm un}(f).$$

Here each binary task uses a uniform label from its two classes, and $L^\ne_{\rm un}$ is the contrastive loss conditional on different positive and negative classes.

In the one-negative latent-class model, for every bounded representation $f$ and either source loss, the population contrastive loss decomposes as

$$L_{\rm un}(f)=\tau L^=_{\rm un}(f)+(1-\tau)L^\ne_{\rm un}(f).$$

If $\tau>0$, the same-class conditional loss obeys

$$1\le L^=_{\rm un}(f)\le1+c_0s(f),\qquad c_0:=\sqrt2\,L_0,$$

where $L_0$ is the common Lipschitz constant of the hinge and logistic losses. If $\tau=0$, then $L_{\rm un}(f)=L^\ne_{\rm un}(f)$ and the model's convention is $s(f)=0$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the one-negative latent-class model with $\tau<1$. Fix either source hinge or logistic loss and a sample size $M\ge1$. Suppose all risks and suprema in the uniform-generalization statement are measurable and that a measurable exact empirical minimizer $\widehat f\in\mathcal F$ exists, meaning $\widehat L_{\rm un}(\widehat f)\le\widehat L_{\rm un}(g)$ for every $g\in\mathcal F$ almost surely. For every $0<\delta<1$, with probability at least $1-\delta$ over the IID triplet sample,

$$\forall f\in\mathcal F,\qquad L^\mu_{\rm sup}(\widehat f)\le\frac{L_{\rm un}(f)-\tau+2\Gamma_M(S,\delta)}{1-\tau},$$

where

$$\Gamma_M(S,\delta):=\frac{2\sqrt{18}L_0R\,\mathcal R_S(\mathcal F)}{M}+3B_{\ell,R}\sqrt{\frac{\ln(4/\delta)}{2M}}$$

is the uniform-deviation quantity for the same sample and loss. This is a guarantee for the average binary task with a uniform label and the class-mean linear classifier.

Let $(\mathcal C,\mathcal C_0,\rho)$ be a measurable probability space and $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ a measurable space. For each class $c\in\mathcal C$, let $D_c$ be a probability measure on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ and assume $c\mapsto D_c(A)$ is measurable for every $A\in\mathcal A$. Assume the displayed mixtures define probability measures. The positive-pair law $D_{\rm sim}$ and negative marginal $D_{\rm neg}$ are specified by

$$D_{\rm sim}(A\times B):=\int_{\mathcal C}D_c(A)D_c(B)\,\rho(dc),\qquad D_{\rm neg}(A):=\int_{\mathcal C}D_c(A)\,\rho(dc)$$

for measurable $A,B\in\mathcal A$. Equivalently, draw $C\sim\rho$ and then draw $X,X^+$ independently with law $D_C$ for a positive pair; draw a fresh independent class $C'\sim\rho$ and $X^-\sim D_{C'}$ for one negative. The class labels are latent: the learner observes the pair and negative data, not their classes.

Let $d\ge1$, $R>0$, and let $\mathcal F$ be a nonempty class of measurable maps $f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^d$ satisfying $\sup_{x\in\mathcal X}\lVert f(x)\rVert_2\le R$. Use either one-negative loss $\ell_{\rm h}(t)=(1+t)_+$ or $\ell_{\rm log}(t)=\log_2(1+e^t)$ from the immediately preceding loss-properties lemma. The contrastive score and population loss are

$$q_f(x,x^+,x^-):=f(x)^\top\bigl(f(x^-)-f(x^+)\bigr),\qquad L_{\rm un}(f):=\mathbb E_{(X,X^+)\sim D_{\rm sim},\,X^-\sim D_{\rm neg}}\bigl[\ell(q_f(X,X^+,X^-))\bigr].$$

For $M\ge1$, an observed sample is $S=((x_j,x_j^+,x_j^-))_{j=1}^M$ of $M$ independent triplets with common law $D_{\rm sim}\otimes D_{\rm neg}$, and its empirical loss is $\widehat L_{\rm un}(f):=M^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^M\ell(q_f(x_j,x_j^+,x_j^-))$. For this sample define the unnormalized vector Rademacher complexity

$$\mathcal R_S(\mathcal F):=\mathbb E_\varepsilon\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\sum_{j=1}^M\sum_{t=1}^d\bigl(\varepsilon_{jt0}f_t(x_j)+\varepsilon_{jt+}f_t(x_j^+)+\varepsilon_{jt-}f_t(x_j^-)\bigr),$$

where every $\varepsilon_{jt0},\varepsilon_{jt+},\varepsilon_{jt-}$ is an independent uniform sign. This is the one-sided convention with no absolute value and no $1/M$ factor.

All vector and matrix expectations in this definition are taken entrywise in finite dimensions. The bound on $f$ makes each coordinate of $f(X)$ and every product defining a covariance entry integrable.

Let $C_+,C_-\sim\rho$ be independent class draws and set $\tau:=\Pr(C_+=C_-)<1$. Assume the diagonal $\Delta:=\{(c,c):c\in\mathcal C\}$ and each $\Delta_A:=\{(c,c):c\in A\}$, $A\in\mathcal C_0$, are measurable. The average binary task draws $(C_+,C_-)$ conditional on $C_+\ne C_-$, then samples a label $Y$ uniformly from $\{+1,-1\}$ and an input $X$ from $D_{C_+}$ if $Y=+1$ or $D_{C_-}$ if $Y=-1$. For a vector representation $f$, a binary linear classifier uses a weight vector $w\in\mathbb R^d$ and loss $\ell(-Yw^\top f(X))$. Define $L_{\rm sup}(f)$ as the average over tasks of the infimum of this risk over $w\in\mathbb R^d$. Write $\mu_c:=\mathbb E_{X\sim D_c}f(X)$ and define the class-mean classifier by $w_\mu=\mu_{C_+}-\mu_{C_-}$; its average risk is $L^\mu_{\rm sup}(f)$. For $\gamma>0$, write $L^\mu_{\gamma,\rm sup}(f)$ for the same mean-classifier risk with margin loss $\ell_\gamma(t):=(1+t/\gamma)_+$ in place of $\ell$.

For $\tau>0$, let $L^=_{\rm un}(f)$ and $L^\ne_{\rm un}(f)$ be the conditional contrastive risks given $C_+=C_-$ and $C_+\ne C_-$, respectively. Let $\nu$ be the class law conditioned on the collision event, namely $\nu(A):=(\rho\otimes\rho)(\Delta_A)/\tau$ for $A\in\mathcal C_0$; for an atomic class law this gives $\nu(\{c\})=\rho(\{c\})^2/\tau$. Define $\Sigma_f(c):=\mathbb E_{X\sim D_c}[(f(X)-\mu_c)(f(X)-\mu_c)^\top]$ and

$$s(f):=\mathbb E_{C\sim\nu}\left[\sqrt{\lVert\Sigma_f(C)\rVert_{\rm op}}\,\mathbb E_{X\sim D_C}\lVert f(X)\rVert_2\right],\qquad \lVert\Sigma\rVert_{\rm op}:=\max_{\lVert u\rVert_2=1}\lVert\Sigma u\rVert_2.$$

The assumed measurability of $\Delta$ and every $\Delta_A$ makes the displayed collision event and conditional class law well-defined; disjoint class sets give disjoint $\Delta_A$, so the formula for $\nu$ is countably additive and has total mass one. Assume also that $c\mapsto\mu_c$ and $c\mapsto\Sigma_f(c)$ are measurable for each $f$, and that the displayed class-conditional risks and random suprema used below are measurable.

If $\tau=0$, there is no collision term; set $s(f):=0$ and use $L_{\rm un}(f)=L^\ne_{\rm un}(f)$. Any empirical minimizer or approximate minimizer used below is separately assumed to be a measurable selector; no selector-existence claim is part of this definition.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the one-negative latent-class model with $\tau<1$. Fix either source hinge or logistic loss and a sample size $M\ge1$. Suppose all risks and suprema in the uniform-generalization statement are measurable and that a measurable exact empirical minimizer $\widehat f\in\mathcal F$ exists, meaning $\widehat L_{\rm un}(\widehat f)\le\widehat L_{\rm un}(g)$ for every $g\in\mathcal F$ almost surely. For every $0<\delta<1$, with probability at least $1-\delta$ over the IID triplet sample,

$$\forall f\in\mathcal F,\qquad L^\mu_{\rm sup}(\widehat f)\le\frac{L_{\rm un}(f)-\tau+2\Gamma_M(S,\delta)}{1-\tau},$$

where

$$\Gamma_M(S,\delta):=\frac{2\sqrt{18}L_0R\,\mathcal R_S(\mathcal F)}{M}+3B_{\ell,R}\sqrt{\frac{\ln(4/\delta)}{2M}}$$

is the uniform-deviation quantity for the same sample and loss. This is a guarantee for the average binary task with a uniform label and the class-mean linear classifier.

In the one-negative latent-class model, for every bounded representation $f$ and either source loss, the population contrastive loss decomposes as

$$L_{\rm un}(f)=\tau L^=_{\rm un}(f)+(1-\tau)L^\ne_{\rm un}(f).$$

If $\tau>0$, the same-class conditional loss obeys

$$1\le L^=_{\rm un}(f)\le1+c_0s(f),\qquad c_0:=\sqrt2\,L_0,$$

where $L_0$ is the common Lipschitz constant of the hinge and logistic losses. If $\tau=0$, then $L_{\rm un}(f)=L^\ne_{\rm un}(f)$ and the model's convention is $s(f)=0$.

derivations.claim: By the definition of $L_{\rm sup}$ as an infimum over all linear weights, its value for $\widehat f$ is at most the risk of the particular mean weight, so $L_{\rm sup}(\widehat f)\le L^\mu_{\rm sup}(\widehat f)$.

On the event in [F2], fix any comparator $f$. If $\tau>0$, [F3] gives $L_{\rm un}(f)-\tau=\tau(L^=_{\rm un}(f)-1)+(1-\tau)L^\ne_{\rm un}(f)\le\tau\sqrt2L_0s(f)+(1-\tau)L^\ne_{\rm un}(f)$. If $\tau=0$, the same inequality is equality under the stipulated convention $s(f)=0$.

Divide the inequality in step 1.2 by $1-\tau>0$ and substitute it into [F2]. Together with step 1.1, this gives the displayed bound for every comparator on the same event, whose probability is at least $1-\delta$.

Assume the displayed mixtures define probability measures. The positive-pair law $D_{\rm sim}$ and negative marginal $D_{\rm neg}$ are specified by

$$D_{\rm sim}(A\times B):=\int_{\mathcal C}D_c(A)D_c(B)\,\rho(dc),\qquad D_{\rm neg}(A):=\int_{\mathcal C}D_c(A)\,\rho(dc)$$

for measurable $A,B\in\mathcal A$. Equivalently, draw $C\sim\rho$ and then draw $X,X^+$ independently with law $D_C$ for a positive pair; draw a fresh independent class $C'\sim\rho$ and $X^-\sim D_{C'}$ for one negative. The class labels are latent: the learner observes the pair and negative data, not their classes.

Let $d\ge1$, $R>0$, and let $\mathcal F$ be a nonempty class of measurable maps $f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^d$ satisfying $\sup_{x\in\mathcal X}\lVert f(x)\rVert_2\le R$. Use either one-negative loss $\ell_{\rm h}(t)=(1+t)_+$ or $\ell_{\rm log}(t)=\log_2(1+e^t)$ from the immediately preceding loss-properties lemma. The contrastive score and population loss are

$$q_f(x,x^+,x^-):=f(x)^\top\bigl(f(x^-)-f(x^+)\bigr),\qquad L_{\rm un}(f):=\mathbb E_{(X,X^+)\sim D_{\rm sim},\,X^-\sim D_{\rm neg}}\bigl[\ell(q_f(X,X^+,X^-))\bigr].$$

For $M\ge1$, an observed sample is $S=((x_j,x_j^+,x_j^-))_{j=1}^M$ of $M$ independent triplets with common law $D_{\rm sim}\otimes D_{\rm neg}$, and its empirical loss is $\widehat L_{\rm un}(f):=M^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^M\ell(q_f(x_j,x_j^+,x_j^-))$. For this sample define the unnormalized vector Rademacher complexity

$$\mathcal R_S(\mathcal F):=\mathbb E_\varepsilon\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\sum_{j=1}^M\sum_{t=1}^d\bigl(\varepsilon_{jt0}f_t(x_j)+\varepsilon_{jt+}f_t(x_j^+)+\varepsilon_{jt-}f_t(x_j^-)\bigr),$$

where every $\varepsilon_{jt0},\varepsilon_{jt+},\varepsilon_{jt-}$ is an independent uniform sign. This is the one-sided convention with no absolute value and no $1/M$ factor.

All vector and matrix expectations in this definition are taken entrywise in finite dimensions. The bound on $f$ makes each coordinate of $f(X)$ and every product defining a covariance entry integrable.

Let $C_+,C_-\sim\rho$ be independent class draws and set $\tau:=\Pr(C_+=C_-)<1$. Assume the diagonal $\Delta:=\{(c,c):c\in\mathcal C\}$ and each $\Delta_A:=\{(c,c):c\in A\}$, $A\in\mathcal C_0$, are measurable. The average binary task draws $(C_+,C_-)$ conditional on $C_+\ne C_-$, then samples a label $Y$ uniformly from $\{+1,-1\}$ and an input $X$ from $D_{C_+}$ if $Y=+1$ or $D_{C_-}$ if $Y=-1$. Define $L_{\rm sup}(f)$ as the average over tasks of the infimum of this risk over $w\in\mathbb R^d$. Write $\mu_c:=\mathbb E_{X\sim D_c}f(X)$ and define the class-mean classifier by $w_\mu=\mu_{C_+}-\mu_{C_-}$; its average risk is $L^\mu_{\rm sup}(f)$. For $\gamma>0$, write $L^\mu_{\gamma,\rm sup}(f)$ for the same mean-classifier risk with margin loss $\ell_\gamma(t):=(1+t/\gamma)_+$ in place of $\ell$.

For $\tau>0$, let $L^=_{\rm un}(f)$ and $L^\ne_{\rm un}(f)$ be the conditional contrastive risks given $C_+=C_-$ and $C_+\ne C_-$, respectively. $$s(f):=\mathbb E_{C\sim\nu}\left[\sqrt{\lVert\Sigma_f(C)\rVert_{\rm op}}\,\mathbb E_{X\sim D_C}\lVert f(X)\rVert_2\right],\qquad \lVert\Sigma\rVert_{\rm op}:=\max_{\lVert u\rVert_2=1}\lVert\Sigma u\rVert_2.$$

derivations.claim: If the negative class equals the positive class, the anchor, positive sample and negative sample all have the same representation. Thus $q_f=f(x)(f(x^-)-f(x^+))=0$ and [F2] gives collision loss $1$.

If the ordered classes are $(a,b)$, the anchor representation is $0$, hence $q_f=0$ and loss $1$. If they are $(b,a)$, then $q_f=1(0-1)=-1$, hence the hinge loss is $0$. The two ordered cases are equiprobable given inequality, so $L^\ne_{\rm un}(f)=(1+0)/2=1/2$.

The collision decomposition weights the two conditional losses by $\tau=1/2$ and $1-\tau=1/2$. Therefore $L_{\rm un}(f)=(1/2)\cdot1+(1/2)\cdot(1/2)=3/4$, with a positive contribution from negative-class collisions.

Conditional on a class collision, [F3] gives score values $2r^2,-2r^2,0$ with probabilities $1/4,1/4,1/2$. Since $r\ge1$, their hinge losses are $1+2r^2,0,1$, respectively. Thus $L^=_{\rm un}(f)=\frac14(1+2r^2)+\frac12=\frac34+\frac12r^2$.

Conditional on distinct classes, the score values are $-2+2r^2,-2-2r^2,-2$ with probabilities $1/4,1/4,1/2$. For $r\ge1$, their hinge losses are $2r^2-1,0,0$. Hence $L^\ne_{\rm un}(f)=\frac14(2r^2-1)=\frac12r^2-\frac14$.

Collision and distinct-class events each have probability $1/2$. Combining steps 1.2 and 1.3 yields $L_{\rm un}(f)=\frac12(\frac34+\frac12r^2)+\frac12(\frac12r^2-\frac14)=\frac14+\frac12r^2$. This tends to infinity with $r$, while step 1.1 keeps the mean-classifier hinge risk zero.

Let $(\mathcal C,\mathcal C_0,\rho)$ be a measurable probability space and $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ a measurable space. For each class $c\in\mathcal C$, let $D_c$ be a probability measure on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ and assume $c\mapsto D_c(A)$ is measurable for every $A\in\mathcal A$. Assume the displayed mixtures define probability measures. The positive-pair law $D_{\rm sim}$ and negative marginal $D_{\rm neg}$ are specified by

$$D_{\rm sim}(A\times B):=\int_{\mathcal C}D_c(A)D_c(B)\,\rho(dc),\qquad D_{\rm neg}(A):=\int_{\mathcal C}D_c(A)\,\rho(dc)$$

for measurable $A,B\in\mathcal A$. Equivalently, draw $C\sim\rho$ and then draw $X,X^+$ independently with law $D_C$ for a positive pair; draw a fresh independent class $C'\sim\rho$ and $X^-\sim D_{C'}$ for one negative. The class labels are latent: the learner observes the pair and negative data, not their classes.

Let $d\ge1$, $R>0$, and let $\mathcal F$ be a nonempty class of measurable maps $f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^d$ satisfying $\sup_{x\in\mathcal X}\lVert f(x)\rVert_2\le R$. Use either one-negative loss $\ell_{\rm h}(t)=(1+t)_+$ or $\ell_{\rm log}(t)=\log_2(1+e^t)$ from the immediately preceding loss-properties lemma. The contrastive score and population loss are

$$q_f(x,x^+,x^-):=f(x)^\top\bigl(f(x^-)-f(x^+)\bigr),\qquad L_{\rm un}(f):=\mathbb E_{(X,X^+)\sim D_{\rm sim},\,X^-\sim D_{\rm neg}}\bigl[\ell(q_f(X,X^+,X^-))\bigr].$$

For $M\ge1$, an observed sample is $S=((x_j,x_j^+,x_j^-))_{j=1}^M$ of $M$ independent triplets with common law $D_{\rm sim}\otimes D_{\rm neg}$, and its empirical loss is $\widehat L_{\rm un}(f):=M^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^M\ell(q_f(x_j,x_j^+,x_j^-))$. For this sample define the unnormalized vector Rademacher complexity

$$\mathcal R_S(\mathcal F):=\mathbb E_\varepsilon\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\sum_{j=1}^M\sum_{t=1}^d\bigl(\varepsilon_{jt0}f_t(x_j)+\varepsilon_{jt+}f_t(x_j^+)+\varepsilon_{jt-}f_t(x_j^-)\bigr),$$

where every $\varepsilon_{jt0},\varepsilon_{jt+},\varepsilon_{jt-}$ is an independent uniform sign. This is the one-sided convention with no absolute value and no $1/M$ factor.

All vector and matrix expectations in this definition are taken entrywise in finite dimensions. The bound on $f$ makes each coordinate of $f(X)$ and every product defining a covariance entry integrable.

Let $C_+,C_-\sim\rho$ be independent class draws and set $\tau:=\Pr(C_+=C_-)<1$. Assume the diagonal $\Delta:=\{(c,c):c\in\mathcal C\}$ and each $\Delta_A:=\{(c,c):c\in A\}$, $A\in\mathcal C_0$, are measurable. The average binary task draws $(C_+,C_-)$ conditional on $C_+\ne C_-$, then samples a label $Y$ uniformly from $\{+1,-1\}$ and an input $X$ from $D_{C_+}$ if $Y=+1$ or $D_{C_-}$ if $Y=-1$. For a vector representation $f$, a binary linear classifier uses a weight vector $w\in\mathbb R^d$ and loss $\ell(-Yw^\top f(X))$. Define $L_{\rm sup}(f)$ as the average over tasks of the infimum of this risk over $w\in\mathbb R^d$. Write $\mu_c:=\mathbb E_{X\sim D_c}f(X)$ and define the class-mean classifier by $w_\mu=\mu_{C_+}-\mu_{C_-}$; its average risk is $L^\mu_{\rm sup}(f)$. For $\gamma>0$, write $L^\mu_{\gamma,\rm sup}(f)$ for the same mean-classifier risk with margin loss $\ell_\gamma(t):=(1+t/\gamma)_+$ in place of $\ell$.

For $\tau>0$, let $L^=_{\rm un}(f)$ and $L^\ne_{\rm un}(f)$ be the conditional contrastive risks given $C_+=C_-$ and $C_+\ne C_-$, respectively. Let $\nu$ be the class law conditioned on the collision event, namely $\nu(A):=(\rho\otimes\rho)(\Delta_A)/\tau$ for $A\in\mathcal C_0$; for an atomic class law this gives $\nu(\{c\})=\rho(\{c\})^2/\tau$. Define $\Sigma_f(c):=\mathbb E_{X\sim D_c}[(f(X)-\mu_c)(f(X)-\mu_c)^\top]$ and

$$s(f):=\mathbb E_{C\sim\nu}\left[\sqrt{\lVert\Sigma_f(C)\rVert_{\rm op}}\,\mathbb E_{X\sim D_C}\lVert f(X)\rVert_2\right],\qquad \lVert\Sigma\rVert_{\rm op}:=\max_{\lVert u\rVert_2=1}\lVert\Sigma u\rVert_2.$$

The assumed measurability of $\Delta$ and every $\Delta_A$ makes the displayed collision event and conditional class law well-defined; disjoint class sets give disjoint $\Delta_A$, so the formula for $\nu$ is countably additive and has total mass one. Assume also that $c\mapsto\mu_c$ and $c\mapsto\Sigma_f(c)$ are measurable for each $f$, and that the displayed class-conditional risks and random suprema used below are measurable.

If $\tau=0$, there is no collision term; set $s(f):=0$ and use $L_{\rm un}(f)=L^\ne_{\rm un}(f)$. Any empirical minimizer or approximate minimizer used below is separately assumed to be a measurable selector; no selector-existence claim is part of this definition.

Write $\ln$ for the natural logarithm and $\log_2 u:=\ln(u)/\ln(2)$ for $u>0$. Define the one-negative hinge and logistic losses by $\ell_{\rm h}(t):=(1+t)_+$ and $\ell_{\rm log}(t):=\log_2(1+e^t)$ for $t\in\mathbb R$, where $r_+:=\max\{r,0\}$. Put $L_0:=1+1/\ln(2)$. Each loss is convex, nondecreasing, $L_0$-Lipschitz, and has value $1$ at $0$. For $R>0$ and either loss $\ell$, define $B_{\ell,R}:=\ell(2R^2)-\ell(-2R^2)$. Then $0<B_{\ell,R}\le4L_0R^2$.

derivations.claim: Since $T(c,n)=n$ and $n$ is uniform independently of $c$, each post-augmentation class law is the same uniform law $U$. The mixture formula gives $D_{\rm neg}=U$ and $D_{\rm sim}(A\times B)=U(A)U(B)$ for all subsets $A,B$ of the finite input space, hence $D_{\rm sim}=U\otimes U$. Thus the observed triplet law is $U\otimes U\otimes U$, independent of the latent task labels, and every score $z=w^\top f(n)$ has the same distribution under both labels.

For each fixed score $z$, if $|z|\le1$ then $(1-z)_++(1+z)_+=2$. If $z\ge1$, the sum is $0+(1+z)\ge2$; if $z\le-1$, it is $(1-z)+0\ge2$. Therefore [F2] gives average risk at least $1$ after integrating over the common input law, and $w=0$ attains $1$. The class coordinate erased by $T$ cannot be recovered by this downstream classifier.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.
