Assume the diagonal $\Delta:=\{(c,c):c\in\mathcal C\}$ and each $\Delta_A:=\{(c,c):c\in A\}$, $A\in\mathcal C_0$, are measurable. The average binary task draws $(C_+,C_-)$ conditional on $C_+\ne C_-$, then samples a label $Y$ uniformly from $\{+1,-1\}$ and an input $X$ from $D_{C_+}$ if $Y=+1$ or $D_{C_-}$ if $Y=-1$. For a vector representation $f$, a binary linear classifier uses a weight vector $w\in\mathbb R^d$ and loss $\ell(-Yw^\top f(X))$. Define $L_{\rm sup}(f)$ as the average over tasks of the infimum of this risk over $w\in\mathbb R^d$. Write $\mu_c:=\mathbb E_{X\sim D_c}f(X)$ and define the class-mean classifier by $w_\mu=\mu_{C_+}-\mu_{C_-}$; its average risk is $L^\mu_{\rm sup}(f)$. For $\gamma>0$, write $L^\mu_{\gamma,\rm sup}(f)$ for the same mean-classifier risk with margin loss $\ell_\gamma(t):=(1+t/\gamma)_+$ in place of $\ell$.

For $\tau>0$, let $L^=_{\rm un}(f)$ and $L^\ne_{\rm un}(f)$ be the conditional contrastive risks given $C_+=C_-$ and $C_+\ne C_-$, respectively. Let $\nu$ be the class law conditioned on the collision event, namely $\nu(A):=(\rho\otimes\rho)(\Delta_A)/\tau$ for $A\in\mathcal C_0$; for an atomic class law this gives $\nu(\{c\})=\rho(\{c\})^2/\tau$. Define $\Sigma_f(c):=\mathbb E_{X\sim D_c}[(f(X)-\mu_c)(f(X)-\mu_c)^\top]$ and

$$s(f):=\mathbb E_{C\sim\nu}\left[\sqrt{\lVert\Sigma_f(C)\rVert_{\rm op}}\,\mathbb E_{X\sim D_C}\lVert f(X)\rVert_2\right],\qquad \lVert\Sigma\rVert_{\rm op}:=\max_{\lVert u\rVert_2=1}\lVert\Sigma u\rVert_2.$$

The assumed measurability of $\Delta$ and every $\Delta_A$ makes the displayed collision event and conditional class law well-defined; disjoint class sets give disjoint $\Delta_A$, so the formula for $\nu$ is countably additive and has total mass one. Assume also that $c\mapsto\mu_c$ and $c\mapsto\Sigma_f(c)$ are measurable for each $f$, and that the displayed class-conditional risks and random suprema used below are measurable.

If $\tau=0$, there is no collision term; set $s(f):=0$ and use $L_{\rm un}(f)=L^\ne_{\rm un}(f)$. Any empirical minimizer or approximate minimizer used below is separately assumed to be a measurable selector; no selector-existence claim is part of this definition.

Write $\ln$ for the natural logarithm and $\log_2 u:=\ln(u)/\ln(2)$ for $u>0$. Define the one-negative hinge and logistic losses by $\ell_{\rm h}(t):=(1+t)_+$ and $\ell_{\rm log}(t):=\log_2(1+e^t)$ for $t\in\mathbb R$, where $r_+:=\max\{r,0\}$. Put $L_0:=1+1/\ln(2)$. Each loss is convex, nondecreasing, $L_0$-Lipschitz, and has value $1$ at $0$. For $R>0$ and either loss $\ell$, define $B_{\ell,R}:=\ell(2R^2)-\ell(-2R^2)$. Then $0<B_{\ell,R}\le4L_0R^2$.

In the one-negative latent-class model, fix a bounded representation $f$ with $\sup_x\|f(x)\|_2\le R$, where $R>0$. Use the hinge loss $\ell_{\rm h}(t)=(1+t)_+$. Suppose that for every class $c$, the centered vector $f(X)-\mu_c$, for $X\sim D_c$, is sub-Gaussian in every direction with proxy $\sigma^2\ge0$. For $0<\epsilon\le1$, define

$$\gamma:=\begin{cases}1+2R\sigma\sqrt{2\ln R+\ln(3/\epsilon)},&R\ge1,\\1+2R\sigma\sqrt{\ln(3/\epsilon)},&0<R<1.\end{cases}$$

Then the contrastive risk conditioned on distinct positive and negative classes satisfies

$$L^\ne_{\rm un}(f)\le\gamma L^\mu_{\gamma,\rm sup}(f)+\epsilon.$$

This comparison is for the hinge contrastive loss and its scaled hinge mean-classifier risk.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the one-negative latent-class model with $\tau<1$. Use the source hinge loss for both contrastive training and the binary mean-classifier task. Fix $M\ge1$, a measurable exact empirical minimizer $\widehat f\in\mathcal F$ satisfying $\widehat L_{\rm un}(\widehat f)\le\widehat L_{\rm un}(g)$ for every $g\in\mathcal F$ almost surely, $0<\delta<1$, and $0<\epsilon\le1$. Let $f\in\mathcal F$ be any comparator whose centered class-conditional representation vectors are sub-Gaussian in every direction with common proxy $\sigma^2\ge0$. Define

$$\gamma:=\begin{cases}1+2R\sigma\sqrt{2\ln R+\ln(3/\epsilon)},&R\ge1,\\1+2R\sigma\sqrt{\ln(3/\epsilon)},&0<R<1.\end{cases}$$

Under the risk and supremum measurability hypotheses, with probability at least $1-\delta$,

$$L_{\rm sup}(\widehat f)\le L^\mu_{\rm sup}(\widehat f)\le\gamma L^\mu_{\gamma,\rm sup}(f)+\epsilon+\frac{\sqrt2L_0\tau s(f)+2\Gamma_M(S,\delta)}{1-\tau}.$$

The uniform-deviation quantity is

$$\Gamma_M(S,\delta):=\frac{2\sqrt{18}L_0R\,\mathcal R_S(\mathcal F)}{M}+3B_{\ell_{\rm h},R}\sqrt{\frac{\ln(4/\delta)}{2M}},$$

where $L^\mu_{\gamma,\rm sup}(f)$ is the average task risk of the class-mean weight $w_\mu$ using the scaled hinge loss $(1-Yw_\mu^\top f(X)/\gamma)_+$. The logistic transfer theorems remain separate; the source margin comparison does not supply their logistic analogue.

The positive-label example $a$ has logistic argument $-w_\mu f(a)=4$, while the negative-label example $b$ has argument $w_\mu f(b)=-8$. Swapping the classes gives the same two losses in reverse order, proving the displayed mean-classifier logistic risk.

For the mean classifier, the two hinge-margin arguments at $\gamma=1$ are $4$ and $-8$, so the losses are $5$ and $0$ and their average is $5/2$. The sub-Gaussian proxy is zero because each class is deterministic, so [F3] gives $\gamma=1$ for every permitted $\epsilon$.

The exponential series has positive terms and $e^4>1+4+4^2/2!+4^3/3!+4^4/4!=103/3>31$. Hence $1+e^4>32$, so $\log_2(1+e^4)>5$; also $\log_2(1+e^{-8})>0$. citations.quote:
Fix integers $M,q\ge1$, set $[M]=\{1,\ldots,M\}$, and write the image space on a fixed patch grid as $\mathcal X=(\mathbb R^q)^M$. A measurable space is a set with a specified sigma-algebra; equip $\mathcal X$ and a finite-dimensional latent space $\mathcal Z$ with such structures. An image is $x=(x_1,\ldots,x_M)\in\mathcal X$, with $q$ real pixel values in each of its $M$ patches. Let $S=(x^{(1)},\ldots,x^{(n)})$ be a finite training set with $n\ge1$. For $u\in\mathbb R^q$, set $\|u\|_2^2=\sum_{r=1}^q u_r^2$. For $V\subseteq[M]$ let $\mathcal Z^V=\{(z_j)_{j\in V}:z_j\in\mathcal Z\}$. For unmasked reconstruction, the encoder and decoder are deterministic measurable maps $E_\phi:\mathcal X\to\mathcal Z$ and $D_\psi:\mathcal Z\to\mathcal X$. For masked reconstruction, the encoder is a measurable deterministic map $(V,(x_j)_{j\in V})\mapsto(z_j)_{j\in V}\in\mathcal Z^V$, and the decoder maps the ordered length-$M$ sequence of encoded visible tokens and mask tokens to an element of $\mathcal X$. Each mask token is one learned vector $m\in\mathcal Z$ reused at every masked position. All maps take finite real values; when implemented by feedforward neural networks, each is a finite computation graph evaluated in the layered order of its vertices.

Let $X:\Omega\to\mathcal X$ be a measurable random image on a probability space. Assume that the displayed squared-loss random variables are measurable. The **population reconstruction risk** is
$$R_{\rm rec}(\phi,\psi;X):=\mathbb E\left[\frac1{Mq}\sum_{j=1}^M\|D_\psi(E_\phi(X))_j-X_j\|_2^2\right]\in[0,+\infty].$$
A stochastic denoising corruption is any measurable random image $\widetilde X:\Omega\to\mathcal X$ on the same probability space as the clean image $X$; their dependence may be arbitrary, with no restriction on support. The **population denoising risk** reconstructs the clean image:
$$R_{\rm den}(\phi,\psi;X,\widetilde X):=\mathbb E\left[\frac1{Mq}\sum_{j=1}^M\|D_\psi(E_\phi(\widetilde X))_j-X_j\|_2^2\right]\in[0,+\infty].$$
These expectations use the extended integral of a nonnegative measurable random variable, so they may be infinite.

The **empirical reconstruction risk** on uncorrupted images is
$$R_{\rm rec}^{\rm emp}(\phi,\psi;S):=\frac1{nMq}\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^M\|D_\psi(E_\phi(x^{(i)}))_j-x^{(i)}_j\|_2^2.$$

A **finite denoising corruption law** assigns to each training image $x^{(i)}$ a finite set $C_i$ of corrupted images and weights $c_i(\tilde x)\ge0$ with $\sum_{\tilde x\in C_i}c_i(\tilde x)=1$. The empirical denoising risk is the finite-support specialization of the population risk:
$$R_{\rm den}^{\rm emp}(\phi,\psi;S,C):=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{\tilde x\in C_i}c_i(\tilde x)\frac1{Mq}\sum_{j=1}^M\|D_\psi(E_\phi(\tilde x))_j-x^{(i)}_j\|_2^2.$$

For masked autoencoding, fix an integer $k$ with $1\le k<M$ and let $\mathcal V_k=\{V\subseteq[M]:|V|=k\}$, a set with cardinality $\binom{M}{k}$. A mask $V$ is sampled uniformly from $\mathcal V_k$; the patches in $V$ are visible and the patches in $[M]\setminus V$ are masked. The encoder receives only the visible patches, with their positions, and no mask tokens. The decoder receives the encoded visible patches and a shared learned mask token at each missing position, with position information for all $M$ slots, and outputs predictions $\hat x_j(\phi,\psi;x,V)\in\mathbb R^q$ for every patch position.

The original-pixel target map is $T_{\rm raw}(u)=u$. The optional normalized-pixel target is defined for $u=(u_1,\ldots,u_q)$ with positive standard deviation by
$$\bar u:=\frac1q\sum_{r=1}^q u_r,\qquad s(u):=\left(\frac1q\sum_{r=1}^q(u_r-\bar u)^2\right)^{1/2}>0,\qquad T_{\rm norm}(u):=\frac{u-\bar u\mathbf 1}{s(u)},$$
where $\mathbf 1=(1,\ldots,1)\in\mathbb R^q$.
The target choice $T$ is one of these maps. Define
$$\mathcal D_{\rm norm}:=\{x\in\mathcal X:s(x_j)>0\text{ for every }j\in[M]\}.$$
For $T=T_{\rm norm}$, the masked-objective formulas below are defined only on $\mathcal D_{\rm norm}$, so a finite empirical objective requires $x^{(i)}\in\mathcal D_{\rm norm}$ for every $i$. For a population objective, require the event $A:=\{X\in\mathcal D_{\rm norm}\}$ to be measurable with $\mathbb P(A)=1$; interpret each loss integrand by its displayed formula on $A$ and by $0$ on $A^c$. Since $A^c$ is null, any other measurable extension there gives the same expectation. The raw target has no such restriction. The **per-example masked-patch mean squared error**, its population objective, and its finite empirical objective are
$$\ell_{\rm MAE}(\phi,\psi;x,V,T):=\frac1{(M-k)q}\sum_{j\in[M]\setminus V}\|\hat x_j(\phi,\psi;x,V)-T(x_j)\|_2^2,$$
$$R_{\rm MAE}(\phi,\psi;X,k,T):=\frac1{\binom Mk}\sum_{V\in\mathcal V_k}\mathbb E[\ell_{\rm MAE}(\phi,\psi;X,V,T)],$$
$$R_{\rm MAE}^{\rm emp}(\phi,\psi;S,k,T):=\frac1{n\binom Mk}\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{V\in\mathcal V_k}\ell_{\rm MAE}(\phi,\psi;x^{(i)},V,T).$$
The population objective averages the expectation over the image law for each fixed mask; equivalently, it is the joint expectation for an independent uniform mask. The finite empirical objective averages over every training image and mask.

Because the encoder input and decoder output depend on $V$ and the loss is evaluated only on $[M]\setminus V$, this is an expectation of a mask-dependent loss. It is not defined as an estimator of the separate full-image risk $R_{\rm rec}$, and no equality or unbiasedness between these objectives is asserted. Neither loss alone guarantees that a learned code retains distinctions needed for a downstream label (semantic sufficiency), uniquely determines an underlying data-generating parameter (identifiability), or improves performance on a specified later task (downstream feature quality).

The **expectation** of a real random variable $X$ on a finite probability space $(\Omega,w)$ is
$$\mathbb E[X]:=\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}X(\omega)w(\omega).$$
For a real constant $c$, the notation $c$ also denotes the constant random variable $\omega\mapsto c$.

derivations.claim: For $p_0$, the mean is $1/4$ and the standard deviation is $1/4$; for $p_1$, they are $3/4$ and $1/4$. Hence [F1] gives $T_{\rm norm}(p_0)=(-1,1)=T_{\rm norm}(p_1)$.

Both patches of either image have this same normalized target. By [F2], each mask leaves exactly one masked patch, and the decoder predicts $(-1,1)$ there. Its squared error is zero, so the per-example loss [F1] is zero for every image-mask outcome. The finite expectation [F3] is therefore zero.

For each fixed visible set $V$, the encoder returns the identical indexed token family $(z_*)_{j\in V}$ for both differently labelled images. Any deterministic classifier applied only to this representation has the same output on both images at that $V$, so it cannot classify both labels correctly. Allowing the classifier to use $V$ does not change this conclusion, since $V$ is independent of the equally weighted label. The constant token map and decoder are permitted finite feedforward maps by [F4], taking zero incoming weights, identity output activations, and fixed biases.

Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A_X,\mu_X)$ and $(\mathcal Z,\mathcal A_Z,\mu_Z)$ be sigma-finite measure spaces; that is, each has a countable measurable cover by sets of finite measure. Let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^{d_\theta}$ and $\Phi\subseteq\mathbb R^{d_\phi}$ be parameter sets of finite dimension. A latent-variable model with parameter $\theta\in\Theta$ consists of a measurable prior density $r_\theta(z)\ge0$ on $\mathcal Z$ and a decoder density $d_\theta(x\mid z)\ge0$ on $\mathcal X$ for each $z$, with
$$\int_{\mathcal Z} r_\theta(z)\,d\mu_Z(z)=1,\qquad \int_{\mathcal X} d_\theta(x\mid z)\,d\mu_X(x)=1.$$

Require the hypotheses of the dominated pathwise-gradient theorem at every parameter value reached by the procedure, and require each update below to remain in its open admissible parameter domain. Let $\mathcal N$ be the union of the theorem's common null set for finite positive log values and its null set on which the sample-path $C^1$ condition may fail; thus $\mathcal N$ is a common $\rho$-null set for all data indices and parameter values.

Set $\eta_0=(\theta_0,\phi_0)$. For each $t=0,\ldots,T-1$:

1. Draw $I_t$ uniformly from $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ and draw $\epsilon_t$ from $\rho$, with $I_t$ and $\epsilon_t$ independent and the pair $(I_t,\epsilon_t)$ independent of all earlier random draws.
2. If $\epsilon_t\in\mathcal N$, set $h_t=0$. Otherwise set $z_t=g_{\phi_t}(\epsilon_t,x_{I_t})$ and evaluate
   $$h_t=\log\gamma_{\theta_t}(z_t;x_{I_t})-\log q_{\phi_t}(z_t\mid x_{I_t}).$$
3. If $\epsilon_t\in\mathcal N$, set $G_t=0$. Otherwise, holding $\epsilon_t$ and $I_t$ fixed, compute the Euclidean gradient
   $$G_t=\nabla_{(\theta,\phi)}\bigl[\log\gamma_\theta(g_\phi(\epsilon_t,x_{I_t});x_{I_t})-\log q_\phi(g_\phi(\epsilon_t,x_{I_t})\mid x_{I_t})\bigr]\big|_{(\theta,\phi)=\eta_t}.$$
4. Update $\eta_{t+1}=\eta_t+\alpha_tG_t$.

Return $(\eta_0,\ldots,\eta_T)$ and $(h_t,G_t)_{0\le t<T}$. This finite procedure specifies stochastic ascent on the finite-average ELBO; it makes no claim that the iterates converge or reach a global maximum.

Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A_X,\mu_X)$ and $(\mathcal Z,\mathcal A_Z,\mu_Z)$ be sigma-finite measure spaces; that is, each has a countable measurable cover by sets of finite measure. Let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^{d_\theta}$ and $\Phi\subseteq\mathbb R^{d_\phi}$ be parameter sets of finite dimension. A latent-variable model with parameter $\theta\in\Theta$ consists of a measurable prior density $r_\theta(z)\ge0$ on $\mathcal Z$ and a decoder density $d_\theta(x\mid z)\ge0$ on $\mathcal X$ for each $z$, with
$$\int_{\mathcal Z} r_\theta(z)\,d\mu_Z(z)=1,\qquad \int_{\mathcal X} d_\theta(x\mid z)\,d\mu_X(x)=1.$$
The decoder is jointly measurable in $(x,z)$, and the joint model density is
$$p_\theta(x,z)=\gamma_\theta(z;x):=r_\theta(z)d_\theta(x\mid z)$$
relative to $\mu_X\otimes\mu_Z$. The decoder is also called the generative model: after drawing $z$ from the prior, it assigns a conditional density to the observation $x$.

For a fixed observation $x$, the evidence density and posterior density are
$$Z_\theta(x):=p_\theta(x):=\int_{\mathcal Z}\gamma_\theta(z;x)\,d\mu_Z(z),\qquad \pi_\theta(z\mid x):=\frac{\gamma_\theta(z;x)}{Z_\theta(x)}.$$
Use this posterior only when $0<Z_\theta(x)<\infty$. A variational encoder is a jointly measurable family of functions $q_\phi(z\mid x)\ge0$ on $\mathcal Z$, parameterized by $\phi\in\Phi$ and normalized by
$$\int_{\mathcal Z}q_\phi(z\mid x)\,d\mu_Z(z)=1$$
for every $(\phi,x)$; the same parameter $\phi$ is used for each observation. For an admissible triple $(\theta,\phi,x)$ require $0<Z_\theta(x)<\infty$ and
$$q_\phi(z\mid x)=0\quad\mu_Z\text{-almost everywhere on }\{z:\pi_\theta(z\mid x)=0\},\qquad \int_{\mathcal Z}q_\phi(z\mid x)\bigl(|\log\gamma_\theta(z;x)|+|\log q_\phi(z\mid x)|\bigr)\,d\mu_Z(z)<\infty.$$
Terms multiplied by $q_\phi=0$ are defined to be zero. The evidence lower bound is
$$\operatorname{ELBO}_{\theta,\phi}(x):=\int_{\mathcal Z}q_\phi(z\mid x)\bigl(\log\gamma_\theta(z;x)-\log q_\phi(z\mid x)\bigr)\,d\mu_Z(z).$$

A pathwise representation of the encoder at $x$ is a probability space $(\mathcal E,\mathcal F,\rho)$ whose law $\rho$ is independent of $\theta$ and $\phi$, together with a measurable map $g_\phi(\epsilon,x)$ such that the law of $g_\phi(\epsilon,x)$ for $\epsilon\sim\rho$ is the measure with density $q_\phi(\cdot\mid x)$ relative to $\mu_Z$. This representation defines how to generate encoder samples; it does not by itself assert that differentiation may pass through an expectation.

$$\mathbb{N} = \omega := \bigcap\,\{\, I : I \text{ is inductive} \,\},$$

which exists and is itself inductive by The natural numbers exist: a smallest inductive set (the
Axiom of Infinity, The Axiom of Infinity: there is a set containing a set with no elements and closed under $y \mapsto y \cup \{y\}$, supplies one inductive set to
intersect within, and Separation, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$, makes the
intersection a set). On $\mathbb{N}$ we take

$$0 := \varnothing, \qquad \sigma(n) := n \cup \{n\},$$

the distinguished element and the successor function. Thus
$0 = \varnothing$, $1 = \{0\}$, $2 = \{0, 1\}$, $3 = \{0, 1, 2\}$, and in general
$n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ is the set of its predecessors.

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. If $0 \in S$ and $\sigma(n) \in S$ whenever $n \in S$, then $S = \mathbb{N}$. For $\theta\in\Theta_\mu$, the **energy-based probability measure** is the

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $\Theta$ be a parameter set,
and for each $\theta\in\Theta$ let $E_\theta:X\to\mathbb R$ be a measurable
energy function. Its **partition function relative to $\mu$** is
$$Z_\theta:=\int_X e^{-E_\theta(x)}\,d\mu(x).$$
The admissible parameter set is
$$\Theta_\mu:=\{\theta\in\Theta:0<Z_\theta<\infty\}.$$
For $\theta\in\Theta_\mu$, the **energy-based probability measure** is the
measure with density $e^{-E_\theta}/Z_\theta$ relative to $\mu$:
$$P_\theta(A):=\frac{1}{Z_\theta}\int_A e^{-E_\theta(x)}\,d\mu(x),\qquad A\in\mathcal A.$$
The restriction $0<Z_\theta<\infty$ is part of the definition; parameters
outside $\Theta_\mu$ do not define a normalized model by this formula.

Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $r$ be a positive
integer and $\theta\in\mathbb R^r$,
and let $E_\theta:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable in $x$ and continuously
differentiable in $\theta$. Define the energy model $P_\theta$ relative to $\mu$
only when
$$0<Z_\theta:=\int_\mathcal X e^{-E_\theta(x)}\,d\mu(x)<\infty,$$
with density $e^{-E_\theta}/Z_\theta$. Let $Q_0$ be a data probability
measure on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ and let $K_\theta$ be a probability kernel
from $\mathcal X$ to itself which leaves $P_\theta$ invariant, meaning
$$\int_\mathcal X K_\theta(x,A)\,P_\theta(dx)=P_\theta(A)\qquad(A\in\mathcal A).$$
Let $\{*\}$ carry its full sigma-algebra, let $G_{0,\theta}(*,A):=Q_0(A)$,
and recursively compose the probability kernel $G_{j,\theta}$ from $\{*\}$ to
$\mathcal X$ with $K_\theta$ to obtain $G_{j+1,\theta}$. Define
$Q_{j,\theta}(A):=G_{j,\theta}(*,A)$; thus $Q_{0,\theta}=Q_0$ and
$$Q_{j+1,\theta}(A)=\int_\mathcal X K_\theta(x,A)\,Q_{j,\theta}(dx),\qquad A\in\mathcal A.$$
Finite probability-kernel composition makes each $Q_{j,\theta}$ a probability
measure. For an integer $k\ge1$, $Q_{k,\theta}$ is the $k$-step reconstruction law.

If $Q_0$ and $Q_{k,\theta}$ have specified nonnegative measurable densities
$r_{0,\theta}$ and $r_{k,\theta}$ relative to $P_\theta$, meaning
$Q_{j,\theta}(A)=\int_A r_{j,\theta}\,dP_\theta$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$
for $j\in\{0,k\}$, and
$$\int|r_{j,\theta}\log r_{j,\theta}|\,dP_\theta<\infty\qquad(j\in\{0,k\}),$$
define their finite contrastive-divergence objective by
$$\operatorname{CD}_k(\theta):=\int r_{0,\theta}\log r_{0,\theta}\,dP_\theta-\int r_{k,\theta}\log r_{k,\theta}\,dP_\theta,$$
where $0\log0:=0$ and $\log$ is the natural logarithm. On a finite state
space where $P_\theta$ has positive mass at every state, write
$p_\theta(x):=P_\theta(\{x\})$ and $q_{j,\theta}(x):=Q_{j,\theta}(\{x\})$.
Then $r_{j,\theta}(x)=q_{j,\theta}(x)/p_\theta(x)$ and the objective equals
$$\sum_{x:q_{0,\theta}(x)>0}q_{0,\theta}(x)\log\frac{q_{0,\theta}(x)}{p_\theta(x)}-\sum_{x:q_{k,\theta}(x)>0}q_{k,\theta}(x)\log\frac{q_{k,\theta}(x)}{p_\theta(x)},$$
since each finite-space integral is the sum of the integrand times the point
mass and $p_\theta r_{j,\theta}=q_{j,\theta}$.

For a positive integer $m$, the procedure takes independent data draws
$x^1,\ldots,x^m$ with common law $Q_0$, a transition sampler for $K_\theta$,
and a learning rate $\eta>0$; the
reconstruction chains are drawn independently conditional on their starts. Its
output is the updated parameter from the **stop-gradient CD-$k$ update**:

1. For each $i$, set $x^{i,0}=x^i$ and draw $x^{i,j+1}$ from
   $K_\theta(x^{i,j},\cdot)$ for $j=0,\ldots,k-1$.
2. Form
   $$\widehat g_k=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\left(\nabla_\theta E_\theta(x^i)-\nabla_\theta E_\theta(x^{i,k})\right).$$
3. Update $\theta\leftarrow\theta-\eta\widehat g_k$.

When $\nabla_\theta E_\theta$ is integrable under $Q_0$ and $Q_{k,\theta}$,
the associated **population CD-$k$ direction** is
$$g_k(\theta):=\int\nabla_\theta E_\theta\,dQ_0-\int\nabla_\theta E_\theta\,dQ_{k,\theta}.$$
The procedure makes no claim that the chain has mixed in $k$ steps. The
parameter derivative of $Q_{k,\theta}$ is not stopped in the scalar objective's
definition; the update above deliberately omits that derivative.

Let $\mathcal X$ be a finite nonempty set. A **probability vector** on
$\mathcal X$ is a family $P=(p_x)_{x\in\mathcal X}$ of real numbers such that
$p_x\ge 0$ for every $x$ and $\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}p_x=1$. Its support is
$\operatorname{supp}P:=\{x\in\mathcal X:p_x>0\}$. Coordinates outside the
support are retained as zeros; they are not deleted from the alphabet.

For another probability vector $Q=(q_x)_{x\in\mathcal X}$, the notation
$P\ll Q$ means $\operatorname{supp}P\subseteq\operatorname{supp}Q$. All
finite sums over $\mathcal X$ use the displayed alphabet and ordinary finite
real arithmetic, extended to $+\infty$ only where a later definition says so.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
(Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property)), neighbourhoods are those of
The $\varepsilon$-neighbourhood and the punctured $\varepsilon$-neighbourhood of a point of $\mathbb{R}$ and limit points those of Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that The $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ limit $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a limit point $c$ of $A$ defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by At a limit point of the domain a function has at most one limit applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why The $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ limit $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a limit point $c$ of $A$ leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
(The $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ limit $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a limit point $c$ of $A$). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of The limit at $c$ depends only on the restriction of $f$ to a punctured neighbourhood of $c$, and passes to any subset of the domain having $c$ as a limit point carries the limit to that restriction.

(Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of If $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L \ne 0$ then $|f| > |L|/2$ on a punctured neighbourhood of $c$; in particular if $L > 0$ then $f > L/2 > 0$ there applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
Carathéodory's characterisation: $f$ is differentiable at $c$ if and only if there is $\varphi : A \to \mathbb{R}$, continuous at $c$, with $f(x) - f(c) = \varphi(x)(x - c)$ for every $x \in A$, and then $\varphi$ is unique and $\varphi(c) = f'(c)$.** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of Sums, scalar multiples, products, absolute values, maxima, minima and quotients with nonvanishing denominator of continuous functions are continuous, as are constants, the identity and every polynomial function.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ (Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$) at which $g$ is differentiable
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $X$ be a set and let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on $X$ (Sigma-algebras). A **measure** on $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a function

$$\mu:\mathcal A\longrightarrow[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$$

such that:

1. $\mu(\varnothing)=0$;
2. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$,
   $$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k),$$
   where the right side is the nonnegative extended sum of Series in the nonnegative extended real line.

The second condition is **countable additivity**. It begins at index $0$ and includes the case in which some term or the total sum is $+\infty$.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ (Measures on sigma-algebras). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** (Measure spaces); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space, $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ a sub-sigma-algebra, and $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ integrable. A **conditional-expectation version of $X$ given $\mathcal G$** is a real, $\mathcal G$-measurable, integrable function $Y$ such that $\int_A Y\,dP=\int_A X\,dP$ for every $A\in\mathcal G$. No completeness of $\mathcal G$ is assumed.

Expectation means the integral of Expectation of a nonnegative or integrable random variable. Integrable representatives use The class $L^1(\mu)$ of integrable functions; quotient notation is introduced after uniqueness.

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$

derivations.claim: Fix a coordinate $j$ and vary only $\theta_j$ in a small interval inside the open set $\Theta$. Since $\mathcal X$ is finite and each energy is real, [F13] makes every $e^{-E_\theta(x)}$ positive; hence [F1] gives $0<Z_\theta<\infty$. The formula for $p_\theta$ then gives positive coordinates summing to one, so it is a probability vector by [F4]. By [F6], [F7] and [F8], differentiating the finite sum gives $\partial_jZ_\theta=-\sum_xe^{-E_\theta(x)}\partial_jE_\theta(x)$. The same chain and quotient rules give $\partial_jp_\theta(x)/p_\theta(x)=-\partial_jE_\theta(x)-\partial_jZ_\theta/Z_\theta=-\partial_jE_\theta(x)+\sum_yp_\theta(y)\partial_jE_\theta(y)$; [F9] identifies the left side with $\partial_j\log p_\theta(x)$. Because $q_0$ is fixed and sums to one by [F4], differentiating $\mathcal L=-\sum_xq_0(x)\log p_\theta(x)$ and summing this identity yields the displayed likelihood-gradient formula.

The recurrence in [F2] gives $q_{j+1,\theta}=q_{j,\theta}K_\theta$, hence $q_{k,\theta}=q_0K_\theta^k$ and $\sum_xq_{k,\theta}(x)=1$. For $k=1$ the product rule [F6] gives $\partial_j(q_0K_\theta)=q_0\partial_jK_\theta$. If $\partial_j(q_0K_\theta^k)=\sum_{s=0}^{k-1}q_0K_\theta^s(\partial_jK_\theta)K_\theta^{k-1-s}$, then entrywise application of [F6] to $q_0K_\theta^kK_\theta$ yields $\sum_{s=0}^{k-1}q_0K_\theta^s(\partial_jK_\theta)K_\theta^{k-s}+q_0K_\theta^k(\partial_jK_\theta)$, which is the same formula with $k+1$ by appending the $s=k$ term. Thus the stated product derivative holds for every $k$. Differentiating $\sum_xq_{k,\theta}(x)=1$ by [F6] gives $\sum_x\partial_jq_{k,\theta}(x)=0$. Strict positivity of $K_\theta$ and nonzero mass of $q_0$ imply $q_{k,\theta}(x)>0$ for every $x$, so the following logarithms are finite.

Put $w(x_0,\ldots,x_k):=q_0(x_0)\prod_{s=0}^{k-1}K_\theta(x_s,x_{s+1})$. These weights are nonnegative. Summing successively over $x_k,\ldots,x_1$ and using the row sums of $K_\theta$ reduces $\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)$ to $\sum_{x_0}q_0(x_0)=1$. The set function $\mathbb P_\theta(A)=\sum_{\omega\in A}w(\omega)$ vanishes on the empty set and is countably additive: a disjoint sequence of subsets of finite $\Omega$ has only finitely many nonempty terms. Thus [F10] makes it a measure, and [F11] makes it a probability measure.

By the quotient rule [F6], $\partial_j(q_{k,\theta}(x)/p_\theta(x))=\partial_jq_{k,\theta}(x)/p_\theta(x)-q_{k,\theta}(x)\partial_jp_\theta(x)/p_\theta(x)^2$; the chain and logarithm derivative rules [F7, F9] then give $\partial_j\log(q_{k,\theta}(x)/p_\theta(x))=\partial_jq_{k,\theta}(x)/q_{k,\theta}(x)-\partial_j\log p_\theta(x)$. Applying the product rule [F6] to each summand of $D_{\rm KL}(q_{k,\theta}\|p_\theta)$ therefore gives $\partial_jq_{k,\theta}(x)(\log(q_{k,\theta}(x)/p_\theta(x))+1)-q_{k,\theta}(x)\partial_j\log p_\theta(x)$. Summing the finite terms, the $+1$ contribution vanishes by step 1.2. Substitution from step 1.1 yields $\partial_jD_{\rm KL}(q_{k,\theta}\|p_\theta)=\sum_x\partial_jq_{k,\theta}(x)\log(q_{k,\theta}(x)/p_\theta(x))+\sum_xq_{k,\theta}(x)\partial_jE_\theta(x)-\sum_xp_\theta(x)\partial_jE_\theta(x)$.

For $s=0$, $K_\theta^0=I$ is row-stochastic and its entries are the length-zero path weights. If the entries of $K_\theta^s$ sum the products along all length-$s$ paths, then $K_\theta^{s+1}(x,y)=\sum_zK_\theta^s(x,z)K_\theta(z,y)$ appends the final transition, so its entries sum the length-$(s+1)$ path weights; also $\sum_yK_\theta^{s+1}(x,y)=\sum_zK_\theta^s(x,z)\sum_yK_\theta(z,y)=1$. Thus $\mathbb P_\theta(X_0=x,X_k=y)=q_0(x)K_\theta^k(x,y)$. The function $g_f$ is finite-valued; for each Borel $C\subseteq\mathbb R$, $\{g_f(X_0)\in C\}=X_0^{-1}(\{x:g_f(x)\in C\})$, so $g_f(X_0)$ is $\sigma(X_0)$-measurable. Both $f(X_k)$ and $g_f(X_0)$ are integrable since $\Omega$ is finite.

Since $q_0$ is fixed, the terms $q_0(x)\log q_0(x)$ in $D_{\rm KL}(q_0\|p_\theta)$ have zero derivative; applying the same product and logarithm rules [F6, F9] and using the log-density formula from step 1.1 and $\sum_xq_0(x)=1$ gives $\partial_jD_{\rm KL}(q_0\|p_\theta)=\sum_xq_0(x)\partial_jE_\theta(x)-\sum_xp_\theta(x)\partial_jE_\theta(x)$. Subtracting step 2.1 cancels the model expectations and yields the stated $\partial_j\operatorname{CD}_k$ formula. By [F3], the algorithm uses only its first two terms; the remaining sum is the derivative through $K_\theta^k$. Comparing with step 1.1 also shows that the algorithm replaces the exact likelihood negative phase $p_\theta$ by $q_{k,\theta}$.

Every event in $\sigma(X_0)$ has the form $\{X_0\in B\}$ for some $B\subseteq\mathcal X$, since these preimages form a sigma-algebra and generate $\sigma(X_0)$. For every such event, step 2.2 gives $$\int \mathbf1_{\{X_0\in B\}}f(X_k)\,d\mathbb P_\theta=\sum_{x\in B}q_0(x)\sum_yK_\theta^k(x,y)f(y)=\int \mathbf1_{\{X_0\in B\}}g_f(X_0)\,d\mathbb P_\theta,$$ where terms with $q_0(x)=0$ vanish. The integrability and measurability from step 2.2 and this event-integral identity satisfy [F12], so $g_f(X_0)$ is the asserted conditional-expectation version.

On a small coordinate interval in the open parameter set, finite nonempty states and real energies give positive finite Z and positive model masses. Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $\Theta$ be a parameter set,
and for each $\theta\in\Theta$ let $E_\theta:X\to\mathbb R$ be a measurable
energy function. Its **partition function relative to $\mu$** is
$$Z_\theta:=\int_X e^{-E_\theta(x)}\,d\mu(x).$$
The admissible parameter set is
$$\Theta_\mu:=\{\theta\in\Theta:0<Z_\theta<\infty\}.$$
For $\theta\in\Theta_\mu$, the **energy-based probability measure** is the
measure with density $e^{-E_\theta}/Z_\theta$ relative to $\mu$:
$$P_\theta(A):=\frac{1}{Z_\theta}\int_A e^{-E_\theta(x)}\,d\mu(x),\qquad A\in\mathcal A.$$
The restriction $0<Z_\theta<\infty$ is part of the definition; parameters
outside $\Theta_\mu$ do not define a normalized model by this formula.

Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $r$ be a positive
integer and $\theta\in\mathbb R^r$,
and let $E_\theta:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable in $x$ and continuously
differentiable in $\theta$. Define the energy model $P_\theta$ relative to $\mu$
only when
$$0<Z_\theta:=\int_\mathcal X e^{-E_\theta(x)}\,d\mu(x)<\infty,$$
with density $e^{-E_\theta}/Z_\theta$. Let $Q_0$ be a data probability
measure on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ and let $K_\theta$ be a probability kernel
from $\mathcal X$ to itself which leaves $P_\theta$ invariant, meaning
$$\int_\mathcal X K_\theta(x,A)\,P_\theta(dx)=P_\theta(A)\qquad(A\in\mathcal A).$$
Let $\{*\}$ carry its full sigma-algebra, let $G_{0,\theta}(*,A):=Q_0(A)$,
and recursively compose the probability kernel $G_{j,\theta}$ from $\{*\}$ to
$\mathcal X$ with $K_\theta$ to obtain $G_{j+1,\theta}$. Define
$Q_{j,\theta}(A):=G_{j,\theta}(*,A)$; thus $Q_{0,\theta}=Q_0$ and
$$Q_{j+1,\theta}(A)=\int_\mathcal X K_\theta(x,A)\,Q_{j,\theta}(dx),\qquad A\in\mathcal A.$$
Finite probability-kernel composition makes each $Q_{j,\theta}$ a probability
measure. For an integer $k\ge1$, $Q_{k,\theta}$ is the $k$-step reconstruction law.

If $Q_0$ and $Q_{k,\theta}$ have specified nonnegative measurable densities
$r_{0,\theta}$ and $r_{k,\theta}$ relative to $P_\theta$, meaning
$Q_{j,\theta}(A)=\int_A r_{j,\theta}\,dP_\theta$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$
for $j\in\{0,k\}$, and
$$\int|r_{j,\theta}\log r_{j,\theta}|\,dP_\theta<\infty\qquad(j\in\{0,k\}),$$
define their finite contrastive-divergence objective by
$$\operatorname{CD}_k(\theta):=\int r_{0,\theta}\log r_{0,\theta}\,dP_\theta-\int r_{k,\theta}\log r_{k,\theta}\,dP_\theta,$$
where $0\log0:=0$ and $\log$ is the natural logarithm. On a finite state
space where $P_\theta$ has positive mass at every state, write
$p_\theta(x):=P_\theta(\{x\})$ and $q_{j,\theta}(x):=Q_{j,\theta}(\{x\})$.
Then $r_{j,\theta}(x)=q_{j,\theta}(x)/p_\theta(x)$ and the objective equals
$$\sum_{x:q_{0,\theta}(x)>0}q_{0,\theta}(x)\log\frac{q_{0,\theta}(x)}{p_\theta(x)}-\sum_{x:q_{k,\theta}(x)>0}q_{k,\theta}(x)\log\frac{q_{k,\theta}(x)}{p_\theta(x)},$$
since each finite-space integral is the sum of the integrand times the point
mass and $p_\theta r_{j,\theta}=q_{j,\theta}$.

For a positive integer $m$, the procedure takes independent data draws
$x^1,\ldots,x^m$ with common law $Q_0$, a transition sampler for $K_\theta$,
and a learning rate $\eta>0$; the
reconstruction chains are drawn independently conditional on their starts. Its
output is the updated parameter from the **stop-gradient CD-$k$ update**:

1. For each $i$, set $x^{i,0}=x^i$ and draw $x^{i,j+1}$ from
   $K_\theta(x^{i,j},\cdot)$ for $j=0,\ldots,k-1$.
2. Form
   $$\widehat g_k=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\left(\nabla_\theta E_\theta(x^i)-\nabla_\theta E_\theta(x^{i,k})\right).$$
3. Update $\theta\leftarrow\theta-\eta\widehat g_k$.

When $\nabla_\theta E_\theta$ is integrable under $Q_0$ and $Q_{k,\theta}$,
the associated **population CD-$k$ direction** is
$$g_k(\theta):=\int\nabla_\theta E_\theta\,dQ_0-\int\nabla_\theta E_\theta\,dQ_{k,\theta}.$$
The procedure makes no claim that the chain has mixed in $k$ steps. The
parameter derivative of $Q_{k,\theta}$ is not stopped in the scalar objective's
definition; the update above deliberately omits that derivative.

only when

$x^1,\ldots,x^m$ with common law $Q_0$, a transition sampler for $K_\theta$,
and a learning rate $\eta>0$; the
reconstruction chains are drawn independently conditional on their starts. Its
output is the updated parameter from the **stop-gradient CD-$k$ update**:

1. For each $i$, set $x^{i,0}=x^i$ and draw $x^{i,j+1}$ from
   $K_\theta(x^{i,j},\cdot)$ for $j=0,\ldots,k-1$.
2. Form
   $$\widehat g_k=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\left(\nabla_\theta E_\theta(x^i)-\nabla_\theta E_\theta(x^{i,k})\right).$$
3. Update $\theta\leftarrow\theta-\eta\widehat g_k$.

When $\nabla_\theta E_\theta$ is integrable under $Q_0$ and $Q_{k,\theta}$,
the associated **population CD-$k$ direction** is
$$g_k(\theta):=\int\nabla_\theta E_\theta\,dQ_0-\int\nabla_\theta E_\theta\,dQ_{k,\theta}.$$
The procedure makes no claim that the chain has mixed in $k$ steps. The
parameter derivative of $Q_{k,\theta}$ is not stopped in the scalar objective's
definition; the update above deliberately omits that derivative.

Let $r$ be a positive integer, let $\mathcal X$ be finite and nonempty, and
let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^r$ be open. For each $x,y\in\mathcal X$, assume
the coordinate partial derivatives of $E_\theta(x)$ and $K_\theta(x,y)$ exist
and are continuous on $\Theta$. Let $K_\theta$ be strictly positive and
row-stochastic, so $K_\theta(x,y)>0$ and $\sum_yK_\theta(x,y)=1$. Use counting
measure as the reference measure, set
$$Z_\theta:=\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}e^{-E_\theta(x)},\qquad p_\theta(x):=e^{-E_\theta(x)}/Z_\theta,$$
let $q_0$ be a fixed probability vector on $\mathcal X$, assume $p_\theta$ is
invariant for $K_\theta$, and fix an integer $k\ge1$. Define
$K_\theta^0=I$, $K_\theta^{s+1}=K_\theta^sK_\theta$, and
$q_{k,\theta}=q_0K_\theta^k$, where vectors are row vectors, and
$$\mathcal L(\theta):=-\sum_xq_0(x)\log p_\theta(x),\qquad \operatorname{CD}_k(\theta):=D_{\rm KL}(q_0\|p_\theta)-D_{\rm KL}(q_{k,\theta}\|p_\theta),$$
where for finite probability mass functions $a,b$ with $b(x)>0$,
$$D_{\rm KL}(a\|b):=\sum_{x:a(x)>0}a(x)\log\frac{a(x)}{b(x)}$$
with $\log$ the natural logarithm and zero-mass terms contributing zero. For each parameter coordinate $j$,
$$\partial_j\mathcal L(\theta)=\sum_xq_0(x)\partial_jE_\theta(x)-\sum_xp_\theta(x)\partial_jE_\theta(x),$$
while
$$\partial_j\operatorname{CD}_k(\theta)=\sum_xq_0(x)\partial_jE_\theta(x)-\sum_xq_{k,\theta}(x)\partial_jE_\theta(x)-\sum_x\partial_jq_{k,\theta}(x)\log\frac{q_{k,\theta}(x)}{p_\theta(x)}.$$

$$\partial_jq_{k,\theta}=\sum_{s=0}^{k-1}q_0K_\theta^s(\partial_jK_\theta)K_\theta^{k-1-s}.$$

terms of the displayed $\partial_j\operatorname{CD}_k$ formula and omits the
explicit derivative through the $k$ transition kernels. It also replaces the
model expectation in the exact negative log-likelihood gradient by the finite
reconstruction law; no equality between these gradients is asserted.

For the finite-state path calculation, let $\Omega:=\mathcal X^{k+1}$ with its
full sigma-algebra, let $X_s$ be the $s$th coordinate map, and define
$$\mathbb P_\theta(A):=\sum_{(x_0,\ldots,x_k)\in A}q_0(x_0)\prod_{s=0}^{k-1}K_\theta(x_s,x_{s+1}),\qquad A\subseteq\Omega.$$
This is a probability measure. For every real $f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R$, set
$$g_f(x):=\begin{cases}\sum_yK_\theta^k(x,y)f(y),&q_0(x)>0,\\0,&q_0(x)=0.\end{cases}$$
Then $g_f(X_0)$ is a version of
$\mathbb E_{\mathbb P_\theta}[f(X_k)\mid\sigma(X_0)]$.

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;

   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a

is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
Carathéodory's characterisation: $f$ is differentiable at $c$ if and only if there is $\varphi : A \to \mathbb{R}$, continuous at $c$, with $f(x) - f(c) = \varphi(x)(x - c)$ for every $x \in A$, and then $\varphi$ is unique and $\varphi(c) = f'(c)$.** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ (Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$) at which $g$ is differentiable
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
(Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property)), neighbourhoods are those of
The $\varepsilon$-neighbourhood and the punctured $\varepsilon$-neighbourhood of a point of $\mathbb{R}$ and limit points those of Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that The $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ limit $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a limit point $c$ of $A$ defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by At a limit point of the domain a function has at most one limit applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why The $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ limit $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a limit point $c$ of $A$ leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
(The $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ limit $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a limit point $c$ of $A$). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of The limit at $c$ depends only on the restriction of $f$ to a punctured neighbourhood of $c$, and passes to any subset of the domain having $c$ as a limit point carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex (Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
(Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$).

Consequently, for $f$ defined on a nondegenerate interval $I$, the symbol
$f'(c)$ is meaningful at **every** $c \in I$, endpoints included. At an endpoint
the difference quotient is taken over the points of $I$ lying on the one side
that is available, so what other texts call a one-sided derivative is, here,
simply the derivative of $f$ on $I$.

Let $X$ be a set, let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on $X$ (a family containing $\emptyset$ and $X$, closed under complements and countable unions), and let $\mu:\mathcal A\to[0,+\infty]$ be a countably additive measure with $\mu(\emptyset)=0$. Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on $(X,\mathcal A)$, meaning countably additive measures with $P(X)=Q(X)=1$. A function from $X$ to a Borel space is measurable when the inverse image of each Borel set belongs to $\mathcal A$. Assume that $P$ and $Q$ have finite-valued, nonnegative, measurable densities $p$ and $q$ with respect to the same measure $\mu$, meaning that $P(E)=\int_E p\,d\mu$ and $Q(E)=\int_E q\,d\mu$ for every $E\in\mathcal A$. In particular, $\int p\,d\mu=\int q\,d\mu=1$.

For a measurable discriminator $D:X\to[0,1]$, put $a(t)=-\ln t$ for $0<t\le1$ and $a(0)=+\infty$, and put $b(t)=-\ln(1-t)$ for $0\le t<1$ and $b(1)=+\infty$. In the products below, define $0\cdot(+\infty)=0$; a positive finite factor times $+\infty$ is $+\infty$. Define the log payoff and the unrestricted discriminator value by
$$
V(D;P,Q):=-\int p(x)a(D(x))\,d\mu(x)-\int q(x)b(D(x))\,d\mu(x),\qquad C(P,Q):=\sup_{D:X\to[0,1]\,\mathrm{measurable}}V(D;P,Q).
$$
The functions $a$ and $b$ are Borel measurable: $\ln$ is continuous on $(0,\infty)$, and each extension assigns $+\infty$ only at one Borel endpoint. Therefore $a\circ D$ and $b\circ D$ are measurable, and the products with $p$ and $q$ are measurable by the pointwise product convention and product-closure result referenced below. Thus both nonnegative integrals are defined.

Each integral is the nonnegative Lebesgue integral, defined as the supremum of the integrals of nonnegative simple minorants, so $V(D;P,Q)\in[-\infty,0]$. The supremum ranges over all measurable functions into $[0,1]$, including boundary values; it is not restricted to a finite-parameter discriminator family.

In the common-density setting, put $m=(p+q)/2$. Additivity and nonnegative homogeneity of the integral give $\int m\,d\mu=1$. Define $r=p/m$ and $s=q/m$ where $m>0$, and define $r=s=0$ where $m=0$; then $0\le r,s\le2$ and $r+s=2$ wherever $m>0$. Let $\phi(0)=0$ and $\phi(t)=t\ln t$ for $t>0$. The density-defined Jensen–Shannon divergence is
$$
\operatorname{JS}_\mu(P,Q):=\frac12\int m\phi(r)\,d\mu+\frac12\int m\phi(s)\,d\mu.
$$
The integrals are finite, and this formula is the average of the two density-relative-entropy terms from $p$ and $q$ to the mixture density $m$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space and let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int f\,d\mu=0 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad f=0 \text{ almost everywhere.}$$

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. If $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ are measurable, then
$$\int(f+g)\,d\mu=\int f\,d\mu+\int g\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

1. If $f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ are measurable and $f+g$ is defined
   pointwise, then $f+g$ is measurable.
2. If $c\in\mathbb R$ and $f:X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, then $cf$ is
   measurable.
3. If $f:X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, then $f^+=\max\{f,0\}$,
   $f^-=\max\{-f,0\}$, and $|f|=f^++f^-$ are measurable.
4. If $E\in\mathcal A$ and $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, then
   $f\chi_E$ is measurable, where this function equals $f$ on $E$ and $0$
   off $E$ (in particular, $0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ here).
5. If $(f_n)$ is a sequence of measurable functions $X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$,
   then $\inf_n f_n$ is measurable; if moreover $f_n\uparrow f$ pointwise, then
   $f$ is measurable.

Let $n\ge1$, let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ be a measurable space, and let
$f = (f_1,\dots,f_n) : X \to \mathbb{R}^n$. Then $f$ is measurable if and only
if each coordinate function $f_j : X \to \mathbb{R}$ is measurable.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$, $(Y,\mathcal{B})$, and $(Z,\mathcal{C})$ be measurable
spaces. If $f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Y,\mathcal{B})$ is measurable and
$g : (Y,\mathcal{B}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable, then
$g \circ f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable.

In particular, if $f$ is measurable and $g$ is a Borel measurable function on
its codomain, then $g \circ f$ is measurable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space and let
$f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ be measurable for the Borel sigma-algebra on
the extended real line. Products of functions use
$\odot_X$ from A total pointwise product for extended-real-valued functions, and $cf$
abbreviates $\underline c\odot_X f$ for the constant function $\underline c$.
The magnitude function is $|f|=\max(f,-f)$ as in
The positive and negative parts of a function. Then:

1. $cf$ is measurable for every real scalar $c$;
2. $\max(f,g)$, $\min(f,g)$, $|f|$, $f^+$, and $f^-$ are measurable;
3. if the partial pointwise sum $f+g$ is defined at every point, then it is measurable;
4. the pointwise product $fg:=f\odot_X g$ is measurable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let
$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable, and let $E\in\mathcal A$. Since
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]]
implies that $f\chi_E$ is measurable, define the **integral of $f$ over $E$**
by
$$\int_E f\,d\mu:=\int f\chi_E\,d\mu,$$
where the integral on the right is the nonnegative Lebesgue integral of
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]].

Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. Its positive and negative parts are
$$f^+:=\max\{f,0\},\qquad f^-:=\max\{-f,0\};$$
they are measurable by
Closure properties of measurable functions used by the integral and
satisfy $f=f^+-f^-$ and $|f|=f^++f^-$.

The **Lebesgue integral of a real measurable function** is defined whenever at
most one of $\int f^+\,d\mu$ and $\int f^-\,d\mu$ is $+\infty$, in which case
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\int f^+\,d\mu-\int f^-\,d\mu.$$
The function is **integrable** when both integrals are finite, equivalently
when $\int|f|\,d\mu<+\infty$.

For a complex measurable function $h=u+iv$ with
$u=\operatorname{Re}h,\ v=\operatorname{Im}h$
(Real and imaginary parts, complex conjugation, and modulus), define $h$ to be
**integrable** when $|h|$ is integrable, and then define
$$\int h\,d\mu:=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$

Let $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\chi_{E_j}$ be a simple representation of a
nonnegative simple measurable function
(Nonnegative simple measurable functions) on a measure space
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$, so the $E_j\in\mathcal A$ are pairwise disjoint and
$c_j\ge0$. Its
**simple integral** is
$$\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mu(E_j),$$
where $\mu$ is the given measure (Measures on sigma-algebras) and the convention
$0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ is fixed once and for all.

The next lemma proves that this value is independent of the chosen simple
representation.

If $s$ is a nonnegative simple measurable function, then its nonnegative
Lebesgue integral equals its simple integral:
$$\int s\,d\mu=\int_{\mathrm{simple}} s\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: Define $\psi(0)=1$ and $\psi(t)=t\ln t-t+1$ for $t>0$. If $0<t<1$, then $\ln t=-\int_t^1du/u>-(1-t)/t=1-1/t$, since $1/u<1/t$ for $t<u\le1$. Also $-1\le\phi(t)\le0$ for $0<t\le1$, by the first inequality and $\ln t\le0$; and $0\le\phi(t)\le t(t-1)\le2$ for $1\le t\le2$, since $\ln t=\int_1^tdu/u\le t-1$. At $t=0$, $\phi(0)=0$ and $\psi(0)=1$. Hence $\psi\ge0$ with equality exactly at $1$, $|\phi(t)|\le2$, and $\psi(t)\le5$ on $[0,2]$.

By [F1], [F7] and [F8], $\int m\,d\mu=\tfrac12\int(p+q)\,d\mu=1$. By [F2], $0\le r,s\le2$. The ratio maps $R(a,b)=2a/(a+b)$ and $S(a,b)=2b/(a+b)$ on $a+b>0$, extended by $0$ at $(0,0)$, are Borel because they are continuous on $\{a+b>0\}$ and separately defined on the Borel singleton $\{(0,0)\}$. The functions $\phi,\psi$ are continuous on $[0,2]$, including at $0$. Thus coordinatewise measurability [F10], composition with these Borel maps [F11], and arithmetic closure [F9] give measurable $m,r,s,\phi(r),\phi(s),\psi(r),\psi(s)$; product closure [F12] then gives measurability of $m\phi(r)$, $m\phi(s)$, and $\tfrac12m(\psi(r)+\psi(s))$. Step 1.1 gives $|m\phi(r)|,|m\phi(s)|\le2m$ and $0\le\tfrac12m(\psi(r)+\psi(s))\le5m$, so they are integrable. On $m>0$, $r+s=2$ and $\phi(t)=\psi(t)+t-1$, so $\phi(r)+\phi(s)=\psi(r)+\psi(s)\ge0$; when $m=0$ both products by $m$ vanish. Linearity in [F6] gives $\operatorname{JS}_\mu(P,Q)=\int \tfrac12m(\psi(r)+\psi(s))\,d\mu\ge0$.

If $\operatorname{JS}_\mu(P,Q)=0$, the nonnegative measurable function $h:=\tfrac12m(\psi(r)+\psi(s))$ has integral zero by step 2.1. By [F5], $h=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere. On $m>0$, both $\psi(r)$ and $\psi(s)$ are nonnegative, so they must each be zero almost everywhere there; step 1.1 gives $r=s=1$ there, hence $p=q$. On $m=0$, nonnegativity and $m=(p+q)/2$ give $p=q=0$. Thus $p=q$ $\mu$-almost everywhere. For each $E\in\mathcal A$, [F1] and [F13] give $P(E)-Q(E)=\int p\chi_E\,d\mu-\int q\chi_E\,d\mu$. These restrictions are integrable because they are bounded by $p$ and $q$, whose integrals are $1$; [F8] and [F6] rewrite their difference as $\int u_E\,d\mu$ for $u_E:=p\chi_E-q\chi_E$. The positive and negative parts of $u_E$ are measurable by [F9, F12] and vanish almost everywhere, so [F5] makes both nonnegative integrals zero. By [F14], $\int u_E\,d\mu=0$, hence $P(E)=Q(E)$.

Conversely, suppose $P=Q$. For positive integers $n,k$, put $E_{n,k}:=\{p-q\ge1/n\}\cap\{p+q\ge1/k\}$, which is measurable by [F9]. Since $\{p>q\}=\bigcup_{n,k\ge1}E_{n,k}$, positive measure of $\{p>q\}$ would make some $E:=E_{n,k}$ have positive measure. On $E$, $(1/k)\chi_E\le(p+q)\chi_E\le p+q$, so [F8], [F13], [F15] and [F16] give $\mu(E)/k\le\int_E(p+q)\,d\mu\le\int(p+q)\,d\mu=2$ by [F1], [F7] and step 2.1; hence $\mu(E)<\infty$. Put $u:=(p-q)\chi_E$. By [F9, F12], $u$ is nonnegative measurable, and $(1/n)\chi_E\le u$, so [F8], [F15] and [F16] give $\int u\,d\mu\ge\mu(E)/n>0$. Also $p\chi_E$ and $q\chi_E$ are integrable since they are bounded by $p$ and $q$; [F1], [F13] and [F6] therefore give $\int u\,d\mu=P(E)-Q(E)=0$, a contradiction. The same argument with $p,q$ exchanged rules out $\{q>p\}$, hence $p=q$ $\mu$-almost everywhere. Then $m\phi(r)$ and $m\phi(s)$ vanish almost everywhere: on $m>0$, $r=s=1$ almost everywhere, and on $m=0$ both products are zero. Their positive and negative parts are measurable by [F9, F12] and vanish almost everywhere, so [F5] makes all four nonnegative integrals zero. Step 2.1 gives their integrability, and [F14] and [F2] therefore yield $\operatorname{JS}_\mu(P,Q)=0$.
Steps 3.1 and 3.2 prove that $\operatorname{JS}_\mu(P,Q)$ is zero exactly when $P=Q$; step 2.1 proves it is finite and nonnegative. These are all claims in the Statement.

Let $X$ be a set, let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on $X$ (a family containing $\emptyset$ and $X$, closed under complements and countable unions), and let $\mu:\mathcal A\to[0,+\infty]$ be a countably additive measure with $\mu(\emptyset)=0$. Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on $(X,\mathcal A)$, meaning countably additive measures with $P(X)=Q(X)=1$. A function from $X$ to a Borel space is measurable when the inverse image of each Borel set belongs to $\mathcal A$. Assume that $P$ and $Q$ have finite-valued, nonnegative, measurable densities $p$ and $q$ with respect to the same measure $\mu$, meaning that $P(E)=\int_E p\,d\mu$ and $Q(E)=\int_E q\,d\mu$ for every $E\in\mathcal A$. In particular, $\int p\,d\mu=\int q\,d\mu=1$.

For a measurable discriminator $D:X\to[0,1]$, put $a(t)=-\ln t$ for $0<t\le1$ and $a(0)=+\infty$, and put $b(t)=-\ln(1-t)$ for $0\le t<1$ and $b(1)=+\infty$. In the products below, define $0\cdot(+\infty)=0$; a positive finite factor times $+\infty$ is $+\infty$. Define the log payoff and the unrestricted discriminator value by
$$
V(D;P,Q):=-\int p(x)a(D(x))\,d\mu(x)-\int q(x)b(D(x))\,d\mu(x),\qquad C(P,Q):=\sup_{D:X\to[0,1]\,\mathrm{measurable}}V(D;P,Q).
$$
The functions $a$ and $b$ are Borel measurable: $\ln$ is continuous on $(0,\infty)$, and each extension assigns $+\infty$ only at one Borel endpoint. Therefore $a\circ D$ and $b\circ D$ are measurable, and the products with $p$ and $q$ are measurable by the pointwise product convention and product-closure result referenced below. Thus both nonnegative integrals are defined.

Each integral is the nonnegative Lebesgue integral, defined as the supremum of the integrals of nonnegative simple minorants, so $V(D;P,Q)\in[-\infty,0]$. The supremum ranges over all measurable functions into $[0,1]$, including boundary values; it is not restricted to a finite-parameter discriminator family.

In the common-density setting, put $m=(p+q)/2$. Additivity and nonnegative homogeneity of the integral give $\int m\,d\mu=1$. Define $r=p/m$ and $s=q/m$ where $m>0$, and define $r=s=0$ where $m=0$; then $0\le r,s\le2$ and $r+s=2$ wherever $m>0$. Let $\phi(0)=0$ and $\phi(t)=t\ln t$ for $t>0$. The density-defined Jensen–Shannon divergence is
$$
\operatorname{JS}_\mu(P,Q):=\frac12\int m\phi(r)\,d\mu+\frac12\int m\phi(s)\,d\mu.
$$
The integrals are finite, and this formula is the average of the two density-relative-entropy terms from $p$ and $q$ to the mixture density $m$.

For two probability measures $P,Q$ with finite-valued nonnegative densities $p,q$ relative to a common measure $\mu$, put $m=(p+q)/2$, $r=p/m$ and $s=q/m$ where $m>0$, and $r=s=0$ where $m=0$. Set $\phi(0)=0$ and $\phi(t)=t\ln t$ for $t>0$. The functions $m\phi(r)$ and $m\phi(s)$ are integrable, and the density-defined Jensen–Shannon divergence $\operatorname{JS}_\mu(P,Q)=\tfrac12\int m\phi(r)\,d\mu+\tfrac12\int m\phi(s)\,d\mu$ is a finite nonnegative real number. It is zero if and only if $P=Q$, equivalently if and only if $p=q$ $\mu$-almost everywhere.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

Let $n\ge1$, let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ be a measurable space, and let
$f = (f_1,\dots,f_n) : X \to \mathbb{R}^n$. Then $f$ is measurable if and only
if each coordinate function $f_j : X \to \mathbb{R}$ is measurable.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$, $(Y,\mathcal{B})$, and $(Z,\mathcal{C})$ be measurable
spaces. If $f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Y,\mathcal{B})$ is measurable and
$g : (Y,\mathcal{B}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable, then
$g \circ f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable.

In particular, if $f$ is measurable and $g$ is a Borel measurable function on
its codomain, then $g \circ f$ is measurable.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ (Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$) at which $g$ is differentiable
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
(Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of If $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L \ne 0$ then $|f| > |L|/2$ on a punctured neighbourhood of $c$; in particular if $L > 0$ then $f > L/2 > 0$ there applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
Carathéodory's characterisation: $f$ is differentiable at $c$ if and only if there is $\varphi : A \to \mathbb{R}$, continuous at $c$, with $f(x) - f(c) = \varphi(x)(x - c)$ for every $x \in A$, and then $\varphi$ is unique and $\varphi(c) = f'(c)$.** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of Sums, scalar multiples, products, absolute values, maxima, minima and quotients with nonvanishing denominator of continuous functions are continuous, as are constants, the identity and every polynomial function.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
limit point of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]). If $f$ is differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) then $f$ is continuous at $c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]).

Consequently, if $f$ is differentiable on a set $S \subseteq A$ then $f$ is
continuous at every point of $S$.

**No converse is asserted, and none holds.** Continuity at $c$ does not give
differentiability at $c$, and the standard witness is worked out on the
companion page.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ (Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point, Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. If $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ are measurable, then
$$\int(f+g)\,d\mu=\int f\,d\mu+\int g\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: Define $F:[0,\infty)^2\to[0,1]$ by $F(a,b)=a/(a+b)$ when $a+b>0$ and $F(0,0)=1/2$. It is continuous on the Borel set $\{a+b>0\}$ and constant on its singleton complement, hence Borel. By [F8], $x\mapsto(p(x),q(x))$ is measurable, and [F9] makes $D^*=F(p,q)$ measurable.

Fix $x$ and write $a=p(x)$ and $b=q(x)$. If $a,b>0$, the function $f(y)=a\ln y+b\ln(1-y)$ on $0<y<1$ is differentiable with $f'(y)=a/y-b/(1-y)=(a-(a+b)y)/(y(1-y))$: the derivative of $1-y$ is $-1$ by its difference quotient, [F4] differentiates $\ln$, [F10] applies the chain rule, and [F11] gives the sum and scalar rules. The denominator is positive; the numerator is positive for $y<y^*:=a/(a+b)$ and negative for $y>y^*$. By [F12], $f$ is continuous on every closed subinterval of $(0,1)$. For any $y\in(0,y^*)$, [F13] on $[y,y^*]$ gives $c\in(y,y^*)$ with $f(y^*)-f(y)=f'(c)(y^*-y)>0$. For any $y\in(y^*,1)$, [F13] on $[y^*,y]$ gives $c\in(y^*,y)$ with $f(y)-f(y^*)=f'(c)(y-y^*)<0$. At $y=0,1$ the payoff is $-\infty$. If $a=0<b$, then $f(y)=b\ln(1-y)\le0=f(0)$, with equality at $y=0$. If $b=0<a$, then $f(y)=a\ln y\le0=f(1)$, with equality at $y=1$. If $a=b=0$, every $y$ gives value $0$. In all four cases, $D^*(x)$ maximizes the pointwise payoff.

For any measurable $D$, step 1.2 gives the pointwise loss inequality $p(-\ln D)+q(-\ln(1-D))\ge p(-\ln D^*)+q(-\ln(1-D^*))$, with zero-density endpoint terms interpreted as in [F1]. These are nonnegative measurable losses by the definition and its measurability dependencies [F1]. Additivity [F14] and monotonicity [F6] therefore give $\int p(-\ln D)\,d\mu+\int q(-\ln(1-D))\,d\mu\ge\int p(-\ln D^*)\,d\mu+\int q(-\ln(1-D^*))\,d\mu$. Taking negatives and using [F1] yields $V(D;P,Q)\le V(D^*;P,Q)$. Since $D^*$ is measurable by step 1.1, the supremum is attained and $C(P,Q)=V(D^*;P,Q)$.

On $m>0$, one has $p=mr$, $q=ms$, $D^*=r/2$ and $1-D^*=s/2$. Using $0\ln0=0$ when $r=0$ or $s=0$, the pointwise optimized payoff is $m\phi(r)+m\phi(s)-m(r+s)\ln2=m\phi(r)+m\phi(s)-2m\ln2$. On $m=0$, both densities and all displayed products are zero, so the same identity holds. The first two terms are integrable by [F3]; [F1] and [F7] give $\int m\,d\mu=1$. Hence [F7], [F2] and $\ln4=2\ln2$ [F5] give $C(P,Q)=2\operatorname{JS}_\mu(P,Q)-\ln4$.

By [F3], $\operatorname{JS}_\mu(P,Q)\ge0$, and it vanishes exactly when $P=Q$. Step 3.1 therefore gives $C(P,Q)\ge-\ln4$ with equality exactly at $P=Q$. The unrestricted density class contains the data law itself, so this value is attained there and no other generator law attains it. The argument establishes only the distribution-space optimum stated here.
