Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $P,Q$ be probability measures with finite-valued nonnegative measurable densities $p,q$ relative to $\mu$, normalized by $\int p\,d\mu=\int q\,d\mu=1$. For every measurable discriminator $D:X\to[0,1]$, define
$$
V(D;P,Q)=\int p\ln D\,d\mu+\int q\ln(1-D)\,d\mu,
$$
extending $\ln0=-\infty$ and making each zero-density term $0\cdot(-\infty)$ equal to $0$. Let $C(P,Q)$ be the supremum of $V(D;P,Q)$ over all such $D$. Put $m=(p+q)/2$, $r=p/m$ and $s=q/m$ where $m>0$, set $r=s=0$ where $m=0$, define $\phi(0)=0$ and $\phi(t)=t\ln t$ for $t>0$, and set $\operatorname{JS}_\mu(P,Q)=\tfrac12\int m\phi(r)\,d\mu+\tfrac12\int m\phi(s)\,d\mu$. Then the measurable discriminator
$$
D^*(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{p(x)}{p(x)+q(x)},&p(x)+q(x)>0,\\[4pt]\dfrac12,&p(x)+q(x)=0\end{cases}
$$
maximizes $V$, and $C(P,Q)=-\ln4+2\operatorname{JS}_\mu(P,Q)$. Consequently $C(P,Q)\ge-\ln4$, with equality if and only if $P=Q$. Over the unrestricted class of probability densities, equality of the generator law with the data law is the unique global distribution optimum. This identity does not assert convergence of finite neural alternating optimization.

In the common-density setting, put $m=(p+q)/2$. Additivity and nonnegative homogeneity of the integral give $\int m\,d\mu=1$. Define $r=p/m$ and $s=q/m$ where $m>0$, and define $r=s=0$ where $m=0$; then $0\le r,s\le2$ and $r+s=2$ wherever $m>0$. Let $\phi(0)=0$ and $\phi(t)=t\ln t$ for $t>0$. The density-defined Jensen–Shannon divergence is
$$
\operatorname{JS}_\mu(P,Q):=\frac12\int m\phi(r)\,d\mu+\frac12\int m\phi(s)\,d\mu.
$$
The integrals are finite, and this formula is the average of the two density-relative-entropy terms from $p$ and $q$ to the mixture density $m$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $P,Q$ be probability measures with finite-valued nonnegative measurable densities $p,q$ relative to $\mu$, normalized by $\int p\,d\mu=\int q\,d\mu=1$. For every measurable discriminator $D:X\to[0,1]$, define
$$
V(D;P,Q)=\int p\ln D\,d\mu+\int q\ln(1-D)\,d\mu,
$$
extending $\ln0=-\infty$ and making each zero-density term $0\cdot(-\infty)$ equal to $0$. Let $C(P,Q)$ be the supremum of $V(D;P,Q)$ over all such $D$. Put $m=(p+q)/2$, $r=p/m$ and $s=q/m$ where $m>0$, set $r=s=0$ where $m=0$, define $\phi(0)=0$ and $\phi(t)=t\ln t$ for $t>0$, and set $\operatorname{JS}_\mu(P,Q)=\tfrac12\int m\phi(r)\,d\mu+\tfrac12\int m\phi(s)\,d\mu$. Then the measurable discriminator
$$
D^*(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{p(x)}{p(x)+q(x)},&p(x)+q(x)>0,\\[4pt]\dfrac12,&p(x)+q(x)=0\end{cases}
$$
maximizes $V$, and $C(P,Q)=-\ln4+2\operatorname{JS}_\mu(P,Q)$. Consequently $C(P,Q)\ge-\ln4$, with equality if and only if $P=Q$. Over the unrestricted class of probability densities, equality of the generator law with the data law is the unique global distribution optimum. This identity does not assert convergence of finite neural alternating optimization.

derivations.claim: For $h\ne0$, $\bigl(L(\theta+h,\varphi)-L(\theta,\varphi)\bigr)/h=\bigl((\theta+h)\varphi-\theta\varphi\bigr)/h=\varphi$, so $\partial_\theta L=\varphi$. Likewise $\bigl(L(\theta,\varphi+h)-L(\theta,\varphi)\bigr)/h=\theta$, so $\partial_\varphi L=\theta$.

Substitution into the update gives $\theta_{n+1}=\theta_n-\varphi_n$ and $\varphi_{n+1}=\varphi_n+\theta_{n+1}=\theta_n$. Thus $x_{n+1}=Mx_n$ for $x_n=(\theta_n,\varphi_n)^\mathsf T$ and $M=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$.
Matrix multiplication gives $M^2=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}$ and $M^3=-I$. Hence $x_{n+3}=-x_n$ and $x_{n+6}=x_n$ for every $n$.

Since $x_0\ne0$, the subsequence $(x_{6k})_{k\ge0}$ is constantly $x_0$ and $(x_{6k+3})_{k\ge0}$ is constantly $-x_0\ne x_0$. These subsequences have different limits, so $(x_n)$ does not converge. The computed cycle is for this explicitly defined toy game; [F1] shows it supplies no conclusion about convergence of GAN neural training.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ (The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann),
On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of The vector space $F^{X}$ of all functions $X \to F$ with pointwise operations, and $F^{n}$ as the case $X = n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
(Vector space over a field). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of Finite sums and finite products, by recursion applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 4 and
Squares of nonzero elements are positive, the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
Integer powers $a^m$) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root (Square roots exist: a unique $\sqrt{a} \ge 0$ with $(\sqrt{a})^2 = a$; the positives are $\{x^2 : x \neq 0\}$).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space (The standard list $e : n \to F^{n}$ with $e_i(i) = 1_F$ and $e_i(j) = 0_F$ for $j \ne i$ is an ordered basis of $F^{n}$; hence $\dim_F F^{n} = n$, and $F^{0}$ is the zero space with basis $\varnothing$ and dimension $0$ clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
$\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and Conventions of this page, the standing $n \ge 1$ hypothesis, and what is taken up elsewhere in the reading order lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ (Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   (Squares of nonzero elements are positive), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of A norm on a real vector space, the induced metric, and the dictionary with the metric axioms
is proved in Cauchy-Schwarz $\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \le \lVert x\rVert_2\lVert y\rVert_2$ with its equality case, the triangle inequality for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$, the parallelogram law and polarisation, where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]). As in
[[def-linear-combination-and-span]], a **finite list** of vectors is a function
$v : n \to V$ on a von Neumann natural $n = \{0, \dots, n-1\}$
([[def-natural-numbers]], [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), written
$v_i := v(i)$, and

$$\sum_{i<n} \lambda_i v_i$$

is the finite sum of [[def-monoid-finite-product]] read additively in the abelian
group $(V,+,0_V)$, applied to the list $i \mapsto \lambda_i v_i$. No second notion
of finite sum is introduced here.

### Independence of a list

A finite list $v : n \to V$ is **linearly independent** when, for every list of
scalars $\lambda : n \to F$,

$$\sum_{i<n} \lambda_i v_i = 0_V \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \lambda_i = 0_F \text{ for every } i < n,$$

and **linearly dependent** otherwise, that is, when some $\lambda : n \to F$ has
$\sum_{i<n}\lambda_i v_i = 0_V$ while $\lambda_j \ne 0_F$ for at least one
$j < n$. Such a $\lambda$ is called a **witness** to the dependence of $v$.

### Independence of a subset

A subset $S \subseteq V$ is **linearly independent** when **every injective**
finite list $v : n \to S$ ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]) is linearly
independent, and **linearly dependent** otherwise, that is, when some injective
finite list into $S$ is linearly dependent.

**The injectivity clause is not decoration.** A linear combination in
[[def-linear-combination-and-span]] is indexed by an arbitrary list $v : n \to S$,
which is **not** required to be injective. If the definition above quantified
over all such lists, then for any $w \in S$ the list $v : 2 \to S$ with
$v_0 = v_1 = w$ and the scalars $\lambda_0 = 1_F$, $\lambda_1 = -1_F$ would give

$$\sum_{i<2}\lambda_i v_i = (0_V + 1_F w) + (-1_F)w = w + (-w) = 0_V$$

with $\lambda_0 = 1_F \ne 0_F$ ([[def-field]],
[[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]), so **every** nonempty subset of
$V$ would be dependent and the notion would be empty. Quantifying over injective
lists is what makes the subset notion the intended one. It costs nothing for
lists: [[lem-independent-list-is-injective]] shows that the vanishing condition
above already forces a list to be injective, so no injectivity hypothesis has to
be carried alongside independence of a list.

### The boundary cases are genuine cases

$\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]), so both of the following are
instances of the definitions and neither is a convention.

- **The empty list is independent.** For $n = 0$ the only list of scalars is the
  empty one, and the condition "$\lambda_i = 0_F$ for every $i < 0$" holds
  vacuously.
- **$\varnothing \subseteq V$ is independent.** The only function $v : n \to
  \varnothing$ is the empty one, with $n = 0$, and it is independent by the
  previous point.
- **$\{0_V\}$ is dependent.** The list $v : 1 \to \{0_V\}$ with $v_0 = 0_V$ is
  injective, and taking $\lambda_0 = 1_F$ gives
  $\sum_{i<1}\lambda_i v_i = 0_V + 1_F 0_V = 0_V$ by the recursion of
  [[def-monoid-finite-product]] and $\lambda 0_V = 0_V$
  ([[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]), while $1_F \ne 0_F$ in a field
  ([[def-field]]). So $\{0_V\}$, and hence every subset of $V$ containing $0_V$,
  is linearly dependent.

For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and all $a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n \in \mathbb{R}$, the
set $\{a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ has a maximum and a minimum (Maximum and minimum of a set).

What is proved below is exactly the displayed statement, by induction on $n$.

The usual reading, that *every nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ has a
maximum and a minimum*, follows once one identifies the nonempty finite subsets
of $\mathbb{R}$ with the sets listable as $\{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$. That
identification is recorded as a stipulation in the Given below, because this page
has no definition of finiteness to prove it against. **It is discharged, not
merely assumed**: The nonempty finite subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ are exactly the listable ones proves that the two
descriptions of a nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ agree. That lemma is
recorded in `justified_by` rather than in `deps`, since it is about the sets this
lemma quantifies over and therefore depends on this one. This is what licenses
the notation
$\max\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ and $\min\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ for finite sets of
**real** numbers from this page onwards.

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ and $m \in \mathbb{R}$.

- $m$ is a **maximum** (or *greatest element*) of $S$ if $m \in S$ and $s \le m$
  for every $s \in S$.
- $m$ is a **minimum** (or *least element*) of $S$ if $m \in S$ and $m \le s$
  for every $s \in S$.

A set has at most one maximum: if $m_1$ and $m_2$ are both maxima then
$m_1 \in S$ gives $m_1 \le m_2$ and $m_2 \in S$ gives $m_2 \le m_1$, so
$m_1 = m_2$ by antisymmetry of the order, which is immediate from the trichotomy
axiom of an ordered field (Ordered field, Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property)).
The same argument applies to minima, so we may write $\max S$ and $\min S$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$. A von Neumann natural is the set of its
predecessors, $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]), so it can be
used directly as an index set. Define

$$\mathbb{R}^n := \{\, x : x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\},$$

and write $x_k$ for $x(k)$, $k < n$. Two elements of $\mathbb{R}^n$ are equal
exactly when they agree at every $k < n$, functions being equal when they have
the same values. For $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^n$ put

$$d_1(x,y) := \sum_{k<n} |x_k - y_k|, \qquad d_2(x,y) := \sqrt{\ \sum_{k<n} (x_k - y_k)^2\ }, \qquad d_\infty(x,y) := \max\{\, |x_k - y_k| : k < n \,\}.$$

All three are well defined: the finite sums are those of [[def-finite-sum]]; the
sum of squares is nonnegative ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]], [[lem-of-square-positive]])
so it has a unique nonnegative square root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]); and
$\{|x_k - y_k| : k < n\}$ is a nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$, because
$n \ge 1$, so it has a maximum ([[lem-finite-set-has-max]], [[def-max-min]]).

**Then $d_1$, $d_2$ and $d_\infty$ are metrics on $\mathbb{R}^n$**
([[def-metric-space]]).

**Why $n \ge 1$.** For $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^0$ has exactly one element,
the empty function, and $d_1$ and $d_2$ are the empty sum $0$ and its root; but
$d_\infty$ would be the maximum of the empty set, which does not exist. The
hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is therefore not decoration, and it is carried by every
statement about $d_\infty$ in this library.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space (Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric).

A subset $U \subseteq X$ is **open in $(X,d)$** if for every $x \in U$ there is a
real $r > 0$ with $B(x,r) \subseteq U$ (Open ball, closed ball and sphere in a metric space). A subset
$F \subseteq X$ is **closed in $(X,d)$** if its complement $X \setminus F$ is
open.

The collection

$$\mathcal{T}_d := \{\, U \subseteq X : U \text{ is open in } (X,d) \,\}$$

of all open subsets is the **metric topology** of $d$ on $X$. A subset of $X$
that is both open and closed is called **clopen**.

**Two sets are open for trivial reasons.** $\emptyset$ is open, because the
defining condition quantifies over no points; and $X$ is open, because
$B(x,r) \subseteq X$ for every $x$ and every $r > 0$. Consequently $X$ and
$\emptyset$ are also closed, and both are clopen.

**A neighbourhood of a point $x$** is any set containing an open set that
contains $x$; an **open neighbourhood** is an open set containing $x$. In a
metric space, a set is a neighbourhood of $x$ exactly when it contains some
ball $B(x,r)$ with $r>0$. Thus $U$ is open exactly when it is a neighbourhood of
each of its points, and metric balls suffice to test this condition.

**The metric, not the set, determines $\mathcal{T}_d$.** Two metrics on the same
set may have different metric topologies, and two different metrics may have the
same one; the systematic comparison is Topologically, uniformly and Lipschitz equivalent metrics on a set.

Let $F$ be an ordered field (Ordered field) with positive cone $P$. For
every $a \in F$ with $a \neq 0$ we have $a^2 > 0$, where $a^2 = a \cdot a$. In
particular, every nonzero square is positive.

Let $a \in \mathbb{R}$, where $\mathbb{R}$ is the ambient ordered field
(Ordered field, Field).

**Natural exponents.** By the recursion theorem (The recursion theorem) applied to
the set $\mathbb{R}$, the starting element $1$ and the function
$f(x) = x \cdot a$, there is a unique function $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$,
written $n \mapsto a^n$, with

$$a^0 = 1, \qquad a^{n+1} = a^n \cdot a \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

Thus $a^1 = a$, $a^2 = a \cdot a$, and so on. Note that this is defined for
**every** $a$, including $a = 0$.

**Negative exponents.** If $a \ne 0$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, set

$$a^{-n} := (a^n)^{-1}.$$

**Why that is legitimate.** The right-hand side presupposes that $a^n$ is
invertible, that is, that $a^n \ne 0$. This is a proof obligation and not an
observation, and it is discharged by claim 2 of Laws of integer exponents: for $a \ne 0$
in a field, $a^n \ne 0$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, proved there by induction on
$n$ from the fact that a field has no zero divisors (A field has no zero divisors: $ab = 0 \Rightarrow a = 0$ or $b = 0$).
That lemma is a statement *about* the operation introduced here, so it depends on
this definition and is recorded in this item's `justified_by` rather than in its
`deps` (SCHEMA §3). Given $a^n \ne 0$, the value $(a^n)^{-1}$ is a single
well-determined element, because multiplicative inverses in a field are unique
(Identities and inverses in a field are unique).

**Integer exponents.** Every integer $m$ (The integers as equivalence classes of pairs of naturals) is either
$n$ or $-n$ for a unique natural $n$, where $n$ in these integer expressions denotes its image under the
embedding $\iota : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z}$ (The naturals embed in the integers,
Arithmetic on the integers). This too is a citation and not a slogan: the order on
$\mathbb{Z}$ is total (The integers form a totally ordered ring), so $m \ge 0$ or $m < 0$; the
image of $\iota$ is exactly the set of nonnegative integers, and each of them is
$n$ for a unique natural $n$ (The naturals embed in the integers); and if $m < 0$ then
$-m > 0$, by compatibility of the order with addition (The integers form a totally ordered ring),
so $-m = n$ and $m = -n$, with $n$ unique because $\iota$ is
injective. The two clauses above therefore define $a^m$ for every
$m \in \mathbb{Z}$ whenever $a \ne 0$, and for every $m \in \mathbb{N}$ for
arbitrary $a$. The two exponent domains are disjoint: the natural clause
handles $m \ge 0$, including $m = 0$, while the negative clause requires
$n \ge 1$ and therefore handles only $m < 0$.
In any field $F$ (Field), for every $a \in F$ we have $0 \cdot a = 0$.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field (Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property)). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

Let $a, b, c : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be sequences of reals, let
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, and let $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, with finite sums and
finite products as in Finite sums and finite products, by recursion. Then:

1. **Additivity.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}(a_k + b_k) = \sum_{k<n} a_k + \sum_{k<n} b_k$.
2. **Scaling.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda a_k = \lambda \sum_{k<n} a_k$; in particular $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda = n\lambda$, where $n$ denotes the canonical field image $n\cdot1_{\mathbb{R}}$ of the natural n (The unique embedding of ℚ into an ordered field, Canonical naturals are positive and strictly increasing).
3. **Splitting.** If $m \le n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k = \sum_{k<m} a_k + \sum_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k$, and $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n} a_k = \Big(\prod_{k<m} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k\Big)$.
4. **Monotonicity.** If $a_k \le b_k$ for all $k < n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k \le \sum_{k<n} b_k$. In particular, if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\sum_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, every single term satisfies $a_j \le \sum_{k<n} a_k$ for $j < n$, and $\sum_{k<n} a_k = 0$ forces $a_k = 0$ for every $k < n$.
5. **Telescoping.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}\big(c_{k+1} - c_k\big) = c_n - c_0$.
6. **Products.** $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n}(a_k b_k) = \Big(\prod_{k<n} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k<n} b_k\Big)$; if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, and if $a_k > 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k > 0$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field (Ordered field). The **absolute value** of
$x \in F$ is

$$|x| \;:=\; \begin{cases} x & \text{if } x \ge 0, \\ -x & \text{if } x < 0. \end{cases}$$

Let $F$ be an ordered field (Ordered field) and let $x, y \in F$, with
$|x|$ the absolute value (Absolute value in an ordered field). Then

$$|x| \ge 0; \quad |x| = 0 \iff x = 0; \quad -|x| \le x \le |x|; \quad |-x| = |x|; \quad |xy| = |x|\,|y|;$$

and, for every $c > 0$, one has $|x| < c \iff -c < x < c$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field (Ordered field) and let $x, y \in F$. Then

$$|x + y| \le |x| + |y|.$$

Let $F$ be an ordered field. For $a, b \ge 0$:

$$a < b \iff a^2 < b^2, \qquad a \le b \iff a^2 \le b^2.$$

More generally, for arbitrary $a, b \in F$, $a^2 < b^2 \iff |a| < |b|$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field (Ordered field) with positive cone $P$, and
let $a, b, c \in F$.

1. If $a > 0$ and $b > 0$ then $ab > 0$.
2. If $a > 0$ and $b < 0$ then $ab < 0$.
3. If $a < 0$ and $b < 0$ then $ab > 0$.
4. If $c > 0$ then $a < b \iff ac < bc$.
5. If $c < 0$ then $a < b \iff bc < ac$ (multiplication by a negative reverses order).
In any field $F$ (Field), for every $a \in F$ we have $0 \cdot a = 0$.

Let $X$ be a set and let $p : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfy the reflexivity
axiom (M1') $p(x,x) = 0$ and the symmetry axiom (M2) $p(x,y) = p(y,x)$ of
Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric. Then:

1. If $p$ satisfies the triangle inequality (M3), then $p(x,y) \ge 0$ for all
   $x, y \in X$.
2. If $p$ satisfies the strong triangle inequality (M3'), then
   $p(x,y) \ge 0$ for all $x, y \in X$.

In particular every metric, every pseudometric and every ultrametric
(Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric) takes only nonnegative values. Nonnegativity is therefore
a theorem about the axiom list this library uses, not a fourth axiom, and no
statement on this page needs to assume it separately.

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. If $0 \in S$ and $\sigma(n) \in S$ whenever $n \in S$, then $S = \mathbb{N}$. Equivalently (property form): if a property $P$ satisfies $P(0)$ and ($P(n) \Rightarrow P(\sigma(n))$) for all $n$, then $P(n)$ holds for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. This is the induction principle, the basis of proof by induction.

derivations.claim: Take a representation $x=\sum_{i=1}^N\lambda_i g_i$ with every $\lambda_i\ge0$ and let $S=\{i:\lambda_i>0\}$. If the sublist indexed by $S$ is dependent, [F2] gives coefficients $c_i$, not all zero, with $\sum_{i\in S}c_i g_i=0$. Reverse all signs if needed so $J=\{i\in S:c_i>0\}$ is nonempty, and set $t=\min_{i\in J}\lambda_i/c_i>0$ using [F4]. Define $\lambda'_i=\lambda_i-tc_i$ for $i\in S$ and $\lambda'_i=0$ for $i\notin S$. For $i\in S$ with $c_i>0$, the minimum choice makes $\lambda'_i\ge0$ and makes at least one such coefficient zero; when $c_i\le0$, $\lambda'_i\ge\lambda_i>0$. Thus every $\lambda'_i\ge0$, the positive support strictly shrinks, and $\sum_{i=1}^N\lambda'_i g_i=x$. Each reduction loses at least one index and adds none to the support, which starts with at most $N$ indices, so after at most $N$ reductions the support is empty or linearly independent; the empty support is independent as well.

Fix a nonempty independent sublist indexed by $S=\{i_1,\ldots,i_s\}$, let $A:\mathbb R^s\to\mathbb R^r$ have these columns, and let $G=A^{\mathsf T}A$. If $Gz=0$, then $0=z^{\mathsf T}Gz=\|Az\|_2^2$, so [F1] gives $Az=0$ and [F2] gives $z=0$. Thus $G$ is invertible by [F3]. Put $B=G^{-1}A^{\mathsf T}$ and $P=AB$, so $BA=I$. The cone $C_S$ generated by this sublist is exactly $\{x\in\mathbb R^r:Px=x,\ (Bx)_k\ge0\text{ for }k<s\}$: if $x=Az$ with $z\ge0$, then $Bx=z$ and $Px=x$; conversely those displayed conditions give $x=P x=A(Bx)$ with nonnegative coefficients. Each coordinate of $Bx$ and $Px-x$ is a finite linear form $\ell(x)=\sum_{j<r}c_jx_j$. For $u\in\mathbb R^r$ and $k<r$, [F7] gives $u_k^2\le\sum_{j<r}u_j^2$; by [F5] and [F8], $|u_k|^2=u_k^2\le\|u\|_2^2$, and both $|u_k|$ and $\|u\|_2$ are nonnegative, so [F8] gives $|u_k|\le\|u\|_2$. For any finite list $a_0,\ldots,a_{n-1}$, induction using the two-term triangle inequality in [F8] gives $|\sum_{j<n}a_j|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_j|$: the empty case is equality and the successor step is the two-term triangle inequality. Applying this, the absolute-value product law, multiplication by nonnegative coefficients, and finite-sum monotonicity in [F7,F8] gives $|\ell(x)-\ell(y)|\le\sum_{j<r}|c_j|\,|x_j-y_j|\le(\sum_{j<r}|c_j|)\|x-y\|_2$. If an equation $\ell(x)=0$ fails at $x_0$, then $C_\ell:=\sum_{j<r}|c_j|>0$: otherwise [F7,F8] force every $c_j=0$, so $\ell$ is identically zero. For $\|x-x_0\|_2<|\ell(x_0)|/(2C_\ell)$, the estimate gives $|\ell(x)-\ell(x_0)|<|\ell(x_0)|/2$, hence $\ell(x)\ne0$. The same positivity of $C_\ell$ holds when an inequality $\ell(x)\ge0$ fails; throughout the ball of radius $-\ell(x_0)/(2C_\ell)$, the estimate gives $\ell(x)<\ell(x_0)/2<0$. Thus every point outside $C_S$ has a ball in its complement; by [F5,F6] that complement is open and $C_S$ is closed. For the empty sublist, $C_\emptyset=\{0\}$: if $x\ne0$, then $d_2(x,0)>0$ by [F5,F9], and every $y$ with $d_2(x,y)<d_2(x,0)/2$ is nonzero, since otherwise the triangle inequality would give $d_2(x,0)<d_2(x,0)/2$. Thus the complement of $\{0\}$ is open by [F6], so $C_\emptyset$ is closed.

By step 1.1, every $x\in C$ belongs to $C_S$ for some independent subset $S$ of the $N$ generators; conversely every such $C_S$ is contained in $C$. There are only finitely many subsets $S$, and the empty subset is included. For any $x\notin C$, each closed $C_S$ has an open complement containing $x$; choosing one positive ball radius for each of the finitely many such complements and taking their positive minimum gives a ball about $x$ disjoint from their union. Thus $C$ has open complement and is closed. For $x,y\in C$, choose coefficients $\lambda_i,\mu_i\ge0$ with $x=\sum_{i=1}^N\lambda_i g_i$ and $y=\sum_{i=1}^N\mu_i g_i$. Then $\alpha x+\beta y=\sum_{i=1}^N(\alpha\lambda_i+\beta\mu_i)g_i\in C$ for all $\alpha,\beta\ge0$, proving the stated closure under nonnegative linear combinations.

citations.quote:
Let $\mathcal X$ be a finite nonempty set. A **probability vector** on
$\mathcal X$ is a family $P=(p_x)_{x\in\mathcal X}$ of real numbers such that
$p_x\ge 0$ for every $x$ and $\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}p_x=1$. Its support is
$\operatorname{supp}P:=\{x\in\mathcal X:p_x>0\}$. Coordinates outside the
support are retained as zeros; they are not deleted from the alphabet.

For another probability vector $Q=(q_x)_{x\in\mathcal X}$, the notation
$P\ll Q$ means $\operatorname{supp}P\subseteq\operatorname{supp}Q$. All
finite sums over $\mathcal X$ use the displayed alphabet and ordinary finite
real arithmetic, extended to $+\infty$ only where a later definition says so.

Let $X=\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}$ be a finite nonempty set with this fixed ordering, and let $p=(p_i)_{i=1}^m$ and $q=(q_j)_{j=1}^m$ be probability vectors on $X$: their coordinates are nonnegative real numbers and $\sum_{i=1}^m p_i=\sum_{j=1}^m q_j=1$. A **coupling** of $p$ and $q$ is a real matrix $\pi=(\pi_{ij})_{i,j=1}^m$ satisfying
$$
\pi_{ij}\ge 0,\qquad \sum_{j=1}^m\pi_{ij}=p_i\quad(1\le i\le m),\qquad \sum_{i=1}^m\pi_{ij}=q_j\quad(1\le j\le m).
$$
Write $\Gamma(p,q)$ for the set of all such matrices. The first index records the source point and the second index records the destination point.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
(Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property), Ordered field) constructed in this
library (The real numbers) and carrying its order (Order on the reals).

Let $X$ be a set. A **metric** on $X$ is a function
$d : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $x, y, z \in X$:

- **(M1) Separation.** $d(x,y) = 0$ if and only if $x = y$.
- **(M2) Symmetry.** $d(x,y) = d(y,x)$.
- **(M3) Triangle inequality.** $d(x,z) \le d(x,y) + d(y,z)$.

A **metric space** is a pair $(X,d)$ consisting of a set $X$ and a metric $d$ on
it. The elements of $X$ are its **points** and $d(x,y)$ is the **distance** from
$x$ to $y$. When only one metric is in play we write $X$ for $(X,d)$; when
several are, the metric is always named.

**The values of a metric are real numbers.** The codomain is $\mathbb{R}$, so
$d(x,y)$ is an honest element of the complete ordered field and every
inequality above is an inequality there. No infinite value is permitted;
Which metric axiom list this library uses, the live naming fork between semimetric and pseudometric, and why extended metrics are not treated here records why extended metrics are not treated in
this library.

**Nonnegativity is deliberately absent from the axiom list.** Many texts add a
fourth axiom $d(x,y) \ge 0$. It is redundant: (M1), (M2) and (M3) already force
it, as Nonnegativity of a metric is a consequence of the other axioms, not an axiom proves. Nothing below assumes it before that
lemma is available.

**Pseudometric.** A **pseudometric** on $X$ is a function
$p : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying (M2), (M3) and the weakening

- **(M1') Reflexivity.** $p(x,x) = 0$ for every $x \in X$

of (M1). A pseudometric may therefore assign distance $0$ to two distinct
points. Every metric is a pseudometric, and a pseudometric is a metric exactly
when $p(x,y) = 0$ forces $x = y$.

**Ultrametric.** An **ultrametric** on $X$ is a metric $d$ that in addition
satisfies

- **(M3') Strong triangle inequality.** $d(x,z) \le \max\{d(x,y), d(y,z)\}$

for all $x, y, z \in X$, where the maximum is that of a two-element subset of
$\mathbb{R}$, which exists and is one of the two elements
(Maximum and minimum of a set, Every nonempty finite set of reals has a maximum and a minimum). An **ultrametric space** is a pair
$(X,d)$ with $d$ an ultrametric.

Let $X$ be a set and let $p : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfy the reflexivity
axiom (M1') $p(x,x) = 0$ and the symmetry axiom (M2) $p(x,y) = p(y,x)$ of
Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric. Then:

1. If $p$ satisfies the triangle inequality (M3), then $p(x,y) \ge 0$ for all
   $x, y \in X$.
2. If $p$ satisfies the strong triangle inequality (M3'), then
   $p(x,y) \ge 0$ for all $x, y \in X$.

In particular every metric, every pseudometric and every ultrametric
(Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric) takes only nonnegative values. Nonnegativity is therefore
a theorem about the axiom list this library uses, not a fourth axiom, and no
statement on this page needs to assume it separately.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$. A von Neumann natural is the set of its
predecessors, $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]), so it can be
used directly as an index set. Define

$$\mathbb{R}^n := \{\, x : x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\},$$

and write $x_k$ for $x(k)$, $k < n$. Two elements of $\mathbb{R}^n$ are equal
exactly when they agree at every $k < n$, functions being equal when they have
the same values. For $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^n$ put

$$d_1(x,y) := \sum_{k<n} |x_k - y_k|, \qquad d_2(x,y) := \sqrt{\ \sum_{k<n} (x_k - y_k)^2\ }, \qquad d_\infty(x,y) := \max\{\, |x_k - y_k| : k < n \,\}.$$

All three are well defined: the finite sums are those of [[def-finite-sum]]; the
sum of squares is nonnegative ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]], [[lem-of-square-positive]])
so it has a unique nonnegative square root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]); and
$\{|x_k - y_k| : k < n\}$ is a nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$, because
$n \ge 1$, so it has a maximum ([[lem-finite-set-has-max]], [[def-max-min]]).

**Then $d_1$, $d_2$ and $d_\infty$ are metrics on $\mathbb{R}^n$**
([[def-metric-space]]).

**Why $n \ge 1$.** For $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^0$ has exactly one element,
the empty function, and $d_1$ and $d_2$ are the empty sum $0$ and its root; but
$d_\infty$ would be the maximum of the empty set, which does not exist. The
hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is therefore not decoration, and it is carried by every
statement about $d_\infty$ in this library.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space (Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric).

A subset $U \subseteq X$ is **open in $(X,d)$** if for every $x \in U$ there is a
real $r > 0$ with $B(x,r) \subseteq U$ (Open ball, closed ball and sphere in a metric space). A subset
$F \subseteq X$ is **closed in $(X,d)$** if its complement $X \setminus F$ is
open.

The collection

$$\mathcal{T}_d := \{\, U \subseteq X : U \text{ is open in } (X,d) \,\}$$

of all open subsets is the **metric topology** of $d$ on $X$. A subset of $X$
that is both open and closed is called **clopen**.

**Two sets are open for trivial reasons.** $\emptyset$ is open, because the
defining condition quantifies over no points; and $X$ is open, because
$B(x,r) \subseteq X$ for every $x$ and every $r > 0$. Consequently $X$ and
$\emptyset$ are also closed, and both are clopen.

**A neighbourhood of a point $x$** is any set containing an open set that
contains $x$; an **open neighbourhood** is an open set containing $x$. In a
metric space, a set is a neighbourhood of $x$ exactly when it contains some
ball $B(x,r)$ with $r>0$. Thus $U$ is open exactly when it is a neighbourhood of
each of its points, and metric balls suffice to test this condition.

**The metric, not the set, determines $\mathcal{T}_d$.** Two metrics on the same
set may have different metric topologies, and two different metrics may have the
same one; the systematic comparison is Topologically, uniformly and Lipschitz equivalent metrics on a set.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty and compact. Every lower semicontinuous function $f:K\to\mathbb R$ is bounded below and attains a minimum. Dually, every upper semicontinuous function $f:K\to\mathbb R$ is bounded above and attains a maximum.

Define $d_{\mathbb{R}} : \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ by
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) := |x - y|$ (Absolute value in an ordered field). Then:

1. $d_{\mathbb{R}}$ is a metric on $\mathbb{R}$ (Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric); it is
   called the **usual metric** of $\mathbb{R}$.
2. For $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and $r > 0$ the open ball is the bounded open interval
   (Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length, Open ball, closed ball and sphere in a metric space)
   $$B(x,r) = (x-r,\ x+r),$$
   and the closed ball is $\bar B(x,r) = [x-r,\ x+r]$.
3. Consequently $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is open in the metric topology of
   $d_{\mathbb{R}}$ (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) exactly when for every $x \in U$
   there is $r > 0$ with $(x-r, x+r) \subseteq U$. This topology is called the
   **usual topology** of $\mathbb{R}$.
4. $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ is not a bounded metric space
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space): no ball contains $\mathbb{R}$, so
   $\operatorname{diam}(\mathbb{R})$ is not defined.

Let $(X, d_X)$ and $(Y, d_Y)$ be metric spaces (Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric), let
$f : X \to Y$ be a function and let $a \in X$.

$f$ is **continuous at $a$** if for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that

$$d_X(x,a) < \delta \;\Longrightarrow\; d_Y\big(f(x), f(a)\big) < \varepsilon \qquad \text{for all } x \in X .$$

$f$ is **continuous** (globally, or on $X$) if it is continuous at every point of
$X$.

**The same condition in balls.** Since $d_X(x,a) < \delta$ says $x \in B_X(a,\delta)$
and $d_Y(f(x),f(a)) < \varepsilon$ says $f(x) \in B_Y(f(a),\varepsilon)$
(Open ball, closed ball and sphere in a metric space), continuity at $a$ reads: for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there
is $\delta > 0$ with

$$f\big[B_X(a,\delta)\big] \subseteq B_Y\big(f(a), \varepsilon\big).$$

Both forms are used below and are the same statement written twice.

**Both metrics matter, and both are named.** Continuity is a property of the
triple $(d_X, d_Y, f)$, not of $f$ alone. When several metrics on the same
underlying sets are in play, as in Topologically, uniformly and Lipschitz equivalent metrics on a set, the metrics are
always written out.

**Quantifier order.** The $\delta$ is allowed to depend on $\varepsilon$ **and on
the point $a$**. Requiring one $\delta$ to work at every point simultaneously is
a strictly stronger condition, uniform continuity; it is defined on a later page
of this library, and at this point in the reading order it is written out in full
where needed (Topologically, uniformly and Lipschitz equivalent metrics on a set).

Let $n\ge1$, let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, let $f:A\to\mathbb R$, and let $a\in A$. Using the Euclidean metric and its balls ($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, Open ball, closed ball and sphere in a metric space), $f$ is upper semicontinuous at $a$ when for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that $f(x)<f(a)+\varepsilon$ for every $x\in A\cap B_2(a,\delta)$.

The function is **lower semicontinuous at $a$** when for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that

$$f(a)-\varepsilon<f(x)\qquad(x\in A\cap B_2(a,\delta)).$$

It is upper or lower semicontinuous on $A$ when the corresponding condition holds at every point of $A$. These are relative notions on $A$; when $A$ is empty, each on-set condition is vacuous. A continuous function (Continuity of a map between metric spaces, at a point and globally, in the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ form) satisfies both conditions.

Let $X=\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}$ be a nonempty finite set and let $d:X\times X\to\mathbb R$ satisfy $d(x,y)=0$ if and only if $x=y$, $d(x,y)=d(y,x)$, and $d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z)$. Let $p=(p_i)_{i=1}^m$ and $q=(q_i)_{i=1}^m$ be probability vectors, so their coordinates are nonnegative and each vector sums to $1$. A coupling is an $m\times m$ matrix $\pi$ with $\pi_{ij}\ge0$, row sums $\sum_j\pi_{ij}=p_i$, and column sums $\sum_i\pi_{ij}=q_j$; write $\Gamma(p,q)$ for the set of all such matrices. Writing $d_{ij}=d(x_i,x_j)$, define the finite-metric 1-Wasserstein transport cost by
$$
W_1(p,q):=\min_{\pi\in\Gamma(p,q)}\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^m d_{ij}\pi_{ij}.
$$

Let $F$ be an ordered field (Ordered field) with positive cone $P$. For
every $a \in F$ with $a \neq 0$ we have $a^2 > 0$, where $a^2 = a \cdot a$. In
particular, every nonzero square is positive.

Let $a \in \mathbb{R}$, where $\mathbb{R}$ is the ambient ordered field
(Ordered field, Field).

**Natural exponents.** By the recursion theorem (The recursion theorem) applied to
the set $\mathbb{R}$, the starting element $1$ and the function
$f(x) = x \cdot a$, there is a unique function $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$,
written $n \mapsto a^n$, with

$$a^0 = 1, \qquad a^{n+1} = a^n \cdot a \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

Thus $a^1 = a$, $a^2 = a \cdot a$, and so on. Note that this is defined for
**every** $a$, including $a = 0$.

**Negative exponents.** If $a \ne 0$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, set

$$a^{-n} := (a^n)^{-1}.$$

**Why that is legitimate.** The right-hand side presupposes that $a^n$ is
invertible, that is, that $a^n \ne 0$. This is a proof obligation and not an
observation, and it is discharged by claim 2 of Laws of integer exponents: for $a \ne 0$
in a field, $a^n \ne 0$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, proved there by induction on
$n$ from the fact that a field has no zero divisors (A field has no zero divisors: $ab = 0 \Rightarrow a = 0$ or $b = 0$).
That lemma is a statement *about* the operation introduced here, so it depends on
this definition and is recorded in this item's `justified_by` rather than in its
`deps` (SCHEMA §3). Given $a^n \ne 0$, the value $(a^n)^{-1}$ is a single
well-determined element, because multiplicative inverses in a field are unique
(Identities and inverses in a field are unique).

**Integer exponents.** Every integer $m$ (The integers as equivalence classes of pairs of naturals) is either
$n$ or $-n$ for a unique natural $n$, where $n$ in these integer expressions denotes its image under the
embedding $\iota : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z}$ (The naturals embed in the integers,
Arithmetic on the integers). This too is a citation and not a slogan: the order on
$\mathbb{Z}$ is total (The integers form a totally ordered ring), so $m \ge 0$ or $m < 0$; the
image of $\iota$ is exactly the set of nonnegative integers, and each of them is
$n$ for a unique natural $n$ (The naturals embed in the integers); and if $m < 0$ then
$-m > 0$, by compatibility of the order with addition (The integers form a totally ordered ring),
so $-m = n$ and $m = -n$, with $n$ unique because $\iota$ is
injective. The two clauses above therefore define $a^m$ for every
$m \in \mathbb{Z}$ whenever $a \ne 0$, and for every $m \in \mathbb{N}$ for
arbitrary $a$. The two exponent domains are disjoint: the natural clause
handles $m \ge 0$, including $m = 0$, while the negative clause requires
$n \ge 1$ and therefore handles only $m < 0$.
In any field $F$ (Field), for every $a \in F$ we have $0 \cdot a = 0$.

Let $a, b, c : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be sequences of reals, let
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, and let $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, with finite sums and
finite products as in Finite sums and finite products, by recursion. Then:

1. **Additivity.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}(a_k + b_k) = \sum_{k<n} a_k + \sum_{k<n} b_k$.
2. **Scaling.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda a_k = \lambda \sum_{k<n} a_k$; in particular $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda = n\lambda$, where $n$ denotes the canonical field image $n\cdot1_{\mathbb{R}}$ of the natural n (The unique embedding of ℚ into an ordered field, Canonical naturals are positive and strictly increasing).
3. **Splitting.** If $m \le n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k = \sum_{k<m} a_k + \sum_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k$, and $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n} a_k = \Big(\prod_{k<m} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k\Big)$.
4. **Monotonicity.** If $a_k \le b_k$ for all $k < n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k \le \sum_{k<n} b_k$. In particular, if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\sum_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, every single term satisfies $a_j \le \sum_{k<n} a_k$ for $j < n$, and $\sum_{k<n} a_k = 0$ forces $a_k = 0$ for every $k < n$.
5. **Telescoping.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}\big(c_{k+1} - c_k\big) = c_n - c_0$.
6. **Products.** $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n}(a_k b_k) = \Big(\prod_{k<n} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k<n} b_k\Big)$; if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, and if $a_k > 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k > 0$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field. For $a, b \ge 0$:

$$a < b \iff a^2 < b^2, \qquad a \le b \iff a^2 \le b^2.$$

More generally, for arbitrary $a, b \in F$, $a^2 < b^2 \iff |a| < |b|$.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field (Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property)). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field (Ordered field). The **absolute value** of
$x \in F$ is

$$|x| \;:=\; \begin{cases} x & \text{if } x \ge 0, \\ -x & \text{if } x < 0. \end{cases}$$

Let $F$ be an ordered field (Ordered field) and let $x, y \in F$, with
$|x|$ the absolute value (Absolute value in an ordered field). Then

$$|x| \ge 0; \quad |x| = 0 \iff x = 0; \quad -|x| \le x \le |x|; \quad |-x| = |x|; \quad |xy| = |x|\,|y|;$$

and, for every $c > 0$, one has $|x| < c \iff -c < x < c$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field (Ordered field) and let $x, y \in F$. Then

$$|x + y| \le |x| + |y|.$$

Let $F$ be an ordered field (Ordered field) with positive cone $P$, and
let $a, b, c \in F$.

1. If $a > 0$ and $b > 0$ then $ab > 0$.
2. If $a > 0$ and $b < 0$ then $ab < 0$.
3. If $a < 0$ and $b < 0$ then $ab > 0$.
4. If $c > 0$ then $a < b \iff ac < bc$.
5. If $c < 0$ then $a < b \iff bc < ac$ (multiplication by a negative reverses order).

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. If $0 \in S$ and $\sigma(n) \in S$ whenever $n \in S$, then $S = \mathbb{N}$. Equivalently (property form): if a property $P$ satisfies $P(0)$ and ($P(n) \Rightarrow P(\sigma(n))$) for all $n$, then $P(n)$ holds for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. This is the induction principle, the basis of proof by induction.

derivations.claim: Define $\pi_{ij}=p_iq_j$. These entries are nonnegative by [F1], and their row sums are $p_i\sum_jq_j=p_i$ while their column sums are $q_j\sum_ip_i=q_j$. Thus $\pi\in\Gamma(p,q)$ and the coupling set is nonempty.

Flatten a matrix into $\mathbb R^{m^2}$ in row-major order, assigning entry $\pi_{ij}$ to library coordinate $k=(i-1)m+(j-1)<m^2$; likewise potential coordinate $f_i$ corresponds to library coordinate $i-1<m$. In any dimension $n\ge1$, for $u\in\mathbb R^n$ and $k<n$, [F11] gives $u_k^2\le\sum_{j<n}u_j^2$; by [F5,F11], $|u_k|^2=u_k^2\le d_2(u,0)^2$, and both $|u_k|$ and $d_2(u,0)$ are nonnegative, so [F11] gives $|u_k|\le d_2(u,0)$. By induction on $n$, every finite list satisfies $|\sum_{k<n}a_k|\le\sum_{k<n}|a_k|$: the empty case is equality and the successor step follows from $|a+b|\le|a|+|b|$ in [F11]. Thus for every finite linear form $L(z)=\sum_{k<n}c_kz_k$, this bound, $|ab|=|a||b|$, the coordinate estimate, multiplication by nonnegative coefficients, finite-sum monotonicity and scaling in [F11] give $|L(z)-L(w)|\le(\sum_{k<n}|c_k|)d_2(z,w)$. The same estimate holds for every affine form $H(z)=L(z)+b$, since the constant cancels in $H(z)-H(w)$. The set $\Gamma(p,q)$ is defined by finitely many affine equalities and weak inequalities. Each row or column equality, after moving its marginal to one side, has $m$ coefficients equal to $1$; each entrywise nonnegativity constraint has one coefficient equal to $1$, so the coefficient sum $C=\sum|c_k|$ is positive for every constraint. If an affine equality $H(z)=0$ fails at $z_0$, then for $d_2(z,z_0)<|H(z_0)|/(2C)$ the estimate gives $|H(z)-H(z_0)|<|H(z_0)|/2$, so $H(z)\ne0$. If an affine inequality $H(z)\ge0$ fails at $z_0$, then for $d_2(z,z_0)<-H(z_0)/(2C)$ the estimate gives $H(z)<H(z_0)/2<0$. Thus every point outside $\Gamma(p,q)$ has a ball in its complement, so [F5,F6] make $\Gamma(p,q)$ closed. Also $0\le\pi_{ij}\le p_i\le1$ by [F1,F2], so the set is bounded. Since $m^2\ge1$, [F6] makes $\Gamma(p,q)$ compact.

For a matrix difference $z-w$, the objective changes by at most $C d_2(z,w)$, where $C=\sum_{i,j}d(x_i,x_j)\ge0$ is finite; the coordinate bound is the same as in step 1.2. For any $\varepsilon>0$, taking $\delta=\varepsilon/(C+1)$ shows that inputs within $\delta$ have output difference less than $\varepsilon$, so the objective is continuous by [F8] and lower semicontinuous by [F9]. It is real-valued because all distances are finite reals; by [F4] and [F1] its values are nonnegative. The nonempty compact set from steps 1.1–1.2 and [F7] therefore give a finite attained minimum, which is $W_1(p,q)$ by [F10].

The set $\mathcal L_1(X,d)$ contains the zero vector. It is closed because its constraints are finitely many linear equalities and weak inequalities: $f_1=0$ has one nonzero coefficient, and writing each $|f_i-f_j|\le d(x_i,x_j)$ as $d(x_i,x_j)-(f_i-f_j)\ge0$ and $d(x_i,x_j)+(f_i-f_j)\ge0$ gives two nonzero coefficients in each inequality when $i\ne j$; when $i=j$ the constraint is the identity $0\le0$. Thus every violated constraint has positive coefficient sum and the strict-violation ball argument in step 1.2 applies using [F5,F6,F11]. Since $f_1=0$ and $|f_i-f_1|\le d(x_i,x_1)$, every $f\in\mathcal L_1(X,d)$ satisfies $|f_i|\le d(x_i,x_1)\le 1+\sum_{k=1}^m d(x_k,x_1)$ by [F3,F4]; thus the set is bounded. Since $m\ge1$, [F6] makes it compact.

The objective $f\mapsto\sum_i(p_i-q_i)f_i$ changes by at most $C'd_2(f,g)$, where $C'=\sum_i|p_i-q_i|\ge0$; taking $\delta=\varepsilon/(C'+1)$ for each $\varepsilon>0$ proves continuity by [F8] and upper semicontinuity by [F9]. The nonempty compact set from step 2.2 and [F7] give an attained maximum.

risk_review.notes: Read and independently checked all five steps and all twenty-three direct supplier statements/definitions, including the complete Euclidean semicontinuous extreme-value proof. The explicit product matrix has both marginals even at zero coordinates. Row-major coordinates cover R^(m^2); coordinate and finite-sum bounds prove affine violation balls and closedness. Entries in [0,1] give Euclidean boundedness, so Heine–Borel applies with m^2>=1. The cost objective is finite and continuous using delta=epsilon/(C+1), also valid when C=0; existence is established before identifying the minimum as W_1. The zero potential is feasible, diagonal constraints are identities, nontrivial constraints have positive coefficient sums, and f_1=0 bounds every coordinate by d(x_i,x_1). Heine–Borel and upper semicontinuous extreme values give the normalized dual maximum, including p=q, singleton X and zero coordinate cases. No uniqueness is claimed and no sequential choice is used. citations.quote:
Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
(Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property), Ordered field) constructed in this
library (The real numbers) and carrying its order (Order on the reals).

Let $X$ be a set. A **metric** on $X$ is a function
$d : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $x, y, z \in X$:

- **(M1) Separation.** $d(x,y) = 0$ if and only if $x = y$.
- **(M2) Symmetry.** $d(x,y) = d(y,x)$.
- **(M3) Triangle inequality.** $d(x,z) \le d(x,y) + d(y,z)$.

A **metric space** is a pair $(X,d)$ consisting of a set $X$ and a metric $d$ on
it. The elements of $X$ are its **points** and $d(x,y)$ is the **distance** from
$x$ to $y$. When only one metric is in play we write $X$ for $(X,d)$; when
several are, the metric is always named.

**The values of a metric are real numbers.** The codomain is $\mathbb{R}$, so
$d(x,y)$ is an honest element of the complete ordered field and every
inequality above is an inequality there. No infinite value is permitted;
Which metric axiom list this library uses, the live naming fork between semimetric and pseudometric, and why extended metrics are not treated here records why extended metrics are not treated in
this library.

**Nonnegativity is deliberately absent from the axiom list.** Many texts add a
fourth axiom $d(x,y) \ge 0$. It is redundant: (M1), (M2) and (M3) already force
it, as Nonnegativity of a metric is a consequence of the other axioms, not an axiom proves. Nothing below assumes it before that
lemma is available.

**Pseudometric.** A **pseudometric** on $X$ is a function
$p : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying (M2), (M3) and the weakening

- **(M1') Reflexivity.** $p(x,x) = 0$ for every $x \in X$

of (M1). A pseudometric may therefore assign distance $0$ to two distinct
points. Every metric is a pseudometric, and a pseudometric is a metric exactly
when $p(x,y) = 0$ forces $x = y$.

**Ultrametric.** An **ultrametric** on $X$ is a metric $d$ that in addition
satisfies

- **(M3') Strong triangle inequality.** $d(x,z) \le \max\{d(x,y), d(y,z)\}$

for all $x, y, z \in X$, where the maximum is that of a two-element subset of
$\mathbb{R}$, which exists and is one of the two elements
(Maximum and minimum of a set, Every nonempty finite set of reals has a maximum and a minimum). An **ultrametric space** is a pair
$(X,d)$ with $d$ an ultrametric.

Let $X$ be a set and let $p : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfy the reflexivity
axiom (M1') $p(x,x) = 0$ and the symmetry axiom (M2) $p(x,y) = p(y,x)$ of
Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric. Then:

1. If $p$ satisfies the triangle inequality (M3), then $p(x,y) \ge 0$ for all
   $x, y \in X$.
2. If $p$ satisfies the strong triangle inequality (M3'), then
   $p(x,y) \ge 0$ for all $x, y \in X$.

In particular every metric, every pseudometric and every ultrametric
(Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric) takes only nonnegative values. Nonnegativity is therefore
a theorem about the axiom list this library uses, not a fourth axiom, and no
statement on this page needs to assume it separately.

Let $\mathcal X$ be a finite nonempty set. A **probability vector** on
$\mathcal X$ is a family $P=(p_x)_{x\in\mathcal X}$ of real numbers such that
$p_x\ge 0$ for every $x$ and $\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}p_x=1$. Its support is
$\operatorname{supp}P:=\{x\in\mathcal X:p_x>0\}$. Coordinates outside the
support are retained as zeros; they are not deleted from the alphabet.

For another probability vector $Q=(q_x)_{x\in\mathcal X}$, the notation
$P\ll Q$ means $\operatorname{supp}P\subseteq\operatorname{supp}Q$. All
finite sums over $\mathcal X$ use the displayed alphabet and ordinary finite
real arithmetic, extended to $+\infty$ only where a later definition says so.

Let $X=\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}$ be a finite nonempty set with this fixed ordering, and let $p=(p_i)_{i=1}^m$ and $q=(q_j)_{j=1}^m$ be probability vectors on $X$: their coordinates are nonnegative real numbers and $\sum_{i=1}^m p_i=\sum_{j=1}^m q_j=1$. A **coupling** of $p$ and $q$ is a real matrix $\pi=(\pi_{ij})_{i,j=1}^m$ satisfying
$$
\pi_{ij}\ge 0,\qquad \sum_{j=1}^m\pi_{ij}=p_i\quad(1\le i\le m),\qquad \sum_{i=1}^m\pi_{ij}=q_j\quad(1\le j\le m).
$$
Write $\Gamma(p,q)$ for the set of all such matrices. The first index records the source point and the second index records the destination point.

Let $X=\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}$ be a nonempty finite set and let $d:X\times X\to\mathbb R$ satisfy $d(x,y)=0$ if and only if $x=y$, $d(x,y)=d(y,x)$, and $d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z)$. Let $p=(p_i)_{i=1}^m$ and $q=(q_i)_{i=1}^m$ be probability vectors, so their coordinates are nonnegative and each vector sums to $1$. A coupling is an $m\times m$ matrix $\pi$ with $\pi_{ij}\ge0$, row sums $\sum_j\pi_{ij}=p_i$, and column sums $\sum_i\pi_{ij}=q_j$; write $\Gamma(p,q)$ for the set of all such matrices. Writing $d_{ij}=d(x_i,x_j)$, define the finite-metric 1-Wasserstein transport cost by
$$
W_1(p,q):=\min_{\pi\in\Gamma(p,q)}\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^m d_{ij}\pi_{ij}.
$$

Let $X=\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}$ be a nonempty finite metric space, and let $p,q$ be probability vectors on $X$. The coupling set $\Gamma(p,q)$ is nonempty and compact in $\mathbb R^{m^2}$, so the finite-metric transport cost $W_1(p,q)$ attains its minimum. The normalized 1-Lipschitz potential set
$$
\mathcal L_1(X,d)=\{f\in\mathbb R^m:f_1=0,\ |f_i-f_j|\le d(x_i,x_j)\text{ for all }i,j\}
$$
is also nonempty and compact, so the linear functional $f\mapsto\sum_{i=1}^m(p_i-q_i)f_i$ attains a maximum on it.

Let $r,N\ge1$ be integers and let $g_1,\ldots,g_N\in\mathbb R^r$. Define
$$
C=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^N\lambda_i g_i:\lambda_i\ge0\text{ for every }i\right\}.
$$
Then $C$ is closed in the Euclidean topology, and for all $x,y\in C$ and all real $\alpha,\beta\ge0$, one has $\alpha x+\beta y\in C$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let $x\notin C$. Then there are $a\ne0$ and $b\in\mathbb R$ such that $\langle a,z\rangle\le b<\langle a,x\rangle$ for every $z\in C$. Thus a hyperplane strictly separates $x$ from $C$ (Supporting and strictly separating hyperplanes in Euclidean space).

For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and all $a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n \in \mathbb{R}$, the
set $\{a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ has a maximum and a minimum (Maximum and minimum of a set).

What is proved below is exactly the displayed statement, by induction on $n$.

The usual reading, that *every nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ has a
maximum and a minimum*, follows once one identifies the nonempty finite subsets
of $\mathbb{R}$ with the sets listable as $\{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$. That
identification is recorded as a stipulation in the Given below, because this page
has no definition of finiteness to prove it against. **It is discharged, not
merely assumed**: The nonempty finite subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ are exactly the listable ones proves that the two
descriptions of a nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ agree. That lemma is
recorded in `justified_by` rather than in `deps`, since it is about the sets this
lemma quantifies over and therefore depends on this one. This is what licenses
the notation
$\max\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ and $\min\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ for finite sets of
**real** numbers from this page onwards.

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ and $m \in \mathbb{R}$.

- $m$ is a **maximum** (or *greatest element*) of $S$ if $m \in S$ and $s \le m$
  for every $s \in S$.
- $m$ is a **minimum** (or *least element*) of $S$ if $m \in S$ and $m \le s$
  for every $s \in S$.

A set has at most one maximum: if $m_1$ and $m_2$ are both maxima then
$m_1 \in S$ gives $m_1 \le m_2$ and $m_2 \in S$ gives $m_2 \le m_1$, so
$m_1 = m_2$ by antisymmetry of the order, which is immediate from the trichotomy
axiom of an ordered field (Ordered field, Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property)).
The same argument applies to minima, so we may write $\max S$ and $\min S$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ (The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann),
On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of The vector space $F^{X}$ of all functions $X \to F$ with pointwise operations, and $F^{n}$ as the case $X = n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations

$$

$$

$$

real $r > 0$ with $B(x,r) \subseteq U$ (Open ball, closed ball and sphere in a metric space). A subset
$F \subseteq X$ is **closed in $(X,d)$** if its complement $X \setminus F$ is
open.

The collection

$$\mathcal{T}_d := \{\, U \subseteq X : U \text{ is open in } (X,d) \,\}$$

of all open subsets is the **metric topology** of $d$ on $X$. A subset of $X$
that is both open and closed is called **clopen**.

**Two sets are open for trivial reasons.** $\emptyset$ is open, because the
defining condition quantifies over no points; and $X$ is open, because
$B(x,r) \subseteq X$ for every $x$ and every $r > 0$. Consequently $X$ and
$\emptyset$ are also closed, and both are clopen.

**A neighbourhood of a point $x$** is any set containing an open set that
contains $x$; an **open neighbourhood** is an open set containing $x$. In a
metric space, a set is a neighbourhood of $x$ exactly when it contains some
ball $B(x,r)$ with $r>0$. Thus $U$ is open exactly when it is a neighbourhood of
each of its points, and metric balls suffice to test this condition.

**The metric, not the set, determines $\mathcal{T}_d$.** Two metrics on the same
set may have different metric topologies, and two different metrics may have the
same one; the systematic comparison is Topologically, uniformly and Lipschitz equivalent metrics on a set.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space (Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric), let $x \in X$ and let
$r \in \mathbb{R}$ with $r > 0$ (Order on the reals). Define

$$B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) < r \,\}, \qquad \bar B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) \le r \,\}, \qquad S(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) = r \,\}.$$

$B(x,r)$ is the **open ball**, $\bar B(x,r)$ the **closed ball** and $S(x,r)$ the
**sphere** of **centre** $x$ and **radius** $r$. The radius is always a strictly
positive real; a ball of radius $0$ or of negative radius is never written in
this library.

- $x \in B(x,r)$, because $d(x,x) = 0 < r$ (axiom (M1) of Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric);
  in particular open and closed balls are nonempty.
- $B(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, and
  $\bar B(x,r)$ is the disjoint union of $B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r)$, by trichotomy of
  the order of $\mathbb{R}$ (Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property), Ordered field):
  each $y$ satisfies exactly one of $d(x,y) < r$, $d(x,y) = r$, $d(x,y) > r$.

produces a point at distance exactly $r$ from $x$. If a metric takes only the

derivations.claim: By [F1], choose an at-most-countable dense set $D\subseteq X$. If $X=\varnothing$, the empty family is a countable basis. Otherwise set $\mathcal U:=\{B(a,1/n):a\in D,\ n\in\mathbb N,\ n\ge1\}$. By [F2], the index set $D\times\{n\in\mathbb N:n\ge1\}$ and therefore $\mathcal U$ are at most countable.

To check that $\mathcal U$ is a basis, let $O$ be open and $x\in O$. By [F4], choose $r>0$ with $B(x,r)\subseteq O$. Apply [F3] to $r/2$ to choose $n\ge1$ with $2/n<r$. Density of $D$ gives $a\in D$ with $d(x,a)<1/n$. Then $x\in B(a,1/n)$, and every $y\in B(a,1/n)$ satisfies $d(x,y)\le d(x,a)+d(a,y)<2/n<r$. Hence $x\in B(a,1/n)\subseteq O$.
By [F5], the at-most-countable basis $\mathcal U$ makes $X$ second-countable.

Equivalently, there are pairwise disjoint measurable sets

Any such display is a **simple representation** of $s$.

$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$, so the $E_j\in\mathcal A$ are pairwise disjoint and

If $s$ is a nonnegative simple measurable function, then its nonnegative
Lebesgue integral equals its simple integral:
$$\int s\,d\mu=\int_{\mathrm{simple}} s\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space, let $F=\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}\subseteq X$ be finite and nonempty with distinct ordered points, and let $f_1,\ldots,f_m\in\mathbb R$ satisfy $|f_i-f_j|\le d(x_i,x_j)$ for every $i,j$. Define
$$\widetilde f(x):=\min_{1\le i\le m}\bigl(f_i+d(x,x_i)\bigr)\qquad(x\in X).$$
Then $\widetilde f$ is 1-Lipschitz on $X$ and $\widetilde f(x_i)=f_i$ for every $i$.

Let $X=\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}$ be a nonempty finite set, let $d:X\times X\to\mathbb R$ satisfy $d(x,y)=0$ if and only if $x=y$, $d(x,y)=d(y,x)$, and $d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z)$, and let $p=(p_i)_{i=1}^m$, $q=(q_i)_{i=1}^m$ have nonnegative coordinates with each vector summing to $1$. Let $\Gamma(p,q)$ consist of matrices $\pi_{ij}\ge0$ with row sums $p_i$ and column sums $q_j$, and let
$$
W_1(p,q)=\min_{\pi\in\Gamma(p,q)}\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^m d(x_i,x_j)\pi_{ij}.
$$
Then
$$
W_1(p,q)=\max_{\substack{f\in\mathbb R^m,\ f_1=0\\ |f_i-f_j|\le d(x_i,x_j)\ \text{for all }i,j}}\sum_{i=1}^m(p_i-q_i)f_i.
$$
Both extrema are attained. Moreover, for every minimizing coupling $\pi$ and every maximizing vector $f$, $\pi_{ij}>0$ implies $f_i-f_j=d(x_i,x_j)$.

A coupling is an $m\times m$ matrix $\pi$ with $\pi_{ij}\ge0$, row sums $\sum_j\pi_{ij}=p_i$, and column sums $\sum_i\pi_{ij}=q_j$; write $\Gamma(p,q)$ for the set of all such matrices. $$
W_1(p,q):=\min_{\pi\in\Gamma(p,q)}\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^m d_{ij}\pi_{ij}.
$$

Let $X=\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}$ be a finite nonempty set with this fixed ordering, and let $p=(p_i)_{i=1}^m$ and $q=(q_j)_{j=1}^m$ be probability vectors on $X$: their coordinates are nonnegative real numbers and $\sum_{i=1}^m p_i=\sum_{j=1}^m q_j=1$. A **coupling** of $p$ and $q$ is a real matrix $\pi=(\pi_{ij})_{i,j=1}^m$ satisfying
$$
\pi_{ij}\ge 0,\qquad \sum_{j=1}^m\pi_{ij}=p_i\quad(1\le i\le m),\qquad \sum_{i=1}^m\pi_{ij}=q_j\quad(1\le j\le m).
$$
Write $\Gamma(p,q)$ for the set of all such matrices. The first index records the source point and the second index records the destination point.

Let $\mathcal X$ be a finite nonempty set. A **probability vector** on
$\mathcal X$ is a family $P=(p_x)_{x\in\mathcal X}$ of real numbers such that
$p_x\ge 0$ for every $x$ and $\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}p_x=1$. Its support is
$\operatorname{supp}P:=\{x\in\mathcal X:p_x>0\}$. Coordinates outside the
support are retained as zeros; they are not deleted from the alphabet.

For another probability vector $Q=(q_x)_{x\in\mathcal X}$, the notation
$P\ll Q$ means $\operatorname{supp}P\subseteq\operatorname{supp}Q$. All
finite sums over $\mathcal X$ use the displayed alphabet and ordinary finite
real arithmetic, extended to $+\infty$ only where a later definition says so.

Let $(X,d)$ be a compact metric space. Write $\mathcal B(X)$ for the sigma-algebra generated by the open sets of its metric topology. A Borel probability measure on $X$ is a countably additive measure on $\mathcal B(X)$ with total mass one. For Borel probability measures $\mu,\nu$ on $X$, let $\Pi_X(\mu,\nu)$ be the set of Borel probability measures $\gamma$ on $X\times X$, with its product topology and Borel sigma-algebra, such that for every $A\in\mathcal B(X)$,
$$\gamma(A\times X)=\mu(A),\qquad \gamma(X\times A)=\nu(A).$$
Define
$$W_1^X(\mu,\nu):=\inf_{\gamma\in\Pi_X(\mu,\nu)}\int_{X\times X}d(x,y)\,d\gamma(x,y)\in[0,+\infty],$$
where the infimum is taken in the extended real line and $\inf\varnothing=+\infty$. The integrand is nonnegative and Borel: the triangle inequality and symmetry give
$$|d(x,y)-d(x',y')|\le d(x,x')+d(y,y'),$$
so $(x,y)\mapsto d(x,y)$ is continuous for the product topology; nonnegativity follows from the metric axioms.

set $\{a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ has a maximum and a minimum (Maximum and minimum of a set).

What is proved below is exactly the displayed statement, by induction on $n$.

The usual reading, that *every nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ has a
maximum and a minimum*, follows once one identifies the nonempty finite subsets
of $\mathbb{R}$ with the sets listable as $\{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$. That

$\max\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ and $\min\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ for finite sets of

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
(Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property), Ordered field) constructed in this
library (The real numbers) and carrying its order (Order on the reals).

Let $X$ be a set. A **metric** on $X$ is a function
$d : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $x, y, z \in X$:

- **(M1) Separation.** $d(x,y) = 0$ if and only if $x = y$.
- **(M2) Symmetry.** $d(x,y) = d(y,x)$.
- **(M3) Triangle inequality.** $d(x,z) \le d(x,y) + d(y,z)$.

A **metric space** is a pair $(X,d)$ consisting of a set $X$ and a metric $d$ on
it. The elements of $X$ are its **points** and $d(x,y)$ is the **distance** from
$x$ to $y$. When only one metric is in play we write $X$ for $(X,d)$; when
several are, the metric is always named.

**The values of a metric are real numbers.** The codomain is $\mathbb{R}$, so
$d(x,y)$ is an honest element of the complete ordered field and every
inequality above is an inequality there. No infinite value is permitted;
Which metric axiom list this library uses, the live naming fork between semimetric and pseudometric, and why extended metrics are not treated here records why extended metrics are not treated in
this library.

**Nonnegativity is deliberately absent from the axiom list.** Many texts add a
fourth axiom $d(x,y) \ge 0$. It is redundant: (M1), (M2) and (M3) already force
it, as Nonnegativity of a metric is a consequence of the other axioms, not an axiom proves. Nothing below assumes it before that
lemma is available.

**Pseudometric.** A **pseudometric** on $X$ is a function
$p : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying (M2), (M3) and the weakening

- **(M1') Reflexivity.** $p(x,x) = 0$ for every $x \in X$

of (M1). A pseudometric may therefore assign distance $0$ to two distinct
points. Every metric is a pseudometric, and a pseudometric is a metric exactly
when $p(x,y) = 0$ forces $x = y$.

**Ultrametric.** An **ultrametric** on $X$ is a metric $d$ that in addition
satisfies

- **(M3') Strong triangle inequality.** $d(x,z) \le \max\{d(x,y), d(y,z)\}$

for all $x, y, z \in X$, where the maximum is that of a two-element subset of
$\mathbb{R}$, which exists and is one of the two elements
(Maximum and minimum of a set, Every nonempty finite set of reals has a maximum and a minimum). An **ultrametric space** is a pair
$(X,d)$ with $d$ an ultrametric.

axiom (M1') $p(x,x) = 0$ and the symmetry axiom (M2) $p(x,y) = p(y,x)$ of

1. If $p$ satisfies the triangle inequality (M3), then $p(x,y) \ge 0$ for all
   $x, y \in X$.
2. If $p$ satisfies the strong triangle inequality (M3'), then

In particular every metric, every pseudometric and every ultrametric
(Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric) takes only nonnegative values. Nonnegativity is therefore
a theorem about the axiom list this library uses, not a fourth axiom, and no

2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the

(Extended-real-valued measurable functions). Its
**nonnegative Lebesgue integral** is
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\sup\left\{\int s\,d\mu:\ s \text{ is nonnegative simple and } 0\le s\le f\right\},$$
where the simple integral on the right is the one from
The integral of a nonnegative simple function.

The set of admissible simple minorants is nonempty because it contains the zero
function, which is simple (Nonnegative simple measurable functions).

$$\int s\,d\mu=\int_{\mathrm{simple}} s\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. If $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ are measurable, then

they are measurable by

$F \subseteq X$ is **closed in $(X,d)$** if its complement $X \setminus F$ is
open.

$$\mathcal{T}_d := \{\, U \subseteq X : U \text{ is open in } (X,d) \,\}$$

that is both open and closed is called **clopen**.

**Two sets are open for trivial reasons.** $\emptyset$ is open, because the
defining condition quantifies over no points; and $X$ is open, because

**A neighbourhood of a point $x$** is any set containing an open set that
contains $x$; an **open neighbourhood** is an open set containing $x$. In a
metric space, a set is a neighbourhood of $x$ exactly when it contains some
ball $B(x,r)$ with $r>0$. Thus $U$ is open exactly when it is a neighbourhood of
each of its points, and metric balls suffice to test this condition.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space (Topology on a set, open and closed sets, clopen sets, the closed-set axiomatisation, and the coarser/finer comparison). The

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by Nonempty intersections of sigma-algebras are sigma-algebras, so the generated sigma-algebra exists and is minimal.

**The product set.** Let $I$ be a set and let $X_i$ be a set for each $i \in I$.
The **product** is

$$\prod_{i \in I} X_i \;:=\; \Big\{\, x : x \text{ is a function with domain } I \text{ and } x(i) \in X_i \text{ for every } i \in I \,\Big\},$$

and we write $x_i := x(i)$, the $i$-th **coordinate** of $x$. Two elements of the
product are equal exactly when they agree at every index, functions being equal
when they have the same domain and the same values. For $j \in I$ the $j$-th
**projection** is

$$\pi_j : \prod_{i \in I} X_i \to X_j, \qquad \pi_j(x) := x_j .$$

**Notation for a finite product.** For $I = n$ a natural number, which is the set
$\{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ of its predecessors, an element of $\prod_{k<n} X_k$ is a
function on $n$ and we write it $(x_0, \dots, x_{n-1})$. In particular $I = 2$
gives the **binary product**, written $X \times Y$ for $\prod_{i<2} X_i$ with
$X_0 = X$ and $X_1 = Y$, whose elements are written $(u,v)$ for the function
$0 \mapsto u$, $1 \mapsto v$. This is the only meaning the symbol $X \times Y$
carries on this page.

**Two facts about when the product is nonempty, stated because they are used and
because they cost something.** If some $X_{i_0}$ is empty then the product is
empty, since no function can take a value in $X_{i_0}$. Conversely, suppose every

- For $I = n$ a natural number, the product is nonempty, and this is a theorem of
