citations.quote: Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space and let $\varepsilon>0$. Then there are an integer $m\ge1$, distinct points $x_1,\ldots,x_m\in X$, a Borel partition $C_1,\ldots,C_m$ of $X$, and a Borel map $Q:X\to F:=\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}$ such that $Q(x)=x_i$ for $x\in C_i$ and $d(x,Q(x))<\varepsilon$ for every $x\in X$. The partition assigns each point to a nearest point of $F$, and ties are assigned to the least index.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space that is compact or second-countable. Let $x_1,\ldots,x_m$ be distinct points, let $C_1,\ldots,C_m$ be a Borel partition of $X$, and let $\varepsilon>0$ satisfy $d(x,x_i)<\varepsilon$ for every $x\in C_i$. Let $\mu,
u$ be Borel probability measures on $X$, set $p_i=\mu(C_i)$ and $q_j=
u(C_j)$, and let $\pi=(\pi_{ij})$ be a finite coupling of the probability vectors $p,q$. Then there is a Borel probability measure $\gamma$ on $X	imes X$ with marginals $\mu,
u$ such that
$$\int_{X	imes X}d(x,y)\,d\gamma(x,y)\le\sum_{i,j=1}^m\pi_{ij}d(x_i,x_j)+2\varepsilon.$$

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space, let $F=\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}\subseteq X$ be finite and nonempty with distinct ordered points, and let $f_1,\ldots,f_m\in\mathbb R$ satisfy $|f_i-f_j|\le d(x_i,x_j)$ for every $i,j$. Define
$$\widetilde f(x):=\min_{1\le i\le m}\bigl(f_i+d(x,x_i)\bigr)\qquad(x\in X).$$
Then $\widetilde f$ is 1-Lipschitz on $X$ and $\widetilde f(x_i)=f_i$ for every $i$.

Let $X=\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}$ be a nonempty finite set, let $d:X\times X\to\mathbb R$ satisfy $d(x,y)=0$ if and only if $x=y$, $d(x,y)=d(y,x)$, and $d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z)$, and let $p=(p_i)_{i=1}^m$, $q=(q_i)_{i=1}^m$ have nonnegative coordinates with each vector summing to $1$. Let $\Gamma(p,q)$ consist of matrices $\pi_{ij}\ge0$ with row sums $p_i$ and column sums $q_j$, and let
$$
W_1(p,q)=\min_{\pi\in\Gamma(p,q)}\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^m d(x_i,x_j)\pi_{ij}.
$$
Then
$$
W_1(p,q)=\max_{\substack{f\in\mathbb R^m,\ f_1=0\\ |f_i-f_j|\le d(x_i,x_j)\ \text{for all }i,j}}\sum_{i=1}^m(p_i-q_i)f_i.
$$
Both extrema are attained. Moreover, for every minimizing coupling $\pi$ and every maximizing vector $f$, $\pi_{ij}>0$ implies $f_i-f_j=d(x_i,x_j)$.

Let $X=\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}$ be a nonempty finite set and let $d:X\times X\to\mathbb R$ satisfy $d(x,y)=0$ if and only if $x=y$, $d(x,y)=d(y,x)$, and $d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z)$. Let $p=(p_i)_{i=1}^m$ and $q=(q_i)_{i=1}^m$ be probability vectors, so their coordinates are nonnegative and each vector sums to $1$. A coupling is an $m\times m$ matrix $\pi$ with $\pi_{ij}\ge0$, row sums $\sum_j\pi_{ij}=p_i$, and column sums $\sum_i\pi_{ij}=q_j$; write $\Gamma(p,q)$ for the set of all such matrices. Writing $d_{ij}=d(x_i,x_j)$, define the finite-metric 1-Wasserstein transport cost by
$$
W_1(p,q):=\min_{\pi\in\Gamma(p,q)}\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^m d_{ij}\pi_{ij}.
$$

Let $X=\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}$ be a finite nonempty set with this fixed ordering, and let $p=(p_i)_{i=1}^m$ and $q=(q_j)_{j=1}^m$ be probability vectors on $X$: their coordinates are nonnegative real numbers and $\sum_{i=1}^m p_i=\sum_{j=1}^m q_j=1$. A **coupling** of $p$ and $q$ is a real matrix $\pi=(\pi_{ij})_{i,j=1}^m$ satisfying
$$
\pi_{ij}\ge 0,\qquad \sum_{j=1}^m\pi_{ij}=p_i\quad(1\le i\le m),\qquad \sum_{i=1}^m\pi_{ij}=q_j\quad(1\le j\le m).
$$
Write $\Gamma(p,q)$ for the set of all such matrices. The first index records the source point and the second index records the destination point.

Let $\mathcal X$ be a finite nonempty set. A **probability vector** on
$\mathcal X$ is a family $P=(p_x)_{x\in\mathcal X}$ of real numbers such that
$p_x\ge 0$ for every $x$ and $\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}p_x=1$. Its support is
$\operatorname{supp}P:=\{x\in\mathcal X:p_x>0\}$. Coordinates outside the
support are retained as zeros; they are not deleted from the alphabet.

For another probability vector $Q=(q_x)_{x\in\mathcal X}$, the notation
$P\ll Q$ means $\operatorname{supp}P\subseteq\operatorname{supp}Q$. All
finite sums over $\mathcal X$ use the displayed alphabet and ordinary finite
real arithmetic, extended to $+\infty$ only where a later definition says so.

Let $(X,d)$ be a compact metric space. Write $\mathcal B(X)$ for the sigma-algebra generated by the open sets of its metric topology. A Borel probability measure on $X$ is a countably additive measure on $\mathcal B(X)$ with total mass one. For Borel probability measures $\mu,\nu$ on $X$, let $\Pi_X(\mu,\nu)$ be the set of Borel probability measures $\gamma$ on $X\times X$, with its product topology and Borel sigma-algebra, such that for every $A\in\mathcal B(X)$,
$$\gamma(A\times X)=\mu(A),\qquad \gamma(X\times A)=\nu(A).$$
Define
$$W_1^X(\mu,\nu):=\inf_{\gamma\in\Pi_X(\mu,\nu)}\int_{X\times X}d(x,y)\,d\gamma(x,y)\in[0,+\infty],$$
where the infimum is taken in the extended real line and $\inf\varnothing=+\infty$. The integrand is nonnegative and Borel: the triangle inequality and symmetry give
$$|d(x,y)-d(x',y')|\le d(x,x')+d(y,y'),$$
so $(x,y)\mapsto d(x,y)$ is continuous for the product topology; nonnegativity follows from the metric axioms.

For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and all $a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n \in \mathbb{R}$, the
set $\{a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ has a maximum and a minimum (Maximum and minimum of a set).

What is proved below is exactly the displayed statement, by induction on $n$.

The usual reading, that *every nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ has a
maximum and a minimum*, follows once one identifies the nonempty finite subsets
of $\mathbb{R}$ with the sets listable as $\{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$. That
identification is recorded as a stipulation in the Given below, because this page
has no definition of finiteness to prove it against. **It is discharged, not
merely assumed**: The nonempty finite subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ are exactly the listable ones proves that the two
descriptions of a nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ agree. That lemma is
recorded in `justified_by` rather than in `deps`, since it is about the sets this
lemma quantifies over and therefore depends on this one. This is what licenses
the notation
$\max\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ and $\min\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ for finite sets of
**real** numbers from this page onwards.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
(Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property), Ordered field) constructed in this
library (The real numbers) and carrying its order (Order on the reals).

Let $X$ be a set. A **metric** on $X$ is a function
$d : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $x, y, z \in X$:

- **(M1) Separation.** $d(x,y) = 0$ if and only if $x = y$.
- **(M2) Symmetry.** $d(x,y) = d(y,x)$.
- **(M3) Triangle inequality.** $d(x,z) \le d(x,y) + d(y,z)$.

A **metric space** is a pair $(X,d)$ consisting of a set $X$ and a metric $d$ on
it. The elements of $X$ are its **points** and $d(x,y)$ is the **distance** from
$x$ to $y$. When only one metric is in play we write $X$ for $(X,d)$; when
several are, the metric is always named.

**The values of a metric are real numbers.** The codomain is $\mathbb{R}$, so
$d(x,y)$ is an honest element of the complete ordered field and every
inequality above is an inequality there. No infinite value is permitted;
Which metric axiom list this library uses, the live naming fork between semimetric and pseudometric, and why extended metrics are not treated here records why extended metrics are not treated in
this library.

**Nonnegativity is deliberately absent from the axiom list.** Many texts add a
fourth axiom $d(x,y) \ge 0$. It is redundant: (M1), (M2) and (M3) already force
it, as Nonnegativity of a metric is a consequence of the other axioms, not an axiom proves. Nothing below assumes it before that
lemma is available.

**Pseudometric.** A **pseudometric** on $X$ is a function
$p : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying (M2), (M3) and the weakening

- **(M1') Reflexivity.** $p(x,x) = 0$ for every $x \in X$

of (M1). A pseudometric may therefore assign distance $0$ to two distinct
points. Every metric is a pseudometric, and a pseudometric is a metric exactly
when $p(x,y) = 0$ forces $x = y$.

**Ultrametric.** An **ultrametric** on $X$ is a metric $d$ that in addition
satisfies

- **(M3') Strong triangle inequality.** $d(x,z) \le \max\{d(x,y), d(y,z)\}$

for all $x, y, z \in X$, where the maximum is that of a two-element subset of
$\mathbb{R}$, which exists and is one of the two elements
(Maximum and minimum of a set, Every nonempty finite set of reals has a maximum and a minimum). An **ultrametric space** is a pair
$(X,d)$ with $d$ an ultrametric.

Let $X$ be a set and let $p : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfy the reflexivity
axiom (M1') $p(x,x) = 0$ and the symmetry axiom (M2) $p(x,y) = p(y,x)$ of
Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric. Then:

1. If $p$ satisfies the triangle inequality (M3), then $p(x,y) \ge 0$ for all
   $x, y \in X$.
2. If $p$ satisfies the strong triangle inequality (M3'), then
   $p(x,y) \ge 0$ for all $x, y \in X$.

In particular every metric, every pseudometric and every ultrametric
(Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric) takes only nonnegative values. Nonnegativity is therefore
a theorem about the axiom list this library uses, not a fourth axiom, and no
statement on this page needs to assume it separately.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable
(Extended-real-valued measurable functions). Its
**nonnegative Lebesgue integral** is
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\sup\left\{\int s\,d\mu:\ s \text{ is nonnegative simple and } 0\le s\le f\right\},$$
where the simple integral on the right is the one from
The integral of a nonnegative simple function.

The set of admissible simple minorants is nonempty because it contains the zero
function, which is simple (Nonnegative simple measurable functions).

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space. A measurable function
$s:X\to[0,+\infty)\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$
(Extended-real-valued measurable functions) is a
**nonnegative simple measurable function** when it has finite range.

Equivalently, there are pairwise disjoint measurable sets
$E_1,\dots,E_m\in\mathcal A$ and coefficients $c_1,\dots,c_m\in[0,+\infty)$
such that
$$s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\chi_{E_j}.$$
Any such display is a **simple representation** of $s$.

Let $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\chi_{E_j}$ be a simple representation of a
nonnegative simple measurable function
(Nonnegative simple measurable functions) on a measure space
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$, so the $E_j\in\mathcal A$ are pairwise disjoint and
$c_j\ge0$. Its
**simple integral** is
$$\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mu(E_j),$$
where $\mu$ is the given measure (Measures on sigma-algebras) and the convention
$0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ is fixed once and for all.

The next lemma proves that this value is independent of the chosen simple
representation.

If $s$ is a nonnegative simple measurable function, then its nonnegative
Lebesgue integral equals its simple integral:
$$\int s\,d\mu=\int_{\mathrm{simple}} s\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. If $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ are measurable, then
$$\int(f+g)\,d\mu=\int f\,d\mu+\int g\,d\mu.$$

Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. Its positive and negative parts are
$$f^+:=\max\{f,0\},\qquad f^-:=\max\{-f,0\};$$
they are measurable by
Closure properties of measurable functions used by the integral and
satisfy $f=f^+-f^-$ and $|f|=f^++f^-$.

The **Lebesgue integral of a real measurable function** is defined whenever at
most one of $\int f^+\,d\mu$ and $\int f^-\,d\mu$ is $+\infty$, in which case
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\int f^+\,d\mu-\int f^-\,d\mu.$$
The function is **integrable** when both integrals are finite, equivalently
when $\int|f|\,d\mu<+\infty$.

For a complex measurable function $h=u+iv$ with
$u=\operatorname{Re}h,\ v=\operatorname{Im}h$
(Real and imaginary parts, complex conjugation, and modulus), define $h$ to be
**integrable** when $|h|$ is integrable, and then define
$$\int h\,d\mu:=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space (Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric).

A subset $U \subseteq X$ is **open in $(X,d)$** if for every $x \in U$ there is a
real $r > 0$ with $B(x,r) \subseteq U$ (Open ball, closed ball and sphere in a metric space). A subset
$F \subseteq X$ is **closed in $(X,d)$** if its complement $X \setminus F$ is
open.

The collection

$$\mathcal{T}_d := \{\, U \subseteq X : U \text{ is open in } (X,d) \,\}$$

of all open subsets is the **metric topology** of $d$ on $X$. A subset of $X$
that is both open and closed is called **clopen**.

**Two sets are open for trivial reasons.** $\emptyset$ is open, because the
defining condition quantifies over no points; and $X$ is open, because
$B(x,r) \subseteq X$ for every $x$ and every $r > 0$. Consequently $X$ and
$\emptyset$ are also closed, and both are clopen.

**A neighbourhood of a point $x$** is any set containing an open set that
contains $x$; an **open neighbourhood** is an open set containing $x$. In a
metric space, a set is a neighbourhood of $x$ exactly when it contains some
ball $B(x,r)$ with $r>0$. Thus $U$ is open exactly when it is a neighbourhood of
each of its points, and metric balls suffice to test this condition.

**The metric, not the set, determines $\mathcal{T}_d$.** Two metrics on the same
set may have different metric topologies, and two different metrics may have the
same one; the systematic comparison is Topologically, uniformly and Lipschitz equivalent metrics on a set.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space (Topology on a set, open and closed sets, clopen sets, the closed-set axiomatisation, and the coarser/finer comparison). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by Nonempty intersections of sigma-algebras are sigma-algebras, so the generated sigma-algebra exists and is minimal.

**The product set.** Let $I$ be a set and let $X_i$ be a set for each $i \in I$.
The **product** is

$$\prod_{i \in I} X_i \;:=\; \Big\{\, x : x \text{ is a function with domain } I \text{ and } x(i) \in X_i \text{ for every } i \in I \,\Big\},$$

and we write $x_i := x(i)$, the $i$-th **coordinate** of $x$. Two elements of the
product are equal exactly when they agree at every index, functions being equal
when they have the same domain and the same values. For $j \in I$ the $j$-th
**projection** is

$$\pi_j : \prod_{i \in I} X_i \to X_j, \qquad \pi_j(x) := x_j .$$

**Notation for a finite product.** For $I = n$ a natural number, which is the set
$\{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ of its predecessors, an element of $\prod_{k<n} X_k$ is a
function on $n$ and we write it $(x_0, \dots, x_{n-1})$. In particular $I = 2$
gives the **binary product**, written $X \times Y$ for $\prod_{i<2} X_i$ with
$X_0 = X$ and $X_1 = Y$, whose elements are written $(u,v)$ for the function
$0 \mapsto u$, $1 \mapsto v$. This is the only meaning the symbol $X \times Y$
carries on this page.

**Two facts about when the product is nonempty, stated because they are used and
because they cost something.** If some $X_{i_0}$ is empty then the product is
empty, since no function can take a value in $X_{i_0}$. Conversely, suppose every
$X_i$ is nonempty.

- For $I = n$ a natural number, the product is nonempty, and this is a theorem of
  ZF: Every natural-number-indexed list of nonempty sets has a choice function on its family of values applied to the function $i \mapsto X_i$ on $n$
  supplies a choice function $g$ for the family of values, and
  $x(i) := g(X_i)$ defines a member of $\prod_{k<n} X_k$.
- For an arbitrary $I$ the assertion "$\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \varnothing$
  whenever every $X_i$ is nonempty" **is** the Axiom of Choice: it is the
  formulation recorded in The Axiom of Choice, and the choice function of
  Choice function is exactly a point of the product of a family by
  itself. Every use of it below is flagged at the step that spends it.

**The box topology.** Now let each $X_i$ carry a topology $\mathcal{T}_i$
(Topology on a set, open and closed sets, clopen sets, the closed-set axiomatisation, and the coarser/finer comparison). Put

$$\mathcal{R} \;:=\; \Big\{\, \prod_{i \in I} U_i \;:\; U_i \in \mathcal{T}_i \text{ for every } i \in I \,\Big\},$$

the family of **boxes**. $\mathcal{R}$ is a basis for a topology
(A family is a basis for a unique topology iff it covers the set and every point of an intersection of two members lies in a member inside that intersection; finite intersections of any subbasis form a basis): it contains $\prod_i X_i$, so it covers the product,
and it is closed under binary intersections, since

$$\Big(\prod_i U_i\Big) \cap \Big(\prod_i V_i\Big) = \prod_i (U_i \cap V_i)$$

and each $U_i \cap V_i$ is open by (T3). The topology it generates is the **box
topology** $\mathcal{T}^{\square}$, and $\mathcal{R}$ is a basis for it
(Basis and subbasis for a topology, and the topology generated by a family of sets).

**The product topology.** The **product topology** $\mathcal{T}^{\Pi}$ on
$\prod_i X_i$ is the initial topology of the family of projections
$(\pi_i)_{i \in I}$ (The initial topology of a family of maps into spaces and the final topology of a family of maps out of spaces, and the subspace topology as the model initial topology): the topology generated
by the subbasis

$$\mathcal{G} \;:=\; \{\, \pi_i^{-1}[U] : i \in I,\ U \in \mathcal{T}_i \,\}, \qquad \pi_i^{-1}[U] = \prod_{j \in I} W_j \ \text{ with } W_i = U \text{ and } W_j = X_j \text{ for } j \ne i .$$

By A family is a basis for a unique topology iff it covers the set and every point of an intersection of two members lies in a member inside that intersection; finite intersections of any subbasis form a basis the finite intersections of members of $\mathcal{G}$
form a basis for $\mathcal{T}^{\Pi}$, and those finite intersections are exactly
the boxes with all but finitely many factors unrestricted:

$$\mathcal{R}^{\Pi} \;=\; \Big\{\, \prod_{i \in I} U_i \;:\; U_i \in \mathcal{T}_i \text{ for every } i, \text{ and } U_i = X_i \text{ for all but finitely many } i \,\Big\}.$$

Indeed the intersection of $\pi_{i_1}^{-1}[U_1], \dots, \pi_{i_n}^{-1}[U_n]$ is
the box whose factor at $i$ is the intersection of those $U_m$ with $i_m = i$ and
is $X_i$ when no $i_m$ equals $i$; and the intersection of no members is the
whole product, the box with every factor $X_i$. Conversely a box with
$U_i = X_i$ off a finite set is such an intersection. Members of
$\mathcal{R}^{\Pi}$ are called **basic product-open** sets, and members of
$\mathcal{R}$ **boxes**. So $\mathcal{R}^{\Pi} \subseteq \mathcal{R}$, with
equality when $I$ is a natural number.

**The empty product.** For $I = \varnothing$ there is exactly one function with
domain $\varnothing$, the empty function, so $\prod_{i \in \varnothing} X_i$ is a
one-point set. A one-point set carries exactly one topology, namely
$\{\varnothing, \{\varnothing\}\}$, since a topology must contain the empty set
and the whole set and there is nothing else to contain
(Topology on a set, open and closed sets, clopen sets, the closed-set axiomatisation, and the coarser/finer comparison); so the box topology and the product topology agree
there, and both equal the discrete topology and the indiscrete topology
(The discrete, indiscrete, cofinite, cocountable, particular-point and Sierpinski topologies), which coincide on a one-point set. There are no
projections to speak of, and the initial topology of the empty family is indeed
the indiscrete one (The initial topology of a family of maps into spaces and the final topology of a family of maps out of spaces, and the subspace topology as the model initial topology).

**Convention.** Unless the box topology is named explicitly, $\prod_i X_i$ always
carries the product topology in this library. That is not a matter of taste: the
product topology is the one with the characteristic property of the next item,
and the box topology has no such property.

derivations.claim: Use [F1] at scale $1$ to obtain a finite net $z_1,\ldots,z_s$. Let $M:=2+\max_{k,\ell}d(z_k,z_\ell)$, whose maximum exists by [F7]. For any $x,y\in X$, choose net points within $1$ of $x$ and $y$; [F8] gives $d(x,y)<M$. Hence an anchored feasible $f$ satisfies $|f(x)|\le d(x,x_0)<M$. For every $x$ and $r>0$, $d(x,y)<r$ implies $|f(x)-f(y)|<r$, so the metric-topology definition makes $f$ continuous; [F13] then makes it Borel. Also $0\le f^+,f^-\le M$. By [F9] and [F10], each nonnegative integral is at most $M\mu(X)=M$, so [F12] makes $f$ integrable and both dual integrals are finite. The zero function is feasible, so the dual objective set is nonempty and its supremum $D_X$ is a finite real number.

Fix $\varepsilon>0$ and use [F1] to obtain distinct net points $x_1,\ldots,x_m$, Borel nearest-center cells $C_1,\ldots,C_m$, and a Borel map $Q$ with $Q(x)=x_i$ on $C_i$ and $d(x,Q(x))<\varepsilon$. Set $p_i=\mu(C_i)$ and $q_i=\nu(C_i)$. Countable additivity and the finite Borel partition imply $p_i,q_i\ge0$ and $\sum_i p_i=\sum_iq_i=1$. Let $c_\varepsilon$ be the minimum finite transport cost between these vectors on $F=\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}$; [F4] ensures that this finite minimum exists and is attained.
By [F4], choose a minimizing finite coupling $\pi^\varepsilon$ and a maximizing normalized finite 1-Lipschitz potential; their common finite primal and dual value is $c_\varepsilon$.

For any $\gamma\in\Pi_X(\mu,\nu)$, set $\pi_{ij}:=\gamma(C_i\times C_j)$. Its row and column sums are $p_i,q_j$ by the marginal identities and finite additivity, so it is a finite coupling. On $C_i\times C_j$, [F8] gives $d(x_i,x_j)\le d(x_i,x)+d(x,y)+d(y,x_j)<d(x,y)+2\varepsilon$. The cells $C_i\times C_j$ form a finite Borel partition of $X\times X$. Integrating the pointwise bounds on these cells and using finite additivity of the nonnegative integral [F11] gives $\sum_{i,j}\pi_{ij}d(x_i,x_j)\le\int d(x,y)\,d\gamma+2\varepsilon$, since $\gamma(X\times X)=1$. Taking the infimum over $\gamma$ gives $c_\varepsilon\le W_1^X(\mu,\nu)+2\varepsilon$.

Let $D_F$ be the maximum finite dual value. By [F4], $D_F=c_\varepsilon$. For any feasible finite potential $(f_i)$, [F3] gives an extension $\widetilde f$; put $h:=\widetilde f-\widetilde f(x_0)$. This anchors $h$ without changing either probability-difference objective. The function $h\circ Q$ is finite-valued Borel simple, so its integrals are $\sum_i p_i h(x_i)$ and $\sum_i q_i h(x_i)$ by [F10]. Pointwise, $|h(x)-h(Q(x))|<\varepsilon$. For either probability measure $\rho\in\{\mu,\nu\}$, let $r=h-h\circ Q$. It is integrable because both terms are bounded Borel functions. Monotonicity [F9] gives $0\le\int(r+\varepsilon)\,d\rho$ and $0\le\int(\varepsilon-r)\,d\rho$; [F10] gives $\int\varepsilon\,d\rho=\varepsilon$, and linearity [F12] yields $|\int r\,d\rho|\le\varepsilon$. Hence each finite objective differs from the corresponding compact objective by at most $2\varepsilon$, so $D_F\le D_X+2\varepsilon$.

Conversely, let $g$ be any feasible compact potential and restrict it to $F$, subtracting $g(x_1)$ to normalize the first coordinate. The finite objective is unchanged by this shift because both probability vectors sum to one. The functions $g\circ Q$ are Borel simple and have the finite sums as their integrals, by [F10]. For each $\rho\in\{\mu,\nu\}$, the integrable difference $r=g-g\circ Q$ satisfies $-\varepsilon\le r\le\varepsilon$; applying the two monotonicity and linearity inequalities detailed in step 2.3 gives $|\int r\,d\rho|\le\varepsilon$. Thus each compact integral differs from its finite sum by at most $\varepsilon$. By the definition of $D_F$ in step 2.3, every restricted finite objective is at most $D_F$, and $D_X\le D_F+2\varepsilon$.

For any $\gamma\in\Pi_X(\mu,
u)$ and feasible compact $f$, the Lipschitz constraint gives $f(x)-f(y)\le d(x,y)$. By step 1.1 and [F13], the functions $f\circ\mathrm{pr}_1$ and $f\circ\mathrm{pr}_2$ are bounded Borel, and the metric cost is bounded and Borel; hence they are integrable. The first-coordinate pushforward of $\gamma$ agrees with $\mu$ on every Borel set by the marginal condition, and the second-coordinate pushforward agrees with $
u$. Equal measures integrate indicators, then simple functions, then all nonnegative Borel functions equally by [F10]; positive-negative decomposition and signed-integral linearity [F12] give equality for bounded signed Borel functions. Thus $\int(f(x)-f(y))\,d\gamma=\int f\,d\mu-\int f\,d
u$. Since $d(x,y)-(f(x)-f(y))\ge0$, [F9]–[F10] give a nonnegative integral for this difference, so [F12] implies the dual value is at most the cost of $\gamma$. Taking the infimum gives $D_X\le W_1^X(\mu,
u)$.

Apply [F2] to the minimizing plan $\pi^\varepsilon$ of step 2.1. It gives a Borel coupling $\gamma^\varepsilon\in\Pi_X(\mu,\nu)$ with cost at most $c_\varepsilon+2\varepsilon$. Hence the coupling set is nonempty and $W_1^X(\mu,\nu)\le c_\varepsilon+2\varepsilon$.

Steps 2.2 and 3.3 give $|W_1^X-c_\varepsilon|\le2\varepsilon$. Steps 2.3 and 3.1 give $|D_X-D_F|\le2\varepsilon$, and step 2.3 gives $D_F=c_\varepsilon$. Combining with step 3.2 yields $D_X\le W_1^X\le c_\varepsilon+2\varepsilon=D_F+2\varepsilon\le D_X+4\varepsilon$. Since this holds for every $\varepsilon>0$, $W_1^X(\mu,\nu)=D_X$.

Let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on a nonempty set $X$ (Sigma-algebras) and fix $x_0\in X$. The **Dirac set function at $x_0$** is

$$\delta_{x_0}(E):=\begin{cases}1,&x_0\in E,\\0,&x_0\notin E,\end{cases}\qquad E\in\mathcal A.$$

The two branches are exhaustive and disjoint. The fact that this set function is a probability measure is proved in A Dirac set function is a probability measure.
For $x_0\in X$, the Dirac set function $\delta_{x_0}$ is a probability measure on every sigma-algebra on $X$.

Let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on a set $X$, let $x_0\in X$, and let
$\delta_{x_0}$ be the Dirac probability measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. For every
nonnegative $\mathcal A$-measurable $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$,
$$\int_X f\,d\delta_{x_0}=f(x_0).$$

Let $X=\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}$ be a nonempty finite set and let $d:X\times X\to\mathbb R$ satisfy $d(x,y)=0$ if and only if $x=y$, $d(x,y)=d(y,x)$, and $d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z)$. Let $p=(p_i)_{i=1}^m$ and $q=(q_i)_{i=1}^m$ be probability vectors, so their coordinates are nonnegative and each vector sums to $1$. A coupling is an $m\times m$ matrix $\pi$ with $\pi_{ij}\ge0$, row sums $\sum_j\pi_{ij}=p_i$, and column sums $\sum_i\pi_{ij}=q_j$; write $\Gamma(p,q)$ for the set of all such matrices. Writing $d_{ij}=d(x_i,x_j)$, define the finite-metric 1-Wasserstein transport cost by
$$
W_1(p,q):=\min_{\pi\in\Gamma(p,q)}\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^m d_{ij}\pi_{ij}.
$$

Let $(X,d)$ be a compact metric space. Write $\mathcal B(X)$ for the sigma-algebra generated by the open sets of its metric topology. A Borel probability measure on $X$ is a countably additive measure on $\mathcal B(X)$ with total mass one. For Borel probability measures $\mu,\nu$ on $X$, let $\Pi_X(\mu,\nu)$ be the set of Borel probability measures $\gamma$ on $X\times X$, with its product topology and Borel sigma-algebra, such that for every $A\in\mathcal B(X)$,
$$\gamma(A\times X)=\mu(A),\qquad \gamma(X\times A)=\nu(A).$$
Define
$$W_1^X(\mu,\nu):=\inf_{\gamma\in\Pi_X(\mu,\nu)}\int_{X\times X}d(x,y)\,d\gamma(x,y)\in[0,+\infty],$$
where the infimum is taken in the extended real line and $\inf\varnothing=+\infty$. The integrand is nonnegative and Borel: the triangle inequality and symmetry give
$$|d(x,y)-d(x',y')|\le d(x,x')+d(y,y'),$$
so $(x,y)\mapsto d(x,y)$ is continuous for the product topology; nonnegativity follows from the metric axioms.

Let $(S,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space, let $P$ and $Q$ be probability measures on it, and let $\mathcal F$ be a nonempty class of real-valued $\Sigma$-measurable functions that are integrable under both $P$ and $Q$. The **integral probability metric** induced by $\mathcal F$ is
$$d_{\mathcal F}(P,Q):=\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\left|\int_S f\,dP-\int_S f\,dQ\right|\in[0,+\infty].$$
It is nonnegative and symmetric, and it may equal $+\infty$; no separation property is asserted for an arbitrary class $\mathcal F$.

Let $X$ be a set and let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on $X$ (Sigma-algebras). A **measure** on $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a function

$$\mu:\mathcal A\longrightarrow[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$$

such that:

1. $\mu(\varnothing)=0$;
2. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$,
   $$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k),$$
   where the right side is the nonnegative extended sum of Series in the nonnegative extended real line.

The second condition is **countable additivity**. It begins at index $0$ and includes the case in which some term or the total sum is $+\infty$.

derivations.claim: For $t>0$, the second row sum $0$ and nonnegative entries force $\pi_{21}=\pi_{22}=0$; the first column sum $0$ then forces $\pi_{11}=0$, and the first row sum $1$ forces $\pi_{12}=1$, which also gives the required second column sum $1$. This is the unique feasible matrix, and [F3] gives finite-space cost $d(0,t)=t$. For $t=0$, the singleton probability vector has unique coupling $(1)$ and cost $0$.

By [F1], $P$ and $Q_t$ are Borel probability measures. If $\gamma$ is any coupling of $P$ and $Q_t$, then $\gamma(\{0\}\times X)=1$ and $\gamma(X\times\{t\})=1$. The complement of their intersection is contained in the union of their two null complements, so finite subadditivity from [F6] gives $\gamma(\{(0,t)\})=1$. A probability measure concentrated on the singleton $(0,t)$ equals its Dirac measure there: sets containing $(0,t)$ have mass $1$, and sets omitting it have mass $0$. The Dirac measure at $(0,t)$ has the required marginals, so it is the unique coupling. By [F2] and [F4], its cost is $d(0,t)=t$, so $W_1(P,Q_t)=t$, including $t=0$.
Every function in the specified $1$-Lipschitz class satisfies $|f(0)-f(t)|\le t$, and $f(x)=x$ belongs to the class and has $|f(0)-f(t)|=t$. By [F5], the IPM is exactly $t$.

If $t>0$, the mixture $(P+Q_t)/2$ assigns mass $1/2$ to each of $0$ and $t$. The finite sum definition gives $\operatorname{KL}(P\|(P+Q_t)/2)=\log2$ and $\operatorname{KL}(Q_t\|(P+Q_t)/2)=\log2$, so $\operatorname{JS}(P,Q_t)=\log2$. If $t=0$, the two laws agree, each KL term is $0$, and the JS value is $0$.

Under the weight bounds, the slope of $f_{a,b}(x)=abx$ has absolute value at most $c^2$. If $c>1$, the allowed choice $a=b=c$ gives slope $c^2>1$. If $0<c<1$, every allowed slope has magnitude less than $1$, so the function $x$ cannot occur. If $c=1$, every member is linear, while $x^2/2$ is $1$-Lipschitz because $|x^2-y^2|/2=|x-y|(x+y)/2\le|x-y|$ on $[0,1]$; it is not linear, since its value at $1$ is $1/2$ and at $1/2$ is $1/8$. These three exhaustive cases prove the stated failure of exactness for every $c>0$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space, fix $x_0\in X$, and let $D<\infty$ satisfy $d(x,y)\le D$ for all $x,y\in X$. Let $\mu$ be a Borel probability measure on $X$, let $(Z,\Sigma,\rho)$ be a probability space, and let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ be open with $p\ge1$. For every $\theta\in\Theta$, let $G_\theta:Z\to X$ be measurable and define its law by $P_\theta(B)=\rho(G_\theta^{-1}(B))$ for Borel $B\subseteq X$. Assume $z\mapsto d(G_\theta(z),G_{\theta'}(z))$ is $\rho$-measurable for every $\theta,\theta'\in\Theta$, and that there is a measurable set $Z_0\subseteq Z$ with $\rho(Z_0)=1$ on which $\theta\mapsto G_\theta(z)$ is continuous. Let $\mathcal F_1(X,x_0)$ be the class of bounded Borel functions $f:X\to\mathbb R$ satisfying $f(x_0)=0$ and $|f(x)-f(y)|\le d(x,y)$ for all $x,y\in X$, and set $V(\theta)=d_{\mathcal F_1(X,x_0)}(\mu,P_\theta)$. Then $V(\theta)=W_1^X(\mu,P_\theta)$ and $V$ is continuous on $\Theta$.

Suppose in addition that for every $\theta_0\in\Theta$ there are an open neighborhood $U\subseteq\Theta$ of $\theta_0$, a measurable $K_{\theta_0}:Z\to[0,+\infty)$ with $\int K_{\theta_0}\,d\rho<\infty$, and a measurable full-measure set $Z_{\theta_0}\subseteq Z$ such that, for every $z\in Z_{\theta_0}$ and every $\theta,\theta'\in U$,
$$
d(G_\theta(z),G_{\theta'}(z))\le K_{\theta_0}(z)\|\theta-\theta'\|.
$$
Then $V$ is locally Lipschitz, with $|V(\theta)-V(\theta')|\le\|\theta-\theta'\|\int K_{\theta_0}\,d\rho$ for $\theta,\theta'\in U$. At any such $\theta_0$ where $V$ is Fréchet differentiable, if the signed dual supremum at $\theta_0$ is attained by $f_{\theta_0}\in\mathcal F_1(X,x_0)$ and $H_{\theta_0}(\theta,z)=f_{\theta_0}(G_\theta(z))$ is Fréchet differentiable in $\theta$ at $\theta_0$ for $\rho$-almost every $z$ with measurable derivative, then
$$
\nabla V(\theta_0)=-\int_Z\nabla_\theta H_{\theta_0}(\theta_0,z)\,d\rho(z).
$$
Here Fréchet differentiability of a scalar function $F$ at $\theta_0$ means there is a linear map $A$ such that $F(\theta_0+h)=F(\theta_0)+A[h]+o(\|h\|)$ as $h\to0$. The attainment and composite-differentiability assumptions are pointwise hypotheses for the gradient formula; compact dual attainment is not asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For every open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and locally Lipschitz map $u:U\to\mathbb R^m$ (each point has a neighborhood on which $|u(y)-u(z)|\le L|y-z|$ for some finite $L$, [[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]]), $u$ is Frechet differentiable outside a null subset of $U$. Here Frechet differentiability at $x$ means that a linear map $A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ satisfies $u(x+h)=u(x)+Ah+o(|h|)$.

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power (Integer powers $a^m$),
so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$
2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges.

The series starts at $k = 0$ and its first term is $r^0 = 1$; in particular
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 2$, while the series starting at $k = 1$ sums to
$1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here.

Let $(X,d)$ be a compact metric space. Write $\mathcal B(X)$ for the sigma-algebra generated by the open sets of its metric topology. A Borel probability measure on $X$ is a countably additive measure on $\mathcal B(X)$ with total mass one. For Borel probability measures $\mu,\nu$ on $X$, let $\Pi_X(\mu,\nu)$ be the set of Borel probability measures $\gamma$ on $X\times X$, with its product topology and Borel sigma-algebra, such that for every $A\in\mathcal B(X)$,
$$\gamma(A\times X)=\mu(A),\qquad \gamma(X\times A)=\nu(A).$$
Define
$$W_1^X(\mu,\nu):=\inf_{\gamma\in\Pi_X(\mu,\nu)}\int_{X\times X}d(x,y)\,d\gamma(x,y)\in[0,+\infty],$$
where the infimum is taken in the extended real line and $\inf\varnothing=+\infty$. The integrand is nonnegative and Borel: the triangle inequality and symmetry give
$$|d(x,y)-d(x',y')|\le d(x,x')+d(y,y'),$$
so $(x,y)\mapsto d(x,y)$ is continuous for the product topology; nonnegativity follows from the metric axioms.

Let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on a nonempty set $X$ (Sigma-algebras) and fix $x_0\in X$. The **Dirac set function at $x_0$** is

$$\delta_{x_0}(E):=\begin{cases}1,&x_0\in E,\\0,&x_0\notin E,\end{cases}\qquad E\in\mathcal A.$$

The two branches are exhaustive and disjoint. The fact that this set function is a probability measure is proved in A Dirac set function is a probability measure.
For $x_0\in X$, the Dirac set function $\delta_{x_0}$ is a probability measure on every sigma-algebra on $X$.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ (Measures on sigma-algebras). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** (Measure spaces); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.
A **random element** of $S$ is a measurable map $$X:(\Omega,\mathcal F)\to(S,\Sigma)$$ in the sense of A measurable function between measurable spaces.
Its **law** or **distribution** is the set function $$\mathbb P_X:\Sigma\to[0,+\infty],\qquad \mathbb P_X(B):=\mathbb P(X^{-1}(B)).$$
Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element. Then $\mathbb P_X$ is a probability measure on $(S,\Sigma)$.
If $g(X)$ is integrable, then $g$ is integrable with respect to $\mathbb P_X$ and the same formula holds: $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space. A measurable function
$s:X\to[0,+\infty)\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$
(Extended-real-valued measurable functions) is a
**nonnegative simple measurable function** when it has finite range.

Equivalently, there are pairwise disjoint measurable sets
$E_1,\dots,E_m\in\mathcal A$ and coefficients $c_1,\dots,c_m\in[0,+\infty)$
such that
$$s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\chi_{E_j}.$$
Any such display is a **simple representation** of $s$.

Let $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\chi_{E_j}$ be a simple representation of a
nonnegative simple measurable function
(Nonnegative simple measurable functions) on a measure space
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$, so the $E_j\in\mathcal A$ are pairwise disjoint and
$c_j\ge0$. Its
**simple integral** is
$$\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mu(E_j),$$
where $\mu$ is the given measure (Measures on sigma-algebras) and the convention
$0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ is fixed once and for all.

The next lemma proves that this value is independent of the chosen simple
representation.

If $s$ is a nonnegative simple measurable function, then its nonnegative
Lebesgue integral equals its simple integral:
$$\int s\,d\mu=\int_{\mathrm{simple}} s\,d\mu.$$

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then there is an increasing sequence of
nonnegative simple measurable functions $(s_n)$ such that $s_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x\in X$.

Let $a=(a_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ take values in $[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$ (The extended real line $\overline{\mathbb{R}} = \mathbb{R} \cup \{-\infty, +\infty\}$, its order, and the arithmetic that is left undefined). Its **partial sums** are the unique sequence $(s_n)$ in $[0,+\infty]$ satisfying

$$s_0=0,\qquad s_{n+1}=s_n+a_n.$$

To apply The recursion theorem with a fixed successor function, use the state space $\mathbb N\times[0,+\infty]$ and the self-map $T(n,s)=(n+1,s+a_n)$, starting from $(0,0)$. Recursion gives a unique state sequence; induction makes its first coordinate $n$, and its second coordinates are exactly the unique $(s_n)$ satisfying the displayed recurrence. Addition of two nonnegative extended reals is always defined, including when either is $+\infty$. The sequence $(s_n)$ is nondecreasing, and its **nonnegative extended sum** is

$$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}a_k:=\sup_{n\in\mathbb N}s_n\in[0,+\infty],$$

whose existence follows from completeness of the extended real line (Every subset of $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ has a least upper bound and a greatest lower bound in $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$, agreeing with the real supremum and infimum on nonempty sets bounded in $\mathbb{R}$). More generally, for $m\in\mathbb N$,

$$\sum_{k\ge m}a_k:=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}a_{m+j}.$$

Finite sums use the same recursion: $\sum_{k<n}a_k=s_n$, so the empty sum at $n=0$ is $0$. A double sum such as $\sum_i\sum_j a_{ij}$ means that the inner nonnegative extended sum is formed first and the resulting nonnegative extended sequence is then summed.

$$\dot z(t)=v_\theta(t,z(t)),\qquad z(s)=z_s,$$

where $s\in I$ and $z_s\in\mathbb R^d$. A trajectory on an interval $J\subseteq I$ containing $s$ is a differentiable function $z:J\to\mathbb R^d$ satisfying both displayed conditions. Here $v_\theta$ is the state-velocity field.

Here a network is a fixed finite directed acyclic graph evaluated in an order in which every edge points to a later vertex: input vertices hold the coordinates of $(t,z)$, each other vertex applies a fixed scalar activation to an affine combination of earlier vertex values, and the output vertices use the identity activation. The weights and biases are specified functions of $\theta$ and may be shared or fixed. No particular depth, width, or hidden activation is prescribed; affine networks with no hidden vertices are allowed.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function

Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $d,T\ge1$ be finite integers, let $I_d$ be the $d\times d$ identity matrix, and let $\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_T\in(0,1)$. Set $\alpha_t=1-\beta_t$, $\bar\alpha_0=1$, and $\bar\alpha_t=\prod_{s=1}^t\alpha_s$. Write $\lambda_d$ for Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^d$ and define, for $v>0$,
$$\phi_{d,v}(y;m)=(2\pi v)^{-d/2}\exp\!\left(-\frac{\|y-m\|_2^2}{2v}\right),\qquad y,m\in\mathbb R^d.$$
The notation $\|z\|_2^2=\sum_{i=1}^d z_i^2$ is the squared Euclidean norm. The displayed function is the Lebesgue density of $N_d(m,vI_d)$.

For each fixed $x_0\in\mathbb R^d$, the forward chain has path density on $(\mathbb R^d)^T$
$$q(x_{1:T}\mid x_0)=\prod_{t=1}^T \phi_{d,\beta_t}(x_t;\sqrt{\alpha_t}\,x_{t-1}).$$
Thus its transition from $x_{t-1}$ to $x_t$ is Gaussian with mean $\sqrt{\alpha_t}\,x_{t-1}$ and covariance $\beta_t I_d$. Each factor is a normalized density, and finite successive integration of the nonnegative product gives a probability density.

For a generic adjacent pair, the two model directions are shown below. The arrows indicate the direction in which each conditional density generates its target state; they assert no equality or inverse relation between the kernels.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=stealth]
  \node (previous) at (0,0) {$x_{t-1}$};
  \node (current) at (4,0) {$x_t$};
  \draw[->] (previous) to[bend left=24] node[midway,above] {$q(x_t\mid x_{t-1})$} (current);
  \draw[->] (current) to[bend left=24] node[midway,below] {$p_{\theta,t}(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)$} (previous);
\end{tikzpicture}
```

A learned reverse Gaussian model consists of finite-valued Borel maps $\mu_{\theta,t}:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ and fixed variances $\sigma_t^2\in(0,\infty)$, for $1\le t\le T$. It is the joint density
$$p_\theta(x_{0:T})=\phi_{d,1}(x_T;0)\prod_{t=1}^T\phi_{d,\sigma_t^2}(x_{t-1};\mu_{\theta,t}(x_t)).$$
Its prior is $p(x_T)=N_d(0,I_d)$, and its marginal density at $x_0$ is
$$p_\theta(x_0)=\int_{(\mathbb R^d)^T}p_\theta(x_{0:T})\,d\lambda_d(x_1)\cdots d\lambda_d(x_T),$$

$Z_j$ for $1\le j\le m$ be mutually independent random elements of
$\mathbb R^{d_j}$. Suppose $Z_j\sim N_{d_j}(a_j,\Sigma_j)$, where each
$\Sigma_j$ is symmetric positive semidefinite. Put
$D=\sum_{j=1}^m d_j$, $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)$,
$a=(a_1,\ldots,a_m)$, and
$\Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(\Sigma_1,\ldots,\Sigma_m)$. Then
$$Z\sim N_D(a,\Sigma).$$

jointly multivariate normal with mean $(a,b)$ and positive-semidefinite block

$$\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}A&C\\C^T&B\end{pmatrix},$$
where $B$ is positive definite. Then
$$S=A-CB^{-1}C^T$$
is positive semidefinite, and for every $y\in\mathbb R^m$ the probability law
$$K(y,\cdot)=N_d\!\left(a+CB^{-1}(y-b),S\right)$$
is defined. The map $K$ is a probability kernel and is a conditional law of
$X$ given $Y$: for all Borel $E\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ and
$F\subseteq\mathbb R^m$,
$$\mathbb P(X\in E,Y\in F)=\int_F K(y,E)\,\mathbb P_Y(dy).$$

singular $B$ is asserted.

Each $\xi_s$ is standard Gaussian and independent of the previous path; since earlier innovations are measurable functions of that path, $\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_t$ are mutually independent for every $t$.

Iterating $X_t=\sqrt{\alpha_t}X_{t-1}+\sqrt{\beta_t}\xi_t$ gives $X_t=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0+\sum_{s=1}^t\sqrt{\beta_s\prod_{r=s+1}^t\alpha_r}\,\xi_s$. Thus each scalar projection of $X_t$ is normal with mean $u\cdot\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0$ and, by independence, variance $u^T\left(\sum_{s=1}^t\beta_s\prod_{r=s+1}^t\alpha_r I_d\right)u$; [F2] identifies its law as multivariate normal with that mean and covariance. Since $\beta_s\prod_{r=s+1}^t\alpha_r=\prod_{r=s+1}^t\alpha_r-\prod_{r=s}^t\alpha_r$, the covariance sum telescopes to $(1-\bar\alpha_t)I_d$.

Its means are $\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}x_0$ and $\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0$, and its covariance blocks are $A=(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})I_d$, $C=\sqrt{\alpha_t}(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})I_d$, and $B=(1-\bar\alpha_t)I_d$. $$\phi_{d,v}(y;m)=(2\pi v)^{-d/2}\exp\!\left(-\frac{\|y-m\|_2^2}{2v}\right),\qquad y,m\in\mathbb R^d.$$
The notation $\|z\|_2^2=\sum_{i=1}^d z_i^2$ is the squared Euclidean norm. The displayed function is the Lebesgue density of $N_d(m,vI_d)$.

$$\int\pi\,d\mu=Z^{-1}\int\gamma\,d\mu=1.$$

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

derivations.claim: The reverse path density is strictly positive and finite at every finite path because every Gaussian variance is positive and each mean is finite. Its path marginal on $x_{1:T}$ is a probability density by successive integration of its reverse kernels and prior. For fixed $x_0$, the decoder density satisfies $p_\theta(x_0\mid x_1)\le(2\pi\sigma_1^2)^{-d/2}$, so integrating against that path marginal gives $p_\theta(x_0)<\infty$. It is strictly positive: on the positive-measure box $[-1,1]^{dT}$, the sets $\{p_\theta(x_{0:T})\ge1/n\}$ for positive integers $n$ cover the box because the density is positive everywhere. If all these sets had measure zero, their countable union would have measure zero, contradicting the positive measure of the box; one set therefore has positive measure, and the integral is positive. Thus $\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid x_0)$ is a proper positive density.

The forward path density is a probability density and is positive everywhere. Its log is the finite sum $\log q(x_{1:T}\mid x_0)=\sum_{t=1}^T\left[-\frac d2\log(2\pi\beta_t)-\frac{\|x_t-\sqrt{\alpha_t}x_{t-1}\|_2^2}{2\beta_t}\right]$. Under $q$, each normalized residual $(x_t-\sqrt{\alpha_t}x_{t-1})/\sqrt{\beta_t}$ has law $N_d(0,I_d)$ and finite second moment $d$ by [F10], so $\mathbb E_q|\log q|<\infty$. Since the reverse density is also positive everywhere, $\pi_\theta>0$ everywhere and the support condition $Q_{x_0}\ll\Pi_{\theta,x_0}$ holds.

Let $\gamma(x_{1:T})=p_\theta(x_{0:T})$ on path space with base measure $\lambda_{dT}$. Step 1.1 gives $Z=\int\gamma\,d\lambda_{dT}=p_\theta(x_0)\in(0,\infty)$ and the normalized target $\pi=\gamma/Z$; step 1.2 gives the support condition, and the Statement's integrability hypothesis together with step 1.2 gives $\mathbb E_q(|\log\gamma|+|\log q|)<\infty$. The direction is $Q_{x_0}\ll\Pi_{\theta,x_0}$, as required by [F8]. Therefore [F3], [F6], and [F9] apply, and [F4] gives the exact log-evidence identity and nonnegative reverse KL.

For $t\ge2$, the Markov property and positive Gaussian densities give $q(x_t\mid x_{t-1})=q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)q(x_t\mid x_0)/q(x_{t-1}\mid x_0)$. Substitute this into $p_\theta(x_{0:T})/q(x_{1:T}\mid x_0)$. The ratios $q(x_{t-1}\mid x_0)/q(x_t\mid x_0)$ telescope, leaving $p_\theta(x_{0:T})/q(x_{1:T}\mid x_0)=[p(x_T)/q(x_T\mid x_0)]p_\theta(x_0\mid x_1)\prod_{t=2}^T p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)/q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)$. Taking the $q$-expectation of the logarithm yields the stated endpoint-plus-step decomposition, with the t=1 term $-\mathbb E_{q(x_1\mid x_0)}\log p_\theta(x_0\mid x_1)$. Each reverse Gaussian log-density factor is bounded above; the assumed integrability of their finite sum makes each factor integrable, and the forward marginals and conditioned laws are Gaussian with finite quadratic moments, so the expectation splits termwise.

For $t\ge2$, substitute $x_t=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\epsilon$ into the posterior mean in [F2]. Using $\bar\alpha_t=\alpha_t\bar\alpha_{t-1}$ and $\beta_t=1-\alpha_t$ gives $\tilde\mu_t(x_t,x_0)=\frac1{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}\left(x_t-\frac{\beta_t}{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}}\epsilon\right)$. The reverse mean is the same expression with $\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)$ in place of $\epsilon$, so $\|\tilde\mu_t-\mu_{\theta,t}\|_2^2=\frac{\beta_t^2}{\alpha_t(1-\bar\alpha_t)}\|\epsilon-\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)\|_2^2$. Both posterior and reverse variances are positive for $t\ge2$, so [F5] applies with $v=\tilde\beta_t$ and $w=\sigma_t^2$; it gives exactly the coefficient $w_t$ and constant $C_t$ in the Statement.

The terminal term remains $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q(x_T\mid x_0)\|N_d(0,I_d))$ in step 2.2 because finite $T$ and $0<\beta_t<1$ give $\bar\alpha_T>0$; the $t=1$ term remains the separate positive-variance decoder log-likelihood. For an explicit counterexample, take $d=1$, $T=2$, $\beta_1=\tfrac14$, $\beta_2=\tfrac12$, $\sigma_1^2=(2\pi)^{-1}$, and $\sigma_2^2=\tilde\beta_2=\tfrac15$. Then $\bar\alpha_1=\tfrac34$, $\bar\alpha_2=\tfrac38$, $w_2=\frac{(1/2)^2}{2(1/5)(1/2)(5/8)}=2$, and $C_2=\frac12(1-1+\log1)=0$. For a fixed datum $x_0$, set $\epsilon_\theta(x_1,1)=(x_1-\sqrt{3/4}\,x_0)/\sqrt{1/4}$ and $\epsilon_\theta(x_2,2)=(x_2-\sqrt{3/8}\,x_0)/\sqrt{5/8}+c$, with any $c\in\mathbb R$. These are finite Borel maps, and their Gaussian log densities have finite $q$-expectations because they are quadratic functions of finite-dimensional Gaussian variables. The first map makes $\mu_{\theta,1}(x_1)=x_0$, so the decoder density at its mean is $(2\pi\sigma_1^2)^{-1/2}=1$; integrating it against the normalized reverse path density gives $p_\theta(x_0)=1$ for every $c$. Under the forward chain, the $t=1$ noise error is zero and the $t=2$ error is $c$, so $L_{\mathrm{simple}}=c^2/2$, while the exact weighted $t=2$ ELBO contribution is $2c^2$ and its prior term is independent of $c$. Taking $c\ne0$ gives $L_{\mathrm{simple}}>0$ but exact negative log-likelihood $-\log p_\theta(x_0)=0$. Thus the unweighted loss is a surrogate, not in general the maximum-likelihood objective.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

In simple mode, the stated finite squared-error expectations make $Y$ integrable, and independence and uniform sampling give $\mathbb E[Y]=(NT)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{t=1}^T\mathbb E_\epsilon\|\epsilon-\epsilon_\theta(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0^{(i)}+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\epsilon,t)\|_2^2=N^{-1}\sum_i L_{\mathrm{simple}}(\theta;x_0^{(i)})$.

In weighted-elbo mode, [F3] and [F4] with $v=1-\bar\alpha_T$, $w=1$, $m=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_T}x_0^{(i)}$ and $n=0$ identify the algorithm's $K_T(x_0^{(i)})$ as the exact terminal KL. The mode's hypotheses are those of [F2], so the decoder log-density and the interior weighted squared errors are integrable. Finite sums over $i,t$ therefore make $Y$ integrable, even though a decoder contribution may be negative. For fixed $i$, averaging the branch values over $J$ and the noise cancels each factor $T$ and counts $K_T$ once, giving $\mathbb E[Y\mid I=i]=K_T(x_0^{(i)})+\mathbb E_{q(x_1\mid x_0^{(i)})}[-\log p_\theta(x_0^{(i)}\mid x_1)]+\sum_{t=2}^T\mathbb E_\epsilon[C_t+w_t\|\epsilon-\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)\|_2^2]=-\operatorname{ELBO}_\theta(x_0^{(i)})$.

Averaging step 1.2 over the uniform index $I$ proves the weighted identity. When $N=1$ the data average has one term, and when $T=1$ only the decoder branch is selected and the interior sum is empty; the terminal term is still counted once. Thus both identities hold throughout the admitted domain.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in Measures on sigma-algebras and A measurable function between measurable spaces; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim: For fixed $u<v$ and Borel $A$, the integrand $1_A(x)p_{T-v}(x)q(T-v,x;T-u,y)$ is nonnegative and jointly Borel in $(y,x)$. Tonelli's parameter-integral clause [F2] makes its integral Borel in $y$; division by the positive Borel function $p_{T-u}(y)$ preserves measurability. For each fixed $y$ the numerator defines a measure in $A$ by countable additivity of the Lebesgue integral.

Taking $A=\mathbb R^d$ in the formula gives $K_{u,v}(y,\mathbb R^d)=p_{T-u}(y)/p_{T-u}(y)=1$ by the marginal identity, so each $K_{u,v}(y,\cdot)$ is a probability measure. The identity kernel at $u=v$ is also a probability kernel.

If $u<v<w$, Tonelli and the two density ratios give $\displaystyle \int K_{v,w}(x,A)K_{u,v}(y,dx)=\frac{\int_A p_{T-w}(z)\int q(T-w,z;T-v,x)q(T-v,x;T-u,y)\,dx\,dz}{p_{T-u}(y)}.$ The inner integral is $q(T-w,z;T-u,y)$ by forward Chapman–Kolmogorov, so the expression is $K_{u,w}(y,A)$. If two adjacent times coincide, composition with the identity kernel gives the same equality.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Fix a probability space
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ with a continuous-time filtration
$(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$ in the sense of
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. All processes in
this definition are real-valued and indexed by $[0,\infty)$; the filtration is
neither assumed complete nor right-continuous. The Axiom of Choice is declared
because the conditional-expectation classes used in clause 3 are supplied by
the Radon--Nikodym interface of [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]],
which assumes it; the countable-choice obligations inherited from that
interface are declared as dependencies of this item.

1. **Adapted.** $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is **adapted** to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when $X_t$
   is $\mathcal F_t$-measurable for every $t\ge0$. This is exactly the notion
   of [[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]].

2. **Stopped process.** For a stopping time $\tau$ for $(\mathcal F_t)$
   [[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]] the **stopped process** is
   $$X^{\tau}_t(\omega):=X_{t\wedge\tau(\omega)}(\omega),\qquad t\ge0,$$
   with the convention $t\wedge\infty:=t$, so no value $X_\infty$ is ever
   required and $X^\tau_0=X_0$ identically. This formula defines a pathwise
   family; adaptedness of $X$ alone does not assert measurability or
   adaptedness of its stopped values. If in addition $\tau\le c$ for a
   deterministic constant $c$, then $X^\tau_t=X_{t\wedge\tau}$, and only the
   values of $X$ on $[0,c]$ enter. Stopping at a stopping time is not the same
   as replacing a process by a modification; it is a pathwise operation.

3. **Martingale.** $M=(M_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **martingale** (an all-pairs
   continuous-time martingale) relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when it is adapted,
   $E|M_t|<\infty$ for every $t\ge0$, and for all $0\le s\le t$
   $$E[M_t\mid\mathcal F_s]=M_s\qquad\text{almost surely}.$$
   The equality is an equality of the almost-everywhere classes of
   [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]]; equivalently, every version
   of the conditional expectation on the left equals $M_s$ off one null set.
   At $s=t$ the identity reduces to the known-variable case. The word
   "continuous-time" refers to the index set only and does not assert path
   continuity.

4. **Local martingale.** $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **local martingale** relative
   to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when it is adapted, $E|X_0|<\infty$, and there exist stopping times
   $(\tau_n)_{n\ge0}$ with $\tau_0\le\tau_1\le\cdots$ and
   $\tau_n\uparrow\infty$ almost surely such that for every $n\ge0$ the stopped process
   $$X^{\tau_n}-X_0=(X_{t\wedge\tau_n}-X_0)_{t\ge0}$$
   is a martingale in the sense of clause 3. The sequence $(\tau_n)$ is called
   a **localizing sequence**. Equivalently, every $X^{\tau_n}$ is a
   martingale: adaptedness makes the integrable variable $X_0$ measurable with
   respect to every $\mathcal F_t$, so the constant process with value $X_0$
   is a martingale and may be added to, or subtracted from, each stopped
   process. The centering merely makes every localized process start at $0$;
   apart from the required integrability of $X_0$, no claim is made that $X$
   is integrable at a positive deterministic time, and no claim is made that
   $X$ has continuous paths.

5. **Path and integrability attributes.** A process has **continuous paths**
   when $t\mapsto X_t(\omega)$ is continuous on $[0,\infty)$ for every $\omega$
   in an event of probability one; the usual almost-sure path conventions of
   [[def-law-modification-and-indistinguishability-of-processes]] apply. A
   martingale $M$ is **square-integrable** when $EM_t^2<\infty$ for every
   $t\ge0$, and **$L^2$-bounded** when $\sup_{t\ge0}EM_t^2<\infty$. These are
   properties of the single process under consideration, not of its versions:
   a modification of a martingale need not be adapted, so every later statement
   names the adapted versions it uses.

The following remarks specify what follows directly from this vocabulary.

1. **A martingale is a local martingale.** If $M$ is a martingale, the constant
   sequence $\tau_n:=n$, $n\ge0$, localizes it: the stopped process $M^{n}-M_0$ is again
   a martingale by the martingale identity applied at the deterministic times
   $s\wedge n\le t\wedge n$. The converse fails; a local martingale need not be
   a martingale, and no such implication is used in this development.
2. **Localization after a separately justified stopping operation.** Suppose
   $(\tau_n)$ localizes $X$, $\sigma$ is a stopping time, $X^\sigma$ is
   adapted, and each $(X^{\tau_n}-X_0)^\sigma$ is a martingale. Then
   $(\tau_n)$ localizes $X^\sigma$. Indeed it still increases to infinity,
   $(X^\sigma)_0=X_0$, and the pathwise identity
   $$(X^\sigma)^{\tau_n}-(X^\sigma)_0=X^{\sigma\wedge\tau_n}-X_0=(X^{\tau_n}-X_0)^\sigma$$
   verifies exactly clause 4. The stopped-piece martingale assertion and
   adaptedness are hypotheses here, not consequences of the unrestricted
   all-pairs definition. They must be established in each application.
   The sequence $(\sigma\wedge\tau_n)$ is not a substitute for $(\tau_n)$:
   its almost-sure limit is $\sigma$, which need not be infinity.

No path continuity, no right continuity of the filtration, and no completeness
of the underlying probability space is imposed by this definition. Choice
enters only through the conditional-expectation interface named above,
whose countable-choice obligations are declared as dependencies of this item.

Assume AC. Let $N\in\mathbb N_0$, $p>1$, and $q=p/(p-1)$. If $X=(X_n)_{n\ge0}$ is a nonnegative submartingale and $X_N\in L^p$, then
$$\left\|\max_{0\le k\le N}X_k\right\|_p\le q\|X_N\|_p.$$
In particular, for a martingale $M$ with $M_N\in L^p$,
$$\left\|\max_{0\le k\le N}|M_k|\right\|_p\le q\|M_N\|_p.$$

Assume AC. Let $(\mathcal F_n)_{n\ge0}$ be a filtration, and let $(D_k)_{k\ge1}$ be real square-integrable martingale differences relative to it. For $1\le i<j$, $E[D_iD_j]=0$, so their real $L^2$ inner product is zero. For every $n\ge0$, $E[(\sum_{k=1}^nD_k)^2]=\sum_{k=1}^nE[D_k^2]$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Fix processes $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ and $Y=(Y_t)_{t\ge0}$ of real random
variables on one probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$: for every
$\omega$ in a measurable event of probability one the paths $t\mapsto X_t$
and $t\mapsto Y_t$ are continuous on $[0,\infty)$
[[def-continuity-real]]. Fix $T>0$ and a deterministic partition sequence
$(\pi_n)$ of $[0,T]$ with mesh tending to $0$
[[def-quadratic-variation-along-a-partition-sequence]]. For each $n$ write
$\pi_n=(m_n,s^{(n)})$ and form the two families of **cross-increment partial
sums**
$$S^{\mathrm{step}}_n(t):=\sum_{\substack{1\le k\le m_n\\s^{(n)}_k\le t}}\bigl(X_{s^{(n)}_k}-X_{s^{(n)}_{k-1}}\bigr)\bigl(Y_{s^{(n)}_k}-Y_{s^{(n)}_{k-1}}\bigr),$$
$$S^{\mathrm{part}}_n(t):=S^{\mathrm{step}}_n(t)+\bigl(X_t-X_{s^{(n)}_{k(t)}}\bigr)\bigl(Y_t-Y_{s^{(n)}_{k(t)}}\bigr)\quad(k(t)<m_n),$$
with $S^{\mathrm{part}}_n(T):=S^{\mathrm{step}}_n(T)$ and $k(t)$ the largest
index in $\{0,\ldots,m_n\}$ with $s^{(n)}_{k(t)}\le t$; these are the cross sums corresponding to the
two conventions of
[[def-quadratic-variation-along-a-partition-sequence]] specialized to the pair
$(X,Y)$, and both are $0$ at $t=0$.

All suprema in probability statements below use measurable versions. For
any finite collection of the processes involved, including a candidate limit,
intersect their measurable probability-one continuity events and set all of
them to zero off that intersection. These representatives have everywhere
continuous paths and retain measurable fixed-time values. The partial-sum
paths are continuous; the step-sum paths are right-continuous on $[0,T)$
with the specified value at $T$. Their uniform distances from a continuous
candidate therefore equal suprema over $(\mathbb Q\cap[0,T])\cup\{T\}$,
which are finite measurable random variables. Another such normalization
agrees on a measurable probability-one event and gives the same probability
limits. Here indistinguishability means agreement at every time on a
measurable probability-one event. No completeness or adaptedness is needed
for this convention.

1. **Existence and value of the covariation.** We say that the **quadratic
   covariation $[X,Y]$ exists on $[0,T]$** when there is a real process
   $t\mapsto[X,Y]_t$ of real random variables with almost-sure continuous
   paths on $[0,T]$ such that for *every* deterministic partition
   sequence $(\pi_n)$ of $[0,T]$ with mesh tending to $0$ both families
   converge to it uniformly in probability on $[0,T]$:
   $$\sup_{0\le t\le T}\bigl|S^{\mathrm{step}}_n(t)-[X,Y]_t\bigr|\longrightarrow0, \qquad \sup_{0\le t\le T}\bigl|S^{\mathrm{part}}_n(t)-[X,Y]_t\bigr|\longrightarrow0,$$
   the convergence being convergence in probability
   [[def-convergence-in-probability]]. The two displayed requirements are part
   of one condition: the same process $[X,Y]$ must arise for every admissible
   sequence and for both conventions. When the condition holds we call
   $[X,Y]_t$ the **quadratic covariation of $X$ and $Y$ at time $t$**, and we
   write $[X]:=[X,X]$ and call it the **quadratic variation of $X$**. For two candidate limits $U,V$, fix a deterministic dyadic partition
   sequence. The triangle inequality bounds $\sup_t|U_t-V_t|$ by the sum
   of their uniform errors against its partial sums. For each
   $\varepsilon>0$ the probability that this supremum exceeds
   $\varepsilon$ is at most the sum of the two error probabilities at
   $\varepsilon/2$, and hence is zero. Taking $\varepsilon=1/j$,
   $j\ge1$, proves uniqueness on one measurable probability-one event; the definition is applied
   separately on each finite horizon, and when the covariations on all
   horizons are compatible we write the resulting process on $[0,\infty)$
   again as $[X,Y]$.

2. **Symmetry and polarization.** Exchanging the two factors does not change
   the definition, so $[X,Y]=[Y,X]$ whenever either side exists. The
   identities
   $$[X+Y]=[X]+2[X,Y]+[Y],\qquad [X-Y]=[X]-2[X,Y]+[Y]$$
   hold on the domain where all covariations appearing in them exist: the
   cross-increment sums are bilinear in the pair, so the displayed identities
   are exact at the level of partial sums for every partition, and probability
   limits pass through finite algebraic identities. In particular
   $[X,Y]=\tfrac12\bigl([X+Y]-[X]-[Y]\bigr)$ and
   $4[X,Y]=[X+Y]-[X-Y]$ on that domain.

3. **Bilinearity and insensitivity to constants.** If the covariations
   $[X_1,Y]$, $[X_2,Y]$ and $[X_1+X_2,Y]$ exist on $[0,T]$, then
   $[X_1+X_2,Y]=[X_1,Y]+[X_2,Y]$ there, and $[cX,Y]=c[X,Y]$ for real $c$;
   moreover $[X+c,Y]=[X,Y]$ for every real constant $c$, because the
   increments of a constant process are zero. These are again exact
   identities of partial sums plus uniqueness of limits.

4. **Zero covariation with a continuous finite-variation process.** Let
   $A=(A_t)$ be continuous on a full-measure event and suppose, for every
   $\omega$ in that event, that $t\mapsto A_t(\omega)$ has bounded variation
   on every finite interval in the sense of
   [[def-bounded-variation-and-total-variation]]. Then for
   each $T$ and each admissible partition sequence, the cross sums of $A$
   against any continuous process $Y$ satisfy
   $$\Bigl|\sum_k\bigl(A_{s_k}-A_{s_{k-1}}\bigr)\bigl(Y_{s_k}-Y_{s_{k-1}}\bigr)\Bigr| \le\Bigl(\max_k\sup_{u,v\in[s_{k-1},s_k]}|Y_u-Y_v|\Bigr)\operatorname{Var}_{[0,T]}(A),$$
   because every sum of absolute $A$-increments is bounded by the path's total
   variation on $[0,T]$; the
   maximum tends to $0$ along vanishing meshes by uniform continuity of the
   continuous path $Y$ on the compact interval $[0,T]$. Hence $[A,Y]$ exists
   and equals the zero process for every such $A$ and every continuous $Y$,
   and in particular $[A,A']=0$ for two such processes. In the notation of the
   page this says that **continuous finite-variation parts contribute nothing
   to quadratic covariation**.

5. **Scope and choice.** The inputs and candidate limits have measurable
   fixed-time values and almost-sure continuous paths. The normalization above
   makes the uniform errors real random variables, as required by
   [[def-convergence-in-probability]]. No filtration or adaptedness is used.
   The algebra in clauses 2--3 passes to limits by the uniform triangle
   inequality and the union bound. In clause 4 the same estimate holds for
   every partial sum, including its terminal partial increment, because its
   intervals are disjoint; it thus proves uniform convergence to zero on the
   common continuity event. For each epsilon, the measurable events that some
   error after index n exceeds epsilon decrease to a null event; continuity
   from above of probability gives convergence in probability. Uniform
   continuity is justified by the choice-free finite-cover argument in
   [[def-quadratic-variation-along-a-partition-sequence]]. The partitions are
   given and normalization uses a finite intersection of supplied full-measure
   events, so no choice axiom is used. Existence for Brownian Ito processes is
   a separate theorem, not a presupposition of this definition.

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

derivations.claim: If $Q$ is a true continuous martingale and $\rho\le T$ is a stopping time, round $\rho$ up to finite-valued grid stopping times $\rho_m\downarrow\rho$. The finite-valued stopping calculation identifies these stopped values as conditional expectations of $Q_T$. They are uniformly integrable: for any sub-$\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal H$, truncating $Q_T$ at $K/2$ gives $E(|E[Q_T\mid\mathcal H]|1_{|E[Q_T\mid\mathcal H]|>K})\le2E(|Q_T|1_{|Q_T|>K/2})$. If $M$ is a local martingale with localizers $\lambda_k$, then $M^{\tau\wedge\lambda_k}=(M^{\lambda_k})^\tau$ is a true martingale by this fact, so $(\lambda_k)$ also localizes $M^\tau$. The stopping-time definition and continuity make $\tau_n$ a stopping time, and the preceding argument shows $M^{(n)}$ is a local martingale. It is bounded by $n$, hence a true martingale: pass its event-integral identities along its localizing sequence by dominated convergence. Every continuous path is bounded on $[0,T]$, so $\tau_n=T$ eventually on each path. It suffices to construct the claimed limit for each bounded martingale $M^{(n)}$ and show the constructions agree on overlaps.

Fix one such bounded martingale $M$, with $|M_t|\le n$, and a deterministic partition $\pi=(t_0,\ldots,t_N)$ of $[0,T]$. For coefficient bookkeeping put $H^\pi_s=M_{t_k}$ for $t_k\le s<t_{k+1}$ and $H^\pi_T=M_{t_{N-1}}$, and set $\displaystyle I^\pi_t=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}M_{t_k}\bigl(M_{t\wedge t_{k+1}}-M_{t\wedge t_k}\bigr),\qquad Q^\pi_t=\sum_{t_{k+1}\le t}(M_{t_{k+1}}-M_{t_k})^2+(M_t-M_{t_k})^2$ when $t_k\le t<t_{k+1}$, with the last partial term omitted at $t=T$. The process $I^\pi$ is a continuous martingale because it is a finite sum of bounded, left-measurable multiples of martingale increments. Orthogonality [F1] gives $E|I^\pi_T|^2=\sum_kE[M_{t_k}^2(\Delta_kM)^2]\le n^2 E(M_T-M_0)^2\le n^4$. Directly expanding each square yields the exact identity $M_t^2-M_0^2=2I^\pi_t+Q^\pi_t$. Hence $\|Q^\pi_T\|_2\le3n^2$, uniformly over all partitions.

For two partitions $\pi,\rho$, take their common refinement $\eta$. Refinement does not change a step sum with a fixed coefficient on each coarse interval, so $\displaystyle E|I^\pi_T-I^\rho_T|^2=E\sum_{[s,t]\in\eta}(H^\pi_s-H^\rho_s)^2(M_t-M_s)^2\le E\left[R_{\pi,\rho}^2Q^\eta_T\right],$ where $R_{\pi,\rho}=\sup_s|H^\pi_s-H^\rho_s|$. Uniform continuity [F3] gives $R_{\pi,\rho}\to0$ almost surely as both meshes tend to zero, and $R_{\pi,\rho}\le2n$. Cauchy–Schwarz [F4] and dominated convergence [F2] therefore make the last expectation tend to zero, using the uniform $L^2$ bound on $Q^\eta_T$ from step 1.2. Thus the terminal sums $I^\pi_T$ are Cauchy in $L^2$; completeness [F2] gives their $L^2$ limit, and Doob's inequality [F2] gives the same Cauchy property for $\sup_{t\le T}|I^\pi_t-I^\rho_t|$; for the continuous-time supremum, apply the discrete inequality on increasing finite rational grids and pass to their union by monotone convergence [F2]. Choose a subsequence whose successive expected squared sup errors are at most $2^{-4k}$. Markov's inequality and the union bound imply that this subsequence converges uniformly almost surely to a process $I$ with almost-sure continuous paths; define its value at each time as the finite pointwise limit of those sums, and zero if that limit does not exist. Since the approximating sums are continuous and adapted, this rule is adapted and progressively measurable, so its stopped values are measurable. The full family converges uniformly in probability to $I$. For fixed subsequence index $m$, the squared path-sup errors from its $m$th term to later terms converge almost surely to $\sup_{t\le T}|I^{\pi_{n_m}}_t-I_t|^2$. Applying monotone convergence to the infima of these tails gives Fatou's inequality; the $L^2$-Cauchy bound then shows these errors tend to zero in $L^2$. The event-integral martingale identities therefore pass to the $L^1$ limit.

The exact identity in step 1.2 shows that the partial-increment sums $Q^\pi$ converge uniformly in probability to $Q_t=M_t^2-M_0^2-2I_t$. A subsequence converges uniformly almost surely, so $Q$ is continuous. The step-endpoint sum differs from $Q^\pi$ by at most the maximal squared oscillation of $M$ over a partition interval; [F3] makes this tend to zero almost surely. Step-endpoint sums are nondecreasing. A uniformly convergent almost-sure subsequence of those sums therefore shows that $Q$ is increasing. Since $2I=M^2-M_0^2-Q$ is a martingale, $M^2-Q$ is a martingale; uniqueness of the partition-limit object follows from uniqueness of limits in probability.

The bounded-stopping fact in step 1.1 makes the two stopped coordinates true martingales, so $M^i+M^j$ and $M^i-M^j$ are local martingales. Apply the scalar result to them and set $\displaystyle [M^i,M^j]=\tfrac14\bigl([M^i+M^j]-[M^i-M^j]\bigr).$ The identity $4xy=(x+y)^2-(x-y)^2$ makes this the limit of cross-increment sums. Taking the same linear combination of the two square-compensated local martingales gives $M^iM^j-[M^i,M^j]$ local martingale.

Let $H$ be a bounded adapted process with everywhere-continuous paths and $N$ a bounded continuous martingale with $N_0=0$. For each partition $\pi$ use $H^\pi_s=H_{t_k}$ for $t_k\le s<t_{k+1}$ (with the last coefficient at $T$), and set $\displaystyle J^\pi_t=\sum_k H_{t_k}\bigl(N_{t\wedge t_{k+1}}-N_{t\wedge t_k}\bigr).$ On a common refinement $\eta$, martingale orthogonality [F1] gives $\displaystyle E|J^\pi_T-J^\rho_T|^2\le E\left[\sup_s|H^\pi_s-H^\rho_s|^2 Q^\eta_T(N)\right].$ The first factor tends to zero in $L^2$ by boundedness, continuity of $H$, and dominated convergence [F2]; the second has uniformly bounded $L^2$ norm by steps 1.2–2.1 applied to $N$. Cauchy–Schwarz [F4] makes the terminal sums Cauchy in $L^2$, whose limit exists by completeness [F2]. Doob's inequality [F2], applied on increasing finite rational grids and then passed to their union by monotone convergence [F2], makes the process sums Cauchy in $L^2$ of the path supremum. A subsequence with summable squared-sup errors converges uniformly almost surely; define the limit at each time where finite and zero otherwise, giving an adapted progressively measurable version with almost-sure continuous paths. Fatou gives $L^2$ convergence of the full process sums to it, so the event-integral martingale identities pass to the $L^1$ limit. This defines $\int H\,dN$ as the left-step limit. Localization extends the construction to continuous local martingales and locally bounded continuous adapted integrands.

Let $X=M+A$ and $Z=N+C$ as in the statement. For a continuous finite-variation path $A$ and a continuous path $N$, summation by parts gives $\sum_k A_{t_k}\Delta_kN=A_tN_t-A_0N_0-\sum_kN_{t_{k+1}}\Delta_kA$, so these left sums converge pathwise to $A_tN_t-A_0N_0-\int_0^tN_s\,dA_s$; this defines $\int A\,dN$ even if $A$ is not adapted. The limiting identity holds simultaneously at rational times and hence, by continuity, on the whole horizon. This proves the product formula without requiring adaptedness of $A,C$.

If $V$ is a continuous finite-variation local martingale with the stated representative convention, put $U=V-V_0$. Along every vanishing-mesh partition, its partial square sums are bounded by the maximal path oscillation times $\operatorname{Var}_{[0,T]}(V)$, which tends to zero almost surely. Let $n \ge 1$, let $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and let $E + h$ be the translate of
$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ (Translation of a subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$). Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(E+h) = \lambda_n^*(E)$ for **every** subset $E$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $E+h$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(E+h) = \lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

**No choice principle is used.** Lebesgue outer measure is defined as an infimum
and the Carathéodory condition is a family of equations between its values, so
all three clauses are statements about objects that exist in ZF; countable
choice is needed to know that $\lambda_n$ is a measure, not to know that it is
translation invariant.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$
