citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Let
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space with a continuous-time
filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. All processes here
are real-valued and indexed by $[0,\infty)$. AC is inherited from the cited
continuous-time-filtration interface, whose separate martingale clause uses
conditional expectation. Once the filtered probability space and stopping
times are given, the progressive and predictable constructions below make no
additional choice: they use only generated sigma-algebras and product
rectangles.

1. **Progressively measurable.** A process $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **progressively measurable** relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when for every
   $t\ge0$ the restricted map
   $[0,t]\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$, $(s,\omega)\mapsto X_s(\omega)$, is
   measurable for the product sigma-algebra
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$
   [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]].

2. **Time-zero and interval generators.** On the product space
   $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$, let $\mathcal P$ be the sigma-algebra generated by
   the family
   $$\mathcal G:=\bigl\{(s,u]\times A:\ 0\le s<u<\infty,\ A\in\mathcal F_s\bigr\}\ \cup\ \bigl\{\{0\}\times A:\ A\in\mathcal F_0\bigr\}.$$
   The interval generators with $s=0$ are included, so $(0,u]\times A$ with
   $A\in\mathcal F_0$ is a generator. The sigma-algebra $\mathcal P$ exists by
   [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]] and is called the
   **predictable sigma-algebra**. A process $H=(H_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **predictable** when the map $(s,\omega)\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is
   $\mathcal P$-measurable. For a finite horizon $T>0$ we write
   $\mathcal P_T$ for the sigma-algebra on $[0,T]\times\Omega$ generated by the
   same family restricted to $u\le T$ together with the time-zero generators;
   this is the trace of $\mathcal P$ on $[0,T]\times\Omega$. Indeed, the
   trace of an interval generator is empty when $s\ge T$, and otherwise is
   $(s,\min(u,T)]\times A$, while time-zero generators are unchanged.
   Conversely every listed finite-horizon generator is such a trace.

3. **Sections, adaptedness, and null sets.** Two structural conventions are
   used repeatedly and are part of the definition.
   (a) Every generator is a measurable rectangle of
   $\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$, hence
   $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$; the time-zero
   generator $\{0\}\times A$ has $dt\otimes P$-measure zero for every $A$. A
   set in $\mathcal P$ has its section at each fixed time $s$ in $\mathcal F_s$:
   sets with that section property form a sigma-algebra, and each generator
   has the property by the increasing-filtration condition. Its section at
   each fixed $\omega$ is Borel in time, by the same sigma-algebra argument.
   (b) If a process is predictable then it is progressively measurable: for
   $s\le t$ the section $\omega\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is $\mathcal F_s$-measurable
   $\subseteq\mathcal F_t$-measurable, and the progressive-measurability claim
   is the restriction of the joint map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$; the restriction
   of a $\mathcal P$-measurable map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$ is measurable for
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$ because every generator with $u\le t$
   lies in that product sigma-algebra and the generators with $u>t$ have
   intersection with $[0,t]\times\Omega$ of the form $(s,t]\times A$ with
   $s<t$ and $A\in\mathcal F_s$, or the empty set when $s\ge t$.
   The time-zero generators also lie in
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$.

The family $\mathcal G$ need not itself contain the whole space, but a finite intersection
of generators is empty or again a generator, or a time-zero generator, because
$(s,u]\cap(s',u']=(s\vee s',u\wedge u']$ and $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_{s\vee s'}$
whenever $A\in\mathcal F_s$, $A'\in\mathcal F_{s'}$, while
$\{0\}\times A$ is disjoint from every interval generator, including
$(0,u]\times A'$. Two time-zero generators intersect in
$\{0\}\times(A\cap A')$ with $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_0$.
Thus the family consisting of the whole space
together with finite intersections of generators is a pi-system generating
$\mathcal P$; this is the structural fact used by the density theorem below.

Because predictability is a measurability requirement for the joint map, it is
preserved by pointwise limits, products and linear combinations of predictable
processes. A deterministic function $h$ of time defines a predictable process
exactly when $h$ is Borel measurable: the sets $C$ for which
$C\times\Omega\in\mathcal P$ form a sigma-algebra containing the intervals
$(s,u]$ and $\{0\}$, hence all Borel sets. Conversely, take any fixed
$\omega\in\Omega$ (a probability space is nonempty) and use the Borel
time-section property from 3(a) on every inverse image of an open set.
This single choice uses no choice axiom. In particular the
indicators $1_{[0,u]}$ and $1_{(0,u]}$ are predictable for every deterministic
$u\ge0$, and the process $s\mapsto 1_{s\le\tau(\omega)}$ for a stopping time
$\tau$ [[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]] is predictable, since
$$\{(s,\omega):s>\tau(\omega)\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}(q,\infty)\times\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}\bigcup_{n>q}(q,n]\times\{\tau<q\}$$
is a countable union of generators: for rational $q>0$ one has
$\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q'<q,\ q'\in\mathbb Q}\{\tau\le q'\}\in\mathcal F_q$. The
complement of that set inside $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$ is the event of the
indicator, so $1_{[0,\tau]}$ is predictable; its left-continuity in the time
variable is the visual form of the same computation.

No completeness of the filtration and no right continuity of $(\mathcal F_t)$
is used or assumed. Apart from the inherited ambient assumption just recorded,
the constructions in this definition are choice-free.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix a finite horizon $T>0$ and a filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{0\le t\le T}$. Let $M$ be a continuous adapted $d$-dimensional local martingale with $M_0=0$. Let $\sigma$ be a predictable process of invertible $d\times d$ matrices, with $\|\sigma_t^{-1}\|\le C$ for a finite deterministic constant $C$ and $\int_0^T\|\sigma_t\|_F^2dt<\infty$ almost surely. Suppose
$$[M^i,M^j]_t=\int_0^t(\sigma_s\sigma_s^{\mathsf T})_{ij}ds.$$
Then predictable elementary sums, completed in the localized bracket-energy norm, define $B=\int\sigma^{-1}dM$. It has an adapted continuous version, is standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion in the given filtration, and
$$M_t=\int_0^t\sigma_s\,dB_s$$
up to indistinguishability. The integral on the right is the localized predictable Brownian integral defined by elementary sums and their $L^2$ completion. This construction on the given finite horizon does not require completeness or right continuity of the filtration, and no continuity of $\sigma$ is assumed.

derivations.claim: If $T=0$, set $B_0=0$; the integral, bracket and finite-horizon Brownian claims are immediate. Henceforth suppose $T>0$. Form left-step approximations to $\sigma$ on deterministic dyadic partitions, retaining $\sigma_0$ at time zero. They are predictable by [F1]. Take their pointwise limit where it exists as a finite invertible matrix with inverse norm at most $C$, and use $C^{-1}I_d$ otherwise; necessarily $C>0$. The resulting predictable $\widehat\sigma$ agrees with $\sigma$ at all times on its full continuity event. Continuity on the compact horizon gives $\int_0^T\|\widehat\sigma_s\|_F^2ds<\infty$ almost surely, and its bracket identity is the given one. Thus [F9] supplies a Brownian motion $B=\int\widehat\sigma^{-1}dM$ adapted to the original filtration, with bracket $tI_d$. This invocation makes no raw stopped evaluation of an unnormalized almost-surely continuous process.

This integral also has the left-step construction required in the Statement. On the augmented, normalized stopped intervals of [F9], put $H=\sigma^{-1}$ and use its bounded deterministic left-step approximations. They converge uniformly on each continuous path and are bounded by $C$. The bracket-energy isometry and maximal estimate proved in [F9], together with dominated convergence [F7] and the integrable stopped bracket trace, give localized $L^2$ convergence of their integrals to the same $B$. Equality with the predictable reconstruction follows from uniqueness in that energy completion. Its original-adapted continuous version and Brownian increment identities are supplied by [F9]; the bracket is $[B^i,B^j]_t=\delta_{ij}t$. Hence every asserted conclusion holds on the given filtration.

Let $T>0$, let $p_t$ be a strictly positive probability density on $\mathbb R^d$ for each $t\in[0,T]$, and let $q(s,x;t,y)$ be a jointly Borel, strictly positive transition density for $0\le s<t\le T$. Assume the marginal identity $p_t(y)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}p_s(x)q(s,x;t,y)\,dx$ and the Chapman–Kolmogorov identity $q(s,x;t,y)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}q(s,x;r,z)q(r,z;t,y)\,dz$ whenever $s<r<t$. For $0\le u<v\le T$ define
$$K_{u,v}(y,A)=\frac{\int_A p_{T-v}(x)q(T-v,x;T-u,y)\,dx}{p_{T-u}(y)}\qquad(A\subseteq\mathbb R^d\text{ Borel}),$$
and set $K_{u,u}(y,\cdot)=\delta_y$. This is the Bayes-reversed transition probability kernel from reverse time $u$ to reverse time $v$; its source state $y$ is the forward-time state at $T-u$ and its output $x$ is the state at $T-v$.

Let $X$ be a continuous Markov process on $[0,T]$ in $\mathbb R^d$ with positive transition densities $q$ and positive $C^{1,2}$ marginal densities $p$. Suppose its marginal and transition identities define the Bayes-reversed kernels. Write $L_r f=b_{r,i}\partial_i f+\tfrac12a_{r,ij}\partial_{ij}f$, with Borel coefficients and symmetric $a$, and $L_r^*z=-\partial_i(b_{r,i}z)+\tfrac12\partial_i\partial_j(a_{r,ij}z)$. Assume $\partial_rp_r=L_r^*p_r$ classically. Put $A_{ij}(r,x)=p_r(x)a_{r,ij}(x)$, suppose its first state derivatives exist, and define $C_i=-p_rb_{r,i}+\sum_j\partial_jA_{ij}$. Impose the following forward analytic hypotheses. For every compact $K\subset\mathbb R^d$,
$$\int_0^T\!\int_K\left[\sum_i|C_i|+\sum_{i,j}p_r|a_{r,ij}|\right]dx\,dr<\infty.$$
For every $t\in(0,T]$ and $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$, the actual forward conditional expectation
$$g_{t,f}(r,x)=\int q(r,x;t,y)f(y)dy,\qquad 0<r<t,$$
has a $C^{1,2}$ version on $(0,t)\times\mathbb R^d$ satisfying the backward Kolmogorov equation $\partial_rg_{t,f}+L_rg_{t,f}=0$. For every $\phi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$, assume the spatial adjoint identity
$$\int p_r\phi L_rg_{t,f}\,dx=\int g_{t,f}L_r^*(p_r\phi)\,dx$$
holds for almost every $r\in(0,t)$; the integrals are finite. These are assumptions on the original forward transition family, not on a reversed process.

Define $D_r\phi=p_r^{-1}\{L_r^*(p_r\phi)-\phi L_r^*p_r\}$, using the classical product rule. Then $Y_u=X_{T-u}$, with its natural reversed filtration $\mathcal G_u=\sigma(Y_v:0\le v\le u)$, has the Bayes-reversed kernels and, for each such $\phi$,
$$\phi(Y_u)-\phi(Y_0)-\int_0^u D_{T-v}\phi(Y_v)dv$$
is a true martingale. In particular $D_{T-u}$ is its extended martingale generator on compact smooth tests. No pointwise small-time transition-quotient limit is asserted.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim: Bayes' formula gives the one-step reversed conditional law: for Borel $A$, the joint density of $(X_{T-v},X_{T-u})$ is $p_{T-v}(x)q(T-v,x;T-u,y)$, while the later marginal is $p_{T-u}(y)$. Their ratio is exactly $K_{u,v}(y,A)$. The kernel is normalized and composes by [F1], so the finite-dimensional reversed laws have the Markov factorization with these kernels.

Put $t=T-u$ and $D_t\phi=p_t^{-1}\{L_t^*(p_t\phi)-\phi L_t^*p_t\}$. Under the additional forward analytic conditions in the Statement, the hypotheses are exactly those of [F2], so that result gives the compensated-test martingale with coefficient $D_{T-u}$. Thus the displayed operator is the extended martingale generator. This argument uses the finite-time product identity for the actual forward transition family.

Under the same additional conditions, [F2] gives for $0\le s<t\le T$ and every bounded Borel $f$ the identity $\displaystyle E\!\left[f(X_t)\left\{\phi(X_s)-\phi(X_t)-\int_s^tD_r\phi(X_r)dr\right\}\right]=0$. Reversed Markov conditioning and [F3] therefore give zero conditional expectation of every compensated increment given $\mathcal G_u$, as required. The explicit bound gives a true martingale, hence a local martingale.

Expanding the adjoint in step 2.1, the drift part contributes $-p b_i\partial_i\phi$. The second-order product rule contributes $\partial_j(pa_{ij})\partial_i\phi+\tfrac12pa_{ij}\partial_{ij}\phi$ after summing and using symmetry of $a$. Divide by $p$ and use $p^{-1}\partial_j(pa_{ij})=\partial_j a_{ij}+a_{ij}\partial_j\log p$ to obtain the stated reverse drift and diffusion matrix.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice as required by the stochastic-integral interfaces
below. Fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$ and finite integers $d,m\ge1$. Work on
a complete filtered probability space
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{0\le t\le T},P)$ whose filtration is
right-continuous and contains every $P$-null subset of $\mathcal F$ in
$\mathcal F_0$ (the usual conditions).

Let $W=(W_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ be a standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion
$d$-dimensional Brownian motion adapted to this filtration, with
$W_t-W_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and distributed as
$N_m(0,(t-s)I_m)$ for $0\le s<t\le T$. Let
$X_0:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$ be $\mathcal F_0$-measurable, satisfy
$E|X_0|^2<\infty$, and be independent of the future Brownian increments.
Explicitly, $X_0$ is independent of the sigma-algebra
$\sigma(W_t-W_0:0\le t\le T)$.

Continuity of a process means continuity on one measurable event of
probability one. We use an everywhere-continuous adapted representative: if
the chosen process is continuous only on such an event $A$, replace it off $A$
by its initial value. Since $A^c$ is a null set and the filtration is complete,
$A^c\in\mathcal F_0$; the replacement preserves adaptedness and changes the
SDE identity only on a null event, hence preserves it up to
indistinguishability.

The drift and diffusion coefficients are jointly Borel maps
$$b:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d,\qquad \sigma:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}.$$
For nonnegative finite constants $L,K$, assume for every $t\in[0,T]$ and
$x,y\in\mathbb R^d$ that
$$|b(t,x)-b(t,y)|+\|\sigma(t,x)-\sigma(t,y)\|_F\le L|x-y|,$$
$$|b(t,x)|+\|\sigma(t,x)\|_F\le K(1+|x|).$$
Here $|\cdot|$ is the Euclidean norm and
$\|A\|_F^2=\sum_{i=1}^d\sum_{k=1}^m|A^{ik}|^2$ is the Frobenius norm.

For an adapted continuous candidate $X:[0,T]\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$,
the vector Itô equation
$$X_t=X_0+\int_0^t b(s,X_s)\,ds+\left(\sum_{k=1}^m\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}(s,X_s)\,dW_s^k\right)_{i=1}^d,\qquad 0\le t\le T.$$
uses a pathwise Lebesgue integral for the drift and, in each coordinate, the
localized Itô integral from
Continuous Brownian Ito processes, clause 2. Require
$\int_0^T|b(s,X_s)|ds<\infty$ and
$\int_0^T\|\sigma(s,X_s)\|_F^2ds<\infty$ almost surely; these are the local
coefficient-integrability conditions in that definition. When a coordinate
integrand has finite expected energy, its integral is the square-integrable
Itô integral of Ito integral for square-integrable predictable processes;
the Picard estimates below establish that stronger condition for every input
in $\mathcal H_T$. Equality of processes means
equality for every $t$ on one measurable event of probability one, that is,
indistinguishability
Process law, modification, and indistinguishability. A **strong
solution on $[0,T]$** is an adapted continuous process satisfying this
integral equation indistinguishably. No moment bound is included in the
definition; the existence theorem proves its $L^2$ path-sup bound.
The usual-filtration, continuity, and finite-coordinate conventions agree
with the multidimensional class of continuous Brownian Itô processes
Continuous Brownian Ito processes. This definition makes no ellipticity,
transition-density, forward-equation, or time-reversal assertion.

Brownian motion here means the finite-horizon version of the cited definition:
$W_0=0$ almost surely, with continuous paths and the stated increments on
$[0,T]$. All cited stochastic-calculus interfaces are used on this interval.
Their constructions require no extension of $W$ beyond $T$: elementary
integrals use only increments between partition points in $[0,T]$, and their
$L^2$ limits and continuous versions are constructed on that same interval.
For a predictable scalar integrand $H$ with finite pathwise energy, localize
at $\rho_n=\inf\{t\in[0,T]:\int_0^t H_s^2ds\ge n\}\wedge T$.
Here $\inf\varnothing=+\infty$.
The stopped integrands have expected energy at most $n$; their continuous
integrals agree up to the smaller stop by the finite-energy stopping identity.
On the full event of finite energy, $\rho_n=T$ for all sufficiently large
$n$, so these integrals paste uniquely on the whole closed interval $[0,T]$,
exactly as in the localized construction of
Continuous Brownian Ito processes. At $T=0$ every integral is zero.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and let $d\ge1$ be a finite integer. An
$\mathbb R^d$-valued process $B=(B_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **standard
$d$-dimensional Brownian motion** if:

1. $B_0=0$ almost surely;
2. for every finite list $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_n$, the vector increments
   $$B_{t_j}-B_{t_{j-1}},\qquad 1\le j\le n,$$
   are mutually independent and have laws
   $N_d(0,(t_j-t_{j-1})I_d)$; and
3. there is one measurable event $A$ with $P(A)=1$ such that
   $t\mapsto B_t(\omega)$ is continuous from $[0,\infty)$ to
   $\mathbb R^d$ for every $\omega\in A$.

Equivalently, its $d$ coordinate processes $B^\alpha=(B_t^\alpha)_{t\ge0}$
are independent standard one-dimensional Brownian motions. Here independence
of the processes means the following precise assertion. Put
$I=[0,\infty)$ and equip $\mathbb R^I$ with its cylinder sigma-algebra. The
maps
$$ \Phi_\alpha:\Omega\longrightarrow\mathbb R^I, \qquad \Phi_\alpha(\omega)(t)=B_t^\alpha(\omega), \qquad 1\le\alpha\le d, $$
are independent random elements.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Let $m,d\ge1$ be finite
integers, let $B=(B^1,\dots,B^m)$ be a standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion,
and let $X$ be an $\mathbb R^d$-valued continuous Brownian Ito process
$$X^i_t=X^i_0+\int_0^tb^i_s\,ds+\sum_{k=1}^m\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s, \qquad i=1,\dots,d,$$
in the sense of [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]], including its usual-filtration and almost-sure coefficient-integrability conventions. Let
$f\in C^{1,2}([0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^d)$, meaning that $f,\partial_tf$,
$\partial_if$ and $\partial_i\partial_jf$ ($1\le i,j\le d$) exist and are
continuous. Then, up to indistinguishability, for every $t\ge0$
$$f(t,X_t)=f(0,X_0)+\int_0^t\Bigl(\partial_tf+\sum_ib^i\partial_if+\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}\partial_i\partial_jf\Bigr)(s,X_s)\,ds+\sum_{i,k}\int_0^t\partial_if(s,X_s)\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s,$$
For the displayed integrands, intersect the measurable full events of continuity and the decomposition of $X$, and of coefficient integrability at all integer horizons. Its null complement belongs to $\mathcal F_0$ under the usual conditions. Set $X,X_0,b,\sigma$ to zero there. These representatives preserve all coefficient classes and the decomposition up to indistinguishability, with everywhere continuous $X$ and everywhere locally finite coefficient path integrals. All displayed integrands use these representatives.

The stochastic integrals are localized Ito integrals of the predictable
locally square-integrable integrands $\partial_if(\cdot,X)\sigma^{ik}$, and
$(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}_s=\sum_k\sigma^{ik}_s\sigma^{jk}_s$. In
differential form,
$df(t,X_t)=\bigl(\partial_tf+\sum_ib^i\partial_if+\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}\partial_i\partial_jf\bigr)(t,X_t)\,dt+\sum_{i,k}\partial_if(t,X_t)\sigma^{ik}_t\,dB^k_t$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Let $B=(B^1,\dots,B^m)$ be a
standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion and let $X=(X^1,\dots,X^d)$ be an
$\mathbb R^d$-valued continuous Brownian Ito process driven by $B$,
$$dX^i_t=b^i_t\,dt+\sum_{k=1}^m\sigma^{ik}_t\,dB^k_t, \qquad i=1,\dots,d,$$
in the sense of [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]], including its
progressive representative, usual-filtration, almost-sure coefficient-integrability and
vector-increment independence hypotheses. Indistinguishability and
measurable suprema use the full-event normalization convention of
[[def-quadratic-covariation-of-brownian-ito-processes]].
All coefficient path integrals below use zero outside the common measurable
probability-one event on which every drift is locally absolutely integrable
and every diffusion entry is locally square-integrable. Such an event is
obtained by intersecting the finitely many coefficient conditions at integer
horizons; its complement belongs to $\mathcal F_0$ under the usual conditions.
On this event, Cauchy–Schwarz makes every product
$\sigma^{ik}\sigma^{jk}$ locally integrable. The normalized covariance
integrals therefore have finite continuous paths and measurable time sections.

1. **Existence and value.** For every pair $i,j$ the quadratic covariation
   $[X^i,X^j]$ exists on every finite horizon in the sense of
   [[def-quadratic-covariation-of-brownian-ito-processes]], and for every
   $t\ge0$
   $$[X^i,X^j]_t=\sum_{k=1}^m\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}_s\sigma^{jk}_s\,ds =\int_0^t(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}_s\,ds$$
   up to indistinguishability, where $(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}=\sum_k\sigma^{ik}\sigma^{jk}$.
   In particular the real continuous Brownian Ito process
   $X_t=X_0+\int_0^tb_s\,ds+\int_0^t\sigma_s\,dB_s$ has
   $[X]_t=\int_0^t\sigma_s^2\,ds$.

2. **Finite-variation parts contribute nothing.** If $A$ is a continuous
   process whose paths are absolutely continuous,
   $A_t=\int_0^ta_s\,ds$, and $Y$ is any continuous process, then the
   covariation of $A$ with $Y$ exists and is the zero process. Consequently in
   the decomposition $X^i=X^i_0+\int_0^tb^i_s\,ds+\sum_k\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s$
   the drift part contributes zero cross sums against every continuous
   process, including against the driving Brownian coordinates.

Let $m,r\ge1$, and let $A\in\mathbb R^m$ and $B,C\in\mathbb R^r$ have a joint Lebesgue density. Suppose this joint density factors as
$$p_{A,B,C}(a,b,c)=p_A(a)f(b-c)p_C(c)$$
almost everywhere, where $p_A$, $f$, and $p_C$ are probability densities on $\mathbb R^m$, $\mathbb R^r$, and $\mathbb R^r$, respectively. Then $D=B-C$ is independent of $A$, has density $f$, and the joint density of $(A,D)$ is $p_A(a)f(d)$.

[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Let $m,d\ge1$ be finite
integers, let $B=(B^1,\dots,B^m)$ be a standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion,
and let $X$ be an $\mathbb R^d$-valued continuous Brownian Ito process
$$X^i_t=X^i_0+\int_0^tb^i_s\,ds+\sum_{k=1}^m\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s, \qquad i=1,\dots,d,$$
in the sense of [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]], including its usual-filtration and almost-sure coefficient-integrability conventions. Let
$f\in C^{1,2}([0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^d)$, meaning that $f,\partial_tf$,

derivations.claim: For $t>t_0$ set $R(x,w,t)=p_t(x)\varphi_{t-t_0}(w)$. In [F3], the $x$-drift and $x$-diffusion terms combine to $\varphi_{t-t_0}(w)L_t^*p_t(x)$. The cross term is $\displaystyle \partial_i\partial_{w_k}(\sigma_{ik}p_t\varphi)=\partial_{w_k}\!\left(\varphi\,\partial_i(p_t\sigma_{ik})\right)=\partial_{w_k}(c_kp_t\varphi),$ which cancels the $-\partial_{w_k}(c_kR)$ term by the definition of $c_k$. The remaining $w$-diffusion term is $p_t\partial_t\varphi$, and $\partial_t p_t=L_t^*p_t$; hence the augmented equation's right side is $\partial_tR$. The initial limit is the law of $X_{t_0}$ times $\delta_0(dw)$ by [F4]. Uniqueness therefore identifies $R$ with the actual joint density of $(X_t,\widetilde W_t)$.

The definition of $\widetilde W$ gives the forward-Itô equation $\displaystyle dX_i=\left(b_i-\sum_k\sigma_{ik}c_k\right)dt+\sum_k\sigma_{ik}\,d^{\mathrm f}\widetilde W_k.$ For $H_{ik}=\sigma_{ik}(X_t,t)$, right-endpoint sums equal left-endpoint sums plus the cross-increment sums defining $[H_{ik},\widetilde W_k]$. Their limits differ by the bracket in [F6]; consequently $\displaystyle \int_s^t H_{ik}\,d^{\mathrm f}\widetilde W_k=\int_s^t H_{ik}\,d^{\mathrm b}\widetilde W_k-\int_s^t\sum_j\partial_j\sigma_{ik}(X_r,r)\sigma_{jk}(X_r,r)\,dr,$ where the superscripts denote left-endpoint forward and right-endpoint backward Itô sums. This fixes the sign of the conversion.

Fix $s\ge t_0$ and condition on $\widetilde W_s=w_s$. Step 1.1 shows that $X_s$ has density $p_s$ independently of $\widetilde W_s$, so the conditional initial density at time $s$ is $p_s(x)\delta_{w_s}(dw)$. The candidate $R_s(x,w,t)=p_t(x)\varphi_{t-s}(w-w_s)$ has that initial limit. The calculation in step 1.1, with $\varphi_{t-s}(w-w_s)$ in place of $\varphi_{t-t_0}(w)$, proves that it solves the conditional augmented equation. By the assumed uniqueness, this is the conditional joint density of $(X_t,\widetilde W_t)$ given $\widetilde W_s=w_s$.

The resulting backward drift in the original time variable is $\displaystyle \widehat b_i=b_i-\sum_k\sigma_{ik}c_k-\sum_{j,k}\partial_j\sigma_{ik}\sigma_{jk}=b_i-\frac1{p_t}\sum_j\partial_j(p_t a_{ij}).$ Indeed, substituting $c_k=p_t^{-1}\sum_j\partial_j(p_t\sigma_{jk})$ and applying the product rule expands the last numerator as $\sum_k\sigma_{ik}\partial_j(p_t\sigma_{jk})+p_t\sum_{j,k}(\partial_j\sigma_{ik})\sigma_{jk}$.

For $s>t_0$, multiplying the conditional density in step 2.1 by the density $\varphi_{s-t_0}(w_s)$ from step 1.1 gives the joint density of $(X_t,\widetilde W_t,\widetilde W_s)$. Apply [F5] with $A=X_t$, $B=\widetilde W_t$, $C=\widetilde W_s$, and $f=\varphi_{t-s}$. For $s=t_0$, the same conclusion follows directly from step 2.1 with the deterministic value $\widetilde W_{t_0}=0$. Thus $X_t$ and $\widetilde W_t-\widetilde W_s$ are independent and the increment has law $N_r(0,(t-s)I_r)$, proving claim 1.

For $0\le u<v\le U$, put $s=T-v$ and $t=T-u$. Then $B_v-B_u=-(\widetilde W_t-\widetilde W_s)$, so by claim 1 this increment has law $N_r(0,(v-u)I_r)$. It is measurable with respect to the forward filtration at time $t$. By the strong restart assumption in the Statement, the future $X$ path, and hence the future $\widetilde W$ increments, are measurable functions of $X_t$ and the future Brownian increments of $W$; those Brownian increments are independent of $\mathcal F_t$ by [F1]. Since $\widetilde W_t-\widetilde W_s$ is independent of $X_t$ by claim 1, it is independent of the pair consisting of $X_t$ and all future Brownian increments, and thus of the entire future segment $(X_r,\widetilde W_r-\widetilde W_t)_{r\ge t}$. The variables $Y_q$ and $B_q$ for $q\le u$ are measurable with respect to that segment. Therefore $B_v-B_u$ is independent of $\mathcal G_u$. The process $B$ is continuous, starts at zero, and has these centered Gaussian increments independent of its past; hence it is standard Brownian motion in $(\mathcal G_u)$.

Reparameterize by $u=T-t$ and set $B_u=\widetilde W_{T-u}-\widetilde W_T$. Right-endpoint sums in forward time satisfy $\int_{T-u}^T H_s\,d^{\mathrm b}\widetilde W_s=-\int_0^uH_{T-r}\,dB_r$: each reversed increment is the negative of the corresponding right-endpoint forward increment. With $t=T-u$, this is exactly the displayed reverse SDE and completes claim 3.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge1$, $T>0$, and let $\mu$ be a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R^d$ supported in the closed ball $\overline B(0,R)$ for some finite $R\ge0$. Let $g:[0,T]\to(0,\infty)$ be continuously differentiable with $0<g_{\min}\le g(t)\le g_{\max}<\infty$, and set $v(t)=\int_0^t g(r)^2\,dr$. On a complete filtered probability space with the usual conditions, take $X_0$ with law $\mu$, measurable at time zero and independent of the future Brownian increments. Let $W$ be a standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion adapted to the filtration, with $W_t-W_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and distributed as $N_d(0,(t-s)I_d)$ for every $0\le s<t\le T$. Let $X$ be the strong solution of $dX_t=g(t)\,dW_t$ with initial value $X_0$. For $a>0$ define the product Gaussian density $\phi_a(z)=\prod_{j=1}^d(2\pi a)^{-1/2}\exp(-z_j^2/(2a))$. For $t>0$ and $0\le s<t\le T$, define

$$p_t(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}\phi_{v(t)}(x-z)\,\mu(dz),\qquad q(s,x;t,y)=\phi_{v(t)-v(s)}(y-x).$$

Then $p_t$ is a finite, strictly positive, normalized Lebesgue density of the law of $X_t$. For each $x$, $q(s,x;t,\cdot)$ is a finite, strictly positive, normalized Lebesgue density, and for all Borel sets $A,B\subseteq\mathbb R^d$,

$$P(X_s\in A,\ X_t\in B)=\int_A\int_B q(s,x;t,y)\,dy\,\mu_s(dx),\qquad \mu_s:=\operatorname{Law}(X_s).$$

For $0\le s<r<t\le T$, these transition densities satisfy

$$\int_{\mathbb R^d}q(s,x;r,z)q(r,z;t,y)\,dz=q(s,x;t,y)\qquad(x,y\in\mathbb R^d).$$

No Lebesgue density for the initial law $\mu$ is assumed.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in Measures on sigma-algebras and A measurable function between measurable spaces; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim: For $u<v<T$, the integrand $1_A(x)p_{T-v}(x)q(T-v,x;T-u,y)$ is jointly Borel and nonnegative; Tonelli [F2] makes its integral measurable in $y$, and countable additivity in $A$ follows from countable additivity of the integral. For $v=T$, the integrand $1_A(x)q(0,x;T-u,y)$ is jointly Borel and nonnegative relative to the finite measure $\mu$, so the same parameter-integral argument applies. All denominators are positive because $T-u>0$.

If $v<T$, the forward marginal identity [A1] gives $\int p_{T-v}(x)q(T-v,x;T-u,y)dx=p_{T-u}(y)$; if $v=T$, the same identity with initial measure $\mu$ gives $\int q(0,x;T-u,y)\mu(dx)=p_{T-u}(y)$. Thus both formulas have total mass one. The equal-time kernel is a probability measure by definition.

For $u<v<w<T$, composing the density ratios cancels $p_{T-v}(x)$, and Tonelli followed by forward Chapman–Kolmogorov [A1] gives $K_{u,v}K_{v,w}=K_{u,w}$. If $w=T$, the same computation leaves $\mu(dz)$ times $\displaystyle \int q(0,z;T-v,x)q(T-v,x;T-u,y)dx=q(0,z;T-u,y),$ so the endpoint formula gives $K_{u,v}K_{v,T}=K_{u,T}$. Cases with equal adjacent times use the identity kernel.

all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that

Let $T>0$, let $p_t$ be a strictly positive probability density on $\mathbb R^d$ for each $t\in[0,T]$, and let $q(s,x;t,y)$ be a jointly Borel, strictly positive transition density for $0\le s<t\le T$. Assume the marginal identity $p_t(y)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}p_s(x)q(s,x;t,y)\,dx$ and the Chapman–Kolmogorov identity $q(s,x;t,y)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}q(s,x;r,z)q(r,z;t,y)\,dz$ whenever $s<r<t$. For $0\le u<v\le T$ define
$$K_{u,v}(y,A)=\frac{\int_A p_{T-v}(x)q(T-v,x;T-u,y)\,dx}{p_{T-u}(y)}\qquad(A\subseteq\mathbb R^d\text{ Borel}),$$
and set $K_{u,u}(y,\cdot)=\delta_y$. This is the Bayes-reversed transition probability kernel from reverse time $u$ to reverse time $v$; its source state $y$ is the forward-time state at $T-u$ and its output $x$ is the state at $T-v$.

Assume AC. Let $X$ be a continuous Markov process on $[0,T]$ in $\mathbb R^d$, with positive $C^{1,2}$ marginal densities $p_r$ and positive transition densities $q(s,x;r,y)$ satisfying the marginal and Chapman–Kolmogorov identities. $$D_rf=p_r^{-1}\{L_r^*(p_rf)-fL_r^*p_r\}=c_r\cdot\nabla f+\tfrac12a_r:D^2f,\qquad c_r=-b_r+p_r^{-1}\nabla\!\cdot(p_ra_r).$$

Suppose there are stopping times $\tau_n\uparrow T$ almost surely such that the finite measures
$$\mu_n(E)=E\int_0^{\tau_n}1_E(u,Z_u)du$$
are absolutely continuous with respect to spacetime Lebesgue measure. No marginal law of $Z$ after time zero is assumed.

Then $Z$ has the same path law as $Y_u=X_{T-u}$. In particular its marginal at $u$ is $p_{T-u}$ and its transition kernel from $u$ to $v>u$ is
$$K_{u,v}(y,dx)=\frac{p_{T-v}(x)q(T-v,x;T-u,y)}{p_{T-u}(y)}dx.$$
Consequently $Y$ solves the local martingale problem for $D_{T-u}$ in its natural reversed filtration. The occupation condition is an explicit hypothesis of this intermediate lemma; its applicability must be proved, not inferred from density notation.

$$\widetilde L_u\phi=\widetilde b_u\cdot
abla\phi+	frac12a_{T-u}:D^2\phi,\qquad \widetilde b_u=-b_{T-u}+
abla\!\cdot a_{T-u}+a_{T-u}
abla\log p_{T-u},$$

abla\!\cdot a)_i=\sum_j\partial_j a_{ij}$. These Bayes-kernel and formal product identities use only the preceding hypotheses.

Each input local martingale below is taken with everywhere-continuous adapted paths; it suffices that its full continuity event belongs to the initial sigma-algebra, so it can first be normalized there. All pathwise stopping operations use these representatives. Let $M$ be a real continuous local martingale on $[0,T]$ with $M_0=0$, where a local martingale means that some increasing stopping times tending to $T$ make the stopped processes martingales. Then there is a unique continuous increasing process $[M]$ with $[M]_0=0$ such that the step-endpoint and partial-increment sums of squared increments along every deterministic partition sequence whose mesh tends to zero converge uniformly in probability to $[M]$. Moreover $M_t^2-[M]_t$ is a continuous local martingale. For a continuous $d$-dimensional local martingale $M$ started at zero, polarization defines continuous covariations $[M^i,M^j]$ with $M^iM^j-[M^i,M^j]$ local martingales. More generally, if $X=M+A$ and $Z=N+C$ with continuous local martingales $M,N$ and continuous finite-variation processes $A,C$, then left-step sums define the localized integrals against $M,N$ and
$$X_tZ_t-X_0Z_0=\int_0^t X_s\,dZ_s+\int_0^t Z_s\,dX_s+[M,N]_t,$$
where finite-variation integrals are pathwise Lebesgue–Stieltjes integrals and local-martingale integrals are the limits of the displayed left-step sums. Stopping a continuous local martingale at a bounded stopping time preserves its local-martingale property; if the stopped process is bounded, it is a true martingale. A continuous finite-variation local martingale is constant.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix a finite horizon $T>0$ and a filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{0\le t\le T}$. Let $M$ be a continuous adapted $d$-dimensional local martingale with $M_0=0$. Let $\sigma$ be a predictable process of invertible $d\times d$ matrices, with $\|\sigma_t^{-1}\|\le C$ for a finite deterministic constant $C$ and $\int_0^T\|\sigma_t\|_F^2dt<\infty$ almost surely. Suppose
$$[M^i,M^j]_t=\int_0^t(\sigma_s\sigma_s^{\mathsf T})_{ij}ds.$$
Then predictable elementary sums, completed in the localized bracket-energy norm, define $B=\int\sigma^{-1}dM$. It has an adapted continuous version, is standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion in the given filtration, and
$$M_t=\int_0^t\sigma_s\,dB_s$$
up to indistinguishability. The integral on the right is the localized predictable Brownian integral defined by elementary sums and their $L^2$ completion. This construction on the given finite horizon does not require completeness or right continuity of the filtration, and no continuity of $\sigma$ is assumed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Let
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space with a continuous-time
filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. All processes here
are real-valued and indexed by $[0,\infty)$. AC is inherited from the cited
continuous-time-filtration interface, whose separate martingale clause uses
conditional expectation. Once the filtered probability space and stopping
times are given, the progressive and predictable constructions below make no
additional choice: they use only generated sigma-algebras and product
rectangles.

1. **Progressively measurable.** A process $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **progressively measurable** relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when for every
   $t\ge0$ the restricted map
   $[0,t]\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$, $(s,\omega)\mapsto X_s(\omega)$, is
   measurable for the product sigma-algebra
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$
   [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]].

2. **Time-zero and interval generators.** On the product space
   $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$, let $\mathcal P$ be the sigma-algebra generated by
   the family
   $$\mathcal G:=\bigl\{(s,u]\times A:\ 0\le s<u<\infty,\ A\in\mathcal F_s\bigr\}\ \cup\ \bigl\{\{0\}\times A:\ A\in\mathcal F_0\bigr\}.$$
   The interval generators with $s=0$ are included, so $(0,u]\times A$ with
   $A\in\mathcal F_0$ is a generator. The sigma-algebra $\mathcal P$ exists by
   [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]] and is called the
   **predictable sigma-algebra**. A process $H=(H_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **predictable** when the map $(s,\omega)\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is
   $\mathcal P$-measurable. For a finite horizon $T>0$ we write
   $\mathcal P_T$ for the sigma-algebra on $[0,T]\times\Omega$ generated by the
   same family restricted to $u\le T$ together with the time-zero generators;
   this is the trace of $\mathcal P$ on $[0,T]\times\Omega$. Indeed, the
   trace of an interval generator is empty when $s\ge T$, and otherwise is
   $(s,\min(u,T)]\times A$, while time-zero generators are unchanged.
   Conversely every listed finite-horizon generator is such a trace.

3. **Sections, adaptedness, and null sets.** Two structural conventions are
   used repeatedly and are part of the definition.
   (a) Every generator is a measurable rectangle of
   $\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$, hence
   $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$; the time-zero
   generator $\{0\}\times A$ has $dt\otimes P$-measure zero for every $A$. A
   set in $\mathcal P$ has its section at each fixed time $s$ in $\mathcal F_s$:
   sets with that section property form a sigma-algebra, and each generator
   has the property by the increasing-filtration condition. Its section at
   each fixed $\omega$ is Borel in time, by the same sigma-algebra argument.
   (b) If a process is predictable then it is progressively measurable: for
   $s\le t$ the section $\omega\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is $\mathcal F_s$-measurable
   $\subseteq\mathcal F_t$-measurable, and the progressive-measurability claim
   is the restriction of the joint map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$; the restriction
   of a $\mathcal P$-measurable map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$ is measurable for
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$ because every generator with $u\le t$
   lies in that product sigma-algebra and the generators with $u>t$ have
   intersection with $[0,t]\times\Omega$ of the form $(s,t]\times A$ with
   $s<t$ and $A\in\mathcal F_s$, or the empty set when $s\ge t$.
   The time-zero generators also lie in
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$.

The family $\mathcal G$ need not itself contain the whole space, but a finite intersection
of generators is empty or again a generator, or a time-zero generator, because
$(s,u]\cap(s',u']=(s\vee s',u\wedge u']$ and $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_{s\vee s'}$
whenever $A\in\mathcal F_s$, $A'\in\mathcal F_{s'}$, while
$\{0\}\times A$ is disjoint from every interval generator, including
$(0,u]\times A'$. Two time-zero generators intersect in
$\{0\}\times(A\cap A')$ with $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_0$.
Thus the family consisting of the whole space
together with finite intersections of generators is a pi-system generating
$\mathcal P$; this is the structural fact used by the density theorem below.

Because predictability is a measurability requirement for the joint map, it is
preserved by pointwise limits, products and linear combinations of predictable
processes. A deterministic function $h$ of time defines a predictable process
exactly when $h$ is Borel measurable: the sets $C$ for which
$C\times\Omega\in\mathcal P$ form a sigma-algebra containing the intervals
$(s,u]$ and $\{0\}$, hence all Borel sets. Conversely, take any fixed
$\omega\in\Omega$ (a probability space is nonempty) and use the Borel
time-section property from 3(a) on every inverse image of an open set.
This single choice uses no choice axiom. In particular the
indicators $1_{[0,u]}$ and $1_{(0,u]}$ are predictable for every deterministic
$u\ge0$, and the process $s\mapsto 1_{s\le\tau(\omega)}$ for a stopping time
$\tau$ [[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]] is predictable, since
$$\{(s,\omega):s>\tau(\omega)\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}(q,\infty)\times\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}\bigcup_{n>q}(q,n]\times\{\tau<q\}$$
is a countable union of generators: for rational $q>0$ one has
$\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q'<q,\ q'\in\mathbb Q}\{\tau\le q'\}\in\mathcal F_q$. The
complement of that set inside $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$ is the event of the
indicator, so $1_{[0,\tau]}$ is predictable; its left-continuity in the time
variable is the visual form of the same computation.

No completeness of the filtration and no right continuity of $(\mathcal F_t)$
is used or assumed. Apart from the inherited ambient assumption just recorded,
the constructions in this definition are choice-free.

Assume AC. On a usual filtered probability space let $W$ be a standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion relative to that filtration: $W$ is adapted, and $W_t-W_s$ is independent of $\mathcal F_s$ with law $N(0,(t-s)I_m)$ for $s<t$. Let
$$Z_t=Z_0+\int_0^t\beta_sds+\int_0^t\Sigma_sdW_s,\qquad 0\le t\le T<\infty,$$
be a continuous $\mathbb R^d$-valued Itô process, with finite $\mathcal F_0$-measurable $Z_0$, progressively measurable $\beta$ and predictable $\Sigma$, and $\int_0^T(|\beta_s|+\|\Sigma_s\|_{\mathrm{HS}}^2)ds<\infty$ almost surely. Suppose $a_s=\tfrac12\Sigma_s\Sigma_s^{\mathsf T}\ge\kappa I$ for $dt\otimes P$-almost every $(s,\omega)$, for a constant $\kappa>0$. For every stopping time $\gamma\le T$ with
$$E\int_0^\gamma(|\beta_s|+\operatorname{tr}a_s)ds<\infty,$$
the finite Borel measure $\mu_\gamma(E)=E\int_0^\gamma1_E(s,Z_s)ds$ is absolutely continuous with respect to $(d+1)$-dimensional Lebesgue measure. In particular there are stopping times $\gamma_n\uparrow T$ almost surely with this property. No moment assumption on $Z_0$ is required.

derivations.claim: For $u<v$, the joint density of $(X_{T-v},X_{T-u})$ is $p_{T-v}(x)q(T-v,x;T-u,y)$. Dividing by the strictly positive later marginal $p_{T-u}(y)$ gives the conditional law of $X_{T-v}$ given $X_{T-u}=y$, exactly $K_{u,v}(y,dx)$. Its normalization and reverse Chapman–Kolmogorov identity follow from [F1], so $Y$ is Markov with those transitions.

Choose an auxiliary nonexplosive continuous solution $Z$ of the assumed reverse martingale problem, with initial density $p_T$. First work in the usual augmentation and normalize continuous paths on its initial-measurable null exceptional set. The stopped event-test argument in [F5] preserves the given continuous local martingales in this augmentation. Compact coordinate cutoffs give $Z=Z_0+\int\widetilde b\,du+N$ locally in state, with $N$ a continuous local martingale. Coordinate-product cutoffs and [F4] identify $[N]_u=\int_0^u a_{T-v}(Z_v)dv$: subtract the two product compensators and use that a continuous finite-variation local martingale is constant. The compact-test integrals make the local drift and trace integrals finite; nonexplosion and continuity exhaust the finite interval, without a bound on $Z_0$. Left-step approximations as in [F6] give a predictable version of $\sigma_{T-u}(Z_u)$, and [F5] constructs the auxiliary Brownian Itô representation with the same drift and bracket. If $C=\sup\|\sigma^{-1}\|$, then $a\ge C^{-2}I$. Stop when $|Z|$ or the accumulated drift-plus-trace energy reaches $n$; the stops exhaust $T$ and the expected stopped variation and trace are finite. Thus [F7] supplies their occupation absolute continuity. Apply [F2], using only the original classical forward equations for $q,p$ and the actual forward path continuity: it identifies the continuous path law, all marginals and Bayes kernels of $Z$ with those of $Y$. For the SDE conclusion, only this path-law identification is used from [F2]; the compact-test identities for $Y$ are transferred on the usual augmented canonical filtration below.

Carry the continuous path law of $Y$ to the canonical space $C([0,T],\mathbb R^d)$ and use its usual augmented coordinate filtration. The law identification in [F2] transfers the compact-test stopped event identities there, where paths are everywhere continuous; normalize the continuous compensated processes before using [F4]. Pulling these versions back to the usual augmentation of the given reversed filtration preserves the identities. All stopping in this step is in that augmentation. Fix $R$ and stop when $|Y|$ first reaches $R$. Compactly supported cutoffs equal to $x_i$ and $x_ix_j$ on the ball of radius $R$ turn the compact-test martingale identities into coordinate and coordinate-product identities. Subtracting the finite-variation drift in each coordinate identity gives continuous local martingales $M^i$. The product formula in [F4] shows that $Y_iY_j-Y_i(0)Y_j(0)-\int_0^{\cdot}(\widetilde b_iY_j+\widetilde b_jY_i)dr-[M_i,M_j]$ is a local martingale. The coordinate-product test shows that the same expression with $\int_0^{\cdot}a_{ij}(T-r,Y_r)dr$ in place of $[M_i,M_j]$ is a local martingale. Their difference is a continuous finite-variation local martingale, hence constant by [F4]; it starts at zero. Thus $[M_i,M_j]_u=\int_0^u a_{ij}(T-r,Y_r)dr$. Letting $R\uparrow\infty$ is valid because the assumed solution is nonexplosive.

To handle the Borel coefficients allowed by the SDE data, choose the predictable representative $\widehat Y$ obtained as follows: take left-step approximations with coefficients $Y_{kT/2^n}$, set their time-zero value to $Y_0$, and take their pointwise limit where finite and $0$ otherwise. These maps are predictable by [F6] and agree with $Y$ at every time on its common continuity event. The pair $(r,\widehat Y_r)$ is predictable, so the joint Borel coefficient gives a predictable matrix $\Sigma_r=\sigma_{T-r}(\widehat Y_r)$; inversion is Borel on invertible matrices, and $\|\Sigma_r^{-1}\|$ is uniformly bounded. Step 3.2 gives $\int_0^T\|\Sigma_r\|_F^2dr=\operatorname{tr}[M]_T<\infty$ almost surely, as well as $[M]_u=\int_0^u\Sigma_r\Sigma_r^{\mathsf T}dr$. Apply [F5] first in the augmented filtration to construct $B=\int\Sigma^{-1}dM$ and prove $M=\int\Sigma\,dB$. To recover an original-adapted Brownian version, use the original predictable sigma-algebra for its elementary approximants, as in [F5], proof 1.2 and 3.1. The original-adapted compensated coordinates are defined using the progressive left-step representative of $Y$ and its drift integral (with zero assigned when that integral is not finite); on the common full event they equal the normalized coordinates. Choose increasing augmented localizers with failure probabilities at most $2^{-n}$ and original elementary inverse-coefficient approximants with stopped sup-error probabilities at most $2^{-n}$ at tolerance $2^{-n}$. Their unstopped sums against those original coordinates are original-adapted and converge uniformly almost surely to the constructed $B$. Defining the limit at each time when finite and zero otherwise gives an original-adapted version. Its increments are Brownian and independent of the earlier original sigma-algebra, a sub-sigma-algebra of the augmented one. Since $\widehat Y=Y$ on a common full event, this is the displayed reverse SDE with its original Borel coefficient. The assumed well-posedness and nonexplosion of the reverse martingale problem identify its law uniquely and complete the theorem.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge1$, $T>0$, and let $\mu$ be a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R^d$ supported in the closed ball $\overline B(0,R)$ for some finite $R\ge0$. Let $g:[0,T]\to(0,\infty)$ be continuously differentiable with $0<g_{\min}\le g(t)\le g_{\max}<\infty$, and set $v(t)=\int_0^t g(r)^2\,dr$. On a complete filtered probability space with the usual conditions, take $X_0$ with law $\mu$, measurable at time zero and independent of the future Brownian increments. Let $W$ be a standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion adapted to the filtration, with $W_t-W_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and distributed as $N_d(0,(t-s)I_d)$ for every $0\le s<t\le T$. Let $X$ be the strong solution of $dX_t=g(t)\,dW_t$ with initial value $X_0$. For $a>0$ define the product Gaussian density $\phi_a(z)=\prod_{j=1}^d(2\pi a)^{-1/2}\exp(-z_j^2/(2a))$. For $t>0$ and $0\le s<t\le T$, define

$$p_t(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}\phi_{v(t)}(x-z)\,\mu(dz),\qquad q(s,x;t,y)=\phi_{v(t)-v(s)}(y-x).$$

Then $p_t$ is a finite, strictly positive, normalized Lebesgue density of the law of $X_t$. For each $x$, $q(s,x;t,\cdot)$ is a finite, strictly positive, normalized Lebesgue density, and for all Borel sets $A,B\subseteq\mathbb R^d$,

$$P(X_s\in A,\ X_t\in B)=\int_A\int_B q(s,x;t,y)\,dy\,\mu_s(dx),\qquad \mu_s:=\operatorname{Law}(X_s).$$

For $0\le s<r<t\le T$, these transition densities satisfy

$$\int_{\mathbb R^d}q(s,x;r,z)q(r,z;t,y)\,dz=q(s,x;t,y)\qquad(x,y\in\mathbb R^d).$$

No Lebesgue density for the initial law $\mu$ is assumed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix $d\ge1$, $T>0$, a finite $R\ge0$, and a Borel probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb R^d$ supported in $\overline B(0,R)$. Let $g:[0,T]\to(0,\infty)$ be continuously differentiable with $0<g_{\min}\le g(t)\le g_{\max}<\infty$, and set $v(t)=\int_0^t g(r)^2\,dr$. On a complete filtered probability space with the usual conditions, let $X_0$ be measurable at time zero with law $\mu$ and independent of future Brownian increments. Let $W$ be a standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion adapted to the filtration, with $W_t-W_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ for every $s<t$, and let $X$ be the unique strong solution of $X_t=X_0+\int_0^t g(r)\,dW_r$. For $a>0$ define $\phi_a(z)=\prod_{j=1}^d(2\pi a)^{-1/2}\exp(-z_j^2/(2a))$. For $t>0$ set

$$p_t(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}\phi_{v(t)}(x-z)\,\mu(dz),$$

and set $\mu_0=\mu$. Let $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$ denote the real infinitely differentiable functions with compact support. For every $t>0$, $p_t$ is positive and infinitely differentiable in $x$. On each interval $[\epsilon,T]$ with $0<\epsilon<T$, it is continuously differentiable in time and satisfies

$$\partial_t p_t(x)=\frac{g(t)^2}{2}\Delta_xp_t(x),\qquad \Delta_x=\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_{x_j}^2.$$

A family $(\nu_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ of Borel probability measures is narrowly continuous when $t\mapsto\int f\,d\nu_t$ is continuous for every bounded continuous real function $f$. It is a weak forward solution with initial law $\mu$ when it is narrowly continuous, $\nu_0=\mu$, and, for every $t\in[0,T]$ and every real-valued function $\psi:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ with continuous first time derivative and continuous spatial derivatives through order two, whose spatial support lies in one compact set for all $s$, it satisfies

$$\int_{\mathbb R^d}\psi(t,x)\,\nu_t(dx)-\int_{\mathbb R^d}\psi(0,x)\,\mu(dx)=\int_0^t\int_{\mathbb R^d}\left(\partial_s\psi(s,x)+\frac{g(s)^2}{2}\Delta_x\psi(s,x)\right)\nu_s(dx)\,ds.$$

Then $(\mu_t)_{0\le t\le T}$, where $\mu_t(dx)=p_t(x)\,dx$ for $t>0$ and $\mu_0=\mu$, is the unique narrowly continuous weak forward solution with initial law $\mu$. No density for $\mu$ at $t=0$ is asserted.

For $a>0$, define the product Gaussian density $\phi_a(z)=\prod_{j=1}^d(2\pi a)^{-1/2}\exp(-z_j^2/(2a))$. The operator norm below is induced by the Euclidean norm on $\mathbb R^d$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the hypotheses of the compactly supported Gaussian smoothing setup: $d\ge1$, $T>0$, $\mu$ is a Borel probability measure supported in $\overline B(0,R)$ for finite $R\ge0$, $g:[0,T]\to(0,\infty)$ is continuously differentiable with $0<g_{\min}\le g(t)\le g_{\max}<\infty$, $v(t)=\int_0^t g(r)^2\,dr$, and $p_t(x)=\int\phi_{v(t)}(x-z)\,\mu(dz)$ for $t>0$. Fix $0<\epsilon<T$. For $t\in[\epsilon,T]$ and $x\in\mathbb R^d$, define the probability measure

$$\nu_{t,x}(dz)=\frac{\phi_{v(t)}(x-z)}{p_t(x)}\,\mu(dz),\qquad m_{t,x}=\int z\,\nu_{t,x}(dz),$$

and the matrix

$$C_{t,x}=\int (z-m_{t,x})(z-m_{t,x})^{\mathsf T}\,\nu_{t,x}(dz).$$

The density $p_t$ is positive and smooth, and its score $s_t(x):=\nabla_x\log p_t(x)$ satisfies

$$s_t(x)=-\frac{x-m_{t,x}}{v(t)},\qquad D_xs_t(x)=-\frac{I_d}{v(t)}+\frac{C_{t,x}}{v(t)^2}.$$

For all $t\in[\epsilon,T]$ and $x,y\in\mathbb R^d$,

$$\|D_xs_t(x)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\frac1{v(\epsilon)}+\frac{R^2}{v(\epsilon)^2},\qquad |s_t(x)|\le\frac{|x|+R}{v(\epsilon)},$$

so $s_t$ is globally Lipschitz in $x$, uniformly over this truncated time interval, with Lipschitz constant at most $1/v(\epsilon)+R^2/v(\epsilon)^2$. No such bound is asserted uniformly as $\epsilon\downarrow0$.

2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Bayes' formula gives the reversed conditional law of $X_{T-v}$ given $X_{T-u}=y$ as $K_{u,v}(y,dx)$; the density supplier's marginal identity normalizes it, and [F3] gives reverse Chapman–Kolmogorov. Put $t=T-u$ and $\delta v=v(t)-v(t-h)$ for $h>0$. For $u+h\le T-\epsilon$, the reverse transition formula gives $\displaystyle K_{u,u+h}\varphi(y)=\frac{1}{p_t(y)}\int \varphi(x)p_{t-h}(x)\phi_{\delta v}(y-x)\,dx.$ The heat-kernel expansion, justified on the compact support of $\varphi$ by [F1, F4], is $\displaystyle \int \varphi(x)p_{t-h}(x)\phi_{\delta v}(y-x)dx=p_t(y)\varphi(y)+\frac{\delta v}{2}\left(\Delta(p_t\varphi)(y)-\varphi(y)\Delta p_t(y)\right)+o(\delta v).$ Since $\delta v/h\to g(t)^2$, the product rule gives $\displaystyle \lim_{h\downarrow0}\frac{K_{u,u+h}\varphi(y)-\varphi(y)}h=g(t)^2\left(\nabla\log p_t(y)\cdot\nabla\varphi(y)+\tfrac12\Delta\varphi(y)\right)=\widetilde L_u\varphi(y).$ The remainder is locally uniform in $y$ and dominated on the compact test support because $t\ge\epsilon$.

Fix $u$, put $b=T-u$, and write $P_cf=\phi_c*f$. For $r>u$, put $a=T-r$. The explicit kernel gives $K_{u,r}\varphi(y)=P_{v(b)-v(a)}(p_a\varphi)(y)/p_b(y)$. Differentiate in $r$, using the heat equation and integrating the Gaussian Laplacian onto the compactly supported function $p_a\varphi$, to obtain $\displaystyle \partial_rK_{u,r}\varphi(y)=\frac{g(a)^2}{2p_b(y)}P_{v(b)-v(a)}\!\left(\Delta(p_a\varphi)-\varphi\Delta p_a\right)(y)=K_{u,r}(\widetilde L_r\varphi)(y).$ Away from $r=u$, differentiation is justified by [F4]: the variance is positive, the spatial support is fixed compact, and $p_a,\partial_a p_a$ and the needed state derivatives are uniformly bounded there for $a\ge\epsilon$. The product rule gives the last equality. By [F2], $|\widetilde L_r\varphi(x)|\le C$ uniformly in $x,r$ on the truncated interval, so the probability-kernel property bounds the derivative by $C$. Integrate from $u+\delta$ to $v$ and let $\delta\downarrow0$: step 1.2 gives $K_{u,u+\delta}\varphi(y)\to\varphi(y)$, while the bound $C$ controls the omitted integral. Thus $K_{u,v}\varphi-\varphi=\int_u^vK_{u,r}(\widetilde L_r\varphi)dr$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix $d\ge1$, $T>0$, a finite $R\ge0$, and a Borel probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb R^d$ supported in $\overline B(0,R)$. Let $g:[0,T]\to(0,\infty)$ be continuously differentiable with $0<g_{\min}\le g(t)\le g_{\max}<\infty$, and set $v(t)=\int_0^t g(r)^2\,dr$. On a complete filtered probability space with the usual conditions, let $X_0$ be measurable at time zero with law $\mu$ and independent of future Brownian increments. Let $W$ be a standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion adapted to the filtration, with $W_t-W_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ for every $s<t$, and let $X$ be the unique strong solution of $X_t=X_0+\int_0^t g(r)\,dW_r$. For $a>0$ define $\phi_a(z)=\prod_{j=1}^d(2\pi a)^{-1/2}\exp(-z_j^2/(2a))$. For $t>0$ set

$$p_t(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}\phi_{v(t)}(x-z)\,\mu(dz),$$

and set $\mu_0=\mu$. Let $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$ denote the real infinitely differentiable functions with compact support. For every $t>0$, $p_t$ is positive and infinitely differentiable in $x$. On each interval $[\epsilon,T]$ with $0<\epsilon<T$, it is continuously differentiable in time and satisfies

$$\partial_t p_t(x)=\frac{g(t)^2}{2}\Delta_xp_t(x),\qquad \Delta_x=\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_{x_j}^2.$$

A family $(\nu_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ of Borel probability measures is narrowly continuous when $t\mapsto\int f\,d\nu_t$ is continuous for every bounded continuous real function $f$. It is a weak forward solution with initial law $\mu$ when it is narrowly continuous, $\nu_0=\mu$, and, for every $t\in[0,T]$ and every real-valued function $\psi:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ with continuous first time derivative and continuous spatial derivatives through order two, whose spatial support lies in one compact set for all $s$, it satisfies

$$\int_{\mathbb R^d}\psi(t,x)\,\nu_t(dx)-\int_{\mathbb R^d}\psi(0,x)\,\mu(dx)=\int_0^t\int_{\mathbb R^d}\left(\partial_s\psi(s,x)+\frac{g(s)^2}{2}\Delta_x\psi(s,x)\right)\nu_s(dx)\,ds.$$

Then $(\mu_t)_{0\le t\le T}$, where $\mu_t(dx)=p_t(x)\,dx$ for $t>0$ and $\mu_0=\mu$, is the unique narrowly continuous weak forward solution with initial law $\mu$. No density for $\mu$ at $t=0$ is asserted.

Assume AC. Fix $T>0$, a compactly supported Borel probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb R^d$, a continuously differentiable function $g:[0,T]\to(0,\infty)$ bounded above and away from zero, and $v(t)=\int_0^t g(r)^2dr$. For $t>0$ put
$$p_t(y)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}\phi_{v(t)}(y-z)\,\mu(dz),\qquad q(s,x;t,y)=\phi_{v(t)-v(s)}(y-x)\quad(0\le s<t\le T),$$
where $\phi_a$ is the centered Gaussian density with covariance $aI_d$. Put $p_0=\mu$ as a probability measure, not as a Lebesgue density. For $0\le u<v<T$ define
$$K_{u,v}(y,dx)=\frac{p_{T-v}(x)q(T-v,x;T-u,y)}{p_{T-u}(y)}\,dx,$$
and for $0\le u<T$ at the singular data endpoint define
$$K_{u,T}(y,A)=\frac{\int_A q(0,x;T-u,y)\,\mu(dx)}{p_{T-u}(y)}\quad(A\text{ Borel}).$$
Set $K_{u,u}(y,\cdot)=\delta_y$. These are the Bayes-reversed kernels of the additive Gaussian smoothing process, including the posterior kernel at the original data time; no density for $\mu$ is required.

Assume AC and the compactly supported Gaussian smoothing setup: $X_t=X_0+\int_0^t g(r)dW_r$, with $X_0\sim\mu$ compactly supported, scalar $g\in C^1([0,T])$ bounded above and away from zero, $v(t)=\int_0^t g(r)^2dr$, $p_t(x)=\int\phi_{v(t)}(x-z)\mu(dz)$ for $t>0$, and forward transition density $q(s,x;t,y)=\phi_{v(t)-v(s)}(y-x)$. Fix $0<\epsilon<T$, put $Y_u=X_{T-u}$ for $0\le u\le T-\epsilon$, and use the Bayes-reversed kernels from the preceding definition. For $s_t=\nabla\log p_t$, define
$$\widetilde L_u\varphi(y)=g(T-u)^2\left(s_{T-u}(y)\cdot\nabla\varphi(y)+\tfrac12\Delta\varphi(y)\right),\qquad \varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d).$$
Then $Y$ is Markov with those reversed kernels, and for every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty$ the process
$$\varphi(Y_v)-\varphi(Y_0)-\int_0^v\widetilde L_r\varphi(Y_r)\,dr,\qquad 0\le v\le T-\epsilon,$$
is a martingale in the natural reversed filtration. The assertion is restricted to forward times at least $\epsilon$; it makes no score or density claim at $t=0$.

For $a>0$, define the product Gaussian density $\phi_a(z)=\prod_{j=1}^d(2\pi a)^{-1/2}\exp(-z_j^2/(2a))$. The operator norm below is induced by the Euclidean norm on $\mathbb R^d$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the hypotheses of the compactly supported Gaussian smoothing setup: $d\ge1$, $T>0$, $\mu$ is a Borel probability measure supported in $\overline B(0,R)$ for finite $R\ge0$, $g:[0,T]\to(0,\infty)$ is continuously differentiable with $0<g_{\min}\le g(t)\le g_{\max}<\infty$, $v(t)=\int_0^t g(r)^2\,dr$, and $p_t(x)=\int\phi_{v(t)}(x-z)\,\mu(dz)$ for $t>0$. Fix $0<\epsilon<T$. For $t\in[\epsilon,T]$ and $x\in\mathbb R^d$, define the probability measure

$$\nu_{t,x}(dz)=\frac{\phi_{v(t)}(x-z)}{p_t(x)}\,\mu(dz),\qquad m_{t,x}=\int z\,\nu_{t,x}(dz),$$

and the matrix

$$C_{t,x}=\int (z-m_{t,x})(z-m_{t,x})^{\mathsf T}\,\nu_{t,x}(dz).$$

The density $p_t$ is positive and smooth, and its score $s_t(x):=\nabla_x\log p_t(x)$ satisfies

$$s_t(x)=-\frac{x-m_{t,x}}{v(t)},\qquad D_xs_t(x)=-\frac{I_d}{v(t)}+\frac{C_{t,x}}{v(t)^2}.$$

For all $t\in[\epsilon,T]$ and $x,y\in\mathbb R^d$,

$$\|D_xs_t(x)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\frac1{v(\epsilon)}+\frac{R^2}{v(\epsilon)^2},\qquad |s_t(x)|\le\frac{|x|+R}{v(\epsilon)},$$

so $s_t$ is globally Lipschitz in $x$, uniformly over this truncated time interval, with Lipschitz constant at most $1/v(\epsilon)+R^2/v(\epsilon)^2$. No such bound is asserted uniformly as $\epsilon\downarrow0$.

Assume AC. Each input local martingale below is taken with everywhere-continuous adapted paths; it suffices that its full continuity event belongs to the initial sigma-algebra, so it can first be normalized there. All pathwise stopping operations use these representatives. Let $M$ be a real continuous local martingale on $[0,T]$ with $M_0=0$, where a local martingale means that some increasing stopping times tending to $T$ make the stopped processes martingales. Then there is a unique continuous increasing process $[M]$ with $[M]_0=0$ such that the step-endpoint and partial-increment sums of squared increments along every deterministic partition sequence whose mesh tends to zero converge uniformly in probability to $[M]$. Moreover $M_t^2-[M]_t$ is a continuous local martingale. For a continuous $d$-dimensional local martingale $M$ started at zero, polarization defines continuous covariations $[M^i,M^j]$ with $M^iM^j-[M^i,M^j]$ local martingales. More generally, if $X=M+A$ and $Z=N+C$ with continuous local martingales $M,N$ and continuous finite-variation processes $A,C$, then left-step sums define the localized integrals against $M,N$ and
$$X_tZ_t-X_0Z_0=\int_0^t X_s\,dZ_s+\int_0^t Z_s\,dX_s+[M,N]_t,$$
where finite-variation integrals are pathwise Lebesgue–Stieltjes integrals and local-martingale integrals are the limits of the displayed left-step sums. Stopping a continuous local martingale at a bounded stopping time preserves its local-martingale property; if the stopped process is bounded, it is a true martingale. A continuous finite-variation local martingale is constant.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(M_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ be a continuous adapted $d$-dimensional local martingale with $M_0=0$. Let $(\sigma_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ be a continuous adapted process of invertible $d\times d$ matrices such that $\|\sigma_t^{-1}\|\le C$ for a deterministic finite constant $C$, and suppose every entry of $\sigma$ is locally square-integrable in time almost surely. Write $[M^i,M^j]$ for the continuous bracket characterized by the local-martingale property of $M^iM^j-[M^i,M^j]$, and assume
$$[M^i,M^j]_t=\int_0^t(\sigma_s\sigma_s^{\mathsf T})_{ij}\,ds\qquad(1\le i,j\le d).$$
Then the stochastic integral $B_t=\int_0^t\sigma_s^{-1}\,dM_s$, constructed as the localized $L^2$ limit of left-step sums, has a continuous version with $[B^i,B^j]_t=\delta_{ij}t$. Consequently $B$ is a standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion relative to the given filtration.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix $d\ge1$, $T>0$, and a Borel probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb R^d$ supported in $\overline B(0,R)$ for some finite $R\ge0$. Let $g:[0,T]\to(0,\infty)$ be continuously differentiable and satisfy $0<g_{\min}\le g(t)\le g_{\max}<\infty$; set $v(t)=\int_0^t g(r)^2\,dr$. On a complete filtered probability space with the usual conditions, let $X_0$ be measurable at time zero with law $\mu$ and independent of future Brownian increments. Let $W$ be a standard adapted $d$-dimensional Brownian motion whose increment $W_t-W_s$ is independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and has law $N_d(0,(t-s)I_d)$ for $0\le s<t\le T$. Let $X$ be the unique strong solution of $X_t=X_0+\int_0^t g(r)\,dW_r$, and write $\mu_t=\operatorname{Law}(X_t)$. For Borel probability laws $\alpha,\beta$ with finite second moments, write $W_2(\alpha,\beta)$ for the square root of the infimum of $\int|x-y|^2\,d\pi(x,y)$ over Borel probability couplings $\pi$ of $\alpha$ and $\beta$. For every $0<\epsilon\le T$,

$$\mathbb E|X_\epsilon-X_0|^2=d\,v(\epsilon),\qquad W_2(\mu_\epsilon,\mu)\le\sqrt{d\,v(\epsilon)}.$$

As $\epsilon\downarrow0$, $X_\epsilon\to X_0$ in probability and $\mu_\epsilon$ converges weakly to $\mu$, meaning that $\int f\,d\mu_\epsilon\to\int f\,d\mu$ for every bounded continuous real function $f$ on $\mathbb R^d$. This estimate controls endpoint truncation only: it gives no bound for learned-score error or numerical-discretization error, and asserts no density or score regularity at $\epsilon=0$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice as required by the stochastic-integral interfaces
below. Fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$ and finite integers $d,m\ge1$. Work on
a complete filtered probability space
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{0\le t\le T},P)$ whose filtration is
right-continuous and contains every $P$-null subset of $\mathcal F$ in
$\mathcal F_0$ (the usual conditions).

Let $W=(W_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ be a standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion
$d$-dimensional Brownian motion adapted to this filtration, with
$W_t-W_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and distributed as
$N_m(0,(t-s)I_m)$ for $0\le s<t\le T$. Let
$X_0:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$ be $\mathcal F_0$-measurable, satisfy
$E|X_0|^2<\infty$, and be independent of the future Brownian increments.
Explicitly, $X_0$ is independent of the sigma-algebra
$\sigma(W_t-W_0:0\le t\le T)$.

Continuity of a process means continuity on one measurable event of
probability one. We use an everywhere-continuous adapted representative: if
the chosen process is continuous only on such an event $A$, replace it off $A$
by its initial value. Since $A^c$ is a null set and the filtration is complete,
$A^c\in\mathcal F_0$; the replacement preserves adaptedness and changes the
SDE identity only on a null event, hence preserves it up to
indistinguishability.

The drift and diffusion coefficients are jointly Borel maps
$$b:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d,\qquad \sigma:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}.$$
For nonnegative finite constants $L,K$, assume for every $t\in[0,T]$ and
$x,y\in\mathbb R^d$ that
$$|b(t,x)-b(t,y)|+\|\sigma(t,x)-\sigma(t,y)\|_F\le L|x-y|,$$
$$|b(t,x)|+\|\sigma(t,x)\|_F\le K(1+|x|).$$
Here $|\cdot|$ is the Euclidean norm and
$\|A\|_F^2=\sum_{i=1}^d\sum_{k=1}^m|A^{ik}|^2$ is the Frobenius norm.

For an adapted continuous candidate $X:[0,T]\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$,
the vector Itô equation
$$X_t=X_0+\int_0^t b(s,X_s)\,ds+\left(\sum_{k=1}^m\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}(s,X_s)\,dW_s^k\right)_{i=1}^d,\qquad 0\le t\le T.$$

In particular the reverse generator has drift $\beta_u(x)=g(T-u)^2\nabla\log p_{T-u}(x)$ and diffusion matrix $a_u(x)=g(T-u)^2I_d$.

First pass to the usual augmentation of the reversed filtration and normalize the continuous processes on their common null exceptional set in its initial sigma-algebra. The continuous compact-test martingales in [F2] remain martingales there: on the finite horizon each is a conditional expectation of its integrable terminal value, hence uniformly integrable; passing its event identities along times decreasing to a fixed time gives the right-continuous extension, and completion adds only null-event identities. All stopping and product-formula uses below are on these normalized representatives. Fix $R_1$ and stop when $|Y|$ reaches $R_1$. Compactly supported cutoffs equal to $x_i$ and $x_ix_j$ on that ball turn the identities in [F2] into coordinate and coordinate-product martingales. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Let $m,d\ge1$ be finite
integers, let $B=(B^1,\dots,B^m)$ be a standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion,
and let $X$ be an $\mathbb R^d$-valued continuous Brownian Ito process
$$X^i_t=X^i_0+\int_0^tb^i_s\,ds+\sum_{k=1}^m\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s, \qquad i=1,\dots,d,$$
in the sense of [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]], including its usual-filtration and almost-sure coefficient-integrability conventions. Let
$f\in C^{1,2}([0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^d)$, meaning that $f,\partial_tf$,
$\partial_if$ and $\partial_i\partial_jf$ ($1\le i,j\le d$) exist and are
continuous. Then, up to indistinguishability, for every $t\ge0$
$$f(t,X_t)=f(0,X_0)+\int_0^t\Bigl(\partial_tf+\sum_ib^i\partial_if+\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}\partial_i\partial_jf\Bigr)(s,X_s)\,ds+\sum_{i,k}\int_0^t\partial_if(s,X_s)\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s,$$
For the displayed integrands, intersect the measurable full events of continuity and the decomposition of $X$, and of coefficient integrability at all integer horizons. Its null complement belongs to $\mathcal F_0$ under the usual conditions. Set $X,X_0,b,\sigma$ to zero there. These representatives preserve all coefficient classes and the decomposition up to indistinguishability, with everywhere continuous $X$ and everywhere locally finite coefficient path integrals. All displayed integrands use these representatives.

The stochastic integrals are localized Ito integrals of the predictable
locally square-integrable integrands $\partial_if(\cdot,X)\sigma^{ik}$, and
$(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}_s=\sum_k\sigma^{ik}_s\sigma^{jk}_s$. In
differential form,
$df(t,X_t)=\bigl(\partial_tf+\sum_ib^i\partial_if+\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}\partial_i\partial_jf\bigr)(t,X_t)\,dt+\sum_{i,k}\partial_if(t,X_t)\sigma^{ik}_t\,dB^k_t$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice (The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Let $X_t$ have continuous paths on $[0,T]$ and be Markov on $\mathbb R^d$, meaning its conditional future law given the past depends only on its current state; nonexplosive means it remains in $\mathbb R^d$ throughout this finite interval. Let it have forward generator
$$L_t\phi=b_t\cdot\nabla\phi+\tfrac12a_t:D^2\phi,$$
where $a_t=\sigma_t\sigma_t^{\mathsf T}$ is symmetric and $L_t^*r=-\partial_i(b_{t,i}r)+\tfrac12\partial_i\partial_j(a_{t,ij}r)$. Assume positive $C^{1,2}$ marginal densities $p_t$ and positive transition densities $q(s,x;t,y)$ satisfy the marginal identity and Chapman–Kolmogorov identity, and that $\partial_t p_t=L_t^*p_t$ and $\partial_tq(s,x;t,y)=L_t^{*,y}q(s,x;t,y)$ hold classically. Assume for every $\phi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$ that the transition-density integrals can be differentiated in time, the resulting derivatives are integrable, and integration by parts in the state variable has no boundary term.

Define $K_{u,v}$ by the Bayes-reversed kernel formula for $0\le u\le v\le T$. Then the reversed process $Y_u=X_{T-u}$ is Markov with transitions $K_{u,v}$. For compact smooth $\phi$, define the formal adjoint candidate operator
$$\widetilde L_u\phi(y)=\frac{L_{T-u}^*(p_{T-u}\phi)(y)-\phi(y)L_{T-u}^*p_{T-u}(y)}{p_{T-u}(y)}.$$
The product rule gives the identity
$$\widetilde L_u\phi=\widetilde b_u\cdot\nabla\phi+\tfrac12a_{T-u}:D^2\phi,\qquad \widetilde b_u=-b_{T-u}+\nabla\!\cdot a_{T-u}+a_{T-u}\nabla\log p_{T-u},$$
with $(\nabla\!\cdot a)_i=\sum_j\partial_j a_{ij}$. These Bayes-kernel and formal product identities use only the preceding hypotheses.

For the martingale conclusion, impose additionally the following forward analytic conditions. For every compact $K\subset\mathbb R^d$, with $A_{ij}(r,x)=p_r(x)a_{r,ij}(x)$ and $C_i=-p_rb_{r,i}+\sum_j\partial_jA_{ij}$,
$$\int_0^T\!\int_K\left[\sum_i|C_i|+\sum_{i,j}p_r|a_{r,ij}|\right]dx\,dr<\infty.$$
For every $t\in(0,T]$ and $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$, the actual forward conditional expectation $g_{t,f}(r,x)=\int q(r,x;t,y)f(y)dy$ has a $C^{1,2}$ version on $(0,t)\times\mathbb R^d$, solves $\partial_rg_{t,f}+L_rg_{t,f}=0$, and satisfies $\int p_r\phi L_rg_{t,f}dx=\int g_{t,f}L_r^*(p_r\phi)dx$ for each compact smooth $\phi$ and almost every $r<t$. All coefficient expressions in these conditions are Borel. These are conditions on the original forward transition family.

Under these additional forward analytic conditions, $\widetilde L_u$ is the extended martingale generator of $Y$: for its natural reversed filtration $\mathcal G_u=\sigma(Y_r:0\le r\le u)$, every compact-test compensated process is a martingale, hence a local martingale. The unconditional formal candidate identity alone makes no martingale or pointwise transition-quotient assertion.

right-continuous and contains every $P$-null subset of $\mathcal F$ in
$\mathcal F_0$ (the usual conditions).
