and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim: By [F1] and the mixture normalization result [F2], each $p_t$ is a probability density with respect to $\lambda$. Positivity makes $u^m=J/p$ well-defined on the open time interval. The hypotheses on $G_K$ are exactly the local domination assumptions of [F3], so the explicitly assumed classical coordinate equation passes to the marginal and $\partial_tp+\operatorname{div}_x(pu^m)=0$.

Let $Q$ be the measure on time, state, and endpoint variables with density $\rho_t(x\mid x_1)$ relative to $dt\,\lambda(dx)\,\pi(dx_1)$. Product measurability from [F1], conditional normalization, and Tonelli [F14] show that $Q$ has total mass one and that its time-state marginal has density $p_t(x)$ relative to $dt\,\lambda(dx)$. In particular, Tonelli gives $\mathcal L_M(\theta)=\int\|v-u^m\|_2^2\,dQ$, so the finite marginal loss makes $v-u^m$ square-integrable under $Q$. The same identity gives $C=\int\|u^c-u^m\|_2^2\,dQ$, so $u^c-u^m$ is square-integrable under $Q$. By Euclidean Cauchy–Schwarz [F9] and random-variable Cauchy–Schwarz [F10], their inner-product term is integrable. At every $t,x$ where the integrals are defined, the definition of $J_t$ and $u^m_t$ gives $$\int_{\mathbb R^d}\rho_t(x\mid x_1)\bigl(u^c_t(x\mid x_1)-u^m_t(x)\bigr)\,\pi(dx_1)=J_t(x)-p_t(x)u^m_t(x)=0.$$ Expanding $v-u^c=(v-u^m)+(u^m-u^c)$ by bilinearity [F4], integrating first over $x_1$, and using Fubini [F5] for the integrable cross term gives $$\mathcal L_C(\theta)=\mathcal L_M(\theta)+\int_0^1\!\int\!\int\rho_t(x\mid x_1)\|u^c_t(x\mid x_1)-u^m_t(x)\|_2^2\,\pi(dx_1)\lambda(dx)dt.$$ The last integral is independent of $\theta$ and is the finite constant $C$ defined in the Statement.

Fix $\theta_0\in\Theta$ and choose a compact parameter ball $H\subset\Theta$ whose interior contains $\theta_0$. For any $\theta\in\operatorname{int}H$, fix $w$ to be either $u^c_t(x\mid x_1)$ or $u^m_t(x)$ and put $a_\theta:=v(t,x;\theta)-w$. For sufficiently small nonzero $\varepsilon$ with $\theta+\varepsilon e_j\in H$, bilinearity and symmetry [F4] give $$\|a_{\theta+\varepsilon e_j}\|_2^2-\|a_\theta\|_2^2=\langle a_{\theta+\varepsilon e_j}-a_\theta,a_{\theta+\varepsilon e_j}+a_\theta\rangle.$$ Dividing by $\varepsilon$ and taking the limit, differentiability of $v$ yields $$\partial_{\theta_j}\|v(t,x;\theta)-w\|_2^2=2\langle\partial_{\theta_j}v(t,x;\theta),v(t,x;\theta)-w\rangle.$$ The functions $G^C_{H,j}$ and $G^M_{H,j}$ dominate the weighted derivatives on $H$. For a sequence of nonzero increments tending to zero in coordinate $j$, the mean value theorem [F6] bounds the weighted difference quotients by the same majorants; the pointwise quotients converge to the displayed derivatives. Dominated convergence [F7] therefore differentiates both objectives under their integrals. Applying the same domination to convergent parameter sequences shows the derivative integrals are continuous in $\theta$, so both objectives are $C^1$.

Step 1.2 proves $\mathcal L_C(\theta)=\mathcal L_M(\theta)+C$ for every $\theta$, with one finite constant independent of $\theta$. Both sides are differentiable by step 1.3, so differentiating this identity gives $\nabla_\theta\mathcal L_C(\theta)=\nabla_\theta\mathcal L_M(\theta)$.

all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The law of a random element is a probability measure makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in The Dirac set function at a point.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$, $m\in\mathbb R^d$, and let $\Sigma$ be a real symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then its law has Lebesgue density

$$\psi_t(z\mid x_1):=\sigma_t(x_1)z+\mu_t(x_1).$$
For each $t$, this map is a diffeomorphism with inverse $\psi_t^{-1}(x\mid x_1)=(x-\mu_t(x_1))/\sigma_t(x_1)$. The unique vector field satisfying
$$\frac{d}{dt}\psi_t(z\mid x_1)=u_t(\psi_t(z\mid x_1)\mid x_1)$$
for every $z\in\mathbb R^d$ is
$$u_t(x\mid x_1)=\frac{\dot\sigma_t(x_1)}{\sigma_t(x_1)}(x-\mu_t(x_1))+\dot\mu_t(x_1).$$

Let $\mu$ be a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R^d$ with finite second moment, mean $\int x\,\mu(dx)=0$, and $m_2:=\int\|x\|_2^2\,\mu(dx)<\infty$. Fix $a\in\mathbb R^d$ and $s>0$, define $T(x):=a+sx$, and let $
u$ be the law of $T(X)$ when $X$ has law $\mu$. For every Borel probability measure $\gamma$ on $\mathbb R^d	imes\mathbb R^d$ whose coordinate marginals are $\mu$ and $
u$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^d	imes\mathbb R^d}\|y-x\|_2^2\,\gamma(dx,dy)\ \ge\ \|a\|_2^2+(1-s)^2m_2.$$
The law of $(X,T(X))$ under $\mu$ attains equality. Thus $T$ is an optimal transport map for the squared Euclidean cost between $\mu$ and its translated dilation $
u$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ (The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann),
On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of The vector space $F^{X}$ of all functions $X \to F$ with pointwise operations, and $F^{n}$ as the case $X = n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations

same set that $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of Finite sums and finite products, by recursion applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 4 and
Squares of nonzero elements are positive, the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
Integer powers $a^m$) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root (Square roots exist: a unique $\sqrt{a} \ge 0$ with $(\sqrt{a})^2 = a$; the positives are $\{x^2 : x \neq 0\}$).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space (The standard list $e : n \to F^{n}$ with $e_i(i) = 1_F$ and $e_i(j) = 0_F$ for $j \ne i$ is an ordered basis of $F^{n}$; hence $\dim_F F^{n} = n$, and $F^{0}$ is the zero space with basis $\varnothing$ and dimension $0$ clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
$\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and Conventions of this page, the standing $n \ge 1$ hypothesis, and what is taken up elsewhere in the reading order lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ (Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   (Squares of nonzero elements are positive), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of A norm on a real vector space, the induced metric, and the dictionary with the metric axioms
is proved in Cauchy-Schwarz $\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \le \lVert x\rVert_2\lVert y\rVert_2$ with its equality case, the triangle inequality for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$, the parallelogram law and polarisation, where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
(Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of If $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L \ne 0$ then $|f| > |L|/2$ on a punctured neighbourhood of $c$; in particular if $L > 0$ then $f > L/2 > 0$ there applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
Carathéodory's characterisation: $f$ is differentiable at $c$ if and only if there is $\varphi : A \to \mathbb{R}$, continuous at $c$, with $f(x) - f(c) = \varphi(x)(x - c)$ for every $x \in A$, and then $\varphi$ is unique and $\varphi(c) = f'(c)$.** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of Sums, scalar multiples, products, absolute values, maxima, minima and quotients with nonvanishing denominator of continuous functions are continuous, as are constants, the identity and every polynomial function.

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

derivations.claim: Since $\sigma_t=(1-t)+t\sigma_{\min}>0$, every affine map $\psi_t$ is invertible. For each $v\in\mathbb R^d$, the projection of $\psi_t(Z\mid x_1)$ is $v^T\mu_t(x_1)+\sigma_t v^TZ$. By [F1], this is normal with mean $v^T\mu_t(x_1)$ and variance $\sigma_t^2\|v\|_2^2$. Thus $P_t(\cdot\mid x_1)$ is multivariate normal with mean $\mu_t(x_1)$ and covariance $\sigma_t^2I_d$, which is positive definite.

By [F2], the Lebesgue density of $P_t(\cdot\mid x_1)$ is $$\rho_t(x\mid x_1)=(2\pi\sigma_t^2)^{-d/2} \exp\!\left(-\frac{\|x-\mu_t(x_1)\|_2^2}{2\sigma_t^2}\right).$$ It integrates to one for every $x_1$ and is continuous in $(t,x,x_1)$ because $\sigma_t>0$. Therefore for any endpoint probability law $\pi$ it is product-measurable and satisfies the conditional-density requirement in [[def-probability-path-and-velocity-field]].

We have $\dot\mu_t(x_1)=x_1$ and $\dot\sigma_t=\sigma_{\min}-1$. Applying [F3] gives $u_t(x\mid x_1)=x_1+\frac{\sigma_{\min}-1}{\sigma_t}(x-tx_1)$. The density formula in step 1.2 and this affine field are continuously differentiable in $(t,x)$ by the algebra, chain, and exponential derivative rules [F6, F7, F8]. Thus $\rho_t$ and each component of $\rho_tu_t$ meet the regularity clauses of the conditional probability-path definition.
At $t=0$ the parameters are $\mu_0=0,\sigma_0=1$; at $t=1$ they are $\mu_1=x_1,\sigma_1=\sigma_{\min}$. Thus the endpoints are the standard Gaussian law and the law of $x_1+\sigma_{\min}Z$.

Put $r=x-tx_1$ and write $\dot\sigma=\sigma_{\min}-1$. We have $\partial_t r=-x_1$ and $\partial_t(\sigma_t^{-d})=-d\dot\sigma\sigma_t^{-d-1}$ by the product and quotient rules [F6]. Applying the chain rule [F7] to $-\|r\|_2^2/(2\sigma_t^2)$ and then the exponential derivative [F8] gives $$\partial_t\rho_t=\rho_t\left(-d\frac{\dot\sigma}{\sigma_t} +\frac{\langle r,x_1\rangle}{\sigma_t^2} +\frac{\dot\sigma\|r\|_2^2}{\sigma_t^3}\right), \qquad \nabla_x\rho_t=-\rho_t\frac{r}{\sigma_t^2}.$$ The field in step 2.1 has $\operatorname{div}_x u_t=d\dot\sigma/\sigma_t$.

The product rule gives $$\operatorname{div}_x(\rho_tu_t) =\langle\nabla_x\rho_t,u_t\rangle+\rho_t\operatorname{div}_xu_t =\rho_t\left(-\frac{\langle r,x_1\rangle}{\sigma_t^2} -\frac{\dot\sigma\|r\|_2^2}{\sigma_t^3} +d\frac{\dot\sigma}{\sigma_t}\right).$$ Adding this to $\partial_t\rho_t$ in step 3.1 cancels each term, so the conditional continuity equation holds.

The standard Gaussian vector has mean $0$ and covariance $I_d$ by [F1]. Summing its $d$ coordinate second moments gives $\int\|z\|_2^2\,N_d(0,I_d)(dz)=d$. The endpoint law is the affine image under $T(z)=x_1+\sigma_{\min}z$. Applying [F4] with $a=x_1$, $s=\sigma_{\min}$, and $m_2=d$ shows that every coupling has cost at least $\|x_1\|_2^2+d(1-\sigma_{\min})^2$, and that the law of $(Z,T(Z))$ attains equality.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge1$, fix $x_1\in\mathbb R^d$, and choose $\sigma_{\min}>0$. Let $Z$ have the standard multivariate normal law $N_d(0,I_d)$. For $t\in[0,1]$, define
$$\mu_t(x_1):=t x_1,\qquad \sigma_t:=1-(1-\sigma_{\min})t,\qquad \psi_t(z\mid x_1):=\sigma_t z+\mu_t(x_1),$$
and let $P_t(\cdot\mid x_1)$ be the law of $\psi_t(Z\mid x_1)$. Then $P_t(\cdot\mid x_1)$ is the Gaussian probability path with mean $\mu_t(x_1)$ and covariance $\sigma_t^2I_d$, and its Lebesgue density is
$$\rho_t(x\mid x_1)=(2\pi\sigma_t^2)^{-d/2} \exp\!\left(-\frac{\|x-\mu_t(x_1)\|_2^2}{2\sigma_t^2}\right).$$
A conditional velocity field for this path is
$$u_t(x\mid x_1)=\frac{\sigma_{\min}-1}{\sigma_t}(x-tx_1)+x_1.$$
For each endpoint $x_1$, these densities and fields form a conditional path in the probability-path definition; hence they can be mixed against any Borel endpoint law. At $t=0$ the law is $N_d(0,I_d)$, and at $t=1$ it is the law of $x_1+\sigma_{\min}Z$, a Gaussian with mean $x_1$ and covariance $\sigma_{\min}^2I_d$. The affine endpoint map $T(z)=x_1+\sigma_{\min}z$ is optimal for squared Euclidean cost between these two laws: every coupling has cost at least
$$\|x_1\|_2^2+d(1-\sigma_{\min})^2,$$
and the law of $(Z,T(Z))$ attains this value.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge1$, fix $x_1\in\mathbb R^d$, and choose $\sigma_{\min}>0$. Let $Z$ have the standard multivariate normal law $N_d(0,I_d)$. For $t\in[0,1]$, define
$$\mu_t(x_1):=t x_1,\qquad \sigma_t:=1-(1-\sigma_{\min})t,\qquad \psi_t(z\mid x_1):=\sigma_t z+\mu_t(x_1),$$
and let $P_t(\cdot\mid x_1)$ be the law of $\psi_t(Z\mid x_1)$. Then $P_t(\cdot\mid x_1)$ is the Gaussian probability path with mean $\mu_t(x_1)$ and covariance $\sigma_t^2I_d$, and its Lebesgue density is
$$\rho_t(x\mid x_1)=(2\pi\sigma_t^2)^{-d/2} \exp\!\left(-\frac{\|x-\mu_t(x_1)\|_2^2}{2\sigma_t^2}\right).$$
A conditional velocity field for this path is
$$u_t(x\mid x_1)=\frac{\sigma_{\min}-1}{\sigma_t}(x-tx_1)+x_1.$$
For each endpoint $x_1$, these densities and fields form a conditional path in the probability-path definition; hence they can be mixed against any Borel endpoint law. At $t=0$ the law is $N_d(0,I_d)$, and at $t=1$ it is the law of $x_1+\sigma_{\min}Z$, a Gaussian with mean $x_1$ and covariance $\sigma_{\min}^2I_d$. The affine endpoint map $T(z)=x_1+\sigma_{\min}z$ is optimal for squared Euclidean cost between these two laws: every coupling has cost at least
$$\|x_1\|_2^2+d(1-\sigma_{\min})^2,$$
and the law of $(Z,T(Z))$ attains this value.

Fix an integer $d\ge1$, a sigma-finite measure $\lambda$ on the Borel subsets of $\mathbb R^d$, and a Borel probability measure $\pi$ on $\mathbb R^d$. Here sigma-finite means that there are Borel sets $E_n$ with $\mathbb R^d=\bigcup_{n\ge1}E_n$ and $\lambda(E_n)<\infty$ for each $n$. A **conditional probability-density path** with endpoint law $\pi$ is a function measurable for $\mathcal B([0,1])\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d)\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d)$ on time, state, and endpoint variables
$$\rho:[0,1]\times\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^d\to[0,\infty]$$
such that, for every $t\in[0,1]$, $\int_{\mathbb R^d}\rho_t(x\mid x_1)\,\lambda(dx)=1$ for $\pi$-almost every endpoint $x_1$. Its **mixture function** is
$$p_t(x):=\int_{\mathbb R^d}\rho_t(x\mid x_1)\,\pi(dx_1).$$
For a vector field $u_t(x\mid x_1)=(u_t^1,\ldots,u_t^d)$ measurable for the same product sigma-algebra, call it a **conditional velocity field** for $\rho$ when, for $\pi$-almost every $x_1$, $\rho_t(\cdot\mid x_1)$ and every component of $\rho_t(\cdot\mid x_1)u_t(\cdot\mid x_1)$ are continuously differentiable in $(t,x)$ on $(0,1)\times\mathbb R^d$, the functions $\rho_t$ and $\rho_tu_t^j$ are locally integrable there with respect to $dt\,\lambda(dx)$, and
$$\int_0^1\!\int_{\mathbb R^d}\rho_t(x\mid x_1)\left(\partial_t\varphi(t,x)+\sum_{j=1}^d u_t^j(x\mid x_1)\partial_{x_j}\varphi(t,x)\right)\lambda(dx)\,dt=0$$
for every continuously differentiable real function $\varphi$ with compact support in $(0,1)\times\mathbb R^d$. Here $dt$ denotes the supplied Lebesgue measure on time, and local integrability means absolute integrability on every compact subset. This is the **conditional continuity equation** for the measures $\rho_t(\cdot\mid x_1)\lambda$. In the Lebesgue-reference case $\lambda(dx)=dx$, its classical form under the stated differentiability is
$$\partial_t\rho_t(x\mid x_1)+\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_{x_j}\!\left(\rho_t(x\mid x_1)u_t^j(x\mid x_1)\right)=0$$
on $(0,1)\times\mathbb R^d$. This unweighted divergence formula is not the convention for a general reference measure. Only the interior-time equation is imposed; no endpoint continuity or existence or uniqueness of an ODE flow is asserted. At any $(t,x)$ where $0<p_t(x)<\infty$ and the numerator is a finite componentwise Lebesgue integral, the **marginal velocity field** is
$$u_t(x):=\frac{\int_{\mathbb R^d}\rho_t(x\mid x_1)u_t(x\mid x_1)\,\pi(dx_1)}{p_t(x)}.$$
This definition assigns no value to the quotient where $p_t(x)=0$ or $p_t(x)=\infty$, or where the numerator is not finite.

Let $\lambda$, $\pi$, and $\rho$ satisfy the conditional probability-density path definition, and for each $t\in[0,1]$ set $p_t(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}\rho_t(x\mid x_1)\,\pi(dx_1)$. Then $p_t$ is a nonnegative measurable function and $\int_{\mathbb R^d}p_t(x)\,\lambda(dx)=1$ for every $t$; hence it is a probability density with respect to $\lambda$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space,
Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
(Continuity of a map between metric spaces, at a point and globally, in the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ form), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below (Lower bound, bounded below, bounded set), and it has a
maximum and a minimum (Maximum and minimum of a set): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
(Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property), Greatest lower bound (infimum)).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

Let $\lambda$, $\pi$, and $\rho$ be as in the conditional probability-path definition, and let $u$ be a jointly measurable vector field. Suppose that for $\pi$-almost every $x_1$, $\rho$ and each component of $\rho u$ are continuously differentiable in $(t,x)$ and satisfy the classical coordinate equation $\partial_t\rho_t+\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_{x_j}(\rho_tu_t^j)=0$ on $(0,1)\times\mathbb R^d$. This is an explicit algebraic hypothesis; for general $\lambda$ it is not the definition of measure transport. Suppose also that for every compact $K\subset(0,1)\times\mathbb R^d$ there is a nonnegative $G_K\in L^1(\pi)$ which, for $\pi$-almost every $x_1$, bounds on $K$ the absolute values of $\rho_t(x\mid x_1)$, $\partial_t\rho_t(x\mid x_1)$, each component of $\rho_t(x\mid x_1)u_t(x\mid x_1)$, and each derivative $\partial_{x_j}(\rho_tu_t^j)(x\mid x_1)$. If $p_t(x)>0$ on $(0,1)\times\mathbb R^d$, define
$$J_t(x):=\int_{\mathbb R^d}\rho_t(x\mid x_1)u_t(x\mid x_1)\,\pi(dx_1), \qquad u_t(x):=\frac{J_t(x)}{p_t(x)}.$$
Then $\partial_t p_t$ and each indicated flux derivative $\partial_{x_j}J_t^j$ exist and are continuous locally in $(t,x)$, and the marginal continuity equation
$$\partial_t p_t(x)+\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_{x_j}\!\left(p_t(x)u_t^j(x)\right)=0$$
holds on $(0,1)\times\mathbb R^d$. The domination hypothesis is a sufficient Leibniz condition for the time and spatial derivatives to pass through the $x_1$ integral.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in The exponential series converges absolutely for every real argument. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of The factorial $n!$ and the falling factorial $n^{\underline{k}}$, defined by recursion in $\mathbb{N}$, $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image (The canonical natural $\iota(n) = n \cdot 1_F$ of a field, Canonical naturals are positive and strictly increasing), and powers and series are those of Integer powers $a^m$ and Series, partial sums, convergence and the sum, divergence, and the tail series.

This is a real power series centred at $0$ (A real power series about a centre, its interval of convergence, and its radius in $[0,+\infty]$). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

For all real $x,y$,
$$\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y).$$
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$

derivations.claim: Apply [F1] to the two endpoints $x_1=a$ and $x_1=-a$. Their conditional densities are positive and continuous in $(t,x)$, as are their time derivatives, fluxes, and spatial flux derivatives; $\sigma_t>0$ throughout $[0,1]$. Hence for each compact $K\subset(0,1)\times\mathbb R$ the finitely many such functions are bounded on $K$ by [F4]. Taking a common bound as the constant function $G_K$ gives an element of $L^1(\pi)$ because $\pi$ has total mass one. Thus [F5] applies. The mixture density is normalized by [F3] and is strictly positive because it is a sum of two positive Gaussian densities.

Put $$A_+(t,x):=\exp\!\left(-\frac{(x-ta)^2}{2\sigma_t^2}\right),\qquad A_-(t,x):=\exp\!\left(-\frac{(x+ta)^2}{2\sigma_t^2}\right).$$ The common Gaussian normalizing factor cancels in the endpoint-weighted mean, so [F2] gives $$m_t(x):=\frac{\int x_1\rho_t(x\mid x_1)\,\pi(dx_1)}{p_t(x)} =a\frac{A_+(t,x)-A_-(t,x)}{A_+(t,x)+A_-(t,x)}.$$ Expanding the two squares gives $A_+/A_-=\exp(2atx/\sigma_t^2)$ by [F7] and [F9]. Multiplying numerator and denominator by $\exp(-atx/\sigma_t^2)$ therefore yields $m_t(x)=a\tanh(atx/\sigma_t^2)$.

For endpoint $x_1\in\{-a,a\}$, [F1] gives $$u^c_t(x\mid x_1)=cx+(1-tc)x_1, \qquad c:=\frac{\sigma_{\min}-1}{\sigma_t}.$$ Taking the endpoint-weighted mean and using step 1.2 gives $u^m_t(x)=cx+(1-tc)m_t(x)$. Since $\sigma_t=1+t(\sigma_{\min}-1)$, we have $\sigma_t-t(\sigma_{\min}-1)=1$ and hence $1-tc=1/\sigma_t$. Substitution gives the marginal velocity formula in the Example.

Fix $t\in(0,1)$ and put $\beta:=a/\sigma_t>0$ and $k:=at/\sigma_t^2>0$. The formula for $\tanh$, the addition formula [F7], and the reciprocal identity [F9] give $\tanh(-y)=-\tanh(y)$, so $u^m_t$ is odd. For $y>0$, [F7] gives $\exp(0)=\exp(0)^2$, and positivity [F9] therefore gives $\exp(0)=1$; strict increase [F8] now yields $r:=\exp(2y)>1$. Put $s:=(r-1)/(r+1)\in(0,1)$. Rewriting $\tanh(y)$ and $\tanh(2y)$ using [F7, F9] gives $$\tanh(y)=s,\qquad \tanh(2y)=\frac{r^2-1}{r^2+1}=\frac{2s}{1+s^2}<2s.$$ Thus for every $x>0$, step 2.1 gives $$u^m_t(2x)-2u^m_t(x)=\beta\bigl(\tanh(2kx)-2\tanh(kx)\bigr)<0.$$ An odd affine function must be linear through the origin, and every such function has $u(2x)-2u(x)=0$. Hence $u^m_t$ is not affine and is nonlinear.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and fix $a>0$ and $\sigma_{\min}>0$. Let the endpoint law assign probability $1/2$ to each endpoint $x_1=-a$ and $x_1=a$. For each endpoint, use the one-dimensional Gaussian path with
$$\sigma_t=1-(1-\sigma_{\min})t,\qquad X_t=\sigma_t Z+t x_1,\qquad Z\sim N(0,1).$$
For either endpoint and each fixed $Z=z$, the conditional particle trajectory is a straight line. The marginal density is
$$p_t(x)=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma_t}\left[ \exp\!\left(-\frac{(x-ta)^2}{2\sigma_t^2}\right)+ \exp\!\left(-\frac{(x+ta)^2}{2\sigma_t^2}\right) \right],$$
and its marginal velocity field, defined by averaging the conditional velocity against the endpoint density at fixed $(t,x)$, is
$$u^m_t(x)=\frac{\sigma_{\min}-1}{\sigma_t}x+ \frac{a}{\sigma_t}\tanh\!\left(\frac{atx}{\sigma_t^2}\right), \qquad \tanh(y):=\frac{\exp(y)-\exp(-y)}{\exp(y)+\exp(-y)}.$$

Fix image and text encoder maps $f_\theta:\mathsf X\to\mathbb R^d$ and $g_\phi:\mathsf T\to\mathbb R^d$ into one shared embedding space, and a real log-scale $\tau$ with $s:=\exp(\tau)>0$. The inputs are an image $x\in\mathsf X$, an ordered nonempty list of distinct class descriptions $C=(c_1,\ldots,c_K)$, and a finite nonempty list of prompt templates $T=(t_1,\ldots,t_M)$, where each $t_m$ maps a class description to a text input. The admissible input conditions are $f_\theta(x)\ne0$, $g_\phi(t_m(c_k))\ne0$ for every $k,m$, and a nonzero average text embedding for every class.

1. Normalize the image embedding: $u:=f_\theta(x)/\|f_\theta(x)\|_2$.

2. For each class $c_k$ and template $t_m$, form the text embedding $v_{km}:=g_\phi(t_m(c_k))/\|g_\phi(t_m(c_k))\|_2$.

3. Average the normalized prompt embeddings in the shared embedding space and normalize the average to obtain the class prototype $q_k:=\left(\frac1M\sum_{m=1}^M v_{km}\right)\big/\left\|\frac1M\sum_{m=1}^M v_{km}\right\|_2$. This is prompt-template averaging; it averages embeddings before classification, not class probabilities.

4. For each class compute the scaled similarity score $z_k:=s\langle u,q_k\rangle$ and softmax probability $p_k:=\exp(z_k)/\sum_{r=1}^K\exp(z_r)$.

5. Return the vector $(p_1,\ldots,p_K)$ and class $c_{k^*}$, where $k^*$ is the least index maximizing $z_k$.

The returned classifier is zero-shot in the precise sense that no labeled examples from the target classification dataset are used to fit its class prototypes or classifier. The encoder maps, log-scale, class descriptions, and templates are fixed inputs to this inference procedure; it performs no training or parameter update. The procedure makes no accuracy or distribution-generalization guarantee.

Let $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$, $(\mathsf Y,\Sigma_Y)$, and $(\mathsf A,\Sigma_A)$ be nonempty measurable spaces. A **source/target pair of joint laws** consists of probability measures $P_S$ and $P_T$ on $(\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y,\Sigma_X\otimes\Sigma_Y)$. For $D\in\{S,T\}$, its input marginal is the probability measure $\mu_D$ on $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$ defined by $\mu_D(A)=P_D(A\times\mathsf Y)$. If $h:\mathsf X\to\mathsf A$ is measurable and $\ell:\mathsf A\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty]$ is product-measurable, then $(x,y)\mapsto(h(x),y)$ is measurable: the preimage of a measurable rectangle $U\times V$ is $h^{-1}(U)\times V$, and such rectangles generate the product sigma-algebra. Taking preimages once more shows that $(x,y)\mapsto\ell(h(x),y)$ is measurable. The domain risk is the extended nonnegative integral
$$R_D(h):=\int_{\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y}\ell(h(x),y)\,P_D(d(x,y)).$$

A **conditional label kernel** for $P_D$ is a specified probability kernel $K_D$ from $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$ to $(\mathsf Y,\Sigma_Y)$ such that, for every nonnegative product-measurable $g:\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty]$,
$$\int g(x,y)\,P_D(d(x,y))=\int_{\mathsf X}\left(\int_{\mathsf Y}g(x,y)\,K_D(x,dy)\right)\mu_D(dx).$$
The pair is under **covariate shift** when conditional label kernels $K_S,K_T$ are supplied, there is a measurable set $N$ with $\mu_T(N)=0$ such that $K_S(x,\cdot)=K_T(x,\cdot)$ as probability measures for every $x\notin N$, and $\mu_T\ll\mu_S$. No existence of conditional kernels is asserted by this definition.

derivations.claim: For every nonnegative $g:\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty]$, $\int g\,dP_S=g(a,0)=\int_{\mathsf X}\int_{\mathsf Y}g(x,y)K_S(x,dy)\mu_S(dx)$, and likewise $\int g\,dP_T=g(b,1)=\int_{\mathsf X}\int_{\mathsf Y}g(x,y)K_T(x,dy)\mu_T(dx)$. Thus the supplied kernels and stated marginals give the two joint laws under the source/target convention.
For $B=\{b\}$, $\mu_S(B)=0$ while $\mu_T(B)=1$, so $\mu_T\not\ll\mu_S$. This violates a required covariate-shift hypothesis in [F2], regardless of whether the two kernels agree.

By [F3], the in-context route keeps the pretrained parameters fixed and changes the prompt input, whereas a parameter-ERM formulation varies $\gamma\in\Gamma$ to minimize the stated sample loss. By [F1], the 2021 report does not supply a general implication from low pretraining loss to low adaptation loss. The finite shift example therefore carries no task-performance guarantee.

finite_smoke.asserts:
Let $K\ge2$, let the feature space be a measurable space $\mathcal X$, and
let the label set be $\mathcal Y=\{1,\ldots,K\}$ with all subsets measurable.
Let $H$ be a training statistic valued in a measurable rule space $\mathcal H$,
and let $s:\mathcal H\times\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y\to\mathbb R$ be a
jointly measurable score rule. The rule is fixed after training and is used
unchanged on calibration and test examples. Given $m\ge0$ calibration examples
$(X_i,Y_i)$ and $0<\alpha<1$, compute
$$R_i=s(H,X_i,Y_i),\qquad k=\left\lceil(m+1)(1-\alpha)\right\rceil.$$
If $k\le m$, sort the calibration scores by the ordered keys $(R_i,i)$ and let
$q$ be the score value at position $k$. If $k=m+1$, set $q=+\infty$. For a
feature value $x$, return the prediction set
$$
C(x)=\{y\in\mathcal Y:s(H,x,y)\le q\}.
$$
For the optional tie-randomized version, use one random variable $U$ that is
uniform on $[0,1]$ and independent of the training information and all
calibration and test examples, shared across the candidate-label scan. For
$r_y=s(H,x,y)$, define
$$p_U(y)=\frac{\#\{i\le m:R_i>r_y\}+U\bigl(1+\#\{i\le m:R_i=r_y\}\bigr)}{m+1},\qquad C_U(x)=\{y\in\mathcal Y:p_U(y)>\alpha\}.$$
The candidate is included in its own tie group. The algorithm defines these
sets; any coverage claim requires separate distributional hypotheses.

finite_smoke.result: On B={9/10}, the correctness event has probability 1 and the confidence integral is 9/10, so top-label calibration fails.
finite_smoke.asserts:
Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $K\ge2$, let
$Y:\Omega\to\{1,\ldots,K\}$ be a random variable, with the label set carrying
the full power-set sigma-algebra, and let
$G=(G_1,\ldots,G_K):\Omega\to\Delta_K$ be a measurable random forecast, where
the probability simplex is
$\Delta_K=\{p\in[0,1]^K:\sum_{j=1}^Kp_j=1\}$. Define the predicted label and
top confidence by
$$\widehat Y=\min\{j:G_j=\max_{\ell\in\{1,\ldots,K\}}G_\ell\},\qquad C=\max_{\ell\in\{1,\ldots,K\}}G_\ell.$$
The smallest-index rule resolves ties. The forecast is **top-label calibrated**
if for every Borel set $B\subseteq[0,1]$,
$$\mathbb P(Y=\widehat Y,\ C\in B)=\mathbb E[\mathbf 1_{\{C\in B\}}C].$$
Thus, among predictions whose top confidence lies in any specified set of
confidence values, the frequency of a correct top label equals the average
reported top confidence.

finite_smoke.asserts:
Fix $K\ge2$. The input is a trained classifier with a measurable, finite-valued
logit map $z:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^K$, a nonempty finite validation sample
$(x_i,y_i)_{i=1}^{n_v}$ with $n_v\ge1$ and $y_i\in\{1,\ldots,K\}$, and a
finite nonempty set of candidate temperatures $\mathcal T\subset(0,\infty)$.
The validation labels were not used to fit the logits. For $T\in\mathcal T$,
compute
$$p_T(j\mid x)=\frac{\exp(z_j(x)/T)}{\sum_{\ell=1}^K\exp(z_\ell(x)/T)}\quad (j=1,\ldots,K),\qquad L_{\mathrm{val}}(T)=-\frac1{n_v}\sum_{i=1}^{n_v}\log p_T(y_i\mid x_i).$$
Choose the smallest temperature among the minimizers,
$$T^*=\min\arg\min_{T\in\mathcal T}L_{\mathrm{val}}(T).$$
and return the forecasts $p_{T^*}(\cdot\mid x)$ and predicted label
$\min\arg\max_j p_{T^*}(j\mid x)$ for each input $x$. This is a
finite-candidate version of validation negative-log-likelihood temperature
scaling. It selects only by empirical validation loss; it makes no finite-sample
calibration guarantee for future data, particularly when the validation and
future data laws differ.

finite_smoke.asserts:
Let $K\ge2$ and let $(\widehat p_i,y_i)_{i=1}^n$ be a nonempty finite
evaluation sample, where $\widehat p_i\in\Delta_K$ and
$y_i\in\{1,\ldots,K\}$. For each $i$, let
$\widehat y_i=\min\arg\max_j\widehat p_{ij}$,
$c_i=\max_j\widehat p_{ij}$, and
$a_i=\mathbf 1_{\{\widehat y_i=y_i\}}$. Fix before evaluating the sample a
finite Borel partition $(B_1,\ldots,B_M)$ of $[0,1]$. For
$I_b=\{i:c_i\in B_b\}$ and $n_b=|I_b|>0$, define
$$\operatorname{acc}(B_b)=\frac1{n_b}\sum_{i\in I_b}a_i,\qquad \operatorname{conf}(B_b)=\frac1{n_b}\sum_{i\in I_b}c_i.$$
The **binned expected calibration error** and **binned maximum calibration
error** for this sample and partition are
$$\operatorname{ECE}_{(B_b)}=\sum_{b:n_b>0}\frac{n_b}{n}\left|\operatorname{acc}(B_b)-\operatorname{conf}(B_b)\right|,\qquad \operatorname{MCE}_{(B_b)}=\max_{b:n_b>0}\left|\operatorname{acc}(B_b)-\operatorname{conf}(B_b)\right|.$$
These are finite-sample, bin-dependent summaries, not the population expected
calibration error. They compare observed top-label accuracy with average
confidence within bins; log loss and Brier loss instead score probability
forecasts directly and are strictly proper.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $K\ge2$, let
$Y:\Omega\to\{1,\ldots,K\}$ be a random variable, with the label set carrying
the full power-set sigma-algebra, and let
$G=(G_1,\ldots,G_K):\Omega\to\Delta_K$ be a measurable random forecast, where
the probability simplex is
$\Delta_K=\{p\in[0,1]^K:\sum_{j=1}^Kp_j=1\}$. Define the predicted label and
top confidence by
$$\widehat Y=\min\{j:G_j=\max_{\ell\in\{1,\ldots,K\}}G_\ell\},\qquad C=\max_{\ell\in\{1,\ldots,K\}}G_\ell.$$
The smallest-index rule resolves ties. The forecast is **top-label calibrated**
if for every Borel set $B\subseteq[0,1]$,
$$\mathbb P(Y=\widehat Y,\ C\in B)=\mathbb E[\mathbf 1_{\{C\in B\}}C].$$
Thus, among predictions whose top confidence lies in any specified set of
confidence values, the frequency of a correct top label equals the average
reported top confidence.

Let $K\ge2$ and let $(\widehat p_i,y_i)_{i=1}^n$ be a nonempty finite
evaluation sample, where $\widehat p_i\in\Delta_K$ and
$y_i\in\{1,\ldots,K\}$. For each $i$, let
$\widehat y_i=\min\arg\max_j\widehat p_{ij}$,
$c_i=\max_j\widehat p_{ij}$, and
$a_i=\mathbf 1_{\{\widehat y_i=y_i\}}$. Fix before evaluating the sample a
finite Borel partition $(B_1,\ldots,B_M)$ of $[0,1]$. For
$I_b=\{i:c_i\in B_b\}$ and $n_b=|I_b|>0$, define
$$\operatorname{acc}(B_b)=\frac1{n_b}\sum_{i\in I_b}a_i,\qquad \operatorname{conf}(B_b)=\frac1{n_b}\sum_{i\in I_b}c_i.$$
The **binned expected calibration error** and **binned maximum calibration
error** for this sample and partition are
$$\operatorname{ECE}_{(B_b)}=\sum_{b:n_b>0}\frac{n_b}{n}\left|\operatorname{acc}(B_b)-\operatorname{conf}(B_b)\right|,\qquad \operatorname{MCE}_{(B_b)}=\max_{b:n_b>0}\left|\operatorname{acc}(B_b)-\operatorname{conf}(B_b)\right|.$$
These are finite-sample, bin-dependent summaries, not the population expected
calibration error. They compare observed top-label accuracy with average
confidence within bins; log loss and Brier loss instead score probability
forecasts directly and are strictly proper.

Fix $K\ge2$. The input is a trained classifier with a measurable, finite-valued
logit map $z:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^K$, a nonempty finite validation sample
$(x_i,y_i)_{i=1}^{n_v}$ with $n_v\ge1$ and $y_i\in\{1,\ldots,K\}$, and a
finite nonempty set of candidate temperatures $\mathcal T\subset(0,\infty)$.
The validation labels were not used to fit the logits. For $T\in\mathcal T$,
compute
$$p_T(j\mid x)=\frac{\exp(z_j(x)/T)}{\sum_{\ell=1}^K\exp(z_\ell(x)/T)}\quad (j=1,\ldots,K),\qquad L_{\mathrm{val}}(T)=-\frac1{n_v}\sum_{i=1}^{n_v}\log p_T(y_i\mid x_i).$$
Choose the smallest temperature among the minimizers,
$$T^*=\min\arg\min_{T\in\mathcal T}L_{\mathrm{val}}(T).$$
and return the forecasts $p_{T^*}(\cdot\mid x)$ and predicted label
$\min\arg\max_j p_{T^*}(j\mid x)$ for each input $x$. This is a
finite-candidate version of validation negative-log-likelihood temperature
scaling. It selects only by empirical validation loss; it makes no finite-sample
calibration guarantee for future data, particularly when the validation and
future data laws differ.

Let $K\ge2$, let $z\in\mathbb R^K$, and let $T>0$. Define
$$p_j(T)=\frac{\exp(z_j/T)}{\sum_{\ell=1}^K\exp(z_\ell/T)}\quad (j=1,\ldots,K).$$
Then $p(T)$ lies in the relative interior of $\Delta_K$ in the affine hyperplane
$\{p\in\mathbb R^K:\sum_jp_j=1\}$ and
$\arg\max_{j\in\{1,\ldots,K\}}p_j(T)
=\arg\max_{j\in\{1,\ldots,K\}}z_j$.
For the finite validation inputs and candidate temperatures specified in the
validation temperature-scaling algorithm, every validation loss is finite and
the stated smallest-minimizer rule returns a unique candidate.

Let $K\ge2$, let the feature space be a measurable space $\mathcal X$, and
let the label set be $\mathcal Y=\{1,\ldots,K\}$ with all subsets measurable.
Let $H$ be a training statistic valued in a measurable rule space $\mathcal H$,
and let $s:\mathcal H\times\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y\to\mathbb R$ be a
jointly measurable score rule. The rule is fixed after training and is used
unchanged on calibration and test examples. Given $m\ge0$ calibration examples
$(X_i,Y_i)$ and $0<\alpha<1$, compute
$$R_i=s(H,X_i,Y_i),\qquad k=\left\lceil(m+1)(1-\alpha)\right\rceil.$$
If $k\le m$, sort the calibration scores by the ordered keys $(R_i,i)$ and let
$q$ be the score value at position $k$. If $k=m+1$, set $q=+\infty$. For a
feature value $x$, return the prediction set
$$
C(x)=\{y\in\mathcal Y:s(H,x,y)\le q\}.
$$
For the optional tie-randomized version, use one random variable $U$ that is
uniform on $[0,1]$ and independent of the training information and all
calibration and test examples, shared across the candidate-label scan. For
$r_y=s(H,x,y)$, define
$$p_U(y)=\frac{\#\{i\le m:R_i>r_y\}+U\bigl(1+\#\{i\le m:R_i=r_y\}\bigr)}{m+1},\qquad C_U(x)=\{y\in\mathcal Y:p_U(y)>\alpha\}.$$
The candidate is included in its own tie group. The algorithm defines these
sets; any coverage claim requires separate distributional hypotheses.

Let $Z_i=(X_i,Y_i)$, $1\le i\le m+1$, be random elements of one measurable
example space $(\mathcal Z,\mathscr Z)$, and let $\mathcal T$ be the training
sigma-field. Suppose the tuple $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_{m+1})$ has a regular
conditional distribution $Q_\omega$ given $\mathcal T$ in the sense of
Regular conditional distribution, whose sections have joint laws
invariant under every coordinate permutation, as in
Exchangeable random elements, for almost every $\omega$. Let $H$ be a $\mathcal T$-measurable
training statistic, and let $s:\mathcal H\times\mathcal Z\to\mathbb R$ be a
jointly measurable split score rule. Use the split set in
Split conformal prediction set at $0<\alpha<1$. Then
$$\mathbb P\{Y_{m+1}\in C(X_{m+1})\mid\mathcal T\}\ge1-\alpha\quad\text{almost surely}.$$
If the tie-randomized set $C_U$ is used with one $U$ of Lebesgue probability
law on $[0,1]$ independent of $\mathcal T\vee\sigma(Z)$, then
$$\mathbb P\{Y_{m+1}\in C_U(X_{m+1})\mid\mathcal T\}=1-\alpha\quad\text{almost surely}.$$
In either case, integration over the training sigma-field gives the same
marginal lower bound or exact marginal coverage.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\to(T,\Tau)$ be a measurable random element and $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ a sub-sigma-algebra. A **regular conditional distribution of X given $\mathcal G$** is a probability kernel $K:(\Omega,\mathcal G)\to(T,\Tau)$ satisfying
$$\int_H K(\omega,A)\,P(d\omega)=P(H\cap\{X\in A\})\qquad(H\in\mathcal G,\ A\in\Tau).$$

“Probability kernel” has the pointwise meaning of Measure kernel and probability kernel: every $K(\omega,\cdot)$ is a probability measure, and every evaluation is $\mathcal G$-measurable. Its evaluations lie in $[0,1]$ and are integrable. Thus the testing identity says exactly that $K(\cdot,A)$ is a conditional-expectation version of $1_{\{X\in A\}}$ in Conditional expectation given a sigma algebra. Conversely, a probability kernel with these version identities satisfies the displayed definition.

The kernel requirement holds at every sample point. Separate eventwise choices of conditional-expectation versions do not imply it and do not by themselves provide one exceptional set valid for all A. When A is empty the testing identity is zero on both sides, and when A=T it is P(H) on both sides. This defines a property of a supplied kernel and makes no existence or AC assertion.

Let $Z_1,\ldots,Z_n$ be random elements, $n\ge1$, of one measurable space
$(\mathcal Z,\mathscr Z)$. Their tuple $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)$ is a random element
of $(\mathcal Z^n,\mathscr Z^{\otimes n})$ by
Coordinate maps and permutations are measurable on finite products,
and its law is the pushforward probability measure from
Law or distribution of a random element. For a permutation $\pi$ of
$\{1,\ldots,n\}$, let $\tau_\pi(z)_i=z_{\pi(i)}$. The tuple is
**exchangeable** if
$$\mathbb P_Z\circ\tau_\pi^{-1}=\mathbb P_Z\qquad\text{for every permutation }\pi.$$

This is invariance of the joint law, not an assertion of independence or identical marginal construction by independent sampling. The coordinate maps $\tau_\pi$ are measurable by the cited finite-product lemma.

For every $K\ge2$ and $p,q\in\Delta_K$, the logarithmic and Brier losses in the definition of finite-label score loss satisfy $\bar S(p,p)\le\bar S(p,q)$, with equality only when $q=p$. The expected logarithmic loss at the truthful forecast is finite, including when some coordinates of $p$ vanish.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because The exponential is a continuous bijection from $\mathbb{R}$ onto $(0,\infty)$ states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

For all real $x,y$,
$$\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y).$$

Let $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$, $(\mathsf Y,\Sigma_Y)$, and $(\mathsf A,\Sigma_A)$ be nonempty measurable spaces. A **source/target pair of joint laws** consists of probability measures $P_S$ and $P_T$ on $(\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y,\Sigma_X\otimes\Sigma_Y)$. For $D\in\{S,T\}$, its input marginal is the probability measure $\mu_D$ on $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$ defined by $\mu_D(A)=P_D(A\times\mathsf Y)$. If $h:\mathsf X\to\mathsf A$ is measurable and $\ell:\mathsf A\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty]$ is product-measurable, then $(x,y)\mapsto(h(x),y)$ is measurable: the preimage of a measurable rectangle $U\times V$ is $h^{-1}(U)\times V$, and such rectangles generate the product sigma-algebra. Taking preimages once more shows that $(x,y)\mapsto\ell(h(x),y)$ is measurable. The domain risk is the extended nonnegative integral
$$R_D(h):=\int_{\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y}\ell(h(x),y)\,P_D(d(x,y)).$$

A **conditional label kernel** for $P_D$ is a specified probability kernel $K_D$ from $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$ to $(\mathsf Y,\Sigma_Y)$ such that, for every nonnegative product-measurable $g:\mathsf X\times\mathsf Y\to[0,+\infty]$,
$$\int g(x,y)\,P_D(d(x,y))=\int_{\mathsf X}\left(\int_{\mathsf Y}g(x,y)\,K_D(x,dy)\right)\mu_D(dx).$$
The pair is under **covariate shift** when conditional label kernels $K_S,K_T$ are supplied, there is a measurable set $N$ with $\mu_T(N)=0$ such that $K_S(x,\cdot)=K_T(x,\cdot)$ as probability measures for every $x\notin N$, and $\mu_T\ll\mu_S$. No existence of conditional kernels is asserted by this definition.

derivations.claim: In the first model, $\widehat Y=1$ and $C=9/10$ almost surely. For $B=\{9/10\}$, the left side of [F1] is $1$ and the right side is $9/10$, so top-label calibration fails despite accuracy $1$. In the single occupied bin, [F2] gives both errors as $|1-9/10|=1/10$.

By [F10], temperature $1$ gives first-class probability $\exp(2\log3)/(1+\exp(2\log3))=9/10$, while temperature $2$ gives $\exp(\log3)/(1+\exp(\log3))=3/4$. The empirical NLL is the log-score risk $\bar S_{\log}(p,p_T)$ under the validation label frequencies $p=(3/4,1/4)$. Strict propriety [F9] therefore makes the value at $(3/4,1/4)$ strictly smaller than at $(9/10,1/10)$, so [F3] selects $T=2$. By [F4], both temperatures predict class $1$. Their one-bin gaps from the observed accuracy $3/4$ are $|3/4-9/10|=3/20$ and $|3/4-3/4|=0$.

In the rare-feature model, $m=1$ and $\alpha=1/2$ give $k=\lceil2(1/2)\rceil=1$, so the threshold is the single calibration score: it is $1$ for a rare calibration feature and $0$ for a common one. Write $Q$ for the finite joint law of the calibration and test pairs; by [A1], $Q(z_1,z_2)=\mu(z_1)\mu(z_2)$, which is unchanged by swapping coordinates. For the trivial training sigma-field, whose only events are $\emptyset$ and the whole space, the constant kernel with value $Q$ satisfies [F7]: the conditional-event integral is zero for $\emptyset$ and is the ordinary law identity for the whole space. By [F8] its section is exchangeable. The finite score rule is measurable, so [F6] applies and yields conditional-on-training marginal coverage at least $1/2$.

If the test feature is common, its true-label score is $0\le q$ for either possible threshold, so coverage is $1$. If it is rare, its true-label score is $1$, which is included exactly when the independent calibration feature is rare, an event of probability $1/10$. Thus subgroup coverage is $1/10$, while marginal coverage is $(9/10)\cdot1+(1/10)\cdot(1/10)=91/100$.

In the clean/corrupted model, the calibration score is always $0$, so $k=1$ gives $q=0$. At the target feature, both candidate labels have scores $1$ or $2$, hence neither belongs to $C(\mathrm{corrupted})$ and target coverage is $0$. The calibration/test pair law assigns mass one to (clean, corrupted) and zero to (corrupted, clean), so it is not invariant under swapping; the exchangeability hypothesis in [F6] fails.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of Integrable real and complex functions, and their integrals, its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

Let $X,Y$ be integrable real or complex random variables on one probability
space.

1. For scalars $a,b$,
   $$\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Y].$$
2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y].$$
3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and let $A\in\mathcal F$.
Then the indicator $\mathbf 1_A$ satisfies
$$\mathbb E[\mathbf 1_A]=\mathbb P(A).$$

In an online decision protocol with horizon $T$, the environment and feedback model specifies how each loss function is chosen and what the learner observes after choosing $x_t$. **Full-information feedback** reveals the entire function $f_t$ (or, for $N$ experts, the full vector of their $N$ losses) after the round-$t$ choice. **Bandit feedback** reveals only the played loss $f_t(x_t)$ after that choice. An **oblivious adversary** fixes the whole sequence $(f_1,\ldots,f_T)$ before the learner's random choices are realized; it may know the learner's rule but not its realized private randomization. A **non-anticipating adaptive adversary** chooses $f_t$ from the history available before $x_t$ is chosen, so $f_t$ may depend on earlier choices and feedback but not on the current choice or the learner's current private randomization. A **reactive adversary** may choose $f_t$ after observing $x_t$, so its round-$t$ loss may depend on that current choice. These adversary classes have different timing and are not interchangeable; a guarantee established for one class is not asserted for another. For the stochastic reward model, let $\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$ be the smallest collection of subsets of $\mathbb R$ that contains every open interval and is closed under complements and countable unions; its members are the Borel sets. A **stochastic finite-arm reward environment** has $N\ge1$ arms, a fixed probability measure $P_i$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$ for each arm $i\in[N]:=\{1,\ldots,N\}$, and finite first moments $\int_{\mathbb R}|y|\,P_i(dy)<\infty$ with means $\mu_i:=\int_{\mathbb R} y\,P_i(dy)$. At each round the learner chooses a measurable arm $A_t$ with values in $[N]$ equipped with its full power set, before the reward $Y_t$ is drawn. The fixed-law condition means that, for every $i$, every event $B$ determined by the history before the reward and the chosen arm with $B\subseteq\{A_t=i\}$, and every $C\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$, $\mathbb P(B\cap\{Y_t\in C\})=\mathbb P(B)P_i(C)$. The model also states explicitly the conditional-mean identity used below: $\mathbb E[\mathbf1_B Y_t]=\mu_i\mathbb P(B)$ for every such $B$. Here $Y_t$ is an integrable real random variable, $\mathbf1_B$ is the indicator of event $B$, and the history-and-arm events are measurable in the common probability space. This stochastic reward model is distinct from adversarial loss models and supplies no regret guarantee by itself.

derivations.claim: For each fixed $t$, the events $E_{t,i}:=\{A_t=i\}$, $i\in[N]$, are a measurable partition of $\Omega$, because $A_t$ takes exactly one value in $[N]$. The conditional-mean hypothesis gives $\mathbb E[Y_t\mathbf1_{E_{t,i}}]=\mu_i\mathbb P(E_{t,i})$. Since $Y_t=\sum_{i=1}^N Y_t\mathbf1_{E_{t,i}}$ pointwise and the sum is finite, linearity of expectation gives $\mathbb E[Y_t]=\sum_{i=1}^N\mu_i\mathbb P(E_{t,i})$.

Pointwise, $\mu_{A_t}=\sum_{i=1}^N\mu_i\mathbf1_{E_{t,i}}$ and $\mu^*=\sum_{i=1}^N\mu^*\mathbf1_{E_{t,i}}$. Thus $\bar R_T=\sum_{t=1}^T\sum_{i=1}^N(\mu^*-\mu_i)\mathbf1_{E_{t,i}}$. Linearity of expectation and $\mathbb E[\mathbf1_{E_{t,i}}]=\mathbb P(E_{t,i})$ yield $\mathbb E[\bar R_T]=\sum_{t=1}^T\sum_{i=1}^N(\mu^*-\mu_i)\mathbb P(E_{t,i})$.

Linearity of expectation and $\mathbb E[\mathbf1_\Omega]=\mathbb P(\Omega)=1$ give $\mathbb E[R_T^{\rm rew}]=T\mu^*-\sum_{t=1}^T\mathbb E[Y_t]$. Substituting step 1.1 and rearranging the finite sums gives $\mathbb E[R_T^{\rm rew}]=\sum_{t=1}^T\sum_{i=1}^N(\mu^*-\mu_i)\mathbb P(E_{t,i})$, which equals the expression in step 1.2.

Since $N_i(T)=\sum_{t=1}^T\mathbf1_{E_{t,i}}$, linearity of expectation and the indicator expectation identity give $\mathbb E[N_i(T)]=\sum_{t=1}^T\mathbb P(E_{t,i})$. Summing these equalities over the finite set of arms with coefficients $\mu^*-\mu_i$ identifies the result from step 1.2 with $\sum_{i=1}^N(\mu^*-\mu_i)\mathbb E[N_i(T)]$ and proves the claimed identity.

citations.quote: Fix a positive integer horizon $T$, a nonempty action set $K$, and, when choices or the environment are randomized, a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$. An online decision protocol has rounds $t=1,\ldots,T$. Before round $t$, the learner has the history $h_{t-1}$ consisting of its earlier choices and all feedback and loss information revealed in earlier rounds. It chooses $x_t\in K$ using only $h_{t-1}$ and any learner-private randomization available by that time. In a randomized protocol, $X_t$ is a measurable random element of $K$, meaning a measurable map from $(\Omega,\mathcal F)$ into $K$ equipped with its declared measurable structure. The environment supplies a real-valued loss function $f_t:K\to\mathbb R$; it may have fixed $f_t$ before the choice or choose it after the choice, as specified by the environment model, but the learner does not observe $f_t$ before choosing $x_t$. The learner incurs loss $f_t(x_t)$ and then receives feedback about round $t$ according to the feedback model. The history $h_t$ adds $x_t$, the feedback received, and any part of $f_t$ explicitly revealed in round $t$. No convexity, boundedness, or regret guarantee is part of this protocol definition.

A **non-anticipating adaptive adversary** chooses $f_t$ from the history available before $x_t$ is chosen, so $f_t$ may depend on earlier choices and feedback but not on the current choice or the learner's current private randomization. Here $Y_t$ is an integrable real random variable, $\mathbf1_B$ is the indicator of event $B$, and the history-and-arm events are measurable in the common probability space. This stochastic reward model is distinct from adversarial loss models and supplies no regret guarantee by itself.

Let a finite-horizon online protocol have horizon $T$, action set $K$, round losses $f_t:K\to\mathbb R$, and learner choices $x_t\in K$. Whenever a minimum below is used, assume it is finite and attained. For a fixed comparator $u\in K$, the realized regret is
$$
R_T(u):=\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(x_t)-\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(u).
$$
The **static regret** is
$$
R_T^{\rm stat}:=\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(x_t)-\min_{u\in K}\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(u).
$$
For randomized learners or environments, **expected regret** is the expectation of the specified regret random variable over their joint randomness, when that random variable is measurable and integrable. In a stochastic finite-arm reward model with means $(\mu_i)_{i\in[N]}$, let $\mu^*:=\max_{i\in[N]}\mu_i$. The **pseudo-regret** is the random variable
$$
\bar R_T:=\sum_{t=1}^T(\mu^*-\mu_{A_t}),
$$
whereas the **realized reward regret** is
$$
R_T^{\rm rew}:=\sum_{t=1}^T(\mu^*-Y_t).
$$

For dynamic comparators, suppose $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ for a positive integer $d$ and fix a norm $\|\cdot\|:\mathbb R^d\to[0,\infty)$, meaning $\|v\|=0$ exactly when $v=0$, $\|\lambda v\|=|\lambda|\|v\|$ for every $\lambda\in\mathbb R$, and $\|v+w\|\le\|v\|+\|w\|$. Given a comparator sequence $u_{1:T}=(u_1,\ldots,u_T)\in K^T$, the **dynamic regret** and its **path length** are
$$
R_T^{\rm dyn}(u_{1:T}):=\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(x_t)-\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(u_t),\qquad P(u_{1:T}):=1+\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\|u_t-u_{t+1}\|.
$$
For a nonempty contiguous integer interval $I=[r,s]$ with $1\le r\le s\le T$, its **interval regret** is
$$
R_I:=\sum_{t=r}^s f_t(x_t)-\min_{u\in K}\sum_{t=r}^s f_t(u),
$$
and the **adaptive regret** is $\max_{1\le r\le s\le T}R_{[r,s]}$. For an algorithm $A$ producing the choices $x_1,\ldots,x_T$, write $R_I(A)$ for its interval regret on $I$. The algorithm is **strongly adaptive** relative to a specified loss, feedback, adversary, and comparator class precisely when there are a stated base algorithm $A_0$, constants $C>0$ and $p\ge0$, and a specified bound $B_{A_0}(n)$ on $A_0$'s static regret at horizon $n$ in that same class, such that, uniformly over every positive horizon $T$ and every environment in that class, for every nonempty contiguous interval $I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,T\}$,
$$
R_I(A)\le C\bigl(\log(eT)\bigr)^p B_{A_0}(|I|),
$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm and $|I|=s-r+1$; $A_0$, $B_{A_0}$, $C$, and $p$ are fixed independently of $T$, $I$, and the environment. The displayed criterion is pathwise, including for randomized protocols. **Strong adaptivity in expectation** instead requires $\mathbb E[R_I(A)]$ to satisfy the displayed bound for every deterministic interval $I$, with measurable, integrable interval regrets and with $B_{A_0}(n)$ an expected static-regret bound in the same class. Almost-sure or high-probability versions must be explicitly qualified: for each horizon, all interval inequalities must hold simultaneously with probability one or at least the stated $1-\delta$, respectively, and the base bound must use the same probability mode with any dependence on $\delta$ specified. Strong adaptivity is a regret property relative to intervals; it does not imply anytime statistical validity.

derivations.claim: The learner's losses are $1/2,1/2,1/2$, so their sum is $3/2$. For any fixed $u\in[0,1]$, the cumulative loss is $u+(1-u)+u=1+u$, whose minimum is $1$ at $u=0$. Thus static regret is $3/2-1=1/2$.
The comparator losses are $f_1(0)=0$, $f_2(1)=0$, and $f_3(0)=0$, so its total loss is zero and dynamic regret is $3/2$. Its path length is $1+|0-1|+|1-0|=3$.

The singleton interval regrets are $1/2$ on each of $[1,1]$, $[2,2]$, and $[3,3]$, because each learner loss is $1/2$ and each corresponding linear loss has minimum $0$. On $[1,2]$ and $[2,3]$, the cumulative loss is identically $1$, as $f_1+f_2=1$ and $f_2+f_3=1$, so both regrets are zero. On $[1,3]$, the cumulative loss is $1+x$, its minimum is $1$, and the learner incurs $3/2$, so its regret is $1/2$. The maximum over these six nonempty contiguous intervals is therefore $1/2$.

$$

derivations.claim: Under each arm law, the coordinate $y\mapsto y$ equals $\mathbf1_{\{1\}}$ almost surely, so its integral is the probability of $\{1\}$: $\mu_1=3/4$ and $\mu_2=1/2$. Thus $\mu^*=3/4$. In the realized process, $Y_1(\omega)=\omega$ has Borel law $P_2$, since both put mass $1/2$ at each of $0$ and $1$ and zero elsewhere, so $\mathbb E[Y_1]=1/2$.

The pre-reward history is trivial and $A_1=2$ deterministically. Thus for arm 2 the history-and-arm events are $B=\varnothing$ or $B=\Omega$, while for arm 1 only $B=\varnothing$ is possible. For every Borel $C$, the fixed-law identity for $B=\Omega$ is $\mathbb P(\Omega\cap\{Y_1\in C\})=P_2(C)=\mathbb P(\Omega)P_2(C)$ by step 1.1; it is trivial for $B=\varnothing$. The conditional-mean identity likewise holds: for $B=\Omega$, $\mathbb E[\mathbf1_B Y_1]=1/2=\mu_2\mathbb P(B)$, and for $B=\varnothing$ both sides are zero.
The sole chosen arm is 2, so $\bar R_1=3/4-1/2=1/4$, $N_1(1)=0$, and $N_2(1)=1$.
The realized reward regret is $3/4-Y_1$. By linearity and $\mathbb E[Y_1]=\mathbb P(\omega=1)=1/2$, its expectation is $3/4-1/2=1/4$.

The gap-weighted count sum is $(3/4-3/4)\mathbb E[N_1(1)]+(3/4-1/2)\mathbb E[N_2(1)]=0\cdot0+(1/4)\cdot1=1/4$. This agrees with the pseudo-regret and realized-regret expectations in steps 2.2 and 2.3, as the finite-arm lemma asserts.

citations.quote: In an online decision protocol with horizon $T$, the environment and feedback model specifies how each loss function is chosen and what the learner observes after choosing $x_t$. **Full-information feedback** reveals the entire function $f_t$ (or, for $N$ experts, the full vector of their $N$ losses) after the round-$t$ choice. **Bandit feedback** reveals only the played loss $f_t(x_t)$ after that choice. An **oblivious adversary** fixes the whole sequence $(f_1,\ldots,f_T)$ before the learner's random choices are realized; it may know the learner's rule but not its realized private randomization. A **non-anticipating adaptive adversary** chooses $f_t$ from the history available before $x_t$ is chosen, so $f_t$ may depend on earlier choices and feedback but not on the current choice or the learner's current private randomization. A **reactive adversary** may choose $f_t$ after observing $x_t$, so its round-$t$ loss may depend on that current choice. These adversary classes have different timing and are not interchangeable; a guarantee established for one class is not asserted for another. For the stochastic reward model, let $\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$ be the smallest collection of subsets of $\mathbb R$ that contains every open interval and is closed under complements and countable unions; its members are the Borel sets. A **stochastic finite-arm reward environment** has $N\ge1$ arms, a fixed probability measure $P_i$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$ for each arm $i\in[N]:=\{1,\ldots,N\}$, and finite first moments $\int_{\mathbb R}|y|\,P_i(dy)<\infty$ with means $\mu_i:=\int_{\mathbb R} y\,P_i(dy)$. At each round the learner chooses a measurable arm $A_t$ with values in $[N]$ equipped with its full power set, before the reward $Y_t$ is drawn. The fixed-law condition means that, for every $i$, every event $B$ determined by the history before the reward and the chosen arm with $B\subseteq\{A_t=i\}$, and every $C\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$, $\mathbb P(B\cap\{Y_t\in C\})=\mathbb P(B)P_i(C)$. The model also states explicitly the conditional-mean identity used below: $\mathbb E[\mathbf1_B Y_t]=\mu_i\mathbb P(B)$ for every such $B$. Here $Y_t$ is an integrable real random variable, $\mathbf1_B$ is the indicator of event $B$, and the history-and-arm events are measurable in the common probability space. This stochastic reward model is distinct from adversarial loss models and supplies no regret guarantee by itself.

Let $N,T\ge1$ be integers, let $[N]=\{1,\ldots,N\}$ be the expert set, and let $\epsilon>0$. At each round $t=1,\ldots,T$, a finite loss vector $\ell_t=(\ell_t(1),\ldots,\ell_t(N))\in[0,\infty)^N$ is revealed after the learner's choice. Initialize $W_1(i)=1$ for every $i\in[N]$. At round $t$, set
$$x_t(i):=\frac{W_t(i)}{\sum_{j=1}^{N}W_t(j)},\qquad i\in[N],$$
Let $\mathcal H_{t-1}$ be the pre-round history sigma-algebra generated by the previously played choices and all previously revealed loss vectors (any random loss vector is assumed measurable on the protocol's probability space). The weights and $x_t$ are $\mathcal H_{t-1}$-measurable. Draw a measurable expert choice $I_t\in[N]$ with conditional distribution
$$\mathbb P(I_t=i\mid\mathcal H_{t-1})=x_t(i)\quad\text{almost surely},\qquad i\in[N],$$
and play $I_t$. After observing the whole vector $\ell_t$, update
$$W_{t+1}(i):=W_t(i)\exp(-\epsilon\ell_t(i)),\qquad i\in[N].$$
The output is the distributions $x_1,\ldots,x_T$, the sampled choices $I_1,\ldots,I_T$, and the final weights. The protocol assumes a probability space carrying the stated measurable draws; no probability-space construction is claimed.

For every real $x$,
$$1+x\le\exp(x).$$
Consequently, if $0\le p\le1$ and $m\in\mathbb N$, then
$$ (1-p)^m\le\exp(-mp). $$

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$

For all real $x,y$,
$$\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y).$$
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because The exponential is a continuous bijection from $\mathbb{R}$ onto $(0,\infty)$ states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

$$

Fix a positive integer horizon $T$, a nonempty action set $K$, and, when choices or the environment are randomized, a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$. An online decision protocol has rounds $t=1,\ldots,T$. Before round $t$, the learner has the history $h_{t-1}$ consisting of its earlier choices and all feedback and loss information revealed in earlier rounds. It chooses $x_t\in K$ using only $h_{t-1}$ and any learner-private randomization available by that time. In a randomized protocol, $X_t$ is a measurable random element of $K$, meaning a measurable map from $(\Omega,\mathcal F)$ into $K$ equipped with its declared measurable structure. The environment supplies a real-valued loss function $f_t:K\to\mathbb R$; it may have fixed $f_t$ before the choice or choose it after the choice, as specified by the environment model, but the learner does not observe $f_t$ before choosing $x_t$. The learner incurs loss $f_t(x_t)$ and then receives feedback about round $t$ according to the feedback model. The history $h_t$ adds $x_t$, the feedback received, and any part of $f_t$ explicitly revealed in round $t$. No convexity, boundedness, or regret guarantee is part of this protocol definition.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of Integrable real and complex functions, and their integrals, its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

derivations.claim: For every $z\ge0$, [F2] gives $\exp(z)\ge1+z>0$, so [F3] gives $\exp(-z)\le1/(1+z)$. Since $(1-z+z^2)(1+z)=1+z^3\ge1$ and $1+z>0$, one also has $1/(1+z)\le1-z+z^2$. Thus $\exp(-z)\le1-z+z^2$ for all $z\ge0$.

Put $S_t=\sum_{i=1}^N W_t(i)$, $m_t=\sum_i x_t(i)\ell_t(i)$, and $q_t=\sum_i x_t(i)\ell_t(i)^2$. By [F3], every factor $\exp(-\epsilon\ell_t(i))$ is a positive finite real. Starting with $W_1(i)=1$, [F1] therefore gives positive finite weights through round $T+1$ by induction, so $S_t>0$ is finite and $x_t$ is a probability vector. This induction is pointwise and does not require the loss sequence to be fixed before randomization. Applying step 1.1 to $z=\epsilon\ell_t(i)$ and summing with weights $x_t(i)$ gives $S_{t+1}=S_t\sum_i x_t(i)\exp(-\epsilon\ell_t(i))\le S_t(1-\epsilon m_t+\epsilon^2q_t)\le S_t\exp(-\epsilon m_t+\epsilon^2q_t)$, where the last inequality is [F2].

Dividing the positive ratios from step 2.1 by $S_t$ and multiplying over $t$, then using [F4] and $S_1=N$, gives $S_{T+1}\le N\exp(-\epsilon\sum_t m_t+\epsilon^2\sum_t q_t)$. For any fixed $i^\star$, [F1] also gives $S_{T+1}\ge W_{T+1}(i^\star)=\exp(-\epsilon\sum_t\ell_t(i^\star))$. Since $N=\exp(\log N)$ by [F6], combining the bounds and applying [F5] yields $-\epsilon\sum_t\ell_t(i^\star)\le\log N-\epsilon\sum_t m_t+\epsilon^2\sum_t q_t$.
Rearranging step 3.1 and dividing by $\epsilon>0$ gives $\sum_t m_t\le\sum_t\ell_t(i^\star)+\epsilon\sum_tq_t+\log(N)/\epsilon$, which is the first assertion.

For losses in $[0,1]$, $q_t\le\sum_i x_t(i)=1$. Since $[N]$ is finite and nonempty, fix $i^\star$ attaining $\min_i\sum_t\ell_t(i)$. If $N\ge2$, then $N>1$ and [F7] gives $\log N>\log1=0$, so $\epsilon=\sqrt{\log N/T}$ is positive; step 4.1 now gives the deterministic mixed-loss regret bound $\epsilon T+\log N/\epsilon=2\sqrt{T\log N}$. If $N=1$, the only sampled expert is the only comparator, so the static regret is zero.

For each $t$, $\ell_t(I_t)=\sum_{i=1}^N\ell_t(i)\mathbf 1_{\{I_t=i\}}$. By [A1], the entire loss sequence is fixed before randomization; [F11] gives the choice-before-feedback order, and [F1] makes every $x_t$ deterministic from the fixed losses and previous updates. Thus [F8]–[F9] give $\mathbb E[\ell_t(I_t)]=\sum_i\ell_t(i)\mathbb P(I_t=i)=m_t$ and $\mathbb E[\sum_t\ell_t(I_t)]=\sum_t m_t$. The bounded losses are measurable by the algorithm's protocol and integrable by [F12]. Subtracting the deterministic best-expert loss proves the expected static-regret assertion from step 5.1 using [F10].
