Let $d\ge1$ be an integer and let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty, bounded, closed, and convex; let $x_1\in K$, let $T\ge1$ be an integer, and fix a step size $\eta>0$. Coordinate and matrix-entry subscripts in this procedure are one-based labels: for $i,j\in\{1,\ldots,d\}$, write $g_i=g(i-1)$ and $G_{ij}=G(i-1,j-1)$ in the underlying zero-based Euclidean and matrix conventions, and use the same relabeling for the other vectors and matrices. Initialize $G_0=0$. For each round $t=1,\ldots,T$, play $x_t$, then receive the full current loss information and its prescribed gradient vector $g_t\in\mathbb R^d$, and set

$$G_t=G_{t-1}+g_tg_t^\top=\sum_{s=1}^t g_sg_s^\top.$$

The accumulated matrix $G_t$ is symmetric and positive semidefinite. Choose either the **full-matrix scale** $H_t=G_t^{1/2}$, the unique positive-semidefinite square root, or the **diagonal scale** $H_t=\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt{(G_t)_{11}},\ldots,\sqrt{(G_t)_{dd}})$. Define $H_t^\dagger$ to be the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse and update

$$y_{t+1}=x_t-\eta H_t^\dagger g_t,\qquad x_{t+1}\in\arg\min_{x\in K}(x-y_{t+1})^\top H_t(x-y_{t+1}).$$

A minimizer exists; if it is not unique, select any minimizer. Return $x_1,\ldots,x_T$. The matrix seminorm notation in the objective means $\|v\|_{H_t}^2=v^\top H_tv$. The diagonal scale here is formed by taking each diagonal entry of $G_t$ and then its scalar square root; in general it is not $\operatorname{diag}(G_t^{1/2})$. This is an update definition only and asserts no regret bound.

For the diagonal AdaGrad choice $H_t=\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt{(G_t)_{11}},\ldots,\sqrt{(G_t)_{dd}})$ with $G_t=\sum_{s=1}^t g_sg_s^\top$, the $i$th diagonal entry is

$$ (H_t)_{ii}=\sqrt{\sum_{s=1}^t g_{s,i}^2},\qquad i=1,\ldots,d.$$

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, and let
$A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$. A matrix $B\in M_{n\times m}(\mathbb F)$ is a
**Moore--Penrose pseudoinverse** of $A$ when

$$ABA=A,\qquad BAB=B,$$

and the two square products are self-adjoint:

$$ (AB)^*=AB,\qquad (BA)^*=BA. $$

When such a matrix exists and is unique, it is denoted by $A^+$.

The four displayed relations are the **Penrose equations**. They are written in
the matrix product and adjoint conventions of
Rectangular matrix multiplication and the identity matrix $I_n$, including zero-sized shapes and
In orthonormal bases, the matrix of the adjoint is the conjugate transpose of the matrix.

Let $d\ge1$, let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty, bounded, closed, and convex, let $H$ be a fixed real positive-semidefinite matrix, and let $y\in\mathbb R^d$. The function $x\mapsto(x-y)^\top H(x-y)$ attains a minimum on $K$. This conclusion allows $H$ to be singular and makes no uniqueness claim.

derivations.claim: The outer product is $G_1=g_1g_1^\top=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$. By [F1, F2], $H_1=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$; the matrix $D=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$ satisfies $H_1DH_1=H_1$, $DH_1D=D$, and both $H_1D$ and $DH_1$ equal the symmetric matrix $D$. By [F3], $H_1^\dagger=D$.

The update gives $y_2=(0,0)-\operatorname{diag}(1,0)(1,0)=(-1,0)$. For $(a,b)\in[-1,1]^2$, $( (a,b)-y_2)^\top H_1((a,b)-y_2)=(a+1)^2$, which is minimized exactly when $a=-1$, with $b$ arbitrary in $[-1,1]$.

Hence the entire minimizer set is $\{(-1,s):s\in[-1,1]\}$, containing distinct points, and the selected $x_2=(-1,0)$ is valid. The metric has a zero eigenvalue, and [F4] independently guarantees existence of at least one minimizer.

Let $(K,U,R)$ be a mirror regularizer with $R$ $m$-strongly convex on $K$ for some $m>0$. Fix an integer horizon $T\ge1$ and a step size $\eta>0$. Admissibility requires the unique minimizer of $R$ on $K$ to lie in $U$; initialize $x_1$ at this minimizer. At each round $t=1,\ldots,T$, play $x_t$ before observing the full current loss $f_t$, with losses and gradients written in the same affine coordinates used for $K$. Use either of these feedback cases:

1. $f_t$ is differentiable and convex on an open convex set containing $K$, and $g_t=\nabla f_t(x_t)$.
2. $f_t$ is convex on a convex set containing $K$, and a supplied vector $g_t$ satisfies $f_t(u)\ge f_t(x_t)+\langle g_t,u-x_t\rangle$ for every $u\in K$.

For each round require that there is a unique $y_{t+1}\in U$ satisfying

$$\nabla R(y_{t+1})=\nabla R(x_t)-\eta g_t.$$

Set $x_{t+1}$ to the minimizer of $B_R(x\|y_{t+1})$ over $x\in K$, and require this minimizer to lie in $U$ so that the next dual update is defined. The Bregman minimizer exists and is unique under the stated strong-convexity and compactness hypotheses. Output the decisions $x_1,\ldots,x_T$; the final $x_{T+1}$ is the internal post-round iterate.

Let $n\ge2$. Coordinates in $\mathbb R^{n-1}$ use the library's function-space convention: for $v\in\mathbb R^{n-1}$ and $1\le i<n$, write $v_i:=v(i-1)$. Let

$$K_n:=\{q\in\mathbb R^{n-1}:q_i\ge0\text{ for all }1\le i<n,\ \sum_{i=1}^{n-1}q_i\le1\},$$

and for $q\in K_n$ put $p_i=q_i$ for $1\le i<n$ and $p_n=1-\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}q_i$. Define $R(q)=\sum_{i=1}^np_i\log p_i$, with $0\log0:=0$. In the independent coordinates $q_1,\ldots,q_{n-1}$, $R$ is continuous on $K_n$, is twice continuously differentiable on its interior, is $1$-strongly convex in the Euclidean norm, and satisfies

$$-\log n\le R(q)\le0.$$

The minimum $-\log n$ is attained at $p_i=1/n$ for every $i$, and the maximum $0$ is attained at each vertex of the simplex.

Let $d\ge1$, let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty, bounded, closed, and convex, and let $(K,U,R)$ be a mirror regularizer with $R$ $m$-strongly convex on $K$ for some $m>0$. Then $R$ has a unique minimizer on $K$, and for every $y\in U$ the function $x\mapsto B_R(x\|y)$ has a unique minimizer $x_+(y)$ on $K$. If $x_+(y)\in U$, then for every $u\in K$,

$$\langle\nabla R(x_+(y))-\nabla R(y),u-x_+(y)\rangle\ge0$$

and

$$B_R(u\|y)\ge B_R(u\|x_+(y))+B_R(x_+(y)\|y).$$

Let $(K,U,R)$ be a mirror regularizer, and suppose $R$ is $m$-strongly convex on $K$ for some $m>0$. For $x,y\in U$,

$$B_R(x\|y)\ge0,$$

with strict inequality when $x\ne y$. For $x\in K$ and $y\in K\cap U$,

$$B_R(x\|y)\ge\frac m2\|x-y\|_2^2.$$

Let $N,T\ge1$ be integers, let $[N]=\{1,\ldots,N\}$ be the expert set, and let $\epsilon>0$. At each round $t=1,\ldots,T$, a finite loss vector $\ell_t=(\ell_t(1),\ldots,\ell_t(N))\in[0,\infty)^N$ is revealed after the learner's choice. Initialize $W_1(i)=1$ for every $i\in[N]$. At round $t$, set
$$x_t(i):=\frac{W_t(i)}{\sum_{j=1}^{N}W_t(j)},\qquad i\in[N],$$
Let $\mathcal H_{t-1}$ be the pre-round history sigma-algebra generated by the previously played choices and all previously revealed loss vectors (any random loss vector is assumed measurable on the protocol's probability space). The weights and $x_t$ are $\mathcal H_{t-1}$-measurable. Draw a measurable expert choice $I_t\in[N]$ with conditional distribution
$$\mathbb P(I_t=i\mid\mathcal H_{t-1})=x_t(i)\quad\text{almost surely},\qquad i\in[N],$$
and play $I_t$. After observing the whole vector $\ell_t$, update
$$W_{t+1}(i):=W_t(i)\exp(-\epsilon\ell_t(i)),\qquad i\in[N].$$
The output is the distributions $x_1,\ldots,x_T$, the sampled choices $I_1,\ldots,I_T$, and the final weights. The protocol assumes a probability space carrying the stated measurable draws; no probability-space construction is claimed.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
(Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of If $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L \ne 0$ then $|f| > |L|/2$ on a punctured neighbourhood of $c$; in particular if $L > 0$ then $f > L/2 > 0$ there applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
Carathéodory's characterisation: $f$ is differentiable at $c$ if and only if there is $\varphi : A \to \mathbb{R}$, continuous at $c$, with $f(x) - f(c) = \varphi(x)(x - c)$ for every $x \in A$, and then $\varphi$ is unique and $\varphi(c) = f'(c)$.** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of Sums, scalar multiples, products, absolute values, maxima, minima and quotients with nonvanishing denominator of continuous functions are continuous, as are constants, the identity and every polynomial function.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ (Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$) at which $g$ is differentiable
(The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because The exponential is a continuous bijection from $\mathbb{R}$ onto $(0,\infty)$ states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

derivations.claim: On $U_n$, differentiating $R(q)=\sum_{i<n}q_i\log q_i+p_n\log p_n$ using [F6, F7, F9] gives $\partial_iR=\log q_i+1-(\log p_n+1)=\log(q_i/p_n)$ and $\nabla^2R(q)=\operatorname{diag}(1/q_1,\ldots,1/q_{n-1})+\frac1{p_n}\mathbf1\mathbf1^\top$. For every nonzero $v$, $v^\top\nabla^2R(q)v=\sum_{i<n}v_i^2/q_i+(\sum_{i<n}v_i)^2/p_n>0$. Thus the Hessian is positive definite on $U_n$; together with [F2] and [F10], this verifies the mirror-regularizer conditions for $(K_n,U_n)$ and the validity of the uniform initialization.

Fix an interior iterate $p_t$ and write $r_{t+1}$ for the full probability coordinates of a prospective dual point $y_{t+1}\in U_n$. In independent coordinates the linear loss is $f_t(q)=\ell_{t,n}+\sum_{i<n}q_i(\ell_{t,i}-\ell_{t,n})$, a differentiable convex function on all of $\mathbb R^{n-1}$ with gradient $g_{t,i}=\ell_{t,i}-\ell_{t,n}$. By step 1.1, the dual equation [F1] becomes $\log(r_{t+1,i}/r_{t+1,n})=\log(p_{t,i}/p_{t,n})-\eta(\ell_{t,i}-\ell_{t,n})$ for $i<n$.

Let $d\ge1$, let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be a nonempty bounded closed convex set with nonempty interior, and let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be an open convex set such that $\operatorname{int}(K)\subseteq U$ and $K\subseteq\overline U$. If a decision set is lower-dimensional in an ambient Euclidean space, take $\mathbb R^d$ to be orthonormal affine coordinates on its affine hull (the smallest affine subspace containing it); thus interior, gradients, Hessians, and norms are relative to that affine hull. A **mirror regularizer** on $(K,U)$ is a real-valued function $R$ on $K\cup U$ that is continuous on $K$, twice continuously differentiable on $U$, agrees on $K\cap U$, and has symmetric positive-definite Hessian $H_R(z):=\nabla^2R(z)$ for every $z\in U$. We call $R$ $m$-strongly convex on $K$ in the Euclidean norm if, for some $m>0$, all $x,y\in K$ and $\lambda\in[0,1]$ satisfy

$$R((1-\lambda)x+\lambda y)\le (1-\lambda)R(x)+\lambda R(y)-\frac m2\lambda(1-\lambda)\|x-y\|_2^2.$$

For $x\in K\cup U$ and $y\in U$, the **Bregman divergence** generated by $R$ is

$$B_R(x\|y):=R(x)-R(y)-\langle\nabla R(y),x-y\rangle.$$

For $z\in U$ and vectors $v,h\in\mathbb R^d$, define the squared **local primal norm** and **local dual norm** by

$$\|v\|_z^2:=v^\top H_R(z)v,\qquad \|h\|_{*,z}^2:=h^\top H_R(z)^{-1}h.$$

Let $(K,U,R)$ be a mirror regularizer with $R$ $m$-strongly convex on $K$ for some $m>0$. Fix an integer horizon $T\ge1$ and a step size $\eta>0$. Admissibility requires the unique minimizer of $R$ on $K$ to lie in $U$; initialize $x_1$ at this minimizer. At each round $t=1,\ldots,T$, play $x_t$ before observing the full current loss $f_t$, with losses and gradients written in the same affine coordinates used for $K$. Use either of these feedback cases:

1. $f_t$ is differentiable and convex on an open convex set containing $K$, and $g_t=\nabla f_t(x_t)$.
2. $f_t$ is convex on a convex set containing $K$, and a supplied vector $g_t$ satisfies $f_t(u)\ge f_t(x_t)+\langle g_t,u-x_t\rangle$ for every $u\in K$.

For each round require that there is a unique $y_{t+1}\in U$ satisfying

$$\nabla R(y_{t+1})=\nabla R(x_t)-\eta g_t.$$

Set $x_{t+1}$ to the minimizer of $B_R(x\|y_{t+1})$ over $x\in K$, and require this minimizer to lie in $U$ so that the next dual update is defined. The Bregman minimizer exists and is unique under the stated strong-convexity and compactness hypotheses. Output the decisions $x_1,\ldots,x_T$; the final $x_{T+1}$ is the internal post-round iterate.

Let $d,T\ge1$ be integers, let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let $D,G\ge0$ be finite real bounds such that $\|u-v\|_2\le D$ for all $u,v\in K$ and $\|g_t\|_2\le G$. Supply an initial point $x_1\in K$. At each round $t=1,\ldots,T$, the learner plays $x_t$ and then receives the full loss function $f_t$ or the prescribed vector $g_t$. The smooth branch takes $f_t:U_t\to\mathbb R$ differentiable and convex on an open convex set $U_t\supseteq K$, with $g_t=\nabla f_t(x_t)$. The nonsmooth branch takes a convex function $f_t:C_t\to\mathbb R$ on a convex set $C_t\supseteq K$ and a supplied $g_t\in\partial f_t(x_t)$, where $\partial f_t(x_t)$ consists of vectors $g$ satisfying $f_t(y)\ge f_t(x_t)+\langle g,y-x_t\rangle$ for every $y\in C_t$; require explicitly that this inequality holds for every $u\in K$.

If $D=0$ or $G=0$, set $x_{t+1}=x_t$ at every round. If $D,G>0$, assume the Axiom of Countable Choice for the metric projection. Set $\eta_t=D/(G\sqrt t)$, put $y_{t+1}=x_t-\eta_tg_t$, and set $x_{t+1}=P_K(y_{t+1})$, the unique point of $K$ minimizing Euclidean distance to $y_{t+1}$. Return the decisions $x_1,\ldots,x_T$. Equip $\mathbb R^d$ with its Euclidean Borel $\sigma$-algebra and $K$ with the relative Borel $\sigma$-algebra. For random inputs, require $x_1$ to be a measurable $K$-valued random element and each $g_t$, whether supplied directly or computed as $\nabla f_t(x_t)$ in the smooth branch, to be a measurable $\mathbb R^d$-valued random element on the protocol's probability space. The vector update is continuous, and the nonexpansive projection is continuous, so each projected update remains measurable.

Let $d\ge1$, let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty, bounded, closed, and convex, and let $(K,U,R)$ be a mirror regularizer with $R$ $m$-strongly convex on $K$ for some $m>0$. and

$$B_R(u\|y)\ge B_R(u\|x_+(y))+B_R(x_+(y)\|y).$$

Coordinate and matrix-entry subscripts in this procedure are one-based labels: for $i,j\in\{1,\ldots,d\}$, write $g_i=g(i-1)$ and $G_{ij}=G(i-1,j-1)$ in the underlying zero-based Euclidean and matrix conventions, and use the same relabeling for the other vectors and matrices. Initialize $G_0=0$. For each round $t=1,\ldots,T$, play $x_t$, then receive the full current loss information and its prescribed gradient vector $g_t\in\mathbb R^d$, and set

$$G_t=G_{t-1}+g_tg_t^\top=\sum_{s=1}^t g_sg_s^\top.$$

The accumulated matrix $G_t$ is symmetric and positive semidefinite. Choose either the **full-matrix scale** $H_t=G_t^{1/2}$, the unique positive-semidefinite square root, or the **diagonal scale** $H_t=\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt{(G_t)_{11}},\ldots,\sqrt{(G_t)_{dd}})$. Define $H_t^\dagger$ to be the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse and update

$$y_{t+1}=x_t-\eta H_t^\dagger g_t,\qquad x_{t+1}\in\arg\min_{x\in K}(x-y_{t+1})^\top H_t(x-y_{t+1}).$$

A minimizer exists; if it is not unique, select any minimizer. Return $x_1,\ldots,x_T$. The matrix seminorm notation in the objective means $\|v\|_{H_t}^2=v^\top H_tv$. The diagonal scale here is formed by taking each diagonal entry of $G_t$ and then its scalar square root; in general it is not $\operatorname{diag}(G_t^{1/2})$. This is an update definition only and asserts no regret bound.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

For $A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$, the **transpose** of $A$ is the matrix
$A^{\mathsf T}\in M_{n\times m}(F)$ defined by

$$(A^{\mathsf T})_{ji}:=a_{ij}.$$

Thus transposition interchanges rows and columns. The transpose of a zero-sized
matrix is the unique matrix of the transposed zero-sized shape.

let $a, b, c \in F$.

$j = 0$, its first term being $2^0 a_{2^0} = a_1$.

The monotonicity hypothesis is equivalent to the consecutive form
$a_{k+1} \le a_k$ for every $k \ge 1$, since it says that the sequence
$b_i := a_{i+1}$, $i \in \mathbb{N}$, is nonincreasing (Nondecreasing, increasing, nonincreasing, decreasing, monotone, and eventually monotone sequences).
It cannot be dropped: the companion page exhibits a nonnegative non-monotone
family for which the two series behave differently.

The series starts at $k = 0$ and its first term is $r^0 = 1$; in particular

(Ordered field, Field).

**Natural exponents.** By the recursion theorem (The recursion theorem) applied to
the set $\mathbb{R}$, the starting element $1$ and the function
$f(x) = x \cdot a$, there is a unique function $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$,
written $n \mapsto a^n$, with

$$a^0 = 1, \qquad a^{n+1} = a^n \cdot a \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

Thus $a^1 = a$, $a^2 = a \cdot a$, and so on. Note that this is defined for
**every** $a$, including $a = 0$.

**Negative exponents.** If $a \ne 0$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, set

$$a^{-n} := (a^n)^{-1}.$$

**Why that is legitimate.** The right-hand side presupposes that $a^n$ is
invertible, that is, that $a^n \ne 0$. This is a proof obligation and not an
observation, and it is discharged by claim 2 of Laws of integer exponents: for $a \ne 0$
in a field, $a^n \ne 0$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, proved there by induction on
$n$ from the fact that a field has no zero divisors (A field has no zero divisors: $ab = 0 \Rightarrow a = 0$ or $b = 0$).
That lemma is a statement *about* the operation introduced here, so it depends on
this definition and is recorded in this item's `justified_by` rather than in its
`deps` (SCHEMA §3). Given $a^n \ne 0$, the value $(a^n)^{-1}$ is a single
well-determined element, because multiplicative inverses in a field are unique
(Identities and inverses in a field are unique).

**Integer exponents.** Every integer $m$ (The integers as equivalence classes of pairs of naturals) is either
$n$ or $-n$ for a unique natural $n$, where $n$ in these integer expressions denotes its image under the
embedding $\iota : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z}$ (The naturals embed in the integers,
Arithmetic on the integers). This too is a citation and not a slogan: the order on
$\mathbb{Z}$ is total (The integers form a totally ordered ring), so $m \ge 0$ or $m < 0$; the
image of $\iota$ is exactly the set of nonnegative integers, and each of them is
$n$ for a unique natural $n$ (The naturals embed in the integers); and if $m < 0$ then
$-m > 0$, by compatibility of the order with addition (The integers form a totally ordered ring),
so $-m = n$ and $m = -n$, with $n$ unique because $\iota$ is
injective. The two clauses above therefore define $a^m$ for every
$m \in \mathbb{Z}$ whenever $a \ne 0$, and for every $m \in \mathbb{N}$ for
arbitrary $a$. The two exponent domains are disjoint: the natural clause
handles $m \ge 0$, including $m = 0$, while the negative clause requires
$n \ge 1$ and therefore handles only $m < 0$.

Let $F$ be a field (Field) with additive identity $0_F$ and
multiplicative identity $1_F$. Define
$\iota : \mathbb{N} \to F$ by recursion on $\mathbb{N}$
(The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann), The recursion theorem):

$$\iota(0) \;:=\; 0_F, \qquad \iota(n+1) \;:=\; \iota(n) + 1_F .$$

$\iota(n)$ is the **canonical natural** of $n$ in $F$. It is also written
$n \cdot 1_F$, and for $n \ge 1$ it is $1_F$ added to itself $n$ times.

**Why the notation is needed at all.** A natural number in this library is a von
Neumann natural, that is a set (The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)), and a set is not an
element of $F$. So $1/n$, $n^{\alpha}$ and $x/n$ are not expressions of $F$ when
$n$ is a natural: what they mean is $1/\iota(n)$, $\iota(n)^{\alpha}$ and
$x/\iota(n)$. The map $\iota$ is what carries a counting number into the field,
and writing it is the whole reason a reader meets $1/\iota(k+1)$ where an
informal text would write $1/(k+1)$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field, with field structure as in Field, and for

$\underbrace{1_F + \cdots + 1_F}_{n}$, defined recursively by $1 \cdot 1_F = 1_F$

- $n \cdot 1_F > 0$ and $(n+1) \cdot 1_F > n \cdot 1_F$;

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ (Measures on sigma-algebras). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** (Measure spaces); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of Integrable real and complex functions, and their integrals, its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. Its positive and negative parts are
$$f^+:=\max\{f,0\},\qquad f^-:=\max\{-f,0\};$$
they are measurable by
Closure properties of measurable functions used by the integral and
satisfy $f=f^+-f^-$ and $|f|=f^++f^-$.

The **Lebesgue integral of a real measurable function** is defined whenever at
most one of $\int f^+\,d\mu$ and $\int f^-\,d\mu$ is $+\infty$, in which case
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\int f^+\,d\mu-\int f^-\,d\mu.$$
The function is **integrable** when both integrals are finite, equivalently
when $\int|f|\,d\mu<+\infty$.

For a complex measurable function $h=u+iv$ with
$u=\operatorname{Re}h,\ v=\operatorname{Im}h$
(Real and imaginary parts, complex conjugation, and modulus), define $h$ to be
**integrable** when $|h|$ is integrable, and then define
$$\int h\,d\mu:=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$

Let $a=(a_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ take values in $[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$ (The extended real line $\overline{\mathbb{R}} = \mathbb{R} \cup \{-\infty, +\infty\}$, its order, and the arithmetic that is left undefined). Its **partial sums** are the unique sequence $(s_n)$ in $[0,+\infty]$ satisfying

$$s_0=0,\qquad s_{n+1}=s_n+a_n.$$

To apply The recursion theorem with a fixed successor function, use the state space $\mathbb N\times[0,+\infty]$ and the self-map $T(n,s)=(n+1,s+a_n)$, starting from $(0,0)$. Recursion gives a unique state sequence; induction makes its first coordinate $n$, and its second coordinates are exactly the unique $(s_n)$ satisfying the displayed recurrence. Addition of two nonnegative extended reals is always defined, including when either is $+\infty$. The sequence $(s_n)$ is nondecreasing, and its **nonnegative extended sum** is

$$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}a_k:=\sup_{n\in\mathbb N}s_n\in[0,+\infty],$$

whose existence follows from completeness of the extended real line (Every subset of $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ has a least upper bound and a greatest lower bound in $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$, agreeing with the real supremum and infimum on nonempty sets bounded in $\mathbb{R}$). More generally, for $m\in\mathbb N$,

$$\sum_{k\ge m}a_k:=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}a_{m+j}.$$

Finite sums use the same recursion: $\sum_{k<n}a_k=s_n$, so the empty sum at $n=0$ is $0$. A double sum such as $\sum_i\sum_j a_{ij}$ means that the inner nonnegative extended sum is formed first and the resulting nonnegative extended sequence is then summed.

$$
\mathbb E\!\left[\exp\!\left(\lambda(X-\mu)\right)\right]\le \exp\!\left(\frac{\lambda^2}{2}\right).
$$
The expectation in this condition is the nonnegative Lebesgue integral of the displayed exponential; the inequality requires it to be finite for every real $\lambda$.

Its mean for arm $i$ is $\mu_i=\int_{\mathbb R}x\,P_i(dx)=\mathbb E[X_{s,i}]$, which does not depend on $s$. The learner may also use a random element $U$ for private randomization, provided $\sigma(U)$ is independent of the sigma-algebra generated by the entire table; a deterministic learner uses a constant $U$.

A non-anticipating policy chooses a measurable arm $A_t\in[k]$ at each round $t\in[n]$ using only $U$ and the previously observed history $(A_1,Y_1,\ldots,A_{t-1},Y_{t-1})$. Write $\mathcal H_{t-1}=\sigma(U,A_1,Y_1,\ldots,A_{t-1},Y_{t-1})$ for that history sigma-algebra. Define the pull count $T_i(0)=0$ and
$$
T_i(t)=\sum_{r=1}^{t}\mathbf 1_{\{A_r=i\}},\qquad Y_t=X_{T_{A_t}(t),A_t}.
$$
Thus each time arm $i$ is selected the learner receives the next unused entry in arm $i$'s reward stack. Set
$$
\mu^*=\max_{i\in[k]}\mu_i,\qquad \Delta_i=\mu^*-\mu_i\ge0,
$$
define the pseudo-regret $\bar R_n=\sum_{t=1}^n(\mu^*-\mu_{A_t})$, and define the realized reward regret $R_n^{\rm rew}=n\mu^*-\sum_{t=1}^nY_t$ and expected reward regret $R_n=\mathbb E[R_n^{\rm rew}]$.

derivations.claim: Partition $B$ by the finitely many past action strings $\alpha=(a_1,\ldots,a_{t-1})\in[k]^{t-1}$. Let $c_j(\alpha)$ be the number of times arm $j$ occurs in $\alpha$, and write $B_\alpha=B\cap\{(A_1,\ldots,A_{t-1})=\alpha\}$. By the recursive non-anticipating policy rule, each $B_\alpha$ is measurable with respect to $U$ and the table entries $X_{s,j}$ with $s\le c_j(\alpha)$: along that fixed action string, those and only those stack entries have been revealed.

If $B_\alpha$ is nonempty then $A_t=i$ on it, and the next reward is $Y_t=X_{c_i(\alpha)+1,i}$. This table entry is distinct from every coordinate determining $B_\alpha$. By [F2] it is independent of the vector of those coordinates, so the event $B_\alpha$ is independent of $\{X_{c_i(\alpha)+1,i}\in C\}$ for every Borel $C$. Its law is $P_i$, hence $\mathbb P(B_\alpha\cap\{Y_t\in C\})=\mathbb P(B_\alpha)P_i(C)$.
The events $B_\alpha$ partition $B$. Summing the identity in step 2.1 over the finite set $[k]^{t-1}$ gives $\mathbb P(B\cap\{Y_t\in C\})=\mathbb P(B)P_i(C)$ for every Borel $C$.

For each $\alpha$, the indicator $\mathbf 1_{B_\alpha}$ is a measurable function of the exposed-coordinate vector. By [F2] and [F4], it is independent of $X_{c_i(\alpha)+1,i}$. Both are integrable by [F3], so [F5] and [F6] give $\mathbb E[Y_t\mathbf 1_{B_\alpha}]=\mu_i\mathbb P(B_\alpha)$. Summing over the finite action strings yields $\mathbb E[Y_t\mathbf 1_B]=\mu_i\mathbb P(B)$.

Fix positive integers $n$ and $k$, write $[k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}$, and let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space. A finite-horizon $k$-armed stochastic bandit in **reward-stack form** consists of probability measures $P_i$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$ with finite first absolute moments, and an independent table of integrable real random variables $(X_{s,i})_{1\le s\le n,\ i\in[k]}$ such that the table entries are mutually independent and each $X_{s,i}$ has law $P_i$. Its mean for arm $i$ is $\mu_i=\int_{\mathbb R}x\,P_i(dx)=\mathbb E[X_{s,i}]$, which does not depend on $s$. The learner may also use a random element $U$ for private randomization, provided $\sigma(U)$ is independent of the sigma-algebra generated by the entire table; a deterministic learner uses a constant $U$.

A non-anticipating policy chooses a measurable arm $A_t\in[k]$ at each round $t\in[n]$ using only $U$ and the previously observed history $(A_1,Y_1,\ldots,A_{t-1},Y_{t-1})$. Write $\mathcal H_{t-1}=\sigma(U,A_1,Y_1,\ldots,A_{t-1},Y_{t-1})$ for that history sigma-algebra. Define the pull count $T_i(0)=0$ and
$$
T_i(t)=\sum_{r=1}^{t}\mathbf 1_{\{A_r=i\}},\qquad Y_t=X_{T_{A_t}(t),A_t}.
$$
Thus each time arm $i$ is selected the learner receives the next unused entry in arm $i$'s reward stack. Set
$$
\mu^*=\max_{i\in[k]}\mu_i,\qquad \Delta_i=\mu^*-\mu_i\ge0,
$$
define the pseudo-regret $\bar R_n=\sum_{t=1}^n(\mu^*-\mu_{A_t})$, and define the realized reward regret $R_n^{\rm rew}=n\mu^*-\sum_{t=1}^nY_t$ and expected reward regret $R_n=\mathbb E[R_n^{\rm rew}]$.

Each $Y_t$ is integrable because it selects one entry of the finite table, so $|Y_t|\le\sum_{s=1}^n\sum_{i=1}^k|X_{s,i}|$ and the right-hand side is integrable. Hence $R_n^{\rm rew}$ is integrable as well.

Let $X$ be an integrable real random variable on a probability space, and write $\mu=\mathbb E[X]$. The reward $X$ is **1-sub-Gaussian** if for every $\lambda\in\mathbb R$,
$$
\mathbb E\!\left[\exp\!\left(\lambda(X-\mu)\right)\right]\le \exp\!\left(\frac{\lambda^2}{2}\right).
$$
The expectation in this condition is the nonnegative Lebesgue integral of the displayed exponential; the inequality requires it to be finite for every real $\lambda$.

In the finite reward-stack model, fix a round $t\in[n]$, an arm $i\in[k]$, an event $B\in\mathcal H_{t-1}$ with $B\subseteq\{A_t=i\}$, and a Borel set $C\subseteq\mathbb R$. Then
$$
\mathbb P(B\cap\{Y_t\in C\})=\mathbb P(B)P_i(C),\qquad \mathbb E[Y_t\mathbf 1_B]=\mu_i\mathbb P(B).
$$
In particular, the reward stack satisfies the fixed conditional reward-law and conditional-mean interface for finite-arm stochastic environments.

In an online decision protocol with horizon $T$, the environment and feedback model specifies how each loss function is chosen and what the learner observes after choosing $x_t$. **Full-information feedback** reveals the entire function $f_t$ (or, for $N$ experts, the full vector of their $N$ losses) after the round-$t$ choice. **Bandit feedback** reveals only the played loss $f_t(x_t)$ after that choice. An **oblivious adversary** fixes the whole sequence $(f_1,\ldots,f_T)$ before the learner's random choices are realized; it may know the learner's rule but not its realized private randomization. A **non-anticipating adaptive adversary** chooses $f_t$ from the history available before $x_t$ is chosen, so $f_t$ may depend on earlier choices and feedback but not on the current choice or the learner's current private randomization. A **reactive adversary** may choose $f_t$ after observing $x_t$, so its round-$t$ loss may depend on that current choice. These adversary classes have different timing and are not interchangeable; a guarantee established for one class is not asserted for another. For the stochastic reward model, let $\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$ be the smallest collection of subsets of $\mathbb R$ that contains every open interval and is closed under complements and countable unions; its members are the Borel sets. A **stochastic finite-arm reward environment** has $N\ge1$ arms, a fixed probability measure $P_i$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$ for each arm $i\in[N]:=\{1,\ldots,N\}$, and finite first moments $\int_{\mathbb R}|y|\,P_i(dy)<\infty$ with means $\mu_i:=\int_{\mathbb R} y\,P_i(dy)$. At each round the learner chooses a measurable arm $A_t$ with values in $[N]$ equipped with its full power set, before the reward $Y_t$ is drawn. The fixed-law condition means that, for every $i$, every event $B$ determined by the history before the reward and the chosen arm with $B\subseteq\{A_t=i\}$, and every $C\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$, $\mathbb P(B\cap\{Y_t\in C\})=\mathbb P(B)P_i(C)$. The model also states explicitly the conditional-mean identity used below: $\mathbb E[\mathbf1_B Y_t]=\mu_i\mathbb P(B)$ for every such $B$. Here $Y_t$ is an integrable real random variable, $\mathbf1_B$ is the indicator of event $B$, and the history-and-arm events are measurable in the common probability space. This stochastic reward model is distinct from adversarial loss models and supplies no regret guarantee by itself.

Let $T,N\ge1$ be integers, let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, and let $A_t:\Omega\to[N]$ be measurable arm choices and $Y_t:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ integrable rewards for $t=1,\ldots,T$. Let $\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_N\in\mathbb R$ be finite arm means and assume the conditional-mean identity
$$
\mathbb E\!\left[Y_t\mathbf1_{\{A_t=i\}}\right]=\mu_i\mathbb P(A_t=i)\qquad(t=1,\ldots,T,\ i\in[N]).
$$
Set $\mu^*:=\max_{i\in[N]}\mu_i$, define the pseudo-regret $\bar R_T:=\sum_{t=1}^T(\mu^*-\mu_{A_t})$, the realized reward regret $R_T^{\rm rew}:=\sum_{t=1}^T(\mu^*-Y_t)$, and the number of pulls of arm $i$ by $N_i(T):=\sum_{t=1}^T\mathbf1_{\{A_t=i\}}$. Then
$$
\mathbb E[R_T^{\rm rew}]=\mathbb E[\bar R_T]=\sum_{i=1}^N(\mu^*-\mu_i)\,\mathbb E[N_i(T)].
$$

Input integers $k,n,m\ge1$ with $mk\le n$, and access to an $n$-round $k$-armed stochastic bandit. The output is the sequence of selected arms $A_1,\ldots,A_n$ and the committed arm $J$.

1. For rounds $t=1,\ldots,mk$, choose arm $A_t=1+((t-1)\bmod k)$ and observe its reward $Y_t$. Thus each arm is explored exactly $m$ times.
2. For each $i\in[k]$, form its exploration mean
   $$
   \widehat\mu_i=\frac1m\sum_{r=1}^m Y_{(r-1)k+i}.
   $$
3. Let $J$ be the least index attaining $\max_{i\in[k]}\widehat\mu_i$.
4. For every remaining round $t=mk+1,\ldots,n$, choose $A_t=J$ and observe its reward.

Let $Z_1,\ldots,Z_q$ be mutually independent integrable real random variables on a common probability space, with means $m_j=\mathbb E[Z_j]$, and suppose each is 1-sub-Gaussian, meaning that $\mathbb E[\exp(\lambda(Z_j-m_j))]\le\exp(\lambda^2/2)$ for every $\lambda\in\mathbb R$. $$

$$

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of random elements
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$. For each $i$, let
$g_i:(S_i,\Sigma_i)\to(T_i,\mathcal T_i)$ be measurable. Then the family
$(g_i\circ X_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent.

The first $mk$ rounds pull each arm exactly $m$ times, and every later round pulls $J$; hence $T_i(n)=m+(n-mk)\mathbf1_{\{J=i\}}$. Taking expectations gives $R_n=m\sum_{i=1}^k\Delta_i+(n-mk)\sum_{i=1}^k\Delta_i\mathbb P(J=i)$.

Fix an optimal arm $i^*$ with $\mu_{i^*}=\mu^*$. On $G$, any later play when its current count is $s$ requires $\widehat\mu_{i,s}+r_s\ge\mu^*$: its selected index is at least the current index of $i^*$, which is at least $\mu^*$. Each such count $s\in\{1,\ldots,n-1\}$ can be charged at most once, since a play increases the count by one. Always $T_i(n)\le n$. Thus pointwise $T_i(n)\le1+\sum_{s=1}^{n-1}\mathbf1_{\{\widehat\mu_{i,s}+r_s\ge\mu^*\}}+n\mathbf1_{G^c}.$

If it is nonpositive, use the bound $1$ in [F5]. Fix positive integers $n$ and $k$, write $[k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}$, and let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space. A finite-horizon $k$-armed stochastic bandit in **reward-stack form** consists of probability measures $P_i$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$ with finite first absolute moments, and an independent table of integrable real random variables $(X_{s,i})_{1\le s\le n,\ i\in[k]}$ such that the table entries are mutually independent and each $X_{s,i}$ has law $P_i$. Its mean for arm $i$ is $\mu_i=\int_{\mathbb R}x\,P_i(dx)=\mathbb E[X_{s,i}]$, which does not depend on $s$. The learner may also use a random element $U$ for private randomization, provided $\sigma(U)$ is independent of the sigma-algebra generated by the entire table; a deterministic learner uses a constant $U$.

A non-anticipating policy chooses a measurable arm $A_t\in[k]$ at each round $t\in[n]$ using only $U$ and the previously observed history $(A_1,Y_1,\ldots,A_{t-1},Y_{t-1})$. Write $\mathcal H_{t-1}=\sigma(U,A_1,Y_1,\ldots,A_{t-1},Y_{t-1})$ for that history sigma-algebra. Define the pull count $T_i(0)=0$ and
$$
T_i(t)=\sum_{r=1}^{t}\mathbf 1_{\{A_r=i\}},\qquad Y_t=X_{T_{A_t}(t),A_t}.
$$
Thus each time arm $i$ is selected the learner receives the next unused entry in arm $i$'s reward stack. Set
$$
\mu^*=\max_{i\in[k]}\mu_i,\qquad \Delta_i=\mu^*-\mu_i\ge0,
$$
define the pseudo-regret $\bar R_n=\sum_{t=1}^n(\mu^*-\mu_{A_t})$, and define the realized reward regret $R_n^{\rm rew}=n\mu^*-\sum_{t=1}^nY_t$ and expected reward regret $R_n=\mathbb E[R_n^{\rm rew}]$.

Each $Y_t$ is integrable because it selects one entry of the finite table, so $|Y_t|\le\sum_{s=1}^n\sum_{i=1}^k|X_{s,i}|$ and the right-hand side is integrable. Hence $R_n^{\rm rew}$ is integrable as well.

Let $X$ be an integrable real random variable on a probability space, and write $\mu=\mathbb E[X]$. The reward $X$ is **1-sub-Gaussian** if for every $\lambda\in\mathbb R$,
$$
\mathbb E\!\left[\exp\!\left(\lambda(X-\mu)\right)\right]\le \exp\!\left(\frac{\lambda^2}{2}\right).
$$
The expectation in this condition is the nonnegative Lebesgue integral of the displayed exponential; the inequality requires it to be finite for every real $\lambda$.

$$
\mathbb P(B\cap\{Y_t\in C\})=\mathbb P(B)P_i(C),\qquad \mathbb E[Y_t\mathbf 1_B]=\mu_i\mathbb P(B).
$$

$$
\mathbb E\!\left[Y_t\mathbf1_{\{A_t=i\}}\right]=\mu_i\mathbb P(A_t=i)\qquad(t=1,\ldots,T,\ i\in[N]).
$$
Set $\mu^*:=\max_{i\in[N]}\mu_i$, define the pseudo-regret $\bar R_T:=\sum_{t=1}^T(\mu^*-\mu_{A_t})$, the realized reward regret $R_T^{\rm rew}:=\sum_{t=1}^T(\mu^*-Y_t)$, and the number of pulls of arm $i$ by $N_i(T):=\sum_{t=1}^T\mathbf1_{\{A_t=i\}}$. Then
$$

Fix positive integers $n$ and $k$, write $[k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}$, and let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space. A finite-horizon $k$-armed stochastic bandit in **reward-stack form** consists of probability measures $P_i$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$ with finite first absolute moments, and an independent table of integrable real random variables $(X_{s,i})_{1\le s\le n,\ i\in[k]}$ such that the table entries are mutually independent and each $X_{s,i}$ has law $P_i$. Its mean for arm $i$ is $\mu_i=\int_{\mathbb R}x\,P_i(dx)=\mathbb E[X_{s,i}]$, which does not depend on $s$. The learner may also use a random element $U$ for private randomization, provided $\sigma(U)$ is independent of the sigma-algebra generated by the entire table; a deterministic learner uses a constant $U$.

A non-anticipating policy chooses a measurable arm $A_t\in[k]$ at each round $t\in[n]$ using only $U$ and the previously observed history $(A_1,Y_1,\ldots,A_{t-1},Y_{t-1})$. Write $\mathcal H_{t-1}=\sigma(U,A_1,Y_1,\ldots,A_{t-1},Y_{t-1})$ for that history sigma-algebra. Define the pull count $T_i(0)=0$ and
$$
T_i(t)=\sum_{r=1}^{t}\mathbf 1_{\{A_r=i\}},\qquad Y_t=X_{T_{A_t}(t),A_t}.
$$
Thus each time arm $i$ is selected the learner receives the next unused entry in arm $i$'s reward stack. Set
$$
\mu^*=\max_{i\in[k]}\mu_i,\qquad \Delta_i=\mu^*-\mu_i\ge0,
$$
define the pseudo-regret $\bar R_n=\sum_{t=1}^n(\mu^*-\mu_{A_t})$, and define the realized reward regret $R_n^{\rm rew}=n\mu^*-\sum_{t=1}^nY_t$ and expected reward regret $R_n=\mathbb E[R_n^{\rm rew}]$.

Each $Y_t$ is integrable because it selects one entry of the finite table, so $|Y_t|\le\sum_{s=1}^n\sum_{i=1}^k|X_{s,i}|$ and the right-hand side is integrable. Hence $R_n^{\rm rew}$ is integrable as well.

derivations.claim: Each arm's law is the point mass at $0$, so both finite means equal $0$. Hence $\mu^*=0$ and $\Delta_1=\Delta_2=0$.
For every policy and every round, $\mu^*-\mu_{A_t}=0$ and the observed reward $Y_t=0$. The defining sums therefore give $\bar R_n=0$ and $R_n^{\rm rew}=0$ pointwise.
Taking expectations of the two identically zero random variables shows that expected pseudo-regret and expected reward regret both equal zero.

Let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on a nonempty set $X$ (Sigma-algebras) and fix $x_0\in X$. The **Dirac set function at $x_0$** is

$$\delta_{x_0}(E):=\begin{cases}1,&x_0\in E,\\0,&x_0\notin E,\end{cases}\qquad E\in\mathcal A.$$

The two branches are exhaustive and disjoint. The fact that this set function is a probability measure is proved in A Dirac set function is a probability measure.
For $x_0\in X$, the Dirac set function $\delta_{x_0}$ is a probability measure on every sigma-algebra on $X$.

Let $\mu$ be a measure and let $c\in[0,+\infty]$. Define the scalar set function $c\mu$ by three disjoint branches:

$$ (c\mu)(E):=\begin{cases}0,&c=0,\\c\,\mu(E),&0<c<+\infty,\\0,&c=+\infty\text{ and }\mu(E)=0,\\+\infty,&c=+\infty\text{ and }\mu(E)>0.\end{cases}$$

Thus neither the zero branch nor the infinite branch forms the undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

For measures $(\mu_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ on the same measurable space and weights $c_k\in[0,+\infty]$, their **countable weighted sum** is the pointwise set function

$$\left(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}c_k\mu_k\right)(E):=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(c_k\mu_k)(E),$$

using Series in the nonnegative extended real line. Finite weighted sums are defined by the corresponding finite partial sum, with the empty weighted sum the zero set function. The fact that all these set functions are measures is Nonnegative scalar multiples and countable weighted sums of measures are measures.

Let $(\mu_k)$ be measures on one measurable space and let $c_k\in[0,+\infty]$. Each scalar multiple $c_k\mu_k$, defined by the zero, finite-positive, and positive-infinity branches of Nonnegative scalar multiples and countable weighted sums of measures, is a measure. Every finite or countable weighted sum $\sum_kc_k\mu_k$ is also a measure.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ (Measures on sigma-algebras). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** (Measure spaces); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space. Let $(E_j)_{j\ge1}$ be a countable measurable partition of $\Omega$, let $c_j\in[0,\infty)$ be finite real numbers, and let $Z:\Omega\to[0,\infty)$ be measurable with $Z=c_j$ on $E_j$. Then, as an extended nonnegative value,
$$
\mathbb E[Z]=\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}c_j\,\mathbb P(E_j).
$$
If this series is finite, then $Z$ is integrable and its expectation is that finite sum.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and let
$(S,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space. A **random element** of $S$ is a measurable
map
$$X:(\Omega,\mathcal F)\to(S,\Sigma)$$
in the sense of A measurable function between measurable spaces.

When $S=\mathbb R$ and $\Sigma=\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$ from
The Borel sigma-algebra of a topological space, the map $X$ is a **real random variable**.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element. Its
**law** or **distribution** is the set function
$$\mathbb P_X:\Sigma\to[0,+\infty],\qquad \mathbb P_X(B):=\mathbb P(X^{-1}(B)).$$

Thus the law of $X$ records the probability of each measurable target set by
pulling it back to an event in the original probability space.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element. Then
$\mathbb P_X$ is a probability measure on $(S,\Sigma)$.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element, let
$\mathbb P_X$ be its law, and let $g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb R$ or
$g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb C$ be measurable.

1. If $g\ge0$, then
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$
2. If $g(X)$ is integrable, then $g$ is integrable with respect to
   $\mathbb P_X$ and the same formula holds:
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in The exponential series converges absolutely for every real argument. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of The factorial $n!$ and the falling factorial $n^{\underline{k}}$, defined by recursion in $\mathbb{N}$, $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image (The canonical natural $\iota(n) = n \cdot 1_F$ of a field, Canonical naturals are positive and strictly increasing), and powers and series are those of Integer powers $a^m$ and Series, partial sums, convergence and the sum, divergence, and the tail series.

This is a real power series centred at $0$ (A real power series about a centre, its interval of convergence, and its radius in $[0,+\infty]$). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.
For every real $x$, the series $\sum_{n\ge0}x^n/\iota(n!)$ converges absolutely. Its power-series radius is therefore $+\infty$.

Let $(a_k)$ be a sequence of reals with $a_k \ge 0$ for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$,
let $s_n = \sum_{k<n} a_k$ be its partial sums and let
$S = \{\, s_n : n \in \mathbb{N} \,\}$ be the range of $(s_n)$ (Series, partial sums, convergence and the sum, divergence, and the tail series).
Then:

1. $(s_n)$ is nondecreasing (Nondecreasing, increasing, nonincreasing, decreasing, monotone, and eventually monotone sequences) and $s_n \ge 0$ for every
   $n$;
2. $\sum a_k$ converges **if and only if** $S$ is bounded above
   (Lower bound, bounded below, bounded set), and in that case
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} a_k \;=\; \sup S ,$$
   so in particular $s_n \le \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} a_k$ for every $n$;
3. if $S$ is not bounded above then $s_n \to +\infty$
   (Divergence to $+\infty$ and to $-\infty$) and $\sum a_k$ diverges.

This is the theorem that makes the nonnegative theory work: for terms of one
sign, convergence is a boundedness question and no candidate limit is ever
needed. Every comparison test on this page is an application of it.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field (The real numbers) and
a **sequence of reals** is a function $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$
(Sequences of reals: bounded, eventually, frequently, tails, subsequences), written $(a_k)$; recall that $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$.

**Partial sums.** Let $(a_k)$ be a sequence of reals. Its **sequence of partial
sums** is

$$s_n \;:=\; \sum_{k < n} a_k \qquad (n \in \mathbb{N}),$$

the finite sum of Finite sums and finite products, by recursion. In particular $s_0 = 0$, the empty sum, and
$s_{n+1} = s_n + a_n$ for every $n$, those being exactly the two recursion clauses
that define the finite sum. Note that $s_n$ is the sum of the $n$ terms
$a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$, so the index $n$ counts terms rather than naming the last
one.

**Convergence, the sum, divergence.** The **series** of $(a_k)$, written
$\sum a_k$, **converges** when the sequence $(s_n)$ of partial sums converges
(Limits and Cauchy sequences of reals), and then the **sum of the series** is

$$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} a_k \;:=\; \lim_{n} s_n .$$

The series **diverges** when $(s_n)$ does not converge. A convergent sequence of
reals has exactly one limit (A sequence has at most one limit), so the displayed symbol names
a single real number and nothing further has to be checked for it to be
well defined.

**Series with a general starting index.** Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $a$ be a
function on $\{\, k \in \mathbb{N} : k \ge m \,\}$, which we call a **family from
$m$** and write $(a_k)_{k \ge m}$. The series

$$\sum_{k \ge m} a_k$$

is by definition the series of the sequence $b_j := a_{j + m}$,
$j \in \mathbb{N}$, which is a genuine sequence of reals; it converges exactly
when that series converges, and its sum is then written
$\sum_{k = m}^{\infty} a_k$. Its partial sums are

$$\sum_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k \;=\; \sum_{j < n-m} a_{m+j} \qquad (n \ge m),$$

in the notation of Finite sums and finite products, by recursion, the value at $n = m$ being the empty sum
$0$. A sequence on $\mathbb{N}$ is the case $m = 0$, and the two readings of
$\sum a_k$ agree there, since $b_j = a_j$.

**This clause is not a convenience.** Sequences in this library are functions on
$\mathbb{N}$ and $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$ (Sequences of reals: bounded, eventually, frequently, tails, subsequences), while many of the
classical series are built from expressions that are undefined at the index $0$:
$1/k$, $1/k^{p}$ and $|a_k|^{1/k}$ all require $k \ge 1$. Writing such a series as
$\sum_{k \ge 1} a_k$ names an honest object, whereas writing it as a sequence on
$\mathbb{N}$ would require a value at an index where the defining expression has
none. Every statement on this page says which starting index it uses.

**Tail series.** For $N \in \mathbb{N}$, the **$N$-th tail series** of
$\sum a_k$ is $\sum_{k \ge N} a_k$, that is the series of the $N$-th tail
$a^{(N)}$ of Sequences of reals: bounded, eventually, frequently, tails, subsequences, whose terms are $a^{(N)}_j = a_{j+N}$. The
$0$-th tail series is the series itself.

Let $a \in \mathbb{R}$, where $\mathbb{R}$ is the ambient ordered field
(Ordered field, Field).

**Natural exponents.** By the recursion theorem (The recursion theorem) applied to
the set $\mathbb{R}$, the starting element $1$ and the function
$f(x) = x \cdot a$, there is a unique function $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$,
written $n \mapsto a^n$, with

$$a^0 = 1, \qquad a^{n+1} = a^n \cdot a \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

Thus $a^1 = a$, $a^2 = a \cdot a$, and so on. Note that this is defined for
**every** $a$, including $a = 0$.

**Negative exponents.** If $a \ne 0$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, set

$$a^{-n} := (a^n)^{-1}.$$

**Why that is legitimate.** The right-hand side presupposes that $a^n$ is
invertible, that is, that $a^n \ne 0$. This is a proof obligation and not an
observation, and it is discharged by claim 2 of Laws of integer exponents: for $a \ne 0$
in a field, $a^n \ne 0$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, proved there by induction on
$n$ from the fact that a field has no zero divisors (A field has no zero divisors: $ab = 0 \Rightarrow a = 0$ or $b = 0$).
That lemma is a statement *about* the operation introduced here, so it depends on
this definition and is recorded in this item's `justified_by` rather than in its
`deps` (SCHEMA §3). Given $a^n \ne 0$, the value $(a^n)^{-1}$ is a single
well-determined element, because multiplicative inverses in a field are unique
(Identities and inverses in a field are unique).

**Integer exponents.** Every integer $m$ (The integers as equivalence classes of pairs of naturals) is either
$n$ or $-n$ for a unique natural $n$, where $n$ in these integer expressions denotes its image under the
embedding $\iota : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z}$ (The naturals embed in the integers,
Arithmetic on the integers). This too is a citation and not a slogan: the order on
$\mathbb{Z}$ is total (The integers form a totally ordered ring), so $m \ge 0$ or $m < 0$; the
image of $\iota$ is exactly the set of nonnegative integers, and each of them is
$n$ for a unique natural $n$ (The naturals embed in the integers); and if $m < 0$ then
$-m > 0$, by compatibility of the order with addition (The integers form a totally ordered ring),
so $-m = n$ and $m = -n$, with $n$ unique because $\iota$ is
injective. The two clauses above therefore define $a^m$ for every
$m \in \mathbb{Z}$ whenever $a \ne 0$, and for every $m \in \mathbb{N}$ for
arbitrary $a$. The two exponent domains are disjoint: the natural clause
handles $m \ge 0$, including $m = 0$, while the negative clause requires
$n \ge 1$ and therefore handles only $m < 0$.

**The factorial.** By the recursion theorem (The recursion theorem) applied to the
set $\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$, the starting element $(0,1)$ and the function
$f(k, v) = (\sigma(k),\, v \cdot \sigma(k))$, and by the same induction on the
first coordinate as in Finite sums and finite products of natural numbers, $\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ in $\mathbb{N}$, there is a unique
$F : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with

$$F(0) = 1, \qquad F(\sigma(n)) = F(n)\cdot\sigma(n) \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

We write $n! := F(n)$. Thus $0! = 1$, $1! = 0!\cdot 1 = 1$, $2! = 1!\cdot 2 = 2$,
$3! = 6$, $4! = 24$, $5! = 120$, $6! = 720$.

**$0! = 1$ is the base clause of this recursion**, not a convention imported from
elsewhere. Nothing about empty products is presupposed; the agreement with the
empty product is proved below, in clause (a), rather than assumed.

**Truncated difference.** Throughout, $n - k$ is the operation fixed in
Finite sums and finite products of natural numbers, $\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ in $\mathbb{N}$: the unique $j$ with $k + j = n$ when
$k \le n$, and $0$ when $n < k$.

**The falling factorial.** For $n \in \mathbb{N}$ define $n^{\underline{k}}$ by
recursion on $k$, by the recursion theorem applied to
$\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$ with starting element $(0,1)$ and
$f(k, v) = (\sigma(k),\, v \cdot (n-k))$:

$$n^{\underline{0}} = 1, \qquad n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}} = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k) .$$

So $n^{\underline{1}} = 1\cdot(n-0) = n$ and $n^{\underline{2}} = n\,(n-1)$, and
for $k \le n$ the value is the product $n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)$ of the $k$ topmost
factors.

**Four facts, proved here because the page uses each of them.**

**(a) The factorial is the product of the first $n$ positive naturals.**
$n! = \prod_{j<n}\sigma(j) = \prod_{j<n}(j+1)$, the $\mathbb{N}$-valued product of
Finite sums and finite products of natural numbers, $\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ in $\mathbb{N}$. Induction (The principle of mathematical induction): at
$n = 0$ both sides are $1$, the empty product and the base clause agreeing; and
$\prod_{j<\sigma(n)}\sigma(j) = \big(\prod_{j<n}\sigma(j)\big)\cdot\sigma(n) = n!\cdot\sigma(n) = \sigma(n)!$.
**So the empty-product reading and the base-clause reading are the same reading**,
and neither was assumed.

**(b) $n! \ne 0$, and $\iota(n!) = \prod^{\mathbb{R}}_{j<n}\iota(j+1)$.** For the
first, $0! = 1 \ne 0$ (The von Neumann naturals form a Peano system) and
$\sigma(n)! = n!\cdot\sigma(n)$ is a product of two nonzero naturals, which is
nonzero: if $xy = 0$ with $y \ne 0$ then $xy = 0\cdot y$
(Zero and one under multiplication) and cancellation gives $x = 0$
(Cancellation for multiplication by a nonzero factor). So $n! \ne 0$ for every $n$ by induction. For the second, apply the bridge clause
6 of that lemma to clause (a) above. This is what makes the factorial of this
page and the real-valued product $\prod_{j<n}(j+1)$ used elsewhere in the library
**one object seen twice**, rather than two unrelated notions.

**(c) $n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)! = n!$ for $k \le n$.** Induction on $k$, for
all $n$ at once. At $k = 0$ this reads $1 \cdot n! = n!$. Assume it at $k$ and
let $\sigma(k) \le n$; then $k \le n$, and writing $d := n - k$ we have
$k + d = n$ and $d \ne 0$, since $k + 0 = k \ne n$; so $d = \sigma(e)$ for a
unique $e$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor), and $\sigma(k) + e = n$, that is
$e = n - \sigma(k)$ (Addition is cancellative). Therefore
$n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}}\cdot\big(n-\sigma(k)\big)! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)\cdot e! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot\big(e!\cdot\sigma(e)\big) = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot\sigma(e)! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)! = n!$,
using commutativity and associativity of multiplication
(Multiplication is associative, Multiplication is commutative) and the recursion
clause for the factorial.

**(d) Boundary values.** $n^{\underline{0}} = 1$ for every $n$, by the base
clause; $n^{\underline{n}} = n!$, since clause (c) at $k = n$ gives
$n^{\underline{n}}\cdot 0! = n!$ and $0! = 1$; and
$n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ whenever $k > n$. For the last, $n - n = 0$ gives
$n^{\underline{\sigma(n)}} = n^{\underline{n}}\cdot 0 = 0$, the clause
$x \cdot 0 = 0$ being definitional (Multiplication of natural numbers), and if
$n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ then
$n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}} = 0$ as well, so $n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ for every
$k \ge \sigma(n)$ by induction.

Let $F$ be a field (Field) with additive identity $0_F$ and
multiplicative identity $1_F$. Define
$\iota : \mathbb{N} \to F$ by recursion on $\mathbb{N}$
(The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann), The recursion theorem):

$$\iota(0) \;:=\; 0_F, \qquad \iota(n+1) \;:=\; \iota(n) + 1_F .$$

$\iota(n)$ is the **canonical natural** of $n$ in $F$. It is also written
$n \cdot 1_F$, and for $n \ge 1$ it is $1_F$ added to itself $n$ times.

**Why the notation is needed at all.** A natural number in this library is a von
Neumann natural, that is a set (The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)), and a set is not an
element of $F$. So $1/n$, $n^{\alpha}$ and $x/n$ are not expressions of $F$ when
$n$ is a natural: what they mean is $1/\iota(n)$, $\iota(n)^{\alpha}$ and
$x/\iota(n)$. The map $\iota$ is what carries a counting number into the field,
and writing it is the whole reason a reader meets $1/\iota(k+1)$ where an
informal text would write $1/(k+1)$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field, with field structure as in Field, and for
$n \ge 1$ let $n \cdot 1_F$ denote the canonical natural number
$\underbrace{1_F + \cdots + 1_F}_{n}$, defined recursively by $1 \cdot 1_F = 1_F$
and $(n+1) \cdot 1_F = n \cdot 1_F + 1_F$. Then for every $n \ge 1$:

citations.quote: In an online decision protocol with horizon $T$, the environment and feedback model specifies how each loss function is chosen and what the learner observes after choosing $x_t$. **Full-information feedback** reveals the entire function $f_t$ (or, for $N$ experts, the full vector of their $N$ losses) after the round-$t$ choice. **Bandit feedback** reveals only the played loss $f_t(x_t)$ after that choice. An **oblivious adversary** fixes the whole sequence $(f_1,\ldots,f_T)$ before the learner's random choices are realized; it may know the learner's rule but not its realized private randomization. A **non-anticipating adaptive adversary** chooses $f_t$ from the history available before $x_t$ is chosen, so $f_t$ may depend on earlier choices and feedback but not on the current choice or the learner's current private randomization. A **reactive adversary** may choose $f_t$ after observing $x_t$, so its round-$t$ loss may depend on that current choice. These adversary classes have different timing and are not interchangeable; a guarantee established for one class is not asserted for another. For the stochastic reward model, let $\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$ be the smallest collection of subsets of $\mathbb R$ that contains every open interval and is closed under complements and countable unions; its members are the Borel sets. A **stochastic finite-arm reward environment** has $N\ge1$ arms, a fixed probability measure $P_i$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$ for each arm $i\in[N]:=\{1,\ldots,N\}$, and finite first moments $\int_{\mathbb R}|y|\,P_i(dy)<\infty$ with means $\mu_i:=\int_{\mathbb R} y\,P_i(dy)$. At each round the learner chooses a measurable arm $A_t$ with values in $[N]$ equipped with its full power set, before the reward $Y_t$ is drawn. The fixed-law condition means that, for every $i$, every event $B$ determined by the history before the reward and the chosen arm with $B\subseteq\{A_t=i\}$, and every $C\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$, $\mathbb P(B\cap\{Y_t\in C\})=\mathbb P(B)P_i(C)$. Here $Y_t$ is an integrable real random variable, $\mathbf1_B$ is the indicator of event $B$, and the history-and-arm events are measurable in the common probability space. This stochastic reward model is distinct from adversarial loss models and supplies no regret guarantee by itself.

Fix a positive integer horizon $T$, a nonempty action set $K$, and, when choices or the environment are randomized, a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$. An online decision protocol has rounds $t=1,\ldots,T$. Before round $t$, the learner has the history $h_{t-1}$ consisting of its earlier choices and all feedback and loss information revealed in earlier rounds. It chooses $x_t\in K$ using only $h_{t-1}$ and any learner-private randomization available by that time. In a randomized protocol, $X_t$ is a measurable random element of $K$, meaning a measurable map from $(\Omega,\mathcal F)$ into $K$ equipped with its declared measurable structure. The environment supplies a real-valued loss function $f_t:K\to\mathbb R$; it may have fixed $f_t$ before the choice or choose it after the choice, as specified by the environment model, but the learner does not observe $f_t$ before choosing $x_t$. The learner incurs loss $f_t(x_t)$ and then receives feedback about round $t$ according to the feedback model. The history $h_t$ adds $x_t$, the feedback received, and any part of $f_t$ explicitly revealed in round $t$. No convexity, boundedness, or regret guarantee is part of this protocol definition.

A **discrete filtered probability space** is $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_n)_{n\in\mathbb N_0},P)$, where $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ is a probability space Probability measures and probability spaces, each $\mathcal F_n$ is a sigma-algebra on $\Omega$ Sigma-algebras, and $\mathcal F_n\subseteq\mathcal F_{n+1}\subseteq\mathcal F$. The sequence $(\mathcal F_n)$ is a **filtration**. Time starts at zero. Neither completeness nor triviality of $\mathcal F_0$ is required.

Restriction of $P$ to $\mathcal F_n$ has total mass one and is countably additive: a disjoint sequence in $\mathcal F_n$ is also such a sequence in $\mathcal F$, with the same union and the same values of $P$. Thus each restriction is a probability measure. This specifies a structure and uses no choice principle. Real-valued processes will be the default.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space, $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ a sub-sigma-algebra, and $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ integrable. A **conditional-expectation version of $X$ given $\mathcal G$** is a real, $\mathcal G$-measurable, integrable function $Y$ such that $\int_A Y\,dP=\int_A X\,dP$ for every $A\in\mathcal G$. No completeness of $\mathcal G$ is assumed.

Expectation means the integral of Expectation of a nonnegative or integrable random variable. Integrable representatives use The class $L^1(\mu)$ of integrable functions; quotient notation is introduced after uniqueness.

space.

1. For scalars $a,b$,
   $$\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Y].$$
2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then

3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

Let a finite-horizon online protocol have horizon $T$, action set $K$, round losses $f_t:K\to\mathbb R$, and learner choices $x_t\in K$. Whenever a minimum below is used, assume it is finite and attained. For a fixed comparator $u\in K$, the realized regret is
$$
R_T(u):=\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(x_t)-\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(u).
$$
The **static regret** is
$$
R_T^{\rm stat}:=\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(x_t)-\min_{u\in K}\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(u).
$$
For randomized learners or environments, **expected regret** is the expectation of the specified regret random variable over their joint randomness, when that random variable is measurable and integrable. In a stochastic finite-arm reward model with means $(\mu_i)_{i\in[N]}$, let $\mu^*:=\max_{i\in[N]}\mu_i$. The **pseudo-regret** is the random variable
$$
\bar R_T:=\sum_{t=1}^T(\mu^*-\mu_{A_t}),
$$
whereas the **realized reward regret** is
$$
R_T^{\rm rew}:=\sum_{t=1}^T(\mu^*-Y_t).
$$

For dynamic comparators, suppose $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ for a positive integer $d$ and fix a norm $\|\cdot\|:\mathbb R^d\to[0,\infty)$, meaning $\|v\|=0$ exactly when $v=0$, $\|\lambda v\|=|\lambda|\|v\|$ for every $\lambda\in\mathbb R$, and $\|v+w\|\le\|v\|+\|w\|$. Given a comparator sequence $u_{1:T}=(u_1,\ldots,u_T)\in K^T$, the **dynamic regret** and its **path length** are
$$
R_T^{\rm dyn}(u_{1:T}):=\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(x_t)-\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(u_t),\qquad P(u_{1:T}):=1+\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\|u_t-u_{t+1}\|.
$$
For a nonempty contiguous integer interval $I=[r,s]$ with $1\le r\le s\le T$, its **interval regret** is
$$
R_I:=\sum_{t=r}^s f_t(x_t)-\min_{u\in K}\sum_{t=r}^s f_t(u),
$$
and the **adaptive regret** is $\max_{1\le r\le s\le T}R_{[r,s]}$. For an algorithm $A$ producing the choices $x_1,\ldots,x_T$, write $R_I(A)$ for its interval regret on $I$. The algorithm is **strongly adaptive** relative to a specified loss, feedback, adversary, and comparator class precisely when there are a stated base algorithm $A_0$, constants $C>0$ and $p\ge0$, and a specified bound $B_{A_0}(n)$ on $A_0$'s static regret at horizon $n$ in that same class, such that, uniformly over every positive horizon $T$ and every environment in that class, for every nonempty contiguous interval $I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,T\}$,
$$
R_I(A)\le C\bigl(\log(eT)\bigr)^p B_{A_0}(|I|),
$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm and $|I|=s-r+1$; $A_0$, $B_{A_0}$, $C$, and $p$ are fixed independently of $T$, $I$, and the environment. The displayed criterion is pathwise, including for randomized protocols. **Strong adaptivity in expectation** instead requires $\mathbb E[R_I(A)]$ to satisfy the displayed bound for every deterministic interval $I$, with measurable, integrable interval regrets and with $B_{A_0}(n)$ an expected static-regret bound in the same class. Almost-sure or high-probability versions must be explicitly qualified: for each horizon, all interval inequalities must hold simultaneously with probability one or at least the stated $1-\delta$, respectively, and the base bound must use the same probability mode with any dependence on $\delta$ specified. Strong adaptivity is a regret property relative to intervals; it does not imply anytime statistical validity.

Let $k>1$ and $n\ge1$ be integers, and let $\eta>0$. Use the finite-arm bandit protocol with rewards in $[0,1]$ and conditional sampling as specified in the bandit importance-weighted estimator definition. Initialize $\widehat S_{0,i}=0$ for each $i\in[k]$. For rounds $t=1,\ldots,n$, perform the following operations:

1. Set
   $$
   P_{t,i}=\frac{\exp(\eta\widehat S_{t-1,i})}{\sum_{j=1}^k\exp(\eta\widehat S_{t-1,j})},\qquad i\in[k].
   $$
2. Draw a measurable finite-valued action $A_t$ with conditional probabilities $\mathbb P(A_t=i\mid\mathcal F_{t-1})=P_{t,i}$, and observe only $X_t=x_{t,A_t}$.
3. Form the loss estimates $\widehat Y_{t,i}=\mathbf1\{A_t=i\}(1-X_t)/P_{t,i}$ and reward estimates $\widehat X_{t,i}=1-\widehat Y_{t,i}$ for every $i\in[k]$.
4. Update $\widehat S_{t,i}=\widehat S_{t-1,i}+\widehat X_{t,i}$ for every $i\in[k]$.

The procedure assumes a probability space carrying the stated measurable draws; it makes no probability-space construction claim. Normalizing the weights $\exp(\eta\widehat S_{t-1,i})$ is the exponential-weights step used by Hedge.

derivations.claim: First fix any positive finite real learning rate $\eta$ and any reward sequence admitted by the algorithm. Initially $\widehat S_{0,i}=0$ is finite for every $i$ by [F18]. Suppose all $\widehat S_{t-1,i}$ are finite. Then each $\exp(\eta\widehat S_{t-1,i})$ is a positive finite real by [F7] and the real-valued exponential definition [F17]. Its finite sum over $[k]$ is positive and finite, so [F1] gives $P_{t,i}>0$ and $\sum_iP_{t,i}=1$. The assumed measurable action draw exists by [F21]; its observed reward is in $[0,1]$. Thus each $\widehat Y_{t,i}=\mathbf1\{A_t=i\}(1-X_t)/P_{t,i}$ and $\widehat X_{t,i}=1-\widehat Y_{t,i}$ is finite, and [F19] makes every $\widehat S_{t,i}$ finite. Induction proves these facts through round $n$. The prescribed loop has the finite index set $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ and each round consists of the finite operations just checked together with an assumed draw, so it completes exactly $n$ rounds. This argument uses only $\eta>0$ and the algorithm's reward range, for either fixed or deterministic past-adaptive rewards. For the rate in the regret clauses, $k>1$, [F10] and [F20] give $\log k>\log1=0$, and [F9] makes $\log k$ real; hence that tuned $\eta$ is also a positive finite real and the same argument applies to it.

For $t=0$, the claimed identity $\widehat S_{t,i}=t-\sum_{s=1}^t\widehat Y_{s,i}$ holds by [F18] and the empty-sum convention. If it holds at $t-1$, then [F19] and $\widehat X_{t,i}=1-\widehat Y_{t,i}$ give
$$
\widehat S_{t,i}=\widehat S_{t-1,i}+\widehat X_{t,i}=t-\sum_{s=1}^t\widehat Y_{s,i}.
$$
Substituting this identity into [F1] and using [F6] factors out the common positive term $\exp(\eta(t-1))$ from numerator and denominator, giving the stated loss-weight formula for $P_{t,i}$.

For each $t$, set $W_t=\sum_{j=1}^k\exp(\eta\widehat S_{t,j})$ and $V_t=\sum_{j=1}^kP_{t,j}\widehat Y_{t,j}^{2}$. By [F1], [F7], and step 1.1, $W_t$ is positive and finite, and $P_t$ is a probability vector.

By [A1] and [F11], each reward vector is fixed at the pre-action history. At each such history, [F3] and $\widehat X_{t,i}=1-\widehat Y_{t,i}$ give the conditional mean $\mathbb E[\widehat X_{t,i}\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]=x_{t,i}$ by the finite conditional sum. Averaging these sums over histories and using [F14] and [F19] gives $\mathbb E[\widehat S_{n,i}]=\mathbb E[\sum_tx_{t,i}]$.
On every round and every action outcome, $\sum_jP_{t,j}\widehat X_{t,j}=1-\sum_jP_{t,j}\widehat Y_{t,j}=1-Y_t=X_t$, because only the sampled arm contributes to the middle sum.

Fix a pre-action history at round $t$. If $A_t=a$, only coordinate $a$ contributes to $V_t$, with value $y_{t,a}^2/P_{t,a}$. Its conditional expectation is therefore $\sum_{a=1}^kP_{t,a}(y_{t,a}^2/P_{t,a})=\sum_{a=1}^ky_{t,a}^2\le k$, since $0\le y_{t,a}\le1$. Averaging over the finite histories and summing the $n$ rounds gives $\mathbb E[\sum_tV_t]\le nk$.

By [F1]–[F2], $W_t/W_{t-1}=\sum_{j=1}^kP_{t,j}\exp(\eta\widehat X_{t,j})=\exp(\eta)\sum_{j=1}^kP_{t,j}\exp(-\eta\widehat Y_{t,j})$. Each $\widehat Y_{t,j}\ge0$, so [F4] with $z=-\eta\widehat Y_{t,j}$ gives $W_t/W_{t-1}\le\exp(\eta)(1-\eta\sum_jP_{t,j}\widehat Y_{t,j}+\eta^2V_t/2)$. Put $u_t=-\eta\sum_jP_{t,j}\widehat Y_{t,j}+\eta^2V_t/2$. By [F5] and $\sum_jP_{t,j}\widehat X_{t,j}=1-\sum_jP_{t,j}\widehat Y_{t,j}$, this is at most $\exp(\eta+u_t)=\exp(\eta\sum_jP_{t,j}\widehat X_{t,j}+\eta^2V_t/2)$.

Multiplying step 3.2 over $t=1,\ldots,n$ and using [F6] gives $W_n/W_0\le\exp(\eta\sum_{t=1}^n\sum_jP_{t,j}\widehat X_{t,j}+\eta^2\sum_{t=1}^nV_t/2)$. Here $W_0=k$ by [F17]–[F18], and $W_n\ge\exp(\eta\widehat S_{n,i})$ for every $i$ by [F19]. Since $k=\exp(\log k)$ by [F9], strict increase [F8] and $\eta>0$ yield $\widehat S_{n,i}-\sum_{t=1}^n\sum_jP_{t,j}\widehat X_{t,j}\le\log k/\eta+(\eta/2)\sum_{t=1}^nV_t$ for every arm $i$.

For the oblivious case set $R_{n,i}=\sum_tx_{t,i}-\mathbb E[\sum_tX_t]$; for the past-adaptive case set $R_{n,i}=\mathbb E[\sum_t(x_{t,i}-X_t)]$. By steps 2.2–2.3, both equal $\mathbb E[\widehat S_{n,i}-\sum_t\sum_jP_{t,j}\widehat X_{t,j}]$. Taking expectations in step 4.1, using [F14]–[F16], and applying step 3.1 gives $R_{n,i}\le\log k/\eta+\eta nk/2$ for every $i$.

Using $\eta>0$ from step 1.1, substitution gives $\log k/\eta=\eta nk/2=\sqrt{nk\log k/2}$. The per-arm bound in step 5.1 therefore equals $\sqrt{2nk\log k}$; taking the finite maximum over $i$ proves both regret bounds in the Statement.

Let $k,n\ge1$ be integers, let $[k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}$, and let
$$
\Delta_k=\left\{p\in[0,1]^k:\sum_{i=1}^k p_i=1\right\}.
$$
On a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$, let $(\mathcal F_t)_{t=0}^n$ be the discrete filtration generated by the complete histories through round $t$, with $\mathcal F_0$ trivial; a complete pre-action history records past reward vectors, actions, and observed rewards. A reward vector is either fixed in advance or a deterministic function of the complete pre-action history. Thus, at a finite horizon with finitely many arms, there are finitely many possible histories. Before action $A_t$ is drawn, the current reward vector $x_t=(x_{t,1},\ldots,x_{t,k})\in[0,1]^k$ and sampling distribution $P_t=(P_{t,1},\ldots,P_{t,k})\in\Delta_k$ are $\mathcal F_{t-1}$-measurable, and $P_{t,i}>0$ for every $i$. The finite-valued measurable action $A_t\in[k]$ has conditional law $\mathbb P(A_t=i\mid\mathcal F_{t-1})=P_{t,i}$. The learner observes only $X_t=x_{t,A_t}$ and sets
$$
Y_t=1-X_t,\qquad y_{t,i}=1-x_{t,i},\qquad \widehat Y_{t,i}=\frac{\mathbf 1\{A_t=i\}Y_t}{P_{t,i}},\qquad \widehat X_{t,i}=1-\widehat Y_{t,i}.
$$
The quantity $\widehat Y_{t,i}$ is the importance-weighted loss estimate for arm $i$, and $\widehat X_{t,i}$ is its corresponding reward estimate. A fixed reward sequence is the oblivious case; allowing $x_t$ to depend on the history available before $A_t$ is drawn gives the non-anticipating past-adaptive case. In either case the current reward vector is chosen before the current action. For finite horizons and finite action histories generated by such a fixed or deterministic history-dependent sequence, all these estimates are finite and integrable.

In the bandit importance-weighted estimator definition, fix a round $t$ and arm $i$, and write $p=P_{t,i}>0$ and $y=y_{t,i}$. Then
$$

A reward vector is either fixed in advance or a deterministic function of the complete pre-action history. Thus, at a finite horizon with finitely many arms, there are finitely many possible histories. Before action $A_t$ is drawn, the current reward vector $x_t=(x_{t,1},\ldots,x_{t,k})\in[0,1]^k$ and sampling distribution $P_t=(P_{t,1},\ldots,P_{t,k})\in\Delta_k$ are $\mathcal F_{t-1}$-measurable, and $P_{t,i}>0$ for every $i$. $$

Let $k>1$ and $n\ge1$ be integers, and let $\eta>0$. Use the finite-arm bandit protocol with rewards in $[0,1]$ and conditional sampling as specified in the bandit importance-weighted estimator definition. Initialize $\widehat S_{0,i}=0$ for each $i\in[k]$. For rounds $t=1,\ldots,n$, perform the following operations:

1. Set
   $$
   P_{t,i}=\frac{\exp(\eta\widehat S_{t-1,i})}{\sum_{j=1}^k\exp(\eta\widehat S_{t-1,j})},\qquad i\in[k].
   $$
2. Draw a measurable finite-valued action $A_t$ with conditional probabilities $\mathbb P(A_t=i\mid\mathcal F_{t-1})=P_{t,i}$, and observe only $X_t=x_{t,A_t}$.
3. Form the loss estimates $\widehat Y_{t,i}=\mathbf1\{A_t=i\}(1-X_t)/P_{t,i}$ and reward estimates $\widehat X_{t,i}=1-\widehat Y_{t,i}$ for every $i\in[k]$.
4. Update $\widehat S_{t,i}=\widehat S_{t-1,i}+\widehat X_{t,i}$ for every $i\in[k]$.

The output is $(P_t,A_t,X_t,\widehat X_t,\widehat Y_t)_{t=1}^n$ and $\widehat S_n$. These operations use exact real arithmetic. The procedure assumes a probability space carrying the stated measurable draws; it makes no probability-space construction claim. Normalizing the weights $\exp(\eta\widehat S_{t-1,i})$ is the exponential-weights step used by Hedge.

Let $N,T\ge1$ be integers, let $[N]=\{1,\ldots,N\}$ be the expert set, and let $\epsilon>0$. At each round $t=1,\ldots,T$, a finite loss vector $\ell_t=(\ell_t(1),\ldots,\ell_t(N))\in[0,\infty)^N$ is revealed after the learner's choice. Initialize $W_1(i)=1$ for every $i\in[N]$. At round $t$, set
$$x_t(i):=\frac{W_t(i)}{\sum_{j=1}^{N}W_t(j)},\qquad i\in[N],$$
Let $\mathcal H_{t-1}$ be the pre-round history sigma-algebra generated by the previously played choices and all previously revealed loss vectors (any random loss vector is assumed measurable on the protocol's probability space). The weights and $x_t$ are $\mathcal H_{t-1}$-measurable. Draw a measurable expert choice $I_t\in[N]$ with conditional distribution
$$\mathbb P(I_t=i\mid\mathcal H_{t-1})=x_t(i)\quad\text{almost surely},\qquad i\in[N],$$
and play $I_t$. After observing the whole vector $\ell_t$, update
$$W_{t+1}(i):=W_t(i)\exp(-\epsilon\ell_t(i)),\qquad i\in[N].$$
The output is the distributions $x_1,\ldots,x_T$, the sampled choices $I_1,\ldots,I_T$, and the final weights. The protocol assumes a probability space carrying the stated measurable draws; no probability-space construction is claimed.

routine_steps.claim: Since $\widehat S_{0,1}=\widehat S_{0,2}=0$, Exp3 starts with probabilities $(1/2,1/2)$. If $A_1=1$, then $Y_1=0$ and $\widehat X_{1,1}=\widehat X_{1,2}=1$, so the next Exp3 distribution is uniform. If $A_1=2$, then $Y_1=1$, $P_{1,2}=1/2$, and $(\widehat Y_{1,1},\widehat Y_{1,2})=(0,2)$; hence $\widehat X_1=(1,-1)$ and the next distribution is $(\exp(\eta)/(\exp(\eta)+\exp(-\eta)),\exp(-\eta)/(\exp(\eta)+\exp(-\eta)))$.
