The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $S$ be a finite set, possibly empty, let $\mathcal R$ be a finite subset of $\mathbb R$, and for each $s\in S$ let $A(s)$ be a finite nonempty set. Here **finite** means bijective with a natural number, and the **discrete sigma-algebra** on a set is its power set. Write $D=\{(s,a):s\in S,\ a\in A(s)\}$. A **finite Markov decision process (MDP)** consists of these sets and numbers $p(s',\rho\mid s,a)\in[0,1]$, indexed by $(s,a)\in D$, $s'\in S$, and $\rho\in\mathcal R$, with

$$ \sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}p(s',\rho\mid s,a)=1 \qquad ((s,a)\in D). $$

Equip each set used here, including $D$, with its power-set (discrete) sigma-algebra. Thus $p$ is the point-mass form of a probability kernel from $D$ to $S\times\mathcal R$: each input assigns a probability measure on $S\times\mathcal R$, and every event section is measurable. The joint law allows the next state and reward to be dependent. Define the expected reward and state-transition probabilities by

$$ r(s,a)=\sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}\rho\,p(s',\rho\mid s,a), \qquad P(s'\mid s,a)=\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}p(s',\rho\mid s,a). $$

If $\mathcal R\ne\emptyset$, put $M=\max_{\rho\in\mathcal R}|\rho|$; if $\mathcal R=\emptyset$, put $M=0$. A stationary Markov policy is a family of probabilities $\pi(a\mid s)\ge0$ with $\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi(a\mid s)=1$ for every $s\in S$. A deterministic policy is a function $\pi$ with $\pi(s)\in A(s)$ for every $s$. When $S=\emptyset$, these families and policies are the unique empty functions and all statewise formulas are vacuous.

Let $S$ be a nonempty finite state set of a finite Markov decision process, let $0\leq\gamma<1$, let $\pi$ be a stationary Markov policy, and let $\mu:S\to[0,1]$ satisfy $\sum_{s\in S}\mu(s)=1$. The function $\mu$ is a fixed state-weighting distribution; it need not be stationary for $\pi$. Let $d$ be a positive integer, let $\phi:S\to\mathbb R^d$ be a feature map, and for $w\in\mathbb R^d$ put $v_w(s)=\phi(s)^\mathsf T w$.

For real functions $f,g:S\to\mathbb R$, write $f\sim_\mu g$ when $\sum_{s\in S}\mu(s)(f(s)-g(s))^2=0$. Let $[f]_\mu$ denote the equivalence class of $f$ and define $\langle[f]_{\mu},[g]_{\mu}\rangle_\mu=\sum_{s\in S}\mu(s)f(s)g(s)$ and $\|[f]_\mu\|_\mu^2=\langle[f]_{\mu},[f]_{\mu}\rangle_\mu$. Let $H_\mu$ be the resulting finite-dimensional real inner-product space, and let $V_\mu$ be the span in $H_\mu$ of the equivalence classes of the $d$ coordinate feature functions.

For $h\in H_\mu$, let $\Pi_\mu h$ be the unique vector in $V_\mu$ whose difference from $h$ is orthogonal to every vector in $V_\mu$. The Bellman-error vector for $v_w$ is $\delta_w=[T^\pi v_w-v_w]_\mu$. Define the mean square Bellman error and mean square projected Bellman error by $\operatorname{BE}_\mu(w)=\|\delta_w\|_\mu^2$ and $\operatorname{PBE}_\mu(w)=\|\Pi_\mu\delta_w\|_\mu^2$.

For a finite MDP, a discount $0\le\gamma<1$, and a stationary Markov policy $\pi$, define the **policy Bellman operator** $T^\pi:\mathbb R^S\to\mathbb R^S$ by

$$ (T^\pi V)(s)=\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi(a\mid s)\left[r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'\in S}P(s'\mid s,a)V(s')\right]\qquad(s\in S). $$

If $S=\emptyset$, this is the unique map from $\mathbb R^S$ to itself.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let a finite MDP have nonempty state set $S$, and let $\pi$ be a stationary Markov policy. Put $E=S\times(\mathcal R\cup\{0\})$ with its discrete sigma-algebra and define, for $x=(s,\eta)\in E$ and $B\subseteq E$,

$$ K_\pi(x,B)=\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi(a\mid s) \sum_{\substack{s'\in S\\\rho\in\mathcal R}}1_B(s',\rho)\,p(s',\rho\mid s,a). $$

Then $K_\pi$ is a probability kernel on $E$. For each initial state $s\in S$, there is a probability law on $E^{\mathbb N}$ whose coordinate process starts at $(s,0)$ and is a time-homogeneous Markov chain with transition kernel $K_\pi$ relative to its natural filtration.

Assume Choice. Let $(E_n,\mathcal E_n)_{n\ge0}$ be measurable spaces, let
$\mu_0$ be a probability measure on $E_0$, and, for each $n\ge0$, let $K_n$ be
a probability kernel from $E_0\times\cdots\times E_n$ to $E_{n+1}$. There is a
unique probability measure $P$ on
$$ \left(\prod_{n\ge0}E_n,\ \bigotimes_{n\ge0}\mathcal E_n\right) $$ whose finite-prefix laws are the prescribed iterated integrals $$ \mu_0(dx_0)K_0(x_0,dx_1)K_1(x_0,x_1,dx_2)\cdots K_{r-1}(x_0,\ldots,x_{r-1},dx_r). $$
In particular, if every $E_n=E$ and
$K_n(x_0,\ldots,x_n,A)=K(x_n,A)$, the coordinate process is a homogeneous
$K$-chain with initial law $\mu_0$.

derivations.claim: The transition matrices, with states ordered as displayed in the Statement, are $P_1=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1/2&1/2\end{pmatrix}$ and $P_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&1/2&1/2\\1&0&0\\0&1/2&1/2\end{pmatrix}$. Every row sums to one. Direct multiplication gives $\mu_1P_1=(1/3,2/3)=\mu_1$ and $\mu_2P_2=(1/3,1/3,1/3)=\mu_2$. The observed feature has mass $1/3$ at $A$ and $2/3$ at feature $B$ in each process.

Represent each MRP as a one-action finite MDP. Under Choice, [F3] supplies a state/reward path law for each fixed initial state; the finite mixture of these laws with weights $\mu_1$ or $\mu_2$ gives the stated random initial state. Let $Y_n=(\psi(S_n),R_{n+1})$ and set $x_A=((1,0),0)$, $x_+=((0,1),1)$, and $x_-=((0,1),-1)$. In MRP 1, the initial state law and its outgoing rewards give probability $1/3$ to each of $x_A,x_+,x_-$; MRP 2 gives the same probabilities. In each process the transition kernel of $Y_n$ is $x_A\mapsto\frac12x_++\frac12x_-$, $x_+\mapsto x_A$, and $x_-\mapsto\frac12x_++\frac12x_-$. Indeed, in MRP 1, $x_A$ comes from state $A$ and the next state is $B$, whose outgoing reward is equally likely $1$ or $-1$; $x_+$ records the transition $B\to A$, so the next observation is $x_A$; and $x_-$ records $B\to B$, after which the next outgoing reward is equally likely $1$ or $-1$. In MRP 2, $x_A$ comes from state $A$, whose next state is $B$ or $B'$ equally; $x_+$ identifies state $B$, whose next state is $A$; and $x_-$ identifies state $B'$, whose next state is $B$ or $B'$ equally. Thus both observed processes have the same initial law $\nu$ and transition kernel $K$, and their finite-prefix laws factor as $\nu(x_0)\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}K(x_k,\{x_{k+1}\})$ by repeated conditioning. By [F4], the path law with these finite-prefix laws is unique, so their observable path laws agree.

In MRP 1 the conditional expected Bellman residual at $A$ is $\gamma b-a$, because $A$ moves to $B$ with reward zero. At $B$, expected reward is $(1-1)/2=0$ and the expected next value is $(a+b)/2$, so the residual is $\gamma(a+b)/2-b$. Weighting their squares by $\mu_1$ gives the stated $\operatorname{BE}_1$. In MRP 2, the residuals at $A,B,B'$ are respectively $\gamma b-a$, $1+\gamma a-b$, and $-1+\gamma b-b=-1+(\gamma-1)b$, which gives the stated $\operatorname{BE}_2$ under $\mu_2$. At $(0,0)$ the first objective is zero and the second is $2/3$.

Since $\operatorname{BE}_1$ is a sum of nonnegative squares and vanishes at $(0,0)$, that point is a minimizer. If it vanishes at $(a,b)$, its first residual gives $a=\gamma b$ and its second gives $b=\gamma(a+b)/2=\gamma(\gamma+1)b/2$. Since $\gamma(\gamma+1)/2<1$ for $0\leq\gamma<1$, $b=0$ and then $a=0$, proving uniqueness.

Let $r_A=\gamma b-a$, $r_B=1+\gamma a-b$, and $r_{B'}=-1+(\gamma-1)b$. Then $3\operatorname{BE}_2=r_A^2+r_B^2+r_{B'}^2$. Its residual matrix is $X=\begin{pmatrix}-1&\gamma\\\gamma&-1\\0&\gamma-1\end{pmatrix}$, with residual vector $X(a,b)^\mathsf T+(0,1,-1)^\mathsf T$. At $(a,b)=(-\gamma/D,\gamma/(2D))$, direct substitution gives $r_B=(\gamma+2)/(2D)$, $r_A=\gamma r_B$, and $r_{B'}=-(\gamma+1)r_B$. Hence $X^\mathsf T(r_A,r_B,r_{B'})^\mathsf T=0$. For any increment $h\in\mathbb R^2$, expanding the squared residual gives $3(\operatorname{BE}_2(w+h)-\operatorname{BE}_2(w))=\|Xh\|_2^2$ at this point. If $Xh=0$, its first two rows give $h_1=\gamma h_2$ and $\gamma h_1=h_2$, so $(1-\gamma^2)h_2=0$; because $\gamma<1$, $h=0$. Thus the objective is strictly larger at every nonzero perturbation and the stated point is the unique global minimizer. Its minimum value is $\frac13\big(\gamma^2+1+(\gamma+1)^2\big)\big(\frac{\gamma+2}{2D}\big)^2=(\gamma+2)^2/(6D)$.

The observable path laws agree by step 1.2, but the Bellman-error functions differ because their values at $(0,0)$ are $0$ and $2/3$. For $0<\gamma<1$, their unique minimizers also differ because MRP 1 has minimizer $(0,0)$ whereas MRP 2 has first coordinate $-\gamma/D<0$. Any quantity determined only by the observable law must be the same for two models with that law; it cannot equal these distinct objectives or, for positive discount, both minimizing parameters. This proves the non-identifiability claims.

The behavior policy has $b(\mathrm{dashed}\mid s)=6/7$ and $b(\mathrm{solid}\mid s)=1/7$ at every state, and the target policy selects $\mathrm{solid}$ with probability $1$. Use the uniform state weighting $\mu(s)=1/7$. For standard basis vectors $e_1,\ldots,e_8$ of $\mathbb R^8$, set $\phi(s_i)=2e_i+e_8$ for $1\leq i\leq6$ and $\phi(s_7)=e_7+2e_8$, and define $v_w(s)=\phi(s)^\mathsf T w$. For a behavior transition $(S,A,S')$, draw $S$ from $\mu$, draw $A$ from $b(\cdot\mid S)$, and draw $S'$ from the stated action transition law. Put $\rho=\pi(A\mid S)/b(A\mid S)$ and $\delta=\gamma v_w(S')-v_w(S)$, and define the expected semi-gradient TD(0) update by $\bar w^+=w+\alpha\,\mathbb E_{\mu,b}[\rho\delta\,\phi(S)]$. Also define the synchronous expected dynamic-programming update by $w^+=w+\frac{\alpha}{7}\sum_{s\in S}\big((T^\pi v_w)(s)-v_w(s)\big)\phi(s)$. For every step size $\alpha>0$, both deterministic update sequences starting at $w_0=(1,1,1,1,1,1,10,1)$ have Euclidean norm $\|w\|_2=(\sum_{i=1}^8w_i^2)^{1/2}$ tending to infinity. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $S$ be a nonempty finite state set of a finite Markov decision process, let $0\leq\gamma<1$, let $\pi$ be a stationary Markov policy, and let $\mu:S\to[0,1]$ satisfy $\sum_{s\in S}\mu(s)=1$. The function $\mu$ is a fixed state-weighting distribution; it need not be stationary for $\pi$. Let $d$ be a positive integer, let $\phi:S\to\mathbb R^d$ be a feature map, and for $w\in\mathbb R^d$ put $v_w(s)=\phi(s)^\mathsf T w$.

For real functions $f,g:S\to\mathbb R$, write $f\sim_\mu g$ when $\sum_{s\in S}\mu(s)(f(s)-g(s))^2=0$. Let $[f]_\mu$ denote the equivalence class of $f$ and define $\langle[f]_{\mu},[g]_{\mu}\rangle_\mu=\sum_{s\in S}\mu(s)f(s)g(s)$ and $\|[f]_\mu\|_\mu^2=\langle[f]_{\mu},[f]_{\mu}\rangle_\mu$. Let $H_\mu$ be the resulting finite-dimensional real inner-product space, and let $V_\mu$ be the span in $H_\mu$ of the equivalence classes of the $d$ coordinate feature functions.

For $h\in H_\mu$, let $\Pi_\mu h$ be the unique vector in $V_\mu$ whose difference from $h$ is orthogonal to every vector in $V_\mu$. The Bellman-error vector for $v_w$ is $\delta_w=[T^\pi v_w-v_w]_\mu$. Define the mean square Bellman error and mean square projected Bellman error by $\operatorname{BE}_\mu(w)=\|\delta_w\|_\mu^2$ and $\operatorname{PBE}_\mu(w)=\|\Pi_\mu\delta_w\|_\mu^2$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice to form the infinite trajectory laws. Fix $0\leq\gamma<1$. An actionless finite Markov reward process (MRP) here means a nonempty finite state set with a joint probability law for next state and reward at each state. Consider the following two MRPs, each with its stated stationary state-weighting distribution, meaning that one transition leaves the distribution unchanged.

In MRP 1 the state set is $\{A,B\}$, with transitions $A\to B$ receiving reward $0$ deterministically and $B\to A$ receiving reward $1$ with probability $1/2$ or $B\to B$ receiving reward $-1$ with probability $1/2$. Its stationary weighting is $\mu_1(A)=1/3$, $\mu_1(B)=2/3$.

In MRP 2 the state set is $\{A,B,B'\}$, with transitions $A\to B$ and $A\to B'$ each receiving reward $0$ with probability $1/2$, $B\to A$ receiving reward $1$ deterministically, and $B'\to B$ or $B'\to B'$ each receiving reward $-1$ with probability $1/2$. Its stationary weighting is $\mu_2(A)=\mu_2(B)=\mu_2(B')=1/3$.

In both processes the observed feature is $\psi(A)=(1,0)$ and $\psi(B)=\psi(B')=(0,1)$, so a parameter $w=(a,b)^\mathsf T$ assigns values $v_w(A)=a$ and $v_w(B)=v_w(B')=b$. Starting from the stated stationary weighting, the two processes induce the same probability law on the observed feature/reward sequence $((\psi(S_n),R_{n+1}))_{n\geq0}$. Their mean square Bellman errors, defined as the stationary-weighted square of the conditional expected one-step TD error, are
$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{BE}_1(a,b)&=\frac13(\gamma b-a)^2+\frac23\left(\frac{\gamma}{2}(a+b)-b\right)^2,\\ \operatorname{BE}_2(a,b)&=\frac13\left((\gamma b-a)^2+(1+\gamma a-b)^2+(-1+(\gamma-1)b)^2\right).\end{aligned}
$$
MRP 1 has the unique minimizer $(a,b)=(0,0)$ and minimum $0$. With $D=1+\gamma+\gamma^2$, MRP 2 has the unique minimizer $(a,b)=\left(-\frac{\gamma}{D},\frac{\gamma}{2D}\right)$ and minimum $\frac{(\gamma+2)^2}{6D}$; also $\operatorname{BE}_2(0,0)=2/3$. For every $0<\gamma<1$ the minimizing parameters differ. Thus the Bellman-error objective and, for positive discount, its minimizing parameter are not determined by the observable feature/reward sequence law. An MRP here has no action-dependent policy; it is not an unseen-action offline-MDP policy-impossibility claim.

At $w=(0,0)$ the MRP 2 residuals are $0,1,-1$, so [F1] gives $\operatorname{BE}_2(0,0)=(0^2+1^2+(-1)^2)/3=2/3$. The MRP pair and common observation law are the $\gamma=1/2$ instance of [F2], whose path-law claim uses [A1], completing the example.

Let $S$ be a finite set, possibly empty, let $\mathcal R$ be a finite subset of $\mathbb R$, and for each $s\in S$ let $A(s)$ be a finite nonempty set. Here **finite** means bijective with a natural number, and the **discrete sigma-algebra** on a set is its power set. Write $D=\{(s,a):s\in S,\ a\in A(s)\}$. A **finite Markov decision process (MDP)** consists of these sets and numbers $p(s',\rho\mid s,a)\in[0,1]$, indexed by $(s,a)\in D$, $s'\in S$, and $\rho\in\mathcal R$, with

$$ \sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}p(s',\rho\mid s,a)=1 \qquad ((s,a)\in D). $$

Equip each set used here, including $D$, with its power-set (discrete) sigma-algebra. Thus $p$ is the point-mass form of a probability kernel from $D$ to $S\times\mathcal R$: each input assigns a probability measure on $S\times\mathcal R$, and every event section is measurable. The joint law allows the next state and reward to be dependent. Define the expected reward and state-transition probabilities by

$$ r(s,a)=\sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}\rho\,p(s',\rho\mid s,a), \qquad P(s'\mid s,a)=\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}p(s',\rho\mid s,a). $$

If $\mathcal R\ne\emptyset$, put $M=\max_{\rho\in\mathcal R}|\rho|$; if $\mathcal R=\emptyset$, put $M=0$. A stationary Markov policy is a family of probabilities $\pi(a\mid s)\ge0$ with $\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi(a\mid s)=1$ for every $s\in S$. A deterministic policy is a function $\pi$ with $\pi(s)\in A(s)$ for every $s$. When $S=\emptyset$, these families and policies are the unique empty functions and all statewise formulas are vacuous.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in Measures on sigma-algebras and A measurable function between measurable spaces; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
$(E,\mathcal E)$ (Probability measures and probability spaces). Their **total variation
distance** is

$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}\bigl|\mu(A)-\nu(A)\bigr| .$$

For every event $A$ the difference $\mu(A)-\nu(A)$ is a real number in
$[-1,1]$, because both measures have total mass one; hence the set being
maximized is a nonempty subset of $[0,1]$ and the supremum lies in $[0,1]$.
The empty event and the whole space give the values $0$ and
$|\mu(E)-\nu(E)|=0$, so the distance is zero when $\mu=\nu$, and it is symmetric
in $\mu$ and $\nu$. This convention carries no factor $1/2$ in the supremum;
it is therefore not the total variation norm of the signed measure $\mu-\nu$,
which is twice the quantity above when that signed measure is considered on a
measurable space where the decomposition is attained. On a countable state
space with its power-set sigma-algebra the supremum equals the half-$\ell^1$
sum $\tfrac12\sum_{x\in E}|\mu(\{x\})-\nu(\{x\})|$; that identity is proved in
Half-$\ell^1$ formula for total variation on a countable space, not assumed here.

Let $E$ be an at most countable set equipped with the power-set
$\sigma$-algebra $2^E$, and let $\mu,\nu$ be probability laws on $E$
(Total variation distance for probability laws). Then

$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}=\frac12\sum_{x\in E}\bigl|\mu(x)-\nu(x)\bigr| ,$$

where $\mu(x),\nu(x)$ denote the singleton masses and the series on the right
is a series of nonnegative numbers in $[0,+\infty]$. The value is finite; it is
$0$ exactly when $\mu=\nu$. The supremum defining the total variation distance
is attained at the event $A_+=\{x\in E:\mu(x)>\nu(x)\}$.

For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and all $a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n \in \mathbb{R}$, the
set $\{a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ has a maximum and a minimum (Maximum and minimum of a set).

What is proved below is exactly the displayed statement, by induction on $n$.

The usual reading, that *every nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ has a
maximum and a minimum*, follows once one identifies the nonempty finite subsets
of $\mathbb{R}$ with the sets listable as $\{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$. That
identification is recorded as a stipulation in the Given below, because this page
has no definition of finiteness to prove it against. **It is discharged, not
merely assumed**: The nonempty finite subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ are exactly the listable ones proves that the two
descriptions of a nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ agree. That lemma is
recorded in `justified_by` rather than in `deps`, since it is about the sets this
lemma quantifies over and therefore depends on this one. This is what licenses
the notation
$\max\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ and $\min\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ for finite sets of
**real** numbers from this page onwards.

Let $F$ be an ordered field (Ordered field) and let $x, y \in F$. Then

$$|x + y| \le |x| + |y|.$$

Let $F$ be an ordered field (Ordered field) and let $x, y \in F$, with
$|x|$ the absolute value (Absolute value in an ordered field). Then

$$|x| \ge 0; \quad |x| = 0 \iff x = 0; \quad -|x| \le x \le |x|; \quad |-x| = |x|; \quad |xy| = |x|\,|y|;$$

and, for every $c > 0$, one has $|x| < c \iff -c < x < c$.

Let the true environment be a finite Markov decision process with nonempty finite state set $S$, nonempty finite action sets $A(s)$, a finite reward alphabet contained in $[0,1]$, and joint next-state/reward probabilities $p(s',\rho\mid s,a)$. Write $D=\{(s,a):s\in S,\ a\in A(s)\}$, and let $r(s,a)$ and $P(s'\mid s,a)$ be the expected reward and next-state probabilities obtained by summing this joint law. A finite learned model on the same state and action sets consists of estimates $\hat r:D\to[0,1]$ and probability distributions $\hat P(\cdot\mid s,a)$ on $S$ for every $(s,a)\in D$. The estimated transition table is a probability kernel on the finite discrete spaces.

For each $(s,a)\in D$, define the reward error $e_r(s,a)=|r(s,a)-\hat r(s,a)|$ and transition error

$$e_P(s,a)=\frac12\sum_{s'\in S}|P(s'\mid s,a)-\hat P(s'\mid s,a)|.$$

For any subset $C\subseteq D$, define $\epsilon_r(C)=\max_{(s,a)\in C}e_r(s,a)$ and $\epsilon_P(C)=\max_{(s,a)\in C}e_P(s,a)$ when $C\ne\emptyset$, and set both quantities to $0$ when $C=\emptyset$. These are uniform expected-reward and total-variation errors on $C$; the learned model definition makes no accuracy assertion.

Induction proves that every $d_t$ is a probability distribution.

Each summand in $J_H$ is nonnegative, and at each time $t$ its sum is at most $\sum_s d_t(s)=1$ because rewards lie in $[0,1]$ by [F1]. The $H$ finite time sums therefore define a real number in $[0,H]$.

Let the true environment be a finite Markov decision process with nonempty finite state set $S$, nonempty finite action sets $A(s)$, a finite reward alphabet contained in $[0,1]$, and joint next-state/reward probabilities $p(s',\rho\mid s,a)$. Write $D=\{(s,a):s\in S,\ a\in A(s)\}$, and let $r(s,a)$ and $P(s'\mid s,a)$ be the expected reward and next-state probabilities obtained by summing this joint law. A finite learned model on the same state and action sets consists of estimates $\hat r:D\to[0,1]$ and probability distributions $\hat P(\cdot\mid s,a)$ on $S$ for every $(s,a)\in D$. The estimated transition table is a probability kernel on the finite discrete spaces.

For each $(s,a)\in D$, define the reward error $e_r(s,a)=|r(s,a)-\hat r(s,a)|$ and transition error

$$e_P(s,a)=\frac12\sum_{s'\in S}|P(s'\mid s,a)-\hat P(s'\mid s,a)|.$$

For any subset $C\subseteq D$, define $\epsilon_r(C)=\max_{(s,a)\in C}e_r(s,a)$ and $\epsilon_P(C)=\max_{(s,a)\in C}e_P(s,a)$ when $C\ne\emptyset$, and set both quantities to $0$ when $C=\emptyset$. These are uniform expected-reward and total-variation errors on $C$; the learned model definition makes no accuracy assertion.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in Measures on sigma-algebras and A measurable function between measurable spaces; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
$(E,\mathcal E)$ (Probability measures and probability spaces). Their **total variation
distance** is

$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}\bigl|\mu(A)-\nu(A)\bigr| .$$

For every event $A$ the difference $\mu(A)-\nu(A)$ is a real number in
$[-1,1]$, because both measures have total mass one; hence the set being
maximized is a nonempty subset of $[0,1]$ and the supremum lies in $[0,1]$.
The empty event and the whole space give the values $0$ and
$|\mu(E)-\nu(E)|=0$, so the distance is zero when $\mu=\nu$, and it is symmetric
in $\mu$ and $\nu$. This convention carries no factor $1/2$ in the supremum;
it is therefore not the total variation norm of the signed measure $\mu-\nu$,
which is twice the quantity above when that signed measure is considered on a
measurable space where the decomposition is attained. On a countable state
space with its power-set sigma-algebra the supremum equals the half-$\ell^1$
sum $\tfrac12\sum_{x\in E}|\mu(\{x\})-\nu(\{x\})|$; that identity is proved in
Half-$\ell^1$ formula for total variation on a countable space, not assumed here.

Let $E$ be an at most countable set equipped with the power-set
$\sigma$-algebra $2^E$, and let $\mu,\nu$ be probability laws on $E$
(Total variation distance for probability laws). Then

$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}=\frac12\sum_{x\in E}\bigl|\mu(x)-\nu(x)\bigr| ,$$

where $\mu(x),\nu(x)$ denote the singleton masses and the series on the right
is a series of nonnegative numbers in $[0,+\infty]$. The value is finite; it is
$0$ exactly when $\mu=\nu$. The supremum defining the total variation distance
is attained at the event $A_+=\{x\in E:\mu(x)>\nu(x)\}$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field (Ordered field) and let $x, y \in F$, with
$|x|$ the absolute value (Absolute value in an ordered field). Then

$$|x| \ge 0; \quad |x| = 0 \iff x = 0; \quad -|x| \le x \le |x|; \quad |-x| = |x|; \quad |xy| = |x|\,|y|;$$

and, for every $c > 0$, one has $|x| < c \iff -c < x < c$.

Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a sequence of reals and $n \in \mathbb{N}$,
with finite sums as in Finite sums and finite products, by recursion and the absolute value as in
Absolute value in an ordered field. Then

$$\Big|\sum_{k<n} a_k\Big| \le \sum_{k<n} |a_k|.$$

Let $a, b, c : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be sequences of reals, let
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, and let $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, with finite sums and
finite products as in Finite sums and finite products, by recursion. Then:

1. **Additivity.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}(a_k + b_k) = \sum_{k<n} a_k + \sum_{k<n} b_k$.
2. **Scaling.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda a_k = \lambda \sum_{k<n} a_k$; in particular $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda = n\lambda$, where $n$ denotes the canonical field image $n\cdot1_{\mathbb{R}}$ of the natural n (The unique embedding of ℚ into an ordered field, Canonical naturals are positive and strictly increasing).
3. **Splitting.** If $m \le n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k = \sum_{k<m} a_k + \sum_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k$, and $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n} a_k = \Big(\prod_{k<m} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k\Big)$.
4. **Monotonicity.** If $a_k \le b_k$ for all $k < n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k \le \sum_{k<n} b_k$. In particular, if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\sum_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, every single term satisfies $a_j \le \sum_{k<n} a_k$ for $j < n$, and $\sum_{k<n} a_k = 0$ forces $a_k = 0$ for every $k < n$.
5. **Telescoping.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}\big(c_{k+1} - c_k\big) = c_n - c_0$.
6. **Products.** $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n}(a_k b_k) = \Big(\prod_{k<n} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k<n} b_k\Big)$; if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, and if $a_k > 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k > 0$.

Let $S$ be a finite set, $n := \lvert S\rvert$ (The cardinality $\lvert A\rvert$ of a finite set), and
let $a : S \to \mathbb{R}$ or $a : S \to \mathbb{N}$, written $a_i$ for $a(i)$.
Choose a bijection $\varphi : n \to S$, which exists because $S \approx n$
(Equinumerous sets, $A \approx B$ and $A \preceq B$), and set

$$\sum_{i \in S} a_i := \sum_{k<n} a_{\varphi(k)}, \qquad \prod_{i \in S} a_i := \prod_{k<n} a_{\varphi(k)},$$

the right-hand sides being the iterated operations of Finite sums and finite products, by recursion when the
values are real and of Finite sums and finite products of natural numbers, $\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ in $\mathbb{N}$ when they are natural.

**Independence of the enumeration, which is the content of the definition.** Let
$\varphi, \psi : n \to S$ be two bijections. Then $\pi := \varphi^{-1} \circ \psi$
is a bijection $n \to n$ (Injection, surjection, bijection), and
$a_{\psi(k)} = a_{\varphi(\pi(k))}$ for every $k < n$. Applying
A finite sum is unchanged by a permutation of its index range: $\sum_{k<n} a_{\pi(k)} = \sum_{k<n} a_k$ for every bijection $\pi : n \to n$ to the list $c_k := a_{\varphi(k)}$
gives

$$\sum_{k<n} a_{\psi(k)} = \sum_{k<n} c_{\pi(k)} = \sum_{k<n} c_k = \sum_{k<n} a_{\varphi(k)},$$

and identically for products. So the value does not depend on which bijection is
used, and $\sum_{i \in S} a_i$ is a single well-determined element.

**No choice principle is involved.** The definition does not select an
enumeration: it asserts that all enumerations give the same value, and that value
is what the notation names. Only one bijection is ever produced at a time, from a
set already known to be nonempty.

**Three clauses, recorded here because the page uses them constantly.**

**(a) The bridge to the old notation.** Taking $S = n$ and $\varphi = \mathrm{id}_n$,
which is legitimate since $\lvert n\rvert = n$, gives

$$\sum_{i \in n} a_i = \sum_{k<n} a_k, \qquad \prod_{i \in n} a_i = \prod_{k<n} a_k .$$

So the new notation **extends** the sum over an initial segment rather than
competing with it, and every law proved for the latter is available for the
former whenever the index set is a natural number.

**(b) Reindexing along a bijection.** If $h : T \to S$ is a bijection of finite
sets, then $\sum_{j \in T} a_{h(j)} = \sum_{i \in S} a_i$, and likewise for
products. Indeed $\lvert T\rvert = \lvert S\rvert = n$ by transport
(The cardinality $\lvert A\rvert$ of a finite set), and if $\varphi : n \to S$ is a bijection then
$h^{-1} \circ \varphi : n \to T$ is one, so
$\sum_{j \in T} a_{h(j)} = \sum_{k<n} a_{h(h^{-1}(\varphi(k)))} = \sum_{k<n} a_{\varphi(k)} = \sum_{i \in S} a_i$.

**(c) The empty index set and a constant summand.** $\lvert\varnothing\rvert = 0$,
so $\sum_{i \in \varnothing} a_i = 0$ and $\prod_{i \in \varnothing} a_i = 1$ by
the base clause of the recursion. And for a constant $c$, clause (a) together
with the constant clause of Laws of finite sums and products in $\mathbb{N}$, and $\iota\big(\sum_{k<n} a_k\big) = \sum_{k<n} \iota(a_k)$
in $\mathbb{N}$, or clause 2 of Laws of finite sums and finite products in $\mathbb{R}$, gives

$$\sum_{i \in S} c = \lvert S\rvert \cdot c \quad (c \in \mathbb{N}), \qquad \sum_{i \in S} c = \iota(\lvert S\rvert)\cdot c \quad (c \in \mathbb{R}),$$

the second with $\iota$ written out because $\lvert S\rvert$ is a natural number
and not an element of $\mathbb{R}$ (The canonical natural $\iota(n) = n \cdot 1_F$ of a field).

derivations.claim: For each state $s$, the policy mixture $K^\pi(s,\cdot)$ is a probability distribution because it is a convex combination of the probability rows $P(\cdot\mid s,a)$; the same holds for $\widehat K^\pi$. The state set is finite discrete, so both row tables are probability kernels by [F2]. Applying [F4] to the common kernel $K^\pi$ gives $\operatorname{TV}(dK^\pi,\widehat dK^\pi)\le\operatorname{TV}(d,\widehat d)$.

Enumerate the finite set $D$ of admissible state-action pairs. For each $x\in S$, the finite-sum triangle inequality [F6] and absolute-value product formula [F5] give $\operatorname{TV}(\widehat dK^\pi,\widehat d\widehat K^\pi)=\frac12\sum_{x\in S}|\sum_{(s,a)\in D}\widehat d(s)\pi(a\mid s)(P(x\mid s,a)-\widehat P(x\mid s,a))|\le\frac12\sum_{x\in S}\sum_{(s,a)\in D}\widehat d(s)\pi(a\mid s)|P(x\mid s,a)-\widehat P(x\mid s,a)|$. The finite sums over $S$ and $D$ can be interchanged: enumerate both sets, expand by additivity [F7], and use the coordinate-swap bijection with enumeration invariance [F8]. This gives $\sum_{s\in S}\widehat d(s)\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi(a\mid s)\frac12\sum_{x\in S}|P(x\mid s,a)-\widehat P(x\mid s,a)|\le\epsilon$. The last inequality uses the row bound on every positive-weight pair; zero-weight terms vanish, and the weights sum to $\sum_s\widehat d(s)\sum_a\pi(a\mid s)=1$ because both rows are probability distributions.

For every $x\in S$, write $dK^\pi(x)-\widehat d\widehat K^\pi(x)=[dK^\pi(x)-\widehat dK^\pi(x)]+[\widehat dK^\pi(x)-\widehat d\widehat K^\pi(x)]$. The scalar triangle inequality [F5], summed over finite $S$ using [F6], gives $\operatorname{TV}(dK^\pi,\widehat d\widehat K^\pi)\le\operatorname{TV}(dK^\pi,\widehat dK^\pi)+\operatorname{TV}(\widehat dK^\pi,\widehat d\widehat K^\pi)$. Steps 1.1 and 1.2 bound the right side by the claim.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let a finite MDP have nonempty finite state set $S$ and finite nonempty action sets $A(s)$. A **finite stochastic shortest-path problem** consists of that MDP, a nonempty goal set $G\subseteq S$, and a constant $c_{\min}>0$ with the following properties. Each goal $g\in G$ has exactly one available action $a_g$, and its joint reward-transition law satisfies $p(g,0\mid g,a_g)=1$ (so $0\in\mathcal R$). For every $s\notin G$ and every $a\in A(s)$, the expected reward satisfies $r(s,a)\le -c_{\min}$. Define the one-step expected cost by $c(s,a)=-r(s,a)$ off $G$ and $c(g,a)=0$ at goals. A stationary Markov policy $\pi$ is **proper** if, from every initial state, the finite-step probabilities of not having reached $G$ tend to $0$: with $q_0(s)=1_{s\notin G}$ and

$$q_{n+1}(s)=\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi(a\mid s)\sum_{s'\in S}P(s'\mid s,a)q_n(s')\quad(s\notin G),\qquad q_{n+1}(g)=0\quad(g\in G),$$

properness means $q_n(s)\to0$ for every $s\in S$. The problem need not have a proper policy unless that is separately assumed.

Assume Choice. Let $(E_n,\mathcal E_n)_{n\ge0}$ be measurable spaces, let
$\mu_0$ be a probability measure on $E_0$, and, for each $n\ge0$, let $K_n$ be
a probability kernel from $E_0\times\cdots\times E_n$ to $E_{n+1}$. There is a
unique probability measure $P$ on
$$ \left(\prod_{n\ge0}E_n,\ \bigotimes_{n\ge0}\mathcal E_n\right) $$ whose finite-prefix laws are the prescribed iterated integrals $$ \mu_0(dx_0)K_0(x_0,dx_1)K_1(x_0,x_1,dx_2)\cdots K_{r-1}(x_0,\ldots,x_{r-1},dx_r). $$
In particular, if every $E_n=E$ and
$K_n(x_0,\ldots,x_n,A)=K(x_n,A)$, the coordinate process is a homogeneous
$K$-chain with initial law $\mu_0$.

For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and all $a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n \in \mathbb{R}$, the
set $\{a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ has a maximum and a minimum (Maximum and minimum of a set).

What is proved below is exactly the displayed statement, by induction on $n$.

The usual reading, that *every nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ has a
maximum and a minimum*, follows once one identifies the nonempty finite subsets
of $\mathbb{R}$ with the sets listable as $\{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$. That
identification is recorded as a stipulation in the Given below, because this page
has no definition of finiteness to prove it against. **It is discharged, not
merely assumed**: The nonempty finite subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ are exactly the listable ones proves that the two
descriptions of a nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ agree. That lemma is
recorded in `justified_by` rather than in `deps`, since it is about the sets this
lemma quantifies over and therefore depends on this one. This is what licenses
the notation
$\max\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ and $\min\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ for finite sets of
**real** numbers from this page onwards.

Let $(x_k)$ be a sequence of reals (Sequences of reals: bounded, eventually, frequently, tails, subsequences) and let
$S = \{x_k : k \in \mathbb{N}\}$ be its range.

1. If $(x_k)$ is nondecreasing (Nondecreasing, increasing, nonincreasing, decreasing, monotone, and eventually monotone sequences) and $S$ is bounded
   above (Lower bound, bounded below, bounded set), then $(x_k)$ converges (Limits and Cauchy sequences of reals) and
   $$\lim_{k} x_k = \sup S .$$
2. If $(x_k)$ is nonincreasing and $S$ is bounded below, then $(x_k)$ converges
   and $$\lim_{k} x_k = \inf S .$$

Both suprema and infima exist under the stated hypotheses: $S$ is nonempty, so
the least-upper-bound property (Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property)) supplies the
first and Every nonempty set bounded below has an infimum the second, and each is unique
(Suprema and infima are unique).

This is the first place in this track where the least-upper-bound property
produces a **limit**. Everything on the sequences page held in any Archimedean
ordered field; the theorem below does not, and the sequence of decimal
truncations of $\sqrt 2$ inside $\mathbb{Q}$ is the standard witness of its
failure there.

derivations.claim: 1.1 If $S=G$, all costs and values are zero, and the theorem follows. Otherwise let $S\setminus G\ne\emptyset$. For any history-dependent policy, finite state/action histories form finite discrete spaces at each time, so the conditional action and transition rules are probability kernels. By [A1] and [F2], the corresponding trajectory law exists with the specified finite-prefix probabilities; this justifies the expectations in the Statement. [given, A1, F1, F2, construct]

1.2 Define the Bellman map $T$ by $(Tu)(g)=0$ on goals and $(Tu)(s)=\min_{a\in A(s)}[c(s,a)+\sum_{s'}P(s'\mid s,a)u(s')]$ off goals. Set $f_0(s)=0$ and $f_{n+1}=Tf_n$. The minimum is attained by [F3]. These are finite-horizon optimal costs: for $n=0$ the continuation cost is zero; if the claim holds at horizon $n$, conditioning on the first action and next state gives the displayed recursion at horizon $n+1$. Any randomized first action gives a convex combination of action costs, which is at least their minimum; a minimizing pure action attains that minimum, so the finite-horizon optimum is the displayed value. [given, F1, F3, construct]

2.1 The recursion is monotone in its value argument because all transition weights are nonnegative, and $f_1\ge f_0=0$; induction gives $0\le f_n\le f_{n+1}$. For any stationary policy $\pi$, let $U=S\setminus G$ and define the substochastic matrix $Q^\pi$ on $U$ by $Q^\pi(s,t)=\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi(a\mid s)P(t\mid s,a)$. The properness recursion gives $q_0^\pi|_U=\mathbf 1$ and $q_{n+1}^\pi|_U=Q^\pi q_n^\pi|_U$, so $q_n^\pi|_U=(Q^\pi)^n\mathbf 1$; since $Q^\pi\mathbf 1\le\mathbf 1$, these survival probabilities are nonincreasing. Let the true environment be a finite Markov decision process with nonempty finite state set $S$, nonempty finite action sets $A(s)$, a finite reward alphabet contained in $[0,1]$, and joint next-state/reward probabilities $p(s',\rho\mid s,a)$. Write $D=\{(s,a):s\in S,\ a\in A(s)\}$, and let $r(s,a)$ and $P(s'\mid s,a)$ be the expected reward and next-state probabilities obtained by summing this joint law. A finite learned model on the same state and action sets consists of estimates $\hat r:D\to[0,1]$ and probability distributions $\hat P(\cdot\mid s,a)$ on $S$ for every $(s,a)\in D$. The estimated transition table is a probability kernel on the finite discrete spaces.

For each $(s,a)\in D$, define the reward error $e_r(s,a)=|r(s,a)-\hat r(s,a)|$ and transition error

$$e_P(s,a)=\frac12\sum_{s'\in S}|P(s'\mid s,a)-\hat P(s'\mid s,a)|.$$

For any subset $C\subseteq D$, define $\epsilon_r(C)=\max_{(s,a)\in C}e_r(s,a)$ and $\epsilon_P(C)=\max_{(s,a)\in C}e_P(s,a)$ when $C\ne\emptyset$, and set both quantities to $0$ when $C=\emptyset$. These are uniform expected-reward and total-variation errors on $C$; the learned model definition makes no accuracy assertion.

Let $S$ be a nonempty finite state set, let $A(s)$ be a nonempty finite action set for each $s\in S$, let $r(s,a)\in[0,1]$, and let $P(\cdot\mid s,a)$ be a probability distribution on $S$ for each admissible pair. A finite-horizon Markov policy of horizon $H\in\mathbb N$ with $H\ge1$ is a family of probability distributions $\pi_t(\cdot\mid s)$ on $A(s)$ for $0\le t<H$. Given an initial state distribution $\mu$, define $d_0=\mu$ and, for $0\le t<H-1$,

$$d_{t+1}(s')=\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{a\in A(s)}d_t(s)\pi_t(a\mid s)P(s'\mid s,a).$$

The finite-horizon expected return is

$$J_H(M,\mu,\pi)=\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{a\in A(s)}d_t(s)\pi_t(a\mid s)r(s,a).$$

The same definition applies to a learned model by replacing $r,P$ with its estimated reward and transition tables. It is the expected sum of the $H$ one-step rewards; no discount factor or terminal continuation value is included.

Let $S$ be a finite nonempty set, let $A(s)$ be finite and nonempty for each $s\in S$, and let $P(\cdot\mid s,a)$ and $\widehat P(\cdot\mid s,a)$ be probability distributions on $S$ for each admissible pair. For distributions $u,v$ on $S$, write $\operatorname{TV}(u,v)=\frac12\sum_{x\in S}|u(x)-v(x)|$. Let $\pi(\cdot\mid s)$ be a probability distribution on $A(s)$ for each state. Define the induced transition rows

$$K^\pi(s,x)=\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi(a\mid s)P(x\mid s,a),\qquad \widehat K^\pi(s,x)=\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi(a\mid s)\widehat P(x\mid s,a).$$

If $d$ and $\widehat d$ are probability distributions on $S$ and, for some $\epsilon\ge0$,

$$\operatorname{TV}(P(\cdot\mid s,a),\widehat P(\cdot\mid s,a))\le\epsilon$$

whenever $\widehat d(s)>0$ and $\pi(a\mid s)>0$, then

$$\operatorname{TV}(dK^\pi,\widehat d\widehat K^\pi)\le\operatorname{TV}(d,\widehat d)+\epsilon.$$

Here $dK^\pi$ and $\widehat d\widehat K^\pi$ are the next-state distributions obtained by applying the indicated transition rows.

Let $E$ be an at most countable set equipped with the power-set

(Total variation distance for probability laws). Then

$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}=\frac12\sum_{x\in E}\bigl|\mu(x)-\nu(x)\bigr| ,$$

where $\mu(x),\nu(x)$ denote the singleton masses and the series on the right
is a series of nonnegative numbers in $[0,+\infty]$. The value is finite; it is
$0$ exactly when $\mu=\nu$. The supremum defining the total variation distance
is attained at the event $A_+=\{x\in E:\mu(x)>\nu(x)\}$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let a finite MDP have nonempty finite state set $S$ and finite nonempty action sets $A(s)$. A **finite stochastic shortest-path problem** consists of that MDP, a nonempty goal set $G\subseteq S$, and a constant $c_{\min}>0$ with the following properties. Each goal $g\in G$ has exactly one available action $a_g$, and its joint reward-transition law satisfies $p(g,0\mid g,a_g)=1$ (so $0\in\mathcal R$). For every $s\notin G$ and every $a\in A(s)$, the expected reward satisfies $r(s,a)\le -c_{\min}$. Define the one-step expected cost by $c(s,a)=-r(s,a)$ off $G$ and $c(g,a)=0$ at goals. A stationary Markov policy $\pi$ is **proper** if, from every initial state, the finite-step probabilities of not having reached $G$ tend to $0$: with $q_0(s)=1_{s\notin G}$ and

$$q_{n+1}(s)=\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi(a\mid s)\sum_{s'\in S}P(s'\mid s,a)q_n(s')\quad(s\notin G),\qquad q_{n+1}(g)=0\quad(g\in G),$$

properness means $q_n(s)\to0$ for every $s\in S$. The problem need not have a proper policy unless that is separately assumed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and let a finite positive-cost stochastic shortest-path problem have at least one proper stationary policy. For any policy $\sigma$ whose action distribution may depend on the entire finite history, use its trajectory law from the initial state $s$ and define

$$J^\sigma(s)=\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\mathbb E_s^\sigma\!\left[c(S_t,A_t)\,1_{\{S_t\notin G\}}\right],$$

where $c(s,a)=-r(s,a)>0$ off the absorbing goal set $G$ and $c(g,a)=0$ at goals. The optimal total cost $f^*(s)=\inf_\sigma J^\sigma(s)$ is finite for every state. It is the unique finite nonnegative function satisfying

$$f^*(g)=0\quad(g\in G),\qquad f^*(s)=\min_{a\in A(s)}\left[c(s,a)+\sum_{s'\in S}P(s'\mid s,a)f^*(s')\right]\quad(s\notin G).$$

The minimum is attained by a deterministic stationary policy that is proper and has total cost $f^*$ from every initial state.

set $\{a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ has a maximum and a minimum (Maximum and minimum of a set).

What is proved below is exactly the displayed statement, by induction on $n$.

The usual reading, that *every nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ has a
maximum and a minimum*, follows once one identifies the nonempty finite subsets
of $\mathbb{R}$ with the sets listable as $\{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$. That

recorded in `justified_by` rather than in `deps`, since it is about the sets this

$\max\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ and $\min\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ for finite sets of

1. If $(x_k)$ is nondecreasing (Nondecreasing, increasing, nonincreasing, decreasing, monotone, and eventually monotone sequences) and $S$ is bounded

2. If $(x_k)$ is nonincreasing and $S$ is bounded below, then $(x_k)$ converges

Both suprema and infima exist under the stated hypotheses: $S$ is nonempty, so

Unupdated errors are unchanged, and goal errors are zero. Thus $0\le E_{n+1}\le E_n$. By [F4], this nonincreasing sequence bounded below by zero has a limit $E_\infty\ge0$.

Goal states do not lie in $I$ because their errors are always zero. Fix $s\in I$. It is updated infinitely often, and its error is constant between updates. Along a subsequence of times when $e_n(s)\to E_\infty$, the most recent post-update error has the same value; those update times tend to infinity, so a subsequence of post-update errors tends to $E_\infty$. Along this subsequence $E_n\to E_\infty$ and $\sum_{s'}P(s'\mid s,a_s)e_n(s')-\delta(s,a_s)\to E_\infty$. The weighted sum is at most $E_n$ and $\delta(s,a_s)\ge0$, so $\delta(s,a_s)=0$ and the weighted sum tends to $E_\infty$. Let a finite MDP have nonempty finite state set $S$ and finite nonempty action sets $A(s)$. A **finite stochastic shortest-path problem** consists of that MDP, a nonempty goal set $G\subseteq S$, and a constant $c_{\min}>0$ with the following properties. Each goal $g\in G$ has exactly one available action $a_g$, and its joint reward-transition law satisfies $p(g,0\mid g,a_g)=1$ (so $0\in\mathcal R$). For every $s\notin G$ and every $a\in A(s)$, the expected reward satisfies $r(s,a)\le -c_{\min}$. Define the one-step expected cost by $c(s,a)=-r(s,a)$ off $G$ and $c(g,a)=0$ at goals. A stationary Markov policy $\pi$ is **proper** if, from every initial state, the finite-step probabilities of not having reached $G$ tend to $0$: with $q_0(s)=1_{s\notin G}$ and

$$q_{n+1}(s)=\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi(a\mid s)\sum_{s'\in S}P(s'\mid s,a)q_n(s')\quad(s\notin G),\qquad q_{n+1}(g)=0\quad(g\in G),$$

properness means $q_n(s)\to0$ for every $s\in S$. The problem need not have a proper policy unless that is separately assumed.

Input: a finite stochastic shortest-path model, a finite value table $V_0:S\to\mathbb R$ with $V_0(g)=0$ on goals, a nonempty finite start set $S_0\subseteq S\setminus G$, a positive integer trial cap $L$, and an infinite supplied start sequence in which each member of $S_0$ occurs infinitely often. For each trial, set the current state to the next supplied start. For at most $L$ decision steps, or until a goal is reached, do the following: at the current nonglobal state $s$, compute

$$q_V(s,a)=r(s,a)+\sum_{s'\in S}P(s'\mid s,a)V(s')\qquad(a\in A(s)),$$

choose uniformly from the nonempty set of actions attaining $\max_{a\in A(s)}q_V(s,a)$ using a fresh tie draw, execute the chosen action in the given MDP and observe the next state, then replace $V(s)$ by $\max_{a\in A(s)}q_V(s,a)$ using the value table from before that backup. Keep every other value unchanged. At a goal keep value $0$. After a trial ends, reset the state to the next supplied start without resetting the value table. The procedure returns the successive value tables and selected actions; it asserts no convergence guarantee by itself.

derivations.claim: Every nonglobal cost is $1$, and the policy choosing $a$ at $s$ reaches $x$ and then reaches $g$ almost surely because each visit to $x$ has probability $1/2$ of moving to $g$. From $y$ and $z$ the goal is reached deterministically. Thus this is a finite positive-cost SSP with a proper stationary policy. At $x$ there is no action choice; its survival probability after $n$ steps is $2^{-n}$, so its expected total cost is $\sum_{n=0}^\infty2^{-n}=2$ by the finite geometric identity and its limit. The deterministic costs at $y,z$ and the sole initial choice at $s$ therefore give $f^*(z)=1$, $f^*(y)=1+f^*(z)=2$, and $f^*(s)=\min\{1+f^*(x),1+f^*(y)\}=3$. The initial table is finite, zero at the goal, and no larger than these optimal costs.

Induct on the number $k$ of completed trials. At the first trial, $f_0(x)=0<2=f_0(y)$. If $y$ has not been visited in the first $k$ trials and $x$ has been backed up $k$ times, then $f_k(y)=2$ and the recurrence $f_{j+1}(x)=1+\frac12f_j(x)$, obtained from the sole action at $x$ and $f_j(g)=0$, gives $f_k(x)=2(1-2^{-k})<2$. Thus action $a$ has cost $1+f_k(x)<3$, whereas action $b$ has cost $1+f_k(y)=3$. Since $V=-f$ and $r=-c$, the RTDP reward-greedy rule is cost-minimizing; it therefore uniquely chooses $a$ at $s$. The next trial moves to $x$ and does not visit $y$. The cap $L=2$ then provides exactly one backup at $x$, completing the induction. Tie-breaking is never invoked at $s$.

Each trial first executes $a$ and moves to $x$. With cap $L=2$, RTDP then executes the sole action at $x$ and backs up $x$ once before the trial ends, whether that transition returns to $x$ or reaches $g$. Thus the recurrence in step 2.1 holds on every trial, and neither $y$ nor $z$ is ever visited or backed up. In particular, the estimate of $z$ remains $0$ forever although $f^*(z)=1$.

For the goal-terminated variant, after any finite total number $m$ of backups at $x$, its cost is $2(1-2^{-m})<2$. Thus every later departure from $s$ still uniquely selects $a$. Each trial then consists of visits to $x$ until its transition to $g$; the probability of at least $n$ self-transitions is $2^{-n}$, which tends to zero, so the trial is finite almost surely. The union over the countably many trials of their zero-probability nontermination events has probability zero by countable subadditivity. On the complementary event every finite trial boundary has only finitely many backups at $x$, so the strict inequality persists. Neither $y$ nor $z$ is ever visited, and $f(z)=0$ forever.

The stationary policy that chooses $b$ at $s$ and then follows the sole actions at $y$ and $z$ has total cost $1+2=3=f^*(s)$, so it is optimal from the designated start $s$ and reaches $z$ with probability one. Hence $z$ is optimal-relevant by the stated definition, but its estimate fails to converge on every capped run by step 3.1 and almost surely on goal-terminated runs by step 3.2. This refutes the claimed almost-sure convergence on all optimal-relevant states, and therefore also refutes the conjunction with the source's claimed eventual optimality on every such state.

Let the true environment be a finite Markov decision process with nonempty finite state set $S$, nonempty finite action sets $A(s)$, a finite reward alphabet contained in $[0,1]$, and joint next-state/reward probabilities $p(s',\rho\mid s,a)$. Write $D=\{(s,a):s\in S,\ a\in A(s)\}$, and let $r(s,a)$ and $P(s'\mid s,a)$ be the expected reward and next-state probabilities obtained by summing this joint law. A finite learned model on the same state and action sets consists of estimates $\hat r:D\to[0,1]$ and probability distributions $\hat P(\cdot\mid s,a)$ on $S$ for every $(s,a)\in D$. The estimated transition table is a probability kernel on the finite discrete spaces.

For each $(s,a)\in D$, define the reward error $e_r(s,a)=|r(s,a)-\hat r(s,a)|$ and transition error

$$e_P(s,a)=\frac12\sum_{s'\in S}|P(s'\mid s,a)-\hat P(s'\mid s,a)|.$$

For any subset $C\subseteq D$, define $\epsilon_r(C)=\max_{(s,a)\in C}e_r(s,a)$ and $\epsilon_P(C)=\max_{(s,a)\in C}e_P(s,a)$ when $C\ne\emptyset$, and set both quantities to $0$ when $C=\emptyset$. These are uniform expected-reward and total-variation errors on $C$; the learned model definition makes no accuracy assertion.

Let $S$ be a nonempty finite state set, let $A(s)$ be a nonempty finite action set for each $s\in S$, let $r(s,a)\in[0,1]$, and let $P(\cdot\mid s,a)$ be a probability distribution on $S$ for each admissible pair. A finite-horizon Markov policy of horizon $H\in\mathbb N$ with $H\ge1$ is a family of probability distributions $\pi_t(\cdot\mid s)$ on $A(s)$ for $0\le t<H$. Given an initial state distribution $\mu$, define $d_0=\mu$ and, for $0\le t<H-1$,

$$d_{t+1}(s')=\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{a\in A(s)}d_t(s)\pi_t(a\mid s)P(s'\mid s,a).$$

The finite-horizon expected return is

$$J_H(M,\mu,\pi)=\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{a\in A(s)}d_t(s)\pi_t(a\mid s)r(s,a).$$

The same definition applies to a learned model by replacing $r,P$ with its estimated reward and transition tables. It is the expected sum of the $H$ one-step rewards; no discount factor or terminal continuation value is included.

For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and all $a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n \in \mathbb{R}$, the
set $\{a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ has a maximum and a minimum (Maximum and minimum of a set).

What is proved below is exactly the displayed statement, by induction on $n$.

The usual reading, that *every nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ has a
maximum and a minimum*, follows once one identifies the nonempty finite subsets
of $\mathbb{R}$ with the sets listable as $\{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$. That
identification is recorded as a stipulation in the Given below, because this page
has no definition of finiteness to prove it against. **It is discharged, not
merely assumed**: The nonempty finite subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ are exactly the listable ones proves that the two
descriptions of a nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ agree. That lemma is
recorded in `justified_by` rather than in `deps`, since it is about the sets this
lemma quantifies over and therefore depends on this one. This is what licenses
the notation
$\max\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ and $\min\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ for finite sets of
**real** numbers from this page onwards.

Let $M=(S,(A(s))_{s\in S},r,P)$ be a finite MDP with nonempty finite state set $S$ and nonempty finite action sets $A(s)$. Its finite reward alphabet is contained in $[0,1]$, so $r(s,a)\in[0,1]$, and $P(\cdot\mid s,a)$ is a probability distribution on $S$ for every admissible pair. Let $\widehat M=(S,(A(s))_{s\in S},\widehat r,\widehat P)$ be a finite learned model on the same domain, with $\widehat r(s,a)\in[0,1]$ and a probability distribution $\widehat P(\cdot\mid s,a)$ on $S$ for every admissible pair. Set $D=\{(s,a):s\in S,\ a\in A(s)\}$. Let $B\subseteq D$ be the pairs observed at least once in a data set, fix a horizon $H\ge1$ and initial state law $\mu$, and let $\Pi$ be any finite nonempty class of deterministic time-dependent Markov policies for that horizon. For a policy $\pi\in\Pi$, compute its expected return under the true model and learned model using $d_0=\mu$,

$$d_{t+1}(s')=\sum_s d_t(s)\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi_t(a\mid s)P(s'\mid s,a),\qquad J_H(\pi)=\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\sum_s d_t(s)\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi_t(a\mid s)r(s,a),$$

and analogously $\widehat J_H(\pi)$ using $\widehat P,\widehat r$. The learned-model occupancy of a pair $(s,a)$ at time $t$ is $\widehat d_t(s)\pi_t(a\mid s)$. A model-optimal policy is any $\widehat\pi\in\Pi$ attaining $\max_{\pi\in\Pi}\widehat J_H(\pi)$. Such a policy **exploits the model off support relative to $B$** if it has positive learned-model occupancy on at least one pair in $D\setminus B$, overestimates its own true return $\widehat J_H(\widehat\pi)>J_H(\widehat\pi)$, and is truly suboptimal within $\Pi$: $J_H(\widehat\pi)<\max_{\pi\in\Pi}J_H(\pi)$. This definition describes a failure mode; it is not a performance claim about every model optimizer.

Input: a finite learned MDP model, a current state $s_0$, a horizon $H\in\mathbb N$ with $H\ge1$, and, for each state $s$, an ordered finite list containing every action in $A(s)$ exactly once; this ordering determines deterministic tie-breaking. Initialize $V_0(s)=0$ for every state. For $h=1,\ldots,H$, compute for every admissible pair

$$Q_h(s,a)=\hat r(s,a)+\sum_{s'\in S}\hat P(s'\mid s,a)V_{h-1}(s'),\qquad V_h(s)=\max_{a\in A(s)}Q_h(s,a).$$

At the current state $s_0$, return the first action in its supplied listing that attains $V_H(s_0)$. The controller executes only this first action in the true environment, observes the next state, and may invoke the procedure again with the new state and a newly supplied learned model. The procedure specifies no model-update rule and makes no guarantee about the true return of the model-selected action.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let a finite MDP have nonempty finite state set $S$ and finite nonempty action sets $A(s)$. A **finite stochastic shortest-path problem** consists of that MDP, a nonempty goal set $G\subseteq S$, and a constant $c_{\min}>0$ with the following properties. Each goal $g\in G$ has exactly one available action $a_g$, and its joint reward-transition law satisfies $p(g,0\mid g,a_g)=1$ (so $0\in\mathcal R$). For every $s\notin G$ and every $a\in A(s)$, the expected reward satisfies $r(s,a)\le -c_{\min}$. Define the one-step expected cost by $c(s,a)=-r(s,a)$ off $G$ and $c(g,a)=0$ at goals. A stationary Markov policy $\pi$ is **proper** if, from every initial state, the finite-step probabilities of not having reached $G$ tend to $0$: with $q_0(s)=1_{s\notin G}$ and

$$q_{n+1}(s)=\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi(a\mid s)\sum_{s'\in S}P(s'\mid s,a)q_n(s')\quad(s\notin G),\qquad q_{n+1}(g)=0\quad(g\in G),$$

properness means $q_n(s)\to0$ for every $s\in S$. The problem need not have a proper policy unless that is separately assumed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and let a finite positive-cost stochastic shortest-path problem have at least one proper stationary policy. For any policy $\sigma$ whose action distribution may depend on the entire finite history, use its trajectory law from the initial state $s$ and define

$$J^\sigma(s)=\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\mathbb E_s^\sigma\!\left[c(S_t,A_t)\,1_{\{S_t\notin G\}}\right],$$

where $c(s,a)=-r(s,a)>0$ off the absorbing goal set $G$ and $c(g,a)=0$ at goals. The optimal total cost $f^*(s)=\inf_\sigma J^\sigma(s)$ is finite for every state. It is the unique finite nonnegative function satisfying

$$f^*(g)=0\quad(g\in G),\qquad f^*(s)=\min_{a\in A(s)}\left[c(s,a)+\sum_{s'\in S}P(s'\mid s,a)f^*(s')\right]\quad(s\notin G).$$

The minimum is attained by a deterministic stationary policy that is proper and has total cost $f^*$ from every initial state.

Input: a finite stochastic shortest-path model, a finite value table $V_0:S\to\mathbb R$ with $V_0(g)=0$ on goals, a nonempty finite start set $S_0\subseteq S\setminus G$, a positive integer trial cap $L$, and an infinite supplied start sequence in which each member of $S_0$ occurs infinitely often. For each trial, set the current state to the next supplied start. For at most $L$ decision steps, or until a goal is reached, do the following: at the current nonglobal state $s$, compute

$$q_V(s,a)=r(s,a)+\sum_{s'\in S}P(s'\mid s,a)V(s')\qquad(a\in A(s)),$$

choose uniformly from the nonempty set of actions attaining $\max_{a\in A(s)}q_V(s,a)$ using a fresh tie draw, execute the chosen action in the given MDP and observe the next state, then replace $V(s)$ by $\max_{a\in A(s)}q_V(s,a)$ using the value table from before that backup. Keep every other value unchanged. At a goal keep value $0$. After a trial ends, reset the state to the next supplied start without resetting the value table. The procedure returns the successive value tables and selected actions; it asserts no convergence guarantee by itself.

Assume AC for existence. If $\mathcal H\subseteq\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ and $X\in L^1(P)$, then $E[E[X\mid\mathcal G]\mid\mathcal H]=E[X\mid\mathcal H]$ and $E[E[X\mid\mathcal H]\mid\mathcal G]=E[X\mid\mathcal H]$ almost surely. Also, if a version of $E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ is $\mathcal H$-measurable, it is a version of $E[X\mid\mathcal H]$.

Let $(x_k)$ be a sequence of reals (Sequences of reals: bounded, eventually, frequently, tails, subsequences) and let
$S = \{x_k : k \in \mathbb{N}\}$ be its range.

1. If $(x_k)$ is nondecreasing (Nondecreasing, increasing, nonincreasing, decreasing, monotone, and eventually monotone sequences) and $S$ is bounded
   above (Lower bound, bounded below, bounded set), then $(x_k)$ converges (Limits and Cauchy sequences of reals) and
   $$\lim_{k} x_k = \sup S .$$
2. If $(x_k)$ is nonincreasing and $S$ is bounded below, then $(x_k)$ converges
   and $$\lim_{k} x_k = \inf S .$$

Both suprema and infima exist under the stated hypotheses: $S$ is nonempty, so
the least-upper-bound property (Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property)) supplies the
first and Every nonempty set bounded below has an infimum the second, and each is unique
(Suprema and infima are unique).

This is the first place in this track where the least-upper-bound property
produces a **limit**. Everything on the sequences page held in any Archimedean
ordered field; the theorem below does not, and the sequence of decimal
truncations of $\sqrt 2$ inside $\mathbb{Q}$ is the standard witness of its
failure there.

derivations.claim: 1.1 Bellman monotonicity and [F2] imply $f_n\le f^*$ after every backup: an updated value is no greater than the same backup of $f^*$, and other values do not change. Put $e_n=f^*-f_n\ge0$ and $\delta(s,a)=c(s,a)+\sum_tP(t\mid s,a)f^*(t)-f^*(s)\ge0$. An update at $s$ gives $e_{n+1}(s)=\max_a\{\sum_tP(t\mid s,a)e_n(t)-\delta(s,a)\}$. Consequently $\max_s e_n(s)$ is nonincreasing and all errors are bounded by their finite initial maximum. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

1.2 We first justify the probability-one recurrence fact used below. At each of the successive opportunities when a fixed pair $(s,a)$ is currently greedy at a backed state $s$, the conditional probability of selecting $a$ is at least $1/|A(s)|$. For any finite number $m$ of such opportunities after a fixed index, iterated conditioning [F4] bounds the probability of avoiding $a$ through all of them by $(1-1/|A(s)|)^m$; for random opportunity times, first stop at a finite horizon and then increase the horizon, so the same inequality holds on the event those opportunities exist. Letting $m$ increase proves that infinitely many opportunities imply infinitely many selections almost surely. At successive selections of a fixed $(s,a)$, the same argument with probability $P(t\mid s,a)>0$ shows that successor $t$ occurs infinitely often almost surely. Countably many tail indices and finitely many states/actions/successors allow one common probability-one event for all these implications. [given, A1, F4, algebra]

2.1 Work on that event. Since there are finitely many states, after some finite index only states in $I$ are backed. An action greedy at infinitely many backups of a state in $I$ is selected infinitely often by step 1.2. Every nonglobal positive-probability successor is then an outcome infinitely often, hence belongs to $I$ by outcome-backup fairness. There are only finitely many remaining state-action pairs, so after another finite index every minimizing action at every backed state has transition support in $I\cup G$. In particular, after this index the errors of any successors used by a minimizing action are errors inside $I$, or zero goal errors. [given, step 1.2, construct]

3.1 Let $E_n=\max_{s\in I}e_n(s)$ after the index in step 2.1. The set $I$ is nonempty because infinitely many backups occur on a finite state set. The maximum is attained on a finite set. Choose any minimizing action at the current backed state; the error identity in step 1.1, evaluated at that action, and step 2.1 give its post-backup error at most $E_n$. Unupdated errors stay fixed. Hence $E_n$ is nonincreasing, nonnegative, and has a finite limit $E$ by [F5]. [given, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Suppose $E>0$ and put $J=\{s\in I:\limsup_n e_n(s)=E\}$. Finiteness and attainment of the maxima imply $J$ is nonempty. Each $s\in J$ is backed infinitely often and its value is constant between backups, so some sequence of its post-backup errors tends to $E$. On a subsequence one fixed minimizing action $a_s$ realizes these backups, since the action set is finite. In the error identity from step 1.1 its successor errors are all at most $E_n\to E$, by step 2.1; attaining limiting error $E$ forces $\delta(s,a_s)=0$, excludes positive-probability goal successors, and forces every positive-probability successor to have limsup error $E$. Thus every successor lies in $J$. [given, F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Select one such $a_s$ at each member of finite $J$ by finite enumeration. These actions are globally Bellman-optimal and keep every finite transition law in $J$. Iterating their Bellman equalities for $m$ steps gives $f^*(s)=\mathbb E_s[\sum_{k<m}c(S_k,a_{S_k})+f^*(S_m)]\ge m c_{\min}$ by [F1] and nonnegativity of $f^*$. This contradicts finiteness of $f^*(s)$ for large $m$. Therefore $E=0$, giving uniform convergence on $I$. [F1, F2, step 4.1, algebra, contradiction]

6.1 Any action greedy at infinitely many backups has support in $I\cup G$ by step 2.1. Along those backups all successor estimates tend to their optimal values by step 5.1, and the updated state estimate does also. Passing to the limit in its finite Bellman backup proves that its slack $\delta$ is zero. There are finitely many state-action pairs, so after some finite index no action of positive slack is currently minimizing at a backed state. Every designated start is nonglobal by [F3] and belongs to $I$. A stationary policy choosing any eventual minimizing action on $I$ has zero Bellman slack and support in $I\cup G$. For any $s\in I$ and $m\ge1$, iterating its Bellman equalities gives $f^*(s)=\mathbb E_s[\sum_{k<m}c(S_k,A_k)1_{\{S_k\notin G\}}+f^*(S_m)]$. If $q_k=\mathbb P_s(S_k\notin G)$, absorbing goals make $q_k$ nonincreasing, and the identity implies $m c_{\min}q_m\le c_{\min}\sum_{k<m}q_k\le f^*(s)$. Hence $q_m\le f^*(s)/(m c_{\min})\to0$. Since $f^*$ is bounded and zero on $G$, $\mathbb E_s f^*(S_m)\le\max_x f^*(x)q_m\to0$; taking $m\to\infty$ in the identity shows that the policy is proper on $I$ and has total cost $f^*(s)$. [F1, F2, F3, F4, step 2.1, step 5.1, algebra]

6.2 Suppose additionally $f_0\le Tf_0$. Whenever $f_n\le Tf_n$, each updated coordinate satisfies $f_{n+1}(s)=Tf_n(s)\ge f_n(s)$, while unupdated coordinates are unchanged, so $f_{n+1}\ge f_n$. Monotonicity of $T$ then gives $f_{n+1}\le Tf_{n+1}$: at the updated coordinate $f_{n+1}(s)=Tf_n(s)\le Tf_{n+1}(s)$, and at every unupdated coordinate $f_{n+1}(t)=f_n(t)\le Tf_n(t)\le Tf_{n+1}(t)$. Induction shows that the tables increase coordinatewise and remain subsolutions. They are bounded above by $f^*$ by step 1.1, so on finite $S$ they converge to a finite $\bar f\le f^*$; continuity of finite minima and sums gives $\bar f\le T\bar f$. Every designated start is nonglobal by [F3], is backed infinitely often by hypothesis, and hence belongs to $I$; step 5.1 gives $\bar f=f^*$ there. [given, F3, F5, step 1.1, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 In goal-terminated trials, every nonglobal executed successor is the next backed state before any reset, so outcome-backup fairness holds pathwise. Capped trials are covered precisely when they satisfy the stated fairness condition; no assumption about unvisited optimal branches follows from fresh ties. This proves the trial-schedule assertions. [given, F3, step 6.1]

7.2 If $\bar f(s)=f^*(s)$ and $a$ is globally Bellman-optimal at $s\notin G$, then $f^*(s)=\bar f(s)\le T\bar f(s)\le c(s,a)+\sum_tP(t\mid s,a)\bar f(t)=f^*(s)-\sum_tP(t\mid s,a)(f^*(t)-\bar f(t))\le f^*(s)$. Equality throughout forces every positive-probability successor to satisfy $\bar f=f^*$, since $f^*-\bar f\ge0$. [F1, F2, step 6.2, algebra]

8.1 Fix an optimal policy $\sigma$ from a designated start $s_0$. Let $\delta(s,a)=c(s,a)+\sum_tP(t\mid s,a)f^*(t)-f^*(s)$, which is nonnegative and zero at goals. For every $n$, [F4] and the conditional transition law give $\mathbb E_{s_0}^\sigma[\sum_{k<n}c(S_k,A_k)1_{\{S_k\notin G\}}+f^*(S_n)]=f^*(s_0)+\sum_{k<n}\mathbb E_{s_0}^\sigma[\delta(S_k,A_k)]$. Because $J^\sigma(s_0)=f^*(s_0)<\infty$ and costs off goals are at least $c_{\min}$, $\sum_{k\ge0}\mathbb P_{s_0}^\sigma(S_k\notin G)\le J^\sigma(s_0)/c_{\min}<\infty$, so these probabilities tend to zero. Boundedness of $f^*$ and $f^*|_G=0$ make the terminal expectation tend to zero; letting $n\to\infty$ in the identity gives $\sum_{k\ge0}\mathbb E_{s_0}^\sigma[\delta(S_k,A_k)]=J^\sigma(s_0)-f^*(s_0)=0$. Thus $\delta(S_k,A_k)=0$ almost surely at every $k$, so every action on a positive-probability prefix of $\sigma$ is globally Bellman-optimal. Starting with $\bar f=f^*$ at $s_0$ and applying step 7.2 along each such prefix proves $\bar f=f^*$ at every state reachable with positive probability under $\sigma$. Since $\sigma$ was arbitrary and $S$ is finite, convergence is uniform on the union of all such reachable states. [given, F1, F2, F4, step 6.2, step 7.2, algebra] ∎

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of Integrable real and complex functions, and their integrals, its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

derivations.claim: In each process, every state-action pair has a valid reward/next-state probability row: the specified reward and next state occur with probability $1$. Under the behavior policy the only possible one-step trajectory is $(s_0,a,0,z)$. Hence each size-$n$ logged dataset consists of the same fixed trajectory tuple in both processes, so its law is the same point mass for every $n\ge1$.

The target policy chooses $b$ at $s_0$, so its one-step expected return is $1$ in $M_+$ and $-1$ in $M_-$. Since action $a$ has value $0$, the unique maximizing action is $b$ in $M_+$ and $a$ in $M_-$. The behavior law gives zero probability to action $b$, while the target law gives it probability $1$; thus full trajectory coverage fails.

Let $T$ be any real-valued estimator of finite expectation computed from the logged dataset. Equality of the two dataset laws in step 1.1 implies $\mathbb E_{M_+}T=\mathbb E_{M_-}T$ by [F1]. Unbiasedness in both processes would require this common expectation to equal both $1$ and $-1$, which is impossible. A data-based action selector has the same output distribution in both processes; if it chooses $b$ with probability $q$, its probability of being correct is $q$ in $M_+$ and $1-q$ in $M_-$, so it cannot identify the unique maximizing action with certainty in both.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the policy-induced path laws below. Let $S$ be a nonempty finite state set, let $A(s)$ be a finite nonempty action set for each $s\in S$, and let $\mathcal R\subset\mathbb R$ be a finite nonempty reward set. A finite Markov decision process here consists of these sets and a joint next-state/reward probability mass $p(s',r\mid s,a)\ge0$, defined for $s,s'\in S$, $a\in A(s)$, and $r\in\mathcal R$, with $\sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{r\in\mathcal R}p(s',r\mid s,a)=1$ for every $(s,a)$. A stationary Markov policy $\sigma$ assigns probabilities $\sigma(a\mid s)\ge0$ with $\sum_{a\in A(s)}\sigma(a\mid s)=1$ at every state.

Fix a horizon $H\ge1$, a discount $0\le\gamma\le1$, and an initial state $s_0\in S$. A trajectory is a tuple $\tau=(s_0,a_0,r_1,s_1,\ldots,a_{H-1},r_H,s_H)$ with $s_t\in S$, $a_t\in A(s_t)$, and $r_{t+1}\in\mathcal R$ for each $0\le t<H$. Write $\Omega_H$ for the finite set of all such tuples. For each stationary policy $\sigma$, let $P^\sigma_H$ be the probability law on $\Omega_H$ whose atom masses are

$$P^\sigma_H(\{\tau\})=\prod_{t=0}^{H-1}\sigma(a_t\mid s_t)p(s_{t+1},r_{t+1}\mid s_t,a_t).$$

For a trajectory $\tau$, its finite-horizon return is $G_H(\tau)=\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\gamma^t r_{t+1}$, and the value of target policy $\pi$ from $s_0$ is $J_H(\pi;s_0)=\int_{\Omega_H}G_H\,dP^\pi_H$. A fixed logged dataset of size $n\ge1$ consists of independent trajectories $(\tau_1,\ldots,\tau_n)$, each with law $P^\mu_H$ for a behavior policy $\mu$; the true behavior propensities $\mu(a\mid s)$ used to generate the data are known. Full horizon coverage means $P^\pi_H\ll P^\mu_H$, so every behavior-null trajectory event is also target-null. In this finite setting, the condition $\pi(a\mid s)>0\Rightarrow\mu(a\mid s)>0$ at every state-action pair reachable under $\pi$ before time $H$ is sufficient for full horizon coverage. A trajectory function is integrable under a law $P$ when $\int_{\Omega_H}|f|\,dP<\infty$. All returns are integrable in this finite-horizon finite-reward setting; importance-weighted return expressions below are used only when they are integrable.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let a finite MDP have nonempty state set $S$, and let $\pi$ be a stationary Markov policy. Fix an initial state $s_0\in S$ and let

$$Z=\{(s,a,r,s'):s\in S,\ a\in A(s),\ r\in\mathcal R,\ s'\in S\}$$

with its discrete sigma-algebra. There is a probability law on $S\times Z^{\mathbb N}$ whose first state is $S_0=s_0$ and whose subsequent coordinates are $Z_n=(S_n,A_n,R_{n+1},S_{n+1})$. For every $m\ge0$ and every feasible finite trajectory $(s_0,a_0,r_1,s_1,\ldots,a_{m-1},r_m,s_m)$, its probability is

$$
\prod_{n=0}^{m-1}\pi(a_n\mid s_n)\,p(s_{n+1},r_{n+1}\mid s_n,a_n),
$$

where the empty product for $m=0$ is $1$.

Its state-reward marginal also has the finite-prefix probabilities

$$
\prod_{n=0}^{m-1}\sum_{a\in A(s_n)}\pi(a\mid s_n)p(s_{n+1},r_{n+1}\mid s_n,a)
$$

for each feasible finite state-reward path $(s_0,r_1,s_1,\ldots,r_m,s_m)$.

$$

if every measurable $\mu$-null set is also $

$$\mu(E)=0\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad

Because every measurable subset of a $\mu$-null set is again $\mu$-null, this is equivalent to requiring $

If in addition $|
