In both cases the derivative is not a distinguished pointwise function: it is determined only up to $\mu$-almost-everywhere equality in the sense of Measure-null sets and almost-everywhere statements relative to a measure.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\lambda$ and $\mu$ be sigma-finite positive measures and let $\nu$ be a
signed measure or a finite complex measure on the same measurable space.
Assume there is an increasing measurable exhaustion $(X_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$
with $\bigcup_nX_n=X$, $\lambda(X_n)<+\infty$, $\mu(X_n)<+\infty$, and
$|\nu|(X_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$, and assume $\nu\ll\mu\ll\lambda$. Then
$$\frac{d\nu}{d\lambda}=\frac{d\nu}{d\mu}\frac{d\mu}{d\lambda}\qquad\lambda\text{-almost everywhere.}$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int g\,d(f\,d\mu)=\int gf\,d\mu.$$

Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. Its positive and negative parts are
$$f^+:=\max\{f,0\},\qquad f^-:=\max\{-f,0\};$$
they are measurable by
Closure properties of measurable functions used by the integral and
satisfy $f=f^+-f^-$ and $|f|=f^++f^-$.

The **Lebesgue integral of a real measurable function** is defined whenever at
most one of $\int f^+\,d\mu$ and $\int f^-\,d\mu$ is $+\infty$, in which case
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\int f^+\,d\mu-\int f^-\,d\mu.$$
The function is **integrable** when both integrals are finite, equivalently
when $\int|f|\,d\mu<+\infty$.

For a complex measurable function $h=u+iv$ with
$u=\operatorname{Re}h,\ v=\operatorname{Im}h$
(Real and imaginary parts, complex conjugation, and modulus), define $h$ to be
**integrable** when $|h|$ is integrable, and then define
$$\int h\,d\mu:=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

derivations.claim: For a complete trajectory atom $\tau=(s_0,a_0,r_1,\ldots,a_{H-1},r_H,s_H)$, [F1] gives $P^\sigma_H(\{\tau\})=\prod_{k=0}^{H-1}\sigma(a_k\mid s_k)p(s_{k+1},r_{k+1}\mid s_k,a_k)$. If this atom has positive target mass, coverage makes its behavior mass positive. The initial state and every transition/reward factor are common, so on every behavior-positive atom the quotient $P^\pi_H(\{\tau\})/P^\mu_H(\{\tau\})$ is exactly $\prod_{k=0}^{H-1}\pi(a_k\mid s_k)/\mu(a_k\mid s_k)$; if the target mass is zero, this quotient is zero.

Fix $t<H$ and project the full trajectory law onto $\Omega_{t+1}$. If a prefix set is behavior-null, its inverse image in $\Omega_H$ is behavior-null; full coverage makes that inverse image target-null, so $P^\pi_{t+1}\ll P^\mu_{t+1}$. The prefix space is finite. Let $\lambda_{t+1}$ be counting measure on it; $P^\mu_{t+1}\ll\lambda_{t+1}$, and the whole prefix space is a common finite exhaustion for $\lambda_{t+1}$, $P^\mu_{t+1}$, and $P^\pi_{t+1}$. By [A1], [F4]–[F6] give the RN density classes and their chain rule. On each behavior-positive prefix, [F1]–[F2] give the atom-mass quotient by cancelling the common initial and transition/reward factors, leaving $\prod_{k=0}^{t}\pi(A_k\mid S_k)/\mu(A_k\mid S_k)$. Thus $W_{0:t}=dP^\pi_{t+1}/dP^\mu_{t+1}$ almost everywhere.

Fix $t<H$ and a real $g$ integrable under $P^\pi_{t+1}$. Step 2.1 supplies the prefix density $W_{0:t}$. Applying [F7] to $g^+$ and $g^-$ gives $\mathbb E_{P^\mu_H}[W_{0:t}|g|]=\mathbb E_{P^\pi_{t+1}}|g|<\infty$ and equality of the two weighted integrals for each part. Subtracting the finite positive and negative integrals by [F8] proves the prefix expectation identity. Taking $t=H-1$ and $g=G$ gives the full-horizon assertion.

derivations.claim: On any input where the algorithm returns numerical estimates, each propensity ratio is finite: when $\mu(A_t^i\mid S_t^i)>0$, it is a quotient of finite probabilities by a positive probability; when both probabilities are zero, the algorithm sets the ratio to zero. Each return and every finite sum in OIS and PDIS is finite because the reward set, horizon, and dataset are finite. The WIS numerator and denominator are finite, and the procedure either divides by a positive finite denominator or returns zero.

An observed pair with $\mu(A_t^i\mid S_t^i)=0$ lies on a behavior-null trajectory atom by [F1]. Since the trajectory space, horizon, and sample size are finite, the event that any observed pair has zero behavior propensity is a finite union of null events. The algorithm therefore returns numerical estimates almost surely under the behavior sample law. Extending the three estimator expressions by any fixed finite values on the `unsupported` null event does not change their expectations.

Fix a logged trajectory index $i$. By [F1], its law is $P^\mu_H$, and [F3] applied to $G_i$ gives $\mathbb E_\mu[W_{i,H-1}G_i]=\mathbb E_\pi[G_H]=J_H(\pi;s_0)$. Linearity [F4] gives $\mathbb E_\mu[\widehat J_{\mathrm{OIS}}]=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nJ_H(\pi;s_0)=J_H(\pi;s_0)$.

Fix $i$ and $0\le t<H$. The reward $R_{t+1}^i$ is a function of the prefix through $(R_{t+1},S_{t+1})$, so [F3] gives $\mathbb E_\mu[W_{i,t}R_{t+1}^i]=\mathbb E_\pi[R_{t+1}]$. Each of the $n$ PDIS trajectory scores in [F2] has expectation $J_H(\pi;s_0)$ by step 3.2. Their finite sample average has the same expectation by [F4], proving $\mathbb E_\mu[\widehat J_{\mathrm{PDIS}}]=J_H(\pi;s_0)$. Step 3.1 proves the ordinary-estimator claim.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the policy-induced path laws below. Let $S$ be a nonempty finite state set, let $A(s)$ be a finite nonempty action set for each $s\in S$, and let $\mathcal R\subset\mathbb R$ be a finite nonempty reward set. A finite Markov decision process here consists of these sets and a joint next-state/reward probability mass $p(s',r\mid s,a)\ge0$, defined for $s,s'\in S$, $a\in A(s)$, and $r\in\mathcal R$, with $\sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{r\in\mathcal R}p(s',r\mid s,a)=1$ for every $(s,a)$. A stationary Markov policy $\sigma$ assigns probabilities $\sigma(a\mid s)\ge0$ with $\sum_{a\in A(s)}\sigma(a\mid s)=1$ at every state.

Fix a horizon $H\ge1$, a discount $0\le\gamma\le1$, and an initial state $s_0\in S$. A trajectory is a tuple $\tau=(s_0,a_0,r_1,s_1,\ldots,a_{H-1},r_H,s_H)$ with $s_t\in S$, $a_t\in A(s_t)$, and $r_{t+1}\in\mathcal R$ for each $0\le t<H$. Write $\Omega_H$ for the finite set of all such tuples. For each stationary policy $\sigma$, let $P^\sigma_H$ be the probability law on $\Omega_H$ whose atom masses are

$$P^\sigma_H(\{\tau\})=\prod_{t=0}^{H-1}\sigma(a_t\mid s_t)p(s_{t+1},r_{t+1}\mid s_t,a_t).$$

For a trajectory $\tau$, its finite-horizon return is $G_H(\tau)=\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\gamma^t r_{t+1}$, and the value of target policy $\pi$ from $s_0$ is $J_H(\pi;s_0)=\int_{\Omega_H}G_H\,dP^\pi_H$. A fixed logged dataset of size $n\ge1$ consists of independent trajectories $(\tau_1,\ldots,\tau_n)$, each with law $P^\mu_H$ for a behavior policy $\mu$; the true behavior propensities $\mu(a\mid s)$ used to generate the data are known. Full horizon coverage means $P^\pi_H\ll P^\mu_H$, so every behavior-null trajectory event is also target-null. In this finite setting, the condition $\pi(a\mid s)>0\Rightarrow\mu(a\mid s)>0$ at every state-action pair reachable under $\pi$ before time $H$ is sufficient for full horizon coverage. A trajectory function is integrable under a law $P$ when $\int_{\Omega_H}|f|\,dP<\infty$. All returns are integrable in this finite-horizon finite-reward setting; importance-weighted return expressions below are used only when they are integrable.

Assume AC for the behavior-policy trajectory law. Input a finite-horizon logged dataset with $n\ge1$ behavior trajectories, a target policy $\pi$, finite real functions $\widehat Q_t(s,a)$ for $0\le t<H$, and finite nonnegative action-weight multipliers $\widehat\rho_t(s,a)$ for $0\le t<H$. Hold the functions and multipliers fixed when taking expectation over the evaluation dataset; they may be conditioned on an independent training sample. Define $\widehat V_H(s)=0$ for every $s$, and for $t=H-1,\ldots,0$ define

$$\widehat V_t(s)=\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi(a\mid s)\widehat Q_t(s,a).$$

For each logged trajectory $i$, set $\widehat W_{i,-1}=1$ and $\widehat W_{i,t}=\widehat W_{i,t-1}\widehat\rho_t(S_t^i,A_t^i)$ for $0\le t<H$. Compute

$$D_i=\widehat V_0(s_0)+\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\gamma^t\widehat W_{i,t}\left(R_{t+1}^i+\gamma\widehat V_{t+1}(S_{t+1}^i)-\widehat Q_t(S_t^i,A_t^i)\right),$$

and return $\widehat J_{\mathrm{DR}}=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nD_i$. When supplied as propensity ratios, the multipliers have the form $\widehat\rho_t(s,a)=\pi(a\mid s)/\widetilde\mu_t(a\mid s)$, with positive denominators on target-positive actions. In the exact-ratio case they equal the target-to-behavior action-likelihood factors $\pi(a\mid s)/\mu(a\mid s)$; the procedure also permits finite fitted multipliers for the correct-value-model case. The fixed terminal value $\widehat V_H=0$ is part of the procedure.

Assume AC and the finite-horizon dataset conditions of the preceding definition, with full horizon coverage $P^\pi_H\ll P^\mu_H$. For $0\le t<H$, let $\Omega_{t+1}$ be the finite set of trajectory prefixes through $(R_{t+1},S_{t+1})$, and let $P^\sigma_{t+1}$ be the marginal law of this prefix under policy $\sigma\in\{\pi,\mu\}$. On a behavior-positive prefix define

$$W_{0:t}=\prod_{k=0}^{t}\frac{\pi(A_k\mid S_k)}{\mu(A_k\mid S_k)},$$

and set $W_{0:t}=0$ on behavior-null prefixes. Then $P^\pi_{t+1}\ll P^\mu_{t+1}$, and $W_{0:t}$ is a version of $dP^\pi_{t+1}/dP^\mu_{t+1}$ up to $P^\mu_{t+1}$-almost-everywhere equality. In particular, for every real $G$ integrable under $P^\pi_H$, the full-horizon weight $W_{0:H-1}$ satisfies

$$\mathbb E_{P^\mu_H}[W_{0:H-1}G]=\mathbb E_{P^\pi_H}[G],\qquad \mathbb E_{P^\mu_H}[W_{0:H-1}|G|]<\infty.$$

The same identity holds prefixwise: for each $0\le t<H$ and every real $g$ integrable under $P^\pi_{t+1}$, with $g$ evaluated on the observed prefix,

$$\mathbb E_{P^\mu_H}[W_{0:t}g]=\mathbb E_{P^\pi_H}[g],\qquad \mathbb E_{P^\mu_H}[W_{0:t}|g|]<\infty.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let a finite MDP have nonempty state set $S$, and let $\pi$ be a stationary Markov policy. Fix an initial state $s_0\in S$ and let

$$Z=\{(s,a,r,s'):s\in S,\ a\in A(s),\ r\in\mathcal R,\ s'\in S\}$$

with its discrete sigma-algebra. There is a probability law on $S\times Z^{\mathbb N}$ whose first state is $S_0=s_0$ and whose subsequent coordinates are $Z_n=(S_n,A_n,R_{n+1},S_{n+1})$. For every $m\ge0$ and every feasible finite trajectory $(s_0,a_0,r_1,s_1,\ldots,a_{m-1},r_m,s_m)$, its probability is

$$
\prod_{n=0}^{m-1}\pi(a_n\mid s_n)\,p(s_{n+1},r_{n+1}\mid s_n,a_n),
$$

where the empty product for $m=0$ is $1$.

Its state-reward marginal also has the finite-prefix probabilities

$$
\prod_{n=0}^{m-1}\sum_{a\in A(s_n)}\pi(a\mid s_n)p(s_{n+1},r_{n+1}\mid s_n,a)
$$

for each feasible finite state-reward path $(s_0,r_1,s_1,\ldots,r_m,s_m)$.

Assume AC for the supplied existence theorem. Write $E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ for the unique class in $L^1(\Omega,\mathcal G,P|_{\mathcal G})$ consisting of conditional-expectation versions of $X$. A chosen real $\mathcal G$-measurable representative is a **version**. Equalities and inequalities involving these classes mean almost-sure equalities and inequalities.

Existence is Conditional expectation exists by radon nikodym and uniqueness is Conditional expectation is unique almost surely, applied to Conditional expectation given a sigma algebra. The quotient is The space $L^p(\mu)$ as the quotient by null functions. If $X=X^{\ast}$ almost surely, Two integrable functions are equal almost everywhere exactly when all of their indefinite integrals agree gives identical event integrals, so the output class is independent of the input representative. The The Axiom of Choice assumption is inherited from RN existence.
Assume AC. For every real integrable $X$ on $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ and every sub-sigma-algebra $\mathcal G$, a conditional-expectation version of $X$ given $\mathcal G$ exists.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space, $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ a sub-sigma-algebra, and $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ integrable. A **conditional-expectation version of $X$ given $\mathcal G$** is a real, $\mathcal G$-measurable, integrable function $Y$ such that $\int_A Y\,dP=\int_A X\,dP$ for every $A\in\mathcal G$. No completeness of $\mathcal G$ is assumed.

Expectation means the integral of Expectation of a nonnegative or integrable random variable. Integrable representatives use The class $L^1(\mu)$ of integrable functions; quotient notation is introduced after uniqueness.

Assume AC for existence. If $X\in L^1(P)$ and $Z$ is bounded real $\mathcal G$-measurable, then $E[ZX\mid\mathcal G]=ZE[X\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. The identity also holds for finite real $\mathcal G$-measurable $Z$ whenever $ZX$ and $ZE[X\mid\mathcal G]$ are integrable. In fact $X,ZX\in L^1$ imply the latter integrability.

Assume AC for existence. For real $X,Y\in L^1(P)$ and $a,b\in\mathbb R$, $E[aX+bY\mid\mathcal G]=aE[X\mid\mathcal G]+bE[Y\mid\mathcal G]$. Conditional expectation is positive, preserves order and constants, satisfies $E(E[X\mid\mathcal G])=EX$, and $|E[X\mid\mathcal G]|\le E[|X|\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. Also $X<Y$ almost surely implies $E[X\mid\mathcal G]<E[Y\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely.

Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. Its positive and negative parts are
$$f^+:=\max\{f,0\},\qquad f^-:=\max\{-f,0\};$$
they are measurable by
Closure properties of measurable functions used by the integral and
satisfy $f=f^+-f^-$ and $|f|=f^++f^-$.

The **Lebesgue integral of a real measurable function** is defined whenever at
most one of $\int f^+\,d\mu$ and $\int f^-\,d\mu$ is $+\infty$, in which case
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\int f^+\,d\mu-\int f^-\,d\mu.$$
The function is **integrable** when both integrals are finite, equivalently
when $\int|f|\,d\mu<+\infty$.

For a complex measurable function $h=u+iv$ with
$u=\operatorname{Re}h,\ v=\operatorname{Im}h$
(Real and imaginary parts, complex conjugation, and modulus), define $h$ to be
**integrable** when $|h|$ is integrable, and then define
$$\int h\,d\mu:=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

derivations.claim: First assume condition 1. For every $t$, the residual $C_t=R_{t+1}+\gamma\widehat V_{t+1}(S_{t+1})-\widehat Q_t(S_t,A_t)$ is a function of the prefix through $(R_{t+1},S_{t+1})$, so [F3] gives $\mathbb E_\mu[\widehat W_{0:t}C_t]=\mathbb E_\pi[C_t]$. The baseline term is the same under both laws because $S_0=s_0$ is fixed.

Now assume condition 2. For each $s$, let $U_t^\pi(s)$ be the expected discounted return over steps $t,\ldots,H-1$ under target policy $\pi$, starting at state $s$ at time $t$, and set $U_H^\pi(s)=0$. The zero-step return gives $U_H^\pi=V_H^\pi$. If $U_{t+1}^\pi=V_{t+1}^\pi$, then conditioning on the finite target action sum and the joint next-state/reward mass gives $U_t^\pi(s)=\sum_a\pi(a\mid s)\sum_{s',r}p(s',r\mid s,a)(r+\gamma V_{t+1}^\pi(s'))=\sum_a\pi(a\mid s)Q_t^\pi(s,a)=V_t^\pi(s)$. Backward induction proves $U_t^\pi=V_t^\pi$ for all $t$, hence $V_0^\pi(s_0)=J_H(\pi;s_0)$. Condition 2 and the algorithm's definition of $\widehat V_t$ then give $\widehat V_t=V_t^\pi$ for all $t$.

Fix $t$ and let $\mathcal H_t$ be the finite sigma-algebra generated by the history through $(S_t,A_t)$. For each positive-probability history atom $h$ ending at $(s,a)$, the path-law formula in [F4] gives $P_\mu(h,(R_{t+1},S_{t+1})=(r,s'))=P_\mu(h)\,p(s',r\mid s,a)$; dividing by $P_\mu(h)>0$ proves that the conditional next reward/state mass is $p(s',r\mid s,a)$. Therefore $E_\mu[C_t\mid\mathcal H_t]=\sum_{s',r}p(s',r\mid s,a)\left(r+\gamma V_{t+1}^\pi(s')-Q_t^\pi(s,a)\right)=0$. The equality follows because $Q_t^\pi(s,a)$ is defined by the same finite sum. Each $\widehat W_{0:t}$ is a finite $\mathcal H_t$-measurable function, since the trajectory space and horizon are finite and the multipliers are fixed. Applying [F6] and then expectation preservation [F7] yields $\mathbb E_\mu[\widehat W_{0:t}C_t]=0$.

For each state $s$, $\sum_a\pi(a\mid s)\widehat Q_t(s,a)=\widehat V_t(s)$, so averaging over the target-law distribution of $S_t$ gives $\mathbb E_\pi[\widehat Q_t(S_t,A_t)]=\mathbb E_\pi[\widehat V_t(S_t)]$. Substituting the density identities from step 1.1 into the expected score, the $\widehat V_t$ terms telescope: $\mathbb E_\mu D=\widehat V_0(s_0)+\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\gamma^t\mathbb E_\pi[R_{t+1}]+\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\gamma^{t+1}\mathbb E_\pi[\widehat V_{t+1}(S_{t+1})]-\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\gamma^t\mathbb E_\pi[\widehat V_t(S_t)]=J_H(\pi;s_0)$ because $S_0=s_0$ and $\widehat V_H=0$. This proves condition 1 without requiring a correct Q model.

Every residual term in $D$ has zero expectation by step 1.3, while the baseline is $\widehat V_0(s_0)=V_0^\pi(s_0)=J_H(\pi;s_0)$ by step 1.2. Hence $\mathbb E_\mu D=J_H(\pi;s_0)$. No coverage or ratio-correctness premise was used in this branch.

Condition 1 implies that one trajectory score has expectation $J_H(\pi;s_0)$ by step 2.1, and condition 2 implies the same by step 2.2. Every evaluation trajectory has this same behavior law by [F1], so linearity of the integral [F8] makes their finite sample average have expectation $J_H(\pi;s_0)$. Thus either exact condition is sufficient.

The set of **natural numbers** is the **smallest inductive set**
(Inductive set),

$$\mathbb{N} = \omega := \bigcap\,\{\, I : I \text{ is inductive} \,\},$$

which exists and is itself inductive by The natural numbers exist: a smallest inductive set (the
Axiom of Infinity, The Axiom of Infinity: there is a set containing a set with no elements and closed under $y \mapsto y \cup \{y\}$, supplies one inductive set to
intersect within, and Separation, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$, makes the
intersection a set). On $\mathbb{N}$ we take

$$0 := \varnothing, \qquad \sigma(n) := n \cup \{n\},$$

the distinguished element and the successor function. Thus
$0 = \varnothing$, $1 = \{0\}$, $2 = \{0, 1\}$, $3 = \{0, 1, 2\}$, and in general
$n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ is the set of its predecessors.

For $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, define the **order** by

$$m \le n \iff \exists k \in \mathbb{N}\ (m + k = n),$$

and the **strict order** by $m < n \iff (m \le n \text{ and } m \neq n)$, using
addition (Addition of natural numbers).

Let $\mathbb{N} = \omega$ be the von Neumann naturals, with $0 = \varnothing$ and
$\sigma(n) = n \cup \{n\}$ (The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)), and let $\le$ and $<$ be
the order defined additively by $m \le n \iff \exists k \in \mathbb{N}\ (m + k = n)$
and $m < n \iff (m \le n$ and $m \ne n)$ (Order on the natural numbers). Then $\mathbb{N}$ is
a **transitive set**: every element of a natural number is itself a natural
number. Moreover, for all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$:

1. $m < n \iff m \in n$;
2. $m \le n \iff m \subseteq n$;
3. $n < \sigma(n)$, and $m < \sigma(n) \iff m \le n$;
4. $0 \le n$, and $0 \in n$ whenever $n \ne 0$.

Consequently $n = \{\, m \in \mathbb{N} : m < n \,\}$ for every $n$: a natural
number is exactly the set of the naturals below it.

**Why this is proved here.** Order on the natural numbers defines the order additively and
records the identification with membership only as an orienting remark, without
proof. The countability arguments on this page use that identification as a
working fact, so it is established here, from the additive order and induction
alone. Nothing below uses ordinals or any later material.

Throughout this page $\mathbb{N}$ is the set of von Neumann naturals
(The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)): $0 = \varnothing$, $\sigma(n) = n \cup \{n\}$, and
$n = \{\, m \in \mathbb{N} : m < n \,\}$ is itself the set of its predecessors,
the order being the additive order of Order on the natural numbers identified with
membership in On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$. Write $A \approx B$ when a
bijection $A \to B$ exists (Equinumerous sets, $A \approx B$ and $A \preceq B$,
Injection, surjection, bijection). A set $A$ is **finite** when
$A \approx n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$ (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable).

**Definition.** Let $A$ be a finite set. Then there is **exactly one**
$n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $A \approx n$, and we write

$$\lvert A\rvert := \text{that } n,$$

the **cardinality**, or number of elements, of $A$. The notation $\lvert A\rvert$
is defined for finite $A$ only, and its value is a natural number.

**Why exactly one, which is the whole content of the definition.** At least one
such $n$ exists: that is literally what "$A$ is finite" says. At most one exists:
if $A \approx n$ and $A \approx m$ with $n, m \in \mathbb{N}$, then $n \approx A$,
because the inverse of a bijection is a bijection, and hence $n \approx m$,
because a composition of bijections is a bijection
(Injection, surjection, bijection); and $n \approx m$ forces $n = m$ by
claim 3 of The pigeonhole principle on $\mathbb{N}$. So $\lvert A\rvert$ names a single natural number
and not a family of choices.

**Four consequences, proved here because everything on this page uses them.**

**(a) $\lvert n\rvert = n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.** The identity map
$\mathrm{id}_n$ is a bijection $n \to n$, so $n \approx n$; thus $n$ is finite and
the unique natural equinumerous with it is $n$ itself.

**(b) $\lvert\varnothing\rvert = 0$, and a finite $A$ satisfies
$\lvert A\rvert = 0$ if and only if $A = \varnothing$.** Since $0 = \varnothing$,
part (a) gives $\lvert\varnothing\rvert = 0$. Conversely, if $\lvert A\rvert = 0$
then there is a bijection $f : A \to \varnothing$; were some $a \in A$, the value
$f(a)$ would be an element of $\varnothing$, and $\varnothing$ has none, so
$A = \varnothing$.

**(c) Transport along a bijection.** If $A$ is finite and $f : A \to B$ is a
bijection, then $B$ is finite and $\lvert B\rvert = \lvert A\rvert$. Indeed
$B \approx A$ through $f^{-1}$ and $A \approx \lvert A\rvert$, so
$B \approx \lvert A\rvert$ by transitivity.

**(d) Equality of cardinalities is equinumerosity.** For finite $A$ and $B$:
$\lvert A\rvert = \lvert B\rvert$ if and only if $A \approx B$. If the
cardinalities agree then $A \approx \lvert A\rvert = \lvert B\rvert \approx B$;
conversely $A \approx B$ gives $\lvert B\rvert = \lvert A\rvert$ by (c).

Let $S$ be a finite nonempty set of hidden states, $A$ a finite nonempty action set available in every state, and $\Omega$ a finite nonempty observation set. Give these sets their power-set sigma-algebras. A finite POMDP with known model consists of a finite reward alphabet $\mathcal R\subseteq\mathbb R$ and a joint probability mass $p(s',\rho\mid s,a)$ on $S\times\mathcal R$ for each $(s,a)\in S\times A$, an observation probability distribution $O(\cdot\mid s')$ on $\Omega$ for each $s'\in S$, and an initial belief $b_0:S\to[0,1]$ with $\sum_{s\in S}b_0(s)=1$. Put

$$T(s'\mid s,a)=\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}p(s',\rho\mid s,a),\qquad r(s,a)=\sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}\rho\,p(s',\rho\mid s,a).$$

At decision time $t$, write $S_t\in S$ for the hidden state, $A_t\in A$ for the chosen action, $R_t\in\mathcal R$ for the realized reward, and $O_{t+1}\in\Omega$ for the next observation. Conditional on $S_t=s$ and $A_t=a$, the joint law of next state $S_{t+1}=s'$, reward $R_t=\rho$, and observation $O_{t+1}=o$ is $p(s',\rho\mid s,a)O(o\mid s')$. Thus the observation depends only on the next state and is not an additional observation of the reward. A policy uses only the past actions and observations; realized rewards are not included in its history. For a horizon $H\in\mathbb N$ and discount $\gamma\in[0,1]$, the objective is to maximize $\mathbb E[\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\gamma^tR_t]$. The model is known; learning its transition, reward, or observation laws is outside this definition.

For a finite POMDP with state set $S$, define its **belief simplex** by $\Delta(S)=\{b:S\to[0,1]:\sum_{s\in S}b(s)=1\}$, with the Euclidean subspace topology and its Borel sigma-algebra. At time $t$, the observed-history random variable is $H_t=(A_0,O_1,\ldots,A_{t-1},O_t)$, and a realized history is $h_t=(a_0,o_1,\ldots,a_{t-1},o_t)$; at $t=0$ both histories are empty. A (possibly randomized) **history policy** assigns to each finite history $h_t$ a probability distribution $\pi_t(\cdot\mid h_t)$ on $A$; a deterministic choice is the point-mass case. Let $\Pr_\pi$ be the induced finite law: multiply the initial belief, these action probabilities, and the one-step factors $p(s',\rho\mid s,a)O(o\mid s')$, and sum out hidden states and unobserved rewards when taking marginals. Thus policy randomization depends only on the observed history and is conditionally independent of the hidden state given that history. The history $h_t$ is **reachable** when $\Pr_\pi(H_t=h_t)>0$. Its **belief state** is

$$b_t(s)=\Pr_\pi(S_t=s\mid H_t=h_t)=\frac{\Pr_\pi(S_t=s,H_t=h_t)}{\Pr_\pi(H_t=h_t)},$$

where both probabilities are finite sums of products of the specified initial, action, transition, joint reward-transition, and observation probabilities, with unobserved rewards summed out. At $t=0$, the empty history has belief $b_0$.

For $b\in\Delta(S)$ and $a\in A$, define the predicted state distribution $\bar b_{b,a}(s')=\sum_{s\in S}T(s'\mid s,a)b(s)$ and, for $o\in\Omega$, the observation probability

$$q(o\mid b,a)=\sum_{s'\in S}O(o\mid s')\bar b_{b,a}(s').$$

When $q(o\mid b,a)>0$, the **Bayes filter** is the probability vector

$$\tau(b,a,o)(s')=\frac{O(o\mid s')\bar b_{b,a}(s')}{q(o\mid b,a)}.$$

When $q(o\mid b,a)=0$, $\tau(b,a,o)$ is undefined; no quotient or filler value is assigned. For each $(b,a)$, the **belief-state transition kernel** on Borel sets $C\subseteq\Delta(S)$ is

$$K(C\mid b,a)=\sum_{o\in\Omega:q(o\mid b,a)>0}q(o\mid b,a)\,1_C(\tau(b,a,o)),$$

and the expected one-step reward at belief $b$ under action $a$ is $\bar r(b,a)=\sum_{s\in S}b(s)r(s,a)$, where $1_C$ denotes the indicator function of $C$.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in Measures on sigma-algebras and A measurable function between measurable spaces; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let $\pi$ be a prior probability on $(E,\mathcal S)$ and let $Q:E\to T$ be a probability kernel dominated by a sigma-finite measure $\nu$ on $(T,\mathcal T)$, with specified nonnegative jointly measurable density $\ell:E\times T\to[0,\infty]$:
$$Q(\theta,B)=\int_B\ell(\theta,y)\,\nu(dy)\quad\text{for every }\theta\in E,\ B\in\mathcal T.$$

Define $m(y)=\int_E\ell(\theta,y)\,\pi(d\theta)$. Under the joint law with density $\ell$ relative to $\pi\times\nu$, a conditional law of the parameter given the observation is
$$K(y,A)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\int_A\ell(\theta,y)\,\pi(d\theta)}{m(y)},&0<m(y)<\infty,\\ \pi(A),&m(y)=0\text{ or }m(y)=\infty.\end{cases}$$

The observation marginal is $m\,d\nu$, and the filled fibres have marginal mass zero. This is a choice-free assertion about the explicit kernel and event identities.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Let $S$ be a finite set, $n := \lvert S\rvert$ (The cardinality $\lvert A\rvert$ of a finite set), and
let $a : S \to \mathbb{R}$ or $a : S \to \mathbb{N}$, written $a_i$ for $a(i)$.
Choose a bijection $\varphi : n \to S$, which exists because $S \approx n$
(Equinumerous sets, $A \approx B$ and $A \preceq B$), and set

$$\sum_{i \in S} a_i := \sum_{k<n} a_{\varphi(k)}, \qquad \prod_{i \in S} a_i := \prod_{k<n} a_{\varphi(k)},$$

the right-hand sides being the iterated operations of Finite sums and finite products, by recursion when the
values are real and of Finite sums and finite products of natural numbers, $\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ in $\mathbb{N}$ when they are natural.

**Independence of the enumeration, which is the content of the definition.** Let
$\varphi, \psi : n \to S$ be two bijections. Then $\pi := \varphi^{-1} \circ \psi$
is a bijection $n \to n$ (Injection, surjection, bijection), and
$a_{\psi(k)} = a_{\varphi(\pi(k))}$ for every $k < n$. Applying
A finite sum is unchanged by a permutation of its index range: $\sum_{k<n} a_{\pi(k)} = \sum_{k<n} a_k$ for every bijection $\pi : n \to n$ to the list $c_k := a_{\varphi(k)}$
gives

$$\sum_{k<n} a_{\psi(k)} = \sum_{k<n} c_{\pi(k)} = \sum_{k<n} c_k = \sum_{k<n} a_{\varphi(k)},$$

and identically for products. So the value does not depend on which bijection is
used, and $\sum_{i \in S} a_i$ is a single well-determined element.

**No choice principle is involved.** The definition does not select an
enumeration: it asserts that all enumerations give the same value, and that value
is what the notation names. Only one bijection is ever produced at a time, from a
set already known to be nonempty.

**Three clauses, recorded here because the page uses them constantly.**

**(a) The bridge to the old notation.** Taking $S = n$ and $\varphi = \mathrm{id}_n$,
which is legitimate since $\lvert n\rvert = n$, gives

$$\sum_{i \in n} a_i = \sum_{k<n} a_k, \qquad \prod_{i \in n} a_i = \prod_{k<n} a_k .$$

So the new notation **extends** the sum over an initial segment rather than
competing with it, and every law proved for the latter is available for the
former whenever the index set is a natural number.

**(b) Reindexing along a bijection.** If $h : T \to S$ is a bijection of finite
sets, then $\sum_{j \in T} a_{h(j)} = \sum_{i \in S} a_i$, and likewise for
products. Indeed $\lvert T\rvert = \lvert S\rvert = n$ by transport
(The cardinality $\lvert A\rvert$ of a finite set), and if $\varphi : n \to S$ is a bijection then
$h^{-1} \circ \varphi : n \to T$ is one, so
$\sum_{j \in T} a_{h(j)} = \sum_{k<n} a_{h(h^{-1}(\varphi(k)))} = \sum_{k<n} a_{\varphi(k)} = \sum_{i \in S} a_i$.

**(c) The empty index set and a constant summand.** $\lvert\varnothing\rvert = 0$,
so $\sum_{i \in \varnothing} a_i = 0$ and $\prod_{i \in \varnothing} a_i = 1$ by
the base clause of the recursion. And for a constant $c$, clause (a) together
with the constant clause of Laws of finite sums and products in $\mathbb{N}$, and $\iota\big(\sum_{k<n} a_k\big) = \sum_{k<n} \iota(a_k)$
in $\mathbb{N}$, or clause 2 of Laws of finite sums and finite products in $\mathbb{R}$, gives

$$\sum_{i \in S} c = \lvert S\rvert \cdot c \quad (c \in \mathbb{N}), \qquad \sum_{i \in S} c = \iota(\lvert S\rvert)\cdot c \quad (c \in \mathbb{R}),$$

the second with $\iota$ written out because $\lvert S\rvert$ is a natural number
and not an element of $\mathbb{R}$ (The canonical natural $\iota(n) = n \cdot 1_F$ of a field).

Let $S$ and $T$ be finite sets and let $a : S \times T \to \mathbb{R}$, or
$a : S \times T \to \mathbb{N}$, written $a_{ij}$ for $a(i,j)$. Then $S \times T$
is finite and

$$\sum_{i \in S}\Big(\sum_{j \in T} a_{ij}\Big) \;=\; \sum_{p \in S \times T} a_p \;=\; \sum_{j \in T}\Big(\sum_{i \in S} a_{ij}\Big),$$

all three sums being the sums over a finite index set of
The sum $\sum_{i \in S} a_i$ over a finite index set, and its product form, carried by Finite sums and finite products, by recursion when the
values are real and by Finite sums and finite products of natural numbers, $\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ in $\mathbb{N}$ when they are natural.

**This is not a clause of The sum rule: a finite disjoint union is finite with $\lvert A \cup B\rvert = \lvert A\rvert + \lvert B\rvert$ and $\lvert\bigcup_{i \in I} A_i\rvert = \sum_{i \in I}\lvert A_i\rvert$, and a sum over a finite index set splits along a partition.** That theorem splits one sum along a
partition of *its own* index set; the identity above exchanges the roles of two
*different* index sets, and it is what an argument that counts a set of pairs in
two ways needs. Both outer index sets may be empty, in which case all three
quantities are $0$ (respectively $1$ for the product form of the underlying
recursion), since a sum over the empty index set is the empty sum.

derivations.claim: For fixed $s,a$, the mass $J(s',\rho,o\mid s,a)=p(s',\rho\mid s,a)O(o\mid s')$ is nonnegative. Summing first over observations gives $\sum_{s',\rho,o}J=\sum_{s',\rho}p(s',\rho\mid s,a)\sum_oO(o\mid s')=\sum_{s',\rho}p(s',\rho\mid s,a)=1$ by [F1]; all index sets are finite, so the reordering is justified by [F6] and [F7]. Thus the joint next-state/reward/observation mass is normalized.

The predicted coordinates $\bar b_{b,a}(s')$ are nonnegative, and $\sum_{s'}\bar b_{b,a}(s')=\sum_s b(s)\sum_{s'}T(s'\mid s,a)=\sum_s b(s)=1$ by [F1], [F2], and finite double-sum interchange [F7]. Hence $\bar b_{b,a}$ is a probability distribution.

Every $q(o\mid b,a)$ is nonnegative, and $\sum_o q(o\mid b,a)=\sum_{s'}\bar b_{b,a}(s')\sum_oO(o\mid s')=\sum_{s'}\bar b_{b,a}(s')=1$ by [F1], step 1.2, and [F7]. Thus $q(\cdot\mid b,a)$ is a probability distribution, so each $q$ is finite and lies in $[0,1]$.

Fix $o$ with $q(o\mid b,a)>0$. Apply [F4] with prior $\pi=\bar b_{b,a}$ on the finite state set, observation kernel $Q(s',\cdot)=O(\cdot\mid s')$, counting measure on finite $\Omega$, and density $\ell(s',o)=O(o\mid s')$. The density is nonnegative and jointly measurable, and its marginal is exactly $q(o\mid b,a)$, which is finite and positive by step 2.1. The theorem's posterior is therefore $\tau(b,a,o)$, with coordinates summing to one. At $q=0$ the Bayes theorem supplies a filler for its everywhere kernel, but the partial update defined here remains undefined and $K$ omits that zero-mass observation.

For fixed $b,a$, the formula for $K$ is a finite nonnegative sum of point masses at the defined $\tau(b,a,o)$. For pairwise disjoint Borel sets $(C_n)_{n\ge1}$, each point $\tau(b,a,o)$ lies in at most one $C_n$, so $1_{\cup_nC_n}(\tau)=\sum_n1_{C_n}(\tau)$ with at most one nonzero term. Since there are finitely many observations, distributing the finite weighted sum over these finitely many nonzero terms gives $K(\cup_nC_n)=\sum_nK(C_n)$. Also $K(\Delta(S))=\sum_{o:q>0}q(o\mid b,a)=1$ by step 2.1. Thus $K(\cdot\mid b,a)$ is a probability measure.

On $\Delta(S)\times A$, the predicted law $\bar K(\{s'\}\mid b,a)=\bar b_{b,a}(s')$ is a probability kernel: step 1.2 gives probability sections, and each evaluation is a finite linear function of $b$ on each discrete action. The function $((b,a),s')\mapsto O(o\mid s')$ is product-measurable, so [F5] makes $q(o\mid b,a)=\int O(o\mid s')\bar K(ds'\mid b,a)$ measurable; its displayed finite formula also shows it is continuous in $b$. On the Borel set where $q(o\mid b,a)>0$, every coordinate of $\tau$ is a quotient of continuous functions with positive denominator and is Borel. For Borel $C$, the function equal to $q(o\mid b,a)1_C(\tau(b,a,o))$ there and zero where $q=0$ is Borel; summing these functions over the finite set $\Omega$ proves that $K(C\mid b,a)$ is Borel measurable. By [F3], $K$ is a probability kernel.

The only conditional law used in step 3.1 is the explicit dominated-kernel formula at a positive finite marginal. The finite history beliefs are ratios on positive-probability atoms, and all other constructions use specified finite sums and kernels; no version selection or arbitrary-family choice is used.

No reverse characterization of when a finite belief update is a probability kernel is stated in this lemma.

risk_review.notes: Independently checked all seven proof steps: sum pO first over observations, then use finite double-sum interchange to normalize predicted states and observation probabilities. Bayes supplier applies to the finite prior, counting measure and specified jointly measurable O; q is finite and the quotient is used only at q>0. K is a finite weighted Dirac measure of total mass one; disjoint-event additivity reduces to finitely many nonzero contributions. Each posterior coordinate is continuous on its positive-normalizer Borel domain; multiplying its indicator by q there and extending the scalar function by zero gives measurable event evaluations. No null-fibre posterior is assigned, no AC is used, and no diagram occurs. Checked current probability-kernel, dominated-Bayes, kernel-integration and finite-sum supplier statements; MIT lines 16–24 and Waterloo slides 4, 7–8 corroborate conventions. maximum and a minimum*, follows once one identifies the nonempty finite subsets

derivations.claim: Fix $h_t$ and $a$ as in the statement. By [F2], $b_t(s)=\Pr(S_t=s\mid h_t)$. Conditioning first on $S_t$ and using the POMDP's specified one-step law [F1] gives $\Pr(S_{t+1}=s',O_{t+1}=o\mid h_t,A_t=a)=\sum_{s\in S}b_t(s)T(s'\mid s,a)O(o\mid s')$. The action selection does not alter $b_t$ after conditioning on $h_t$, because its randomization depends only on that history and is conditionally independent of the hidden state.

Summing the joint probability in step 1.1 over $s'$ yields $q(o\mid b_t,a)$ by [F2]. If this is positive, dividing the joint mass by it gives $\Pr(S_{t+1}=s'\mid h_t,A_t=a,O_{t+1}=o)=\tau(b_t,a,o)(s')$; if it is zero, the observation event has probability zero and no conditional quotient is used. By [F3], these positive branches form the probability kernel $K$.

Conditioning the immediate reward on the current hidden state and chosen action gives $\mathbb E[R_t\mid h_t,A_t=a]=\sum_{s\in S}b_t(s)r(s,a)=\bar r(b_t,a)$ by [F1] and [F2]. Thus the conditional immediate reward and next-belief law depend on the history only through $b_t$ and $a$, which proves the stated controlled belief-state transition and reward description.

We prove the finite-horizon recursion by induction on $n$. With no decisions remaining, the reward sum is empty, so $V_0(b)=0$. Suppose the optimal $n$-step continuation value is the function $V_n$ of the current belief. If action $a$ is taken at belief $b$, its immediate expected reward is $\bar r(b,a)$ by step 2.2, and for each positive-probability observation $o$ the remaining belief is $\tau(b,a,o)$ by step 2.1. Conditional expectation over the finite observation set therefore gives the $n+1$ step action value $Q_{n+1}(b,a):=\bar r(b,a)+\gamma\sum_{o:q>0}q(o\mid b,a)V_n(\tau(b,a,o))$. The set $\{Q_{n+1}(b,a):a\in A\}$ is a nonempty finite image of $A$ in $\mathbb R$, so [F4] gives an attained maximum. Taking that maximum gives the displayed $V_{n+1}(b)$. The expression depends only on $b$, completing the induction and proving history sufficiency for every finite horizon.

If the action at a history is randomized with probabilities $\lambda_a$, its expected action value is $\sum_{a\in A}\lambda_a Q_{n+1}(b,a)$, where $Q_{n+1}$ is the finite action value from step 3.1, $\lambda_a\ge0$, and $\sum_a\lambda_a=1$. Since each $Q_{n+1}(b,a)\le\max_{c\in A}Q_{n+1}(b,c)$, [F5] gives $\sum_a\lambda_a Q_{n+1}(b,a)\le\max_{c\in A}Q_{n+1}(b,c)$. Randomization cannot improve the finite-horizon value.

Give these sets their power-set sigma-algebras. A finite POMDP with known model consists of a finite reward alphabet $\mathcal R\subseteq\mathbb R$ and a joint probability mass $p(s',\rho\mid s,a)$ on $S\times\mathcal R$ for each $(s,a)\in S\times A$, an observation probability distribution $O(\cdot\mid s')$ on $\Omega$ for each $s'\in S$, and an initial belief $b_0:S\to[0,1]$ with $\sum_{s\in S}b_0(s)=1$. Put

$$T(s'\mid s,a)=\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}p(s',\rho\mid s,a),\qquad r(s,a)=\sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}\rho\,p(s',\rho\mid s,a).$$

At decision time $t$, write $S_t\in S$ for the hidden state, $A_t\in A$ for the chosen action, $R_t\in\mathcal R$ for the realized reward, and $O_{t+1}\in\Omega$ for the next observation. Conditional on $S_t=s$ and $A_t=a$, the joint law of next state $S_{t+1}=s'$, reward $R_t=\rho$, and observation $O_{t+1}=o$ is $p(s',\rho\mid s,a)O(o\mid s')$. Thus the observation depends only on the next state and is not an additional observation of the reward. A policy uses only the past actions and observations; realized rewards are not included in its history. For a horizon $H\in\mathbb N$ and discount $\gamma\in[0,1]$, the objective is to maximize $\mathbb E[\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\gamma^tR_t]$. The model is known; learning its transition, reward, or observation laws is outside this definition.

$$\tau(b,a,o)(s')=\frac{O(o\mid s')\bar b_{b,a}(s')}{q(o\mid b,a)}.$$

$$K(C\mid b,a)=\sum_{o\in\Omega:q(o\mid b,a)>0}q(o\mid b,a)\,1_C(\tau(b,a,o)),$$

and the expected one-step reward at belief $b$ under action $a$ is $\bar r(b,a)=\sum_{s\in S}b(s)r(s,a)$, where $1_C$ denotes the indicator function of $C$.

Input a finite POMDP, a horizon $H\in\mathbb N$, and its discount $\gamma\in[0,1]$. A depth-zero policy tree is the empty continuation and has the zero vector $\alpha_0:S\to\mathbb R$. Recursively, a depth-$(h+1)$ policy tree consists of a root action $a\in A$ and one depth-$h$ continuation tree for each observation $o\in\Omega$. If the continuation vectors are $(\alpha_o)_{o\in\Omega}$, assign the tree the vector

$$\alpha_{a,(\alpha_o)}(s)=r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'\in S}T(s'\mid s,a)\sum_{o\in\Omega}O(o\mid s')\alpha_o(s')\qquad(s\in S).$$

Set $\Gamma_0=\{\alpha_0\}$. For each $h=0,\ldots,H-1$, form $\Gamma_{h+1}$ from every action $a\in A$ and every tuple $(\alpha_o)_{o\in\Omega}\in\Gamma_h^{\Omega}$ using the displayed formula, treating $\Gamma_{h+1}$ as a set so equal vectors are stored once. Return $(\Gamma_0,\ldots,\Gamma_H)$. This procedure exhaustively enumerates finite policy-tree vectors; it does not perform linear-program witness pruning and makes no bit-complexity or polynomial-time claim.

Let a finite POMDP with known model be fixed. A deterministic history policy chooses an action from the finite action set using only preceding actions and observations; a randomized history policy assigns an action distribution using only that history, with its randomization conditionally independent of the hidden state. For every positive-probability history $h_t$ with belief $b_t$ and every action $a$ having positive conditional selection probability at that history,

$$\Pr(S_{t+1}=s',O_{t+1}=o\mid h_t,A_t=a)=\sum_{s\in S}b_t(s)T(s'\mid s,a)O(o\mid s').$$

Consequently the observation probability is $q(o\mid b_t,a)$, the next belief is $\tau(b_t,a,o)$ whenever that probability is positive, and the conditional expected reward is $\bar r(b_t,a)$. The controlled belief-state model has the fully observed Borel state space $\Delta(S)$, action set $A$, transition kernel $K$, and reward $\bar r$; under a policy depending only on the current belief, the belief process is Markov. For every remaining finite horizon $n$, the optimal value depends on the history only through $b$ and satisfies

$$V_0(b)=0,\qquad V_{n+1}(b)=\max_{a\in A}\left[\bar r(b,a)+\gamma\sum_{o:q(o\mid b,a)>0}q(o\mid b,a)V_n(\tau(b,a,o))\right].$$

3. **Splitting.** If $m \le n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k = \sum_{k<m} a_k + \sum_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k$, and $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n} a_k = \Big(\prod_{k<m} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k\Big)$.
4. **Monotonicity.** If $a_k \le b_k$ for all $k < n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k \le \sum_{k<n} b_k$. In particular, if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\sum_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, every single term satisfies $a_j \le \sum_{k<n} a_k$ for $j < n$, and $\sum_{k<n} a_k = 0$ forces $a_k = 0$ for every $k < n$.
5. **Telescoping.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}\big(c_{k+1} - c_k\big) = c_n - c_0$.
6. **Products.** $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n}(a_k b_k) = \Big(\prod_{k<n} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k<n} b_k\Big)$; if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, and if $a_k > 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k > 0$.

For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and all $a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n \in \mathbb{R}$, the
set $\{a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ has a maximum and a minimum (Maximum and minimum of a set).

What is proved below is exactly the displayed statement, by induction on $n$.

The usual reading, that *every nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ has a
maximum and a minimum*, follows once one identifies the nonempty finite subsets
of $\mathbb{R}$ with the sets listable as $\{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$. That
identification is recorded as a stipulation in the Given below, because this page
has no definition of finiteness to prove it against. **It is discharged, not
merely assumed**: The nonempty finite subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ are exactly the listable ones proves that the two
descriptions of a nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ agree. That lemma is
recorded in `justified_by` rather than in `deps`, since it is about the sets this
lemma quantifies over and therefore depends on this one. This is what licenses
the notation
$\max\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ and $\min\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ for finite sets of
**real** numbers from this page onwards.

Throughout this page $\mathbb{N}$ is the set of von Neumann naturals
(The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)): $0 = \varnothing$, $\sigma(n) = n \cup \{n\}$, and
$n = \{\, m \in \mathbb{N} : m < n \,\}$ is itself the set of its predecessors,
the order being the additive order of Order on the natural numbers identified with
membership in On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$. Write $A \approx B$ when a
bijection $A \to B$ exists (Equinumerous sets, $A \approx B$ and $A \preceq B$,
Injection, surjection, bijection). A set $A$ is **finite** when
$A \approx n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$ (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable).

**Definition.** Let $A$ be a finite set. Then there is **exactly one**
$n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $A \approx n$, and we write

$$\lvert A\rvert := \text{that } n,$$

the **cardinality**, or number of elements, of $A$. The notation $\lvert A\rvert$
is defined for finite $A$ only, and its value is a natural number.

**Why exactly one, which is the whole content of the definition.** At least one
such $n$ exists: that is literally what "$A$ is finite" says. At most one exists:
if $A \approx n$ and $A \approx m$ with $n, m \in \mathbb{N}$, then $n \approx A$,
because the inverse of a bijection is a bijection, and hence $n \approx m$,
because a composition of bijections is a bijection
(Injection, surjection, bijection); and $n \approx m$ forces $n = m$ by
claim 3 of The pigeonhole principle on $\mathbb{N}$. So $\lvert A\rvert$ names a single natural number
and not a family of choices.

**Four consequences, proved here because everything on this page uses them.**

**(a) $\lvert n\rvert = n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.** The identity map
$\mathrm{id}_n$ is a bijection $n \to n$, so $n \approx n$; thus $n$ is finite and
the unique natural equinumerous with it is $n$ itself.

**(b) $\lvert\varnothing\rvert = 0$, and a finite $A$ satisfies
$\lvert A\rvert = 0$ if and only if $A = \varnothing$.** Since $0 = \varnothing$,
part (a) gives $\lvert\varnothing\rvert = 0$. Conversely, if $\lvert A\rvert = 0$
then there is a bijection $f : A \to \varnothing$; were some $a \in A$, the value
$f(a)$ would be an element of $\varnothing$, and $\varnothing$ has none, so
$A = \varnothing$.

**(c) Transport along a bijection.** If $A$ is finite and $f : A \to B$ is a
bijection, then $B$ is finite and $\lvert B\rvert = \lvert A\rvert$. Indeed
$B \approx A$ through $f^{-1}$ and $A \approx \lvert A\rvert$, so
$B \approx \lvert A\rvert$ by transitivity.

**(d) Equality of cardinalities is equinumerosity.** For finite $A$ and $B$:
$\lvert A\rvert = \lvert B\rvert$ if and only if $A \approx B$. If the
cardinalities agree then $A \approx \lvert A\rvert = \lvert B\rvert \approx B$;
conversely $A \approx B$ gives $\lvert B\rvert = \lvert A\rvert$ by (c).

Let $A$ and $B$ be finite sets and write

$$A^{B} := \{\, f : f \text{ is a function } B \to A \,\}.$$

Then $A^{B}$ is finite and $\lvert A^{B}\rvert = \lvert A\rvert^{\lvert B\rvert}$,
the power being the $\mathbb{N}$-valued exponentiation of Exponentiation of natural numbers, $m^{n}$, and its agreement with the integer power in $\mathbb{R}$.

Both degenerate cases are covered and neither is a stipulation. If
$B = \varnothing$ there is exactly one function $B \to A$, the empty function, so
$\lvert A^{\varnothing}\rvert = 1 = \lvert A\rvert^{0}$ **even when
$A = \varnothing$**. If $A = \varnothing$ and $B \ne \varnothing$ there is no
function at all, so $\lvert A^{B}\rvert = 0 = 0^{\lvert B\rvert}$ with
$\lvert B\rvert \ge 1$.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$. By the recursion theorem (The recursion theorem) applied to
the set $\mathbb{N}$, the starting element $1$ and the function
$f(x) = x \cdot m$ (Multiplication of natural numbers), there is a unique function
$\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, written $n \mapsto m^{n}$, with

$$m^{0} = 1, \qquad m^{\sigma(n)} = m^{n} \cdot m \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

Both the base and the value are natural numbers, so $m^n \in \mathbb{N}$ for all
$m, n$. In particular $m^{1} = m^{0}\cdot m = m$ and $m^{2} = m \cdot m$.

**Why a new item is needed.** Integer powers $a^m$ defines $a^{n}$ for a
**real** base $a$, so its value is a real number. The counts on this page,
$\lvert A^{B}\rvert$ and $\lvert\mathcal{P}(A)\rvert$ among them, are natural
numbers, and an identity between them has to be an identity in $\mathbb{N}$. The
two operations are related by clause (d) below and by nothing weaker.

**(a) $0^{0} = 1$ and $0^{n} = 0$ for $n \ge 1$.** The first is the base clause.
For the second, $0^{\sigma(n)} = 0^{n}\cdot 0 = 0$, the clause $x \cdot 0 = 0$
being definitional (Multiplication of natural numbers), and every $n \ge 1$ is a
successor.

**(b) $1^{n} = 1$ for every $n$.** Induction: $1^{0} = 1$, and
$1^{\sigma(n)} = 1^{n}\cdot 1 = 1^{n}$ (Zero and one under multiplication,
The principle of mathematical induction).

**(c) $m^{p+q} = m^{p}\,m^{q}$ and $(m p)^{q} = m^{q} p^{q}$.** Both by induction
on $q$, using associativity and commutativity of multiplication
(Multiplication is associative, Multiplication is commutative). For the first, at
$q = 0$ we have $m^{p+0} = m^{p} = m^{p}\cdot 1 = m^{p}m^{0}$, and
$m^{p+\sigma(q)} = m^{\sigma(p+q)} = m^{p+q}\cdot m = (m^{p}m^{q})\cdot m = m^{p}\,m^{\sigma(q)}$,
using $p + \sigma(q) = \sigma(p+q)$ (Addition of natural numbers). For the second, at
$q = 0$ both sides are $1$, and
$(mp)^{\sigma(q)} = (mp)^{q}(mp) = m^{q}p^{q}mp = m^{\sigma(q)}p^{\sigma(q)}$.

**(d) The bridge into $\mathbb{R}$.** With $\iota : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$
the canonical natural (The canonical natural $\iota(n) = n \cdot 1_F$ of a field) and $x^{n}$ the integer power
of Integer powers $a^m$,

$$\iota\big(m^{n}\big) = \iota(m)^{n} \qquad (m, n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

Induction on $n$: at $n = 0$ both sides are $1$, since $\iota(1) = 1$; and
$\iota(m^{\sigma(n)}) = \iota(m^{n}\cdot m) = \iota(m^{n})\,\iota(m) = \iota(m)^{n}\iota(m) = \iota(m)^{\sigma(n)}$,
the second equality being the multiplicativity of $\iota$ (clause 0 of
Laws of finite sums and products in $\mathbb{N}$, and $\iota\big(\sum_{k<n} a_k\big) = \sum_{k<n} \iota(a_k)$) and the last the
recursion clause of Integer powers $a^m$.

**(e) $m^{n}$ is a constant product.** $m^{n} = \prod_{k<n} m$, the
$\mathbb{N}$-valued product of the constant list
(Finite sums and finite products of natural numbers, $\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ in $\mathbb{N}$). Induction: at $n = 0$ both sides are $1$,
and $\prod_{k<\sigma(n)} m = \big(\prod_{k<n} m\big)\cdot m = m^{n}\cdot m = m^{\sigma(n)}$.

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. If $0 \in S$ and $\sigma(n) \in S$ whenever $n \in S$, then $S = \mathbb{N}$. Equivalently (property form): if a property $P$ satisfies $P(0)$ and ($P(n) \Rightarrow P(\sigma(n))$) for all $n$, then $P(n)$ holds for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. This is the induction principle, the basis of proof by induction.

derivations.claim: At horizon $h=0$, there is one empty-continuation policy tree and the backup returns $\Gamma_0=\{0\}$. Its conditional value is zero at every state, and the optimal zero-step value is $V_0(b)=0=\sum_s b(s)0$ for each belief. Thus $P(0)$ holds.
Fix $h\in\mathbb N$ and assume $P(h)$.

A depth-$(h+1)$ policy tree is a root action $a$ and a depth-$h$ continuation tree $\pi_o$ for each $o\in\Omega$. From initial hidden state $s$, its expected immediate reward plus discounted continuation value is $\sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}\sum_{o\in\Omega}p(s',\rho\mid s,a)O(o\mid s')\bigl(\rho+\gamma\alpha_h^{\pi_o}(s')\bigr)$. By the induction hypothesis [L1], each continuation vector $\alpha_h^{\pi_o}$ is represented in $\Gamma_h$. Since the continuation is selected from $o$ alone, not from the unobserved reward $\rho$, finite-sum linearity and reindexing [F5], together with $\sum_oO(o\mid s')=1$ from [F1], rewrite this expectation as $\sum_{s',\rho}\rho p(s',\rho\mid s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}\bigl(\sum_\rho p(s',\rho\mid s,a)\bigr)\sum_oO(o\mid s')\alpha_h^{\pi_o}(s')$. The first term is $r(s,a)$ and the inner next-state marginal is $T(s'\mid s,a)$ by [F1], so this is exactly the vector formed by [F3]. Conversely, each tuple generated by [F3] has a depth-$h$ tree for each continuation vector by [L1]; since $\Omega$ is finite, choose these finitely many trees successively and adjoin the root action to obtain a depth-$(h+1)$ tree. Therefore $\Gamma_{h+1}$ is exactly the set of distinct conditional-value vectors of those trees. The candidate set $A\times\Gamma_h^{\Omega}$ is finite by [F8]–[F9], so its image $\Gamma_{h+1}$ under the vector formula is finite; it is nonempty by the nonempty action set and a constant continuation tuple.

For each depth-$(h+1)$ tree $\pi$, conditioning on the initial hidden state gives value $\sum_s b(s)\alpha^\pi_{h+1}(s)$ from belief $b$. Every deterministic history policy is such a tree: its first action is the root and its restriction after each observation is the corresponding subtree; conversely every tree prescribes such a policy. Since $\Gamma_{h+1}$ is finite and nonempty by step 2.1, its value set $\{\sum_s b(s)\alpha(s):\alpha\in\Gamma_{h+1}\}$ is a nonempty finite image in $\mathbb R$, so [F6] gives an attained maximum. By [F4], randomized policies cannot improve it. Hence $V_{h+1}(b)=\max_{\alpha\in\Gamma_{h+1}}\sum_s b(s)\alpha(s)$. This completes $P(h+1)$.

The base step 1.1 and successor steps 2.1–3.1 prove $P(h)$ for every natural $h$ by induction. The recursion in [F3] depends only on the preceding stage, so a call with horizon at least $h$ has the same $\Gamma_h$ as a call with horizon exactly $h$. In particular, the displayed alpha-vector representation holds for every $0\le h\le H$.

For each $\alpha\in\Gamma_h$, its maximizing region $R_\alpha$ is the simplex intersected with the finitely many half-spaces $\sum_s b(s)(\alpha(s)-\beta(s))\ge0$, one for each $\beta\in\Gamma_h$. These regions cover $\Delta(S)$ because the maximum in step 4.1 is attained, and on $R_\alpha$ the value equals the linear function $b\mapsto\sum_s b(s)\alpha(s)$. This proves piecewise linearity.

For arbitrary $b,c\in\Delta(S)$ and $\lambda\in[0,1]$, the vector $\lambda b+(1-\lambda)c$ is again in $\Delta(S)$ by [F2]: its coordinates are nonnegative and sum to $\lambda+(1-\lambda)=1$. Finite-sum linearity [F5] gives $\sum_s(\lambda b(s)+(1-\lambda)c(s))\alpha(s)=\lambda\sum_s b(s)\alpha(s)+(1-\lambda)\sum_s c(s)\alpha(s)$ for each $\alpha$. Taking the maximum over $\Gamma_h$ and bounding each summand by the corresponding maxima gives $V_h(\lambda b+(1-\lambda)c)\le\lambda V_h(b)+(1-\lambda)V_h(c)$. Thus $V_h$ is convex.

Define $\Gamma_h^{\rm wit}=\{\alpha\in\Gamma_h:\exists b\in\Delta(S),\ \sum_s b(s)\alpha(s)=V_h(b)\}$. For arbitrary $b$, [F6] gives a maximizing $\alpha_b\in\Gamma_h$; that same $b$ witnesses $\alpha_b$, so $\alpha_b\in\Gamma_h^{\rm wit}$. Therefore $\max_{\alpha\in\Gamma_h^{\rm wit}}\sum_s b(s)\alpha(s)=V_h(b)$; deleting all vectors with no witness preserves the value at every belief.

Let $\mathcal P_0$ contain only the empty continuation and $\mathcal P_{h+1}=A\times\mathcal P_h^{\Omega}$. A depth-$(h+1)$ tree is uniquely its root action and a function from observations to depth-$h$ trees. By [F8]–[F9], these sets are finite and their cardinalities satisfy $N_0=1$ and $N_{h+1}=|A|N_h^{|\Omega|}$; [F10] fixes the natural-power convention. The map from trees to conditional-value vectors has image $\Gamma_h$, the set of distinct exhaustive candidates by step 2.1. Enumerating the $N_h$ trees shows that this image has at most $N_h$ vectors, and the witness vectors form a subset, so their count is no larger.
In the case $|A|=2$, $|\Omega|=1$, let $Q(h)$ be the claim $N_h=2^h$. The base case is $N_0=1=2^0$.
Fix $h$ and assume $Q(h)$. Step 5.4 gives $N_{h+1}=2N_h=2\cdot2^h=2^{h+1}$ by the natural-power recursion [F10], so $Q(h+1)$ holds.
The base and successor steps prove $N_h=2^h$ for every $h$ by [F11]. Thus exhaustive tree candidates can grow exponentially, although duplicate vectors or pruning may reduce the stored set.

The induction conclusions in steps 4.1 and 7.1, together with the envelope and convexity arguments in steps 5.1 and 5.2, witness pruning in step 5.3, and the general tree count in step 5.4, establish all claims. No Axiom of Choice is used: branches are selected only over the finite observation set, maxima are attained in finite sets, and the cited sufficiency, finite-sum, finite-function-set, product, and induction arguments make no arbitrary-family choice.

citations.quote:
Let $S$ be a finite nonempty set of hidden states, $A$ a finite nonempty action set available in every state, and $\Omega$ a finite nonempty observation set. Give these sets their power-set sigma-algebras. A finite POMDP with known model consists of a finite reward alphabet $\mathcal R\subseteq\mathbb R$ and a joint probability mass $p(s',\rho\mid s,a)$ on $S\times\mathcal R$ for each $(s,a)\in S\times A$, an observation probability distribution $O(\cdot\mid s')$ on $\Omega$ for each $s'\in S$, and an initial belief $b_0:S\to[0,1]$ with $\sum_{s\in S}b_0(s)=1$. Put

$$T(s'\mid s,a)=\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}p(s',\rho\mid s,a),\qquad r(s,a)=\sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}\rho\,p(s',\rho\mid s,a).$$

At decision time $t$, write $S_t\in S$ for the hidden state, $A_t\in A$ for the chosen action, $R_t\in\mathcal R$ for the realized reward, and $O_{t+1}\in\Omega$ for the next observation. Conditional on $S_t=s$ and $A_t=a$, the joint law of next state $S_{t+1}=s'$, reward $R_t=\rho$, and observation $O_{t+1}=o$ is $p(s',\rho\mid s,a)O(o\mid s')$. Thus the observation depends only on the next state and is not an additional observation of the reward. A policy uses only the past actions and observations; realized rewards are not included in its history. For a horizon $H\in\mathbb N$ and discount $\gamma\in[0,1]$, the objective is to maximize $\mathbb E[\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\gamma^tR_t]$. The model is known; learning its transition, reward, or observation laws is outside this definition.

For a finite POMDP with state set $S$, define its **belief simplex** by $\Delta(S)=\{b:S\to[0,1]:\sum_{s\in S}b(s)=1\}$, with the Euclidean subspace topology and its Borel sigma-algebra. At time $t$, the observed-history random variable is $H_t=(A_0,O_1,\ldots,A_{t-1},O_t)$, and a realized history is $h_t=(a_0,o_1,\ldots,a_{t-1},o_t)$; at $t=0$ both histories are empty. A (possibly randomized) **history policy** assigns to each finite history $h_t$ a probability distribution $\pi_t(\cdot\mid h_t)$ on $A$; a deterministic choice is the point-mass case. Let $\Pr_\pi$ be the induced finite law: multiply the initial belief, these action probabilities, and the one-step factors $p(s',\rho\mid s,a)O(o\mid s')$, and sum out hidden states and unobserved rewards when taking marginals. Thus policy randomization depends only on the observed history and is conditionally independent of the hidden state given that history. The history $h_t$ is **reachable** when $\Pr_\pi(H_t=h_t)>0$. Its **belief state** is

$$b_t(s)=\Pr_\pi(S_t=s\mid H_t=h_t)=\frac{\Pr_\pi(S_t=s,H_t=h_t)}{\Pr_\pi(H_t=h_t)},$$

where both probabilities are finite sums of products of the specified initial, action, transition, joint reward-transition, and observation probabilities, with unobserved rewards summed out. At $t=0$, the empty history has belief $b_0$.

For $b\in\Delta(S)$ and $a\in A$, define the predicted state distribution $\bar b_{b,a}(s')=\sum_{s\in S}T(s'\mid s,a)b(s)$ and, for $o\in\Omega$, the observation probability

$$q(o\mid b,a)=\sum_{s'\in S}O(o\mid s')\bar b_{b,a}(s').$$

When $q(o\mid b,a)>0$, the **Bayes filter** is the probability vector

$$\tau(b,a,o)(s')=\frac{O(o\mid s')\bar b_{b,a}(s')}{q(o\mid b,a)}.$$

When $q(o\mid b,a)=0$, $\tau(b,a,o)$ is undefined; no quotient or filler value is assigned. For each $(b,a)$, the **belief-state transition kernel** on Borel sets $C\subseteq\Delta(S)$ is

$$K(C\mid b,a)=\sum_{o\in\Omega:q(o\mid b,a)>0}q(o\mid b,a)\,1_C(\tau(b,a,o)),$$

and the expected one-step reward at belief $b$ under action $a$ is $\bar r(b,a)=\sum_{s\in S}b(s)r(s,a)$, where $1_C$ denotes the indicator function of $C$.

Let a finite POMDP be fixed, let $b\in\Delta(S)$ and $a\in A$, and put $\bar b(s')=\sum_{s\in S}T(s'\mid s,a)b(s)$, $q(o)=\sum_{s'\in S}O(o\mid s')\bar b(s')$, and, when $q(o)>0$, $\tau(o)(s')=O(o\mid s')\bar b(s')/q(o)$. For Borel $C\subseteq\Delta(S)$ define $K(C)=\sum_{o:q(o)>0}q(o)1_C(\tau(o))$. Then the joint next-state/reward/observation mass in the POMDP definition is normalized; $\bar b$ and $q$ are probability distributions; every defined $\tau(o)$ is a probability distribution and is the conditional law of the next state given observation $o$; and $K$ is a probability measure. Moreover, $(b,a)\mapsto K(C\mid b,a)$ is Borel measurable for each Borel $C$, so $K$ is a probability kernel from $\Delta(S)\times A$ to $\Delta(S)$. No Axiom of Choice is used.

Let $S$ be a finite set, $n := \lvert S\rvert$ (The cardinality $\lvert A\rvert$ of a finite set), and
let $a : S \to \mathbb{R}$ or $a : S \to \mathbb{N}$, written $a_i$ for $a(i)$.
Choose a bijection $\varphi : n \to S$, which exists because $S \approx n$
(Equinumerous sets, $A \approx B$ and $A \preceq B$), and set

$$\sum_{i \in S} a_i := \sum_{k<n} a_{\varphi(k)}, \qquad \prod_{i \in S} a_i := \prod_{k<n} a_{\varphi(k)},$$

the right-hand sides being the iterated operations of Finite sums and finite products, by recursion when the
values are real and of Finite sums and finite products of natural numbers, $\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ in $\mathbb{N}$ when they are natural.

**Independence of the enumeration, which is the content of the definition.** Let
$\varphi, \psi : n \to S$ be two bijections. Then $\pi := \varphi^{-1} \circ \psi$
is a bijection $n \to n$ (Injection, surjection, bijection), and
$a_{\psi(k)} = a_{\varphi(\pi(k))}$ for every $k < n$. Applying
A finite sum is unchanged by a permutation of its index range: $\sum_{k<n} a_{\pi(k)} = \sum_{k<n} a_k$ for every bijection $\pi : n \to n$ to the list $c_k := a_{\varphi(k)}$
gives

$$\sum_{k<n} a_{\psi(k)} = \sum_{k<n} c_{\pi(k)} = \sum_{k<n} c_k = \sum_{k<n} a_{\varphi(k)},$$

and identically for products. So the value does not depend on which bijection is
used, and $\sum_{i \in S} a_i$ is a single well-determined element.

**No choice principle is involved.** The definition does not select an
enumeration: it asserts that all enumerations give the same value, and that value
is what the notation names. Only one bijection is ever produced at a time, from a
set already known to be nonempty.

**Three clauses, recorded here because the page uses them constantly.**

**(a) The bridge to the old notation.** Taking $S = n$ and $\varphi = \mathrm{id}_n$,
which is legitimate since $\lvert n\rvert = n$, gives

$$\sum_{i \in n} a_i = \sum_{k<n} a_k, \qquad \prod_{i \in n} a_i = \prod_{k<n} a_k .$$

So the new notation **extends** the sum over an initial segment rather than
competing with it, and every law proved for the latter is available for the

$$T(s'\mid s,a)=\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}p(s',\rho\mid s,a),\qquad r(s,a)=\sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}\rho\,p(s',\rho\mid s,a).$$

At decision time $t$, write $S_t\in S$ for the hidden state, $A_t\in A$ for the chosen action, $R_t\in\mathcal R$ for the realized reward, and $O_{t+1}\in\Omega$ for the next observation. Conditional on $S_t=s$ and $A_t=a$, the joint law of next state $S_{t+1}=s'$, reward $R_t=\rho$, and observation $O_{t+1}=o$ is $p(s',\rho\mid s,a)O(o\mid s')$. Thus the observation depends only on the next state and is not an additional observation of the reward. A policy uses only the past actions and observations; realized rewards are not included in its history. For a horizon $H\in\mathbb N$ and discount $\gamma\in[0,1]$, the objective is to maximize $\mathbb E[\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\gamma^tR_t]$. At time $t$, the observed-history random variable is $H_t=(A_0,O_1,\ldots,A_{t-1},O_t)$, and a realized history is $h_t=(a_0,o_1,\ldots,a_{t-1},o_t)$; at $t=0$ both histories are empty. A (possibly randomized) **history policy** assigns to each finite history $h_t$ a probability distribution $\pi_t(\cdot\mid h_t)$ on $A$; a deterministic choice is the point-mass case. Its **belief state** is

$$b_t(s)=\Pr_\pi(S_t=s\mid H_t=h_t)=\frac{\Pr_\pi(S_t=s,H_t=h_t)}{\Pr_\pi(H_t=h_t)},$$

where both probabilities are finite sums of products of the specified initial, action, transition, joint reward-transition, and observation probabilities, with unobserved rewards summed out. At $t=0$, the empty history has belief $b_0$.

For $b\in\Delta(S)$ and $a\in A$, define the predicted state distribution $\bar b_{b,a}(s')=\sum_{s\in S}T(s'\mid s,a)b(s)$ and, for $o\in\Omega$, the observation probability

$$q(o\mid b,a)=\sum_{s'\in S}O(o\mid s')\bar b_{b,a}(s').$$

When $q(o\mid b,a)>0$, the **Bayes filter** is the probability vector

$$\tau(b,a,o)(s')=\frac{O(o\mid s')\bar b_{b,a}(s')}{q(o\mid b,a)}.$$

$$K(C\mid b,a)=\sum_{o\in\Omega:q(o\mid b,a)>0}q(o\mid b,a)\,1_C(\tau(b,a,o)),$$

and the expected one-step reward at belief $b$ under action $a$ is $\bar r(b,a)=\sum_{s\in S}b(s)r(s,a)$, where $1_C$ denotes the indicator function of $C$.

Input a finite POMDP, a horizon $H\in\mathbb N$, and its discount $\gamma\in[0,1]$. A depth-zero policy tree is the empty continuation and has the zero vector $\alpha_0:S\to\mathbb R$. Recursively, a depth-$(h+1)$ policy tree consists of a root action $a\in A$ and one depth-$h$ continuation tree for each observation $o\in\Omega$. If the continuation vectors are $(\alpha_o)_{o\in\Omega}$, assign the tree the vector

$$\alpha_{a,(\alpha_o)}(s)=r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'\in S}T(s'\mid s,a)\sum_{o\in\Omega}O(o\mid s')\alpha_o(s')\qquad(s\in S).$$

Set $\Gamma_0=\{\alpha_0\}$. For each $h=0,\ldots,H-1$, form $\Gamma_{h+1}$ from every action $a\in A$ and every tuple $(\alpha_o)_{o\in\Omega}\in\Gamma_h^{\Omega}$ using the displayed formula, treating $\Gamma_{h+1}$ as a set so equal vectors are stored once. Return $(\Gamma_0,\ldots,\Gamma_H)$. This procedure exhaustively enumerates finite policy-tree vectors; it does not perform linear-program witness pruning and makes no bit-complexity or polynomial-time claim.

Fix a finite POMDP, horizon $H\in\mathbb N$, and discount $\gamma\in[0,1]$. For $0\le h\le H$, let $\Gamma_h$ be the finite alpha-vector set returned by the exhaustive backup, with set semantics for duplicate vectors. Then, for every belief $b\in\Delta(S)$,

$$V_h(b)=\max_{\alpha\in\Gamma_h}\sum_{s\in S}b(s)\alpha(s),$$

where $V_h$ is the optimal expected $h$-step discounted reward. Thus $V_h$ is the upper envelope of finitely many linear functions on $\Delta(S)$: it is linear on each region $R_\alpha=\{b\in\Delta(S):\sum_s b(s)\alpha(s)\ge\sum_s b(s)\beta(s)\text{ for every }\beta\in\Gamma_h\}$ and is convex. Define a **witness belief** for $\alpha\in\Gamma_h$ to be any $b\in\Delta(S)$ with $\sum_s b(s)\alpha(s)=V_h(b)$. Removing every vector with no witness belief leaves $V_h$ unchanged. the unique natural equinumerous with it is $n$ itself.

**(b) $\lvert\varnothing\rvert = 0$, and a finite $A$ satisfies
$\lvert A\rvert = 0$ if and only if $A = \varnothing$.** Since $0 = \varnothing$,

2. **Scaling.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda a_k = \lambda \sum_{k<n} a_k$; in particular $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda = n\lambda$, where $n$ denotes the canonical field image $n\cdot1_{\mathbb{R}}$ of the natural n (The unique embedding of ℚ into an ordered field, Canonical naturals are positive and strictly increasing).

For a finite POMDP with state set $S$, define its **belief simplex** by $\Delta(S)=\{b:S\to[0,1]:\sum_{s\in S}b(s)=1\}$, with the Euclidean subspace topology and its Borel sigma-algebra. At time $t$, the observed-history random variable is $H_t=(A_0,O_1,\ldots,A_{t-1},O_t)$, and a realized history is $h_t=(a_0,o_1,\ldots,a_{t-1},o_t)$; at $t=0$ both histories are empty. A (possibly randomized) **history policy** assigns to each finite history $h_t$ a probability distribution $\pi_t(\cdot\mid h_t)$ on $A$; a deterministic choice is the point-mass case. Let $\Pr_\pi$ be the induced finite law: multiply the initial belief, these action probabilities, and the one-step factors $p(s',\rho\mid s,a)O(o\mid s')$, and sum out hidden states and unobserved rewards when taking marginals. Thus policy randomization depends only on the observed history and is conditionally independent of the hidden state given that history. The history $h_t$ is **reachable** when $\Pr_\pi(H_t=h_t)>0$. Its **belief state** is

$$b_t(s)=\Pr_\pi(S_t=s\mid H_t=h_t)=\frac{\Pr_\pi(S_t=s,H_t=h_t)}{\Pr_\pi(H_t=h_t)},$$

where both probabilities are finite sums of products of the specified initial, action, transition, joint reward-transition, and observation probabilities, with unobserved rewards summed out. At $t=0$, the empty history has belief $b_0$.

For $b\in\Delta(S)$ and $a\in A$, define the predicted state distribution $\bar b_{b,a}(s')=\sum_{s\in S}T(s'\mid s,a)b(s)$ and, for $o\in\Omega$, the observation probability

$$q(o\mid b,a)=\sum_{s'\in S}O(o\mid s')\bar b_{b,a}(s').$$

When $q(o\mid b,a)>0$, the **Bayes filter** is the probability vector

$$\tau(b,a,o)(s')=\frac{O(o\mid s')\bar b_{b,a}(s')}{q(o\mid b,a)}.$$

When $q(o\mid b,a)=0$, $\tau(b,a,o)$ is undefined; no quotient or filler value is assigned. For each $(b,a)$, the **belief-state transition kernel** on Borel sets $C\subseteq\Delta(S)$ is

$$K(C\mid b,a)=\sum_{o\in\Omega:q(o\mid b,a)>0}q(o\mid b,a)\,1_C(\tau(b,a,o)),$$

and the expected one-step reward at belief $b$ under action $a$ is $\bar r(b,a)=\sum_{s\in S}b(s)r(s,a)$, where $1_C$ denotes the indicator function of $C$.

2. $m \le n \iff m \subseteq n$;
3. $n < \sigma(n)$, and $m < \sigma(n) \iff m \le n$;
4. $0 \le n$, and $0 \in n$ whenever $n \ne 0$.

proof. The countability arguments on this page use that identification as a
working fact, so it is established here, from the additive order and induction
