Let $S$ be a finite set, possibly empty, let $\mathcal R$ be a finite subset of $\mathbb R$, and for each $s\in S$ let $A(s)$ be a finite nonempty set. Here **finite** means bijective with a natural number, and the **discrete sigma-algebra** on a set is its power set. Write $D=\{(s,a):s\in S,\ a\in A(s)\}$. A **finite Markov decision process (MDP)** consists of these sets and numbers $p(s',\rho\mid s,a)\in[0,1]$, indexed by $(s,a)\in D$, $s'\in S$, and $\rho\in\mathcal R$, with

$$ \sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}p(s',\rho\mid s,a)=1 \qquad ((s,a)\in D). $$

Equip each set used here, including $D$, with its power-set (discrete) sigma-algebra. Thus $p$ is the point-mass form of a probability kernel from $D$ to $S\times\mathcal R$: each input assigns a probability measure on $S\times\mathcal R$, and every event section is measurable. The joint law allows the next state and reward to be dependent. Define the expected reward and state-transition probabilities by

$$ r(s,a)=\sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}\rho\,p(s',\rho\mid s,a), \qquad P(s'\mid s,a)=\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}p(s',\rho\mid s,a). $$

If $\mathcal R\ne\emptyset$, put $M=\max_{\rho\in\mathcal R}|\rho|$; if $\mathcal R=\emptyset$, put $M=0$. A stationary Markov policy is a family of probabilities $\pi(a\mid s)\ge0$ with $\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi(a\mid s)=1$ for every $s\in S$. A deterministic policy is a function $\pi$ with $\pi(s)\in A(s)$ for every $s$. When $S=\emptyset$, these families and policies are the unique empty functions and all statewise formulas are vacuous.

Let $S$ be a finite set, $n := \lvert S\rvert$ (The cardinality $\lvert A\rvert$ of a finite set), and
let $a : S \to \mathbb{R}$ or $a : S \to \mathbb{N}$, written $a_i$ for $a(i)$.
Choose a bijection $\varphi : n \to S$, which exists because $S \approx n$
(Equinumerous sets, $A \approx B$ and $A \preceq B$), and set

$$\sum_{i \in S} a_i := \sum_{k<n} a_{\varphi(k)}, \qquad \prod_{i \in S} a_i := \prod_{k<n} a_{\varphi(k)},$$

the right-hand sides being the iterated operations of Finite sums and finite products, by recursion when the
values are real and of Finite sums and finite products of natural numbers, $\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ in $\mathbb{N}$ when they are natural.

**Independence of the enumeration, which is the content of the definition.** Let
$\varphi, \psi : n \to S$ be two bijections. Then $\pi := \varphi^{-1} \circ \psi$
is a bijection $n \to n$ (Injection, surjection, bijection), and
$a_{\psi(k)} = a_{\varphi(\pi(k))}$ for every $k < n$. Applying
A finite sum is unchanged by a permutation of its index range: $\sum_{k<n} a_{\pi(k)} = \sum_{k<n} a_k$ for every bijection $\pi : n \to n$ to the list $c_k := a_{\varphi(k)}$
gives

$$\sum_{k<n} a_{\psi(k)} = \sum_{k<n} c_{\pi(k)} = \sum_{k<n} c_k = \sum_{k<n} a_{\varphi(k)},$$

and identically for products. So the value does not depend on which bijection is
used, and $\sum_{i \in S} a_i$ is a single well-determined element.

**No choice principle is involved.** The definition does not select an
enumeration: it asserts that all enumerations give the same value, and that value
is what the notation names. Only one bijection is ever produced at a time, from a
set already known to be nonempty.

**Three clauses, recorded here because the page uses them constantly.**

**(a) The bridge to the old notation.** Taking $S = n$ and $\varphi = \mathrm{id}_n$,
which is legitimate since $\lvert n\rvert = n$, gives

$$\sum_{i \in n} a_i = \sum_{k<n} a_k, \qquad \prod_{i \in n} a_i = \prod_{k<n} a_k .$$

So the new notation **extends** the sum over an initial segment rather than
competing with it, and every law proved for the latter is available for the
former whenever the index set is a natural number.

**(b) Reindexing along a bijection.** If $h : T \to S$ is a bijection of finite
sets, then $\sum_{j \in T} a_{h(j)} = \sum_{i \in S} a_i$, and likewise for
products. Indeed $\lvert T\rvert = \lvert S\rvert = n$ by transport
(The cardinality $\lvert A\rvert$ of a finite set), and if $\varphi : n \to S$ is a bijection then
$h^{-1} \circ \varphi : n \to T$ is one, so
$\sum_{j \in T} a_{h(j)} = \sum_{k<n} a_{h(h^{-1}(\varphi(k)))} = \sum_{k<n} a_{\varphi(k)} = \sum_{i \in S} a_i$.

**(c) The empty index set and a constant summand.** $\lvert\varnothing\rvert = 0$,
so $\sum_{i \in \varnothing} a_i = 0$ and $\prod_{i \in \varnothing} a_i = 1$ by
the base clause of the recursion. And for a constant $c$, clause (a) together
with the constant clause of Laws of finite sums and products in $\mathbb{N}$, and $\iota\big(\sum_{k<n} a_k\big) = \sum_{k<n} \iota(a_k)$
in $\mathbb{N}$, or clause 2 of Laws of finite sums and finite products in $\mathbb{R}$, gives

$$\sum_{i \in S} c = \lvert S\rvert \cdot c \quad (c \in \mathbb{N}), \qquad \sum_{i \in S} c = \iota(\lvert S\rvert)\cdot c \quad (c \in \mathbb{R}),$$

the second with $\iota$ written out because $\lvert S\rvert$ is a natural number
and not an element of $\mathbb{R}$ (The canonical natural $\iota(n) = n \cdot 1_F$ of a field).

Let $S$ and $T$ be finite sets and let $a : S \times T \to \mathbb{R}$, or
$a : S \times T \to \mathbb{N}$, written $a_{ij}$ for $a(i,j)$. Then $S \times T$
is finite and

$$\sum_{i \in S}\Big(\sum_{j \in T} a_{ij}\Big) \;=\; \sum_{p \in S \times T} a_p \;=\; \sum_{j \in T}\Big(\sum_{i \in S} a_{ij}\Big),$$

all three sums being the sums over a finite index set of
The sum $\sum_{i \in S} a_i$ over a finite index set, and its product form, carried by Finite sums and finite products, by recursion when the
values are real and by Finite sums and finite products of natural numbers, $\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ in $\mathbb{N}$ when they are natural.

**This is not a clause of The sum rule: a finite disjoint union is finite with $\lvert A \cup B\rvert = \lvert A\rvert + \lvert B\rvert$ and $\lvert\bigcup_{i \in I} A_i\rvert = \sum_{i \in I}\lvert A_i\rvert$, and a sum over a finite index set splits along a partition.** That theorem splits one sum along a
partition of *its own* index set; the identity above exchanges the roles of two
*different* index sets, and it is what an argument that counts a set of pairs in
two ways needs. Both outer index sets may be empty, in which case all three
quantities are $0$ (respectively $1$ for the product form of the underlying
recursion), since a sum over the empty index set is the empty sum.

Let $a, b, c : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ be sequences of reals, let
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, and let $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, with finite sums and
finite products as in Finite sums and finite products, by recursion. Then:

1. **Additivity.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}(a_k + b_k) = \sum_{k<n} a_k + \sum_{k<n} b_k$.
2. **Scaling.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda a_k = \lambda \sum_{k<n} a_k$; in particular $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} \lambda = n\lambda$, where $n$ denotes the canonical field image $n\cdot1_{\mathbb{R}}$ of the natural n (The unique embedding of ℚ into an ordered field, Canonical naturals are positive and strictly increasing).
3. **Splitting.** If $m \le n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k = \sum_{k<m} a_k + \sum_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k$, and $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n} a_k = \Big(\prod_{k<m} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k=m}^{n-1} a_k\Big)$.
4. **Monotonicity.** If $a_k \le b_k$ for all $k < n$ then $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n} a_k \le \sum_{k<n} b_k$. In particular, if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\sum_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, every single term satisfies $a_j \le \sum_{k<n} a_k$ for $j < n$, and $\sum_{k<n} a_k = 0$ forces $a_k = 0$ for every $k < n$.
5. **Telescoping.** $\displaystyle\sum_{k<n}\big(c_{k+1} - c_k\big) = c_n - c_0$.
6. **Products.** $\displaystyle\prod_{k<n}(a_k b_k) = \Big(\prod_{k<n} a_k\Big)\Big(\prod_{k<n} b_k\Big)$; if $a_k \ge 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k \ge 0$, and if $a_k > 0$ for all $k < n$ then $\prod_{k<n} a_k > 0$.

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. If $0 \in S$ and $\sigma(n) \in S$ whenever $n \in S$, then $S = \mathbb{N}$. Equivalently (property form): if a property $P$ satisfies $P(0)$ and ($P(n) \Rightarrow P(\sigma(n))$) for all $n$, then $P(n)$ holds for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. This is the induction principle, the basis of proof by induction.

Fix $t<T$ and assume [L1]. Every term in the recursion for $\mu_{t+1}(s')$ is nonnegative by [F1]. Step 1.1 proves the base case and step 1.2 proves the successor case, so [F5] gives nonnegative normalized vectors $\mu_t$ for every $0\le t\le T$.

Every term in $d_\pi(s)$ is nonnegative. Summing over $s$ and using the finite-sum scaling law [F4] gives $\sum_s d_\pi(s)=T^{-1}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\sum_s\mu_t(s)=T^{-1}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}1=1$, because there are exactly $T$ indices and $T\ge1$. Hence $d_\pi$ is a probability vector.

Fix a finite Markov decision process with nonempty finite state set $S$ and finite nonempty action set $A(s)$ at each state, a positive integer horizon $T$, and an initial probability vector $\mu_0$ on $S$. A **policy** is a stationary Markov policy $\pi(a\mid s)$; a **deterministic expert** is a function $\pi^*:S\to\bigcup_{s\in S}A(s)$ with $\pi^*(s)\in A(s)$. For a policy $\pi$, let $\mu_t^\pi$ and $d_\pi$ be the finite-horizon state and average-occupancy probability vectors defined by the finite recursion in the preceding lemma.

Let $c_t(s,a)\in[0,1]$ be the task cost at time $t$ for $0\le t<T$. Define the total expected task cost by

$$J(\pi)=\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\sum_{s\in S}\mu_t^\pi(s)\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi(a\mid s)c_t(s,a).$$

Define the expert cost-to-go recursively by $V_T^*(s)=0$ and, for $0\le t<T$,

$$Q_t^*(s,a)=c_t(s,a)+\sum_{s'\in S}P(s'\mid s,a)V_{t+1}^*(s'),\qquad V_t^*(s)=Q_t^*(s,\pi^*(s)).$$

For a learner policy $\pi_\theta$ indexed by a parameter $\theta$ in a nonempty set $K$, define its expert-action disagreement probability at $s$ by $e(s,\theta)=\sum_{a\in A(s):a\ne\pi^*(s)}\pi_\theta(a\mid s)$. An **expert surrogate loss** is a function $\ell:S\times K\to[0,1]$ satisfying $\ell(s,\theta)\ge e(s,\theta)$ for every $s\in S$ and $\theta\in K$. The average surrogate loss under a policy's own state occupancy is $\mathbb E_{s\sim d_{\pi_\theta}}[\ell(s,\theta)]=\sum_s d_{\pi_\theta}(s)\ell(s,\theta)$.

**Behavior cloning** fits a learner policy using expert labels on states sampled from $d_{\pi^*}$. **DAgger** (Dataset Aggregation) is the interactive alternative: at iteration $i$, it rolls out a mixture $\pi_i=\beta_i\pi^*+(1-\beta_i)\hat\pi_i$, where $\hat\pi_i=\pi_{\theta_i}$ is the current learner with parameter $\theta_i\in K$ and $\beta_i\in[0,1]$ is the expert-use probability at each decision, queries the expert on the visited states, aggregates those labeled states with prior data, and updates the learner. For a positive integer $N$ of iterations, in the infinite-sample analysis define $L_i(\theta)=\sum_s d_{\pi_i}(s)\ell(s,\theta)$. When the minimum is attained, define $\epsilon_N=\min_{\theta\in K}N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N L_i(\theta)$ and the learner's average regret $\gamma_N=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N L_i(\theta_i)-\epsilon_N$. Fixed demonstrations do not in general provide expert labels for every learner-visited state; if they cover those states, their labels can be reused without new expert interaction.

Let a finite Markov decision process have a nonempty finite state set $S$ and finite nonempty action sets $A(s)$, with state transition probabilities $P(s'\mid s,a)$ obtained by summing its joint reward-transition law over rewards. Let $T\ge1$ be an integer, let $\mu_0:S\to[0,1]$ satisfy $\sum_{s\in S}\mu_0(s)=1$, and let $\pi(a\mid s)$ be a stationary Markov policy. Define recursively

$$\mu_{t+1}(s')=\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{a\in A(s)}\mu_t(s)\pi(a\mid s)P(s'\mid s,a),\qquad 0\le t<T.$$

Then each $\mu_t$ is a probability vector on $S$, and the finite-horizon average occupancy

$$d_\pi(s)=\frac1T\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\mu_t(s)$$

is also a probability vector. This construction uses only finite sums and does not require an infinite-path probability extension.

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. If $0 \in S$ and $\sigma(n) \in S$ whenever $n \in S$, then $S = \mathbb{N}$. Equivalently (property form): if a property $P$ satisfies $P(0)$ and ($P(n) \Rightarrow P(\sigma(n))$) for all $n$, then $P(n)$ holds for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. This is the induction principle, the basis of proof by induction.

derivations.claim: Put $q=1-\beta$. The transition matrix of the mixed policy is $P_{\pi_\beta}=qP_{\hat\pi}+\beta P_{\pi^*}$ by finite-sum distributivity. For each $t\le T$, we show $\mu_t^{\pi_\beta}=q^t\mu_t^{\hat\pi}+r_t$, where $r_t$ has nonnegative coordinates and total mass $1-q^t$. At $t=0$, take $r_0=0$. If the formula holds at $t<T$, the recursion gives $\mu_{t+1}^{\pi_\beta}=q^{t+1}\mu_{t+1}^{\hat\pi}+\underbrace{q^t\beta\mu_t^{\hat\pi}P_{\pi^*}+r_tP_{\pi_\beta}}_{r_{t+1}}$. The two terms defining $r_{t+1}$ have nonnegative coordinates, and their total masses are $q^t\beta$ and $1-q^t$, so $r_{t+1}$ has mass $1-q^{t+1}$. Induction proves the decomposition for every $t\le T$.

Since $0\le q\le1$, for each $t<T$ one has $q^t\ge q^T$. Thus $r'_t:=r_t+(q^t-q^T)\mu_t^{\hat\pi}$ is nonnegative and has mass $1-q^T$. Averaging over $t=0,\ldots,T-1$ gives $d_{\pi_\beta}=q^T d_{\hat\pi}+r'$, where $r'=T^{-1}\sum_{t<T}r'_t$ has mass $1-q^T$. If $1-q^T>0$, normalize $r'$ to a probability vector $\nu$; then for $g:S\to[0,1]$ the difference of expectations is $(1-q^T)(\sum_s\nu(s)g(s)-\sum_s d_{\hat\pi}(s)g(s))$, whose absolute value is at most $1-q^T$. If $1-q^T=0$, the occupancies are equal and the same bound is zero.

The Bernoulli inequality $q^T=(1-\beta)^T\ge1-T\beta$ follows by induction: it is equality at $T=0$, and multiplying $q^n\ge1-n\beta$ by $q\ge0$ gives $q^{n+1}\ge(1-n\beta)(1-\beta)=1-(n+1)\beta+n\beta^2\ge1-(n+1)\beta$. Also $1-q^T\le1$, so $1-q^T\le\min\{1,T\beta\}$. Combining this with step 2.1 proves the Statement.

Let a finite-horizon imitation-learning problem have the finite MDP, initial state distribution, positive integer horizon $T$, deterministic expert $\pi^*$, learner class $\{\pi_\theta:\theta\in K\}$, and expert surrogate loss $\ell(s,\theta)$ defined previously. Initialize the aggregated training dataset as the empty multiset $\mathcal D_0=\varnothing$.

1. Set $\hat\pi_i=\pi_{\theta_i}$. For the rollout policy, at each decision time of every trajectory, independently draw an expert-use coin with success probability $\beta_i$. At current state $s$, if the coin succeeds, execute $\pi^*(s)$; otherwise sample an action from $\hat\pi_i(\cdot\mid s)$ and execute it. This per-decision stochastic policy is $\pi_i=\beta_i\pi^*+(1-\beta_i)\hat\pi_i$.
2. Run $m$ trajectories of length $T$ from the specified initial distribution using $\pi_i$. At every visited state $S_{ij t}$, for $1\le j\le m$ and $0\le t<T$, query and record the expert label $\pi^*(S_{ij t})$. Append these labeled pairs to $\mathcal D_{i-1}$, with multiplicity, to form $\mathcal D_i$. The expert label is recorded for training and is not executed unless the mixture in step 1 selected the expert.
3. Define the empirical round loss on every candidate parameter by

   $$\hat L_i(\theta)=\frac1{mT}\sum_{j=1}^m\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\ell(S_{ij t},\theta).$$

4. Update by Follow-the-Leader on the cumulative empirical loss: set $\theta_{i+1}$ to the supplied selector's choice from $\arg\min_{\theta\in K}\sum_{r=1}^i\hat L_r(\theta)$.

The procedure requires an interactive expert capable of labeling learner-visited states.

Let $d,N\ge1$ be integers, let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty and convex, and define $\|x-y\|_2=(\sum_{r=1}^d(x_r-y_r)^2)^{1/2}$. Let $G\ge0$ and $\mu>0$. For each $i=1,\ldots,N$, let $L_i:K\to[0,1]$ be $G$-Lipschitz, meaning $|L_i(x)-L_i(y)|\le G\|x-y\|_2$, and $\mu$-strongly convex, meaning

$$L_i((1-\lambda)x+\lambda y)\le(1-\lambda)L_i(x)+\lambda L_i(y)-\frac{\mu}{2}\lambda(1-\lambda)\|x-y\|_2^2$$

for all $x,y\in K$ and $\lambda\in[0,1]$. For $n=1,\ldots,N$, assume $F_n:=\sum_{i=1}^nL_i$ attains a minimum on $K$. Let $\theta_1\in K$ and, for $n=1,\ldots,N$, let $\theta_{n+1}$ be the unique minimizer of $F_n$. Define $H_0=0$ and $H_n=\sum_{j=1}^n1/j$ for $n\ge1$. Then

$$\sum_{i=1}^N L_i(\theta_i)-\min_{\theta\in K}\sum_{i=1}^NL_i(\theta)\le1+\frac{4G^2}{\mu}H_{N-1}.$$

Let a finite-horizon MDP have positive integer horizon $T$, and let $\pi^*$ and $\hat\pi$ be stationary Markov policies. For a stationary policy $\pi$, define its state transition matrix by $P_\pi(s,s')=\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi(a\mid s)P(s'\mid s,a)$; for a state vector $\mu$, define $(\mu P_\pi)(s')=\sum_{s\in S}\mu(s)P_\pi(s,s')$. For every function $g:S\to[0,1]$, its finite-horizon average occupancies satisfy

$$\left|\sum_{s\in S}d_{\pi_\beta}(s)g(s)-\sum_{s\in S}d_{\hat\pi}(s)g(s)\right|\le1-(1-\beta)^T\le\min\{1,T\beta\}.$$

Here $d_\pi=T^{-1}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\mu_t^\pi$ is the normalized average of the state marginals from the common initial distribution.

Let a finite-horizon MDP, horizon $T\ge1$, initial distribution, deterministic expert $\pi^*$, learner policy $\pi_\theta$, task cost $J$, expert cost-to-go $Q_t^*$, expert value $V_t^*(s)=Q_t^*(s,\pi^*(s))$, occupancy $d_{\pi_\theta}$, and surrogate $\ell(s,\theta)$ be as defined previously. Let a finite-horizon imitation-learning problem have the finite MDP, initial state distribution, positive integer horizon $T$, deterministic expert $\pi^*$, learner class $\{\pi_\theta:\theta\in K\}$, and expert surrogate loss $\ell(s,\theta)$ defined previously. Let $N\ge1$ and $m\ge1$ be integers giving the number of training rounds and trajectories per round, let $\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_N\in[0,1]$ be expert-use probabilities, supply an initial parameter $\theta_1\in K$, and supply a deterministic selector for attained minimizers of the cumulative losses. Require that each cumulative training-loss function below attains a minimum on $K$; when the minimizer is unique the selector returns it.

Initialize the aggregated training dataset as the empty multiset $\mathcal D_0=\varnothing$.

For each round $i=1,\ldots,N$:

1. Set $\hat\pi_i=\pi_{\theta_i}$. For the rollout policy, at each decision time of every trajectory, independently draw an expert-use coin with success probability $\beta_i$. At current state $s$, if the coin succeeds, execute $\pi^*(s)$; otherwise sample an action from $\hat\pi_i(\cdot\mid s)$ and execute it. This per-decision stochastic policy is $\pi_i=\beta_i\pi^*+(1-\beta_i)\hat\pi_i$.
2. Run $m$ trajectories of length $T$ from the specified initial distribution using $\pi_i$. At every visited state $S_{ij t}$, for $1\le j\le m$ and $0\le t<T$, query and record the expert label $\pi^*(S_{ij t})$. Append these labeled pairs to $\mathcal D_{i-1}$, with multiplicity, to form $\mathcal D_i$. The expert label is recorded for training and is not executed unless the mixture in step 1 selected the expert.
3. Define the empirical round loss on every candidate parameter by

   $$\hat L_i(\theta)=\frac1{mT}\sum_{j=1}^m\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\ell(S_{ij t},\theta).$$

4. Update by Follow-the-Leader on the cumulative empirical loss: set $\theta_{i+1}$ to the supplied selector's choice from $\arg\min_{\theta\in K}\sum_{r=1}^i\hat L_r(\theta)$.

The finite-sample output is the sequence $\hat\pi_1,\ldots,\hat\pi_N$ and the aggregated labeled multiset $\mathcal D_N$. The population-loss idealization replaces each empirical $\hat L_i$ by $L_i(\theta)=\sum_s d_{\pi_i}(s)\ell(s,\theta)$; it is used only for the infinite-sample theorem. The procedure requires an interactive expert capable of labeling learner-visited states.

Let $d,N\ge1$ be integers, let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty and convex, and define $\|x-y\|_2=(\sum_{r=1}^d(x_r-y_r)^2)^{1/2}$. Let $G\ge0$ and $\mu>0$. For each $i=1,\ldots,N$, let $L_i:K\to[0,1]$ be $G$-Lipschitz, meaning $|L_i(x)-L_i(y)|\le G\|x-y\|_2$, and $\mu$-strongly convex, meaning

for all $x,y\in K$ and $\lambda\in[0,1]$. For $n=1,\ldots,N$, assume $F_n:=\sum_{i=1}^nL_i$ attains a minimum on $K$. Let $\theta_1\in K$ and, for $n=1,\ldots,N$, let $\theta_{n+1}$ be the unique minimizer of $F_n$. Define $H_0=0$ and $H_n=\sum_{j=1}^n1/j$ for $n\ge1$. Then

The minimizers are unique because $F_n$ is $n\mu$-strongly convex. The first policy $\theta_1$ may be any supplied point of $K$.

Let a finite-horizon MDP have positive integer horizon $T$, and let $\pi^*$ and $\hat\pi$ be stationary Markov policies. Applying [F3] samplewise gives $\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\hat L_i(\theta_i)\le\hat\epsilon_N+\frac{1+\frac{4G^2}{\mu}H_{N-1}}N$.

Flatten the pairs $(i,j)$ in round-major order. Put $\mathcal G_0=\mathcal F_{1,0}$ and, for $r=(i-1)m+j$ with $1\le i\le N$ and $1\le j\le m$, put $\mathcal G_r=\mathcal F_{i,j}$; for every $r>mN$, put $\mathcal G_r=\mathcal G_{mN}$. Within each round the sigma-algebras are nested, and at round boundaries $\mathcal F_{i,0}=\mathcal F_{i-1,m}$, so $(\mathcal G_r)_{r\ge0}$ is an infinite filtration. Define $D_{(i-1)m+j}=L_i(\theta_i)-\bar\ell_{ij}(\theta_i)$ for the sample indices and set $D_r=0$ for $r>mN$. For each fixed round $i$, the policy probabilities are Borel functions of $\theta$, the finite occupancy recursion uses only finite sums and products, and $\ell(s,\cdot)$ is continuous by its Lipschitz property. Thus [F15] makes $L_i(\theta)$ Borel, so $L_i(\theta_i)$ is measurable with respect to $\mathcal G_{(i-1)m}=\mathcal F_{i,0}$ and hence with respect to each $\mathcal G_{r-1}$ in round $i$. Since the state set is finite and each statewise loss is continuous, $(s,\theta)\mapsto\ell(s,\theta)$ is measurable; the revealed states and preceding measurable parameter therefore make each $\bar\ell_{ij}(\theta_i)$ measurable with respect to $\mathcal G_r$. By [A1] and the probability-occupancy property in [F1], both $L_i(\theta_i)$ and $\bar\ell_{ij}(\theta_i)$ lie in $[0,1]$, so each sample increment is integrable and in $[-1,1]$; the zero extension has the same properties. For $r=(i-1)m+j\le mN$, [A3], [F13], and [F14] give $\mathbb E[D_r\mid\mathcal G_{r-1}]=L_i(\theta_i)-L_i(\theta_i)=0$. For $r>mN$, [F14] gives $\mathbb E[0\mid\mathcal G_{r-1}]=0$. Thus $D$ is an infinite adapted martingale-difference sequence by [F6], using the filtration and process conventions [F8, F9, F11].

Put $q=1-\alpha$ and $k=k_\alpha$. For every integer $n\ge1$, $(1+\alpha)^n\ge1+n\alpha$: equality holds for $n=1$, and if it holds for $n$, then multiplication by $1+\alpha>0$ gives $(1+\alpha)^{n+1}\ge(1+n\alpha)(1+\alpha)=1+(n+1)\alpha+n\alpha^2\ge1+(n+1)\alpha$. Thus [F16] gives $(1+\alpha)^k\ge1+k\alpha\ge2$. Also $q(1+\alpha)=1-\alpha^2\le1$, so $q\le(1+\alpha)^{-1}$ and $q^k\le1/2$. For block $j\ge0$, let $I_j=\{jk+1,\ldots,(j+1)k\}$. Taking $t=\sqrt{2mN\ln(1/\delta)}$ makes this probability at most $\delta$. Fix a finite Markov decision process with nonempty finite state set $S$ and finite nonempty action set $A(s)$ at each state, a positive integer horizon $T$, and an initial probability vector $\mu_0$ on $S$. A **policy** is a stationary Markov policy $\pi(a\mid s)$; a **deterministic expert** is a function $\pi^*:S\to\bigcup_{s\in S}A(s)$ with $\pi^*(s)\in A(s)$. For a policy $\pi$, let $\mu_t^\pi$ and $d_\pi$ be the finite-horizon state and average-occupancy probability vectors defined by the finite recursion in the preceding lemma.

Let $c_t(s,a)\in[0,1]$ be the task cost at time $t$ for $0\le t<T$. Define the total expected task cost by

$$J(\pi)=\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\sum_{s\in S}\mu_t^\pi(s)\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi(a\mid s)c_t(s,a).$$

Define the expert cost-to-go recursively by $V_T^*(s)=0$ and, for $0\le t<T$,

$$Q_t^*(s,a)=c_t(s,a)+\sum_{s'\in S}P(s'\mid s,a)V_{t+1}^*(s'),\qquad V_t^*(s)=Q_t^*(s,\pi^*(s)).$$

For a learner policy $\pi_\theta$ indexed by a parameter $\theta$ in a nonempty set $K$, define its expert-action disagreement probability at $s$ by $e(s,\theta)=\sum_{a\in A(s):a\ne\pi^*(s)}\pi_\theta(a\mid s)$. An **expert surrogate loss** is a function $\ell:S\times K\to[0,1]$ satisfying $\ell(s,\theta)\ge e(s,\theta)$ for every $s\in S$ and $\theta\in K$. The average surrogate loss under a policy's own state occupancy is $\mathbb E_{s\sim d_{\pi_\theta}}[\ell(s,\theta)]=\sum_s d_{\pi_\theta}(s)\ell(s,\theta)$.

**Behavior cloning** fits a learner policy using expert labels on states sampled from $d_{\pi^*}$. **DAgger** (Dataset Aggregation) is the interactive alternative: at iteration $i$, it rolls out a mixture $\pi_i=\beta_i\pi^*+(1-\beta_i)\hat\pi_i$, where $\hat\pi_i=\pi_{\theta_i}$ is the current learner with parameter $\theta_i\in K$ and $\beta_i\in[0,1]$ is the expert-use probability at each decision, queries the expert on the visited states, aggregates those labeled states with prior data, and updates the learner. For a positive integer $N$ of iterations, in the infinite-sample analysis define $L_i(\theta)=\sum_s d_{\pi_i}(s)\ell(s,\theta)$. When the minimum is attained, define $\epsilon_N=\min_{\theta\in K}N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N L_i(\theta)$ and the learner's average regret $\gamma_N=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N L_i(\theta_i)-\epsilon_N$. Fixed demonstrations do not in general provide expert labels for every learner-visited state; if they cover those states, their labels can be reused without new expert interaction.

derivations.claim: Under the expert, the state remains $g$ at every decision time, so $d_{\pi^*}$ is the point mass at $g$. The learner's action-disagreement probability at $g$ is $\epsilon$, hence its behavior-cloning surrogate loss averaged under $d_{\pi^*}$ equals $\epsilon$.

Put $q=1-\epsilon$. The probability that the learner is at $g$ at time $t$ is $q^t$: it is $1$ at $t=0$, and if it is $g$ at time $t$ it remains there at the next state with probability $q$, while if it is $b$ it remains $b$. Thus the probability at time $t+1$ is $q^tq=q^{t+1}$. At decision time $t$, expected cost is $q^t\epsilon+(1-q^t)=1-q^{t+1}$. Summing for $t=0,\ldots,T-1$ gives the displayed cost.

For each integer $k\ge1$, $(1-\epsilon)^k\ge1-k\epsilon$: the case $k=1$ is equality, and if it holds at $k$, multiplication by $1-\epsilon\ge0$ gives $(1-\epsilon)^{k+1}\ge(1-k\epsilon)(1-\epsilon)=1-(k+1)\epsilon+k\epsilon^2\ge1-(k+1)\epsilon$. Therefore $1-q^k\le k\epsilon$.

If $T=1$, the displayed cost is $\epsilon$, which lies between $\epsilon T^2/8$ and $\epsilon T^2$. Now assume $T\ge2$, so $0<\epsilon\le1/2$. Then $(1-\epsilon)^{-1}\ge1+\epsilon$ because $(1-\epsilon)^{-1}-(1+\epsilon)=\epsilon^2/(1-\epsilon)\ge0$. Also $(1+\epsilon)^k\ge1+k\epsilon$ for all $k\ge1$: it is equality for $k=1$, and multiplication by $1+\epsilon>0$ gives $(1+\epsilon)^{k+1}\ge(1+k\epsilon)(1+\epsilon)=1+(k+1)\epsilon+k\epsilon^2\ge1+(k+1)\epsilon$. Fix a finite Markov decision process with nonempty finite state set $S$ and finite nonempty action set $A(s)$ at each state, a positive integer horizon $T$, and an initial probability vector $\mu_0$ on $S$. A **policy** is a stationary Markov policy $\pi(a\mid s)$; a **deterministic expert** is a function $\pi^*:S\to\bigcup_{s\in S}A(s)$ with $\pi^*(s)\in A(s)$. For a policy $\pi$, let $\mu_t^\pi$ and $d_\pi$ be the finite-horizon state and average-occupancy probability vectors defined by the finite recursion in the preceding lemma.

Let $c_t(s,a)\in[0,1]$ be the task cost at time $t$ for $0\le t<T$. Define the total expected task cost by

$$J(\pi)=\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\sum_{s\in S}\mu_t^\pi(s)\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi(a\mid s)c_t(s,a).$$

Define the expert cost-to-go recursively by $V_T^*(s)=0$ and, for $0\le t<T$,

$$Q_t^*(s,a)=c_t(s,a)+\sum_{s'\in S}P(s'\mid s,a)V_{t+1}^*(s'),\qquad V_t^*(s)=Q_t^*(s,\pi^*(s)).$$

For a learner policy $\pi_\theta$ indexed by a parameter $\theta$ in a nonempty set $K$, define its expert-action disagreement probability at $s$ by $e(s,\theta)=\sum_{a\in A(s):a\ne\pi^*(s)}\pi_\theta(a\mid s)$. An **expert surrogate loss** is a function $\ell:S\times K\to[0,1]$ satisfying $\ell(s,\theta)\ge e(s,\theta)$ for every $s\in S$ and $\theta\in K$. The average surrogate loss under a policy's own state occupancy is $\mathbb E_{s\sim d_{\pi_\theta}}[\ell(s,\theta)]=\sum_s d_{\pi_\theta}(s)\ell(s,\theta)$.

**Behavior cloning** fits a learner policy using expert labels on states sampled from $d_{\pi^*}$. **DAgger** (Dataset Aggregation) is the interactive alternative: at iteration $i$, it rolls out a mixture $\pi_i=\beta_i\pi^*+(1-\beta_i)\hat\pi_i$, where $\hat\pi_i=\pi_{\theta_i}$ is the current learner with parameter $\theta_i\in K$ and $\beta_i\in[0,1]$ is the expert-use probability at each decision, queries the expert on the visited states, aggregates those labeled states with prior data, and updates the learner. For a positive integer $N$ of iterations, in the infinite-sample analysis define $L_i(\theta)=\sum_s d_{\pi_i}(s)\ell(s,\theta)$. When the minimum is attained, define $\epsilon_N=\min_{\theta\in K}N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N L_i(\theta)$ and the learner's average regret $\gamma_N=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N L_i(\theta_i)-\epsilon_N$. Fixed demonstrations do not in general provide expert labels for every learner-visited state; if they cover those states, their labels can be reused without new expert interaction.

Let a finite-horizon imitation-learning problem have the finite MDP, initial state distribution, positive integer horizon $T$, deterministic expert $\pi^*$, learner class $\{\pi_\theta:\theta\in K\}$, and expert surrogate loss $\ell(s,\theta)$ defined previously. Let $N\ge1$ and $m\ge1$ be integers giving the number of training rounds and trajectories per round, let $\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_N\in[0,1]$ be expert-use probabilities, supply an initial parameter $\theta_1\in K$, and supply a deterministic selector for attained minimizers of the cumulative losses. Require that each cumulative training-loss function below attains a minimum on $K$; when the minimizer is unique the selector returns it.

Initialize the aggregated training dataset as the empty multiset $\mathcal D_0=\varnothing$.

For each round $i=1,\ldots,N$:

1. Set $\hat\pi_i=\pi_{\theta_i}$. For the rollout policy, at each decision time of every trajectory, independently draw an expert-use coin with success probability $\beta_i$. At current state $s$, if the coin succeeds, execute $\pi^*(s)$; otherwise sample an action from $\hat\pi_i(\cdot\mid s)$ and execute it. This per-decision stochastic policy is $\pi_i=\beta_i\pi^*+(1-\beta_i)\hat\pi_i$.
2. Run $m$ trajectories of length $T$ from the specified initial distribution using $\pi_i$. At every visited state $S_{ij t}$, for $1\le j\le m$ and $0\le t<T$, query and record the expert label $\pi^*(S_{ij t})$. Append these labeled pairs to $\mathcal D_{i-1}$, with multiplicity, to form $\mathcal D_i$. The expert label is recorded for training and is not executed unless the mixture in step 1 selected the expert.
3. Define the empirical round loss on every candidate parameter by

   $$\hat L_i(\theta)=\frac1{mT}\sum_{j=1}^m\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\ell(S_{ij t},\theta).$$

4. Update by Follow-the-Leader on the cumulative empirical loss: set $\theta_{i+1}$ to the supplied selector's choice from $\arg\min_{\theta\in K}\sum_{r=1}^i\hat L_r(\theta)$.

The finite-sample output is the sequence $\hat\pi_1,\ldots,\hat\pi_N$ and the aggregated labeled multiset $\mathcal D_N$. The population-loss idealization replaces each empirical $\hat L_i$ by $L_i(\theta)=\sum_s d_{\pi_i}(s)\ell(s,\theta)$; it is used only for the infinite-sample theorem. The procedure requires an interactive expert capable of labeling learner-visited states.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function

derivations.claim: Fix one state $s$. Write $\Delta_a=q_s(a)-p_s(a)$; since both distributions have mass one, $\sum_a\Delta_a=0$. The set $B=\{a:\Delta_a\ge0\}$ consists of the nonnegative differences. The positive and negative parts of $\Delta$ therefore have equal sum, each equal to $\frac12\sum_a|\Delta_a|$. For every subset $C\subseteq A(s)$, $|\sum_{a\in C}\Delta_a|$ is at most this common sum, and $C=B$ attains it. Thus the event-supremum total variation in [F2] equals $\operatorname{TV}_{A(s)}(q_s,p_s)$.

Apply [F3] to the probability measures $q_s$ and $p_s$ on the finite power-set space, and use step 1.1. This gives $\operatorname{TV}_{A(s)}(q_s,p_s)\le\sqrt{D_{\rm KL}(q_s\|p_s)/2}$, including the infinite-divergence case.

If $K=+\infty$, the asserted inequality holds because each total-variation term is at most one. Suppose $K<\infty$ and put $m=K/2$. When $m=0$, step 2.1 gives $D_{\rm KL}(q_s\|p_s)\ge2\operatorname{TV}_{A(s)}(q_s,p_s)^2\ge0$ for every state. Since their $d$-weighted sum is zero, every state with $d(s)>0$ has zero divergence, so step 2.1 also gives zero total variation there. When $m>0$, for every $x\ge0$ the square $(\sqrt{x}-\sqrt m)^2\ge0$ gives $\sqrt{x}\le(\sqrt m+x/\sqrt m)/2$. Apply this with $x=D_{\rm KL}(q_s\|p_s)/2$ for states with $d(s)>0$, multiply by $d(s)$, and sum. Since $\sum_sd(s)=1$ and $\sum_sd(s)x_s=m$, the result is $\sum_sd(s)\sqrt{x_s}\le\sqrt m$. Let $M=(S,\mathcal R,(A(s))_{s\in S},p)$ be a finite Markov decision process with nonempty state set $S$ and finite nonempty action set $A(s)$ at each state. Put $\mathcal X=\{(s,a,\rho,s'):s\in S,\ a\in A(s),\ \rho\in\mathcal R,\ s'\in S\}$. Let $\mu$ be a probability distribution on $S$, let $\gamma\in[0,1)$, let $m\ge1$ be an integer, and for each $i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$ let $b_i\in\mathbb R$, $C_i\ge0$, and $c_i:\mathcal X\to[-C_i,C_i]$. A **finite discounted constrained Markov decision process (CMDP)** is the tuple consisting of $M$, $\mu$, $\gamma$, and the bounded transition-cost functions and thresholds $(c_i,b_i)_{i=1}^m$. Its immediate reward signal is $r(s,a,\rho,s')=\rho$.

For a stationary Markov policy $\pi$, define the state-mass sequence recursively by $\mu_0^\pi=\mu$ and

$$\mu_{t+1}^\pi(s'):=\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{a\in A(s)}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}\mu_t^\pi(s)\pi(a\mid s)p(s',\rho\mid s,a).$$

This recurrence defines nonnegative finite-time masses; the result that each $\mu_t^\pi$ is a probability distribution is established separately.

Let $S$ be a finite set, possibly empty, let $\mathcal R$ be a finite subset of $\mathbb R$, and for each $s\in S$ let $A(s)$ be a finite nonempty set. Here **finite** means bijective with a natural number, and the **discrete sigma-algebra** on a set is its power set. Write $D=\{(s,a):s\in S,\ a\in A(s)\}$. A **finite Markov decision process (MDP)** consists of these sets and numbers $p(s',\rho\mid s,a)\in[0,1]$, indexed by $(s,a)\in D$, $s'\in S$, and $\rho\in\mathcal R$, with

$$ \sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}p(s',\rho\mid s,a)=1 \qquad ((s,a)\in D). $$

Equip each set used here, including $D$, with its power-set (discrete) sigma-algebra. Thus $p$ is the point-mass form of a probability kernel from $D$ to $S\times\mathcal R$: each input assigns a probability measure on $S\times\mathcal R$, and every event section is measurable. The joint law allows the next state and reward to be dependent. Define the expected reward and state-transition probabilities by

$$ r(s,a)=\sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}\rho\,p(s',\rho\mid s,a), \qquad P(s'\mid s,a)=\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}p(s',\rho\mid s,a). $$

If $\mathcal R\ne\emptyset$, put $M=\max_{\rho\in\mathcal R}|\rho|$; if $\mathcal R=\emptyset$, put $M=0$. A stationary Markov policy is a family of probabilities $\pi(a\mid s)\ge0$ with $\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi(a\mid s)=1$ for every $s\in S$. A deterministic policy is a function $\pi$ with $\pi(s)\in A(s)$ for every $s$. When $S=\emptyset$, these families and policies are the unique empty functions and all statewise formulas are vacuous.

Let $S$ be a finite set, possibly empty, let $\mathcal R$ be a finite subset of $\mathbb R$, and for each $s\in S$ let $A(s)$ be a finite nonempty set. Here **finite** means bijective with a natural number, and the **discrete sigma-algebra** on a set is its power set. Write $D=\{(s,a):s\in S,\ a\in A(s)\}$. A **finite Markov decision process (MDP)** consists of these sets and numbers $p(s',\rho\mid s,a)\in[0,1]$, indexed by $(s,a)\in D$, $s'\in S$, and $\rho\in\mathcal R$, with

$$ \sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}p(s',\rho\mid s,a)=1 \qquad ((s,a)\in D). $$

Equip each set used here, including $D$, with its power-set (discrete) sigma-algebra. Thus $p$ is the point-mass form of a probability kernel from $D$ to $S\times\mathcal R$: each input assigns a probability measure on $S\times\mathcal R$, and every event section is measurable. The joint law allows the next state and reward to be dependent. Define the expected reward and state-transition probabilities by

$$ r(s,a)=\sum_{s'\in S}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}\rho\,p(s',\rho\mid s,a), \qquad P(s'\mid s,a)=\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}p(s',\rho\mid s,a). $$

If $\mathcal R\ne\emptyset$, put $M=\max_{\rho\in\mathcal R}|\rho|$; if $\mathcal R=\emptyset$, put $M=0$. A stationary Markov policy is a family of probabilities $\pi(a\mid s)\ge0$ with $\sum_{a\in A(s)}\pi(a\mid s)=1$ for every $s\in S$. A deterministic policy is a function $\pi$ with $\pi(s)\in A(s)$ for every $s$. When $S=\emptyset$, these families and policies are the unique empty functions and all statewise formulas are vacuous.

Let a finite discounted CMDP and a stationary policy $\pi$ be given. The **column transition matrix** $K_\pi$ has entry

$$K_\pi(s',s):=\sum_{a\in A(s)}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}\pi(a\mid s)p(s',\rho\mid s,a),$$

so that its column indexed by $s$ gives the next-state distribution from current state $s$. With the state-mass column vectors $\mu_t^\pi$ from the CMDP definition, the **normalized discounted state occupancy** is

$$d^\pi(s):=(1-\gamma)\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^t\mu_t^\pi(s).$$

This normalization is part of the definition; the occupancy is a probability distribution by the separate well-definedness result below.

Let a finite discounted CMDP have initial distribution $\mu$, discount $\gamma\in[0,1)$, $m$ bounded transition signals $c_i$, thresholds $b_i$, and finite-time state masses $\mu_t^\pi$ under a stationary policy $\pi$, as defined in the CMDP model. For any bounded transition signal $g$ on $(s,a,\rho,s')$, define its **expected discounted sum** under $\pi$ by

$$J_g^\pi(\mu):=\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^t\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{a\in A(s)}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}\sum_{s'\in S}\mu_t^\pi(s)\pi(a\mid s)p(s',\rho\mid s,a)g(s,a,\rho,s').$$

The expected discounted reward is $J^\pi:=J_r^\pi(\mu)$ for the immediate reward signal $r(s,a,\rho,s')=\rho$, and the $i$th expected discounted cost is $J_{c_i}^\pi(\mu)$. The policy $\pi$ is **feasible** for the discounted-cost constraints exactly when $J_{c_i}^\pi(\mu)\le b_i$ for every $i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$. Feasibility constrains these expectations; it does not assert a per-trajectory bound.

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power (Integer powers $a^m$),
so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges (Series, partial sums, convergence and the sum, divergence, and the tail series) and
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$
2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges.

The series starts at $k = 0$ and its first term is $r^0 = 1$; in particular
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 2$, while the series starting at $k = 1$ sums to
$1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here.

Let $M\ge0$, $0\le\gamma<1$, and let $(\rho_j)_{j\ge1}$ be any real sequence with $|\rho_j|\le M$. Then the series

$$ \sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\gamma^j\rho_{j+1} $$

converges absolutely; write $G$ for its sum. Every partial sum and the limit satisfy

$$ \left|\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}\gamma^j\rho_{j+1}\right|\le\frac{M}{1-\gamma}, \qquad |G|\le\frac{M}{1-\gamma}. $$

For every integer $N\ge0$,

$$ \left|G-\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}\gamma^j\rho_{j+1}\right|\le\frac{M\gamma^N}{1-\gamma}, $$

where the partial sum at $N=0$ is empty and $\gamma^0=1$, including when $\gamma=0$.

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. If $0 \in S$ and $\sigma(n) \in S$ whenever $n \in S$, then $S = \mathbb{N}$. Equivalently (property form): if a property $P$ satisfies $P(0)$ and ($P(n) \Rightarrow P(\sigma(n))$) for all $n$, then $P(n)$ holds for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. This is the induction principle, the basis of proof by induction.

derivations.claim: The initial vector $\mu_0^\pi=\mu$ is nonnegative and sums to one. If $\mu_t^\pi$ is a probability distribution, then the recurrence and [F2]–[F3] give nonnegative next masses and $\sum_{s'}\mu_{t+1}^\pi(s')=\sum_s\sum_{a\in A(s)}\mu_t^\pi(s)\pi(a\mid s)\sum_{s',\rho}p(s',\rho\mid s,a)=\sum_s\mu_t^\pi(s)=1$. By [F8], every $\mu_t^\pi$ is a probability distribution.

By step 1.1, $0\le\mu_t^\pi(s)\le1$ for every $s,t$, so each coordinate series in [F4] converges by comparison with the geometric series [F6]. Since $S$ is finite, its coordinate series can be summed termwise, giving $d^\pi(s)\ge0$ and $\sum_s d^\pi(s)=(1-\gamma)\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^t\sum_s\mu_t^\pi(s)=(1-\gamma)\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^t=1$ by [F6]. Thus $d^\pi$ is a probability distribution.

For each $t$, the finite transition weights $\mu_t^\pi(s)\pi(a\mid s)p(s',\rho\mid s,a)$ are nonnegative and sum to one by step 1.1 and [F2]–[F3]. Hence their weighted sum of $g$ has absolute value at most $B$. Apply [F7] to this bounded sequence of time-$t$ signal sums; the series in [F5] converges absolutely and its absolute value is at most $B/(1-\gamma)$.

Thus $K_\sigma^t$ is column-stochastic for every $t$, and its induced matrix $1$-norm $\|A\|_1:=\max_s\sum_{s^{\prime}}|A(s^{\prime},s)|$ is one. Every entry of $K_\sigma^t$ lies in $[0,1]$, so each of the finitely many coordinate series $\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^t(K_\sigma^t)(s^{\prime},s)$ converges by comparison with [F4]; their limits give convergence of the matrix partial sums in this finite-dimensional norm. The same identity with multiplication on the other side shows $G_\sigma=(I-\gamma K_\sigma)^{-1}.

By [F1], for each coordinate $s'$ of $(K_{\pi'}-K_\pi)d^\pi$, the triangle inequality gives $\sum_{s'}|((K_{\pi'}-K_\pi)d^\pi)(s')|\le\sum_{s,a,s'}d^\pi(s)|\pi'(a\mid s)-\pi(a\mid s)|P(s'\mid s,a)=2\sum_s d^\pi(s)\operatorname{TV}_s(\pi',\pi)$, because $\sum_{s'}P(s'\mid s,a)=1$.

derivations.claim: Fix a policy $\sigma$. For each $t$, let $e_t^\sigma$ be the finite transition-mass sum of $g$ at time $t$, and let $h_t^\sigma:=\sum_s\mu_t^\sigma(s)f(s)$. By [F1] and the definition of $\delta_f^g$, the finite sum of $\delta_f^g$ at time $t$ is $e_t^\sigma+\gamma h_{t+1}^\sigma-h_t^\sigma$. Summing after multiplication by $\gamma^t$ for $t=0,\ldots,N$ telescopes to $\sum_{t=0}^N\gamma^t e_t^\sigma-h_0^\sigma+\gamma^{N+1}h_{N+1}^\sigma$.

The remainder satisfies $|\gamma^{N+1}h_{N+1}^\sigma|\le\gamma^{N+1}\|f\|_\infty\to0$ by [F4] and [F5]. Also $|\delta_f^g|\le\|g\|_\infty+(1+\gamma)\|f\|_\infty$, so [F4] makes its discounted series convergent. Passing to the limit in step 1.1 and using [F2]–[F3] gives $J_g^\sigma(\mu)=\sum_s\mu(s)f(s)+(1-\gamma)^{-1}\sum_s d^\sigma(s)\bar\delta_f^{g,\sigma}(s)$.

Apply the identity in step 2.1 to $\sigma=\pi'$ and $\sigma=\pi$ and subtract; the initial terms $\sum_s\mu(s)f(s)$ cancel. Add and subtract $\sum_s d^\pi(s)\bar\delta_f^{g,\pi'}(s)$. The first resulting term is $L_{\pi,f}^g(\pi')$ by its definition, and the second is $\sum_s(d^{\pi'}(s)-d^\pi(s))\bar\delta_f^{g,\pi'}(s)$. Dividing by $1-\gamma>0$ gives the claimed identity.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

$$\sum_{s\in S}d(s)\operatorname{TV}_{A(s)}(q_s,p_s)\le\sqrt{K/2},$$

Let $M=(S,\mathcal R,(A(s))_{s\in S},p)$ be a finite Markov decision process with nonempty state set $S$ and finite nonempty action set $A(s)$ at each state. Put $\mathcal X=\{(s,a,\rho,s'):s\in S,\ a\in A(s),\ \rho\in\mathcal R,\ s'\in S\}$. Let $\mu$ be a probability distribution on $S$, let $\gamma\in[0,1)$, let $m\ge1$ be an integer, and for each $i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$ let $b_i\in\mathbb R$, $C_i\ge0$, and $c_i:\mathcal X\to[-C_i,C_i]$. A **finite discounted constrained Markov decision process (CMDP)** is the tuple consisting of $M$, $\mu$, $\gamma$, and the bounded transition-cost functions and thresholds $(c_i,b_i)_{i=1}^m$. Its immediate reward signal is $r(s,a,\rho,s')=\rho$.

For a stationary Markov policy $\pi$, define the state-mass sequence recursively by $\mu_0^\pi=\mu$ and

$$\mu_{t+1}^\pi(s'):=\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{a\in A(s)}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}\mu_t^\pi(s)\pi(a\mid s)p(s',\rho\mid s,a).$$

This recurrence defines nonnegative finite-time masses; the result that each $\mu_t^\pi$ is a probability distribution is established separately.

Let a finite discounted CMDP have initial distribution $\mu$, discount $\gamma\in[0,1)$, $m$ bounded transition signals $c_i$, thresholds $b_i$, and finite-time state masses $\mu_t^\pi$ under a stationary policy $\pi$, as defined in the CMDP model. For any bounded transition signal $g$ on $(s,a,\rho,s')$, define its **expected discounted sum** under $\pi$ by

$$J_g^\pi(\mu):=\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^t\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{a\in A(s)}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}\sum_{s'\in S}\mu_t^\pi(s)\pi(a\mid s)p(s',\rho\mid s,a)g(s,a,\rho,s').$$

The expected discounted reward is $J^\pi:=J_r^\pi(\mu)$ for the immediate reward signal $r(s,a,\rho,s')=\rho$, and the $i$th expected discounted cost is $J_{c_i}^\pi(\mu)$. The policy $\pi$ is **feasible** for the discounted-cost constraints exactly when $J_{c_i}^\pi(\mu)\le b_i$ for every $i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$. Feasibility constrains these expectations; it does not assert a per-trajectory bound.

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power (Integer powers $a^m$),
so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges (Series, partial sums, convergence and the sum, divergence, and the tail series) and
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$
2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges.

The series starts at $k = 0$ and its first term is $r^0 = 1$; in particular
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 2$, while the series starting at $k = 1$ sums to
$1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $M=(S,\mathcal R,(A(s))_{s\in S},p)$ be a finite Markov decision process with nonempty state set $S$ and finite nonempty action set $A(s)$ at each state. Put $\mathcal X=\{(s,a,\rho,s'):s\in S,\ a\in A(s),\ \rho\in\mathcal R,\ s'\in S\}$. Let $\mu$ be a probability distribution on $S$, let $\gamma\in[0,1)$, let $m\ge1$ be an integer, and for each $i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$ let $b_i\in\mathbb R$, $C_i\ge0$, and $c_i:\mathcal X\to[-C_i,C_i]$. A **finite discounted constrained Markov decision process (CMDP)** is the tuple consisting of $M$, $\mu$, $\gamma$, and the bounded transition-cost functions and thresholds $(c_i,b_i)_{i=1}^m$. Its immediate reward signal is $r(s,a,\rho,s')=\rho$.

For a stationary Markov policy $\pi$, define the state-mass sequence recursively by $\mu_0^\pi=\mu$ and

$$\mu_{t+1}^\pi(s'):=\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{a\in A(s)}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}\mu_t^\pi(s)\pi(a\mid s)p(s',\rho\mid s,a).$$

This recurrence defines nonnegative finite-time masses; the result that each $\mu_t^\pi$ is a probability distribution is established separately.

Let a finite discounted CMDP have initial distribution $\mu$, discount $\gamma\in[0,1)$, $m$ bounded transition signals $c_i$, thresholds $b_i$, and finite-time state masses $\mu_t^\pi$ under a stationary policy $\pi$, as defined in the CMDP model. For any bounded transition signal $g$ on $(s,a,\rho,s')$, define its **expected discounted sum** under $\pi$ by

$$J_g^\pi(\mu):=\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^t\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{a\in A(s)}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}\sum_{s'\in S}\mu_t^\pi(s)\pi(a\mid s)p(s',\rho\mid s,a)g(s,a,\rho,s').$$

The expected discounted reward is $J^\pi:=J_r^\pi(\mu)$ for the immediate reward signal $r(s,a,\rho,s')=\rho$, and the $i$th expected discounted cost is $J_{c_i}^\pi(\mu)$. The policy $\pi$ is **feasible** for the discounted-cost constraints exactly when $J_{c_i}^\pi(\mu)\le b_i$ for every $i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$. Feasibility constrains these expectations; it does not assert a per-trajectory bound.

Let a finite discounted CMDP, a stationary policy $\pi$, and a bounded transition signal $g$ be given. For $s\in S$, let $\delta_s$ be the initial distribution assigning probability one to $s$. The **state value** is $V_g^\pi(s):=J_g^\pi(\delta_s)$. For $a\in A(s)$, define the **action value** and **advantage** by

$$Q_g^\pi(s,a):=\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}\sum_{s'\in S}p(s',\rho\mid s,a)\bigl(g(s,a,\rho,s')+\gamma V_g^\pi(s')\bigr),\qquad A_g^\pi(s,a):=Q_g^\pi(s,a)-V_g^\pi(s).$$

Taking $g=r$ gives reward values and advantages; taking $g=c_i$ gives the value and advantage for the $i$th cost. These quantities are finite because the signal is bounded, $0\le\gamma<1$, and the transition law is normalized.

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the theoretical average-KL comparison, and let a finite discounted CMDP have cost signals $c_1,\ldots,c_m$ with thresholds $b_1,\ldots,b_m$. Let $\theta\mapsto\pi_\theta$ be a stationary policy family on an open set $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ with fixed common support, where $d\ge1$ and the current parameter $\theta_k$ lies in $U$. Assume its policy coordinates are twice continuously differentiable on a neighborhood of $\theta_k$. Choose a trust radius $\delta>0$, a backtracking factor $\beta\in(0,1)$, and a finite backtracking budget $L\ge0$. At iteration $k$, the finite data batch consists of $N\ge1$ rows $(s_j,a_j,\omega_j,\widehat A_j^r,\widehat A_{1,j}^c,\ldots,\widehat A_{m,j}^c)$ from trajectories generated in the CMDP under the current policy $\pi_{\theta_k}$, where $\omega_j\ge0$, $\sum_j\omega_j=1$, and $\pi_{\theta_k}(a_j\mid s_j)>0$. The advantage estimates are real numbers held fixed during the update, and the batch also includes real baseline-cost estimates $\widehat J_{i,k}$. The weights and estimates may come from any fixed rollout or critic estimator; this procedure assumes no accuracy property for them. It specifies the exact finite-data trust-region subproblem and line search; implementations that approximate the subproblem solve are discussed separately.

For every $\theta\in U$, define the finite sample surrogates

$$\widehat L_r(\theta):=\sum_{j=1}^N\omega_j\left(\frac{\pi_\theta(a_j\mid s_j)}{\pi_{\theta_k}(a_j\mid s_j)}-1\right)\widehat A_j^r,\qquad \widehat L_i^c(\theta):=\sum_{j=1}^N\omega_j\left(\frac{\pi_\theta(a_j\mid s_j)}{\pi_{\theta_k}(a_j\mid s_j)}-1\right)\widehat A_{i,j}^c.$$

and $\widehat K(\theta):=\sum_j\omega_jD_{\rm KL}(\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid s_j)\|\pi_{\theta_k}(\cdot\mid s_j))$. Put $g=\nabla\widehat L_r(\theta_k)$, $u_i=(1-\gamma)^{-1}\nabla\widehat L_i^c(\theta_k)$, $H=\nabla^2\widehat K(\theta_k)$, and $q_i=\widehat J_{i,k}-b_i$. The update procedure is:

1. If $H$ is not symmetric, or if some nonzero $x\in\mathbb R^d$ satisfies $x^THx\le0$, return `no-step`. Otherwise form the local quadratic program

   $$\max_{x\in\mathbb R^d} g^Tx\quad\text{subject to}\quad q_i+u_i^Tx\le0\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\qquad \frac12x^THx\le\delta.$$

2. If this program is feasible, let $x^*$ be its lexicographically least global maximizer. The feasible set is a closed subset of the compact ellipsoid, so the maximizer set is nonempty and compact. Minimize the first coordinate on that set, restrict to its nonempty compact minimizers, and repeat for each coordinate; the resulting point is the lexicographically least maximizer. If the program is infeasible and $m=1$, compute $v=H^{-1}u_1$. If $u_1=0$, return `no-step`, since the linearized cost cannot be reduced. Otherwise $u_1^Tv>0$ by positive definiteness, and use the cost-recovery proposal $x^*=-\sqrt{2\delta/(u_1^Tv)}\,v$. If the program is infeasible and $m>1$, return `no-step`.

3. For $j=0,\ldots,L$, set $\theta_j=\theta_k+\beta^jx^*$. Accept the first $\theta_j$ in the policy family's parameter domain for which $\widehat K(\theta_j)\le\delta$ and every sample cost estimate $\widehat J_{i,k}+(1-\gamma)^{-1}\widehat L_i^c(\theta_j)$ is at most $b_i$. If no candidate passes this sample check, return `no-step`; otherwise output the accepted parameter as $\theta_{k+1}$.

For finite constants $D_i\ge0$, optional nonnegative bounded transition signals $\Delta_i:\mathcal X\to[0,D_i]$ may be included in the supplied cost-advantage and baseline estimates by estimating the shaped costs $c_i+\Delta_i$. The exact theorem concerns exact policies and expectations; the line search above checks only the supplied sample estimates.

Let a finite discounted CMDP, a bounded transition signal $g$, a bounded function $f:S\to\mathbb R$, and stationary policies $\pi,\pi'$ be given. For each state define

$$\bar\delta_f^{g,\sigma}(s):=\sum_{a\in A(s)}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}\sum_{s'\in S}\sigma(a\mid s)p(s',\rho\mid s,a)\bigl(g(s,a,\rho,s')+\gamma f(s')-f(s)\bigr),\qquad \sigma\in\{\pi,\pi'\}.$$

Set $\epsilon_f^g(\pi'):=\max_{s\in S}|\bar\delta_f^{g,\pi'}(s)|$ and

$$L_{\pi,f}^g(\pi'):=\sum_{s\in S}d^\pi(s)\bigl(\bar\delta_f^{g,\pi'}(s)-\bar\delta_f^{g,\pi}(s)\bigr),\qquad D_{\pi,f}^{\pm,g}(\pi'):=\frac{L_{\pi,f}^g(\pi')}{1-\gamma}\pm\frac{2\gamma\epsilon_f^g(\pi')}{(1-\gamma)^2}\sum_{s\in S}d^\pi(s)\operatorname{TV}_s(\pi',\pi),$$

where $\operatorname{TV}_s(\pi',\pi):=\frac12\sum_{a\in A(s)}|\pi'(a\mid s)-\pi(a\mid s)|$. Then

$$D_{\pi,f}^{-,g}(\pi')\le J_g^{\pi'}(\mu)-J_g^\pi(\mu)\le D_{\pi,f}^{+,g}(\pi').$$

These total-variation bounds are choice-free. Under the additional Axiom of Choice, define

$$\overline D_{\rm KL}^{\pi}(\pi'\|\pi):=\sum_{s:d^\pi(s)>0}d^\pi(s)D_{\rm KL}\bigl(\pi'(\cdot\mid s)\|\pi(\cdot\mid s)\bigr),$$

using natural logarithms and $+\infty$ when the first action law is not absolutely continuous with respect to the second. The same inequalities hold after replacing $\sum_s d^\pi(s)\operatorname{TV}_s(\pi',\pi)$ by $\sqrt{\overline D_{\rm KL}^{\pi}(\pi'\|\pi)/2}$; when the average KL is infinite, these KL-form inequalities are interpreted as the trivial extended bounds $-\infty\le J_g^{\pi'}(\mu)-J_g^\pi(\mu)\le+\infty$. Taking $g=r$ gives the reward bound, and taking $g=c_i$ gives the corresponding bound for each discounted cost.

derivations.claim: The old expected cost is $J_c^\pi(\mu)=1/100$, while the proposed expected cost is $J_c^{\pi'}(\mu)=1/5$. Since $1/5>1/20$, the exact cost constraint rejects $\pi'$.

By [F4], the average KL at the single state is $K=(1/5)\log20+(4/5)\log(80/99)$. The second logarithm is negative. Also [F5] gives $\log20=\int_1^{20}dt/t<19<20$, so $K<(1/5)20=4=\delta$. Thus the proposal satisfies the exact average-KL radius despite violating the exact cost limit.

The ideal CPO cost advantage under $\pi$ is $A_c^\pi(s,\text{risky})=1-1/100=99/100$ and $A_c^\pi(s,\text{safe})=0-1/100=-1/100$. Its exact surrogate is therefore $J_c^\pi+(1-\gamma)^{-1}\mathbb E_{a\sim\pi'}A_c^\pi(s,a)=1/100+(1/5)(99/100)+(4/5)(-1/100)=1/5>1/20$. By [F7], this is the proposed policy's exact expected cost at $\gamma=0$.

Under $\pi$, one sampled action is `safe` with probability $99/100$. On that event the observed cost is zero; choosing the corresponding supplied baseline-cost estimate and cost-advantage estimate as zero makes the sample cost surrogate at $\pi'$ equal zero. Since $0\le b$, the line search in [F6] accepts this sample check if $\pi'$ is proposed, even though step 1.1 gives its exact expected cost $1/5$.

Assume its policy coordinates are twice continuously differentiable on a neighborhood of $\theta_k$. Choose a trust radius $\delta>0$, a backtracking factor $\beta\in(0,1)$, and a finite backtracking budget $L\ge0$. At iteration $k$, the finite data batch consists of $N\ge1$ rows $(s_j,a_j,\omega_j,\widehat A_j^r,\widehat A_{1,j}^c,\ldots,\widehat A_{m,j}^c)$ from trajectories generated in the CMDP under the current policy $\pi_{\theta_k}$, where $\omega_j\ge0$, $\sum_j\omega_j=1$, and $\pi_{\theta_k}(a_j\mid s_j)>0$. The advantage estimates are real numbers held fixed during the update, and the batch also includes real baseline-cost estimates $\widehat J_{i,k}$. The weights and estimates may come from any fixed rollout or critic estimator; this procedure assumes no accuracy property for them. It specifies the exact finite-data trust-region subproblem and line search; implementations that approximate the subproblem solve are discussed separately.

For every $\theta\in U$, define the finite sample surrogates

$$\widehat L_r(\theta):=\sum_{j=1}^N\omega_j\left(\frac{\pi_\theta(a_j\mid s_j)}{\pi_{\theta_k}(a_j\mid s_j)}-1\right)\widehat A_j^r,\qquad \widehat L_i^c(\theta):=\sum_{j=1}^N\omega_j\left(\frac{\pi_\theta(a_j\mid s_j)}{\pi_{\theta_k}(a_j\mid s_j)}-1\right)\widehat A_{i,j}^c.$$

and $\widehat K(\theta):=\sum_j\omega_jD_{\rm KL}(\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid s_j)\|\pi_{\theta_k}(\cdot\mid s_j))$. Put $g=\nabla\widehat L_r(\theta_k)$, $u_i=(1-\gamma)^{-1}\nabla\widehat L_i^c(\theta_k)$, $H=\nabla^2\widehat K(\theta_k)$, and $q_i=\widehat J_{i,k}-b_i$. The update procedure is:

1. If $H$ is not symmetric, or if some nonzero $x\in\mathbb R^d$ satisfies $x^THx\le0$, return `no-step`. Otherwise form the local quadratic program

   $$\max_{x\in\mathbb R^d} g^Tx\quad\text{subject to}\quad q_i+u_i^Tx\le0\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\qquad \frac12x^THx\le\delta.$$

2. If this program is feasible, let $x^*$ be its lexicographically least global maximizer. The feasible set is a closed subset of the compact ellipsoid, so the maximizer set is nonempty and compact. Minimize the first coordinate on that set, restrict to its nonempty compact minimizers, and repeat for each coordinate; the resulting point is the lexicographically least maximizer. If the program is infeasible and $m=1$, compute $v=H^{-1}u_1$. If $u_1=0$, return `no-step`, since the linearized cost cannot be reduced. Otherwise $u_1^Tv>0$ by positive definiteness, and use the cost-recovery proposal $x^*=-\sqrt{2\delta/(u_1^Tv)}\,v$. If the program is infeasible and $m>1$, return `no-step`.

3. For $j=0,\ldots,L$, set $\theta_j=\theta_k+\beta^jx^*$. Accept the first $\theta_j$ in the policy family's parameter domain for which $\widehat K(\theta_j)\le\delta$ and every sample cost estimate $\widehat J_{i,k}+(1-\gamma)^{-1}\widehat L_i^c(\theta_j)$ is at most $b_i$. If no candidate passes this sample check, return `no-step`; otherwise output the accepted parameter as $\theta_{k+1}$.

derivations.claim: First consider $d\ge1$ and symmetric positive definite $H$. By homogeneity, [F2] gives $x^THx\ge c\|x\|_2^2$ for all $x$, with zero handled directly. Put $C=\sum_{a,b}|H_{ab}|$. Coordinate bounds in [F6] and the identity $x_ax_b-y_ay_b=(x_a-y_a)x_b+y_a(x_b-y_b)$ give $|x^THx-y^THy|\le C\|x-y\|_2(\|x\|_2+\|y\|_2)$, so the quadratic form is continuous. The ellipsoid $E=\{x:x^THx/2\le\delta\}$ is therefore closed and contained in the ball of radius $\sqrt{2\delta/c}$, hence compact by [F3]. Each linear functional $x\mapsto v^Tx$ is continuous because $|v^T(x-y)|\le\|v\|_2\|x-y\|_2$. Thus the feasible set $F=E\cap\bigcap_i\{x:q_i+u_i^Tx\le0\}$ is a closed subset of $E$, and is compact.

If $F$ is nonempty, [F4] gives an attained maximum $M$ of $g^Tx$ on $F$. Its maximizer set $K_0=\{x\in F:g^Tx=M\}$ is nonempty and compact by closedness and [F3]. Successively for coordinates $h=1,\ldots,d$, let $a_h$ be the minimum of coordinate $h$ on $K_{h-1}$ and set $K_h=\{x\in K_{h-1}:x_h=a_h\}$. Each minimum exists by [F4], and each restriction remains nonempty and compact by [F3]. After $d$ restrictions all coordinates are fixed, so $K_d$ is a singleton. For any other maximizer, the first coordinate where it differs from this singleton must be greater, by the construction of that coordinate's minimum. The singleton is therefore exactly the unique lexicographically least maximizer. As a member of $F$, it satisfies all stated constraints.

If $Hz=0$, then $z^THz=0$ and positive definiteness forces $z=0$. Thus [F5] supplies $H^{-1}$. In the single-cost recovery branch write $u=u_1\ne0$, $v=H^{-1}u$. Then $v\ne0$, $Hv=u$ and $a=u^Tv=v^THv>0$. For every $x\in E$, nonnegativity of the quadratic form at $x-(u^Tx/a)v$ gives $0\le x^THx-(u^Tx)^2/a$, using symmetry. Consequently $u^Tx\ge-\sqrt{2\delta a}$. For $x^*=-\sqrt{2\delta/a}\,v$, direct substitution gives $(x^*)^THx^*=2\delta$ and $u^Tx^*=-\sqrt{2\delta a}$, attaining the bound. If another point attains it, equality in the preceding inequalities gives $(x-(u^Tx/a)v)^TH(x-(u^Tx/a)v)=0$, hence $x=(u^Tx/a)v=x^*$ by positive definiteness. The recovery proposal is therefore unique, and its linearized cost is $q_1-\sqrt{2\delta a}$. Since it is the minimum over $E$, infeasibility implies that this last value is strictly positive, rather than implying feasibility.

The remaining proposal branches are the explicit returns in [F1]: non-positive-definite $H$, infeasible single-cost problem with $u_1=0$, and infeasible problem with $m>1$ all return `no-step`. If $d=0$, the only parameter displacement is the zero vector, so a feasible program has that unique maximizer, and in the infeasible case all $u_i=0$ and one of the specified no-step branches applies. Thus zero dimension introduces no missing proposal case. Together with steps 2.1 and 2.2, every branch either gives one uniquely specified proposal or returns `no-step`.

For a proposal $x^*$, the candidates $\theta_k+\beta^jx^*$ for integer $j=0,\ldots,L$ form a prescribed ordered list of $L+1$ points. The parameter-domain check precedes evaluation of the policy tests, so no value outside the domain is required. On the domain, the finite common-support policy probabilities define the empirical KL and surrogates in [F1]. Either there is a least passing index in this finite list, or there is none; [F1] returns its candidate or `no-step`, respectively. Inspecting successive indices therefore terminates in at most $L+1$ candidate tests. The definition of passing supplies exactly the stated sample inequalities. All choices and returns are single-valued by steps 2.1, 2.2 and 3.1 and this least-index rule, establishing the asserted output and finite-search properties. A **discrete filtered probability space** is $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_n)_{n\in\mathbb N_0},P)$, where $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ is a probability space Probability measures and probability spaces, each $\mathcal F_n$ is a sigma-algebra on $\Omega$ Sigma-algebras, and $\mathcal F_n\subseteq\mathcal F_{n+1}\subseteq\mathcal F$. The sequence $(\mathcal F_n)$ is a **filtration**. Time starts at zero. Neither completeness nor triviality of $\mathcal F_0$ is required.

Restriction of $P$ to $\mathcal F_n$ has total mass one and is countably additive: a disjoint sequence in $\mathcal F_n$ is also such a sequence in $\mathcal F$, with the same union and the same values of $P$. Thus each restriction is a probability measure. This specifies a structure and uses no choice principle. Real-valued processes will be the default.

On a filtered probability space Filtration and filtered probability space, a **real stochastic process** is a sequence $(X_n)_{n\in\mathbb N_0}$ of real random variables Random elements and real random variables on the same space. It is **adapted** when $X_n^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal F_n$ for every $n$ and every real Borel set $B$. It is **integrable** when $E|X_n|<\infty$ for every $n$, using Expectation of a nonnegative or integrable random variable.

An integrable adapted process satisfies both conditions at each fixed time. Integrability here does not mean $\sup_nE|X_n|<\infty$: the deterministic process $X_n=n$ has $E|X_n|=n<\infty$ at every time but unbounded supremum. Measurability and finiteness of each integral are separate requirements. No versions, limits or choices are selected.

On a discrete filtered probability space Filtration and filtered probability space, a real process $(H_n)_{n\ge1}$ is **predictable** if $H_n$ is $\mathcal F_{n-1}$-measurable for every $n\ge1$. Real means finite-valued, as in Random elements and real random variables. There is no $H_0$ convention and predictability alone imposes neither integrability nor boundedness.

Since $\mathcal F_{n-1}\subseteq\mathcal F_n$, every Borel preimage of $H_n$ is also in $\mathcal F_n$. Thus predictability implies adaptedness at the positive times. This is a preimage inclusion, requiring no choice or conditional expectation.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{t\in\mathbb N_0},P)$ be a discrete filtered probability space and let $(\theta_t)_{t\geq1}$ be a real target process with each $\theta_t$ measurable with respect to $\mathcal F_t$. For $\alpha\in(0,1)$, a sequence of random closed intervals $C_t=[L_t,U_t]$, with finite real $\mathcal F_t$-measurable endpoints at each $t\geq1$, is a **$(1-\alpha)$ confidence sequence for the target process $(\theta_t)$** if
$$P\!\left(\theta_t\in C_t\text{ for every }t\geq1\right)\geq1-\alpha.$$
The target may be random and may vary with time; the definition asserts only simultaneous coverage under the specified probability law.

Inputs are real bounds $a\leq b$, a nominal error level $\delta\in(0,1)$, an observation stream $(X_t)_{t\geq1}$ with $X_t\in[a,b]$ almost surely and $X_t$ measurable with respect to $\mathcal F_t$, a forecast stream $(\widehat X_t)_{t\geq1}$ with $\widehat X_t\in[a,b]$ almost surely and $\widehat X_t$ measurable with respect to $\mathcal F_{t-1}$, and, when $c=b-a>0$, an evaluation procedure for a Borel one-sided sub-exponential uniform boundary $u_{\delta/2,c}$ with crossing probability $\delta/2$ and scale $c$. The output is one interval $C_t$ at each positive integer time $t$.

1. If $c=0$, return $C_t=[a,a]$ at each time.

2. If $c>0$, initialize $\bar X_0=0$ and $V_0=0$. After receiving forecast $\widehat X_t$ and then observation $X_t$, update
$$\bar X_t=\left(1-\frac1t\right)\bar X_{t-1}+\frac{X_t}{t},\qquad V_t=V_{t-1}+(X_t-\widehat X_t)^2.$$
Return
$$C_t=\left[\bar X_t-\frac{u_{\delta/2,c}(V_t)}{t},\;\bar X_t+\frac{u_{\delta/2,c}(V_t)}{t}\right].$$

The procedure uses observations only through time $t$. The accumulated quantity $V_t$ is the observed sum of squared forecast errors; it is not a predictable conditional-variance process.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

A **real kernel** on a set $X$ is a function $k:X\times X\to\mathbb R$. It is **positive semidefinite** if it is symmetric and, for every integer $n\ge1$, every $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in X$, and every $c_1,\ldots,c_n\in\mathbb R$,

$$\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n c_i c_j k(x_i,x_j)\ge0.$$

A **real reproducing kernel Hilbert space with kernel $k$** is a real Hilbert space $\mathcal H$ of functions $X\to\mathbb R$ such that, for each $x\in X$, the section $k_x:=k(\cdot,x)$ lies in $\mathcal H$ and $\langle f,k_x\rangle_{\mathcal H}=f(x)$ for every $f\in\mathcal H$. Consequently $\langle k_z,k_x\rangle_{\mathcal H}=k(z,x)=k(x,z)$.

For the canonical construction, let $E_0$ be the real vector space of finitely supported functions $a:X\to\mathbb R$, write $\delta_x$ for the function supported at $x$ with value $1$, and put

$$B(a,b):=\sum_{x\in\operatorname{supp}(a)}\sum_{z\in\operatorname{supp}(b)}a(x)b(z)k(x,z).$$

Let $N:=\{a\in E_0:B(a,a)=0\}$. Under the Axiom of Countable Choice, the canonical space is formed by giving $E_0/N$ its induced inner product and taking a norm completion; the image of $\delta_x$ is denoted $k_x$. For an element $h$ of that completion, its associated function is $x\mapsto\langle h,k_x\rangle$. The quotient, completed inner product, and function identification are justified by the local construction theorem.

Set $\tau=n\lambda$ and define the mean-square empirical objective

$$J(f)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-f(x_i))^2+\lambda\lVert f\rVert_{\mathcal H}^2. $$

For any finite real symmetric positive-semidefinite matrix $G\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$, define its regularized kernel prediction system by $a_G=(G+\tau I_n)^{-1}y$ and $u_G=Ga_G$, where $I_n$ is the $n\times n$ identity matrix. The original training system uses $G=K$. The same definition applies to any positive-semidefinite matrix approximation $\widetilde K$ of $K$, with $a_{\widetilde K}=(\widetilde K+\tau I_n)^{-1}y$ and $u_{\widetilde K}=\widetilde K a_{\widetilde K}$. In either case $u_G=y-\tau a_G$. The scalar $\tau=n\lambda$ fixes the normalization between mean-square loss and the unnormalized finite linear system.

A **real kernel** on a set $X$ is a function $k:X\times X\to\mathbb R$. It is **positive semidefinite** if it is symmetric and, for every integer $n\ge1$, every $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in X$, and every $c_1,\ldots,c_n\in\mathbb R$,

$$\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n c_i c_j k(x_i,x_j)\ge0.$$

A **real reproducing kernel Hilbert space with kernel $k$** is a real Hilbert space $\mathcal H$ of functions $X\to\mathbb R$ such that, for each $x\in X$, the section $k_x:=k(\cdot,x)$ lies in $\mathcal H$ and $\langle f,k_x\rangle_{\mathcal H}=f(x)$ for every $f\in\mathcal H$. Consequently $\langle k_z,k_x\rangle_{\mathcal H}=k(z,x)=k(x,z)$.

For the canonical construction, let $E_0$ be the real vector space of finitely supported functions $a:X\to\mathbb R$, write $\delta_x$ for the function supported at $x$ with value $1$, and put

$$B(a,b):=\sum_{x\in\operatorname{supp}(a)}\sum_{z\in\operatorname{supp}(b)}a(x)b(z)k(x,z).$$

Let $N:=\{a\in E_0:B(a,a)=0\}$. Under the Axiom of Countable Choice, the canonical space is formed by giving $E_0/N$ its induced inner product and taking a norm completion; the image of $\delta_x$ is denoted $k_x$. For an element $h$ of that completion, its associated function is $x\mapsto\langle h,k_x\rangle$. The quotient, completed inner product, and function identification are justified by the local construction theorem.

Let $p,d\ge1$, let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $W\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, and let $f:\Theta\times W\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$ and $g:W\times\Theta\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$. Here $C^1$ means continuously differentiable on the open domain, and $C^2$ means that the derivative map is itself continuously differentiable. Gradients are column vectors, vector norms are Euclidean, and the norm of a matrix or linear map is the induced Euclidean operator norm.

For $(\theta,w)\in\Theta\times W$, define the inner stationarity residual $F(\theta,w):=\nabla_w f(\theta,w)\in\mathbb R^d$, its state Jacobian $H(\theta,w):=D_wF(\theta,w)\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$, and its parameter Jacobian $B(\theta,w):=D_\theta F(\theta,w)\in\mathbb R^{d\times p}$. Thus $H$ is the inner Hessian and $B$ is the mixed derivative of the inner gradient. A point $(\theta_0,w_0)$ is stationary when $F(\theta_0,w_0)=0$. If a $C^1$ map $w^*:P\to Q$, for open neighborhoods $P\subseteq\Theta$ of $\theta_0$ and $Q\subseteq W$ of $w_0$, satisfies $w^*(\theta_0)=w_0$ and $F(\theta,w^*(\theta))=0$ for all $\theta\in P$, it is a local stationary branch. The associated outer objective is $J(\theta):=g(w^*(\theta),\theta)$, and its column gradient $\nabla_\theta J$ is called the hypergradient of that branch. The definition of a local stationary branch imposes no global-minimality requirement.

For $\mu>0$, the phrase globally $\mu$-strongly convex in $w$ means that $f(\theta,\cdot)$ is defined on all of $\mathbb R^d$ and, for every $u,v\in\mathbb R^d$, satisfies

$$f(\theta,v)\ge f(\theta,u)+\nabla_w f(\theta,u)^T(v-u)+\frac{\mu}{2}\|v-u\|_2^2.$$

Let $m,n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{m+n}$ be open, and let
$F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$.  Suppose $(a,b)\in U$, $F(a,b)=0$, and the
**partial derivative in the second block**

$$D_yF(a,b):\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n,\qquad D_yF(a,b)v:=DF(a,b)(0,v),$$

is invertible.  Put similarly $D_xF(a,b)u:=DF(a,b)(u,0)$.  Then there are open
neighbourhoods $P$ of $a$ and $Q$ of $b$, and a unique $C^1$ map
$\varphi:P\to Q$, such that

$$F(x,y)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y=\varphi(x)\qquad((x,y)\in P\times Q).$$

After shrinking $P,Q$ if necessary, $D_yF(x,\varphi(x))$ is invertible and

$$D\varphi(x)=-D_yF(x,\varphi(x))^{-1}D_xF(x,\varphi(x)).$$

Let $m,n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{m+n}$ be open, and let
$F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$.  Suppose $(a,b)\in U$, $F(a,b)=0$, and the
**partial derivative in the second block**

$$D_yF(a,b):\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n,\qquad D_yF(a,b)v:=DF(a,b)(0,v),$$

is invertible.  Put similarly $D_xF(a,b)u:=DF(a,b)(u,0)$.  Then there are open
neighbourhoods $P$ of $a$ and $Q$ of $b$, and a unique $C^1$ map
$\varphi:P\to Q$, such that

$$F(x,y)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y=\varphi(x)\qquad((x,y)\in P\times Q).$$

After shrinking $P,Q$ if necessary, $D_yF(x,\varphi(x))$ is invertible and

$$D\varphi(x)=-D_yF(x,\varphi(x))^{-1}D_xF(x,\varphi(x)).$$

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

derivations.claim: Put $F(\theta,w)=\nabla_w f(\theta,w)$. Since $f$ is $C^2$, this residual is $C^1$ on the open product domain; it vanishes at $(\theta_0,w_0)$ and its state derivative is the invertible matrix $H(\theta_0,w_0)$. Applying [F2] gives open neighborhoods and a unique $C^1$ local branch $w^*$ through that point.
The derivative clause of [L1], evaluated along this branch after shrinking its parameter neighborhood, gives $Dw^*(\theta)=-H(\theta,w^*(\theta))^{-1}B(\theta,w^*(\theta))$.
The map $\theta\mapsto (w^*(\theta),\theta)$ is $C^1$, so [F3] applied to $g$ and this map yields $\nabla_\theta J=\partial_\theta g+(Dw^*)^T\nabla_w g$.
Substitute step 2.1 into step 2.2 and use $(H^{-1}B)^T=B^TH^{-T}$. This is the asserted column-gradient hypergradient formula.

In the stated global regime, fix any $\theta\in P$ and any stationary point $u\in\mathbb R^d$, so $\nabla_w f(\theta,u)=0$. For every $v\ne u$, the strong-convexity inequality gives $f(\theta,v)\ge f(\theta,u)+\frac{\mu}{2}\|v-u\|_2^2>f(\theta,u)$. Thus this arbitrary stationary point is the unique global minimizer, proving the claim for every stationary point wherever the global regime holds.

Here $C^1$ means continuously differentiable on the open domain, and $C^2$ means that the derivative map is itself continuously differentiable. Gradients are column vectors, vector norms are Euclidean, and the norm of a matrix or linear map is the induced Euclidean operator norm.

For $(\theta,w)\in\Theta\times W$, define the inner stationarity residual $F(\theta,w):=\nabla_w f(\theta,w)\in\mathbb R^d$, its state Jacobian $H(\theta,w):=D_wF(\theta,w)\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$, and its parameter Jacobian $B(\theta,w):=D_\theta F(\theta,w)\in\mathbb R^{d\times p}$. Thus $H$ is the inner Hessian and $B$ is the mixed derivative of the inner gradient. A point $(\theta_0,w_0)$ is stationary when $F(\theta_0,w_0)=0$. If a $C^1$ map $w^*:P\to Q$, for open neighborhoods $P\subseteq\Theta$ of $\theta_0$ and $Q\subseteq W$ of $w_0$, satisfies $w^*(\theta_0)=w_0$ and $F(\theta,w^*(\theta))=0$ for all $\theta\in P$, it is a local stationary branch. The associated outer objective is $J(\theta):=g(w^*(\theta),\theta)$, and its column gradient $\nabla_\theta J$ is called the hypergradient of that branch. The definition of a local stationary branch imposes no global-minimality requirement.

For $\mu>0$, the phrase globally $\mu$-strongly convex in $w$ means that $f(\theta,\cdot)$ is defined on all of $\mathbb R^d$ and, for every $u,v\in\mathbb R^d$, satisfies

$$f(\theta,v)\ge f(\theta,u)+\nabla_w f(\theta,u)^T(v-u)+\frac{\mu}{2}\|v-u\|_2^2.$$

Let $p,d\ge1$, let $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $W\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, and let $f:\Theta\times W\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$ and $g:W\times\Theta\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$. Here $C^1$ means total differentiability with continuous derivative, and $C^2$ means the derivative map is $C^1$. Define $F(\theta,w)=\nabla_w f(\theta,w)$, $H(\theta,w)=D_wF(\theta,w)$, and $B(\theta,w)=D_\theta F(\theta,w)$. Suppose $F(\theta_0,w_0)=0$ and $H(\theta_0,w_0)$ is invertible. Then there are open neighborhoods $P\subseteq\Theta$ and $Q\subseteq W$ of $\theta_0$ and $w_0$ and a unique $C^1$ local stationary branch $w^*:P\to Q$ through $(\theta_0,w_0)$, meaning $w^*(\theta_0)=w_0$ and $F(\theta,w^*(\theta))=0$ for every $\theta\in P$. After shrinking $P$ if necessary, $H(\theta,w^*(\theta))$ is invertible and

$$Dw^*(\theta)=-H(\theta,w^*(\theta))^{-1}B(\theta,w^*(\theta)).$$

Write $H^{-T}:=(H^{-1})^T$. For $J(\theta)=g(w^*(\theta),\theta)$, where $\partial_\theta g$ holds $w$ fixed and gradients are column vectors, the hypergradient is

$$\nabla_\theta J(\theta)=\partial_\theta g(w^*(\theta),\theta)-B(\theta,w^*(\theta))^T H(\theta,w^*(\theta))^{-T}\nabla_w g(w^*(\theta),\theta).$$

The local branch need not be a global inner optimizer. In the separate global regime where, for every $\theta\in P$, $f(\theta,\cdot)$ is defined on all of $\mathbb R^d$ and, for some $\mu>0$, satisfies $f(\theta,v)\ge f(\theta,u)+\nabla_w f(\theta,u)^T(v-u)+\frac{\mu}{2}\|v-u\|_2^2$ for every $u,v\in\mathbb R^d$, each stationary point is the unique global minimizer.

The implicit sensitivity at a state $z$ is $S(z)=-A(z)^{-1}B(z)$. Suppose the local inverse $\Psi$ of $z\mapsto R(z,\theta_0)$, supplied near $z_*$ by the implicit function theorem, is defined on a convex residual neighborhood containing $0$ and $r=R(\tilde z,\theta_0)$, with $\|D\Psi(y)\|\le\kappa$ along their segment. Suppose also that the segment from $z_*$ to $\tilde z=\Psi(r)$ lies in a convex neighborhood where $\|A(z)^{-1}\|\le M$, $\|B(z)\|\le B_0$, and $A,B$ are Lipschitz with constants $L_A,L_B$. Then
$$\|S(\tilde z)-S(z_*)\|\le\kappa\bigl(M^2L_AB_0+ML_B\bigr)\|r\|.$$

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Here $C^1$ means total differentiability with continuous derivative, $C^2$ means the derivative map is $C^1$, and all graph evaluations must remain on one unique strict branch.
